text: Inefficiencies in various parts of the shipping world continues to keep freight on a tight leash.  The strength is coming from a strong arb, tight shipping availability driven by Panama Canal restrictions and subsequently with both ballast and laden legs increasingly routed via Cape. TS Edouard's impact is reportedly limited to the Sabine Pass.  With August loadings complete, routing shows roughly 30 of 110 departures via Cape to discharge East, against Panama Canal auction fee levels and transit uncertainty.  Whilst there are only a couple September vessels left, fixing activity pivots to October. The October position list now shows 2 first-decade, 7 second-decade, 1 third-decade. In other words, very tight availability for spot shipping.

North Sea After a long weekend activity has been slow on the pick up. Natural dates 8-10 window but with a number of relets around and stems a little thin charterers are able to take their time. US market looks to have bottomed and with Mediterranean market looking softer we may see drive to ballast towards the US again after a quiet few days on that front. Slow but steady.  Mediterranean Activity stalled at the end of last week which has rebuilt the early part of the list. Activity has picked up again at the start of the week but the increased tonnage has changed the sentiment for now and charterers have managed to pushed the market down. Natural window pushing into the 2nd decade with tonnage to clear which in the short term may lead to some more weakening before we find the bottom.

Summer holidays in Europe are over and chartering activity has returned, with September laycans in the U.S. largely covered now and the gaze raising to October. Surplus vessels remain but as enquiries begin to build, there has been renewed interest for periods covering winter. Rate expectations are a significant discounts to average traded levels for modern vessels for this time of year, and reflect the growing sense that weak shipping fundamentals will override high LNG pricing and trading opportunities. Whether the Winter bid continues to improve remains to be seen, but a bridging of the wide bid/offer spread suggests a softer view of winter and that portfolios continue to edge to the long side heading into a Q4 where Qatari supply is still stranded and DES markets East and West keep putting off demand until it really hits. The Pacific has now corrected with challenging supply/demand balance, and unfortunately for owners the market has come off rather than the Atlantic market picking up. The few multi-month fixtures reported suggest that several players see this as the bottom of the market – so perhaps rates can only strengthen from here?

The Supramax market remained mixed and largely directionless, with activity picking up selectively across both the Atlantic and Asia. The Atlantic saw pockets of strength, particularly around the USG and South Atlantic, supported by steady demand for grains, petcoke and minor bulks, while Asia remained active but positional with varied tonnage availability between areas. Handysize trading was generally subdued, although fundamentals remained healthy in parts of the Pacific and South Atlantic. The US Gulf continued to show relatively firm conditions despite limited fixing, while the Continent and Mediterranean markets remained softer. Overall, sentiment across both sectors remains cautious, with regional tonnage positioning and pockets of enquiry driving the market rather than any clear broader trend. There is good appetite for period with quite a few fixtures reported past weeks.

Capesize is heating up across all segments, with both C3 and C5 trade routes posting some of the highest numbers seen this year. Last done on C3 Brazil/China today was seen at USD 40.9, setting a new benchmark which hasn't been seen since the peak of 2021. FFAs are up for the coming quarter, Baltic C3 prints USD 40.2 today and C5 is also showing strong activity with last done in the mid USD 16s and rumors of a fixture at USD 17 flat (yet to be confirmed). C5 West Australia/China prints USD 16.5 today on the Baltic, jumping 7.59% today, overtaking C3 Brazil/China as the higher earner per day between C3 and C5. With an uptick of ballasters headed for Brazil toward the end of September, we may see some pressure in the Atlantic for late September and early October laycans. Overall sentiment is bullish but cautious as limited fresh demand to absorb growing supply.

Despite Suezmaxes regaining competitiveness against VLCCs following last week’s sharp correction, a front-heavy tonnage list and muted activity have continued to weigh on the rates in West Africa. Meanwhile, Aframaxes remain firmly in the driving seat across the Atlantic. That said, the improved economics of the Suezmaxes appear to be attracting renewed interest, with activity showing signs of picking up.

The Panamax market has firmed steadily through the week, with the gains broadening across both basins as the index pushed higher over successive sessions. In the Atlantic the tone is constructive: transatlantic business remains well bid on the back of a replenished cargo book and a tightening nearby tonnage list, while fronthaul has been slower to follow, with owners holding above charterers' ideas on US Gulf and South American grain. The Pacific has been the stronger of the two, where a steady flow of Australian and Indonesian coal alongside North Pacific grain has left prompt tonnage short and charterers chasing owners' levels rather than the reverse. Period interest has picked up markedly, with a good spread of owners collecting for both short and twelve-month cover and bids increasingly obliged to follow last-done rather than set it, although the forward curve continues to price modest backwardation beyond the prompt. We expect the tone to remain sideways-to-firmer into next week, with the main question being how much of the recent move reflects genuine incremental demand rather than positioning ahead of the autumn grain programme.

The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is becoming more precarious by the hour as the US-Iran conflict has intensified again. Several tankers have been hit, and reports suggest that a fully laden VLCC has been abandoned by its crew. The possibility of a major oil spill would of course be a natural disaster but will also bring more focus on the condition of ships which do make it through and their safety when it comes to performing ship to ship operations. A number of discounted Somo tenders never made it through the strait resulting in some failures of fixtures done in the last couple of days at inflated rates. With that some of the immediate pressure has eased slightly, but the position list still remains wanting and rates are unlikely to go much down any time soon. The Atlantic position list is even more challenging, and the likes of oil major Petrobras reportedly only had 1 offer yesterday for a Brazil/China enquiry by the deadline, on and ex d/d ship which wasn’t workable. There’s also reports of another Brazilian export cargo working off the market. Add to that a couple of charterers sniffing ex West Africa and a tender or two USG/Eastbound and it’s a perfect “storm”. Arguably the Suezmax market has seen a drop lately and will eventually cap the upside for their bigger sisters.

Record profits in the crude space continue to fuel rampant tanker buying appetite. Lofty valuations, even for this market, are being met by buyers who are targeting prompt tonnage, often bypassing usual concerns such as yard or survey dates. The suezmax sector has seen particular action this week with new benchmarks being set across the curve. Scrubber fitted CAPE BENAT (156k dwt Rongsheng 2010) sold at USD 62.5M to Lila Global, and SS due ANTIGUA I (157k dwt New Times 2016) sold for USD 90M.    The dry bulk market action is more modest by comparison, but still healthy for this time of year. Owners are in a luxurious position of having the option to sell ageing tonnage at firm valuations, or indeed just keep operating their ships in healthy earnings environments. The supramax sector was busiest this week with a flurry of transactions, helping to price the older end of the curve. With the Q4 supra/ultra futures curve sitting around the USD 20K/day mark, buyers are clearly plentiful. The 20-year-old benchmark was set with SPAR SCORPIO (53k dwt Chengxi 2006) sold for USD 11.5M despite surveys being due in October of this year.

The September list is down to 10 vessels, and October dates are starting to come into view. Panama NB/SB fees remain a real dissuader, and it's showing up in the routing split: ballasters from Asia are now going 50/50 Cape versus Panama, up from roughly 25% back in June and July. Fixture activity has been quiet this week, just a handful done, with owners' ideas mid/low USD 260's.

The Supramax market remained largely subdued and stable. The Atlantic was mixed, with the Mediterranean gradually softening while the Continent saw some fresh enquiry and the US Gulf and South Atlantic remained broadly balanced. In the Pacific, activity was stronger in the NOPAC and parts of Southeast Asia, while Indonesian coal activity was relatively limited. The Handysize market showed a modestly firmer tone, supported by improving cargos in East Coast South America, tighter prompt tonnage in parts of the Pacific and better sentiment in the US Gulf. While the US Gulf was still soft in the short term despite expectations of improvement ahead.

This week on Capesize we saw strong demand from Pacific C5 as three majors were seen in the market alongside a healthy showing of supportive operators. Recent bids seen at mid to high USD 15 levels and today a Newcastlemax fixed at low USD 15 C5 equivalent. Ballasters are looking to get ahead of yet another Typhoon forecasted to hit the coast of southeast China (near Fujian) around late Thursday to early Friday and recent fixtures ex West Australia have been reported in high USD 14s. Atlantic C3 Brazil/China has also seen healthy activity with rumors expecting even higher levels for October. With a flurry of fixtures yesterday, C3 ex Brazil reported levels for 2h September laycans in mid/high USD 37s with one stem reported at USD 38 for late September. Offers today reported in high USD 37 and mid USD 38s for early October laycans ex Brazil. The North Atlantic shows some fronthaul and transatlantic demand ex Seven Islands for later September dates and tonnage remains healthy in the North. A recent fixture ex Seven Islands to India was reported in low USD 42 for end September.

There has been reasonable activity to start the week. However, the market remains very much oversupplied, with 17 FOC and 7 ETS 5 day window ETA West Africa by 10 September. On the flip side, there are plenty of cargoes to move in the second decade from both Guyana and West Africa. For the time being, however, charterers do not appear to be under any pressure to work much beyond two weeks forward from these regions. In addition, the Aframax market stateside appears to be heavily oversupplied, with Aframaxes pricing Suezmaxes out of USG/TA moves on a USD/bbl basis, which further incentivises charterers to sit on their hands.

Spot activity remains broadly muted although the list of developing requirements has begun to build in both basins, giving some much needed encouragement to. High LNG prices prove a double-edged sword in a market predominantly controlled by subletters; whilst some prefer to hold back, the cost of idling and boil-off for others is of greater concern than negligible rates of hire and this has been a factor in rates falling so fast on the back of weak sentiment and high competition. The supply and demand fundamentals have reached a particularly soft level in recent weeks thanks to fewer cargoes, shorter distances and substantial fleet growth being felt in the Atlantic, where the majority of modern vessels have been positioned. The resistance shown in the East is proving to be more of a lag than a snag and rates look set to fall further unless more demand emerges for September laycans. There remains a real possibility that availability becomes constricted by tonnage warming up, with insufficient opportunities East of Suez and unattractive econs further West.

No material change in the VLCC market, still strong by any measure. However, there are signs which could suggest it’s levelling out, which would not be too surprising. Risk/reward does start to play a part at these historically high levels – how much to push? Is another couple of points worth losing out and risk waiting? Daily returns up to and into USD 200k/day also means it “costs” the same to idle and wait to load. In the words of the late Dolly Parton, may she rest in peace: "The way I see it, if you want the rainbow, you gotta put up with the rain."

The Panamax market has firmed steadily through the week, with the index posting consecutive gains and sentiment improving across both basins. The Pacific has been the clearer engine: NoPac and Australian grain and coal demand has absorbed the prompt tonnage that had been weighing on the market, and owners are now comfortable holding their levels while charterers chase. In the Atlantic the North has been the steadier of the two, supported by a healthy coal and minerals programme into the Continent that has kept fronthaul well bid, while the South Atlantic has traded more sideways as the market looks toward the next grain window and owners show little urgency to discount. Period enquiry has picked up noticeably, with a wider range of owners and operators willing to engage on one-year business, although bids continue to sit modestly behind owners' ideas. With paper firmer and tonnage tightening into September, we expect the tone to remain sideways-to-firmer in the near term.

North Sea After the large number of vessels we have seen ballast towards the US the North Sea list has been left with a reduced number of natural candidates for North Sea business. Dates have pushed into early September with rates picking. The flow of tonnage leaving for the US is currently less as that market has softened on the back of vessels arriving but with the Mediterranean also pushing up tonnage will continue to move out. First decade North Sea stems are a little on the light side which may limit the firming of rates.  Mediterranean Activity in the Mediterranean remains consistent with dates pushing into September and cargoes from certain ports pushing out to the 5th. Like the North Sea the Mediterranean had seen vessels leaving for the US which has helped owners push for increases in rate levels. List remain interesting with some tonnage compromised due to trading history.

The disruption in the tanker market shows no sign of easing, and arguably we are at one of the furthest points from resolution we’ve seen so far in the USA-Iran conflict. The prevailing factors are tightening lists and causing rates to surge. Incredible returns are there to be made, seen in the confidence shown from an unknown buyer rumored to have bought the VLCC HELLSTUGUTINDEN (299k dwt Universal 2003) for a sensational USD 57M.   While the tanker market keeps making headlines, the dry space is bringing in consistent returns, keeping prices firm. Capesize rates have strengthened in recent weeks, which will attract buyers at both ends of the age curve. Pricing the older end of the curve, we have JIAN FA (175k dwt SWS 2004) sold this week at USD 18.5M. A quiet week, otherwise, due to holiday season.

Fixture activity continued this week, with several concluded, all for September dates. The position list has tightened further, down to 14 ships from yesterday's 17. Positions are stacking as: 5 ships second decade September, 6 last decade September, and 3 first decade October. FOB interest is reported for first decade September, but with no ships currently sitting in that window, it may get pushed into the second decade, adding further pressure to an already thin 5-ship count there. Fixing levels have been choppy, ranging between USD 255 and 280pmt this week, (subject to vessel type and routing options) though levels have firmed back toward USD 270pmt more recently. With fresh fixtures and a tightening list, we believe freight will stay flat. Panama Canal costs remain a live factor in routing decisions: yesterday a northbound slot auction cleared at USD 4.2m, with a southbound auction at USD 851k.

We’re in “stop the press” territory now with VLCC rates galloping in all areas in tandem with the Suez- and Aframax segments. In the Atlantic we saw a stonking WS 197.5 fixture Brazil/China yesterday, up from a WS 182.5 just done a bit earlier! An unconfirmed report suggests WS 210 has been done West Africa/East, but whether true or not tallies with the last Brazil rate, if not higher. Fujairah-Oman/East cargoes have followed suit sniffing on the WS 200 mark or above. Position lists are thinning by the hour both east and west of Suez so today’s “expensive” fixture might very well look “cheap” tomorrow. Time and tide wait for no man.

On the one hand we have prompt replacements & 1-5 window cargoes working Suezmax, VLCC levels also in runaway mode with TD15 fixing circa 260KT x WS 200 and their USG list almost devoid of tonnage within the next 30-day. Thus expectations of strong West Africa demand to carry the Suezmax market in the 2nd decade could sustain this spike. On the other, we are fully priced out of the USG market with 2 enquiries withdrawing yesterday & Aframaxes USD 2.5/BBL cheaper, and basis latest cargo counts ex West Africa we may be down to our final 6 stems in the 1st decade once present enquiry is cleaned out.  The list has 8 natural options FOC up to the 5th, 4 discharging presently, 3 at disport waiting and overall 12 natural ETS within the next 5 days/22 natural ETS within the next week. It's not hugely extensive & CPC players are not going to change their tune whilst TD6 is paying in the WS 500s either. Given the confidence a low-VLCC count should give owners in the 2nd decade, even if 1st decade demand falls off a little towards the end of the week, we are not anticipating owners to suddenly become pushovers.

Supramax market remained broadly steady, with limited movement across most regions and only modest gains in the Atlantic. The Continent and Mediterranean continue to face pressure due to ample tonnage and limited fresh cargo input, while the South Atlantic remains more balanced but somewhat positional. In Asia, sentiment is improving, supported by better activity in NoPac and Southeast Asia, although this has yet to translate into significant rate gains.  Handy market wise- another subdued session overall, with the Continent and Mediterranean remaining soft amid limited cargo volumes. The South Atlantic and USG were broadly stable, with little change in fundamentals. Asia remained the strongest area, supported by tighter prompt tonnage and steady cargo flow, although activity remained relatively limited.

The complete collapse in the Atlantic freight market continues, with owners and subletters having to battle not only against a considerable number of competing vessel but also against sharp FOB economics. The fall in headline rates is stark and is highly unusual outside of the shoulder months, but reflects a dynamic often seen in the LNG spot market: when rates begin to move one way or the other, they can accelerate so rapidly as subletters see the same market signals. There are signs that some players will prefer to hold on to tonnage rather than sublet in this market, although this is likely to support a modest floor rather than materially raise rates at this stage. The Pacific is still considerably higher, although it is somewhat illiquid and deals have been concluded at surprisingly high rates given the number of available vessels (mainly due to cargo-specific restrictions). Looking a little further forward, there is more tonnage emerging in September and with less motivation to ballast back West this may apply some downward pressure. If the spread does close, will it be led by an Atlantic revival or a softening Pacific?

Panamax sentiment has turned more cautious this week, with the index giving back part of its recent gains and both basins trading with a softer bias. The Pacific has led the correction: prompt tonnage has accumulated across the North and South while fresh NoPac grain and Australian and Indo coal enquiry has been slow to absorb it, leaving charterers in control and the market still in search of a floor. The Atlantic has held up rather better, with ECSA fronthaul remaining the firmer leg and Continent tonnage still reasonably tight, although bid/offer have widened and fixing volumes are thin as charterers wait for the north to settle. Period discussion remains active across both Kamsarmax and Panamax, but owners are resisting the softer nearby curve and bids have yet to close the gap, so relatively little is concluding. We would expect a sideways-to-softer tone into next week, with any recovery contingent on a fresh injection of grain and coal cargo in the Pacific; in the meantime the Atlantic should continue to offer owners the better alternative.

This week markets are showing slight pressure with limited fixing today on Capesize across all segments, however markets are consistent on C3 Brazil/China with the main decline seen in Pacific C5. FFAs show slight positive sentiment in the long term although above average laden to ballast ratio of vessels heading toward the Atlantic gives a slight bearish outlook in the near future. This week sentiment has had a softer tone in the Pacific and today saw a decline on paper. Earlier fixing concluded around and just below the USD 14 range for West Australia/Qingdao. Today, two miners reported fixing at USD 13.4 yesterday and latest bids are mixed and around USD 13 to USD 14 for early September laycans. In the Atlantic, levels have remained consistent however South Brazil and West Africa to China remains subdued with limited bids and offers reported today. C3 Brazil/China sees bids and offer reported in low USD 36 levels with last done in high USD 34s on C3 for West Africa and another reported in the USD 37 range on Friday for a Newcastlemax.

North Sea The North Sea list has been greatly reduced with vessels heading to the US. The amount of vessels in ballast to the US so far in August is the largest amount we have seen in the same period in any previous month. The North Sea market has remained steady even with the clearing of the list holding around the WS 200 level. Dates are starting to push towards the end of the month which should see some increase in activity and itineraries will be important for B/L dates which may allow owners to chase a slight premium.  Mediterranean Activity in the Mediterranean has been consistent with a few replacement requirements also coming into the mix. The US has attracted vessels from the West Mediterranean along with some compromised vessels has kept the tonnage available to charterers interesting. Rates have firmed around WS 15 points from last week and heading to the end August/early September fixing window we may still see some more firming.

Nothing quite sums up the current value environment quite like the sale of 2-year-old scrubber fitted Suezmax BRISTOL (157k dwt Hyundai Samho 2024) at USD 123M. This figure sees former owners CMB.Tech banking a gain of USD 56.9M on the asset it purchased in 2021 at a reported total cost of USD 66.4M. Not only is the gain noteworthy, but the confidence in this tanker market is such that there are also willing buyers at these levels. Not to be outshone, the clean market was also the stage for a significant transaction this week with ON PROSPER/PROMISE (50k dwt HHI 2026) sold at USD 59M each to GEM. This will effectively reprice modern MR tanker values.   A fairly uneventful week in the dry market as we enter prime summer holiday time in Southern Europe. Pricing across the market has remained firm alongside consistent earnings, and buyers are there to snap up any available tonnage. Vessels from good yards will be main beneficiaries as seen the sale of GRAMOS (61k dwt NACKS 2019), sold to Greek buyers for USD 34.5M. Older panamax bulkers continue to fetch a premium, seen in 18-year-old FRANCESCO CORRADO (77k dwt Oshima 2008) bought by Korean buyers for USD 15M.

WEST Activity has picked up compared to last week, with several fixtures reported after a quieter run. The near-term list remains tight and heavily relet-dependent, with positions stacking up as follows: 2 ships last decade August, 1 first decade September, 6 second decade September, and 8 last decade September. Freight is sitting around USD 280pmt, underpinned by recent fixing levels. Adding to the pressure on owners weighing routing options, this week's Panama Canal northbound slot auction cleared at a record USD 4m, making the Cape an increasingly attractive routing.  EAST East of Suez, activity remained thin, with just one fixture reported, an STS Vadinar deal concluded at USD 170pmt RT/C equivalent. With so little else crossing the tape this week, it's hard to draw much of a broader trend from a single fixture.

The Atlantic spot market remains muted, with a small number of requirements seeing a considerable number of open vessels. Rates have cooled considerably and with the ongoing lack of liquidity, what bids there are suggest the trend will continue downwards for a while yet. However, where the West is quiet, the market East of Suez has gained momentum and seen a steady stream of firm requirements and subsequent fixtures to keep owners and subletters busy. This activity has helped whittle down the availability list and softened the decline, although it has not been enough to see rates reverse their recent fall. Charterers’ cargo-specific preferences are often dictating the vessel fixed rather than price tag, so average rates remain relatively firm across the tonnage classes versus the drops seen in the Atlantic. The growing delta between the basins is significant enough that owners with ships redelivering in the East, or who had plans to ballast West, may now opt to stay put and trade in the more active Pacific spot market.  The multimonth market continues to point the way through winter, and that way looks to be relatively flat. High LNG prices and low European storage may not come to Owners’ rescue in the coming months, as the bearish fundamentals are finally winning through.

North Sea The stems through the 2nd decade have been depleted for Aframaxes with some Suezmax activity and a few relets in the mix. With a limited amount of fixtures the market has steadily fallen over the last week by around 20 points. US markets are strengthening and pulling tonnage out of the North Sea, so we may have started to bottom out, and heading into the 3rd decade date wise we could start to see some pinch points which will see rates bounce.  Mediterranean A steady week activity wise so far but rates have been eroded. Natural window pushing into 3rd decade with a list that has been trimmed but still looks relatively healthy for charterers. With the issues in the Black Sea, tonnage that wouldn’t normally look X-Mediterranean is recalibrating.  Early West Mediterranean positions are looking at turning right and heading for the land of opportunity across the pond.

There’s no lack of VLCC activity judging from a long list of ships reported fixed or on subs. Details of which are few and far in between, these days motivated further not wanting to advertise to hostile elements where and when the ship in question will be appearing in the wider Middle East. This makes navigating the market even more difficult, although if there were deals done considerable different from “last done” levels I am sure it would have been alluded to. There is huge money to be had for the risk takers out there, of which there are not too many for the top prize inside MEG load. But Fujairah-Oman load still pays a decent premium and Yanbu/East even more as the Houthis continue to attack Saudi controlled ships and installations – although third party ships/owners have not yet been targeted. The MEG position list is balanced, albeit littered with oil company and trader relets so what is really available, or not, remains to be tested. With a solution of the US-Iran conflict looking increasingly further away, and soaring refinery margins, logic dictates Atlantic eastbound interest will increase going forward, albeit as of now several ships ballasting west on spec has kept a lid on rates.

The Panamax market has held a constructive tone through the week, with the index grinding higher after a brief pause mid-week and both basins now pointing in the same direction. The Atlantic remains led by the fronthaul, where steady South American and Black Sea grain programmes together with a thinner list of prompt North Atlantic tonnage have allowed owners to hold their ideas and to resist on shorter transatlantic business as well. In the Pacific, sentiment has improved on the back of a fuller NoPac grain order book and firmer Australian coal demand into North Asia, with Indonesian volumes providing a steady if less dynamic floor; the gap between available tonnage and cargo requirement is narrowing and charterers are having to work harder to cover. Period enquiry is genuinely active across both Kamsarmax and Panamax, with a clear preference for index-linked structures, although owners' ideas continue to sit above where charterers are prepared to bid. We expect the market to remain sideways-to-firmer into next week, with the fronthaul retaining a healthy premium over backhaul and tonnage supply the main variable to watch.

The Supramax market began the week on a subdued note, with limited fresh activity and sentiment generally steady across most regions. The Atlantic showed signs of increased enquiry, particularly in the Mediterranean, although a widening gap between bids and offers and softer nearby positions suggested some caution. The Continent remained largely unchanged, while Asian markets were mostly flat, with backhaul activity correcting and regional demand remaining muted.  Handysize conditions were similarly quiet, with sentiment remaining cautious in both basins. Europe faced pressure from an increase in available tonnage and limited fresh cargoes, while the USG continued to struggle with weak demand and ample vessel supply. The South Atlantic showed early signs of improvement due to a more balanced cargo-to-tonnage ratio. In Asia, demand remained steady but insufficient to materially tighten the market, resulting in an overall soft but stable tone.

This week in the Capesize market we see the lowest tonnage congestion in China following Typhoon Dolphin. The typhoon hit the coast of China later last week and has since weakened, moving inland. Ballasters heading for Brazil on C3 (Brazil/China) were welcomed to a fresh injection of cargoes this week ex Brazil and West Africa. Last night fixes concluded in the USD 35-35.5 range, with owners offering USD 36.5 and traders bidding USD 35 for C3 mid-late September dates. Today rates are flat/slightly down with Baltic printing USD 35.93 and latest offers in low USD 36 range. Pacific C5 ex West Australia/China saw significant activity yesterday in the basin with three majors in the market. One fixture was done at USD 15.5 for late August dates and an East Australian stem fixed in the mid-high USD 31s for early September. Today the Pacific has also seen a slight dip on paper with Baltic down 2% today. Latest offers are in the low mid USD 14s for late August and early September. Last fixture concluded a late August Dampier stem at USD 14.25.

Activity continues to build across August and September dates in the West. While vessel availability remains reasonable on paper, the tonnage to cargo ratio continues to tighten, strengthening owners’ leverage and limiting their willingness to move first. In addition, September CPC stems are expected to be released imminently. With rates reaching astronomical levels, owners capable of trading in the Black Sea are likely to prioritise CPC cargoes over adjacent markets.

ADNOC’s expansion of their fleet is once again the headline story, as more details emerge from their ongoing buying spree. An en bloc deal on two Frontline VLCCs FRONT HUMBER/VEFSNA (297/298k dwt Hyundai Samho/HHIC 2017) for USD 270M stands out for the sheer size of transaction, but importantly it shows that experienced owners are willing to sell units in this market in order to crystalise gains following the recent prolific rise in values. Regarding the earnings market, talks are open between Iran and Oman on a ‘Navigation Plan’ for Hormuz, so we could potentially see some easing of the vast inefficiencies being experienced by tanker owners and charterers, time will tell. Older units are still being sold for huge premiums, with this week GRIT (298k dwt Daewoo 2003) sold for USD 50M.  Dry remains a very open avenue for liquidity, with plenty of action in the 10–15-year-old age range. There is a precarious feel to macro fundamentals, however, which is likely to impact dry charter rates going forward. A sustained high energy cost scenario would potentially weaken the overall manufacturing space, and it feels we are a long way from any solution from the main cause of this (USA/Iran). Capesize values appear to be softening slightly, with SS passed ORANGE TIGER (181k dwt Imabari 2011) bought by Mercuria for USD 36.5M.

The USG activity remains muted with only one fixture concluded this week at USD 280 pmt H/C. Albeit the Baltic LPG3 print have started sliding downwards, owners' and traders' freight ideas to charter out, are yet to follow. We expect more activity in the USG and USEC for September as there are a mere five fixtures concluded thus far for next month. It's worth to note that the first and second decade of September only have ten vessels open for spot (five fixed as of now for September) whereas the average number of fixtures in 2026 per first and second decade every month is twenty one(!).

The Supramax and Handymax markets remained relatively stable this week. The US Gulf continued to see the highest activity, while the Continent/Mediterranean remained balanced despite limited fresh enquiry. South America softened slightly as cargo volumes eased, and Asia remained quiet with rates edging lower. Overall, the market remains steady, although fresh cargo demand will be needed for further improvement.

Geopolitical tensions continue to fuel the volatility in rates. Houthi attacks are now starting to restrict movements and transits into the Red Sea. Owners willing to transit are able to attract healthy premiums over the standard Fuj/East run. USG barrels were a flash in the pan last week with not many ships actually getting fully fixed.

Atlantic rates have come under considerable pressure, with a growing availability list chasing relatively few requirements and competing not just against each other but also against aggressive FOB structures. The impact on spot rates has been dramatic, to the extent that the Pacific basin now commands a premium for the first time this year. The market East of Suez has also had to contend with excess tonnage, but so far rates have been supported by the premiums charterers are prepared to pay for larger, more modern vessels. There is more likely to be further downward pressure in both basins, as Atlantic sublets try to accommodate their own backstops dates while Pacific vessels are at risk of warming up; unless more cargoes emerge to fill the gap between now and the early-September requirements, the list of ships requiring cool-down threatens to grow substantially. There have also been several multi-month fixtures, spanning periods through this winter out to the end of next year, at rates that suggest a muted winter season. There has been some discussion as to whether the winter freight market will be buoyed by higher LNG prices and thus attractive LNG trading dynamics or weighed down by soft fundamentals; the signs today suggest the latter trends may dictate the coming months.

North Sea Market has quietly been covering the 1st half of the month with freight levels remaining relatively steady. Ballasting has slowed with softer surrounding markets but is still attractive rather than accepting waiting time. The Suezmax market has softened which may rekindle charterers' appetite for larger vessels with Aframax activity potentially coming under pressure.  Market looks like it will remain steady/soft through mid month unless we see a jump in activity.  Mediterranean Very busy Mediterranean market after the corrections of last week. Rates have found a floor and are hovering around last-done levels, but the position list is slowly becoming thinner. Volumes are remaining high as Syria and Sidi are pumping additional volumes at the moment keeping the market interesting.

The Panamax market firmed steadily through the week, with momentum broadening across both basins and owners increasingly able to hold their ground. In the Atlantic, the fronthaul grain trade remained the principal driver – a healthy flow of South American and US Gulf cargoes against a tightening tonnage list kept sentiment constructive and lifted end-month levels, even against continued charterer resistance. The Pacific firmed in tandem, underpinned by tight prompt tonnage, a steadier stream of North Pacific grain alongside Australian and Indonesian coal, and some weather-related disruption that lent owners additional confidence. Period interest was active and the bid-offer gap narrowed over the week, though owners continued to price forward cover with a firm hand and a modest premium on shorter durations. With cargo replenishment healthy in both basins and the forward curve holding a shallow backwardation, we enter next week on a constructive footing.

After yesterday's downward correction it comes as no surprise that we have a lengthy mystery list this morning, along with more enquiries on the sheet, given the overall fixing hiatus from charterers the week prior. The uptick in activity will help to stabilise sentiment, however, there are still 15+ ‘natural’ vessels capable of making both Guyana and West Africa by 20th August. Owners should remain pragmatic in fixing their vessels away, particularly as the flow of tonnage remains consistent heading into the third decade.

The Capesize market began the week on a solid footing and has continued to strengthen throughout the week setting a positive trajectory. South Atlantic and West Africa continue to underpin improvements on C3 and healthy demand also pushed rates on C5 West Australia/China. In the Atlantic, the charge was led again this week on C3 Brazil/China with a flurry of fixtures in the low-mid USD 35s yesterday and today we see owners bidding in the mid USD 35s up to USD 36 for Brazil and West Africa stems for first half September laycans. In the Pacific, some ballasters are forced to delay as Typhoon Dolphin brings severe weather off the coast of China. C5 West Australia/Qingdao shows good support with four new fixtures from one miner today as the Baltic jumps by 6.9%. Refreshed offers for late August laycans are between USD 16.5-17 and one fixture was reported at low to mid USD 16s. First half September stems see offers ease to high USD 15 levels.

ADNOC has made a splash in the VLCC market this week, acquiring at least five units for use in their own trading operations. The deals have prompted debate over whether the prices paid are representative of the wider market or instead reflect the lucrative and highly specific employment intended for the vessels. It remains to be seen, however, whether other owners will view these levels as grounds to raise their own price expectations.  Dry bulk earnings remain healthy, giving Sellers little incentive to soften their price expectations. Despite firm asset values, liquidity remains elevated in the 15-year-old space, with several transactions reported this week. Kamsarmax sisters ARTVIN/ORDU (81k dwt HMD 2012/2011) were sold en bloc to Korean buyers for USD 39m.

Freight softened this week, with two fixtures reported at USD 280 H/C and at USD 268 H/C, both end August. Activity remains quiet ahead of the Pertamina tender result, which will likely set the tone. We see only two ships end August while we start to look to September (10 first decade, 4 second decade, 4 last decade). Panama canal auction premiums held elevated, with three NB slots clearing above $3m and two SB slots at $2.6m and $1.46m. Middle East tension remains a wildcard that could change sentiment quickly.

This week on Capesize, we have seen a slow retreat across major Atlantic and Pacific basins. Pacific C5 West Australia/China saw relatively limited fresh cargo out of Australia with two main active miners in play. Latest last done levels on C5 reported at low-mid USD 12 levels with the most recent fixture reported at USD 12.25 for mid August dates. Refreshed ideas today are at high USD 11s and low USD 12s for mid August. C3 Brazil/China and West Africa also saw softening this week, in part due to easing oil prices earlier in the week. Charterers took a more patient approach amid the weaker market levels with bids hovering around the USD 33s for late August dates and offers aiming in the mid-low USD 34s. Ideas moving to September are rumored in the USD 32s signaling potential further softening. Atlantic activity has remained subdued this week following limited fresh interest. Transatlantic stems saw a slight increase in cargo volume but levels are below owners' expectations. Charterers are hopeful for rate corrections before committing and owners continue to discount prompt vessels in order to secure employment. Transatlantic paper has increased marginally today with C8 transatlantic valuing USD 44,500 per day.

North Sea Market activity has been limited as we push into August stems with cargoes covering quietly with relets and some Suezmax in the mix. The front end of the list has some natural North Sea tonnage on it for the first time in a couple of weeks. There has been some prompter questions but natural window now likely heading toward the end of the first decade. Surrounding markets are steady / softer but still attractive for tonnage to ballast out of the area.  Mediterranean Midway through this week and there has been hardly any local Mediterranean runs from the usual suspects. The tonnage list is long with the prompt West Mediterranean positions ballasting towards USG but equally the Red Sea/Arabian Sea vessels keep feeding Mediterranean with ballasters. Fundamentals are pointing towards a correction while the short-term inefficiencies and sentiment might help rates remain at significant high levels for this period of the year.

A lack of requirements to work and a sensitive arbitrage has continued to pressure Atlantic rates, and with abundant tonnage there is likely to be strong competition among owners for the emerging fresh cargoes. Rates have been bound within a fairly narrow range for several months, but it is likely the next round of fixtures will align closer with the bid than the offer. Conversely, in the East recent requirements have been covered at steady levels that suggest a balanced or even slight undersupplied spot market, aided by owners opting to relocate vessels West to take advantage of premium rates. However, there remains high competition for smaller cargoes among the TFDE fleet, with owners showing sharp numbers to attract Charterers' attention.    The Middle East situation remains tense and seemingly at a stalemate, and LNG prices have been edging higher - trading strategies that account for a higher LNG price through winter will be gaining traction. The multimonth market has remained active with several tenders underway or recently concluded and levels are broadly flat or trending down, so reducing risk by forward fixing winter coverage at today’s softer rates is clearly attractive to certain charterers.

* CPC has been tested, with W430 on subs with only 3 offers being received, as owners are clearly pricing in the risk following the recent drone attacks.  * On the other hand, we have a market quote for Med/Skorea that received 8 offers. Therefore, despite this elevated rate from the Black Sea, it seems unlikely to translate across the wider market or offset the bearish supply fundamentals, as the majority of owners will continue to avoid the Black Sea. * We have plenty of vessels available in the prompt window for WAF, with tonnage either opening locally or sitting FOC from UKCM positions. In addition, towards the back end of the fixing window, we have a fleet of ballasters from the East heading towards the Cape. * In terms of volume, there will be cargoes to move in the 2nd decade, but a downward test is anticipated before any congestion emerges.  * Even then, owners are expected to remain pragmatic given the aforementioned supply outlook. Owners will be banking on the re-emergence of CPC activity and improved safety assurances to counterbalance the bearish market sentiment.

Petrobras continue to face the brunt of the volatility that this market has to offer. They fixed 50 points down and 40 points up, all within a span of 2 weeks. Owners who are able to transit the Gulf of Aden, albeit with conditions have done well with being able to achieve WS 297.5 for Red Sea to Korea voyage. With the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab El Mandeb being tricky to transit, suppliers are now looking to off load the oil via the Sumed pipeline and load out of Sidi Kerir. Charterers in the USG seem to be taking some cover by taking ships on subs but not much has come to fruition as most of them have failed.

The Panamax market softened over the course of the week, with the index easing and sentiment turning more cautious across both basins amid the seasonal summer lull. The Atlantic set the softer tone – transatlantic and fronthaul enquiry stayed thin, prompt tonnage was discounted to secure employment, and a widening gap between owners' ideas and charterers' bids kept activity subdued, even as the Continent and Western Mediterranean remained comparatively tight on prompt vessels. The Pacific was the more constructive corner late in the week, steadying off recent lows as North Pacific grain enquiry improved and charterers returned to cover weather-disrupted positions, though an ample tonnage list and still-elevated Chinese stockpiles capped the recovery. Period interest remained active, with charterers continuing to pursue Kamsarmax cover for one- to two-year employment, but bid and offer stayed apart and owners of modern eco tonnage were reluctant to chase the market lower. On balance we would characterise the tone as soft but stabilising into month-end, with near-term direction hinging on whether the Pacific's tentative firming can broaden and Atlantic cargo replenishment comes through.

Supramax/Ultramax market remained under pressure, extending its recent downward trend as fresh cargo enquiry stayed limited across most regions. Atlantic sentiment continued to soften, with increasing vessel availability weighing on in despite occasional stronger fixtures. Asia remains relatively quiet. Overall, the market remains cautious with little sign of a near-term improvement in the coming weeks. The Handy market was largely unchanged, with sentiment continuing to be driven by vessel positioning rather than any meaningful shift in demand. The Continent/Mediterranean remained balanced but subdued, while the Atlantic softened further as an expanding tonnage list outpaced fresh cargo volumes. Activity in the Pacific was generally quiet, with limited fixing keeping momentum subdued.

Never a dull moment in the tanker market as this week oil eclipsed USD 100/bbl for the first time since May, amid renewed involvement in the general conflict by the Houthis. Threats and attacks against vessels transiting the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait mean that we are presented with a two-chokepoint problem, which would exacerbate the already extraordinary market conditions tankers (and global oil flows) are facing. Wider economic fears are shaking markets, with most hoping that a resolution can be found quickly so that we are not faced with a sustained high oil price environment. Buyers are cautiously watching the unfolding situation, with second-hand sales effectively grinding to a halt. This week STST J19 EVA HONGKONG (19k dwt Usuki 2017) sold for USD 30M.    Amid the headline grabbing tanker market, dry has remained consistent. Earnings have not budged for the past few weeks, and sellers of tonnage are largely able to set lofty price targets for any buyers willing to meet them. The allure of these earnings are enough for some buyers, as we are seeing a steady stream of sales. China remains one of the prime destinations for second hand capes as this week sisters AANYA/AASHNA (179k dwt HHIC 2012) sold for USD 75M en bloc to Chinese buyers. The sale that stole the show this week, however, is ultramax SEACON TOKYO (66k dwt Tsuneishi Zhoushan 2023) selling for USD 41.6M, a figure that will have owners and brokers rethinking their values.

WEST The arb has been widening all week, and freight is following; where we saw ~250 $/mt end of last week, we now see last done at high 280s $/mt and Owners last ideas between 290 and 300+. US propane stocks rose by 6.3mn/b per EIA weekly stats. Fixing activity in the West has been focused in last decade August dates, with one first decade September fixture reported. There are still a handful of ships able to meet august dates.  EAST East activity continues to be limited with some owners still waiting for any change in the Strait transits.

Petrobras managed to chip off another 15 and a bit points off their last done Brazil/East enquiry yesterday, down 51 points from the high in the better part of a week, and the likelihood is they’ll manage a bit more on their next enquiry as owners shy away from potential danger in the Middle East and head west. On the other side, now that both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait are fast becoming a “no go zone” focus must change to alternative supply from the likes of USG and West Africa, and punchy Suez- and Aframax rates will encourage economy of scale both transatlantic and eastbound. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a meeting of Southeast Asian foreign ministers today that the US is still willing to negotiate an end to the Iran crisis, but Tehran is not serious about talks. Where there’s a will there’s a way they say, but where it leads right now is anyone’s guess. One day (hour) at the time….

North Sea North Sea and Mediterranean markets have settled down activity wise in the early part of the week after what had been a very active couple of weeks. The North Sea list remains on the thin side but natural dates now pushing into August with the potential for relets to come back into the frame. The list will be further depleted especially the early part with tonnage heading off to the very firm US markets. For a Summer market rates remain strong giving owners very healthy returns.  Mediterranean Rates in the Mediterranean continue in the high WS 300s with a bit of underground activity so far this week but slower compared to the chaos of last week. At first look tonnage list is long however delays in Trieste, vessels ballasting from the Red Sea-East and potentially ballasting towards USG might keep it more balanced. Returns are too good for owners to say 'no', if a small discount is required but sentiment remains strong. Black Sea disruptions are expected to negatively affect the rates if loadings will get cancelled.

High fixing activity has cleared the long list of active requirements seen over the past weeks in the Atlantic. As the market pauses for breath and the number of firm cargoes thins, headline rates have dipped slightly - while still maintaining a significant premium to the East. Availability has widened for mid/late-August laycans, but Charterers requiring worldwide redelivery flex will be constrained by Autumn backstops for most opening tonnage.  A slowdown in Pacific requirements and fixing activity has bolstered the TFDE availability lists in the East. Conversely, with 2-strokes being enticed West, securing larger tonnage for 2H August laycans proves more of a challenge. Competition for cargoes is putting downward pressure on TFDE rates, with 2-stroke owners also needing to sharpen to compete for smaller cargoes.  Delivered LNG price continues to rally, and this week saw the most expensive cargo per MMBtu since 2022, at USD 21.88. These levels are justifying charter rates at a significant premium to the levels otherwise expected in a market that is structurally oversupplied. With pricing unlikely to dip significantly as we head towards Northern Hemisphere winter, it will be a fascinating second half of the year.  Certain portfolio players continue to release tonnage on multi-month and 1-year bases, with fixing rates below current spot rates. This does signal bearish sentiment into next year, although it is not clear-cut yet how different trading strategies will play out in the coming months and thus whether there will be more demand building as LNG players shape up for winter.

This week on Cape, we saw quieter activity in the Pacific and Atlantic basins. All markets overall have fallen since last week levels with some signals of improvement. Pacific C5 sees limited miner activity and growing competition from owners. West Australia stems are limited with owners seeing low USD 11s and others claiming to see low USD 12s for first half August. Latest fixture from West Australia/Qingdao was done at USD 11.1 for August 7-9 dates. C3 Brazil/China and West Africa stems also saw slow activity this week so far, and rising bunker prices may further affect freight rates going forward. Today's offers so far are in the low-mid USD 33s for mid August dates, and ideas in the high USD 32s for end August laycans. Yesterday we heard rumors of a West Africa stem fixed in the USD 31s. North Atlantic is also quiet and we see growing tonnage lists building. The North is mostly confined to a couple transatlantic stems, and a few fresh fronthaul stems. Last night we heard of a fixture for early August in mid USD 42 levels ex Sept-Iles/Qingdao for 6-15 August on a standard Cape.

The Supramax and Handysize markets remained subdued with limited fresh activity reported. Atlantic sentiment was mixed, with North America under pressure from longer tonnage lists, while the East Mediterranean remained relatively firmer. In Asia, conditions were mixed with softer sentiment in the North but improved activity in Southeast Asia and steady Indian Ocean demand. Handysize market remained balanced in Europe, while the US Gulf and South Atlantic continued to face pressure from tonnage availability. Overall, both markets are awaiting stronger cargo flow and increased activity for clearer direction.

Stronger USG Aframax rates are expected to improve the sentiment across the Atlantic, while limited VLCC availability in West Africa ahead of the 10th prohibits their crash from disrupting volume in the present window. That said, any disruption to CPC exports could lead to more tonnage seeking employment in the Atlantic basin & VLCC rates look like they are on a collision course, and at the very least encourage 2nd decade charterers to utilise them at higher rates than we have become accustomed to. Looking ahead, continued tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and growing uncertainty surrounding Aden transits are encouraging more vessels to ballast West, which may place some pressure on the Atlantic markets going forward, but demand fundamentals ex West Africa (12MBBLS 1st decade / 26MBBLS 2nd decade uncovered) could counterweight this.

The Panamax market has drifted softer through the week, with sentiment turning cautious across both basins as the index eased and owners found bids reluctant to follow their ideas. In the Atlantic the tone has been subdued – transatlantic business is holding together rather better than fronthaul, but the constraint is one of cargo volume rather than tonnage, and a build-up of ballasters arriving from the East has left forward positions in the South under pressure and the basin trading two-tier, with prompt units still commanding a premium. The Pacific has been the weaker of the two, as thin fresh grain and coal enquiry out of North Pacific, Australia and Indonesia has allowed prompt tonnage to accumulate and charterers to sit back and bid below last-done. Period remains the steadier corner of the market, with one-year business still concluding, though a backwardated forward curve and firmer bunkers on Middle East tensions are keeping owners measured rather than assertive. We look for a sideways-to-easier tone into next week, with the eventual ramp-up in new-crop grain out of the US Gulf and South America the most likely source of support later in the quarter.

Further escalation in the Middle East is a worrying scenario as much for the global markets as it is for tanker owners and operators. Production shut-ins, lower export capacities, and eventually higher oil prices are hardly things the global economy needs right now, and the effect on tanker rates should be negative as cargoes dwindle. Rates have however, remained resilient so far during the disruption and are at very healthy levels, meaning we are unlikely to see softening in tanker values anytime soon. Sizeable premiums are still being paid on older units, seen in the sale of 2x Ice class 1A suezmax pair ALASKA/ARCHANGEL (163k dwt Hyundai 2006) at USD 50.75M each.  Quiet week once again on the dry second-hand front, likely a combination of the exasperating conditions in the Middle East and the beginning of summer holidays. The general situation on dry is rosy, with earnings consistent across all sectors, and values firm. Some action to report this week as Meghna continue their ultramax buying spree with scrubber fitted pair BRITTA/BENJAMIN OLDENDORFF (62k dwt Oshima 2020) at just over USD 37M each.

WEST We have seen a lot of activity on shipping in the West during the last few weeks, and current fixing count for August now stand at 25 deals (10/10/5 by decade). Last done commercially clean deal at USD 235 HCvP on a Neo type ship, but as we still see several uncovered cargos in both 2nd and 3rd decade of August, owners latest ideas at USD 250+ HCvP.  EAST East of Suez market is again facing increased turmoil as the ceasefire between Iran and US have been broken. The relatively newly established and increasingly active STS-Sohar market may meet less willingness from owners as the market is yet again forced to reassess risk.

The Handy and Handymax market remained active this week, supported by a healthy mix of spot and short-period opportunities across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. Cargo flow remained steady, with active tonnage circulation across key regions. Demand was primarily driven by grain, coal, fertilizer, and petcoke trades. The Atlantic basin, particularly South America, continued to generate the majority of activity, while Asia provided consistent short-haul employment opportunities.  The Supramax and Ultramax markets remained firm, although spot cargo demand has started to ease, with market attention shifting toward late July and August positions. East Coast South America (ECSA) continues to offer significantly stronger returns than West Africa, and despite the widening spread between the two regions, the U.S. Gulf market remains broadly balanced. Owners have remained selective in their voyage choices, particularly when considering repositioning opportunities as the USG continues to rise.

The Atlantic market strengthened further during the week, with modern 2-stroke rates pushing towards the $100,000/day mark and TFDE tonnage from the East seen covering outstanding Atlantic requirements in the first half of August. Availability appears healthy but is typically tighter once flexibility between basins is required. A growing theme is the disconnect between spot freight rates and cargo economics, with the same flexibility sought by FOB buyers also attracting a premium on the cargo side.  The Pacific has seen one of its busiest weeks in recent memory with fixtures East of Suez touching double digits, although rates have so far remained relatively contained. Activity from West Africa has also picked up noticeably. While it is too early to determine whether this signals a repeat of the production growth that drove the market higher in Q4-25, it is a development worth monitoring.   Looking ahead, the balance of the year remains backwardated with multimonth interest increasingly price sensitive as availability builds and both owners and subletters seek coverage into 2027. For the traditionalists, the idea of Winter trading at a discount to Summer remains difficult to reconcile. With geopolitical uncertainty persisting, and in some regard increasing, there remains a credible case behind both sides of the bid-offer spread.

North Sea All of the western Aframax markets are active and firm putting upward pressure on rates. North Sea rates have jumped 30+ points so far this week and the pressure looks likely to remain on charterers for the balance of the month stems. The list has also been depleted with early tonnage heading out of the area both to US and Mediterranean with owners looking to lock in longer voyages at high daily returns. Next natural North Sea stems now in the 28-30 window.  Mediterranean Who would have said that TD19 will be printed at over WS 300 in the middle of summer. Expensive Suezmaxes, fuel inquiries and a bit of forward fixing have pushed rates probably at all-time high for the month of July. Charterer are trying to find viable solutions while owners from surrounding areas are ready to ballast into the Mediterranean with the dates pushed slowly even to August.

This week on Capes, fresh activity emerged earlier this week mostly centered around Brazil and West Africa stems with strong fixtures in the first half of the week. Today activity on C3 Brazil / China saw less activity, although players are still rating at similar levels seen earlier in the week. Latest offers on C3 Brazil/China seen for early August at mid USD 34 levels, and later dates posting offers in the high USD 32s. The Baltic exchange shows that all basins are a tick down, as well as C3, falling slightly after bunker prices saw an overnight jump.  North Atlantic trade this week has been more centered around West Africa fronthaul stems, with a fixture yesterday reported in low USD 36 levels, equivalent to USD 76.3K a day on C9.   In the Pacific, we saw a slightly suppressed tone earlier in the week, and flat market today on C5 West Australia / China, with offers in the low USD 14s and High USD 13s range for end July dates and last done levels posting low USD 13s for end July. August outlook is expected to decrease as rumours of low-mid USD 12 and low USD 13s reported.   Overall, markets look toward the bearish direction going forward across major segments, with C3 Brazil / China posting a higher daily earning potential over C5 West Australia / Qingdao.

The mystery list is piling up again, much like last week. This implies that the majority of rates have been in and around last-done levels. Despite the eased supply at the week's outset, healthy demand has counteracted this and kept the market in equilibrium. The list has now tightened slightly but unless charterers have very prompt dates in hand, owners on the front end are expected to remain pragmatic, as there are a reasonable number of vessels currently on berth in the West, as well as tonnage arriving from the East for the forward window. In isolation, Suezmaxes appear steady. However, there are reports that East-bound enquiries have reignited in the Atlantic in response to heightened tensions in the Middle East, while the Aframaxes are firming in the West - this is bringing Suezmaxes closer to being competitive, albeit not quite there yet.

The Panamax market held a firm but consolidating tone through the week, with the index trading broadly sideways at historically elevated levels after the sharper gains of recent weeks. In the Atlantic, fronthaul remained the engine - steady mineral and grain demand out of the US Gulf, North Coast South America and the northern basins kept owners confident on the longer east-bound legs, while East Coast South America held its ground and better-supplied transatlantic rounds left the North Atlantic waiting on fresh cargo to set the next direction. The Pacific was the steadier of the two basins, underpinned by a deep North Pacific grain book, a consistent flow of Australian and Indonesian coal, and a gradually tightening prompt list as tonnage was drawn south toward South American loading; sentiment stayed constructive and owners largely held their offers, leaving charterers to chase. Period enquiry remained active and reasonably well bid, though owners' ideas and charterers' bids stayed some way apart and the forward curve continues to sit in modest backwardation. Overall the tone is constructive-to-steady heading into next week, with firmer bunker prices and a quieter North Atlantic the principal watch-points.

The market never sleeps of course, and ships are being picked off quietly, but the sense is nevertheless that things have slowed down as hostilities have worsen in the Middle East. President Trump reimposed a naval blockade on all Iranian ports and Tehran launched strikes on US infrastructure in the region. Early today, the US began a fresh round of strikes to continue degrading Iranian capabilities used to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and any further escalation involving the Strait of Hormuz or additional sanctions on Iranian exports could quickly tighten ‌market sentiment ⁠and add further risk premiums. Iran's army also said that it had launched drone attacks against US positions at Jordan's Azraq base and targeted weapons and storage facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait. War risk insurance is back in the melting pot, to the extent it is available, and with that rates reported are not necessarily comparable like for like. The devil is in the detail as the saying goes. Fujairah and Oman are now back as priority number one in addition to Yanbu of course, where possible additional risk is added as the Houthis have started saber-rattling again. Although the Atlantic has seen a bit more action as far eastern refineries seek alternative supply the market in general is left searching for direction.

Strait of Hormuz crossings have almost ground to halt as USA and Iran trade blows once again, proving the fragility of the MOU. While disruption can boost earnings, tanker owners still need the free flow of cargo, and the new strikes are a cause for concern. This week, scrubber fitted GH HOLIDAY (157k dwt New Times 2016) was sold for USD 81M to GNMTC, setting a new benchmark in this sector.   Like on the wet, dry owners and charterers will be closely observing the deteriorating situation in Hormuz. Earnings in the meantime have remained consistent, and values too are strong, which will certainly keep owners happy. There is a “school’s out” feel in the market this week with less second-hand activity than usual, and buyers perhaps taking a step back in these complicated conditions. On the modern front, ultramax WF ARTEMIS (63k dwt Iwagi Zosen 2020) sold to Meghna for USD 36.5M.

Sentiment in the VLGC sector improved markedly during the week, pushing USG–East TCEs above USD 100,000/day after a sharp rebound from the lows recorded last week. In the West, an active fixing pace has significantly reduced prompt tonnage availability, leaving only a handful of July positions open. As a result, freight levels have moved higher, with H/C rates climbing from the low USD 160s to around USD 210. Owners remain optimistic on the near-term outlook, supported by improving MEG demand and an increasing preference for Cape routing over Panama. At the same time, the firmer MEG outlook continues to shape decisions, with vessel positioning increasingly reflecting expectations of stronger Middle East activity and sustained support for freight levels.

As storms brew in the Pacific, strong demand continues on C5 West Australia/Brazil trade routes with offers between low-mid USD 13s. Earlier in the week we saw a series of stems for second half July dates fixing in low-mid USD 13s while other majors fixed C5 in low USD 13s and one reported selling 13 flat for end July dates. Today fresh fixtures were seen, all in low USD 13 levels. Further uncertainty awaits as Typhoon Maysak is expected to bring continued storms to already flooded regions of southern and central China, which may lead to further discharge disruptions. C3 Brazil/China trades are also at potential risk of discharge disruptions in the coming days, however markets have seen stronger offers this week, with offers in the mid USD 32s and low USD 30s for August dates. Others have seen bids in low USD 32 levels and fixtures have been reported in mid USD 32 levels for end July and early August laycans. North Atlantic activity has also picked up this week, with a recent transatlantic stem ex West Africa to Arzew fixing in the USD 10s (about USD 49.5k/day equivalent to opening Gibraltar). C8 has +5.77% gains today on paper, while C3 and C5 routes are down slightly compared to yesterday.

Two steps forward and one step back. Iran and the US have been at it again trading airstrikes. And Washington has also reimposed crude sales sanctions on Tehran. You could have been fooled to think we were back to normal in the last few days with numerous enquiries and fixtures inside the MEG and rates have strengthened accordingly, but the exchange of fire underlines how fragile the situation still is. Players are likely to take a breather to see where we go from here. It will probably “blow over” but you never know after President Trump today indicated that the tentative ceasefire with Iran is over. Having been largely "dormant" lately, barring Brazilian export, focus could again change to the Atlantic for alternative supply.

The Panamax market remains firm in the Atlantic, where limited prompt vessel availability, particularly in the North, continues to support owner sentiment and keep charterers under pressure for coverage. In the Pacific, it is more balanced, with quieter activity and ample tonnage offset by more cargos from the NOPAC. Indonesian demand remains soft, while potential weather disruptions around Taiwan and South China may temporarily tighten tonnages. Overall, the Atlantic is providing the main support to the market, while the Pacific remains broadly stable but regionally mixed.

Outstanding West Africa volume for the third decade is likely nearing 10 mbbls, with 4–5 Guyana cargoes still to cover and likely a similar number from CPC. Further Brazilian volumes may also emerge, with VLCC availability remaining short in the Atlantic for July laycans. The front end of the Suezmax Atlantic list is fairly balanced; however, renewed Middle East tensions could see vessels waiting on MEG business ballast towards the Cape, offering charterers more end-July/early-August options. Conversely, if strikes persist, Asian buyers may turn to the Atlantic again, renewing forward buying and helping absorb any excess tonnage.

North Sea The main headline this week has been vessels ballasting. Tonnage list in the North Sea has been trimmed with tonnage heading mainly to USG but by the middle of the week heading to the Mediterranean with the busy firming market becoming the destination of choice. North Sea has remained steady so far with not enough activity to be affected by the smaller tonnage list.  Natural dates should start to push towards 3rd decade.  Mediterranean We are slowly heading into 3rd decade of July and rates for local runs are close to the WS 200 mark. Multiple factors are positively affecting the market and the owners have built some proper summer sentiment for now. There are still outstanding cargoes for the 2nd decade and rates are expected to remain under further upward pressure.

Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have put LNG directly in the firing line, but the freight market has held its nerve - spot rates remain broadly stable for now. Steady fixing since the start of the month has eroded the long availability lists of recent weeks and longer voyages driven by the open arbitrage has created some tightness in the early August window in the Atlantic. Rates for modern tonnage in the West are therefore increasing, albeit at a modest pace and still within the bounds we have seen in recent months. TFDEs in the East have seen some downward pressure, but rate levels for modern tonnage remains resilient, supported by firming DES prices and thinning availability. Current availability is concentrated on the prompt to mid-July, while demand on both sides of Suez sits early August onwards - leaving owners to absorb idle time to bridge the gap into their next employment. In contrast to recent weeks, a broad spread of firm requirements is being worked, keeping all participants busy. Charterers continue to pay up for worldwide redelivery flexibility, with the economics of sending Atlantic cargoes East still justifying the premium.

On Supramax, US Gulf remains firm- demand is healthy and tonnage tight. ECSA holds steady with firmer levels for index dates, while West Africa has strengthened on a thin tonnage list plus ongoing weather delays along the coast. The Continent stays lacklustre on limited scrap volumes, and the Mediterranean, though quieter, shows signs of firming as tonnage thins. Asia remains subdued overall on weak mineral demand from Australia and Southeast Asia and limited NOPAC grains, though backhauls and renewed Indonesia x India demand are propping the region up. Handy sentiment is softer and positional across the board, with wide bid-offer spreads in the Atlantic pushing owners to reassess expectations lower, while Asia sees tonnage lengthening and rates flat. Overall tone: Atlantic cautiously positive in pockets, Asia waiting on fresh impetus.

The tanker market continues its watchful approach to the second-hand space in the aftermath of a fragile reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Owners will be tested through the remainder of the 60-day MOU, where volumes are unlikely to move much. Rates in general are coming under downward pressure, with crude buyers not rushing to replenish in the short term. Across the clean market, particularly in the Atlantic, MR rates have returned to normal levels following an intensely profitable period, as lower volumes result in ships outweighing the number of cargoes available. This week Y/Knot emerged as buyers of LR2 JAG LOKESH (105K dwt HHI 2009) for USD 44.1M.   The dry market is providing the liquidity this week, albeit at levels that give a cautious feel. The global macro situation, despite a lower oil price potentially helping the outlook, is still very unpredictable. Rising interest rates and a much-speculated over-inflated stock market will cast some doubt into the minds of buyers, which could fuel a bearish feel to the market. That said there is still plenty of opportunity for those willing to invest at these levels. This week, ADNOC bought SS passed HAATO (61K dwt Shin Kasado 2011) for USD 23.5M.

Several deals have been concluded ex US this week from end July into 1H August, bringing total July fixtures to 23 deals and 8 for August. Freight sentiment has strengthen considerably within the last 24 hours, from last concluded fixture yesterday at around $170 HCvP, to high 180s - low 190s being reported today. In the East, there have been talks of ships subfixed to load ex MEG for July, but no deals appear to have finally been done.

All segments up today on Cape after a flat start to the week, C5 rates recovered as all major miners returned to market with healthy cargo volumes. High USD 10s have been most recent fixtures, with highest so far today done at USD 10.85 for a West Australia/China stem for 15-17 July, and USD 10.75 for 16-18 July dates ex Hedland/Japan. C3 Brazil/China rates have climbed over the last 3 days, with activity sharply picking up yesterday, setting a positive sentiment and more constructive tone. Latest offers on C3 have seen around USD 33 levels for 11-20 July dates, and last done was a standard Cape in the USD 31s for end July ex Brazil. Earlier week fixtures were in the mid/high USD 28-29.4 levels ex Brazil/China. Transatlantic activity picked up as of yesterday following one operator fixing a fronthaul from Sept-IIes to Taiwan for early August dates at USD 36 which is equivalent to around USD 66.7 C9 basis. Transatlantic demand continues across late July and early August dates and healthy tonnage sits tighter in end July dates. C3 21-31 July last done USD 31. C5 15-17 July last done USD 10.3, 17-19 July last done USD 10.75, 19-21 July last done USD 10.35.

Whilst the Middle East remains opaque supply & demand in the West are all working in owners favour presently, although with potential for seismic shifts down the line there is plenty of nuance. Multiple CPC stems versus what just 2 ships FOC or ETS within 5 days ex Mediterranean tilts TD6 towards the bulls. Supplemented nicely by Brazil enquiry, with 2-4 Liza working over the past 24H and 24MBBLS untouched in the 3rd decade ex West Africa, the Atlantic basin is also strong. However, VLCC trajectory on freight is not miles away from rendering them competitive on 1MBBL stems, utilisation of 3x VLCC this week ex West Africa in our window & potential for corrections in crude pricing that could bring back Chinese demand may all undermine Suezmax volumes. Over the past 6 decades we have averaged a colossal 25MBBLs per decade, which has been a significant market driver, particularly during this period when USG volumes are almost solely reserved for Aframaxes. This has halted further progress, and the risk of an Armada of ballasters ex East down the line (24-31 window) only serves to underline this. Charterers on the front end still have a tough job, but we are pretty much working 3 weeks out and with crude pricing, VLCC freight & Suezmax supply (both ex East and ex UKC if we have time to wait) potentially alleviating pressure there will be reluctance to work the forward window.

The Panamax market remained firm, supported by improving demand in both the Atlantic and Pacific. In the Atlantic, prompt tonnage remains relatively tight despite the emergence of more early July vessels, with strong transatlantic, mineral fronthaul and East Coast South America demand continuing to support sentiment. Owners are maintaining a firm stance, although an increase in ballasting vessels into ECSA may gradually improve tonnage availability. In the Pacific, stronger demand from Australia and the NOPAC, combined with fewer owners committing to longer trips, has tightened effective vessel supply and kept market sentiment positive.

North Sea North Sea so far this week has seen almost no Aframax activity. The first decade of July is almost covered with a combination of Suez and relets taking what was on paper a light decade stem wise. Rates will be tested by charterers. Surrounding markets have been steady although not overly inspiring for owners. Ballasting out of the North Sea if you have missed the dates is still the option to take.
