Mediterranean One step forward two steps back feels to be the situation for the Mediterranean market where activity remains healthy, tonnage list has shortened in a way but still a bunch of vessels prompt. Days keep pushing ahead and we slowly reaching mid-July dates for all ports. As a correction is expected or rumoured done already in the US market, the future doesn't look promising for European markets either.

As many had feared, hopes for resumed safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz in the near future were once again dented as further attacks on commercial shipping were followed by retaliatory strikes on Iran over the weekend. The brief window of free transit enjoyed by LNG Carriers last week is back on hiatus and there was an immediate reaction in the LNG market, with pricing into Asia ticking higher and the arbitrage widening. It is clear now if it wasn’t before, that there will be no quick fixes and there remains a lot of risk heading into the second half of the year and through winter. For now though, despite continued uncertainty, the summertime lull in the spot market is apparent: availability lists are quite thin but there are also a relative lack of requirements, so there is a slight oversupply of tonnage putting downward pressure on 2-stroke and TFDE rates. This is more pronounced East of Suez than West where there is considerable premium, although Atlantic rates dipped below $90k/d for the first time in months off the back of a rush of QatarEnergy sublets. Looking further ahead, there has been little change for multimonth periods and rates have remained fairly flat through to 1Q 2027.

The owning community has done well keeping rates at elevated levels, but the resolve is starting to show cracks as volumes have subsided and are unlikely to see much improvement for the remainder of the 60-day MOU between the US and Iran. Arguably we have seen a bit more production emerging in the MEG, but a far cry from pre-war levels and transit through the Strait is still precarious. A rumour suggest that WS 250 has been done for an inside MEG loading for east. Whether true or not there’s seldom smoke without fire and direction of travel is evident. However, TD3C paper for July is currently pegged each side of WS 250 which could indicate a floor. Rates for “outside” loading continue to be under pressure as well with WS 159 last done for a Korea destined cargo, and the enquiry in question had 10 punters competing for it, the balance of which are left looking for employment. The Atlantic remains quiet barring almost daily Brazilian export requirements, but competition for same is naturally also tightening. All said and done however, a summer market in the WS 100-150 range is not something the tanker market has been used to historically. As always, it’s all in the eye of the beholder.

The Supramax/Handysize market remained mixed, with the Atlantic showing signs of improvement while Asia continued to soften. Sentiment in the US Gulf and South Atlantic strengthened, reported better enquiry and improving momentum, particularly for transatlantic business, while the Mediterranean also saw a increase in activity, providing support to the basin. In contrast, the Pacific market remained under pressure as a lack of fresh cargo demand, particularly from South Asia, led to increasing prompt tonnage.

Tanker rates are grabbing headlines in the aftermath of the confusing yet tangible progress which has been made on opening the Strait of Hormuz. The market is offering some levels of correction to the extraordinarily high levels that we have seen in the last months, however at numbers that will satisfy owners. In the shadow of continued newbuild ordering, a quieter week in the second-hand space as buyers observe how the next phase of the Middle East saga plays out. In the specialised market, STST J19 GREENWICH PARK (19k dwt Fukuoka 2011)* SSDD due 06/26 was sold to Vietnamese buyers at USD 22.8M.  Easing, though fragile, conditions in the Strait of Hormuz are a positive for the dry market. Lower and more consistent crude pricing will give confidence for the general macro demand outlook, while an open Strait will release trapped cargoes and allow countries within the Gulf to resume dry trading. Rates though appear to be looking on the toppy side, with the market understandably cautious about 2H 2026. Still, plenty of liquidity in the second hand space, most notably scrubber fitted capesize LADY DEENA (182k dwt JMU 2020) selling to Chinese buyers at USD 70M. Scrubber fitted 2020 blt capesize units have increased in value by 10% in the past year, seen against the sale of last done unit ex BULK GINZA (182k dwt Imabari 2020) which sold to GENCO at USD 64M in May 2025.

More of the same in the VLCC market, lots of under the radar fixing, and with all this “need to know only", very few do know, although the different camps are trying their best to influence direction of travel by divulging snippets or half truths if you like. Loading inside MEG now pays everything from WS 400 to almost WS 900 depending on destination and who you choose to listen to, but tracking still suggests volumes going through the Strait of Hormuz are limited and mostly existing inventories. A bit of Fuj-MAF and Yanbu continue to keep the flame burning and being mostly prompt liftings underpin the current rate level. All in all, the map does not fit the terrain at the moment, but that isn’t a first in our industry. As for the Atlantic, thank the Lord for Brazil continuing to pump and export, and to a degree compensating lack of appetite for WTI and West African grades in Asia.

This week on Capesize we have seen flat levels across the pacific earlier in the week with marginal decline today on C5. Physical fixtures for C5 West Australia/China have seen last done levels in the USD 11.25 range for early July dates and USD 11.75 for mid July. Earlier week fixtures were hovering between mid USD 11s-11.75 range for July dates. On C3 Brazil/China, a more active on fronthauls from Brazil, with active fixing yesterday. Latest fixtures today indicate levels hovering in the USD 31s with the latest stem fixed for late July dates. Earlier week fixtures were seen between mid USD 31s-33s, however Baltic today is down again slightly. In the North, tonnage demand has remained healthy with support through July dates, though transatlantic levels remained flat over the last week. West Africa cargoes have been an attractive substitute for limited fronthauls in the north. Recent fixtures ex West Africa are shown in mid USD 31 levels, with last being fixed at USD 31.5 from West Africa to China. Daily earning spreads for C3 vs C5 show stronger earning potential on C3 Brazil/China, with the latest spread around USD 8671 per day.

After weeks’ of “will they, won’t they” in the Middle East, an agreement to try to work towards an agreement has finally emerged and will be heavily scrutinised as more details emerge. It does appear that some of the key pillars should lead to the resumption of merchant traffic through the Strait of Hormuz (without tolls or hinderance); however, the devil will be in the detail and the detail is sorely lacking at this stage. One of the Articles refers to a resumption of traffic within 30 days, although the same Article does note there are challenges including mines that could impact that timeline, and of course there will be operational matters to handle in production itself.   Nonetheless, this is a welcome development and markets have reacted accordingly. Prices are already lower and the inter-basin arbitrage has been squeezed. How this will shape the LNG shipping market in the weeks and months to come remains to be seen, but we may expect some temporary disruptions and tightening East of Suez as scheduling is reworked to accommodate the additional volume while further out. Further out into winter, the competition between Europe and Asia for US volume should ease and lead to lower peak pricing and also to a softer market than we could have seen, yet while we work through the uncertainties and until we see more concrete steps it is unlikely there will be major changes to shipping strategies.  Thus, the markets in all basins have remained broadly steady. There are a number of multimonth requirements being worked and these should provide interesting data points for winter tonnage, although as mentioned last week there is a divergence of views for winter trading split between those pricing in weak freight fundamental versus a strong trading environment and we may see these plans revisited across the board in the days ahead.

On Supramax, market lost some momentum after recent gains, with sentiment becoming more cautious across both basins. In the Atlantic, owners largely maintained a firm stance, although activity slowed and the market appeared increasingly positional. Elsewhere, the region seemed to be taking a natural breather following a stronger run, while arbitrage opportunities became less prominent. In Asia, limited fresh enquiry and wider bid-offer gaps weighed on sentiment, resulting in a quieter and more subdued environment. Overall, the sector remains supported by underlying optimism in the Atlantic, but short-term direction appears less clear as owners and charterers alike adopt a wait-and-see approach.   The Handy market continued to display a steady-to-firm tone overall. Atlantic regions, particularly the South Atlantic and US Gulf, remained supported by healthy demand and positive sentiment, helping maintain a constructive outlook. The Continent and Mediterranean saw more limited activity, with conditions broadly unchanged. In Asia, a balanced supply-demand picture and consistent cargo flow helped keep the market stable, with charterers generally maintaining a positive approach. Overall, the sector remains on a solid footing, supported by steady fundamentals and resilient sentiment across most regions.

North Sea rates have held relatively flat over the past week with last-done levels being repeated at WS 145. Activity has been healthy and a steady flow of ballasting has helped thin out the list, although positions are gradually pushing into end/early fixing windows. We expect the traditional TA players to continue heading West, with sentiment leaning towards a firmer US market, in turn lending some support to TD7 going forward.  The Mediterranean market has had a softer week, with charterers capitalising on a long tonnage list to push rates lower, while some deals have been concluded quietly under the radar. Despite overall healthy activity, availability has remained too high to be fully absorbed, keeping downward pressure on rates. A handful of prompt vessels remain, and the balance looks weak as we settling into July stems. Owners, now, may look to resist further erosion of current levels, although without a fresh wave of stems it is difficult to see a meaningful recovery.

Subdued activity in the VLGC market so far this week. The vessel balance in USG/USEC remains largely unchanged, however, a narrowing arbitrage has halted any new activity. In the East, we have started to see more enquires ex MEG appear following a handful of deals fixed STS Sohar week prior, but so far nothing reported fixed.

The Panamax market has remained uneven this week, with the Atlantic showing more life as fresh inquiry improved across both fronthaul and transatlantic trades. However, direction remains divided and the tonnage list looks less tight than last week. Owners are still managing to hold firmer ideas in certain pockets where prompt tonnage is tighter, but the wider basin feels broadly balanced rather than outright firm. The Pacific remains under pressure, with supply still outweighing demand despite better activity and some fresh cargo appearing, while owners are showing more resistance, particularly on longer-duration business and better-spec units. Overall sentiment remains soft, with the market continuing to ease, though the pace of decline appears to be slowing.

The market has resumed its upward trajectory this week, building on the momentum seen at the end of last week. CPC/Mediterranean rates have broken through the WS 250 barrier, and TD20 looks set to move above WS 240. Tonnage availability, both in the West and among vessels committed via the Cape of Good Hope, remains thin, and charterers look set to face increasingly emboldened owners, particularly given that there are still cargoes to cover for the second decade in both the Atlantic and ex-CPC.

While not a full deal per se, the framework agreed and signed this week between USA and Iran will provide the tanker market with lower supply side risk, and hopefully some seldom seen stability. It is likely we will see a tug of war between owners and charterers over the next few weeks as the situation unfolds, though what is certain is that the market will be carefully watching the fortunes of laden crude tankers in their attempts to leave the Gulf. Buyers are still there to meet sellers’ lofty expectations on crude tonnage, seen in suezmax COSMO SAIL (159K dwt Hyundai Samho 2007) selling for USD 49.5M.   News coming from the Middle East will be positively received by the dry bulk market, hoping increased crude supply side security will keep oil prices at more sustained and manageable levels, allowing more general macro investment confidence and activity. Rates remain strong across dry and as usual there is a consistent stream of transactions. This week, MONT BLANC HAWK (81K dwt Imabari 2017) was sold for USD 32.2M.

This week on Cape we saw a decline with Pacific C5 markets remaining flat over the last days. Bids were initially reported in the low USD 10s but thanks to good support from miners, levels recently have raised to USD 10.6-10.7 levels in Pacific and last done for early July at USD 10.85. Atlantic sentiment has weakened with C3 declining sharply over the last week. Bids reported in the USD 30s with offers hovering around USD 34 for mid July dates, capping activity in the Atlantic. North Atlantic also sees softer sentiment. Recently a Newcastlemax fixed close to USD 35 on a C3 Brazil/China fixture. Baltic today is at USD 31.75 which is still marginally over the average so far this year, yet decreased 2.63% today. C5 today was flat with Baltic printing USD 10.73, slightly below the year to date average. The latest spread for Atlantic vs Pacific is USD 11400 in favour of C3 Brazil/China. C3 Brazil/China 21-30 June seen offers USD 37.25, 1-10 June seen offers USD 36.75, 11-20 July last done USD 35 Newcastlemax. C5 West Australia/China 1-3 July last done USD 10.85, 4-6 July last done USD 10.5, 7-9 July last done USD 11.1.

North Sea North Sea market has taken a hit this week with WS 140 on subs for a North Sea – Baltic cargo and it feels like more to come. On paper relets should come back into the fixing window, and we expect a fair amount of programming to occur, as with all Western Aframax markets being softer, ballasting doesn’t necessarily give you an outlet, and reducing waiting times will be key.  Mediterranean Market has adjusted downwards after 1-2 market quotes, but we haven't seen it collapsing. There is still underground activity that is taking out tonnage quietly but at the same time there is a couple of vessels stuck prompt hoping for earlier dates. We are more or less done for Ceyhan June dates and Libya hasn't much cargoes left either, so owners need to think about their next move while there aren't many alternatives.

"Much Ado About Nothing". Friday can’t come quick enough, in more ways than one. In the meantime, players are sitting on their hands in anticipation of the Strait of Hormuz opening. However, even if US and Iran put pen to paper we doubt we’ll see an immediate rush inbound any time soon. Seeing is believing and so on. Priority will likely be to get ships stuck in the Gulf out. The immediate urge for impulse oil buying may also be curbed as there are still tens of millions of barrels of crude stuck onboard those trapped ships in the Gulf, and refineries will need to process and digest this backlog first. There’s of course a rate out there for anything, money always talks, but the spread between what those owners willing to break the mould would want and what charterers would be willing to pay is going to take a broking job and a half to bridge. With the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow now becoming more tangible owners are naturally also pricing up all other less precarious alternatives as well. He who blinks first…

Over the past week, sentiment in the Supramax and Handysize sectors remained broadly positive, led by continued strength across the Atlantic basin. The US Gulf and South Atlantic markets consistently provided support, with improving confidence and healthy cargo demand underpinning activity despite limited reported fixtures. Mediterranean conditions also firmed gradually, benefiting from steady enquiry and better cargo coverage. In contrast, Asian markets were generally more balanced, with sentiment ranging from stable to mildly positive. While demand remained present, particularly for regional and long-haul employment, momentum appeared less pronounced than in the Atlantic. Overall, owners retained a positive outlook, supported by tightening vessel availability in Atlantic regions and a steady flow of cargo requirements across both vessel segments. Period appetite remains however very few fixtures reported past week.

The Panamax market presents a mixed picture, with the Atlantic outperforming the Pacific. In the Atlantic, activity has improved with better cargo replenishment, steady transatlantic and fronthaul demand, and tighter prompt tonnage supporting sentiment and helping rates remain stable. Meanwhile, the Pacific remains under pressure due to limited grain and mineral demand, an oversupply of prompt vessels, and a lack of fresh cargoes. Overall, Atlantic strength is providing some support to the broader market, but Pacific weakness continues to weigh on sentiment.

Subdued activity in the VLGC market this week as the world anxiously awaits further developments around the Straight of Hormuz. The vessel balance in USG/USEC remains largely unchanged, however, a narrowing arbitrage is halting new activity unless freight drops significantly from last done levels of mid USD 260’s basis HCvP. On the back of the shear volatility in the product market seen in the recent month or so and the arbitrage movements parallel to a potentially opening of the Straight of Hormuz, it is hard to be adamant of short term freight movements should an opening delay further.

Fairly active start to the week in the West, with the East beginning to see increased attention amid growing chatter around a potential Iran/US deal. While West Africa supply remains healthy for now, a thin list of local openers in USG continues to leave charterers reliant on UKCM ballasters, effectively drawing on the same tonnage that would otherwise service West Africa. Growing expectations of a deal appears to support the sentiment, with more vessels likely to remain positioned in the East in anticipation of a potential opening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Tanker market earnings may be cooling slightly but transactions this week prove that buyers’ confidence in this disrupted market remains sky high. CMBTech owned scrubber fitted suezmax pair BREST/BRUGGE (157K dwt Hyundai Samho 2023) are reported sold at USD 112M each, well in excess of the last Korean built resale units (albeit with later delivery) which were sold to Teekay in May at USD 95M each. Numbers like this are sure to make every modern suezmax owner think twice about their youngest units. As a result of this pricing, newbuilding remains a popular choice for investors, with healthy numbers being reported.   Those expecting an avalanche of deals to be reported after the Posidonia week will be slightly disappointed, however it is worth remembering that the general market fundamentals have not changed, and the overall geopolitical position is arguably at it’s most tense in weeks. Sellers of older capesize units are being rewarded for their patience, seeing excellent exits such as KERKIS (176K dwt Namura 2007)*SSDD due in November 26, sold for USD 25.5M.

A softer week on Cape with Pacific basins down from recent highs over the last week with further downward pressure expected. June C5 West Australia/China fresh fixtures indicate last done levels in the low USD 12 range with late June last done seen USD 12 flat and end June seeing USD 12.35. For Atlantic, both C3 Brazil/China and North Atlantic are trading firm with mixed sentiment. C3 Brazil/China stems see offers for late June dates in the low USD 37 range and early July offers at mid USD 36 levels. One fixture reported today was 11-20 laycan fixing USD 35 on a Newcastlemax. With strong demand and limited fresh tonnage in the North Atlantic, transatlantic routes remain firm as owners hold out for premium fronthaul rates to return amid continued tightness in the basin. C3 Brazil/China 21-30 June offers USD 37.25, 1-10 July bids USD 34, offers USD 36.5, 11-20 June last done (Newcastlemax) USD 35. C5 West Australia/China 19-21 June last done USD 12, 25-27 June last done 12.35.

Ships continue to disappear under the radar on the VLCC front and the position lists both sides of Suez are becoming wanting in the front end, which should dictate a further uptick in rates. Capping that is lack of transparency. A tight supply/demand picture is one thing but not having a pricing reference is clouding proceedings. If owners really want to push this, they will have to start leaking a bit more information – real time – if not the assumption will be that it’s just more of the same. Rumours suggest there is still prompt interest from Fuj/Oman from the likes of Admic and KPC et al., and not much to choose from with WS 140 eastbound seemingly a “given” if nothing else comes to light. Petrobras keeps the flame burning from the Atlantic with almost daily cargo quotes Brazil/East and rates have inched up a couple of points north of the WS 115 mark. Sinkor is back in buying mood if we are to believe reports, the Maxim being the latest to be added, at a stonking price for an older lady ('11 built). Never have so many had one player to thank for so much to paraphrase Churchill, without Sinokor’s big market share and restraint in fixing we wouldn’t be even close to current levels.

The Supramax market maintained a positive tone, supported by stronger enquiry in the Atlantic and improving activity across Asia. Market reported firmer sentiment in the US Gulf and South Atlantic, while growing backhaul demand in North Asia helped support overall vessel demand. The Handysize also strengthened, with tighter tonnage availability and balanced supply-demand conditions contributing to a firmer market environment. Activity remained steady across most regions, with the US Gulf and Asian markets showing the most encouraging signs of improvement.

WEST Spot fixing activity has been subdued in the West this week, except from one Asian major fixing a ship at around USD 250 HCvP for 3rd decade July via tender. Forward fixing out of the US Gulf remains limited, with just 8 spot fixtures recorded so far for July loading (3/4/1 by decade). This is a marked slowdown compared to previous months and highlights the current lack of visible cargo flow. Meanwhile, prompt ship availability remains tight, with only two VLGCs available for loading up to 10th July, and just a handful of ships for 10-15 July window. This constrained availability suggests that the market retains upside potential and could quickly firm once more cargoes emerge.  EAST MEG exports remain constrained amid the ongoing Iran situation, limiting conventional cargo flow. However, alternative setups have recently created some business, with STS cargoes reported off Sohar at premium rates. These have been fixed around USD 215 RT/CH.

The Panamax market remains divided between a gradually improving Atlantic and a weakening Pacific. Atlantic sentiment has turned slightly more constructive, supported by better transatlantic activity, firmer fronthaul demand, and increasing NCSA enquiry, although ample tonnage and wide bid-offer spreads continue to cap gains. In the Pacific, limited cargo volumes, a growing tonnage list, and cautious charterers are keeping pressure on rates, particularly on Indonesian business. While vessel tightness indicators still point to near-term softness, strong shipment volumes, supportive demand fundamentals, and a coal forward curve now moving into slight backwardation suggest the market could find better support as July approaches.

A busy first half of the week, with an enormous amount of off market activity alongside some reported fixtures. Tonnage in the West has tightened, however, supply should remain healthy enough to prevent aggressive upside. With this level of activity, the demand outlook has also been somewhat undermined. We are likely down to the last 5 mbbls to cover in West Africa for June, with a similar volume remaining out of Guyana for the month. Naturally, with July stems only just entering the 3 week window, charterers may opt to take a step back from fixing into July.

The persistent arbitrage to head East and a relative lack of available vessels should be squeezing the spot market, but the Atlantic looks to be holding steady at best or slightly softening. A clear-out of tonnage for prompt dates in the Pacific has resulted in some uplift for TFDE’s, despite pocket lengths on modern tonnage being priced aggressively. Higher LNG prices and a more volatile trading environment will present traders and portfolios with opportunities and this should lead to higher freight, which is certainly the case where any real flexibility is preserved for charterers, yet there is a natural counter to this with lost volume and weak shipping fundamentals. The interplay between these competing forces is driving the bid/offer spread at the moment, and many freight discussions are run in parallel with traders looking at FOB sales so there is a cap on spot rates. Interestingly, this dynamic is already leading to divergent strategies for winter. Most market participants see the same factors (less volume, more ships, higher LNG prices, buyers competing), but while some see the potentially strong trading dynamics as a basis for taking on additional tonnage others see the weak fundamentals as a reason to hold off - markets are always more active and much more interesting when there are such different views.

North Sea The market has remained stable through the 2nd decade in the low WS 150’s. Natural window is now moving into the 3rd decade and with relets still in the mix taking stems activity has been limited. With surrounding markets also looking softer there isn’t much in the way of pressure on charterers so steady as we go for the near future.  Mediterranean A Libyan cargo on Monday managed to attract 6-7 offers in and as a result cross Mediterranean runs corrected by 15 points which was then repeated multiple times. Activity has been consistently healthy, but the fundamental issue is the excess tonnage supply as 70% of the total LR2's on the water are trading in DPP with majority in the West of Suez markets. US markets took a blow yesterday however the flow of ballasters is expected to remain steady from Europe. Overall, steady/softer with owners to try and stop the downfall.

No second-hand transactions are reported in the tanker market this week, though not due to any change in sentiment, which remains strong. Newbuilding continues to be the preferred outlet for investors in this sector, with activity particularly focused on larger crude tonnage.    Earnings across dry are in keeping with the overall buoyant shipping markets, with the lower than usual reported sales likely due to Posidonia 2026 taking place in Athens this week. SSDD due Supramax AE MARS (53K DWT Yangzhou Dayang 2006) was sold for USD 9.05M.

Rates continue to stay buoyant across the basins, as both Atlantic and Pacific markets enjoy increased liquidity over spot and term periods.  Several competing requirements in the East for 2H June have made availability among TFDEs appear tight for the first time in some weeks, which is reflected by gently increasing headline rates.  The Atlantic market looks increasingly tight for July, driven mainly by a sustained arbitrage pulling ships out of the intra-basin trade flows to which we have become accustomed.  These patterns show little sign of slowing down, as both developing and firm requirements for 1H July have already hit the market.  Layer on to the current market dynamics the continuing difficulties resolving the conflict in the Middle East, and the firmness we're seeing today looks set to persist for the foreseeable future.

North Sea The majority of the first decade stems are now covered with little in the way of actual market activity. Rates fell to WS 145 at the end of last week but with US and Mediterranean markets picking up the North Sea should have stabilized and with tonnage expected to ballast away may have bottomed. With some Norwegian field maintenance now over the 2nd half of June on paper looks to be busier than the first half which should give owners some optimism.   Mediterranean The end of last week was very busy with charterers fixing both ahead in dates and ahead of Posidonia. This week has remained active with a mixture of new business and some replacement business which has pushed the market up over 40 points very quickly. The list is on the tighter side of balanced for good itinerary tonnage and some ports are experiencing some delays which is helping to keep it balanced. Sentiment is firm from owners. We may see some vessels ballast from the North Sea but probably not enough to change the momentum for this week at least.

The Panamax market opened the week on a softer note, with Posidonia and regional holidays keeping activity limited and many players still reassessing direction. The Atlantic remains under pressure, with limited fresh mineral and grain enquiry meeting a growing prompt tonnage list in the Continent and Mediterranean, forcing earlier-position owners to trim expectations. ECSA is broadly flat but feels toppy for index dates, with spot tonnage still discounted due to limited cargo volume. In the Pacific, Indonesia and Australian mineral flows continue to provide some support, but sentiment has turned more cautious as tonnage builds and fresh requirements remain thin. Overall, near-term indicators still point bearish, while coal demand and potential Chinese weather disruptions remain the main upside risk.

This week on Capesize, C3 Brazil/China remains firm but thin fresh activity, with ideas hovering around USD 38 today for July stems. With slightly softening forward curve and lack of prompt tonnage we expect to see slight easing for Q3 stems. The Atlantic remains hot for another week, with transatlantic C8 pushing USD 58,000 per day and C9 at USD 76,972 reflecting strong front haul demand and limited prompt tonnage in continent. Ballasters are still favouring Brazil/China C3 but North Atlantic continue to command premium rates. C5 Pacific still remains firm but slightly off the recent highs. Some forward softness is expected coming into late June. Owners ideas are currently hovering around USD 16 and bids reported in the mid USD 15s for June 18-22 stems. C3 Brazil/China last done USD 38 21-30 June. C5 West Australia/China last done USD 15.85 16-18 June, last done USD 15.7 22-24 June.

Despite Posidonia & regional holidays around, market continued to exhibit a generally constructive tone. In the Atlantic, sentiment remained positive, particularly in USG where tightening vessel avails continued to support owners’ expectations. ECSA maintained firm underlying fundamentals, although fresh business remained limited. In Asia, it was a mixed picture, with stronger demand evident in the north while ample prompt tonnage weighed on sentiment further south. The Handy sector showed comparatively firmer momentum across Asia, supported by tightening vessel supply and steady cargo demand, helping offset the subdued activity seen across much of the Atlantic basin. With the upcoming monsoon season in India, demand is expected to slowdown in the coming weeks. Period activity remains limited with very few fixtures reported in the region.

USG market remains quiet with limited visible fixing. Two deals reported at USD 270, with broader Apr/May activity at 48 liftings ex-Houston. Forward July coverage is still thin at just four fixtures, split between USD 270 and USD 285, pointing to a firmer tone. Most activity this week has been done discreetly, masking underlying positioning. An Asian oil major tender is currently in play and could set the next benchmark. Baltic sentiment remains stable-to-firm, supporting the view of gradual upside.

A noticeably quiet week for VLCCs, shaped by industry participants’ temporary migration to Greece for Posidonia. Activity has slowed, position lists fairly balanced, but ships disappearing quietly with no details. Prompt cargoes in the Middle East showing signs of paying extra, but a slightly softer feel in the Atlantic with USG/East holding for above 16 million for the time being.

High off market activity pruned lists, primarily characterised by Mediterranean/West Africa fixtures whilst the US still fails to pull its weight. Charterers eagerness for simple deals pre/during-Posidonia and with the easy excuse last Friday of the "risk" of a resolution in the Middle East spiking sentiment lead to high activity countering weak supply fundamentals and stagnating rates. CPC enquiry is working but plenty of ships are keen to cover it, some pointing towards Canakkale on spec. West Africa is fixed into the 3rd decade with over 10 natural & pushed FOC vessels despite high erosion. Charterers can now sit and enjoy the remainder of their Athens escapades and let availabilities rebuild.

Scorpio this week announced the sale of 4x scrubber fitted LR2 units STI CONDOTTI/BROADWAY/WINNIE/LAUREN (109K DWT Daehan 2014/15) for a total of USD 285.8M, representing a figure of xs USD 70M per vessel. In this context it is worth remembering that only a month ago, the market was in shock at scrubber fitted 2018 blt Japanese Afras being sold in the mid USD 70M range. Deadlock in the Middle East, plus the disruption that entails, and the potential booming aftermath of a resolution is seemingly more than enough for buyers to justify the levels being paid today. Longer term question marks remain over the increased fleet growth we will see in the coming years, however this feels like a distant worry for owners and buyers alike as the short-term uncertainty reigns supreme.   There is unrelenting momentum in the dry bulk market, with average capesize spot rates climbing 12% from last week alone to a high of USD 46K/day on Thursday. Buyers still see legs in this bulk run, despite total demand growth reaching 6%, which is usually seen around the peaks of dry cycles. This confidence is seen in the fact 20 buyers registered interest in Tess 82 KEY HUNTER (82K DWT Tsuneishi 2011), which was eventually sold to Greek buyers for USD 21M. Elsewhere, the benchmark has been set for 10 year old capesize units, with scrubber fitted EHIME QUEEN (181K DWT Imabari 2016) selling for USD 59M to Chinese buyers.

A relatively quiet week in the VLGC market, despite the underlying tightness in vessel availability for the US Gulf. Freight levels remain at, or near, record highs. Activity has been notably subdued across regions, largely influenced by Monday’s holiday in Europe and yesterday’s holidays in both Singapore and the Middle East, resulting in limited fresh enquiry.

The Panamax/Kamsarmax market opened the week cautiously after the holidays, with sentiment still lacking conviction despite some firmer undertones. The Atlantic appears broadly balanced, with prompt tonnage largely absorbed, slimmer lists in the Continent/West Mediterranean and ECSA supported by firmer paper, while the Pacific looks more constructive on stronger Australian minerals and steady Indonesia/China demand, with owners showing more resistance. That said, the broader indicators remain bearish near-term: shipment volumes are only modestly ahead of fleet growth, coal contango has widened, and both Pacific and South Atlantic tightness indicators point to potential softening, suggesting any upside may remain fragile unless fresh cargo volumes build quickly.

After many weeks of static rates in the West and a slow softening in the East, there is now clear momentum building in the spot market. A modest yet sustained arbitrage for cargoes heading out of the Atlantic into Asia has put a little more pressure on the fleet, and although there are not a vast number of requirements there are even fewer ships to meet them. The upwards pressure on rates is thus supply driven, and will remain sensitive to trade flows and the availability of sublets. Traders and schedulers are being kept busy by the continuing uncertainty in the Middle East, fuelled by repeated contradictory hype of an impending “deal” and an unusual ceasefire in name only. It is clear the LNG and LNG shipping markets will be impacted well into 2027, and after a brief pause there has been more activity in the multi-month space. Control of tonnage will be key to navigating what could be a strong winter, and we expect more appetite for charterers to take on tonnage for longer periods.

Again we started the working week with a ‘workable vessel count’ well above average, eta West Africa within 3 weeks. First decade West Africa appears to be nearing completion, while second decade demand has also thinned amidst fresh VLCC fixtures/outstanding cargoes, and additional Suezmax mysteries. The ongoing influx of Eastern ballasters remains a key pressure point on TD20. With limited options elsewhere, there is a willingness for such vessels to secure coverage without much resistance. Whilst the US local list remains short therefore reliant on ballasters, the smaller 2nd decade CPC programme is expected to push an increasing number of vessels into the Atlantic ex-Mediterranean.

This week on Capesize we saw firming across all major segments, with strong Pacific activity driving sentiment higher throughout the week. Pacific C5 markets remain firm and well supported, with activity yesterday fixing in the USD 16.10-16.5 range for early and mid June stems ex West Australia/Qingdao. With a stable to slightly bullish market, owners are holding ideas around last done levels for Pacific stems. Atlantic markets remain firm but slightly cautious, with C3 today bidding in the high USD 37s and last done at USD 38 for late June dates. Sentiment is firm yet somewhat cautious with good support despite limited fresh prompt tonnage. In the North Atlantic, we saw a quiet start to the week with slow activity. Strong fronthaul demand has caused tight transatlantic tonnage as owners continue to push for premium returns on fronthaul. C3 Brazil/China 21-30 June last done USD 38. C5 West Australia/China 7-9 June last done USD 16.25, 10-12 June last done USD 16.1, 13-15 June last done USD 16.25.

All mouth and no trousers still when it comes to a deal to reopen the now famous Strait. In the meantime, nothing material has changed, although a few ships managed to “escape” the MEG over the weekend. Going the other way, however, is no more likely than it was last week. Tonnage has “disappeared” in the area, likely heading for Oman (outside) or Yanbu to load, but not quite enough to ease the pressure on alternative cargoes in the Atlantic. That said, had you offered 3 digits for a June load Atlantic/East to the owning community a few moths back they would probably have eaten your hand - so, all about perspective. Much of the activity has gone under the radar and unless directly involved it is difficult to find out what happened and definitely not in real time – and the lack of transparency has made it much harder to gauge the market. That said, if it’s up, or more likely down, it tends to be leaked - but lack of context makes it a less credible benchmark.

North Sea North Sea dates are slowly moving into June. The first 5 days stems are not that populated and we have seen a lot of programming which explains the muted start to the month activity wise. Even with a continued softer US market the North Sea list is being kept balanced with vessels ballasting. Market looks like it will remain steady/soft likely through the first decade.  Mediterranean Rates are hovering around last-done levels with decent levels of activity and the tonnage list looking much better compared to last week. Sentiment is the issue these days as owners seem to have accepted last done and at the same time fundamentals aren't helping them either.

The market opened this week on a relatively balanced but gradually softer footing, as parts of Europe was off on Monday - with activity mainly centred around TCT and short-period employment. In the Atlantic, continued South America grain movements supported cargo demand into both regional and Atlantic destinations, although increasing vessel availability and flexible positioning kept pressure on rates. The Supra/Ultramax segment saw a steady flow of prompt June openings globally, contributing to a more competitive tonnage list and allowing charterers to apply increased pressure in negotiations. In Asia, trading activity remained focused on regional distribution within Southeast and Northeast Asia, with cargo flow steady but insufficient to significantly tighten market conditions. Period enquiry remained active across short and long durations, though a persistent gap between owners’ ideas and charterers’ bids continued to slow longer-term conversions. Overall, the Handy and Supra markets remained stable but leaned slightly in charterers’ favour, as balanced cargo flow, ample tonnage supply and cautious fixing activity kept rates largely range-bound across most regions.

Those in the market wondering what the top and bottom of the VLCC values curve looks like are in luck this week, as we report sales of 2002 and 2026 built units. Granted these are different countries of build, but the picture is as clear as it can be for owners and prospective buyers of this size of tanker. LAS PALMAS (306K DWT Hengli 2026) has been purchased by Trafigura for USD 163M, while Scrubber fitted ABIE (302K DWT Samsung 2002) was sold at USD 40.5M. Those on the selling side are happy to exit at these historic levels, so long as buyers continue to chase these units; a scenario that shows no signs of letting off. This tanker market is feeding off the lingering Hormuz disruption, and there is more than enough uncertainty to prolong the higher earnings environment while any bearish arguments can be countered with a potential post Hormuz resolution bounce.    The dry market has generally been the substory in the shipping world of late, but rates and values are surging upwards. The high volume of reported transactions this week is likely a culmination of recent weeks but still represents significant dealmaking and notable buyer confidence in this market. As usual among dry, we are seeing transactions centred around 10–15-year-old + age range with a couple of modern units sprinkled in. Of those modern units, in a rare mini cape transaction, Asyad bought LOWLANDS AMBER/CRIMSON (100KDWT OSHIMA 2021/20) for USD 75.M en bloc.

There has been sufficient activity across Black Sea-USG-Guyana-West Africa to keep lists fairly balanced for 1st decade cargoes. There should still be reasonable volume to come for 1st decade West Africa, given the lack of VLCC fixing, and as we move into next week, 2nd decade dates should also begin to work. Similarly, there has been fairly limited interaction from the larger units in the forward window as well. For West Africa, there will of course be the usual pragmatism from vessels coming from the East that are unable to fix elsewhere, which may weigh on the market. However, the wider Atlantic-Mediterranean-Black Sea market appears well supported.

The market opened this week on a mixed and increasingly positional footing. In the Atlantic, sentiment remained divided view underlying demand increasing in US Gulf, although widening bid/offer spread kept activity selective. The South Atlantic softened amid easing demand and growing tonnage, while Asia saw slower momentum overall with prompt vessels in the south weighing on sentiment despite pockets of enquiry further north. Overall, both Supra and Handy market lacked clear direction as cautious trading and regional imbalances continued to dominate market sentiment.

The Atlantic market had been showing early signs of a typical summer slowdown, driven in part by an overhang of prompt tonnage following the impact of production issues at Freeport. However, this softer sentiment has proven short lived, as  prompt requirements have emerged including additional production in West and North Africa. As a result, vessel availability has tightened at the front end. Overall rate levels remain firm. While isolated fixtures have been concluded at marginal discounts where availability has been more constrained, these appear to be exceptions rather than a broader trend. Charterers continue to demonstrate a willingness to pay a premium to secure operational flexibility, particularly for multi-voyage employment and/or redelivery into Asia. The prompt forward curve remains supported, although visibility further out is becoming increasingly limited. There is discernible interest in covering positions across the next two quarters; however, the absence of meaningful 12 month bidding suggests a degree of caution. This has, in effect, introduced a pronounced backwardation extending into 2027. Beyond the near term, the outlook remains highly uncertain. Much will depend on the evolution of geopolitical factors, including the ongoing and unresolved disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. In this context, further volatility cannot be ruled out. At the same time, the broader balance of global gas supply remains under scrutiny, particularly with several traditionally quiet buying regions expected to return to the market ahead of peak demand in the second half of the year.

North Sea North Sea sentiment has continued to soften on the lack of activity and surrounding markets also remaining relatively soft. Early vessels have had to make the decision to ballast out after missing natural dates with a mixture heading Mediterranean and USG. Natural window in the North Sea pushing into 28-30 window and with a long weekend coming up, end May and very early June dates will most likely need cover this side of the weekend. Market steady for now.  Mediterranean We are close to get sold-out for May dates in the Mediterranean with end-month cargoes now being worked. Tonnage list has become a bit more balanced considering that a couple of vessels in the list will either ballast to US or to Baltic. Reports of WS 180 done for Libya/Augusta might put some extra pressure on the rates but otherwise it feels we have bottomed as owners start to not make sense of lower rates.

The spot VLGC market activity is hampered by scarce vessel availability for June laycans ex USG. As a result, the few fixtures that have been concluded during the last week have seen levels yet again setting new all time high records on a per ton basis. As of today, around twenty fixtures have been concluded for June ex USG and USEC whereas April and May saw a total of about thirty more deals done for freight. The way things are looking at the moment, it seems this situation will continue well into July and thus keep the market on a tight leash.

Two Chinese laden VLCC have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz southbound and heading for the homeland, accompanied by a Trafigura controlled ship heading for Korea. Reports also suggests that Eastmed’s Grand Lady has gone the other way, enroute to load inside. Combined with chatter of a “deal” between the US and Iran (yet again) being close it could possibly indicate that things could slowly move towards a solution of sorts.. Here’s hoping, but we’ve been disappointed before. We need the waterways to open, that’s for sure, both for the shipping industry and no less so for the world economy. In the meantime, it’s more of the same in the market, the little there is - owners showing great resolve in holding back and rates on a steady sideways “trajectory”.

Panamax sentiment has turned softer, with the recent rally now looking increasingly tired. The Atlantic is losing support as fronthaul activity and ECSA enquiry slow, while a fuller tonnage list in the Continent and Mediterranean is adding pressure on owners’ ideas. In the Pacific, the tone is also more defensive, with limited fresh cargo, weaker paper, and prompt tonnage beginning to build, particularly in the North. Owners are still trying to hold close to last-done levels, especially for better-positioned modern units, but charterers are cautious and bids are drifting lower. Overall, the market looks close to a near-term peak, and without a fresh injection of cargo in either basin, further downside feels likely.

After a fairly quiet end to last week in the Pacific, Capesize demand rebounded on Monday as Port Hedland and Dampier basins firmed for June stems, with last done at USD 15 for 7-8 June dates. Pacific C5 markets are currently firm but steady with multiple trades reported in the mid USD 15 range. Tighter tonnage coming into June appears to keep levels near current highs, setting a balanced market tone for Pacific, though forward curves suggest possible easing beyond mid-June laycans. In the Atlantic, we saw exceptionally strong demand for transatlantic trade in the early week. Levels have subsided today and are active and well supported with C8 at USD 46,875/day (-10.69% compared to yesterday) and fronthaul C9 at USD 73,639 thanks to tight tonnage in the north and strong mineral demand. Ballasters continue to favour Brazil stems over transatlantic, further constraining supply. C3 Brazil/China is stable but thin today on fresh fixtures, with ideas hovering in the mid USD 36s. C3 Brazil/China 1-10 June bid USD 37 offer USD 37, 11-20 June last done 33.8, 21-30 June offer USD 36.75, 1-10 July bid USD 36 offer USD 36. C5 West Australia/China 1-3 June last done USD 15.35, 3-5 June last done USD 15.5, 4-6 June last done USD 15.

The tanker market continues to defy the broader geopolitical uncertainty, with sentiment underpinned by firm earnings and a steady flow of buyers prepared to meet owners’ price expectations. That said, crude buyers seem to have taken a breather this week as ever increasing pricing pushes more would be buyers into the yards. In the MR sector, Turkish buyers committed USD 20.8M for ice-classed ROYAL JASMINE (53K DWT GSI 2008), while AUTAN (51K DWT SPP 2009) changed hands at USD 23.5M. The pricing achieved for these vintage units further reinforces the depth of demand for mid-aged tanker tonnage, particularly where prompt trading flexibility or niche specifications are involved.  A busy time indeed across the dry market as earnings remain firm. This week saw a cluster of modern handysize resales emerge from Ciner, with CLACTON, MARGATE, EASTBOURNE and PORTSMOUTH (40K DWT Jiangmen Nanyang 2024) reportedly sold to Norden at USD 30.5M apiece. The sellers in this transaction represent the target blueprint for buyers seeking modern units in this market, in the sense they have a modern fleet with a stacked orderbook, and are more likely to listen to potential suitors. Chinese buyers were particularly active this week, acquiring both JOY (81K DWT Chengxi 2019) for USD 31.5M and HUAYANG LILY (63K DWT China Shipping 2016) at USD 25.2M. Elsewhere, Greek buyers secured SUMAQ QUEEN (51K DWT Imabari 2017) for USD 25M.

Surface level and off market activity has been reasonable, with the tonnage overhang easing. We still have around a dozen vessels in ballast capable of making end‑month laycans in West Africa. That said, following yesterday’s sharp drop, owners are likely to be reluctant to concede further ground, and on the flip side, considering the number of cargoes quoted today we may see upside. Stateside, Aframax sentiment has weakened further, with USD/bbl on a last-done basis now clearly favouring the smaller units on USG/TA, which is likely to limit 145kt volume to some extent. In the East, opportunities have been few and far between amid a continued flow of ballasters heading West. A cargo quoted ex‑Red Sea yesterday attracted 10+ offers, despite the ongoing exodus of tonnage.

The Supramax and Handysize markets remained generally firm, with sentiment supported mainly by steady activity in Asia where balanced tonnage and cargo demand continued. The Atlantic market remained largely positional, particularly in the Continent and Mediterranean where fresh enquiry was still limited and tonnage availability remained ample. The South Atlantic showed signs of gradual improvement, while the US Gulf stayed relatively stable, although some softer sentiment was in the Supramax.

Open, not open, open, not open. The market spent the week caught between softening fundamentals and stubbornly resilient sentiment (as has been past few weeks), with Hormuz disruption still dictating flows. Early in the period, lack of volume and a widening East list pointed to downside risk, but the Atlantic steadily firmed as Brazil and USG exports paid up. Despite no real progress on US-Iran and no reopening of Hormuz, the market was holding together far better than many expected, with very few genuinely open ships in the West.

The Panamax market has continued its firm trajectory through the week, with momentum building across both basins. In the Atlantic, fronthaul remains the engine – strong NCSA grain demand is keeping cargo volumes healthy and owners confident, with the strength on longer east-bound legs allowing them to hold firm on shorter Atlantic business as well. The Pacific has moved in tandem, driven by tight prompt tonnage, improving NoPac grain stems and a steady flow of Australian and Indonesian coal; charterers are having to chase. Period interest is active but bid and offer remain apart. The overall tone is constructive heading into next week.

Some significant LNG shipping developments in the Middle East over the past week, as both QELM and ADNOC vessels are reported to have transited the Strait of Hormuz on laden voyages. This marks the first LNG cargoes loaded within the Gulf to exit via the Strait of Hormuz since conflict began in late February. While this is not a signal that regular LNG transits are on the horizon, and the scope of the agreements (if any) between the counterparties and Iran are unknown, it gives some hope that Qatari and Abu Dhabi volumes are not beyond reach.   In the East, sparse May cargoes coupled with ample supply has led to hot competition across the tonnage classes for prompt requirements. Owners that are able to call Qalhat are somewhat insulated from the quieter SEA market, and continue to enjoy a steady stream of opportunities to load Omani volumes at premium freight rates. Requirements are emerging for June but currently these are stacked towards the second half of the month, giving owners the dilemma of fixing forward and absorbing idle time, or waiting and risking unemployed vessels. Requirements out of the US East Coast and especially West Africa have been able to entice tonnage to reposition from the East, offering attractive utilisation and a rate premium to Pacific cargoes. While Kitimat’s schedule remains uncertain, Barossa loadings are expected to be resume, which the market hopes will boost liquidity East of Suez.   The Atlantic market has proved very stubborn, with rates remaining tightly bound in the mid-$90k/d range when accounting for vessel specifications. The requirement list has been a little lumpy though, with relatively few cargoes in early June set against an extensive list from mid-June onwards. We may therefore see a little more variability as charterers face more or less competition for individual requirements, but the fundamentals and in particular the situation in the Middle East are showing no signs of change in the coming weeks.   Following the trend we have seen through the past few weeks, multi-month coverage through Q3/Q4 remains of interest but charterers have eased back on taking on tonnage. The bullish sentiment of the major portfolio players has trickled through the market and we do see some additional subletters hoping to lock-in utilisation, and this may explain the “wait and see” approach among charterers now.

Freight rates continue to surge to fresh highs despite an increasingly challenging arbitrage backdrop, underscoring that control has firmly shifted in favour of shipping. June spot activity remains exceptionally limited, with the current fixture count at just 18 liftings (8/7/3 by decade), a stark contrast to the high‑40s average observed over the past two months. Although some incremental volumes may still materialize as voyage itineraries firm up, the availability of June U.S. positions remains critically constrained. This persistent tightness is expected to sustain upward pressure on freight levels in the near term.

This week on Capesize, we see firmer markets overall today with increases in every route. June demand on C3 Brazil/China remains firm while C5 West Australia/China takes a more balanced tone as C5 improves today after being relatively flat early week (however levels have jumped 4.7% on paper today). Pacific C5 West Australia/China sees more activity today with multiple stems fixed between USD 15.15-15.30s from West Australia to Qingdao. Despite a softening FAA curve moving forward, spot sentiment remains bullish on tight tonnage and if momentum holds, late May laycans are expected to climb around USD 16s levels. On C3 Brazil/China remains the stronger leg with firm demand coming into June with multiple fixtures done in the USD 36.25-37 range for mid-June laycans. West Africa stems are slightly lower at mid USD 35 levels. Atlantic sees stronger transatlantic activity over the last few days, supporting overall market levels and promoting strong demand for prompt tonnage. Sentiment remains bullish for short term transatlantic and fronthaul positions out from Atlantic. C3 1-10 June: bids at USD 37, 11-20 June: last done USD 33.8. C5 13-15 May: last done USD 15.8, 25-27 May: last done USD 16.6, 28-30 May: last done USD 15.15.

North Sea A slow start to the week activity wise. Natural window 19-21 dates. North Sea sentiment has softened on the lack of activity and the softening of surrounding markets, making ballasting not the sure opportunity it was. Market remains soft as charterers will try and find some more points. 3rd decade does look busier stem wise.  Mediterranean Activity is still moderate in the Mediterranean while tonnage list remains long with several vessels available within the next 7 days. Owners are watching one market after another correcting in the West leaving them without any get-out-of-jail-free card now. We are still looking for the bottom, but owners need to pull the brakes first.

Resolution of the conflict in the Middle East seems no closer despite some encouraging headlines this week. That said, there appears to be a steady supply of buyers willing to transact at current levels, while giving owners attractive exit points across the size and age curve. All the confusing ongoing diplomacy aside, values show no signs of softening with suezmax tankers this week setting new levels for mid aged ships as 15-year-old STELLA (164K DWT Hyundai 2011) sold for USD 67M.    The BDI crossed the 3000-point mark for the first time since 2023 on the back of the recent run, whilst contending with perhaps a quieter week than usual due to holidays in China. There appears to still be room for even higher levels on the larger sizes, with some predicting Capesize will hit the USD 50K/day mark in the coming weeks. The majority of second-hand activity is limited as usual to the rgn 15-year-old tonnage, with the exception of 85K DWT wide beam Kamsarmax pair SEACON NOLA/HAMBURG (85K DWT Huangpu Wenchong 2023) begin sold for USD 36M each.

VLGC freight market remains tight with Owners latest ideas pushing into $300s HCvP for US business. We count 14 spot fixtures in June thus far (8/5/1 by decade), compared to 48 deals seen in May and 47 in April. We currently see less than a handful of ships that can be worked firm today for June, and it remains to be seen where the next deals will be fixed at.

We started Tuesday with a lengthy supply, eta West Africa prior 25th. However, an active day helped to trim down the front end of the list, bringing supply down to a level more akin to stability rather than aggressive downside. There are likely still some prompt cargoes that may present themselves in West Africa, given lack of buying appetite. Additionally, there is still a large chunk of 3rd decade volume to cover with cargoes prior 25th firmly in the window. CPC is likely coming towards the end for May dates, with stems not expected to be released for another week or so. As a result, we do not anticipate a significant boost in demand from here. However, in the USG, despite Aframaxes continuing to slide, USD/bbl economics still lean in Suezmaxes’ favour, leaving the demand outlook from across the pond optimistic.

Supramax market started the week quieter, with sentiment generally steady but lacking fresh momentum. The Atlantic showed some positivity, particularly for fronthaul demand from USG, while other areas remained slow. Handy followed a similarly subdued tone overall, though the Atlantic saw pockets of improved demand, especially in the USG and South Atlantic. In contrast, the Continent and Mediterranean continued to soften with limited fresh cargo. Asia remained relatively stable, supported by tighter tonnage and steady demand despite the slow start. Looking back to the prior session, both segments were already losing steam ahead of the holidays, with weak activity in the Atlantic and limited cargo flow in Asia. Overall, the market remains cautious, with sentiment varying by region.

The dormant spot market East of Suez has been somewhat roused this week by a number of requirements firming up for late May through mid-June. Qalhat liftings continues to feature heavily, with wide disparities in additional war risk premia playing a key role in assessment of candidates. Uncertainty on production across various load terminals in Australia as well as Canada continue to stall prompt transactions and stifle liquidity.  After a very quiet long weekend covering a number of public holidays, the West is now enjoying a far more active spot market, and is continuing to command a premium on freight rates for the May-June fixing window. This comes despite recent disruptions at Freeport LNG leading to several cancelled cargoes, and subsequent unexpected short-term length from scheduled lifters. Although open tonnage feels a little sparse, firm requirements have seen interest from 2-stroke owners but not with sufficient competition to force rates significantly lower, while a preference for worldwide redelivery optionality is supporting the price floor. Despite the Atlantic liquidity, players on both sides of the transaction will be keeping one eye on spot, and one eye on the quarter ahead …  A rush of activity from the portfolio players resulted in a flurry of term fixtures late last week, as charterers sought coverage into Q1 2027. Modern 2-strokes with worldwide redelivery are the vessels of choice, owing to charterers’ need for maximum geographical optionality as a hedge against a bullish LNG price outlook. A widening arbitrage and the highest levels of Inter-basin cargoes in over a year, coupled with low EU storage levels and injections down 20% on last year, is signalling strong East-West jostling for volumes and subsequent LNG price volatility. We’re now in a strange situation where forward 2-stroke availability is tightening while we experience fleet oversupply on the spot. Owners seem to be following the trend, opting to market their multimonth length rather than pure spot availability. Let’s see if other market participants take heed and look to bolster their fleets ahead of Q3.

This week on Capesize, we see strengthening across every segment, with C3 and C5 remaining well supported near future. C5 leads the charge as of yesterday as the highest time charter earner, today gaining an additional 6.5% on paper. Recent fixtures for C5 West Australia/China have been reported in the mid-high USD 14 for second half May stems and early June bids are coming in the mid USD 15s with offers in the range of USD 15.75-16. Overall, the Pacific market is outperforming index with firm bids and rising offers looking positive with potential for future gains coming into June. For C3 Brazil/China, market remains firm but slightly capped with fresh offers in the mid USD 37s for early June stems. West Africa stems are still in circulation with no distinct premiums over Brazil stems. North Atlantic transatlantic remains firmly bid, supported by strong mineral demand and limited prompt tonnage. Sentiment remains positive as the North Atlantic continues to outperform paper, underpinned by healthy Coal and Iron Ore flow. C3 11-20 May offer USD 30.75, 1-10 June offer USD 36, 11-20 June offer USD 37.25. C5 19-21 May bid USD 15.3 / offer USD 15.85 / last done USD 15.9.

This week the Panamax market has turned firmer after a quieter start, with sentiment improving across both basins. In the Atlantic, early pressure from a longer Continent tonnage list and limited transatlantic demand has eased as NCSA grain activity picked up, giving owners more confidence and pushing fronthaul levels higher, while ECSA remains supported by steady demand and tighter prompt tonnage. USG activity is still relatively flat and transatlantic volumes remain thin, but the tone is clearly more constructive. In the Pacific, the market remains firm despite some Golden Week disruption, with Australia and Indonesia coal/mineral demand providing the main support, prompt tonnage looking tight, and modern/premium units in particularly short supply. With China back in the market and Japan returning, activity is picking up and owners are again showing stronger resistance.

North Sea Activity has stagnated in the North Sea and given that tonnage has built over the long weekend and relets are absorbing the available volume, we could see rates test further down. A lot depends on activity levels in the USG, which are also under pressure at the moment.   Mediterranean The natural fixing window has moved into the back end of May now. The Mediterranean is in a similar predicament to the North Sea with a long tonnage list after the long weekend. Owners are to be tested as the market will likely experience further downward pressure for the rest of the week.

“We have mutually agreed that, while ‌the ⁠Blockade will remain in full force and effect, Project Freedom ... will be paused for a short period of time to see whether or not the Agreement can be finalized and signed," Trump wrote on social media yesterday. This follows comments to the Congress that Operation Epic Fury has ended. There’s been no immediate reaction from Tehran, but reports suggest the two parties are closing in on a one-page memo to end war. Yes, we’ve heard it all before, but oil prices have nevertheless dropped more than 10% on the back of it. However, as the blockade/s persist, and being actively "defended", there’s no material change for the tanker market, nor is it likely to be for some time. Lack of volume is now starting to bite in earnest, and with that rates continue to be under pressure. VLCC daily earnings have dropped but still hover close to USD 100k/day, but there’s no denying the direction of travel short term.

Confidence in the strength of this crude tanker market shows no signs of waning as buyers continue to pay the ever increasing price asks. Monte Nero are reported to have paid USD 140M en bloc, for scrubber fitted suezmax pair FRONT ULL/FRONT IDUN (156K DWT Rongsheng 2014/15), a figure well in excess of the price these ships were ordered for over a decade ago. Owners expectations on Aframax pricing are also being met, with scrubber fitted Aframax pair SOUTHERN REVERENCE/PUSAKA BORNEO (108K DWT Tsuneishi 2018) sold for USD 75M and USD 78M respectively. These are only the second and third transactions in the eco Aframax space this year, setting well needed benchmarks for this vintage.   While not quite at the towering heights of the tanker market, the dry space is still providing healthy returns and strong values. Buyers are not shying away either, this week GENCO purchased scrubber fitted capesize LOWLANDS SPIRIT (182K DWT Imabari 2019) for USD 67M, which interestingly represents the most modern capesize sale of the year so far. Modern dry deals have been hard to come by, perhaps we are now at a price point where we might see a few more sellers coming to the table.

text: Saudi Aramco announced May CP at $750 for C3 and $800 for C4, a rollover from April, which lagged behind the recent spike in oil price, amid concerns over middle East supply disruptions.   Arbitrage strengthened this week with improved premium on CFR FAR EAST, with FEI/Lst spread widening to $376 for May and $308 for June. However terminal fee for Jun lifting US FOBs declined further against soaring freight and higher Panama transit costs. Mid Jun lifting 2/2 spot cargo was reported traded in low 20 cpg, while 4/0 was discussed at low teens only. U.S. propane/propylene inventories declined by 1.1 mmt barrels to 78.8 million barrels in the week ended 24th Apr, leaving stocks remained 67% higher year on year.   On Thursday window, a 23/0 parcel for 2h Jun delivery basis Chiba was changed hand at May FEI plus $8, equivalent to Jun FEI plus around $83. Outside window, a couple of 4/0 parcels for 2h Jun delivery basis Chiba were reported traded at May FEI plus $2-$3. Separately, a few lots of 4/0 parcels for 1h Jun delivery basis Ningbo were concluded at May FEI plus mid 40s reportedly. One SChina PDH procured a 2/0 lot for 1-20 Jun delivery, Australia stem, at Jun FEI plus $190 reportedly. Another EChina petchem player also tendered to buy similar cargo for Jun delivery into Ningbo. China PDH run rates reduced to 44% this week, marking a record low. This being said, several PDHs are expected to restart in late May/Jun, and have started inquiring on Jun feedstock.

We have registered 7-8 fixtures this week for June. The market continues to tighten, underpinned by a scarcity of available vessels from end May/early June onwards. Based on current BLPG 3 levels, modern conventionally fueled VLGCs are now generating round‑trip earnings of approximately USD 130,000 per day, marking the strongest market returns since the latter part of 2023. Owners and trader relets are increasingly testing higher ideas, with ideas shown up to USD 260 per tonne HC on Pmax ship. Given the absence of meaningful tonnage availability through at least 10 June, downside risk to freight remains limited. The return of a more standard five‑week fixing window next week should help sustain momentum and drive further fixtures. In contrast, the MEG market remains quiet, with uncertainty persisting around the Straits of Hormuz and the timing and scale of any cargo flow resumption.

The market remains fairly active, however, rates in the West have started to show greater stability. Tonnage is relatively balanced, and additional volume will be required for owners to push the market further. At this juncture, for cargoes beyond the 15th, both stateside and in West Africa, charterers may opt to pull the handbrake to curb any building momentum and allow the list to rebuild going into next week.

The Panamax market opened the week with a clear Atlantic/Pacific split. The Atlantic remains under pressure, with more tonnage appearing in the North Continent and limited fresh TA demand, leaving both round and fronthaul levels exposed. USG/NCSA enquiry has been patchy, while ECSA remains the one firmer pocket for forward dates, though prompt ships still face pressure to discount or wait. In the Pacific, sentiment remains more positive, supported by steady Indo/Australian coal and mineral demand ahead of Golden Week, with charterers gradually moving closer to owners’ ideas. Overall, the Atlantic feels cargo-short, while the Pacific remains better balanced and firming.

This week on Capesize, C3 Brazil/China market remains firm but tense. Owners are resilient, holding offers in the USD 33-33.75 range for second half May, with last done at USD 31.9 for 21-31 May. The C3 FFA is reported to soften after May, adding pressure on later positions. Currently C3 is the stronger market compared to C5 with a dollar per day differential of USD +914 on C3. The C5 market also remains active and bullish with current spreads at sub USD 13 bids vs USD 13.1-13.3 offers. Multiple stems were cleared yesterday, and cargo lists from West Australia remain healthy. C5 is leading sentiment with solid grain stems and strong demand, while C3 market remains rangebound but supported. North Atlantic market is strong this week with fronthaul C9 stems commanding USD 67,000/day. FAA May is at USD 16.35 for C7 Bolivar/Rotterdam while Baltic sets C7 at USD 18.96 reflecting tight tonnage in the basin. With tight tonnage in the North and limited fresh fixtures reported, bullish sentiment remains amongst owners. C3 11-20 May: offer USD 33.25, 21-31 May: last done USD 31.9, 1-10 June: offer USD 33.5, 11-20 June: bid USD 32.5, offer USD 33.5. C5 14-16 May: bid USD 12.9, offer USD 13, last done USD 13.5, 17-19 May: bid USD 12.85, offer USD 13.35, last done USD 13.1.

The VLCC market eased over the course of the week as MEG disruption continued to displace tonnage and intensify competition across the remaining trading options. The East was pressured by a growing availability list. A Yanbu/Korea market quote attracted 8 offers and was concluded at WS 145. Activity from Brazil/USG remained steady with combination of charterers scheduling own tonnage and some market quotes. USG requires some incremental volume to stabilise levels.

North Sea The anticipated strengthening of the US markets has happened which is pulling tonnage from the early part of the North Sea available list.   Activity for early May has been steady with Suezmax also in the mix from WCN. Natural dates are pushing towards the end of the first decade with a tighter list and firmer sentiment.  Mediterranean It's sentiment versus fundamentals so far this week in the Mediterranean with the USG activity pushing owners' resistance in Europe too. Tonnage list for local candidates in the Mediterranean is fairly balanced but possible delays in strategic discharge ports might make it look tighter. Hovering around last-done levels for now, but if activity picks up things might change quickly.

The period market remained active this week, with demand centred on short to medium-term employment. Charterers continued to prioritize flexibility, while longer-term discussions remained selective and focused mainly on modern, fuel-efficient tonnage. Interest was strongest for versatile vessels offering flexible trading, grain-clean holds, GOA transit, and suitability for steel and project cargoes. Tonnage availability remained ample across both Atlantic and Pacific basins, with a steady flow of prompt and forward positions, including modern eco vessels and newbuildings. Owners remained disciplined, particularly for quality employment, maintaining a noticeable bid-offer gap as charterers continued to test lower levels, especially for one-year business. Modern, efficient vessels continued to command the strongest interest, while older or less flexible units faced increased competition. Overall, market conditions remain constructive, with steady enquiry and healthy fixing activity, although longer-term commitments continue to be approached cautiously.

There is unmissable irony in the description of spot charter rates for modern tonnage as “healthy”, given the ongoing crisis in the LNG market where the world’s largest single supplier continues to be cut off from its global customer base. Despite the forcibly idle tonnage unable to reach home base in the Middle East, levels continue to show resistance around a similar range as long-term charter rates.   Whilst the worst of the conflict is hopefully behind us, what lies ahead remains wholly uncertain. However, amongst strong activity in the spot market, some consensus has also emerged for periods covering the balance of the year and into Q1-27. Portfolios are taking positions down the curve at rates largely in line with current Atlantic spot, supported by higher LNG prices and anticipation of competition between basins in the second half of the year.    We continue to see signs of weak underlying fundamentals in the spot market, with length beginning to build on TFDE’s in the East and new requirements often flushing out fresh 2-stroke availabilities for short spot employment in the Atlantic. However, the same cannot be said for term availabilities, where 2-strokes are beginning to thin out and TFDE’s under independent control are less forthcoming when asked to lock in prevailing spot levels for longer period. It remains to be seen which strategy will pay off but with summer looming and speculation that tonne-miles could take another boost in the third quarter, we are eager to see how this plays out.

Scorpio are accounting for most of the action this week with the announcement of 6 sales across their MR and LR2 fleet. They have been consistent over the last 6 months in selling out assets, taking advantage of the scarce availability of these vessels and the elevated prices on offer. Buyers are ready to pounce on these opportunities as once you start looking at more modern units, the high pricing usually encourages potential suitors to the newbuilding yards instead. Despite various extensions of ceasefires, the situation in the Middle East remains largely the same, with brent crude trading today at its highest levels in ceasefire conditions, meaning that the market will need a little more than a fragile ceasefire in order to normalise.   A relatively slow week for dry liquidity, understandable given a strange combination of near-term strength and longer-term uncertainty in the market. Earnings are strong across the size ranges for now, while long term macro sentiment is being eroded as the war in the Middle East drags on. Some rare modern transactions this week with Niovis purchasing 2x resale ultramax units (64K DWT New Dayang 2027) for USD 36.5M each.
