comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Oil and gas prices surged amid escalating strikes on key energy infrastructure in the Middle East. At the time of writing, April CP was traded at $620 for C3, with the C3/C4 spread assessed at $5. FEI spiked up on heightened supply concerns after Targa declared force majeure, with delays reportedly ranging from 7 to 10 days. April FEI was traded at $1,010, with the April/May FEI spread at $160 latest. Following this, US-FAR EAST arbitrage widened significantly to over $500 for Apr and over $400 for May in extreme volatility. One late Apr lifting full propane cargo was reported being traded at 42 cpg.  U.S. propane/propylene inventories rose by 810,000 barrels to 72.5 million barrels in the week ended 13rd Mar, leaving stocks remained 67.2% higher year on year.  In window one 23/0 parcel for 1h May delivery basis Chiba was bid at Apr FEI plus $30, and similar parcel for 2h May bid at May FEI plus $130, while no offers seen. Several petchem players with term supply and spot supplement in existing inventory continue to maintain run, max out downstream yields, and captured front margins; while the others plan to carry out maintenance or take a wait-n-see approach before procuring spot in later Apr or May as downstream price yet to keep pace with the surge in feedstock costs.

North Sea After a brief correction last week North Sea bounced back almost straight away with a busy end to last week. Natural dates have moved towards end month with a limited amount left to cover in March. With US and Mediterranean markets remaining interesting, rates have remained steady in the North Sea, even with the limited activity we have seen so far this week. At the returns the Aframax markets are providing in the current window, waiting time is a big consideration and will also influence owners to ballast out for longer sustained returns whilst limiting downtime.  Mediterranean Market in the Mediterranean/Black Sea remains steady and firm with WS 340 being the go-to rate for medium-large local flat rates. Window has pushed out to end-month now and we will be sold-out of March cargo before the end of this week. The list remains thin but with ballasters from the North Sea expected to join the party. Steady as it goes rate wise with very healthy returns for owners.

This week in Capesize, C5 is currently steady to slightly firmer, however West Australia is facing cyclone concerns in the coming days, with category 5 Cyclone Narelle expected to hit the East Coast by Friday before potentially veering to the West mid next week, which may lead to tightening for West Australia. Levels are currently balanced but slightly under pressure, with early April fixtures previously done at USD 12.80 for and latest fixtures for early April heard USD 12.25 on a Newcastlemax. In the Atlantic, C3 remains firm. Latest fixtures for early April are at USD 28.75-29 and Newcastlemax fixtures at USD 30.9 for 11-20 April dates. West Africa options are still in play but there is limited fresh demand. In the North Atlantic, tonnage remains tight and patchy demand maintains elevated rates. C3 1-10 April fixed USD 28.75, 11-20 April fixed USD 30.9. C5 1-3 April fixed USD 12, 7-9 April offers USD 13.5.

West Africa supply remains nuanced, with a low ownership spread, several relets and a limited number of vessels expected to sail by Monday. On the demand side, there may not be much left to cover for the 1st decade of April in West Africa; however, UKCM tonnage should remain busy with USG and Guyana cargoes, which are still underfixed for April. Within this pool, several are CPC players, where earnings remain attractive, making it difficult to draw owners across the Atlantic or down to West Africa. Given that stateside supply is devoid of tonnage, charterers will likely rely on UKCM vessels. There is also the potential for a false sense of security in the West, even with indices in the red. Aframaxes remain the top pick for USG/TA and VLCCs for Atlantic/East, but signs are improving at least for the current window. Aframaxes have plenty of cargoes outstanding and limited ballasters, and VLCCs eta USG in the next 30 days are few and far between.

The Strait of Hormuz remains shut for all practical purposes and any fixture for inside MEG loading, promptly and widely reported, smells more of a paper play than a realistic view to load/transit. Thus, please be warned that the Baltic TD3C estimate is and will continue to be academic under the current circumstances – and it is not a reflection of owner’s current earnings. Yanbu and Oman are still on the menu and although rates for this have slid into the WS 200’s, uncertainty remains as the loading window opens and closes depending on hostilities at any given time. The disparity between the Middle East and the Atlantic has continued to grow and rates from the latter is now printing below the WS 150 mark eastbound, being the only safe area and more and more ships are heading west. The USG did spring to life yesterday, partly of the back of bidding for a Taiwan delivering tender, but with a WTI/Murban spread of around USD 10+ trading opportunities have also become viable. Unconfirmed reports suggest USD 24m has been concluded for the benchmark USG/Ningbo run.

Market volatility has eased this week, perhaps as the reality of a prolonged conflict in the Middle East has sunk in and the opposing bull and bear factors surrounding the curtailment of Middle East supply is now beginning to shape up. A lack of liquidity in the Atlantic spot market and mystery shrouding a handful of Qatari fleet fixtures towards the end of last week saw implied levels pare back considerably before finding some support in the low-mid $100kpd's. Fresh fixtures have been few and far between as elevated cargo and freight costs jostle for position, keeping bid/offer spreads wide. East of Suez, fixing activity has been higher, led by continued Omani flows and strong volumes from other regions producing excess cargoes. Whilst levels have trended lower overall, TFDE and 2-stroke rates remain healthy and there is even life for some steamers finding spot employment. Whether, or not, the reappearance of previously underutilised or idle tonnage and the arrival of newbuildings will outweigh tonne mile increases amidst trade flow disruptions, remains to be seen. However, uncertainty and volatility on high LNG prices leave no doubt as to the value of flexible modern tonnage in the short term.

The Panamax market has shown a steadier and more constructive tone this week, with the Atlantic improving on the back of better fronthaul and Transatlantic enquiry, allowing owners to push firmer ideas despite a tonnage list that is still by no means tight. The North Atlantic has benefited from improved replenishment and better support out of USG/USEC, while ECSA remains the softer pocket, particularly for prompt ships, although forward April positions appear more stable. In the Pacific, sentiment has also strengthened, helped by a shorter spot list, decent demand out of Indonesia and Australia, and a touch more period interest, but bunker volatility continues to cast a shadow over negotiations and remains the key variable shaping sentiment across both basins.

Supramax and Handy markets remained under pressure over the past couple of sessions, with sentiment largely subdued across both basins. Limited fresh enquiry and steady to growing tonnage availability continued to weigh on rates, particularly in the Atlantic where demand remained thin. The Continent–Mediterranean region showed little change, with muted activity and largely stable conditions. In Asia, sluggish trading persisted as weaker cargo volumes and cautious charterer activity kept momentum in check. Elevated bunker costs and uncertainty further dampened sentiment across regions. Overall, the market continues to drift with softening fundamentals and no clear signs of recovery in the near term.

As predicted in this report last week, we are seeing a slowdown in reported transactions while the ongoing conflict in the Middle East unfolds. Spot earnings, while having cooled off on the larger crude tonnage this week, continue to be extremely elevated and highly volatile. In a market with more questions than answers at the moment, one thing has been made clear; Iran will keep disrupting the Hormuz Strait so long as this conflict is active. Of course, this tactic is not without blowback on Iran’s own crude export markets but is a steadfast disruption tactic against its aggressors and the global shipping markets. This week, high spec scrubber fitted IMOII MR sisters FINNANGER/FJELLANGER (46K DWT HMD 2009/10) were sold for USD 48M en bloc.   The conflict has given the dry market a rude awakening. Prior to the beginning of March, dry was looking like the darling of the shipping markets following a stellar start to the year and a widely reported rosy outlook for the rest of 2026. However, now we are imagining the consequences of a sustained high oil price environment – something that could lead to a general macro/dry slowdown. Second-hand availability lists remain tight at this stage, something that would potentially keep prices firm as buyers fight it out over sales candidates. An example of this is seen this week in ultramax ABILITY (64K DWT Shin Kurushima 2021) which was sold for USD 37M with delivery SSDD passed to Greek buyers.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Middle East tensions have intensified amid escalating attacks, causing extreme volatility in oil prices. At the time of writing, April CP was traded at $583 for C3 and $578 for C4. So far, three vessels carrying Iranian LPG have transited the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the conflict.  The ongoing supply disruptions pushed the US–Far East arbitrage wider to -$350 for April and one Apr lifting US FOB was reported traded at 37 cpg. U.S. propane/propylene inventories fell by 1.7 mil barrels to 71.7 million barrels in the week ended 6th Mar, leaving stocks remained 58.4% higher year on year.  Supply concerns continued to mount as no clear signals pointing to a near-term end on Middle East conflict. South and Southeast Asian buyers have prioritized LPG for residential consumption over the petrochemical sector, given limited spot availabilities on US butane cargoes. Some cargoes with butane grade were reportedly sold into India at Apr CP plus over $300 for prompt delivery. Meanwhile, Hyosung Vina was heard to award a 4/0 cargo for 1H May delivery at CP plus nearly $200. A couple of bids for 23/0 2h Apr delivery basis Chiba were shown in window at Bal Mar FEI link plus low-mid single digit, with no offers not seen. Separately, a couple of 4/0 parcels for Apr delivery were reported being placed into China at Mar FEI plus high teens or Apr FEI plus 100s. Meanwhile, FPCC issued tender to secure LPG for 2h Apr delivery for cracker use in Mailiao, due to Napatha supply crunch.

Panamax activity remained relatively muted this week, with fixing across both basins still somewhat limited as volatility in bunker prices continues to complicate negotiations and keep many players cautious. In the Atlantic, the market remains under pressure with a lack of fresh fronthaul and transatlantic enquiry and a growing list of prompt tonnage, leaving owners competing more aggressively for the few stems in the market. In the Pacific, while cargo demand appears reasonably steady, the balance has started to loosen as more vessels come open, creating a wider bid–offer spread and slowing the pace of concluded business. Overall sentiment has softened slightly, and although underlying shipment volumes remain supportive, the latest tightening indicators in both the Pacific and South Atlantic suggest that the recent upward momentum may struggle to extend much further without a fresh pickup in cargo flow.

Volatility remains the key theme as conflict in the Middle East continues. The questions posed in last week’s report remain largely unanswered and the swings seen on crude pricing after fresh assaults on Gulf region assets over the weekend have added another layer of uncertainty for LNG trading. This, along with many vessels marketed for sublet, has led to a cautious mood with more bearish undertones. Nevertheless, after a softening from the initial reactive spike we saw last week, rates appear to have held with prompt availabilities commanding strong charter rates around $200kpd for 2-strokes and above $100k for TFDE’s in both basins. There is a sense of charterers holding off for now as they hope for more clarity for laycans further out in the fixing window, especially with the emergence of more sublets and potential competition; however, every day brings fresh turmoil and we are now facing the prospect of mines in the Straits of Hormuz and several vessels have been struck by projectiles in the region. So while the early days of the attack saw charterers typically scrambling to charter in, reshuffle or sell FOB, the more recent days have been shaped by caution due to the underlying length in the market and the increasing number of availabilities shown. Where the LNG and the LNG shipping markets go in the coming days is still uncertain.

This week on Capesize, C5 remains steady but softening tone. Fresh bids for early April stems are heard at USD 11.00 and late March seen at mid USD 11s. The tone is softening compared to early week highs (up to mid USD 12). Overall outlook in the Pacific is bearish as bunker price volatility combined with easing oil prices weigh on the previous bullish forecast. C3 (Brazil/China) sentiment is holding firm with ideas above USD 28. Forward positions in mid-April are seeing offers in the USD 31 range. The North Atlantic sees strong front haul sentiment but limited fresh cargo. C3 21-32 March offers USD 27, 1-10 April fixtures at USD 26.35, 21-31 April bids at USD 28. C5 25-27 March last done USD 11.3, 28-31 March offers at USD 11.5.

North Sea After a quiet week rates have taken a correction. WS 195 on subs admittedly for a vessel that will deliver on time charter after the voyage, but the correction has happened. Natural dates are starting to push into the 3rd decade. There are a few relets around and with US markets softening the draw to ballast may not be as strong, so list should start to grow again and remains to be seen if new floor has been established.  Mediterranean Mid way through this week and the Mediterranean market has been quieter after the correction in the USG and North Sea. There are still outstanding cargoes which need to cover and charterers want to test it down as Mediterranean now is still providing much higher returns compared to surrounding markets. Remains to be seen where the owners will draw the line.

West Africa was tested yesterday with WS 267.5 on subs for Angola/Mediterranean. In amongst this, a solid number of vessels were clipped from the list, rendering supply fairly balanced, leaning on tight. Considering there are very few local ships stateside, US charterers will be reliant on UKCM tonnage, although some recalibration of rates may be required for Suezmaxes to compete with Aframaxes for USG/TA. The main question mark regarding West Africa relates to vessels ballasting from the East. After being cancelled, these units will be keen to fix in this healthy market while also minimising waiting time. They may be more practical compared to UKCM tonnage, who have the pick of Americas–CPC–Mediterranean etc. In the East, with a week of trading Yanbu under owners’ and charterers’ belts, it is evident more owners are willing to trade the Red Sea whilst gargantuan returns are present.

The VLCC market continued the rollercoaster ride in the week gone by as suppliers look for alternative ways to ship oil out and refiners are scrambling for it. Consequently Asia is shutting down one significant production line after another due to lack of feedstock. Guidance from Saudi Aramco suggests the East-West pipeline to Yanbu in the Red Sea will reach full capacity in the next couple of days as tankers arrive to load, upwards to 7 million bbls per day, and with that every existing C/P intended for MEG load can- and have been re-negotiated for loading in Yanbu. The Strait of Hormuz remains “inaccessible” now with the added risk of mines, however, Fujairah and Mina Al Fahal in Oman are still a vague possibility. The Atlantic has seen a downward rate correction with USG export eastbound now priced sub USD 25 million, and West Africa or Brazil/East around the WS 220 mark – although still yielding USD 250k/day in daily return give or take. Rates from the Middles East are on paper double of that from the Atlantic but an owner will only be paid if the ship physically loads and performs the intended voyage. In the meantime, the only certainty is uncertainty.

The Supramax and Handysize markets showed mixed conditions with a generally softer tone in the Atlantic and steadier activity in Asia. In the Continent and Mediterranean, both markets remained relatively balanced with stable demand. However, the US Gulf and South Atlantic faced increasing pressure due to a growing tonnage list and limited cargo demand, leading to weaker sentiment. In contrast, the Asian market remained comparatively firmer, supported by steady trading activity and tighter vessel availability in some areas, although rising bunker prices and fuel constraints made some charterers more cautious.

EAST With Middle East practically remaining closed, more vessels continue to gather outside of the Strait of Hormuz. Activity across the rest of the Eastern market has also been limited so far this week. Much now hinges on whether conditions in the Middle East shift - if at all.  WEST After a handful of US fixtures were concluded last week at premiums to last‑done levels, the market paused briefly before activity resumed early this week, with a flurry of fixtures emerging in the low USD 130s. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz is expected to trigger a meaningful repositioning of MEG tonnage towards the USG. As a result, the impact is likely to be most pronounced on USG liftings from late April onwards, potentially increasing tonnage availability and influencing rate direction. So far, 21 April spot fixtures have been concluded, comprising 11 in the first decade, 8 in the second decade, and 2 in the final decade.

Clearly, a lot has changed since the previous report last Friday. A long-predicted US-Israel bombing campaign on Iran commenced over the weekend to leave tanker owners (particularly crude owners) bracing themselves for heavy disruption. Most would have expected rates to rise, though few would have dreamed of the highs we are now seeing. A monstruous $696,803/day is being reported for scrubber fitted KALAMOS (317K DWT SWS 2010), which has comfortably set the record for highest rate recorded on a spot VLCC voyage. Shockwaves are being felt in the second-hand market, where already elevated price asks are shooting up in response to the new earnings norm, that is, if candidates are still being considered for sale. Sales reported this week are likely to be some of the last with a ‘pre-war’ pricing, and we would expect the number of sales reported to fall sharply as the market adjusts to what is going on. Time will of course tell in this very unpredictable environment. This week Scrubber Fitted Aframax GREEN ATTITUDE (112K DWT COSCO 2018) was sold for USD 70M.    The dry market finds itself in a curious spot. A buoyant Q1 means that values are rising steadily, but sellers are disincentivised to part ways with tonnage. This is due to healthy rate predictions for the rest of the year and into 2027, and the fact that replacement tonnage is so hard to come by. Thus, if you sell your 15-year-old ship, yes you will receive a nice sum in return, but there is no guarantee you can find a 5-year-old equivalent to reinvest in, one would only be left with newbuildings as an option to deploy capital. Competition is fierce on any available candidates particularly quality tonnage (Japanese built units), with a rumoured 15 interested parties in SPIRIT OF HO-PING (82K DWT Tsuneishi 2011) which was eventually bought by Greek buyers for USD 19.4M. All this leaves dry with an ever growing list of buyers, and a seemingly shrinking list of candidates, something that will only influence values one way.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: The Middle East conflict that erupted over weekend has disrupted oil and gas export flows through the Strait of Hormuz. No spot deals or market discussions have been heard amid the prevailing uncertainty on geopolitical tensions. Swap values continued to surge on supply concerns, and by the time of writing, Apr CP was traded at $591/mt for C3 and $590/mt for C4 respectively.  U.S.–Far East arbitrage widened sharply to around minus $270s for April, as supply disruptions in the Middle East pushed landed costs higher. Terminal fees for April liftings surged to around 27 cpg, with sellers targeting higher margins from the wider arbitrage amid softening freight on the US–Chiba route. U.S. propane/propylene inventories rose by 819,000 barrels to 73.4 million barrels in the week ended Feb. 27, although stocks remained 50.7% higher year on year. The build came as a surprise to the market, as most had expected a decline.  Both Mar and Apr FEI and cash premiums surged amid tightening supply. A 23/0 parcel for 1h Apr delivery basis Chiba was concluded in window at Apr FEI plus $105, and similar parcel for 2h Apr delivery was traded at Mar FEI plus high single digit. A 46/0 parcel for 2h Apr delivery basis Chiba was also reported traded at Mar FEI plus mid-teens.  Asian refiners and petchem plants are reportedly cutting rates or shutting units due to feedstock shortages. China’s PDH operating rate is expected to fall from the current 64% to around 54% in the next two weeks, facing rising feedstock costs amid supply tightness. The resulting demand loss could exceed 2mmt of propane per month, which might partly offset Middle East supply disruptions and easing some tightness. However, India and some Southeast Asian buyers are more severely impacted, with few alternative butanes available for prompt Mar delivery. Some US exports are expected to be diverted into these markets, though arrivals will likely be mid/2h Apr range.

The Panamax market remains clearly split between the two basins this week. In the Atlantic, fundamentals continue to soften as limited fresh enquiry and a growing list of prompt tonnage keep pressure on owners, with transatlantic activity subdued and overall sentiment cautious. Some support is still seen from ECSA and firmer fronthaul demand, particularly for forward dates, but the basin remains largely oversupplied. In contrast, the Pacific continues to firm, with tight spot tonnage and steady cargo flow out of Indonesia and Australia keeping owners in the driving seat and maintaining upward pressure on rates.

North Sea Although not directly impacted yet the North Sea is reacting to the surrounding markets and the uncertainty created by the ongoing situation in the MEG. With more vessels ballasting out of the area, the list remains relatively short and is keeping market sentiment firm. Natural dates have moved into the 2nd decade and with a lack of Suezmax / VLCC in the area / Atlantic Basin, focus will remain firmly on Aframax in both North Sea and US, keeping markets firm and giving owners options.  Mediterranean Same as in the North Sea and USG, the Mediterranean market is climbing with owners trying to push for more on every fixture. Sentiment prevails at the moment but also people are ballasting towards the USG and the list in the Mediterranean could suddenly look very short.

The Handysize market levels softened a touch, but have generally remained steady. Fewer fresh orders and fewer concluded trips, as owners continue to push period rates, whilst it seems like many operators have filled up their tonnage books for now. For the Supramax and Ultramax market owners have continued to favor USG and ECSA, but might take a turn as fronthaul orders from Mediterranean/Black Sea are likely to route via Cape of Good Hope. Generally speaking, with the ongoing geopolitics, market remains hesitant with no clear direction for the time being.

This week on Capesize, both C3 and C5 are showing upward momentum, with C5 supported by limited March tonnage as well as bunker spikes. The C5 (West Australia/China) front is active and bullish, with mid-March fixtures reported at USD 11.5, driven by rising fuel costs and tight West Australia tonnage. C3 (Brazil/China) market is firm with bullish undertones. Bids have been seen at USD 26 for full April dates, and early April fixture seen at USD 27. In the Atlantic, activity is thin, but sentiment is strong, supported by coal demand. Overall tone is firm to strong, with both basins showing upward pressure. C3 11-12 March fixed USD 23.25, 21-31 March fixed USD 23.5. C5 16-18 March fixture USD 11.30, 19-21 March fixture USD 10.8.

The LNG and LNG shipping markets are suffering seismic shocks in the wake of military actions in the Middle East. The geopolitical situation is very fluid and information is flowing fast and is not always subject to validation, but it is increasingly apparent that there is no quick resolution on the horizon and the disruptions we are seeing to the LNG trade are likely to persist for some time. How long will Middle Eastern production remain offline? How will Asia adapt to reduced supply? When will Europe seek to replenish low storage levels? How will US volume be distributed between importers? It is too early to answer these questions with much certainty, but these past days have shown charterers are willing to pay rates of 10 times the levels from last week to secure prompt tonnage, and there is interest for multi-month periods up to a year in the six figure range – unthinkable as we prepared our report last week. Underpinning the frantic trading, chartering and operational activity that is keeping us all very busy, we are grateful to the brave seafarers working in increasingly challenging situations across all sectors.

Conflict in the MEG has intensified an already fundamentally strong Suezmax market, supported by spillover volumes and elevated market sentiment. The limited number of owners willing to call the Red Sea have been fixed at exceptionally high rates, while owners in the West have leveraged these levels to secure record‑setting fixtures. There continues to be significant eastbound enquiry in both the Mediterranean and the Atlantic, in addition to the customary flows.

It’s all about the war in the VLCC segment. Rate estimates, and paper, for loading MEG or Saudi Red Sea have skyrocketed although no cargoes have been physically lifted since the war broke out, so Baltic rates are so far academic and purely a guestimate by the broking community of what it could be as, if, and when. Ships are piling up on both sides of the Hormuz Strait and it’s all a stalemate. On the back of the MEG situations Atlantic rates have also increased substantially as charterers seek alternative oil supply to the MEG. However, thus far the rate spread between east and west is still substantial, but current daily returns are nevertheless still in the mid USD 200k/day and above for eastbound voyages from eg. Brazil and the USG.

EAST The Middle East is facing unprecedented turmoil, with conflict disrupting the entire region. Ship insurers have withdrawn coverage, and head owners are refusing to send vessels into or out of the Gulf. As a result, we are witnessing a surge of cancellations, with ships unable to meet their previously fixed laycans. At the same time, no new fixtures or negotiations are taking place, leaving future deals completely stalled. Meanwhile, there have been some discussions for cargos loading in the Red Sea.  WEST A handful of fixtures have been concluded in the USG for both April and March laycans. Amidst MEG turmoil and a jumping arbitrage, freight has yet to really take off, however, rates are still solid. Worries that the USG position list for second half April will grow substantially is apparent, although, for the same to happen the MEG has to stay closed for a somewhat longer period of time.

The sky really is the limit it seems for the tanker market as earnings go from strength to strength. Last done VLCC rates are being eclipsed by the following fixtures, leading to a game of cat and mouse between owners and charterers. Those who have waited will be the beneficiaries of the rates squeeze, while others who locked in TCs below USD 100K/day will now be feeling slightly hard done by. Buyers this week are paying more attention to the smaller crude sizes, where values have been steadily pushing north so far this year. Buyers in this space need to move quickly and be gutsy in order to capture this earnings environment, as it will feel they are chasing a runaway market. This week Scrubber fitted STENA SUNSHINE (159K DWT Samsung 2013) was bought by Thenamaris for USD 61M.   The Capesize sector has garnered the most attention in the dry space so far this year, and those who have yet to move are running out of time. Owners are seeing TC rates rise steadily, and unless buyers are there to match the ever-increasing prices, owners will be more than happy to withdraw candidates and accept the healthy returns. Modern ships are the hardest to come by, so generally buyers are restricted to the c.15-year-old range. Outside of the largest sizes, the dry sector is still providing an outlet for buyers looking for steel on the water. Competition is rife, and a rumoured 10 buyers were fighting out for Kamsarmax THREE SASKIAS (82K DWT JMU 2014), which eventually sold for USD 26.75M, setting a new benchmark in this sector.

EAST An issue at Ras Tanura Terminal currently causing disruptions to trade flows. It remains to be seen how severe and long lasting this situation will be. On a monthly basis Ras Tanura export about 7-10 VLGC cargos. Close to half of these are usually lifted by Indian PSUs. A disruption to exports could lead Saudi lifters to source product elsewhere, likely USG, which could increase ton-miles. At the same time, less Saudi Exports will also mean less volumes coming on water. So far, a Japanese importer has secured a ship on subs loading early second half of March with freight some 16 dollars below last done levels.  WEST Toward the end of last week, activity resumed in earnest following the CNY holiday. A handful of fixtures concluded West of Suez helped lift sentiment, pushing rates back up to around USD 150 pmt on a Houston/Chiba via Panama Canal basis, while further thinning the available position lists. With a few March cargoes still expected to emerge, owners are hopeful that the current momentum will carry into next week, potentially opening the door for additional April fixing and further firming of rates.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Saudi Aramco declared force majeure and cancelled March liftings from the Juaymah NGL facilities, which account for around 75% of Saudi exports. At the time of writing, the market was still awaiting the March CP announcement, while March CP swaps surged to around $550 for C3 and $545 for C4 amid the Saudi supply disruption. March/April C3 CP structure also narrowed to near flat, compared with a $13 backwardation in the previous session.  Following the Saudi incident and the resulting supply loss, the U.S.–Far East arbitrage widened further to around minus $260s for March and minus $220s for April. Terminal fees for March loaders were assessed at around 12 cpg. Meanwhile, U.S. propane/propylene inventories fell by 1.7 million barrels to 72.5 million barrels in the week ended Feb. 20, although stocks remained 40.7% higher on a year-on-year basis.  Cash premiums for April delivery strengthened subsequently. In the window, a 23/0 parcel for 1H and 2H April delivery basis Chiba was bid at April FEI plus $47 and plus $39 respectively. A 46/0 parcel for 1H and 2H April delivery basis Ningbo was bid at April FEI plus $40 and plus $38 respectively. However no offers were shown as sellers also monitoring the supply disruption situation. Earlier of the week, FIC reportedly awarded a buy tender for a 4/0 Canadian cargo for April delivery at April FEI plus the high $80s.

All load regions from East to West have firmed, with the MEG and CPC leading the charge. The others appear undervalued and ready to pop, especially with prompt cargoes continuing to emerge – particularly out of West Africa driven by the abundance of unsold barrels. Tonnage remains very tight in both hemispheres and, with VLCCs continuing their Sinokor‑driven bull run, we should expect further split‑VLCC stems to explore Suezmaxes.

The VLCC market has continued on an upward trajectory in the week gone by and Sinokor Maritime has begun to capitalize on their huge investment in the segment as daily earnings have moved beyond USD 200k/day. The MEG dominates the demand, and the front end of the position list is shrinking by the hour, leaving charterers with few other alternatives to choose from but the South Korean giant. West Africa and not least Brazil is also offering owners a profitable option, and paradoxically Brazilian freight now top USG exports as WTI crude struggle to compete in the East. Heightened tensions between Iran and the US have also added upward pressure, particularly for paper, which again has given opportunities to hedge period deals now north of USD 100k/day for 12 months T/C. Expect more of the same short term.

The Panamax market continues to show a clear split this week, with the Atlantic remaining under pressure while the Pacific maintains a firm tone. In the Atlantic, prompt tonnage is building amid limited fresh enquiry, keeping competition among owners high and rates under gradual pressure, particularly on transatlantic routes, while the lack of grain support from NCSA and the USG remains notable. Some support is seen in ECSA forward dates, which are still trading at a premium, but overall sentiment remains cautious. By contrast, the Pacific is holding well on the back of tight vessel availability and steady cargo flow from Indonesia, Australia, and the North Pacific, allowing owners to maintain firm ideas and pushing charterers to cover at stronger levels. Forward indicators and vessel tightness continue to point toward a constructive near-term outlook into March, although seasonal factors suggest some moderation may emerge later in the spring.

This week on Cape, both basins showing forward upward pressure, with C3 leading strong and forward curves firming. C3 (Brazil/China) saw March fixtures in the high USD 23s, with offers heard in the mid to high USD 25 range for April dates. West Africa remains in play, but Brazil is dominating the C3 market. Overall tone shows tight tonnage for end of March. In the Pacific, C5 sentiment remains steady to firm. Last done fixtures for early March is at USD 9.90. Overall tone in the Pacific region is slightly easier, with sub USD 10 trading, but tight tonnage in March is keeping sentiment balanced, with an expected upside into the second half of March firming above USD 10, setting a positive sentiment into April. C3 11-20 March offers USD 25, 21-31 March fixes at USD 25.2, 1-10 April offers USD 25.65. C5 10-12 March fixtures at USD 9.9, 13-15 March fixtures seen USD 10.3.

The Handysize market levels remain steady and unchanged. Few more fixtures concluded this week as regional tightness continues to press, supporting firmer rates, especially in the Americas. For the Supramax and Ultramax market, regional divergence has become even more pronounced – clearly showing owners favouring USG and ECSA FHs rather than any FHs from West Africa. The Atlantic continues to outperform the Pacific basin, showing stronger and firmer support. Period rates on Handies up to Ultramaxes continues to increase, sending positive vibes through the market.

The LNG shipping markets East and West of Suez have been moving in different directions lately, and the trend has continued this past week with rates softening in Asia and the Middle East while firming in the Atlantic. In the East, there continues to be a steady flow of requirements but competition among owners and subletters is giving charterers the edge in negotiations especially for those that can work with smaller vessels. The basis for the rising market in the Atlantic is well understood, with off-takers working hard to mitigate weather-related disruptions and delays. The market has climbed considerably week-on-week, and with portfolios holding on to tonnage there are some windows showing no availability at all. While there is speculation over whether the spot market will correct as these disruptions unwind, the multimonth market for periods through summer suggests a higher floor than we saw in January.

North Sea Clearing out the remaining stems for February at the end of last saw the market firm to WS 195. So far this week we have seen limited activity in what looks like a relatively small program for early March. Relets are coming back into the window which should cover the majority of the first 5 days North Sea stems. List remains on the shorter side which is keeping the market steady at the moment.  Mediterranean Correction has been on the cards since last week as owners were pilling up in the front end, dates moved forward and the market was very quiet for 2-3 days. Rates remain at very healthy levels - even if corrected downwards - and with some more activity till the end of this week they should find a new equilibrium. Supply of tonnage has more than enough vessels though for rest of the 1st decade March with a bunch prompt but some of them on their way to the USG.

The Sinokor machine continues to gather momentum this week as we enter a new era for the VLCC space. Such a singular concentration of vessel ownership has not been seen in the history of this market, and the South Korean outfit are showing no signs of letting up as 11 Dynacom VLCCs were confirmed this week. TC rates are quickly surpassing last done levels, from USD 90k/day to USD 100K/day reported for one year, which is justifying the historically high valuations for VLCCs. It’s not just the larger ships that are benefitting, sentiment is also engulfing most tanker segments, where sellers are increasingly confident to hold their positions.    Predictably, with Lunar New Year celebrations in full swing this week, the dry market has taken a breather. It is a rosy picture otherwise across the sector, as rates are expected remain strong throughout 2026. While not having the dramatic movement of the tanker market, dry is being seen as a safe bet and provides buyers with a more accessible entry point. This week ultramax ONLY YOU (60K DWT Sanoyas 2017) was sold for USD 28.3M.

EAST Following a subdued start to the week, slowed by public holidays across much of Asia, spot activity picked up pace on Thursday. Several cargoes were quoted for March loading out of the Middle East Gulf, bringing with it a renewed boost of optimism for freight. Saudi acceptances are yet to be released at the time of writing, but we are already seeing expectations of further gains on freight as tonnage availability already have started to slim down.  WEST Players short shipping ex USG during last decade March quickly realized today that in order to secure freight before the market ran out of availability, one had to make a move. Although levels have come down a bit, freight has settled around USD 150 per ton and a handful of deals were concluded today. We believe there is more potential for freight increases as the MEG and USG currently are battling for the same vessels.

Panamax market opening the week with a clear Atlantic/Pacific split, with the Atlantic losing some momentum as activity slows, prompt demand eases and tonnage lists become more balanced, keeping sentiment cautious and upside limited for now. Fronthaul and ECSA remain subdued, with wider bid/offer gaps and owners holding firm on ideas. By contrast, the Pacific continues to set the tone despite the holiday period, supported by steady cargo flow, tight prompt supply in parts of Asia and improving period interest, which is also lending support to the backhaul. Overall, fundamentals remain healthy and point toward a more constructive post-Chinese New Year market if Pacific strength persists.

The momentum reported last week has continued in both basins, albeit in fits and starts, with spot rates in the Atlantic basin now edging higher than in the Pacific and Middle East. The primary driver in what is still a fundamentally over-supplied Atlantic market has been scheduling disruptions, mainly linked to cold weather impacting cargo operations as well as storm and adverse sea conditions. The result is several mis-matches between cargo dates and vessel arrival times, which has added to the usual steady stream of requirements and pushed rates back above $30,000 per day. The tight spell is currently within the middle decade of March, but if disruptions continue and if more requirements emerge this is likely to spread through towards the end of March. The markets East of Suez are a little quieter as expected through the holidays, although recent fixing levels are struggling to hold steady due to a healthy availability list. Multimonth activity is also a little more muted this past week, although with the interest shown in recent candidate vessels this is surely just a pause.  And for those celebrating, we hope you have enjoyed the holidays!!!

VLCC rates continue to go from strength to strength, upwards to the mid WS 150’s for MEG/eastbound cargoes at the writing moment, and on relatively thin volumes as the Far East are off celebrating Lunar New Year. 2026 is the year of the horse – and it is galloping at full speed as far as the tanker market goes. Traders have also started taking cover medium and long term, paying upwards to USD 90k+/day for 1 year T/C and low USD 60’s k/day for 3 years. Very few clouds on the sky short term with Sinokor now controlling about 25% of the compliant fleet, leaving charterers with very slim pickings for alternatives. Iran and the US continue talks aimed at resolving their longstanding nuclear dispute, but analysts remained skeptical about the potential for further progress. In the meantime, both sides are rattling sabres adding uncertainty and additional upward pressure on rates.

We are down to just a couple of natural FOC options for TD20 runs, and although the USG market looks very well stocked with local sailers and is unlikely to drag further ships across the Atlantic, Guyana was busy last night and West Africa has circa 10MBBLs outstanding in the 1st decade. Basis present crude dynamics, Asian appetite and thus VLCC erosion of West African grades in the 2nd decade should be muted, with the same applying for WTI. All of these contrive to build a bullish demand outlook. With CPC and AFRA spillover also sponging Mediterranean tonnage, strong MEG volumes trimming potential Eastern ballasters and weather delays up north, an already constricted supply side should also remain firm. Outside of the USG, where AFRAs also corrected down followed by a flurry of local activity, Suezmaxes are on strong footing, underlined by a tight VLCC market.

North Sea A relatively slow week so far activity wise but vessels have been clearing the area which has kept the rates steady. Relets have come back into the frame taking various stems out into the third decade. List is slowly building again, but if US markets remain activity, more will ballast, keeping the North Sea availability balanced. Owners are able to be a bit more selective on which cargoes they want to look at. Early March window is not expected to be that busy on paper so we don't expect big swings on the rates however some delays here and there might change things pretty quickly.  Mediterranean After the busy end of last and start of this week we are done now for February dates in the Mediterranean and March dates will be worked from today. Feeling top-ish? I would say so, as owners repeated the rates on the last busy window and if 01-05 March isn't that busy they should be happy to do it again or even leaving a few points on the table. Weather expected to clear out from this weekend onwards and more vessels will come back open next week.

On Capesize for this week, we saw C3 holding firm and C5 showing a slightly softer tone, with forward pricing signalling a potential rebound after Chinese New Year. C3 (Brazil/China) remains steady to firm. Physical orders have been seen in the mid USD 24-25s for full stems. Ballaster lists are growing, with several ships headed for Tubarao for end March and early April dates. North Atlantic is showing tight tonnage, with fronthaul C9 at USD 54,333/day, indicating a strong tone with solid demand. C5 (West Australia/China) is quieter this week, but owners are holding firm. Sentiment is slightly softer as bids remain in the USD 9.25-9.50 range. FFA premiums heading into March suggest forward optimism, implying a USD 1 premium coming into March. Overall tonnage is tight ex-China for early March, however less fresh C5 stems keep the market balanced.   C3 11-20 March offers at USD 25, 21-31 March offers seen at USD 24. C5 04-06 March last fix USD 9.5 with offers seen at USD 9.9.

The Supramax market remained subdued with limited fresh enquiry and softer sentiment in the US Gulf, while the South Atlantic appeared finely balanced and fronthaul interest showed signs of slowing. The Continent and Mediterranean stayed relatively supportive but with scarce fixing activity. In Asia, activity was mixed, with some coal and minor bulk business reported but overall momentum remained patchy. Period activity is picking up and few fixtures reported for SP up to 1 year duration.  Handysize also saw a lacklustre session, with Lunar New Year holidays continuing to dampen Asian demand, although the Atlantic showed some resilience with steady interest from the Continent and East Coast South America. The US Gulf remained firm but with limited new fixtures, and overall sentiment in Asia stayed weak amid ample tonnage supply.

While Sinokor has stolen the headlines so far this year with its raid on VLCCs, the increased liquidity and pricing have spurred many others into action to crystalise gains at these levels. One could argue that the turbulent geopolitical situation isn’t going anywhere, particularly during the current US administration, and there could be further upside for tanker owners, but prudent shipowners have sold vessels into buyers willing to take the exposure at these levels. On modern units, buyers are paying for the prompt delivery and long life of the asset, whereas those operating at the other end of the age curve are taking on more risk at these elevated levels. This week Thenamaris purchased scrubber fitted suezmax pair EMERALDWAY/SUNRISEWAY (158K DWT SWS 2022) for USD 88M each en bloc. In the mid aged LR2 space, scrubber fitted sisters FS DILIGENCE/ENDEAVOR (108K DWT Namura 2012) were sold for USD 43M each en bloc.   Lunar New Year celebrations will likely curtail what has been a strong start to the year for the dry market. Many analysts are touting a healthy 2026, so a slowdown will surely prove to only be temporary. Capesize demand has been relentless over the past 12 months, and we have seen values rise accordingly. This week EPIC (182K Odense 2010) was sold to European buyers at USD 32.3M while CAPE BRAZIL (177K DWT SWS 2010) was sold for USD 31.2M. There was some action in modern Ultramaxes, with BERGE TATEYAMA (63K DWT Shin Kasado 2020) sold to Turkish buyers at USD 34.5M.

text: Cash differentials for evenly split March lifting cargoes fell to minus $20s against March CP, pressured by weakening demand and elevated freight costs. A similar parcel for April lifting was offered via window at April CP minus $4. At the time of writing, March CP was assessed at $537/mt for C3 and $527/mt for C4, with the March/April structure trading at a $15 backwardation. The U.S.–Far East arbitrage widened to minus $208, and terminal fees for March loaders were pegged at 7–8 cpg. Meanwhile, U.S. propane/propylene inventories declined by 5.4 million barrels to 77.3 million barrels in the week ended Feb. 6, though stocks remained 31.2% higher on YOY basis. In the window, 23/0 parcels for Mar delivery basis Chiba were bid at March FEI plus $56 and plus $39 for 1H and 2H respectively. A similar parcel for 1H April was bid at April FEI plus $37. Despite these bids, offers remained scarce. Outside the window, a flurry of tenders emerged this week, but only limited volumes were awarded. Notably, one South China PDH plant secured a March-delivery 4/0 cargo via tender at March CP plus high $80s. Likewise, another Chinese importer also procured similar non U.S. cargo for Mar delivery at similar price.

The Supra/Handy market is showing signs of improvement, with sentiment strengthening in the Atlantic as tighter tonnage availability supports firmer rate discussions, particularly from the US Gulf. While the South Atlantic remains more balanced, activity levels are gradually improving. In Asia, demand remains softer with ample vessel, though some pockets of stability are emerging. Overall, market tone is positive, with owners gaining confidence as momentum slowly builds across key regions.

Strong levels for ECC/UKCM underpin the market - Afra’s were holding out in WS 330s which allowed 2 suezmaxes to swoop in. This should keep USG/TA rates at a minimum of 145kt x WS 150, and with US list short on local tonnage, potential ballasters should, in theory, be able to leverage this to keep TD20 above WS 160. February is a short month, and although there have been rumours of March enquiries on both sides of the Atlantic, nothing concrete has emerged. With less West Africa volumes absorbed by the VLCCs for 1st decade March, we expect activity to pick up. Prompt cargoes continue to surface in the MEG, keeping levels firm with possible upside. This should also limit the number of vessels ballasting West.

After a highly successful LNG2026 in Doha, it is London’s turn to be in the spotlight with International Energy Week and it feels appropriate that the focus shifts to the Atlantic. After a rollercoaster winter that saw rates surge well into the six digits before crashing down below $10,000 per day just weeks later, the region is enjoying a bounce in charter rates for early March with levels around double what they were this time last week. Turbulent weather is still impacting schedules and is leading to a tightening availability list, and with several uncovered cargoes right in the fixing window there is more likelihood the renaissance will continue than it will stall. The Middle East and Pacific regions are holding steady and are still at a premium to the Atlantic, although it there is a fair chance the situation will be reversed within days if current momentum holds. All this will give owners some comfort, yet the landscape remains challenging and will not be helped by the number of sublets being show for multimonth periods. We wouldn’t unbuckle the seatbelts just yet.

The Panamax market has started the week on a firmer tone, with sentiment improving across both basins despite fundamentals remaining mixed. In the Atlantic, better near-side TA cover and steady ECSA grain, supported by USG/NCSA stems, are helping owners hold levels, although thin mineral volumes and ample tonnage continue to limit upside. North Atlantic replenishment has been more active, but charterers remain selective. In the Pacific, firmer paper and improved NoPac grain demand have lifted confidence, allowing owners to defend numbers, while Indo/Australian minerals stay quiet. With Chinese New Year approaching and tonnage tightening slightly, we expect prompt fixing to remain supportive in the near term.

This week in Capesize we saw both C3 and C5 trending firmer, supported by tightness in the Atlantic and FFA strength. In the Atlantic, Brazil & West Africa remains firm but capped, with physical bids seen around USD 22 mark for mid-March, while offers hover around the mid to high USD 23s. Some owners are hinting at higher prices with hints around USD 24+ for late March. Ballaster lists are growing with several vessels headed for Tubarao in early March. In the Pacific, the C5 remains firm but range bound, with a strong forward curve coming into March. Sentiment has a positive undertone, with FFA indicating in the USD 10s in March, however fixtures in the low to mid USD 8s for early March. Overall market tone is firm to bullish. C3 1 to 10 March offers USD 23, 11 to 20 March offers USD 23.8 and ideas USD 24. C5 25 to 28 Feb fixtures at USD 8.25.

North Sea Last cargoes of the 2nd decade are being covered so far this week with rates varying depending on the nature of the voyage. Local players are enjoying colossal returns and they are trying to hit cargoes on the right dates. Balanced list compared to the amount of activity we see although with the very firm US markets vessels will continue to head across keeping itineraries at a premium in the North Sea, rates likely to hover around last done.  Mediterranean Market has had room to correct on the back of an expanding tonnage list for local candidates. Activity still remains robust but Ceyhan dates have now pushed towards the end Feb window. Libya is lagging as always and expected to attract interest from vessels. A couple of ballasters heading out of the area and levels for local runs might stabilize now however charterers still seem to be gaining a few points.

EAST Halfway through the week and so far very little to write home about. Indeed a small handful of cargos have been looked at, but at the time of writing only one of these have materialized into actual fixtures. Most Middle East suppliers have released their acceptances for March barring only Aramco. Despite this, we are currently counting just March spot fixture in the East.  WEST Market has slowed down this week with IE week London in full force, and we have only seen one fixture ex USG reported. Last done remain in the high USD 150s HCvP and we count 28 spot fixtures thus far in March (10/15/3 by decade). We still see many potentially uncovered FOBs in the last decade of March, while freight remains relatively tight for same period.

The VLCC market has been trading in a band between WS 130-140 MEG/East in the week gone by with healthy daily earnings upwards of USD 120k/day and above. Geopolitical tension persists, no less so between the US and Iran, which in worse case could threaten safe passage in the Strait of Hormuz should it escalate. Sinokor’s continued appetite for tonnage, and by and large pricing the spot market higher than the prevailing rate level has underpinned the strong sentiment and left charterers with slim pickings for alternatives. T/C rates have soared as oilco’s and traders hedge their bets, paying upwards of USD 90k/day for one year, also made possible by a strong paper market capping the downside. The MEG February program is at the last leg but those charterers with leftover cargoes should be careful to assume that the owning community has softened their stands significantly. The position list is still wanting and some of the end month MEG ships will more than likely slip into March. Arguably, the immediate upward pressure has subsided a bit and some “profit taking” is to be expected at these levels. Strong Suez- and Aframax segments have also left little wiggle room. In short: all to play for.

This week’s sales are not representative of the raucous undercurrent of the present tanker market. The high level of enquiry and numerous ongoing discussions suggest that more second hand activity is to come. Pricing remains firm and shows no signs of respite, which may encourage prospective investors to seek better value down the newbuilding avenue. This week, scrubber fitted MARAN PYTHIA (158K DWT HHI 2009) was sold to Greek Buyers for USD 46M. The excitement isn’t limited to the crude space, MRs and LR1s have seen an uptick in demand, particularly in the mid age (rgn 15-year-old) bracket. SSDD passed sisters ELANDRA BALTIC/FJORD (51K DWT HMD 2011) were sold for USD 24.5M each en bloc.   A relatively quiet week in the dry market despite the strong start to the year. Predictably, China remains the source of much of the buying interest for ageing bulk carriers. Upcoming Lunar New Year may curtail this demand for the coming weeks, but this will likely be a temporary blip as appetite remains high across the range of sizes from Chinese buyers. In the only ECO transaction of the week, MGJ bought DARYA TAPTI (35K DWT Shikoku 2015) for USD 18.9M.

text: Cash differential for Mar lifting evenly split cargos is assessed lower at Mar CP minus teens amid thin trades, particularly with Mar/Apr CP being traded at $15 backwardation. By the time of writing, Mar CP swap was assessed at $535 for C3 and $527 for C4.   Mar ARB from US to FAR EAST maintained at $190s, however terminal fee declined in response to soaring freight. 46/0 parcel for 2h Mar lifting was changed hand at 6.5 cg reportedly, vs last week’s 8cpg. U.S. propane/propylene stocks declined by 6.2 million bbl to 82.7 million bbl on the week ended January 30, leaving inventory 34.7% higher on YOY basis.  A flurry of deals was concluded for 2/0 parcels on March delivery basis Chiba. 2/0 parcels for 1H March delivery were traded at March FEI plus the high $40s to mid $50s, while 2H March trades at Feb FEI plus $1 to $2.5. On Thurs window, 2/0 parcels for 1h and 2h Mar delivery were bid at Mar FEI plus $51 and $33 respectively, however no offers surfaced. 12/12 parcel was offered in window at Mar CP plus $81 basis Yantai, yet to entice buyer. Bal Feb/March spread widened from high $20s into the $40s, underscoring front-month strength.   Meanwhile, a couple of Us 46/0 cargoes for 2H March delivery were placed into EChina at March FEI plus the mid-high $30s to low $40s, while non-Us stem sold basis SChina at Mar CP plus $70s. One SChina based PDH are still inquiring for 23/0 parcel for Mar delivery while another NChina based PDH are procuring Mar and Apr lots. Additionally, some butane cargos were reportedly sold into South China at March CP plus $60s.

EAST The daily Baltic print keeps rising to new highs on the back of a rock solid West market coupled with an ever slimming position list in the East due to same. Two Indian cargos was fixed yesterday at around 100 RT/C equivalent basis and two more Australian cargos are being worked at the time of writing. Market in the East is expected to remain firm with more near term upside.  WEST  Activity in the Western hemisphere has picked up again after a quiet start to the week, and a handful of vessels are reported on subs at rates higher than what we saw last week. Current fixing ideas are hovering around very high 150s to low 160s pmt HCvP. Laycans fixed are thus far focused around the first two decades of March, and within a week or two, we expect that the entire month will be done and dusted.

North Sea The weather has improved from last week but is still causing some issues with some vessels getting delayed and subsequent replacement requirements. Natural window has pushed into the 2nd decade and with a longer / firmer looking list market sentiment has cooled and softened with a correction in freight levels from the highs of last week. Surrounding areas have also softened which although still attractive to ballast now isn’t the sure thing it was.  Mediterranean Rates have moved sideways this past week but with a softer tone after some quiet days in the local Mediterranean market. Levels however are providing hefty returns for the owners still especially fixing on the right dates. With surrounding markets still providing decent support we might not see the Mediterranean market correcting too much more in the next couple of days.

North of a dozen cargoes were worked in the West yesterday, with additional details emerging today, resulting in a much‑needed trimming of the list. Despite a few Suezmax failures stateside yesterday, the Aframaxes firmed back up to our equivalent levels, which will further underpin the market. There is certainly a sensitive feel to the market, and with impending third‑decade volume expected to work from both sides of the Atlantic, the list will not be as simple to navigate; as such, there is potential for the market to heat up again. The MEG market remains tight on tonnage and was fairly active yesterday, and ongoing geopolitical tensions will continue to bolster sentiment in the region.

The LNG shipping market appears to have paused for breath after the highs and lows of winter volatility, with enough activity to keep owners and charterers busy but with rates across all three major regions broadly steady. The status quo is for very low rates in the Atlantic and there doesn’t seem to be much respite in the near future for owners or sub-letters seeking to capture value in their open positions; there may be some more opportunities as US producers get back on track after the recent weather-related disruptions, but competition among 2-stroke tonnage remains fierce. The markets East of Suez still command a premium for now despite some softening sentiment, and players will be watching the ongoing spot tenders with interest. If there is a light on the horizon for owners, it is the multimonth/multiyear market for which recent fixtures price in a strengthening market later in the year. For those visiting Doha for LNG 2026, we hope you all enjoy a successful trip among old friends, with particular credit to our Qatari hosts for once again providing a fabulously warm and friendly welcome!

Panamax sentiment remained cautious this week, with subdued Atlantic activity and a mixed Pacific keeping market conditions fragile. Limited transatlantic and fronthaul enquiry, well-covered charterers, and growing tonnage lists continued to weigh on Atlantic rates, while ECSA softened as supply increased. In the Pacific, thinner NoPac and East Australia volumes were partly offset by firmer grain demand and renewed period interest, maintaining a two-tier market where modern, larger units command a premium. While near-term sentiment remains soft, forward indicators suggest scope for improvement later in the quarter, albeit tempered by seasonal factors and Indonesian policy uncertainty.

This past week on Capesize saw a slight softening compared to the surge of previous week fixtures, with C3 easing and C5 losing ground. In the Pacific, fixing has been steady with firmer sentiment. Charterers are targeting low USD 8s, but owners are resisting sub USD 8.50s for front end Hedland stems. West Australia/Qingdao C5 fixtures are done at USD 8.35 - 8.40 with some late Feb cargoes still circulating. On the Atlantic front, C3 (Brazil/China) we saw easing with end Feb fixtures in the low USD 25s. The North Atlantic remained steady yet quiet with growing tonnage lists adding pressure. Brazil and West Africa market remains softening, with C3 last done at USD 24.5. Owners ideas going into later March are still around USD 26 however this has little traction. C5 19-21 Feb fixtures at USD 8.75, 25-27 Feb seen bids at USD 8.5. C3 1-10 March seen offers at USD 27s, 11-20 March seen offers at mid USD 27.5s.

The Supramax market experienced a subdued start to the week, with limited fresh fixing activity reported. Atlantic sentiment remained relatively firm with a few cargoes ex USG. The South Atlantic stayed positional but showed signs of improving momentum. In Asia, trading was slow, with recent strength in the North easing while southern areas remained comparatively stable. Period activity offered some support, with a couple of period deals reported. Overall sentiment was marginally positive.

The VLCC market took off end of last week, partly pre-empting a possible US attack on Iran, which did not materialise. However, yesterday the US shot down an Iranian drone, and armed Iranian boats approached a US-flagged vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, rekindling fears of an escalation in tensions between Washington and Tehran. The rate hike was also underpinned by South Korean kingpin Sinokor controlling a large portion of the available fleet in the front end and pricing it accordingly. Paper has been trading in tandem with the physical market and has to some extent been front running proceedings, notably also lifting the forward curve. Monday followed suit with a few MEG/East fixtures logged at WS 142.5. However, come mid-week the upward trajectory has stalled a bit, and some charterers have turned to the more vintage fraternity with corresponding discounts. TD numbers came off a smidgeon as well, with yesterday’s TD3C logged at WS 139 and change. Very little of note to report from and in the Atlantic barring a continues flow of Brazilian export, largely sourcing from the same pool as the MEG.

Despite crude tankers dominating tanker activity since the start of the year, this week as seen a flurry transactions in the product space with eight MR units changing hands. The chinese controlled resale LIANYUNGANG WUZHOU WZ465 (49k DWT 2026) was sold for USD 45M, in line with the last comparable transaction concluded in November 2025, despite it offering a prompter delivery. Notably, SEAWAYS MADELEINE/GRACE (49k DWT HMD 2008) were sold en bloc at USD 16.8M each, compared to same-age sisters from the same owners that achieved USD 16.2M in December 2025. This suggest heighten price volatility for older units, while modern tonnage remains more stable. Elsewhere, ARISTARCHOS (79k DWT Onomichi 2017) was sold for USD 44M, establishing a welcome new benchmark in an otherwise illiquid segment.   Dry bulk asset values continue to remain stable this week, with underlying chartering market  proving to be resilient throughout the start of this year. Stealing the headlines this week was Spar’s acquisition of NANTONG XIANGYU XY149/XY150 (63k DWT 2026), purchased en bloc for USD 72m.

text: Saudi Aramco announced Feb CP at $545 for C3 and $540 for C4, up by $20 respectively, reflecting the earlier tightness on Feb FOBs supply. However, spot differentials for Mar lifting FOBs declined sharply with expectations of increasing US 2/2 arriving in Mar. Mar lifting 2/2 was reported traded at low mid-single digit discount to Mar CP. Qatar Energy was reported to have awarded their sale tender for a 22-27 Feb lifting 2/2. By the time of writing, Mar CP was traded at $536 for C3, and $523 for C4.   ARB from US to FAR EAST remains firm this week, supported by strong front market against supply disruptions caused by previous delays, coupled with strong crude price. Feb LST/FEI widened to -$220 and Mar at -$180ish. This being said, Feb activities remained thin amid limited spot availability, and 4/0 for mid Mar lifting was reported being changed hand at 8cpg. U.S. propane/propylene stocks declined by 4.7 million bbl to 89 million bbl on the week ended January 23, leaving inventory 34% higher on YOY basis.   Cash premium for Mar delivery plunged this week by nearly $20-30, indicating an easing in supply tightness, especially for 2h Mar arrival. On Thurs window, 23/0 parcel for 1h Mar delivery basis Chiba was bid at Mar FEI plus $37, while 4/0 parcel basis Yantai for 2h Mar delivery was traded at Feb Fei plus $9, equates to Mar FEI plus $36. Outside window, 23/0 parcels for 2h Mar delivery basis Chiba were reported traded at Feb FEI plus $2-3. Meanwhile, several 4/0 parcels for 1h to mid Mar delivery were placed into China, with price being concluded at Feb FEI plus mid high single digit or Mar FEI plus mid high 30s. Other than normal cargos, two Iranian cargos of heavy propane ratio for 2h Feb delivery are being offered via tender, which will close by this Sunday reportedly.

EAST Despite most of the action taking place in the USG and less so in the Middle East Gulf - Owners' freight ideas have been coming up the past couple of days also in the East. We are currently looking at mid month laycans, fitting for ships which also in theory could be in the USG from early March onwards depending on routing. As long as earnings remain strong in the West, freight in the East looks set to continue firming in order to be able to attract ships to the area.  WEST This week opened much the same way last week ended: with 6-7 open February positions and very few cargoes circulating in the market. Cold weather across the US and reports of cargo delays added another layer of uncertainty. However, activity picked up sharply as both last‑decade February and first‑decade March fixing gained momentum. Over the past 72 hours, a flurry of 15-16 cargoes have been concluded, with freight levels ranging from the mid‑USD 120s to mid USD 150s pmt H/C v PC. At the time of writing, sentiment is firming and the market is busy. February positions are now close to being fully absorbed, and coverage for the first half of March is close to complete.

The Supramax market saw a rather subdued day from the Atlantic, with demand from the Mediterranean–Continent largely matched by tonnage supply, while the US Gulf remained fairly steady despite some feeling it was still a bit toppy. The South Atlantic continued to be seen as positional with limited fresh enquiry. In the Handysize, a firmer market tone improve overall, with improved reported in the South Atlantic and US Gulf, while the Continent, Mediterranean, and Asia remained mostly steady amid limited fresh activity.

Surface activity in West Africa remains limited, however, the USG continues to pay well for UKCM openers. With Aframaxes also in good shape stateside, the wider strength in the Americas has helped underpin Suezmax ideas. This should keep TD20 sentiment supported and continue drawing potential West Africa contenders away. Supply is now short enough that an influx of 2nd‑decade cargoes in West Africa could give owners the impetus to push, and while cargo counts suggest more should still be left to move, it remains to be seen whether it materialises this side of the weekend. The MEG has also seen supply trimmed through recent enquiries and vessels heading to the Cape of Good Hope. However, the relet‑heavy VLCC list remains a concern and, with their rates taking a hit, sentiment on adjacent sizes may be affected in the medium term.

North Sea The weather coming through the Continent has caused significant delays for vessels over the last week disrupting itineraries. Vessels have continued to head out of the area to take advantage of very firm markets both in US and Mediterranean which along with weather delays has reduced the available tonnage. With a few replacement cargoes off relatively prompt dates freight levels has firmed seeing around WS 70 points increase. The first decade of February stems are a little light month on month and with the weather hopefully passing through market should start to at least steady with a softer sentiment for the next natural window.  Mediterranean Weather continues to be poor across the Mediterranean and Portugal-North Spain range delaying vessels in loading or discharging but still with some safe positions to choose from sentiment is a little softer. Market has had an initial test on a cargo with many offers but owners didn't back down. Market is still not to be underestimated while other regions are still holding strong as well.

The Panamax market has steadied this week following last week’s weather-led disruption in the North Atlantic, which briefly tightened prompt supply and supported transatlantic grain. That momentum has now eased, with charterers stepping back and owners showing limited urgency despite tonnage still available, keeping Atlantic rates broadly unchanged. Grain continues to outperform minerals, while ECSA remains steady with some support for Feb/March business but no clear breakout yet. In the Pacific, conditions are largely unchanged, with cautious sentiment, limited South Pacific mineral demand and activity focused on North Pacific grains and forward Indo stems. Overall sentiment is improved week-on-week, though gains remain selective rather than market-wide.

The Capesize market saw a significant rebound over the last week, with Atlantic routes leading the surge, indicating acute tightness in the North Atlantic and increased activity in Brazil and West Australia. On the C5 route, overall sentiment improved with a comfortable tonnage supply, led by Australian miners returning with volume, with fixtures reported at USD 8.70-9.15 range. Market tone is balanced to slightly soft with charterers in control for prompt tonnage. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, sentiment also firmed throughout the week due to a thinning tonnage list. Tonnage ballasting from the East continues to weight on forward positions, with February trading at a firm but slightly capped tone. Fixtures reported in the USD 23.75-24.5 range. 11–20 Feb bids at USD 22 with offers at USD 25. 21–31 Feb offers at USD 26.

VLCC rates have been on a steady downward trajectory in the week gone by, dipping below the WS 100 mark both east and west of Suez for eastbound cargoes and currently pegged at low-mid WS 90 depending on the voyage/ship in question. Charterers will continue to test owner’s resolve, but the market never sleeps and quite a few ships have been tucked away under the radar in the last 24 hours, which could, repeat could signal support to keep things staring with a 9, although we would not be surprised to see someone tempted to do a smidgen less. Still, daily earnings in the USD 70’s k/day is not to be sniffed it. USG export cargoes east continue to be few and far between with ton-mile considerably down despite a steady flow from Brazil spiced with a few West Africa liftings. MEG volumes are holding on par with previous months but signals from OPEC+ suggest the group will keep the pause on oil output increases for March at their upcoming meeting on February 1st.

Last week we wrote of plummeting rates in the Atlantic, and this week we write of… plummeting rates in the Atlantic. While it was clear then that momentum was only going one way, the brakes have barely been applied as levels fell rapidly through the teens and now into the single digits. There are several more requirements within the traditional fixing window, but there are few signs of a recovery at this stage and competition remains fierce for each cargo. Our report also suggested that a reverse arbitrage could see some Asian cargoes heading into Europe and this has occurred, but it will probably not be a feature of the market going forward. The Pacific and Middle East regions are still trading at considerably higher levels than the Atlantic, and East of Suez there are TFDE vessels fixing out at higher rates than modern 2-stroke vessels are achieving in the Atlantic. All of this presents a challenging environment for owners; however, several 1-3 year fixtures have been concluded at levels that suggest a stronger second half of the year and should give encouragement to those with redelivering tonnage.

Following an explosive start to the year, tanker activity has somewhat flattened this week. Rates remain firm, with owners confidently holding strong on their price expectations. Values for mid-aged MR tankers remain resilient, reflected in the sale of GREEN PLANET (50K DWT Dae Sun 2014), which achieved USD 31M. In the Handy tanker market, the HTM EVEREST (37K DWT HMD 2010) was sold for USD 20M establishing a welcomed benchmark in a relatively illiquid second hand market.  On the dry cargo front, volumes remain high with FRONTIER KOTOBUKI (174K DWT Namura 2011) sold to Global Chartering at USD 31.4M, a correction from last done sale of the MIRACLE (180K DWT Tsuneishi Cebu 2011) at USD 32M, suggesting that Cape values of similar vintage may have reached their peak.

EAST  It has been an active week in the East, with freight levels spanning nearly USD 25 between the highest and lowest fixtures concluded. The market remains highly date‑dependent, with several late quotes; two end‑Jan quotes ex‑MEG and one ely-Feb quote ex-Yanbu, currently being negotiated and expected to command strong premiums. However, looking into the second decade of February, sentiment appears to be softening as more ships come open and the position list begins to lengthen.  WEST The West market is currently in a wait-and-see mode with limited activity to report. We count 29 fixtures for Feb (12/9/8 by decade) but still see about 10-11 ships that can make Feb laycans. Meanwhile, delays at a couple of US terminals appear to be creating hesitation among Charterers. Last done was fixed in the low-mid $130s HCvP, and the general consensus in market is for ideas to start coming off versus levels seen in the last couple of weeks.
