comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Spot differential for Feb lifting 2/2 split cargo was assessed at $20s to Feb CP, in lack of fresh deals. Indian HPCL was reported to have awarded one Mar FOB 2/2 ratio at Mar CP plus mid-single digit. With more US butane expected to flow into EAST in Mar, cash premium for AG Fobs has since softened. QatarEnergy also issued a sale tender for a 2/2 split loading 22-27 Feb. By the time of writing, Feb CP was assessed at $540 for C3 and $531 for C4. Feb/Mar C3 CP was assessed at $17 backwardation.   US FOB resale prices were reportedly surged to 14ish cpg for late-February loading and 10 cpg for early March loading, underpinned by strong cash premiums into the Far East and softening freight rates. However notional netback to Asia fell sharply as Arbitrage to EAST narrowing, driven by higher LST prices due to the cold snap in US. On Thurs, Feb FEI/Lst plunged from $200s to $180s and Mar narrowed from $170s to $160s.   Cash premium for Feb and 1h Mar delivery into FAR EAST remains firm, supported by extended front-end tightness due to US delays. On Thurs window, 23/0 parcel for 1h Mar delivery basis Chiba was bid at Mar FEI plus $49 while 2h Mar at plus $33. One 46/0 parcel for 2h Feb delivery basis Chiba was bid at Feb FEI plus $22. Outside window earlier this week 46/0 parcels for 1h Mar delivery were changed hand at Feb FEI plus high teens to low 20s reportedly.   A flurry of buy tenders from Chinese players emerged this week, with most seeking feedstock amid insufficient term supply. While some were cancelled amid high or no offers, at least 250kt propane was concluded reportedly.  Deals were heard at plus 80s on Non-Us stem, to Feb and Mar delivery month CP respectively; and Feb FEI plus low 30s for 1h Mar delivery on Us stems, which equates to Mar FEI plus around 60. General inventory in China remains low as only 2.5mmt LPG tracked for Jan delivery, which is around 500kt less than last Dec or monthly average in Y2025.

Panamax sentiment has strengthened this week across both basins, supported by improving demand and firmer bidding. In the Atlantic, trans-Atlantic rates continue to edge higher and fronthaul enquiry remains supportive, with grain employment still commanding a premium over mineral business. While tonnage is still visible across the Continent and Mediterranean, the supply–demand balance is tightening, adding upward pressure into end-Jan/Feb, and ECSA remains firm as nearby tonnage thins. In the Pacific, momentum is also improving with a shorter spot list and fresh NoPac and Indonesia RV requirements, as charterers pay up on shorter runs to retain modern tonnage and discourage owners from ballasting toward the Atlantic.

For Cape this week we saw C5 rates were supported by both miners and operators, while overall sentiment remained cautious. Newcastlemax interest continues however premiums have flattened relative to last week as ample tonnage weighed on the market. Pacific demands showed signs of improvement late last week, reflecting firmer bids and a tightening offer side compared to the softer tones at the beginning of January with Hedland fixtures at low USD 8s and RTS fixing at mid USD 7s. For C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, sentiment also strengthened later last week, supported by a tightening list in South Brazil/West Africa. Tonnage from the East remains heavy for the coming weeks, setting a balanced tone in February with fixtures reported in the low USD 21 to USD 22 range and Baltic Exchange posting USD 21.95 today. 10-20 Feb market is at low USD 21 for Nuke and low-mid USD 21 to mid USD 21 for std capes. 20 Feb onw - offers in xs USD 22. 1-10 Mar - bids generally low USD 21s.

TD20 has printed down to WS 156.67, marking another aggressive drop. However, we still have very few vessels FOC (the majority are one owner), and several ports across Europe are closed and experiencing poor weather until end‑month. Additionally, there are still unsold barrels for West Africa 1st decade February, which aligns with our counts suggesting the program is not yet complete (possibly 4-6 more to cover). It seems premature to write off the market, particularly given that CPC SBM 3 is restarting (all going well) and the USG/Guyana market will need to factor in greater sea margin due to weather for ballasters, which may prompt owners to seek higher returns. We do have a number of vessels ballasting toward the Cape of Good Hope, offering a potential outlet for the forward window and implying downward pressure could emerge in the MEG, but the market still has scope for volatility prior to these being within the working window.

The Handy and Supra markets have continued to improve, and charterers are losing their leverage - strongly supported by a healthy flow of fresh enquiries and slimmer tonnage lists. Overall conditions remain mixed in terms of wide ranges of hire and freight ideas; however the spread-gap has continuously become smaller and negotiations clearly showing owners getting back on the horse.  In the Handy segment, sentiment has become firmer in Atlantic and Pacific, providing better support to rates. Owners continue to test higher levels where cargo flow allows, though some resistance persists from charterers.  The Supramax/Ultramax market was notably more busy throughout the week. Owners continued to stand their ground and holding out on negotiations and trading until reasonable numbers were seen. Charterers continue to resist the upward pressure, but seems to have been given in to owners demands as LC’s have been more spot and non-negotiable. Overall sentiment is firm, but the market remains sensitive to regional cargo availability.

The VLCC market has strengthened further in the past week, up from around WS 100 MEG/East mid last week and culminating at WS 130 for same at the writing moment. Yesterday saw a bit of a wobble, led by a Brazil/China fixture logged down from last done level, but the owning community at large took little notice. The front end of the MEG position is bordering on tight leaving little reprieve for those charterers still exposed with early February cargoes. Shorter voyages to, for example, the west coast of India have paid upwards to WS 170. Looking further out on the curve things look more palatable for the charter-in community but the here and now is nevertheless priced according to the here and now. Strong Suez- and Aframax segments are also propping up their bigger sisters and capping the downside both east and west of Suez short term.

North Sea Market has moved up over 20 points through the first half of the week as positions are very tight for anything loading prior to the end of the month.  Tonnage continues to leave the area shortening the available tonnage for what has been a relatively active market. Tonnage will start to come back for loading into February but with the US and Mediterranean markets remaining very firm the North Sea list will be kept on the shorter side while tonnage looks at alternative options. Weather in the North Sea / Mediterranean and Atlantic is causing issues with schedules and adding further uncertainty.  Mediterranean So far this week activity has been somewhat slower in the Mediterranean but with high numbers still being paid. The weather conditions in the Mediterranean are really harsh and several load and discharge ports are closed delays and uncertainty. With USG market still on fire, we expect more vessels to ballast out from Western Mediterranean.

This week has seen a bit of an ebb after the deluge of spot fixtures seen last week, when the number of ships placed on subjects hit double digits in the Atlantic Basin alone. Despite that fixing frenzy, spot charter rates have plummeted further into levels many had not expected to see in January, but such is the unpredictability of the LNG shipping market that this is just a mirror image of the spike seen in Q4, which also caught many by surprise. Market fundamentals may not always tell the full story, but the oversupply of modern tonnage has been fuelled by European gas prices soaring and a prevailing sense that tonne mile demand will take a hit in the short term. Such is the price disparity that options to deliver cargoes originating East of Suez into Europe have been sought by a number of players looking to capture value in a game of increasingly fine margins. Whilst this may be great for those managing to achieve it, there is not likely to be a significant impact for the overall fleet balance and now, more than halfway through January, the steady churn of new buildings from the yards is picking up again which is weighing further on sentiment for short multimonth periods. And regarding newbuilds, two fresh orders have been placed this week and the early signs suggest this may be a strong year for the shipyards.

The frenzied start to the year continued in the tanker market this week, not only due to the emergence of further Sinokor deals but other transactions cementing these new price levels. The Sinokor activity is impacting values across the crude space, and sellers are now more confident than ever that their price asks will be matched. For anything 5 years or older, this provides an attractive exit for owners. Scrubber fitted VLCC pair HUNTER/SERENDIPITY (299K DWT Hyundai Samho 2021) were bought by Trafigura for USD 125M each, while Scorpio continue take advantage of these favourable prices with the sale of scrubber fitted LR2 STI KINGSWAY (109K DWT Sungdong 2015) for USD 57.5M to Paragon Mobility.  On the dry bulk side, the excitement seems more measured. By this we mean seeing the usual premiums on more modern ships with a long trading life ahead of them, and a busier, more opportunistic environment at the other end of the age curve. Buyers have been in hot pursuit of Newcastlemaxes over the past 6 months and have had to pay premium levels for modern ships, seen in the sale this week of scrubber fitted NORD PALLADIUM (209K DWT SWS 2021) at USD 76.25M to Zhejiang Shipping. Further to this, ultramax STARRY NIGHT (61K DWT NACKS 2022) received a firm USD 32.5M from undisclosed buyers.

EAST With all February acceptances released, barring Aramco, we have shifted focus into next month fixing in the Middle East Gulf this week. At the time of writing three deals have been confirmed since Monday in the region. At the same time there are some chatter about at least one more January cargo that may come to market soon from an Indian PSU. So far this week freight rates in the East remain stable at about $2,000 USD per day discount to the earnings seen in the West.   WEST After a very active period last week the market has calmed down in the West. We count 27 spot fixtures thus far in February ex US (12/9/6 by decade), with last done fixed at around mid $140s HCvP. But as we have started to see more ships appearing on the positions list for 2H Feb, mainly from the traders, we expect next deals to be done sub last done subject to vessel type.

text: Cash premium for evenly split on an Feb AG Fob, stands firm in low $30s to Feb CP, underpinned by tightening spot availability. Earlier, Indian spot buy tenders were awarded a couple on FOB basis at CP plus $30s for Feb and plus mid-high single for March, and some on CFR basis at CP plus $50s–60s for Mar and below $50s for April, according to market sources. Demand remained robust, with another Indian PSU issuing a tender to secure one evenly split monthly cargo for Feb to April delivery, on either FOB AG or CFR basis. At the time of writing, Feb CP was traded at $528 for C3 and $514 for C4, while the Feb/Mar CP C3 traded at $18 backwardation, reflecting the front strength.  US FOB values for Feb lifting surged amid widening ARB to EAST. At the time of writing, Arb to East was traded at $209 for Feb and $190 for Mar. Evenly split ratio for Feb lifting was reported traded at 10cpg, as players actively procured such for Indian and SEA market, driven by better economics with declining MB butane price. While 4/0 for Feb lifting was assessed at 9cpg. U.S. propane/propylene stocks fell by 2.4 million bbl to 95.7 million bbl on the week ended January 9, leaving inventory 23% higher on YOY basis.  Cash differentials for Feb delivery soared up further with acute supply tightness, partly due to the previous delays caused by fog closures in late dec/early Jan loadings ex US. 23/0 parcel for 2h Feb delivery basis Chiba was bid at Feb FEI plus $36 while similar cargo with narrower laycan and specific origin/region was bid upto plus $50, yet to attract offers. 46/0 lot for 2h Feb delivery basis Ningbo was bid at Feb FEI plus $33. Outside window, Pertamina was said to award their buy tender for Mar delivery evenly split cargo at Mar CP plus 50$. Befar also issued buy tender for similar ratio on Mar delivery. Chinese spot purchase slowed down this week, as most have already secured minimal tons for feedstock/consumptions for Feb delivery in last two weeks, and stepped back from the intense bids in window. PDH rates declined further this week to below 70%, due to glitches, scheduled maintenance and weak margins.  Other than petchem, residential prices in SChina/EChina spiked up as of shortage in supply. Up to 4 VLGCs of Iranian stems are floating outside SChina, as vessels having issues for berthing due to sanction and old ages, etc.. This being said, over 1mmt tons is expected to arrive in China for Jan delivery. However, as disruptions on supply due to Iran turmoil, we might see a significant decline on exports into China for Feb and even into 1h Mar delivery.

Stronger rates reported from both the USG and West Africa yesterday/this morning. We still have healthy volumes to cover in West Africa for 1st decade Feb, in addition multiple February cargoes expected from Guyana, Brazil and the USG. Supply stateside is incredibly short in addition to thin tonnage in Europe with more poor weather inbound - the tug of war for tonnage will continue and heat up further. Expect owners in the East to keep options open for both MEG and West Africa fixing, and off the back of VLCC sentiment above us, owners will have wind in their sails. Expect Venezuelan, Iranian & Black Sea volatility to bolster sentiment further.

On the C5 front, focus is on end January dates as we see participation from miners and operators with more interest for Newcastlemaxes. Some tick forward enquiries excess of 18 days out as well. Volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the Pacific improved slightly overall. Spot tonnage opening Far East is abundant. Standard Cape offers on C5 are generally at the mid USD 7 pmt levels by midweek while Newcastlemaxes command a premium at low USD 8 pmt levels. On C3 and ex West Africa, month on month wise general contango as we compare Feb vs Mar. 1-10 Feb – mid USD 19s done. 10-20 Feb – USD 19.00 done. 20-28 Feb – General bid offer spread at sub USD 19 v mid USD 19s. Mar generally trading xs USD 20. Ballasting tonnage generally remain heavy for Feb dates.

Looser market fundamentals are reasserting influence on the spot side this week, as despite a slightly gentler decline in rates than some had predicted the downward pressure is growing. There is still an impressive amount of volume being produced and at the time of writing, there remains a healthy handful of requirements to be worked in both basins; however, despite the fixing frenzy continuing any fresh requirements are matched with fresh availabilities. Rising tensions between Iran and the US, along with colder weather across Europe, have led to a narrower TTF/JKM spread and a firmly closed Arb for Atlantic cargoes to the East. Uncertainty on scheduling in Egypt and the ongoing risk of bad weather in the Atlantic remain potential disrupters, but portfolios are confident enough to show the length that had all but disappeared through parts of Q4. Discussions for longer period remain active, with the soft front months blurring into concerns of a repeat of last winter on both owners and charterers minds. The busier streak in the newbuilding space continues with multiple orders being finalised, whilst several owners are leaning towards more speculative plays in anticipation of large-scale projects applying further upward pressure on prices.

The Panamax market has started the week on a quiet and somewhat cautious note, with Atlantic activity evident but fundamentals remaining heavy as open tonnage continues to build across the Continent and West Mediterranean, keeping rates largely anchored around last-done levels. While ECSA is offering slightly better support for end-January dates, overall cargo volume remains thin and insufficient to drive a clear recovery. In the Pacific, sentiment has softened further as tonnage accumulates, particularly in the North, with charterers reluctant to bridge the gap to owners’ ideas despite steady mineral enquiry. Looking ahead, forward-looking indicators remain constructive and point to a firmer bias and higher volatility into the coming weeks, although near-term seasonal headwinds are likely to persist.

North Sea Unlike other areas North Sea has remained relatively slow and steady. The early part of the week has seen a little action including some replacement business with the majority being covered at last done levels. Mediterranean market has firmed rapidly this week and US markets remain active and firm which is and will continue to pull tonnage away from North Sea. Natural window now 22-25 window.  Mediterranean As of midweek almost nothing outstanding at the moment in the Mediterranean/Black Sea market as all cargoes up to the 25th are covered now. Almost zero prompt vessels in the area for local business but with some open in the ARA-WCUK discharging now. It's a bit early for now but list is expected to replenish again with vessels open 20th and onwards. Rest of January's cargoes should be covered around last-done levels give or take some points with sentiment staying strong.

The VLCC market has gone from strength to strength in the week gone by and the owning community is now aiming well into 3 digits MEG/East supported by similar daily returns USG and West Africa/East. WS 102.5 has already been booked on subs according to reports. The sentiment is underpinned by geopolitics, Korean owner Sinokor’s unstoppable appetite for tonnage - buying and T/C in - and paper bets, all seemingly trumping supply/demand projections. The January MEG program is largely a wrap and scared by recent rate hike charterers are already out soliciting for early February, although Saudi stems are unlikely to be out this side of the weekend. If US President Trump follow up threats towards Iran with military action it could of course be a game changer. Failing which and all things equal it’s worth reminding of the old saying “buy the rumour – sell on news."

The Handy and Supra markets have improved in terms of spot activity across both basins this week, supported by steady demand and a consistent supply of tonnage. Overall conditions remain firm but mixed, with freight and hire ideas showing a wide range. While activity levels have improved, negotiations continue to reflect charterers upper hand and owners holding vessels to the very last minute.  In the Handy segment, sentiment has edged slightly firmer in Atlantic and Pacific, providing some underlying support to rates. Owners continue to test higher levels where cargo flow allows, though resistance persists from charterers on shorter voyages and lower-quality stems, keeping gains in check.  The Supramax/Ultramax market was notably busy and broadly balanced throughout the week. Owners maintained a constructive stance and continued to push rate ideas, particularly on longer-haul business. Charterers, however, remained disciplined and resisted upward pressure on shorter or less attractive cargoes. Overall sentiment is cautiously firm, with pockets of strength emerging, but the market remains sensitive to regional fundamentals and cargo availability.

Few would have expected this start to the new year. Rumours have been swirling around the market from Monday this week on a huge VLCC deal involving various new TCs, extended TCs and 2nd hand S&P transactions to Sinokor. Details continue to emerge on number of ships sold, and quantity/length of the TCs, though what has caught the eye is that many of the ships were not known sales candidates, and they come from a vast spread of counterparties. Frontline, CMB Tech, TMS, Capital, Dynacom and Advantage are among the known sellers thus far, proving that in this market everything is for sale at a price. Elsewhere beyond the Sinokor excitement, Greek buyers have acquired zinc coated scrubber fitted MR pair MARITIME TRANQUILITY/COMITY (49K DWT GSI 2020) for USD 39.2M each.    No such fireworks in the dry market this week but it is worth noting this could be a fruitful period for dealmaking in this sector this year. With many market analyst touting great things across dry throughout 2026, the seasonal Q1 lull up to and including Chinese New Year could provide buyers the opportunity to increase their market exposure at potentially the softest prices they will see all year. Levels are still historically high, but owners will be open to taking money off the table to themselves reinvest or expand further. The mid-aged capesize second hand space is proving ever busy with MINERAL HONSHU (181K DWT Koyo 2012) selling for a firm USD 37.1M.

Barely a week into 2026 and we have already seen some fairly drastic shifts. The unpredictable nature of geopolitics right now is raising all manner of questions, but even if we just focus on our more genteel LNG shipping market we will still have plenty to think about. Starting in the Atlantic, there has been a growing sense of a falling market with several vessels opening but very few new requirements. Charterers have generally been comfortable holding out in the circumstances, and some have been rewarded by securing much softer rates; however, the see-saw may already be tipping the other way with a number of fresh enquiries emerging and a much more balanced market, at least on paper. The Pacific basin has been a little more predictable, with downward pressure leading to a steady decline in fixing levels albeit from a lower base than in the Atlantic. The Middle East remains a more active region than has traditionally been seen, but with the build up of tonnage the premium for ballasting across is also coming under pressure. The question for many in these past weeks has been how the market will react to a weaker environment into Q1, and although it’s fair to say that things are cooling there is still some fight left in this market. The shipyards have also been very busy in closing out 2025, and we will provide a full summary in our next Quarterly Update – watch this space!

EAST  A small handful of January cargos remain uncovered East of Suez. At the time of writing, ideas currently seem too far apart between Owners and Charterers. Currently we’re counting 17 spot fixtures on January dates (4/11/2 by decade). Notably, the first February spot requirement has already been quoted today - four weeks out in time - which usually is a positive indicator for freight.  WEST The West market kicked off the week on a strong note, with nine spot fixtures concluded out of the US Gulf alone. Freight levels have firmed, climbing from the high $130s earlier in the week to the mid/high $140s today. The current February spot count stands at 19 fixtures (split 9/8/2 by decade), compared to a monthly average of 29 in 2025. At present, at least 2–3 cargoes are actively being worked. On the tonnage side, we see 2–3 open ships in the 1–10 February window and 5–6 vessels available in the 10–20 February window. However, with the arb currently sitting at around $10, market activity has slowed from the pace seen during the first two days of the week.

“No” is also a complete sentence and with WS 50 give/take having been repeated MEG/East a few times it seems the owning community has finally drawn a line in the sand as daily earnings have been falling dramatically in the last few days, close to OPEX in some cases. However, even if the rot has stopped there’s still a bit of cleaning up to do before we can see some meaningful rate gains from the MEG, although early third decade January requirements might have to tempt with an extra point or two to get across the line, not to mention the likes India's state owned IOC having quoted a replacement job off the 11th of January. The Atlantic, however, should have some legs with VLCC looking to cannibalise on still healthy-ish Suezmax rates.

The Panamax market has shown a clear improvement in tone this week after a subdued post-holiday start. In the Atlantic, activity remains uneven but sentiment is more constructive, with the transatlantic appearing to have found a floor and ECSA showing early signs of firming as tonnage gradually tightens. In the Pacific, last year’s owner sell-off has largely cleared, fixing activity has absorbed much of the prompt supply, and owners are now holding firmer ideas amid a slowly improving cargo count. Overall sentiment is cautiously positive, with near-term support likely as long as fresh demand continues to emerge.

The Handy and Supra markets have experienced a subdued start to the year, broadly in line with expectations. Vessel supply continues to outweigh cargo demand, maintaining a charterer-driven environment. In the Handy segment, activity remains focused on completing carryover business from late last year, with limited spot cargoes being fixed at levels favorable to charterers. Charterers interest is gradually extending into mid-January positions, reflecting continued opportunistic coverage. While charterers retain the upper hand, owners are showing some resistance in their rate ideas.  A similar dynamic is evident in the Supra/Ultramax segment, where market sentiment remains soft. Owners are attempting to defend rate levels, while charterers continue to push for more competitive terms. A small number of tenders and spot enquiries have surfaced, particularly on routes from the ECSA, West Africa, and India to the Mediterranean, mainly for mid- to late-January laycans. Overall, sentiment across both segments remains cautious and largely flat, with limited signs of near-term improvement.

TD20 has now fallen to WS 117.5 on a 2008-built vessel. After multiple weeks trading at higher lump-sum levels compared to VLCCs, Suezmaxes have finally corrected down to a level where taking a VLCC with a part cargo is no longer viable in the West. During this period of irrational pricing differences, VLCCs have taken a greater share of West Africa cargoes compared to normal conditions. In the MEG, VLCCs also continue to absorb cargoes both long and short. Although VLCCs show some stability and possible upside, Suezmax owners will still need to adjust ideas downward to claw back cargoes. Pure fundamentals aside, geopolitics will certainly have a positive effect on sentiment - we shall see what transpires.

North Sea A slow start to the new year so far with only a couple of enquiries in the first half of the week. Natural window pushing to 16-18 window with relets and Suez taking a lot of the available stems prior to mid month. US markets remain steady which is encouraging owners to ballast especially for those that have missed the dates and are looking at waiting time. Softer market sentiment but will steady out with vessels leaving the area.  Mediterranean Despite the massive tonnage list a week ago and still a couple of ppt vessels, rates in the Mediterranean seem to have find a floor or be near there. 2026 flats have been tested and established now with owners happily fixing around last-dones. Balance of 2nd decade isn't expected to be that busy so a small correction is on the cards however US market will play its role attracting ballasters.

On the C5 front, we see enquiries from miners and operators for end January dates. Volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the pacific have been flat since last week. Spot tonnage opening Far East is abundant. Fixtures concluded at around USD 8 mark by midweek. On C3 and ex West Africa, market is in backwardation corresponding to the number of ballasters on dates. End Jan - low to low-mid 22s C3 done. 1-10 Feb - low-mid 21s C3 done. 10-20 Feb - general offers are at low-mid to mid 21s C3. Ballasting tonnage generally heavy for Feb dates.

WEST Despite the festive season there has been an active couple of days in the West this week. Freight now appears to be relatively tight going into February and last done has been fixed at around USD 136-137 on a NEO type. We saw 36 spot fixtures concluded ex US in January (2 deals shy of Apr-25 which ended up being the most active month of the year), and we currently count 9 spot fixtures 1st decade of February. Meanwhile we see 3-4 open ships in 1-10 Feb and 5-6 open ships in 10-20 Feb window.

North Sea As the year draws to a close North Sea levels remain steady with some replacement fixing early January caused by weather delays in the Baltic discharge program.  With some relets and Suezmax in the mix the natural window is pushing out to 9-11 dates. US markets are still attractive but sentiment in the US is a bit softer which may lessen the ballasters.  Mediterranean Market has been busy post Christmas but with some cancellations from the Black Sea and a healthy list for Charterers rates have softened with fixtures concluded basis 2026 Worldscale. 1st decade looks fairly well covered after the recent activity and will push into 2nd decade when market resumes on the 2nd.

Resulting from a populated list and a number of oil co. relets, the market is at half the earnings it was at about a week or so ago. Lack of activity in West Africa and USG has not helped the cause. We should be close to the bottom if not at the bottom.

Last week Western Australia fixtures were active, with multiple Capesize vessels fixed for Hedland/Qingdao and Dampier/Qingdao routes at rates mostly between USD 8.50 and USD 8.80, while some early ships achieved USD 8.95. On C3 there was  steady activity with rates mostly in the low-to-mid USD 23s, while some fixtures and bids hinted at softening sentiment compared to earlier highs. West Africa flows remained active.

This week the Panamax market closed on a steady but cautious note. In the Pacific, activity was thin with most fresh stems pushed into mid-January, leaving owners under pressure. The Atlantic saw some support from ECSA grains and USEC coal, but overall sentiment remained soft as ballasters continued to weigh on the list. Period interest was muted, with charterers testing lower levels while owners held back, hoping for a post-holiday rebound. Overall, the tone was flat with limited fixtures and a wide bid-offer spread, suggesting a slow start to the new year.

As we put down A Christmas Carol for another year, we can pick up another Dickens novel to see in the New Year. 2025 initially appeared to be a year of lows for LNG shipping, until a late surge in Q4 served as a timely reminder of the market’s capacity for sharp swings. The uptick, driven primarily by additional LNG supply, suggests there may be more opportunities ahead, though the path forward will be far from smooth. A 50% orderbook-to-fleet ratio highlights the growing pains of rapid expansion, while uncertainty over a potential medium-term LNG glut adds further complexity. In this multidirectional, technologically tiered, and fast-evolving market, volatility remains the only constant. So whether a charterer enjoying low rates but stung by this winter spike or an owner suffering the soft market but locking in historically high numbers of fixtures, 2025 really did see the best of times and the worst of times, and we all look forward to 2026 with Great Expectations.

The Handy and Supramax markets remain under pressure as activity continues to slow ahead of the Christmas holidays, with prompt tonnage outweighing demand and charterers firmly in control. In the Handysize sector, sentiment is weak across both basins, with the Continent, Mediterranean, US Gulf and South Atlantic all seeing limited enquiry and softening rates, while Asia remains subdued as owners lower expectations to secure employment. The Supramax market reflects a similarly negative tone, particularly in the Atlantic and US Gulf where a lack of fresh cargoes and a growing tonnage list continue to weigh on rates, while the Mediterranean, South Atlantic and Asia lack momentum despite some minor interest from the Indian Ocean. Overall, sentiment across both segments remains cautious to bearish, with little indication of near-term improvement during the holiday period.

Some further activity yesterday on suezmaxes has helped to trim a healthy amount of tonnage off the front end of the list. However, as laycans push into 3rd decade January supply does replenish a reasonable amount. Unfortunately, with VLCCs continuing to slide with TD3 paying equivalent to 130kt x 104 and TD15 equivalent to 130kt x 115 it is hard to foresee any turn around in the near term. It seems possible we will see a similar downward correction as we did early this week. This is despite fairly stable fundamentals, in isolation from VLCCs.

In our first Weekly Report of 2025, we brazenly asserted that “we can be sure that 2025 will be just as interesting as was 2024”. In what turned out to be our most accurate forecast to date, this year has indeed had it all. As we head into Christmas Day, however, it isn’t armed conflicts or trade wars that that are exerting the most influence on our market, rather it’s the reminder that shipping is a derived demand, and when there’s more LNG to be shipped, there’s more LNG carriers needed to ship it. Like most of the market, we were caught out by the dramatic jump in Atlantic exports in Q4, and the resultant strain on LNG shipping fleets which took us into the six-figure winter fixing mode. Whilst these rates had been par for the course in many previous years, they weren’t meant to appear this year, and the fact that the market still hasn’t properly corrected underlines the structural nature of this winter’s rate rise. This root cause has significant ramifications for 2026, with many charterers carrying recent reminders that being short shipping in LNG can be costly. So, whilst most owners won’t get to unwrap a clean term TCP tomorrow morning, those with available 2-strokes coming up on their books will be feeling considerably more Christmas cheer than they would have only two months ago.  There’s no shortage of festivities at the yards either, with Hudong-Zhonghua securing a hat-trick of Newbuilds for a producer’s fleet renewal needs, whilst Samsung have reportedly bagged a brace on the back of more long-term tender business. Merry Christmas, everyone!

It was said in this report a few weeks ago that owners would be hard pressed to ignore buyers willing to transact at current levels, and it appears that some have caved to the extensive amount of enquiry in the market. Larger owners, for example Scorpio, have been wisely executing sales of sub 10 year old assets while simultaneously ordering new ships, ensuring fleet modernisation whilst cashing in on historically strong values of older units. This week they announced the sales of scrubber fitted STI GALLANTRY/GOAL (109K DWT GSI 2016) for USD 52.3M each. Elsewhere, SFL took money off the table with the sale of suezmax pair SFL OTTOWA/THELON (159K DWT Bohai 2015) for USD 57M each.   A quieter than usual week in the second hand dry market, and for good reason. Robust earnings over the last few months have resulted in strong pricing, and with seasonal softening expected in Q1 2026, buyers are more likely to wait. That said, the market goes into the winter break in a strong position, leaving owners hoping for more of the same in the new year. This week, kamsarmax THERESA HAINAN (81K DWT Sainty 2013) was sold for USD 16.8M.

North Sea Natural dates pushing towards end month with a slimmer list of available tonnage due some quiet fixing and vessels ballasting. Market has been steady and unless we see a push in activity or the weather that is hitting this week causes more issues than looks likely at the moment the balance of 2025 should remain relatively steady.    Mediterranean  Last stems of December are being covered at last-done levels in the Mediterranean too. A couple of different owners around still looking for the best dates to fix which will be soon into January. With some relets around in the mix too we will probably see rates being repeated till the end of this week.

As we race closer to the end of the year, the rush to cover requirements for the first half of January is starting to slow down and there is a corresponding softening in rates. The flagging momentum may suggest the winter spike is over, but there is still some shape to the curve and considerable volatility, particularly for earlier laycans in the Atlantic for which rates remain very much in the six-figures. Further out into the second half of January and into February, fixing levels are lower but is this due to a general market easing or have charterers fixed well-ahead, before the upcoming holidays? Regardless, the feeling remains that we will see a gradual decline in rates rather than an abrupt fall. Longer periods remain in limbo as independent owners and subletters seek to capture the recent strength while charterers hold off for the excitement to fade, but it is likely that levels will settle a little higher for multi-month and multi-year charters next year than they were through much of this year.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Cash premium for Jan lifting evenly split grades is holding firm in the $50s to Jan CP, due to limited spot availability, and with last deal changed hand at $45. Saudi acceptance has been released with no major cuts or delays reported. Buy tenders from India and Indonesia are continuously supporting spot differentials for the front market. By the time of writing, Jan CP was traded at $499 for C3 and $492 for C4.   US ARB to EAST market maintained wide at $160s-170 for Jan FEI/Lst, but narrowed down to $150s for Feb only, reflecting the front strength. Terminal fee for late Jan-early Feb liftings was discussed at 7-8 CPG. US propane/propylene inventory fell by 1.77 mil barrels to 100 mil barrels on the week ended 12nd Dec, leaving 11% higher on YOY basis.  Cash premium for CFR EAST on Feb arrival plunged on Thurs with one 23/0 parcel for 1h Feb delivery basis Chiba was traded at Feb FEI plus $19, which equates to Jan FEI plus small premium only at the time of trade. Similar parcel for 2h Jan delivery was shown at Jan FEI plus $17 via window, yet to be lifted. Earlier of the week, a couple of 4/0 lots for 1h Feb delivery was changed hand at Jan FEI plus hi single to low teens.   A handful of Chinese buy tenders were cancelled this week, with one reported receiving offer quoting Jan FEI plus 20s for Feb delivery, while the others no offers for requested laycan/ratio. One Canadian stem for Jan delivery was sold into SChina at Jan CP plus mid 70s reportedly. One Oil major was reported awarded their sale tender for 18-20 Jan lifting evenly split cargo ex Dampier, details remained sketchy. Indonesia Pertamina reissued tender for two evenly split cargos on Feb delivery.

EAST Indian PSUs are expected to quote a couple of cargoes to the market soon. Some suggest 1-10 January, while others indicate 8-12 onwards. Rates are likely to be on the higher side regardless, with earlier dates likely resulting in higher premiums. Yesterday, we saw relatively slow activity, with only one fixture reported in the MEG at USD 80 RT/C.  WEST Flurry of fixtures ex USG last week has left freight very tight for the remainder of January. Last done range from low USD 130s HCvP on NEO ships and USD 140 HCvP on Pmax. We count 36 spot fixtures ex US in January (11/13/12 by decade), just 2 deals short of April-25 which ended up being the most active month of 2025. February fixing should be imminent as term lifters will get their final nominations over next couple of days. We expect freight ideas to remain firm for the next fixing window.

The segment has shown firming tendencies in the last days, primarily led by Atlantic strength and steady Pacific support. Brazil demand and tightening tonnage lists have been key catalysts, while miner activity in the Pacific maintained stability. Spot benchmarks climbed, with C5TC moving into the low USD 30k range and C3 advancing sharply on robust Brazil flows. Fixtures like Tubarao/China at USD 25 and Kamsar/China at USD 26.50 reinforced bullish sentiment. Going forward, bearish seasonality should kick in so we expect the downtrend to resume.

The VLCC market is searching a bit for direction at the moment, illustrated among other things with eg TD3C paper this morning at WS 110 vs WS 123 for the balance of the month. As always, the “mind game” between pushing for rate change and wishing to clear the deck before the Christmas holidays is present this time of year. Early January MEG stems are now out, sure to be tweaked a bit, but so far little if anything has been done for January loading baring the normal China Inc scheduling. Assuming a bit of left over lolly for December the 35 odd ships free of cargo on the water we counted this am will all be needed, and maybe then some. Oilco/trader relets being pushed to some degree tend to be just window dressing. The Atlantic is still dominated by Brazil and relets and Suezmaxes appear to have the hegemony for everything else.

The Supramax market remained under pressure across all basins, with limited fresh enquiry and ample tonnage continuing to drive rates lower. The Handysize sector also stayed soft, as holiday-related inactivity and cautious sentiment allowed charterers to retain the upper hand. Overall, seasonal slowdown and lack of momentum kept both markets subdued with no clear status for recovery.

Vessels quietly dropped off the list yesterday, and additional cargoes floated today, starting to fill the glut of West Africa volume for January that has been highlighted over the past couple of days. WS 135 has been done for TD20 (2+ points north of BDTI yesterday), and the list suggests we may see higher rates paid. It seems many of these January barrels were struggling to find a home last week, which explains why they didn’t move amid the activity from the States. Poor weather in the Atlantic, combined with some in the Mediterranean, is keeping supply tight and uncertain. This may force charterers either to pay for a solid itinerary or play it slow and steady, hoping that by the end of this week owners still with vessels on the water will cooperate, as they want to shut up shop before Christmas.  Stateside, there are still a couple of stems rumoured to be outstanding, supposedly not attracting much interest. Despite this, taking a breather may be the play, as US cargoes have reached unprecedentedly far forward, so sitting tight and letting local vessels emerge could be the best option.

The Panamax market remained under pressure this week as thin fixing activity across both the Atlantic and Pacific continued to hand control to charterers, with owner resistance steadily softening. In the Atlantic, prompt demand has largely been absorbed, bids are slipping below last-done levels and increased ballaster supply from a weaker Pacific is weighing further on P6, while ECSA is mostly covered into early January. The Pacific remains seasonally soft, with ample prompt tonnage and limited fresh cargoes keeping sentiment firmly charterer-led. Overall, despite the current weakness, owner behaviour and forward signals suggest the market is moving closer to a base rather than facing a materially deeper correction.

With the festive season now in full swing, owners will be reflecting on 2025 and looking ahead to next year. For the tanker market, owners will be hoping this current market can sustain for as long as possible, however will know that volatility in earnings works both ways. MRs appear to be at the top of buyers' wishlists, having seen increased TC appetite that makes sense of current value levels. Sisters SEAWAYS OLIVE/STAR (49K HMD 2008) were sold at USD 16.2M each.  The usual healthy liquidity is seen in the bulk market this week. As has been the story all year, buyers from the Far East appear to be dominating this market and have been the destination for many European owned ships. There has been particular appetite for Capesize bulkers, which have pushed in value over the recent period. This week DENSA SHARK (179K DWT Hyundai 2012) was sold to chinese buyers for USD 32.5M with TC attached until June 2026. Elsewhere, Ultramax IVS WINDSOR (60K DWT Oshima 2016) was sold to Greeks at USD 26M.

EAST ADNOC acceptances were released last night, with no indications of cuts so far. Market chatter suggests that early January cargoes have largely been allocated to Indian PSUs. While the US Gulf has seen a sharp increase in activity over the past three days, the East remains subdued, with only a single January cargo quoted at the time of writing.  WEST Activity has picked up this week, as we have registered 13 spot deals ex USG. This brings total December fixtures to 30 (11/11/8 by decade) and January fixtures to 31 (11/13/7 by decade). After a tender cargo got fixed sub USD 120 HCvP eqv. in the previous week, the market started this week at USD 120s and has now firmed to around USD 130. The position list shows only one vessel open for December and remains tight for January dates too. Heading into 2H January, there are less than a handful actual ships open, but with a potential for more as ship schedules get firmed up. We expect rest of January and early February to be covered soon with Christmas holidays coming up, but levels subject to Arb econs which has been challenging lately.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Cash premiums for Jan AG FOB evenly split cargos, continued to soar up with active bids against tight supply. Indian HPCL covered two lots of such grades for Jan and one each for Feb and Mar reportedly. Last spot deal was concluded at Jan CP plus $20s. Nevertheless, one producer trading arm bid through window for Jan open date FOB 2/2 at the fixed price of $555, which equates to Jan CP plus $30 for C3 and $38 for C4, yet to entice offers. Another trader also called similar buy tender. There are some delays reported for ADNOC acceptance, understanding most lifters would like to ask for early month loading to cover front demand. Market participants are still awaiting Saudi’s acceptance to have a full scheme on Jan supply. By the time of writing, Jan CP was traded at $525 for C3 and $517 for C4. Jan/Feb C3 CP was traded at $13 backwardation.   Arbitrage for Jan FEI/Lst widened to 160s, supported by the firming CFR FAR EAST demand for Jan delivery. US FOBs for earlier Jan lifting were changed hand at around 8cpg while discussion for later days subdued, in view of narrowing ARB and backwardation. US propane/propylene inventory fell by 1.78 mil barrels to 101.770 mil barrels on the week ended 5th Dec, leaving 9% higher on YOY basis.  Supply shortage persisted for Jan arrival and bids for CFR FAR EAST Window continued surging up. 23/0 parcel for 1h and 2h Jan delivery basis Chiba were bid at Jan FEI plus $35 and Bal Dec FEI plus $6 respectively, which equates to Jan FEI plus $40. Similar parcel for 1h Feb delivery was bid at Jan FEI plus $3, equivalent to Feb FEI plus $26. 46/0 parcel for 2h Jan delivery basis Chiba was bid at Jan FEI plus $21. Outside window a flurry of buy tenders seeking propane for Jan and Feb delivery, total up to 184kt demand. Among such one tender was reported awarded for a 23/0 parcel on Feb delivery basis Schina at Feb CP plus high 80s. Butane for Jan delivery into Asian market are also in high demand, as Indonesia Pertamina keep reissuing buy tender for three even split cargos for Jan delivery.

The festive season is in full swing in London, but that hasn’t led to a slowdown in the markets with fresh cargo sales and shipping requirements emerging almost daily. There has definitely been more for owners to celebrate in recent months and there is a little more optimism than there was for next year, but sentiment in the spot market has been more measured this week. Finding tonnage for prompt laycans is still challenging, but further out there are more ships emerging and some players are seemingly more open to subletting. Many of the key drivers for the current market strength remain in place including high production levels and FOB sales, so perhaps we are seeing the results of the fleet being worked harder. Despite this, rates in the Atlantic remain solidly in the six figures for laycans within December and although there is a steady softening into the new year, there have been very few fixtures concluded to give benchmarks for the second half of January. In contrast, the Pacific has been remarkably quiet on the prompt and rates have been moving sideways, with only distant requirements for second half January being considered. However, the Middle East continues to be a very hot market with tonnage being pulled into the region and Owners also considering ballasting to West Africa to lock in rates at the Atlantic premium.  On the newbuilding front, activity remains strong, with several deals in progress.

On the C5 front, we see enquiries for miners and operators for end December dates. Level of enquiries from players decreased as we approached midweek. Volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the pacific are low. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, focus is on early to mid January dates. Ballasting tonnage is more abundant for first half January. Spot tonnage out of Far East is increasingly abundant. Fixtures concluded at sub USD 11 pmt levels by midweek. C3 concluded in the mid-high USD 22 pmt levels for early to mid January.

North Sea Some activity and programming has covered almost all the 2nd decade stems with rates remaining on the whole steady. For the right cargo a softer feel but downside limited so far. With Vessels continuing to Ballast both TA and to the Med the available tonnage has remained balanced and helped maintain rates.  Mediterranean  Very busy week in the Mediterranean/Black Sea with some 3rd-decade local cargoes worked too but rates still hoovering around last done levels. Activity should remain healthy heading into next week and owners will have the chance to push unless they are already in Christmas holiday mood.

The Panamax market eased again this week, with the Atlantic still outperforming but losing some momentum as charterers kept the pressure on. The North Atlantic held up reasonably well on tighter prompt supply and the possibility of Cape splits adding support, while the South Atlantic stayed thin with sentiment clearly leaning toward charterers. In the Pacific, the slide continued, with growing prompt tonnage and cautious bidding creating a challenging environment as owners look to secure longer cover ahead of the holidays. Looking ahead, the near-term trend remains soft into year-end, but the broader indicators we track still point to healthier conditions and a potential rebound as we move into January.

VLCC rates remains at status quo in the low W120’s for MEG/east, more or less identical to last Wednesday. Owners had a go at pushing rates up yesterday, eg. offering at W150 level on a MEG/Vietnam requirement, and only a handful of punters at that. However, it landed at W123.5, albeit on a 16-year-old lady and a voyage calculating better than your standard TD3C in comparison. Notably none on the oilco/trade relets supposedly available offered in, make of that what you like. The list is still balanced, bordering on tight if relets shown is just window dressing, and although it feels more like rates are just holding some charterers may get caught out if they wait too long or must revisit and existing fixture. The Atlantic continues to lag barring the continuous flow of Brazilian export, shedding a point or two on each successive fixture, albeit on relets.

The Supramax segment continued to show a positional tone, with the USG seeing some resistance while the South Atlantic softened amid weaker sentiment. Asia remained under downward pressure with further easing reported, and the Indian Ocean stayed finely balanced despite some activity. For Handy, overall conditions were quiet with limited fresh enquiry and a slight softening across most Atlantic regions as open tonnage increased. The South Atlantic and US Gulf carried a weaker undertone, while Asia held largely steady though a longer tonnage list applied mild pressure. Rates across both basins generally hovered around last-done levels with no major shifts.

It’s been a busy start to the week, with more than 20 vessels on subs overnight and no details across the board. The recent uptick in off market activity in the Atlantic has taken out a solid chunk of Suezmaxes in the West. Despite this erosion, the list of available tonnage in the current fixing window in WAF appears sufficient. As a result of recent activity, the question of how much December volume is left to move in the USG and WAF remains. Looking ahead to next week, the January programme for West Africa will fall within the natural ‘three-week window’, and likewise the CPC January programme will be released and is expected to come into play. In the MEG, the list has tightened and rates have remained fairly stable; however, demand-wise, with the number of fixtures and reports that Indian market quotes are closed out for the month, we may have a quiet end to the week in the region.

The small number of sales being reported this week in the tanker market somewhat underplays the current market conditions. Yes, large older crude tonnage is still in demand seen in the sale of TOWADA (305K DWT Mitsubishi 2006) but behind the scenes, there is even more interest swirling around scarcely available modern units, with buyers increasingly keen to transact. Price asks are still toppy, which explains why many are choosing the newbuilding route, but with geopolitical influences more changeable than ever, sellers would be short sighted to hold out against firm buyers in such historically high markets.   The dry market is still looking very prosperous with many underlying factors signalling this prosperity is going nowhere. Underlying market demand growth is on an upswing, while commodities prices are looking bullish. Second hand vessel demand remains strong, and there is more liquidity on modern tonnage than in other sectors. This week Blumenthal purchased ice 1C URSULA MANX (82K DWT Tsuneishi Zhoushan 2021) for USD 33.85M.

EAST After an active first half of the week with 6 spot fixtures concluded from Middle Eastern ports the past 2 days have slowed down East of Suez. With 19 total fixtures concluded on December dates in total - there should be room for more fixing before we shift focus into next year laycans. Tonnage availability looks slightly long towards the end of the month - but with some ships sailing West coupled with an expected cargo out of West Africa the market might balance out nicely.  WEST A handful of cargos in play 1st half of January ex USG this week with last done around 123-124 HCvP. But as Arb econs remain challenging, some of the deals done ended up failing subs.  One Asian major currently in the market for a 2nd decade January loader into Indonesia, while some other potential Charterers are taking a step back to reassess levels. We count 17 fixtures in Jan thus far; 10/7/0 by decade.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Supply tightness extended further, driven by increased demand for January evenly split cargoes. The latest deal was concluded at January CP plus mid-20s, with limited firm offers available. HPCL is seeking four 2/2 ratio cargoes via tender, with two for Jan and one each for Feb and Mar, either on FOB or CFR basis; while IOC is looking for monthly AG FOB 2/2 cargoes for Jan to Dec delivery. By the time of writing, Jan CP was traded at $501 for C3 and $491 for C4. Jan/Feb was assessed at $3 backwardation.   Terminal fee for Jan US liftings softened this week to 6ish cpg, as ARB to FAR EAST narrowing down due to unaffordability from petchem players seeing eroding margins. US propane/propylene inventory fell by 687,000 barrels to 103.5 mil barrels on the week ended 28 Nov, lesser draw than expectations and leaving it 7% higher on YOY basis.   Cash premium for Jan delivery propane continued to soar up with strong bids from traders covering shorts. 23/0 for 1h Jan delivery was bid at Bal Dec FEI plus $10, which equates to Jan FEI plus $26 while similar cargo for 2h Jan was bid at Jan FEI plus $17. Outside window a flurry of tenders was issued to seek butane. Pertamina issued buy tender for 2/2 late Jan delivery. Hyosung Vina tendered to buy 1/1 for 2h Jan to early Feb delivery. HTC closed their tender for 0/2 2h Jan delivery but no offers received reportedly.  Other than that, one SChina importer secured a Jan delivered 4/0 at Jan CP plus 70s. Another 23/0 parcel for Jan delivery was also reported placed into SChina at low 80s. Similarly, 1/1 for early Jan delivery basis SChina was also reported traded at similar level.

December has started in a slightly softer mood in the Atlantic, as the recent flurry of relatively prompt fixtures has relaxed into requirements a little further out into January and thus towards some lower rates. Interestingly, the decline in levels hasn’t been as rapid or as sharp as some may have expected. Seasonal spikes have historically lasted little more than four weeks so whilst it’s natural to expect a downturn before too long, the recent rise has not come on the back of a cold snap or a regional demand swing. The main driver has been increased production and this is not likely to reverse anytime soon, instead the market will be seeing the benefits of sharper optimisations and the delivery of more newbuildings to help rebalance the picture. As the Atlantic eases a little, the Pacific remains a little quiet with very few requirements or fixtures and rates holding firm. Instead, we look to the Middle East again as the region has returned to the foreground with a number of spot requirements and FOB cargo sales, and therefore firming rates. If it feels a little quiet just look left or right or give it a day or two, it’s still a very busy market out there.

North Sea Market levels remain steady with limited activity through the first half of the week.  We have seen some bigger vessel take volume out of stems in the 2nd decade which will reduce the available cargoes for Afra. Rates / Activity likely to remain steady through the first half of December. 2nd half of the month does look to be busier stem wise.  Mediterranean Position list remains balanced with rates moving sideways. Limited activity so far this week and sentiment / rates likely to remain unchanged pushing into next week. Natural window working towards mid month now North Africa and CPC well into 3rd decade.

The VLCC market has seen a downward rates adjustment in the week gone by from high W130’s to low-mid W120’s MEG/east as much of the activity has gone under the radar. But despite all the smoke and mirrors owners have shown a stoic restraint, fought “gravity” and held the line at now last done levels, and even trying for a bit more when an opportunity presents itself. The tonnage situation is still balanced, and tonnage is controlled on few hands. Baltic estimates came in last night with very little change from the day before which suggests that the broking community is similarly inclined, despite maybe voicing the opposite. Another Brazil export cargo was quoted this morning, and quickly concluded at W107.5 (2.5 points down from last done) but other than that not very much to write home about in the Atlantic, and Suezmax rates are also on the defensive giving charterers more optionality .

The headline deal from yesterday was W105 for ECM/Spain, albeit off fairly prompt dates, so possibly the reduced waiting time compared to the natural window justified the discount. W115 was also done on a prompt replacement, so in theory W110 seems like a ‘sensible’ call for natural dates. UKCM openers will be firmly focused on West Africa at these levels, with TCE parity for such vessels achieved at approx. W127.5 for TD20, which is well below last done. Considering both sides of the pond, we are long on tonnage, it is hard to argue against rates coming off at this juncture. In the East, an MEG/WCI cargo received 8 offers, eventually going on subs at W165. Tonnage there is also long, and we expect rates to come off here as well.

Supramax segment continued to soften in the Atlantic, with both North and South regions seeing further pressure amid limited enquiry, while the cont-med stayed balanced. Asia and the Indian Ocean remained the comparatively firmer. Influx of the iron ore cargoes ex Indian Ocean helped balance out the sentiment. The handy market on another hand held a more positive tone, supported by gains in the BHSI and a firming Atlantic driven by tight tonnage in the U.S. Gulf and South Atlantic. The Cont–Med saw limited activity with only marginal movements, while Asia stayed muted as players adopted a wait-and-see approach. We will see the year end rush soon with charterers flooding the market with enquiries before the end of the year.

On the C5 front, we see enquiries for miners and operators for mid to end December dates. Level of enquiries from players are generally healthy. Volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the pacific are tick down from last week. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, focus is on late December dates with growing interest for early January as we approach midweek. Ballasting tonnage is very tight for December dates and relatively more tonnage available for first half January. Spot tonnage out of Far East is tight.

Sentiment has shifted into correction mode this week as building tonnage lists across both basins hand leverage back to Charterers. While NOPAC remains sluggish and the Atlantic drifts lower on quiet USG activity, a surging Capesize market is offering a vital lifeline via cargo splits. The one bright spot in the Pacific is Aussie coal, where a shortage of immediate tonnage is forcing operators to pay premiums. Technically, our indicators suggest this softer trend persists through year-end, but with coal futures signaling a January rally and copper supporting asset values, we view this as a temporary dip before a Q1 rebound.

The tanker market is flying into the festive period with healthy earnings across the board. This will put buyers at the mercy of sellers, who will be rethinking their price expectations accordingly. The Russia-Ukraine conflict was rather the catalyst of this current overall tanker market run throughout the last few years, however, this week market analysts and owners alike are imagining a market beyond the conflict, after positive talks between US and Ukrainian officials. It still feels a long way away, but peaceful resolution could drastically reshape the tanker market.    The BDI hit its highest levels since December 2023, as rates hold firm. Capesize rates are leading the way, and the strong demand for second hand candidates is only increasing. Tonnage hungry buyers are acting quickly and decisively, particularly in the c.15 YO range, which is encouraging owners of such units to see what bids they can attract. Values are changing rapidly; this week NGM sold PACIFIST (181K DWT Koyo 2011) for USD 32M (SSDD due January 2026), this is compared to SSDD freshly passed 1-year older scrubber fitted sister SEAUNITY (181K DWT Koyo 2010) sold at USD 30.5 at the start of the month

text: While market participants awaiting Saudi Cp, cash premium for Dec lifting evenly split cargo continue to strengthen, with bid in window for mid Dec lifting shown at $530 for C3 and $515 for C4, equivalent to Dec Cp plus $30s. By the time of writing, Dec Cp was traded at $497 and C3/C4 at $17.5.  Supported by the strong Dec and Jan CFR EAST market, US Arbitrage widened with terminal fee for Jan lifting discussed at 7ish cpg.  Japanese and Korean importers actively buying for winter stockpiling, which substantially keep driving up cash premiums in the window. 23/0 parcel for 1h Jan delivery was once traded at Jan FEI plus $15 and continuously bid up to $21. Similar cargo for 2h Jan delivery was bid at Jan FEI plus $15, yet to entice seller interests.  Outside window, FIC was reported to award two 4/0 and one 2/0 cargos for Jan delivery at Jan FEI plus low teens. One 4/0 for 1h Jan delivery basis Chiba was heard traded at FEI plus $20s. Similarly, one 4/0 for 1h Jan delivery basis Ningbo was also reported done at similar range. One NChina importer tendered to buy Jan delivered evenly split cargo basis Tianjin. Another PDH importer reissued tender to buy propane for late Dec to Jan delivery.

EAST & WEST After a relatively quiet period East and West, we’ve seen about 5+ fixtures each in both basins. Last done in US at around USD 120 HCvP (plus one modern Pmax fixed in the mid-120s), while Eastern rates remain at a theoretical premium with last done in the high 60s RT/C. With Thanksgiving weekend about to start the market may take a breather for now, but we do expect freight ideas to remain around last done.

The VLCC market has gone from strength to strength in the week gone by, culminating just north of W145 MEG/east. Arguably the first 10 days of December in the MEG is now all but a wrap, barring what may need revisiting for some reason or another. Moving into second decade the position list is a bit more palatable for charterers but nothing which would indicate a dramatic weakening. However, the spread between east and west still needs bridging seeing as both West Africa and Brazil source from the same pool of ships as the MEG. Daily earnings on the current TD3C estimate far outperform those of TD15, albeit the latter being a longer commitment. The upcoming Thanksgiving holiday will likely slow trading down the next couple of days so we’re probably going to see a bit of a Mexican standoff short term.

Whilst consistent fixing keeps the front of the Atlantic basin tonnage availabilities tighter, the forward window looks a little softer, both with increased appetite to ballast ex east via Cape of Good Hope on the back end, and in the medium term a big delta between USG and Guyana TCEs offer versus TD20 for ballasters from the continent. As such rates have been chipped away, 150 achieved ex Nigeria for UKCM, minus 2.5 for Angola load, but last done for West Africa/US Atlantic Coast was in line with a 152.5 TD20 (over 2.5 over market) and utilised an ex West Africa itinerary to achieve this. USG last dones in the region of 120 earn a good USD 6K less PDPR for Rotterdam ballasters, with both USG & Liza markets using local tonnage to push the market down, unable to charm UKC ships. MEG has also dropped off a little, 160 last done albeit on an EX DD ship. We have a good 5 or so FOC ships pointing towards Cape of Good Hope, partly wary of this, and the VLCC trajectory is looking a little softer also which undermines confidence in the eastern markets. Overall, expecting further incremental erosion, but it is a slow decay not a violent one.

North Sea An active first half of the week has seen dates push out covering up to the 4-6 window and with relet tonnage coming back into the frame next natural window likely to be 7-9 dates. Front end of the position list has been depleted through fixing early tonnage and vessels heading out of the area. Rates have firmed a little and if we see some continued activity have room to push further. Thanksgiving will take activity out of the US markets at the end of the week but may well lead to a backlog to be covered early next week.  Mediterranean So far activity has been moderate on the surface but busier under the radar in the Mediterranean/Black Sea with owners repeating last-done levels. As dates are moving further into 1st decade of December, the tonnage list consists of enough candidates for rest of 1st decade on paper. Seems fair for now to repeat rates around current levels but things might change as we are slowly approaching 2nd-decade dates.

The Supramax and Handysize markets showed a mostly subdued tone across both basins, with sentiment generally flat and activity limited. In the Atlantic, Supramax levels softened – particularly from the U.S. Gulf and East Mediterranean – while the West Mediterranean and parts of South America saw only modest enquiry. Asia remained slightly more positive for Supramaxes, supported by steady demand from the south, though overall momentum was still muted. The Handysize sector likewise experienced quiet conditions, with balanced markets in the Continent and Mediterranean and softer expectations emerging in the South Atlantic and U.S. Gulf. Asian Handy activity was also restrained, influenced in part by regional holidays, leaving both segments stable but lacking strong directional drivers.

The spot market gains seen in recent weeks continue with significant increases across all basins, although trying to report any of these regions under a single headline rate may give a false impression of a smooth and steady rise. The reality has been a much more volatile climb that may surge one day then soften the next, and although this has appeared mildly chaotic at times we do now see an overarching curve through winter. In the Atlantic, the lack of 2-stroke tonnage has led to some very tight periods in which majors are allowing ships to be pried from their portfolios…at a premium. When there has been competition among owners and sub-letters, this has merely acted as a fluttering brake rather than an abrupt cliff edge. And yet, as we look ahead to the end of December and beyond, rates are clearly easing from the mid-December highs but do remain at elevated levels and this suggests a soft landing into 2026. The Pacific basin has also seen more activity and at higher levels, but with considerably less volatility than in the West. This may be because ST and TFDE vessels offer more of a relief valve when 2-strokes disappear (something we address in our recent LinkedIn post), but there is also much more opportunity to optimise shorter voyages. Amidst these two major basins, the Middle East has again asserted itself as a strong demand source and has been a focal point with a spate of new requirements and fixing levels that are attractive enough to pull ships in from Asia.

On the C5 front, we see enquiries for miners and operators for mid December dates. Volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the pacific are tick up from last week. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, focus is on second half of December dates with some forward interest for January dates. Ballasting tonnage is tightening for mid December. Spot tonnage out of Far East is tight. Fixtures concluded at USD 11.00 pmt levels by midweek. C3 concluded at low-mid USD 24 pmt levels for end December dates.

The Panamax market has held a firm, steady tone this week, with the Atlantic supported by solid grain and coal demand out of the U.S. Gulf and East Coast, keeping fronthaul sentiment positive despite a wider gap between bids and offers on nearby trans-Atlantic business. South Atlantic indicators softened a touch, but the North Atlantic remained well underpinned with limited prompt tonnage. In the Pacific, activity stayed strong as Indonesian and Japanese demand met a tightening list, keeping owners confident and charterers competing to cover early positions. While Chinese buying has eased slightly, the overall setup remains constructive, and the forward curve still suggests room for further upside heading into year-end.

Sky high sentiment in the tanker market is driving activity forward with some unexpected results. Okeanis have purchased scrubber fitted resales NORTH STAR/VIKING STAR (157K DWT Daehan 2025/2026) for USD 97M per unit, setting a new benchmark for the sector. These units were ordered by Atlas in 2023 for USD 84M each, and the owners will reap significant upside by delivering the units into a strong, tonnage hungry market. This will only add fuel to the fire of the current ordering, as owners bet on future strong markets. Elsewhere in the clean sector, MR rates and activity continue to push higher. It will be interesting to see how the market will react to an extensive number of deliveries in Q1 26.    The story is similar on the dry side, sentiment high as a result of robust and consistent earnings. 2020 Bulkers this week sold off the last of their vessels in a deal worth USD 145.5M, Scrubber fitted Newcastlemax pair BULK SYDNEY/SANTOS ( 208K DWT New Times 2020) acquired by Genco. Buyers have been clambering for Newcastlemaxes in the last few months to try and capitalise on healthy long term employment opportunities in this sector. Staying in the larger sizes there is significant demand around the 15-year-old mark, mostly form Far Eastern buyers. LAKE DOLPHIN (179K DWT Hanjin Hi 2011) was sold for USD 30.5M, while FORTUNE VIOLET (181k DWT Imabari 2012) achieved USD $34M.

EAST The week got off to an active start in the Middle East on the back of Saudi Acceptances with 3 deals confirmed and 1 failed. Levels are currently being concluded in the low USD 70s. As of writing, we count five spot fixtures for December, all in the first decade. Additionally, an Indian spot cargo is currently being worked for mid-December dates, suggesting that Indian PSUs may have completed their spot program for the first decade.  WEST After some eventful weeks, fixing activity has calmed down in the West. We count 27 deals done thus far in December (11/11/5 by decade), while we still see a handful of uncovered stems off end December. Last done at around USD 118-119 pmt bss HCVP. We expect some of the term lifters to receive their January nominations by today, and this could potentially spark activity for next fixing window.
