text: Cash premiums for Dec lifting evenly split cargoes have surged further to CP plus $30s range, driven by tight supply and recent active spot purchases. A Middle East producer has cut tolerance on propane for term liftings and canceled one cargo reportedly. By the time of writing, Dec CP was traded at $486 for C3 and Dec C3/C4 at $15. Dec/Jan CP C3 narrowed to flattish vs last week’s $9, reflecting front strength.   US FOBs remain strong, with December FOB cargos changed hand at 7-8 cpg, supported by the strong CFR Asian market for front December and January delivery. ARB to Asian market for Dec and Jan were traded at around $161 and $155 respectively.   Sentiments for Asian market strengthened, with cash differentials firmer for both Dec and Jan discussions. In window 2/0 parcel for 2h Dec delivery basis Chiba was once traded at Dec FEI plus $9. 4/0 parcel for earlier Jan delivery was bid at Dec FEI plus $2, equates to Jan FEI plus $7 basis Yantai, and Jan FEI plus $5 basis Ningbo, respectively. Outside window 4/0 parcel for 2h Dec delivery into Ningbo was changed hand at Dec FEI plus $12 reportedly. One Chinese PDH procured a late Dec delivered Canadian propane at Dec CP plus 70s. Pertamina was reported to award their buy tender for 1/1 or 2/2 for last decade dec delivery at Dec CP plus $60s. One Schina importer tendered to buy 1/1 or 2/2 for Jan delivery, result is yet to be known. Similar offers into N.China ranged from Jan CP plus $90s to $100, yet to hear any deal concluded. Other than spot, a couple of PDH users have issued buy term tenders to secure next year term supply, which offers are expected to edge up in view of front supply tightness.

The market showed a mixed tone, with firmness in parts of the Atlantic set against quieter patches elsewhere. In the Supra segment, the USG softened after earlier support, while the South Atlantic and Continent–Mediterranean stayed largely steady and positional. Asia held a firm underlying tone despite lighter fixing. Handy saw similar regional contrasts, with the Continent–Mediterranean steady and the South Atlantic and U.S. Gulf maintaining underlying strength even as activity slowed. Across Asia, conditions remained muted, keeping rates broadly flat.

VLCC rates continue to trade in a band between W125-130 MEG/East for modern unhampered tonnage. However, most of the activity has gone underground which has left it up to players’ artistic freedom to peg the market and speculate on who’s done what to whom. TD3C came in at W126.67 last night and being an average of submissions indicates big differences of opinion out there. Position lists remain on tighter side of balanced both east and west of Suez, albeit with an over representation of oil company and trader relets. The battle of mind of mater is likely to continue short term. Some profit taking is always to be expected, however, the downside should be capped and rates likely to remain well supported at 3 digits with corresponding daily earnings north of USD 100k.

On the C5 front, we see enquiries for miners and operators for early December dates. Volumes out of East Australia are flat from last week. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, focus is on mid December dates with some forward interest for January dates. Ballasting tonnage is tightening for early and mid December. Spot tonnage out of Far East is tight as well as we see inclement weather over the weekend/early this week. Fixtures concluded at mid-high USD 10 pmt levels by midweek. C3 concluded at mid USD 24 levels for mid December dates.

The Panamax market this week felt steadier than last, with overall indicators turning slightly more bullish even as day-to-day activity remained mixed. In the Atlantic, early negativity gave way to a marginal improvement as North Atlantic tonnage cleared and fresh USG grain and USEC coal inquiries supported December sentiment, though Trans-Atlantic rounds stayed quiet and ECSA softened toward the mid-sixteens. The Pacific was the softer side of the basin, with abundant tonnage and thin Australia and North Pacific demand keeping offers in the high-seventeen to eighteen region while bids slipped into the mid-fifteen to sixteen range, suggesting a near-term correction before a potential floor. Despite the softer physical tone, forward indicators such as reduced coal contango, rising spot prices, and a firmer South Atlantic tightness signal point to a sideways market with scope for the P5TC to approach year-to-date highs toward year-end.

A substantial number of vessels went on subs yesterday in the West, helping to clear what had been a large supply at the start of the week. The tonnage complexion is now on the sensitive side. Conversely the demand side has shifted the other way - VLCCs have taken more stems for the 1st decade December than initially expected, and relets have dropped off the list in swathes, removing additional volume. We estimate roughly around 7 stems still to cover for 1st decade December West Africa. Additionally, with Aframaxes weakening stateside, charterers focus may shift to the smaller class, reducing the likelihood of the USG continuing to pull Suezmaxes from this side of the Atlantic. Despite this, VLCCs remain very healthy and sentiment may carry over to Suezmax, as evidenced by MEG rates holding despite friendlier supply.

North Sea On the surface has been quiet through the first half of the week as relets come back into play to cover a lot of stems in the 23-27 window. With some bad weather effecting offshore programs we may see some requirements for STS to alleviate delays to the offshore vessels. List is arguably balanced and even though surrounding markets have come under pressure and softened through the first half of the week ballasting still remains an option to mitigate waiting days suffered in the North Sea.  Mediterranean As expected and with fundamentals pointing the way the correction in the Mediterranean has happened for the last stems of November. Tonnage list has cleared out on the front end but majority of the expected positions are opening between 21st and 26th of November which will be bang for the next fixing window. Rates might lose a bit more ground but equally owners are expected to dig their heels and try and establish a new floor in the ws190s depending on the type of run.

Spot charter rates in the Atlantic continued their ascent on an even steeper trajectory through the end of last week as a small number of prompt requirements were met with scant supply. Those able to release tonnage were able to capture large increments to last done, breaking the six-digit mark and by a considerable distance in at least one case. This has only added to the uncertainty around forward pricing, where better availabilities for end Dec look fairly evenly matched with requirements at the end of the fixing window. Owners in the Pacific have also notched up a few new highs for the year as firm availabilities have remained relatively tight, although charterers with more forward dates are beginning to pause and question whether the recent run has legs, given a healthy number of expected redeliveries. On the newbuilding front, Hyundai Samho, announced they signed a $507 million contract with a North American company, scheduled for delivery in the 2H 2028.

High spirits this week as much of the tanker market gathered in Dubai for Bahri week, in a time where earnings are holding strong into the winter months. Unsurprisingly in the second-hand space, good spec suezmax units with prompt delivery are attracting a significant amount of market interest. A number of offers were seen on Scrubber fitted STENA SUNSHINE (159K DWT Samsung 2013), which eventually sold to Greek buyers at USD 58M. Despite this, it is worth pointing out that in a period of little over a month, there have been 30 new VLCC and nearly 20 Suezmax orders, showing that plenty of other buyers in the market prefer to focus on newbuildings, rather than compete at these premium levels in the second-hand market. Otherwise, it was the MR market which saw further liquidity, with Montfort purchasing pumproom pair MAERSK MARU/MISSISSIPPI (48K DWT Iwagi Zosen 2011/10) for USD 44M en bloc.   A busy week, as ever, in the dry market. In an overall sense, the momentum is with this market despite the incoming usual seasonal slowdown. It will be interesting to assess whether this slowdown will affect asset values in any way, or whether the underlying optimism of the next year or so will carry values over this period. In the ultramax space, GRACE HARMONY (60K DWT Onomichi 2015) was sold for USD 24.8M.

The spot market remains firm in the West, with rates hitting year-to-date records and the idea of a six-figure fixture may no longer be a wild fantasy. There are requirements emerging including some relatively prompt loadings out of West Africa and US Gulf cargoes within the second half of December, giving some rate support at the end of the current fixing window. Additional volumes marketed by producers are struggling a bit to find homes in the absence of suitable modern tonnage, and much of the underlying ship length remains tied up on longer laden legs with portfolios yet to turn towards chartering out to capture the trading value.    However, amidst all the bullish market talk there are clear reasons for caution; although the prompt market remains tight there are vessels redelivering in December and more availability is emerging, and we cannot expect the weather to help this year with mild conditions forecast in importing regions both East and West. There remains a large discount in the Pacific where rates for both 2-strokes and TFDE lag well behind the Atlantic, while the premium for 2-strokes over TFDEs is also widening, despite fewer requirements calling for larger ships East of Suez. The question of how long this firmer market lasts has to yet be answered, but for now it seems clear that the answer has been deferred at least another week.

text: Cash premium for Dec lifting FOBs ex AG soared up especially for evenly split grade, due to tight spot supply, coupled with robust Indian buying demand. Two oil majors were reported cancelled their Dec FOB AG buy tenders. No fresh deals were reported after last deal into India which was concluded at CP plus teens level.   One producer trading arm was bidding in window for Dec FOB 2/2 at $490, which equates to Dec CP plus mid-teens, yet to entice offers. Indian IOC issued buy tender for monthly one evenly split cargo for Q1 delivery, either FOB AG or CFR India. Market participants are awaiting acceptance to know the full scheme, especially if any ratio/quantity adjustments from Saudi Aramco. By the time of writing, Dec CP was traded at $480 for C3 and C3/C4 at $10.   Arbitrage for US exports to Asia narrowed sharply this week, as Lst/Fei for Dec and Jan once traded at below $150. However, due to the softening freight, terminal fee for Dec liftings improved to 6ish cpg and a couple of spot deals reported traded at around such level.   A flurry of cargoes changed hand in Asian market, supported by strong demand from both heating and petchem segments. Supply tightened for 1h Dec delivery as Japanese and Korean importers are actively buying, together with traders covering shorts. Cash differentials for 23/0 parcels surged up into positive premium, vs last week’s deep discounts, with CFR 1h Dec being bid at Dec FEI plus $8 while 2h Dec at Bal Nov FEI minus $0.5, which equates to Dec FEI plus $3.5. 4/0 parcel for Dec delivery basis Chiba was heard traded at Dec FEI minus mid-single, and similar parcel basis Ningbo for 2h Dec delivery was bid at Dec FEI plus $3.5. Two PDHs have awarded their buy tenders to secure non-US 4/0 cargoes for Dec delivery at Dec CP plus high 60s basis Schina and Echina respectively. One cracker canceled their buy tender seeking 1h Dec delivery propane into Ningbo as limited offer, while the other managed to procure a 4/0 for Dec at Dec FEI plus $1.

EAST The MEG market remains relatively subdued, largely due to the industry event in Dubai. Outside of that, activity has been limited to one cargo each from WAF and WC Canada. Sentiment in the East continues to be weak, with a few vessels still open for end-November dates. Meanwhile, the shrinking West market premium has made ballasting via the Cape to the US less appealing. As of writing, only 15 spot fixtures have been recorded out of MEG (including Yanbu) for November - seven fewer than the 2025 monthly average. Given this shortfall, it wouldn’t be overly optimistic to expect a few more cargoes to emerge for the very end of the month.  WEST After peaking in the mid USD 140s at the end of last week, the market has softened by approximately USD 20-25/mt over the past few days, based on 4-5 fixtures concluded in the last 3 days. Despite the correction in rates, TCE earnings remain robust at around USD 50,000/day on the basis of the latest fixtures. We now count 22 spot fixtures for December, with the majority fixed for the first half of the month. The current position list appears balanced to slightly long for the remainder of the month, suggesting that market levels are likely to hold steady to firm in the near term.

Atlantic showing firmer sentiment across both Supramax and Handysize sectors amid tightening tonnage and improved enquiry, particularly from the US Gulf and South Atlantic. In contrast, the Asian market remained more subdued, with an extended tonnage list and limited activity keeping rates broadly steady. Overall, fundamentals appeared balanced, with the Atlantic maintaining a positive tone while the Pacific held steady, and some Supramax owners showing interest in short and long period.

The VLCC market saw a bit of a downward adjustment at the end of last week as charterers held their nerve and only drip-fed cargoes into the marketplace. Rates held around the W100 mark, although TD3C dipped marginally below on Monday. However, as market players descended on Dubai for the yearly Bahri get-together things heated up and suddenly charterers were scrambling for tonnage and W110 has just been concluded for a MEG/east. The position list of available ships able to do November cancelling in the MEG is thinning by the hour and several cargoes remain uncovered. The Atlantic market has also been ticking along nicely underpinned by an increasing flow of Brazil export cargoes, and the USG has also kept on giving despite the west/east arb suggesting otherwise. This has and will continue to attract tonnage away from the MEG, eroding the position list there for early December liftings and suggesting a further strong market going into the last month of 2025. Santa Claus is coming to town.

There have been rumours circulating about a couple of stems working in West Africa; however, the majority of activity has been attributed to other regions. Fundamentally, we remain firm, with the list still fairly short and cargo coverage lacking for the 25–30 November window, as well as for December where we’ve seen VLCCs failing. The safe ships currently on the list are mostly ETA Bonny around 25-26 Nov, so a cargo around this window may result in a few points being chipped off, as waiting days carry a significant cost in this market. However, with each passing day the flexibility for charterers to sit on stems will diminish. In theory, we should begin to see December dates worked next week, which will congest the market. Additionally, VLCCs in the MEG have rebounded with MEG/East on suezmax also paying up to w180 (albeit with a ‘new’ charterer). This will likely keep attentions of vessels opening in the East.

North Sea A relatively quiet week up to middle of the week with some replacement business keeping rates at the WS 160 level for North Sea. Natural dates are pushing into 3rd decade which on paper looks likely to be busy stem wise. Tonnage still looking outside the area which is keeping the available tonnage interesting. Rates could still have firming potential for an active 3rd decade unless bigger-size vessels continue to take out volume.  Mediterranean Quiet week in the Mediterranean as well so far as dates have been pushed forward enough for the charterers to take a step back. Prompt position which lost the window are either ballasting towards USG or choosing some other alternatives to fix. With a couple of relets around for the next window and enough positions for the balance of the month rate could have hit the ceiling for November dates and take a breather but it remains to be seen.

The Panamax market maintained a constructive tone this week, with both basins showing firmer sentiment and a sense of underlying support. In the Atlantic, trans-Atlantic activity gained traction on improved grain demand, while fronthaul business remained limited but balanced by a tightening tonnage list in the North. ECSA values held steady with early December demand slowly building, aided by a firmer Pacific. In Asia, momentum persisted on the back of healthy enquiry ex-Australia and Indonesia, a shorter tonnage list, and continued period interest lending further confidence. Paper markets have also been trending higher, reflecting a generally optimistic outlook as owners retained the initiative heading into the second half of November.

On the C5 front, we see enquiries for miners and operators for late November and early December dates. Volumes out of East Australia are a tick up. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, focus is on December dates. Ballasting tonnage is heavily weighted on first half of December with some prompt ships. Spot tonnage out of Far East is abundant. Fixtures concluded at mid USD 9 pmt levels by midweek. C3 offers seen are sub USD 23 pmt levels and bids in the USD 21 pmt levels.

Barhi week will take centre stage over the next week, and in general owners will be attending with smiles on their faces given the sustaining strength in the tanker market. Liquidity on modern ships has slowed yet continues, with Tankerska purchasing Scrubber fitted LR2 PLATANOS (114K DWT Namura 2019). Elsewhere in the product space, an active week for Scorpio with the announcement of the sale of 4x 2014 blt scrubber fitted MR units to Torm and the acquisition of 4x scrubber fitted MR resales from Jingjjiang Nanyang shipbuilding.    Much of the market were in Hamburg this week for Eisbein, where there is a mix of optimism and excitement for the next dry market run. Despite this optimism, there is still a disconnect between asset prices and earnings. New candidates in the market are expected to beat last done, and owners will not be rushed into accepting the first bid that comes their way. Competition is particularly rife within the c.15yo supramax sector, where eight sales were reported this week. Scrubber fitted Capesize SEAUNITY (181K DWT Koyo 2010) was sold for USD 30.5M, helping price an abundance of candidates in this area of the market.

EAST Market activity has slowed noticeably since yesterday, with no new freight enquiries in the market. After last week’s sharp rate increases, we are now seeing signs of a stabilising market. East spot fixing for late November may still have a few uncovered cargoes in store, but the current spot count is trailing monthly averages by 7 to 8 fixtures. As it stands, November is shaping up to fall below average.  WEST Momentum from last week’s strong fixing activity has carried into this week, with 9 spot fixtures and 2 COA deals already concluded. Rates continue to firm, climbing another $12/mt, pushing TCE earnings to approximately $65,000/day on a standard VLGC. With only two vessels remaining open for November, the market is tight. We now count 36 spot fixtures for November and an impressive 17 already booked for December loading. Given the limited tonnage and sustained demand, market levels are expected to remain steady to firm in the near term.

text: Despite limited spot trades, cash premium for Dec AG FOB, particularly 2/2 grade, stands firm. BPCL issued tender to buy Nov or Dec split cargo, either FOB or CFR, but was heard no Nov offer received but Dec stems only and asking at CP plus teens. By the time of writing, Nov CP was traded at $464 and Nov C3/C4 at $9.   Netbacks for FOB ex US on Dec lifting declined, with ARB to EAST narrowing down against soaring freight. Terminal fee for Dec spot was assessed at around 5cpg however under downward pressure, as CFR Asian market being traded at deep discounts.   A 23/0 parcel for 1h Dec delivery basis Chiba was traded in window at Dec MOPJ minus $86, which equates to Dec FEI minus $6. A 4/0 parcel for 1h Dec delivery was bid at Bal Nov FEI minus $7, which equates to Dec FEI minus around $15. Outside window a flurry of spot buy tenders for late Nov/Dec delivered propane are ongoing. Jinneng was reported to award two cargos, with one at Dec FEI minus mid high single for US origin, while the other at Dec FEI plus 30s for Non-US origin. FIC cancelled their buy tender for Ningbo PDH as offers are higher than expected in view of weakening downstream margins. Kingfa procured one cargo for 1h Dec delivery into Panjin at Dec FEI minus mid-single and issued another tender to secure 2/0 or 4/0 for 1h Dec delivery into Ningbo. The shrinking propane/propylene spread has led to some PDH shutdown or rate cuts, due to negative economics.   China has announced that it will suspend the additional 24% tariff imposed on US goods for one year, while maintaining 10% levies. Chinese importers have reconsidered taking US cargos in latest tenders, if the cost with 10% additional tariff levied is more competitive than non-us stems. Meanwhile, the global shipping market remained unsettled, as market players are still cautiously awaiting the official announcement on US-China port fee truce.

North Sea  A small downward correction for the local North Sea runs was fixed yesterday as a market quote put a bit of pressure on the owners. More vessels are ballasting towards USG/ECC and some of them might keep an eye on any Mediterranean enquiries as well. Rates in the North Sea are expected to hover around last-done levels give or take some points depending on the voyage in question.   Mediterranean  Local runs in the Mediterranean have experienced a small downward correction this week. Dates keep being pushed forward as charterers are taking the chances on tight itineraries that can result in replacement jobs. Tonnage list remains balanced but at the same time there aren't that many candidates which are ticking all boxes, so sideways with a firm sentiment depending on cargo dates.

The West remains extremely short on tonnage, with this tightness reflected in aggressive rates from the US Gulf: USD 7.25 million on subs for USG/WCI and WS140 on subs for USG/UKCM, both marking significant increases on last done. We have yet to see similarly aggressive movements in TD20 rates, but owners will be keen to replicate the gains seen across the pond and will undoubtedly use them as leverage. Adding to bullish supply fundamentals, demand is expected to accelerate, with very little covered from West Africa or Guyana and CPC December cargoes entering the natural window. This is without factoring in seasonal weather changes, which typically add further volatility to tanker markets as conditions cause vessel delays. The MEG remains very strong as well; however, VLCCs appear to be cooling slightly, which may weigh on sentiment. That said, ahead of the Bahri festivities next week, a potential surge in demand could prevent significant losses and may even trigger a rebound. Overall, a perfect storm is developing for owners as we approach year-end.

W127.5 was logged MEG/China end of last week, and despite balanced position lists east and west of Suez VLCCs got a punch in the snout as W115 was logged for a MEG/China cargo yesterday on a trader relet, after which TD3C came in at W113 and change. A cargo being traded at the time of writing has seen punters firm at very low teens against low W100’s from the charterer. That said, barring Chinese “system liftings” we have hardly seen any fixtures concluded in the 20-30/11 window from the MEG and if we extrapolate there should be another 50 odd cargoes to cover before November is a wrap, and a relative short time to do it seeing as most players head for Dubai next week for the yearly Bahri get together, after which December dates will come into play. So, in as much as we may see a bit more profit taking the downside should be capped and rates hold in 3 digits with corresponding daily earnings at USD 100k/day or more. West Africa and Brazil exports have parred the MEG with W110 conclude for a TD15 run.

The Capesize market began the week on a soft note before gaining momentum midweek, though this improvement tapered off amid lighter activity in both the Atlantic and Pacific. Early pressure on rates was offset from midweek onward as increased cargo inquiry and firmer fixing on key routes, particularly C3 and C5, helped stabilize sentiment and lift levels. In the Pacific, steady demand from the miners supported gradual rate improvement, while the Atlantic experienced tighter tonnage lists, which in turn bolstered both Transatlantic runs and fronthaul employment. Market confidence was further supported by reports of a one-year trade truce between the U.S. and China.

The market saw a positional day with sentiment in Asia remaining weak amid limited enquiry and ample prompt tonnage keeping pressure on rates. The Atlantic, however, showed signs of improvement as activity from the US Gulf hinted at a possible turnaround, with stronger discussions emerging on TA runs. Owners appeared slightly more optimistic in the region, though elsewhere charterers continued to hold the upper hand. The South Atlantic and Mediterranean basins remained subdued with little fresh enquiry. In Asia, sentiment stayed soft as limited fixtures surfaced, and overall, the market tone remained cautious despite early signs of recovery in parts of the Atlantic.

The bubbling momentum in the spot markets for loadings through the end of November and early December has continued through this week, despite some uncertainty following news of some lost cargoes out of the US Gulf; however, the resulting prompt length does not really come into play for later laycans in the Atlantic and so rates have continued to firm. With many of these requirements now covered, focus shifts a little further back and we enter into speculative territory: how many of the FOB sales will take in tonnage? How many of the optimisations will play out? How many fresh firm requirements will hit the market? In short, owners and charterers are assessing how long will the current freight imbalance last and when the market will start to soften. The firming market in the East is trailing that in the West, and the dynamic quite different. Named positions are few and far between but equally, open requirements remain scarce.

The Panamax market saw another week of correction, with sentiment softening across both basins as vessel supply continued to outpace demand. In the Atlantic, the South held relatively steady on the back of activity from East Coast South America and South Africa, while the North lost ground as trans-Atlantic demand thinned and tonnage availability increased. Fronthaul demand provided only limited relief, with the overall tone turning more cautious. In the Pacific, charterers maintained pressure on rates despite a brief uptick in midweek activity, and owners showed resistance while covering short trips in hopes of a rebound. Coal demand offered some seasonal support, but the broader trend remained downward amid growing vessel lists and weaker sentiment.

After the recent run on modern tonnage, the tanker second hand market has had a much more subdued week. Overall bullish earnings sentiment remains however, and VLCCs are leading the way with several fixtures reported well in excess of USD 100K/day. Owners will be hoping these levels sustain into a healthy winter market. In the clean space, Ice 1A SEAWAYS GATUN/HERUN (47K DWT HMD 2007) sold to Champion tankers for USD 12.7M each, the conservative price levels owing to strict KYC from the sellers.   A US - China trade ‘truce’ will excite the dry market after talks between the two nations took place this week in Busan, South Korea. Tariffs will be trimmed but crucially for panamax owners, China have agreed to buy 12 million metric tonnes of soybeans through January and 25 million tonnes annually for the next 3 years. This soybean deal is one thing, but the wider market will welcome easing tensions and general stability between the two nations. In the standout transaction of the week, ultramax CMB BRUEGEL (63K DWT Shin Kasado 2021) was bought by Meghna for USD 32.8M, this follows up these buyers’ purchase of DRAFTDODGER (66K DWT Mitsui 2016) at USD 26.2M last month.

EAST Following the mutual suspension of trade penalty fees between the US and China, the VLGC freight market is showing renewed strength. With Chinese vessels no longer confined to the ME, shipowners have revised their freight ideas upward. Asking levels on the RT/C route are already into $60/ton and above - over $10 higher than yesterday’s last done. Where actual fixtures will settle remains to be seen at the time of writing.  WEST Following a highly active close to last week, expectations were for a quieter start to this one. However, the market has defied those forecasts, with 11 USG fixtures already concluded this week. Rates have responded positively, climbing approximately $12/mt from recent lows. So far, 34 spot fixtures have been booked for November loading dates which is a notable increase from the 22 fixtures concluded in all of October, signalling a strong uptick in demand. Despite this surge in activity and firming rates, the USG still has 6-7 vessels open and ready to fix for November. This available tonnage is likely to cap further rate increases, keeping levels steady in the near term.

text: Saudi Aramco reduced Nov CP to $475 for C3 and $460 for C4, down by $20 and $15 respectively. Given they are still in the process of term renewal, market participants expect such a decline on CP, but the announcement is slightly set on high end versus swap value. Cash premium for evenly split cargos remained firm with robust Indian and Chinese demand, coupled with tighter US butane supply to EAST in winter typically. By the time of writing, Dec CP rallied up to $490 for C3 and $ for $473 for C4.  Spot sentiments for US FOBs strengthened with arbitrage into Asia widening from $150s to $160s for both Nov and Dec lifting. Notional FOB netbacks into EAST improved to 5ish cpg and some late Nov lifting FOB was reported changed at 5.75 cpg. US propane/Propylene inventory increased by 2.5mml barrels, much higher than expected.  Asian price rebounded, following the stronger CP price announced and relief on trade tensions after US/China talk. 46/0 parcels for 1h Dec delivery basis Chiba was offered via window at Dec FEI minus $7 and 23/0 for 2h Dec was bid at $518, which equates to Dec FEI minus $4. Outside window a handful of term tenders are under negotiations. One Chinese petchem players was reported awarded their buy propane tender for US stems at FEI minus high single, and non US stems at CP plus $60s. Another two Chinese importers also issue similar tenders to procure open origin propane. Indonesia Pertamina was reported to award some evenly split cargos via new term tender at CP plus 20s range. Similarly, some Philippines importers award their term tender for 1/1 split at CP plus 30s. Spot activities slowed down as players are awaiting CP, however one 2/2 for Dec delivery was reported sold into SEA at CP plus 30s, which reckoned to be US stem. Whereas another Non US 2/2 was placed into China at Dec CP plus 80s reportedly. Huayi cancelled their propane buy tender for Nov/Dec delivery, hearing offer at the premium of 80s as well.

The market continued to soften as both the Supramax and Handymax faced further downward pressure. For the Supramax, sentiment remained weak across both basins, with the US Gulf leading the decline amid limited fresh enquiry and growing prompt tonnage. The Continent–Mediterranean and South Atlantic also saw subdued activity, while Asia offered little support despite demand from North Pacific and Australia. For the Handymax, trading was similarly lacklustre as Greek holidays slowed European activity, and the US Gulf and South America lost ground on thin demand. Period activity remains relatively quiet with very few fixtures reported.

The Panamax market eased this week, with both basins showing signs of topping out. In the Atlantic, the North Atlantic and U.S. Gulf rounds lost steam as fresh inquiry dried up and tonnage lists grew, leaving charterers firmly in control. Fronthaul demand was patchy at best, with most players waiting on the outcome of the upcoming U.S.–China meeting before committing. South America held steady but failed to gain momentum despite some late November interest. In the Pacific, activity was reasonable midweek but rates edged lower as owners softened ideas against a growing list and limited fresh cargo. Overall, sentiment turned cautious, with the market looking due for a correction after recent highs.

On the C5 front, we see enquiries for miners and operators for early/mid November dates. Volumes out of East Australia remain flat from last week with a tick up in enquiries from others fronts of the pacific. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, focus is on end November dates with some exchanges for early December. Ballasting tonnage is heavily weighted on second half of November with some prompt ships. Spot tonnage out of Far East is accumulating due to overall lower pacific fixing volumes this week. Fixtures concluded at low-mid USD 9 pmt levels by midweek and mid USD 22 pmt levels is traded on C3.

North Sea North Sea hasn’t reached the activity levels we have seen in the Mediterranean, some fixing combined with relets and some bigger vessels has pushed dated beyond the first 5 days. Rates pushed up at the end of last week and have remained steady so far into November. With limited activity in the North Sea we continue to see vessels mainly heading South into a firm Mediterranean market and the US market has also been strengthening with both giving appealing results returns wise for Owners.  Even if we see a lack of activity in the North Sea there is very limited scope for downside while Owners continue to have other options.  Mediterranean Mediterranean market remains busy and as a result rates aren't taking a step yet. We are more or less sold out for the 1st decade and possibly sold-out for November ex CPC. Tonnage list is pretty balanced but with some LR2's willing DPP it seems a tad longer, however these vessels aren't expected to give big discounts. As USG is also on the rise again Mediterranean should hoover around last-done levels for the balance of the week.

Stateside, 2 charterers were sniffing around for USG/Transatlantic off 10-15/11. Local availabilities remain extremely low, with nothing in ballast or sailing within 10 days. As of COB yesterday, there was only 1 UKCM ballaster that could arrive in the USG prior to 15/11. TCEs stateside will certainly continue to pull vessels across the Atlantic and reinforce a floor of at least WS 140 on TD20. In truth, even if we didn't have a strong USG market, safe tonnage remains very short for West Africa, and CPC will continue to attract the attention of UKCM vessels. With limited downside expected going into the third decade and the window approaching rapidly, if you have a West Africa/East in hand, forward coverage on an Eastern ballaster is advised. In the MEG, VLCCs have picked up with w110 rumoured on subs - despite a longer list of Suezmaxes in the region, sentiment should maintain rates if not bolster them.

The short-term supply/demand picture in the MEG is now not far off 1:1 and we are approaching a “pick a number” territory. W122.5 has been printed for a MEG/China run and owners will peg it north of that now for sure. The Atlantic is following suit, USG/east reported paid USD 13 million a couple of times despite the arbitrage not supporting such numbers, and Brazil-West Africa export is probably in 3 digits eastbound too. Attempts to talk about things balancing further out on the curve are met with a deaf ear by the owning community. Winter is coming!

The market through most of the year has remained quite flat and weekly reports had a sense of déjà vu; yet a glance back to our last report shows that a week can also be a very long time in LNG, and that a month ago can feel like ancient history. Rates across the three major regions have all moved higher, with Atlantic rates perhaps even entering “surging” territory, having more than doubled in recent weeks. One trigger for this tightening can be linked to delays discharging into Egypt and the knock-on impact on scheduling, but this was maybe only a starting gun for a winter upturn that many had thought would never come. There are now signs of an improving cargo market in Asia that is enticing for portfolios and traders, and ships are being pulled back from availability lists. East of Suez, there are very few 2-strokes available and TFDEs are now supporting the market at higher rates. It is often the case that a long freight market is only skin deep, and scratching the surface can quickly reveal a more complicated picture; that appears to be the case here. The opposite can happen too though, if the cargo market softens then recent gains can disappear even quicker. How long this upturn lasts is already a big topic of discussion.   There have been no new orders or project FIDs this week, but the announcement that Totalenergies have lifted the Force Majeure on Mozambique LNG was a very welcome step. There will be more challenges ahead but we wish the project well as they target first production by the end of the decade.

Seasonally stronger crude markets, combined with an increasing US sanction effort against Russia has buoyed the tanker earnings market as selected owners are reporting VLCC rates breaching the USD 100K/day mark. This push in rates is expected to filter into the rest of the sector, which will likely keep second hand values looking strong towards the end of the year. ASYAD have offset their recent spending spree with the sale of scrubber fitted VLCC SAIQ (299K DWT Universal 2011) for USD 57M with TC attached until April at USD 41K/day. This is while another similar vintage VLCC scrubber fitted NAVE CONSTELLATION (296K DWT Dalian 2010) was sold for USD 52.5M, showing there is plenty of demand for this vintage of VLCC at these levels, despite their age. Elsewhere MRs PTI HUDSON/NILE (49K DWT SPP 2016) were sold to Chinese buyers with TC attached at USD 33M.   A busy week across the dry market sees market players jostling for position and tonnage. Q3 rates remained consistent and there is widespread optimism for the years ahead, so one could speculate the bottom of the market from a values perspective is firmly in the rearview mirror. A notable variable that will need to be dealt with in 2026 however, is vessel deliveries. Certain subsectors are in line for high growth, particularly Kamsarmax and Ultramax, so buyers will be hoping for some opportunity here. In the standout transaction this week, EBE Belgium purchased scrubber fitted Newcastlemax BULK SAO PAOLO (208K DWT New Times 2020) for USD 72.75M. There has been a recent spike in demand for Newcastlemax units as owners look to take advantage of longer employment opportunities on offer for these vessels.

text: Cash premium for AG 2/2 FOB cargo soared up further, with one Nov FOB being traded at Nov CP plus high teens reportedly. Dec parcels are also in heated discussion, with IOC reported to award a Dec cargo at Dec CP plus $7 via tender. By the time of writing, Nov C3 CP was traded $460, following the crude, and Nov/Dec C3 CP in $10 contango.   FOB trading activities ex US for Nov slightly improved, as some players try to utilize their ships and procure spot cargos. ARB to EAST stabilized this week at $140ish and $150 for Nov and Dec respectively, whilst netback to Asia edged up to 5cpg with softening freight. Us Propane and propylene stock rose by 800k barrels, and inventory increased by 1.4% versus last year.   Asian price surged up with Nov FEI being traded at $500, and Nov FEI/CP enlarged by $15 to $40 versus last week. 23/0 parcel for 2h Nov delivery basis Chiba was bid at Nov FEI minus $15 and similar parcel for 1h Dec was bid at Dec FEI minus $9 in the window. Outside window FPCC was reported awarded their buy tender for two Dec lots, with 4/0 concluded at Dec FEI minus mid/high single and 2/0 at Mopj linked price. Shenghong was also reported to award their buy tender for non-Us flexible ratio LPG delivered during 10/Nov to 20/Dec, but details remained sketchy. A couple of non-Us stem for Nov delivery was reported placed into China, with 1/1 parcel at Nov CP plus 70 basis SChina and 2/0 heard at 80 range.

EAST Activity in the East is beginning to show signs of recovery, with several fixtures reported in the MEG and one out of Australia for November loading. The regional position list is gradually rebalancing, though sentiment remains subdued. A more pronounced shift is unlikely unless a surge of Indian PSU tenders materializes as so far, only one has emerged for early November. Freight levels appear to be stabilizing, but the overall tone remains soft.  WEST The VLGC market in the West has seen a noticeable uptick in activity over the past week, with 11–12 fixtures concluded. This signals a modest recovery in momentum, although monthly fixing volumes in both hemispheres remain slightly below the year-to-date average. In the US Gulf, the landscape has shifted. Vessels are now arriving open and ready to load on prompt dates, a scenario not observed for some time. This development points to a loosening of the previously tight tonnage situation, granting charterers greater flexibility. Despite the increase in fixture activity, the market continues to face downward pressure, with freight rates softening and sentiment remaining cautious. TCE earnings are currently approximately USD 43,000–45,000/day, offering owners a respectable return amid an otherwise uncertain environment. For now, the market appears to have found a temporary floor, supported by the recent burst of hiring activity.

The tighter market conditions in the Atlantic persists still driven by uncertainties on discharge schedules, and 1H November is now effectively sold out. Bids have continued to improve to meet the offer and interestingly, sentiment remains strong enough to support a number of more forward fixtures at prevailing levels, including some rumoured for longer period closing out the remainder of the year. The pressing question for both Owners and Charterers now is whether these levels are maintained through year-end of whether the market eases again; for now, we're likely faced with a wait and see approach for liftings further out.  East of Suez, charter rates have also been lifted on the back of this shift, helped too by improved fundamentals with more supply online from Australia and a steadier flow of Canada volumes. Lots of opportunities for owners to assess although it remains to be seen if there will be sufficient to keep all available TFDE's moving.

The week saw a rather subdued market overall, with limited fresh enquiry across most regions. The Atlantic remained under pressure as the USG faced ample prompt tonnage and softer demand, while the South Atlantic also lacked momentum. The Continent–Mediterranean showed mixed tones, with some activity from the East Mediterranean but others feeling levels had plateaued. In contrast, Asia maintained a slightly firmer tone, supported by steady Indo rounds and consistent demand from North. Period activity remains slow with very few deals reported past week.

Despite the upward trajectory having stalled, the VLCC market remained firm for the past few days in the W90-95 range MEG/east (pending of the ship/voyage in question). However, charterers played good game of hide and seek, trying to feed a narrative that a big portion of the first 10 days of the MEG November program was already covered, but cargoes have continued to trickle in. The position list did nevertheless widen, but owners withstood temptations to slip up - until today. NSRP quoted a preferred MEG/Vietnam voyage today and managed to secure a ships at W85 which tested owner’s confidence and direction of travel, albeit in $/day better than your average TD3C voyage. This was followed up by a MEG/Taiwan fixture at W82.5, and with that further downward pressure is evident. The Atlantic also saw a bit of a rate adjustment, with eg. Brazil/China concluded at W86, however, supported TD15 being priced just shy of the W90 mark. That said, with MEG/east having shed the better part of 10 points the Atlantic is likely to follow suit. On a positive note, the west/east arb has improved which may reignite player’s interest USG/east.

The Panamax market was split this week, with the Pacific driving positive momentum while the Atlantic remained mixed. Asian sentiment was firm, supported by strong Indonesian demand and fresh cargo requirements. This, combined with a tightening tonnage list, forced charterers to "pay up" to secure vessels, pushing rates higher. In contrast, the Atlantic lacked clear direction; the North held flat, supported mainly by steady Transatlantic volumes absorbing spot ships, while the ECSA market remained quiet and uninspiring, stalled by a wide bid-offer spread and minimal activity.

North Sea North Sea is fixing End month and like all the western Aframax markets North Sea has firmed albeit more slowly. Tonnage has been leaving the area for better returns keeping pressure on available tonnage. Sentiment will remain firm even if limited activity heading into November in the North Sea while surrounding areas give other options and remain firm.  Mediterranean The market in the Mediterranean remains firm as TD19 has almost reached the ws200 mark up nearly 40p from last week. Local tonnage list remains thin however vessels from the UKC have open eyes down there and try to fix anything that makes more sense than a North Sea run. Owners are tempted to do some profit taking on the right dates and at the same time Suezmaxes are also monitoring if anything makes sense for them.

On the C5 front, we see enquiries for miners and operators for early November dates. Volumes out of East Australia remain flat from last week with a tick up in enquiries from others fronts of the pacific. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, focus is on mid and end November dates. Ballasting tonnage is slowly thinning and chipping away. Spot tonnage out of Far East is slightly tighter, influenced by cold winds hitting the North of China. Fixtures concluded at mid-high USD 10 pmt levels by midweek and low USD 24 pmt levels is traded on C3.

A number of vessels have been tucked away off market in the East and West, but surface level activity remains muted. Charterers do not seem rushed into fixing 2nd decade TD20/Guyana/USG as they allow tonnage to build. It does feel as though a slight downward correction could be in order from the highs of last week but overall fundamentally speaking we remain fairly healthy, so do not expect an implosion. Additionally, the part cargo avenue remains in the Mediterranean if Suezmaxes see value in Afra dates / time killer’s. The 3 week window is now out to 12 November so expect the conversations to pick up as charterers seek coverage.

Buyers expecting modern tanker values to drop have their hopes firmly dashed by now. The recent rush of modern tanker transactions has continued with a headline deal between Metrostar and Delta Tankers, the latter purchasing suezmax sisters CRUDE ZEPHYRUS/LEVANTE (156K DWT New Times 2021) for USD 156M. This is interesting as it represents an age of asset which would have been ordered for substantially less than it is worth today, while having had almost 5 years of trading in mostly strong tanker markets. Representing a very understandable decision to take money off the table on desirable assets, this sale could encourage others to do the same. Elsewhere, PNSC have been busy acquiring Scrubber fitted STAVANGER POSEIDON (50K DWT Hyundai Vietnam 2020) for USD 44.15M, and scrubber fitted aframax pair NAFSIKA (112K DWT Sumitomo 2022) / LORAX (109K DWT Sumitomo 2022) for USD 75M each.   While the China-USA port fee battle has caused more than its fair share of headaches this week, it is unlikely to have a notable impact on the overall market. Sales in the dry market appear to have taken a brief pause, perhaps while the market makes sense of the new rulings, but it is worth remembering that overall sentiment is high and many sales candidates are reflecting this in their price ask.

text: Cash differentials for Nov evenly split FOB cargos ex AG hover at teens level to Nov CP, driven by the strong butane demand, especially with Indian importer like IOC and HPCL calling tender for Nov and/or Dec cargos. Additionally, the tightening sanction on Iranian fleets and tensions over US-China tariff talks have diverted more buy interests on normal AG stems, which consequently lends further support to cash premiums. By the time of writing, Nov C3 CP was traded at $450 and C4 traded 5$ higher to C3.   US FOB netbacks for Asian market slightly improved as of the softening freight. However, the deep discounts on CFR East market on front market have dampened the lifting incentives, and a couple of late Oct and Nov liftings are reported cancelled when arbitrage deteriorated earlier this week. Bids for Nov delivered propane parcels basis Chiba are shown at Nov FEI minus $20s on the window. The uncertainties over US-China tariff talk and the additional imposed rival port fees move, have disrupted the traditional trade operation and leave the market unsettled.   Outside window a handful of tenders are floating this week. One NChina PDH awarded their spot tender by securing two US 4/0 cargos for earlier Nov delivery at Nov FEI minus low 20s and also issue term tender to secure monthly 4/0 including Us origin, for next year. FPC also issued similar term tender to procure monthly 4/0 des Mailiao. Another two importers only tendered for non-Us 2/0 or 0/2 or 1/1 parcels for next year. A couple of Korean importers issued spot tender to buy LPG with butane grade for Nov delivery. Outside tender, non-Us 4/0 or 2/2 parcels were reported placed into China at Nov CP plus 80s range.

The VLGC market has shown signs of renewed activity over the past week, particularly in the Western hemisphere. While the monthly fixing count in both the East and West remains slightly below the year-to-date average, the pace of fixtures has picked up compared to previous months. Notably, seven fixtures for November loading ex-USG have already been recorded—an encouraging sign of forward momentum. In the US Gulf, vessels are now arriving open and ready to load on prompt dates, a scenario not seen in quite some time. This shift suggests a loosening of the tight tonnage situation that has recently characterized the region, potentially offering more flexibility for charterers.  Despite this uptick, the broader market continues to be weighed down by ongoing trade tensions between the US and China. The uncertainty surrounding the scope and enforcement of sanctions has led market participants to adopt a more cautious approach. In response, many are securing vessels that fall outside the affected jurisdictions to avoid potential disruptions to trading and delivery operations. Nevertheless, TCE earnings remain relatively stable, hovering around the USD 50,000/day mark—still a respectable return for owners navigating an otherwise uncertain environment.  East of Suez, November acceptances are nearing completion, with one fixture already concluded via a vessel swap. However, a significant overhang of October tonnage is expected to carry into November, keeping freight rates under pressure and limiting upside potential in the short term. Looking ahead, any further developments in the US-China trade landscape could quickly reshape market dynamics. That said, given the inherently supply-driven nature of the VLGC market, we expect a swift adjustment to any new trading norms as players adapt to evolving conditions.

North Sea Dates pushing out toward the final 5 days of October. Positions have remained tight with a mixture of delayed Itineraries and vessels heading out of the area.  With the tight list even though activity has been muted rates have held and allowed owners to be a bit more selective in what they offer for. Heading into the last 5 days of October window market remains balanced and could easily tip in a firmer direction.  Mediterranean Activity is still strong in the Mediterranean/Black Sea as fixing window reaches end-month dates soon and some ports already sold-out for October. Tonnage list will refresh a bit with some natural local vessels returning in position but overall, it remains thin. No downside for the rates and repeating last dones should be there as some owners are keen on profit-taking as returns are healthy.

This week, the Panamax market was characterized by a distinct disconnect between a rallying paper market and a subdued physical segment, a dynamic driven by the escalating US-China tariff situation. This was evident in both basins; in the Pacific, bullish FFA sentiment failed to translate into significant physical activity as charterers remained hesitant, though the market found a floor from steady intra-regional coal and mineral demand. A similar story unfolded in the Atlantic, where a positive start to the week gave way to slow activity and a wide bid-offer spread as participants globally adopted a cautious wait-and-see approach. Despite the geopolitical headwinds, underlying fundamentals remain stable, with the South Atlantic in particular showing signs of future vessel tightness heading towards the end of the month.

The VLCC market is still trying to find its footing post China tariffs on US linked tonnage and operators. A W88 was concluded MEG/east yesterday, and a W90 today on “vintage” and/or ex d/d units so not representative of the general market, whereas modern unhindered tonnage is offering well into 3 digits on prospective cargoes. Albeit balanced there’s no shortage of ships so it’s more a battle of will than supply/demand dictating proceedings short term. Strong earnings from the MEG, whatever they settle on, has prevented owners from sending ships west, leaving charterers with Atlantic enquires to source from ships already in the area, and a strong Suezmax market has left no “safety valve”, supporting a strong sentiment.

Western markets remain piping hot with multiple cargoes still outstanding and supply that is extremely short and barely extends. Typically, when we reach these elevated levels, profit-taking tends to kick in from the owners’ side; however, so far they remain steadfast in pushing the market above and beyond the year’s highs. Additionally, several owners have opted not to extend subs, and with further questionable itineraries being taken, there’s potential for additional replacement cargoes to enter the market. We did see a brief flurry of VLCC cargoes for West Africa first decade November, but most appear to have been withdrawn - suggesting that using VLCCs as a release valve has not borne fruit. The MEG has overall been quiet, but sentiment should be healthy amidst strong Western markets and as a result further vessels exiting contention to the Cape of Good Hope.

The Supramax market remained relatively muted with sentiment mixed between basins. In the Atlantic, activity was steady but with an overall soft undertone as the U.S. Gulf was thought to have found a floor, while the Pacific showed a firmer tone with improving enquiry, though limited fixing. Handysize sentiment also remained steady across most regions, with Europe and the U.S. Gulf showing stable conditions, the South Atlantic softening slightly due to a growing tonnage list, and Asia holding firm as market activity gradually picked up following recent holidays.

We have seen less liquidity in the Atlantic spot market this week with several requirements sitting in the window for longer than usual in 2025. Ongoing strikes in Europe and deferrals in Egypt continue to create uncertainty in discharge schedules and subsequent vessel availabilities, resulting in limited firm candidates showing for outstanding first decade November cargoes. Whilst charterers’ expectations have increased week on week leading to a couple of fixtures, the gap between bid and offer remains wide, with owners’ ideas firming amid a thin availability list. However, fundamental vessel oversupply and weak sentiment is casting a shadow over hopes of a winterish bump into November, as portfolios still see value in keeping their fleet utilised in the low $20s RT. Meanwhile, market participants are evaluating the potential implications of recent geopolitical developments and their possible impact on LNG shipping. No newbuilding orders have been reported this week, with prices remaining stable.

The Capesize market started the week on a strong note but lost direction as confidence faded toward the end. Early optimism in the Pacific, driven by consistent miner activity, gave the market a solid lift, while the Atlantic struggled to maintain momentum amid quieter inquiry and weaker sentiment. Activity from Brazil and West Africa remained subdued, suggesting limited fresh demand. Although fundamentals were still supportive, the mood in the market shifted as traders reacted to rising geopolitical tension, particularly China’s decision to impose new port fees on U.S.-linked vessels. By the end of the week, confidence had clearly softened, with sentiment rather than demand setting the tone.

The modern transactions this week have taken the tanker market by surprise, setting fresh valuation benchmarks across several segments. The scrubber fitted ECO BEL AIR/BEVERLY HILLS (157K DWT Hyundai 2019) were sold en bloc to Performance for USD 152M, marking the first modern suezmax sale since the NORDIC THUNDER (157K DWT Hyundai 2017) achieved USD 66M in June 2025. Scrubber fitted VLCC LANDBRIDGE PROSPERITY (308K DWT Dalian 2016) changed hands for USD 85M.   In the dry bulk market, liquidity remains strong for both modern and older tonnage. The scrubber fitted MINERAL SHOU GANG INTERNATIONAL (206K DWT Qingdao Yangfan 2019) was sold to Chinese buyers for USD 65.5M, adding to the recent wave of modern newcastlemax sales. Demand for modern ultramaxes continues to stay high with scrubber fitted IMABARI QUEEN (60K DWT Sanoyas 2016) being sold at USD 23.7M, a price that appears favourable for buyers British Bulkers. In the handysize sector, BEN 1 (35K DWT Jiangdong 2015) changed hands for USD 14.7M.

text: Spot differentials for Nov FOBs ex AG are evaluated at mid high single digit premium to Nov Cp. Qatar Energy was reported to sell two mid Nov lifting fobs, one 2/2 and one 4/0 at such level. By the time of writing, Nov Cp was traded at $470 and Nov C3/C4 at $2.   Spot discussions for Nov Fobs ex US are subdued as economics to EAST still at cancellation level with narrowing arbitrage, among plentiful propane supply against bearish demand. Terminal fee for Nov liftings was heard being offered at below 4cpg but little buying interests.   CFR Asian window fell further with offers of 23/0 parcels for 2h Nov delivery basis Chiba being shown at Nov FEI minus $19 while bid at minus $23. Outside window similar parcel for 1h Nov delivery was said changed hand at minus low 20s. Nov FEI swap dropped further to $494 at the time of writing. The widening FEI/MOPJ however stimulated cracking demand. Lotte Chemical was reported to procure a 2/2 for Nov delivery at Nov MOPJ minus 30s.  With Chinese back from long holidays, market participants are expecting the demand revived as petchem margins improved by cheaper feedstock prices. However with the uncertainty on US-China tariff talk, Chinese buyers are still cautious on cargo origins. Huayi issued buy tender for non Us 23/0 delivered for late Oct to Nov delivery basis Schina.

EAST There’s been a modest resurgence in the Eastern market this week, with at least four spot cargoes quoted from the Middle East so far. As October draws to a close, a flurry of offers was seen for the end October stems seen on Thursday, pushing freight rates down into the low $60s RT/C. Looking ahead, it’s difficult to dispute that the market appears oversupplied with tonnage.  WEST Activity on freight finally revived following an adjustment in Owners ideas for November. Last done now stand at $132 HCvP on a modern pmax, and $124.50 HCvP on a Neo type ship. Arb econs still remain challenging however, and with most of the remaining positions in October being ‘Owner controlled’ we are yet to see any further fixtures in this window. Current spot fixture count in October at 21 (8/9/4 by decade), while we have seen 2 deals in 1st decade of November.

A relatively muted week on spot in the Atlantic as a gap between bids and offers has emerged for 1H November loadings, with most owners not in a rush to lock in vessels for what might be their final rotation before the year’s end. The potential for seasonal demand spikes and for further geopolitical disruptions to European gas supplies during the winter, such as the TTF uptick following the Qatari disruptions this week (later confirmed to have no effect on LNG shipping), may explain some of the hesitation ahead of December TTF/JKM pricing next week; however, the fundamentals are still winning out and longer periods are priced largely flat through to Q1 and even beyond well into 2026. There has been an uptick in activity in the Pacific this week with a number of vessels on subs for prompt employment, and although levels remain higher than in the Atlantic they are under downward pressure.   Long-term sentiment is underpinned by a good number of structural requirements from fleet renewal and the huge wave of supply coming towards the end of the decade, including further progress on pre-FID projects. However, the immediate outlook is hampering discussions for multiyear periods starting in the next 6-12 months.

The Panamax market firmed as the week progressed, overcoming the early-week slowdown caused by Asian holidays. In the Atlantic, a tightening tonnage list in the North has lifted sentiment and rates, with grain fronthauls commanding a premium over quieter mineral runs, while the South Atlantic held largely steady. The Pacific also strengthened, particularly on North Pacific rounds where limited spot tonnage forced charterers seeking prompt cover to pay above last-done levels. Although overall inquiry was muted early in the week, owners have regained confidence, and with fresh demand expected to return, both basins look set to maintain a firmer tone heading into mid-October.

Tonnage in the west remains extremely tight this side of the weekend so expect owners to have the bit between their teeth. Considering the number of private/public deals we have seen in the West it does appear that we are approaching the conclusion of Octobers’ West Africa program so this avenue may start to close - with the current dynamic reaching into November dates seems illogical. However, we have yet to hear a peep from CPC or Stateside so if these markets kick start West Africa charterers may not have much time to play with. The MEG has seen a gradual erosion of vessels and the West continues to draw boats out of contention, expect this to lend stability albeit a test is needed for both East and Westbound routes.

The VLCC market has seen a steady slow decline in the week gone by, culminating with a WS 69 fixture MEG/China reported this morning. With much of the Far East on holiday activity has gone under-ground. Ships have been fixed off in a steady tempo but few if any details leaked to the market has fuelled a fear-of-missing-out sentiment. However, daily returns are still in the USD 55-65k range depending on the voyage/ship in question and although we might see a bit more profit taking, independent owners have started stepping on the break paddle. The Atlantic has also sprung back to life again, with USG/east rates back up to USD 10.5 million for the benchmark Ningbo discharge, largely down to very few ships having ballasted west on spec so charterers must make do with what’s already in the area.

North Sea Rates in the North Sea have been fairly steady even though the tonnage list is still short for local candidates. A couple of relets around on hold for internal needs.  Demand will set the tone but if we see any delays with forward deliveries the list will remain tight heading into what looks like a fuller 3rd decade program. Tonnage also looking to head out of the area which will continue to keep pressure on the available tonnage for North Sea cargoes.  Mediterranean Mediterranean has been busy with vessels taken quietly all week and WS 155 repeated many times for the benchmark TD19. Tonnage list has cleared out in the front end with few ppt/safe vessels available. We are seeing some itineraries slip which is also keeping pressure on the list. Dates are well into the 3rd decade now for all ports as charterers try and secure early safe tonnage and pressure from the owners' side doesn't seem to be fading.

The Handysize and Ultramax markets opened the week on a subdued and mostly positional tone, with activity levels muted across the board. In the Atlantic, the Continent and Mediterranean regions remained steady, supported by a consistent flow of cargo, while the South Atlantic and U.S. Gulf showed signs of softening amid slower demand. Sentiment in Asia was equally quiet, largely impacted by widespread holidays, keeping both owners and charterers in a wait-and-see mode. Overall, the market remains balanced but cautious.

Quieter start to the week on all basins due to Golden week and Korea off as well. Activity level picked up as we approached midweek. On the C5 front we see operators out for late Oct dates with miners present as well. Several forward enquires for Nov/Q4 as well. On the tonnage side, we see typhoon affecting vessel itineraries, causing an overall thinning of available tonnage 14-18 days out. This coupled with recovered activity midweek led to a steady climb to mid USD 9 pmt levels done. Other fronts of the pacific remain relatively quiet. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, we see enquiries for early up to mid November dates. Operators seem to be in risk averse mode. Offers are generally in the USD 24 pmt levels and up range, bids generally at sub USD 23 to sub USD 24 pmt levels. C3 remains quiet this week.

Mixed sentiment this week across the larger crude sizes, and a range of opinion on the strength of Q4 earnings. On the back of the recent rally, where VLCCs have seen spot rates of around USD 100K/day, it seems bizarre to question earnings but softer FFAs and a quiet Chinese market with the beginning of Golden Week has people thinking on the resilience of this crude market. On second hand tonnage, modern, large transactions remain at a premium, but it is the clean space that is picking up once again. MRs enjoyed plenty of liquidity at the beginning of the year, and this looks to be returning as prices appear to have bottomed out. T MATTERHORN (47K DWT Iwagi Zosen 2010) sold for USD 20M, with SSDD due in Dec 25 and TC attached until Q1 26.   The dry market appears to be flourishing; values have corrected upwards across the sector very rapidly and there is a healthy amount of buying interest across each subsector. While there are some submarket fundamentals that warrant this buoyant outlook, other subsectors are seeing values increase despite potentially testing times ahead. To this point, the ultramax sector has a reported 179 ships to be delivered in 2026, the highest number in a decade, but values and demand for candidates are both still very strong. This week ANDIAMO (63K DWT Shin Kasado 2019) sold for USD 30.5M, against last done 2019 ultramax MONA LISA (63K DWT Imabari 2019) at USD 29.5M back in August.

The VLGC shipping market activity has been subdued both east and west of Suez so far this week. Narrowing arb econs and the annoucement of CP hasn’t helped, however, following year-to-date fixing history there should be room for more business to be done.  Whilst the MEG position list may look long at first glance, more than half of these available vessels are also potential US candidates via Cape from 1H November onwards.   We currently count 12 spot fixtures ex MEG in October (4/6/2 by decade) and 20 spot fixtures ex US in October (8/9/3 by decade). November fixing is yet to begin, however, some questions surrounding freight have submerged for early November with bids hoovering the mid USD 120’s with no takers yet.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Saudi Aramco cut Oct Cp to $495 for C3 and $475 for C4, which fall shorts of market expectations as earlier recommendation reported at over $540 for C3. The surprising price reduction is reckoned as strategic move to spark term buyer interest, especially when Indian NOCs issued buy term tender for US stems. Forward month Cp swaps immediately dived and at the time of writing, Nov Cp C3 was only traded at $468. The price drop stimulated the buying interests and cash differential for AG FOB Nov rapidly changed from minus mid single digit to teens premium.    Comparatively, US fobs remained illiquid as of the narrowing ARB. Cp link AG cargos are more affordable especially to Chinese players. Notional netback to CFR Asia is assessed at 3ish cpg which is close to cancellation level and we’ve heard a couple of late Oct lifting parcels were reported cancelled.   CFR Asia market is in great volatility with spot price extend losses as of dull demand over uncertainties. 23/0 for 1h Nov delivery basis Chiba was offered at Nov FEI minus $13 yet to attract bid. HTC was reported to award their buy tender for 23/0 for late Nov delivery at Oct FEI plus small digit. E1 also issued spot tender to procure a 2/2 for Nov delivery.

The VLCC market, as with everything else, is all about perception, what you think you see versus what it really is. The perception the last couple of days is that we are in for a downturn and charterers are going to play the Golden Week holiday, starting today, for all it’s worth in trying to soften owner’s resolve. And yes, the market has shed 10-15 points MEG/east, but then again China's largest charterer - knowing more than most - reportedly repeated a WS 90 MEG/China without much further ado yesterday. We’ve seen very little concluded mid-October onwards and if we are to end up with 155 or more fixtures for the month it could prove to be a restless holiday. The west/east arb momentarily opening up with a couple of corresponding fixtures has added some optimism in the Atlantic too. We might of course see a bit more shaved off rates both east and west before it levels off, but there’s always more to it than meets the eye.

As we approach Golden week, quieter on all ends of the pacific.  Some players are out seeking for mid October C5 dates.  Activity for East Australia coal has generally fallen this week.  On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, we see a build up of ballasters and bids are a rare sight.  Prompt tonnage is accumulating out of the pacific which might create more downward pressure for early November C3 dates.  Fixtures concluded at sub USD 9 pmt levels for C5 and low USD 23 pmt levels for Oct/Nov split dates C3.

The Supramax/Ultramax market ended September on a relatively muted tone as holidays in Asia slowed activity, leaving sentiment in the East soft with charterers maintaining the upper hand. The Atlantic, however, retained a firmer footing, though some questioned whether the recent push from the US Gulf had already peaked. The Continent and Mediterranean were seen as steady, while the South Atlantic stayed finely balanced. In Asia, prompt tonnage continued to weigh on sentiment, with rates slipping lower across both regional and Indian Ocean positions. As the monsoon season comes to an end, we however do see more cargoes volumes ex West Coast India. Period interest surfaced, though with mixed levels compared to previous reports and the bid/offer spread is too wide in present levels. Overall, the index average started correcting, reflecting softer conditions despite steady demand from the Atlantic.

The steady flow of requirements in the Atlantic appears to have absorbed much of the modern tonnage willing or able to show flexibility off October dates, with the remaining time- or price-sensitive availabilities held back for now. The most recent fixing levels suggest a floor may have been reached and also interest in multimonth requirements imply some charterers are now ready to snap up tonnage for winter, but the year has taught us not to get ahead of ourselves… either way, an immediate rebound in rates is unlikely given the overall supply imbalance. Requirements further out are yet to garner much interest at the lower end of the rate range of recent weeks, but we shall see how the market shapes up as we approach the fixing window. The Pacific continues to lag somewhat with lower liquidity, as challenges for owners remaining cold seem more likely to curb oversupply as opposed to a resurgence of requirements.   There is still a lot of interest in the medium- and long-term space, with some interesting pricing signs for existing and newbuild tonnage emerging for the remainder of the decade.

So far this week the silence has battered sentiment despite supply and demand fundamentals that at the week's outset suggested some form of stability. 2nd decade West Africa appears to have been covered on the most part with very few reported deals, and Guyana seems to be heading the same way.  However, we start today with 7 vessels on subs in the USG - that leaves 0 in ballast with just 3 sailing in the next 10 days. As a result outstanding USG/Guyana cargoes will have to drag vessels from this side of the Atlantic and will likely face renewed bullishness. Owners will be hoping this translates to corresponding markets.  Aside from an Indian quote the MEG was quiet yesterday. Tonnage has grown and overall sentiment has declined as VLCCs have trended downwards.

The Panamax market has struggled this week with sentiment firmly on the back foot. In the Atlantic, a lack of fresh mineral demand and thinning trans-Atlantic volumes have weighed on rates, while fronthaul interest out of the US East Coast has not been enough to absorb the growing tonnage list across the Continent and Mediterranean. East Coast South America continues to slide as charterers push levels down despite owners’ resistance. In the Pacific, Golden Week has drained activity with most Chinese requirements already covered, leaving limited fresh demand and spot ships struggling to find employment. With FFA support also absent, fixtures are being concluded below last done and the near-term outlook remains soft.

North Sea After a flurry of activity at the end of last week clearing the last of the September requirements October has started on the slower side.  The available tonnage remains thin but with relets available  and at least so far a lack of activity the market is likely to remain steady as we push into the 2nd decade fixing window.  US markets continue to pull tonnage away but this is relatively balanced with tonnage coming  back laden.  Mediterranean  Market has been active under the radar with vessels being picked up quietly by Charterers at more or less last-done levels. We are approaching mid October dates for all ports. Tonnage list is still balanced considering the amount of cargoes and the fixing window being forward now.  Rates are voyage / date sensitive with Owners able to be selective on cargo choice.

Liquidity in the tanker market is still an issue, with modern units particularly difficult to come by. That said, sentiment is buoyant, leading some to even wonder if perhaps we are at the beginning of a supercycle. Sentiment, however, is one thing, and owners know there are plenty of deliveries and much potential uncertainty ahead. In the afra sector, YINGHAO CONFIDENCE (107K DWT Tsuneishi 2010) was sold for USD 36M.  Headlines were stolen this week with Asyad purchasing scrubber fitted Newcastlemax trio BULK SANTIAGO/SANDEFJORD/SHENZHEN (207K DWT New Times 2019/2020) en bloc at USD 209M, with delivery in early 2026. Newcastlemax units have experienced a sharp spike in demand over recent months, with a handful of deals concluded recently and enquiry still high. The dry sector is seeing a general rise in value, particularly illustrated in the Ultramax sector where sales are beating last dones. BULK CASTOR (66K DWT Mitsui 2015) was sold for USD 24.2M and BEAUTY LILY (63K China Shipping Jiangsu 2015) sold at USD 22.25, showing the 10-year-old benchmarks for the sector and the current delta between Japanese and Chinese built units.

EAST The first ten days of October in the MEG have seen subdued spot activity, with freight rates softening from the high $70s/ton to the low $70s/ton. The MEG market is also becoming more segmented, with a growing divide between India-bound and non-India-bound business. This bifurcation, combined with USTR developments, continues to shape rate dynamics and vessel positioning strategies.  WEST The USG market remains underfixed for October, with spot activity trailing the year-to-date monthly average of 29 fixtures. While freight rates are fundamentally driven by the balance of supply and demand, the current landscape is heavily influenced by fleet concentration. Notably, BW LPG and Helios control eight of the twelve VLGCs on the position list. This consolidation of tonnage has effectively capped downward rate pressure, as these owners show limited willingness to entertain levels in the low USD 150s/ton.
