comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Cash differentials for FOB AG remain strong, firmly backed by the Indian buying demand. BPCL tendered to procure up to 3 lots of 2/2 evenly split cargo for Nov and Dec delivery, either FOB AG or CFR. One 18-20 Oct lifting 2/2 cargo was changed hand at Nov CP minus mid-teens, which equates to Oct CP minus small single digit. 1st round Oct CP recommendation was heard at $540 to $560 for C3, and C3/C4 spread at $20. By the time of writing, Oct CP was traded at $541, Oct C3/C4 at $22 and Oct/Nov CP was traded at $16 contango.  Terminal fee for Oct lifting FOBs ex US was assessed at 4ish cpg amid subdued activities. Arbitrage to EAST market narrowed down as MB stands firmer against the softening FEI. US propane/propylene stock rose by 1m bbl., lower than expected.    Spot discounts for CFR east market plunged further, with 23/0 for 2h Oct delivery basis Chiba being traded at Oct FEI minus $17, vs last week’s minus $11. Similar parcel for 1h Nov delivery was bid at Oct FEI minus $2.5. Outside window such parcels were traded at Oct FEI minus $0.5/0.75 or Nov FEI minus mid high single digit reportedly. Two Chinese PDH players have issued buy tender for propane delivery during 2h Oct to 1h Nov delivery, with one excluding US origin, with uncertainties over US-China tariff talk. Other PDH yet to move, partially discouraged by the negative margins which lead to potential maintenance. One NChina importer issued term tender to secure 6 or 12 propane cargos, including US origin for next year delivery.

Spot charter rates have continued their decline this week despite a few more requirements emerging, mainly due to the oversupply of modern tonnage particularly in the Atlantic Basin. A handful of players had suggested a possible floor on freight at which traders would see more value in arbitrage opportunities to go East rather than subletting; however, with FOB bids pricing in-house tonnage very low, spot shipping is having to compete ever more aggressively and the result is yet more downward pressure. The Pacific Basin remains awash with idle tonnage and fresh multimonth enquiries from the Middle East saw competitive offers across vessel sizes and types. The prospect of a firming winter now seems very remote, with both FFAs and offer for physical tonnage holding fairly flat through until early 2026.  Whilst the long-term views coming from Gastech this year were wholly positive and have been bolstered by fresh reports of FIDs for new U.S. projects this week, reconciling the soft market of today and the likely conditions through the interim period remains challenging. There are a handful of requirements for periods bridging that stark contrast in sentiment. However, the gap between bid and offer for structural availabilities is likely to remain wide for the time being.

On the C5 front, we see miners and operators out seeking for early up to mid October dates. Periphery volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the pacific have held up since last week. Overall healthy levels as fixtures concluded at high USD 10 pmt levels for C5. On the buy side, we see strong volumes with excess of 10 spot fixtures ex West Australia concluded yesterday, typical daily average is 6-7. On sell side, upside is further exacerbated by typhoon in South China and increasing attractiveness to ballast, resulting in fewer candidates in the pacific. On the C3 ex Brazil and West Africa front, enquiries are primarily for end October and October/November split dates. Number of ballasters is thinning across all dates. Fixtures have concluded in the high USD 25 pmt levels, up more than USD 1 pmt from mid last week.

A few mysteries coming to light today as charterers continue to pick off vessels for 2nd decade West Africa. Availabilities remain reasonable albeit extension over the weekend isn’t huge. The balance between available tonnage, remaining stems and how forward we are working indicates a bit of mounting pressure albeit not substantial. If we had demand impetus from CPC and USG we would argue on the contrary but with strong coverage in the Black Sea and cheaper Aframaxes in the states these regions may not offer support right away. The VLCCs in the MEG continue to fix at healthy levels despite some ‘cheaper’ rumours earlier this week. Expect this heightened sentiment to trickle down to Suezmaxes, despite a healthier list for the smaller ladies.

Supramax sentiment in the Atlantic stayed firm, led by continued strength in the US Gulf and steady demand further north, though some felt the South Atlantic was looking a bit toppy. In contrast, Pacific remained under pressure with charterers in control and owners cautious about repositioning, as negative sentiment remained. The Handysize market showed a mixed tone: the South Atlantic stayed strong, the Continent and Mediterranean were stable with a slightly firmer bias, the US Gulf was quieter with only marginal gains.

The week gone by has been a roller coaster ride in the VLCC market. The whole of last week saw a continued upward trajectory culminating at W105 MEG/east, repeated several times. West Africa and Brazilian exports followed suit, helped further by USG exports paying into the $12 million for the benchmark Ningbo discharge. However, Monday came with a couple of surprise fixtures reported done at W95 MEG/China for a couple of oil company relets. A Mexican stand off followed with independent owners refusing to recognise these as relevant to the market. The stubbornness paid off with Baltic’s TD15 estimate coming in at W102 and change yesterday evening. We have yet to see same printed, but the downside appears firmly capped with several fixtures concluded around the W100 mark since. However, the sky is not without clouds. The surge in shipping costs and WTI premiums has all but shut the US-Asia oil arbitrage putting a damper on the Atlantic market.

The Panamax market has been split this week, with the Atlantic struggling to find momentum while the Pacific has shown a firmer tone. In the North Atlantic, limited fresh inquiry and a growing list of available tonnage continue to weigh on sentiment, with charterers pushing levels down and owners holding back from deeper discounts. South America has been steadier, with grain flows helping to absorb some of the nearby tonnage, though forward positions remain flat. By contrast, the Pacific has been more active, with steady demand from Indonesia and Australia, charterers covering ahead of Golden Week in China, and weather delays tightening supply in parts of the basin, all lending a more positive outlook compared to the Atlantic.

North Sea A slow first half of the week clearing out the last few September stems. Available tonnage does still remain relatively tight but early October stems aren’t overly populated and tonnage will start to come back into position. We have seen a fair amount of tonnage ballast out recently both to US and Mediterranean. US markets had softened and were quiet but have seen an uptick in activity and rates look like they have hit bottom and likely to bounce back firmer which will encourage more ballasting. Market looking likely to remain stable heading into October fixing.  Mediterranean Cargo flow has remained healthy in the Mediterranean as the early part of the 1st decade in the Mediterranean and Black Sea is almost sold-out. Despite a couple of vessels being picked up, there are still enough around for local or longer runs. USG activity is busier and it's likely that will attract more to ballast going forward in the hope of a bounce back.

The story on tanker market remains largely the same this week, though with increasing anticipation of a strong period of earnings for crude tonnage. Modern units remain at a premium, shown in the sale of LR2 SILVERSTONE (113K DWT SWS 2025), bought by Transpetrol for USD 75M. Liquidity is increasing at the other end of the age curve with OLYMPIC SEA/SKY (104K DWT SWS 2008) being sold at USD $29.5M each.   Several ships taking offers this month has provided the dry market with somewhat of a recalibration. Firstly, in the ultramax sector, BULK CASTOR (66K DWT Mitsui 2015) took offers on Tuesday and is rumoured to have seen levels in the mid 24Ms. The final figure is likely to exceed this, given the reported sale of scrubber fitted AFRICAN CHEETAH (66K DWT Mitsui 2014) at USD 24M, following the same bidding process. Capesize WAKAYAMA MARU (181K DWT Koyo 2013) was bought by Asyad for USD 37M, setting the new benchmark for a non eco Japanese cape. Spot rates across the smaller sizes are at similar levels to the peaks of last year, and comparative asset prices suggest there could be some further upside for owners in what is now a seller’s market.

The Panamax market softened this week as sentiment turned negative across both basins, with the approach of the final quarter weighed down by muted US soybean demand into China and softer coal dynamics as the heat-driven rally faded. In the Atlantic, trans-Atlantic and fronthaul activity remained thin with fresh demand lacking, leaving owners and charterers increasingly divided on levels as the bid-offer gap widened. South America also slowed, with owners discounting to chase limited interest. In the Pacific, momentum stalled despite steady cargo counts ex-NoPac and Australia, with charterers holding back and selectively fixing while offers drifted lower, leaving the market direction uncertain and dependent on fresh replenishment to halt the slide.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: Cash differentials for Oct FOBs ex AG have edged up with strong butane demand from both India and China. Qatar Energy is reported to award their late Oct FOB 2/2 sale tender to a producer trading arm at Oct CP minus $5. HPCL also issued buy tender to secure 2/2 either FOB or CFR for Oct and Nov delivery. By the time of writing, Oct C3 CP was traded at $545 and C3/C4 at $23, Oct/Nov C3 CP at assessed at $12 contango.   While on the other hand, US fobs are less attractive amid firm MB price against solid freight, with netback of Oct and Nov lifting for EAST market at 4ish cpg only. US propane and propylene stock increased by 1.3 mil bbl, which is lower than expected and leaving inventory almost flat YOY basis.   On CFR Asia window, spot differentials fell further with a number of 23/0 parcels for 2h Oct delivery basis Chiba, being traded from Oct FEI minus $5 to minus $8/9ish. 46/0 parcel for 2h Oct delivery basis Chiba was offered at Oct FEI minus $15 vs bid at minus $19. Outside window discussions are less active as soaring costs for non-US stems into China eroded the petchem margins. Both Huayi and FIC were reported to cancel their tenders for non-Us propane for Oct delivery, with few favourable offers. FIC reissued tender to procure 23-46kt C3 for 2h Oct delivery into Ningbo including US origin, and FPC also tendered to buy flexible ratio for late Oct to Nov delivery into Mailiao. One 11k C3 non-Us for Oct delivery was heard sold into SChina at $590s and one 46kt C3 parcel for Oct delivery basis Ningbo was reported done at Oct FEI minus high single.

EAST With Saudi acceptances released last night, October programs are now being finalized. Freight earnings in the East are currently trailing the West market by approximately $10 per metric tonne. September fixing appears to have wrapped up, with a final fixture concluded today by a Middle Eastern producer. October fixing is expected to begin imminently. However, with just two weeks remaining before October and minimal fixing activity so far, one possible explanation being speculated is that these cargoes are held by Indian Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs).  WEST We have seen 18 deals ex US for October (8/9/1 by decade) and currently count about 10+ open ships left for the month. Owners’ ideas have ranged from low/mid usd 150s to 160+ depending on dates, but no deals have really been concluded since market reached a high last week. While Arb has narrowed overnight, we are still seeing potentially 4-5 cargos being looked at ex USG either as FOB sellers or freight buyers.

The market opened the week on a muted tone, with sentiment remaining firmer across the Atlantic while Asia saw softer activity, particularly from the south. The US Gulf continued to show a positional feel, though seems like demand for fronthauls was easing. The South Atlantic stayed balanced, with fundamentals in the Continent and Mediterranean largely unchanged. In Asia, northern demand persisted, but opportunities further south appeared more limited for owners. Period activity emerged in the Atlantic, showing some continued appetite from charterers despite the quieter backdrop. Overall, the Atlantic held its ground while Asia remained under pressure.

The market is pushing into China's Golden Week, in line with usual seasonal developments. October FFA is trading over 30.000 USD pd, with C5 reportedly done above 11 USD pmt and C3 remains around 24 USD pmt. Normally, there is a market correction following the Golden Week.

We’re normally strapping ourselves in for spot rates’ annual trip to the moon at this time each year, but it appears as though the shuttle has been grounded in 2025. With an endless stream of uncovered cargos to be shipped, the hope for Owners is that vessel supply starts to dry-up as portfolios horde their tonnage as an insurance policy against any weather driven (or geopolitically driven) spikes. Unfortunately for those who are long tonnage, this has not happened. To focus on the positives, the spot market is working exactly the way it’s meant to - and this is great news for the handful of Charterers who are not also Owners. For everyone else (which is actually everyone else…) who is reliant upon a winter premium to balance the books in 2025, there’s just way too much vessel supply on offer to make this a plausible outcome for now. Of course, this is the cyclical nature of LNG shipping and whilst we need to brace for a couple of years of low spot rates, as mentioned in last week’s circular, the long-term outlook for the industry is very bullish. Reviews from Gastech have highlighted the sheer number of portfolios looking for long-term tonnage and this means that there’s more than enough work to keep Owners and Charterers busy for now. And whilst it might only be jam tomorrow for Owners, it at least provides some line of sight to better times ahead for all of us.

"Show me the money honey" - Rates have continued to firm since in the week gone by and VLCC owners are now seeing earnings at $90-100k per day and above, which is in Word Scale terms is circa W105 for MEG/eastbound voyages. The MEG cargo count for September came in north of 165 in the MEG, up from the previous month, and the October program promises to be higher still. USG-East movements have also increased and the list of candidates for the current loading window is very slim. There are  question marks whether current levels are sustainable into the winter months, but the here now show no sign of weakening.

Within the current fixing window in WAF, we currently have abt. 12 vessels in ballast, with an additional of 20 vessels expected to supplement the list by Sunday. In terms of cargo coverage, we likely have sub 10 mbbls remaining. Despite the significant number of vessels expected to sail in the coming days and limited 1st decade cargoes left to cover in WAF, we expect that there should still be sufficient activity elsewhere in the West to help balance the list. Additionally, if the current strength on the VLCC’s continues, we expect that the sentiment may override the underlying fundamentals.   In the AG, the tonnage list is comparatively tighter and prospects remain strong, with VLCC’s holding at elevated levels. We are likely to see further VLCC stems split into Suezmaxes.

NSEA Dates are pushing well into 3rd decade and available tonnage for natural nsea owners is on the light side for balance of the month.  Rates have moved up since last week and we could still see some tight points which may see owners make further gains.  MED A couple of cargoes off end-month dates worked yesterday in the market or quietly with Owners pushing above last-done on some specific ones. Tonnage list is getting shorter but expected to replenish a bit despite some few more ballasters to the States and at the same time we are closer to be sold-out for September.

Despite the ongoing support from the underlying freight markets, tanker SnP activity remains subdued. Modern assets remain particularly challenging to transact with a resilient bid/offer spread, while values of older tonnage appear to have bottomed out, leading sellers to hold back and reassess. In the mid-aged VLCC market, the scrubber-fitted FPMC KNIGHT (301K DWT Universal 2011) was sold for USD 55M.  Dry cargo markets are also yielding better-than-expected returns for owners. Although we are witnessing higher second-hand activity including more modern vessels changing hands, current rates are similarly consolidating sellers' expectations.  This week, Precious Shipping secured the wide beam ultramax sisters JAL KALPAVRIKSH/KALPATARU (66K DWT, Mitsui 2021) for USD 32.55 million each.

text: Cash differentials for Oct FOB AG evenly split grade grew firmer, supported by strong butane demand. Buyers are bidding at CP minus low teens, yet to attract offers. IOC was reported to award their Q4 buy tender for evenly split cargo, with some on CFR basis at CP plus 40s, which lent support on netbacks to Oct FOBs. HPCL also issued buy tender to secure similar parcel for Oct and Nov delivery. By the time of writing, Oct CP was assessed at $550 and C3/C4 at $25. Oct/Nov CP was traded at $10 contango structure.   Spot terminal fee softened from earlier 5ish cpg to 4ish cpg for Oct liftings FOBs, as of strong freight. However, players are still actively lifting tons in view of current arbitrage to EAST and contango structure for forward months.    Window discussions slightly improved. 23kt C3 parcel for 1h Oct delivery basis Chiba was changed hand at Oct FEI minus $8.0, while similar parcel for 2h Oct delivery bid at minus $7.5 yet to entice seller appetite. Outside window limited talks on spot market as of ongoing Appec meetings. Most discussions are centered around changes on new trade flows, term negotiations due to the US-China tariff and USTR 301.

EAST The earnings gap between East and West continues to widen, driven by robust US fixing activity and a relatively quiet week in the East, where many market participants are attending APPEC events and meetings in Singapore. A noticeable shift is emerging as more Chinese-controlled vessels seek cargos in the East, aiming to avoid exposure to US and the upcoming USTR penalties. With USTR measures expected to take effect in just over a month, a new normal in the East-West earnings spread may be expected to persist for a while. Meanwhile, the recent attack on Qatari soil is currently looking unlikely to impact security in the Strait of Hormuz, though the situation remains under close observation.  WEST An under fixed October US market took a run at the start of the week following the fixing spree in the Middle East week prior. Shipping positions East and West of Suez goes hand in hand as long as the majority of vessels ballast via Cape, leaving little or no surprises when it comes the visibility of vessel ETAs. At the time of writing there are very few relets in the USG for second half October, which subsequently sets expectation of a strong market to continue throughout the month.

After having roared into the WS 80’s MEG/East rates have dropped back into the low WS 70’s, by and large led by oilco-trader relets taking a less aggressive stand, simultaneously making it more palatable when having the “buyer” hat on. That said, an offer a few weeks back of something starting with a 7 for September loading dates would have endangered the offering hand. However, the question is whether it’s sustainable or if we’ll see a further downward pressure. The “official” cargo board was wanting this morning and with a fixture count around the 140 mark we’re approaching the end of the month’s program with October stems not due out before next week. The Atlantic, however, is still a healthy alternative with USG exports continuing to “pump, baby, pump”, albeit date sensitive. And geopolitical tensions are not making predictions any easier to say the least.

With the party makers and Gastech shakers currently plying their trade throughout Milan, the market can be forgiven for its somewhat lacklustre performance in the first half of this week. Of course, seasonally a lull is expected at this time of year, and one assumes that this annual gathering of LNG protagonists is timed accordingly to combat depressing rate levels with some industrywide bonhomie. Rejuvenated and reseated at their desks next week, the hope is that the powers that be will ensure that trading volumes recover in time to provide Owners with the Christmas present they so justly deserve. This might sound like wishful thinking from a shipbroker who is wading through the market doldrums, but with Corpus Christi, LNG Canada and Barossa all set to push additional volumes onto the water in Q4, all that’s needed is a prolonged cold snap to flip the current market sentiment on its head. It’s also worth noting that spot shipping is just the very visible tip of the market in which we all operate and as observant readers of Tradewinds will have noted, vessel recycling, LNG bunkering and long-term tendering activities are all continuing apace. In short, whilst those of us operating in the short-term chartering market might be agitating for increased levels of activity, when the LNG shipping market is considered as a whole, we’ve probably all never been busier. Enjoy the rest of your week!

The Atlantic Supramax and Handysize markets showed a generally firm tone, though momentum varied across regions. In the US Gulf, Supramax sentiment remained positive with stronger levels being discussed, while Handysize activity was subdued and continued to trend softer. The South Atlantic was the standout, where both sizes benefited from tighter tonnage lists and healthy demand, supporting firmer sentiment and encouraging charterers to bid higher. The Continent–Mediterranean remained finely balanced, with little fresh cargoes in the Supramaxes and only modest improvements on the Handysize side.

The Panamax market sustained its upward momentum this week, with the Atlantic continuing to show strong fundamentals. Tight nearby tonnage and firm mineral demand from the USEC, Colombia, and Baltic supported higher ideas, while ECSA remained more balanced but still saw P6 supported by October spot requirements. In the Pacific, fresh demand from NoPac and Australia, coupled with consistent Indonesian coal activity, kept sentiment buoyant, with charterers actively chasing coverage and owners holding the upper hand. Although some resistance remains on the bid side, the overall tone across both basins is firmly bullish, underpinned by resilient demand and limited tonnage availability, with market participants watching October volumes closely to assess whether current strength can be sustained.

A handful of cargoes have been worked so far this week in the North Sea and rates have been corrected downward. Still some prompt vessels that needs to find employment, but some of them might find alternatives in the USG where rates been pushing up again for a usg/ta run. But even with some ships ballasting towards usg, we don’t expect rates in the North Sea to change anytime soon.  The Mediterranean market has been going sideways with limited activity and charterers reaching a bit datewise with some already looking for cover well into the 3rd decade of September. The tonnage list looks fairly balanced with some vessels ballasting out of the area and some ballasting in from a lackluster Cont market. Trend is still sideways, but with a downward pressure unless we see an increased activity level.

Despite lacklustre volumes overall ex West Africa (we are on track to take at least 10MBBLs less on Suezmax - close to 20% - in September, compared to a standard month) upsizing US Gulf stems on top of Liza & Brazil moves have contrived to sustain market levels, whilst active CPC and MEG markets continue to fire, all keeping lists condensed. The front end remains very sparse for TD20, just 5 ships roughly FOC, but with supplementation inbound over the weekend and dates fixed sufficiently forwards that charterers will be reluctant to pay up further than WS 110-112.5 levels which have fixed this week. Whilst in the US Gulf, Aframax levels are unlikely to drive further spillover, VLCC rates remain strongly in excess of Suezmax on a 1 parcel basis and additional export volume from the MEG may drive more USG/TA moves and TD20 runs which could help sustain the market in the medium term. From an earnings perspective levels ex West Africa are sufficient to underline owners attempts to keep the MEG at WS120 eastbound on modern tonnage and circa WS 60 westbound via COGH.

On the C5 front, we see miners, operators and some tenders alike out for late September to early October dates. Volumes out of other fronts of the Pacific are rather flat. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, cargo enquiries remain for split dates and second half of October dates primarily. Spot tonnage out of Far East is beginning to tighten. On ballasters, we see some vessels left for split dates and heavily weighted on first half October dates. We see C5 concluding at tick above mid USD 10 pmt levels. On C3, fixtures concluded at mid USD 23 pmt levels for split dates.

Only a trickle of tanker sales to report in the first week back since the official end of summer. Overall, the underlying factor remains, particularly across more modern tonnage, that asset values are on the high side compared to current achievable TC rates. On spot however, there is a mixed story with VLCCs ending the week strongly, while products experience more variable conditions. In the Aframax market, scrubber fitted BLUE PRINCE (109K DWT Hudong Zhonghua 2009) sold for USD 32.7M.    A seemingly extremely busy week in the dry market. This is likely due in part to many returning from summer holidays, with broker channels and information streams up and running once again, but also perhaps a symptom of the overall perception that brighter times are on the horizon for the dry market, with the hope that the TC market will mirror the current buoyant spot earnings. The majority of sales have occurred in the 10+yo space, with investors sensing now is the time to strike for a potential asset play. In the only modern transaction, open hatch LILAC HARMONY (38K DWT Tsuneishi Cebu 2020) sold for USD 25.05M.

WEST Freight in the West is following the East’s trend; we have seen 2 fixtures in the market this week. Fixtures in the East have left the West tighter than what was thought at the beginning of the week, which could support freight in the West. There are currently 10 ships open for the first decade and 2 for the second decade, just over half of these are ballasting via Panama, leaving uncertainty for USG dates. This marks a shift from last week when most open ships were routing via the Cape.  EAST Freight has continued to come off, with one fixture at the beginning of the week reported just below $80 and at least two more suggesting levels in the mid $70s. Attention is likely to soon shift to the final decade of September, as the first two decades have aligned with annual averages - 7 to 8 fixtures. Vessel positions for the remainder of the month shows many ships being available in both the East and the West - as such it looks like the balance of the month may be less long than current sentiment suggests.

Terminal fee for FOB Oct ex US was heard offered at 6 to 7ish, with expectation on winter seasonal demand increment. However, the narrowing ARB and uncertainty US-China tariff talk for Nov onwards, refrained buyers’ appetites on spot trades.  As for the EIA statistics, the 3.2mmbbl build was higher than expected, though the build month-on-month, though a slight decrease of 2.7% year-on-year of 93.1mm. bbls now resides in primary storages, which is 99% of the same time last year.   CFR east window is active with 23/0 for 1h Oct delivery basis Chiba being traded at Oct FEI minus $9.5. Similar parcel for 2h Oct delivery was bid at minus low teens. 4/0 for 1h Oct delivery basis Ningbo was offered at $544, equates to Oct FEI minus small digit.    Outside window a tender galore before the upcoming APPEC meeting. Around 250kt propane were placed into China for end Sep to Oct delivery for feedstock use, with two Canadian stems reported at Oct CP plus 30s and 40s and AG stem at 50s or equivalence basis South/Echina, whereas US origin into NChina at Oct FEI minus mid single digit. One SChina player was reported to buy a 1/1 for late Sep to Oct delivery at Oct CP plus 50s. FPCC also procured one 46/0 for 2h Oct delivery into Mailiao at Oct Mopj minus 50s. HTC was said to buy a late Oct delivered 2/0 at Sep FEI plus low single.

text: The Capesize market has softened this week, with both basins under pressure as sentiment turns cautious. In the Pacific, activity from the majors has been sporadic, with C5 slipping back toward USD 10.00, while in the Atlantic a growing ballaster list and thin enquiry has weighed on C3, despite owners trying to hold mid USD 24,000s. Fundamentally, Chinese steel mill margins have weakened, with rebar profitability turning negative, and the near-month iron ore futures curve in contango - both pointing to downside risks ahead. Iron ore imports remain strong but have eased slightly, while Guinea bauxite exports have picked up, signaling the seasonal low is behind us. With coal markets also cooling, the outlook feels more bearish than last week, and the best of this year’s strength may now be behind us.

A long overdue West African splurge has only served to underline how squeezed TCE parity across all regions is. With the MEG continuing to fix in the realm of 130kt x 120 eastbound, TD20 at 107.5-110 and firm, and the USG short on local availabilities owners are spoilt for choice. To some extent profit taking may curtail real progress from here but with the VLCC market holding over the past 24H both West Africa/MEG markets should benefit with continue appetite. For TD20, we are down to just 3-4 FOC options making 2nd decade dates and just 6-7 overall (provided all are still there today). Most of those ships are ex East as well and not keen to gift already squeezed earnings or fix shorter Nigerian flats westbound. Ball in owners court as we only have a half dozen ETS in the next 24H with further sailers projected/uncertain.

The Panamax market has entered September on a softer note, with both the Atlantic and Pacific struggling to find momentum. In the Atlantic, enquiry has been thin, particularly from ECSA, leaving charterers with the upper hand and owners increasingly willing to discount to secure employment. Transatlantic demand has slowed, while front-haul is offering only limited support, leaving rates under pressure across the basin. The Pacific story is much the same, with an overhang of tonnage against limited Australian and NoPac demand pushing values steadily lower. Despite some ballasting to the West, oversupply remains the dominant theme, and owners are finding it challenging to resist charterers’ pressure. Overall, sentiment is weak, and the market looks set to remain under strain in the near term unless volumes pick up.

Spot charter rates have come under pressure this week with vessel oversupply in both basins leading to fixtures concluded at close to $30,000 pd on modern tonnage. Additional requirements are naturally being shown as charterers look to dip into the weaker sentiment for Atlantic loadings throughout October. Extended periods are still valued at some premium whilst the spot fluctuates within a relatively tight range. Independent owners’ share of the short-term market is likely to continue growing through the balance year with an increase in redeliveries from term charters, as the gap between bid and offer for periods covering 2026/27 remains too wide in most cases. That said, there are a handful of structural requirements coming forward which may lead to more manageable levels for owners in that one-to-two-year space, though competition remains strong. On the longer-term side, fleet replacement and a healthy year for new FID’s continue to fuel discussions for long term coverage following the massive increases in LNG supply set to come online later in the decade.

The V-market is very busy, and ships are being picked off at a breathtaking pace leaving the position list both East and West of Suez wanting. What’s remaining is dominated by oil company and trader relets, and although the perception is they are more logistically- than price focused nobody is going to say no to a bit extra dosh. With a MEG/Taiwan run clocked at WS 65 today we’d venture that TD3C is now well north of WS 65 rather than yesterday’s WS 60.83 Baltic gauge. Like the song goes; “what a difference a day makes”. The USG continues to fire on all cylinders dragging West Africa and Brazil with it, and enticing ships to ballast from the East, further depleting MEG availabilities. A report suggests that OPEC+ are considering another production hike when they meet on September 7th and TD3C paper is trading north of WS 70 for September. A perfect storm brewing?

In the North Sea this week we saw a downward correction in rates. This was anticipated as a local run out of WCN was quoted, attracting a couple of offers from predominantly relets. The supply of tonnage is more than sufficient given the current activity levels, with about half a dozen vessels ready and waiting free of cargo for the next load window. Relets are continuing to absorb early 2nd decade stems, meaning independent owners might feel a bit more pressure with a tonnage list dominated by relets.   Moving on to the Mediterranean, rates have been relatively stable so far this week. Activity has been a bit slower compared to last week, largely because charterers had covered their cargoes well in advance. The tonnage list looks balanced and there should be sufficient supply of available tonnage covering any inquiries in the 14-20 September window.

The market showed firm momentum through past weeks, supported by steady enquiry from the USG, South Atlantic, and balanced sentiment in the Continent–Mediterranean, with Asia also holding positive tone amid tighter northern tonnage. Rates and activity remained healthy, with both spot and period fixtures reported. Starting this week, we saw sentiment stall as US Gulf enquiry slowed and the South Atlantic steadied, while Asia turned softer with prompt tonnage building against limited fresh demand. The Handysize market held a positive tone, with both the Atlantic and Asian basins showing firm sentiment and balanced conditions.

text: US Despite generally softening WTI values, and despite the healthy propane inventory builds that have been seen in recent weeks – those which have bolstered stock levels in the US to an overall total of 93mmbbls – MB propane values continue to firm, perhaps on the heels of gains that have most recently been achieved in the Asian markets or, perhaps, simply an end-of-the-month spike in the pricing structure.  The EIA data shows that overall US production levels remain strong at 2.835mmbbls/day, where conversely the export volumes were sub-average (YTD 2025) at 1.732mmbbls/day.  That combination – if it continues – should allow propane stocks to reach beyond 100mmbbls by the conclusion of the traditional ‘build’ season.  Terminal fees for spot FOB USGC transactions have subsided from the upper 5s cts/gal range to not much more than 5cts/gal at present.

EAST Although activity saw a slight increase this week, freight rates have failed to maintain previous levels. A total of four Indian PSU tenders and a few additional cargoes have been fixed, bringing the fixture count to seven at the time of writing. However, with a still extensive and relet-heavy position list, overall market sentiment remains subdued.  WEST This week has seen increased activity out of the US Gulf, with four fixtures reported - two for the last decade of September and two for the first decade of October. One fixture was also seen out of WAF with the Soyo tender. Freight has softened, fixing levels between $149.5 and $150.5. A significant portion of the VLGC fleet is either sailing or expected to sail via Cape (laden and ballast respectively) which in turn supports freight for prompt activity given that the market is tight on vessel supply and confined to few players controlling the available tonnage. Additionally, concerns over Panama Canal congestion are contributing to the preference for Cape routing.

Activity levels in the Atlantic spot market have been somewhat lacklustre of late, though a slower August can certainly be forgiven in a year when the number of spot fixtures to date already totals close to 300. The resulting sentiment in the West has been a little mixed, with laycans moving out beyond marketed availabilities. Prompter enquiries for end September continue to emerge, though corresponding availabilities are largely untested with many requirements optimisation-led or linked to cargo purchases. All in all, this makes for a rather sideways trajectory for charter rates, as supported by the levels reported for an interbasin fixture for October implying minimal upside priced through the balance of Q4.  Rates have begun to soften in the Pacific despite a small number of fixtures. Tonnage continues to build up on TFDE’s and whilst new volumes are expected online in the next couple of months, current conditions are challenging with additional length brought about by maintenance at one Australian export terminal and limited activity out of the Middle East. New volumes from Barossa expected online in the next couple of months and further LNG Canada ramp up are needed to bring more balance.

The week opened on a firm note for both the Supramax and Handysize segments, with sentiment strengthening across the Atlantic and Asia. In the Atlantic, the Continent–Mediterranean showed improvement on fresh demand, while the South Atlantic and US Gulf gained momentum as a tight tonnage list continued to pressure charterers into higher bids. Asia was notably more active in the Supramax sector, where renewed enquiry lifted rates above last-done levels, while the Handysize market saw a quieter session but maintained a positive state.

Despite Baltic rates easing slightly yesterday and tonnage increasing over the long weekend, the West remains in good shape. In West Africa, both VLCCs and Suezmaxes remain light on second-decade September fixing. Although the tonnage profile may appear to lean on the softer side, prospective demand should be sufficient to counterbalance this. Additionally, CPC, USG, Brazil, and Guyana are expected to draw from the same pool of tonnage, meaning charterers cannot rest on their laurels. The market has the potential to turn quickly, especially with three days remaining before the weekend.  The East, on the other hand, despite showing signs of promise, has a reasonable amount of supplementation of vessels able to make laycans prior September 15th. This has left the market with a steadier feel.

NORTH SEA After a busy couple of weeks with the North Sea rates pushing up over 20 points, this week started slowly.  The loading schedules for the first decade September look a little light on volume, and with relets and Suezmax coming into play we could see a slow down in market activity.  Available tonnage is still on the tighter side which even with a slow down in activity may mean the downside potential on rates is somewhat limited.  MEDITERRANEAN Busy start to the week in the Mediterranean with rates correcting and charterers have taken tonnage at the lower rates for the 1st decade.  Tonnage list has cleared up but dates are also pushing forward for now. Surrounding areas are holding strong so we don’t foresee further correction on the rates for local Mediterranean runs for now.

The Panamax market has carried a steady and constructive tone into this week, with support coming from both Atlantic and Pacific basins. In the Atlantic, coal demand from the USEC and Baltic continues to soak up tonnage, leaving the nearby position list tight and giving owners the confidence to push ideas higher. South America has also remained well-supported, though some charterers have stepped back as the week progresses. In Asia, demand ex-Australia and NoPac has helped underpin the market, keeping sentiment positive even as charterers show some resistance on numbers. On the fundamentals side, grain flows remain clouded by Trump’s trade war, with US corn exports hitting record highs to non-Chinese buyers, while soybean demand is muted as China leans on inventories and South American supply. Coal, meanwhile, continues to provide a solid backbone for Panamax demand. All in all, the market tone remains firm, and owners’ sentiment is buoyant as we move further into the week.

After having been on an upward trajectory in the week gone by the Baltic Index shed a bit across the board yesterday although probably more down to lack of reported deals than anything else > (perceived) inactivity = (perceived) lower rates. On the flip side there’s been a couple of Indian marked cargoes which, if not a King’s ransom, has had to dig deep. Among them a short MEG/WC India run reportedly paid WS 100 and a WS 68 equivalent was concluded for a West Africa/WC India cargo. However, the “emperor’s new clothes” strategy will struggle unless the owning community can back it up with widely reported confirmed fixtures. That said, a MEG/East market in the mid WS 60’s was probably more than most expected it to be before we even turn the page from the summer to autumn calendar. But as some author once said “Desire is an odd thing. As soon as it’s sated, it transmutes. If we receive golden thread, we desire the golden needle”.

On the C5 front, we see miners and operators alike out seeking for mid September dates. Volumes out of other fronts of the Pacific have held up fairly well. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, cargo enquiries are primarily for 20 September onwards to split dates. Spot tonnage out of Far East is beginning to tighten. Ballasting tonnage is heavily weighted towards end September dates with a handful still able to meet mid September dates. We see C5 concluding at low to mid USD 10 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at high USD 24 pmt levels for end September dates with USD 25 pmt levels done for mid October dates.

text: US With only a couple of recent transactions on which to base a terminal fee price assessment, it is clear – despite calculated netbacks - that the Gulf Coast market ranges from 5.50-6.00cpg for September.  October values are likely just on the higher end of that range and are seen at 6.00cpg and above.  Aside from those few deals, very little is occurring as holidays, vacations, and events have many regular market participants away from their desks. As for the EIA statistics, the 2.6mmbbl build was a surprise to many, but in any case an overall total of 91.20mmbbls now resides in primary storages, which is 99% of the same time last year.   Production levels in the U.S. remain entirely robust at 2.851mmbbls/day – 98% of the historical maximum level.  Export volumes at 1.719mmbbls/day continue at just below the 2025 YTD average of 1.835mmbbls/day, but are expected to increase as the newly installed Flex capacity has by now been engaged.

EAST The MEG market has so far this week been the one and only driver of activity in the VLGC market. At the end of last week, big question were looming around what’s next for freight in the wake of the Saudi acceptances for September being released the coming Sunday; since Monday, five fixtures have been concluded for laycans in the 1st decade of the month and unless there are further discharge port delays or sudden fixing appetite from the USG that tightens the vessel availability, the market looks set to continue hovering the high USD 80s per ton on a Ras Tanura/Chiba equivalent basis.  WEST The fixing count in the USG for September has reached 26 deals and as such is slightly behind being on par with previous months’ fixing records. At the time of writing for September there are still four out of seven vessels on both position lists, which purports to explain why rates (in both basins) remain resilient. It is likely that we will see a few more September deals being done in the USG and October fixing should not be far away. There is a cargo tender ex Angola for loading end September which is likely to attract attention during next week. Activity has picked up in the 2nd and 3rd decades of September, with a total of 20 fixtures registered between the two periods. Little to no activity this week since the Pertamina tender earlier this week, while broader sentiment remains subdued as players await clearer market direction following Aramco’s September acceptances. In general, shipping activity has otherwise been muted, awaiting further cargo availability.

Yesterday was very busy, with Guyana, CPC, and West Africa all firming. Expect owners to continue to have the bit between their teeth today. We do have around 16 West Africa contenders sailing over the weekend, but considering the 3 week window reaches out to the 15th September on Monday, charterers do not have time on their side to sit on cargoes.  Activity in the East has been strong this week and supply remains stretched on the front end - the likelihood for vessels to choose to head to COGH also remains high. Market continues on a strong footing as we approach the weekend.

VLCC rates have held up remarkably well over the past couple of weeks during a generally lacklustre summer period. Increased OPEC+ output coupled a working West-East arb has boosted owners’ confidence and MEG/East rates have fluctuated in the WS 50-60 band, albeit struggled to break through the WS 60 mark in earnest. Charterers are doing their utmost to keep a lid on proceedings by targeting a limited selection of ships quietly under the radar. To quote Dalai Lama; "A lack of transparency results in distrust and a deep sense of insecurity." However, as the regular run of the mill early month cargo program is coming into play for September there’s now a real potential for MEG/East rates to establish themselves in the WS 60’s. Increased USG exports eastbound in addition to an ever-growing Brazilian export program has also underpinned demand and balanced tonnage availability geographically.

The ebb and flow of a soft summer market continues across all basins. In the Atlantic, after the record-breaking July followed by a much quieter August, the market is now beginning to pick up again although rates remain stubbornly range-bound. The Pacific basin had taken up a bit of the slack offered by the Atlantic but without coming close to matching the hectic pace of fixing in the West, while the Middle East has also been a little quiet of late following the surge of activity earlier in the summer that emphasised how important the region has become. For periods a little longer, the bid (and to an extent, the offer) suggests a fairly flat winter and one in which charterers will likely feel comfortable with a little more spot exposure… so we may be in for a busy winter.  After a quiet few months at the shipyards, this week felt like a bonanza with six orders reported by Samsung on behalf of two owners, for delivery between November 2027 and September 2028. The specifications remain under wraps for now so direct comparisons to previous orders are a little unclear, but all the indications are that pricing resists downward pressure despite relative inactivity this year.

On the C5 front, we see miner and operators out seeking for early September dates with some tenders for early to mid September dates. Peripheral volumes ex East Australia and other fronts of the Pacific have held up as well. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, cargo enquiries are primarily for end September dates. Spot tonnage out of Pacific is relatively abundant. Ballasting tonnage is getting heavy for mid to end September dates. We see C5 concluding at USD 9.00 pmt levels at mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at mid USD 23 pmt levels for very end September dates.

The market displayed mixed sentiment across basins, with the Atlantic showing a persistent North–South divide. The US Gulf was supported by positional demand though some felt rates were topping, while the South Atlantic remained subdued with little fresh enquiry. The Continent–Mediterranean was steady but lacked clear momentum, with activity varying by sub-region. In Asia, the Pacific maintained a firmer tone, underpinned by steady cargo flows and improving sentiment from Southeast Asia and Australia. Overall, the index remained stable, reflecting a generally steady-to-firm undertone across the week.

The Panamax market held broadly sideways this week, with the Atlantic showing more resilience as steady USEC coal demand and a firming ECSA market for September dates kept sentiment supported, even as prompt tonnage faced pressure. Transatlantic business remained largely flat, with Baltic coal lending stability, while the North Atlantic continued to lack momentum. In Asia, a lengthening tonnage list and quieter chartering interest saw sentiment soften and fixtures ease slightly, though activity levels across Australia and Indonesia routes stayed healthy. Overall, the basin remains finely balanced, with the Atlantic better supported than the Pacific for now.

NORTH SEA With some vessels ballasting and steady activity firm positions for anything prior to the end of August are looking tighter.  Stem dates are pushing towards end month with charterers looking to cover out to end of the month prior to the long weekend. Window remains tricky for charterers and owners sentiment is firmer at least to end month dates.  Coming to the end of the summer period activity should also start to pick up going into Autumn although we may also see larger vessels spoiling the activity for Aframaxes.  MEDITERRANEAN By usual standards the Mediterranean so far this week has been relatively quiet and the majority of uncertain vessel positions have started to firm up, which has put some pressure on rates seeing TD19 drop to WS 140.  The position list still contains vessels that may not from trading history be for everyone, but with dates heading into September steady/softer seems to be the tone.

Spot activity has eased off slightly over the past week, as could be expected after breakneck speed with which requirements were covered during July. Atlantic fixtures have continued to trickle through with little direction or movement on charter rates and whilst availabilities look patchier further forward, charterers are in no hurry expecting redeliveries to repopulate position lists in due course. The Pacific has remained quiet, and rates have come under further pressure with a single spot fixture for early September seeing plenty of offers.   Whilst we may have finally reached holiday mode on the spot, the long-awaited summer lull has not killed longer term discussions. Preparations are being made for some structural shorts next year, against growing availability profile from independent owners looking to take short term coverage before anticipated tightening later in the decade. Fresh newbuilding orders remain muted year-to-date though yards are comfortable with large orderbooks and a healthy pipeline of prospective requirements from the LNG space and other segments alike.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US The market is largely inactive due to a couple of industry outings, and the holiday schedule is now fully engaged.  That said, the few who remain in office are eyeing a buy/sell range of 4.75-5.75cpg for FOB USGC spot parcels. Cancellation talk has been growing in the meanwhile, as the freight market continues to absorb any uptick in the arb, leaving the terminal fee market perilously close engagement. The EIA yesterday reported a well-received 3.9mmbbl build, which brought overall US propane stock levels to 88.60mmbbls, or about 98% of both last year and two years ago.  The US inventory levels are poised to reach the upper 90mmbbl level by end Oct, which would be satisfactory in terms of both domestic winter supplies and exports, which at this point are being well supported by domestic US production levels.

EAST There have been very few fixtures into India for August, which could result in a heavier concentration of spot activity early September. Aramco acceptances are still pending, and we will likely hear more Monday. While the position list may appear long, it may be somewhat misleading. A number of vessels currently listed are ballasting via the Cape, which could significantly reduce actual availability. One fixture ex AG this week bringing the total number of Aug fixtures from the Middle East (inc. Yanbu) to 28, rates have remained flat at $89 excluding one fixture out of Yanbu at $115 which carries a risk premium for GOA passage.  WEST 21 deals registered ex US thus far in September (6 / 9 / 6 by decade), versus an average of 29 deals/month year to date. The first open ships bss USG currently from 18th September onwards, however this could potentially change if / when ship schedules gets affected by northbound Panama transits.  We’ve seen a handful of deals concluded in the 3rd decade of September this week with last done ranging from $152-153 HCvP. Activity on shipping has otherwise been quiet as we await market direction post Aramco’s acceptances for September.

Despite not many FOC boats, 9–10 vessels are safe to work today for West Africa, i.e. berthed or firm prospects to sail by the weekend. Given we are virtually closed out for August West Africa volume, USG is unlikely to draw tonnage, and vessels ex-East are either committed to COGH or showing willingness; as a result, both supply and demand fundamentals have weakened. We did see TD20 test down to WS 112.5 yesterday - it seems likely quoting of September dates will see more losses realized.  CPC may however lend a hand - the number of CPC candidates isn’t particularly long, especially off early September. Expect vessels ex-UKC to be in contention given greater stability for the route compared to TD20.   The MEG also experienced a downward correction yesterday on an opts cargo. Tonnage remains healthy and owners will need more enquiry to end the week to lend stability.

The Panamax market saw a mixed week, with the Atlantic continuing to drift amid scarce fresh inquiry, limited grain and coal volumes, and a growing tonnage list pressuring rates, particularly on transatlantic and ECSA runs. Fronthaul demand showed only tentative improvement and has yet to lift sentiment. In contrast, the Pacific showed firmer signs, supported by healthy Indonesian coal flows to China and fresh Australian demand, with some tightening in southern tonnage lists and premiums being paid for prompt positions, although spot ships still discounted where laycans missed key requirements. Overall, Pacific sentiment remained positive, while the Atlantic stayed under pressure, leaving the broader market in a cautious balance.

Having been on an upward trajectory through the whole of last week MEG/East rates peaked at WS 57.5 on Friday, up more than 25%. This week rates have been under pressure again as the last of the August MEG cargoes have found their match. There are still a couple of cargoes left to cover while we’re waiting for September stems to be announced. Rates are still holding north of the WS 50-mark from both MEG and the Atlantic eastbound but set to be tested. However, contrary to last months wrap-up we do not foresee a landslide back into the low WS 40’s or below now that OPEC+ have hiked production again from September onwards.

On the C5 front, we see miner and operators out seeking for split dates/early September dates. Slight increase in peripheral volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the Pacific since last week. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, cargo enquiries are primarily for early September and end September dates. Spot tonnage out of the Pacific is loosening. Ballasting tonnage is slowly lengthening for end September, remains relatively tight for end August and early September dates. We see C5 concluding at sub USD 10 pmt levels as we approach mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at low USD 25 pmt levels for early September dates and mid-high USD 24 pmt levels for end September dates.

The Supramax market saw a split in sentiment, with the Atlantic remaining firm from the US Gulf and Continent–Mediterranean on steady enquiry, while the South Atlantic struggled for momentum. In Asia, activity stayed slow, with more prompt positions keeping rates contained. The Handysize sector was generally subdued, a quiet but balanced South Atlantic, and the Asian market showing downward pressure in the south while holding steady in the north.

NORTH SEA The list has been thinned on the early side with tonnage leaving the area and some quiet fixing taking out tonnage and stems into the 3rd decade. Downside on rates is limited with viable alternatives coming into play.  The projected list does show a few relets coming back into position which may limit the market activity out toward the end of the month.   MEDITERRANEAN The available tonnage on paper looks plentiful for demand out to the end of August, but on closer inspection there are a number of vessels that wont be favorable for a number of cargoes and charterers.  Rates sideways, but date and voyage sensitivity will come into play.

EAST At the time of writing three spot fixtures have been concluded in the Middle East this week. One of which was a re-quote due to a ship failing technical clearance. Same ship was quickly re-fixed for another cargo on slightly later dates. We reiterate the fact that there’s only been two Indian PSU fixtures so far despite August being a record month in terms of spot fixtures. With two Indian, only idle SIRE, owned ships waiting to go on to long term employment – these could put a dampener on any big jumps in freight going forward.  WEST This week we've seen 6 fixtures for the 2nd decade of Sep, leaving 3 ships open (2 via Panama, 1 via Cape). Prices have varied between 140 and 150 this week with last done at 150. We see 7 ships open for the last decade of September, 5 of which via Cape and 2 via Panama. Owners might start to consider ballasting more and more via Cape if congestion continues. Though many ships have booked slots, there are still 9 ships waiting in Balboa, and an additional 8 that can meet the dates for the next auction slot on the 14th of Aug. With auction fees closing in on USD 1 million this week, we might just see fees go above that.

text: MEG Spot differentials improved as of better butane demand. comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US The US Gulf Coast FOB market is generally thin, with many abstaining in recent days/weeks due to tariff-related uncertainty.  As the arbs and netbacks have ebbed/flowed, a generally wide range is being seen in terms of the terminal fee pricing structure.  Where buy-side interest is in the mid/upper 4cpg range, sell side ideas are at/near 6cpg – and very little is being done in the middle.  The EIA data report this week showed a disappointing 1.2mmbbl increase in propane stocks as of 1st August which brought overall stock levels to 84.70mmbbls – or just over 96% of last year’s level.   It is thought that while production levels are at near record levels, exports were also seen to have improved (thanks in part to Energy Transfer’s newly installed “flex” capacity) which thus allowed for only a modest build.   Based on historical build averages (but barring any unforeseen events) stock levels are on course to reach some 97mmbbls by the end of Oct.

The Panamax market showed a fragmented picture this week. The North Atlantic continued to soften with limited fresh demand and a subdued tone, while the South Atlantic showed glimpses of support but lacked follow-through, leaving sentiment largely flat. The Pacific saw a more dynamic shift mid-week, with improving demand from Australia and Indonesia and firmer paper prompting some owners to pull back offers. Although the tonnage list remains long and charterers are still highly selective, there’s been a noticeable pickup in momentum, particularly on the period front. Overall, while the market remains cautious, there are early signs of renewed interest and a more optimistic undertone developing in the East.

The VLCC market started with a bang on Monday with a handful of quoted cargoes before we’d finished the morning coffee. Probably in part spurred by OPEC+’s decision to boot production further on Sunday’s meeting. Rates inched up ending the day at WS 47 MEG/East. Tuesday and today have followed suit with a steady flow of cargoes and the position list thinning by the hour. A strengthening Atlantic market has and will entice owners to look West as well, thinning the list further. A WS 48 has been concluded on an ex D/D ship MEG/Korea today and a "regular" one at WS 53.5 for a Singapore discharge, so nobody will be surprised if TD3C tests the WS 55 mark before long. President Trump’s tariff-shenanigans in general and further potential Russian/Indian ones in particular continues to create uncertainty. That said, should India be pressured to stop import of Russian oil and buy “conventional” instead it would probably favor VLCCs more than most.

The Atlantic market saw limited fresh activity, though the US Gulf remained the key positive driver, with some stronger numbers emerging for both TA & FH. The Continent-Mediterranean Supramax market saw mixed sentiment, likely influenced by firmer US Gulf outlooks. From Asia, the North-South divide persisted, with some solid fixtures ex NOPAC. Period market remains active with a few fresh enquiries in the market and couple fixtures reported past week. While there's no aggressive upswing on the horizon, the market shows signs of gradual firming.

A continuation of last week’s themes as spot activity in the Atlantic remains high, with the fixing window stretching out to mid-September, although there has been a notable lack of movement on charter rates as underlying length amongst portfolios continues to absorb the bulk of requirements. On paper the market would appear tight with more enquires than there are marketed vessels, but with the fixing window stretched much further out it is likely that ships redelivering from charter or shaken out of schedules will emerge and competition should keep rates in check. The situation is somewhat reversed in the Pacific since there are more vessels available and few requirements to be worked, so the end result is the same. The term market continues to draw in resources with ongoing requirements for multi-year periods, and although pricing suggests a fairly flat winter this year the curve does trend upwards thereafter.

A manic day on the Suezmaxes, with West Africa and CPC seeing immense gains after a combination of replacements, difficult option cargoes, and a list devoid of available vessels. Charterers have attempted to approach VLCCs for UKCM runs, but seemingly without success. The larger class has also picked up and appears destined to make gains, albeit more incrementally than the Suezmaxes. The lifting of the VLCC ceiling should assist owners in the East — supply has been tight in the region, but the VLCCs have done their best to hoover up available volume.

On the C5 front, we see miner and operators out seeking for 20 August onwards dates. Peripheral volumes out of East Australia have held relatively constant since last week. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, cargo enquiries are primarily for September dates. Spot tonnage out of the Pacific is getting tight. Ballasting tonnage is slowly lengthening. We see C5 concluding near mid USD 10 pmt levels. On C3, bids are generally at low to mid USD 23 pmt levels while offers are in the USD 24 pmt levels and up.

NORTH SEA Out to the 15th August crude stems are all but covered.  Majority of the stems utilizing relets with a few Suezmaxes also in the mix from WCN with rates remaining steady around the 115-117.50 level.  The last few days in July and this first week in August have seen a good number of vessels ballast from the area, especially to the US where freight levels have jumped 50 points in the last week although this looks like it will be tested by charterers.  Outlook for the next fixing window in the North Sea remains steady.  MEDITERRANEAN Mediterranean is steady/sideways this week with most of the activity taking place under the radar and charterers trying to get levels lower than last-done. Tonnage list remains balanced and demand for tonnage will define the direction.

Sales activity in the tanker sector was limited this week, with the only reported transaction being the sale of the MR SEAWAYS MIA (49k dwt HMD 2008) at $16.5 million. Despite the subdued volume, the deal underscores continued liquidity in the MR segment and suggests a slight firming in values for MRs of this age.  On the dry side, activity remains robust. Notable sales include the HERUN ZHEJIANG (181k dwt SWS 2017), sold for $48 million - marking the second eco Capesize sale recorded this year. Eco Ultramaxes continue to change hands with Belships rumoured to offload the four Chinese blt units BELATLANTIC/BELINDA/BELMONT/BELSOUTH* (63k dwt Jiangsu Hantong 2016/2015*) for $83.6 million en bloc to Singaporean Buyers.

EAST A very active week in the East with almost a dozen spot fixtures concluded at the time of writing. This brings the total tally for August dates up to 25, at par with the most active months so far this year (March and June). After seeing BLPG1 dropping 5 bucks at the beginning of the week, freight is now back to where we left off on Friday in the mid 80s. With very few (only two so far) Indian PSU spot cargos fixed, there should be more in store for August fixing still.  WEST One very end August cargo was booked at $140 on a pmax this week. Fixing window now mainly in September where we have seen a handful of players in market today for 2nd decade. Rates have trended somewhat down for the later dates, but still firm in the mid/high 130s HCvP. We count three deals in the 1st decade of September / two deals in 2nd decade thus far.
