comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US The US Gulf Coast LPG market is practically stagnated, since a large number of market participants are either taking holiday or – up to now – leery of the outcome of the tariff situation. By now it is known that the existing tariffs will remain in place for another 90 days, but basis the arb and current netbacks (both of which are rather poor), not much is expected.  The EIA, meanwhile, reported a modest and less-than-expected build of 1.2mmbbls for the week ending 25 July, and primary propane stocks stand at 83.50mmbbls – 96% of last year.  The market had largely been anticipating a build of some 2.5-3.0mmbbls based on strong production but somewhat limited exports.  Production was strong (2.822mmbbls/day against an all-time high of 2.897mmbbls/day) but exports over the week declined to 1.629mmbbls/day (against a YTD 2025 average of 1.839mmbbls/day.  Terminal fees presently range rather widely, with buy-side interest in the mid/upper 4cts/gal, but sellers (those who have shown themselves, anyway) are coming from 6cts/gal, and as a result very little is known to have been accomplished.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco cut Aug CP to $575 for C3 and $520 for C4, both by $55, reflecting the front length. One evenly split cargo for 2h Aug lifting was offered at Sep CP minus mid-teens, and similar ratio cargo for Sep lifting was also offered at Sep CP minus $10, which barely attract buyer interest in terms of netbacks. By the time of writing, Sep C3 CP was traded at $530 and C3/C4 at $15.  FAR EAST Cash differentials for Sep delivery are still discussed in heavy discounts. 23/0 for 1h Sep delivery basis Chiba was offered at Sep FEI minus $11, and similar parcel for 2h Sep delivery was bid at Aug FEI minus mid-single digit or Sep FEI minus $20. Outside window, a couple of 46kt C3 was reported changed hand for 1h Sep delivery, with one traded at Aug FEI minus mid-single digit basis Ningbo.   As US-China tariff trade talks are still ongoing, Chinese importers are cautiously taking non-Us stems, avoiding the potential tariff hikes. One EChina importer procured a 23/0 (non US) for Sep delivery into Ningbo at FEI plus 10s via tender reportedly.    Following the crude rise, Aug and Sep FEI/MOPJ widened rapidly and cracking demand improved with a handful of buying inquires emerged for butane. One Korean petchem player was reported to award a 0/23 for 7-13 delivery at Aug MOPJ minus 40s. Another Korean importer also issued butane buy tender for Sep delivery. Two Schina petchem buyers also issued butane buy tender but cancelled in the end as offer prices are not favorable.

Rates have continued to slip over the past week and are unable to find a bottom. The summer market continues and seems owners just want to get through it for now. Rates have slipped to a lever where shorter voyages are being preferred in all areas. Owners are shying away from committing to longer voyages and may start asking for small premiums. But for now, there is not enough volume to put an upward spin on the rates.

Another bumper week for spot fixtures worldwide, with the focus shifting back towards the Atlantic. Apart from a few discounted deals on outstanding prompt positions, charter rates for intra-Atlantic spot voyages have held steady in the mid $30s. The crowded requirement list for end-August should imply a firming market, but depending how each individual requirement matches with some tight restrictions on vessel availabilities there are still some trades being discussed at lower rates. That said, the pricing of worldwide flexibility and even longer periods through October/November remains flat in the low-mid $40s and we are entering what is typically the seasonal uplift. The gap for modern 2-stroke coverage through Q4 and into Q1 still requires some bridging, although this may be challenging considering a growing consensus that spot will remain accessible and range-bound through the Winter months, thanks to ample vessel supply on paper.   It's been another good week for the U.S. Energy sector and LNG producers, following Trump's deal with the EU, which has also seen the announcement of successful FID by Venture Global on their CP2 project. Whilst this creates additional demand for long-term shipping, current sentiment sees very limited new orders on the Newbuilding side as the market grapples with a large orderbook and stagnated demand growth in the immediate years.

NORTH SEA Steady activity so far this week and dates are pushing out towards the end of the 1st decade. With surrounding markets looking firmer tonnage will be pulled out of the area to look at alternative business which in turn should put pressure on North Sea both availability and rates levels.   MEDITERRANEAN Continued activity, rates have been moving sideways in the early part of the week. Tonnage list has shrunk on the front end but fixing window is late 1st/early 2nd decade for most of the ports. As USG market has jumped 25p since Monday we expect to see some ballast from the West Mediterranean.  Which again will put pressure on the Mediterranean rates.  Like the North Sea likely to firm.

The tides are turning in the West for the Suezmaxes. Since Monday a vast clearout of tonnage has occurred, FOC availabilities are down and supplementation over the weekend is minimal. Charterers x-CPC have already begun reaching and realistically charterers x-West Africa should also do so as downside seems out of the question. This sensitivity is further compounded by a USG market that will continue to poach UKCM boats as few local vessels remain and USAC delays persist.   In the East, despite a good level of enquiry and a list that has seen some erosion, as long as the VLCCs linger in the mid WS 40s positive momentum will be capped.

The Supramax and Handysize segments seeing limited fresh enquiry and soft sentiment across most regions. Activity in both the North and South Atlantic was minimal due to the ongoing summer holiday period, and tonnage availability continued to build. In Asia, the market held steady but sluggish, with Southeast Asia showing some interest yet lacking momentum. Overall, sentiment was flat, with few signs of immediate improvement and little fresh cargo driving rates forward.

On the C5 fronts, we see miner and operators out seeking for mid August dates. Peripheral volumes out of East Australia have dipped since last week. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, cargo enquiries are primarily for September dates while operators are looking to optimize dates/vessel sizes for August. Spot tonnage out of the Pacific is fairly well balanced with cargo volume. Ballasting tonnage is getting very thin for end August and early September dates.We see C5 concluding at mid-high USD 9 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, fixtures are concluding at high USD 22 pmt levels for end August dates.

The Panamax market saw a notable correction this week, with bearish sentiment prevailing across both basins. In the Atlantic, limited transatlantic and front-haul activity saw owners adjusting ideas downward amid cautious charterers and weaker EC South America demand. The Pacific market remained sluggish, with Indo and East Australian cargoes providing some activity, but overall demand failed to absorb the long tonnage list - particularly around Indonesia - resulting in softer rates and widened bid/offer gaps. With the TA index retreating and P6 continuing to weaken, owners are increasingly opting to stay in the Pacific rather than ballast, awaiting clearer direction.

These summer periods tend to give time for reflection for those in the tanker markets, and, generally speaking, this summer is no different. Crude earnings have dropped off since a spike in June, and product rates are languishing. This has resulted in a well-documented reshuffling in the products market, with very healthy liquidity in the MR space, particularly in the c.15-year-old range where values appear to have hit a floor. This sentiment seems to have spread into the Aframax/LR2 space which is attracting added attention from opportunist investors. Scrubber fitted BLUE PRINCE (109K DWT Hudong Zhonghua 2009) was sold this week for USD 32.25M, as part of three vessels sold in this size range.    Dry cargo charter brokers hoping to enjoy their summer break have been glued to their desks this week in a flurry of activity in the charter market. Healthy returns are spurring owners into action to capture these earnings in what has mostly been an uninspiring sector over recent times. The supramax – ultramax sector has seen a bump in SNP activity this week, as pricing has fallen into line for investors. CP CHONGQING (63K DWT Chengxi 2016) was sold this week for USD 21M, in line with other similar units sold. Elsewhere, scrubber fitted Capesize PACIFIC WEST (175K DWT Jinhai 2012) sold for USD 23.2M, in line with last done similar unit scrubber fitted GOLDEN ZHOUSHAN (175K DWT Jinhai 2011) sold at USD 22M earlier this month.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US: The freight market has adeptly captured the widened US/Asia arb and simultaneously managed to retain much of its strength, even in the face of its narrowing.  This has kept US spot FOB terminal fees in the 5.00-5.00cpg range for August, though trade has been thin. While the Sep market has yet to fully develop, asking-levels at present are mildly higher and in the 6cpg range.   The EIA yesterday released its propane inventory findings and its data surprised the market with a half-million barrel decline for an overall US stock level of 82.30mmbbls – still within striking distance of the 100mmbbl mark at the end of Oct, but nonetheless revealing the strength of the US export market. Where the highest export month is pegged at 2.335mmbbls/day, the EIA reported that last week’s outbound volumes totaled 2.095mmbbls/day.  Conversely, production levels have not reacted to waning crude prices and at 2.871mmbbls/day is just off the high-water mark of 2.897mmbbls/day.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: A couple of 2h Aug lifting evenly split cargo was offered in window at Aug CP minus $20s yet to attract buyer interests, as last trade concluded at minus $40s. Qatar Energy issued sale tender to market one 3/1 and one 2/2 cargo for 23/28 Aug lifting. By the time of writing, Aug CP was traded at $530 for C3 and C3/C4 at $18. Aug/Sep CP was traded at $5 contango.   FAR EAST: Cash differentials for 2h Aug and 1h Sep delivered propane were still in heavy discounts. On Thurs window 23/0 parcel for 1h Sep CFR Chiba was changed hand at Aug FEI minus $7.5, equivalent to Sep FEI minus mid-teens. Similar parcel for 2h Aug delivery was offered at Aug FEI minus $27 but barely see bids.  Outside window a flurry of tenders is floating, especially from petchem procurement in view of the improved margins. FIC procured a 23/0 parcel for 2h Aug delivery into Ningbo at a fixed price around $550 via tender. Grand resources awarded their buy tender Sep arrival propane at CP plus 10s. Sailboat cancelled their last buy tender for 1h Aug delivery as few suitable offers but awarded their new tender for flexible ratio delivered from Aug to Sep. Korean HTC was reported to award 23kt C4 for early Sep delivery at Aug MOPJ minus 40s. Sinobenny also issued buy tender for 1/1 or 0/ delivered from late Aug to end Sep.

EAST One market tender bound for India was fixed yesterday in the mid-$80s and an FOB tender towards the end of August is due later today, also attracting shipping interest. Freight is rising in both basins with the East currently leading the way with higher earnings. With cargo dates being relatively widely spread we do see a date dependent freight market.  WEST Shipping activity west of Suez remains robust. A total of nine cargoes have been fixed for the third decade of August, bringing the total number of August USG fixtures to 29. Notably, this week also saw the first September fixture concluded, coming in slightly ahead of July levels.  Currently, only two ships remain open for August laycans. Over the past 24 hours, market rates have risen from USD 135 to above USD 140, reflecting tightening tonnage and sustained demand. Looking ahead, market conditions are expected to remain firm, underpinned by limited vessel availability and continued chartering interest.

On the C5 front, we see miners, operators, and tenders for early August dates. Periphery volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the Pacific saw a sustained level of enquiries. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, we see a handful of enquires for first half of August dates with most enquires second half of August and early September. Spot tonnage out of the Pacific seems to be relatively balanced with buy side enquiries. Ballasting tonnage is thinning for early to mid August dates. Count for late August and September ballasters are starting to accumulate. We see C5 concluding at USD 10 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at USD 24 pmt levels for mid August dates.

The Panamax market showed signs of softening this week, with sentiment waning across both basins. The North Atlantic held relatively steady with some support from fronthaul demand, though rising tonnage and limited fresh cargo are capping momentum. In contrast, the South Atlantic lost steam, especially for second-half August dates, as increased ballaster presence pressured rates. In the Pacific, activity slowed further with an oversupply of prompt tonnage and insufficient cargo flow, keeping rates under pressure and sentiment flat to soft. Although North Atlantic routes offered some positive momentum, overall sentiment across the market remains cautious and positionally driven, awaiting clearer direction.

The Atlantic market saw a steady decline in demand, especially from the US Gulf and South America, contributing to weaker sentiment. Some minor support was noted from the Continent-Mediterranean, but fresh activity remained limited. In contrast, Asia maintained healthier momentum, with consistent demand from both North and South supporting stable to slightly firmer rates. Fixtures were limited across both basins. Period market remains active with quite a few fixtures reported in the market past week.

The summer doldrums have set in, and It’s been a dismal week in the VLCC segment with every successive fixture shedding a tad off the previous. TD3C came in marginally above WS 50 yesterday, but few will be surprised to see the WS 50 mark broken before the week is over. Rates for USG export cargoes, both transatlantic and East bound, has fared better, albeit for loading dates limiting the tonnage supply to ships already in the area. However, rates from the likes of West Africa and Brazil have followed suit with the MEG as sourcing tonnage from the same pond. Expect more of the same short term.

NORTH SEA July dates are all but covered and the market has remained flat for the last couple of weeks.  The first 5 days of August stems are looking a little light on volume, especially from ECUK.  With relets anticipated to come back into the frame for early August and surrounding markets not looking that favourable for Aframax, the outlook remains steady both in activity levels and rates.  MEDITERRANEAN Activity has been slow so far this week as most of the end July and some early August stems had been covered last week quietly. Tonnage list still has prompt vessels, some with firm itineraries in the front end and it slightly opens up from 28th onwards but charterers need to take their chances. Rates for CPC inched higher and it remains to be seen if X-Mediterranean runs will do the same. Ceyhan loadings have halted for now as some cargoes seem to have been contaminated.

Whilst spot requirements in both basins continue to provide a steady flow of chartering activity, there has been little change in market direction or sentiment and rates have continued their slow drift down. There is surplus supply in the Atlantic and with most cargoes pointing to Europe and no arbitrage opening up, there are few signs of material changes as we approach the start of the shoulder months. Perhaps it is too early to call whether this persists through the Northern Hemisphere Winter, although September laycans being discussed at only very slight premiums to August suggests the seasonal uptick is at the very least a little late in coming this year. The premium we have seen for requirements East of Suez remains in place but is under pressure. Multi-year requirements continue to be worked and rumours abound with regards fixed laycans, periods and rates; as details emerge, new benchmarks will guide players for the years ahead.  On the newbuilding front, we may soon be able to point to the first “US-built” LNGC in a very long time: Hanwha Philly Shipyard secured an order from their parent company, although it remains to be seen how this will work in practise – the bulk of the construction will be in Korea and then finished in the US. Many questions remain, but it is certainly an interesting development.

Tonnage for West Africa remains in healthy supply, with strong relet presence and a couple of ‘cheaper’ boats dropped back into the market. Demand wise we have not seen a huge amount of 2nd decade bbls worked on the surface. However, with the three-week window reaching out to 13 August, charterers are not feeling time pressure and can afford to fix cargoes at a measured pace.   Across in the USG, rates continue to flatline. Tonnage is not long, however, drip-fed demand hasn’t allowed owners to push on. In addition, the Aframaxes remain working at eq, 145 x 58 so do offer a cheaper alternative. Despite no movement in rates, with TD20 poised to come off and local supplementation minimal expect some owners to ballast TA.   Reasonable activity this week, albeit for MEG/India runs. The mystery list is long, hinting that a good amount of cargoes in the fixing window have already been covered. In addition, the draw of West Africa is becoming weaker meaning a greater proportion of tonnage in the region may focus on MEG business.

KMG of Kazakhstan are reported to have bought scrubber fitted LR2 resale pair LAMU / DUNE (113K DWT COSCO Yangzhou 2025) at USD 72M each, in line with non scrub LR2 HESPERIA TIDE (115K DWT Zhoushan Changhong 2025), bought last week by Polembros for USD 70M. In the MR sector, despite the less than exciting rates on offer, buyers are still seeing value in 15–17-year-old units. There has been a large amount of liquidity in this age bracket with buyers taking a chance that those bumper spot earnings seen last year will return.    The dry market is showing resilience, with healthy returns across the sector. These elevated rates are already fuelling an increase in buying interest, though sellers will be keen to extract as much value as possible and units will be priced accordingly. It was a busy week in the Kamsarmax sector, seeing five sales. Scrubber fitted ULTRA LION (81K DWT Tsuneishi Zhoushan 2015) was sold for a better than anticipated price of USD 24.8M, signalling a potential recovery in pricing for this sector, which corrected so sharply towards the end of 2024.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US Mont Belvieu propane values have softened on the heels of yesterday’s EIA report which showed a larger-than-expected inventory build.  Where a +2.5mmbbl increase was forecast, the EIA reported a 4.40mmbbl build for an overall stock level of 82.80mmbbls.  That, in turn, puts the US in position to potentially reach over 100mmbbls at end-Oct, but the startup of Energy Transfer’s expanded marine terminal capacity will likely have an impact on the outcome.  Meanwhile, the August market remains at between the 5.00-6.00cpg terminal fee level, depending on timing and ratio, etc.  The declining MB market, though, has allowed the arb to improve but whether terminal fees will rise or the freight market will capture that differential is presently in limbo.  The freight market has been quick and nimble and largely able to have remained on top of the changes in the market, but some FOB sellers have begun to (proverbially) draw a line in the sand and are offering at no less than 6cpg.

EAST A strong West market is now catching up with theoretical earnings in the East making it increasingly attractive to send vessels for longer haul voyages. This is likely to affect the market in the East in form of higher asking levels. Once Saudi Aramco’s August program is finalized we should see increased demand in the Middle East as well.    WEST Despite the latest ARB being less favorable for traders, shipping activity has remained robust. Over 10 cargoes are currently in play for the third decade of August ex-US, marking a highly active week.  This brings the total number of spot fixtures for August to 28—matching July’s overall count.  At present, fewer than a handful of ships remain open for August laycans. Looking ahead, market conditions are expected to stay firm, supported by tight vessel availability and sustained demand.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG   Slim interest on FOB AG discussion and discounts dampened, and one evenly split cargo for 2h Aug lifting reported at Aug CP minus $50. By the time of writing, Aug propane was traded at $544 and C4 at $20 cheaper. Aug/Sep CP was traded at flat.  Seeing front weakness, Indian PSUs are actively negotiating to secure next year FOB/CFR supply.   FAR EAST Cash differentials crashed further amid sluggish demand against bountiful supply. At the time of writing, 23/0 for 2h Aug delivery basis Chiba was changed hand at Aug FEI minus $20, whereas 46/0 parcel traded at Bal Jul FEI minus $10, which equates to Aug FEI minus $24.   Outside the window a handful of tenders were concluded. Taiwan FPCC awarded two 46/0 cargos for Aug delivery into Mailiao at Aug MOPJ minus close to $50, which assumed Us stems, and FIC also secured one 23/0 for Aug delivery into Ningbo close to $560. Whereas another EChina importer was rumored to procure two 23/0 parcels for mid Aug delivery at Aug CP plus teens. Other PDH players are conservative, despite the PDH margins slightly improved. Butane demand is expected to increase with better margins in MTBE gasoline additives. HTC was also said to award their buy tender for 0/23 late Aug delivery.   Other than these, Iranian cargos for Aug delivery were reported concluded at Aug CP minus 10/teens level.

Waf availabilities have been chewed through over the past 48 hrs, provisional list limited foc vessels eta prior 5th August - there is solid supplementation over the weekend but the demand potential remains strong. Our counts show roughly 15 (confirmed) to 28 mbbls cvrd across VLCC+SMAX segments in the first decade so charterers will have to tread carefully, and dates dictate any straggling cargoes within 1-5 window will have to move this week.   The Mediterranean/Black Sea has also started to show signs of positive momentum with TD6 at WS 92.5 and a x-med cargo failing to garner too much interest. Additionally, there is a very prompt CPC replacement that paid up at 97.5 and provides more wind in owners' sails.  On the contrary, the USG is struggling. Yes we did see rates rebound to the mid WS 60s off end month, however, the Aframaxes have dropped to eq.145 x 60 and will likely take the bulk of the remaining 3rd decade volume.   The MEG has seen a few fixtures helping to shorten the list slightly. A steadier feel at these levels with rates repeating, however, for stability to remain activity must persist and with VLCCs weak cannibalisation is on the horizon.

The Panamax market started the week firmly supported by tight tonnage and strong grain-driven enquiry, particularly in the North Atlantic and ECSA regions, though overall fixture volumes remained limited. However, by mid-week sentiment softened globally, with the Atlantic basin seeing widening bid-offer spreads and subdued activity, as charterers pulled back amid uncertainty and weaker FFAs. In the Pacific, rates also turned softer despite steady demand, as negative paper sentiment and rising tonnage availability pressured owners into narrowing their ideas. Market conditions are currently positional, and much depends on the forthcoming grain activity from South America, which will heavily influence both Atlantic and Pacific directions in the short term.

The spot market has continued to drift lower, confounding any thoughts of revival off the back of a number of Atlantic requirements towards the end of August. The relatively high level of activity across all basins has applied a brake to more significant downward pressure on rates; nonetheless, fixing levels across the key benchmarks of 2-strokes West of Suez and TFDEs East of Suez are down week on week. The Pacific premium is unusual this time of year, and is a sign of a challenging trading environment that hasn’t really seen much of an arbitrage pulling ships out of the Atlantic for some time. Those hoping for a recovery won’t be seeing many encouraging signs, other than increased energy demand due to above average temperatures, so for now “utilisation” remains the name of the game. If there is a silver lining for owners, it is the growing interest in multimonth/multiyear tonnage. Rate expectations will be muted, but securing business through this weaker market will hold some appeal.  On the cargo side, Venture Global will supply 2 MTPA of LNG from its Calcasieu Pass 2 project to Eni over 20 years. This deal marks Eni’s first long-term LNG contract from the U.S. On the Newbuilding front, there were no reported conventional LNGC orders over the last week and prices remain stable.

NORTH SEA The trend of relets and bigger vessels has continued into this week which has send both the sentiment and physical market soften.  Very little market activity is pushing owners to look for alternatives but with the US markets also taking a hit on the Afra only the Mediterranean looks like a viable alternative at the moment.  Very much a summer market at the moment.  MEDITERRANEAN End month July dates are being worked quietly ex Libya with rates hovering around WS 130. The tonnage list has shortened and vessels with the right cargo and trade history are few and far between which in a busier market could give some upside pressure. But for now rates are moving sideways.

Handsome daily gains for the big ships as in particular Atlantic activity picking. List of ballasters shrinking rapidly whilst ever more demand for August loaders ex Brazil, West Africa and North Atlantic appearing – further improvements to be expected in coming days/weeks by the looks of it. Far East developing similarly although more moderate, much driven by major miners picking multiple units for the  West Australia/China trade. Index lagging - conference route Brazil/China realistically at USD 22 pmt and West Australia/China at close to USD 9 pmt, giving actual daily earnings at excess USD 20k for round voyages, closing in on USD 23k on wide average, and climbing.

A combination of possible tightening of US sanctions on Russia, increasing OPEC oil production and being slightly behind the curve on the MEG end July program spurred owners to push rates up from WS 50 level MEG/East into the mid WS 50’s in the week gone by, despite ample tonnage supply suggesting otherwise. However, as US President Trump kicked the can down the road for 50 days on further sanctions and early August Saudi stems yet to have materialize, confidence within the owning community is showing signs of weakening. The West/East arb remain firmly closed and although the tonnage situation in the Atlantic is tighter than the MEG, inter-Atlantic movements have done little to add significant pressure.

The Supramax sector continued to firm, supported by ongoing demand from the US Gulf and South Atlantic alongside limited prompt tonnage, allowing owners to maintain higher rate ideas across the Continent and Mediterranean while Asian markets remained firm despite a growing bid-offer gap on certain routes. In the Indian Ocean, steady inquiry and a tightening tonnage list underpinned sentiment, adding upward pressure to rates. The Handysize market also sustained a positive tone, with the Atlantic benefiting from fresh demand and improving confidence, while in Asia, a shift in the cargo-to-tonnage ratio supported gradual gains.

The pre summer rush appears to have been short lived, with only a handful of reported sales this week. Standing out, however, is resale LR2 HESPERIA TIDE (115K DWT Zhoushan Changhong 2025), bought by Polembros for USD 70M, adding to the 4 other LR2 units they have on order at the same yard. Old VLCCs continue to see relatively high levels of enquiry, with CITY OF TOKYO (303K DWT Universal 2004) selling at a firm USD 41.5M, despite earnings being in the usual summer lull. Elsewhere, the LR1 KOI (74K DWT STX 2010) was sold to Greek interests at USD 23.3M, following a sharp correction in values in this sector.   Usually, the excitement and volatility are reserved for spot cape earnings, however, this week all sizes across dry are enjoying a rush in spot returns. Rates particularly in the panamax sector are firming sharply, sitting at USD 15k/day, having spent the majority of the year closer to USD 10K/day. This will likely disincentivise sellers of tonnage, frustrating buyers who are now seeing the price asks of potential candidates rising. In the Kamsarmax sector, the attractiveness of yard is plain to see this week with sale of the Tess 82 ULTRA PUMA (81K DWT Tsuneishi 2016) selling at USD 25M versus a younger yet Chinese built AVICL ATERMIS (81K DWT Jiangsu Jinling 2019) being sold at USD 24.5M.

EAST A total of five ships, East and West, were placed on subs yesterday. Three of these were done in the Middle East, bringing the total spot count in the region up to 23 for July. Six of these are so far Indian PSU cargos, and we do hear some talks that at least one more Indian July cargo might come to market at a later stage. With an already high spot count in July, there might not be a whole lot of cargos left for this month, but given what’s left of ships just a few more cargos is enough for the balance to remain tight.  WEST Spot fixing activity out of the US Gulf (USG) remains steady, even as traders continue to describe the market as challenging. July positions are largely covered, while August has already seen 17 spot fixtures concluded in the mid-to-high $120s to $130 HCvP range—9 in the first decade and 8 in the second. The emergence of an anticipated market cargo has helped stimulate further activity. Vessel availability appears balanced for the remainder of the month, with major owners currently dominating the position list. Looking ahead, the market is expected to remain firm.

text: The EIA this week reported yet another propane inventory build which has overall US stocks resting at 78.40mmbbls, which is effectively on par with last year’s stock level, but more importantly, well beyond the 5yr average for the 27th week of the year.   It was only a few months ago when serious doubts were expressed as to whether 2025 inventories would rise to sufficient levels.    However, if historical averages are employed to calculate the balance of the inventory build season (which concludes 31 Oct) for 2025, stocks should then be at 99mmbbls – well above the 5yr average of 92.3mmbbls.  However, it is believed that operations have now begun at Energy Transfer’s Nederland terminal which should elevate export volumes, thus impacting overall propane inventory levels.  As for the Gulf Coast terminal fee market, where July is largely concluded, the August market is pretty well pegged at between 5-6cpg, depending on timing, ratio, etc.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: FOB discounts for Aug lifting FOBs dampened as of ample supply against lukewarm demand and weak netback on CFR basis. One evenly split cargo was reported traded at Aug CP minus high 30s/$40. By the time of writing, Aug CP for C3 was traded at $565, and C3/C4 narrowed down to $20 from last week’s $26 as seasonal demand improved for butane and additional cracking demand.   FAR EAST: Cash differentials slide further this week with limited propane buying inquiries. Several parcels for 23/0 for 2h Aug delivery basis Chiba were changed hand at Aug FEI minus $5 or Jul FEI minus $0.5 to $1.5. And offers are still under downward pressure. 46/0 for similar delivery range was assessed at Aug FEI minus mid-teens. Outside window PDHs are hesitant to move, with tentative turnaround schedule in Aug and bearish outlook on downstream demand. Only one PDH major issued tender to buy non-Us propane for Aug delivery so far.   Despite the slim interest on propane, cracking inquiry surged up as FEI/MOPJ widened, following the crude rise. Two Korean importers are reported to award their butane buy tender for Aug delivery at Aug MOPJ minus around $40. One more Korean company also issued tender to buy upto 44kt flexible ratio for Aug delivery into their Indonesia cracker. Several petchem players didn’t award their Aug butane buy tender as offers not attractive. CPC also issued tender to buy 1/1 split for last decade Aug delivery.

Even though the tonnage list is fairly populated, owners seem to have resolved to not let this market slip through their fingers. Charterers are trying to keep a lid on things by working under the radar and picking ships off quietly. At the time of print we are working end month dates and still about 20-25 cargoes to be fixed before august dates start coming into play.   West has been a bit active overnight and if some owners decide to ballast West, the MEG list will thin putting more upward pressure on the rates.

Off market activity continues to dominate in the West. Very few cargoes leaked to the market yet 10+ vessels have gone on subs over the past 2 days. Albeit not an exact science given the cloak and dagger nature of the market, however, the aforementioned indicates that a healthy chunk of the 20-25 July window ex-West Africa has been covered with rates seemingly remaining flat. The list has shortened on the front end, however, off 25-31 July window there still remains plenty of candidates to cater for prospective demand.   So far this week the USG has yet to kick into gear, and as a result tonnage has built to a point where any sensitivity has faded. There is just 1 stem rmrd working off 3rd decade. With an armada of Aframax ballasters heading over charterers will be incentivized to wait and fix the smaller class if they have the flexibility to do so.   A few more vessels were clipped off in the East yesterday… once again off market. Per yesterday's tonnage count there should be enough vessels present to prevent any upside from materializing.

The positive momentum continued across most regions, with the 11TC average climbing up steadily. In the Atlantic, US Gulf transatlantic rates held strong, with limited fresh fixing but firm sentiment. The South Atlantic saw improved levels amid tight tonnage, while the Continent and Mediterranean also noted gains despite scarce visible activity. Asia remained buoyant, driven by steady backhaul demand and healthy cargo flows from Indonesia and Australia. Overall, the market reflected growing confidence, even as reported fixtures remained relatively sparse.

On the C5 front, we see miners, operators, and tenders for late July dates. Periphery volumes out of East Australia saw a sustained level of enquiries while it is reasonably quiet on other fronts of the Pacific. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, we see a handful of enquires for end July dates with most enquires for August. Towards mid-week, we start seeing enquiries for forward September dates. Spot tonnage out of the Pacific is relatively abundant and well balanced with buy side enquiries. Ballasting tonnage is heavily weighted for the first half of August with several ballasters left for end July dates. We see C5 concluding at low-mid USD 7 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at sub mid USD 18 pmt levels for 1-10 August dates. For mid August dates, bids are generally in the low USD 18 pmt levels while offers are generally in excess of USD 19 pmt levels.

NORTH SEA  North Sea stems have been quietly covering out to around the 20th – Not much in the way of market activity with a lot of programming taking a large portion of available cargoes.  The list isn’t being boosted as much this month with a lower level of vessels arriving from the US but with still a good  number of oil company relets in the mix it looks like activity will remain subdued heading into the 3rd decade.  MEDITERRANEAN  Rates have been kept under pressure as the available tonnage has been seeking employment. Market has been activity this week, but with the 2nd decade almost sold out for local loads and tonnage replenishing any upside potential does not seem to be on the cards, especially with the surrounding areas not looking promising.

After a slightly quieter spell in the spot markets both East and West of Suez, rates have been softening and there has been a sense that the turnover of requirements was easing. That seems to have been a little premature, with a few early August requirements in the Pacific basin and a handful of fresh enquiries in the Atlantic basin for the second half of August. Given there is prompt tonnage but perhaps less availability further out, this has echoes of the tight patches that have emerged throughout this year; during these periods, the competition for prompt business drove down levels but further out rates rebounded, as especially as ships were gradually fixed out. We shall see whether this trend repeats itself in the coming weeks, but for now the East premium remains in place. In contrast, the term market hasn’t shown much sign of slowing down; while liquidity is naturally lower for longer periods, there have been several fixtures of one or two years reported and several enquiries remain ongoing. On the Newbuilding front, there we no reported conventional LNGC orders over the last week and prices remain stable. However, Samsung Heavy Industries has reportedly secured a contract for a 3.5mtpa FLNG production unit at $637m for Eni’s Coral Norte project offshore Mozambique, with the unit expected to be operational by 2028.

The Panamax market has gained significant upward momentum this week, primarily fueled by a robust Atlantic basin. Strong demand from ECSA for late July and early August loadings has drawn in tonnage and tightened availability in the North Atlantic, leading to firmer rates for both transatlantic and front-haul voyages. This Atlantic strength has had a positive spillover effect, stimulating the previously quiet Indonesian market and lending support to a firmer tone in the Pacific. While the North Pacific remains more mixed, a healthy cargo count and tightening tonnage in the South have emboldened owners, who are holding for higher rates against a backdrop of positive FFA and overall bullish sentiment.

MR tankers continue to be the focus of investors with values having stabilised in recent weeks, following a notable correction since the peak of summer 2024. Sellers have done extremely well over the last few years in terms of earnings, so despite the fact they are not selling at the peak, units are leaving fleets likely having repaid their initial investment and more. PTI HUANG HE (50K DWT SPP 2016) was bought by Greek buyers, which will help price units in this range.   The dry market  has had a bumper week in activity but the story remains the same. That is, there is healthy liquidity across older units but a lack of supply on more modern ships. The unusually high amount of activity may be attributed to the incoming summer holidays, with much of Northern Europe taking time away from the desk over the coming weeks. A significant range of sizes transacted this week gives little away in terms of buying preference, which could support the narrative that buyers are seeking tonnage to position themselves for potentially better markets over the next year. Interestingly, capesize GOLDEN ZHOUSHAN (175K DWT Jinhai 2011) sold for USD 22M, below many price expectations.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US Propane at Mont Belvieu softened after the release of the EIA data for the week ending 27 June which showed a mostly larger-than-anticipated build of 3.1mmbbls and brought overall US primary stock levels to 75.70mmbbls – almost exactly 100% of the level recorded last year. Production levels were effectively flat at 2.8mmbbls/day, but still above the YTD 2025 average of ~2.5mmbbls/day.  That compares to the export rate of 1.868mmbbls/day which itself is just slightly above the YTD 2025 average of 1.852mmbbls/day. Terminal fees, meanwhile, have softened.  After a series of transactions reportedly in the low/mid 5cpg range, a deal today was reported to have been concluded in the mid 4cpg range for an Aug cargo.

EAST A market bid brought the sleeping Middle East market back to life finally seeing the first deal of the week concluded almost 10 dollars below last done from the previous week. An ongoing FOB tender is still in the works and will only be finalized tomorrow. Currently several Charterers are sniffing for freight against same. This combined with a scorching hot West market have flushed out cargos from other load ports in the East outside the MEG as well. With West earnings now catching up with the East we could be near a floor on freight and next deals could well be slightly above last done.  WEST U.S. LPG inventories increased by 3.0 million barrels compared to last week, lending support to the arbitrage, which remains steady.  The first decade of August continues to show a consistent stream of fixtures and inquiries, driving freight rates into $130 at time of writing. This week, eight deals have been concluded in the mid-to-high $120s per metric ton (Houston–Chiba via Panama), leaving approximately 5–6 vessels open for the August 1–10 loading window.  Looking ahead, we may see additional ships ballasting via the Cape for mid-to-late August loadings, as activity in the Eastern market has recently slowed.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced their Jul Cp at $575 for C3 and $545 for C4, which is much below market expectation, but reflecting the long fob supply. Due to the regional uncertainty, some lifters to refer to sell fob instead of self lifting, avoiding the freight risk and sluggish CFR demand. KPC also issued tender to sell a 22/22 FOB cargo for 18/19 Jul lifting. By the time of writing, Aug C3 Cp was traded at $558 and C4 at $532.   FAR EAST Market sentiment was weak, seeing a handful of importers resales. During the week two lots for 23/0 for 1h and 2h Aug delivery basis Chiba changed hand at Jul FEI minus $1.5, equates to Aug Fei minus mid single at the time of trades. The discounts dived further, with 23/0 2h Aug bid on thurs shown at FEI minus high single, while no bids shown for 1h Aug but offers at minus $7.5.   Several Jul prompt cargos were concluded at Aug Cp plus single digit, or similar equivalence. FIC awarded their buy tender for 2 lots of 23/0 at $560s for late Jul early Aug delivery. We are expecting petchem users to emerge for Aug feedback purchase soon with declined flat price and better margins.  Other than this, IOC was reported to award their Aug 2/2 buy tender on CFR basis at Cp plus 20s. One Korean player also tendered to buy 23kt butane for Aug delivery.

Congratulations to all those involved in the LNG Canada project as the newly commissioned export terminal shipped Canada's first LNG export cargo this week. A significant milestone for the LNG market as new volume directly enters the Pacific region free of Panama Canal risk or diversion to Europe. Whilst the ramp up this year will not be enough to absorb excess supply on the shipping side, it brings a new dynamic to the market in the East.   Most of the past week's chartering activity has also taken place East of Suez with a pair of Middle East fixtures levelling out what had become a hotspot for activity amidst rising geopolitical tensions. Rates have pulled back slightly, and competition remains for outstanding requirements in the Pacific, nonetheless at healthier levels than observed year to date. The Atlantic has been more muted with the lack of activity and a growing availability for prompter tonnage to load end July into 1H August leaving rates to drift downward. There are additional requirements further forward in both basins with some premiums expected for interbasin trade.    There has been an increasing interest in term tonnage in recent weeks, and several ships are now on subjects and a couple more requirements remain uncovered for now. The fundamentals remain unchanged although rates appear to be edging higher, so we are braced for interesting times ahead.

This week saw a subdued Panamax market with limited momentum across both basins. In the Atlantic, sentiment remained cautious, as uncertainty over true market levels led to widening gaps between owners and charterers, particularly for forward cargoes off the Continent and NCSA. Fronthaul cargoes continue to underpin activity, but volumes need replenishing to sustain current rate stability. Further south, activity eased slightly, reflecting softer bids and more flexible owners. Asia opened mixed but gradually softened, with charterers gaining confidence and owners beginning to face resistance, especially on forward dates. Australian coal remains supportive, but elsewhere Pacific activity has quietened. Overall, the market feels delicately balanced, with cargo replenishment critical to maintaining momentum in the weeks ahead.

On the C5 ex West Australia front, we see an uptick in the level of enquiries from operators, miners and tenders alike for mid July dates. Some operators out looking for August coverage as well on index and fixed rate basis. Peripheral volumes out of East Australia have improved as well, though it is quieter on all other fronts of the Pacific. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, primary interest are for 20 July onwards and first half August dates. Pacific spot tonnage is fairly well balanced with a notable number of vessels choosing to ballast due. Ballasting tonnage is heavy for July and early August dates. We see C5 slowly recovering this week and reached low USD 7 pmt levels at mid-week. On C3, mid to mid-high USD 18 pmt levels have been done for late July/early August dates.

West Africa is under pressure with 30+ ETS within 5-days or already FOC, but 8 of the 13 FOC ships are ex-UKC and finding USG/TA suitors off 19-20 window trying to tempt them across so perhaps this props it up a little. With TD20 around 85 and under downward pressure, USG/TA for 20th onwards is capped at 72.5 with pressure to hit 70, but the prompt window in the USG is conversely very tight. Within the mid-hi 60s Aframaxes provide a spongy base, as we suspect they are prone to softening as owners look to lock in healthy earnings through the summer. The Black Sea has been active under the surface in the interim, a few East Mediterranean ships off the list, a few UKC-GIB vessels heading EMED/CANAK indicative that deals have been snuck away. East of Suez we are valued higher than a single VLCC, a quandary which plagues Aframaxes also on TD8 - as such don't expect heavy levels of action unless rates realign into the 90s.

After the war Iran/Israel conflict finally settled, it seems that the summer market seems to have kicked in.  Tonnage in the East is now at its peak that it's been all year. We seem to be heading into the territory where charterers will be spoilt for choice and "if he does not take it, we will just go to someone else" .   On the other hand, tonnage in the West has thinned but there has not been much volume there either. This will attract some ballasters from the East but until the volume picks up, we don't see the rates picking up. The West-East arb does not seem to be working which does not help the cause.

The Supramax market remained firm despite slow fresh enquiry, with the Atlantic slightly more positive, while Asia had a slower start and the Indian Ocean stayed quiet. Meanwhile, the Handysize market was subdued and mostly flat across all regions, with the Atlantic and South Atlantic holding steady, the US Gulf under downward pressure due to prompt tonnage and limited enquiry, and Asia showing a modest upward trend on a slight cargo-to-tonnage improvement, though overall the market lacked significant momentum.

NORTH SEA The majority of the first decade July stems have been covered with a lot of programming and limited market activity. Stem wise the 2nd decade looks similar in volume to first 10 days.  Surrounding markets not providing much in the way of opportunity for tonnage.  We should see tonnage availability continue to climb and if we continue to see the lack of activity market levels likely to be tested by charterers.  MEDITERRANEAN Rates are moving sideways with a softer tone as dates now are well into the 2nd decade for all ports. Owners seem to be less resistant as returns are decent for this period of the year and activity isn't that strong so far this week. Balanced tonnage list for local runs with still enough vessels to choose from.

The tanker market has absorbed recent news developments and geopolitical tensions with little disruption and volatility. There was a brief spike in VLCC spot rates, however this has since fallen away with the market normalising. This week, Yasa acquired scrubber fitted VLCC C.SPIRIT (313K DWT HHI Gunsan 2013) for USD 67.5M, against last done 2013 scrubber fitted VLCC CAPTAIN X KYRIAKOU (300K DWT HHI Ulsan 2013) sold in September 2024 for USD 80M. Elsewhere MRs continue to change hands given the recent correction on pricing with 4 further sales this week. Most notably, NORD OCEANIA (49K DWT Onomichi 2018) sold for USD 36.5M, levels that this time last year restricted buyers to non eco tonnage.   Emerging news of a US-China trade deal being struck will have not only the global stock markets rallying but could also provide some life to the steady yet unexciting dry market. Earnings have been stable for the most part, aside from the usual capesize rollercoaster, with many touting a stronger 2026. This trade agreement could be the first green shoots of the next prosperous period for dry owners. Brave maritime continue their run on Japanese tonnage this week as they picked up ARIES SAKURA (39K DWT Shin Kurushima 2020) for just under USD 26M. Elsewhere, scrubber fitted capesize PACIFIC EAST (176K DWT SWS 2012) sold for USD 27.5M.

EAST The gap in earnings between East and West narrowed on Thursday after a few days with a more stable situation in the Middle East. A market tender was concluded some 5-6 dollars below last done levels despite a relatively tight shipping market illustrating the diminishing risk premium in the region. Looking ahead the freight market for mid July dates look set to stabilize around $80.  WEST In July, we have recorded 27 spot fixtures, distributed as 11 in the first decade, 6 in the second, and 10 in the third. Additionally, one spot fixture has been registered for the first decade of August. Current arbitrage economics do not support the high $120s - $130s levels being sought by most Owners, but we did however see one spot fixture today on an ex DD ship at lower levels. Otherwise market is still in a holding pattern.  While the remainder of July appears tight in terms of available tonnage, some of these vessels may ultimately roll into August. At present, we anticipate around 8 or more open ships for the first decade of August.

text: US With much volatility and uncertainty, Mont Belvieu propane has, since the start of June, seen a 10cpg swing in pricing but seems now to be finding some footing in the mid 70cpg range.  It was immediately assumed with the release of this week’s EIA inventory which showed a 5.1mmbbl increase in propane stocks, that further relaxation would occur.  But considering all of the other factors currently competing with one another the market remains essentially flat. The larger-than-expected inventory build brought the overall total stock level at 72.60mmbbls, or 99% of last year’s 2H Jun level, and puts the U.S. inventories in a position to reach well in to the high 90mmbbl level by the end of Oct – the conclusion of the traditional ‘build’ season.   Meanwhile, the spot FOB terminal fee market continues to compete with freight and has been held largely to either side of the 5cpg level.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Muted discussion on FOB trades and spot differentials for Jul lifting 2/2 was estimated at Jul CP minus 50 or more, reflecting latest FOB deal done into India and the depressed CFR netback. However, such discounts have enticed buyer interest and we’ve seen Indian BPCL issued term tender early to procure upto 82 VLGC cargos of evenly split grade on FOB AG for Y2026.  First round CP recommendation was heard at $590 for Jul C3 and $25-30 cheaper for C4. By the time of writing, Jul CP was traded at $592 and Jul/Aug CP backwardation at $22.   FAR EAST Swap prices extended the loss under selling pressure. On Thurs window, 23/0 CFR basis Chiba for 2h Jul delivery was changed hand at Jul FEI flat and similar parcel for 1h Aug delivery done at fixed price $535, equates to Aug FEI flattish. Cash differentials for 2h Aug continued to weaken, with offer at Aug FEI plus $3 vs bid at minus $4.   Outside window several butane related cargos traded. Indian IOC was reported to buy an evenly split cargo at CP plus single digit for Aug delivery via tender. Another evenly split cargo for 2h Jul delivery was sold into SEA market at Jul CP plus mid-single. Lotte Chemical also reportedly bought a 0/2 for Jul delivery into Indonesia at MOPJ minus 50s reportedly.   Other than normal stem, quite a handful of special origin cargos for Jul delivery remained unsold and offered via tender, however limited buying interest left. At the time of writing, we’ve tracked min 600kt volume will reach China within 1st to 2nd decade Jul.

Welcome news of a ceasefire in the latest Middle East conflict this week has helped to settle concerns over LNG supply leading to a softening of Asian LNG prices. However, the situation appears far from stable and continues to highlight the speed with which sentiment can change in LNG shipping. A strong premium remains for charters loading from the region though plenty of owners are seeing this as business worth pursuing, which may lead to slightly softer levels achieved for the latest round of enquiry vs. prompter requirements last week.    Whilst there appears to be ample supply on paper, with all eyes on the Middle East, Pacific rates have firmed as offers are less forthcoming. Meantime, the Atlantic has been comparatively quiet thus far this week with Arb closed, further availabilities firming up and charterers with spot exposure holding off as the geopolitical situation shows signs of easing.    Nonetheless the term market remains abuzz with activity for periods covering 1-3 years with reports of a couple of the ongoing requirements closing this week. Further deadlines loom and sentiment is strong for 2-stroke tonnage providing coverage through next year.   On the LNG supply side, Cheniere announced it had taken FID on the final phase of its Corpus Christi phase 3 expansion which will see the producer’s volumes reach around 70mt by time of completion. Orders for newbuildings remain fairly muted this year but firmer sentiment on the prompt may encourage firmer discussions in that space.

It's been some week for VLCCs as rates shot up along with the missiles. Although MEG/East rates touched 3 digits, very few deals were actually confirmed other than those done in the WS 70's. And if we are to believe reports a deal has already been concluded in the WS 70's again today as the ceasefire seems to hold and the risk premium evaporates. If paper is anything to go by there's more downside in stall with TD3c July currently at WS 52.25 vs WS 52.5 (bid/ask). As the old saying goes, you do not really panic if you are the first one out the door... On the plus side for owners bunker prices have been tumbling in tandem with the oil price.

The Panamax market maintained its positive momentum this week, holding firmly around the USD 12k index mark, supported by consistent seasonal trends and steady enquiry across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. Atlantic sentiment strengthened further, particularly up north, where robust front-haul activity has tightened tonnage lists, pushing rates towards the mid-USD 19k level basis BKI. Transatlantic rates held steady despite lighter volumes, largely due to limited spot availability. Meanwhile, the Pacific showed solid gains, driven by increased cargo flows from Australia and Indonesia, with premium rates now comfortably in the USD 12-14k region for quality tonnage - especially ex-NoPac and Indo rounds. Although fundamental cargo volumes haven’t shown significant growth, current conditions feel well-balanced, and sentiment remains cautiously upbeat heading into next week.

NORTH SEA  Stems steadily covering in the first 5 days of July although actual market activity has not been that busy.  Market remains relatively steady and prompt vessels now looking to have to absorb a fair amount of waiting time. A slightly unusual fuel oil cargo has paid a premium which has given some uplift in owner sentiments.  The 5-10 July window stem wise doesn’t look to be that full so for the time being we anticipate market to remain on an even keel.  MEDITERRANEAN Activity in the Mediterranean has been steady and strong as rates are moving sideways under some upward pressure. Dates are moving way too forward now and we might see a couple of quiet days until the end of this week. Also, replacement jobs might be needed for some tight fixing but there are still enough vessels around to protect.

On C5 ex West Australia, we observe limited activity this week, no miners were in and very limited fixtures done for tender and operators alike. As we approach mid-week, we see slightly more operators out seeking for mid July dates. On peripheral fronts such as East Australia, we see a tick up on volume of enquiries.   On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, we note backwardation in the market due to tightening of tonnage for before 20 July dates. Operators are out seeking for second half of July to full August dates.   Pacific spot tonnage is slowly increasing with a notable number of prompt vessels.   No fixed rate C5 fixtures heard this week, fixed rate offers are generally in the low to mid USD 9s. On C3, we see mid-high USD 22 pmt levels done for mid-late July dates.

The market gained modest momentum over the past week, largely driven by firmer activity from the Asia, particularly in the NoPac and Indonesia trades. In contrast, the Atlantic remained muted overall, with the US Gulf continuing to face limited enquiry and downward pressure. The South Atlantic stayed balanced with little change in fundamentals, while some improved sentiment was noted in the Continent-Mediterranean. Period interest picked up, with a few short-term fixtures reported, though details were scarce.

TD20 finally got tested yesterday with WS 90 on subs for Bonny/Pembroke on an 06built. Quite a few mysteries have been uncovered overnight with the tonnage profile tightening a reasonable amount. We will have a good chunk of 2nd decade volume to come, however, we expect that charterers will be hesitant to reach further into 15-20 July window this week as the tonnage-list does open up again over the weekend and if all stays calm in geopolitics, sentiment should also become more grounded. For now we expect rates to remain steady.   In the USG despite tonnage tightening up significantly, little gains have been made by owners. Considering the number of vessels we have seen taken on subs it is likely that the majority of first decade July cargoes have been accounted for. Furthermore, with Aframaxes now reaching into the 5-10 July window, we also expect a quiet end to the week for the Suezmaxes on the other side of the Atlantic.   After a quieter day geopolitically in the Middle East, seems that the sentiment is starting to cool off, at least on the VLCCs. Despite, the softer outlook on the larger ladies, recent activity on the Suezmaxes have cleared out the front-end of the tonnage-list and the market is now looking stronger fundamentally speaking. Albeit, much can change in a matter of hours as seen over the past fortnight.

Headlines in the tanker market have been stolen by two rare modern transactions this week. On the VLCC front DHT reported their acquisition of the the scrubber fitted VLCC PAPALEMOS 320K DWT HYUNDAI 2018 for USD 107 million while Delta Tankers have reportedly purchased the NORDIC THUNDER 157K DWT HYUNDAI 2017 for USD 65 million. Both transactions setting some welcomed benchmarks across both crude segments in an ever-evolving geopolitical landscape. In the product sector ADNOC have sold their LR1 sisters BANI YAS and YAMILAH-III 75K DWT STX 2010/2011 for USD 22.2 million each. A notable decrease from the last comparable transaction of FLAGSHIP WILLOW 75K DWT SPP 2012 at USD 27.8 million in February 2025.   Dry markets were equally active this week with CMB selling their Newcastlemax MINERAL HIROSHIGE 208K DWT IMABARI 2019 basis a forward delivery for USD 65 million while the scrubber fitted Capesize BULK GINZA 182K DWT IMABARI 2020 was sold to Genco for USD 64 million. Lastly In the handysize sector the NY TRADER III 39K DWT JIANGMEN NANYANG 2016 was sold by clients of Nisshin to a European buyer for USD 16.8 million.

text: MEG Saudi acceptance was released late but no cuts or restrictions on propane reported. However, uncertainties over potential disruption on Middle East supply lent support to the front CP, coupled with the soaring crude. By the time of writing, Jul CP for C3 was traded at $603 and C3/C4 at $30.   Slim buying interests for Jul liftings FOBs seen this week, as freight soared up since the Israel-Iran conflict. Evenly split cargo was offered at ard Jul CP minus 40s but no bids heard. HPCL tendered to buy upto three evenly split grade for Aug and Sep lifting or delivery.   Earlier this week we’ve heard Iranian suppliers expediated the loadings and tried to deplete the storage. Our shiptrack shows over 900kt LPG on the water now and some prompt cargos for late Jun/early Jul arrival basis Schina are still on sale.   FAR EAST Cash premium for 23/0 2h Jul delivery basis Chiba softened this week, traded from plus $4 to $2. A similar parcel for 1h Aug delivery was traded at Jul FEI plus $1.5. 46/0 for 2h Jul delivery basis Ningbo was changed hand over window at Jul FEI plus $3.   Outside window demand has dampened by soaring flat prices and negative petchem margins, especially Jul FEI surged up by $40, which refrained Chinese buyers from taking any more US stems given additional 10% tariff. Additionally, there are prompt propane cargo was offered into China at Jul CP plus single digit. FPC cancelled their buy tender for propane on Jul to Aug delivery and butane on 2h Aug delivery into Mailiao, as offers not attractive. HTC just issued buy tender for 23kt butane delivered 3-9 Aug.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US With the recent geopolitically oriented and tension-based gains seen in crude oil, which have brought WTI to its highest levels since January, propane itself has been quick to move in lock-step and has also now risen to its highest point since the first part of the year.  Where that had allowed the relationship between MB c3 and WTI to reach as much as 56%, by now the differential has relaxed to a more palatable 45% in recent trading days.  The EIA this week released its propane inventory data which showed a generally agreeable 1.5mmbbl build to an overall total of 67.50mmbbls as of 13 Jun.  Production levels in the US remain at high levels (2.880mmbbls/day) while export volumes were off just a bit at 1.911mmbbls/day.  This is believed to be due to recent weather-related issues which impacted the electrical systems at a couple of the terminals and caused single-digit days delays which are now being addressed.  Based on 5-yr averages, Week 25 should see a build of ~1.6mmbbls, though the longer-term outlook over the summer build season rests in the hands of production rates and export volumes, some of which could be impacted by the weather.

EAST Since the first attacks on Iran last Friday we have so far only registered one single spot fixture intended to load inside of the Middle East Gulf. Aramco acceptances are now finalized, and whether this will flush out cargos from the Middle East Gulf right away, or if we will continue to see Charterers on the fence remains to be seen. So far only one uncovered cargo is being worked in the Middle East and we are just one and a half week away from July.  WEST The West VLGC freight market continues to be closely tied to the state of the arbitrage, which remains a primary driver of rate direction. Recent weeks have seen periods where rate momentum has been more pronounced in the MEG than in the U.S., and this trend has continued into the current week.  At present, the highest level fixed stands at USD 128 basis HCvP, despite RT/C levels trading in the USD 80–90 per metric ton range—indicating a spread of USD 12,000–14,000 per day between the two markets.  For July loading, owners and relets fixing in the West seem more focused on locking in 80–90 day round voyages at firm levels, rather than chasing the shorter 20–40 day voyages prevailing in RT/C.  To date, 24 fixtures have been reported in the USG, with only 6–8 ships remaining prompt for the balance of the month. This increasingly tight tonnage list points to possible upward pressure on rates if more freight demand emerges.

NORTH SEA Despite a very active market in the North Sea the past week we saw a small downward correction on rates. We are currently reaching to end-month loading dates for local runs. Tonnage availability looks sufficient and with a handful of relets still around we don’t expect any dramatic changes on rates in the current fixing window.    MEDITERRANEAN After a few days with a firmer sentiment, owners and relets both decided to move yesterday and fix any available cargoes in the market. Rates vary for different routes and the benchmark for Ceyhan/Mediterranean runs for end-early dates is still priced around WS 135 levels. Tonnage list looks more plentiful in the current fixing window, but keep in mind a couple of vessels will focus on areas outside the Mediterranean/Black Sea and rates could move sideways.

This week, the Panamax market appears to be nearing a short-term peak, with softer spot activity hinting at potential downward pressure on the 5TC index, possibly pushing it back towards the mid-10k levels in the weeks ahead. The Atlantic market has seen patchy activity; limited visibility persists in the North Atlantic, while South America shows a softer undertone despite still commanding some premiums on prompt transatlantic rounds. The Pacific market has maintained selective firmness, supported notably by consistent Japanese tender activity and steady East Australian enquiry, though a clear two-tiered dynamic has emerged, with some pockets of tonnage oversupply tempering overall sentiment. Owners might consider fixing coverage while current levels hold, whereas charterers should stay alert for opportunities as market sentiment shifts cautiously weaker.

The week gone by has been an eventful one for tanker owners. On the back of the Israel/Iran conflict MEG/East rates have surged 25 points, or more than 50% since last Wednesday. There are two schools out there now as to where the market is. One is “take the money honey” arguing that WS 69-70 has now been repeated a few times, and the other that it’s still got legs what with the uncertainty surrounding the war and possible US involvement – and Saudi July stem dates are still not out. However, it is fair to say that most agree that it’s not going down. The Atlantic market is ticking along with eg a USG/China run logged at USD 7.25 million, and some suggest upwards to USD 7.5 million has been paid, considerably up from last done levels, albeit still not quite on par with Brazil and West Africa/East earnings where rates are more linked to the MEG.

A busier day yesterday and today with a good number of ships taken on subs in the West. Per our counts we have approximately 9-10 mbbls left to move for first decade West Africa with a list that appears healthy enough to limit any aggressive upside. Considering the delta in TCEs for a UKCM opener when comparing USG/TA and TD20 we are likely to see such tonnage avoid ballasting over to the States.   Across in the USG, WS 72.5 was paid on a cargo that had been hanging over since last week. Tonnage is reasonably healthy but with the absence of ballasters there is some sensitivity to demand. However, the Afra last done sits at eq.145 x 67.5 so for remaining June stems and possibly early July stems those charterers that can quote basis 70kt will be incentivized to do so.   In the MEG, WS 115 has been reported for an eastbound cargo. Tonnage remains fairly balanced; however, with ongoing uncertainty and threats in the region, rates may continue to rise.

The LNG shipping market is rarely immune from the influence of geopolitical events, though with Middle East tensions boiling over into further direct conflict, the risk posed by the potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz affecting more than 20% of global LNG supply, brings a degree of uncertainty rarely seen in the industry. The reality of weak supply/demand fundamentals has kept rates subdued for the year to date, but sentiment has continued to firm this week with security of supply on the shipping side paramount in case of significant disruption to trade flows. On an operational level, owners face increased AWRP and greater vigilance when transiting high risk areas, and some additional logistical measures to limit time within the region, but it is business as usual for now for loadings out of the Middle East. Further international involvement would of course bring additional complexity to an already fragile situation.   Chartering activity remains robust with numerous fresh spot requirements being worked in all three major hubs, East, Middle East and West, and there remains a premium for vessels West of Suez. The end of July is looking a little tighter on paper, and combined with the backdrop in the Middle East sentiment is firming. Whilst charterers have been comfortable with spot exposure through the year thus far, there is now more incentivise to lock in tonnage for multimonth period against the backdrop of firming rates on the prompt and further forward

In the Pacific, a growing list of available tonnage is beginning to weigh on sentiment, even as trading volumes remain relatively active. On C5, Rio Tinto was heard fixing at USD 9.60 pmt for 1–3 July dates, a modest uptick that suggests demand is holding, though supply-side pressure may start to cap further gains.  In the Atlantic, the South remains light on ballast traffic, offering some support, while the North Atlantic continues to tighten as we move into the second half of June. On C3, sentiment has cooled somewhat from the highs - CSN was reported fixing in the low USD 25s basis their terms, for mid July loading. While this reflects a firmer tone than recent benchmarks, forward momentum appears stalled for now.

The Supramax and Handysize markets remained relatively subdued, with the Atlantic showing more resilience compared to Asia. The US Gulf continued to support firmer sentiment in both segments, while the South Atlantic maintained steady demand, contributing to a more optimistic outlook. In contrast, the Continent and Mediterranean regions faced ongoing pressure due to limited fresh inquiry. The Pacific markets remained quiet across both sectors, with an extended tonnage list and soft cargo availability leading to a cautious tone. Overall, while the Atlantic offered some support, broader market activity was muted with few signs of momentum building in the Pacific.

Almost a clean sweep for MRs this week as the sector remains the focus of second-hand tanker buyers. This has been the story on tanker S&P throughout the last months primarily due to the recent correction in pricing, but also the anticipated deliveries to take place this year. Most of the MRs sold this week are SS due, indicating sellers will take market offerings in order to avoid spending more on SS due units. Scrubber fitted NORDTOKYO (50K DWT Samsung HI Geoje 2020) was sold for USD 38.2M, against last done scrubber fitted EDEN (49K HMD 2020) at USD 40M back in March of this year.   A much quieter than usual week on dry, where liquidity has not been an issue so far this year. The underlying story, however, remains the same where majority older ships are transacted amongst the rare modern sale. Values have been sliding gradually against the consistent yet uninspiring earnings market, seen in scrubber fitted BRIGHT PEGASUS (82K DWT Tsuneishi Zhoushan 2013) which sold for USD 17.8M this week, against scrubber fitted BRIGHT GEMINI (82K DWT Tsuneishi Zhoushan 2013) from same sellers which sold for USD 23M back in September 2024.

A rush of activity late last week saw the number of Atlantic spot fixtures reach double digits through the preceding seven days. Although many of these requirements were for intra-basin voyages with the usual cap on tonne-mile demand, there may be an outsized impact on the market due to some tonne-time affects; the Egypt and Jordan cargo sales drove much of the shipping demand and there are sometimes delays and uncertainty around discharge slots into the FSRUs. A large Argentina tender has the same effect of prompting lifters to seek additional tonnage in the Atlantic Basin, and flexibility around discharge dates remains key.   Despite the large volume of activity for July laycans in the Atlantic, we see spot charter levels fairly flat week-on-week and rates have settled only slightly higher than what was seen at the beginning of this quarter. Whether this small upward trajectory will continue throughout the summer remains to be seen, especially with limited signs of life in the arbitrage trades East, but there are several enquiries for near-term multi-month charters which should provide further support in the coming months.   The bid-offer remains wide on longer term periods, but there are now a number of open enquiries across a range of charter lengths so it will be interesting to see how rates converge.   Away from the day-to-day activities on the LNG shipping market, there are some promising noises from the US around a softening in tone regarding US-built LNGCs lifting US volume. This is an entirely practical and pragmatic development that many have expected, so although it may not be a surprise it is nonetheless a welcome step in removing uncertainty for projects, Owners and Charterers alike.
