comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US Despite a robust (but generally anticipated) propane inventory build reported by the EIA this week, the Mont Belvieu propane market defied gravity yet again and closed up by over a penny on the day.  The 4.1mmbbl increase brought overall propane stocks in the US to 66mmbbls, or more than 94% of the same time last year, which is why the market saw the increase as a potential avenue toward a wider arb.   This was not to be the case, however, and even as of this writring the arb from the East remains in the high $-140s/mt.  Furthermore, with freight inching slightly higher with each of the next fixtures, the netback has been subdued. At present there are bids in the low 4cpg range, but inasmuch as the last done was vastly nearer to 5cp – sellers are standing their ground as terminal fees continue to hover just above cargo cancellation levels.

EAST June spot fixing is already on par with March (25 spot deals ex MEG including Yanbu) – the strongest spot lifting month(s) so far this year. Market expects a few more deals towards the very end of the month before July fixing takes the focus. The open end June ships in the East might eventually be absorbed by US cargos, meaning although there’s a selection of open ships still off June dates – freight is set to remain stable.  WEST USG/East freight is currently trading at parity with MEG/East rates. As of today, 16 spot fixtures have been concluded for July. Based on historical monthly trends, this implies that approximately 14 cargoes remain to be fixed for the month.  U.S. gas production data released yesterday showed a build of 4 million barrels—the second consecutive week of higher-than-expected inventory growth. Despite this, the East arbitrage has not widened as anticipated, largely due to hedging activity in the paper market. As a result, freight levels are holding just a few dollars below the last done rate of USD 122/mt

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Spot differentials for Jul liftings are under pressure as of subdued interests. BPCL was reported to award their buy tender for a Jul evenly split FOB cargo at Jul CP minus 40s. At the time of writing, Jul CP C3 was traded at $585 and C3/C4 was traded at $30.   FAR EAST Cash premium for Jul delivery propane softened this week. Despite some hiccups in Us loadings, cargos for Jul delivery are still in ample supply as importers reselling in window. A couple of 46/0 cargos for 2h Jul delivery basis Ningbo was traded at Jul FEI plus mid-single digit. And several parcels of 23/0 for 2h Jul delivery basis Chiba were changed hand at Jul FEI plus $3 and afterwards $1.5.   Outside window one PDH importer was reported to secure two lots of 46/0 for end Jul delivery into Echina and NChina at Jul FEI plus mid-high and high single digit respectively, which cargos are reckoned to be US origin. With additional 10% tariff into China, US stems are still affordable to import compared to non-Us stem, with minimal price advantages.   Other than propane, butane demand restored for petchem cracking, together with some speculative purchase. HTC was reported to secure 0/2 for late Jul delivery at Jul MOPJ minus 30s, which is the 3rd butane parcel procured for Jul delivery. Similarly, FPC was reported to award similar cargo at Jul MOPJ minus 40s. One Jul delivery butane cargo was heard traded into China at fixed price of $510, equates to Jul CP minus 40s roundabouts, has stimulated other Chinese players’ buying interests.

On the Pacific side, we note a build-up of tonnage in the region, though trading volumes remain decent across the board. On C5, Rio was heard fixing at USD 9.45 pmt for end June dates, reflecting steady demand despite the increase in ships on the offer. South Atlantic remains thin on ballasters, while the North Atlantic looks increasingly tight heading into the second half of June. On C3 hearing offers in the mid USD 21's pmt for end July dates, with very low USD 21's being last done on those dates, we can see sentiment cautiously firming on the back of limited prompt tonnage.

The market remained broadly flat over the week, with soft sentiment prevailing across both the Atlantic and Asia. Holidays and limited activity in Europe and Asia contributed to sluggish demand, while tonnage availability remained high. The Atlantic saw some isolated fixtures, but overall momentum was lacking. In Asia, owners continued to reduce rates amid an oversupply of vessels and limited cargoes. Fixing activity was thin, with a few notable fixtures reported but lacking full details and period market remains relatively quiet.

NORTH SEA North Sea continues on a sideways path with a softer undertone. Dates now pushing to very end of the 2nd decade with little sign of any upturn in activity. Vessels continue to leave the area rather than take the inevitable waiting time where to ballast to isn’t as clear as it usually is.  July stems are out and look healthier in volume than June with Teesport back after maintenance.  MEDITERRANEAN A dozen plus ships is on subs/hold since Monday as the expected busy 3rd decade has kicked off properly. After the necessary small correction, rates should have hit bottom now with a proper clear-out being done on the tonnage list. The busy Mediterranean will attract North Sea ballasters and relets so potentially could move sideways for now.

Western markets remain oversupplied with tonnage, with rates across the board in the red with little sign of the rot stopping today. July dates are starting to move into the natural window in West Africa, however, charterers will not be inclined to flood the market with volume as plenty of vessels are due to supplement the list heading into next week. Yes, WS 85 was achieved off prompter dates on a cargo that required a big lifter, however, given the downward correction we have seen in the Mediterranean and rumored out of Brazil it seems even more likely TD20 will land close to WS 77.5.  In the USG prompt boats are starting to pile up with bearish fundamentals resulting in a 5 point decrease in rates from last done off prompter dates. With the VLCCs busy off end June/early July and Aframaxes 20th June onwards piling up as ballasters arrive, its hard to see where the Suezmaxes get the opportunity to turn their fortunes around.   The tonnage complexion in the East is tighter week on week. Yesterday there were reports of multiple Basrah cargoes working, however, all the noise died out with relets in position and the inevitable VLCCs lurking in the background likely keeping Suezmax owners' ideas realistic. Hard to see where there is much room for growth despite the tighter list.   Overall, even if we see a run on Suezmaxes, the VLCCs in the West and East have resupplemented and rates remain at rock bottom. As long as this dynamic remains it is hard to see any prospect for growth for smaller sizes.

The VLCC market remains in a lethargic state with little change to speak of from the MEG in the week gone by. A sputter of activity is keeping the flame from being extinguished, but rates are going sideways - at best - and held up more from stubbornness on the owners’ part than supply and demand. The Atlantic, however, has seen a bit of a tonnage clear-out, albeit on falling rates, but with two third of the US export program yet to be tackled, a continues flow from Brazil and a bit of West African seasoning, there could possibly be potential for slight a turnaround as we move further out on the curve. Hope is eternal.

The Panamax market held firm this week, supported by steady mineral and coal demand, especially out of Asia and the North Atlantic, while grain flows from Brazil and the US provided some underlying stability despite overall flat growth in major commodities. North Atlantic tonnage remains tight, with fronthaul activity and bullish sentiment keeping rates steady to slightly higher, though the South Atlantic was more stable. In the Pacific, fresh tenders and solid coal volumes out of Australia and Indonesia fueled growing confidence, with bid/offer spreads widening as owners push for higher rates. Overall, the market looks poised for sideways to slightly firmer movement in the week ahead, with fundamentals largely unchanged but sentiment remaining upbeat across both basins.

As much of the market descended on Oslo for Norshipping the story in the tanker second hand market remained the same, with MRs still providing the majority of activity. Values appear to be stabilising, having corrected significantly from the heights of the market during summer last year. Torm continued the sell out of their older units, with Chemsea acquiring TORM DISCOVERER/VOYAGER (45k dwt Brodotogir 2008) for USD 34M en bloc. Elsewhere, Navios provided the market with a new benchmark in the Afra sector, acquiring resale sisters (115k dwt Zhoushan Changhong 2026) for USD xs 67M each, from Pro Tanker Investment.  Similarly this week was not one of great change for the dry bulk market. Rates on the smaller and medium size tonnage are unremarkable, and capesize returns have calmed down somewhat after a recent spike. This is resulting in a consistent story for the second-hand space, with occasional modern transactions and mostly c.15-year-old ships being sold into Far Eastern buyers. In the one modern transaction this week, Greek buyers picked up scrubber fitted Kamsarmax AOM SOPHIE II (81k dwt Sanoyas 2020) for USD 31.5M, in line with last done units. In the Capsesize sector, Costamare bought IMPERATOR AUSTRALIS (176k dwt Shanghai Jiangnan Changxing 2012) for USD 25.5M, from Japanese sellers.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US After having been fixed in the upper 4cpg range (twice), a low 5cpg transaction was recorded – all for Jun 4:0 parcels – the FOB USGC terminalling fee market seems to be very slowly edging upwards.  Calculated netbacks as of this writing are in the 6cpg range, though trade is thin as the number of offers vastly exceeds willing buyers.  That, combined with an undercurrent of strength in the near-term freight market may be keeping a lid on things, though. The EIA this week revealed a surprisingly large propane inventory build – one that was much needed, as it has been hoped that a wider arb could help activity levels improve.  As of 30th May stock levels increased by 6.8mmbbls to an overall total of 61.90mmbbls.  This is on the heels of record-level production levels of 2.897mmbbls and a soft weekly export level of just 1.231mmbbls/day (against a maximum of 2.335mmbbls/day).   This, in turn, is likely the result the reshuffling that came about on the news of tariffs, which when announced gave cause for a host of lifters to swap from 4:0 parcels to 2;2 cargoes in their attempts to deliver to non-Chinese destinations.

EAST Market looks flattish with few deals done East of Suez this week. A small handful of uncovered cargos are being floated and with West taking the lead, second half June may remain stable although spot volumes might not match the strong first half.  WEST A handful of deals reported fixed in the US this week with last done at $119. Owners latest ideas north of last done, supported by improved arb economics overnight. However, one can argue that freight availability still looks healthy from 2H July in the USGC/USEC region.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Discounts for Jul lifting FOB on evenly split ratio continued weakening and was assessed at minus $40 to Jul CP, yet no deals done. BPCL issued tender to buy one evenly split cargo for Jul lifting, which reckoned will be discussed in deeper discounts, in view of slim buying interest on butane. At the time of writing, Jul CP was traded at $580 for C3, and C3/C4 at $30.   FAR EAST Cash premium for Jul delivery propane surged up due to the unexpected disruptions on US loadings, and potential replacement for ethane as US export curbs into China. 23/0 1h Jul delivery basis Chiba was traded at Jul FEI plus $11 and similar bid for 23/0 2h Jul was at $9 vs offer at $14. Outside window a couple of 46/0 bss EChina for Jul delivery was changed hand at Jul FEI plus low mid-teens.   Several PDHs have issued buy tender to secure Jul feedback, with price reported at Jul CP plus 20s, and then softened to 10s on non Us stems basis SChina. One NChina-based player procured a Us stem at Jul FEI plus ard $20 reportedly, which equates to Jul CP plus hi 20s after additional 10% tariff. Sinobenny was said to cancel their Jul butane buy tender as offers not attractive, reported at certain premium over Jul C4 CP. Most butane buyers expected to achieve certain discounts to Jul C4 CP as of long butane supply. Hanwha Total was reported to procure 2 lots of 0/23 and 1 lot of 2/0 for Jul delivery via tender, with C4 at MOPJ minus 30s and C3 at FEI plus single digit respectively.

NORTH SEA With US and Mediterranean markets pushing up we have seen a lot of tonnage leave the area, but with a lack of activity in the North Sea  we still have prompt natural tonnage available which is now looking at waiting time with cargo window now heading towards  mid month.  MEDITERRANEAN Mediterranean/Black Sea markets slowly climbed this week as USG spike improved sentiment in Europe as well while activity in the Mediterranean was strong. Owners are enjoying good returns as the summer just started and it remains to be seen for how long this will happen.

A busier day above and below the surface. Tonnage remains tight for early 2nd decade with a couple of cargoes outstanding on the front end that are being shown punchy numbers. However, we have seen a good number of charterers reach forward and poach tonnage for end June loadings which may damage the long term prospects for TD20. Additionally, although VLCCs have seen reasonable activity out of Brazil tonnage is still aplenty and the threat that the larger ladies cannibalize Suezmax stems remains.   Over in the USG we have an extreme discrepancy in pricing across all three vessel classes. A VLCC is on subs at USD 2.5m for USG/UKCM which freights USD 300k better than taking an Aframax bss last done, thus expect VLCCs continue to poach stems where possible. Although Aframax and Suezmax are tighter in the West, these illogical market dynamics at some point have to cause rates to cool.

The Panamax market remained relatively stable this week, with fundamentals balanced across both the Atlantic and Pacific. In the Atlantic, grain continued to drive activity alongside occasional coal shipments, while charterers tried to pressure rates lower. The Pacific saw a gradual improvement in sentiment, as increased inquiries helped clear spot tonnage and boosted optimism. Activity in Asia was slower due to regional holidays, but overall rate levels were maintained, with the market now looking for renewed demand to sustain its current footing.

It’s starting to feel very Summery in this market, although perhaps we can lay some of the blame at the feet of Nor Shipping, which has lured a number of chartering protagonists into Oslo this week. Whatever the reason, there’s been a noticeable reduction in spot market activity, and this has in turn seen us reduce rates in the East for both 2-Strokes and TFDEs (we won’t comment on Steam ship rates…). With a growing number of disponent owners now marketing their July availability, one assumes that the next done in the Pacific will be hotly contested, especially when factoring in the independently controlled tonnage that’s currently idling within the basin. In the Atlantic, and on term, we’ve decided to keep everything on hold and whilst this does leave one-year 2-Stroke rates trading at a ~25% premium to spot, there’s no sign of any MEGI/MEGA/XDF owners discounting their tonnage for 12 months of coverage just yet. This is partly explained by the low base we’re starting from (there’s little incentive for portfolios to release their best ships at these levels) but it’s also the case that there are a number of term requirements for owners to choose from (we count ~15 for delivery in 2025 and at least the same again basis delivery from 2026). Given this smorgasbord of charterers, periods and trades on offer, it’s little wonder that Owners are ignoring current spot rate levels and placing their hopes in the various suppliers of jam for tomorrow. Of course, not all ships are created equally so whilst it’s been difficult to close the bid-ask spread for the newest 2-strokes, those charterers who are able to make use of TFDEs for their trade have been shown some competitive offers and this is likely where the best value sits for now.   Turning to the Newbuild market, there’s been no new conventional orders placed these past seven days, but there has been further growth in the SSLNG fleet with United Bunkers confirming a second 20k LNGBV order from CIMC SOE at the end of last week.

The Supramax and Handysize markets remained subdued across both the Atlantic and Pacific, weighed down by limited fresh demand and oversupply of tonnage. In the Atlantic, Supramax activity was mostly flat, with only minor improvement in the Continent-Mediterranean, while the South Atlantic and US Gulf remained soft. Asia saw reduced activity due to regional holidays and weak sentiment. Similarly, the Handysize market continued to weaken in the Continent and Mediterranean, with firming limited to the US Gulf. The South Atlantic stayed under pressure, and Asia remained quiet with little new inquiry and a growing tonnage list.

Things have gone from bad to worse in the VLCC-market in the week gone by, with now even Aframaxes being paid more than VLCCs for USG/transatlantic runs, pretty much summing up the dismal state of affairs. Ships continue to be picked off en mass on the quiet from the MEG, and with no details leaking we can only assume they are on par with last done, or possibly a tad lower. And with information delayed that ships have been taken care of the count becomes skewed which in turn exacerbate the problem when players realize enquiries, they though were still there, are in fact long gone.

On the West Australia front, we see healthy volumes from miners and operators alike for 20 June onwards. Enquiries for East Australia coal have moved a tick up as well. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, we see a handful of enquiries for end June dates with operators out for first half of July dates. Some interested as well for more forward second half of July dates. Tonnage opening Far East is getting a tick tighter. Same can be observed for ballasting tonnage. On C5, we reached high USD 9 pmt levels by mid-week. For C3, sentiment is uptick as we see mid-high USD 21 pmt levels done for early-mid July dates.

MR sales continue to provide liquidity to the tanker second hand market. Despite some recent stability on values basis last dones, it would not be surprising to see values correct further amid significant deliveries to come throughout the rest of 2025. At the older end of the spectrum, PS CAPRI (49K DWT STX Jinhae 2011) sold for USD 18M, in line with last done GLENDA MELODY (49K HMD 2011) at USD 17.9M. Younger units NORD JEWEL*/JOY (49K JMU 2018) *scrubber fitted, sold for just under 74M en bloc to Paragon Mobility, in line with last done en bloc transaction PS ATENE/MILANO (49K DWT HMD 2018).    Further question marks over the legality and implementation of President Trump’s sweeping tariffs this week mean a similar story of uncertainty in the shipping markets. That said, the dry market remains consistent and active, although unexciting. Competition is still fierce for large handy bulkers, seen in BUNUN ORCHID (37K DWT I-S Shipyard 2021) bought by Stealth for USD 25M. Elsewhere, Indian buyers acquired the Kamsarmax trio CL GRACE/MONA/TIFFANY (81K DWT Yangfan 2012/2013) for USD 45M en bloc.

EAST/WEST There have been a handful of cargo enquiries in both the East and the West this week and largely freight is maintaining momentum in both basins. MEG fixing activity (albeit somewhat scarce number-wise this week) is keeping US freight ideas firm around the USD 110-115 per ton mark. Slowly but surely the West market is starting to focus on July enquiries whilst there are seemingly still some June fixing left. With the expected US FOB expansions from the Nederland terminal, there’s more in store for the VLGC market going forward.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Jun CP at $600 for C3 and $570 for C4, down by $10 and $20 respectively, which unsurprisingly higher than expectation. Jun C3/C4 enlarged to $30, reflecting long supply on butane. Evenly split cargo for Jun lifting was assessed at Jun CP minus $60s or even lower, in view of thin discussions, heavy backwardation into Jul and downward CFR bids. After Jun CP announced, Jul C3 CP surged to $575.   FAR EAST Slim window after CP set, with 23/0 for 1h Jul delivery bid at Jul FEI plus $3 and yet to see offers. Earlier this week a handful of buyers are trying to cover shorts for 23/0 2h Jun delivery basis Chiba and bid once surged to Jun FEI plus $9.   Outside window a flurry of tenders floating. Indonesia Pertamina awarded their buy tender for mid Jul delivered evenly split cargo at Jul CP plus $10 reportedly. Lotte Chemical cancelled their buy tender on heavy butane cargo for Jul delivery as price not attractive versus napatha for cracking reportedly. One SChina cracker user awarded their buy tender for 11-22 kt C4 before 10/Jun delivery at Jun CP minus single digit, while another Chinese reported to buy 23 kt C4 for Jul delivery at the equivalence price of Jul CP minus single digit. CPC also issued tender to procure a 1/1 parcel for Jul yet to hear result. Despite active butane inquiry, a handful of heavy butane cargos lifted ex AG are reported unsold and buying appetite inhibited as of slow consumptions.   Propane discussions are healthier but with softened premium on non-US stems. HTC tendered to buy 23/0 for last decade Jul delivery. A couple of PDH users have issued tenders to secure Jul delivery propane (excluded US stems), which awarded at Jul CP plus high 20s to mid-high 30s range based on different location. We are expecting a few more petchem players buy tender next week to secure Jul feedstock. However importers refrained from speculative buying and higher operation motivation due to negative margins.   Other than normal stems, we’ve seen over 900kt special origin cargos arrived in China for both Apr and May, 20% up than average in Q1 2025.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US Sellers heavily outnumber buyers in the US FOB market.  Offers of all varieties litter the market, both in June and into July, and are priced accordingly.  Most sellers have reduced their asking prices to the low 5cpg range, but the last known transaction was accomplished for a late-Jun 4:0 at 4.75cpg, nearer to the calculated netback level, and setting a new bar.    Freight rates are playing a crucial role in the matter and seem to have the upper hand at the moment as a rise in spot shipping levels results in a corresponding decline in terminal fees.  Some market participants had this week sidelined themselves after the holiday on Monday but were eagerly awaiting the data revealed today by the EIA.  A large propane inventory build was both hoped and anticipated as a higher build would likely allow Mont Belvieu c3 values to relax and thus open the arb and improve netbacks.  However, despite exceedingly robust production levels, exports were also strong and the EIA reported a 2.00mmbbl propane inventory increase to an overall total of 55.1mmbbls.

If last week could be characterised by rates drifting away slightly due to a lack of firm interest, the market has woken back up this week with nearly ten spot requirements being worked worldwide at the time of writing. The bulk of activity in the West is centred around July laycans, though there are still one or two end June requirements to be covered. Any relatively prompt cargoes would likely see a lot of competition in the Atlantic and thus lower rates, but further out the balance appears to shift and levels are looking like creeping back upwards. Flexibility for deliveries into Asia and thus through the remainder of Summer continue to command a slight premium. The Middle East and Pacific regions also burst back to life with post-WGC activity and rise are firming, although competition is likely to keep a lid on rates. The collective exposure to the spot market is unrivalled compared with recent years and despite some corners of the market expecting weaker tonne mile demand due to European LNG pricing in Winter, there are still few players willing to release tonnage beyond the shoulder months as of now.   No sooner does one industry gathering end and another is on the horizon: Nor shipping returns next week and much like WGC, a healthy turnout is expected. For those joining us in Oslo, we wish you safe travels.

NORTH SEA A short week started slowly and with maintenance affecting Ekofisk production in June and a smattering of Suezmax in the frame has meant early stems for Afra have been slightly lacking in the market.  Surrounding areas have also been on the slower, softer side limiting the ability to head away for better markets.  On paper June looks like it will be a challenging month for Aframaxes in the North Sea.  MEDITERRANEAN The short week started quiet and mid way through it, owners are on the lookout for any opportunities to fix their vessels. With a long tonnage list in the Mediterranean/Black Sea of more than 20 vessels open by the end of the coming weekend - excluding Red Sea positions - owners' resistance will be tested sooner or later. Surrounding areas do not provide great alternatives and the safe haven of USG took another hit yesterday evening.

We see a reasonable level of enquiries from miners and operators alike for early-mid June dates. Peripheral volumes out of other fronts of the Pacific are slightly lackluster. Enquiries out of C3 ex Brazil and West Africa are primarily for second half of June dates with multiple operators seeking for July dates forward buying. Far East spot tonnage is slowly tightening. Ballasting tonnage is slowly thinning for second half of June and July. Fixtures concluded at low-mid USD 8 pmt levels by mid-week and in the low USD 19 pmt levels for Brazil for mid June dates.

The week began on a softer note, with sentiment remaining weak across both the Atlantic and Asian markets. In the Atlantic, limited fresh enquiry and a lack of support from the south continued to weigh on rates, while the US Gulf held relatively steady but lacked momentum. Asia remained under pressure, particularly in the south, where an oversupply of tonnage and scarce cargo availability kept the market subdued. Overall, activity was muted and confidence remained low. By the end of the week, the tone across both basins was soft, with the 11TC average reflecting the weaker conditions. Limited activity on period side.

The Panamax market saw little improvement this week, with long tonnage lists and weak demand keeping sentiment bearish across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. In the Atlantic, sluggish activity after the UK and US holidays led to softer rates, with charterers firmly in control as fresh cargoes remained scarce and fixtures often slipped below previous benchmarks. The Pacific basin mirrored this trend, as a steady stream of open vessels and a lack of new enquiries saw owners under increasing pressure to accept lower levels, especially on Indonesian coal runs and Australian trips. Overall, with limited fresh business and oversupply of ships in both basins, owners are facing another challenging week ahead unless demand picks up meaningfully.

Fairly active start to the week in West Africa, with a spread of 2nd decade dates worked. With tonnage lists looking more balanced and more volumes expected to come, it appears that fundamentals are leaning in owners favor. Hence, despite WS 76 standing as last done for West Africa/UKCM, do not expect other owners will be there to break WS 80 as easily - we expect rates to keep steady with potential for upside.  Across the pond we are still short on local availabilities and it is unlikely we see UKCM vessels ballast TA given the gulf in TCEs when comparing USG/TA Vs TD20. However, a weak Aframax floor (eq.145kt x 55.5 has been repeated) and the presence of relets on the front end means we may not see rates respond accordingly.    In the MEG, we have seen a few deals surface, however, owners need to see more volume this week before any momentum can build. Basrah/West candidates are not in huge supply, however, rates remain subdued as owners and relets alike have strong appetite to reposition back west. For Eastbound, the tonnage complexion is far friendlier with rates under continued pressure.

VLCC activity has been slow in the week gone by, at least on the surface, and oil company/trader relets have led the charge in pushing rates down in all areas. A lot of reported internal programming by charterers, China Inc “Uber” bookings, and position lists still littered with relets has left, at least a perception, that there’s less to choose from for the independent owning community. Add to that a scarcely populated cargo board from where we’re at on the curve and we’re on the verge of ”catching a falling knife” territory, if not already there. Further downward potential evident: eyes closed, nose pinched, going once…

The Product sector continues to see a healthy amount of activity with three MR sales to report this week. The GLENDA MELODY 47K DWT HMD 2011 l) was sold for $17.9 million to after nearly a year on the market. Enquiry levels for older vessels remains strong in the Crude sector with GMS being the reported buyers of the scrubber-fitted VLCC M. STAR 314K DWT KAWASAKI 2008 for $46 million, still offering a compelling exit opportunity for owners of similar vintaged VL’s.   Far eastern players continue to drive activity in the dry bulk sector with KEY ACTION (82K DWT TSUNEISHI ZHOUSHAN) ending up in Chinese hands for $15.1 million - a price reflective of the segment’s subdued earnings experienced throughout this year. Conversely, modern tonnage remains scarce, compelling buyers to compete for the limited candidates available.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US The global LPG market is softening on all fronts and is led by the declines being seen in the US domestic market where propane, having rallied earlier in the month, seems to be succumbing under the weight of the latest EIA report. For the week ending 16 May total US primary stock levels rose by 2.7mmbbls to an overall total of 53.10mmbbls, or about 83% of last year’s total in mid May.  As anticipated, the EIA data showed production levels at 2.833mmbbls/day (against a high of 2.852mmbbls/day and a 5yr average of 2.440mmbbls/day).  Likewise, however, the export number revealed a decline which on its own was not surprising.  Total exports were listed at 1.690mmbbls/day, which is still above the 5yr average, but well off the 2.335mmbbl/day overall high-water mark.  This is thought to be the result of a host of parties switching export cargo ratios from full propane to 50:50 lots.  That, in turn, is because of the US-led tariffs. Meanwhile, terminal fees on the Gulf Coast have been hovering just over cancellation economics as the arb from Asia remains depressed and netbacks – in consideration of robust, healthy freight levels – have been held down.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Butane supply is pretty long especially plenty of evenly split cargo available for sale on Jun liftings. KPC was reported to sell another 0/4 cargo for 18-23 Jun lifting, which is the 2nd pure butane cargo sold via tender for Jun loader. Qatar Energy was also said to award their sell tender for a 2/2 or 3/1 cargo on 26-29 Jun lifting, at CP minus 40s reportedly. On Thur window, one oil major offered a 19-20 Jun lifting 2/2 at a fixed price $555 for C3 and $525 for C4 as well, which equates to Jun CP minus $30s.   By the time of writing, Jun CP was assessed at $587 for C3 and $562 for C4. Jun/Jul CP was assessed at $30 backwardation.   FAR EAST  Active bids for propane delivered from 2h Jun to 2h Jul surged in window, but few offers seen. Earlier this week 23/0 parcel for 2h Jun was traded at Jun FEI plus $4.5 and similar parcel for 1h Jul was traded at Jun FEI plus $1.5. A couple of 46/0 for 2h Jun delivery basis NChina were changed hand at Jun FEI plus mid-high single digit. Similar cargo for 1h Jul delivery basis Ningbo was bid at Jun FEI link plus low single digit in window, and bid for 2h Jul 4/0 basis Yantai was at Jun FEI flattish.   Indian IOC was reported to buy monthly one 2/2 for Q3 at CP plus 20s-30s range, which help relieved butane selling pressure for Jul onwards but not front market. A couple of 0/4 cargos been loaded for late Jun/Jul delivery into Far East, which exerted pressure on butane sales. 2/2 for Jun delivery into China was traded at Jul CP plus 20s reportedly this week.    Comparatively, propane is still discussed in better premium. However, importers are evaluating costs between FEI link US stem with additional tariff and CP link Non-Us stem. One NChina PDH player issued a tender to procure 33kt or 46kt C3 excluding US origin for late Jun to Jul delivery. Despite the eroded margin, we are expecting some PDHs return from scheduled maintenance in late May/Jun, which might incite some buying inquiries, but at a weakening premium.

EAST The Middle East market is taking a drop as it looks like freight climbed too much too quickly. The gap in TCE earnings between East/West have seemingly become too big while the Arb is shut ex US, and we are seeing $ ideas coming into the mid-60s RT/CH from a peak of low 80s RT/CH at the beginning of the week on an India bound fixture.   WEST Most of the attention on freight has been East of Suez with no deals reported in West this week. We have been hovering around cancellation levels in the US lately, and two players were reported to have cancelled liftings in May and June earlier today. Nevertheless, a couple of players have tested the market for freight in end June and early July, but it remains to be seen where the next deal is at.

End of last week the stars looked aligned, and the MEG VLCC market poised for an uptick. Arguably MEG/East rates did inch into the WS 60’s, with a couple of prompt and/or replacement fixtures at WS 64 and 64.5 for short East, but failed to gain further traction. Charterers have played a good game and picked off a number of ships under the radar suggesting a bigger difference between the map and the terrain than the general perception, and with that yesterday saw a downward correction. NSRP got off at WS 59.5 for a MEG/Vietnam run, but this does calculate a few points better than your bog standard TD3C earning wise, and a WS 59.5 done by Formosa for MEG/Taiwan was concluded on an oil company relet ex d/d. So, good, or bad? All in the eye of the beholder. Formosa did manage to book a second ship at WS 59.5 as well, but again an oil company relet turned 15 years old. However all said and done, any upward pressure appears to have evaporated and it’s now all about holding the line for the owning community. Patience is a virtue not particularly prevalent but then again charterers cannot sit on their hands for ever either.

As many market participants gather for the World Gas Conference in Beijing this week, one may be forgiven for expecting market activity to come to a halt as in previous years, but the LNG shipping spot market is a different beast in 2025. We have perhaps seen a downturn in fresh requirements building over the past week in the Atlantic; however, fixing activity remains quite brisk for June cargoes, although increased competition among owner and sub-letters has erased some of the gains seen over the past couple of months. East of Suez, several prompt positions have found employment though there remains an overhang of modern tonnage likely to reposition to the Atlantic, and a further decline in rates has been observed for June dates. Overall though, this past week has felt more like a drift downwards rather than a serious fall.   Rates for multimonth periods covering the coming Winter remain higher than prompt spot levels, and with interest for such periods building there is some consensus of late-Summer or Winter uptick. Longer tenures through 2026 are largely flat though, and the following Winter is still proving tricky to price for owners and charterers.    Whilst unconfirmed, there is growing noise around further large-scale Newbuilding orders for deliveries before the end of the decade. There have been very few new orders this year and prices have eased, but Shipyards sit comfortably with long forward orderbooks and this latest news may alleviate downward pressure on prices.

NORTH SEA An active end to last week and the beginning of this week covered the majority of the remaining May stems reducing the available tonnage and pushing rates to rebound slightly from the lows of last week.  Natural tonnage will come back around for early June stems, and if we see the trend for larger vessels continue into June mixed with a reduced stem count caused by maintenance, it could be a challenging start to the summer for Aframax in the North Sea.  MEDITERRANEAN The Mediterranean/Black Sea market picked up the torch from North Sea since Monday with more than 10 vessels subs/fixed and a couple of relets on hold. Supply vs demand for tonnage is pretty balanced at the moment as dates are moving forward and the pool of candidates slowly replenishing. Also, Suezmax are not in the best condition setting the ceiling low for the Aframax.

Another quiet day in the West yesterday on the surface with rates softening across the board in the Atlantic. Yet to see a rate for a West Africa/UKCM run, but after the P66 and Petrobras numbers charterers should be pushing sub WS 80. Demand wise we have covered approximately 13 stems for 1st decade, therefore we are close to closing out the window with plenty of tonnage still present. With the incoming long weekend for the UK I would expect charterers to start reaching into 2nd decade today onwards.   It seems unlikely CPC will draw too many West Africa players given the tonnage dynamic in the Mediterranean, however, the USG appears poised to do so. The local list is not particularly long and is short on safe supplementation. Additionally, we have already had UKCM openers expressing willingness to fix at last done levels for USG/TA. Although VLCC activity has picked up a little for June overall exports are still very light which hints that there could be more volume than usual shovelled the way of the adjacent vessels classes. Of course it is not a certainty that exports will pick up but charterers should be aware of the pull the US may have for European openers. We had a similar dynamic last week where West Africa contenders were sponged on mass for Americas cargoes leading to end May TD20 cargoes having a tough time and eventually paying up.    The MEG has experienced a small dent in tonnage, however, downward pressure is still present as evidenced by MEG/EC India fixing down. Albeit we are not at crossover levels yet the Aframax floor sits at eq.130 x 89 for MEG/East. We will need to see greater volume from today for any stability to emerge.

We see a reasonable level of enquiries from miners and operators for early June dates. Peripheral volume out of other fronts of the Pacific are still present, albeit a tick lower form last week. Enquiries for C3 ex Brazil and West Africa are primarily for second half of June dates. Far East spot tonnage seem to be on the tighter side. Ballasting tonnage is slowly thinning for June dates. Fixtures concluded in the low USD 8 pmt levels for C5 and around mid USD 18 pmt levels for mid June dates in Brazil.

The Supramax/Ultramax market began the week on a quieter note, with limited fresh activity across most regions. In the Atlantic, the US Gulf maintained a firm tone, though signs suggest it may be nearing a peak, while the Continent-Mediterranean remained under slight downward pressure and the South Atlantic held steady in a balanced state. In contrast, the Pacific showed a firmer outlook, supported by a tightening tonnage list in Southeast Asia and modest improvements in demand further north. The Indian Ocean and Middle East regions were more subdued, with activity levels stable but lacking momentum. Overall, the market reflected a stable yet regionally uneven sentiment, with Pacific areas generally showing more strength than the Atlantic.

The Panamax market experienced additional softening this week, driven primarily by limited Atlantic activity where growing tonnage lists pressured transatlantic rates downward. Fronthaul trades from NCSA offered some resilience, though a lack of fresh cargoes keep fundamentals broadly bearish. In contrast, the Pacific provided some optimism, benefiting from stronger activity ex-East Australia and NoPac and an increasingly balanced tonnage supply. Looking ahead, the market’s direction will largely depend on the upcoming grain seasons in the Black Sea and US, weather conditions in Asia during the summer, and notably, any shifts in US-China trade dynamics. With ECSA grain season winding down, these factors will become increasingly critical for market sentiment.

Sellers of tankers are not pressed to sell, and it seems that eventually one will find a buyer in spite of current high asset values. Long time sales candidate NEW NAXOS (299K DWT Universal 2003) has changed hands this week for USD 33M, beating last done AUSTRALIS (299K DWT Universal 2003) which sold earlier in the year at USD 28M. Despite the healthy returns available in the earnings market, these levels provide an attractive exit point for owners, exhibited by Teekay selling suezmax pair ASPEN SPIRIT/CASCADE SPIRIT (156K DWT Rongsheng 2009) for USD 37.5M each to Nigerian buyers. The story is not quite so rosy in the products market, where we continue to see price correction. SEAWAYS CITRON/SEAWAYS FRONTIER (49K DWT HMD 2007) sold for USD 14M each, a far cry away from the USD c.25M they were seeking last summer.   The dry market continues its unremarkable run this week, that said in these uncertain times, owners will be very satisfied with the reliable returns they are seeing. HMM are back in a purchasing mood with the acquisition of scrubber fitted Newcastlemax LUISE OLDENDORFF (207K DWT Hyundai 2015) for USD 51M, otherwise it appears that the most likely buyers for second hand bulk carriers are located in China. In the capesize sector THALASSINI AVRA (182K DWT Universal 2011) sold for USD 29M, to Chinese buyers.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Slim discussions on evenly split cargos for Jun loaders this week and cash differentials deepened further as lack of buying interests. KPC was reported to sell their 0/4 cargo for 6-10 Jun lifting at Jun CP minus 30s to a SEA player. Indian IOC tendered to buy monthly one evenly split cargo for Q3 period on FOB or CFR basis, which might lend support to Q3 FOB discussions. By the time of writing, Jun C3 CP was traded at $584 and C3/C4 assessed at $25. Jun/Jul CP C3 are in $25 backwardation.   FAR EAST:  Cash premium for 23/0 1h Jun delivery basis Chiba improved to Jun FEI plus $7.5, as of a lack of offers for 1H period. Similar package for 2h Jun delivery was traded outside window at Jun FEI plus $6/7 reportedly.  With the US-China tariff agreement, Chinese importers have reconsidered to import US cargos, by comparing costs with additional 10% tax, vs Non Us origin. However, due to the eroding margins, a handful of petchem plants have cut rates, refrained from additional buying for Jun cargos. Cash differentials therefore softened, with 46/0 non Us origin reported sold into SChina at Jun CP plus $40 only, a dramatic drop from last week’s 60s . And a couple of US origin 46/0 parcels for Jun delivery basis EChina and NChina were changed hand at Jun FEI plus mid high single digit.   Compared to propane, butane was heavily discounted vs propane, with offers slashed to CP plus teens level basis delivery into China. Traditional importers struggled with high CP costs vs slow distribution. Other than normal stem, another special origin cargo sale tender is available, offering two evenly split and two heavy propane grades for 2h Jun delivery basis SChina.

EAST One Oil Major wiped out three early June ships yesterday. Freight jumping into mid-high 60’s and Owners asking now starting at $70. A few additional re-lets have emerged on the back of increased freight earnings – but so far that has done little to put any dampener on the rising freight market.  WEST June fixing in the USG/USEC is well underway and is currently somewhat in a standstill as charterers’ bids versus owners’ offers are off by 3-5 USD per ton. In the wake of the US/China tariff exemption discussions, the arb improved and parallel to tight vessel supply, freight ideas have been on the rise. At the time of writing, June vessel availability is relatively scarce and despite some relets popping up during second half of the month, it has yet to put a dampener on freight ideas. Increases in RT/C is more or less directly affecting the US freight ideas, however, thus far, there has only been done three fixtures above USD 110. There are talks of some FOB availability and although a few cargoes have changed hands, it has yet to bring actual fixing forward.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US: The EIA this week recorded a 2.2mmbbl primary propane inventory gain which brought overall stocks to 50.40mmbbls, or just over 81% of the same time last year.  Current calculations, which are based on 5yr average weekly builds/draws, project that propane inventories will peak in late October in the 87-88mmbbl range – or just below the 90mmbbl average level for the 49th Week of the year.  Aside from potential weather-related production disruptions over the pending summer there is little impeding the lofty production rates in the U.S., which at more than 2.83mmbbls/day as of this week’s EIA report continues to push up against the 2.85mmbbl/day maximum.  Export volumes, meanwhile, are presently departing at 2.2mmbbls/day (against a maximum recorded rate of 2.335mmbbls/day).  Spot FOB USGC terminal fees are pretty squarely established at 6cpg, as a small handful of activity has been recorded at just above and below that level for June.  The tariff relief – temporary though it may be – brought freight back to life which is thus keeping a lid on spot terminal rates.

Despite an influx of end May MEG cargoes yesterday rates didn’t move much. Although the MEG May program is now all but a wrap there’s still a handful of leftover cargoes if we are to believe reports, and with a starting point at WS 60 give/take MEG/East rates should be set for an uptick when June cargoes emerge in earnest. There are already rumours suggesting some charterers are out sniffing well into the 1st decade which does signal a certain nervousness if true. The position list appears balanced, and tonnage is controlled on fewer hands than prior to last month’s program. "Buy cheap buy twice” the saying goes, or three times when it comes to Petrobras’ end May Brazil export cargo, having now replaced it for the 3rd time at WS 61, albeit a couple of points off what they started out at. The position list in the Atlantic tilts more in favor of charterers as June USG export cargoes have so far been few and far in between.

The wheels keep turning in the LNG shipping spot market as fresh requirements flow in steadily and plenty of fixtures placed on subjects in the last week. Rate levels have softened somewhat in the Atlantic, although this seems to be driven more by well-matched cargo dates and motivated sub-letters with very tight vessel availability than by a generally weaker trading environment. As such candidate vessels are fixed out the market, rates are likely to stabilise again especially as fresh requirements are emerging for the second half of June. The Middle East and the Pacific basins are also softening slightly, with some tentative requirements to work but little firm business for owners to get their teeth into.   There remains plenty of interest on longer periods through 2025-26, with a slight uptick in sentiment also observed in small part due to improved spot conditions but underpinned by the widely anticipated fundamental tightening in years to come. With a couple of recent fixtures being reported, there may be a little momentum building in this segment and owners and charterers will be considering their next steps quite carefully.  There were no newbuildings ordered in the past week, but with further positive news on US project developments and some softening in the rhetoric and implementation of tariffs, it has broadly been a “good news” week for LNG shipping.

Charterers have successfully managed to limit the upside by tucking away vessels under the radar. While lists are tightening at the front-end, we also expect that a decent amount of 3rd decade volumes have been taken out in the Atlantic. However, with an equally large June CPC program expected, and 1st decade laycans just over two weeks out, we expect activity to tick up. It feels as though as the market has bottomed in the West.  In the States, quite a few Suezmaxes have been poached for Liza and USG runs ex local positions in addition to vessels from Europe. The backlog of tonnage has been chewed through bringing us back down to a more balanced complexion. The Aframaxes are however on increasingly shaky ground. With the number of ballasters arriving for 3rd decade and the eerily quiet market it feels as though sentiment may begin to falter - likely charterers will have the smaller class in their sights for the remainder of May cargoes.   The MEG has seen bearish fundamentals materialize with MEG/East on subs WS 97.5 on a modern boat. Owners will be hoping that more vessels ballast out of the region to COGH as the list remains plagued with modern, old, xdd and Basrah suitable vessels. The region has however been busier this morning with a couple of Basrah stems working. With stem releases around the corner owners will be hoping for demand to sustain.

The Panamax market has continued its downward trajectory this week, with both Atlantic and Pacific regions under pressure. In the Atlantic, sentiment remains bearish amid growing tonnage and limited fresh demand, particularly from NCSA, leading to wider bid-offer spreads and sub-index fixtures for transatlantic runs. ECSA offered some short-term support due to tighter spot tonnage in May, but ample June supply could weigh on rates. In the Pacific, the market remains flat with bearish sentiment as long tonnage lists persist, and new cargoes remain scarce. Fixing levels are holding in the high USD 9,000s to low USD 10,000s for Pacific rounds, though some owners are showing resistance in anticipation of a correction. Overall, while ECSA grain continues to lend some support, weak coal markets and macroeconomic headwinds suggest limited near-term upside.

NORTH SEA Lack of activity this week with rates softening from last week.  Natural window now pushing into 3rd decade in the North Sea.  Activity has been subdued on the Aframax side with own vessels being programmed and some Suez action taking out stems as well.  Prompter tonnage will be looking to other areas for support to avoid the inevitable waiting time.  MEDITERRANEAN  Rates on a freefall in the Mediterranean as the excessive amount of tonnage is forcing owners to drop the rates further down. The balance of May will see rates hovering around current levels or possibly lower as there is no escape for the owners at the moment.

The Atlantic market maintained a generally positive tone throughout the week, with steady demand and stronger numbers particularly from the US Gulf and South America. The Continent/Mediterranean region remained subdued with limited fresh inquiry. In contrast, the Asian market continued its slow decline amid a lack of activity, though the Indian Ocean stood out with consistent demand, especially from South Africa. Several fixtures were reported across various regions, supporting localized strength. With the monsoon season incoming, the cargo volumes in WC India will go down eventually in the weeks to come. There remains interest on the period side but very little reported in the market this past week.

We see a reasonable level of enquiries from miners, operators, and tender for very end May and early June dates. Peripheral volume out of East Australia has held up from last week with some tenders in market as well.  Enquiries our of C3 ex Brazil and West Africa are primarily for first half of June dates with some operators out for second half of June.  Far East spot tonnage seems to be relatively abundant. Ballast tonnage is slowly thinning as earlier ships are chipped away but remains relatively heavy for June dates. Fixtures concluded at low-mid USD 7 pmt levels on C5 this week and sub USD 18 pmt levels for early June Brazil dates.

The search for renewed benchmarks in the tanker market has been a fruitless task for a while now, however, this looks to be changing at least in the MR space. An Increased liquidity is driving the ongoing value correction, indicating more activity in the segment as these corrected levels continue to attract the attention of opportunistic players. Pumproom MR ANNA M (47K DWT Iwagi Zosen 2010) sold in xs of USD 17M, almost 35% less than what she could have expected this time last year.  There remains healthy activity across the dry market despite a somewhat dreary outlook for the rest of 2025. Most will be well placed to ride out this current storm, with rates remaining comfortably above OPEX for the time being. The next few months could see an increase in buying interest, as buyers look to position themselves to catch potential predicted upside in 2026-2027. That said, modern tonnage remains at a premium and these buyers will likely need to beat last done on these units in order to secure tonnage. In the modern ultramax space, scrubber fitted AQUAVITA LIME (63K DWT Nantong Xiangyu 2021) sold for USD 30.5M.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Butane surplus has deepened the FOB netback discounts to teens level for evenly split grade, while propane stands firm in premium. By the time of writing, Jun CP was traded at $574 for C3 and $547 for C4. Jun/Jul C3 CP was traded at $28 backwardation.   FAR EAST Propane demand remains strong amongst active stockpiling and cracking buying from Japanese and Koreans importers, together with traders covering shorts. A handful of 23/0 for 1h Jun delivery actively was changed hand at Jun FEI minus $6 and $7, and 4/0 basis China was traded at minus $8. On Thurs, bids for 23/0 parcel for 1h Jun and 2h Jun delivery improved to Jun FEI minus $4 and $5 respectively, while few offers seen.   China markets are relatively slow compared to last week, as players are waiting for upcoming US-China trade talks. Petchem players refrained purchase by cutting run rates, as soaring costs on CP and cash premiums eroding margins. Despite such, Jun delivered propane are still traded at CP plus 50s/60 into China reportedly, in view of tight supply on non-US stem. However, butane was heavily discounted vs propane, as of ample supply against limited buying and high inventory from receivers. On special origin, there are two heavy propane and two evenly split cargo cargos for end May to mid-Jun delivery being offered via tender.

EAST Two Indian PSU deals done yesterday at a small premium to Baltic. Another Indian cargo got rolled over and will be worked today together with a non-Indian cargo meaning there are two uncovered cargos currently in play. A major fixed a relatively prompt cargo today at mid-50s which we assess as being outside the fixing window and hence the premium. A small uptick in activity have so far managed to pull freight up slightly in the Middle East but how much further upside there is to this market remains to be seen.  WEST The week started off with the ever lasting question of the arb being open or closed and parallel to freight, who dictates who. Knowingly or unknowingly, the US market have for the time being adopted a ‘one week on-one week off’ schedule whereby lack of activity both on product and freight pushes the Baltic downwards and same with the arb. Nevertheless, freight has yet again been able to withstand most downward resistance and the market remains flat despite the arb values trying to suggest otherwise. Last done HCvP deal is at USD 103 per ton, however, it feels as if further momentum is relatively lackluster. A handful of vessels were fixed this week off first half June dates at 3-digit freight, and there are still a few left by the looks of it.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US Tariff-related market uncertainty continues, and very little is being accomplished unless necessary since no one wants to lock in a trade which might later prove to be unwise.  As such, while there was a rash of activity on the announcement of the tariffs – mostly attempts to secure 2:2 volumes (in place of 4:0 cargoes and/or fix pre-tariff deadline laycans) – the June market is now littered with both buyers and sellers.  There exists a divide, however, and where buyers are more apt to place value in the 4cpg range, sellers are reluctant to break below 6cpg.  Netback calculations presently show value at 5cpg.    The EIA this week reported a 1.0mmbbl propane inventory increase which brought stocks to a total of 48.20mmbbls, or ~81% of last year’s total, and just ~78% of two years ago.  The modest build was on the lower end of expectations but overall considered a step in the right direction.  It is anticipated by some that the recent switching from 4:0 cargoes to 2;2 cargoes could have an impact on stock levels, though terminal owners have indicated that in some other cases they’re seeing maximum propane volumes being nominated.  This speculation is largely related to the expectation that propane stocks may not rise to sufficient levels.  That, in turn, is a price-driver, and that, in part, determines the arb.  Armed with the ongoing uncertainty of whether or not trade deals will be achieved, the market naturally remains in limbo.

NORTH SEA After the long weekend the market managed to get going so far.  The early positions on the available tonnage is seeing vessels ballast  both to USG and Mediterranean to minimize waiting and take opportunities in busier markets. Activity in the natural window has suffered from relet programming and bigger vessels taking stems limiting what is actually there to fix.  With dates pushing further out and the list growing we will see more ballasting and rates will be tested by charterers.  MEDITERRANEAN A busy start to the week with some relatively prompt cargoes left from last week, but the growing tonnage list is pushing the rates downwards. Competition for cargoes is increasing with vessels ballasting from North Sea, but with activity also looking stable/active 2nd half May in the USG we may see some a few vessels head off.

Owners blinked first. The cycle seems almost predictable. Owners had their run past couple of weeks and were cruising around the WS 70 mark on TD3C. It is amazing what a few quiet days coupled with a bank holiday does to the sentiment. Charterers let the tonnage list build up and managed to take some wind out of the sails, with TD3C now in the low WS 60s. At circa 8.8m USG/East continues to attract ballasters from the East should help balance East and West. That and OPEC+ announcing that would unwind some cuts for June should put some positivity back in owners' camp and help.

The market remained largely subdued over the past week, with activity dampened by widespread holidays and limited fresh enquiry in both the Atlantic and Asian regions. The South Atlantic showed signs of sporadic strength, though momentum remained inconsistent, while the US Gulf continued to see minimal fixing. In Asia, sentiment weakened further as prompt tonnage increased and new cargoes remained scarce. Isolated fixtures were reported from the Indian Ocean and South East Asia, but they were not enough to shift the overall tone. Rates held mostly steady. Period market is relatively quiet with not many fixtures reported.

There has been no shortage of chartering activity in the LNG shipping market this year, and the action didn’t let up last week. There hasn’t been a huge increase in rates over the record lows seen in the first quarter, but the recovery has been fairly well-sustained by emerging enquiries and a relative lack of modern tonnage. Lower landed LNG prices in Europe have encouraged interest from Asian importers and the subsequent tonne mile boost coincides with strong U.S. production, which is supporting charter rates through the summer months. Amidst all the uncertainty within and around the U.S. economic proposals, there has been good news on projects, with Woodside announcing FID on Louisiana LNG and the potential advancement in the delayed commissioning of Golden Pass LNG. With ongoing debates about the timing and extent of the anticipated tighter market towards the end of the decade, these developments present a positive outlook for LNG freight in the medium term. We remain cautious for the near term given the weak fundamentals on paper, though demand for the most modern ship types is certainly driving some of the recovery and this segment is leading the way in edging rates higher. TFDEs are continuing to find a role in the market with several fixtures recently, although the differential to 2-strokes is wide and likely to grow over time, while steam turbines are struggling with few attractive requirements and most focus being on Sale and Purchase transactions. Much of this has been expected, although uncertainty remains as to how quickly this rebalancing will take place and whether the recent uptick will be sustained considering the fleet growth still to be seen this year.

Pretty ugly yesterday, replacements in the USG underlining softness there that saw levels drop to 145x85 to replace a 95, numbers that may be challenged in due course of inquiry is not forthcoming and we start working the TA ballaster window. Aframaxes dropped to 145x72.5 levels, and though a solid half a dozen TA options appear to have been sponged, ballaster interference looks likely to counter any inflationary pressure this may otherwise have built. Volume there is clearly solid in the near term (2 more clipped off on Suezmax on a private basis) but both markets undermined on the supply side.  For West Africa 130x90 on an 08-built O/O a No Sire lady some argued was a little misleading on what will presumably be a pretty naff flat rate for Nigeria/Spain, but directionally it was spot on. With the Black Sea still coming in overvalued previously it may take a day or so for the remainder of the market to align with that level, but it is certainly logical when you consider the supply side softness (still conservatively 20+ FOC, plus about 15 options sailing within 5-day window). That being said, we are now in a window where dates dictate the 3rd decade has to start pulling tonnage in. Given the issues with selling West Africa BBLS you would anticipate this means continued activity off prompter dates with high optionality required. Now we have the added boon of increased competitiveness versus VLCCs we should also get a bigger piece of the pie. The rot won’t stop overnight but those who haven’t been sat prompt for a few days may wish to hold fire rather than pile on pressure.   For TD6 the drag effect is there and only 8 stems remaining off third decade infers we'll see 120 challenged in the near term. East of Suez equally looks overtonnaged and overvalued, albeit ships still for some reason are ballasting to COGH in spite of TD20 dumping.

The Panamax market opened on a muted note this week, with trading activity limited by holidays and mixed sentiment across both basins. The Atlantic saw modest stability, particularly in the North, supported by tight spot tonnage and consistent grain demand from NCSA, though ECSA remains quiet with limited fresh inquiry. Conversely, the Pacific faced downward pressure as tonnage continued to build, especially in the Far East, while bids weakened amid limited NoPac activity and sluggish Aussie rounds. With the Pacific struggling to find direction, attention shifts to Atlantic premium routes to help absorb surplus tonnage in the short term.

We see a reasonable level of enquiries from miners, operators and tender for 20 May onwards dates. Peripheral volume out of East Australia has held up from last week as well. Enquiries are thin for C3 ex Brazil and West Africa for end May dates with more operators starting to focus on June dates. Far East spot tonnage seems to be tightening a tick as we approach mid-week. Ballast tonnage remains heavy for second half of May and first half of June dates.  Fixtures concluded at high USD 7 pmt levels on C5 this week while bid to offer spread for Brazil is at USD 18 pmt levels verses high USD 19 levels for June dates.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US Market conditions have by now deteriorated to the point where US cargo cancellations are being considered.  The nearly nonexistent arb and poor netbacks have pushed term lifters to the brink and it is being predicted that cancellations might occur as soon as this week.  All of this comes as a result of the trade tariffs which have disrupted global LPG market trade.  When, if, and how things might be resolved is a topic of ongoing debate, but in the meanwhile most regular market participants have adopted a ‘shelter-in-place’ approach so as to minimize potential exposure.  Those that can have already swapped as many 4:0 cargoes to 3:1 or – better – 2:2 parcels in order that non-Chinese destinations can be availed, though despite the best efforts the tariff-related barriers are proving most difficult.  On the domestic front, the EIA this week posted a weak build of just 600,000bbls, bringing overall US primary propane stock levels to 47.20mmbbls, or about 83% of the same time last year.  This is despite another record-level production figure provided by the EIA of 2.852mmbbls/day.  Mont Belvieu propane pricing on 1st April were 92cts/gal but by 1st May have fallen to 77cts/gal, a 16% decline over the month-long period.

The VLCC space continues to provide liquidity to the tanker second hand market amid a strong spot market earnings environment. China’s buying appetite for VLCCs is also showing no respite, as LAYLA (317K DWT Hyundai 2007) sold for USD 46.75M. Chinese buyers are also being linked to at least 2 of the 3x scrubber fitted VLCCs sold from CMB.Tech this week, HAKATA/HAKONE (302K DWT Universal 2010) & IRIS (314K DWT HHI 2012) which generated a profit for the Brussels listed owner of USD 96.7M, though no official sale price has been disclosed. In the face of weakening, yet historically still above average, rates and an influx of newbuildings to come this year, there is an ongoing correction in MR values. In this space, CELSIUS PHILADELPHIA/PORTSMOUTH (50K DWT Jiangsu Newyangzi 2021) were sold to IMS with TC attached at USD 35.5M each.   In the face of widely reported bearish sentiment, the dry market is delivering solid yet unremarkable returns. The all too familiar feeling that no one is pressed to sell remains a barrier to entry for opportunist buyers but will provide comfort to owners and investors with skin already in the game alike. That said, there is still a fair level of liquidity ranging across sizes and subsectors. This week, Turkish buyers were reported on the sale of ANSAC MOON BEAR (33K DWT Shin Kurushima 2017)*Open Hatch at USD 18.7M.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced May Cp at $610 for propane and $590 for butane, which is surprisingly above market expectation, especially C3/C4 spread is not as wide as expected amid the long butane supply. Fob netbacks for Jun loaders vary widely depending on ratios. As in lack of discussions, cash differentials for heavy propane are reckoned at high single to teens premium while evenly split at discounts only.  By the time of writing, Jun Cp was traded at $565 for propane and $543 butane respectively.   FAR EAST Trading activities slowed down as of labour holiday, coupled with uncertainties on US-China trade talks. 23/0 parcel for 1h Jun delivery was offered at Jun FEI minus $8 on Friday window but no bids seen. Outside window similar cargo was traded at Jun FEI minus $5 earlier. Despite the deviation cost, full cargo 4/0 are now reckoned with higher premium vs 2/0 from 2H May delivery onwards, said to be supported by Japanese and Korean buyings.   No official announcement from China yet, but likely product like ethane might be granted with tariff exemptions, and China is also evaluating the tariff impacts in different industries. Most Chinese importers have managed to sell their US Stems/buy non US stems or bookout with their suppliers for May cargos. For Jun delivery, premium for non-Us propane extended the strength, and was assessed at Jun Cp plus 60s, as of rigid petchem demand. However, discussions for non-Us butane are in stalemate as in lack of demand. Ningbo Huatai cancelled their buy tender for 1st decade Jun delivered propane as of few offers. One petchem player cancelled their butane buy tender for May-Jun delivery as offers not attractive. One NChina PDH importer was reported to award their Aug to Dec mini term buy tender for monthly one heavy propane cargo at Cp plus 40s.

EAST In the first half of the week, freight sentiment gradually started to look negative in the Middle East as it was becoming apparent that the market was lacking spot demand in May. However, we have seen more spot cargos 2 half of May dates. At the time of writing, whether this will bring the market up again, remain to be seen.  WEST With Golden week holidays and Labor Day observance, fixing activity kicked off for 1st decade June beginning of the week. Time of writing we have seen 8 deals concluded in this window with last done fixed just shy off $100 HCvP. Freight rates have held up until now, despite Arb trying to suggest otherwise.

The Panamax market showed signs of weakening this week, with limited upside as seasonal grain exports from the US and Canada began to decline and vessel counts to Indonesia fell. In the Atlantic, the North saw a modest pickup in transatlantic activity on fresh spot demand from NCSA, while the South remained quiet, partly due to the Geneva dry conference. Tonnage in the Mediterranean is building, though sentiment remains cautiously firm. In the Pacific, the market continued to soften amid an oversupplied tonnage list and slow cargo replenishment, with rates easing further across NoPac and Australia trades. Support from ECSA grain volumes remains a key stabilizing factor.

The headwinds predicted came to fruition with demand ex-West Africa tailing off, albeit it took this a while to be reflected in BDTI, ultimately culminating in a sharper [delayed] drop in TD20 yesterday. With USG crudes struggling to sell Eastbound there has been more transatlantic inquiry in the past few days and although rates have failed to push on beyond WS 95, local availabilities have been eroded. The underlying TCE for USG/TA on a Rotterdam ballaster would hit parity with TD20 earnings should TD20 drop to WS 110 - that's probably where we wind up this week, but after this the future is less transparent. Aframaxes are not going to provide spillover inquiry in the Gulf at present levels, but equally the ongoing struggle to source buyers for Nigerian crudes is leaving prompt barrels on the table. This has been reflected in lagging West Africa counts for VLCCs in the 3rd decade, with only 8MBBLS covered thus far, and whether we hit standard volumes on VLCC or not remains opaque. If we do, and if Aframaxes fail to recover in the USG, today's count of 20 FOC natural and willing West Africa candidates on the water would tend to infer further softening of TD20 below WS 110.

On the West Australia front, we see a healthy level of enquiries from miners, tenders, and operators alike for mid to late May dates. Other fronts of the Pacific see a tick up in volumes as well. On C3 ex Brazil and West Africa, enquiries are primarily for second half of May and early June dates. We see a tightening of number of spot vessels opening in Far East while number of ballasters remain lengthy for May dates. Fixtures concluded at USD 8.00 pmt levels and low USD 19 pmt levels for West Australia and Brazil round, respectively.

After a rate rally last week culminating in the mid WS 70’s for MEG/East runs this week started with a whimper. It’s been very quiet on the surface in the last couple of days, with charterers holding back and/or reaching out on the curve hoping to leave an impression that the second decade MEG program is more covered than what meets the eye. If today proceedings proves equally uneventful sentiment might start to shift in favor of charterers again - but it could also backfire. If in fact the second decade is as “untouched” as lack of reported fixtures suggest, when and if we see a correction, we could see charterer tumble in on top of each other and rates turn back up. Summed up; a battle of mind over matter. Let’s see who blinks first.

Rates have remained steady in the North Sea even with limited activity to start the week. As we move into May, although 2nd decade stems do look a little busier than the 1st, rates may come under downward pressure with a growing position list and relets/bigger sizes still there to absorb volume quietly. Still, there are opportunities to ballast for some owners as surrounding areas remain in a better state.   Rates in the Mediterranean following a softer trend as dates are continually moving forward for the main ports of Libya and Ceyhan. Tonnage is still quite balanced but the additional competition coming from the North Sea is adding pressure. With a bank holiday early next week some more cargoes are expected to enter the market sooner or later.

Another active week in the spot market on LNG shipping where the crunch on tonnage for end May dates in the USG remains the topic of conversation since our last report. Charter rates have appreciated more quickly than has been seen at any point this year with 2-strokes in the Atlantic around the $40,000 pd mark on certain date ranges. Requirements continue to crop up on the back of cargo diversions away from Europe. Several lifters of U.S. volumes are strategically short whilst portfolios are also redelivering ships and replacing on a weak spot market, the resulting rush for tonnage highlights the potential for pockets of tightness to appear in the right trading environment, despite the overarching weaker fundamentals. The Pacific is yet to make up the widening gap in charter rates due to a lack of firm requirements of late, though with several ships sure to ballast back to the Atlantic we may see some rebalancing further forward.  On the period side, further interest in multiyear charters is being worked in the market this week although the story remains that whilst there are plenty of willing sellers for 2026, offers for longer period are more limited and priced accordingly.

The Supramax and Handysize markets remained largely subdued, with minimal fresh activity and a lack of clear direction across both basins. In the Supramax market, the South Atlantic continued to offer a glimmer of optimism, supported by steady demand, while the US Gulf and Asian markets remained flat amid limited enquiry. The overall tone was muted, reflecting a cautious sentiment from both owners and charterers. The Handysize market followed a similar pattern, with the South Atlantic standing out as the most stable region, backed by consistent transatlantic cargo flows. In contrast, the Continent, Mediterranean, and US Gulf faced downward pressure due to oversupply and weak demand, while Asia remained stagnant amid a build-up of tonnage and scarce fresh enquiries. Both segments showed marginal movements in their respective indices, reflecting the overall lack of momentum in the market.

Tanker headlines this week were stolen by scrubber fitted VLCCs LANDBRIDGE GLORY/WISDOM 307K DWT Dalian 2019/20, which sold to Oman Shipping co (Asyad) for USD 205M. This timing is seen as somewhat curious for Chinese built VLCCs given uncertainty over USTR and the evolving, yet potentially easing, tariff situation. MRs it appears, are close to bottoming out, seen in SS/DD due TAMIAT NAVIGATOR (46K DWT HMD 2010) at USD 18M, a unit that would have transacted closer to USD 30M this time last year.   Easter holidays are likely to have had an impact on the lower-than-average number of dry sales this week, although this is coinciding with fewer firm enquiries in the market on the back of the much-reported growing uncertainty and general geopolitical instability. That said, rates remain consistently above opex levels, though doing little to excite potential investors. In a rare transaction of a modern handy, NORD ABIDJAN (37K DWT Minaminippon 2020) *OHBS was sold for USD 25.5M.

EAST / WEST  Since the Easter break, the market has been asleep in the midst of various geopolitical developments relating to shipping tolls, tarrifs and general market directional factors. The much talked about arbitrage ex USG/USEC has yet to stabilise and as such received a lot of attention, which it normally does when the shipping market is quiet. The ship availability remains largely unchanged from last week. There have been few attempts to to fix vessels this week and last done remains at H/C via Panama at USD 103. One vessel was subfixed ex Soyo this week, however, it is still on technical subjects reportedly. Lately, we have seen a trend in the market of a few busy fixing days followed by a quiet week or more, when the Baltic suddenly rid any momentum gained during the busy days and numbers keep coming off, simply due to inactivity.
