text: MEG Spot discounts for Feb FOBs still stay in teens level. One evenly split cargo loading in Feb was heard traded at Feb CP minus mid-teens, to one producer trading arm. Qatar Energy was also reported to award their sale tender for a 3/1 of 16-23 Feb lifting to a Chinese player but price was sketchy. At the time of writing, Feb CP was traded at $636 and C3/C4 spread at $9. Feb/Mar CP was assessed at $7 backwardation.   FAR EAST Cash premium eased off but flat price stands firm, following the strong swap prices especially the surge on MB price due to the cold weather and big inventory draw. 23kt propane parcel for 2h Feb delivery was offered in window at Feb FEI plus $10, and off window such parcel was traded at plus $8 reportedly. Meanwhile, a couple of 46kt propane parcels for Feb delivery was placed into China at Feb FEI plus mid high single digit, to different regions.   Butane price also inched up owing to the sharp price increase on MB, narrowing the ARB to FAR EAST. CPC issued buy tender for late Feb delivered 11/11 cargo. On special origins, one evenly split cargo and one heavy propane cargo, both for 1st decade Feb delivery basis SChina, were reported concluded at Feb CP minus 20s.   Other than spot, Tianjin Bohai called a mini term tender to secure 46kt propane monthly from Mar to Jun delivery into Tianjin, whose PDH is currently under maintenance and expected to restart after CNY. The PDH margins eroded further due to the rising cost, but we still expect the run rate to improve slightly with some units returning from glitches. However, the sluggish downstream demand still refrains plants from ramping up rates.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US It should come as no surprise at this time of year that the weather is playing a crucial role in the US propane market, and given both the current temperatures and the forecast over the next 7-10 days, there is little doubt that this is exactly the case.  “Freeze-Off” – the threat that sustained cold weather can negatively impact field production -  is the term of the day, and at present there is both sustained and cold weather in the Permian region of West Texas.  Simultaneously the robust crude oil market (which is being driven by the additional sanctions on Russia) is the combination that is driving the MB pricing structure.  Rising MB pricing against a more modestly behaved Far Eastern market has allowed the F/E arb to shrink to the $140s/mt range, and that is what has caused terminal fees to fall to single-digits on the buy side, and low double-digits on the offer side.  As for the domestic US propane inventories, stocks came in at the end of last week at 77.90mmbbls, a 4.7mmbbl decline from the week prior.   Still, though, current levels are ~102% of both last year and 2023, so there is little worry from that perspective – particularly since production levels – at 2.631mmbbls/day – remain satisfactory and exports have so far in 2025 averaged 1.790mmbbls/day (against a cal 2024 average of 1.757mmbbls/day).

Market participants could be forgiven for looking at the bigger picture on LNG shipping this week, with the spot market firmly in the doldrums and the widening supply-demand imbalance this year means there is broad consensus for the near-term outlook. The week saw plenty of spot activity but availabilities have been creeping upwards and putting pressure on levels in both basins, and current charter rates have dipped below the December averages. For the most part, multimonth charter ideas have found a floor for the timebeing, well in excess of spot rates and it seems this separation is likely to persist with both charterers and owners preferring to play spot rather than meeting the others’ ideas. On to that bigger picture, as the final week of the Biden administration plays out the seemingly ever-present threat of geopolitical influence on the LNG market is impossible to ignore. Whilst President Trump’s DoE takes shape, so too the optimism grows for future export projects pending FID and/or approval from the FERC to proceed. However, the nearer term impact of trade and sanctions policies are far less predictable, and yet will be wide-ranging in their implications. Europe further mulls its own sanctions of Russian LNG despite finding its current storage dwindling and the lack of an immediate replacement amidst sustained high prices. European refilling demand during the Summer will keep pricing into Europe relatively high, and whether Asia will compete for flexible volumes remains one key element of uncertainty which could provide the volatility needed to partially absorb excess shipping this year, but all this remains to be seen.  Several more vintage units have been marketed for sale, with cash buyers the likely suitors in most cases. There have been no recent newbuilding orders.

On the Supra/Ultra segment, a negative sentiment dominating across both the Atlantic and Asian markets. Limited fresh enquiry and abundant tonnage supply kept rates under pressure, though we believed the US Gulf may have found a floor for transatlantic runs. Activity remained subdued in the Continent-Mediterranean and Asia, with charterers holding an upper hand due to weak demand. Over the three days, the 11TC average dropped steadily, ending at USD 10,092. On the Handy side, rates under pressure across both basins due to oversupply and weak demand. In the Atlantic, the US Gulf and South Atlantic showed slight activity but remained insufficient to absorb excess tonnage, while the Continent and Mediterranean markets stayed subdued. Asia saw continued soft dynamics, with limited fresh cargo availability pushing rates lower as owners adjusted expectations. Period markets remain relatively quiet for the time being with very few fresh enquiries.

This week, the Panamax market experienced continued weakness across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, with rates declining further due to oversupply and subdued demand. In the Atlantic, limited activity from South America weighed heavily on sentiment, leaving ballaster positions under pressure, while thin visibility in the North led to fixtures at discounted rates. The Pacific offered slightly better volumes, particularly on NoPac runs, but shorter routes remained under significant pressure, with owners discounting heavily to secure cover. Grain trades in the East provided some support, but this was insufficient to counter the overall negative sentiment. A recovery is unlikely before the Chinese New Year, with market hopes focused on increased coal trades and the seasonal ramp-up of South American soybean exports to boost activity.

With the first full week of 2025 in full swing markets are adjusting to the new Worldscale schedule. Activity has been limited so far which is adding pressure on rates with fixing window already pushing into the end of the 2nd decade. US markets are picking up which may bring opportunities, but so far the year remains on the softer side rate wise.  Inactivity through the start of the week along with Suezmaxes absorbing Afra parcels created a very long list of prompt vessels and a steady stream continually coming back around. Summer fundamentals in the middle of Winter has had a negative impact on sentiment and it seems that it will take a while before we see any change to the current situation.

Lest we forget, the main driver behind the Q4 2019 bull-run emanated in the East, with those same fundamentals bearing a striking resemblance to what we're seeing today. This conspired to produce enormous VLCC freights which ultimately forced splits onto Suezmax, and the rest, as they say, is history (market went nuts). Hitherto 2019, the Eastern Suezmax market offered zero in terms of global impact , but as we know, that changed dramatically and the Atlantic was awoken from its winter slumber, not by delays in the Turkish straits, but by an East market that savagely spiked. This present market smells rather similar, although in order not to get to carried away, we are at the embryonic stage of this upswing, but exciting it is, nonetheless. Since the Ukraine war, we have been conditioned to look to the US Gulf as the main driver, with Afra's, wagging the tail, as it were, which had flipped previous market analysis on its head. With recent OFAC sanctions and probably more in the offing (scratch that, definitely more sanctions coming), this market is likely to revert to type with the lead being taken from VLCCs (top down), and the butterfly effect, as in 2019, likely further support Suezmax. As of going to print, this segment has no downside in either hemisphere.

The V-market continued its upward trajectory yesterday, and as predicted WS 70 was logged MEG/East numerous times, with corresponding daily earnings upward to USD 50k/day give/take. Saudi stems are still not out thus most of what has been concluded is either intended for other load configurations, pre-empting, or taken as a hedge. However, at current rates corresponding demurrage rates are starting to bite should charterers not get the laycan they were banking on, so we’d not be surprised to see some charterers taking a more “wait and see” attitude until stem confirmations are out. The flip side is of course that as and when we could have another rush to take cover, which could spur rates further up the scale. The Atlantic sprang to life again as well yesterday, with emphasis on USG export which saw an influx of cargoes emerging. Rates similarly soared, upwards to USD 10 million for the benchmark USG/Ningbo route, although by and large now yielding same daily returns as cargoes from West Africa and Brazil, albeit over a longer period. The market may take a breather to take stock of recent developments. However, the downside seems firmly capped as with the old Yazz hit; The only way is (probably) up.

On the West Australia front, we see a reasonably healthy volume from miners, operators and tenders primarily for early February dates. Volumes out of East Australia and other fronts of the Pacific remains relatively flat from last week. On C3 ex Brazil to China, players are seen enquiring for late January dates up till full February. On the West Africa front, enquiries have tapered off since last week. Far East spot tonnage is abundant. Ballasting tonnage is tight for end January dates and heavily weighted for first half of February. On C5, the week has been flat at mid USD 6 pmt levels since start of the week. On C3, we observe some backwardation with end January at USD 19 pmt levels, early February at mid USD 18 pmt levels, and mid-high USD 17 pmt levels for rest of February.

It feels too soon to make sweeping statements on the fate of the 2025 tanker second hand market, but the sale of the LR2 SUVRETTA (109k DWT STX 2008) for USD 31.5M is certainly a sign of things to come for non eco tanker tonnage. This age of Aframax for example would have been asking in excess of USD 40M at its peak in 2024. Non eco ships however are still in a historically good position, and there remains plenty of money on the table for those who invested shrewdly over the past cycle. What will be interesting to watch is how eco tonnage holds up against potentially volatile price swings across non eco ships.   Usual seasonality dictates a somewhat subdued start to the year in the dry market, and 2025 is no different. Enquiry remains healthy, though buyers are adjusting their budgets to reflect the quieter times. This should help pricing fall into line with the earnings environment, an issue that caused significant disillusionment with the second-hand market last year. Eco tonnage will remain highly sought after, especially that of Japanese build, and buyers will be monitoring the markets closely for any fresh candidates. Handy IYO SEA (37k DWT IMABARI 2015) was sold for USD 17.5M to Greek buyers, a pattern which is likely to repeat itself over the course of the year.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco lowered Jan CP by $10 for propane to $625 and $15 for butane at $615, reflecting the weaker demand on delivered market, especially Jan FEI/CP being traded in negative values. Qatar Energy issued sale tender for a 3/1 cargo loading 16-23 Feb. FOB for feb lifting was assessed at mid/high teens discounts amid muted discussions. By the time of writing, Feb CP was traded at $627 and Feb/Mar CP traded at $12 backwardation.    FAR EAST Very lively window this week with three deals concluded. 46kt propane for 2h Feb delivery basis Yantai was traded at Bal Jan FEI minus $1.28, and 2 lots of 23kt propane for 1h Feb delivery were done at Feb FEI plus $9 and $10. Similar parcel for 2h Feb delivery basis Chiba was bid at $7ish, yet to see offers. Outside window a flurry of 46kt propane parcels were also placed into China for Feb delivery at Feb FEI plus mid high single digit, in terms of the new startup PDHs, completion of maintenance and anticipated demand recovery after holiday. HTC also issued tender to buy 23kt butane for late Feb delivery.   One of the heated topics this week is China’s Shangdong Port Group banned US-Sanctioned tankers to call its ports and players are worrying if same would affect in LPG carriers. As per our tracking, around 1mmt Iran cargos was imported into Shandong, accounting for 11% among 8.8 mmt total imports into China. And only 9 VLGCs are listed in SDN list, which means other fleets can still be alternatives to continue the flows.

EAST To date, only 14 spot deals have been concluded in January for Middle East loadings which still leaves some hope for more to be done, before focus fully moves into February. Even if it would turn out to be a fair amount of uncovered cargos on January dates, there is no getting away from the fact that the position list looks long.  WEST We have seen a few spot deals concluded in the Western hemisphere this week with last done in the low $100s H-C via Pan. All of the deals have been done on traders relets, and the position list for 1H Feb is now dominated by two pure shipowners. In total we count 13 spot fixtures for February dates ex USG/USEC - 9 first decade and 4 second decade.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The lull of the holidays has by now abated and buyers and sellers of Feb parcels have begun to emerge.  There is not much in the way of fixtures to report, however, as the volatility in the front of the curve has most playing things cautiously.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, have softened as the arb has narrowed, and at present an FOB Feb 4:0 is offered at around the 12(ish) cpg range, with buyers generally talking at the lower limits of double-digits.    Meanwhile, the EIA data revealed this week that stock levels as of the 3rd of Jan are pegged at 82.60mmbbls, a decline of 2.4mmbbls from the end of Dec levels, but still 104% of last year, and 105% of two years ago.  Production levels continue to hover at the 2.6-2.7mmbbls/day level, which is the average recorded for 2024.  Export volumes are also about average at 1.719mmbbls/day.

Whilst supply side fundamentals were weak in West Africa half a dozen stems from one Charterer in a couple days buoyed sentiment with rates bouncing off of a TCE earnings base of 62.5 WS2024. Whether Owners can hold onto these gains remains to be seen, with MED/BSEA seeing similarly corrections, TD6 fixing down to 80 on WS2024 / 75 level on WS2025 with pressure to lower rates today. Certainly USG / TA TCEs must look favourable for UKC ballasters now on Suezmax, but a deluge of Aframaxes undermine the forward window for USG / TA and consequently our capacity to move up from 145kt x 55 WS2025. East of Suez muted activity has hurt sentiment, and the collapse of West Africa means there is no release valve for the pressure mounting on Owners.

This week, both the Handysize and Supramax markets experienced subdued activity and downward pressure on rates due to holiday effects and limited demand across the Atlantic and Asia. In the Atlantic, sentiment was weak with oversupply in the Continent-Mediterranean, South Atlantic, and US Gulf regions keeping rates soft. Asia showed a two-tiered market, with prompt vessels under pressure while others adopted a wait-and-see approach. Despite attempts to stabilize in the North Atlantic, further activity is needed to lift sentiment up.

Whilst many in the market return to their desks to start the New Year this week, we salute those who have kept their noses to the grindstone to fix over the festive period. While some of these fixtures are being closed out now, a further handful of short term fixtures have already been concluded and levels in the Atlantic are a little higher than they were before the break. Things remain a little sluggish East of Suez, with most activity focussed on the Middle East, and rates have been fairly flat as a result. With the arrival of additional tonnage and reduced risk of being short shipping, we expect a continued increase in spot activity this year. We are beginning to see date sensitive volatility within the Atlantic spot market where requirements stack up on a similar window, although the range within which rates ebb and flow seems likely to be narrow. Looking ahead, the LNG market may present some challenges for inter-basin trade, as European supply concerns due to the end of Russian gas flows via Ukraine and increased drawdown of storages in the prevailing cold weather is pushing summer prices higher. This mismatch between robust LNG prices and historically low charter rates for modern tonnage may present a buying opportunity for producers and large portfolios, though. The increasing acceptance of index-linked rates as well as a convergence on fixed rates should encourage further charters for multimonth periods.

With the first full week of 2025 in full swing markets are adjusting to the new Worldscale schedule. Activity has been limited so far which is adding pressure on rates with the fixing window already pushing into the end of the 2nd decade. US Markets are picking up which may bring opportunities but so far the year remains on the softer side rate wise.  Inactivity through the start of the week along with Suezmaxes absorbing Afra parcels created a very long list of prompt vessels and a steady stream continually coming back around. Summer fundamentals in the middle of Winter has had a negative impact on sentiment and it seems that it will take a while before we see any change to the current situation.

The Panamax market began the year on a weak note, with challenges across both basins. In the Atlantic, initial firmness due to limited New Year tonnage gave way to flat levels as more vessels replenished the basin, while in the south, oversupply prompted owners to discount to secure cover. Spot vessels available for prompt loading continued to command premiums, but forward fixing remained cautious. In the Pacific, rates struggled, particularly ex-Indonesia, where limited volumes and a growing tonnage list kept pressure on the market. NoPac grains and petcoke cargoes provided some support, but Aussie rounds lagged behind. With ballasters now repositioning toward Brazil, anticipation is building for a spot market recovery during February’s soybean export season.

Last year ended on a weak note which usually means January ends up being even weaker. So far that seems to be the case. However, there are several pointers toward a rebound starting around the middle of February. There is currently a record number of VLOCs sailing toward Brazil, which is a good indication that a Capesize rally will materialize. The previous four times the count was similar to now were in late August last year, early September 2023, and late August 2022. However, most of the vessels are still positioned in the Pacific or Indian Ocean, so it will take time before the vessels have loaded and freed up space for Capes. Further, the iron ore price leads shown below indicate a firming market from late Feb and through March.

VLCC daily earnings continue to be under pressure, about $20k/day for the best of them on a MEG/east round voyage with no waiting time, whereas the older contingency struggle to cover OPEX. However, it would appear that the rot has stopped if nothing else, stabilising in the low W40’s. Increased activity in the Atlantic as well, with the west/east arb encouraging eastern buyers. Even North Sea bbls are said to be in play in addition to USG, Wafr and Brazil. So far not made a positive rate impact but the list is shortening and is not really being topped up by ballasters from the east on spec. Paper trading up.

The strange year that was 2024 is behind us now and for some, that will be quite a relief. The relatively flat cargo market and excess freight were widely anticipated, but it has still been a bruising ride for those that have enjoyed the benefits of a strong trading environment in previous years; naturally, the flip side is true for the net charterers these past months, and they will hope for more of the same in 2025! That simple narrative ignores many of the quirks and challenges of the year that really kept everyone busy though, such as an open arbitrage in summer that caused an unseasonal spike, and a subsequent collapse that saw a strange winter trough. The regulatory environment was also a major topic for owners and charterers alike, as both EU and IMO regulations rippled through markets, economics and charterparties: the EU ETS scheme kicked in a year ago today, and also the IMO EEXI and CII schemes were having a tangible effect on certain vessels.       It is likely that 2025 will also be a challenging year, with the trading environment again looking tough and the entry into force of the complex FuelEU regulations likely to cause some headaches, but periods like this can be beneficial to the longer-term health of a market. We will see growth following the commissioning of some new trains late in 2024, with congratulations to Cheniere and Venture Global, and we will likely see at least some of the following: a shift to index-linked deals rather than traditional fixed charter rates; more SnP activity; increased recycling of vintage tonnage; renewed focus on technical improvements to ship design and retrofitting; more project FIDs; the return of some speculative newbuild ordering; new entrants as both commodity traders or end-users; consolidation, etc. Add in to the mix the range of geopolitical and economic issues on the horizon, and we can be sure that 2025 will be just as interesting as was 2024.   Wishing you all a very successful year ahead!

As the holiday season continues for many, the LNG shipping market has remained relatively stable since our last update. Spot fixtures have been recorded in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, but without significant movements in charter rates, despite the seemingly tightened availability of two-stroke tonnage in the US Gulf towards the end of January. In the East of Suez, firm opportunities have been limited, with the majority of shipping requirements appearing out of the Atlantic basin for intra-AB trades with arbitrage opportunities remaining scarce. Meanwhile, multi-month and term charter discussions have taken more of a focus, with several deals being executed in the past week, as players look to capitalise on attractive rates that are becoming more achievable across market. With the next seven days expected to be relatively quiet as the market slowly returns from the holiday period, we will see if any end-of-year surprises emerge. No newbuilding orders for conventional LNG carriers have been reported this week, with newbuilding prices holding.

What goes up must come down’ has been the feel in the tanker market this year, resulting in a struggle for liquidity throughout 2024. Correcting values are keeping prospective investors on their toes, and it is likely we will see increased activity once the market returns from winter breaks. CHIBA (45K DWT Shin Kurushima 2007) sold for USD 17M, representing a new benchmark for Japanese blt pumproom MRs.   The Dry market has been the avenue for the majority of second hand investment this year, this is despite an underwhelming Q4 and a mixed outlook on 2025. 15 year old capesize units are still proving popular with Far Eastern buyers as Korea Line acquired scrubber fitted FEG SUCCESS (182K DWT Kawasaki 2010)*ss/dd due for USD 28M. In a rare eco Newcastlemax transaction, Oldendorff sold scrubber fitted LINDA OLDENDORFF (207K DWT HHI 2014) for USD 48.3M to Bohai.

EAST With the late release of Saudi acceptances yesterday the East market remained surprisingly inactive at the beginning of the week - especially considering Christmas is right around the corner. We have yet to see any spot fixtures concluded for January dates ex Middle Eastern ports if we exclude Yanbu (three deals done), but at the time of writing we observe two uncovered cargoes out there for early Jan – one being an Indian PSU.   WEST A spot tender out of the US Gulf was concluded earlier this week several dollars below last done, which has pushed Western freight rates slightly lower, and now we are seeing spot deals being done around USD 110 H/C. Fixing activity in the first and second decade of January is seemingly finished with currently no available vessels left this period. In the last decade there still remain 7-8 open positions before the market shifts focus into February where we already have seen one vessel fixed for early dates.

text: AMERICAS Activity levels have dulled in recent days as many regular market participants have either retreated to the sidelines in an effort to preserve any profits achieved in 2024, or have begun to depart for the holidays.  However, a few transactions are known to have been achieved including a recently concluded 17.50cpg 4:0 January FOB deal which has effectively set market levels.  Meanwhile, many await the results of a term tender which may well set the forward path.  December is now concluded and only a handful of January offers are known to exist, but depending on arb levels (which continue to hover around the $200/mt level) – and freight to the East (which seems to be waffling at just over $100/mt) – this could change.  Little is anticipated in the coming days – even weeks, however – due to the holidays.  Otherwise, the EIA yesterday reported a 3.0mmbbl decline in overall propane stock levels for an updated total of 90.10mmbbls, which is 96% of last year and 103% of two years ago.  The draw was not surprising as several industry contacts accurately assessed the decline prior to its release.  Now the Days of Supply stands at 66 days (down from 75 days at last week’s report), production remains robust at 2.667mmbbls/day (against a 2024 average of 2.668mmbbls/day) while export levels were reported at 1.987mmbbls (versus a YTD average of 1.751mmbbls/day).

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco released Jan lifting acceptance with one cargo rumored cancelled, some suspecting the “cancelled” cargo might be less favored ratio or not needed by term lifter. Qatar Petroleum awarded their sell tender for 29-30 Jan lifting evenly split cargo at Jan FEI link minus teens to a Korean importer reportedly. By the time of writing, Jan C3 CP was traded at $625 and Jan C3/C4 at $5. Jan/Feb CP was traded at minus $13 backwardation.   FAR EAST Cash differentials fell further as in lack of buying inquiries, hence Jan FEI/CP traded at minus $20, edged down from last week’s minus $16. 23/0 parcels for 2h Jan delivery into FAR EAST was changed hand at Jan FEI minus $3 off window. And subsequently similar parcel was offered at FEI minus $3ish while bid at minus $7 only.   Outside window a flurry of tenders were seen this week. NChina-based Jinneng was reported to procure a 46/0 parcel for 2h Jan delivery at Jan FEI minus 2/3 via tender. HTC was said to award their buy tender for 11/0 on late Jan delivery at Jan FEI plus low teens while the 0/2 for early Feb arrival yet to know result. BASF also tendered to buy 0/2 for 2h Jan to 1h Feb basis Caojing, EChina. FIC issued term tender to secure six to eight 46/0 parcels basis Ningbo.  Despite the drop on flat price, the improved margins yet to incite more speculative/stockpiling buying from petchem players, foreseeing waning downstream consumption.   Additionally, a handful of special origin stems for prompt and Jan delivery remained unsold. Latest we’ve heard spot level was concluded at CP minus 50s basis SChina. Our shiptrack showed the arrival volumes into China will exceed 1mmt, accounting for 1/3 of the total import for Dec. However some cargos are still floating to find home and probably will be rolled into Jan arrivals.

Don't call us Scrooge, but the week prior to Christmas normally heralds a buyer’s market, and this year is unlikely to be the exception. Whilst there has been positive market chatter relating potential upside in the US Gulf, we conclude that December is done (or close to) with zero pressure on early January dates.TD6 remains under downward pressure with WS 87.5 on subjects for a 13-15/January stem, leaving owners on a backward footing for now. West Africa has a slew of ships lining up to fix mid/high WS 80's which suggests that a correction is likely on the cards, moderate as that may be. In the East, BOT/UKCM last traded WS 52.5 (Cape) with a steady feel.

Requirements have kept rolling in during the build-up to the Christmas period. The Atlantic spot market remains the most liquid, although sufficient supply is keeping a lid on rates for laycans through January. There are still a handful of opportunities for the second half of January and the slight arbitrage may lead to some scheduling challenges as we head into 2025, but sentiment is fairly well contained for now and charterers seeking slightly longer coverage are also seeing quite a flat horizon. The coming days should see some interesting price points for inter-basin trade as well as for multimonth charters. In short, while rates are proving stubborn the level of activity is keeping players busy, and ships trading.

The Panamax market has faced further downward pressure this week, with rates continuing to slide amid weak sentiment and oversupply across both the Atlantic and Pacific regions. In the Atlantic, despite slightly improved transatlantic volumes, the abundance of available tonnage - particularly in the East Mediterranean - has kept rates under strain, while fronthaul routes remain depressed due to limited Black Sea activity and pressure from ballasting towards Gibraltar. The Pacific saw minimal cargo replenishment, with bid-offer spreads narrowing further as vessel oversupply continues to dominate. Owners are under pressure to accept lower rates, with no clear floor yet in sight. Looking ahead, optimism is pinned on record-high Brazilian soybean exports expected to begin early next year, but for now, the market remains subdued as it heads into the holiday season.

Rates in the North Sea look likely to remain in a sideways trend for the time being with the majority of volume for the rest of December being covered on relets and Suezmax. Tonnage has balanced out somewhat, but the potential for things to tighten as vessels continue to ballast to the US is still there, though it will take a certain increase in activity for pressure on rates to materialize in this market.  With December dates selling out owners in the Mediterranean have marginally pushed rates higher showing caution to keep a safe distance from larger vessels. Activity and USG ballasters has significantly thinned out tonnage, and further to this the number of ballasters from UKC to the US has been substantial of late, and as a result Continent positions have been fixed out of West Mediterranean. The fate of Aframax moving forward looks to be in the hands of Suezmax for one more time this year.

Activity remained limited, with very few new fixtures reported. Pacific markets consistently struggled with negative sentiment and declining activity. The 11TC average steadily declined throughout the week, signaling weak overall market conditions. In the Atlantic, the ECSA and US Gulf showed occasional signs of stability with some fresh volumes, however the long list of tonnage did not help with pushing up markets. Across all regions, fresh enquiry and fixing activity remained sparse, contributing to a subdued tone. Period market remains quiet with not being much reported in the past week.

On the West Australia front, miners and operators enquiring primarily for early January dates. Overall, the number of players enquiring for freight have dropped compared to last week. Volumes out of East Australia remain flat with a decent number of WCSA enquiries for late January to early February dates. For C3 ex Brazil to China, some operators are out primarily for second half of January. On the West Africa front, there seems to be some delays experienced. Far East spot tonnage remains heavy for prompt, spot and several positions coming up for forward dates. Ballasting tonnage level remains ample for full January with some still able to make late December dates. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at low-mid USD 7 pmt levels on Monday, retreating to mid-high USD 6 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at low-mid USD 16 pmt levels for mid January.

The VLCC market has remained sideways all week, with daily returns close to OPEX for the older guard, and it's been hard for charterers to drive it down any further. Earnings at this time of a year are uncharacteristically low but here we are! Current returns on TD3C have forced owners will big fleets to explore further away in hope for a more active Western market, which has failed to deliver too. As a result, west tonnage list coupled with lack of activity resulted in rates being driven down to 6.5m for a USG/East voyage. As things stand, Saudi stem dates are expected within today/tomorrow and charterers are running against time to clear their desk before the holidays kick in next week. This leaves a window of 4-5 days to cover their requirements and clear subjects. We expect owners to push back now and take advantage of this situation to try and achieve low WS 40's at least. And as we know, in a market things can turn quickly and suddenly we are in the mid WS 40's. That’s the best it seems owners will get this year, and we start with a new slate in 2025.

Scrubber fitted DHT SCANDINAVIA (317K DWT HHI Samho 2006) was sold in line with last done despite the dreary VLCC market. It is a winter of discontent so far, and most buyers on large crude tonnage are likely to wait for pricing to fall further before considering this segment.   Likely a result of busy social calendars across the market, and the inbound winter holidays, but the dry market has not provided its usual high liquidity this week. Capesizes though, are still proving popular. OTSL ARTEMIS (177K DWT Shanghai Jiangnan Changxing 2008) & OTSL ATHENA (174K DWT SWS 2007)*scrubber fitted, sold for USD 24.5M each, firm pricing considering recent sale of younger scrubber fitted CAPE DREAM (179K DWT HHI Ulsan 2011) at USD 28M. Elsewhere, Premuda sold FOUR NABUCCO (34K DWT SPP 2010) at USD 11.8M.

text: MEG FOB discounts for Jan lifting evenly split cargos deepened further to minus $20, reflecting recent trade discussions with slim buying inquiries. Despite such, Jan CP swaps remained firm, which traded at $630 by the time of writing, and Jan C3/C4 at $5. Jan/Feb CP was traded at $10 backwardation.   FAR EAST Cash differentials for Jan discussion into FAR EAST has edged down to discounted level this week, with a handful of offers available against limited bids. 23/0 for 2h Jan delivery was once traded at Jan FEI minus $1, and it’s expected to slide further as of lengthy supply. 46/0 for 2h Jan delivery into Yantai was bid at Jan FEI minus $3 in window. Off window similar cargo was placed into Qingdao at Jan FEI minus small single digit reportedly, at the equivalence of CP minus mid-teens, as Jan FEI/CP traded at -$16.    A flurry of buy tenders issued this week but only partial awarded. FPCC was reported to cancel buy tender to procure one 46/0 for next Aug delivery into Taiwan, assuming discounts not favorable yet. One SChina PDH player only procured 11kt C3 for Jan delivery at Jan FEI minus low single, despite their original tender asking for 2/0 or 4/0. HTC issued tender to buy 11kt C3 for late Jan delivery. And CPC tendered to buy 11/11 for late Jan delivery as well.  Compared to normal stems, special origin cargos are reckoned to be discussed at least 20 bucks cheaper, especially with three cargos unsold from prompt delivery to 1st week of Jan basis SChina. From our shiptracks, exports into China this year maintained similar at close to 9mmt vs last year, however at more prompt discussion via spot tenders.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Spot FOB USGC terminal fees have found a range – at least temporarily – as the last known transactions have been right at/around 18cpg for 4:0 parcels.  Butane fees are vastly softer and assessed at around a nickel.  Therefore, a 2:2 cargo is valued in the +,- 12cpg range.  Few actual transactions are occurring, however.  As for Mont Belvieu, propane values have ebbed and flowed over the past 6 weeks, having taken a generally similar path as WTI, though as a percentage, there have been recent moments when propane has topped 50% of WTI.  Presently, however, the propane-to-WTI ratio is around the 46-47% level.  With regards propane inventories, the EIA yesterday reported a draw of 2.9mmbbls for an overall total of 93.10mmbbls.  or 97% of last year’s level, and 103% of two years ago.  Export volumes declined for the week ending 6th Dec, having been at 2.190mmbbls/day last week, but 1.611mmbbls in the more recent reporting period.  Production levels in the US continue to outperform and at 2.742mmbbls (as of 6 Dec) is above both the annual average (2.668mmbbls/day) and the Q4 average of 2.727mmbbls/day.

EAST Increased activity in both East and West so far this week has pulled up freight in both regions. Adnoc acceptances for January was published on Tuesday, and while we still awaiting Saudi acceptances, we start to see more fixing into January already. While itineraries will be clearer, for January ships in the East, next week and as such we can expect more ships appearing on the list for this window as we go – currently it looks like there could be more upside to freight in the East as freight rates are still lagging behind West and the list does not look exceptionally long.  WEST Since Monday, over a dozen of vessels have been placed on subs in the Western hemisphere. The position list has been slimmed down and at the time of writing we only find 2 vessels left able to work 1H January dates in the USG – one of them being prompt open. Fixing in 2H January is also well underway, and vessel supply for this period appears relatively tight. Freight rates have been strengthened significantly the last few days as we find last done around mid $110s H/C.

This week in the Panamax market, slight improvements in tonnage balance were noted across both the Atlantic and Pacific, though the fundamental outlook remains fragile. In the Atlantic, marginal gains on transatlantic routes were driven by steady demand and a tighter tonnage list, while fronthaul trips faced downward pressure due to limited fresh demand and owners competing on rates for longer voyages. The South American grain season continues at a seasonal low, with vessel demand anticipated to rise in the coming weeks, while the US grain season has already peaked, resulting in a notable decline in vessel activity. In the Pacific, China’s coal import market remains under strain from record-high inventories and unseasonably warm weather, further weakening demand and posing risks to fundamentals moving forward. Limited cargo replenishment from key origins compounded the challenges, leaving the basin oversupplied and rates under pressure despite early signs of stability at the start of the week. Confidence in lasting improvements remains low, leaving the market constrained by muted sentiment and cautious activity across both basins.

Whilst it could be argued that healthy tonnage lists in the Atlantic have conspired to allow charterers a smoother path to competitive rates, an even more compelling argument to support this general lethargy, is the distinct lack of positive sentiment on the owning side. There are exceptions to this of course but unless there is a mad pre-Christmas rush, we envisage rates gently softening.  The East market has been peppered with dribs and drabs of enquiry from the Gulf, but nothing that would signal a reversal in fortunes for now. Steady/soft.

The VLCC market has gone from bad to worse in the week gone by with returns now getting dangerously close to OPEX. TD3C is still hovering marginally north of WS 40 but is sure to be tested as charterers look to wrap up the last bits and pieces of the December MEG program and start looking into the new year. The Atlantic is not faring much better with plenty ships having ballasted West on spec to choose from. However, with some of the voyages in question being a longer commitment into the tail end of Q1 ‘25 there’s a tad more resistance on the owners’ part to lock in a poor result. Aframaxes and Suezmaxes are outperforming their bigger sisters by a country mile, but if things do not pick up, VLCCs will at some stage eat into their turf, even on a part cargo basis if and where possible. It is said that the darkest hour of the night comes before the dawn – hope springs eternal.

On the West Australia front, we see miners and operators alike out seeking for primarily end December dates. Some were out seeking for early January dates. Overall, the number of players enquiring for freight have dropped a tick below last week. Volumes out of East Australia remain flat, but we saw an increased number of enquiries for other fronts of the Pacific, such as NoPac, for January and early February dates. For C3 ex Brazil to China, enquiries for second half of December are very limited as most operators are out seeking for January dates. On the West Africa front, we see an uptick compared to last week for mid to end January dates. Far East spot tonnage, both prompt and on dates, are heavy. We see some forward positions popping up as well. Ballasting tonnage remains heavy overall with a notable number of ships still able to make late December dates while first half of January numbers is building up. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at mid USD 7 pmt levels when the week started but retreated to sub USD 7 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at low-mid USD 17 pmt levels for first half of January dates.

The Supramax market has been more active this week with improved cargo volumes across basins, however the rates still remain low. With long list of tonnage in position, all the fresh volume got absorbed and concluded well below last done levels. In the Pacific, we see steady flow of the Indonesia-India and Indonesia-China coal stems. The volumes in WC India-MEG region still remain low. In the ECSA we see more TA stems with minerals. With Christmas season coming up, owners and traders alike would cover their positions before year-end holidays and expect some leftover volumes in the market before end of the year. Overall, the sentiment is not uplifting given the long tonnage list and lack of cargo volumes. Period market is relatively quiet with very few reported fixtures.

After the inclement weather last weekend, the early part of the week saw a fair amount of replacement activity. The prompt part of the list has been heavily depleted with tonnage ballasting to US markets. Even with the activity and depleted tonnage rates have remained relatively stable although good itinerary vessels are trying to push rate levels with WS 135 done as a replacement off prompt dates. Natural dates now pushing out to end 2nd/early 3rd decade.  An anticipated correction with rates for local Mediterranean runs breaking the floor of WS 140, as owners were on the lookout for opportunities after a couple of prompt vessels opened earlier in the week. Tonnage is looking more balanced now compared to the start of the week but still a healthy amount to choose from. Ballasters over to the States are limited and that seems to be adding a bit to the downward pressure.

Spot chartering activity continues apace as we head into the final weeks of 2024, across a fixing window stretching from the out through to the end of January. There has been tightness on the front end in the Atlantic but rates are remaining stubbornly flat for TFDE's and 2-strokes. A little further out, charterers with January requirements have looked to get ahead of their remaining Christmas shopping and a good number of ships have been placed on subjects. In spite of this forward fixing, last week’s marginal rate increase does not yet feel embedded into the market and may be tested again. In the same vein, Pacific requirements seeking modern tonnage for end January have revealed healthy availabilities with levels under pressure as portfolios complete deliveries into Asia on effectively sunk shipping.

Another muted, yet unpredictable, week in the tanker second hand market as reported sales vary in subsector from week to week and seemingly no longer follow any pattern. There remains a healthy level of enquiry behind closed doors, and owners are keen to take money off the table, however buyers are in the driving seat when it comes to discussing price. Saying that, more specialised sectors are holding firm with scrubber fitted J19 SONGA BREEZE (19K DWT FUKUOKA 2009) selling at USD 24M and WINTER (13K DWT 21st CENTURY 2009) at 13.5M.  Sharply dropping earnings in the dry market could be the reason for lower volumes, but certain sectors are still proving attractive to buyers. Capesize particularly is falling under that banner with Far Eastern buyers securing 3 candidates this week. Now could be a smart time to move, so long as you are willing to ride out the slightly gloomy sentiment and likely slowdown over Chinese New Year, as competition could be fierce market units come Q1/Q2 25. As in any market correction, older ships are feeling the pinch with STRATTON (74K DWT HUDONG ZHONGHUA 2004) sold at USD 7.1M to Chinese buyers, a noticeable downtick on the USD 12M sellers were seeking earlier in the year for the vessel.

text: AMERICAS The FOB market on the Gulf Coast, while having declined from earlier high levels upwards of 30cpg, appears to have settled in the mid-teens at this point for January volumes.  There are a series of offers at present, but buyers seem reluctant and as a result very little has been accomplished.  Meanwhile, the EIA this week reported that propane stock levels in the US declined by a rather paltry 700,000bbls – where expectations ranged wildly from -1.25 to -4.0mmbbls.  Overall inventories now reside at 96mmbbls, or about 99% of the same time last year, and 107% of two years ago.    As the holiday season is now in full swing and year-end events are now regularly taking place many have retreated to the sidelines in an effort to preserve not only the profits that have been achieved thus far in 2024, but also any year-end bonuses.

EAST Main focus on shipping this week has been in the West market with only two deals done in the East so far since Monday. Next fixing window in the East should now be around last decade December where we so far have registered three deals. While there are very few ships on the Middle East position list that are restricted or very likely only want to stay in the area - the amount of ships potentially piling up in the West could eventually make it equally attractive to do a shorter East of Suez voyage.  WEST The first January cargo was covered on Monday and since then we have seen a handful of spot fixtures concluded. However, there are still a few vessels available for December dates ex USG with one being prompt open. The last deal was concluded in the low USD 100s H/C, but the downside may be limited as the ones controlling the length in January will look to seek alternative outlets if ideas on freight are too low.

text: MEG Owing to limited buying interests, cash differentials further weakened, with discounts for Jan lifting evenly split cargo plunging to mid-teens level vs small single digit last week. By the time of writing, Jan CP was traded at $626 and C3/C4 assessed at $4. Jan/Feb CP was backwardated by $10.  FAR EAST On CFR FAR EAST window, 23/0 for 1h Jan delivery was traded at Jan FEI plus $1, while similar parcel for 2h Jan delivery was offered at Jan FEI plus $2 yet to trigger interest. 46/0 parcels for 1h Jan delivery were reported done at Jan FEI minus $2.5 basis Chiba, and Jan FEI plus mid high single into Echina and Nchina, with deviation factored in.  However general demand remains sluggish, despite the winter coming and petchem margins improving. We’ve seen FIC’s buy tender solely for 4/0 Jan delivery this week, and the rest are cautious about buying spot, in view of upcoming CNY holidays and uncertainties over downstream consumption growths.  Special origin 3/1 cargo, for prompt Dec delivery was heard traded at Dec CP minus 30s basis SChina, which .

On the West Australia front, miners and operators alike were out for mid/end December dates. Overall, the number of players enquiring for freight have dropped since last week. Volumes out of East Australia have ticked up slightly but overall remains very limited. Same may be said for other fronts of the Pacific. For C3 ex Brazil to China, we see limited enquiries for late December with most operators looking at early January dates. On the West Africa front, some enquiries remain for late December, but many seem to have own tonnage behind and seeking opportunities for arbitrage. Far East spot tonnage is heavy. We see a considerable number of prompt ships. Ships on dates are ample as well with more and more forward positions popping up. Ballasting tonnage remains heavy for second half of December. On C5, fixtures concluded at mid/high USD 7 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see fixtures concluding at sub USD 19 pmt levels for end December dates.

Some steady activity in the North Sea with dates pushing into the 2nd decade.  A lot of programming of tonnage but placing Bbls still proving tricky for charterers so we could well see some delays. Rates are flat at the moment but with USG firming we will see pressure on availability as tonnage heads out of the region.  List now looking well established and relets are in the region. Prompter vessels are locking in on opportunities in front of them allowing charterers to squeeze some points out of last done rates. CPC somewhat lacks suitable candidates but with relets in the picture and the window reaching end-month dates rates won’t be under pressure. Bad weather due in the region might yet have some influence.

West Africa tonnage tightened towards the back end of last week, charterers having fixed openly off natural dates and pushed TD20 to WS 85-87.5 region, but also fixing off market on the forward window to sponge ballasters. As such although lists remain on the tighter side lack of serious volume probably stops us ballooning. Keep in mind though that the USG market has reignited in the wake of Thanksgiving. UKC ships have a nice floor with local USG options dwindling, surely forcing charterers to pay transatlantic tonnage for their services. This puts a tighter spin on our West Africa list and should enable owners to sustain TD20 in the high WS 80s or push on, albeit significant gains remain unlikely given the cheap alternatives that VLCCs have become! In the Mediterranean/Black Sea it has been a quiet week as CPC stems closed out December last week, similar to the Aframax market. In the MEG, eastbound runs have corrected into the low WS 90s with USD/mt competitiveness enabling us to cannibalize Aframax volume after VLCCs did the same to Suezmaxes, whilst we have seen less pronounced erosion on Basrah levels into the low WS 50s on non-compromised units.

The Supramax and Handysize markets remained quiet, with slow activity and mixed views across the Atlantic and the Pacific. In the Atlantic, the South Atlantic felt balanced, the US Gulf rates might have hit the bottom. The Continent and Mediterranean stayed sluggish, with little fresh interest and plenty of ships putting pressure on rates. In the Pacific, things didn’t look much better. Both markets faced weak demand and longer tonnage lists, with no real change in sentiment. As the festive season kicks in, the slowdown seems to be taking hold, and rates struggled to find any upward momentum.

The VLCC market is like catching a falling knife right now and there aren’t many signs in sight of an uptick any time soon. Daily returns are in the teens for the best of them at prevailing rates, and for the older end of the spectrum OPEX is under threat. Questions are being asked if we are witnessing a paradigm shift in the market, or if it’s just the same old game of hide and seek? The latter is probably the likely explanation, at least that’s been the conclusion the last few months when looking in the rear-view window. China Inc. is becoming more and more dominating on both the ship and cargo side which has clouded she supply-demand picture further. However, volumes are relatively stable month on month and the fleet has not increased. Looking ahead, however, an ageing fleet and a market not even remotely encouraging new orders will all things equal lead to a boom. What comes around goes around – eventually.

The Panamax market faced another challenging week, with weak fundamentals persisting across both basins. In the Atlantic, limited grain and coal inquiries from the US Gulf and Baltic, along with oversupply of tonnage and a lack of fresh cargo, kept rates under pressure despite some support from South Africa coal activity. ECSA remained relatively stable, aided by South Africa absorbing spot ballasters, but the overall tonnage imbalance left owners struggling to maintain last-done levels while charterers secured lower bids. The Pacific fared no better, as Indonesian coal and Japanese tenders offered minimal relief against a backdrop of high vessel availability. Bid-offer spreads widened, and rates continued to ease across key routes, with the market searching for a floor and no signs of recovery in sight.

The flurry of activity in the Atlantic last week saw a modest increase in spot LNG charter rates, which has continued into this week as 2-stroke availability for December cargoes has all but disappeared. Portfolios keen to maintain or gain flexibility amidst uncertainty on optimal cargo destinations has tightened availability considerably and prompted several other requirements to emerge for later in January. It remains to be seen whether this tightness will lead to anything resembling a spike on freight or, as we are seeing for the moment, a slight uptick. Similarly, East of Suez sees a healthy amount of enquiries both from the Middle East and APAC with requirements still being worked at the time of writing. On the surface, the market remains oversupplied with TFDE’s but with independent owners holding most positions, Charterers who require vessels to reposition and seek flexibility on charter period have less bargaining power with rates already at relatively low levels. There is also a sense of convergence on multimonth and multiyear levels, although the delta is still a little wide for now. With owners and charterers travelling around for the festive period and possibly preparing for CWC, it’s likely we’ll see some progress on these medium term periods in the coming weeks.

Slow week again for second hand tankers, though there is increased appetite being shown from Far Eastern buyers, particularly on larger tonnage. Whether or not this translates into increased liquidity is yet to be seen, however, with the winter market noticeably absent, it is not expected that these buyers will rush to transact. On smaller sizes, handy tanker MAERSK BERING (29K DWT GSI 2005)*ice 1C was bought by Chinese buyers for USD 15.55M.   A clear direction for Dry cargo markets with consensus among most market players that there is still some way to go for this ongoing correction. Sentiment which is keeping liquidity high with some Sellers deciding to catch the falling knife at what remain historically attractive levels, while Buyers seeing increasing value in these correcting benchmarks. This week has seen flurry of capesize activity with scrubber fitted capesize sisters K.CONFIDENCE/K. VICTORY (181K SASEBO 2012-13) inviting offers this week and being traded around USD 32-33M each, while the scrubber fitted CAPE DREAM (179K DWT HHI ULSAN 2011) was sold at USD 28M to Chinese buyers.

EAST Next round of spot fixing out from Middle Eastern ports are expected from second half December onwards. How much spot volume we can expect prior to 20th December remains to be seen. The next Indian PSU VLGC cargoes being talked about is already into last decade December dates. That said, these dates are still rather far out and with CP for December still not published one can hope a few more players finally will surface into the market soon. Last done at low 50s.  WEST A few spot fixtures have been done so far this week, both out of US and West Africa. In total we now count 28 spot fixtures in December ex USG/USEC and there are still a couple uncovered cargoes out there for end December dates. Currently we still find 5-6 positions left open before moving into January. Freight rates are currently moving sideways with latest deals done around 105 H/C.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Dec propane CP at $635 and butane at $630, a rollover from Dec. Propane is in line with swap value, but butane is higher than most expectations, especially in view of ampler butane supply compared to Nov liftings. Evenly split cargo for Dec was assessed at CP flattish level amid limited discussions. By the time of writing, Jan CP was traded at $630 and Jan C3/C4 was traded at $7.   FAR EAST A couple of 23/0 parcels on 2h Dec delivery was changed hand at Dec FEI plus $2/2ish last Friday, and discussions have shifted to Jan program. In window several 23/0 parcels for 1h Jan delivery was traded at Jan FEI plus mid-single digit. However, outside window the sluggish demand has exerted further pressure on FEI, with Jan FEI/CP was traded depressingly at -$13. Chinese petchem players hold off on spot procurement, with bearish outlook on downstream consumption before CNY (starting end Jan) and uncertainties on delays of restart up from maintenance. We’ve only seeing one Vietnam based importer issue buy tender for one 3/1 or 2/0 or 1/1 for 1h Jan delivery.    Other than normal stems, one 2/2, special origin, for 1h Dec arrival basis Schina was reported done at Dec CP minus $20. And three more heavy propane cargos for Dec arrival are reported unsold amid thin trades. Till Nov we’ve seen over 8mmt tons been placed into China, similar vs last year, whereas the trades are more spot tender related, causing more volatility in cash differentials than before.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The US LPG market has been very subdued this week due to the U.S Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday.  Many regular market participants have been away from their desks and little has occurred.  The EIA inventory report, however, was released yesterday amid earlier predictions of a 1.10-1.40mmbbl draw.  Where the 5-yr average for Week 47 shows an average draw of 224,000bbls, for the week ending 22 Nov the EIA reported a draw of 1.0mmbbls, bringing the overall propane total stock level in the U.S. to 96.70mmbbls, or about 98% of the same time last year but 107% of two years ago.  There are presently 87 Days of Supply, versus a 2024 average of nearly 83 Days of Supply and a Q4 average of nearly 99%.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, are in the mid teens at this point, though an 18cpg 4:0 transaction was reported earlier in the week, though most buyers balk at such lofty levels and point to calculated levels at 14-15cpg.

The VLCC market has gone from the doghouse to the outhouse with rates plummeting across the board in all areas in the week gone by. TD3C (MEG/China) came in at WS 48.7 yesterday, but there’s been deals concluded at considerably less, albeit spearheaded by older tonnage some of which hampered by being ex dry-dock etc. The rot has spilled over into the Atlantic market too, but thus far eastbound rates have clung on just north of WS 50 from both West Africa and Brazil. Although there are few signs of a turnaround this side of the weekend resistance is becoming more evident the further down the scale we’ve come so the likelihood of a much further decline is limited.

Bad weather caused some issues at the beginning of the week but seems to have settled a bit more now. Activity in the first half of the week has been limited with some fixing/failing. Dates covering into the first 5 days and rates look like they will remain steady and in certain date ranges could come under some downward pressure. US Market not enticing much in the way of ballasting just yet.  An interesting Mediterranean/Black Sea market where the intervention of bigger ships is not extensive, but attractive returns have put them in the mix occasionally. Fixing window is pushing well forward with finding safe itineraries now at the forefront of charterers minds. The North Sea remains weak and the USG not giving much support; owners will look to keep one foot in the Mediterranean and with some requirement will likely push for higher than last done, but with Suezmax watching closely.

The Atlantic market normally relies heavily on the US Gulf for any green shoots, but on this occasion, West Africa has managed to step up, albeit, moderately. TD20 bottomed out at WS 75 with owners now holding for WS 80 plus. With a flurry of cargoes entering the market today, there's a reasonable case to be made for this region adding a few more points (prior to the weekend). Meanwhile, TD6 looks likely to trade variations of WS 90's as owners look to leverage on improved sentiment.  In the East, it's been very quiet, at least on the surface. The good news is that the list of FOC available ships has fallen with rates likely to trade WS 90's for an East run.

Rates continue to fall quicker than autumn leaves, and growing position lists in all areas shows no sign of respite for the owning community. Cargo volumes remain low across basins. The oversupply of tonnage continues to exert downward pressure on the rates. The usual Indonesia-China coal is being fixed at USD 9,000 levels. Indonesian coal volumes continue to keep up. MEG-EC India trips being concluded at USD 10k/d levels. MEG/WC India volumes have not picked up as yet. ECSA volumes remain low and whatever hit the market was covered away quietly with the available tonnage. Period activity is rather slow and not much being reported in the market.

The Panamax market experienced persistent weakness this week, with soft fundamentals and declining sentiment in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. In the Atlantic, grain volumes remained significantly lower than the same period last year, and coal demand weakened as high inventories in China and India, coupled with mild temperatures and limited trade. While mineral cargoes provided some support on transatlantic routes, fronthaul fixtures struggled due to an oversupply of tonnage heading East, with rates falling below index levels. A lack of demand from key origins such as NoPac kept rates under pressure in the Pacific despite some activity from southern mineral cargoes and Japanese tenders. An oversupply of vessels gave charterers the upper hand, with bid-offer spreads narrowing further as rates declined another USD 250–300. Modest FFA gains and a clearing of spot tonnage provided slight optimism, but sustained recovery will require more substantial grain volumes and improved demand across regions.

There has been little change to rates and sentiment in spot LNG shipping over the past week, with a handful of fixtures spread between the two basins at levels largely unchanged week-on-week. Although as a word of caution for those claiming winter has already passed us by, storage levels in Europe are being drawn down quickly and Korea is experiencing record snowfall for this time of year. Traction on multi-month and mid-term charters remains limited though we could see some moves for periods in the range 12-24 months before the end of the year.   There are more positive notes for long-term LNG growth as President Trump and his team continue to outline plans for their return to the White House. The rapid restart of new U.S. export permit approvals featured prominently in a broad energy package floated this week, which is likely to support new long-term offtake agreements next year.   There has also been some moves on the FSRU front, with reports that the Energos Eskimo is heading to Egypt for a 10yr charter to EGAS once she finishes up duty in Aqaba, Jordan in mid-2025. EGAS is also looking for another FSRU in the near-term to support a widening gap between domestic gas production and expected growth in power consumption.

On the West Australia front, we see much more activity from miners but fewer operators and tenders for mid December dates. Volumes out of East Australia and other Pacific fronts remain limited. Slightly more enquires ex South Africa this week to Far East and a back haul cargo was seen as well. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see very limited enquiries for first half of December and slightly more for second half of December. In the Far East, we still see some prompt vessels while a notable number of ships experienced itinerary delays due to typhoon. Ballasting tonnage is stacking up for the second half of December with a handful still able to meet first half of December dates. On C5, fixtures concluded at sub USD 10 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see lower level of fixing activity this week as owners and charterers adopt a more passive and wait and see approach. Fixtures although limited, concluded at low-mid USD 22 pmt levels on C3 equivalent for early December and circa USD 23 pmt levels for end December dates.

Although spot rates have improved somewhat this week, the tanker winter market continues to be elusive. Enquiry on larger crude tonnage remains tentative as a result, but despite this, any discussion will be taken very seriously by owners who are keen to exit positions at these elevated levels. What is uncertain is the extent to which values will correct following this ongoing slump. As expected, values for non-eco aframaxes, around the 15-year age bracket, are the first to feel the heat as uncertainty takes hold. Tellingly, the sale of SOFIA II (105k DWT Sumitomo 2008) at USD 32.2M is a rude awakening for owners still stuck with yesterday’s price expectations. History has shown however, that bids accepted in a falling market may prove to be a smart move once the dust settles.  It can be argued that the reason for the well documented disconnect between values and rates has been driven by sentiment, rather than by genuine market fundamentals in this year’s dry market. Despite this somewhat lacklustre earnings environment, investors are still keen to pursue opportunities in this sector. Sellers, for the same reason, are willing to service this enquiry even as values are correcting. This is demonstrated in the sales of scrubber fitted capesize sisters NORD ENERGY/POWER (178k DWT HHIC Phil 2012) to Hayfin at USD 31.8M each, 6 months after the same owners sold a year older ship scrubber fitted unit NORD FERRUM (179k DWT HHIC Phil 2011) for USD 34.3M (in May).

EAST So far this week we have seen several deals done from ports East of Suez at various freight levels. In total we now count 8 spot fixtures conluded for December dates ex MEG. Despite the recent activity there still remain a few open vessels in the first decade of the month and the position list in the East continues to appear lengthy.  WEST Western freight rates have remained relatively flat this week with the latest deals concluded a bit above 105 H/C. Among the vessels still on the position list for December dates, the majority are controlled by two major shipowners, while the remaining three are trader relets. In total we count 24 spot fixtures in December ex USG/USEC – YTD avg at 28 spot.

European gas prices surged at the end of last week on the back of renewed concerns around Russian supply disruption, making headlines in mainstream media with recent winters still fresh in the region’s memory. Coupled with a sharp decline in JKM, Europe has rubber stamped its position as the premium destination for U.S. LNG in the near term, and now cold weather will increase drawdown on storages. The reality for LNG shipping this winter is starkly different, as bolstered regasification capacity and phenomenal growth in vessel supply this year fail to alleviate the bearish tonne-mile scenario brought by heavily-favoured intra-basin trade. Combined with no contango to support tonne-time, there really hasn’t been much to alleviate this ongoing weak freight demand scenario. Competition for uncovered December shipping requirements in the Atlantic has hence been fierce, with the slight gains on freight of last week erased in a flash. The Pacific continues to see a steady flow of requirements with charter rates for modern tonnage aligning with those in the West. There are also certain requirements being worked with more vintage sizes although the surplus of early spec ST and TFDE tonnage is piling pressure on rates, with fixing levels forced below OPEX in some cases.  Naturally, at this point in the cycle there will be discussions on laying older ships up or scrappage. The announcement by a Korean Ship Owner of the scrapping of four 25-year old steamships is likely to be the start of a trickle of such deals rather than a surge, although the prospect of a prolonged lay-up and the evolving regulatory framework may accelerate these decisions.

text: MEG Spot differentials for Dec FOBs edged lower, assessed at Dec CP minus small single digit for evenly split grade, as in lack of buying interest. Saudi Aramco released their Dec lifting acceptance, with some reported to be cut on propane tolerance and some evenly split ratio changed to heavy butane. This is quite surprising as Nov butane was restricted on plus tolerance. Qatar Energy tendered to sell an evenly split cargo for 19 to 22 Dec lifting. With such additional butane length, Dec C4 quickly fell and Dec C3/C4 traded at $13 vs last week’s $4.  FAR EAST Cash premium improved as cargo length slowly been absorbed. Despite the slim buying interests from China, a couple of 46/0 parcels for 2h Dec delivery basis Chiba were changed hand at Dec FEI minus mid-single digit. And in the window 23/0 parcel for 2h Dec delivery was bid at $1.5 to Dec FEI while offer at $3.5. Similar parcel for 1h Jan delivery was offered at $7.5 to Jan FEI. Dec FEI/CP was relatively volatile, traded from minus $12.5 on Monday and narrowed down to minus $3.5 by the time of writing.   HTC tendered to buy 23/0 for last decade Jan delivery but result remains sketchy. One NChina PDH issued buy term tender for 46/0 monthly delivery into Tianjin. Despite the weakening flat price, China PDH overall run rates still at below 65%, due to scheduled maintenance and unexpected glitch. We expect rate to be improved by end Nov, as a couple of PDHs will resume operation. Other than petchem, disappointingly residential demand yet to rebound in China, and the market is overwhelmed with a handful of unsold special origin stems for Dec delivery.
