comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The EIA this week reported a modest draw of 300,000bbls which brought overall US stocks to 101.5mmbbls, or almost exactly100% of the same period in 2023, and 115% of the total achieved in 2022.  As before, there are sufficient stocks of propane in the domestic US market.  Production is most recently listed at 2.754mmbbls/day, which is well above average for the year (and the quarter), and exports are, for the most recent reporting period, actually below average at 1.578mmbbls/day (against a YTD average of 1.724mmbbls/day).  While those numbers are being absorbed, propane at Mont Belvieu continues to outperform crude, the evidence being the sharp rise in the c3/WTI ratio, which moved from 42% at the front of October to 50% at the close of business yesterday.    Terminal fees, meanwhile, are solidly robust through Nov, but there is very little remaining on offer.  It is then that the market softens, and rather suddenly.  Where Nov transactions were solidly in the mid 20cpg range, December is bid at a dime less, though offers are – for the moment - still in the upper teens.

EAST A couple of spot fixtures for last-decade November laycans have already been completed ahead of Diwali. In total we now count 4 deals done this week – all being Indian PSUs which brings the total for the month to 9 which is a couple cargoes above the monthly average. Hence, Indian programs are likely soon wrapped up for November. Looking at current tonnage availability versus expected remaining cargo volumes you may quickly become a bit less optimistic for near term spot freight in the East.  WEST The BLPG3 index has now fallen below the 100 dollar mark. December fixing out of the US Gulf is underway, with the first fixture completed earlier this week. Several trader relets are beginning to appear on the US position list for first decade December laycans, though there are still 5 vessels available for November - all in control by two major shipowners. We currently count 29 spot fixtures for November dates which is 1 more than the YTD avg ex USG/USEC.

Slow start to the week. Past week has been relatively quiet except for the fresh influx of cargoes especially in west Africa early this week - cargo covered well below last done levels given ample tonnage in the region. In Asia, the market picked up start of the week with fresh volumes taking up the available tonnages. The Handysize market remained positive, however the Continent and Mediterranean remains relatively weaker. Market fundamentals in the US Gulf and South Atlantic stay strong, contributing to a positive outlook. With the grain season coming up, we expect more volumes out of ECSA in the coming weeks. Period market is slow with fewer fixtures reported this week.

Unseasonably, VLCC-rates continue to fall quicker than autumn leaves, and growing position lists in all areas shows no sign of respite for the owning community short term. Chinese charterers are increasingly looking to local tonnage for their requirements, leaving less choice for “third party” owners, but more importantly creating less transparency and more opportunity for the larger oil company-trader community to dictate the narrative. The MEG has led the downward trend, thus enticing more modern tonnage to ballast west on spec. This has added additional pressure in the Atlantic, which resulted in a 6.5-point drop for TD15 yesterday. Falling bunker prices is the only saving grace for owners right now, to the extent ships are not already filled up that is. One possible "positive" is a typhoon brewing in the East with potential port closures and delays as a result. This could trim the MEG position list somewhat further out on the curve.

Q4 has a distinctly Q3 feel to it which is rather unnerving considering the optimism that pervaded this segment less than a month ago. Where do we go from here? The bane of the market remains that much vilified class of vessels, well, vilified by some in the owning community who ironically TC their vessels out, that being the humble relet. With an enormous chunk of the Suezmax fleet now in the hands of oil companies, there is a natural cap on freight whilst charterers are content to profit from the delta between chartering in and out, which caps the downside to some extent (a silver lining of sorts).  For now, TD20 will do well to stay in the WS 90's whilst MEG/East will trade WS 112.5-115 with a softer underbelly.

Where did October go? A handful of spot fixtures have been concluded since our last report, with a similar number of requirements on the horizon or being worked at the time of writing.   Charterers continue to pile pressure on headline rates on the prompt, although with sustained activity there has been some resistance from subletters and levels appear to have bottomed out in the high-teens for modern 2-strokes in the Atlantic, at least for the time being.  With sentiment at its weakest, the fixing window is moving right out to cover periods into January and throughout the first quarter 2025 in some cases. Whilst we would typically expect a healthy premium for forward fixing, particularly at this time of year, rate increments appear minimal despite requirements effectively locking away vessels for the remainder of the traditional Winter period. Competition for similar requirements is likely to remain strong.  Yearly highs on European LNG prices and minimal arbitrage opportunities continue to ensure the bulk of flexible volumes remain in the Atlantic, skewing already weakening fundamentals in favour of oversupply. That said, with freight at such depressed levels there are plenty of fixing opportunities on spot and an increase in 1-2 year charters may soon follow. Whilst most discussions thus far have been on index-linkage, a correction in fixed price charter rate ideas for 2025 onwards could spur additional demand for the safe haven of period coverage.

This week's Panamax market reflects a cautiously mixed outlook shaped by regional variations and upcoming seasonal shifts. While coal demand for winter could catalyze a rate rebound, the market remains broadly moderate with two more weeks of expected sluggishness. In the North Atlantic, grain trades continue to command a premium, while a moderate tonnage supply has supported slight transatlantic gains, with time charter rates around USD 9,500. Fronthaul, however, remains static as owners continue to prefer trip-out fixtures, limiting immediate upside potential. Asia presents a similarly muted landscape, with limited trades and mixed sentiment suggesting a soft floor but insufficient demand to lift rates. Meanwhile, East Coast South America faces noticeable tonnage oversupply, compelling owners to settle for lower rates on November liftings. Without a sustained push in cargo flow, fundamentals will likely stay constrained, especially in the Atlantic basin, where fresh demand will be critical to supporting any rate improvements.

On the West Australia front, we see enquiries from miners, operators, and tender for mid November dates and some operators expressing interest for first full December forward dates. Volumes out of East Australia is relatively healthy and held up from last week. Relatively little activity on other fronts of the Pacific. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see operators enquiring primarily for second half of November dates as well as first half of December dates. West Africa volumes remain relatively robust. Far East spot tonnage is abundant with a notable number of prompt vessels. Ballasting tonnage is heavy for second half of November. On C5, the week started with fixtures concluding at mid USD 8 pmt levels and remained flat till mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at low-mid USD 20 pmt levels. We see some resistance with bids in the USD 19 pmt levels and offers at USD 22 pmt levels for second half of November dates.

After activity covering the last stems in October, the market has quietened again; the first decade in November is looking light on Aframax stems with own tonnage being programmed. With the Mediterranean and US markets also softening ballasting looks less attractive which will keep vessels in the area. On a positive note, US markets are starting to look busier again so need to watch that space.  The Mediterranean/Black Sea market experienced an inevitable correction with rates trending downwards. Weak activity in the 1st decade ex North Africa, Ceyhan, and CPC covered ahead and a lengthy tonnage list due to ballasters into the area have been the main factors. The question now is where the floor will be set, as there are still plenty of vessels seeking employment.

The tanker market this week continues to slide in unfamiliar fashion as firm buyers are finding themselves inundated with possible candidates, particularly in the 10YO+ age range. These buyers though, will likely be rewarded for showing patience while sellers begin considering interest at well below last done levels. Modern units however, continue to show resilience to this story. C.15yo MR tankers are under pressure in terms of value due to the persisting flat sentiment, however it is worth remembering that most owners of these units have enjoyed buoyant earnings and will be exiting positions well in the money. Helping price this part of the age curve AHINOS (53k DWT GSI 2007) which was sold for USD 22M.   The disconnect between values and rates persists across the dry sector, with many buyers waiting in the wings at tomorrow’s prices. Owners for the most part are resilient and are not so inclined to drop their price ideas despite a lacklustre earnings environment. That said, there is still a fairly healthy amount of liquidity within the market, particularly when those price ideas are reduced. For example, scrubber fitted Ultramax pair ALWINE/AUGUST OLDENDORFF (63k DWT JMU 2014/2015) were sold SS/DD due en bloc at USD 51.5M to Greek Buyers, having failed at c.USD 30M per vessel during the summer. In the modern Ultramax sector GREENWICH PIONEER (63k DWT Nantong Xiangyu 2020) was sold for USD 32.5M with TC attached until March 2026.

Little change in sentiment on LNG shipping this week. Spot requirements in both basins continue to be covered for prompt liftings at levels below last done, with charter rates for all conventional vessel types converging at historical seasonal lows. Weak downstream demand for LNG combined with tonnage oversupply has led portfolios to aggressively bid on FOB cargoes to keep their vessels moving, resulting in negative implied freight economics. Nonetheless there is a reasonable amount of spot activity, and we expect further fixing opportunities throughout the remainder of Q4 albeit amongst strong competition.   As the steady flow of newbuildings continues to add pressure on overall fleet utilisation in the near term, the multi-month space is likely to remain muted. However, discussions around a redistribution of next year’s length are ongoing, as a handful of players show appetite to take on tonnage for additional trading flexibility, although it may be some time before we reach alignment on hire rate and structure.  Newbuilding activity has been limited this week although Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) have announced the long term charter of their ordered newbuilding FSRU with storage capacity of 200,000m3 to Singapore LNG.

EAST 6 spot fixtures have been done in the Eastern market so far this week – 4 of these are Indian PSUs with 1 more currently in the works.  In total 7 spot deals have been done in the first decade of Nov ex MEG which is the same as the average for the last three months. The market is expected to shift focus to the second decade of November soon, although there are still several vessels available for the first decade. The position list in the East may shorten as some ships are expected to ballast West, but whether this will stabilize the market remains uncertain.  WEST  Several ships have been placed on subs in the West so far this week. With that said we now count 28 spot fixtures for November dates out of the US. Freight rates have been gradually declining over the past couple of weeks but now seem to have found a floor at around 105 H/C. There still remain 8 vessels able to work November dates ex USG.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The Nov Gulf Coast terminal fee market has maintained much of its strength from Oct as current rates remain in the mid 20cpg range where several transactions are known to have occurred for all-c3 parcels.    Mixed ratio cargoes are discounted and priced in the upper teens, but buy-side sentiment for Dec 2:2's is in the mid/upper teens range.  Yesterday the EIA reported a  1.3mmbbl draw which was viewed as mildly surprising as most had anticipated a small build as a result of ongoing production strength and - in recent weeks - some export disruptions.  Current overall US stocks as of 18 Oct stand at 101.8mmbbls, or 99.4% of last year's mid-Oct level.  NWE While a handful of unmet window bids allowed large cargo CIF ARA propane values to rise during the first half of the week, a global slide in LPG prices which tracked the losses of crude resulted in the marking down of large cargo values by $8/ton to $594/mt where they stand as of Wednesday evening. Looking structurally at the curve, it will be difficult for importers to purchase and store propane due to significant backwardation, especially juxtaposed with belvieus modest contango. The propane / naphhta spread, now marked at -$50/ton, is nearing the levels of theoretical demand destruction for propane, due to thin margins, however several PDH plants including the new 437,000 ton/year plant that opened this year on the coast of Poland, have shown little signs of slowing down yet. As we approach the season of increased heating demand, it will be interesting to see how regional buyers bolster inventories, faced with such significant backwardation.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Despite limited inquiries this week, cash premium for Nov lifting evenly split cargo maintained at CP plus $18-20. Saudi Aramco was said to cut the plus 5% tolerance on butane for Nov lifting while no changes for propane. At the time of writing, Nov C3 CP was traded at $628, and C3/C4 was traded at $7.    FAR EAST Cash differentials softened further this week with a couple of 46/0 for 2h Nov delivery offered in window at Nov FEI plus low single digit basis Yantai or minus low single basis Chiba, but no bids seen. 23/0 parcel for 1h Dec delivery was bid at Dec FEI plus $3.5 while offered at $5.5. Outside window a handful of 46/0 for 1h Dec delivery was placed into EChina and NChina at Nov FEI plus mid single digit.    At the same time, a flurry of tenders was concluded this week. Taiwan Formosa was reported to procure a 23/0 into Mailiao at Nov MOPJ minus teens, and a 46/0 into Ningbo at Nov FEI flattish, both for Nov delivery respectively. Huayi was reported to procure two parcels through their tender for 10 Nov to 1h Dec delivery, with one at Nov CP plus mid high 20s. Inpex was reported to sell via tender, a 3/1 for 11/12 Nov lifting on CFR Chiba basis at Nov FEI plus mid high single digit to a trader. Another 23kt butane for early Dec lifting ex Port Bonython was offered via Santo tender this week.    Other than normal stems, there are 4 Iranian cargos available for Nov delivery, offered via tender, among which 2 for heavy propane and 2 evenly split ratios. Last tender for heavy propane delivered in Nov was reported concluded at Nov CP plus low teens. However since Nov FEI/CP narrowed to $25, plus limited buying appetites, we believe the differential will have to decline significantly to award.

The market saw a mixed week. In the Atlantic, the US Gulf continued to show demand for fronthaul business, but transatlantic rates softened as recent gains stalled. The Mediterranean showed improved demand. In Asia, the gradual decline continued, with limited fresh inquiry and minimal changes in the Indian Ocean. The Handysize market remained positive, with rates edging higher in the Atlantic, particularly in the Continent and Mediterranean. Market fundamentals in the US Gulf and South Atlantic stayed strong, contributing to a positive outlook. In the Pacific, the market remained stable with some new orders, but tonnage availability increased.

On the West Australia front, we see enquiries primarily from miners and tenders primarily for early November dates. Lesser activity was seen from operators this week though some have started enquiring for second half of November forward dates. Volumes out of East Australia have picked up from last week. Relatively little activity on other fronts of the Pacific. Reasonably healthy volume out of South Africa with few tenders. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see operators enquiring for primarily second half of November dates. Far East spot tonnage is abundant with a notable number of prompt vessels deciding to ballast. Resulting ballasting tonnage is heavy for November. On C5, the week started off with fixtures concluding at high USD 8 pmt levels and dropping to mid USD 8 pmt levels the day after. Approaching mid-week, there is a bounce back to mid-high USD 8 pmt levels. On C3, fixtures concluded at low-mid USD 21 pmt levels but retreated to low USD 20 pmt levels by mid-week.

Throughout the 20th century, Wednesday has been especially referred to as hump day in an effort to liven up the drudgery of the workweek, although it won’t necessarily cheer up the owning community today. The market for the big ships is not bad by any measure, but with rates having been pushed up towards the WS 60 mark for MEG/East runs in the week gone by, there’s a danger that it’s reach the top of the hump as we turn the corner towards the weekend - with a possible slide down the other side in stall. Charterers have showed resistance leaving owners wondering if “that was it” for the first decade November in the MEG. Few believe that is the case of course, but where there is doubt… one bird in the hand and so on. A few failings have stalled things a bit in the Atlantic too. However, even if rates could be in for an adjustment, seasonal demand should dictate a temporary setback.

A combination of vessels ballasting leaving a tighter list and a relatively active spot market for end/early dates has seen X-North Sea firm up 25 points since this time last week. Pushing into November stems, and with levels giving much improved returns, we may not see as much ballasting out in the short term and natural tonnage will come back into the frame which should rebalance the available tonnage.  Small correction on the benchmark of TD19 to equal Suezmax levels that have capped the Aframaxes. Tonnage list is still well populated with quite a few different owners and vessels up until the end of the month. November dates in North Africa slowly coming into play, and the 2nd decade ex CPC is also anticipated. Some relets are being utilized on own cargoes.

The Atlantic has a steady feel with no evident downside. West Africa is busy with sustained enquiry in a narrow window, which may see rates gently nudge upwards prior to the weekend. In the Mediterranean, despite a lengthy list of TD6 candidates, there appears to be some resistance from owners to drastically softening their ideas, especially as charterers still insist on early Canakkale cancelling.  In the East, it's been a mixed bag with last done rates rarely being repeated. BOT/UKCM (cogh) might trade down due to an abundance of FOC ships who will be looking to reposition West.

This week in the Panamax market started slow, with owners reducing their rate expectations as tonnage lists grew in both the Atlantic and Pacific regions. The Indonesian market held up better, but a long tonnage list for ECSA added pressure. The general sentiment remained negative, with expectations of further rate erosion despite some improvement in Atlantic enquiries and softening conditions in the East.

There is a feeling in the tanker market that beating last done is no longer the expectation for sellers, as buying interest wanes given a calming charter market and potentially impactive events to come in the near future (i.e. the US Election). That said, levels slightly below the last done will still provide owners with extremely healthy returns on their initial investments.   A flurry of new candidates on the market coupled with a sharp correction on spot rates has dampened sentiment in the dry market. Buyers are being encouraged to either wait or are testing owners on levels very much at tomorrow’s pricing rather than yesterday’s. It remains to be seen whether owners will embrace this new pricing sentiment or endure the uncertain charter market and rely on the vessel supply story to support elevated values. There was healthy activity in the Capesize sector, particularly focused around the 15 year old mark, which will help price the increasing list of units in the market.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Cash premium hovers above $20 for Nov lifting evenly split cargos, as in lack of spot availability. Earlier this week one trader also bid for similar cargo in window at Nov CP plus $20 but no offers seen. By the time of writing, following the crude drop, Nov C3 CP was traded at $625 but still resilient to drop further.   FAR EAST Cash differentials inched up and 23kt C3 for 2h Nov delivery was bid at Nov FEI plus $3.5 while similar cargo for 1h Dec at Dec FEI plus $7.5.   Outside window a couple of 46kt C4 for 2h Nov delivery was changed hand at Nov FEI plus $5-6 basis Echina. However petchem inquiries from end users are limited, owing to the waning margins. A handful of PDHs were reported to cut rates or consider shutdown in Nov. This week so far only one SChina PDH user was heard to procure two 46/0 parcels for 1H and 2H Nov delivery, at Nov FEI plus 7ish and CP plus 40s respectively. Other than that, Taiwan FPCC issued tender to buy a Dec lifting Us 4/0 into Mailiao.    A couple of Iranian 3/1 parcels for early Nov delivery basis SChina, were reported to trade at Nov CP plus teens. Given the increasing tensions, recent Iranian LPG programs/offers are delayed until vessels loaded for sail and for sale.  However, Oct delivery into China is estimated to rebound over 700kt, from 594kt in Aug and 660kt in Sep.   Other than spot, One NChina Major importer issued term tender to secure monthly supply propane. Taiwan CPC also issued a FOB/DES swap tender as usual to secure the logistics supply next year.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Product availability remains limited from the US – particularly from the terminals themselves - and spot FOB terminal resale fees continue to be robust, with October having closed out at above 30cts/gal, and a more recent 4:0 transaction was just seen in the mid-20cpg for November.    One of the supporting factors has been the relatively soft freight market, which has disallowed vessel owners from grabbing a larger share of the arb, which on its own has retained the bulk of it strength.  Today the EIA reported that US propane inventory levels rose sharply as of 11th Oct – and above expectations – to 103.10mmbbls, a 3.3mmbbl week-over-week build, where estimates ranged from +1.8 to +2.6mmbbls. This should motivate buy-side interest as it will likely cause MB to soften.  NWE From the end of September until last week, large cargo propane pricing surged by $61/t to $627.25/mt CIF Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp as markets braced for a possible retaliation from Israel following a missile attack from Iran. The price for large cargos swung from -$10/mt discounts versus swaps to plus $13/mt premiums,  That quickly led to the narrowing of the propane naphtha spread at the beginning of October.  Large cargo butane values also shot up by $44/mt to $625/mt across over the same time frame, as seasonal blending demand leapt while US exports to the region feigned.   This week however, the market has come off some, closing yesterday at $583/metric ton, effectively widening the propane/naphtha spread to  -$46/mt, from an the 18 month low of  -$30pmt seen at the beginning of the October.   In the North Sea, LPG exports remain on hold as maintenance at fields at Karsto is reduced to 70% until  26 October.

EAST We have seen one spot fixture in the East so far this week, but the market remains largely in wait mode pending Saudi acceptances which are expected to come out within Friday. Sentiment is trending downwards as the position list before 10 November appears well supplied – including a good number of trader relets. However, the outlook could change quickly if a wave of cargoes suddenly emerge.  WEST The last available position for October is finally gone after being fixed as the only spot fixture so far this week. The first open vessel in USG will be from 9 November onwards, and we see a further 6-7 ships open in the second decade. We have seen 18 spot fixtures ex USG/USEC so far for November; 10 in 1st decade and 8 in 2nd decade, but 3rd decade remains unexplored. Charterers are not in a hurry to move for this window yet as rate sentiment keep coming off.

Prompt available positions are still being depleted with vessels ballasting mainly to the Mediterranean, but there is currently still sufficient tonnage to keep the rate levels steady.  Relets and own program cargoes are still limiting the market activity which looks to continue in at least the short term.  Activity in the Mediterranean has been reflective of a tentative feel to the market of late, but owners’ sentiment looks to remain positive with lower numbers ex North Africa being trumped as Ceyhan dates move into early November loads. With North ships maybe preferring a USG ballast there is scope for lists in the Mediterranean to shorten if activity continues to tie up tonnage. Delays in the straits should help Black Sea fixing and Suezmax look to be moving out of the way.

Sustained liquidity has contributed to a further reduction in spot charter rates in both basins this week. Oversupply of tonnage is felt most heavily in the Atlantic despite numerous requirements within the first half November window.    We expect 2024 to be a record-breaking year for the number of spot fixtures; however, the active start of the year has tailed off and the number of spot fixtures continues to slide each month. In part, this is due to a soft LNG market that is seeing tendered cargoes hoovered up by those with length in their portfolios, resulting in few firm requirements. The opportunities that do emerge are fought over keenly, and this trend doesn’t look like easing in the near future: rumours of sub-fixtures below all-time-lows for 2-strokes circulate at the time of writing.   There has also been further correction in the Pacific where competition for spot employment remains fierce. One sub-fixture reported on modern tonnage sees levels tracking the decline observed in the West.    The short- to mid-term period space has remained quiet with limited transactions seen since August. Further delays to two projects that had been expected to deliver first cargoes to long-term off-takers by the start of 2025 has not helped to alleviate any of this pressure. In addition to independent Owners, there remain a good number of sub-let tonnage over the next 12 to 24 months before the market is expected to tighten through 2027 and beyond.

Last week saw TD20 inexplicably drop (like a stone) from about WS 100 down to WS 82.5 before immediately rebounding. There's been very little pause for breath this week with the Atlantic positively poised due to a number of West Africa cargoes, that had hitherto been trying to work quietly, being smoked into the open market.  The East Suezmax market remains positive with no evident downside with MEG/East likely to trade WS 115-120.

VLCC owners have done well to hold their ground in spite of charterers trying to work under the radar. Even when proceedings were a bit slow while waiting for November dates, rates did not slip too much, and the owning community continued to resist. At the time of writing rates are holding firm around WS 55 for MEG/Far East with upward pressure evident and a number of cargoes in play. Activity in the Atlantic has also picked up today including a Petrobras export quote and also with oil prices falling USG bbls are starting to come to the forefront now, so the stage could be set for rates to firm further.

This week in the Atlantic, the market saw limited activity, with only slight improvements as cargoes cleared some tonnage. Tonnage count remains lengthy. TA on a Supra is around USD 10,000 per day. With fresh enquiries, USG was holding up. FH is well paying, Supramaxes earned around USD 23,000 per day. Fresh enquiries also coming up on the West Africa mineral cargoes which are being covered at last done levels. Meantime on the Pacific side, increased demand for Australian and North Pacific grains suggests stronger sentiment for the coming weeks. The market in MEG-WC India remains weak at the moment due to oversupply of tonnage and lack of cargo volumes. With market firm in Pacific, owners are not keen to reposition in WC India. Overall, both Atlantic and Pacific markets saw mixed activity with positive prospects ahead.

This week the Panamax market saw a continued decline in rates driven by weak fundamentals and oversupply in both the Atlantic and Pacific regions. In the Atlantic, early vessels faced difficulty securing employment, leading to aggressive discounts amid scarce cargo volumes, especially in the USEC and USG. Although US grain exports offered some support, volumes were insufficient to balance the oversupply of tonnage, particularly in the South Atlantic. In Asia, despite the end of recent holidays, demand from key routes like NoPac and Australia remained weak, further depressing rates. Seasonal factors, such as Indian coal imports and Brazilian corn exports, underperformed, and worsening macroeconomic conditions in Europe and the US added to the negative sentiment. A potential rebound hinges on increased coal demand for winter, but overall market sentiment remains pessimistic as charterers delay fixing in hopes of securing lower rates.

On the West Australia front, we see enquiries from miners, some operators, and a notable number of tenders primarily for very end October to early November dates. Volumes out of East Australia started off flat beginning of the week but picked up as we approach mid-week. Relatively little activity on other areas in the Pacific. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see operators enquiring for various November dates. Far East spot tonnage is abundant with a notable number of prompt vessels deciding to ballast. Ballasting tonnage is heavy for November. On C5, the week started off with fixtures concluding at low-mid USD 10 pmt levels but retreated to low-mid USD 9 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, fixtures concluded at mid to high USD 24 pmt levels for end November dates and low USD 24 pmt levels for early-mid November dates.

While the story on modern tanker tonnage remains steady, older units are once again in the spotlight as geopolitical turmoil continues to pose questions to investors. There is a real sense of unpredictability over escalating conflict in the Middle East, and the US elections getting ever closer. Record prices on modern MRs are being crystalised in the form of scrubber fitted MARITIME VERITY/INSPIRATION (49K DWT GSI 2021), where not long ago, NB prices were in line with these levels now seen on almost 4 year old ships.    A quieter week in terms of reported transactions in the usually busy dry sector has been interestingly coupled with what has felt like an avalanche of new candidates on the market. The 10-15 y.o. Capesize sector seems particularly active, where confidence in the iron ore demand story is waning in the wake of a strong period for owners and charterers. Values and rates on the smaller sizes however, seem fairly consistent for the time being, despite a recent slight softening on the increasingly liquid Ultramax market where OCEAN AMBITIOUS (63K DWT China Shipbuilding 2016) was sold for USD 25.5M.

EAST The East market remains rather quiet, but it has still been the most active trade area this week. We have seen one Indian PSU done for end Oct dates at mid 60s and two Australian cargoes done around the 70 dollar mark. There's a rumor of another Indian PSU cargo for October, but beyond that the market seems to be holding off as we await November acceptances.  WEST Sentiment in the Western freight market has seemingly softened slightly after a busy week of fixtures. In total we have seen 18 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC for November dates - 10 first decade and 8 second decade. One vessel still remain available for the first decade (prompt open), while 7-8 ships are ready for the second decade. We have yet to see any fixtures in last decade November, but we should expect some activity very soon. Last done fixture concluded at low 120s H/C range.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Cash premium for evenly split for Nov liftings stand firm, with deal being concluded at CP plus low mid 20s for trader’s short into India. Even without new tenders from Indian importers, a couple of traders are also seeking similar grade for SEA or FAR EAST delivery.   By the time of writing, Nov C3 CP was traded at $637 and Nov C3/C4 was traded at $10.   FAR EAST During mid-week, one 23/0 parcel for 2h Nov delivery was traded at Nov FEI plus $6 in the window. Outside window, similar cargo was traded at $5.5 reportedly. A couple of 46/0 parcels for Nov delivery was traded at Nov FEI plus mid-high single digit into N.China.   Buying sentiment remained low after the China Golden holidays. Despite on the China fiscal stimulus, downstream product ie. PP lagged the soaring FEI, and petchem players have refrained buying interest, or even considered on maintenance. This week only one SChina PDH user issued tender and awarded for one Nov delivered 46/0 based SChina at the combination of 50% CP plus 50s and 50% FEI plus mid high single digit.   Indonesia PERTAMINA issued another term buy tender for monthly 2/2 from Jan to Dec delivery. Earlier they are reported to secure some volumes for next year at CP plus less than $30.  And lately they were reported to procure two evenly grade cargos for Nov delivery at Nov CP plus 50s. Similarly, Hyosung Vina was reported to buy 23kt butane for Nov delivery instead of 11/11 at Nov CP plus 60s.

The Supramax was mixed. In the Atlantic, activity remained positional, with differing views on whether the US Gulf had reached its bottom. However, the USG seems to be picking up slowly. The Mediterranean-Continent region saw some activity, but fresh inquiries were limited, while the South Atlantic stayed balanced but quiet. In Asia, sentiment was more positive, though demand remained weak however there has been a supply of prompt tonnage. Overall, the market didn’t see much change. The Handysize was similarly quiet, with limited activity in the Atlantic. Some fresh demand surfaced in the South Atlantic, while the US Gulf held steady. The Pacific was more active, with tight tonnage availability supporting decent rates.

Bearing in mind the time of year (on the cusp of Winter Market etc) combined with escalations in the Middle East, we remain optimistic, however after a 30 percent spike in the Atlantic last week, profit taking has dragged rates back to the WS 80's for TD20.

Freight levels have moved up from last week but earnings are still lagging behind the Mediterranean and US markets. Natural dates are now into the 15-20 window.  We are still seeing prompter vessels ballasting out of the area which is reducing the front end of the position list but so far not enough to affect levels unduly.  The window for some key ports in the Mediterranean is now fixing well-ahead but with Libyan exports returning to the market and with tonnage in the region shortened on the front end, Owner’s sentiment is positive as they push for higher returns on earlier cargoes. Suezmax are watching on closely for any opportunity with the two segments working in tandem for some routes.

On the West Australia front, we see enquiries from miners, operators, and tender primarily for last October dates and some operators enquiring for forward November dates. Volumes out of East Australia remained flat from last week and picked up slightly as we approach mid-week for late October to early November dates. Some activity on the ex Indonesia and North Pacific front for late October dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China, a majority of operators were seeking for November dates while some still enquiring for late October dates. Far East spot tonnage is abundant with availability of prompt and early vessels. Ballasting tonnage is thinning for late October and heavily weighed on first half of November. On C5, the week started with fixtures concluding at mid-high USD 10 pmt levels and retreated to low USD 10 pmt levels and subsequently to mid-high USD 9 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see fixtures concluding at low USD 26 pmt levels for early November and sub USD 26 pmt levels for end November.

The everyday dilemma of “Middle Eastern headlines” moving like a pendulum between “ceasefire talks” and “further escalation in attacks” continue to distract players from reality. Although uncertainty remains and potential swings in war risk insurance premiums is an incalculable risk, short term fundamentals remain strong regardless. MEG rates have steadily ticked up in the week gone by, culminating with a WS 60 paid yesterday for a Taiwan bound cargo. The position list remains balanced and strong Atlantic activity has enticed tonnage away from the area. However, “published” enquiries are few and far in between at the writing moment playing into a “after a storm comes calm” narrative, which could encourage some profit taking on the owner’s part. Sentiment tends to trump all, but it is a fine balance. All it takes is 2-3 cargoes on top of each other in the same loading window and the owning community will dictate the narrative again.

The LNG Shipping market has come to life this week led by a burst of predominantly Atlantic Basin activity which saw at least seven fresh requirements emerge in the past seven days.  A welcome sight for those with length although the wide window of uncovered dates spanning late October to end November dampens hopes of any immediate recovery in charter rates.  Nevertheless, a healthy amount of liquidity ensures good competition, and we see several other cargoes which should be covered in the coming days, with Charterers keen to lock in freight for laycans over 45 days ahead. A few requirements have also played out in the Pacific across November dates with Tri-Fuels and Steamers the preferred taste of Charterers. Most modern ships are preparing to ballast back to the Atlantic Basin to compete for longer utilization through Winter.  The short and mid-term space remains muted with limited interest to bring in additional vessels on the prompt as the market awaits to see whether any semblance of the “Winter” we have come to take for granted hits during Q4-24/Q1-25.

The Panamax market saw modest gains this week, with fronthaul rates in the Atlantic improving due to strong activity from the US East Coast and Gulf regions, particularly for coal and grain exports. Asia showed steady demand growth, especially from Southeast Asia, despite the impact of Chinese holidays. However, challenges persist, including weaker Brazilian soy and maize exports, low industrial demand in Europe, and only modest increases in India’s coal imports and US grain exports.

With much of Asia taking holiday this week, one would have predicted a more subdued few days, however the increasingly volatile geopolitical landscape jolted the tanker market into life. The questions on the longevity of record asset prices have been put to one side, at least for now, as spot rates and tanker stocks both received sizeable boosts this week. Sentiment had been, that price ideas on second hand tanker tonnage would begin to soften, however owners and investors alike will be closely monitoring the earnings market as the situation in the Middle East unfolds. Appetite for older MRs remains firm as MR HAFNIA ANDROMEDA (50K DWT GSI 2011) was sold for USD 31M.   A combination of extreme weather and Golden Week in China has not disrupted the liquidity in the bulk market, as demand for units remains strong. What continues to challenge investors though, is the disconnect between asset values and charter rates. Granted, there is cause for optimism on news of the incoming China stimulus, but overall demand and consumer confidence is still an issue in this major global market driver. Ultramax demand is high, and liquidity appears to be increasing, particularly on more modern units where BEECHGATE (63K DWT IWAGI ZOSWEN 2019) was sold at USD 35.6M.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco raised up Oct CP by $20 for C3 at $625 and by $25 for C4 at $620, reflecting the strong demand in Oct butane especially from India. Entering Nov, the buying inquiries for Nov lifting slowed down but still assessed at teens premium to Nov CP.    Following the Middle East conflicts, Nov CP traded firmer alongside the rising crude. By the time of writing, Nov CP was traded at $630 and Nov C3/C4 at $8.   FAR EAST Cash differentials for Nov inched higher with active trader’s bids in window. 23/0 parcels for 1h Nov delivery and 2h Nov delivery was bid at Oct FEI plus $6/6ish, and similar cargo for 1h Dec delivery was traded at Nov FEI plus $1.88 which equates to Dec FEI plus hi single digit.   During the Golden week holiday, Inquiries from China are muted. However, the volatile swap price, especially the soaring FEI flat price, up by roughly $20 , might raise concerns on motivated rate cuts for PDHs and some resales. At the time of writing, Nov FEI was traded at $670 and offers for full propane cargo basis Echina were reported at the premium of teens level but barely heard bid range.    Other than propane, Indonesia PERTAMINA reissued their buy tenders for two 2/2 cargos delivered during mid and late Nov respectively, seeking better offers. Hyosung Vena also issued buy tender for 11/11 split CIF in Nov delivery.

EAST Although most attention has been on the Western market this week, there has still been some things going on in MEG with a few spot fixtures done. As US Gulf rates have surged, we have seen corresponding adjustments in the East, with the BLPG1 index rising by over $30 since Monday. With that said we could expect second half October to fully start moving as charterers could be tempted to secure shipping this period very soon. Some owners are now aiming 80 dollars for freight.  WEST Freight has jumped significantly this week with almost 40 dollars on the BLPG3 index route. Close to 20 spot fixtures have been done this week and we now find last done in the mid 120s H/C. First half November ex USG is nearly sold out, with only a few open positions remaining, and a couple players reportedly still searching for freight. The vessel supply in 2H is looking more balanced. At the time of writing, we count 17 spot fixtures ex USG/USEC for November dates. There still remain one prompt open ship.

A new month in a new quarter but a continuation of recent themes in LNG shipping this October 2024 as weak fundamentals weigh heavily on short to medium term sentiment. There remains a degree of activity in both basins on the spot side although availability lists have continued to grow more quickly than ships have found spot employment. The spot-fixing window is becoming more prompt, typical of a looser freight environment. Whilst a handful of prompt fixtures have been seen, this is more likely an indicator of Charterers’ confidence in vessel supply, rather than an uptick in demand.  In the Atlantic, several prompter positions have been cleared out with charter rates largely stable. However, interest in multi-month coverage into Q1-25 has evaporated, with the East/West Arb firmly shut since traders returned from Gastech. There is a long list of modern tonnage available for early November liftings against next to no firm enquiry at present.  The oversupply on the prompt is more apparent in the East where several vessels are redelivering from period charters. Spot rates have shown some decline in response to renewed activity for end October dates. Visibility on November positions is more limited although with several cargoes seemingly heading inter-basin despite the closed Arb, the list is likely to be repopulated in due course.  The biggest, in all senses, news in the newbuilding space this week is MOL’s order at Hanwha Ocean for an FSRU to be delivered by October 2027. The unit, which will be utilized in Singapore, was reportedly contracted for $413.7mn and will feature high spec low-emissions and fuel-efficiency elements.

North Sea market remains an area of limited activity with the natural working window pushing into the 2nd decade of October. With the prospect of production in Libya due to resume and a volatile US market, available vessels for North Sea business will reduce as vessels ballast out of the region for better returns. A thinning position list means freight levels will come under pressure and with some activity and vessels heading out there is potential for further rises.  Owners have drawn a line in the sand of the Mediterranean in anticipation of a return of Libyan production. The tonnage list is still balanced with stable activity in the region, but with the surging USG market already attracting ballasters from West Mediterranean, if supply was to surge, then we might suddenly find ourselves in a tighter position, especially for uncompromised vessels.

With events in the Middle East providing enormous geopolitical uncertainty, the question, as always, is where are rates heading? Coinciding with recent exchanges in the Middle East, the US Gulf appears to have already reacted with other regions surely to follow the trend.  With latent volatility being a prized market ingredient, owners are in prime position to take advantage.

Despite fundamentals suggesting otherwise V-rates were under pressure for the most part in the week gone by. However, recent geopolitical events have changed focus, and still underpinned by a balanced supply/demand picture, will add upward pressure. The front end of the MEG position list of unemployed modern ships free of cargo has shrunk, and tonnage is controlled on fewer hands than seen for some time. Preempting a tightening market, most of the Chinese fleet has been tied up to local Chinese charterers. Oil prices have surged and corresponding bunker prices with it, and owners will seek to be compensated on top of any risk premiums. Many market players have adopted a “wait and see” attitude, but as and when proceedings kick off again in earnest rates could surge exponentially.

On the West Australia front, we see enquiries from miners, operators, and some tenders primarily for mid to late October dates. Volumes out of East Australia have dropped compared to last week with few of the limited orders seen seeking for prompt dates. On the Pacific and west coast South America front, some enquiries were present for mid October and late October dates, respectively. On C3 ex Brazil to China, operators were seeking for late October to early November dates. Far East spot tonnage is moderate with some availability of prompt vessels. Ballasting tonnage is reasonably heavy for late October. On C5, fixtures concluded at mid USD 11 pmt levels as the week started and retreated to low USD 11 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see fixtures concluding at high USD 26 pmt levels for end October dates and low/mid USD 27 pmt levels for early October dates.

This week in the Panamax market, despite strong fundamentals such as shipment volume growth outpacing supply growth, the market continues to face a notable downtrend, contrary to typical seasonal patterns. The weakness is largely attributed to the absence of a cyclical recovery in industrial demand from the US and Europe, which has prevented any substantial uptick in rates. Earlier hopes for a recovery in Q3 have now shifted to the beginning of 2025, further dampening sentiment. Activity in the North Atlantic has been limited, with rates softening as vessel availability increases. Meanwhile, holidays in Asia have also contributed to the overall slowdown in trading, keeping the market under pressure. Even with some demand emerging from Australia, rates have continued to ease, and bearish sentiment remains the dominant theme.

The Supramax market continued to remain sluggish in the Atlantic, with limited new inquiries, especially from the US Gulf and South America. Although mineral cargoes offered some support, the volume of sugar and grains remain low, and there is a clear oversupply of vessels. In contrast, the Pacific market is more stable, fueled by stronger demand from India. Activity in the Pacific Handy market was minimal, however seeing increased demand in the Atlantic. The South Atlantic and US Gulf markets faced pressure from growing tonnage lists and limited inquiries. In the Pacific, the market is slow in view of the holidays in China. Overall, while some regions experienced slight improvements, both segments began the week in a cautious and largely positional manner.

In the standout transaction of the week, Evalend took 2x Hengli scrubber fitted VLCC resales due for delivery in 2026 for USD 127M each. While modern ship values are holding fairly steady, there is much debate on the fate of older units and whether buyers are still there to pay yesterday’s prices.  That said, undercutting the last done on c.10-year-old tanker could provide owners with a straightforward way to take some money off the table at extremely healthy historical levels. This is just what Advantage tankers did, with VLCC ADVANTAGE VIRTUE (296K DWT BOHAI 2009) being sold to Chinese buyers at USD 51M.   There are a number of stories to contend with on dry bulk this week. Extreme weather has spurred the capesize market onward, where a single day jump of 8% was registered on Thursday this week. This is while supramax values hinted that there may be an imminent correction. ZEN-NOH GRAIN PEGASUS (55K DWT OSHIMA 2010) sold for USD 15M, this is at a sizeable discount to last done similar VISAYA (56K DWT MITSUI 2010) at USD 16.8M. Levels that will excite buyers in what is a very liquid sector. Elsewhere, Newcastlemax MINERAL CLOUDBREAK (205K DWT HHIC-Phil 2012) was sold to Chinese buyers for USD 38.5M.

text: MEG Despite the recent decline in crude oil price, Oct CP still maintained the strength and traded at $618 for C3 and $616 for C4, by the time of writing. This is in line with the 1st round recommendation which submitted mid-week at $610-625 for C3 and $620-635 for C4 reportedly. In window one trader was bidding evenly split cargo for any Oct lifting at $615 for C3 and $645 for C4.  FAR EAST Cash premium slightly strengthened compared to last week, with 23/0 parcel for 2h Oct delivery basis Far East traded at Oct FEI plus low mid single digit level. And a couple of 46/0 parcels for 2h Nov delivery basis Ningbo was offered at Nov FEI plus $14.    Importers refrained their buy interests, especially seeing swap value surging up on Thurs due to ET planned maintenance and potential impact under new hurricane. Some resales for Oct delivery were heard from NChina players but volumes have been well absorbed and barely see the premium declined much. This being said, we yet to see any new major shutdowns apart from scheduled maintenances.  One SChina PDH player just issued spot tender to procure propane for Nov delivery, and meanwhile they’ve awarded their term tender for monthly 46/0 at odd and even month to two different sellers. FPC was also reported to secure a 23kt propane for 2h Oct delivery into Mailiao at Oct MOPJ minus small digit via tender, which equates to Oct FI flat at the time of conclusion. HTC also issued tender to purchase a 23/0 parcel for late Nov delivery.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The combination of domestic NGL production, (effectively) capped exports and corresponding inventory levels has had an impact on MB propane prices, which are off by more than 6cpg (or ~$33/mt) since the beginning of September.    However, the relationship to crude oil seems to show that propane has consistently aligned itself less on the fundamentals and more alongside WTI, the ratio of which continues to be maintained in the 41-43% range.  Meanwhile, as to the inventories, the market was taken aback yesterday as the EIA reported a 1.5mmbbl decline in stocks to an overall total of 97.60mmbbls, or 96% of last year, and 118% of two years ago.  The market had mostly been anticipating a small build more in line with the 5-yr historical build rate of ~475,000bbls.  Terminal fee offers continue to be robust, though buy side interest has rarely peaked above what seems to be the psychologically important 30ct/gal threshold.  NWE An array of competing factors makes it difficult to summarize the current NWE propane market or make clear of what’s to come.   As we approach the tail end of what looks to be a record setting month for imports into the region (680,000mt) the economic incentive to crack propane over naphtha sits at its lowest of the year. The propane/naphtha spread ended Tuesday for September at -$53/mt, all while the North Sea processing facilities - both on and offshore - grapples with unplanned delays as they come out of a period of maintenance.   Due to the delays in the North Sea upstart, it is expected that October will mandate yet another month of significant delivers from the US.

EAST US activity picked up earlier this week, seeing freight already trading at more than 2x earnings there vs MEG, this should eventually pull up East freight. We think we are hovering around bottom in the MEG and we are seeing potential upside around the corner. Currently we have seen 11 spot fixtures ex MEG (Incl 3x Yanbu) - four of these 11 deals are from Indian PSUs. Next deals should be around mid / second half October.  WEST The Western market has been quite active this week, counting more than a dozen spot fixtures which brings the total to 23 spot deals for October dates ex USG/USEC. Freight rates have seemingly found a floor with several deals done in the mid-80s Houston-Chiba range, and the latest edging closer to 90 dollars. November fixing is also underway with one deal done so far and others beginning to show interest.

On the West Australia front, we see a healthy level of enquiries from miners, operators, and some tenders alike largely for early/mid October dates. Volumes out of East Australia continued to hold steady this week with orders for mid October dates as well. On the Pacific and west coast South America front, enquiries were for early October and late October/early November dates respectively. On C3 ex Brazil to China, enquiries were primarily for first half of October second half of October dates with some operators starting to seek for early November. Far East spot tonnage is moderate. Ballasting tonnage is tight for first half of October and heavily weighs on second half of October. On C5, fixtures concluded at mid/high USD 11 pmt levels at the start of the week and retreated slightly to mid USD 11 pmt levels by mid-week.   On C3, we see offer indications in the mid USD 28 to USD 29 levels for second half October and bid ideas in the low/mid USD 27 levels for late October to early November.

This week in the Panamax market saw mixed activity across regions. The Atlantic remained subdued, with limited fresh demand and a widening bid/offer spread, particularly in the ECSA where October liftings started to show divergence. The North Atlantic showed a slight uptick in tonnage availability against a quieter US grain market, keeping rates buoyant but lacking significant upward momentum. USEC coal cargoes provided minimal support, while the Baltic and Black Sea regions remained largely inactive. In contrast, Asia displayed more strength, with firmer rates across trades, especially from Australia, where some exceptionally strong rates were agreed, reinforcing a positive sentiment for the region. Despite these developments, the overall market remained cautious, with no major rallies expected, although steady support in both regions continued.

NORTH SEA North Sea natural window has moved into October with the first 5 days already looking relatively well covered.  A combination of own program scheduling and stems being worked into Suez and VLCC has limited the availability of market cargoes. Rates continue at the similar levels that they have been for a few weeks now and with both Mediterranean and US markets subdued there isn’t any area giving support West of Suez.  MEDITERRANEAN Ceyhan and CPC continue to push through October fixing with activity out of Sidi Kerir also, although some recent cargoes there have been scooped up by Suezmax. CPC is the only area that owners can attempt to hold with delays in the Straits working in their favor. Libya is still deficient and tonnage is there to work in the region leaving sentiment somewhat lacking in positivity and hopeful of a North Africa comeback.

The global Suezmax market can be divided into areas of stability, such as the Middle East Gulf and US Gulf, and areas of weakness, such as West Africa and the Black Sea.   On closer inspection, the US Gulf could have indeed added some weight this week with some cargoes tight on tonnage and light on offers, therefore the question has to be asked, are owners analyzing lists or going with the flow? USG/UKCM trades WS 65 levels for now with no real support from other segments.  TD20 has been very quiet this week and will require sustained enquiry in order not to fall beneath WS 77.5 whilst the Black Sea is an Enigma. Northbound Turkish Straits delays have increased but rates have conversely fallen down to WS 85 for TD20.

The Supramax market remained subdued in the Atlantic, with minimal fresh inquiries, particularly from the US Gulf and South America, though coal cargoes provided some support. The Pacific market showed improvement, driven by stronger demand from Indonesia and India. The Handysize experienced mixed activity, with stronger demand in the Continent and Mediterranean. The South Atlantic and US Gulf markets remained under pressure due to growing tonnage lists and limited inquiries. The Pacific market saw a quieter start, impacted by holidays in Japan. Overall, while some regions saw marginal improvements, both segments faced a largely positional and cautious start to the week.

After days of upward rate trajectory, the sentiment in the VLCC market took a turn for the worse yesterday. This time last week MEG/East rates were hovering around the WS 55 mark, but a tight front end position list, made shorter by bad weather and delays in the East, left charterers scramble for tonnage as the early October program finally came into play. Thereafter rates ticked steadily up for every successive fixture. However, despite reports yesterday morning of a strong WS 62 having been paid MEG/Taiwan, a sole early second decade cargo attracted a multitude of punters and the first counter at WS 57.5 were taken out without much of a fight. They say you do not panic if you are the first one out the door, and not long after a flat WS 57 was done for a shorter voyage, unimpressed by a report of a WS 65 having been done earlier for a similar voyage. And with that we’re likely “back to start”, and as in the game of Monopoly not collecting.   The last three peaks in the MEG have been at about the same level of earnings. Something to watch going forward.

As players in the shipping industry resume their normal work pace following Gastech, the LNG shipping market continues to exhibit subdued activity, mirroring the trends of previous weeks. There are few transactions and ample vessel availability in both basins, alongside limited shipping demand. In the Atlantic, freight rates have remained flat, with no significant fluctuations observed and while several fixtures were reported last week, the arbitrage remains volatile. In contrast, the market East of Suez has experienced a more challenging week; activity has slowed due to a lack of firm requirements and owners competing for the various FOB cargo tenders, and so rates have softened.  The multi-month term charter market has also remained relatively stable for another week, although there is a noticeable softening in sentiment primarily due to the increasing likelihood of a fairly flat winter. While several candidate vessels are available, charterers aren’t showing much interest at this stage.  On the newbuilding front, Peninsula has signed an agreement with Hyundai Mipo to construct a new LNG bunkering vessel with a capacity of 18,000m3, expected to be delivered in 2027. Conversely, there have been no new orders for conventional LNGCs this week, despite indications of softening prices in the newbuilding market.

Despite the buoyant levels seen in transactions this week, there is an emerging sense of caution among second hand participants in the tanker market. Rates have been lacklustre in recent weeks, but given the winter markets are just around the corner, perhaps this caution will be short lived. In the J19 market, TC rates dipping below $20K/Day have done little to discourage investors. Woojin bought HORIN TRADER (19K DWT USUKI 2015) at USD 32.5M, a premium to last done 1 year younger and scrubber fitted TRF J19s which sold at the same price.  CHEM STREAM (19K DWT SHITANOE SHIPBUILDING 2010) also sold at a firm USD 25.3M to Chinese buyers, showing the unrelenting appetite of Far Eastern buyers for this vessel type. VLCC SAKE (300K DWT IHI KURE 2005) selling at USD 40M will likely entice more owners of older tankers to consider exiting those positions, however it is worth adding that VLCCs have been of more interest to buyers over suez-afra sizes.   While modern bulkers remain atop the shopping lists of most owners, older ships are cause for discussion among brokers and investors. A correction in value in the panamax/kamsarmax sector is potentially acting as a cautionary tale for those thinking these record asset values are here to stay. Tellingly, several Japanese owned Kansarmaxes in the 10 yr bracket have been withdrawn for sale as offers received were deemed too low. Kamsarmax sisters AM QUEBEC/HAMBURG (81K DWT NEW TIMES 2013) were bought by Chinese buyers at USD 18M each, a level that will correct similarly aged units by at least 10%. It is as yet unseen whether similar corrections will take place in other sub sectors, with most sellers not willing to be the first to reduce price ideas. What is sure though, is that asset players will be watching this sector very closely.

EAST The week began with China, Japan, and Korea off due to public holidays, and so far we have only seen two spot fixtures being reported - both Indian. Freight rates have dropped significantly recently and September laycans should mostly be concluded by now. Currently we have seen 4 spot fixtures for Oct dates with last done at mid 30s RT/C.  WEST A handful of vessels have been placed on subs so far this week, bringing the current spot fixture count for October dates ex USG/USEC to 11. The number of spot cargoes in the market remains very low compared to the available vessels and western freight is currently in free fall with last done at low 70s H/C.

text: MEG Spot differentials for Oct evenly split fobs remained strong, due to the Indian continued robust demand for Q4 delivery. Such fob was assessed at Cp plus 20s but offers barely seen. We’ve hearing much higher number shown into Indian PSU tenders but yet to be awarded.   By the time of writing, Oct C3 Cp was traded at $611 and C4 at $7-9 higher.   FAR EAST A handful of deals concluded in window this week, mainly trader shorts covered. Premium for 23kt C3 for 2h Oct delivery into far east softened, traded from FEI plus $5 earlier and declined to 3ish. 46kt lot for 2h Oct delivery basis Yantai was offered at Oct FEI plus $10 while similar parcel for 1H Nov delivery was bid at Nov FEI plus $6.5.   Comparatively, propane demand from end user outside window is less active, mainly resulted by the squeezed margins. FIC awarded their buy tender for 4/0 delivered during 1-20 Oct basis Ningbo at Oct FEI plus high single. However Tianjin Bohai was said to cancel their buy tender for 4/0 2h Oct delivery as offer received at similar high single range.   Well butane is another story. Taiwan CPC and SChina Sinobenny both issued buy tender for late Oct to early Nov delivery evenly split cargo respectively, which reported concluded at Cp plus $60s but details are sketchy.   Other than spot inquiries, Huayi issued term buy tender to secure monthly 46kt C3 into Qinzhou in 2025. Pertamina called 2025 term buy tender for 2/2 split volumes. Equinor also tendered to buy 2/2 into Port Klang for 1H 2025 delivery.

The October fixing window tends to act as a bellwether for the ensuing Winter market, and whilst it's too early to talk fireworks today, there are very few areas of weakness and definitely areas that are beginning to exhibit all the hallmarks of an exciting market.  The US Gulf remains the trend setter for all markets, and whilst Aframaxes remain flat, there are signs of life on Suezmax with rates gently firming and on the cusp of hitting 145kt x WS 70 (although at the time of going to press last done trades WS 67.5.)  In the East, there's a rumor of 130kt x WS 115 on subjects for MEG/East which suggests that owners have the bit between their teeth.

This week’s Panamax market began with slow activity, showing minimal movement and limited visibility across most routes. In Asia, regional holidays led to a quieter market with reduced activity, and rates continued to erode as nearby tonnage chased lower offers to secure deals. Meanwhile, the Atlantic basin, particularly in the North, saw some positive momentum, with rates gaining support. Overall, the market started the week sluggishly, with little progress in bids and offers, as both sides hesitated to commit, influenced by mixed views on market value and the impact of holidays in both Asia and the Middle East.

The rates have continued to creep up and owners are feeling they are now in a position to try and push this further. Holidays in the Far East combined with waiting for the new dates have kept proceedings slow paced, but the hang over of tonnage from the previous September would seem to be lesser than it has been in the past few months. New stem dates have been rolled out and we will see charterers coming to the market today onwards albeit under the radar in order to try and keep a lid on the sentiment. One early October cargo has attracted 7 offers and charterers are taking their time to cover.   In the West, short voyages are attractive so much so that they are being discounted just so owners have kept their ships in the West to try and make the most of Q4. Long East voyages are still attracting a premium. Petrobras are in the market which will be a good test of the levels.

As Gastech draws the attention of players in the LNG industry this week, the LNG shipping market remains in a fairly muted state. There have been relatively few firm requirements and there is an extensive availibity list across both basins. However, there have been sporadic signs of activity with several fixtures being reported last week and into this week, triggering a slight tick up in charter rates for larger tonnage in the Atlantic. Outside of the flutters of optimisation demand, a multi laycan requirement in the Atlantic will keep market players engaged this week. With the opening of the November fixing window and the prospect of cooler weather in the northern hemisphere on the horizon, both Owners and Charterers will be eagerly watching on for an indication of which direction charter rates will develop and whether we see an improved demand for winter shipping coverage typical for this time of year.  There have not been any LNGC newbuilding orders this week and prices remain stable. Separately, it is reported that Golar LNG has entered an EPC agreement with CIMC Raffles to convert Fuji LNG (148,000 cbm) into a MK II FLNG production unit with a liquefaction capacity of 3.5MTPA for delivery in Q4 2027 for approximately $2.2bn.

NORTH SEA Nothing much has changed in the North Sea as dates move forward with some prompt vessels still looking for employment. Relets continue to replenish the area as activity remains moderate. The tonnage list is on the shorter side with non-local/non-relet vessels continuing to look outside of the region for employment, the ballast to the USG still the preference despite softer trends in that sector.  MEDITERRANEAN The prolonged lack of activity from Libya seems to have capped owners’ bullish sentiment for the time being, with rates in the Mediterranean repeating as we move into early October fixing dates. Delays in the Straits and itineraries will define rates moving forward, but with vessels piling up for the next window we could possibly be looking at taking a step backwards.

Seeing more activity this week with healthy volume of cargo across basins. However, with ample vessels, we see cargo being covered basis last done levels. The usual South Africa/China route is being fixed at 18,000 + BB on an Ultramax. A trip from WC India to China is paying USD 11,000 levels on a Supra. The ECSA activity has picked up with quite a few cargoes popping up for direction Mediterranean, some fronthauls. ECSA fronthaul on an Ultra fixed at USD 15,000 + BB.  Period interest is healthy, and hearing Ultramax opening China fixed at USD 17,000 levels for 5/7 months. With Q4 and grain season around the corner, we will see more cargoes until end of this year.

On the West Australia front, we see enquiries from miners and operators for early October dates. Volumes out of East Australia have held up from last week with the presence of some tenders as well seeking from early October to mid/late October dates. On the Pacific and West coast South America front, enquiries were for late September to late October/early November dates respectively. On C3 ex Brazil to China, enquiries were primarily for first half of October dates with interest slowly building for second half of October dates. Far East spot tonnage is moderate for early October dates. Ballasting tonnage is dwindling for first half of October dates and tonnage weighs primarily on second half of October dates. On C5, fixtures concluded at mid/high USD 11 pmt levels at the start of the week and retreated to mid USD 11 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see offer ideas in the USD 27s pmt levels and bid ideas in the low to mid USD 26 pmt levels for October.

Ice 1B JAG LALIT (158K DWT Hyundai Samho HI 2005) is the first suezmax tanker to be sold since June 24 as it was transacted this week at USD 33M. Not only suezmax, but tanker sales in general have stuttered this year, with historical high pricing giving potential investors much to consider. This sale will catch the attention of those owners who are placing the increasing number of ageing tanker candidates in the market. MR tankers continue to provide consistent liquidity to the market, with this week TENACITY (50K DWT GSI 2014) selling in line with other market candidates at USD 40M to Greek buyers.   Dry liquidity is somewhat bolstered this week by a 7 ship en bloc transaction of the entire Dasin Holdings supramax fleet for USD 80M to Hai Tong of China. There continues to be a healthy amount of activity on second hand capesize units, as rates remain firm. ALPHA PRUDENCE (178K DWT SWS 2008) was bought for USD 24.75M, a slight increase on last done OCEAN COURTESY (178K DWT SWS 2008) which sold in July 24 for USD 24M.  Overall, attitude on dry remains bullish, with a rapidly ageing fleet, despite some reported economic uncertainty in China.

text: MEG FOB strength extended further this week, with IOC keep re-tendering buy tender for monthly evenly split cargo in Q4. Assessment for such ratio is at CP plus mid-teens to $20s but barely see offers. Thanks to the robust demand, Oct CP barely moved despite the crude loses. By the time of writing, Oct C3 CP was traded at $602 and C4 was assessed at $5 higher than C3.    FAR EAST With the APPEC conference ongoing, market players kicked off next year term negotiation, with the concerns over limited supply expansion against foreseeable demand increment. Petchem players addressed the worries on the resilient LPG feedstock price and olefins oversupply weighing on slow downstream consumptions, whilst traders are sensitive on next year petchem performance.  In terms of spot discussion, Oct FEI swap softened this week, alongside the crude losses and Oct FEI/CP narrowed down from $37 to $23. In the window we’ve seen bid for 2h Oct 23/0 basis Chiba at Oct FEI plus $5.5 whereas offer at $8.5. Outside window a flurry of buy tenders ongoing. Indonesia PERTAMINA tendered to buy 2/2 or 1/1 parcel for 6-25 Oct delivery. CPC also sought 1/1 for last decade Oct delivery via tender. Other than butane, one NChina PDH also issued buy tender to secure 46/0 for 2h Oct delivery and we’ve seen a couple inquire the same privately.
