comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Q3 2024 has seen the MB non-TET propane price decline by 20cpg, while correspondingly a 21% drop in crude oil has been recorded over the same period.  The ratio of propane to WTI has remained neatly in line and continues at around 42-44%.  It might have been assumed that MB finally reacted to the weight of the propane inventory levels, but the evidence shows that propane is walking in lockstep with WTI values.  As for the EIA report itself, as of 30 Aug a weekly increase of 1.1mmbbls was recorded, where the market was anticipating an approximate 1.5mmbbl rise, so slightly disappointing but not altogether unsettling.  This puts US propane stocks on track to conclude the summer build season at ~102mmbbls.  Production levels, say the EIA, are 2.702mmbbls/day, or just above both the quarterly and YTD annual averages.  Export volumes, meanwhile, are also robust, and at 1.833mmbbls/day beat the YTD annual average of 1.728mmbbls by 105,000bbls/day, but most are of the opinion that exports are unlikely to trend higher until some of the capacity improvements commence.  With regards the terminal fees, the market remains robust.  Hot, in fact, as firm offers of 30cpg presently exist.  Buy-side ideas, however, are in the ~27cpg range – and while this might be viewed as a standoff, there is legitimate logic and rationale from both sides of the spectrum.  Freight is slowly waning; the arb is up and there is little product to be had other than via trading houses.  From the buy side, however, 30 cents is a tough psychological barrier.   NWE September is set to be the busiest month this year for imports into Europe, due largely to scheduled annual maintenance on the North Sea’s largest LPG export terminal, Kaarstoe which has sidelined the facility for last 3.5 weeks. In Q2 of this year, the facility exported just shy of 70,000mt/month, thus requiring added imports from the US to make up for lost volume.   Elsewhere after multiple weeks of unmet offerings, a major petchem finally sold what’s thought to be the last of the September ToT cargoes, marking the conclusion of a very slow month in Window activity, and a turn in attention to a typically busier October.   At present, October Pro/Nap is marked at $59 and CIF ARA is quoted at $530, up along with the rest of the market since Tuesday’s slide, but off $18 from MTD average.

EAST Over halfway through the week, the East has so far failed to bring much excitement in the spot market. There are reportedly one or two Indian cargoes remaining on September dates – and statistically we could hope for one or two additional cargoes before we look to October. Even with an optimistic view on remaining volumes it looks like freight has more downside, and with the APPEC conference still in full swing in Singapore, it’s rather unlikely that activity will pick up just yet.   WEST A few of deals have been concluded in the West so far this week bringing the total to 7 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC for October dates – 3 first decade and 4 second decade. There are still 14 available ships before 15th October in the US Gulf. That said, shipping is currently looking a bit long for the time being with few available spot cargoes in the market. Freight rates are on its way down with last done deals at 105-108 H/C range.

This week the Panamax market saw modest gains in the Atlantic, particularly in fronthaul routes, though the North remained weak due to excess tonnage. In contrast, the Pacific showed positive sentiment, driven by firm demand in the region despite wide bid-offer spreads. The US Gulf saw steady cargo activity, but many owners are waiting for better rates. Although the coal market remains bearish, seasonal demand for grains and coal is expected to rise in Q4, which could provide some market support.

The Handysize and Supramax markets saw a mixed performance with limited fresh activity across regions. In the US Gulf, there were slight signs of improvement with a better cargo book, but the tonnage-to-cargo imbalance continued to pressure rates. The South Atlantic experienced a gentle decline due to minimal new inquiries. In Asia, the market remained largely flat, though some interest in nickel ore trades emerged, with a few fixtures reported. Rates in the Continent and Mediterranean held firm despite long tonnage lists and thin demand.

The LNG market remains flat, with few transactions as bearish fundamentals and minor index fluctuations continue to keep netbacks unattractive. Spot demand is generally limited to optimisations and cargo tenders, and the margins available for shipping are not very generous, especially with ample vessel supply. While a winter upturn is still expected, it’s unlikely to match the peaks of previous years. The approach of a major conference is often associated with a quieter spell in the spot market, and we will see whether the present lull persists through Gastech.  In contrast to the spot market, longer-term requirements are keeping owners occupied and it’s likely that discussions in Houston next week will see more enquiries emerge or firm up.   Six more QC-Max LNG carriers have been placed on order by QatarEnergy. And while prices remain stable, the heavy 2024 delivery schedule could face delays later in Q4.

The front end of the MEG menu has thinned substantially both in numbers and in who controls the tonnage. Arguably there are question marks as to the fixture count and remaining volumes for September, but with the October program just around the corner anyone exposed into the early part of “next” month should be careful to rest on the laurels. TD3C is likely now priced at minimum WS 55 and few will be surprised to see something north of WS 60 before the week is over. Falling oil prices will also whet the appetite for more spot purchasing from both the MEG and the Atlantic. The WTI-Dubai spread, adjusted for slight backwardation is back at levels where USG-East activity was much higher earlier in the year. Worse case sideways – upwards risk evident.

On the West Australia front, we see enquiries from miners and operators for late September to very early October dates. Volumes out of East Australia seen an uptick from last week with the presence of some tenders as well. On the Pacific and west coast South America front, enquiries were for mid to late September dates and October dates respectively. On C3 ex Brazil to China, very limited enquiries for late September dates with operators and some miners interested in first half of October dates. Far East spot tonnage is abundant albeit some impacted by Typhoon Bebinca. Ballasting tonnage is dwindling for second half of September and heavily weighted on first half of October. On C5, fixtures concluded at mid to high USD 11 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see bids in the mid USD 25 pmt levels for early October dates and fixtures concluding at high USD 27 pmt levels.

There's a feeling of renewed optimism in the wider Atlantic as relatively cheaper oil hits the market. This should kick start firmer freight rates due to the cheaper WTI pricing coinciding with October fixing dates, a month that has historically set the scene for the winter. In the here and now, TD20 remains fairly flat but we envisage the market staging a recovery in the next couple of weeks due the aforementioned fundamentals.  The East has flattered to deceive. After a couple of headline MEG/East rates last week, the region is very quiet with mainly Indian market cargoes providing the only above radar action. MEG/East will trade WS 105-110 and BOT/UKCM needs a test but probably trades WS 50's via Cape.

For the last few weeks, the North Sea market has remained stable at around the WS 115-120 level. Activity has been limited with a lot of stems covering either on Suezmax or own tonnage. US markets remain soft, but is anticipated to pick up towards the end of the month, and with Libya barrels starting to flow again and Mediterranean market firming, tonnage does have an alternative which could attract tonnage out of the area and start to affect North Sea rates if tonnage thins.  Mediterranean Aframax have seen rates rise from the bottom giving a sense of better days to come. It might take a while for things to kick on but the increase in barrels from a functioning Libya should at least bring some stability to the region. Window is edging towards mid-third decade and prompter vessels will be hoping for an influx from North Africa. CPC fixing is also there to progress with the added implications of increased delays at the Turkish Straits.

There is a ‘back to school’ feel in the market this week, with most players returning from their seasonal holidays. In the tanker space, MRs are continuing to hold value against last done deals in the market, with Scorpio selling the scrubber fitted sisterships STI SAN ANTONIO / TEXAS CITY (50K DWT SPP 2014) at an enbloc price of USD 85M. Levels that are becoming increasingly attractive for owners that so far have resisted the temptation of these historical highs. A sentiment particularly well illustrated by the increase in availability on older large tankers, with some owners looking to exit positions they likely fought aggressively for 18 months ago.    The dry space continues to dominate in terms of S&P activity, with the sector being the preferred avenue second only to newbuildings, for profit reinvestment for owners. While COSCO made the headlines revealing a 42-ship newbuilding order, there appears to be an increase in Japanese controlled bulkers, which will help set pricing benchmarks going forward for the rest of the year. Much of the liquidity remains in the older units, particularly this week on the capesize front. Surveys due AZURE OCEAN (180K DWT IMABARI 2007) was sold to Chinese buyers for USD 25M.

EAST Sentiment on freight has shifted from being on the rise two weeks ago to cooling off in the past week. This is now moving the fixing window closer in time and as such we have seen a vacuum in fixing activity over the course of the past 10 days or so. So far this week we have seen a couple spot fixtures for last decade Sep - both done around the 60 dollar mark.  WEST The western position list is still showing 5 open vessels in September but we could likely see some of them roll over into first decade October where the vessel supply is looking tight with only 5 available positions. In total we have only seen 4 spot fixtures so far for Oct dates ex USG/USEC. Using latest Baltic print, the West is trading at a premium of approx. 8 dollars before waiting in Panama.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Premium for Oct lifting evenly split cargos still stands firm at mid-teens level, with vigorous demand from India and Indonesia. IOC was reported award their buy tender for Oct and Nov lifting evenly split cargos at CP plus low-mid teens and continued to secure monthly one cargo for Q4 delivery. Meanwhile, BPCL also tendered to buy monthly 20kt heavy butane cargo and 45kt evenly split cargo for Q4 delivery.   At the time of writing, Oct C3 CP was traded at $607, lagging crude losses. Oct C3/C4 was at $5 but it’s expected to narrow down further. Oct/Nov CP was traded at flattish level.    FAR EAST Active bids in window this week, with 23/0 parcels for 1h Oct delivery traded at Oct FEI plus $5.5 and $6. Similar parcels for 2h Oct delivery was bid at plus $5 while offer at $7.5. 46/0 lot for 2h Oct delivery was bid at plus $2.18 basis Dongguan, SChina and plus $5.68 basia Tianjin, NChina.   Outside window a handful of 46/0 parcels were placed into China at Oct FEI plus mid-single digit basis Ningbo reportedly, majority for trader shorts. Despite the talk on rate cuts caused by squeezed margins, we are still seeing PDHs emerge to explore Oct spot or Q4 supply. One SChina PDH user re-issued buy tender for 23/0 for Sep to Oct delivery or 46/0 for mid/2h Oct delivery. Other than spot, another NChina PDH player have issued term procurement tender for 46/0 monthly delivery in 2025.   Apart from propane, butane demand was unexpectedly strong, given few demands on cracking. One Korean importer tendered to buy 11kt butane for 1h Oct delivery. One European trader also issued buy tender for 23kt butane in Oct delivery into EChina but canceled in the end. PERTAMINA also issued buy tender to secure two evenly split cargos for early and mid Oct delivery but was reported only award one parcel at Oct CP plus around hi 50s.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The month of August 2024 has seen very little in the way of propane pricing changes, as on Aug 1 non-TET c3 at Mont Belvieu was posted at 76.875cts/gal and on Aug 30 values were marked at 76.0625, a net decline of a little more than three-quarters of a cent.    However, a loss of over 2.5cpg has been seen in the first days of September, much of which was realized today after the EIA posted its inventory findings for the week ending 30 Aug.  And where the market was anticipating an approximate 1mmbbl build, the EIA data revealed a surprising 2.6mmbbl propane stock increase which brought overall US to 95.70mmbbls, or 99.7% of last year.  It is anticipated that the flat-price decline will continue to incentivize exports, which are still at (effectively) maximum levels.  Meanwhile, production of propane in the US remains robust, with a YTD average of 2.648mmbbls/day which compares to this week’s 2.689mmbbl/day production level.

Very limited activity in the North Sea with a lot of programming of oil company tonnage taking a lot of the stems for the first half of the month. Rates have been stable with soft undertones in the first half of the week and with surrounding markets both in the US and Mediterranean not providing support/alternatives, the market looks likely to remain where we are in the short term.  The situation in Libya has had its effect on the Mediterranean Aframax market and where owners have been left with few alternatives, X-Mediterranean rates have borne the brunt of the uncertainty. History has shown that an influx of cargoes should hit the market once the dust settles and with this, owners will look to put pressure on rates as the tonnage gets put to work.

Market has been quiet past week as cargo volumes were very limited. Towards the end of monsoon season, we will see more cargoes in the market in the Indian ocean region. There is a clear oversupply of tonnage across basins and cargoes are being covered well below last done levels. As for ECSA, couple’ fronthaul cargoes in the market. With a relatively slow start to the grain season, we see less cargoes coming out in the Mediterranean/Continent region as well. Meantime, there is healthy demand on the period side on the Supra/Ultra segment.

Is it the calm before the storm? You would like to think so and there are indeed reasons to be optimistic, but that's for the weeks ahead. Playing what's in front of us, there is a weaker feel in the Atlantic with a number of ships on the cusp of missing the natural fixing window, which is most noticeable in West Africa. Conversely, one region that feels a little undervalued is the US Gulf, which has fallen to 145kt x WS 60's for a TA run, suggesting owners haven't been monitoring the lists and if they had been, they might have held out for something closer to WS 70's.   WS 115 is last done Fujairah/Singapore which pegs a MEG/East run at WS 110.This jump is due to a tight list of FOC ships which are in the hands of just a few owners. We also have less ships being recycled onto the East list due to West/East arb' issues.  Momentum with owners in this region.

The calendar has turned the page to meteorological autumn and logic should dictate a firmer seasonal market, however, the current situation in the VLCC market can be summed up in one word: lethargic. Rates have stabilized in the low to mid WS 40’s for MEG/East runs, for now, but mostly down to the owning community having drawn a line in the sand. However, lack of perceived demand could support further downside risk. Activity has largely gone underground, but lack of reported details suggests no game changing fixtures have been concluded. In the Atlantic, the cargo flow is behind the curve, but tumbling oil prices will support the West/East arb. Quiet before the storm?

As anticipated, the LNG spot market started this week relatively sluggishly, with persistently low demand leading to flat levels. The availability of prompt tonnage remains extended, likely sufficient to cover any immediate shipping needs. While several spot requirements have emerged from ADP cargoes or FOB tenders, the number of developing requirements in both basins remains limited.  The pace of discussions on multi-month and short-term charters has also slowed. However, we anticipate movement as both charterers and owners work to bridge gaps in periods and rates. Some activity is evolving in the second-hand market for older steamers, and we anticipate there will a surge in this segment as more vessels come off long-term charters.   The LNG product market remains balanced, with production shortages offset by comfortable inventory levels in importing regions. Despite limited demand, spot cargo prices continue to fluctuate within double digits, potentially encouraging spot market activity and potentially more shipping activity in the near term.  Despite relatively strong newbuilding prices, shipyards have not seen many new transactions for some time now. A few long term tenders could, however, end up with new orders.

On the West Australia front, we see active participation from miners, operators and some tenders primarily for the second half of September dates. Volumes out of East Australia have decreased slightly compared to last for late September dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see limited enquiries for late September dates with most players interested in early October dates. On the West Africa front, activity level is relatively low. Far East spot tonnage is relatively abundant while ballasting tonnage is mainly for second half of September and early October. On C5, fixtures concluded at mid to high USD 11 pmt levels at start of the week but sold down to low USD 11 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see bid ideas at sub USD 27 pmt levels and offers in the USD 28 pmt levels for October dates.

This week in the Panamax market, there are signs of potential improvement with the grain season underway, leading to an increasing number of vessels heading to the US, which could serve as a bullish trigger. However, the BPI5TC index remains below the Handy7TC and BSI58 indices, indicating a slower market rebound. In the Atlantic, the North continues to suffer from an oversupply of tonnage and minimal fresh demand, particularly for transatlantic routes, while fronthaul routes from the US Gulf show better prospects for October dates. In South America, September volumes are under pressure, but the outlook for October remains uncertain. In Asia, while coal demand remains low and the Indian monsoon season is expected to last longer, mineral demand from Australia and Indonesia has slightly improved market sentiment. Despite this, charterers continue to hold the upper hand, with the overall market still weak due to tonnage oversupply and slow demand growth.

An unsurprisingly slow week in terms of SnP transactions as markets are slowly finding their post-holiday rhythm. Subdued summer freight markets are consolidating a relatively cautious sentiment with a number of players anticipating a possible value correction on the short term especially on older tonnage. A dynamic that would see owners exploring potential sales in hope to capture last done levels that remain historically attractive. A consensus that however remains far from negative with a widely shared positive long-term sentiment. On the Tanker front only one sale to report this week with the 20 year old Aframax “SILVERA” (Abt 115k dwt Hyundai 2004 ) being sold at Usd 27m. Levels that remain in line with recently concluded business.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco raised Sep C3 CP to $605, up by $15 and C4 CP to $595, up by $25. This is in line with the swap value, reflecting the tightness for Sep supply against strong demand for evenly split cargo from India and Indonesia. This being said, some end receivers are discontented about the high flat price during summer season. Cash premium for such 2/2 FOB Oct is offered at CP plus teens level. By the time of writing, Oct CP was assessed at $606 for C3, and C3/C4 traded at $10. Oct/Nov CP was traded at flat level.  FAR EAST Cash differentials softened on Oct delivered tons during the week. 23/0 for 1h Oct CFR FAR EAST was reported concluded at Oct FEI plus mid-single digit, and similar parcel for 2h Oct was offered at Oct FEI plus $5 vs bid at $3. Apart from propane, one 0/23 parcel for end Sep early Oct delivery was offered at Sep propane FEI minus $5. Outside window one 23/0 2h Oct delivery was traded at Sep FEI plus $2 reportedly.  Discussions for Oct trades into China slowed down also. A handful of 46/0 for 1h Oct delivery was traded at Oct FEI plus mid/high single basis North and East China. However, the surging propane costs and squeezed petchem margins refrained some players from buying. Several PDHs unexpectedly shut down due to glitch and we expect it extend the maintenance due to negative margin, while some others are considering cutting rates. Meanwhile, cash premium for special origin stems on Sep delivery still hovered at CP plus 40s basis Schina, which has driven some Nchina players to procure normal stems instead.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Volumes of LPG direct from the marine terminal owners remains limited, but this is not to imply that product is not available since offers for October are littered across the calendar.  Most talks for Oct are centered around the 21-23cpg range, depending on timing/location, etc.  Meanwhile, Nov talks are still thin but early days values are pegged right at about 20cpg.  Initial talks for Dec are in the upper teens, but nothing is yet known to have been accomplished.  With regards the US stock report of yesterday, the EIA revealed a 1.00mmbbl build to an overall total of 93.10mmbbls as of 23 Aug, or about 97.5% of last year.  The 5-yr historical average build for Week 34 was 2.8mmbbls, so from that angle the data was disappointing.  However,  a large number of market observers were calculating a build of a half-million barrels, so from perspective the data appeared to be more accurate than not.    In any case, on a Days of Supply basis, the EIA report a current level of 110.9 days, which compares to the 2024 YTD average of 73 days, the 2023 average of 85 days, the 2022 average of 61 days, and an average of 49 days in 2021.  In short, there is a sufficient volume of propane in tank, but further to the point, the current Quarterly average (for Q3 2024) is 107 days, which is the second-highest Quarterly average since 2020.    NWE LPG imports for august totaled 550,000mt, the majority of which has gone toward feeding petchem plants in the region. The strong imports are likely one of catalysts for the European propane market steep drop seen Wednesday- as large cargo values dropped to CIF ARA flat from +27 the day prior, following an unmet offer from a major regional petchem on Wednesday.    In the North Sea, Karsto’s gas processing will see output cut in half, starting today, before a full shutdown tomorrow (August 30th) for yearly maintenance that will extend until the 20th of September.   At time of writing, the August propane/ naphtha spread has come in from-100pmt to -50pmt, theoretically dissuading the further imports, but so far the LPG crackers have continued to operate at high rates.

EAST There have been a few cargos mentioned in the East so far this week and we only count one spot fixture this side of Suez. This deal was an Indian PSU cargo which means 6 out of the 14 spot fixtures for September dates ex MEG have been Indian. The East / West earning spread is at about five dollars West premium before calculating potential additional waiting times in Panama and it looks like freight is stabilizing currently in the East.   WEST A few vessels have been fixed out in the West this week. We now only find one vessel left able to work 1st and 2nd decade September dates. There still remains 5-6 vessels left in the last decade of September, but we could see some of these roll over into first decade Oct where we currently only find 4-5 open positions. There are a couple players out looking 1H Oct dates ex USG as we find Owners freight ideas above 120 H/C.

This week's Handy and Supramax markets presented a mixed view . The Supramax experienced positive momentum in the US Gulf, where increased activity led to slightly higher rates, although options were limited for vessels opening in the South Atlantic. In contrast, the Continent and Mediterranean regions faced softer sentiment due to ample available tonnage following the clearing of most August stemsThe Handy market was generally quiet, with limited activity and negative sentiment in the South Atlantic, but the US Gulf showed signs of improvement as fresh demand entered the market.

Following a long weekend, with London closed on Monday, the negative sentiment in the VLCC market has continued on from last week. MEG/east rates have dipped below the WS50 mark, and likely to be tested further. Charterers are by and large sitting on their hands and whether or not the 1st decade MEG September program is a wrap or not it nevertheless nourishes the perception that only crumbles remain. And with that the doom and gloom chatter increases in volume. The picture is not improved by Atlantic volumes being behind the curve. But something has got to give and if VLCC cargoes from the likes of Wafr and USG do not materialise then logic dictates that the Suezmax segment will benefit. As politicians like to say to managed expectations; it could get worse before it gets better.

Last week saw a good number of fixtures, although they were insufficient to support rates, which continue to be under pressure. This week commenced with a relatively quiet Monday due to the UK bank holiday. However, over the past few days, several spot enquiries emerged for both basins, with cargoes requiring ships for end September and October. There is an ample supply of ships available promptly and in the upcoming months, and we can anticipate fixtures going forward. Owners are generally holding out for longer-term charters of at least one year, rather than fixing only for the winter months, to avoid being idle during the “shoulder months” of March, April, and May.  Regarding multi-year charters, there are ongoing enquiries, of which owners would be eager to secure long-term charters for their modern and newbuilding vessels. Meanwhile, there are more steam turbine vessels being circulated for sale, coinciding with the end of their current long-term charters. There have been no newbuilding purchases this week, as prices have not softened despite having no orders of LNG vessels at the shipyards for some time now.

On the West Australia front, we see participation from miners and operators primarily for mid to second half of September dates.  Volumes out of East Australia have held up since last week with charterers enquiring for mid to late September dates.  On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see interest for second half of September onwards with several operators seeking for first half of October dates.  Far East spot tonnage is relatively abundant while ballasting tonnage is thinning for second half of September with limited vessels still able to meet first half of September dates.  On C5, we see fixtures concluding at low to mid USD 11 pmt levels.  On C3, we see fixtures concluding at low USD 27 pmt levels for late September.

This week in the Panamax market, the overall activity remained subdued, particularly following the UK bank holiday, which contributed to a slow and uneventful opening. In the Atlantic, rates continued to decline as a result of increasing tonnage and weak demand, especially with the ongoing absence of US grain and mineral shipments. The market in the Pacific also remained quiet, with little activity reported, as the start of the US grain season has yet to begin, although there is speculation that conditions may improve in September. Notably, the Kamsarmax index has dropped significantly below the BSI58 index, a trend which, since 2018, has typically been followed by a market rebound, suggesting potential recovery ahead.

Market remains stable rate wise with moderate activity pushing into the first decade. Tonnage remains balanced but with soft markets both in the Med and US and a relatively light North Sea program in the first decade, market looks like it will remain flat in the short term.  There is a softer feel in the Mediterranean Aframax market as rates slowly slip further and the lack of supply remains limited with Libyan exports remaining up in the air. Vessels continue to rotate back into position for the next window and so if force majeure is applied in Libya, then a further blow to rates will be seemingly inevitable.

Last week saw Owner Sentiment gently nudge rates up in Wafr, Whilst this week,  sentiment and improved fundamentals have converged.  At the time of going to press, TD 20 trades minimum WS 80 with the fixing window focused on the 15-20 September window.  USG/TA  has traded a couple of times at  WS 70 before retreating back to WS 69.75. We think this is a momentary blip with rates likely to head back to WS 70'ish very soon.  In the East, the majority of activity is mainly short haul Indian cargoes which hasn't been enough to thin out the list although rates remain stubbornly healthy with reported last done MEG/East at WS105 NHC. BOT/UKCM needs a test but should trade W50-55 COGH.

After some optimism last week tanker rates again face some overall pressure. That is, however, not out of the ordinary for this time of the year, and everything looks set for normal seasonality to the upside in coming weeks and months. TC rates have not been immune to these summer doldrums but hold at overall solid levels – especially for longer durations. This bodes well for values in the near to medium term, however any disappointment in earnings will put values for the older ones firmly at risk.  Values for modern tankers are, and will remain resilient but we see rather limited upside potential from present levels. Tangible deals for the very modern ones are few and far between but following its acquisition of three modern VLCC’s from Korean owners in May, Bahri made another swoop this week for nine modern, scrubber-fitted units from Capital Group reportedly for abt Usd 1 bn en-bloc. Prices agreed are in line with our value estimates.  Earnings in the Capesize and Ultramax segments are at solid levels, whereas Kamsarmax earnings continues to slide. However, the imminent US and Canadian grain season could reverse this trend. Coal demand in Asia will eventually improve in Q4, so earnings in the Ultramax and Kamsarmax segments will likely average in the mid or even high teens through the remainder of this year. In the Capesize segment, the weakening fundamentals in China could result in a near-term correction in earnings. However, seasonal factors like Indian coal demand and increased Guinean bauxite shipments should support the market in Q4.  We have seen a bumper dry SNP actitivity YTD and with this expected back-drop on earnings, the briskness should continue once the holiday season has passed.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Bids for evenly split cargos for Sep liftings softened due to higher freight however offers still maintained at mid-teens premium to lifting month CP, as of strong demand from India and Indonesia. Despite the loss in oil price, Sep CP was traded resiliently at $595, and Sep/Oct CP traded at flat to small contango.    FAR EAST Earlier in window 23/0 parcel for 2h Sep delivery was traded at Sep FEI plus $5 and bids continue to edge up. Similar cargo for 1h Oct was bid at Oct FEI flattish to $1, yet to entice sellers’ interest. Off window a handful of 46/0 lots for 2h Sep delivery was traded into EChina and NChina at Sep FEI plus mid high single last Friday, and a couple of similar cargo for 1h Oct delivery was also been placed into East and NChina, at Oct FEI plus mid single digit basis Ningbo reportedly.   This being said, still quite a few tenders were cancelled due to high offers. One SChina cracker user cancelled their buy tender for evenly split or heavy butane cargo for Sep delivery, another SChina PDH didn’t award their tender for Sep to Oct delivery propane either, with both offers reported at delivery month CP plus 50s range. FPC also cancelled their 3rd buy tender for 23/0 or 46/0 late Sep delivery into Mailiao. PERTAMINA issued another buy tender to procure two evenly split cargos for mid Sep and early Oct delivery.   Special origin for Sep delivery was reported done at CP plus low 40s basis Schina, which barely have any price advantage vs normal stem and some players already diverted to normal cargo purchase.   Other than spot inquiries, Chinese importers started to secure next year term supply in view of recent soft freight. One China traditional importer have concluded their annual term tender and secured monthly cargo and quarterly cargo reportedly. Another China major petchem player also issued term tender to secure monthly cargo (heavy propane) basis Ningbo and Maoming and even Chiba.

EAST September spot rates have risen from the 40s and into the 60s in just over a weeks’ time. So far this must be said to be due to the continuously prosperous West market which have been leading the way. The Eastern market has been staying quite active so far this week with 6 spot deals done - 3 of which are Indian PSU cargos. That said, we now count 11 spot fixtures for September dates out of the Middle East Gulf. Last done at mid 60s RT/C.  WEST So far this week we have only seen 2 vessels fixed out in the West although there have been several out looking both in the US and WAF. In total we count 19 spot fixtures in September out of the USG/USEC compared to an average of 27 spot fixtures YTD 2024. The position list appears relatively balanced as we see a few uncovered cargoes out there. Last done concluded at mid 110s H/C.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The EIA yesterday revealed a weekly build of 2.00mmbbls, bringing total US propane stocks to 92.10mmbbls, which is almost exactly the same as last year, but 135% of two years ago.  On a Days of Supply basis, there are 121 days of supply as of last Friday’s reckoning, which is vastly greater than the 73-day average for 2024.  At the risk of repetition, propane inventories in the U.S. are solidly sufficient and can easily accommodate all fashions of demand.  It is calculated that US stocks will reach to between 102-105mmbbls at the first week of October, which would be the highest level in 10 years.  The pricing shows Sep MB propane as presently trading at over 78cpg and at a ratio of 45% of WTI.  There is very little pricing subsidence through Q1 2025 as the forward curve doesn’t allow for anything less than 78cpg until Mar of next year.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, remain solidly robust – though there is a bit of fade into Q4.  It is reckoned that Sep is effectively complete, as a mid-Sep 2:2 was fixed at a reported 21cpg.  Oct avails are offered in the low/mid 20cpg range, while Nov is offered in the very upper teens for a 4:0.  NWE In the first half of August, Europe's LPG market experienced a significant downturn, with prices sliding approximately $20 from August 1st to 15th. This decline was primarily attributed to steady supply  from US exports and more consistent output from the  North Sea.   The East-West spread narrowed and While seasonal demand loomed on the horizon, the market remained in a lull, as almost half a million tons of LPG discharged at Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp (ARA) ports for the period July 15- August 15.   However, as of mid week this week, the propane market in Northwest Europe has showed signs of stabilisation CIF ARA propane has risen to $572/metric ton, up by $6/mt. The large-cargo CIF ARA propane market maintained a steady assessment at +$21/mt to September quotes.   Looking ahead, the European LPG market though well-supplied, could occur if maintenance is required in the North Sea or if temperatures drop.

On the West Australia front, there was active participation from the likes of miners and operators primarily for first half of September dates. Some were seen seeking forward second half September dates. Volumes out of East Australia have improved since last with players enquiring for prompt dates to mid-late September dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see interest for full September dates. Lesser activity was seen on West Africa. Far East spot tonnage tightening while ballasting tonnage is thinning for September with limited vessels still able to meet late August dates. On C5, we see an uptick in numbers with fixtures concluding at USD 11 to low USD 11 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see fixtures concluding at low USD 25 pmt levels for mid September.

This week, the Panamax market has been characterized by continued weakness and limited activity, with no fundamental changes observed in either basin. While the Atlantic basin saw long tonnage lists, the Pacific was more balanced, with some owners considering ballasting to ECSA rather than fixing Indonesian round voyages. Despite the current lull, there is potential for a market rally next month, driven by the imminent US grain season, increased coal demand from India, and higher corn shipments from Brazil. However, China’s coal import market remains quiet, with a possible rebound dependent on the steel sector's recovery.

Another quiet week in the market so far, at least on the surface. Seasonality indicates this week being the bottom for the geared market. With the upcoming grain season in USG, the markets in Atlantic will pick up. Over the past week, very little cargo enquiries ex ECSA and likewise, also in the Pacific. Chinese coal demand remains low.  The usual South Africa-China/Japan trips on an Ultra are priced at USD 22,000 + BB. ECSA fronthauls on top of the shelf Ultra done at USD 23,000 levels. EC India-China trips are being fixed at USD 11,000 levels on Supra. Period market is not very active at the moment as everyone is waiting for a further ‘drop’ in the markets. Last reported on period side was an Ultra opening in Pacific last week covered at USD 17,000 levels for about 8/10 months period. Market sentiment remains flat with expectation of an upswing in Q4.

The beginning of the end? Is the so called 'summer market' soon to be behind us? It's showing signs is the answer. Guyana cannot take VLCCs from September until April. This is going to add 10 or so more cargoes a month and it's worth adding that the VLCC list in general in the West is not long. USG rates have already started to slowly rise and that will only assist. In the Mediterranean and West Africa there is still early tonnage but you can sense a bit of optimism from owners. MEG has been busier. For Basrah liftings the list is shorter so watch this space. The Suezmax market is showing signs of improvement.

It’s counterintuitive to be dropping rates as we charge ahead into the Q4 fixing window, but the conservative world of LNG appears to be shaking off the shackles of conventional wisdom these days. The main focus this week has been down the curve, with a handful of Charterers looking for big ships with laycans in the second half of this decade. This has kept the smiles on the faces of the fortunate owners who have Newbuild tonnage (or slots) on offer, and helps distract from the paucity of demand in the short term market. The latter is completely justifiable when the fundamentals are examined, but we’ve become so used to sentiment calling the shots that it seems unfaithful to write the rest of 2024 off too quickly. What we do know is that volumes on the water always spike in Q4 and this means that shipping utilisation will also go up. Will it be enough to turn a five-figure market into a 200k per day bonanza? Maybe not. But this certainly looks to be a buying opportunity for modern tonnage and if too many savvy charterers pick up on this, anything is possible. No newbuilding orders this week, but this will need to change soon also.

When the dust settled, August turned out to be a big month enabling rates to recover from the mid WS 40s in a matter of days, with WS 62.5 the highest paid for a MEG/Singapore run. MEG 1-10 September is far from done and owners will be trying to keep the momentum up. With Q4 around the corner, the shorter MEG/East runs are preferred over West Africa or Brazil, as owners want to keep short and are reluctant to lock in for longer voyages at the current levels (depending on the fleet size of course). As a result, West Africa, Brazil and the USG - heading East, are attracting a premium and it should be noted the tonnage situation in the West is also slim pickings.  Owners went into September riding on the wave of WS 60s. But the usual tactic of drip feeding cargoes often played by charterers has been prevalent so far this week and this will strain owners confidence. Our view next week - East softer, West warmer.

With the majority of August North Sea stems covered, activity has been limited as rates maintain at WS 120 level. So far this week we have seen around 10 vessels heading out of the area to benefit from busier markets in the USG and Mediterranean; unless North Sea market activity increases, we expect more to follow. One charterer has now reached into September dates and by the end of the week, with a UK holiday on Monday, a few more stems in September should be worked.    Last done levels look to have been repeated at least for the meantime as September dates begin to work. The lack of volume from Libya and the steady flow of ballasters from the North into the area has recently capped the market, and with supply of tonnage seemingly balanced for the 1st decade of September, it would take a surge of activity to tighten the list and move things on.

EAST It looks like a substantial portion of first decade September FOBs being controlled by Indian PSUs could help explain the lack of shipping interest for next month so far. Bar a couple of Yanbu fixtures and the end of last week UAE fixture the spot market have up until today been pretty muted on September dates. With West freight on the rise and with East still being a discount market we expect there could be upside ahead and more activity just around the corner.  WEST Since Monday the Western freight market has increased almost 20 dollars on the Houston-Chiba route after having seen a dozen of deals done this week. With that said, we now count 17 spot fixtures (with latest sub deals incl.) out of the USG/USEC for September dates. The position list is now looking tighter with only 3 open positions left for 1H Sep dates while 2H Sep currently showing 10 available vessels (5 relets). Last done at 108 H/C.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS After having declined over most of July, Mont Belvieu non-TET propane values have – alongside a modest uptick in the crude arena – turned a corner and found a home at just below 80cts/gal, the current going rate.  The lock-step nature of propane to WTI has kept the ratio between the two in the low 40-percentile range.  The maintenance of the propane pricing structure continues to confound, particularly in view of the fundamental factors.  It is summertime, after all, and export volumes are effectively capped until the expansions begin to emerge late next year.  Furthermore, stock levels of propane are indeed robust, having on yesterday been reported at 90.10mmbbls for the week ending 9th August.  This is 99.5% of last year’s level and puts the US on a trajectory to reach ~103mmbbls at the first week of October, which is entirely sufficient for all varieties of demand which regularly occur.  Meanwhile, as to terminal fees, they remain strong as they continue to be supported by a healthy arb, unfettered passage to the East via Panama Canal, limited terminal avails and – for the moment, at least – generally cheap freight.  September transactions are largely concluded by now, and October volumes are being discussed in the low/mid 20cpg range.  It is presently anticipated the Nov and Dec will likely commence trade soon, and then probably in the upper teens, though nothing is known to have been concluded yet.  NWE The European LPG market got off to a strong start in August, crossing the $600/mt mark for the first time in over a year, with physical premiums extending $6/mt higher still. But It has come off sharply on the back of comfortable stocks, bolstered by US exports and growing Norwegian output- as North Sea exports have increased, along with production, up 18 percent on the year.   Furthermore, while propane remains the more competitive feedstock in relation to naphtha, it’s been observed that steam crackers, have turned toward Naphtha as of late despite the spread (-$89/mt), in efforts to minimize Ethylene length. As of yesterday, OPIS report that 460,000 metric tons of LPG have discharged in NWE on the month, a level that the market finds more than sufficient given storage levels and demand at present.

With limited requirements observed across both basins, the LNG shipping market has seen a quiet week, resulting in limited demand for spot charters. Few requirements are being worked, and these are predominantly East of Suez. The lack of activity has resulted in a softer sentiment for the upcoming winter. Vessel availability is slightly long against the requirements seen in the market and ships opening prompt may see a discount for a spot voyage against present rate levels.  It remains unclear if this trend will dampen sentiment further down the curve into Q4, although in contrast to last winter, there is limited interest in securing tonnage for multi months despite more ships being available. However, the premium to charter a larger modern vessel is still present and with spot cargo prices currently stable, it’s likely to incentivise charterers to prioritise such vessels ahead of the cheaper tonnage for the upcoming “peak season”. Newbuilding prices remain stable and no recent transactions have been recorded this week.

This week in the Panamax market, the sector saw continued rate declines in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins, with limited demand and some slight improvement in Pacific demand offering minimal support. The market is still under pressure, particularly in Asia, despite potential drivers such as US grain, Indian coal, and Brazilian corn shipments, while China's weak coal import market shows little immediate promise of recovery without a rebound in its steel sector. The outlook remains cautious, with expectations of further rate corrections.

On the West Australia front, we see enquires from full suite of miners for late August dates and operators for late August to September dates. Volumes out of East Australia remained flat from last week with some operators enquiring for early September dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see interest for full September dates in particular for early to mid September. Lesser activity was seen on West Africa. Far East spot tonnage is tightening slightly while ballasting tonnage weighs heavily on first half of August with few still able to meet late August dates. On C5, we see an uptick in numbers with fixtures concluding at high USD 10 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see fixtures concluding at mid USD 25 pmt levels for early September while offers are in the USD 26 pmt levels for mid to late September dates.

The lackluster market form in the North has continued into this week with activity limited and freight rates steady at WS 120 for X-Nsea. USG and Mediterranean markets have also softened which has made ballasting out of the area less attractive, leaving a good supply of tonnage for a relatively small amount of activity.    Some activity this week in the Mediterranean, but charterers keeping the pressure on rates. Lots of tonnage has been committed though ships are willing to fix down from the North and so attention turns to what’s left in the region. With mid-3rd decade being worked and end month stems around the corner the hope is that September stems bring renewed backing for the region. Suezmax tipped to progress also which should allow Aframaxes in the Mediterranean to work without the threat of Suezmax.

If you quote a cargo in this market, you're likely to receive 4, 5, possibly 6, 7 offers. That goes for nearly every region. Owners therefore have little else other than their own TCEs to use as the reason for resistance. The ships which have missed cargoes off their dates are left with a decision to sit and wait for the winds of change or fix at a number which involves a fair amount of waiting, which in turn will yield little returns. When we say little, we're talking in the teens for TCE equiv. Therefore, the tonnage list is slowly squeezing rates down but it's not going anywhere fast. Information in these markets is harder to come by because owners will do what they need to do to fix but there's no point in talking about it. In our opinion, the tonnage lists suggest there's at least another 10 days before ships begin to thin out. That's the earliest we can hope for change in a positive direction for rates.

The last couple of days the MEG has been in that twilight zone in between months with Saudi September stems reportedly due tomorrow. However, as it turned out August was far from “sold out” and proceedings kicked off this morning with a few end month cargoes and a couple of early September stems from the likes of Kuwait and UAE, charterers seemingly sensing the potential upside. The Atlantic also showed signs of picking up yesterday with a handful of USG export cargoes emerging, and we got a Brazilian export cargo this morning. There’s currently very little disparity TCE wise between MEG- and West Africa/East. The extra 5 points give/take for the longer voyage mostly cover the extra cost, so owners with ships ballasting from the East will be reluctant to lock in a long commitment into a perceived stronger autumn/winter marker at current low returns – and as ships naturally open in the Atlantic becomes absorbed logic dictate rates will have to come up. Position lists both East and West of Suez are relatively balanced, but more importantly the front end is controlled on fewer hands which narrows the scope. When you are at the bottom of the hill the only way is up.

This week's market for Supramax and Handysize vessels remained generally subdued, with limited fresh activity and a cautious sentiment prevailing across regions. In the Supramax sector, the US Gulf saw recent gains for transatlantic runs stall, while the South Atlantic stayed balanced with little change in rates. The Continent-Mediterranean routes lacked new momentum, and Asian markets remained lethargic, with only a few fixtures reported. The Handysize segment mirrored this trend, with mixed signals from the South Atlantic and slightly firmer sentiment in the US Gulf, but overall activity remained low.

A slump in activity is being felt across chartering and S&P in the tanker space this week as the summer market takes hold. This is likely not distracting owners from their holidays while they enjoy the historically strong position the market is in. In the only sale this week VLCC APOLLO HARMONY 301K DWT IHI KURE 2010 was bought by Smart Tankers for USD 58M, with an end of year delivery.   The dry market too is suffering symptoms of the summer, with a fall in activity this week. This is likely only temporary while owners take a breather before the typically hectic Q4. Despite the lower activity, values have remained steady, with Capesize SEA TRIUMPH 181K DWT KOYO 2012 sold in line with last done at USD 36M.

Market activity remains high this week on both spot and term requirements, with several Charterers pursuing tonnage for winter. There are more enquiries emerging for September laycan and beyond, although such requirements are still competing with cargo deals leaving the market in a somewhat volatile state. We have seen an inversion in the shipping rates, where in the past month there has been a large premium in rates in the West compared to the East, it has now flipped with the East fetching a higher premium particularly on modern 2-stroke vessels. While there is speculation on whether this will push rates higher across the basins, the prompt availability list remains quite long especially for steamships in the East, so competition should keep rates in check, for now.  There have been no new orders this week. However, all eyes are peeled on rumours that a wave of large orders might be on the horizon.

EAST The last done fixture in the East demonstrates reluctancy from owners to keep fixing very low 40 levels. Most owners are now aiming for mid 40s level and above signaling a more optimistic near-term outlook despite a continuously challenging length. Current spot fixture count for August now stands at 20 versus a monthly average so far this year of just above 23 fixtures.   WEST A few September fixtures have already been done, but we still find a couple ships left able to work August dates.  There are reports that several players in the US are looking to buy FOBs in the middle of September. In addition, we expect an Asian spot tender to be quoted early next week for second decade September dates. Last done fixture concluded at 90 H/C.

text: MEG Cash premium for Sep lifting evenly split cargos hover at high single digit. The premium stabilised amidst the weak freight and strong demand into India specifically. One Indian major issued tender to buy upto 4 cargos for Sep to Nov delivery. At the time of writing, Sep Cp was traded at $590 and Sep/Oct traded at flattish level.   FAR EAST 23kt propane for 1h Sep delivery was traded bid at Sep FEI plus $7, while similar cargo for 2H period was bid at Sep FEI plus $3.5 vs offer at $6.  Owing to the squeezed margin, spot inquiries was relatively thin this week. One Korean petchem player was reported to procure a late Sep delivered 23kt propane at FEI plus low single digit, and they’ve issued new tender for mid Sep delivered 23kt butane parcel. One SChina based PDH tendered to buy 23kt or 46kt propane for Sep delivery. Another EChina PDH user was said to buy some propane for 1H Sep delivery at Sep FEI plus high single.   Pertamina reissued their buy tender for an evenly split cargo for mid Sep delivery as last offer at Cp plus 40s higher than target, but yet to hear result.

North Sea market remains steady with limited activity so far this week and rates maintaining at 80 x WS 120 for X-North Sea.  We are still seeing tonnage ballast out but with surrounding markets also on the softer side opportunities are limited at the moment.  Charterers in the Mediterranean have managed to utilize willing participation from vessels exiting the North Sea market as well as Suezmax interaction to hold owners around the 80 x WS 135-140 mark for X-Mediterranean. As we head towards the 3rd decade a healthy stem count could help to support owner’s incentives if the Suezmax are not there to cannibalize. For now, we expect activity to remain subdued and for rates to hold around current levels.

On the West Australia front, volumes started off flat at start of the week and increased gradually as we approached mid-week with miners, some operators, and tenders for second half of August dates. Volumes out of East Australia held up and players were mainly seeking for late August to early September dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China, enquiries were heavily weighted on very late August and first half of September dates. A sizable number of operators were seeking for second half of September dates. On West Africa, enquiries were primarily for first half of September dates. Far East spot tonnage is slightly tighter while ballasting tonnage weighs heavily on first half of September dates with some still able to meet late August dates. We see fixtures concluding at mid-high 9 pmt levels/mid 17 pmt levels/high 23-low 24 pmt levels on C5/C17/C3, respectively.

Healthy activity in the Atlantic basin with a few fresh sugar stems on geared sizes. MEG/Indian Ocean region also remains active with usual South Africa-India coal, and some backhaul cargoes as well. ECSA-Mediterranean trip was fixed at around USD 19,000 levels on a Supra. ECSA-Algeria trip reportedly fixed at USD 15,000 levels on a Handy. South Africa-China trips being done at USD 21,000 levels. The usual Indonesia-China coal runs stand at around USD 12,000 levels basis Supra. Indonesia-India trips going for USD 10,000 levels as usual. There is still appetite for period, and last done was in high USD 17,000 levels for SP on an 63k Ultra opening in WC India. As pointed out by our research team, several macro indicators suggest that the positive momentum will continue until the end of the year. This does at least suggest market levels will not go much lower than where it is currently. The USG grain season could act as a trigger and push the markets to firm up.

Plenty of VLCC tonnage around, especially in the West, have resulted in USG/East rates reducing 2-300k in about a week’s time. Hardly any ballasters from the East though, but the list is well stacked with ships opening on UK/Continent. It shows that there are enough ships to cover the little enquiry at hand as the arb seems shut for Far Eastern voyages from the West. With just the past week seeing about 4-5 ships failing from USG/West Africa load. The MEG market struggling to find a proper bottom, with tighter list then last week. Cargoes seeing fewer offers, but still managing to cover around mid WS 40s mark. The Summer doldrums still present as owners are patiently waiting for the activity to pick up, especially from the West, to help push the market in the East on the back of a 'tighter' MEG list.

This week, for the Panamax segment, the market has continued to decline, deviating from seasonal patterns seen in previous years. The US Gulf grain and Brazilian corn shipment seasons are positive factors, though coal markets remain quiet. Normalizing Panama Canal water levels are not seen as bearish but limit potential gains. Earnings are expected to be higher than last year, with a possible rally in September driven by US grains. However, the market is marked by low demand and increased tonnage, with charterers holding the upper hand and reducing bids, leading to weaker sentiment in both the Atlantic and Asian markets.

After a slow start to the week, the Atlantic has finally showed some basic signs of life with a decent volume of ships on subjects. TD20 should still have circa 8-10 cargoes for the third decade with confirmed "last-done" pricing WS 77.5 with a chance of rates nudging up a pip or two by Friday. The US Gulf is still fairly flat, but the positive news is that rates appear to be scraping the bottom at about WS 60 for a T/A run.  To a large extent, the East remains fairly opaque and what cargoes we have seen either flirted with going on VLCC's or went VLCC. We freight MEG/East low WS 90's with a flat trend. BOT/UKCM has suffered at the hands of VLCC's and we're pasting WS 50 cogh against that run today.

Despite the usual seasonal slump and lacklustre earnings environment, there remains a healthy amount of activity on the dry S&P front. This only amplifies questions on the disconnect between asset values and earnings, particularly on modern ships. It hasn’t however, deterred Alpha Bulkers acquiring DD due capesize HERUN GLOBAL SWS 2016 at USD 49.5M, in line with recently done COURAGEOUS (181K DWT SWS 2016). Kamsarmax trio THERESA HEBEI/JINLIN/GUANGDONG (81K DWT SAINTY YANGHZHOU / JIANGSU EASTERN HI 2012) were sold en bloc at USD 19M each to a Chinese buyer, a premium versus the USD 17.5M paid for YU QIANG (81K DWT PLA4807 2012) by a Greek buyer.   MRs continue to dominate activity within tanker S&P market as GREEN SEA (50K DWT DAE SUN 2014) was sold this week at just under USD 39M, with SS/DD passed.  A price that when compared with recent transactions is Illustrating particularly well the premium that HMD built units still command over their Korean counterparts.  Liquidity for large mid aged tankers remains resilient as EMERALD I (104K DWT SAMSUNG HI 2007) sold for USD 38M, this is in contrast to older c.20yo afra and suezmax tankers where the number of available candidates is growing steadily.

text: MEG:  Saudi Aramco raised Aug propane CP by $10 to $590 and butane CP by $5 to $570 respectively. Despite the heated discussions on evenly split cargo, Aug C3/C4 widened from $15 to $20, partially due to Saudi’s tight supply on propane in August. However, it was said that AG producers might have more propane available for Sep liftings and Sep C3/C4 narrowed down to $8. BPCL was reported to awarded one or two Sep lifting evenly split cargo at Sep CP plus mid high single digit.   At the time of writing, Sep C3 CP was traded at $597 and Sep/Oct was traded at $5 contango.   FAR EAST:  23kt propane parcel for 1h Sep delivery basis Chiba was bid at Sep FEI plus $6 while similar cargo for 2h Sep delivery bid at plus $3. 46kt full lot basis Tianjin was bid at $5 yet to see offers in window. Nevertheless, off window a handful of propane cargos for early/1h Sep delivery were concluded into China, with price ranging from FEI plus high single to low teens based on different locations. One EChina importer reckoned current premium higher than expectation hence cancelled their buy tender of 46/0 for 1h Sep dleivery, while another Echina cracker user still issued buy tender for 4/0 des Ningbo 6-15 Sep. despite the eroded margins, we are seeing some PDHs plan to restart up in Aug, in the hope of stronger downstream demand in coming Sep and Oct.   Apart from propane cargos, premium over butane related cargos also remained strong, regardless the softening freight. One Australia stem of evenly split cargo for 8-22th Sep delivery basis Chiba was heard sold at Sep FEI plus high single. However, a couple of tenders were cancelled reportedly due to high offers. PERTAMINA was said to have cancelled their buy tender for an evenly split cargo for 19/23 Sep delivery as offers asking Sep CP plus 40s. Similarly, one SChina player cancelled their buy tender for late Aug to late Sep delivery evenly split cargo. Other than normal stems, latest special origin cargo for late Aug delivery into SChina was heard done at Aug CP plus 40s, which barely have any price advantage over normal stems.   As per our shiptrack, China July VLGC import reached record high hitting 3.8mmt, up by 14% MOM and 20% YOY.  According to China Custom data, China import in 1H increased by 1.8 mmt YOY, and we believed the increment from 2H will be higher, due to new demand from the released of new capacity in petchem.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: US: Cargo transactions concluded in recent days include a purchase at 21.50cts/gal, another at 21.75cts/gal, another at 22.50cts/gal and – the highest (as yet) – 23.50cts/gal.  And while these lofty levels might seem extraordinary – and they are – they are supported by the arb to the East.  Freight rates and robust Far East market values are the primary causes, since it is relatively cheap to transport product to the high-priced Asian markets.  Freight, in turn, has softened as a result of the more readily available slots at the Panama Canal, though this is often referred to as a ‘wild card’ these days since it is uncertain if delays might again occur as they did last October.  In the domestic market propane continues to track almost exactly with crude, at least on a percentage basis, and 42% was the average ratio during July.  So, as crude prices fluctuate, so go MB propane values.  Mont Belvieu propane concluded July at 78.25cts/gal – about 8% lower than on the first of July, and that compares neatly to the 8% decline in WTI pricing during the same period.  Meanwhile, as to the propane inventory levels in the U.S., this week the EIA posted a 2.9mmbbl build, which caught most by surprise as expectations were well lower.  In any case, overall US stocks are recorded as of 26 July to be 87.40mmbbls, or nearly 99% of last year’s end-July figure.  Based on 5-yr average builds for August and September, it is calculated that US propane inventories will quite easily breach 100mmbbls, and likely stand at ~104mmbbls at the first week of October.  Again, it is repeated that this level will be entirely sufficient for both domestic and international requirements.  Perhaps too much, in fact.

EAST: Seemingly more than half way through August fixing in the Middle East we now stand at 14 concluded spot fixtures. Available ships for the second half of the month has been building up, not necessarily because of a lack of spot cargos but, simply due to too many vessels now likely ending up in the region. This can partly be explained by Owners preference for shorter voyages at current freight levels - although USG is now being fixed at a theoretical premium of about 2-3 dollars.  WEST: August fixing gained some momentum this week, albeit at rates steady around low USD 90s basis Houston/Chiba via Panama and low USD 50s basis Houston/Flushing. The current fixture count is up to 24 spot deals which remains more or less at par with the last few months' development. At the moment, the product market is stronger relative to shipping and the market is in need for a drying up of shipping length in order to gain momentum. The Panama Canal Authority announced that it will be back to normal within the next couple of months, however, in terms of shipping outlook, we remain positive for US activity once the terminals catch up any backlog and start exporting at full capacity again.

This week, the Supramax and Handysize markets experienced subdued activity across all regions. In the Atlantic basin, the Supramax market remained lacklustre with minimal fresh inquiries, particularly in the US Gulf where rates faced negative pressure. The South Atlantic also saw reduced interest and weakening rates with a few fixtures reported close to last done levels. Similarly, the Handysize segment reported limited action, though there were indications of slight resistance from owners in the Continent. The Asian markets for both vessel sizes experienced a decline due to a lack of fresh inquiries, with both owners and charters adopting a 'wait and see' approach. The Indian Ocean saw a bit more activity for Supramax sizes with sulphur shipments driving the market, but it has not significantly impacted the overall market sentiment. The general mood was cautious, with limited new fixtures and mixed opinions about potential upward pressure in specific regions.

This week in the Panamax market saw rates decline further in both basins, with the Atlantic experiencing a notable lack of activity, especially due to an underwhelming South America market affecting both Atlantic and East positions. In the North Atlantic, limited mineral voyage business and cheaper rates contributed to negative sentiment, though there was a positive outlook regarding the volume of grain from NCSA and USG, expected to stabilize levels for the week. Asia showed slightly better activity, but rates continued to fall, with some owners discounting shorter runs to minimize exposure to low rates. Both basins exhibited a cautious approach with mixed views on market value, and the summer season adding to the uncertainty.

Last week we wrote about the upswing in the market, green shoots and Worldscale numbers with 40% increases. This week however, it is quite the opposite. We are back in the WS 40's for MEG/East and it highlights that even the best laid plans of owners can be thwarted or rewarded purely by the timing of their vessels open dates. Still, we are in the heart of the Northern hemisphere summer and the TCE's still look a lot better than summers past. TD3 sits mid WS 40's with downward pressure from the Oil Co. relets and a building tonnage list.   The Atlantic has taken a back seat this week and tonnage has built accordingly which is dissuading ballasters for now. West Africa/East sits low WS 50's to test and USG/Ningbo you'll likely get change from USD 7.3m. Tin hats to remain on for now.

As we move into a new month, the market has been busy firming up and working spot and multimonth requirements. The end of last week saw a number of clean fixtures or vessels get placed on subjects in both basins, with the Atlantic basin remaining at a premium to the Pacific, while this week the spot market has quietened down and attention has been more on the longer term opportunities, with several ongoing requirements seeing indicative offers due. Thus, LNG players will be eager to see where rate levels will settle for the winter months. On the availability front, the list of prompt Steam vessels continues to grow, presenting a challenge in finding suitable charter requirements for these vessels as they warm up and await opportunities. Additionally, a number of 2-stroke vessels are expected to become available in upcoming months in both basins. On the cargo side, Freeport has resumed operations at all three of its liquefaction trains and this will draw down some of the prompt tonnage.  Meanwhile, there have been no new orders this week.

Listening to market chatter, one would be forgiven for thinking that Suezmax's, and in particular, the Atlantic Suezmax market, is on its knees. It's not. The comparative year on year August fixing window base is extremely healthy and will provide a huge springboard for owners once Summer comes to a close and we start staring down Q4. Evidently, there have been corrections, with a Ghana/UKCM trading WS 82.5, but if you'd guaranteed an owner these summer rates in February, the majority would have probably taken that number. Nonetheless, there might be a few more points to come off that rate, but that's the summer market for you.  In the East, it's more of the dreary same I'm afraid. The MEG market has become even more opaque which has curiously helped owners. Whilst charterers have tended/preferred to work off market, they have inadvertently been keeping rates in an elevated state. Had they looked at the list in recent months, one can conclude that an open market quote would have delivered cheaper freight.

The North continues to be quiet on the forefront and with bits happening under the radar. Demand is expectedly weak exhibiting the traits of a traditional summer market with relets being on hold for internal cargoes and owners looking for the best options available to them. Even with the USG softening, ballasting out is still a safe option for some of the players in position.  In the context of a summer market the Mediterranean has seen some increased activity this week. Owners have been content fixing last done numbers, but with tonnage being worked through they might feel empowered moving forward if opportunities in the second decade keep coming. Suezmax are soft in West Africa and USG so maybe some potential to interject with a few vessels open in the region.

On the West Australia front, the week started off quiet but picked up gradually as we approached mid-week with enquiries from some miners and operators for primarily mid to late August dates. Volumes out of East Australia also picked up throughout the week for mid August to September dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see enquiries heavily weighted on second half of August and some seeking for early September dates. On West Africa, we see some interest for second half August and first half of September dates. Far East spot tonnage is abundant while ballasting tonnage weighs heavily on second half of August dates with very limited ballasters able to meet first half of August dates. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at low-mid USD 9 pmt levels. On C3, offers are generally in the sub USD 24 pmt to low-mid USD 25 pmt levels and bids are generally at sub USD 24 pmt levels for second half of August dates.

MRs, particularly older MRs this week, continue to be a popular investment despite the well documented rise in asset prices over the last 18 months. This is likely due to the low barrier to entry and the healthy returns on offer. The rise in pricing shows no sign in stopping as BAHRI sold DD Due NCC TABUK 45K DWT HMD 2006 for USD 20.7M, a slight rise on their last done DD Due NCC TIHAMA 45K DWT HMD 2006 at USD 20.5M. Several other sales have been or are close to being concluded, with Navios rumored having sold their NAVE EQUATOR 50k DWT, SPP 2009 at USD 26M to Soechi with slightly forward delivery and prompt dock due. A handful of similar aged MRs we understand being discussed with owners now aiming in the high 20s for both DD passed and due.  Elsewhere, China continues to be a destination for older Afras, with Thenamaris’ DD Due SEAQUEEN 115K DWT SAMSUNG HI GEOJE 2004 sold to Victory Global Navigation at USD 30M.   South Korean buyers continued their run on modern dry tonnage with two notable transactions this week. Scrubber fitted Newcastlemax FOMENTO TWO 206K DWT DAEHAN HAENAM 2017 was bought for USD 60M by Pan Ocean, while HMM provided Densay the opportunity for a rare modern asset flip, purchasing SSI DARING 36K DWT SHIKOKU 2017 for USD 2.7M more than they paid for it in March 2024, at USD 26.7M. We also observe this week the progress in pricing on the Kamsarmax front, XING DE HAI 82K DWT OSHIMA 2017 being bought by Tolani at USD 37M, versus the last notable comparable sale in August 2023 of ALAM KEKAL 82K DWT OSHIMA 2018 at USD 31.8M.

EAST Increased waiting times in Indian ports looks to cause troubles for some Indian PSUs who has been quoting a couple of very prompt cargos. In the first decade of August alone we have seen five Indian PSU cargos out of nine spot cargos in total. After two formidably quiet weeks this week has been much more active. On the back of a handful of prompt quotes in the Middle East we see some optimism in the front of August. Realistically and keeping in mind the West market still being under pressure we still believe freight has a way to go before any sustainable upside will find root.  WEST So far this week we have only seen a couple spot fixtures out of the West. The first available relet we find from 14 August onwards, but there are still six vessels left before then, five of which are for end July dates. We currently observe a couple uncovered cargoes in the USG for 2H August with last fixture concluded at USD 90 to low 90s H/C.
