text: MEG Cash premium for Aug lifting evenly split cargo stabilized at mid-high single digit. One trader was bidding end Aug lifting 4/0 FOB AG at $589. One Indian major was reported to award their buy tender for Dec 2/2 FOB AG at CP minus low-mid single digit.  1st round CP recommendation was heard at $580-595 for C3 and $565-590 for C4. Despite the decline in oil price, Aug C3 CP edged up to $584 and C3/C4 assessed at $9. Aug/Sep CP was traded at flattish to small contango.  FAR EAST A couple of deal was concluded in window, with 23kt propane parcel for 2h Aug and 1h Sep delivery basis Chiba traded at Aug FEI plus $6.5 and $2 respectively. Outside window similar bid for 2h Aug maintained at FEI plus mid single digit but few offers seen.   PDH buying inquiries remains muted, but some PDH which under turnaround plan to restart in Aug and we are expecting more spot procurement if the startup materialized. However cracking inquiries are relatively active. One SChina cracker user awarded their buy tender for a heavy butane cargo at Aug CP plus 40s. Another EChina cracker user also procured a late Aug delivered propane at Aug FEI plus low teens.   On the other hand, Sep discussion have started, seeing one Vietnam based importer tendered to buy 3/1 or 1/1 or 23/0 for 1h Sep delivery and one Korean importer tendered for 0/2 delivered end Aug early Sep.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS While the recent storms and disruptions along the Texas Gulf Coast have (mostly) passed and things have begun to settle down, there remain lingering aftereffects which some of the Gulf Coast terminals continue to have to work around.  Delays of between just a few days and just over a week are reported, and in the case of the Freeport shipping channel, draft restrictions of 39 feet are expected to remain in place for a period.  Otherwise, with no Atlantic basin hurricanes forming, things should return to normal by around the end of July.    That said, August availability is tight.  Most of the available laycans are in the hands of resellers, each of whom is pointing to the robust US/FarEast arb and relatively relaxed freight market while offering product in the 22-23cpg range – which is where a series of transactions are known to have recently occurred.  Meanwhile, stock levels of propane in the US continue to climb.  Per the EIA report for the week ending 19 July, overall inventories now stand at 84.50mmbbls – or just about 99% of last year at the same time, and 137% of what was recorded in 2022.  And based on average build levels over the past 5 years, the latest calculations point to an overall total of ~103mmbbls at the first week of October, which (to be repetitive) is entirely sufficient given the demand from the export market, the petchem arena, and the remaining domestic US requirements.  Product values have not entirely succumbed to the pressures of the growing stock levels, though, and at around 77cts/gal, propane is still 40+ percent of WTI.

At the beginning of the week, the Atlantic Suezmax market looked like it was on the edge of a precipice, but owners have managed to avert all an out rate-capitulation (at least as far as the US Gulf is concerned). A key insight into owners’ resolve was a USG/TA fixture that traded marginally down on last done from WS 82.5 to WS 81.25, crucially staying above the WS 80 barrier.  In West Africa, all eyes are on ENI West Africa/UKCM 10-11th August which is likely to test TD 20 down a tad, although having been in the market for days now, natural dates might start to work past them.  Non-Indian flagged vessels have had to watch from the sidelines as circa 80 percent of Indian cargoes were awarded to Indian flagged vessels. There is a long list of FOC vessels and MEG/East rates are under downward pressure.

A busy end-month window in the North Sea with charterers securing tonnage in the market willing to do last done rates and reset positionally within the region. The 1st decade of August is soft on paper and with a balanced position list moving forward, it is hard to envisage any big swing on rates in the short-term.  Rates have ticked along in the Mediterranean with deals being done on or off the market and rates being repeated. Owners have held their ground through a tricky period of fixing where the summer lull in activity has been all encompassing. Still fair returns for owners and activity is steady with the tonnage list remaining balanced, despite vessels being fixed for voyages that will take them outside of the area.

The doom and gloom of the past few weeks quickly dissipating over the last few days, as MEG rates improving by 40%, and the swinging WS 60’s potentially in view. The usual busier start to the month meant charterers fell over themselves chasing tonnage and owners were able to help each other out by leaking deals into an increasingly warming market. At the time of writing, WS 59 done short East and WS 58 to Korea. Expect a Chinese freeze on anything prior to mid-month August laycans in an effort to cool the market, and some profit taking on prompter dates very likely. But sentiment is strong right now and we count just 27 vessels free of cargo in the East at this moment in time.  The Atlantic, the earlier vessels booked what they can, minimizing waiting and a lack of ballasters from the East means this market may continue an upward trajectory in the short term. USG to China fixed at USD 7.35m, T/A at USD 3.15m. A sense of resistance on the Suezmaxes taking hold also.

On the West Australia front, the week started off with depressed volumes but slowly picked up as we approached mid-week with enquiries from some miners and operators. Players are primarily seeking for first half of August dates, and we see buying activity from operators for second half August albeit limited enquiries. Volumes out of East Australia are a tick up. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see enquiries for full August dates while things were quiet on the West Africa front. Far East spot tonnage is abundant. Ballasting tonnage is thinning for first half of August and heavily weighted on second half of August. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at sub USD 9.50 pmt levels. On C3, fixtures were concluding at mid to high USD 24 pmt levels by mid-week for late August and early September dates.

This week in the Panamax market, Asia experienced balanced conditions with increased cargo flows despite potential disruptions from incoming storms and typhoons. The Atlantic market displayed notable strength, driven by a tightening tonnage list in the North Atlantic and additional cargoes in the South Atlantic. The index saw positive movement, bolstered by low tonnage availability and modest demand from NCSA and Black Sea grain. The ECSA market found stability, trading around the 16,500/17,000 BKI level. While overall activity in the Atlantic was subdued, the North Continent's tight tonnage and a well-balanced ECSA market maintained stable levels with slight gains despite the broader market's cautious stance.

It has been a bit of a mixed bag when it comes the sentiment of this week’s LNG shipping market. There has been robust chartering activity with multiple new spot requirements in both basins, which coupled with the partial restart of Freeport would usually mean a “full-steam ahead” in our ship order telegraph. However, on the other hand we have seen a flurry of new vessels been shown as available for various periods, especially from Asian subletters, causing some to question whether shipping demand is going to hold firm through the winter. But as ever, no one has the crystal ball to see how things will play out, and like so many previous cycles we must brace ourselves for some rate volatility in the months to come. As we currently stand, the Pacific spot rates have almost caught-up with the Atlantic rates; however, the exception remains for inter-basin rates, since most subletters are reluctant to show tonnage with worldwide flexibility from the Atlantic. On the newbuilding front, it has been a quiet week with no new orders, but we are almost at the end the “holiday month” so expect to see more activity going forward.

Overall quiet/flat week in the Atlantic with little to report, but we did see a few fresh orders ex ECSA and Atlantic basin. The past week saw fresh enquiries with sulphur cargo as (sulphur) commodity prices saw improvement. Slow & steady, we also see more orders ex Indian ocean.   Large Ultramax reportedly fixed at USD 15,000 level for EC India-China run. The Indonesia-China Supra runs going at around 18/19k levels. ECSA fronthauls on Supra/Ultra paid around USD 22,000 levels as usual.   We see fresh appetite for period tonnage especially for Supra/Ultra sizes.

Despite the market entering the usual summer lull, capesize bulkers remain an attractive investment as 2 further units were reported sold this week. Pricing remains firm, with CAPE MATHILDE 178K DWT MITSUI 2010 achieving close to USD 30M and scrubber fitted GENCO HADRIAN 169K DWT SUNGDONG 2008 being sold for USD 25M. This price environment seems for good reason too, with Vale reporting this week they increased iron ore production in Q2 and expect to reach the upper end of their 2024 guidance. Scrubber fitted kamsarmax KRISTIAN OLDENDORFF 82K DWT JIANGSU NEW HANTONG 2024 saw the first transaction of a Chinese kamsarmax in xs of USD 40M, sold at USD 40.85M, showing the value of a new ship on the water.   Scrubber fitted sisters PACIFIC JEWELS/TREASURES 115K DWT DAEHAN 2016 were reported sold to Vietnamese buyers in the high USD 60Ms, this represents a strong firming in the market following from two sales in February of scrubber fitted 2018 built sisters POLAR BRIGHT/ACE 109K DWT DAEHAN 2018 for 65.5M USD. NAVE EQUATOR 49K DWT SPP 2009 was bought by Soechi at USD 26M, riding the high of the increasingly strong market with a near 20% rise in values since last year. Clearly buyers are backing this market, with TORM further establishing market position in a cash plus shares deal for 8x 2014-2015 MRs valued at USD 340M.

Market activity remains high this week and all eyes are on spot rates as requirements for August firm up. The imbalance between rates in the East and West persists, with the West still seeing higher levels than the East although the delta has narrowed. On vessel availability, more 2-Stroke vessels are expected to become open starting from the end of July in the West. Conversely, the East sees little emergence of these vessels. Although the list of prompt Steamers is growing in the East, the challenge lies in finding suitable requirements for these vessels. Additionally, Charterers have started seeking tonnage to cover their Winter needs. While there are some emerging requirements for September in both basins, most of these are tentative and expected to firm up soon. Meanwhile on the cargo front, Freeport LNG is expected to restart its first train this week, following disruptions by Hurricane Beryl.    There have been no new orders this week.

EAST  Saudi acceptances were released yesterday, but we have yet to see any activity in the Eastern market. As we move into the second half of July, the first August spot fixture is still pending. With the current weak sentiment in the freight market, charterers appear to be in no rush to secure deals, taking their time as the market keeps muted.  WEST  So far this week we have seen a few deals done both for end July and early August dates done at around mid 90s H/C. In addition, the position list has been trimmed down with a couple trader relets being internally programmed, but we still find 5 positions left in July. At the time of writing, we count 11 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco released their Aug lifting acceptance with small delays heard. comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS With the passing of Hurricane Beryl last week, the US Gulf Coast LPG terminals – and the corresponding waterways – conducted assessments and soundings, which resulted in relatively modest overall delays of days (not weeks).  There are some lingering after-effects, and product remains tight, but no physical hardware damage is known to have occurred.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, have remained robust and transactions are known to have occurred at (and above) 20cpg.  Current offers are seen in the low 20cpg range for Aug and into September.   Given the general weakness in the freight arena, the arbitrage to the East supports these price levels, and until either product becomes more readily available or freight turns in a different direction, more of the same is expected.  Meanwhile, the EIA yesterday reported that overall US propane stock levels rose by 4.6mmbbls – well beyond the 5-yr historical average for Week 28 of +1.7mmbbls, but this is directly related to the power outages which came as a result of Hurricane Beryl.   It is presently calculated that US propane stocks will reach to between 101-104mmbbls as of the first week of October, the conclusion of the traditional US stock building period.  And this is considered an entirely ample supply, which might only be bolstered further if crude strength carries on and domestic production remains robust.  NWE Two unmet bids in yesterday's window echoed the sentiment of tightness across the European LPG market, as North Sea maintenance, reduced Russian LPG exports, and steep competition from high FEI netbacks, lifted CIF ARA premiums into the double digits.  The tightness has been cause for concern for some European buyers looking to bolster inventories in the build up to strong seasonal demand- but help is on the way. Following a slow start to July imports from the US, over 200,000 tons is expected to discharge in the region in the balance of July, bringing the total number close to 500,000 tons, up almost 100,000 tons compared to June.  Whether or not the increase in US imports will be sufficient- remains to be seen, but for now, strong premiums and a narrowing propane/ naphtha spread seem to paint a picture of tightness in the short term.

Another quiet/flat week in the Atlantic as it seems the market running out of steam with low activity, despite of few fresh mineral orders and EX Ukraine grain. The tonnage vs cargo is more of less balanced, but any further gain requires new replenishment of cargo. ECSA market has a positive sentiment with fresh inflow of cargoes to Mediterranean as well as fronthauls. Pacific market - there are many fresh enquiries and sufficient tonnage which can take it. There still remains appetite for period across Handy to Ultra. Market will adjust in coming days and will remain flat.

On the West Australia front, we see a drop in overall volumes and limited enquiries from miners, operators, and tenders. Players in market seeking are primarily for early August dates and some operators for second half of August dates. Volumes out of East Australia slowly picked up as the week progressed. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see enquires primarily for second half of August dates with fewer looking for early August dates. West Africa volumes remain relatively flat. Far East spot tonnage is building up whereas ballasting tonnage is increasingly heavy for mid August and relatively tight for early August. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at low USD 9 pmt levels. On C3, fixtures were heard concluding at USD 25 pmt levels for second half of August.

This week's Panamax market saw a decline in support from ECSA due to fewer vessels heading there, while increased loadings in the Pacific and seasonal Black Sea grain volumes provided market support. In the Atlantic, activity dropped, particularly in the North, with a wider bid/offer gap and mixed rates. The market remained flat with balanced tonnage and cargo, and ECSA saw limited fresh orders and slight owner discounts. Meanwhile, in the Pacific, despite a recent surge in vessel loadings and good demand replenishment, activity was subdued, especially in Asia, due to a national holiday in Japan. Overall, fundamentals remain bullish with ton-time growth outpacing supply growth and industrial metal prices indicating higher averages for the second half of the year.

From an owner’s perspective, the less said about the past week the better, with rates drifting into the lower WS 40’s for a TD3 run, which on a TCE basis leaves a Baltic vessel teetering around the USD 20k TCE. Others will be dipping firmly into the teens. This, despite healthy activity for end July/early August dates which had failed to light up the market. BUT, and it is a big but, there seems to be some green shoots of a gentle recovery. A number of early August stems looking to Korea and some Chinese enquiry at least giving the owners some choice. The drawback remains that a long list with plenty of overhang and the prevalence of relets interspersed within said list will weigh heavy.   Bit brighter in the MEG then, but the Atlantic, reporting a few failings with ships handed back to owners in a dropping market is never a good sign. Possible fewer ballasters will head to the Cape due to the lower numbers will help down the line, but in the short term, little demand for oil in the Atlantic basin will mean lower numbers. Roll on the Autumn.

Whilst the Atlantic market continues to deliver bumper Summer returns (relatively speaking), you could be forgiven for asking, what are the fundamentals that are keeping this market so high? The answer is sentiment, because when you count ship/cargo ratios, the supply/demand argument doesn't stack up. We're now fixing August dates with TD20 at close to the WS 100 mark, so ostensibly, there hasn't been a Summer market and when compared to the same time last year, it's up nearly 30 percent.  The East is another market that has weathered this quiet period extremely well. Despite VLCCs eating into the 1MB market share, you won't find a Suezmax owner today willing less that circa WS 102.5-107.5 for a MEG/East run whilst BOT/UKCM is steady in the WS 50's (COGH).

The North Sea market has softened with demand for tonnage weak and activity levels suffering. Hands are being forced with ballasting out of the region high on the agenda for owners heading out to try their luck elsewhere. Despite the exodus, vessels are still around to be picked up with fixing off the right dates seemingly the only thing that can save Owners Day.  Activity is lacking in the Mediterranean with vessels piling up on the tonnage list. Owners may well try to explore possible alternatives. Dates are up to end month now and a continued correction downward seems inevitable in the current climate. Even if activity picks up quickly, a proper clear-out is mandatory if we are to see a turning of the tide.

Capital is capturing the headlines this week with the purchase of Scrubberfitted Newcastlemax BERGE BOBOTOV (207K DWT BOHAI 2021) at $75m which marks an appreciation in values since last done “TRUST SHANGHAI/QINGDAO (209K DWT SWS 2021) at $73m - a price highlighting the continued strong appetite for larger tonnage. Elsewhere in the dry market, a flurry of Handysize transactions across all ages, most notably the MAESTRO EMERALD (39K DWT SAIKI 2020) fetching $30m from Turkish buyers, as well as Nisshin Shipping, who is rumoured to have offloaded 4 x handies, WESTERN DURBAN/LIMA/MIAMI/PARIS (39K DWT JIANGMEN 2015) at $19.75m each to Precious shipping. To no surprise, the activity in the tanker market continues to be subdued. Prices for older tankers remain resilient as the PGC COMPANION (72K DWT HUDONG-ZHONGUA 2005) fetched $18m. Buying enquiry remains high for product tankers with three transactions to report this week, most notably the ZEZE START (50K DWT HMD 2009), which is sold basis surveys due to Indonesian buyers for $27m.

text: MEG With the declining freight, FOB premiums improved further this week. We’ve heard seller asking teens premium for Aug lifting evenly split cargo however yet to hear deals concluded. Indian majors have started to procure term supply next year, with IOC asking for one cargo monthly in Q1’25, and BPCL looking for 62 VLGC cargos in total for next year delivery, for evenly split ratio. Aug CP was traded at $587 at the time of writing, and Aug C3/C4 was traded at $15. Aug/Sep CP was traded at $2.5 contango.   FAR EAST Delay on supply caused by the hurricane doesn’t lend much support to the CFR market, due to the lackluster demand and the softening freight. 23kt propane for 1h Aug was rumored changed hand at Aug FEI plus mid single digit, and similar cargo for 2h Aug delivery was bid at plus $3.5-4.5. 46kt propane parcel for Aug delivery was bid at Aug FEI minus $4 basis Chiba and plus $5-6 basis NChina.   Outside window market appears quiet this week, especially the high flat price cost discouraged petchem buying interests. Till Thursday one SChina PDH awarded tender to secure 23kt upto 46kt C3 des Qinzhou in 1-25 Aug delivery at Aug FEI plus low single reportedly. One NChina PDH was said to procure an Aug delivery propane basis Panjin at Aug FEI plus low teens. Other bids for similar cargos basis Ningbo were heard at Aug FEI plus low mid-single this week. With current margins, China PDHs are unlikely to ramp up rates further, which was reported at around 75%.

EAST The East market keeps quiet while we are awaiting the remaining acceptances for August. Sentiment is relatively stable but with signs of more potential downside as we haven't seen any spot deals done in the East this week so far. Charterers seem to have time on their side and currently we find ourselves in a bit of a waiting game.  WEST After an Asian spot tender came out in the market earlier today we have seen a few players out checking freight options both in the US and WAF. Most terminals in the USG are now reportedly back online after the hurricane forced them to close down. Freight rates have decreased to mid-90s HCvP which is currently last done out of the US Gulf.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The biggest news in July has been the effects on the US Gulf Coast LPG terminals after Hurricane Beryl made landfall early Monday morning.  The eye of the storm hit just south of Freeport at Matagorda Island, but the counterclockwise rotation of the storm absolutely pummeled the City of Houston where more than 1m people remain without electricity or connectivity.  All of the terminals were shut down at some point, though Energy Transfer’s Nederland facility escaped the brunt of the high winds and rain.  Enterprise and Targa – whose terminals are positioned along the Houston Ship Channel – suffered power outages and were out of commission for a period which resulted in the declaration of Force Majeure.  While both facilities are now operational, delays of around 3 and 6 days (respectively) are being reported.  Meanwhile, the P66 terminal at Freeport, TX – which was nearest to Beryl’s landfall location – is indicating today (Thu) that power has been restored and the Port of Freeport is technically open but there remain draft and daylight restrictions.  Additional assessments are pending today.  As to the market itself, Mont Belvieu propane values remain in the low 40-percentile range against WTI, which is very near to the average established for 2024 but some 5% above the 2023 average of ~38%.  Flat prices today are in the low 81cpg range, so approximately a nickel below the start of July.  Therefore, there is a lingering sentiment that MB propane has potential downside – particularly as demand levels during the summer months are traditionally lower.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, have spiked hard.  There were transactions at the end of June in the low teens, but since then – and so far in July – offers have been recorded at the mid-teens, the upper teens, and as of this writing offers are known to exist at 20cpg (and even above).

A subdued start to the week with lack of exchanges and limited fixture report. The volume cargo is thin at both ECSA & the Pacific. Combined with nearby oversupply of tonnage, giving the owners little support than drop ideas further to cover. A similar pattern in the Indian ocean with monsoon season setting in and very low cargo volume giving the charters upper hand to maintain low bids. Rates continued their slow decline throughout last week.  Market is weak.

On the West Australia front, we see a general dip in overall volumes in market as we approach mid-week with enquires from miners and some operators primarily for second half of July dates. We see some forward enquiries and interest for August dates as well. Volumes out of East Australia and other Pacific business picked up gradually as we progressed through the week.  On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see enquires primarily for August dates with very few looking for late July dates. West Africa volumes remain relatively flat. Far East spot tonnage is increasingly abundant. Ballasting tonnage is increasingly heavy for first half of August dates. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at sub USD 10 pmt levels. On C3, fixtures were heard concluding at USD 26 pmt levels for early August.

More of the same on VLCC’s this week as subdued enquiry and the smoke and mirrors tactics continue. In addition, we near the twilight zone as the end July MEG cargoes are fixed and we wait for the early August stems (dates released early next week). Claims from China of multiple modern owners willing WS 46 may need to be taken with a pinch of salt, but little argument the market is soft and their remains a lack short term cheer. Outliers are there to be found on prompter cargoes with a replacement rptd at WS 49. TD3C likely sits around the WS 47 level, but a test required.   The Atlantic is usually the knight in shining armor for the VL market but flattering to deceive at present. Recent deals done transatlantic at USD 3m, and USD 7.4m to USG/Far East. Given the state of the current MEG, more modern vessels opening in the East will point towards the Cape. Still, summertime! Although a glance out of a London window and you wouldn’t think so.

The Panamax market is experiencing a subdued week with mixed signals and no substantial improvement despite gains in the FFA market. In the Atlantic, minimal transatlantic activity and a flat market in the South characterized the week, with rates expected to continue falling due to a lack of demand. Asia also saw little change, with insufficient demand causing rates to drift and initial hopes of stabilization from South America not materializing. The overall sentiment remained negative, with limited trade reported and inactive regions like NCSA and USEC, combined with an oversupply of tonnage, giving charters the upper hand to maintain low bids. This has resulted in a weak market outlook overall, with owners facing pressure to lower their ideas further to cover.

Summer rates (the troughs, not the peaks) haven't been wildly different from some of the winter/spring rates that we saw earlier in the year, although of course the market has been less volatile. TD 20 is holding steady at WS 97.5 for a straight run with the fixing window now chasing down the balance of the end month cargoes.  The East market is becoming more opaque by the week which has bizarrely played into owner hands with rates probably a touch above where should be had charterers been bothered to quote a cargo and go wide.

Market remains steady with a few quiet fixtures taking tonnage, but general market activity remains limited. Tonnage availability remains healthy with forward dates being replenished.  Natural window heading towards 3rd decade dates.  US markets still attractive to ballast from North Sea.  Mediterranean market has ticked along in a steady fashion with some business being done, but rates holding fast in the region for now. Tonnage outlook is plentiful at the moment and with ships engaging from the North down it will take some increase in volume to see significant pressure mount on rates.

Following last week’s charter rate rally in the Atlantic, it is the Pacific's turn this week. Several requirements were hitting the market for 2H July and 1H August laycans. To this end, we are seeing a slow, but steady increase in rates and consolidation of RT econs in the Pacific basin, yet the delta between Atlantic rates remains notably wide. Activity in the Atlantic is continuing albeit at a slightly slower pace, as there is an expectation of more 2-stroke tonnage emerging through August and the arbitrage remains volatile.  The short-term market has remained relatively quiet, as Charterers weighing their options. The arbitrage may test the market in coming weeks, but for now the landscape remains flat. Newbuilding prices have remained stable this week.

Ice 1c ARISTOFANIS 115K DWT DAEHAN 2020 was the latest modern afra/LR2 to be reported this week, sold to Azerbaijan Caspian Shipping Co for USD 78.8M, this represents a significant rise in the last done STIRLING 112K DWT COSCO 2021 which sold at USD 70M back in May of this year. Rumour still surrounds Japanese controlled PUSAKA JAVA 108K DWT TSUNEISHI 2018, with uncertainty related to both price and direction.    Transactions this week in the dry market are typical of the current environment; modern ships hard to come by resulting in an increased focus on 10-15yo units. Despite a somewhat lull in earnings, supramax values remain firm with NORDIC STAVANGER 56K DWT MITSUI 2011 selling for USD 18M. Elsewhere, Jinhui Shipping, a strong believer in the capesize market as they make another purchase, OCEAN CONFIDENCE 178K DWT SWS 2008 for USD 24M.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Jul CP at $580 for C3 and $565 for C4, a rollover from Jun, which is cheaper than swap values. Following crude, Aug CP surged up to $592 and C3/C4 maintains $15. Owing to the softening freight and decent CFR price, Aug FOB discussions also inched up and turned into premium, with seller asking Aug CP plus $3 for Aug lifting evenly split cargos in window while bids outside window in discounted level.   FAR EAST The upcoming hurricane have raised up concerns on current US Gulf loadings, which affects on the Aug delivery supply. 23/0 for 1h Aug delivery was traded earlier at Aug FEI plus $7, higher than curve value, then weakened to $5 on the time of writing. 46/0 parcel for Aug delivery basis Ningbo was bid at Aug FEI plus $5, and similar cargo basis Chiba was bid at Aug FEI minus $3.5.  Outside window FIC awarded their buy tender for 46/0 1-10 Aug delivery at Aug FEI plus mid high single and they issued another tender for 46/0 2h Aug delivery. Similarly, Huatai also reported to award 23/0 for early Aug delivery at Aug FEI plus mid single. Tianjin Bohai also tendered to buy 23/0 or 46/0 for 1h Aug delivery, which is still within validity. Despite the fact that there are still some more feedstock procurement demand, the soaring flat price has eroded the margins and we are expecting some new PDHs or units under maintenance might defer startup/re-startup.   Apart from regular stems, there are still two special origin evenly split cargos, for end Jul delivery basis Schina are for sale via tender.

EAST July has been strong in terms of spot volumes especially in the first two decades of the month. The next couple of weeks will reveal if we will see an equally strong third decade and a month performing above the typical month. The average monthly spot count from Middle Eastern ports (inc. Yanbu) for the first half of 2024 stands at just below 23 spot fixtures vs July so far at 23 (10 in first, 9 in second and 4 in third decade). We expect more to come on July dates still, especially considering we only have seen four spot deals in the last decade (one of which rep still on com subs).   WEST In contrast to last week the West has been more active than the East in terms of fixing activity with 7 spot deals done. So far we count 4 spot fixtures for August dates ex USG/USEC with the last few deals done around 110 H/C. Although August fixing in the USG is well underway, we still find a chunk of July vessels seeking employment. In addition, the position list for 1H August is starting to build up which could limit the upside.

Uninspiring would be the buzz word for the week, with new lows for MEG/East runs - as a shorter voyage to Thailand agreed at WS 47 (albeit a 15-year+ vessel). Few charterers would be contemplating anything starting with a 5, even on a modern, regardless of where in the East they may discharge, as the summer doldrums remain firmly in place.   Atlantic quiet on the surface and softer on other sizes. For the VL’s, we remain low on the cargo count – July 72 Atlantic wide, whereas June at this stage was 83 (although, the opaqueness of the current market does make this trickier to read). With 4th July holidays imminent, likely the US market this week will finish with a whimper. Unlike the potentially catastrophic hurricane Beryl. USG/Rok-Ningbo today sits around USD 7.7m and 3.3m transatlantic.

As we close out Q2, charter rates have rallied in the Atlantic especially for 2-strokes, although Owners across all propulsion types are enjoying improved levels and interest. Yet this week, the market seems more divided as some question the longevity of this early summer rally. In recent years, this strength had led to numerous multi-month fixtures being concluded, yet so far we haven’t seen the same dynamic. At the time of writing, there appears to be a slight rebalancing, with a little less activity and some more potential tonnage emerging. The delta between the Atlantic and the Pacific is historically high and is encouraging 174,000m3 tonnage to ignore pacific requirements and head West without delay. Historically, in this instance vessels located in the Pacific become the focus of Atlantic requirements and there is a balancing effect, yet it is quite clear that currently without sufficient demand to head back to the Pacific region the economics don’t stack up, thus we continue to see a price disconnect between the two basins. How the rest of 2024 will play out is a very intriguing discussion. Cargo pricing suggests limited contango or arbitrage and although we can expect a busy few months, it is not straightforward to anticipate how high rates will go. With both canals essentially out of action, there is scope for volatility yet cargo demand appears to surface on a very prompt basis. Perhaps unsurprisingly given these uncertainties, the LNG freight market is unlikely to drop as fast or as far as some may predict, and perhaps we will see a broadly flat market; however, as winter nears this dynamic will be tested for sure.   Looking at asset values, newbuilding prices remain stable whilst second-hand interest remains very robust.

Very little to report as markets across basins remain quiet. Markets remain under pressure due to lack of cargo volumes. ECSA saw little activity end of last week and early this week which was promptly covered tick below last done levels. Similar story to report on West Africa stems. Lack of cargo volumes coupled with ample tonnage in position driving the pattern. In the Indian Ocean region, the usual sulphur, salt, and aggregates cargoes are out in the market, but all covered up. With the monsoon season hitting Western coast of India, we expect less activity in the region for the next 2 months. Limited cargo activity in the Pacific region as well. On the period side, no fresh enquiries and rates remain very high hovering around 18k levels for longer periods. Hopefully the grain season in the Atlantic picks up in the coming weeks and possibly bring in some well needed push in the freight markets.

A slow start to the week in the North Sea with very limited activity coming to the market has seen rates take a hit and fall by a further 10 points. Tonnage availability remains healthy. The USG markets took a hit but bounced very quickly. Independence Day celebrations will limit the activity this week but should be active again at the start of next week.  The market has seen some action this week but steady, with any movement in rates to be incremental in this stagnant market. Slow moving and in a sideways trend with still a few candidates there for charterers to take out, but an increase in activity could see upward pressure put on to rates with tonnage lists looking thinner on the front end and some vessels stuck in discharge ports.

Ground Hog Day in the Atlantic. TD 20 ended last week feeling overvalued at WS 112.5 but has now corrected down to circa WS 100 (theoretical rate based on most recent West Africa/USAC trades). We expect rates to scratch the floor in the low/mid WS 90's against the backdrop of a marginally over-tonnaged list and from there we envisage a cut and paste of the last 12 months (moderate bounce) based on a USG market that is exhibiting some green shoots.  In the East, there's been a flurry of off market fixing but not enough to prevent further falls. We expect next done MEG/East to trade at WS 110 (+/- 2.5) with downside bias. BOT/UKCM needs a test but we're calling it mid WS 50's via COGH.

The Panamax market is experiencing weakness, particularly in the Atlantic. Rates are eroding due to lack of demand, especially for longer round trips. While fundamental indicators suggest potential growth in the second half of the year, the current market lacks support. Coal markets have softened, and grain activity from South America remains subdued. Owners are willing to discount rates to secure coverage before a potential summer lull. Overall sentiment is bearish, with expectations of further rate declines in the near term.

On the West Australia front, we see a drop in overall volume in market as we approach mid-week with enquiries from miners, some operators, and limited tenders for primarily second half of July dates. Volumes out of East Australia and other Pacific businesses have dwindled. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we still see some enquires for late July and split dates with majority of enquiries for forward August dates. West Africa volumes are relatively flat from last week with enquiries for late July and early August dates. Far East spot tonnage is increasingly abundant. Ballasting tonnage remains extremely tight for any July dates but heavy for first half of August dates. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at high USD 10 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, fixtures were heard concluding at USD 30+ pmt levels for July dates. For August, we see resistance between charterers to bid up to owners’ ideas.

Softer sentiment across the tanker charter market won’t be of too much concern to owners as the overall picture remains strong. Tanker SNP has lagged behind dry this year in terms of liquidity, and it seems unlikely to change anytime soon particularly as we enter the summer months. The Japanese controlled scrubber fitted Aframax PUSAKA JAVA 108K DWT TSUNEISHI 2018 invited offers on 25.06.24 and is now understood to have been committed at rgn USD 68M to EPS. Elsewhere, Kyklades Maritime bought the scrubber fitted C. PROSPERITY 313K DWT HHI ULSAN 2009 at USD 53M, a slight discount against last done given the ship has her special surveys due.   Despite a slower week on the spot market, dry values continue to push upwards. Belships announced this week that along with declaring a purchase option on BELMAR 63K DWT SHOEI KISEN 2021, they have agreed to also purchase an unnamed Japanese built 2024 64K DWT Ultramax at USD 41M, setting the pace for the rest of the market and showing that there are genuine buyers at levels only previously speculated. In other news, Pioneer have followed up their recent supramax purchase with the acquisition of two Newcastlemax sisters MINERAL CHARLIE/MAUREEN 205K DWT HHIC PHIL INC 2012 at USD 81.6M en bloc.

text: MEG 1st round Jul CP idea was heard recommended at $575 for C3 and $540 for C4. However, paper swap inched higher and at the time of writing, Jul C3 already traded at $590 and C3/C4 at $20. Jul/Aug CP was traded at $4 backwardation. Final CP was expected to come out this Sunday.  Qatar Energy awarded their heavy propane cargo for 22/23 Jul lifting, reported at Jul CP minus around $10 but cannot be confirmed. One AG producer was offering heavy butane cargo for Jul lifting at $585 for C3 and $550 for C4 via window.   FAR EAST Inquiries for 23kt propane for 2h Jul delivery was subdued, and such parcel was traded at Jul FEI plus mid-single digit this week. Similar cargo for 1h Aug delivery was bid at Aug FEI plus $1 while offer at $5.   Cracking spread enlarged further with C3 FEI/MOPJ traded at -$70 and -$60 for Jul and Aug respectively. One Korean importer have tendered for Aug delivery propane and butane. Another Korean importer also issue term tender to secure monthly 2/2 for 2025 delivery. Taiwan FPC also issued prompt tender for Jul delivered propane, however cancelled as the offer discounts not reached target yet, will refresh and likely tender next week.   Other than cracking demand, Hyosung Vina was reported to award a heavy propane cargo for 1h Aug delivery. One Schina cracker procured a 11kt propane at Jul CP plus around $50. Another EChina petchem user also purchased 23kt butane for 1st decade Aug delivery. Taiwan CPC also tendered to buy 11/11 for mid Aug delivery which yet to know result.

EAST This week most of the cargos worked has been in and around the second decade of July ex Middle East. Last decade July deals are starting to be looked at but after a flurry of fixtures in the beginning of the week Charterers could prefer to see things cool down a bit before jumping on to the next train of fixing. Come next week vessel itineraries will also become more clear for this window.  WEST Activity on freight in the West remains uneventful as market fundamentals still not there time of writing, despite East fixing picking up. One Indonesian major is however expected to quote an early August cargo at some point, which will provide a usual benchmark of where freight is at. Fixture count ex US in July stands at 19 deals (6 first decade/9 second decade/4 third decade) compared to a monthly average of 30 deals so far in 2024.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICA All eyes are on the US export market, but with tightness at the terminals (which is the combined result of back-to-back-to-back storms in/around Houston as well as reduced load rates due to maintenance) it is the re-sellers who are in control at present.  And with a lengthy Gulf Coast freight market, offers for 1H Aug range from 13cpg (for a 2:2) to ‘mid’ teens for a 4:0.    The market did seem to sigh in relief with the release of yesterday’s EIA data which showed a solid 2.1mmbbl build.  The market had been anticipating something like 1.75mmbbls, but in hindsight it is thought that perhaps this week’s data included corrections from weeks past, during which time lower-than-expected builds were recorded.  At present US propane inventories are listed at 73.5mmbbls, which is 92.5% of last year, and 136% of two-years ago.  Current estimates for the end of the 2024 ‘build’ season (which traditionally concludes the first week of Oct)  have total overall stocks pegged at a about 99mmbbls – which would be sufficient for the winter season and anticipated export volumes.  Meanwhile, the Mont Belvieu market continues to be priced at stubbornly high levels.  Non-TET MB propane today is marked at ~84cpg, or just over 43% of crude oil which – in its own right – continues to make upward strides

On the West Australia front, we see a drop in overall volumes compared to last week from miners, fewer operators, and some tenders primarily for mid to end July dates. Volumes out of East Australia and other Pacific business held steady from last week with players seeking for mid July tonnage.  On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see a majority of enquiries for second half of July dates with some enquiring for forward early August dates. West Africa enquiries remain relatively robust for late July to early August dates.   Far East spot tonnage remains increasingly abundant while ballasting tonnage is increasingly tight for full July. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at mid USD 10 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see fixtures concluding at low USD 27 pmt levels for mid July dates.

The LNGC spot market continues to show a significant regional imbalance, bubbling over in the Atlantic while remaining a little flat in the Middle East and Pacific basins. The arbitrage driving Atlantic volume into Asia is modest but still present, and the resulting conveyor belt taking ships East is making the summer far more interesting than many would have expected (and also, more than some would have liked). Taken globally, the fleet is more than capable of handling current LNG production levels with quite some length to spare; however, trying to find certain vessels for specific dates out the US Gulf is now proving very difficult – hence the spike in rates. There are some signs that the Pacific may feel a modest knock-on impact as disponent owners price tonnage off Atlantic levels, but this is not likely to push levels much higher since competition remains strong.   The multi-month market up to periods of a year has continued to firm up, although there is a sense of “wait and see” from some players on winter tonnage, whether chartering in or out. For multiyear business, sentiment is softening slightly mainly due to anticipated delays in project start-ups. Yet as today’s spot activity shows, a surplus of global tonnage does not necessarily mean a dull market.  Looking to geopolitics, there was a fresh round of sanctions adopted against Russian reloads from European terminals, but there is a considerable phase-in period and the overall impact will likely be small. There were no newbuildings ordered this week.

The North Sea market has had to tolerate a lull in activity this week and it feels like it’s poised for a further downward correction. The tonnage in the region looks balanced with relets and local ships off the front end and a steady flow inbound off the back of TA runs. With the lack of activity, vessels continue to ballast to the USG despite the softer correction over there.  An active week in the Mediterranean with a number of fixtures enabling a necessary clear out of units. Rates have repeated off the right dates and the tonnage list has thinned as the market looks to turn around. Summer market is still governing the region for the time being, but things could get interesting as we move forward.

The arb for West/East moves is more or less shut which will see the majority of Atlantic basin barrels stay local. Focusing on West Africa, there remains a glut of unsold barrels which suggests there will be some prompt requirements that will help support rates with TD 20 currently trading last done at WS 112.5.  Across the pond, the softening oil price will not bring about an SPR release anytime soon, therefore any uptick will have to come from other sources.  In the East, despite a flurry of enquiry, tonnage is beginning to build and on that basis we are calling MEG/East WS 115-120 and BOT/UKCM WS 60-65 via Cape.

The summer doldrums continue. Slow demand, Chinese ships for Chinese cargoes, and many other deals remain mysteries with no rates reported. The few deals with details attached sees MEG/East ticking down into the high WS 40’s. However, it is not all doom and gloom. The MEG volume count is normal for this time of year, rates are often softer and the paper numbers for 2nd half 2024 are trading WS 62. Owners need to ride out the summer.   As for the Atlantic market, there is a possibility of an SPR release to ease gasoline prices prior to the driving season, but this will be for domestic consumption. Additionally, there is little incentive for spot barrels West to East now due to recent strengthening and steepening backwardation in Brent and WTI pricing. Petrobras a lot quieter for Far East discharge than previous months and any USG activity is noticeably quieter. Rates for USG/Ningbo soft around the USD 8m level.

This week, the Panamax market saw a continued downward trend in rates across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. Limited activity, particularly in the Atlantic, and an underwhelming South American market contributed to the decline. The Pacific arena remained lethargic, with owners discounting shorter runs to minimize exposure to depressed rates. Despite firm fundamentals, including ton-time growth outpacing fleet growth, the market lacked sufficient cargo influx to halt the slide. The Kamsarmax index dropped below the Supramax index, suggesting limited downside from current levels. Holidays in Greece added to the subdued market sentiment, with little indication of an immediate turnaround.

Last week's short-lived excitement of a more robust market has slowly vaporized. While there is currently a downward pressure on rates in the Atlantic due to limited activity, particularly for the transatlantic round voyages, the increased activity on fronthaul routes from the Black Sea and the Continent is a promising sign. With more activity, we can see a meaningful impact. However, we need more demand to see the desired change. The South Atlantic, with more tonnage available for July dates, is experiencing the pressure on the rates. USG also started to feel the pressure; the owner’s expectations to push rates further up are not materializing, and we see rates fixing below “last done”. Ultramax 63‘ dwt delivery USG for a trip with pet-coke fixed at around USD 29,000. Trip from USEC to UK with wood pellets was reported to fix on Supra at USD 20,000. Trip from ECSA to the Far East paying around USD 17,000 + USD 700,000 GBB. The Pacific has good cargo volume and has increased activity from last week. Supra 55‘ dwt delivery S China via Indonesia, fixed USD 12,500 pd for a trip to S China. Pacific round voyages are fixed at around USD 15,000 pd, depending on the vessel’s position. We anticipate the market will be flat coming into Europe's Holiday season unless substantial cargo volume overrides market prediction.

The dry market continues to benefit from increased levels of interest as shipowners look for ways to deploy their capital. Once again, anything ECO is deemed to be extremely desirable, and this is reflected in the price. In the standout transactions this week, 2x 2016 Chinese blt Capesizes sold either side of USD 50M. We would have to look back November 2023 for the sale of the last 2016 Chinese capes with scrubber fitted CHOW/COMANCHE 180K DWT SWS 2016, which sold to Genco for 43.1M each. Considering the premium applied to scrubber fitted units, this would mean the market has pushed ~20% in value in the last 8 months. Greek buyers in these transactions would indicate there is room for these values to increase further.   A lacklustre week all round in the tanker market with stuttering spot rates and only one sale to report. Away from the second-hand market however, investment is still being poured into tanker newbuildings, with owners backing the legs of this bull run. In the only transaction this week, Greek Buyers bought LR1 AVRA PATROS 75K DWT Sungdong Shipbuilding 2008.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco released their Jul FOB acceptance with max 0% tolerance on propane as of tightness, but butane remains in ample supply. comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The Mont Belvieu propane market remains robust at ~80cpg for July, and is being bolstered in tandem by both the strong crude market (which this week pushed through resistance levels of $81.55/bbl and is today at $82.34/bbl), as well as recent domestic US inventory levels which have revealed less-than-expected builds.  In this week’s data, the EIA reported that stock levels increased by 1.6mmbbls to a total of 71.4mmbbls, where the average build for Week 24 is 2.2mmbbls and expectations were calling for upwards of 2.5mmbbls.  Those predictions were based on the notion that export levels were off a bit after a series of storms over the past month battered the City of Houston and caused periodic and temporary power outages.  It is believed that July cargoes are at this point sold out, save for one potential cargo which is offered at 14cpg.  Most of the activity which occurred for July took place at between 10.00 and 12.50cpg.

The market continues to show a high level of activity, building on the record start to the year in terms of number of fixtures. In the Pacific spot market, things have been a little quieter and the open West-to-East arbitrage has delivered an increase in availability ahead, but there are now more firm requirements emerging towards 2H July and 1H August. Meanwhile, in the Atlantic, interest in tonnage remains strong and this has pushed rates higher, since the arbitrage has stretched some fleets a little too thinly. As we approach the middle of the year,  the number of spot fixtures has almost reached the total for all of 2023 already.  Prompt vessel availability has slightly decreased across all basins this week, and the imbalance due to the arbitrage will play out in the coming weeks. Those vessels needed back in the Atlantic will need to take the long way around, although notably, the first LNG carrier (a steam-turbine vessel) since mid-January has now embarked on the Red Sea-Suez route.  The term charter market remains highly active as charterers seek to secure tonnage in preparation for winter, with several requirements already firm and expected to be worked in the coming weeks. On the newbuilding front, prices have remained stable with no new orders reported this week.

EAST Baltic printing higher than actual last done out from the Middle East suggests a more optimistic sentiment. That said, based on current volumes (7 spot deals) we are approaching the end of first decade July fixing and with at least five ships that could be East candidates for the same period there is a considerable length still. Currently it looks like the East/West earning spread could be set to widen as we see it likely that freight is stagnating in the East before any eventual upside.  WEST Since the beginning of last week, the VLGC rates took a tumble in the midst of lack of activity and a narrowing arb. Once freight found its feet again, the majority of this week’s fixtures have been concluded around the USD 120 mark on a Houston/Chiba via Panama basis.  As of today, the current fixing count ex US in July now stands at 19 deals (6 first decade/9 second decade/4 third decade) compared to a monthly average of 30 fixtures thus far in 2024. Although the number of spot open vessels is diminishing and owners’ freight ideas are on the rise parallel to a widening arb, the distribution of arrival timing in the USG and uncovered cargoes remaining is not matching and it remains to be seen how 1H July will be cleared out. At the moment, the product side is the frontrunner relative to shipping.

Market has remained busy in the West with a steady supply of cargoes in most sectors, and this time it’s not on the back of the Aframax markets which hasn’t seen any movement, but some positive signs are starting to emerge from the US Gulf. TD20 should be around the WS 110 to 112.5 levels, whilst for TD06 we think WS 122.5 will still stand. Middle East Gulf has remained pretty slow with a weaker feel, 4.0m has been concluded for sts Kaz to US Gulf, and estimate going east should pay close to WS 120, possibly a tad less.

On the West Australia front, we see a tick drop in enquiries from operators while those of miners and tenders have held up for first half of July dates. East Australia coal volumes have held up as well while enquiries for other parts of the Pacific remain relatively flat. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, we see enquiries for full July dates. Far East spot tonnage is increasingly abundant while ballasting volume is relatively healthy for first half of July dates. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at mid USD 10 pmt levels at mid-week. On C3, we see a stronger sentiment compared to last week with fixtures concluding at low to mid USD 26 pmt levels for the first half of July.

Slowly but surely the July stems come trickling into the VL market. As we cast a cursory glance back at June, it shows a light month with below 140 cargoes. But given the veil of secrecy currently sitting over the market, cargo counting can become a little arbitrary. Still, it is certainly a lighter month, but this is not abnormal, as summer cargo counts are often 10+ cargoes below the cold, dark, Northern winter. Rates have struggled over the week, but are showing signs of levelling out at the WS 50 level for TD3. Indeed, one Chinese charterer at the time of writing only gathering 4 offers for early July dates. Significantly lower than the 10+ offers seen on cargoes last week.    The Atlantic has tightened. Assisted by a recent clear out and owners turning the speeds down to 10-11 knots. Ballasters will therefore take that little longer and we see just the 6 vessels heading for Cape at present. No spring backs imminent, but owners should be able to halt the slide. USG/ Ningbo staying stubbornly around USD 8.2m.

This week, the Panamax market began quietly, influenced by holidays in Singapore and the start of Eid, resulting in limited activity and sparse information. The North Atlantic was largely stable with a wide bid/offer spread, while South America saw softer bids and some owners willing to accept lower rates. Following the holidays, grain and mineral activities increased slightly, balancing cargo and tonnage but requiring more volume to keep rates steady. Asia showed mixed rates with a surplus of tonnage in the South. Despite the subdued start, the market outlook remains cautiously positive, with expectations of an upturn driven by seasonal trends and upcoming grain shipments from the Black Sea.

NORTH SEA Levels continue to move sideways for the time being in the North Sea market as tonnage lists remain balanced for the natural fixing window, but there is a buzz of activity under the radar as relets make their presence known. With opportunities for non-relet/non-local vessels hard to come by, some vessels are expected to ballast out towards USG which is still offering high returns.  MEDITERRANEAN Activity in the Mediterranean continued to soften throughout the week as owners and charterers searched for the bottom of this cycle. Owners have had to work in a competitive nature to secure business with the front end of lists being busy and providing charterers with options, but as vessels fix out, owners are on the cusp of being able to hold some ground on numbers as we push into mid-end 3rd decade fixing.

There is no significant change from last week's sentiment; the market generally has healthy activities in all geographical basins. Grain and minerals led the commodity movements in the Atlantic. The cargo volume is well balanced with the tonnage supply, giving flat rates with little chance to improve. Despite BSI showing green pillars, we need more cargo volume to increase this market. USG had an incredible push, and rates rose to a high number at the end of last week, but it is more stabilized now. The USG fixtures to Singapore/China were reported at USD 28,000 pd and USD 25,000 pd on Supra. On transatlantic routes, the grains trade to the Mediterranean trading around USD 18,000 pd on Supramax and about USD 20,500 pd on Ultramax. The trips to the Continent paying premium and Ultra was covered at USD 24,000 pd. Indian Ocean and South Africa markets remained stable, with rate keeping a similar level; Ultamax were reported fixed delivery South Africa for trips to China at USD 22,000 pd plus USD 220,000 GBB. The Pacific market remains stable. Supramax trading Pacific coal RV was able to obtain around USD 14,000 pd.

Headlines about the tanker second hand market have provided little in terms of variance in the past few months (slowing activity amid high prices), however, the reported sales this week confirm there are still those willing to buy and sell at these levels. Prices in general have continued to firm despite few transactions to prove it, shown here with scrubber fitted FRONT THOR 159K DWT JIANGSU RONGSHENG 2010 selling in the low USD 48Ms. Suezmax transactions around this age bracket have been hard to come by, however, Frontline’s ability to dispose of their 2010 blt Rongsheng series at better than last done on each occasion is a prime example of the underlying positivity in the tanker space. MRs also continue to gain in value, with ALHENA 52K DWT GSI 2012 selling to Greek buyers at USD 32.2M.  Quite an unremarkable week in the dry market with the usual activity of players jostling for position on older units. Capes remain strong, with scrubber fitted NYMPHE 180K DWT DSME 2009 sold to Hayfin at USD 29.3M, just slightly up on last done 2009 CORINTHIAN PHOENIX 179 K DWT HHI 2009 at USD 29M. Otherwise, it is tough to see where the potential asset play is in the dry bulk space. Modern eco ships are scarcely available and priced to represent that, and older bulkers are often priced in excess of any justifiable calculation from an investment standpoint.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Volatility is the key descriptor of the MB propane market this week.  Crude strength and exterior influences such as hedge funds and price-shavers (i.e., not fundamental factors) have conspired and lifted values to near 80cts/gal, and propane/WTI ratios have reverted up to the low 40-percentile range.    How long this will remain the case is as-yet undetermined, but the present situation was exacerbated by the data revealed by the EIA for the week ending 7th June which showed a rather paltry 1mmbbl week-over-week increase to a total of 69.80mmbbls, or 92.5% of last year.  The market had generally been anticipating something nearer to a 2.5mmbbl build.  Nonetheless, stock levels remain on track for an early-October total of right around 100mmbbls, which – based on current production and, separately, export levels – would be deemed sufficient.  Meanwhile, terminal fees remain buoyant.  10cts/gal was fixed at least a few times, 11cts/gal was seen done, as was 11.50 and 12.00cts/gal.  At present the remaining (and by now limited) avails are offered at 14cts/gal, presumably to close in the 13s.  NWE    European propane price realized gains this week following a reduction of imports from the North Sea due to gathering plant outages, increased steam cracking margins in the region and crude gains in the wake of OPEC’s meeting.   Buyers have actively bid the window during four consecutive sessions for both propane and butane and while 250,000mts of LPG has already arrived in Europe in June (so far), only 30-40,000 metric tons is scheduled for the second half of the month, thus the moderately bullish sentiment in the NWE LPG market for now.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG FOB value for Jul lifting was assessed at Jul CP minus around $10. BPCL was reported to award their buy tender for such cargo at Jul CP minus high single digit. KPC awarded their sale tender for 3-4 Jul lifting 2/2 to another producer trading arm at Jul CP minus 10ish reportedly. Subsequently similar cargo for Jul open dates was bid at CP minus low mid teens while offer at high single discounts.  Jul CP was traded at $569 for C3 and C3/C4 was traded at $17. Jul/Aug C3 CP was traded at $5 backwardation.   FAR EAST Cash premium for 23kt propane parcels during 2h Jul CFR FAR EAST softened this week, from mid teens trades on FEI link to high single digit offers. Similar cargo for 1h Aug delivery was traded at Jul FEI link plus $1.68.   Outside window a handful of 46kt propane for 2h Jul delivery was traded, at the price of Jul FEI plus mid single digit basis chiba, or FEI plus low mid teens basis Ningbo.  Due to the ease of panama congestion and declining freight, one EChina cracker even awarded their buy tender for 46/0 des Ningbo 16-25 Jul at Jul FEI plus high single digit only. There are still a couple of Jul feedstock demand uncovered and shall call out buy tender next week.   Other than normal stems, three Iranian cargos for end Jun/1h Jul delivery of evenly split or heavy propane ratio were reported sold at Jul CP plus 40s basis SChina, and we expect more cargos for 2h Jul delivery shall be available soon.

EAST Freight came down significantly last night as a result of a narrowing arb in the West and a bearish outlook on cargo supply in the East for end of June and early July. Several ships offered in quite aggressively on the only June cargo quoted so far this week and consequently freight took a hit. An early July fixture, also from an Indian PSU, quickly followed suit a couple of bucks further down. A non-Indian spot fixture was also concluded around similar levels last night.   WEST After a big drop in the Western market we now find last done at 120 H/C v Pan which is 20 dollars below where we found freight rates last week.  At the time of writing we count 15 spot fixtures ex USG/USEC for July dates - 10 in the first half and 5 in the second half. On the position list there are 5-6 vessels available in the first half of July and 8 in the second half. The first relet we find in the middle of July.

On the West Australia front, we see a drop in enquiries compared to last week from miners, fewer operators, and some tenders primarily for late June to early July dates. Volumes out of East Australia saw a tick increase while enquiries for other Pacific businesses remain relatively flat. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see limited buying for end June dates with a majority focusing on July dates. Volumes out of West Africa remain reasonably robust. Far East spot tonnage is increasingly abundant while ballasting tonnage is heavily weighted on first half of July with some still able to make late June dates. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at low USD 10 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see fixtures concluding at low/mid USD 25 pmt levels for early July and sub USD 25 pmt levels for late June.

Ground hog day again in the US Gulf, with rates firming and last printing 145KT x WS 107.5 with no evident downside against the backdrop of a very tight list. The wider Atlantic, and in particular TD20, should benefit from this upswing and uptick in tandem with the States.  In the East, it's been relatively quiet with rates for a MEG/East run likely to trade down to WS 120's whilst BOT/UKCM will trade in and around last done; WS 70.

NORTH SEA A steady start to the week both in terms of activity and rates. The available tonnage list remains relatively tight with some uncertain itineraries; some cargoes being sold off deferred dates and with the US market continuing to firm, tonnage will look to leave the area in search of greater returns.  Natural North Sea owners can be selective on which cargoes they want to offer, but so far for the right type of voyage rates have remained fairly stable. Natural working window pushing into last decade June.  MEDITERRANEAN An active market in the Mediterranean this week but rates have continued to soften albeit gradually. The USG market is strong and helps to add some robustness to owner’s ideas, but with a lot of the plentiful tonnage in the region open C.Mediterranean/E.Mediterranean, very few ballasters have head in the direction of USG, leaving plenty of options for charterers to work through and some competitiveness in the market. Expect rates to continue in a softer trend until we can find a bottom to this cycle.

The Panamax market anticipates a rally within 1 to 3 weeks, driven by increased grain shipments from the Black Sea and rising coal demand in Asia. This could potentially push the BPI5TC to around USD 19,000 per day within a month. In the Atlantic market, there are significant discrepancies between bids for grain and mineral trips. The North Atlantic seems bullish with tight tonnage and expectations of rising rates, while the South Atlantic remains stable but firm due to plentiful cargo volumes. In contrast, Asia remains quiet with limited activity and a weaker overall tone. The slow start to the week is attributed to holidays in parts of Asia, with sentiment remaining bearish and minimal overall market activity despite some stronger bids for grain transatlantic round trips.

After the eventful Posidonia events last week, we see that the Atlantic market has become more alive; there is more fresh requirements and better cargo volume.   All eyes are on USG and USEC recovery, with rates pushing up USD 3,000 plus from last week's fixtures. The fixture was reported MV Belinda 63’ dwt fixed delivery SW Pass trip India USD 24,000 pd. Another fixture was reported for Supra delivery NCSA for trip to UK with coal USD 17,000 pd. The scrap from the Baltic/Continent also pays a premium to last done, and owners hold back to fix better rates. Transatlantic will improve further as the current index is low and spot rates are improving. The Far East market remains stable. There is a good balance of cargo and tonnage supply. Supramax delivering to North China for coal round voyage fixed at USD 14,000 pd. The Ultramax 61’ dwt delivering Indonesia fixed at USD 18,000 for a trip to China.

As players in the shipping industry return to their normal work pace following Posidonia, the LNG shipping market has also reverted to the levels of activity observed in previous weeks, predominantly in the West. So far this week, various spot requirements have emerged to cover July loadings out of the Atlantic basin, and several fixtures are currently being worked. The demand for both two-stroke tonnage and mid-sized vessels, combined with a tightening availability list, has increased pressure on charter rates in the Atlantic and strengthened market sentiment. Conversely, East of Suez, activity has slowed due to a limited number of firm requirements, with the focus so far this week being directed to FOB cargo tenders and the growing number of developing requirements for the second half of July and August loadings. In view of the current market conditions in the East, owners may begin to consider positioning their vessels to the Atlantic with a potentially improved chance to reduce idle time and to capitalize on potential arbitrage opportunities. On the newbuilding front, prices remain stable as no new orders have been reported so far this week.

News filtering across from other desks of a firmer Aframax market & Suezmaxes climbing upwards… But here on the VLCC’s the downward pressure continues to build. Limited cargoes on the open market. Presently, a Vietnamese cargo working and able to cater for a wider range of tonnage on a voyage that calculates better than most, so lower numbers remain imminent. Charterers also reaching out already into July dates is not a good sign, but likely some infilling of end June to come. MEG/East very low WS 50's.  As for the Atlantic, the oversupply of tonnage will likely continue the softer run ahead. Given the opposite direction of the Suezmaxes, there will be some toe stepping on the smaller vessels as TD20 moves towards the WS 120 level, and it is likely some VL’s have already muscled in on the West Africa/UKC run. Little cheer for owners at present.

A predictably quiet week, with the majority of the market gathered in Athens for the latest instalment of Posidonia. Despite the slow week, the good times in the tanker market continue to roll on. MRs GUNMETAL JACK/PARADISE CITY 50K DWT SPP 2009 were both sold to Greek buyers at USD 28M, as this market continues to rise in terms of asset values.   A more subdued, yet surprisingly active week in the dry market. In the standout deal, the Stefanou brothers (Sea Gate Navigation/Bright Navigation) took 3 Laskaridis Panamax units THISSEAS/ICARUS/ATLAS 75K DWT PENGLAI 2012 en bloc for USD 52.5M. Elsewhere, the Far East remains a likely place for older capes to end up as China’s Pioneer paid USD 32.5M for CAPE KEYSTONE 179K DWT HHI ULSAN 2011.

EAST Indian tenders finally came out as expected, with rumors of additional PSUs potentially coming later, though this is yet to be confirmed. So far, we have observed only 3 fixtures in the third decade of June in the MEG, suggesting that a few more cargoes may appear before early July. However, the market has been generally quiet in both the West and East, primarily due to the ongoing Posidonia Maritime event this week.  WEST It has been a rather slow week in the Western market, with only two spot fixtures registered so far - both concluded below last done levels. With that said we now count 8 spot deals for July dates ex USG/USEC. There are still a couple ships available for the end of June, while the first half of July appears well-supplied, with a few shipowners controlling the majority of the available positions during this period.
