comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Harshly cold weather across the entirety of the US both last week and this has given cause for the EIA to report a decline in domestic propane stock levels of 2.8mmbbls, and thus bringing overall stock levels as of 12 Jan to 76.3mmbbls, or almost exactly the same as last year.   The arctic weather this week will no doubt cause yet another decline in stocks, but thereafter a warming trend is being forecast which should relieve some of the pressure.   Meanwhile, Mont Belvieu propane values have increased by over 14cts/gal since the start of the month despite the (still) relatively robust stock levels.  Current market values are pegged at over 84.00cts/gal, up from the upper 60s on the first of December.   Terminal fees have been seen in the mid/upper 6cts/gal for Jan and Feb, with the number of offers exceeding the number of bidders.  NWE The cold snap in Europe is coming to an end, keeping the TOT window at a $5/MT discount to February CIF ARA for 2H February arrivals. January imports to the region are expected to reach 486,000MT. There is hope that restocking will occur in February after this recent cold weather, but in general Europe remains in a low demand environment. Healthy North Sea production is expected to continue as Dutch TTF values remain below propane and butane on an MMbtu basis. The large cargo butane market remains subdued, assessed at 84% February Naphtha.  MED Trans-Atlantic imports to the region remain high even though VLGCs are no longer transiting the Suez Canal. Over 550,000MT will be imported to the region in January, a 13 month high, with large imports from Dortyol to Mohammedia.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their sale tender for a 25-28th Feb lifting split cargo at CP minus mid-teens level. Saudi Aramco released their Feb acceptance with details remain sketchy, but we don’t expect producer to have spot avails as its trading arm was heard to buy Feb spot previously. At the time of writing, Feb C3 CP was traded at $580 and C4/C3 at $10, Feb/Mar CP was assessed at $9 backwardation.   FAR EAST The market seems more balanced this week after the hectic buyings from Chinese last week, which quite well absorbed the excess tons. Less offers were seen in window but more bids shown for 23kt propane parcels delivered in 2h Feb and 1h Mar. Cash differentials have improved from last week’s discount to premium level, with a couple of 23/0 parcels for 2h Feb delivery changed hand at Feb FEI plus $3 to $5 level. Feb FEI/CP narrowed down further this week to $23 only, down by 18$ vs last Monday, partly due to the decline in freight. Fei/MOPJ widened recent and some cracker are seen switching to LPG from Napatha for feedstock, however subject to run rates and ethylene margins. One SChina based cracker has issued tender to secure 11kt upto 45kt propane for late feb/1h Mar delivery.   The drastic drop in freight have also enticed some term discussion interests. Indonesia PERTAMINA called new term tender for split grade cargo monthly delivery from Apr to Dec. Last week a couple of PDH buy term tenders have heard awarded with details yet to know, but premium edged down as of cheaper logistics costs.

EAST Since Monday Eastern freight rates have fallen 25 dollars and now trades close to parity with the West. Although not usually the biggest driver, with current direction in the market there has been little incentive for charterers to make a move prior to Aramco dates. Tonnage availability should be plentiful once fixing gets restarted, but with Panama still being a somewhat accessible alternative for vessels going in ballast back to US, charterers need to keep in mind that vessels able to catch early February laycans in MEG soon may start their journey in the opposite direction.  WEST With the few latest fixtures done ex USG at levels from 100 and 105 H/C v Pan there are some signs of the western market possibly finding its feet again, but the vessel supply for what’s left of February still looks relatively lengthy. There are currently a handful of uncovered cargoes out there and some are already looking first decade March dates.

With January closed out and February yet to really kick off, rates in the MEG remain in limbo. Each consecutive deal able to chip a little off last done. TD3 sits at a little under WS 70, but deals are being confirmed a point or so below. Charterers looking to pick a target and enter the market quietly and efficiently. Therefore, without any open influx of February stems, rates may continue to feel the pressure as the MEG list looks well balanced.  Subtracting from the above-mentioned MEG list are a few unfixed ballasters (we count 9 or 10) heading for Cape, all by different owners. Therefore, increased competition will play a part. Low USD 10m's from the USG are earnings too good to turn down, the same argument applies to USD 9m. But USG/Caribs/Venezuela volumes for February have been low, we counted 30. Yes, February is a shorter month, but both December and January had 50+. Without returns to those levels, further softening of rates likely. But, given the Red Sea, this market can change quickly and Suezmaxes certainly showing little downside.

It has been a rather quiet start to 2024 on the cargo side. However, lots of activity on period front and operators are rushing to take in tonnage on the Handy and Supra market. 60/61k dwt vessels being fixed at around USD 14,000-15,000 levels for 1 year duration and Handy market hovers around high USD 11,000/12,000 for 1 year. Meantime, the usual Indonesia-India Supra being fixed around 8k levels, Indonesia-China on a Supra around USD 12,000. Pacific RV on Supra being done at low USD 10,000 levels and at mid to high USD 8,000 levels on Handy. Far East to Indian ocean/MEG on an Ultra paying around 7-8k levels and a backhaul trip around 7k on a Supra. Overall, market sentiment remains positive. Market will see some correction amidst the various geo-political developments over the past weeks.

The Panamax market is currently demonstrating a mixed outlook, influenced by regional dynamics. In the Pacific basin, robust coal shipments are helping maintain market levels. In contrast, the Atlantic region is facing varied trends: the North Atlantic is showing a softer trend due to excess tonnage despite a slight increase in demand, while the South Atlantic, particularly ECSA, is firmer with rising bids and showing signs of stabilization. The market overall is expected to remain stable in the coming weeks. However, concerns are growing due to recent attacks in the Red Sea, drawing significant industry focus and adding an element of caution as the market closely observes these developments and their potential implications.

NORTH Very quiet week in the North Sea with hardly any fixtures done for local runs. Owners ballasting to better returns in surrounding areas as both USG and Mediterranean more active and very firm. Sentiment says that rates should be under upward pressure as vessels depart, but so far rates have remained steady in the fixing window.  Increased activity needed to allow owners to push levels.  MEDITERRANEAN Activity in the Mediterranean this week with the positive USG trends translating into the Mediterranean; tighter tonnage and weather delays helping to firm the market. Black Sea rates have pushed up to a point where Suezmax have looked twice and steadied the Aframax drive, though with Suezmax markets looking positive there may still be some small gains to be had on the Aframaxes. Sentiment somewhat steadier but forward potential.

Houthi maritime attacks are beginning to impact the market with firmer numbers reported for MEG/West (this trend is likely to continue). Red Sea transits have been a cash cow for insurers and there is a case to be made that they won't push AWRP much higher as this risks driving all their business around the Cape, therefore we envisage a sweet spot approaching close to present levels.  The Atlantic is poised to push on from present levels with TD20 last done reported at WS 144 with no downside supported by a strong US market and spill over sentiment from the Red Sea.

We see a drop in overall C5 enquiries this week. Miners and some operators were seeking primarily late January to early February dates. On the East Australia coal and Pacific front, volume has somewhat maintained from last week. On South Africa and Indian business, we see several interests for early February dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, we see an uptick in enquiries for early to mid February dates. Far East tonnage is building up. Ballasting tonnage is heavily weighted for February. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at mid to high USD 7 pmt levels by midweek. On C3, we see offers at 21 pmt levels for early February and sub 20 pmt levels for mid February. There is resistance with bids seen at mid to high 18 pmt levels.

A subdued week for the tanker S&P market with a number of deals on hold behind the scenes. The unfolding situation in the Red Sea raises the question whether Sellers of large Crude tonnage could hold out and receive premium rates/price levels. This is coupled with the fact that without a very prompt delivery, Buyers would miss out on the best of the winter returns and would be unwilling to pay a premium to do so – resulting in a standoff. Smaller product carriers were the movers this week with ice 1A Handy Tankers DINAH/PLUTO 37K DWT HMD 2008 being sold by Tufton for USD 41.75M en bloc, booking them a sizeable profit on the units. Elsewhere, MR SOCHRINA 46K DWT SUNGDONG 2008 was bought by Besiktas for USD 24M.  A busy week in the Dry sector but in general the story remains the same, which is one of a significant lack of liquidity on modern tonnage. Rates are experiencing a seasonal dip, however, this does not translate to lower values. Quite the contrary for those available modern market units, with some owners taking advantage of the scarcity of candidates and indeed increasing their price expectations. With that in mind, in the one standout modern transaction of the week, scrubber fitted Newcastlemax MINERAL QINGDAO 206K DWT Qingdao Yangfan 2020 was bought by Winning for USD 54.25M. Otherwise Kamsarmax SUPER LUNA 81K DWT JINHAI HI 2016 sold to Modion at USD 22.6M, part of a very active week for ships of this size. Further down the size curve activity thrived with a number of Supramax units blt 07-12 transacted, helping price other candidates in which is a very competitive corner of the market.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS While an approximate 2.5mmbbl US propane inventory draw had generally been anticipated, the EIA this week reported a decline of 3.5mmbbls which brought the overall total stock level to 79.10mmbbls, or (just) 101% of last year’s total at the same time.  The reported figures came on the heels of a corrected set of data which was revealed two weeks ago and at that time brought inventory levels down by 9mmbbls, a rather staggering drop.   It should therefore be of little surprise that MB propane values have – over the same period of time – made their way up from the mid 60cpg range to the over 77cpg as of this writing, and most are of the impression that with a looming large-scale winter storm that is set to bring North American temperatures to sub-freezing levels over the next week should very likely result in yet still further pricing gains.   Meanwhile, the market has been reeling from wildly volatile arb levels and fantastic declines in freight rates, which are the result of issues at the Panama Canal and, more recently, at the Suez Canal in the Red Sea.    Terminal fees, all the while, have been resting around the mid 6cpg range for late Jan through late Feb business, and while a few transactions have been reported, it is generally a thinly traded market.  NWE An offer in the TOT window has pushed the physical discount to CIF ARA -$8/MT for 20-24 January delivery. Continued offers in the TOT window for January deliveries continue to put pressure on physical values. Forecasted cold weather is expected to reach the region is keeping the demand picture positive. The relative low value of natural gas has Dutch TTF prices below CIF ARA propane and butane values on an MMBTU basis. Supporting North Sea LPG exports rather than rejecting LPG into the gas stream. Butane value has been steady for some time through lack of deals, remaining at 81.5% January Nahptha  MED A change in Morrocan import pricing formula for 2024 reflects the ratios of imports in 2023. Imports tedners have been released with pricing wieghted 70% towards MT Belveiu pricing and 30% CIF ARA.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Discussions on evenly split cargo for Feb lifting softened this week with offer heard at CP minus mid-single digit. A Feb FOB was rumored to change hand at CP minus 20, which is yet to be confirmed. At the time of writing, Feb C3 CP was traded at $578 and C4 at $10 higher. Feb/Mar CP was traded at -7$ backwardation. ADNOC released their term lifting schedule with no cuts heard but some got advanced. And Qatar Petroleum tendered to sell a late Feb lifting 22/22 cargo.   FAR EAST The decline in flat price finally enticed the buying interests. A flurry of tenders from China have been floating in the market this week. At least five lots of 46kt propane have been sold into China at the range of Feb FEI minus high single to low teens level basis East to NChina. There is another buy tender for Feb propane into SChina ongoing and we are expecting at least one more PDH player to procure Feb feedstock. As Feb FEI/CP narrowing down, the CFR east value is in equivalent to CP plus around $20 only, which is more favored now compared to Iranian cargo with less price advantages. In addition to the Chinese purchase, several traders were bidding in window for 23kt propane parcel basis Chiba of 2h Feb delivery at Feb FEI minus mid single digit.   Apart from spot tenders, the drastic drop in freight have also attracted the attention on term discussions. We’ve seen three term buy tenders, with one inquiring for monthly 46kt propane from Feb to Jun delivery into NChina, one for monthly 23kt or 46kt propane from this Mar to next year Mar delivery into SChina, and the last for monthly 11/11 from Mar to Dec delivery basis SChina also.

EAST The East market took a nosedive yesterday following the trend in the West. Considering East is still trading at a premium the risk remain on the downside. Adnoc dates was published yesterday with reports of some advancements. February fixing would likely commence next week. With the risk of sounding repetitive, although most of the ships on the East position list could look west, the down trending market coupled with excess tonnage is bound to keep freight in a negative spiral.   WEST With the arb narrowing a lot lately we have also seen freight in free fall as a result. On Tuesday we recorded the biggest ever drop on the BLPG3 route at 33 dollars while we yesterday found western freight rates at its lowest since August 2023. In total we have only seen 8 spot fixtures for February dates ex USG/USEC - same time last year we had seen over twice as many for Feb.

We see a drop in C5 enquiries this week, mostly with late January dates. On the East Australia coal and Pacific front, volume remains steady from last week. On South Africa and Indian business, we see limited enquiries for late January dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, we see dampened volumes as well; majority of outstanding enquiries have first half of February dates. The Far East and ballasting tonnage seem to be building up. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at low to mid USD 8 pmt levels by midweek. On C3, we see limited fixtures concluding at high USD 23 pmt levels for early to mid-February dates. One known fixture of a 179k dwt, 2010-build, non scrubber for 9 to 11 months at USD 23,800 per day.

All eyes have been on the USG market as the candidates for local runs look few and far between. Owners continue to push rates higher though with predominantly relet based tonnage we haven't seen the full effects of the USG pull as we have done in the Mediterranean. It remains to be seen if 3rd decade stems will be busy in this region, as dates push out, owners are hoping rates will move upwards too.  The Mediterranean Aframax market continues to show the potential for positive trends in rates, with poor weather affecting itineraries on the few ships that are not being enticed by trade over in the States. Lack of supply or business done off market might stem the increase in rates but should demand increase, then pressure on rates is likely to continue to strengthen the market. Black Sea trade was tested up this week and may well continue with inclement weather causing delays/closures in the Turkish Straits.

Based on the latest reports, thermal coal demand in Asia remains subdued. Additionally, the South American grain export season has yet to start. These factors have contributed to the weakening of the market as expected.  Regarding the seasonal average market development, the market is expected to reach a bottom in either week 5 or week 6. However, it is important to note that the market is subject to fluctuations and can be influenced by a variety of factors.

Start of 2024 is unfolding as expected and with the fixing window moving into February, we see the LNG commodity market itself is weakening. The Pacific basin was active this week, with several requirements throughout February; however, there is abundant vessel availability so charter rates continue to soften. Fixing activity in the Atlantic basin remains quiet, marked by a lack of firm requirements and there is considerable uncertainty regarding the market's direction in the weeks ahead. There are ongoing issues around scheduling due to weather conditions causing delays and missed laycans, although the flurry of activity around the new year appears to have resolved the most urgent situations. Furthermore, the situation in the Red Sea remains a challenge for the shipping industry. Many charterers have chosen to use the Cape route to mitigate the risk of attacks. Northern Europe is experiencing very low temperatures, although with current storage levels at 84% it's unlikely to have a major impact in the short-term. On the project side, Energos has purchased two 2021-built 174,000m3 FSRUs from Dynagas, and Nakilat is engaging in fleet renewal and expansion with an order for two 174,000m³ LNG carriers in Korea.

For another week, we see a steady decline in rates for Supra–Ultramax tonnage. Though the cargo flow from the US Gulf and South America remains steady, charterers keep pushing the rates down due to the extensive number of ships opening in the area. Trips from ECSA to Far East fixing at USD 16,000 pd plus USD 600,000 GBB pd. Transatlantic trips pay USD 27,000 pd on modern Ultra basis delivery USG. Oversupply of tonnage in the Continent and Black Sea areas significantly decreased spot rates. Supramax fixing scrap from the North Continent to Turkey at USD 18,500 pd. There are undoubtedly fewer spot cargoes, and the holiday season has an impact on the slow and bearish market. Trips from Mediterranean to ECSA are fixed at a low USD 10,000 pd. Supramax 55’ dwt fixed TCT to China at USD 22,000 pd.

A busy, breathless week. Plenty of fixing as WS rates moving up WS 10 points since the start of the year. Mainly due to the Atlantic excitement. At the time of writing, TD3C sits just below WS 70, but the MEG market taking a back seat. January volume is closing out with a healthy figure close to the 140 level, so another 10 or so deals to come. We are nearing the end of January dates and the quieter twilight zone between months, so rates likely to level out for the time being.  However, the Atlantic holding all the cards. Sinokor beginning to flex their Atlantic muscles, having taken 5-6 ships on spot voyages, quick subjects, with no cargoes attached. They now ready to work these vessels, fixing one ex EC Mexico to India, but a few more still to fix. With highest they paid at USD 9.7m USG to Ningbo, providing any potential demurrage bill is minimalized, they should be in the money, as we rating TD22 USG/Ningbo at USD 10m. USD 5m has been paid USG/UKC, and West Africa reports at WS 75 done, but not widely believed, as Bitr TD15 still around the WS 72.5 level. Rates? – We are still low on fixture volume for February in both West Africa and USG, and a lot will depend on Sinokor frame of mind and charterers attitude. Likely a little steadying in the short term but certainly little downside.

The East market has been quiet on the surface with the vast majority of business being done off market, which has done nothing to support rates in the region (OTC markets require noise otherwise they die). Despite the best efforts of tanker-terrorists in the Red Sea, TD 23 continues to soften with last done pricing WS 80 (23 flats). MEG/East appears stuck in limbo with a MEG/China run likely to trade circa WS 130-135 (24 flats).  In the West, the USG/East arb is still wide open which has resulted in a deluge of enquiry from the US Gulf being smoked into the open market. This will further support rates in the wider Atlantic with no evident downside for now.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Generally speaking the domestic US market has seen a slow start to 2024 as market participants have returned to the desk but have so far been engaged in finalizing their respective 2023 books.    While there has lately been in North America some weather-related demand, and export volumes are at a respectably healthy 1.720mmbbls/day (off from 1.882mmbbls in the previous EIA report), overall US stock levels for the week ending 29 Dec were given at 82.6mmbbls, or 2.1mmbbls lower than the previous week’s reported data.  Market expectations varied widely, but in the end a pragmatic prediction of an approximate 2.5mmbbl decline was deemed reasonable, and thus the 2.1mmbbl drop was considered appropriate.  As such, Mont Belvieu propane prices for Jan have not reacted much and remain in the upper 60cpg range.  Terminal fees, though largely untested so far this year, are expected to have remained in the mid/single digit range of around 6cpg.  NWE The TOT window has been quite to start the year, the reduction of US exports transiting the region as they avoid the Suez Canal has reduced window offers. Also causing the East West spread to narrow from $165/MT yesterday to $158/MT today. An increase in petchem demand in the region from 340,000MT in November to 420,000MT in December is a welcome boost of demand as mild winter weather has kept seasonal demand low. An increase in North Sea LPG production, due to LPG’s premium to Natural Gas halted rejection, has accounted for part of this new petchem demand. Large cargo butane trades have been absent from the market leaving value assessed at 81.5% January Naphtha.  MED The mild temperatures for the most part this winter have kept stocks in the region at healthy levels. While the large volume US imports have been accounting for any new demand.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco set Jan C3 and C4 CP at $620 and $630, up by $10 respectively. Some end users reckoned the price is lower than expectation with the anticipation of less supply due to oil cuts and rumored maintenance ex Yanbu liftings.    At the time of writing, Feb C3 CP was assessed at $617 and C4 at $10 higher. Feb/Mar was traded at $10 backwardation. Evenly split cargo for Feb lifting was assessed at CP flattish level without fresh deals reported since last done before new year holiday.    FAR EAST Muted activities in window as most players are away from holidays. 23kt C3 parcel for 2h Feb delivery was bid at the equivalence of Feb FEI minus mid/high single digit, while outside window similar parcel for 1h Feb delivery was heard changed hand at Feb FEI minus small single digit. 46kt parcel was reported sold into Ningbo at Feb FEI minus 5$ with sketchy details, while other bids for similar parcel at high single discount.   Outside window one EChina petchem player issued buy tender for 46kt C3 delivered during 4-10th Feb, which is believed shall receive aggressive offers as limited players willing to import during/before CNY period. We have a couple of new PDHs expected to start up in Jan, hopefully can run stable and import regularly from 2h Feb or Mar onwards, with sustainable margins, if any.

EAST January fixing should be more than halfway through, and we are currently seeing cargoes fixed around the 20th of January. The positions list looks relatively populous, but many are expected to sail West - at least while East is still trading at a discount. Acceptances for February are also looming but so far there should be more deals done for end January dates before we jump into next month.   WEST On the current position list more or less every ship arriving US the first 20 days of February are coming in ballast via Cape. There is still one ship left in the very end of Jan and she is coming via Panama as she is a Pmax. We currently count 6 spot fixtures for Feb dates ex US with last done at mid 260s H/C v Cape. The west is still trading a premium of approximately 5 dollars.

With stormy weather hitting the North Sea we have seen some weather delays over the Xmas and New Year’s period. Charterers have searched the tonnage list for vessels with safe itineraries to avoid delays. This combined with a firming USG market with tonnage likely to ballast out of the area, will maintain rates at current levels, at least up to mid-month January dates.   It’s a tough start to 2024 in the Mediterranean with supply coming slow. Tonnage is top heavy with a mass of prompt ships that will look for opportunities elsewhere with the Mediterranean yet to spark excitement. Not much hope for owners this side of the weekend with rates to remain steady with downward pressure whilst demand continues to outweigh supply, making a rising USG market all the more enticing for owners.

There is not much action in the market on the first trading week after the New Year celebrations. The soft tone presents, where USG seems to be most affected. Oversupply in the Atlantic and slow demand in the Pacific decreased the rates. Escalating conflict in the Red Sea and the Black Sea adds to the uncertainty in the market direction. The evidence of less demand in USG and South Atlantic putting pressure on rates. The Baltic BSI routes on S1 and S4 dropped by approx USD 2,000 pd a day. In the Pacific, a similar situation with weak demand and a slow start of the year pushed owners to accept lower rates. Inter Pacific trading around USD 10,000 pd.

We see fresh enquiries from miners and operators on C5 for mid-late January dates. On the East Australia coal and Pacific front, volume seems to be dampened. On South Africa and Indian business, we see some enquiries primarily for late January stems. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, we see a healthy volume for late January to February dates. Far East tonnage levels seem to be on the rise. Ballasting tonnage weighs on late January to early February. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at low to mid USD 10 pmt levels over the course of the week. On C3, we see limited fixtures concluding at USD 29 pmt levels for 2nd half of January. There is resistance between bids and offers with many adopting a wait and see approach.

A shorter week as 2024 kicks in and rates continue to drift further south. At the time of writing, MEG/China clings to the WS 50’s (on 2023 flats), but this line in the sand will likely be tested as the week draws on. Tonnage is plentiful and TCE’s remain decent, so there is scope for owners to consider below last done. Charterers continue to pick targets from the shadows, so deals going unreported, but January is already up to 100+ deals and the 3rd decade yet to be touched.   The Atlantic is a little different. Plenty of ships still (we count 12 sitting prompt), but owners are trying to play the waiting game. Aframaxes firming in the USG, and Suezmaxes also starting to move positive. So, dollars/bbl could soon look attractive on a VLCC. Mind you, there are quite a few VL’s there to soak this up. A West Africa cargo being worked, attracting few offers, and the Petrobras deal fixing a vessel from the US West coast at WS 55.25 East and WS 64 UKCM, dragging us onto the new 2024 WS rates. The smaller sizes need to move up a bit quicker to help out their bigger sisters.

It has been a quiet start to the New Year in the West, with a lack of firm requirements in the basin and general muted market activity following the public holiday period. This is typically the period when rates come off, although the lull could be short lived following the harsh weather that is prevailing through North West Europe, which has been and is expected to continue disrupting schedules. Moreover, with the ongoing challenges in the Red Sea, it will be interesting to see how shipping activity in the Atlantic responds and whether we see a response over the coming days as players seek prompt tonnage to address interferences. Such circumstances have the potential to disrupt the current softening market rates, given the shortage of modern vessels available in the West, especially if Owners withdraw tonnage amidst prevailing uncertainties.   The picture in the East is quite different, as Owners finds themselves engaged with several firm requirements for tonnage across various sizes and specifications, whilst potential developing opportunities also draw attention. With vessel availability high East of Suez, there has been a corresponding lowering in charter rates. While the possibility of a slowing decline exists if the cold weather persists in North Asia and demand increases, the current trend is marked by heightened competition. On the term side, the past week has seen limited activity. However, as charter rates become more attractive to Charterers, we can expect to see increased interest in term vessel availability over the coming weeks. There were no reported LNG newbuilding orders this week, however, we note a USD 1.5 billion order for a FLNG unit at Samsung. LNG newbuild prices remain stable.

The year begins with a downward trend in the Panamax market, particularly in the Atlantic, where tonnage oversupply has led to a drop in rates. Fleet distribution is skewed with a historic low West of Suez. A rebound is expected in February with the South American grain exports.  The market is muted in both basins, with a decrease in tonnage in the North and thin spot rates in the South. The general sentiment is cautious, awaiting market direction after the holiday lull.

The Suezmax market is slowly waking from its holiday slumber, with an emphasis on "slowly". In the East, there has been a less than auspicious start with the only signs of life coming from short-haul Indian cargoes. TD23 "should" have been the big story to kick start 2024, with the Red Sea slap bang in the middle of the headline. But thus far, and despite the furore, rates are unlikely to reflect much upside (if any). We are pricing that run at circa WS 80 (2023 basis flatrates).  Despite an overtly well stocked tonnage list, the Atlantic is a tad more positive with present TD20 rates holding up well (WS 107.5 basis 2023 flatrates). Support also comes from the USG where TA runs may yet bring some further New Year cheer.

Whether it’s due to the holiday season or it’s simply the normal murkiness that pervades our market, things are especially opaque in LNG Shipping at present. This has led to some significant spreads between fixtures concluded over the last few weeks, and in turn it further complicates the picture for Charterers who are looking to take tonnage now. In the West, at least one party is seeking a vessel for 2H January but with a comparable last done concluding at under $100k pdpr (on a 2-Stroke) it’s hard to reconcile the mid $100k numbers being shown on similar dates. It might be that geopolitical risks are to blame here, and just as we see shipping stocks rise and fall on the news of “who is and who isn’t avoiding the Suez”, so too are Owners and Charterers fixing ideas affected. In the East, recent business has been steam ship centred, and this might explain the sizeable discount to the fixtures completed in the Atlantic, but with another Pacific charterer now looking to cover a beginning of February cargo on a bigger vessel, we should have a new price point with which to commence proceedings in 2024. As always, a number of moving parts in this business and we are constantly reminded that every requirement is unique!  Putting the market aside for now, we thank you all for your support during 2023 and we wish you a peaceful and prosperous 2024. Happy Fixing!

A lot more activity on the Indian Ocean and the Pacific side last week prior holiday season with more cargo orders flowing in. Hearing WC India-China Supra voyages being fixed at last done levels. The usual Indonesia-India trips being fixed around 10k levels. ECSA-Far East Supra trips being fixed around 23k levels. With the coal & grain season coming to an end, we can expect to see a seasonal slowdown in the coming weeks. Position lists still have plenty on offer, especially in the Pacific, but even here rates are holding well – however, people are happy, or resigned, to pay what it says on the ticket. As we near the end of the holiday season, we can expect more activity in the coming week.

We see volumes holding consistent with enquiries from miners and operators on C5 for mid-January dates. On the East Australia coal and Pacific front, we see several fresh enquiries and an uptick in volumes from previous week. On South Africa and Indian business, we see limited enquiries primarily for mid to late January stems. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, we see enquiries for mid to late January. Far East tonnage seems to be slightly tight. Ballasting tonnage weighs heavily on mid-January onwards. On C5, we see conclusions at high USD 10 pmt at start of week and mid USD 10 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we see limited fixtures concluding at USD 25 pmt levels for 2nd half of January and several adopting a wait and see approach.

Geopolitical events continue to wreak havoc in the Red Sea as charterers increasingly ask for Cape of Good Hope options causing thirsty refineries in the West to quickly reorganize their import schedules. Backhaul rates are the main beneficiary of this disruption with Cape rates probably trading close to WS 85-90.  In the Atlantic, there will be some positive spillover from events in the Red Sea at some stage, but with the market stuck in the twilight zone (betwixt Christmas and New year), we will have to wait for the market to properly awaken from its holiday slumber in early January to see the full benefits.

A quiet Christmas break for the VLCCs as tonnage has risen for the next 30 days over the festive period. Still there are early cargoes being worked ex MEG. Second decade barely touched, and we should see some more activity here over the next few days. Middle East troubles continue with reports of a drone which has been reported to have been fired from Iran, hitting a tanker in the Indian Ocean. Let's hope it doesn’t escalate any further, but this market could fly at any moment with tensions still high, but for the time being we still should see a weaker market in general going forward. West volumes lagging especially from USG, but a lifeline from the smaller siblings (Suez/Afra) could help owners as there are relatively few ballasters from the East at the time of writing.

As the year draws to a close, market has been quiet this week and there is not much activity to report East or West. Market looking strong with last done deals at mid 270s H/C v Cape and mid 130s RT/C.

The Panamax market has shown mixed signals over the past week, with a correction due to abundant available tonnage and limited inquiries. Freight rates from the Continent to the Far East remained stable at USD 39/tonne. Since July, the Panama Canal's reduced transit capacity to 32 daily transits (regular daily transit is between 38 and 40) has significantly influenced the market. Additionally, the market in the Pacific was subdued, with limited fresh inquiry from Asia, notably from Indonesia and NoPac, affecting rates and demand. This overall decline in demand and the continuous decrease in Panamax ballasters highlight the current challenges with a simultaneous decline in supply and demand. This can lead to a more balanced or stagnant market rather than a clear benefit to owners or charterers.

Last week of the year and the activity in both the North Sea and the Mediterranean has been slow after last week's fixing frenzy that helped owners to push rates higher than last-done levels on every fixture. Sentiment is positive but with charterers having fixed well-ahead into next year we might see some quiet days next week. Overall, the end of the year find owners enjoying healthy returns while the uncertainties and geopolitical risks that are growing could add more fuel to the fire.

The unfolding situation in the Red Sea, coupled with the upcoming festive break, meant the S&P market had a rather quiet week. Sellers can be forgiven, as the ramifications of the Red Sea disruption could yet dramatically change price expectations when the market returns to full capacity in the New Year. In a sub-sector that has largely struggled for liquidity in the latter half of the year, scrubber fitted Suezmax SERENEA (158K DWT SAMSUNG HI 2009) sold this week for USD 45.5M. Elsewhere, a trio of 2008-2009 blt MRs sold, helping price other units circulating in the market.  Modern tonnage in the dry market has been hard to come by for most, and this week’s transactions are symptomatic of this. That said, there remains much optimism in the sector going into the New Year, with Capesize rates ticking along around USD 20k/day. The hope will be that momentum can be maintained despite the upcoming Chinese New Year celebrations in early February.

EAST Christmas is just around the corner which usually slow things down for a bit, and the last Baltic print for the year will be this coming Friday the 22nd of December.   Yesterday proved to be a day of heightened activity, and currently, a few cargoes remain uncovered. The prevailing sentiment indicates a growing momentum that suggests an upward trajectory in freight rates today. While there's a cargo on End December dates in the works, the primary focus has swiftly shifted to the middle of January. At the time of writing, we have recorded 9 spot fixtures - 3 of these concluded by Indian PSU.  WEST This week we have seen a good amount of spot fixtures in the west, and we can now count 30 deals for January dates ex USG/USEC. Recent challenges in the Red Sea, coupled with draught issues in Panama, have forced most Owners to send their vessels via Cape from the East to the US. Freight rates are on the rise and the vessel supply is looking tight before shifting focus towards February fixing and Christmas Holidays.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The resiliency of MB propane prices is remarkable given that in spite of this week’s EIA inventory data which revealed a 2.2mmbbbl draw, it brought overall US stock levels to 93.7mmbbls, or 107% of last year and 134% of two years ago.  This is without mentioning that the weather outlook for North America through the balance of December is calling for generally un-winter-like temperatures and for only limited levels of precipitation.  MB non-TET propane is today valued at ~67cpg, having dipped to around 65cpg in mid-Dec.  Crude values are providing support, but WTI prices are effectively unchanged over the balance of December, and propane export volumes are recorded this week at 1.812mmbbls/day – which is up from last week, but off from the more than 2mmbbls/day reported earlier in the month, and overall volumes are not expected to see a surge of any kind through the end of ’23.  Meanwhile, terminal fees were seen at 7.50cpg for end-Dec – and while 1H Jan has seen little (or no) activity, 2H Jan values are off just a bit, with offers presumably in the 7cpg range, and lower for a mixed-ratio parcel.  Otherwise, the ongoing issues at the Panama Canal and, more recently, in the Red Sea, have conspired to force overwater volumes to the longer, more expensive Cape of Good Hope route, which – when paired with a generally weak Asian market - has made for a difficult trading period and forced some participants to the sidelines.  NWE  Few VLGCs will go East via Suez due to the risk of attack reducing the number of large cargo offers into the region, by traders hoping to get their vessels back promptly. Import volume for December is expected to be around 370,000 MT, low for the time of year, with January import volumes projected to be similar. Though TOT bid for a mid-Jan delivery is supporting the market somewhat, the physical tons remain discounted, assessed at January CIF ARA -$2/MT. A  repeated large cargo butane offer in the window has pushed values down from 92.5% balance December Naphtha to 82.5% today.   MED  Higher than average temperatures in the region are keeping demand in check. The reduction of VLGCs transiting the region due to the risk of attack in Suez will see less transitory offers.

This week's Panamax market shows a general downtrend due to the off-season for coal and grain shipments, and uncertainties in soybean exports. Minor uplifts may arise from China's cold weather and slight recoveries in grain shipments. The North Atlantic remains quiet with limited cargo, while the Pacific faces challenges with an oversupply of ships. The Atlantic shows modest improvements in rates, especially for deferred positions, but overall market corrections are evident due to an excess of available tonnage and limited demand.

We see volumes holding consistent with enquiries from miners and operators on C5 for early January dates. On the East Australia coal and Pacific front, volumes have increased slightly from previous week albeit scarce. On South Africa and Indian business, we see limited enquiries primarily for mid-January stems. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, we see enquiries for full January with a heavy focus on mid-January. Far East tonnage is moderately tight. Ballasting tonnage is increasing and weights heavily on mid-January onwards. On C5, activity level is healthy with fixtures concluding at low to mid USD 12 levels by midweek. On C3, we see fixtures concluding at USD 24 levels for early January and resistance between offers and bids for mid to late January.

NORTH An active end to last week, and the start of this week has seen the natural North Sea tonnage with safe itineraries being picked off, tightening the list and pushing dates out towards end month. We have seen some weather delays, and with surrounding areas looking attractive and firming tonnage is likely to ballast out of the area, this combination will further tighten the list and put some more pressure on freight rates.   MEDITERRANEAN A flurry of activity has firmed Mediterranean Aframax throughout this week. With the activity and lists at least off prompter dates beginning to tighten, owners look to keep the pressure on for higher numbers though that being said, next week could be quiet and this time of year always leaves room for a ship to be wrapped up at last done rates in time for Christmas. Continued consistent supply has potential for higher numbers as rates are only moving in one direction.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Premium for evenly split cargos rebounded this week, with Feb lifting FOBs traded at CP flattish level reportedly. The reason being was the tighter supply due to crude cuts and some planned maintenance from AG producers, which volume affected yet to be known. At the time of writing, Jan C3 CP was assessed at $617 and C4 at $15 higher. Jan/Feb CP was traded at $2 contango.   FAR EAST Spot discounts deepened amid muted discussions. Off window 23kt propane for 2h Jan delivery was reported traded at Jan FEI minus mid 20s, and bids or offers were barely seen in the window, perhaps due to the coming holiday.   Outside window several petchem players emerged to procure feedstock propane for Jan to early Feb delivery. One SChina PDH user secured 46kt propane for Jan delivery at Jan CP plus high 40s, while another two Echina based players procured 23kt propane each at Jan FEI minus mid-teens. One Korean importer also tendered to buy 23kt propane for early Feb delivery.   To the contrary of spot discussion, term negotiations in China are stagnant as of the high cash differentials caused by the rising freight and potential supply deficit. The poor margins in both petchem and residential segment have refrained the buying interests and we might see active spot inquiries for later Feb delivery (after CNY period).

At last, some life in the Western markets, and the USG has finally got going from the doldrums where we were last week. Last done for this market now is 145 x WS 82.5 over to West Africa, and it’s slowed down somewhat as we move into early January laycans with the charterers keeping quite some mild pressure on the rates. Last done we have seen in Angola/UKCM fix at WS 90 off the 1st of January, but we are expecting the market to move up a touch given the positive sentiment amongst the Suezmax owners here in the West. There are bouts of bad weather in the North and over the Atlantic which will undoubtedly help owners to push on for more with the delays/impacts the weather will have on tonnage. Over in the MEG, the rates have firmed significantly for any MEG/West cargoes transiting the Red Sea, which is no surprise given developments there. We have seen the Basrah/UKCM market jump some 20 points over the week to 140 x WS 90 levels now for 1st decade January fixing. MEG/East remains steady in the 130 x WS 155-120 range.

Positions seems to be covered ahead of holidays approaching therefor market been rather flat with bear action both in the Atlantic and the Pacific. There were fixtures done at below last done in USG while ECSA seemed to still hold up due to some tight laycans and lack of tonnage for those dates. Bit more cargo flows from NoPac otherwise flat in the East as well. All eyes on Red Sea situation and how that would eventually start impacting the market going further.

The winter spot market this year has proven to be notably subdued when compared to recent years, lacking any significant spikes.  Sentiments have softened again, marked by spot fixtures concluded at levels lower than the preceding week. The current lack of demand and limited arbitrage opportunities has contributed to an increase in vessel availability, exerting downward pressure on spot rates. Subletters with shipping capacity are actively pursuing opportunities and vying for cargoes. LNG prices have also decreased, primarily attributed to ample inventories despite declining temperatures in the North Asia region.  In contrast, the escalating daily situation in the Red Sea has encouraged an increasing number of companies to redirect their vessels away from the Suez Canal and sail via the Cape of Good Hope. This heightened risk of further attacks may result in a temporary surge in tonne/miles and might create additional demand for shipping. With a weaker spot market, rate projections for multi-month and up to one-year term periods have also softened. As the year draws to a close, market participants remain on the sidelines, anticipating decisions for the upcoming year. No new orders were reported this week, however newbuilding prices remained stable.  In closing, for those celebrating Christmas, wishing you a celebration filled with joy and happiness.

A bit of an East/West divide has developed in the V-market over the week. A tightening tonnage list in the East, with plenty going on under the radar and several ships on subs with no details attached. Rates are still mid WS 50's TD3C, but there is limited downside. Only 29 modern ships on the water free of cargo, which should spur any owner to head straight up to the MEG when passing Galle as opposed to ballast towards the Atlantic on spec. Albeit marginally, Baltic numbers all came in green yesterday so a possible uptick for MEG/East could be in the cards in the coming days, once the Christmas holiday has passed. Tonnage supply in the Atlantic is a tad more plentiful. However, both the Suezmax and Aframax segments is showing promise, which should rub off on their larger sisters eventually.

Much of the tanker story this week was to do with an attack on Norwegian owned STST tanker STRINDA 20K DWT FUKUOKA 2006, which was struck by a missile in the Red Sea. Fortunately, there were no injuries sustained but the narrative here is one of increased disruption to a very busy shipping lane, and further unpredictability in an already mercurial market. Aframax AEGEAN POWER 115K DWT SAMSUNG HI 2007 was privately sold at a very firm price of USD 41M, which will fuel speculation over whether this is a new benchmark, or whether there were other factors at play. Elsewhere ice 1B handy tanker BLUE TRADER 37K DWT HMD 2005 sold to Turkish Buyers at USD 17.4M.  Eagle Bulk shares were the big winner this week in the dry market following the announcement of an all-stock acquisition by Star Bulk. The combined company will boast a total fleet of 169 bulkers and over USD 2BN in market cap. On the vessel side, 7 sales kept the market ticking over with the most significant being 3x Capesize units MINERAL TEMSE/DESTELBERGEN/BRUGGE 175K DWT NEW TIMES 2010/2011 bought by EGPN for total of USD 63.5M. With seasonal slowdown expected over Christmas/New Year and then Chinese New Year, market players will be keen to tie up as many deals as possible in the next week.

text: MEG Evenly split cargo for Jan lifting is still assessed at CP minus low teens. Sentiment subdued with no fresh buying inquiries from India. Swap value swings in high volatility following the crude. By the time of writing, Jan C3 CP was traded at $604 and C4 at $15 higher, Jan/Feb was at $10 backwardation.   FAR EAST With limited spot buying inquiries, cash differentials plunged further. 23kt propane parcel for 1h Jan delivery was offered Jan FEI minus $23, and similar parcel for 2h period at minus $18 while bid at minus $40. Off window a couple of full propane cargos placed into EChina was reported done at FEI minus mid teens level.   One NChina PDH importer awarded four cargos for monthly 46kt propane from Mar to Jun delivery at FEI plus mid high teens via term tender reportedly. And we are still waiting another three petchem players’ term tender result, however it is reckoned that the discussed premium would be higher than this year, at teens level mostly to FEI, as of higher freight and uncertainties over Panama transits, together with tighter supply against new demand from petchem expansions.    Other than propane, PERTAMINA was reported to award an evenly split cargo for mid Jan delivery at Jan CP plus 60s. And Hyosung Vina was reported to buy a heavy propane cargo for Jan delivery also at Jan CP plus mid high 50s.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The EIA this week reported an overall propane inventory total of 95.9mmbbls, revealing a 1.1mmbbl decline from the previous week.  The market had generally been anticipating around a 2mmbbl draw, but while export volumes were off (1.7mmbbls/day from 2.0mmbbbls/day), domestic demand requirements increased and thus only the modest drop.  The reduced export rate may also be related to overland deliveries to Mexico, which – due to lower production there – has recently given cause for additional rail/truck/pipe deliveries.   At the same time last year US propane stock levels were 90.3mmbbls.  In spite of many market expectations, the weight of the inventory levels has not (yet) caused Mont Belvieu propane values to commensurately decline as crude continues to mill about on either side of $70/bbl and weather-related demand is simultaneously providing domestic support.   Meanwhile, terminal fees were notionally bobbing along in the mid-single-digit range until a late Dec fixture confirmed the level.  Very little has been accomplished for 1H Jan, but a mid/2H Jan fixture was reported in the upper single-digits, prompting offers to be significantly increased amid a late-breaking demand flurry.  NWE No bids or offer were shown in the TOT window this week, leaving the physical market assessed at December CIF ARA minus $5/MT. December import volumes are expected to be low, around 260,000MT due to the mild winter so far and low petchem demand. For comparison 475,000MT of LPG were imported in November while 550,000MT were imported in October. While imports are low the physical TOT discount shows demand is being covered and reflects the low demand environment. The arb from the US is open, and we expect to see a larger volume of imports in January. Butane demand remains firm with levels at 92.5% December Naphtha.     MED US VLGC imports to the East Med have been rising with 3 VLGCs set to arrive in Dortyol in the last decade of December. The West of the region has been relatively quiet, the mild start to winter reducing demand

EAST With a handful of remaining vessels available on December dates, there might be questions why freight rates are not declining further. However, a $20 discount in the East appears to have established a freight floor. It's important to be reminded of the increasing number of ships sailing via the Suez Canal, leading to a potentially misleading impression of freight availability. While there are few cargos fixed into next month so far, ongoing discussions are now primarily focused on January dates.  WEST Western freight rates are on the rise again and we are currently seeing a few uncovered cargoes out there. 8 of the 17 ships on the western position list for Jan (+ end Dec) are also MEG candidates. In total we have seen 18 spot fixtures ex USG/USEC for January dates - avg last three months at 32 spot fixtures. Last done at 250 H/C v Suez and 206 v Pan.

Strong Atlantic market keeps positive trend though the number of ballaster continues to increase. Fronthaul in USG on Ultra was fixed for a trip to India with Petcoke above USD 60,000 pd and about USD 50,000 pd for clean cargo to the Far East with a long duration. Trips across the Atlantic were paying in the region USD 50,000 pd for the trip with coal to Continent and low USD 30,000 pd for grain cargoes with longer duration. All other markets in the Atlantic, including ECSA, Black Sea, and Continent, have good demand, and rates are firm. Fronthaul on Ultramax delivery Brazil was fixed at USD 17,500 pd + 750,000 GBB to China. In Far East, though, we had a very short life of a good market before it started to soften again. Rates fall by USD 2,000-3,000 pd on most of the Pacific routes. Nopac RV with grain was fixed at USD 13,000 compared to the fixture, which was reported a week ago at USD 17,000. The same Indonesia-China RV is now fixed at USD 10,000 pd compared to USD 13,000 pd from last week.

The Panamax market is experiencing diverse trends. In the North Atlantic, a surplus of vessels has led to a softer market, giving charterers the upper hand to negotiate lower rates and favorable terms. This scenario contrasts with the South Atlantic, which is performing well due to increased activity and higher rates driven by regional demands. In Asia, the market is mixed with pressures on Indonesian coal routes, yet there's potential for growth in the southern regions. Overall, the market is cautious, shaped by regional disparities in supply and demand.

NORTH A very quiet week so far in the North Sea Aframax market. This is mainly due to the bigger sizes taking a fair share of the December volumes away and also too many available relets being programmed for own cargoes. Some cargoes being worked under the radar or being worked on forward dates. Despite this coupled with some owners looking to ballast to the USG, we still need more activity to put upward pressure on rates.    MEDITERRANEAN Despite some premium inclined vessels ballasting out of the Mediterranean, tonnage remains sufficient for the time being, as dates begin to move forward. Suezmax have absorbed a significant amount of Ceyhan bbls for December and as a result Afra's look to seek out alternatives. Rates feel bottomy in the Mediterranean though with continued ballasters a burst in activity could turn the tide.

One could argue this week has been a bit of a fire sale. Looking at the Atlantic, owners consistently fixing below last done, despite plenty of volume. Lists don’t lie and due to a few weeks of quiet in the region, tonnage has built, leaving owners little choice but to aggressively compete. Rates for USG/Ningbo drifting from USD 9.5m last week to present rates at around the USD 8m level. One could argue there is also a desire for both owners and charterers to clear their desks before the Christmas period.   As for the Middle East liftings, we have seen rates drift from the mid WS 60’s to current levels of 10 points less. Still, TCE’s remain very respectable across the board, so it's all relative. At present, we sit in the gap between December and January (with a few charterers already dipping their toes in to the new year) so owners will hope for an influx prior to the Christmas break, to at least arrest any further declines. But likely a little more pain before the tide turns.

Global high inventory levels, coupled with a significant decrease in freight and gas prices, raise the question of whether winter has already passed. The widening delta between the Pacific and Atlantic persists. The possibility of more tonnage shifting westward from the Pacific could be contemplated given there seems more enquiry there, but the challenge lies in the time lag associated with redirecting vessels to the Atlantic, especially when both the Panama and Suez Canals routes are unpredictable. While rates have decreased with most fixtures in the East, it's worth noting that some prompter requirements have encountered difficulties in securing shipping particularly in the West. Despite the time available for a potential recovery before holidays commence in most countries, the prospect of a significant surge in activity seems highly unlikely at the moment. Although no newbuild orders have been placed at the yards this week, prices remain robust.

The East Suezmax market remains remarkably resilient to quiet periods and almost none reactive to busier ones (relatively speaking). That possibly defines it as steady with most participants happy to go with the flow on both sides of the phone. MEG/East modern trades WS 115-120 and TD23 is maximum WS 65-67.5.  In the West, there doesn't appear to be a solid support mechanism with a degree of softening likely to occur this side of the weekend. One could argue that with the USG/East arb' being wide open, Suezmax's will definitely be dragged into the lightering fray, but we don't feel this will be in sufficient volumes to significantly move the dial.  In isolation, West Africa (TD 20) doesn’t really offer many positives. The list is lengthy and dates will shortly move into early January, with a number of ships on the cusp of missing the natural fixing window. Eni has just quoted Bonga/Mediterranean 28-29/12 and all will soon be revealed. Freighting this run mid/high WS 90's.

We see volumes holding consistent from miners and operators alike on C5 for end December dates. On the East Australia coal and Pacific front, volumes have dampened from last week. On South Africa and Indian business, we see several fresh enquiries for late December to mid-January 2024. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, we see enquires for full January. Far East tonnage is relatively tight. Ballasting tonnage has lengthened slightly and weighs heavily on early to mid-January dates. On C5, activity level has generally ticked upwards with fixtures concluding at low to mid USD 14 levels at start of the week to low to mid USD 13 levels by mid-week. On C3, we see resistance between offers and bids with conclusions at high USD 23 to low USD 24 levels for mid-January.

The Dry market, despite the recent uptick in earnings, still lacks liquidity. Market players will need to see this earnings surge sustained for at least a few months before we see any significant changes in buying impetus, and with Chinese New Year swiftly following the Christmas holidays, this seems unlikely. The few sales that are reported this week are useful in the sense they help benchmark a number of candidates on the market, such as Supramax ERMIONE (56K DWT IHI 2008) sold by Byzantine for USD 14M, and handy VULLY (35K DWT Shinan 2011) selling for USD 13.2M.   VLCCs are making the most noise on the tanker front, with three sales reported this week. Scrubber fitted VLCC ATHENIAN FREEDOM (299K DWT HHI 2013) was bought by Greek interests at USD 73.5M, however it is the behind the scenes candidates that have been igniting conversations at festive industry get togethers. One thing is for sure, should the modern candidates being discussed transact at their rumoured levels, the modern VLCC market will witness a significant jump in values. At the other end of the age curve, HARAD (303K DWT Samsung 2001) sold for USD 30M to Chinese buyers, still well above scrap levels and a staggering delta of USD c.100M to current newbuild price ideas. Elsewhere, Greek interests picked up LR1 LEON APOLLON (75K DWT HMD 2009) for USD 28.5M.

EAST A so far dull week in the East with nothing much to report in terms of fresh fixtures or cargo enquiries. One deal from last week failed tech subs yesterday and this cargo will reportedly go back domestically meaning we at the time of writing actually count one less spot fixture compared to last week (14 down from 15).  We still have some 3 and 1/2 weeks left on the calendar this year and we expect that some additional December cargoes will appear towards the tail end of the month before we start to focus on 2024 cargoes. That said, with the current sentiment in both East and West we see further downside on freight from Middle East right now and charterers seems to be taking their time.  WEST The Western freight rates continue falling and the BLPG3 has dropped almost 25 dollars so far this week. It is the first time in over 40 days we find it below the 200-dollar mark. In total we have seen 28 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC for December dates and 10 for January. The position list still showing a couple vessels left open in December while potentially seeing 7 open in 1H Jan – but a few ones could go into own program making actual count of vessels slimmer.

text: AMERICAS  At the cusp of Nov and Dec the prompt MB propane market took a sharp step upwards, having risen from the mid 60cpg range to over 71cpg in just a couple of days.  This is attributed to a couple of things, but most prominently to investor short positions which were in need of being covered.  By now the market has begun to subside and has retreated back to the 67-68cpg range after those positions were covered.   Meanwhile, though, LPG market sentiment continues to feel cautious, and many regular participants remain in retreat on the sidelines.  Ongoing delays (and costs) associated with the lack of rain in Panama persist and do not appear to be abating soon.  Crude oil values have seen losses of more than $20/bbl since the start of Q4 which, when coupled with the recently rising propane values have given cause for the propane/WTI spread to rise to above 40%.   Looking at the Jan cargo roster, there are presently believed to have been two cancellations, with two more which are pending decision.  Terminal fees have softened and for 2H Jan are notionally in the 5-6cpg range  NWE The TOT window was not bid for the first time on over a month, reducing the assessed premium for TOT deliveries from a $6/MT to a $3/MT premium to December CIF ARA. VLGC have been transiting the Panama Canal with more ease in December so far compared with previous months, bringing the January East West spread down to +$154/MT. Butane has risen to 95.5% to December Naphtha through strong buyside interest, and remains attractive after the large drop in crude oil and naphtha values seen Wednesday. The butane rise coupled with fewer aggressive offers from transiting VLGCs has seen European netback values improve. With US Gulf FOB cargo values assessed between 5-6cpg the arb to Europe is open for both propane and butane. On paper the European market is an attractive home for US tons, though the low petchem demand and slow rise in winter demand continues to make it a challenge to place tons in the region.  MED Crude oil price volatility saw trade discussions take a back seat. Fewer forecast LPG transits through the Suez Canal helped support values in the region while seasonal demand is beginning to support values in the region.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Value for evenly split cargo on Jan lifting has dived into negative territory at CP minus high single, as of subdued interests from India and Indonesia. Jan C3 CP was traded at $600 at the time of writing and C4 assessed at $14 higher. Jan/Feb C3 CP was traded at $14 backwardation.   FAR EAST Cash differentials plunged further this week as limited buying interests on 23kt propane parcel basis Chiba. Such parcel for 1h Jan delivery was offered at Jan FEI minus low 20s, while similar parcel for 2h Jan is in better contango, with bid at minus mid teens versus offer at minus mid single.   To the contrary, active inquiries from China this week as of improved margin against the declined flat price on feedstock coupled with good discounts. Several full propane cargos for Jan delivery were changed hand and placed into East and North China at FEI minus from high teens to low/mid 20s this week. And there are another two spot buy tenders ongoing for in total 96kt C3 during Jan delivery into Ningbo. With shortage of term supply, we might expect active spot inquiries from Petchem players on spot market, on the premise of normal operation. Other than spot, the descent in freight have triggered importers to negotiate on next year term supply. We have seen three Chinese importers emerged this week for term inquires, mainly to secure petchem feedstock.

Owners are holding the market together remarkably well, despite charterers tactics of holding off and fixing quietly off market (19 deals done over the week passed with no details attached). At the time of writing, an MEG/Vietnam run just on subs at WS 64. It looks lower on a WS basis, but freights well and equates similar to a WS 67.5 for like TD3C and WS 66.5 also just done ex Basrah to China. Given last Wednesday MEG/China was at WS 68.5, it shows the lack of excitement, so a small points victory for charterers then.   As for the Atlantic, despite the bright spot of Venezuela reappearing as a loading destination (and the welcome million plus premium on freight - we will see how long that continues), the lower export volumes, notably in the USG have stressed owners resolve. The Atlantic tonnage list builds, perhaps discouraging potential ballasters which likely have a knock-on effect on the MEG market. Continued lack of support from Suezmaxes and Aframaxes does not help. It is not all doom and gloom as owners holding the line and of course, hope springs eternal, as there remains appetite from charterers for T/C. But for modern, scrubber, it will cost in excess of USD 50k/day. So, evidence from all sides the market will remain strong.

We see volumes present on C5, East Australia, and the Pacific with enquires from miners and operators for mid to end December dates. On C3 ex Brazil to China, we see enquiries for primarily January stems. Volume remains moderate on South African and front haul business. All in all, market sentiment increased moving into end of last but tapered off moving into mid week. Tonnage in Far East is moderately tight. Ballasting tonnage is heavily weighted on early to mid January dates. On C5, we see fixtures concluding at high USD 11 pmt levels by mid-week. On C3, we saw an uptick of rates to upwards of USD 30 pmt for late December dates. For January, we see offers at USD 28 and USD 25 pmt levels for early and mid January stems respectively.

The Panamax market is facing volatility, influenced by stable fundamentals but tempered by cautious sentiment due to fluctuations in the FFA market. This has led to a pause in charterer activity and a noticeable gap between charterers' and owners' rate expectations. Despite these challenges, the market remains resilient, though it is subject to ongoing adjustments and external market pressures.

The Suezmax market remains fairly flat in both hemispheres. Interesting to note that whilst the East has experienced very little surface activity (in recent weeks), this lack of market noise has not resulted in an all out rate-capitulation, with rates remaining comparatively resilient. TD 23 should trade WS 67.5-70 with a MEG/East run trading circa WS 115-120 for a modern unit.  Thus far, the Atlantic basin has failed to deliver an end of year bull run with all major load zones failing to fire on all cylinders. TD 20 is likely to trade out the balance of the week at about WS 100-102.5 with the only real support mechanism coming from confusion over who should shoulder the burden of EU/ETS  payments. Early deals suggest this will be baked freight rates for now.

Handy: The USG market remains firm. Furthermore, scarcity of tonnage is pushing rates higher and owners continue demanding premium. USG-Continent fixture reported at mid 26k levels. More activity seen in the ECSA market with multiple cargoes in market, however owners shy away from fronthaul biz with the market booming in Atlantic. On the Pacific side, we see the usual Indonesia-China run being fixed at mid 9k levels.   Supra/Ultra: With the boom in the USG-ECSA market, rates for a Supra doing ECSA-China run reported around USD 23k levels and the USG-Continent route paying upwards of USD 33k. The Pacific markets are also firming up with increased activity. The usual Indonesia-China runs paying USD 17k levels and the WC India-China route going upwards of USD 20k.  Overall, although we see a slight correction in the FFA market, physical market shows positive momentum which is expected to continue until the onset of holiday season. Given the continued scarcity of tonnages in the USG-Atlantic market, we expect the rate to remain stable in the region. As for the Pacific side, with the NOPAC grains season now we expect more activity and expect slight improvement in rates for the usual trade routes.

As we enter the final weeks of the year, there is no doubt that the bulls are a little quieter than the bears right now. A couple of softer spot fixtures particular in Asia have dampened hopes of a stronger winter, and with the recent cold spells having barely any impact on LNG prices there aren’t many signs of a turnaround. It was natural then, that one of the main topics of conversations at last week’s CWC gathering in Athens and at the festive parties this week has been where the market will go from here (even taking airtime away from emissions clauses and the impact of ETS!). Some will be looking back exactly a year to the crash in the LNG spot market from those record highs, while others may point to fixtures already done for January at levels similar to those seen for November and December. Either way, the discussions are around the pace of change rather than the direction. The same is true for multimonth and multiyear charters: sentiment is softening and there are several candidate vessels, yet charterers are a little reluctant to move at this stage. To finish on a more positive note, with 2023 seeing a drop in the number of fixtures versus 2022 (and 2022 in turn seeing fewer than 2021), a consistent view is emerging of an expected increase in liquidity next year. There should be plenty to keep us busy! At the yards, there were no newbuildings reported this week and prices remained stable.

North Sea market saw a busy start to the week with a few cargoes entering the market first thing Monday, but by the middle of the week activity has slowed.  Dates pushing out well into to the 2nd decade with rates remaining relatively steady.  With stem dates pushing out and limited activity the US markets has again attracted prompter tonnage to ballast.  No real significant changes in the Mediterranean/Black Sea region this week. Supply has been slow with a healthy amount of tonnage picking up the slack. Owners are happy to repeat last done levels with dates now pushing out to mid-month continuing this sideways trend for now.

The dry market rally continued this week as Capesize earnings saw their biggest daily jump since 2010, this was particularly prevalent in the North Atlantic market where tonnage is most scarcely available. Scrubber fitted Capesize duo CHOW/COMANCHE 181K DWT SWS 2016 are primed to take advantage of this rally, being bought by Genco for USD 41.3M each. Smaller sizes are also seeing a welcomed push in rates as a result, after a fairly uneventful Q3. This bump in rates, if sustained, will begin to justify the comparatively firm price expectations across the bulk market. This could also entice more cash rich owners looking to diversify, such as Pyxis, who bought scrubber fitted Kamsarmax PEDHOULAS CHERRY 82K DWT JIANGSU NEWYANGZI 2015 at USD 26.5M.    News of OPEC+ production cuts rather dampened the festive sprit in the Tanker market as rates will likely see a dip in the short term, but in the medium to longer term result in higher ton miles. In reality, these cuts won’t drastically change the overwhelmingly positive overall tanker story. MR tankers have been making headlines this week as some units have reported TCE earnings in excess of USD 100K/day, no wonder there is a swell of interest here with a number of ongoing discussions behind the scenes, surely to set new price benchmarks once completed.

EAST With a descending West market the AG freight floor has followed and we are now seeing both regions trading closer to parity. It looks like we are more than half way through second decade of December fixing while the last decade likely will be the focus of next week. Seeing a good selection of both Owner controlled vessels and Trader re-lets available for second half of December might mean we still need freight to adjust a bit further before Charterers are tempted to move forward.  WEST There are still a few open positions left in December USG although the majority of this weeks deals have been done for January dates. In total we now count 26 spot fixtures for December and 8 for January.  After the arb recently narrowed about 30 dollars we have seen western freight rates drop almost 20 dollars on the BLPG3 index route this week. Despite this drop we are seeing Panamaxes trade at a huge premium of 40-50 dollars to Houston/Chiba via Pan route and three have been fixed the last few days - one of which almost two months ahead.
