text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Dec CP at $610 for C3 and $620 for C4, a rollover from Nov CP. Although no increment into winter season, it’s still higher than expectation as of front length supply amid sluggish demand, probably at the anticipation on further OPEC cuts. At the time of writing, Jan C3 CP was traded at $605.   FAR EAST  A handful of offers for Jan delivered propane emerged in window this week. 23kt propane for 1h Jan delivery was offered at Jan FEI minus $4, and similar cargo for 2h Jan period was offered at minus $1 while bid at minus $4.5. Off window such parcels for 1h Jan delivery was reported concluded at Jan FEI minus $5/6. Following this, Dec FEI slashed by $20 vs the start of the week, seeing players relentlessly selling either in physical or paper market.   On Monday four Chinese PDH players tendered to buy Jan and Feb delivery propane at max 230kt in total. At the time of writing, two SChina players were reported to award one 46kt each at Jan CP plus high 50s and 60s respectively. One was canceled due to few offer to up NChina port. Another one is still ongoing. Meanwhile, Hanwha Total also reported to procure 23kt propane for 2-8 Jan delivery at some discounts to Dec FEI via tender. One Japanese importer also said to award their buy tender for 46kt propane delivered in 2h Feb to 1h Mar.   With the declined in flat price and heavy discounts for 46kt propane into EChina, we might expect some more Chinese PDHs to replenish their feedstock. This being said, there are still a couple of Iranian heavy propane cargos for Dec delivery unsold, which might exert further pressure to the front.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Much of the domestic US LPG market has gone quiet as the wait for winter-related weather demand has commenced.  While there have been recent, large-scale storms, nothing sustained has occurred as yet.    Meanwhile, propane stocks in the US fell by a generally anticipated 600,000bbls as of the week ending 24 Nov, and now total 98.7mmbbls, or about 109% of last year and 136% of two years ago.  At this point stock levels are sufficient in the event of a long, cold winter – as well as export volumes, which were most recently reported by the EIA to be 1.594mmbblss/day, but which are down from last week’s 1.787mmbbls.   As for terminal fees, the high levels seen for Dec transactions have receded, but buy-side ideas have declined more sharply and at this point – for Jan – interest levels is tentatively in the mid single-digit levels while offers (thin as they are) remain hopeful for double-digits.   At the forefront of it all remain the issues at the Panama Canal, and transit auctions have commanded between $1m and (nearly) $4m in recent weeks, which has, in turn, given cause for Eastbound alternatives such as the Suez Canal and the Cape of Good Hope, thus adding ton-miles which, in turn, has kept freight rates resilient.  NWE The first wave of cold weather has arrived in Europe and with it disappeared the TOT window offers. Leaving only BP bidding for a Dec 20-24 delivery, pushing the physical premium up to December CIF ARA +$4.25/MT. The region still looks well supplied and with a large percentage of US LPG exports heading East likely to transit the region over the next few months due to Panama Canal restrictions, expected to be in place until April 2024. Butane values in the region have increased to 83% December Naphtha, though large cargo butane activity has been scarce.   MED The region continues to see tons offered on VLGCs in transit to the Suez Canal. So far there has been no uptick in weather related demand.

A week that has flattered to deceive. The fundamentals were there for a jump in rates - a tight list, strong sentiment, a reawakening Venezuela - but a combination of levelheaded chartering and the tactic of working in the shadows has enabled rates to stay pretty stagnant with perhaps a small, gentle uptick. In the MEG, we saw reports of a Unipec TD3C run at WS 69, but so far proved unfounded. Lower numbers have been agreed on better freighting voyages to Vietnam, or vessels on the cusp of 15 years. December cargo count has crept up to 75+, so we well over halfway, but likely unobserved deals have skewed this total lower than what is perhaps correct.  A number of ships reported fixing ex Venezuela have assisted a lackluster USG market. One deal reported Venezuela/China at USD 11m, so a USD 1m premium on the USG. How long this premium lasts is a debate as more owners willing the call. West Africa quieter on the whole but the list of natural vessels in the Atlantic is tight, and getting tighter.   Opec+ meeting tomorrow and oil prices moving upwards. Someone spooked perhaps, but any increased cut seems unlikely, as African producers and the UAE keen to increase. Let's see tomorrow.

Laden vessels in the Pacific are at all-time highs, and laden vessels in the Indian Ocean are slightly down from all-time highs. The market has tightened considerably in the Atlantic, where like in the other segments earnings is comparable to the heights of 2021 and 2022. This ongoing late-year rally strongly suggest fundamentals will be firm far into next year in our opinion, as it is unusual to see a rally at this time of year. The forward curve is likely to continue being bid in the coming months.

This week's Panamax market shows a high number of laden vessels, particularly in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific, suggesting strong market fundamentals. The Atlantic market has seen a notable drop in vessels, but prices have doubled since November. The market is cautious with limited activity, but fundamentals remain unchanged, supporting further price rises. The physical market remains firm, with major routes trading around the low-mid 16k level and the Atlantic market attracting vessels from the Pacific. Period market rates are in the mid 15k-16k range, bolstered by the strong FFA and Capesize markets.

The spot LNG shipping market has been relatively subdued of late, with only a slow trickle of firm requirements and fixtures in the past week. Despite the reduced activity in the market and an abundance of available vessels, the sentiment regarding rates remains resilient. We are almost at the time of year when the market dropped in the last couple of years, yet there are no discernible signs of a market collapse this year. Disponent owners of available vessels have maintained offers at market levels when responding to the limited vessel requirements that have been issued, and numbers out to January suggest a healthier tale end to the winter than we've seen in recent years. The current week has seen a little more demand for ships, primarily driven by prompt deliveries and January loadings. This uptick in demand raises the possibility of a "double-peak" in rate levels for this winter season, or at least a steady plateau.   Simultaneously, there are no indications suggesting any softening in the shipbuilding market. Consequently, the rate expectations for a long-term charter remain robust among owners with vessels available. Given that shipyards are operating at near-full capacity for the foreseeable future, the industry is constrained to working with existing vessels or those already under order. Notably, there have been no new orders this week, as newbuilding prices continue to hold firm.

NORTH In the North Sea, we have seen very limited activity for early December and rates have fallen as a result.  Fixing window now into the 5-10 December window.  After the quiet start to December fixing the balance of the month beyond the 10th does look like it should be more active with a relatively large North Sea program.  MEDITERRANEAN Activity this week has helped to clear the way for some firming looking forward on the Mediterranean Afras with owner’s keen to quickly close the gap up to the Suezmax.  Black Sea fixing mid-month with the window X-Mediterranean slightly earlier off end/early first decade dates; with a predicted increase in supply through December.

We see consistent volumes on C5, East Australia, and the Pacific, with enquiries from miners, operators, and several tenders this week for mid December dates. On West Africa and C3 ex Brazil to China, we see healthy volumes for the second half of December and several enquiries for early January. Volume remains moderate on front haul, Indian, and South African business. All in all, market sentiment is rising as we move into December. Far East tonnage is moderately tight. Ballaster count is heavily weighted on end December and early January with a few operators willing to perform swaps for mid December dates. On C5, rates strengthened tremendously compared to last week, concluding at high USD 11 to low USD 12 pmt levels. On C3, we see an uptick of rates with fixtures concluding in the mid USD 28 to low USD 29 pmt range for mid December. On early January stems, we see offers at mid USD 25 pmt to USD 26 pmt levels while awaiting charterers bids. One known fixture of a 203k dwt 2013-build non scrubber for 1 year at USD 19,500 per day.

The Eastern Suezmax market has been extremely quiet this week and would have been deemed dead, without a pulse, had it not been for a trickle of short haul MEG/India enquiry and the odd fuel stem. South East Asia and Red Sea are also conspicuously quiet, which says more about the underlying Afra market than anything else. MEG/China will trade WS 110-112.5 on modern and TD23 likely to dip under WS 70 if it remains quiet.  In the Atlantic, it's difficult to pinpoint without specifics, but having spoken to multiple owners with USG exposure, there is possibly more going on off market than meets the eye which will act as a support mechanism, not just to this region, but to the wider Atlantic in general. Hence, TD20 will hold minimum high WS 90’s with owners looking to nudge rates upwards towards the WS 100 mark.

Whether it was celebrated or not, tanker market players would have been giving thanks this week for the fortuitous position they find themselves in as the sector remains hot. Although a relatively quiet week, behind the scenes there are rumours of a 2019 eco VLCC seeing interest in the region of USD 110m levels that would recalibrate valuation models across the sector. Older Aframax tankers have received a boost this week with AEGEAN MYTH (115K DWT 2006 SAMSUNG) being transacted at USD 37.5M to Chinese buyers, showing that current freight rates are proving hard to resist. Elsewhere, Chinese interests secured J19 ALBATROSS TRADER (19K DWT 2015 USUKI) for USD 29.3M.    Rallying chartering markets on the Capesize front is building up anticipation for an ever-increasing level of enquiry. NGM securing in time the Capesize sisters GLORY/HONOR (179K DWT 2011 HHI) for USD 26.5M per unit from compatriots Unisea - levels that most would consider a relative bottom in light of ever bettering earnings. Final price on Ultramax ZEYNO (63K DWT 2014 DAYANG) was revealed to be USD 22M, rather in line with market expectations. With most players cautiously heading into 2024, the busy nature of the S&P market in this year-end suggests sentiment is mending across segments with hope that these invigorated earnings are here to stay.

EAST With few signs of early December cargos remaining uncovered in the AG the fixing window is moving in to the second decade of the month. Many of the early December ships are also about to reach their deviation point for East/West – meaning availability for the first 10 days of December soon will become very limited. Japan and US are off Thursday for Thanksgiving and we could expect a big crowd off for long weekend which might mean we are in for a quiet end to this week. Second half December laycans and onwards in the East is still comfortably far out for Charterers and while sitting back waiting vessel itineraries for this window will soon firm up.   WEST A second Pertamina tender came out in the market this week, now for end December dates, and it was done to an Indonesian Owner at arnd 230 H/C v Pan eqv. At the time of writing we see 2 vessels left in the second decade of Dec – one in each end. For the third decade we see potentially 8 ships left – 3 of which are relets all with NB slot booked. The rest is coming via Suez or from West discharge. So far we have seen 26 spot ex US for December and 1 for January.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Discussing level for evenly split cargo softened as Indian and Indonesia demand were covered gradually. Latest BPCL was heard to have awarded Jan and Feb liftings at small premium to CP. However, similar grade sold into Indonesia was reported done on CFR basis, at a equivalence of discounts to CP.   Dec C3 CP was assessed at $600 at the time of writing. And due to front butane inquiries, Dec C3/C4 still maintained at -$15. Dec/Jan C3 was traded at $8 backwardation.    FAR EAST 23/0 parcel for 2h Dec was heard changed hand at Dec FEI minus mid-single digit, while some Cananda origin parcels for same period were sold at minus low-mid teens basis Chiba reportedly. Similar cargo for 1h Jan delivery was bid at Jan FEI plus $6 in window and was heard traded at plus $8 off window.   A handful of tenders are floating this week. PERTAMINA was reported awarded their Jan procurement tender at Jan CP plus $90s to $100 on CFR basis. One Vietnam-based PDH plant issued tender to buy 23/0 or 46/0 for Dec to 1st decade Jan delivery. One EChina petchem player tendered to buy 0/23 for 1st decade Jan delivery. One EChina cracker issued new tender to procure 23/0 or 46/0 for 3-10 Jan delivery into Ningbo, which had secured 46/0 for 2h Dec delivery at Dec FEI minus mid-teens via previous tender. Taiwan FPCC tendered to procure 0-22kt C3 and 22kt C4 for 2h Dec delivery. One 33/11 for end Dec lifting ex Australia was reported placed into Japan. As limited term been signed for next year, we will expect active spot inquiries from petchem players, on the premise of maintaining basic operating rates.

The main driver for the Atlantic market remains the USG, which commenced the week with an influx of four Monday cargoes. With Thanksgiving on Thursday, the condensed trading week was to be expected and this probably fed into sentiment and corresponding rate uptick. As of going to print we think WS 105 TA is last done with older, regurgitated rates coming to the surface.  TD20 was the main beneficiary of the USG uptick and has now settled at WS 100'ish, where it's likely to stay for the balance of the week. We count circa five stems prior end first decade December (yet to work).  In the East, there's a steady feel with low WS 70's repeated multiple times for TD23 and MEG/East modern probably in the WS 120's.

Quiet patches rarely go unnoticed in the VLCC market and as such, tonnage slowly building off the back of the lull in activity. TD3C losing the grip on the WS 70’s as charterers looking lower than last done. Latest deals at WS 68 done to China and at the time of writing, just Formosa and KPC on the board in the MEG. Therefore, as the East drifts a touch, we may see a few more modern ladies turning left at Rondo and ballasting to the Cape.   At present, we see 5 unfixed ships now ballasting in that Rondo to COGH corridor, down from 9 on Monday. Therefore, tonnage is tightening a touch, with 11 vessels in next 30 days for the USG (which is pretty average), so likely rates steady here a touch, but watch for the ballasters. IOC ex Mex quoting and Petrogal still taking their time ex Brazil will test the market. Still unconfirmed reports of the Eco Petrol cargo at USD 10.2m ex Covenas (likely prompter dates) is a strong statement, and more reported Venezuela business will stretch the ton mile. All a little cooler, but owners unlikely to worry.

Chartering activity remains limited for yet another week. In the Atlantic, there is still demand for 2H December tonnage but there hasn’t been much fixing, due to the limited number of available vessels in the basin. With European natural gas prices correcting, a inter-basin arbitrage has opened offering some opportunities on the paper markets, but with physical demand yet to follow, any such exercises seem rather opportunistic at the moment. In the Pacific, there is also a lack of new firm requirements, and in the Middle East most activity is centered around FOB cargo sales. In short, there is still a lot of uncertainty over the winter months and portfolios seem to be reluctant to release any tonnage at present. The term market is a little more active, with vessels being reported fixed for Q2 2024 deliveries, however rates have started their downward trend reflecting the typical shoulder months. There have been no NewBuilding orders reported this week and NB prices have remained stable.

This week Supramax market is heading only in one direction – North. Strong rates in the Atlantic pushed indexes with substantial gains. Fronthaul in USG on Ultra was fixed for a trip to India with petcoke at USD 47,500 pd and USD 32,000 pd was paid on 63’ dwt with grain cargo to China. Trips across the Atlantic were paying in region USD 30,000 pd. ECSA remains firm, with demand for December loaders increasing. Supramax was rumored fixed at USD 16,000 pd with delivery from West Africa, loading Brazil to the Continent. In the Pacific, rates increased as well, though not at the same speed as in the Atlantic. We see charterers paying a premium of about USD 1,000-2,000 pd in most routes. A 57,000 dwt with delay Indonesia fixed at USD 13,000 pd for a trip via Indonesia to China, a 63,000 dwt delivery Singapore fixed at USD 14,500 pd for a trip via Indonesia to South China. Period appetite has increased in the last couple of weeks, and we see an aggressive approach from Garin House taking long-period deals paying premiums for nice Ultramaxes. Tess 64/2020-built was fixed at USD 14,000 pd for one year charter.

The Panamax market is experiencing a notable rise in sentiment, led by a tight supply of North Atlantic ships pushing rates up. The South Atlantic showed potential for higher rates, while the Pacific market, especially around NoPac and Australia, remained strong. The market started the week slowly but held a firm outlook, with the Atlantic basin seeing significant growth due to limited tonnage availability, particularly in the East Mediterranean/Black Sea area. The market has benefited from improved dry bulk fleet efficiency earlier in the year due to reduced port congestion. However, with congestion returning to normal levels, vessel availability has slowed, creating a favorable market balance for owners. This supply-demand imbalance and active period business suggest a stable and bullish market trend.

With surrounding areas losing ground the North Sea market has followed suit, softening further so far this week. Tonnage lists remain balanced as the number of ballasters out of the area declines. Overall, activity has been muted for the end of the 3rd decade November stems. Looking at the published December stems the North Sea looks like it should be active.  Activity has been relatively slow so far this week. With surrounding areas lackluster we have seen less ballasters out of region adding to the excess of available tonnage continuing to add downward pressure. More vessels are slowly coming back into the picture as Fos resumes operations, and with November dates sold-out, owners look to face a tough situation for the 1st decade of December. Tonnage is plentiful in this region with rates soft.

We see volumes holding up on C5, with enquiries from miners, operators, and tenders for early to mid December dates. On East Australia and the Pacific, the week started with scarce volume and picked up slightly midweek. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, we see healthy volumes for second half of December. Volume remains moderate on front haul and Indian business. All in all, market is softening from last week’s optimistic sentiment. Far East tonnage is moderately tight. Ballaster count is scarce for early December with most vessels having mid December to early January 2024 dates. Atlantic tonnage is tight. On C5, rates dipped slightly from las week with fixtures concluding at low 9 pmt levels. On C3, we see conclusions between high 20 to mid 21 pmt levels for late December stems. Bid offer spread is wide at low 22 pmt versus 20 to 21 pmt levels as owners and charterers adopt a wait and see approach.

Tankers have taken a breather this week as the Dry bulk segment dominates the S&P market. Headlines were stolen by Transmed sale of their AGIS (182k dwt Namura 2023) to Arcelor Mittal, what is considered a very firm $67m. Among other Capesize transactions was the sale of the FRONTIER BRILLIANCE (181k dwt Imabari 2013), which was sold for $30.6m with SS/DD due. Elsewhere, benchmarks are also being set on modern Kamsarmax front with the resale of the AP LOVRIJENAC (82k dwt Hantong 2024) to NNC for $37.62m. In the Ultramax segment, the GLORY HARVEST (63k dwt Hantong 2014) was sold for $21.5m. This sale includes a 1-year time charter to Pan Ocean, explaining the slightly higher than expected price. There have been several Handysize sales, with the most noteworthy being the sale of the APRILIA (36k dwt Jiangdong 2017) to Greek buyers for $20.2m.  In the wake of last week’s numerous tanker transactions, we have recorded 3 Aframax sales supporting last week's activity. One of these was the IRIDESCENT (112k dwt New Times 2009) which was sold for $40m. Following last week's purchase of 8 LR2’s, Torm has this week sold 2xLR1’s, the TORM ESTRID and scrubberfitted TORM ISMINI (74k dwt HHI 2004) en bloc for $40m. Lastly some activity in the MR segment with the sale of the SEAWAYS LORAIN (51k dwt STX 2008) for $24.5m and the FALCON SEXTANT (50k dwt STX 2009) for $25.5m.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Although it is now raining in Panama, the declining water levels in Lake Gatun (which feeds the insatiable appetite of the Canal itself) have taken center stage and become an entirely global issue as the number of daily transits has been reduced (and is scheduled in the coming months to continue falling) SHARPLY.  That has led to competition for the remaining slots which are being auctioned and a much wider use of the alternative routes: the Suez Canal and the Cape of Good Hope.  In each case, prices and freight rates have increased wildly.  Auction payments of $2m, $3m, and as much as $4m are known to have been made, while a $100/mt premium is being placed over the standard Baltic Hou/Chi (via Panama) rate for the ~15-20 additional sailing days which are required for passage via Suez or Good Hope (respectively).  The combined impact of these issues has led to downward pressure on US spot terminal fees which have been halved over the course of November.  Previous offers were seen at around the 15cpg mark, but buyers have been reluctant to engage beyond the mid/single digits.  Meanwhile, the EIA reported this week – after a week’s hiatus - that domestic US propane inventories as of 10 Nov stand at 99.7mmbbls, or about 14% higher than mid-Nov last year.  Stock levels are clearly beyond the 5-year high levels and expected to be fully sufficient for both export volumes and winter-related requirements.  NWE The TOT window continues to be active, with both bids and offers being show. So far delivery dates have not lined up for a deal to get done, TOT cargoes valued at CIF ARA November flat. November imports split between petchem feedstock 270,000MT and retail 170,000MT. Increased winter retail demand has not started. The drop in Brent will narrow the propane naphtha spread though this is unlikely to affect the largely stable low petchem demand. Panama Canal issues will keep the East / West spread wide, December E/W $205/MT today, as traders continue to offer tons into the region en route East via Suez. The butane market has been very quiet and remains at 81% Novmeber naphtha.  MED LPG values in the region are likely to remain under pressure as VLGCs pass through the region to head East, offering their tons if values make sense as they go. For now low heating, Autogas and petrochemical demand in the region means most vessels will pass on through.

EAST Freight in the East is gradually climbing upwards with a small handful of deals done or on subs at around USD 150 RT/C. We are yet to see a large demand increase as a result of Adnoc, and we are still awaiting Aramco dates - as such we expect there’s still a good amount of cargoes remaining, also in the first decade of December. Freight availability is also dependent on how many ships finally ending up in the West, and we continue to see more vessels passing MEG on the way to US giving a somewhat false assurance that there are plenty of ships available in the East.   WEST Western freight rates continue moving upwards and we now see a daily TCE of approximately USD 145k on the Houston/Chiba route according to the latest Baltic print. We are no longer seeing any vessels left in 1H December USG as we count 21 spot fixtures for that month so far - YTD average at 31 spot. Current position list showing 2 vessels left in second decade December and potentially 6-8 open positions in the third decade. Last done at 250 H/C.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Qatar Petroleum was reported to sell a 4-15 Dec lifting full propane cargo to a Japanese importer. Evenly split cargo for Dec lifting was assessed at CP plus $10 though yet to hear any deal concluded. At the time of writing, Dec C3 CP was traded at $609 and C4 was traded at $12 higher. Dec/Jan CP was traded at $6 backwardation.   FAR EAST  Cash differentials continued to fall on weak sentiment. A couple of 23kt propane parcels for 2h Dec was offered in window at Dec FEI minus 1, while off window earlier such parcels were changed hand at Dec FEI plus small digit.   Outside window trades still in slow motion, as of depressing petchem demand against the negative margins, coupled with uncertainties on route diversion for US loadings. One cracker issued buy tender to secure 23/0 des Ningbo during 21-30 Dec, while the rest petchem players remain quiet and wait-and-see. On the other hand, butane demand remains robust with both Indian and Indonesian importers buying. Indonesia PERTAMINA reissued tender to secure an evenly split cargo for 16-20 Dec FOB ex AG or CFR 1-5 Jan. Indian BPCL also issued buy tender for monthly two and a half cargo from Dec to Feb delivery.

As traders come back after long Diwali weekend, we are seeing more action in the market and lots of cargoes in the MEG-India range for the geared vessels. FFA is pushing but physical markets are still low. On Supramax, Indonesia-China leg being fixed at 14,000 levels. The Atlantic market remains around USD 11-12,000 levels. Although slow start to the week with holiday season, we expect to see an upswing in the coming weeks before the year end.

Nsea has seen rates slip by around 15 ws points in the early part of the week.  Surrounding areas also looking softer which has limited opportunities for ballasting.   Available tonnage has started to thin especially for natural Nsea tonnage.  Dates moving into 3rd decade.  The Med has continued in a downward trend throughout the week. Stems for the month are all but covered with Owners on the lookout for early December stems. Natural tonnage in the Med lacks conviction off prompter dates but seems ready to pick up the influx of December supply of which we expect to see an increase. Suezmax market still weak and will have have further effect on Aframax freight levels. Sentiment is soft with additional corrections in this region in mind.

The Panamax market dynamics varied across regions, with the Atlantic market showing strength, especially in transatlantic voyages, and the Pacific market remaining robust due to fresh orders and a strong paper market. The BPI time-charter index experienced a notable 15% increase week-to-week, largely driven by gains on the transatlantic route.  In the Pacific, we witnessed a rise in China's coastal freight rates and higher vessel activity in Australia and Indonesia. With the continued congestion West of Suez, notably in Brazil, and China's potential purchase of 3 million tons of US soybeans, should result with markets continue to rise near-term.

Plenty of chartering opportunities are coming to market yet the lack of available vessels has dampened freight activity this week. The result so far this week - only a handful of vessel are being fixed! The lack of availability, particularly on the prompt, likely means most potential requirements will pass without taking shipping, although those that do conclude will be at charter levels equalling 2023 previous highs.    A wide spectrum of news stories emerged this week; reports of a power outage at Freeport saw concerns rise on the supply side, whilst seasonal bad weather effected European ports and the ability for vessels to discharge on time, potentially providing needed respite to terminals that remain almost at full capacity. Despite glimpses of colder temperatures appearing for brief intervals, high storage levels mean Mediterranean terminals are offering attractive reload parcels which seek homes further down the curve or in the East; however, Pacific cargo demand still appears limited and opportunistic. So, all-in-all there is plenty of uncertainty and control of tonnage remains valuable and priced at a premium.   In the Atlantic, 170,000m3 plus vessels showing December availability could be viewed as  “Unicorns”, and charterers are now looking to open vessels in the East for Atlantic loads as US gulf FOB tenders are offered to market. Not an easy exercise as rates in the pacific remain on par with those in the Atlantic. The next week will be an intriguing one for the LNG spot shipping market!   Newbuilding prices rose this week on the back of two orders placed at HHI with delivery Q1 2028.

We see volumes holding up on C5, East Australia coal, and Pacific trades for late November and first half of December. On C3 ex Brazil to China and West Africa, there has been an uptick in volumes as operators and miners’ surface with primarily first half of December stems. On South Africa, activity volumes remain subdued with little to no fresh enquiries. Volume remains moderate on front haul and Indian business. All in all, market optimism from last week continues.   Far East tonnage is moderately tight. Ballaster count is scarce for early December with most vessels having mid December onwards dates. On C5, rates held up with fixtures concluding at very high 9 to mid 10 pmt levels. On C3, fixtures concluded at low 22 to 23 pmt levels for early December stems. We notice a wait and see approach between owners and charterers for mid December onwards stems.   One known fixture of a 180k dwt 2011-build non-scrubber for 4 to 6 months at BCI 5TC*107 percent index linked basis.

As the post Dubai dust settles, we saw no major jumps this year, but there is certainly an upward trajectory in the week after. As December stems start to filter in the MEG, charterers sentiment is starting to drive rates up. Paper came out this morning, jumping up to 72 for TD3C (a 10 point move in 2 days). At the time of writing MEG/Singapore on subs at WS 72.5 and TD3C now naturally starts with a 7. Older vessels and, or better, freighting voyages able to encourage numbers still in the WS 60’s. As more stems are confirmed, it is likely owners can keep this trajectory in their favor.   Atlantic yet to really move. We see 9 vessels controlled by 6 different owners coming to the Cape, but the activity in the East will likely assist in higher numbers in the near future. A safe bet now is a USD 10m USG/Ningbo - touch either side depending dates, but with the Venezuela business coming back on line (at present paying a million dollar premium), should increase volumes and push us higher in the coming weeks.

Whilst the global Suezmax market has experienced significant downward corrections over the last week, the East market hasn't suffered to the same extent as the Atlantic, which saw a calamitous 50 point fall. TD23 has now repeated mid WS 70's with MEG/East stable in the WS 120's and that's how we see it playing out the rest of the week.  TD20 is still at the mercy of a lengthening list with further falls on the cards. Charterers will be looking to slow trade in a falling market but will likewise be wary of the VLCCs, which are on the upturn. We are freighting this run WS 90's to be tested.  The wider Atlantic is still without structural support and yet to find a bottom.

A busy week again across S&P dominated by Tanker sales, despite a significant proportion of the market occupied in Dubai for Bahri week. On the larger crude tonnage, New Shipping took C. CHALLENGER (313K DWT DALIAN 2013) & C. SPIRIT (313K DWT HHI 2013) for USD 65M and USD 67M respectively, these were sold with tc attached hence the slightly lower than expected price. In the Afra/LR2 sector TORM were extremely busy this week, taking in 8 LR2 tankers built between 2010 – 2012 built at Hyundai Samho for a combination of USD 239M and 5.5M shares (roughly equating to USD 399M), and selling scrubber fitted LR2 TORM MARINA (109K DWT DALIAN 2007) for USD 36.2M to Chinese buyers. This sector is very busy behind the scenes, with more deals likely to emerge before the end of year. Activity continued further down the size curve, with CHEMTRANS URANUS/MERCURY/LEO (37K DWT HMD 2006) selling for USD 18M each to Middle East buyers.  A fairly uneventful week on the Dry front as asset values remain relatively high compared to the available earnings in the market. Buyers are therefore encouraged to go bargain hunting in order to have a more attractive investment case, but this of course relies on a motivated seller. Liquidity is still there however, with NIPPON MARU (55K DWT MITSUI 2011) selling for USD 17.3M, and MARLIN V (61K DWT IWAGI ZOSEN 2013) for USD 21.3M. Elsewhere, Genco are rumoured to be the buyers of scrubber fitted Capesize CHOW (181K DWT SWS 2016), which sold in October for USD 41.3M, after releasing an announcement they are due to take delivery of a scrubber fitted SWS 2016 Cape this month.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS  Without the benefit of an EIA propane inventory report this week (due to system maintenance/upgrades), it is generally assumed that propane stocks in the US likely declined by around a modest million barrels, though the government data will be revealed next week when the systems it employs are returned to service – at which point another million barrels or so may have been consumed domestically as a result of cooler temperatures across the US and ongoing export activities.  If that is the case US stock levels will have declined to below the 100mmbbl mark.   Meanwhile, all eyes are on the Panama Canal where reduced transits – which have come as a result of a drought in Panama – have forced shipping to seek alternatives, most of which are more time consuming and, therefore, expensive.  A couple of recent deviations (both North and Southbound) are evidence of the disruption, and perhaps a sign of things to come in 2024.   The abrupt changes, combined with what has been described as a chaotic Asian market and an overbought European market wherein winter-related demand has yet to commence, are allowing for a wider arb, but simultaneously high freight costs, which have resulted in pressure on the US terminal fee market.  Those values, from the sell-side perspective, are now pegged in the mid/low teens but -as of this writing – buy-side ideas are more in the upper single digits.  NWE The TOT window continues to be active the latest activity an end November offer equating to CIF ARA November -$10/MT vs an early December delivery bid equating to CIF ARA November -$8.5/MT. Cold weather has yet to increase demand while petchem run rates remain low. A slide in crude oil values the week added to the bearish sentiment in the region. As winter approaches and TTF Natural Gas values rise, we will start to see maximum LPG rejection into the natural gas stream, reducing local LPG production. Dutch TTF average $13.40/MMBtu while Propane $9.45/MMBtu and butane $10/MMBtu. The butane market continues to be very quiet and remains assessed at 81% November Naphtha.   MED Imports to the region in November are likely to set a 1 year record. Traders continue to look to place in the region due to the difficulties in transiting the Panama Canal. A slide in crude values has added bearish sentiment to the already oversupplied propane and butane markets.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG While we are waiting for Dec lifting acceptance, we’ve seen Dec CP rose from $600 to $616. Dec C4 was assessed at $12 higher, reflecting the better demand on evenly split cargos driven mainly by India and Indonesia residential segments. And it’s believed that the premium over Dec loadings will stand firm as Pertamina issued tender to buy two evenly split cargos for 16-25 Dec liftings ex AG or CFR during 1-10 Jan.  Dec/Jan CP was traded in $10 backwardation. There are rumors circulating on one AG producer might carry out maintenance during Q1 but the exact timeline not clear yet.    FAR EAST The recent Panama transit restrictions have disrupted the delivery program and lifters or owners are diverting the vessels for other routes. The increased ton miles and rising auction fees undoubtedly support the FEI value, hence widen the arbitrage.   Due to negative margins, a bunch of PDHs users are advancing maintenance or cutting run rates, which resulted in cargo resales or book-out for propane delivered in 2h Nov to 1h Dec. This being said, the cargos have been well absorbed, to traders covering shorts, who faced with cargo delays; and to Japanese or Korean importers for stockpiling on winter demand.    With the rising feedstock costs eroding margins, we might not expect any active spot buying inquiries from China petchem plants. Such might prevail until Panama situation eased or when lifters have clear program with less uncertainties. Nevertheless, the petchem players are issuing term tender to secure term supply for next year, with concerns over volatility on spot market.   Apart from above, a handful of 23kt propane for 2h Dec delivery changed hand at Dec FEI plus $2-3, softening from earlier at $5-6 as of limited buying interest.

EAST November fixing in AG seems to be nearing an end with year to date lowest monthly spot count so far (16 fixtures). December has kicked off early with four confirmed deals at the time of writing - two of which are from Indian PSUs. This even before Adnoc acceptances for December has been published point to a continuously strong market. While the Panama situation evolves more and more vessels will pass by Middle East ports on the way to USG via Suez or Cape and as such we will see a longer theoretical position list in the East which could mean we will more often than not see East trading at a discount to the West going forwards.  WEST At the time of writing, three spot fixtures have been observed in the West this week, bringing the total count to 18 deals out of the US Gulf/US East Coast for December dates. On the Western position list, only one vessel remains open for 1H December. Between 20-30 December, only 2 spot fixtures have been concluded, and the vessel supply this period is looking relatively tight. Every vessel on the West list is currently ballasting via Suez or Cape. The last done Neo-VLGC ex US Gulf was a few dollars below 240 H/C, while the latest Panamax fixture closed at 270 H/C. January fixing is already underway.

North Sea market has seen steady fixing with prompter tonnage being picked off for mid-month stems - rates have held steady at WS 195.  List is starting to thin which may start to have an impact heading into the last decade.  US Markets still attractive to owners so we continue to see vessels ballasting away.  Activity has been ticking over slowly but nothing of great significance. Western Suezmaxes have shown signs of weakness and may look for part cargoes putting a strain on Afra rates. Maintenance in some ports due next week; this will be factored in when chartering a vessel pushing dates out to early 3rd decade Nov. Rates should continue in a steady motion with delays now being the main influence in keeping these levels afloat. Volume should pick up as we proceed through Q4 but no upward trajectory we predict anytime soon. Rates sit steady/soft for now.

We see an uptick in volumes for C5, East Australia coal, and Pacific trades for mid to late November. On C3 ex Brazil to China, there is little activity as vast majority of November stems seem to have been covered and we await December prospects. On West and South Africa, volumes are scarce with little fresh enquiries. On the Atlantic front, we see several new stems this week but high resistance for bids and fixing of ships. On a whole, market optimism has ticked upwards albeit unstable. Far East tonnage is moderately tight. Ballaster count is sizable with a large majority of vessels going for first half of December dates. On C5, fixtures concluded at mid to high USD 9 pmt levels mid-week. On C3, little fixtures were concluded with a huge spread of low 20 pmt versus mid to high USD 21 pmt levels.

A different story for Dubai week 2023. This time last year rates were jumping and owners’ sentiment climbed like the mercury in an Emirati morning. At present, deals will certainly be getting done under the surface, but unlikely charterers will be accepting of a last done. Certainly no major drops on the horizon, but given the lack of open activity, rates will be chiseled at and TD3 likely sits just below WS 70.   The Atlantic, although promising much, is yet to deliver. With little done for USG exports in December the expectation is for more activity, but with little to work with or shout about, owners unable to drive up from the USD 10.2m levels. Again, any charterer will be aiming lower.  Undoubtedly it is busier than it seems, but with ‘over the dinner table’ deals likely taking the lions share, we will have to wait and see how the Dubai dust settles for true market levels.

Touch more positive sentiment from USG, where Ultramax was fixed to India at about USD 38,500.  From east there was bit more fresh orders. Indo-China rounds have been done around USD 12,000.  In big picture still sideways to downwards trends seem continue most likely through year-end. Shipment volumes remain around all-time highs but the weakness in the Pmx/Kmx segment continue to weigh heavily.

What to say, what to say, what to say.... There's not been a market cargo fixed in West Africa, Brazil, or the US yet this week that we know of, so I think it's fair to say this market is well and truly softer without actually anything to show for it. Tonnage has now built up and we're due a reset on rates. Earnings for owners are still good but the dizzy heights of WS 160 level for TD20 are not sustainable. Right now it's fast looking like this market will reach WS 120s soon.  The MEG hasn't exactly been busy either. Relets are there to fix and the assessment above goes for all Suezmax markets. Rates will drop.

The Panamax market this week has seen limited activity and uncertain pricing in the Atlantic, rates have remained steady due to lower prompt tonnage, but cargo volume is low as charterers wait for clearer market direction. In Asia, rates have varied, but overall, the sentiment is weaker as tonnage count increases. The Pacific market had a brief improvement in sentiment but is now slowing down. Overall, the market lacks a clear direction with some fluctuations in sentiment and activity levels.

After a few weeks of relative calm in the shipping market, things got pretty busy pretty quickly last week. Many of the leading indicators of a tight shipping market have been flickering to life recently, such as increasing ballast speed and more FOB/DES and swapping activity on the cargo market, so it’s not surprising that some sublets are being pulled and the availability list is shrinking. This hasn’t led to an increase in fixing levels yet, and it may not do at all while LNG storage levels are high and pricing remains subdued, but it has led to more shipping enquiries as participants look for opportunities in the spot market. Likewise for term charters, there are more enquiries as traders and portfolios look to take advantage of what has hitherto been considered a buying opportunity next year. That being said, Panama Canal disruption, geopolitical tensions, uncertainty around the future of steam ships and the start of the EU ETS are all theoretically bullish 2-Strokes. Conversely, the wave of redelivering tonnage from Q1 next year should provide commercial opportunities for those who are more agnostic when it comes to propulsion, size and vintage. All in all, it’s hard to do anything other than sit on the fence this week! There were no newbuilding orders placed within this reporting cycle.

Quite simply, the S&P world at the moment is a very busy one. Conflict, adverse weather, and humanitarian crises dominate the headlines, impacting long and short-term strategy, all while market players rush to conclude deals before the end of the calendar year. In the only large crude transaction, VLCC JIU YUE (305K DWT DSME 2007) sold for USD 48M. Behind the scenes on the large crude tonnage there is swell of activity, which will dominate reports to come over the next few weeks. Elsewhere, Scorpio sold scrubber fitted MR STI AMBER (49K DWT HMD 2012) for USD 33.9M, which will help price other units in the market.  The Dry market is proving tough to measure as the BDI hit a seven-week low, but appetite on the asset side remains high. There is a steady flow of Japanese built units hitting the market, but mostly on the older end of the size curve, with buyers being forced to either wait for younger Japanese units or shift their attention to modern Chinese built bulkers. An example of this is Ultramax FJM GLORY (61K DWT COSCO Dalian 2019) selling for USD 29.6M. In the largest sub size, Capesize OCEAN CORONA (180K DWT Koyo 2009) was sold for USD 20.8M and SATORI (177K DWT Mitsui 2007 ) sold for USD 18.5M, these were to Chinese and Turkish buyers, respectively.

text: EAST The East market has been a bit slow so far with only two spot fixtures ex MEG this week. At the time of writing, we are still counting only 16 spot fixtures for the whole November ex MEG and Yanbu, so it wouldn't be too optimistic to expect a few more cargoes hitting the market for November dates. The position list so far looks balanced for the remainder of November, but it could change quickly if early December ex MEG also kicks off. The widening arbitrage out of US may attract more vessels towards the West as well which again could give strength to the East market.  WEST From November 3rd 2023 to February 1st 2024 we will see the number of daily transits in the Panama Canal be reduced from 25 to 18. With this recent news the market reacted with the arb widening approximately 50 dollars overnight and we now find freight 35 dollars higher than the start of the week. In total we have seen 15 spot fixtures ex US for December dates and there is currently a tight vessel supply in the West with an arb very supportive of today’s freight level. Bullish sentiment.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Massive volatility in the global markets, underpinned by the calamity at the Panama Canal, gave cause for the Asian arb to spike sharply, only to then be met with wide gains in the freight market which, in turn, caused terminal fees to subside from the high levels that were previously being asked.  Current offers are seen in the mid teens, but asking levels at one point were as high as 20cpg.  Meanwhile, the EIA this week reported that domestic US propane stock levels declined from 102.4mmbbls by 1.2mmbbls to an overall total as of 27 Oct of 101.2mmbbls.  Generally speaking this was of little surprise since the market had been anticipating a draw of around a million barrels.  This was based on domestic demand levels which are believed to have improved as a result of early winter weather and relatively widespread early snowfall across North America.  In any case, US propane inventories are presently the highest they’ve been since at least 2015 for end-October, and remain about 15% higher than at the same time last year, and 33% higher than in 2021.  NWE Large cargo propane pricing has come off rapidly this week, as multiple new offers have been shown in the window. The high Panama Canal auction fee of almost $3 million caused many traders with US Gulf loadings in December to see if they could place hteir cargoes in the European market. Rapidly pushing TOT values to a $4/MT discount to November CIF ARA, down from an $8/MT premium Tuesday. Petchem demand remains low and winter demand yet to increase substantially the European market will remain discounted with multiple offers. The butane market has been creeping up this week as bids have pushed value up towards 83% November Naphtha.   MED The region has also seen a swath of offers due to the Panama Canal risk, pushing propane prices down, while butane values in the region remained steady.

NORTH The North Sea Aframax market has been generally slow this week with rate levels taking a slight dip.  Stem dates pushing into 2nd decade November, and with surrounding areas still showing strength we will see more vessels ballasting out keeping positions on the tighter side. This will be off set with vessels arriving from US, although weather causing some delays, and we may just see these vessels head straight back out of the area.   MEDITERRANEAN Aframax trading in the Mediterranean have seen a significant rate increase week on week. Owners remain bullish in their approach and there is not much to sedate their appetite. With prompter vessels in the Mediterranean coming up short, rates can only remain steady/firmer off earlier dates. However, any firming going forward one would think might be incremental as tonnage seems more balanced off a window of around 15-20 dates. Itineraries can be problematic now with the winter weather delays in the straits now reported at 5 days.

This week Supramax market is heading in the same direction as in previous weeks. The Baltic index is accelerating downward purely due to a lack of volume and growing tonnage counts in the loading areas. USG and ECSA still keeping momentum however rates seem softening. TA trip from USG is getting fixed close to USD 20,000 pd, while trips to Singapore-Japan direction still able to obtain close to high USD 20,000 pd. Demand in the Pacific is reduced and we see owners accepting very low USD 10,000 pd for Indonesian coal or Nopac grains. There are slightly better rates fixed from South East Asia direction India-MEG though little fixtures surfaced. We expect a further decline to be evident this week.

The global Suezmax market is well into winter mode with the Atlantic market exhibiting all the signs of volatility. During the last few weeks, West Africa has found it impossible to benchmark itself with rates failing to settle on a particular number. As of going to print, last done Angola/UKCM priced WS 162.5, with TD20 likely to trade closer to WS 170 with the fixing window focused on 20-25 November.  In the East, Basrah/UKC has just been booked at WS 90 which is the highest rate we have seen thus far for Q4, whilst MEG/China needs a test on modern but unlikely to be below WS 130's.

We see scarce volume for mid November C5, East Australia, South Africa, West Africa, and Indian business. On C3 ex Brazil to China, large majority of November stems seem to be covered. Miners and operators are out in market with late November and December stems, but we see high resistance for bids and taking of ships. On the bright side, we see several fresh stems and enquiries in the Atlantic. On a whole, market optimism has further diminished from last week. Far East tonnage is abundant with a substantial number of owners opting to ballast, leading to further increase in ballaster count. On C5, fixtures concluded at mid USD 8 pmt levels. On C3, fixtures concluded at high USD 20 to low USD 21 pmt levels.

A busy few days in all areas. Last week, the MEG market jumped 10-15 WS points and the past few days owners have not only held those gains and been able to push for a few additional points up through the WS 70’s. At present WS 69 done on a Vietnam run (freighting 3ish points better than a TD3C) and with TD3 paper currently at 67.5-70 (buy/sell) for November, shows many feel we finding a level.  The Atlantic was a little toppy yesterday and we saw a correction USG/East down to USD 10.2m USG/East (albeit a relet). The list is lengthy, with 10 ballasters heading Cape, BUT…. with Dubai on the horizon (we all know what can happen there) and we’ve seen only 4 deals done so far ex USG in December (usually there are around 40 a month), there is plenty of oil to come. This time last year we had the USG frenzy up to USD 15m paid USG/East, and a repeat of such remains unlikely, but owners likely be looking at earning more than last done. The VL’s have also enjoyed plenty of support from the smaller sizes.

The LNG shipping spot market has strengthened particularly in the West, driven by a surge of firm requirements and fixing activities. Partly as a result of this and also charterers having to manage uncertainties in their own scheduling, the availability of vessels has noticeably reduced and there are barely two-stroke vessels available in the spot market for the upcoming month. However, Europe's storage levels remain at 99.24% capacity and with Asia also experiencing high inventories, there is little prospect of a sustained arbitrage. Unless the cargo market sparks into life and drives demand, there is unlikely to be a big upturn in spot rates.  On the projects side, it has been reported that MISC has agreed to convert an old steam-powered LNG carrier, the Puteri Delima Satu, into an FSU for Petronas. This conversion is set to become operational in 2025 under a 20-year contract. Furthermore, BP plans to launch the Tortue FLNG project in the first quarter of 2024, located in Mauritania and Senegal. There were no new buildings ordered last week.

The Panamax market is facing a downturn due to a lack of demand and increasing vessel supply, particularly in the Atlantic, with cargo volumes low and rates falling. In the Pacific, activity is subdued, with charterers bidding low and owners hesitant to accept, leading to a quiet market. Coal supply issues in Indonesia persist; China’s demand is low, but India’s demand remains strong. The Baltic Panamax Index (BPI), which fell -10,2% week-to-week, suggests overvaluation with a potential further decline due to low volume and rising tonnage counts. Overall, the market sentiment is gloomy, with an immediate need for fresh orders to stabilize the market.

A fairly volatile week in the Tanker market takes nothing away from the overall picture that good times are here to stay in this sector. Aframax spot rates are driving increased interest in this size, with some routes paying a mouth-watering USD 100k/day+. Little coincidence then, that the headline transaction this week comes in the form of ice 1A LR2 HIBERNIAN TIDE (108K DWT 2019 SWS), to Minerva at USD 65.5M. VLCC TIMMUS (318K DWT 2002 HHI), sold at USD 32M, a softening on last done, GOOD NEWS (319K 2002 HSHI) at USD 34.75M.  A softer week in the Dry market and a subsequent correction in the recent strong rates hasn’t discouraged buyers, as liquidity remains strong. Otherwise, a rather unremarkable week in the sector as the reported sales do little to raise eyebrows. Japanese tonnage is at the top of most buyers’ shopping lists, with modern tonnage still tricky to acquire, hence the older sales as below. In the most modern of the transactions, Ultramax ATLANTIC ISLAND (61K DWT 2014 IWAGI ZOSEN) sold for USD 24M to Greek buyers while Capesize FRONTIER BRILLIANCE (180K DWT 2013 IMABARI) sold at USD 30M.

EAST A widened arbitrage between US and FEA has pulled up the West market which has had a spillover effect on the East. The robust West market has been leading ships away from the Middle East in view of longer voyages and stronger earnings. As second half November fixing in the AG is well underway Charterers are faced with a tighter market and fewer competitive offers than we saw earlier last week. Looking at the balance of November we are now fixing far out and as such there may be additional candidates appearing later on but in conclusion consensus seems to agree that the market is again pointing upwards.  WEST We have seen 10+ deals concluded in the West during the week, both off end-November and well into 1H December laycan’s. Last reported deal in the market was fixed at usd 198 H-C, but Owner’s idea are now well above usd 200 H-C as the position list is getting tighter and current arb still there to support same. We expect the fixing window to gradually shift towards mid-December onwards, and count 8 deals concluded in December so far.

text: MEG Bids for evenly split cargo edged up this week, as of firm bid in window for late Nov lifting at $615 for C3 and $635 for C4 respectively, which equates to CP plus $15 approximately.   At the time of writing, Nov C3 CP was traded at $600 and C4 CP at $10 higher. But Nov/Dec CP was traded at -$3 backwardation from earlier flattish level.     FAR EAST A couple of full propane cargos for 1h Dec delivery were changed hand. One 46/0 for 1h Dec delivery basis Chiba were said to be placed into Japan, rumored at Dec FEI minus high single digit. And similar parcel for 1h Dec arrival into Ningbo was said concluded at Nov FEI plus $3.5 late last week, which equates to Dec FEI plus around $5-6 by then. 23kt propane parcel was bid in window today at Dec FEI flat while off window deal concluded at mid-single digit reportedly. HTC was also reported to award their spot buy tender to secure 23kt propane for early Dec arrival.   Other than this, spot inquiries for Dec tons especially demand from China remained thin amid weak margins. However, term tenders are under active discussion. One Chinese importer is reported to have awarded their tender for monthly heavy propane or evenly split ratio cargo at FEI plus single digit and CP plus 50s. Another three petchem players are still in the process of negotiation, likely will reach higher premium in general due to foreseeable tight supply amid strong freight next year.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS At 102.4mmbbls the domestic US propane inventory has wholly eclipsed the 5-year high level for mid-October (the previous high-water marks were 98.3mmbbls in 2020 and 99.6mmbbls in 2016.  The EIA report for the week ending 20 Oct showed a modest 100,000bbl weekly increase, which was regarded by the market as rather low as expectations ranged from a build of 250,000bbls to as much as +1.4mmbbls.  This puts the Days of Supply at 113 days, and the YTD 2023 average Days of Supply at 85 days, which is well beyond the previous (2016) high of 76 Days.  Stocks are high.  That said, exports were recorded at 1.843mmbbls/day, which is just below the highest weekly export volume on EIA record, and which occurred just two weeks ago (2.129mmbbls/day on 6 Oct 2023).  This is despite the various and sundry terminal-related export issues which continue to plague the Gulf Coast.  Meanwhile, as there is now winter weather to contend with in North America, heating-related requirements will follow.  Simultaneously there is winter-related demand now being seen in Northwest Europe and – it is now being reported – previous length in Chinese inventories has been drawing down, so in each case demand for US-sourced product should continue to prop up terminal fees, which moved from 10cts/gal earlier in the month to 13cts/gal more recently, and then to 16cts/gal where a transaction is believed to have been concluded.  Asking levels are indeed even higher, with known offers at 20cts/gal for December volumes.  With Eastern arb levels in the $320s and $330s, these types of rates are (at least temporarily) rationally supported.  NWE  The 1st decade November TOT market in the region is very tight. Constant bidding by multiple parties has pushed premiums up to November CIF ARA +$21/MT, a level last seen in March. The prompt market looks tight, partly due to the reduced US export volumes due to terminal loading delays over the last few weeks. Another reason for the tightness in Europe was the tightness in the VLGC market, which led to a larger volume of imports on MGCs rather than VLGCs for October and early November imports. The propane naphtha spread narrowed to multi-month lows as crude oil coming off dragged naphtha down, while prompt propane remains bullish. If the petrochemical sector was receiving any more than the minimum required volume, they would be reselling physical tons at these premiums. Butane in Europe has been quiet in the physical window and values remain at 79% November Naphtha.   MED  The region continues to be in a low demand environment and cannot keep up with the strong premiums innorthwest Europe.

The Panamax market reveals a significant fleet positioned West of Suez, hinting at a potential upturn if Pacific demand rises. The Pacific activity increased slightly over the week; while coal demand is robust, supply issues persist in Indonesia. Asia presents an unpredictable market with a notable bid/offer spread.  The Atlantic reports modest gains in the south, while the north lags. The week in the Atlantic started slowly, dominated by grain, and the North Atlantic shows reduced activity with widening rate disparities. The ECSA remains stable, with the 10-20 November window emerging as a hot spot with notable rates. Overall, the sentiment leans towards optimism despite the slow pace.

The geared market had a slow start this week with activity picking up early today and lots of cargoes coming out of the Pacific and the Atlantic alike.   As for Handysizes, vessels being fixed at USD 10,000 levels for SP. EC India-Far East runs fetching around USD 9k levels and in the Atlantic (Brazil-Med/MEG) around low-mid 20ks. On the Supra/Ultra segment, owners asking in the range of USD 13k/11k for about 1 year. Indonesia-India Supra runs going around 10k levels and Indonesia-China runs seen mid 15k’s this week. The FFA markets have been flat this week starting with a correction seen today, however expect market to remain in the high until end of last quarter 2023!

NORTH In the North Sea, the start of the week has seen some outstanding end month stems being covered some fresh and some replacements mixed in with stems in the first 5 days of November. Very tight early positions have enabled the market to push up with freight rising a further 30 WS points from an already strong positions at the end of last week.  The balance of the week should see the balance of the first decade November cover.  We will see vessels recirculate into position, but available tonnage will remain fairly tight keeping the freight market strong.  MEDITERRANEAN It was an energetic start to the week in the Mediterranean market with an uncharacteristically busy Monday clearing most of the end month stems and pushing us in to first decade of November fixing dates. Rates have remained steady with little change w-o-w with TD19 in at 218.67, the same time last week showing 219.44; tonnage for the most part has been available to cover demand. Although West Mediterranean positions of late have been tighter and surged rates somewhat, we still view the market to be around 80 x WS 215 for Ceyhan-Mediterranean with a steady outlook as we move in to a 1-5/11 fixing window, where natural end month itineraries could bring stability or maybe test rates if supply continues.

The LNG shipping market has been relatively quiet this week with few new firm requirements in either basin, although there are a fair number of cargo tenders. Taking the Atlantic, the lacklustre mood might be a fair reflection of a weakened prompt cargo market, as TTF slipped due to minimal demand off the back of storage levels reaching near capacity in Europe. It was a similar story East of Suez, with a lack of demand from Asian buyers keeping the cargo market flat. Thus, without huge cargo revenues or a strong contango, tendered volumes are mostly going to those with excess shipping length. This leaves the shipping market at the mercy of weather conditions in both Asia and Europe for the weeks ahead, and perhaps this represents a return to normality! On the newbuilding front, it was reported that Celsius have declared two options for 180,000 cbm LNG carriers at China Merchants Heavy Industry Jiangsu with delivery of the vessels scheduled for Q1 and Q4 of 2027.

The Atlantic Suezmax market continues to take the lead in this segment with TD20 last trading WS 140. If you look purely at the numbers, there is a case to be made that VLCCs should cap Suezmax, but on further examination, it's obvious that the Suezmax fixing window in West Africa (15-20/11) is simply too early to be impacted by VLCC cannibalization (at least for now). The USG and wider Atlantic are following the same trajectory.  In the East, there's a mixed bag of rates with TD23 last trading WS 75, but with possible upside simply due to sentiment spillover from the Atlantic. MEG/China on modern tonnage should trade WS 130's for now.  This is a sentiment driven market, and we envisage no downside this week.

We see volumes thinning for mid November C5, East Australia, South Africa, and Indian business. On C3 ex Brazil to China, volumes are scarce as miners have limited November slots left and are adopting a wait and see approach. On West Africa, there are several enquiries for mid to late November stems, but we see a lack of bids and resistance to take a ship.  On a whole, market has moved downwards with diminishing optimism. Tonnage is abundant in Far East with an uptick in ballasters. On C5, fixtures concluded at low USD 10 pmt levels. On C3, fixtures concluded at high USD 24 pmt levels for late November stems with operators. One known fixture of a 210k dwt 2023-build non scrubber for 18 to 21 months at USD 23,000 per day.

VLCC has taken a turn for the worse in the week gone by, down some 10 WS points for a MEG/East run since same time last week. In the Atlantic, recently the main catalyst for an upswing the VLCC sector, their smaller sisters have dominated the headlines as Suez- and Aframax rates have gone from strength to strength: However, given a chance VLCCs will put a spanner in the wheels. Even on a part cargo basis freight now supports going the V-route all things equal but thus far the fixing window is out of sync. A domino effect of fixing and failing from the USG has added to the list of ships committed to the area looking for a home. Until VLCCs come back into flavour vis a vis the smaller segments we expect more of the same short term.

Much of the market has been left scratching their heads as LR1s AESOP/SIENA (74K DWT 2012 HMD) were purchased by Naftomar for a very firm price of USD 41.5M each. Details are yet to emerge on the transaction, so pricing on existing market candidates of that age remain unchanged for now. With the ongoing situation in the Middle East on a knife edge, it would appear that tanker sentiment will remain firm for some time. NAT purchased Suezmax CHEROKEE (158K DWT 2016 HYUNDAI SAMHO) for USD 72M from CM Lemos, the firm price highlighting the relative lack of available candidates in the market.   Liquidity continues to be a feature of the dry market, as market players jostle for position. Despite a recent uptick, the market is still relatively low in terms of asset values, so there is much opportunity for those looking to divest into Dry. In the rather traditional pattern for this stage of the dry cycle, a number of Japanese ships went into Greek buyers – ROYAL FUKUYAMA (82K DWT 2013 TSUNEISHI) was sold for USD 23M, and Ultramax SANTA FRANCESCA (61K DWT 2016 SHIN KASADO) sold for USD 26.8M. Elsewhere, scrubber-fitted Capesize CYMONA IRON (176K DWT 2011 SWS) was sold for USD 26M.
