comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Terminal fees for full propane cargoes from the US continue in the mid teens and show little sign of abating in the face of a now $300/mt arb to the East.  Some have recently predicted that the arb will rise to as high as $315/mt, which only bolsters the notion that terminal fees might be maintained at current levels well in to Q4.  Mixed ratio cargoes are believed available at a modest discount to all-propane cargoes, but there is little demand at present for anything other than 4:0 VLs.  And while the arb is wholly robust, so are freight rates.  In fact, the Hou/Chi route has today been established by the Baltic Index at $220/mt.  Overall export volumes are generally steady, with 1.694mmbbls/day recorded by the EIA last week, and 1.547mmbbls in its most recent report, that for the week ending 01 Sep.  As for inventories, the EIA reported a 500,000bbl week-over-week inventory increase for a current overall total of 96mmbbls.  This is nearly 130% of the same time last year – week 35 – and nearly 137% over two years ago at the same time.  This took the market by surprise as most had calculated an estimated 2.3mmbbl increase.  That estimate was based on historical averages, current petrochemical consumption levels and export volumes over the past week.  Over the past 5 years the average build for week 35 was 2.394mmbbls.  NWE  The region is finding it hard to attract trans-Atlantic VLGCs as netback values stand 5cpg below the East. The low demand environment due to reduced petchem run rates, is making it possible for traders to fill European demand on smaller size vessels. The October Propane vs Naphtha spread of $103/MT keeps propane the favoured feedstock, a bounce back from below $100/MT earlier this week. A TOT bid for end September arrival continues to be shown, with assessed value at September CIF ARA +$2.5/MT. The butane market has been quiet this week, keeping assessed value 83.5% September Naphtha.   MED  Turkey imprted a record 418,000MT LPG in August. Another 400,000MT of LPG on VLGCs is aimed at the region in September already, although it is difficult to predict if the volume will stay in the region or head East. The Panama Canal delays and auction costs above $2million USD are pushing VLGCs through Suez on both laden and ballast legs.

North Sea Aframax rates continued its downward trend this last week. Lack of activity and healthy tonnage lists giving charterers the needed leeway in the current fixing window. Much the same can be said about the Mediterranean/Blsea market, just not been enough activity to keep rates from following that downward curve. For the time being owners are stuck in that equilibrium as surrounding markets unfortunately not offering much better alternatives. We don’t expect any notable surprises for the balance of the week.

The East of Suez Panamax fleet has hit low levels, presenting an upside if Asian demand, notably from China, rebounds. The Atlantic continues to underperform, particularly in the North, although South Atlantic regions offer a glimmer of hope. Market sentiment in Asia remains generally buoyant, partially offsetting subdued activity in the U.S. and North Atlantic. Rates are fluctuating across the board, and charterers appear hesitant in both coal and grain sectors. The BPI is down -3.7% week-on-week. The landscape is mixed but tilting towards cautious optimism, demanding vigilant monitoring for imminent market shifts.

With VLCCs and Aframax in the doldrums, one would have logically presumed that the Suezmax market would exhibit similar frailty. Not so. Charterers have been very quick to swoop on early third decade ships for their TD20 requirements which has stabilized rates in the low WS 70's. Balmo paper has curiously been trading at WS 76, so make of it what you will. This is all the more bizarre considering how quiet the general Atlantic market has been, therefore we will have to put this down sentiment.  The East saw a replacement TD23 cargo trade at WS 62.5, but for the natural window, we are pinning mid/high WS 50's on this run with a flat feel.

New lows across the board this week as the market reflects the new norm of lower OPEC volume and the now fashionable method of fixing in silence and hiding the details. Owners feeling the need to clear ships off their desks at or just below last done levels and then worry about the next one. We have seen MEG/East in the WS 30’s back in May this year, but then the bunker prices were USD 70-80 lower than they are now and so TCE’s drift further towards the red. But, at the time of writing, it seems owners are drawing a line. Non-eco vessels are a few thousand dollars above OPEX and non-scrubbers are almost on it. Given the length of lists in all areas, the market is unlikely to do any spring loaded rebound, but charterers may find owners less accommodating, if their ideas sit below last done. As we stand now, it is likely a bottom, unless bunker prices decrease. MEG/East is at WS 37, Wafr/East at WS 44’ish and USG/Ningbo down to USD 7.25m.

The Supramax market is slowly gaining its confidence. The Pacific market remains stable however the Atlantic is paying reasonable premiums to last done. All main loading areas in the Atlantic see big demand for September tonnage. In Asia, due to the recent typhoon in the southeast region, many ships needed to be replaced for those ships missing cancellation date. Rates were very much mixed depending on the position and ships able to make laycan.   Period activity picked up as charters interest increased, as we saw more demand for good spec tonnage in the Atlantic. Owners are asking for a premium for Atlantic delivery.   The Darya Mira 61’ dwt opened in Finland on 6/11 September, fixed for a trip redelivery Singapore-Japan range with grains at USD 17,500 to Lighthouse Navigation. The Bulk Prudence 61’ dwt open Gresik 2 September was reported fixed for a trip via West Australia redelivery Vietnam with grains at USD 14,000 to Western Bulk.

Volumes remain consistent for mid-late September C5, East Australia, and Pacific business, contributing to slight improvement in optimism. Slight improvement in volumes on South Africa and India business. Volumes remain scarce on West Africa, C3 ex Brazil/China and North Atlantic. Far East tonnage remains abundant while ballasters continue to remain substantial. C5 levels improved slightly and we see a slight uptick to high USD 7 pmt levels. C3/West Africa fixtures are limited and experienced further decline to sub USD 19 pmt levels. On period, we see 180k dwt 2011-build non-scrubber fixed with narrow spread of 4-6 months at high USD 13,000/day.

A slow week across the sale and purchase market sees only one sale reported in the tanker sector with CAPT THANASIS 40K DWT HMD 2004 selling at just under USD 18M. Across the larger units, despite much of the market returning from holidays, S&P discussions are yet to regain momentum given a limp sentiment in the spot market.   The dry market is similarly quiet with only three sales to report. The most notable being NORD PACIFIC 61K DWT SHIN KURUSHIMA 2018 selling for USD 27.15M. The last transaction of a 2018 blt Japanese unit was in July when KK PROGRESSION 64K TSUNEISHI 2018 achieved USD 28.5M which reaffirms the gradual softening in values for these younger Japanese built units.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS MB propane market levels have improved alongside the gains seen in the crude arena, but the percentage of propane-to-WTI continues in the 34-35% range, giving some cause to believe that propane is undervalued – particularly going into the winter.  Prior to that, however, crop drying demand is not expected to reach average consumption levels due to the general lack of rain in the MidWest and the scorching heat which continues to plague most of North America.  Meanwhile, in consideration of the OPEC crude cuts which have limited LPG output in that region of the world, much of the focus is now on the US Gulf Coast as an alternative source of supply.  However, with limited marine terminal capacity and burgeoning demand – not to mention ongoing limitations related to shipping availability – terminal fees have ramped up solidly.  Transactions are known to have occurred at above 15cts/gal for 1H Oct spot FOB deals, with talk of any remaining volumes at still higher levels.  As for propane inventories, the EIA report for the week ending 25 Aug stocks built by a surprising 3.2mmbbls for an overall total of 95.5mmbbls – well beyond what was achieved last year in late August when stocks were recorded at 72.2mmbbls.  With yet another four weeks in the traditional build season, it is well within reason that propane stocks will easily exceed 100mmbbls prior to what is now expected (by some) to be a colder-than-normal winter period.  NWE The TOT window has been consistently offered with no bids corresponding bids for a 2H September propane cargo. Leaving the physical discount at September CIF ARA -$7.50/MT. Propane naphtha lost almost $10/MT as propane gained whilst naphtha came off. Now at -$106/MT for September propane remains the favoured feedstock. The current issue is the continued reduced run rates and maintenance at petchem plants, which is shrinking the size of the European market. The September East/West spread has widened to +$107/MT. Though with Panama Canal transit costs and waiting times some traders see Europe as a safe option keeping US tons flowing across the Atlantic. Butane values tracked naphtha down and are assessed at 89% September Naphtha quotes.  MED Sonatrach prices were posted at $530/$550 for propane and butane respectively. Split ratio VLGCs continue to head to the West Med from the US as Turkish demand remains high.

EAST At the time of writing only one Indian PSU cargo has been fixed out of AG so far on September dates versus an average just above 5 the previous past three months. A second India cargo was quoted today flushing out a couple of other cargos which led to a race between charterers to secure the few ships that was left for their cargo laycans. With few vessels and a fierce competition for vessels freight have now spiked up by more than 20 dollars from last done previously this week.  WEST We have seen a good amount of spot activity in the western market this week and now we count 23 spot fixtures for October ex USG/USEC – all done in 1H of the month. The first open position we find from 6 Oct onwards which also is the only position left for 1H Oct. For the vessels coming up in 2H Oct dates are still a bit uncertain for most of them and by the looks of it the vessel supply is very tight, but this period is still far ahead and we can therefore expect a couple more vessels to appear on the list when schedules are firm. Last done fixture concluded at low 180s H/C.

As the market gets ready to descend on Singapore for what is looking like being a very busy Gastech, the past week hasn’t seen the usual “pre-conference” surge in activity although there remains a number of enquiries to keep people occupied between meetings. Uncertainty still rules the market, with the Australian labour dispute edging closer and the potential impact of El Nino set against high storage levels in both basins and a relatively flat forward curve. As such and unsurprisingly, many enquiries have fallen or will fall away as optimisations and tenders and cargo swaps play out. So, what next? This uncertainty may have resulted in less activity but it hasn’t stopped fixing levels rising earlier this year than we have seen in recent years, and although few expect rates to spike as they did last year, we are now on the cusp of the floating window. Let’s hope there are enough breakout areas at Gastech, just in case… There were no newbuilding orders placed last week.

The MEG market is busy and September MEG stems have flown by, fixture count now into the 70’s. You would expect rates to reflect this buoyant hive of activity, but in reality, with most cargoes now fixed under the radar with no details attached, we sit at the WS 42-43 level for MEG/China. The only “official” benchmark fixtures leaked into the public domain are rarely representative of the top tier. With lack of prospects in the MEG, turning left at Rondo – or opting for the Suez transit option - has become even more appealing for the owning community, in turn putting pressure on Atlantic rates too, which have thus far having resisted the rot. Wafr/East sits around the WS 50 level and USG around USD 8m to Ningbo. For assistance, the big ships can look to their smaller sisters for support, but only flickering signs of improvement and unlikely sufficient buzz for an immediate turn around.

There has been an uptick in volumes for mid-September C5 and East Australia/China, contributing to an increasingly optimistic sentiment. Volumes continue to remain low on South Africa, West Africa and C3 ex Brazil/China route. Tonnage is still readily available in Far East with a substantial number of ballasters. C5 levels held up from last week, concluding at mid to high USD 7 pmt levels. Limited C3 fixtures has been concluded while we see owners hesitate to take charterer bids and Vale remains quiet. On period, we see 176k dwt 2011-build non-scrubber fixed with wide spread 10-18 months at USD 15,200/day.

The share of the fleet east of Suez has dropped noticeably the last few weeks, which perhaps could trigger upside as Asian coal demand is set for a seasonal upturn in the coming months. China’s demand has been low the last weeks but rising industrial metal prices could indicate that demand is about to rise going forward.  If the above scenario plays out remains to be seen, but what is clear is that the market will be supported in the near-term by the high ECSAM grains activity and the upcoming USG grain season.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Sep CP at $550 for C3 and $560 for C4, up by $80 and $100 respectively. The CP surge is resulted by the tight supply especially on butane grade, one reason owing to the oil cuts, and the other on Indian import increments.  Oct C3 CP was assessed at $570 at the time of writing, $20 higher than Sep, reflecting the strong forward market. One Indian importer was reported to cancel their buy spot tender for Oct lifting due to high offers.  FAR EAST Muted discussions on 23/0 for 2h Sep and 1h Oct delivery in the window. Off window 46/0 for 1h Oct delivery was concluded between traders at Oct FEI minus low single digit.   In contrary to the quiet window, a handful of tenders are floating in the market this week. Despite the squeezed margins, petchem players emerge to secure feedstock for late Sep and Oct or even Q4 delivery.   One NChina PDH secured a 46/0 for Oct delivery at Oct FEI plus high single digit via tender reportedly. Another EChina PDH user also managed to secure some propane parcels for Q4 delivery into Yantze river at FEI plus double-digit premiums. One SChina PDH also tendered to buy 23/0 for late Sep/early Oct delivery into Qinzhou, which is due next week. Taiwan FPCC issued two buy tenders to secure one 44/0 parcel des Ningbo in Oct and one flexible ratio on C3/C4 delivered to Mailiao during late Sep to early Oct, which was reported only awarded the propane parcel at Oct FEI plus high single digit. With soaring costs, some PDH users might consider rate cuts but again new capacity released in Q4 might somehow offset the demand loss.

The Nsea Aframax market, despite lack of activity this week, is looking a bit more interesting from an owner’s perspective. This is mainly due to delays at disport with vessels sitting off discharge port waiting to discharge. Also, more tonnage leaving the area either in ballast or laden condition. As a result, there aren’t as many natural North Sea positions to choose from for any cargoes loading in the 10-15 September window and rates could tick up slightly. Rates in the Med/BSea moved sideways with a softer tone last week as activity was slower. Supply of vessels in the area is expected to increase in the short term as we see an overflow of vessels from NSea and USG to discharge there, which will put rates under downward pressure. As a result, we expect charterers to push for lower rates in September and it will be up to the owners to show the necessary resistance.

After a dynamic start post-UK holiday, the Panamax market is experiencing mixed sentiment across regions. The BPI timecharter index is USD 13,689, a 3.2% increase week-on-week, primarily buoyed by gains in the FFA market and firm sentiments in the North Atlantic and South America. Meanwhile, typhoons near China's coast raise potential concerns for port congestion. Despite some positive indicators, a gap remains between owners' asking prices and what charterers are willing to pay, especially in the Pacific market.

The healthy gains experienced by the Atlantic last week have now stalled due, in part, to the lull in market activity created by a UK Bank Holiday (Monday). This has created a false impression of underlying softness, which could be very misleading for those not paying close attention. The West African list has been trimmed by a steady procession of west Med'/Cont' ships that continue to ballast transatlantic. A number of these vessels are privately on subjects or fully fixed which further distorts the picture. Therefore, we are calling the Atlantic close to the bottom with little downside.  In the East,  it's  active but soft for now. A couple of Kuwait fuel oil cargoes will help to keep MEG/East in and around WS 90 levels, whilst TD23 is likely to trade down to low/mid WS 50'S.

Asset players are driving a surge in genuine buying interest across the Dry market. Where perhaps purchase enquiries over the last few months seemed like more of an information gathering exercise, buyers are now ready to capitalise on the recent market price correction. Despite this surge in buying interest, many subsectors are still facing weakened returns at least in the short term, thus justifying lower price levels. Capesize continues to dominate in terms of liquidity with 5 sales reported this week. Of those, IANTHE (180K DWT DSME 2009) sold for USD 21M while YUAN FU STAR (176K RONGSHENG 2011) sold to Middle Eastern buyers at USD 22.3M. Elsewhere lower down the size curve, ongoing deals are the talk of the market, likely to have significant impact on prices once completed.   Discussions on Tankers at the upper end of the size curve appear to be resuming after the summer hiatus, however, at levels lower than initially proposed. That said, general outlook across the sector remains bullish especially as the winter months approach. Activity was restricted to the smaller sizes this week with Union selling MR BRUNSWICK (45K DWT SHIN KURUSHIMA 2010) to PV TRANS for USD 24M, and Maritime Asset Partners selling Handy Tanker ACAMAR (37K DWT HMD 2011) for USD 23.4M.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS After languishing in the mid single-digits earlier in the summer, spot FOB terminal fees on the Gulf Coast rapidly rose to the mid-teens after a well-noted transaction.  Some moderation has been noted, but at present 13-14cpg is likely the most representative range for October.  This is in part due to the somewhat reduced avails on the Gulf Coast (which comes as a result of the ongoing and sweltering heat as well as a couple of recent mechanical tie-ins), but is also representative of the delays at the Panama Canal which has kept freight aloft.  To that, a recent $2.41m Northbound Canal transit payment has given cause for speculation as to additional return voyages via the Cape of Good Hope which would be seen as bullishness in the freight arena.  The EIA Wednesday reported that stocks during the week ending 18 Aug rose by 1.7mmbbls to an overall total of 92.3mmbbls, which compares to the 5-yr average of 72.3mmbbls and is 135% of the same time last year.  It is likely – based on 5-yr averages – that by next week propane inventories will total ~95mmbbls, and – barring any unforeseen events - put Sep overall totals in a position to rather easily eclipse the 100mmbbl mark.  Meanwhile, the relationship between WTI and propane continues to hover in the low/mid 30% range – well below the 52% overall average recorded since Jan 2021.  The rolling YTD average in 2023 has been on a slow decline, having started the year at just above 42% but as of now is ~39% of WTI.  NWE A recurring TOT window offer this week has kept pressure mid-September arrival tons, now assessed at Sept CIF ARA -$2/MT, with no public buying interest shown. The European market continues to import large volumes from the US, but with the September East/West spread nearing $100/MT European buyers will have to up their ideas to continue to do so. With almost 600,000MT set to be imported in August the region has done well to draw tons this summer. Refiners are beginning their blend-up period in order to meet raised winter gasoline pressure requirement. Supporting butane levels at 89.5% balance August Naphtha.    MED  US and northwest European imports continue to supply Moroccan demand, which continues to rise. In the East Med further Algerian and Russian LPG has been heading to Turkey as Autogas demand continues to be strong. 440,000MT is set to be imported to Turkey in August, a record since 2016.

Outside of a small number of isolated spot requirements released early in the week in the East, fresh demand in the spot LNG shipping market has remained light. However, recent gains resulting from an improving cargo market have been retained for larger, more efficient vessels and some see this as "winter coning early". Competition between owners with older tonnage vying for business in Asia has led to a cooling for steamships in the region. In the Atlantic, we continue to see a sizeable bid ask spread between owners of modern tonnage and charterers, however, it’s only a matter of time before we see this gap shrink as availability tightens in the weeks ahead. This is likely to be exacerbated while the labour disruption endures in Australia. There are no newbuild orders to report this week and prices remaining unchanged.

EAST Although freight rates seem steady in the US at the moment, the MEG market appears a bit weaker as the tonnage availability for early September is currently outweighing available cargoes. Considering the spot count for first decade of Sep now stands at 5 v 1 in second decade, there could be a few more cargoes requiring spot fixing before the second decade of Sep.   WEST We are currently seeing several uncovered cargoes out there for 1H Oct dates in USG as we count 9-10 spot fixtures in total for October (all in first decade). There are still a few vessels left in end Sep, but they might also be candidates for 1-10 Oct dates as we only see 2 firm open position left there this period. Further out for 10-20 Oct dates the position list continues looking tight, but we have at the time of writing yet to see a spot fixture this decade as it is still 6-7 weeks out.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Premium for butane grade softened as a few evenly split cargo shorts covered, which earlier reported dealt or offered at CP plus 30s for Sep lifting but bid interest subdued to mid-teens only this week. Sep C3 CP was traded at $535 and C4 at flattish level. However forward market still appears strong especially with one Indian major inquiring for Nov and Dec butane cargos. Sep/Oct C3 CP was traded at $17, also reflecting the coming winter demand. Producers are said to have delayed some butane loadings, resulted by the increased liftings into India with optional cargos, plus max tolerance.  FAR EAST Limited activities in window this week, 23kt propane parcels for 2h Sep delivery was traded at Sep FEI flattish level reportedly. Similar parcel for 1h Oct delivery was bid at Oct FEI minus low-mid single yet to attract offers, especially with uncertainty in Panama transits on skyrocketing costs.  Off window a handful of propane for Sep delivery were changed hand between traders, indirectly placed into China, at Sep FEI plus mid/high single digit basis EChina or mid teens basis NChina. One SChina cracker covered a 2h Sep delivered 46kt propane at an average of Sep CP and Oct FEI plus 40s via tender. Another EChina cracker secured 23kt propane at Sep FEI plus low single digit for late Sep delivery basis Ningbo. One NChina PDH player called tender to procure two full propane cargos for 2h Sep and 1h Oct delivery, respectively. Similarly, one Vietnam based PDH user also tendered to secure propane for 2h Sep to 1st decade Oct delivery.   Other than spot inquiries, one SChina based PDH user tendered for monthly 23/0 from Oct to Mar delivery which due to close on this Friday.

The wider Atlantic market is exhibiting subtle signs of what is to come this winter. Owners have defied the lists and managed to push up rates with ease in West Africa as TD20 jumped 10 points in less than a week, with that run now trading comfortably at WS 75 and no downside. Across the pond, steady enquiry has trimmed the early side of the list with the USG susceptible to further gains.  In the East, there has been very little surface activity with all routes requiring a proper test.

Volumes are comparatively lower than last week on front haul, Indian business, South and West Africa.  Abundant tonnage available in Far East caps possibility of any potential gains. We see a substantial number of vessels choosing the alternative option of ballasting.  C5 seen a drop from last week, with fixtures concluding in the mid to high USD 7 pmt range as opposed to low USD 8 pmt last week.  More resistance seen on C3 with low charterer willingness to bid. Week started off with USD 20 pmt levels for 5-15 September as opposed to low to mid USD 21 pmt levels for mid-end September concluded last week.   Period activity remains low apart from a single known 1-year fixture on 2020-built 179,000 dwt scrubbered vessel at USD 17,300.

A quiet start of the week compared to the exciting market from last week. The negative FFA trading added some nervous volatility, especially among period interest.   Although the Atlantic remains tight on nearby tonnage unless, with spot inquiries, charters rather wait as the feel for an adjustment could be the case this week.   The Pacific market taking a dive and rates falling sharply.

The Panamax market presents mixed signals this week. On the one hand, the coming months might see an upward trend, aided by the US grains season. On the other, vessel activity to Asia, especially China, is declining. European holidays have limited market exchanges, but the market remains robust. The North Atlantic tonnage is tight, with notable gains in the Baltic area due to August demands. Furthermore, a strong September demand in ECSA has shipowners confidently asking for higher rates, even amidst an overall slow market and a dip in the Baltic Exchange Index for Panamax.

More of the same it seems (at least for now), as the Atlantic continues to hold, with USD 8.375m USG/Ningbo (with a TA option at USD 3.375m) paid. A repeat, on a replacement deal. With Smaxes improving in Wafr, the rates for Wafr/East on VL’s (Bitr at the WS 52.5 level) feels a little light, certainly for prompter dates as few vessels either opening in the Atlantic or making the ballast from the East. However, it is well worth noting that there is significant tonnage (23-24 vessels) opening in the UKC in Sept dates, and we will start seeing ballasters now.  Therefore, given the state of the MEG market, little sign of the chasm in rates between East and West closing in the immediate future. September liftings are flying by and plenty more vessels on subs ex MEG no dets, but unlikely exciting in numbers. TD3C in the mid WS 40’s with little upward pressure for now. Still, many owners will have seen worse summers.

Finally some sign of life in the North Sea Aframax market with rates being fixed at higher levels than last done. Owners have managed to push rates higher as the tonnage list looks tighter with ships delaying in discharge port and others ballasting away from the area. So charterers haven’t had as many natural positions to choose from for the early September stems. Aframaxes in the Med/BSea also gained some momentum as activity picked up and replacement jobs helped the owners to fix at higher levels. Sentiment is building, but it remains to be seen if we will see further upward pressure in the area as preliminary volumes for September in the area are expected to be weaker. However, it was a positive weak for the owning community after a disappointing August.

In what has otherwise been an uneventful week in the tanker S&P markets, UK buyers are reported to have acquired scrubber fitted Suezmax NAMSEN 157K DWT NEW TIMES 2016 for USD 67M. The last comparable sale was in June when EPS paid USD 75M for scrubber fitted ELANDRA OSPREY 157K HHI 2018.  The downwards correction of dry values is gathering pace as the transaction liquidity begins to pick up . Capesize ARIADNE 180K DWT DSME 2009 was hotly contested, and eventually sold at USD 21.25M to UK buyers. Demand is growing in the 2008-2014 built range of Capesize as opportunistic owners look to find a bargain asset play. Capesize MOUNT APO 176K DWT RONGSHENG 2012 was bought by Peter Doehle for just under USD 25M, helping price similar assets in this sector. Elsewhere, MBA GIOVANNI/ROSARIA 93K DWT JIANGSU NEWYANGZI 2010/11 sold to Samudera for 33.5M en bloc.

EAST The Eastern market has been quiet this week compared to the West. Positions still look healthy before 10th September in MEG, but about half of them are coming out of India (dates may be deferred) and some may go to West, so eventually it could be balanced. So far we have only seen two spot fixtures in the first decade of September, but with Saudi acceptances expected by tomorrow we should expect more activity to come.  WEST We are no longer seeing any ships left in the end of August and the first available position in the USG we now find from 19-20 Sep onwards. This position is followed by a small handful of about 5 workable ships in the last decade of the month where 3 of them are still candidates for MEG. At the time of writing, we count 25 spot fixtures for September ex USG/USEC with last done concluded at 170 H/C and high 90s H/F. Seeing the arb still wide and delays caused by both the Panama Canal and extreme weather, in addition to a relatively tight position list, we can expect today’s strong freight rates to maintain.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS  WTI values have seen a $2/bbl decline since the start of August, and propane values have also weakened over the same period – from 68cts/gal on the 1st to below 62cts/gal at present.  The ratio of WTI to propane values, though, has weakened from just over 35% to 32%, perhaps signaling that MB propane values have room to again advance in the near-term.   Terminal fees, meanwhile, have made remarkable gains this month and moved from somewhere in the 6cts/gal level to 8cts/gal, then to 10cts/gal, followed by a 12.5cts/gal deal and – finally – a 15+ cts/gal transaction that was recorded earlier this week.  Asking levels have correspondingly increased, but buy-side interest at this point remain in the lower end of the double-digit range.   As for inventory levels, the EIA reported this week that stock levels as of 11 Aug had built by 700k bbls to a total of 90.6mmbbls.  The week-over-week increase was well below the 2.2mmbbl 5-year average build for the 32nd week, but inventories are now 133% of the same time last year and 135% of two years ago. Many are now rightly anticipating that propane inventories in the US will handily eclipse the 100mmbbl level by the beginning of October.    As the excessive heat of the North American summer continues and ocean water temperatures continue to post at record levels the threat of tropical storms and/or hurricanes has now intensified.  NOAA forecasters have just recently increased their Atlantic hurricane season predictions to ‘above normal’.  NWE  The region saw a significant rise in imports month on month, from 425,000MT in July to 582,000MT expected in August. Surprising as the netback to Asia has been considerably stronger during this period. The August Propane / Naphtha spread rose $10/MT to $126/MT, and remains the preferred feedstock. Though with many petchem plants on maintenance, shutdown or running reduced rates due to weak olefins markets feedstock demand fluctuations do not represent a huge volume. The TOT window is assessed at a double digit discount to September CIF ARA, public bids and offers have been scarce. Butane continues to be strong now at 87% September Naphtha as refinery demand beings to increase to meet adequate vapor pressures before blending season.  MED  The East Med has been buoyed by the wide arb from the US. Morocco importing 115,000 MT in the first half of August already, 60% of US origin. In the West Med Turkey has been importing a large volumes of LPG, and continues to look for prompt tons. As the summer driving season is keeping autogas demand high.

A bizarre set of circumstances have recently seen a Suezmax ballast from the Mediterannean to the MEG to perform a TD23 voyage. So dismal were the returns West of Suez, that this actually made sense. That was last week, and whilst the list for 20T crane vessels remains fairly balanced, it's unlikely we will see a repeat of this scenario in the near future. Otherwise, the East has been quiet on the surface and likely to trade flat.  In the Atlantic, charterers have worked off market to secure a large volume of vessels for first decade West Africa stems, suggesting they think it's bottomed at about WS 65. A market quote has just entered the fray which will set the scene for the balance of the week.  Elsewhere, in the USG there has been steady enquiry with the early side of the list thinning out therefore we are calling USG/UKCM 145KT x WS 54-55 with no downside.

As we roll into 2H August, we find ourselves with a quieter spot market to start the week with no new requirements or spot fixtures recorded as of yet. Although the case, we still do see momentum with ample activity in the background as market participants continue to test levels for various winter periods and attempt to narrow the still gaping bid-ask spread. Most notably in the East, albeit a healthy degree of availability on the prompt and otherwise, we understand that end-September / beg-October laycans are still struggling to attract the needed tonnage, prompting an increase in our rates this week accordingly. On the term side of the equation, a 22-month charter on a 2-Stroke delivering in November has been concluded circa the mid-$120k region, further softening and pulling term rates down across the board. Otherwise, newbuild prices remain flat this week and we have no new orders to report.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Following the crude, Sep C3 was traded lower this week at $517 and C4 at $5 higher than C3 by the time of writing. Sep/Oct CP enlarged rapidly from Monday’s flattish to $13 contango on Thursday, partly reflecting the softening front as several buyers have covered their demand for evenly split cargos from AG producer’s trading arm, which reported at Sep CP plus high 20s-30s range.   FAR EAST Premium for 23kt propane on 2h Sep delivery fluctuates. Bids softened to low single digit in window on thur, while similar parcels was concluded at FEI plus $5-6 earlier this week , following the volatile time spread.   One Oil Major issued sale tender for a mid Sep lifting evenly split cargo from Dampier and result is yet to know by the time of writing. And Taiwan FPC withdrew their buy tender for an 22/22 cargo during 20-30 Sep delivery, as offers too high. Buying interests from other petchem units are muted owing to the squeezed margins. Several China PDHs shut down due to glitches or annual scheduled turnarounds, and some expected to extend the duration in view of the poor margins.

Various holidays across the world hindering real action. The USG and ECSA stood out with tick more fixtures represented. A grain run on a Supramax was fixed for del South Brazil to Far East around 13k + 300k bb, and sugar to Nigeria around mid teens.   Continent/Mediterranean rather few fresh requirements. Some of the pmx coal stems out of Baltic being priced on Supras now.  From the East, overall sentiment remained positive, but it was experienced a small stand off and wider gap between bid offers with more positive expectations towards market.

Still disappointing considering time of year, but finally some fundamental positives for the big ships. Slightly improved physical volumes, partly assisted by smaller segments and paper sentiment, have sent spot rates for two main iron ore trades ticking modestly up. West Australia/China conference rates gaining more than USD 0.50 pmt to exceed USD 8.00 pmt, showing improved returns of around USD 15k/day. Similarly on the Brazil or West Africa/China run, latest conclusions are markedly up at USD 22 pmt or close, making ballasting a more attractive alternative for prompt Far East units. Period activity remains low except for index-linked deals giving some potential for possible upside, for fixed-level conclusions latest appears 208,000 dwt/built 2019 done for about 12 months at USD 21,500 to major traders.

Aframax rates in the North Sea area are currently being fixed at bottom levels for yet a consecutive week. At time of writing, the market is WS 95 for a cross North Sea voyage. We need to see more vessels ballast away from the area before we will see any improvement in rates. In the Mediterranean/Blsea, rates picked up slightly over the last week with benchmark route TD19 currently trading around WS 100 level. A steady flow of enquiries from main Libyan hubs keeps the area alive. The tonnage list is still looking fairly healthy, giving charterers some leverage. We expect the market to remain steady/firm in the near term.

All in all, a quietish week, exacerbated by a few public holidays around the world and many major players away from their desks. In addition, we are sitting in the twilight zone between August MEG cargoes closing out and the influx of the September stems. By everyone’s count, August has been a quiet month - sub 130 deals and few to come. Some of this can be blamed on the cuts in OPEC production, but really, that should have shown in June/July too. We believe the higher volume for June (162) & July (149) was probably due to a combination of (slight) inventory draw, but also lower Afra/Suez exports month-over-month, and some 'cheating' on quotas! As for rates, ticking down, WS 26 MEG/West and mid WS 40’s East.  However, with few willing to commit to a long voyage from the West to East (so far), the Atlantic market has held its ground. Brazilian market quotes receiving 2-3 offers each time, USG exports holding last done levels (USD 8.3m USG/Ningbo), and West Africa only falling off a point to the WS 51 level. Interesting to see the interest in a forward-reaching Brazil cargo in the market at the time of writing.

The North Atlantic continues to experience a limited tonnage supply, leading to gains for owners, especially in the Baltic area for TA and fronthaul. Delays at the Panama Canal hint at further improvements. Meanwhile, the South Atlantic's demand remains robust in September, with owners in ECSA confident in asking prices above previous rates. Additionally, in Asia, there's been an uptick for owners due to limited tonnage and steady enquiries from regions like NoPac, Australia, and Indonesia.

With the summer in full swing, many Tanker S&P discussions have found themselves on hold. Buying interest has more or less dried up, which has forced sellers of the decidedly thin number of candidates circulated in the market to reevaluate their price expectations. This has coincided with rates slipping across the larger end of the size curve, putting buyers back in the driving seat. It seems, for now at least, the next transactions will not eclipse last done but instead will provide the wet market with a much-needed correction in values. This week’s sales are dominated by smaller tankers with Celsius continuing to offload their older units, this time in the form of MR2 CELSIUS ROSKILDE (46K DWT 2009 HMD) for USD 25M. Elsewhere, scrubber fitted Suezmax MONTE TOLEDO (150K DWT 2004 UNIVERSAL) sold for USD 35M.  The Dry sector price correction, something which has been discussed in the market since Q4 2022, is finally taking hold with market candidates attracting interest at c.10-15% lower than original asking price. That said, there hasn’t been a rush of sales candidates to meet the ever-increasing enquiry. Japanese built eco units are still at the top of buyers’ shopping lists but the lack of replacement ships being delivered from yards are stifling those looking for a potential bargain. In a rare example of a modern Japanese ship changing hands, Meadway Shipping picked up scrubber fitted Ultramax NORD AMAZON (64K DWT 2020 OSHIMA) for USD 32M. Furthermore, in the Ultramax sector, SSI FORMIDABLE (63K DWT 2017 JINLING) sold for USD 27M.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Premium on evenly split ratio for Sep lifting stands firm with bid seen in window at CP plus $15. Off window hearing one producer might have a heavy butane grade for early Sep lifting can sell and asking at teens premium too.   At the time of writing, Sep Propane Cp was assessed at $530 and Butane at $10 more, reflecting the front strong demand.    FAR EAST Cash differentials turns into positive territory as of traders shorts in window against the delays caused by Panama congestion. 23kt propane parcel for 2h Sep delivery was bid at minus small single digit while off window plus small premium was reported done.   Sep FEI/Cp continued to enlarge and by the time of writing it was traded over $100. This being said, importers especially petchem players are holding back buying interests and some are planning for rate cuts. A few Chinese PDHs are even scheduling for annual turnarounds as well. One Vietnam based PDH user issued buy tender for Sep delivery propane but the result was not clear yet, as the previous procurement tender cancelled due to high offers. 46kt propane for Sep delivery into Ningbo was placed at Sep FEI plus low single digit and discussing level increased furthermore due to limited offers as well. Other than such, there were three 1h/mid Sep arrival Iranian cargos available via tender this week and some Chinese players are eyeing on such instead of looking at non-Iranian origins which priced at $40 higher easily.

EAST With most of the action so far this week being focused in the West, the East remains relatively quiet. Singapore was off for a National day on Wednesday while Japan has a national holiday on Friday. This together with a populous position list has so far led to a pretty slow week in the East market. Adnoc is likely to release their acceptances Thursday/Friday, but the current market balance is not forcing charterers to rush into far forward fixing, and we do expect some more cargoes to be fixed on August dates before the focus fully shifts into Sept laycan in the East.  WEST Fixing activity in the US market is largely focused around the first two decades of September and currently we have seen around fifteen to sixteen vessels fixed. Gradually though, a tendency to book last decade's September cargoes is building momentum on the back of Panama congestion and typhoons in the Eastern hemisphere lurking around the corner, leaving the market relatively date dependent and in search of firm itineraries. We expect the market to keep its current pace going forward despite seeing some shipping length in the first half of the month posing an imminent threat of waiting time for the owner, which is largely due to a lack of shipping inquiries and slim to none FOB availability. Freight rates remain flat across the board at around mid to mid/high USD 160's H/C and mid/high USD 90's for H/F.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Following the upwardly trending crude markets which are rising primarily due to pending production cutbacks in the Middle East, the Mont Belvieu propane market rose by more than 20cts/gal over the course of July with non-TET values presently pegged at around 73cts/gal.  The reduced LPG output in the other primary supply region is putting the spotlight on the US and, predictably, spot FOB terminal fees have also increased – particularly since freight rates have stalled.   Where just a short while ago September business was being talked in the mid single-digit range, notional terminal fee ideas rose quickly as an 8cpg transaction was quickly followed by a 10cpg deal, after which price ideas rose to as high as 12cpg – all for the mid/2H Sep market.  Buyers are now known to be assessing values in the low 10cpg range, but little product is believed to be on offer.  This is partially due to a pair of mechanical tie-ins which have recently been undertaken – one of which is related to PDH efforts, the other to a terminal capacity improvement project.    Meanwhile, stock levels this week were recorded by the EIA to have risen by 1.3mmbbls for an overall total of 89.9mmbbls as of the end of the first week of August.  The increase fell short of the market’s expectations, but nonetheless propelled stock levels nearer to eclipsing the 100mmbbl mark by the end of September.   Over the past 5 years propane inventory levels have gained an average of over 15mmbbls during Aug and Sep which, if applied to the current 89.9mmbbl stock total, would put total US stocks at over 105mmbbls as of the end of Sep.  NWE Approximately 150,000 mt of US Origin LPG are scheduled to arrive in NWE first half August on VLGC's,  along with 70,000 mt on LGCs, along with a handful of MGC's also. All that to say, NWE is seemingly well supplied at present however the market still saw a bid for a September cargo in yesterday's window. It went unmet. European butane steadied after a sharp rise over recent weeks which saw prices at a 6-month high, however the arbitrage is expected to come in as blending season arrives.  MED This month will see the highest ever US origin imports into the region, totaling nearly 550,000 tons, and thus nullifying the need for more product at present. The bulk of the demand has been driven predictably by Morocco and Turkey, while Spain will import 140,000 tons also, contributing to the record levels.

As Singapore celebrates its 58th birthday, it’s testament to the role the country now plays in the LNG market that things have been very quiet in the East today. Of course, this is naturally a quiet time in the market anyway, as the holiday season continues across the Northern Hemisphere, gas storage continues to fill up in Europe and LNG tanks remain near their tops in NE Asia. The upshot of this supply build-up is that the contango that had previously kept 2H 2023 2-Stroke term fixtures ticking over has now contracted, and we return to a very wide bid-ask spread between Owners and Charterers. Turning to the prompt, we’ve seen fixtures in both basins this week and the main take-away is that owners are expecting rates to double in October. With the fixing window now in September, this has proven a sticking point in spot negotiations – especially when the charter period strays into October. Consequently, a handful of October requirements remain uncovered because even though Charterers have been keen to fix before rates shoot up, Owners (primarily portfolio players) see no benefit in locking in a fixture now when the market could roof again when we hit Q4. In any event, we’re printing higher rates this week as we close in on Q4 and we wait with interest to see who gives first on the next October fixture – Owners or Charterers? Newbuild prices remain flat this week and we have no new orders to report.

Aframax rates in the North Sea area hit bottom levels due to slow activity and the tonnage list building up for 2nd decade loading dates. Some owners are ballasting towards the USG, but we need to see some of the early positions be fixed away before we might see some improvement in rates. We have seen healthy activity levels in Med/BSea for mid-month dates. List looks somewhat tighter, and owners been holding back for higher freight levels rather than just rolling with a repeat of last done - this again has resulted in a slight uptick in freight levels in the area. We expect the area to remain steady/firm in the current fixing window.

Another positive day for the Atlantic market, as volume continues to prevail absorbing prompt/spot tonnage. The Baltic volumes for mineral have been very active within August loader adding extra tightness to North Continent tonnage. ECSA, after the recent pause we are seeing more September inquiries after with better levels exchanges resulting further improvement.

Supramax market stabilized, and BSI closed by 3 points for the first time after many days of negative gains. The Baltic 10TC average closed at USD 7,580 yesterday. With Singapore National holiday today, we see less inquiry in Far East. Atlantic is more positive with some better fixture reporting in South Atlantic with more cargoes surfacing in ECSA. In the Pacific, an Ultramax asking above USD 10,000 pd for Pacific RV. A smaller Supra 53,000 dwt was rumored fixed basis delivery Indo a trip redelivery CJK-North China in the mid USD 10,500 pd. Even though some may say that USG market is improving, we still see very low fixtures of Ultramax 63,000 dwt fixed USD 9,000 pd for TCT loading Miss River redly NCSA. Solid fixture was reported from ECSA M/V CMB FLORIS fixed close to USD 14,500 pd plus USD 450,000 GBB.

Capesize overall, average value coming off some USD 500 to present USD 14,500. The C5 market has improved on back of the cyclones, having affected port operations and ships at sea. T/C levels in the Pacific are unchanged from last week. In the South Atlantic, the majors have been busy and are expected to be so also for the near future. Freight rates being fixed are around USD 20,50 being up from low USD 20,00 last week. The T/C rates in the Atlantic have been coming off, after a positive spike last weeks, number of new cargoes has been limited.

Activity on Suezmax have gone drastically down the last couple of weeks. Mostly due to oil being shipped on other sizes (especially V's), but also some production issues in Wafr, especially Forcados. At the same time, tonnage list in the West have been building up, and there have been a shift in balance East/West. It does seem like we have hit the bottom around low-mid WS 60's in Wafr, as we have seen a bit more activity ex Brazil and USG this week. The East is looking fairly balanced still. MEG rates have remained decent even with the West dropping like a stone, due to a shorter list of tonnage in the area. Going forward we expect rates in the West to slightly improve, although this will not happen overnight.

At the time of writing, a certain Korean cargo working 25-27 laycan and they are usually market setters (as in down). They have been assisted by a fresh MEG/China run on subs at WS 47, and likely any other charterers will now await a result - see what they do and hang off the coat tails. Plenty of ships fixing away off market, but also plenty to offer in (10 offers on recent stems). Yesterday’s Bitr sat at WS 48 and change, but next done will slice a few points off that. Still, only just over 100 fixtures for the month, so volume to come, but the cuts are likely starting to bite.   An active Atlantic, with mid Sept USG stems holding the market up at USD 8.3m to Ningbo. Wafr a touch softer, with TD15 down to WS 53.5 level and a softer MEG will push more vessels West. Petrobras working now, but with prompter dates, not inundated with offers. Owners perhaps not willing to fix out their Q4 at these numbers. We will see.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Aug C3 CP at $470 and C4 at $460, up by $70 and $85 respectively, which is in line with curve value and market expectation. The decrease in exports and increased demand from India lend support to the strong CP, and at the time of writing, Sep CP was traded at $517 for C3 and $511 for C4.  Butane is in favored due to seasonal demand. Earlier one end Aug lifting 2/2 was said to be concluded at CP plus high single digit. Similar grade for Sep lifting was bid in window at $525 for C3 and $520 for C4 respectively, which equates to CP plus high single digit. And outside window mid-teens bid was heard as well.    FAR EAST 23kt propane parcel for 1h Sep delivery was bid at Sep FEI minus mid-single digit and outside window low single digit discount was traded reportedly. In addition to this, a handful of 46kt propane parcels were reported to change hand at Sep Fei minus low single basis EChina or plus small premium basis NChina. One EChina PDH user was reported to only award their tender for 2h Sep delivered propane at FEI plus teens, paying the higher premium into river port and dead freight. Other PDHs yet to call procurement tender for Sep delivery, particularly seeing the eroding margins on soaring costs.    One China Major importer issued term tender to secure monthly one propane cargo from Q4 2023 to Q3 2024 delivery. Similarly, another Indian Major also tendered to buy max 2335kt evenly split or heavy butane cargo for AG FOBs in 2024. Previously one Indian major is reported to award their 2024 annual term tender on some AG FOB volumes at CP minus teens level.   One European Major also tendered to buy evenly split cargo for CFR Port Klang during late Aug to Sep delivery or FOB AG in Sep lifting, but was said not awarded eventually. Another SChina traditional importer tendered to buy a 11/11 or 0/23 for mid/2h Sep delivery.

EAST Although we’ve only seen 20 spot fixtures in August ex AG  so far (v. 28 average for the past three months), the question now is what’s actually left of spot demand for the rest of the month. OPEC continues to reduce production which means, even with healthy Natgas production, we could see decreased tons ex AG this month. The position list for last decade of August in AG still looks pretty healthy, although some vessels obviously may choose to go US or elsewhere. With some weather delays and some cargos popping up outside of just US and AG, maybe freight in the East will manage to stay put a while longer.  WEST The first available vessel in USG we find from 28 Aug onwards. Some players already looking at mid Sep dates, but with only 5-6 spot fixtures concluded for September we still see a large chunk of open vessels available at earlier dates. For the first half of September the position list looks balanced with an even split of trader relets and shipowner-controlled vessels. With Panama delays to increase combined with incoming Typhoons/Hurricanes and a still widening arb we should expect todays strong rates to stay put.

Once again, the LNG spot shipping market has experienced a subdued week. While some developing cargoes have emerged, there are very few new firm requirements seen. Vessel availability remains steady at present; nevertheless, as the seasonal breeze carries us closer to winter, a subtle shift is anticipated. Vessels primarily controlled by subletters may be withdrawn, leaving the market tighter. The West-to-East Arbitrage and the winter contango are currently open, hinting at forthcoming trade opportunities which should improve shipping rates further going into the final months of the year. A handful of charterers are still actively seeking tonnage for this period; however, closing the Bid-Offer spread remains a challenge as the current lack of spot activity is not giving much scope to optimise any spot length as a result. On the longer-term side, there remains considerable attention driven increasingly by fleet renewals.  In the newbuilding market, Evalend Shipping was reported to have placed an order for two 174,000km3 LNG carriers with Korean Shipbuilder Hyundai Heavy Industries. The vessels are due for delivery in late 2027.  Another Japanese shipowner was also heard to have place an order for one LNG carrier with another Korean Shipbuilder, Hanwha Ocean. The newbuilding is due for delivery around February 2027.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Expectations of crude oil production cuts in the Middle East has put pressure on the US supply system, and with August effectively sold out and September avails limited, terminal fees have been on the rise.  Where at the end of July the market was hovering around the 6cpg range for the remaining Aug volumes, an 8cpg Sep deal is known and 9cpg is being asked – and justifiably since the arb is supportive.  Talk of a 10cpg offer for Sep was heard but is not known to have been concluded.   Part of the reason that dock space is limited is due to a couple of domestic mechanical tie-ins; the first being Targa’s terminal capacity expansion by a pair of monthly 4:0 VLGCs, the second being Enterpise’s PDH start-up.  In all cases, however, the ongoing and rather dreadful heat wave which continues unabated is slowing the flow of product, which – at +40C ambient temps – is making it difficult to achieve -42C refrigeration levels.   As for the stock levels, is not the volume of available propane supplies that is in question, but the limited dock space – particularly for 4:0 cargoes.  The EIA this week again posted an inventory gain, this time a build of 2.9mmbbls for an overall US stock total of 88.6mmbbls – or nearly 140% of the total seen at the same time last year.  The build was well beyond most expectations, particularly as compared to the 5-year average build for week #30 of 1.7mmbbls.

Capesizes have been gradually more positive over the last week. The c5 has reached well into the 8s, before getting a correction again towards the end of the week.  The same trend has been seen for the c3 market with last done excess USD 20 pmt.  All in all, the average Capesize rate is 14,997 today compared to 14,937 one week ago, so all in all flat.

A slow start to the week especially in the West with a tonnage list getting longer than we have seen for some time. In addition, several prompt vessels free of cargo are seen in all areas.TD 20 are trading around the WS 67.5 mark, and we do expect it to soften further due to lack of activity and more VLCC being fixed ex West Africa. On a positive note, TD 23 been very active last few days, so we don’t see many vessels ballasting from East towards West.

A positive week as sentiment continues to be positive on back of fresh inquiries and thinner prompt tonnage.   Market stays balanced with optimism next week opening.   Further south looks better, and we still see end August/September lifting to cover market is stable rising.

Once again, the West is providing the much needed support required to keep this market buoyant. USG export and West Africa cargoes continue to work and attract ships from the East.  A USG/East cargo was reported at 8.3m and also another deal was reported at 7.9m although on an oil co. relet. In the MEG, charterers are managing to keep things steady by taking out candidates who are challenged fixing/do no fix out of the West. One does suspect if ships keep turning left at Galle, it could put some downward pressure in the West too, potentially improving things in MEG. However, it all feels a bit sideways for now. Firmer bunker prices have also helped keep the rates steady.  Typhoon in Taiwan, Philippines, and South China is also likely to delay a few ships.

The whole European Aframax market has been under downward pressure for more than two weeks with returns for owners being as low as 20k/day right now. Premium players cannot find Russian cargoes as Urals are trading above price cap, supply of oil in general in the West is lower the last couple of weeks and a bunch of vessels looking for employment has sent rates tumbling all across the board. Short-term future will be tough for the owners as all signals are bearish and the summer market is here to stay.

The summer holidays in Europe starting to influence market activity. The trend across all markets remain unexcited despite some areas having seen more fresh requirements. Rates in the Atlantic remain flat. Fronthaul from USG fixing USD 12,000 pd, and trips within the Atlantic improved from sub USD 10,000 pd to low USD 10,000 pd. The Black Sea and Mediterranean markets see a downward due to the Black Sea grain deal terminated by Russia. Rates from Med to West Africa directions with clinker is about USD 8,000 pd. The South African market has seen a bit better volume, and a few fixtures have been reported Ultramax fixing delivery Port Elizabeth-Richards Bay range for trips to Far East at the level USD 13,000 plus USD 250,000 GBB. The market in the Pacific basin has regular cargo flow, however rates remain unchanged. Supra fixed delivery China for South Asia coal run fixed at USD 9,000 pd.

EAST As expected freight is continuing its descent and last done in the East have now dropped below the $100 mark. Currently we are counting 15 spot fixtures on August dates and the positions list is still looking relatively long. Thus, we would need to see quite some healthy spot cargo volumes to maintain freight at current levels.  WEST Compared to last week, this week has been fairly active with a good amount of spot fixtures both in the East and in the West. August fixing in the West looks to soon be finished seeing only a couple open candidates left in the very end of the month. September fixing ex USG/USEC is well underway and we have already registered a fixture in the beginning of the second decade which was done at mid-low 170s H/C. Vessel supply for the first half of September looks relatively balanced to tight and the arb is still widening.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS  Despite a widening arb to the East little activity has been noted as August is mostly sold out, save for a couple of lingering parcels which are being offered either CFR or include butane.  Sep is presently subdued but talks have begun to surface as early winter-related demand requirements emerge.   US propane inventories were recorded by the EIA at 85.7mmbbls as of 21 Jul, an increase of 1mmbbls over the week prior.  The average build for the 29th week of the year is 1.716mmbbls, and expectations were calling for stocks to rise by some 1.9mmbbls.  The relatively weak stock build is likely due (in part) to tie-in’s at Targa (due to its expansion efforts) and Enterprise (due to its PDH-related efforts).  Furthermore, the ongoing and persistent heat wave in Texas has made it difficult to achieve -42c, the temperature at which fully refrigerated vessels load most efficiently.   Meanwhile, terminal fees continue to plod slowly upwards (and in a relatively quiet environment), with a reported fixture in Aug of 6.75cpg.  Talks for Sep start in the 7s and will work from there, but buy-side interest seems to remain in the 6s for the moment.    Latin American demand levels are muted, as Southern Hemisphere winter-related requirements are being satisfied by term contract deliveries.  NWE The TOT window continues to be well offered with two 1H August delivery parcels being shown. One of the offers was from the petrochemical sector, which lent a bearish feel to the mid-August European market. Strong crude oil has supported European LPG paper values and kept the trans-Atlantic Arb open. The European market remains in a low demand environment and though the arb is open cargoes are finding it difficult to find homes. Another factor has been the low natural gas price, which has pushed Dutch TTF below propane and butane. This will increase North Sea LPG production as LPG will no longer be spiked into the natural gas stream. Which is starting to be seen, North Sea exports are expected to be 335,000MT in July, up from an average of 255,000MT in Q1 2023. Butane values remain at 69% August Naphtha, though outright value has increased with stronger naphtha values.   MED Butane in the region has been strengthening this week, pulled up by crude and naphtha rises. There are areas of North African demand, although these are not being worked with any urgency.

We are halfway through a key week where rates in the Atlantic have traded down to the lowest levels seen, thus far, in 2023. Last done TD20 is WS 75 with the fixing window focused on mid August dates. The question is, if you're a charterer sitting on similar dates, do you swoop and grab a ship in and around these levels, or gamble on lower? We think they will take the former option.  In the US Gulf, there's expected to be a raft of lightering enquiry enter the market on the back of last month’s VLCC fixtures, which should start to tie up the early side of the list and stop the rot.  In the East, a prompt TD23 cargo has paid WS 65, but for natural window it's more likely to price WS 55-60 whilst MEG/China probably finds a home at WS 107.5-110.

NSea rates softened last week as activity in the area was slow due to the lower volumes for early August dates combined with the large amount of relets in the area. Barely any fixtures were done and reported, and with surrounding areas not offering any better alternatives we expect the market to remain flat but downward pressure will be applied soon. Med/BSea was more active with a couple of fixtures done but with rates keep hovering around WS 120 levels for local runs. Tonnage list is balanced, and no surprises are expected in the near future with rates moving sideways unless we see a burst of activity on a certain window.

We are now almost at the end of July, and it has in actual fact felt like a proper summer (holiday) week in the markets. Aside from the many industry players reading this week’s reports from their hammocks, the relatively quiet 7 days can be attributed to the general lull in the cargo market. The Southern Europe heatwave has caused some increases in European gas pricing, but this seems to have been relatively well controlled.  We have had a few spot requirements concluded in the Atlantic with levels indicating a “balanced” market, whereas the Pacific (where people, paradoxically, aren’t on holiday yet) has stayed very quiet. Surprisingly, we have seen a few short voyages out of the Middle East emerge, with some charterers looking to capitalise on summer sentiment for Q4 liftings in order to optimise freight. Term and multi-month discussions continue in the background, as the market tries to price the contango into winter. Vessel availability has also stayed more or less balanced in both basins whilst on the newbuilding side there are some discussions on new orders, which should be announced out of China soon. Furthermore, it was reported that NYK has found lengthy term charters on their recent orders.

What a difference a day makes, as the song goes. After a few days of a steady slow decline the Atlantic gave the VLCC market a shot in the arm yesterday. An ECMex/Korea run was booked at USD 8.3 million, dictating rates north USD 8 million for TD22, a good quarter million improvement over last done, and Wafr and Brazil loads likely to follow in the footsteps. To what extent the MEG, where downward pressure persists, will follow suit remains to be seen, but it should encourage owner to dig their heals in at the WS 50+ mark for MEG/East. A major typhoon expected to hit Taiwan, Philippines, and South China this week could cause delays, with possible replacements needing to be arranged and tightening the front end of the position list.

text: MEG Bids for full cargo propane during late Aug lifting ex AG surged up at $470 in Thursday window. This week barely see any spot tenders and fobs for later Aug lifting were assessed at high single digit premium to Aug Cp.   Some idea for 1st round Cp was heard at $460 for C3 and $445 for C4 which is in line with curve value but it’s unpredictable on what actual cp will be set.   At the time of writing, Aug C3 Cp was traded at $460 and Aug/Sep Cp at $38 contango.  FAR EAST Several 23kt propane parcels for 2H Aug delivery were reported changed hand at Aug FEI minus $3/4 and discussions moved into Sep range. Similar cargo for 1h Sep delivery was bid at Sep FEI minus high single yet to see offers. Aug FEI/CP enlarged further to $122.  Most Chinese players have finished their Aug procurement with some petchem players skipped due to high inventory and unexpected glitch. Some are exploring with suppliers to swap for a later delivery cargo reportedly. Other than such, Hyosung Vina was reported to cancel their propane buy tender for late Aug/1H Sep delivery.

The Supra/Ultra vessel market remains subdued globally, with limited progress in the Atlantic region and strong tonnage availability in the North Atlantic. South Asia faces tightened tonnage availability in early August, and notable transactions include Iseaco Grace and Federal Indus securing new ventures. However, a decline in fresh US Gulf enquiries and low sentiment in the South Atlantic have led to the BSI falling to 753, with the 10TC average at USD 8,278. There are glimpses of potential recovery in South Asia due to ongoing activity, but cargo inquiries remain limited, prompting some owners to consider reduced bids to secure business.

The Panamax market has experienced a slow start due to a lack of fresh orders, and there is an oversupply of tonnage in the Continent/Gibraltar area. The South American market remains subdued, impacting not only Atlantic committed and ballaster positions but also opportunities in the East. In the northern Atlantic, there are rumors of more accessible rates compared to previous periods. Despite the improved activity in the Asia region, the market still lacks a definitive floor, leading to easing rates and some owners offering discounts on shorter runs to mitigate exposure to challenging rates.

Capesize rates have overall been holding steady with a small improvement towards the end of the week: In the Pacific with improved c5 rates up to 7.65 and in the Atlantic due to tighter supply of ships. The Pacific market may be affected by the upcoming cyclone. C3 out of Brazil however pretty much remains unchanged.

EAST Four spot fixtures have been concluded in the East this week - two of them Indian cargoes at healthy premiums which brings the spot count for the first decade of August to eight. In addition to these there is one more Indian cargo in the works the first ten days of August. Focus will eventually shift into second decade of August now where availability so far is looking decent. The past five months we have seen on average 27 monthly spot deals from Middle Eastern ports and the pace of spot cargo demand in August seems to be following suit so far.   WEST This week we have only seen one spot fixture in the west and with that said we count 24 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC so far for August dates – seven first decade, eight second decade and nine last decade. There is still one vessel left open in the first decade in addition to two relets open for swap. In the second decade we only see one vessel open in the very end while the last decade still showing five to six available vessels. Last done concluded at mid-low 170s H/C and low 100s H/F.
