comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Jun CP at $450 for C3 and $440 for C4, down by $105 and $115 respectively, which is totally out of expectation. Jul C3 CP was traded at $440 at the time of writing. Freight is still soaring up, especially when a major producer trading arm was rumored to have over 10 cargos for Jun lifting still, and so far we’ve seen 8 fixtures on shipping by them.   FAR EAST Earlier this week 23kt propane for 1h Jul delivery was traded at Jul FEI plus mid single digit while same parcel for 2h Jul period at Jul FEI minus $1-2. Thurs window similar parcel for 1h Jul bid up at Jul FEI plus $7 while offer at Bal Jun FEI plus $10, which equates to Jul FEI plus $14. 11/11 parcel (inclu. US origin) was offered at Jul FEI plus $10.8 yet to see bids.   One Korean importer issued term buy tender to secure monthly 23/23 or 0/23 from Jan to Dec delivery at Mopj link pricing. Cal 24 FEI/MOPJ is assessed at -60s which is indeed a good timing to secure LPG for cracking use.   However, most PDH users yet to come for Jul purchase due to the poor margin for downstream PP etc. Some PDH is reported to cut rates and slow down feedstock procurement program. For residential segment, hot weather and unexpected decline in Jun CP have resulted in slow consumption and the inventory loss for importers hence less speculative buying so far but keep wait-and-see.

A long weekend in many places saw the week start with a mini rush. Some observers may have expected a turn-around or at least a levelling out, however, a couple of "market" fixtures were concluded in both the MEG and the Atlantic squashing any perception of a turnaround, in spite of decent volume. With resistance evaporating charterers took the opportunity to pick off ships in the shadows - presumably at/around similar levels. At the time of writing, MEG/East sits in the mid WS 40’s – WS 45 rptd to China, and a WS 43.5 to Korea on favorable terms.   The Atlantic market – Wafr/East took a hit overnight, dropping to a rptd WS 44. Brazil/East at WS 42.4, but it was just one of 5 VLCCs on subs ex Brazil yesterday, coupled with an active fresh quote today, underlining the active nature. However, Suezmaxes continue to offer little support, with my colleague describing it as “low & slow”.

North Sea Aframax rates moved sideways the past week, and as we approach the middle of the week there are very few fresh fixtures to report. The market needs to be tested, but with a lack of activity and the tonnage list building up, we expect spot earnings to come off slightly in the next fixing window. It’s been a quiet start to the week in the Mediterranean as well, and with tonnage lists in favor of charterers we have seen a downward correction in freight levels. We don’t foresee any drastic changes near term and expect the area to remain soft if anything.

After a calm conclusion to the previous week and an extended weekend, the Suezmax market has begun the current week at a sluggish pace. The list of available tonnage in the Western region continues to increase steadily each day, while cargo activity remains notably slow.  Within the last 24 hours, TD20 rates have dropped from WS 115 to low WS 100's, with the possibility of the market further declining into double digits. In the Eastern region, the majority of cargoes this week have consisted of short-haul shipments between the Middle East Gulf (MEG) and India. There are still some fuel cargoes available for MEG/Spore, but overall, the Eastern market appears to be experiencing a weakened demand as well.  Moving forward, we anticipate a further decline in the Suezmax market. However, one positive aspect we can derive from this market situation is the relatively swift fixing window, which could indicate more cargoes left for this week.

Rates are still coming off and new low's are reached in the Pacific where c5 is being fixed below mid 7s. The Atlantic is lacking support and there has been some fixtures concluded equivalent to a zero TCE. Vale have emerged out of Brazil, but so far not demanding a big number of ships, and rates on this route is as well dropping day by day.

Following a long weekend for many, the Panamax market started the week lethargically with little activity. The Atlantic, with a distinct lack of activity in both the north and the south of the arena, sentiment remained weaker with rates continuing to slide. Asia returned a mixed bag, with talk so far this week of better demand ex Indonesia and Australia but offset against a long tonnage list, the market largely remained flat to kick off the weekend.

LNG as a fuel is back in vogue this week. Those shippers fortunate enough to control DF cargo ships are inundating their bunker suppliers with fuel stem requests. As one established LNG bunker provider put it, “Christmas has come early this year”. It’s a stark reminder for those of us on conventional chartering (who have been bemoaning the collapsed Contango) that every cloud has a silver lining. Like the owners of LNG fuelled container ships, price sensitive buyers have switched back to sea gas in recent weeks, helping to repair some of the demand destruction our chosen commodity has suffered over the last few years. Even though this exacerbated buyers’ market is unlikely to survive the next winter, this current period of competitively priced restocking in both basins will go some way to restoring LNGs role in the fuel mix. So, whilst this may not be a great time for those who are long product and / or shipping, it is a fantastic market for those buyers who can purchase at current spot market levels. Given where those prices were in August last year, it seems only fair that the pendulum has now swung so far in this direction.

The Supramax market slid further down with rates dropping by more than 10% from last week. The outlook is negative for the upcoming summer months. June is trading below at USD 10,000 and Q3 is just about USD 10,000 pd mark.   Far East market trading below USD 10,000 for Pacific trips on modern Ultramax, while Supra obtaining much less. Owners accepting APS rate with 2-3 days ballast to load port. 52,000 dwt fixed delivery CJK for a trip via South Kalimantan back to CJK around USD 6,500 pd. The Atlantic market had a poor week with very few cargoes surfacing the market while the tonnage count building up. Ultramax reported fixed loading grains in USG at USD 22,000 pd for trip to Far East with grains. Petcoke cargoes from the same area pay a small premium and fixing at USD 23,000- 24,000 pd. Very limited activity was reported in ECSA. Ultramax reported fixed at USD 15,000 pd + USD 500,000 GBB basis delivery Brazil for a trip with grains to Singapore-Japan range. The Continent and Mediterranean markets dropped further last week, and now charts indicate around low USD 10,000 for trips with scrap or clinker.

EAST First half June spot cargoes are still being fixed and freight in this window is significantly higher than what is currently achievable in the second half of the month. Second half of the month is still facing some uncertainties on itineraries which could be part of the reason why less charterers have started to work these dates as of now. With a strong momentum spilling over from the early part of the month, we expect the fixing window to remain quite far out.  WEST Freight market keeps firm in the West with current fixing window concentrated around 1H July in US. Last done deals have been done at mid 150s H/C and mid 90s H/F. As freight has kept on rising one could start to see activity cool off at some point (as players try to manage their positions internally), but time of writing we have seen 5-6 deals fixed or on subs so far this week.

text: MEG: KPC was reported to award their sale tender for end Jun lifting 3/1 ratio at Jun CP minus low 40s. And there are a couple of late Jun and July lifting evenly split cargos were offered via window. Given the soaring freight, players are hesitant to take FOB positions and the FOB netback is much lower than recent tender levels.    Jun C3 CP was traded at $497 at the time of writing, and C4 CP at $10 less. Jun/Jul CP was traded at $8 backwardation at the moment.   FAR EAST:  Cash premium surged up for 23/0 delivered in 2h June, and a few traders covered such shorts at Jun FEI plus mid-teens, which mostly from Japan or Korean importers’ resales. Similar cargo for 1h Jul delivery was bid at Jul FEI plus $2, yet to entice interest. 46/0 for 1h Jul delivery was reported changed hand at Jul FEI minus small digits basis Chiba, or high single digit basis Ningbo.   One Korean importer was said to procure two propane cargos for 2h Jun and 1h Jul delivery, respectively. Another Korean importer also tendered to buy 23kt butane for 6-12 Jul delivery. One evenly split cargo was said placed into SChina at Jun FEI flat by a producer trading arm.  Petchem margins eroded as downstream consumption demand yet to recover, hence concerns over the PDH run rate cuts and demand for Jul delivery looming in the market. Some PDH was said to resell their Jun arrival propane, amid high inventories even.

Vintage tanker plays are still making headlines with New Shipping doubling their investment on the VLCC GOOD NEWS (319K DWT SAMHO HI 2002) at USD 43M to undisclosed buyers. It is too soon to tell whether the flagging and insurance issues plaguing vintage tanker operator Gatik will impact the level of buying enquiry for older tanker tonnage, but it is worth monitoring, as registries and P&I clubs begin to scrutinize trading patterns of these older units.    Sentiment in the dry sector is waning at least in the short term, as global worries over Chinese demand increase. Nevertheless, despite more market players adopting a wait and see approach to second hand vessel acquisitions, there has been a steady stream of transactions reported this week. In the modern Ultramax sector TAURUS/ARIES CONFIDENCE  (63K DWT NEW DAYANG 2018) were sold to Spar Shipping for USD 28.5M per unit. With Chinese units generally much more available than their Japanese equivalents, it will be interesting to see whether this transaction sparks a run on the available Chinese built units in the market. Capesize BAO MAY (178K DWT SWS 2010) was sold for USD 25.5M, perhaps showing that slightly younger units are being considered by market players, following the recent spike in demand for vintage Capesize units.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: NWE  TOT window saw some activity with a 1st decade June offer which equated to CIF ARA +$2.75/MT. Early June buying looked to be almost done in the region and the offer level was seen as more hopeful than actual market level. The main issue is that the petrochemical buyers are well supplied during that timeframe and retail buyers are adding minimal demand. The June propane naphtha spread is $175/MT, and continues to improve through propane’s weakness, so petchem buying will remain at a maximum. The East vs West spread of $85/MT is side so US spot cargoes will head East. Butane remains assessed at 75% naphtha with little buying interest.  MED  The region had seen a rise in butane buying interest early week due to naphtha’s strength propping up butane values. With crude oil values off today discussions are likely to stall until these settle.  US Mont Belvieu propane prices declined overnight on the weight of rapidly growing inventory levels, which the EIA yesterday reported to have reached 66.7mmbbls as of 19 May, 2023, or 144 and 151% more than the third-week of May 2022 and 2021, respectively.  The 3mmbbl build this week is the second largest since 2019 and well ahead of the 1.4mmbbl 5-year average.  In short, stock levels of propane are increasingly rapidly, which is then having a predictable impact on the pricing structure.  That said, the value of propane at Mont Belvieu has been – with a couple of notable exceptions - in decline since the start of 2022, loosely mirroring (but modestly outpacing) the softening crude oil market.  The propane-to-crude ratio has been descending all the while and has been hovering on either side of 37%, which is below the 2023 YTD average of 43%, and well off the 54% average established since Jan 2021.  In order to incentivize exports, propane prices will need to continue the existing downward trend, and thus the ratio to crude will continue to decline, perhaps to unprecedented levels.  With regards terminal fees, offers are on the table in June in the low 5cpg range, with July being offered in the mid-5cpg range.  August offers currently exist at between 5.50 to 6.00cpg

Cape rates are under pressure despite relatively ok demand in the Pacific. On the main route c5, the miners have been present, but rates have not been going anywhere, rather slightly down. Overall index is off a couple of thousands, and the biggest drop is in the most volatile par; the Atlantic. Sentiment is dull, but analysts are forecasting an upturn will be coming, along with the summer.

Supramax market falling for yet another week. With various public holidays in Europe and the lack of cargo volume, the rates reduced even further. The S10TC at USD 11,151 and FFA all forward value falling sub USD 12,000 for the balance of 2023.  In the Pacific, Ultramax 64‘ dwt fixed delivery Singapore prompt dates for a trip via Indonesia to China at about USD 15,000 ,and the Supramax 55‘ dwt delivery South China for a round voyage via Indonesia to China was fixed below USD 10,000.  In general, Supramax trading in the Indian Ocean and Pacific basin trading below index value.  The Atlantic market looks healthier though all indications showed a weakening market.  Ultra 63’ dwt was fixed delivery Brazil for a trip to Chittagong at USD 16,750 pd plus USD 675,000 BB. USG market lacking cargo orders, while prompt tonnage building up. Rates are down by USD 2,000-3,000 pd for all directions.

The Atlantic so far appeared to be lacking in any fresh demand with opinion divided following the end of last week’s mini push ex EC South America, whilst limited talk of improved mineral demand ex Australia, otherwise Asia experienced a muted week.

With the 1-10 June window drawing to a close in the MEG, the volume count is up to the mid 50’s for month and we have only scratched the 10-20 window. However, the recent quiet days are never a good sign for owners, and sentiment rarely avoids taking a hit as patience is tested. It is likely a cargo working now on the open market would test both owners resolve and the WS 50 level for TD3C too. However, the Atlantic has kept decent volume, noticeably West Africa awakening from a recent slumber, with rates up to the WS 55.5 level Wafr/East (on a deal likely concluded last week). But, with OPEC+ cuts, many owners have pointed vessels to the West/USG to avoid the group and therefore dilution is a concern. On the VL’s it is looking like a tough summer, but plenty of light at the end of the tunnel.

The Suezmax market has spent the best part of eight months peaking in and around the WS 130's for TD20, before steadily coming off again into WS 90-100 levels. This pattern is on the cusp of being repeated this week, with last done rates reported at the WS 115 level. Whether the fall is as precipitous as previous crashes comes down to whether owners buy the pattern or fundamentals. If they're looking at the fundamentals, then there's a case for the brakes to be applied but sentiment is more likely to triumph. The main support base in the USG has all but dried up for now and the Black Sea continues to be pinned down by a continuous stream of vessels coming through the Suez Canal, either on spec' or discharging off the back of TD23 voyages. MEG/East has repeated WS 127.5 several times, but we expect this to be tested downwards as softer sentiment from the Atlantic infects the East. TD23 will find a home in the WS 60's with a softer trend.

During the past week, a handful of vessels have been placed on subjects but support for rates has been minimal. For “Owners”, each successive fixture has been lower than the last, which is especially telling in a sublet-dominated market. In short, the floor, which some envisaged the portfolios would not breach, has opened; now, keeping vessels cold and moving is more important than securing better rates. Accordingly, and despite a slight decrease in vessel availability, spot rates are softer this week, affording Charterers the confidence of securing spot tonnage as required in both basins. On the term front, all eyes are on the contango into Q4 which, when open, exponentially increases the demand for 2H 2023 2-strokes but whilst closed, sees Charterers defer their winter procurement activities until absolutely necessary. The gulf between the spot and term markets persists, but as period-flexible tonnage hits the spot fixing window, the Bid-Ask spread closes and another term deal is generally concluded.  This keeps the premium for term fixtures alive as the availability – especially from independent owners – of tonnage that can cover all of this coming winter is limited at best. Given that there are more requirements still under discussion, one expects that Q3 delivering term fixtures will be concluded at a premium to those we’ve seen on the prompt. No newbuilding orders have been placed this week; however, prices remain elevated with some yards now booked out until 2028.

The North Sea Aframax market finally showed some sign of life this week. Rates have slowly firmed during the month of May, and at the time of writing last done in the area is WS 157.5. Also, other areas still pay a higher TCE per day for those willing to ballast out of the area. Owners will try to push for more as the tonnage list for cargoes loading end May/early June looks tight on paper. But moving forward, the market looks a bit more balanced in terms of supply and demand, and we don’t expect rates to continue moving north. In the Med and Bsea market, the owners gained some momentum as the tonnage list thinned out for end month loading dates. Moving forward we expect the market to remain firm unless Suezmax would be an alternative for charterers capping Aframax.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Domestic US propane inventory levels – as reported by the EIA – are at the forefront of many conversations, and many have been left with the impression that corrective data will again be required in order that a truer picture might be revealed.  In any case, stock levels this week were said to have risen by 2.3mmbbls this week where expectations of ~1.4-1.5mmbbls was anticipated.    Most notably, however, was the 700,000bbl decline in PADD I stocks when there has been little demand pressure.  Overall stocks are presently 143% of the totals achieved in 2022 and 2021, respectively, and the second highest since 2015.  This has led to questions regarding potential late-summer containment, and whether there is sufficient above-ground brine storage capacity.  Most agree, however, that the owners/operators of MB storage are monitoring the situation but at present see no cause for alarm.   As for market levels, MB propane is off by about 6cts/gal from the start of May and presently marked in the mid-64cts/gal range.  And while WTI crude oil values have also declined over the past couple of weeks, the relationship between the two has declined from around 40% to approximately 37%, against the YTD 2023 average which is in the 43-44% range.   Terminal fees remain at modest levels and most talk for June and July is in the mid/upper-5cpg, having risen from the upper 4s and low 5s, but through the summer levels are slowly improving to the 6cpg range.  NWE The region has not been competitive vs the East on a netback basis from the US for a sometime. This has not stopped large volumes of LPG being imported 650,000MT in April and 600,000MT in May. This pushed the May/June contango out to $6/MT and though CIF ARA values have been weak they did track crude oil values upwards Wednesday. This was surprising after consecutive larger than expected build in US inventories. Petrochemical continues to buy their maximum potential volume with the  propane naphtha spread at $160/MT in May. The TOT window has been quiet with discounts assessed at May CIF ARA minus $12/MT. Butane is valued at 75% May Naphtha which has butane at a higher outright of TTF Natural Gas for the first time this year, while propane remains below.   MED US imports have been filling the Moroccan butane demand. Turkey is set to received 300,000MT in May, down from 320,000MT in April.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Though crude rallied up, Jun C3 CP was still traded below $500 and at the time of writing at $493, and C4 was assessed at $5 less as long supply out of AG.  FOB discounts deepened further, against the lukewarm demand and soaring freight. Evenly split ratio for Jun lifting was assessed at CP minus 30s even into 40s. Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their sale tender for 19/20th Jun lifting heavy propane at FEI netback value. And one Oil major also tendered to sell an evenly split cargo for mid Jun lifting.   Saudi Aramco finally released their Jun lifting acceptance, and again players have concerns over their surplus spot sales.   FAR EAST Cash premium slightly inched up in window and 23kt propane for 2h Jun delivery was bid at Jun FEI plus $5, partially due to the rising freight. However off window buying inquiries appear thin, as most have finalized June program and domestic consumption slowed down for the coming slack season amid high inventory for residential sector .   One producer trading arm was said to have placed a mid-Jun arrival propane this week at CP plus less than $30, and it was seen to have fixed at least three vessels for Jun liftings ex AG. One full propane parcel for 2h Jun delivery was placed into Echina at Jun FEI plus high single digit.   PDH margins seems healthy for now, and the run rates in China have improved to 80% in general. Two new PDHs each 600kt/y, located in SChina and EChina respectively, have started trial run and produced on spec propylene this week. However, one Schina PDH accidentally shut down and might need one month for maintenance and it was reported reselling their propane for Jun arrival.

Scrubber-fitted Aframax SOUTHERN GLORY (108K DWT TSUNEISHI 2019) is the standout transaction in the wet market, purchased by Eastern Pacific for USD 66M, thus affirming value for Aframax units of this age following the recent sales of SPERCHIOS and ARISTOKLIS. Otherwise, it was the familiar tale of older tonnage achieving firm prices, often at huge premiums to the previous purchase price. No transaction represents this better than WONDER POLARIS/BELLATRIX (115K DWT SAMSUNG HI 2005/2006) selling en bloc for USD 72M, compared to their respective purchase prices of USD 13.6M (06/22) and USD 18.15 w/TC attached (12/21). In the only VLCC transaction of the week, having failed previously at USD 53M, BALITC SUNRISE (309K DWT HHI ULSAN 2005) sold to Chinese buyers at USD 51.5M.    Units at the top end of the size curve are the flavour of the week in the Dry market, making up the majority of transactions. There appears to be a run on vintage Capesize units, with levels on 2004 built vessels exceeding last done on a 2006 built. VICTORIUS/OLYMPIUS (171K DWT HYUNDAI SAMHO 2004) sold en bloc for USD 17M per vessel to Dubai based buyers, which surpasses the USD 16.3M spent earlier in May on the younger C H S SPENDOR (170K DWT IHI 2006). TASIK MELATI (180K DWT KOYO 2004) sold for USD 15.5M, perhaps a slightly lower price than the VICTORIUS/OLYMPIUS due to the manner of sales process (sealed bids/outright offers). Elsewhere in the dry sector owners around the market are reporting disappointing results largely due to the lower earnings environment for the first half of 2023, adding to a widely softening sentiment.

EAST Aramco acceptances was published Wednesday night and we are seeing cargos being quoted continuously both East and West. Owners' freight ideas remain strong although so far 2H June positions in the East looks relatively balanced for now. That being said we so far only count 3 confirmed deals in the second decade of June versus an average this year of 7 for the same period.   WEST We have seen cargoes being worked both in end June and early July in the USG this week with rates rising from around 140 H/C to mid-high 140s H/C, but we still see the West trade at a pretty big discount of approximately 10k per day to the East. June fixing looks to soon be finished as we only see 2 vessels left for last decade and time being we count 27 spot fixtures for the month ex USG/USEC. So far for July we count 6 spot deals and with the Western position list still looking tight we expect the strong rates to stay put for now.

The LNG spot shipping market has seen subdued activity this week. The emergence of a small number of spot requirements has highlighted the lack of opportunities relative to the size of the availability lists; the majority of potential vessels provided offers, suggesting that the market is quiet across both the Atlantic and Pacific basins. Despite the muted spot market, LNG industry participants are actively engaged in managing internal fleets, including optimizing their portfolios, strategic vessel repositioning, cargo swaps, or time charter extensions to address operational requirements. Looking ahead, the second half of 2023 is anticipated to bring about a tightening of the market. Rates for multi-month charters during the winter season and multi-year charters spanning multiple winters are expected to remain at elevated levels, indicating that market participants anticipate strong demand and potential supply constraints during this period.  In terms of newbuilding LNG vessels, prices have maintained their firmness in recent times. The limited availability of the newbuilding slots is anticipated to keep newbuilding prices at higher levels, consequently exerting upward pressure on corresponding long-term charter rates. Shipowners with existing modern LNG vessels, influenced by the expectation of high newbuilding rates, are likely to maintain their rate level expectations or demand rates close to those required by newbuilding vessels.

Recent sluggishness seen in the tanker charter market seems to have spilled into the S&P space, as the sector registered an unremarkable week. Asset values remain strong however, with Suezmax CLASSIC (159K DWT HHI 2005) transacting for USD 36.8M, more than double what Seven Islands paid for the unit back in December 2020. Aframax PS PISA (108K DWT Hudong Zhonghua 2010) was sold for USD 36.5M, issues with the vessel condition explaining the lower than market price on the unit. With an enticing rates environment, vintage MRs continue to be in high demand, MR SYMPHONY (46K DWT STX 2004) fetching just under USD 18M. Tanker owners across the size curve are likely asking themselves the same question; how far can this market go?   The dry market remains a target for most market players, seen in the competitiveness for the Capesize DENSA COBRA (180K DWT STX 2011) which had a rumoured 6-7 buyers. This, however, did not prevent the sale from failing, with the unit being circulated around the market once again. There seems to be a run on older Capesize units, seen in TASIK MELATI (180K DWT KOYO 2004) taking offers this week and attracting levels of xs USD 16M, which is well over the last done for a ship of this vintage (C H S Splendor). In the even more competitive Ultramax space, scrubber fitted VOKARIA (63K DWT COSCO YANGZHOU 2020) sold for USD 32M.

EAST Adnoc acceptances was released earlier this week with reports of some disparity between nominated and actual dates received by Charterers. This could require some reshuffling on the product side before more requirements hit the shipping market, but still a bit early to say. Availability in the front of June is tight and with market keeping active in West and other regions freight is maintaining momentum.   WEST With a couple spot tenders out in the market this week, in addition to a good handful of cargoes in the USG, there have been several things happening West of Suez this week. For the rest of June the current position list is looking tight with only about 5 ships ships left open. Counting 23 spot fixtures (14 first half and 9 second half) so far for June ex USG there should be room for more to be done as we find the monthly YTD average at above 30 spot fixtures.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS MB propane prices have drifted since the start of May, but so have WTI values – each by more/less 6%.  That has left the ratio of propane to crude static at between 38-39%, which is considered a relative bargain.  The much higher-than-expected propane inventory build as reported by the EIA yesterday took the market by surprise as an increase of around 1.8mmbbls was expected, but a 3.1mmbbl build was reported.  Now stock levels have risen to 61.40mmbbls, or roughly 140% of early May in both 2022 and 2021.  The 5-year average stock level for the first week of May is 47.5mmbbls, where the 5-year average weekly build for this time of year is 2.254mmbbls.  Along with the soft crude market, this is surely adding to the bearish sentiment within the MB complex.  Netbacks from both the East and from NWEurope have remained relatively flat, as well (~7-9cpg to the East and ~2-4cpg to NWE), but the number of transactions has been limited – mostly due to the ever-tightening freight market, which continues to push buyers to the sidelines.  Northern tier LatAm demand seems satisfied, with contractual volumes having met the existing requirements.  Nonetheless, Southern tier winter-related demand is now on the horizon and will perhaps reveal spot requirements.  NWE The weight of imports are being felt in the region, pushing CIF ARA into a steepening contango, May/June at $5/MT. 500,000MT are on the water for arrival in May, and new deliveries continue to point to the region form the US. Cargoes now heading to Europe are thought to be term deliveries as the May East vs West spread is wide at -$89/MT. Additionally the TOT window is a assessed at May CIF ARA -$12/MT whereas the Ginga window is as June FEI +$1.5/MT, so any spot cargoes should head East. The propane Naphtha spread remains wide, $153/MT in May, and keeping petrochemical demand for propane high. Butane has been quiet in the region and remains at 76% May Naphtha.  MED  Tight freight in the region with delays discharging in Tunisia is impacting deliveries. Causing traders to venture into the spot market for CFR deliveries in the West Med.

The effect of the Easter Holidays kept markets at low activities and rates softened further. The Atlantic market in main loading areas from USG and ECSA is well positioned and rates for FH pay a premium, though trips within the Atlantic are reduced slightly. An Ultramax loading Mississippi River was fixed close to USD 23,000 pd for a trip to Japan with grains.  While Ultramax still getting premium to load in draft-restricted ports, a smaller tonnage of 56 000 dwt is fixed at USD 15,000 pd for a trip across the Atlantic. The Black Sea and Continent markets are very quiet due to a lack of fresh cargo and supply of prompt tonnage. Cont-Med trade rates are ranging from USD 14,000 pd to USD 16,000 pd depending on trip duration and delivery port. Activity from Russian ports was slowing due to a lack of cargo at Russian ports due to the inland logistic challenges. A Supramax was reported at USD 16,500 pd basis delivery Atlantic Spain via Russian Baltic to India with fertilizers. The Far East market still lacks coal demand thus rates remain low.  In Asia, we see rats only at low USD 10,000 pd no matter of vessel size or direction. Pretty gloomy market. The 1 mill USD question – do we believe in dramatic improvement during the upcoming summer?

Market is overall up a few thousands on average from last week. The Atlantic is stronger with last fixture concluded close to USD 30,000 daily. The c3 route is more or less unchanged week on week, whilst improved activity in the pacific has boosted the c5 mildly. Also the Australian coal has been more active recently. All in all it looks good, but some more Brazilian iron ore would be needed in order to lift rates up to next level.

Following holidays in the UK, it returned a tedious opening for the Panamax physical market with fundamentals largely unchanged with rates drifting lower. This despite an active and positive move in the FFA markets which created some consternation in parts, but overall had little impact so far. The North Atlantic was still widely gapped between the grain and mineral trades whilst trade ex-South America remained slow. The outlook ex Asia from the outset looked tonnage heavy with the smaller/older units discounting still for the quick Indonesia round trips, whilst there was muted talk of better bids being touted around for the longer rounds, but the market remained a watching brief.

After news broke of a replacement cargo fixing TD23 135kt x WS 130, charterers appear to have been smoked into the MEG market en-masse. They have inexplicably interpreted this as a green light to jump in with four cargoes, straddling the last seven days of the month. What makes this even more curious, is that the morning after news of this juicy rate filtered through, the rate was universally dismissed as an aberration and owners were all talking maximum mid WS 60's, but those rates are no longer there thanks to the generous state of the cargo board and now likely start with a seven. In the Atlantic, there was much talk of VLCC's capping Suezmax, but rates have pushed on despite this, with TD20 likely to surpass WS 110 by the end of the week. With a number of unsold West African cargoes and a limited number of European ports that can accommodate VLCC's, charterers are unable to fully commit to VLCC's unless they know exactly where the cargo will end up. US Gulf is looking positive, and we expect support from lightering and Aframax' to further underpin TA rates.

It is likely the VLCC market has found the base around the WS 40-41 level MEG/China and a little below that for voyages with better freights, and things are looking up. With many vessels fixing under the radar there is certainly more going on than meets the eye and as such ships disappearing off a (albeit long) list. In these situations, it is often an uptick in volume of USG cargoes that drive the market upwards and right on cue for owners, we have seen 10 or so cargoes fixing ex USG in the last few days. This, coupled with a busy Suezmax market and the clear temptation for VLCC’s to move in on their smaller sisters turf. Wafr UKC fixing at WS 52.5 and USG/East at USD 6.6m.

Activity in the Nsea Aframax market has been quite decent, but rates have only moved slightly up on the back of this increased activity. The tonnage list is slowly thinning as ships also ballast or fix outside the Nsea basin. If the current activity level remains, then we could see rates firm a bit more. The Med/BSea market has been relatively slow this week with moderate activity and a balanced position list. As a result, we see owners willing to fix premium cargoes ballasting to Baltic while others just looking for a local cargo before fixing window move too forward. We expect rates to move sideways in the short term with a potential to move higher if fixing activity increases.

We have finally had a somewhat "normalised" week as Japan and China both returned from their lengthy holidays. However, any expected boost for LNG demand was short-lived, as buying remains muted and as a result, JKM prices continue to test new lows.   On the LNG shipping side, the spot market continued to soften despite some new activity and regular tender cargoes. We even witnessed a spot fixture going below "roundtrip econs", which until now has been a strong support level. The softening can be attributed to the ongoing slump in LNG prices (and constantly regenerating sublet availability). However, it's a completely different story in the term market, as demand remains very healthy and new requirements appear every week. Unfortunately, closing the Bid-Ask spread is now more challenging due to the wide gulf between spot and term rates. Looking ahead, we expect spot market activity to pick up once we get the contango back into play. As ever, it will be a volatile road up to winter!  Turning our attention to the yards and no fresh newbuilding orders were placed this week - which has provided the sector with a well deserved breather.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Jun propane CP was traded at $508, and butane assessed at $500. One producer trading house was reported to fix over 14 vessels for May lifting, which lent support to the freight whereas exerted pressure on CFR June market with plentiful supply.  Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their 8-9 Jun lifting evenly split cargo, which assessed at CP minus mid high 20s against the soaring freight. ADNOC released their Jun lifting acceptance, and it is believed that the freight rates will gain further in view of the front tightness in shipping.   FAR EAST Window is muted with limited bid and offers. Off window a couple of 23kt propane for 2h Jun delivery were changed hand at FEI plus $1-2. Apart from that, a handful of 46kt propane parcels into China for similar period were reported concluded at June FEI plus $6-7, mostly for PDH use. Cracking wise, one China major managed to cover a late Jun delivered propane cargo into Hainan reportedly. And another Korean importer also tendered to buy a late Jun delivered 23kt butane. Other than petchem use, a couple of players in Schina are also inquiring for evenly split cargos.   Additionally, offers for Iranian cargo into China is reported to edge higher and some traditional users shifted purchase from such origin to normal stems, which help absorbed the abundant supply from both AG and US. With limited vessel availability and unstable program, we believe importers will keep eyes on non-Iran origins at a competitive price.

Tanker values showing no signs of abating. Another week with pricey Aframax sales; WONDER AVIOR (108K DWT 2004 HHI) achieved USD 30.1m and the one year younger and scrubber-fitted SONGA CORAL (107k 2005 KOYO) is reported sold for USD 35m. To put this into perspective, WONDER AVIOR was purchased by the Sellers in May 2021 for just below USD 10m. Expecting further activity in the sector with the modern scrubber fitted Aframax SOUTHERN GLORY 2019 Tsuneishi seeing a number of buyers getting outright in view of the upcoming offers which are invited on 10th May.  Dry values are moving sideways as seen by the sale of Capesize DENSA COBRA 2011 STX at USD 27.7 which, adjusted for yard, falls is line with the sale in mid-April of STELLA ADA 2011 Dalian at USD 25.6 mill. Japanese owners remain notably absent from the sales lists.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Three significant events have occurred over the course the past week:  First, crude oil values declined by $4/bbl, mostly on economic fears based on the recent large bank closures (and the ongoing fear of additional problems).  Second, propane prices at Mont Belvieu softened by up to 5cts/gal as a direct response to the crude oil weakness.  Third, terminal fees have weakened as buy-side interest has retreated.  Current June offers are seen at 5cpg but buyers remain agnostic, even when shown that there is plenty of room for negotiation.   Meanwhile in rather a surprising fashion, the EIA reported that propane stocks as of the week ending 28 April actually fell by 600,000bbls to 58.30mmbbls from 58.90mmbbls.  This leaves current stock levels at 143% of those recorded last year and 140% of end April 2021.  This week’s data release is widely viewed as a correction from the week prior when a 3.4mmbbl stock increase was published.   If – in fact – that is the case then presumably the traditional ‘build’ season should resume with next week’s report.  In any case, at this point stock levels of propane in the US are well above the 5-year average and remain closer to the 5-year high’s, which in some cases has become worrisome in the sense that brine containment issues later in the season are now becoming a consideration.  NWE Large import volumes continue, around 600KT in April and 350KT set to arrive in 1H May. Despite the drop in crude LPG values the propane naphtha spread remains at a healthy -$144/MT in May. The spread continues to keep petchem demand at high levels which is driving this spring market. Additionally production in the region is increasing, though re-injection into the natural gas stream continues. The butane market has been quiet over the last few weeks and continues to be valued at 76% May naphtha which has lost significant value this week in line with crude.   MED  The butane market has come off relative to naphtha with decreasing seasonal demand.

EAST Despite many players being kept away from the office during Golden Week, the market in the East was very active yesterday - mainly thanks to one big supplier. So far at least five ships was placed on subs for 2H May dates ex AG on Wednesday, in addition to that there is now one India tender cargo that have been rolled over until to today. Sentiment is now looking strong on the back of a shorter position list and increased activity. There should still be enough ships available for the rest of May – but many of the remaining vessels are likely West candidates and the obvious East candidates is slimmed down quite significantly now.  WEST Freight rates in the Western market has come off from mid-$130’s to $130 within the last week, but it now seems that freight rates are on the rise again on the back of a widening arb and relatively tight availability of ships. We continue to see large exports on VLGCs from the US and with April ending at close to 90 liftings and a consistent ratio of around 70% for East destinations, this increases the ton mile significantly for the sailing fleet and supports the bullish freight environment we have witnessed so far this year.

The LNG shipping market has seen a quiet week resulting in low demand for spot charters. However, there is interest in securing tonnage for longer periods, as more Charterers are seeking to prepare for the upcoming winter season. While spot rates have remained unchanged in all basins, multi-month and multi-year period deals have been observed, with more expected to follow. This trend is likely to reduce term availability and increase sentiment for term charters. It is always a question of where winter spot rates will be, and this will eventually be factored into longer-term rates as Charterers look to compromise on longer periods at the right price to cover this winter. At present, many Independent Owners are reluctant to fix for short periods and are instead enticing Charterers with better rates for longer-term charters. However, for now, some are struggling to find a bridge between the spread, but it is expected that either parties will bite soon. Despite the current subdued state of the spot LNG shipping market, the increased interest in longer-term charters suggests a positive outlook in the coming months. On the newbuilding front, prices remain firm with reports this week that an Owner have secured two 200,000m3 LNG carriers at around US$277M a vessel from Hyundai Heavy Industries for delivery in late Q4 2027.

The North Sea Aframax market remained relatively flat at the start of the week with relets dominating the tonnage list. But we see somewhat increased activity in surrounding areas. The local market is looking balanced right now, but we might see rates firming as Owners could push for higher rates in the North Sea area due to better alternatives ballasting out of the area.After tumbling the last two weeks, Med/BSea market touched bottom early this past week as tonnage list started clearing away from prompt vessels. Owners gained some momentum as tonnage list became thinner and managed to earn some extra Worldscale points. Moving forward we expect market to remain firm with the Suezmaxes being the only threat capping Aframaxes.

Bizarrely, despite two vessels being apprehended by the Iranians  and a chunk of vessels disappearing  in the last 72 hours, rates and sentiment have not improved, at least not for now. Thus far, we have seen an ex dry dock vessel fix a touch below WS 50 for TD23 whilst MEG/China on modern needs a proper test, but for now, we're freighting it in the WS 110'S. The Atlantic has a degree of stability with a similar scenario to the East, where a large volume of ships have fixed with no details. On the surface, we have seen TD20  repeatedly fix at WS90 which is how we envisage the rest of the week playing out. The USG has seen sustained enquiry for transatlantic runs at the back end of the second decade which edged rates up to WS 82.5 for a UKC run. If Aframax rates start to show promise by the weekend, then a further support mechanism will come into play.

With holidays looming over the tanker market this week, the activity was perhaps unsurprisingly subdued. Those cargoes that did come into the market were fixed quietly with minimal fuss, and clearly, if the rates paid on these had been exciting in any form, Owners/Charterers would have tried their best to at least hint at it (?). TD3C at the time of writing looks likely to dip below the ws50 level and will probably have done so at the time of going to press. West Africa/East numbers also look likely to do similar. The USG remains quiet and focussed on the smaller vessels due to the WTI pricing.  With the Iranian Revolutionary guard flexing their muscles in the Straits of Hormuz, in times of old, we would have seen a big shift in Owners attitude. At present however, little if any effect on rates. At least for now. Fingers crossed for a swift and peaceful resolution.

EAST A decent amount of deals have been concluded this week but freight levels seems to show little direction either up or down – if anything a bit softening. Fixing window gradually moving into the very last decade of May in the Middle East and with about 4 weeks to go it seems like many players don’t feel any reason to move this far out just yet. Last done concluded at mid 70s RT/C.  WEST We have registered approximately twice as many fixtures in the West this week than the week before and we are now counting 27 spot fixtures in May ex USG with only one available ship left in the very end of month. With last spot deal done 4-5 dollars pmt below the two ones fixed right before we get the feeling that freight might be topping out, but vessel supply is still looking relatively tight 1H June in the West as only 8 spot fixtures have been done so far this period. Last done at 130 H/C.

text: MEG CP recommendation was reported at $555 for C3 and C4 at flattish or $5 cheaper, and it is expected to be announced by this Sunday. At the time of writing, May C3 CP was traded at $554 and C4 at $551. Jun CP was traded at $6 backwardation to May. Discounts for evenly split cargo lifting in Jun were assessed at minus 20s to CP.   FAR EAST Quite thin discussion in window this week. 23kt propane parcel for 1h Jun delivery was bid at FEI plus $4 while offer at plus $9, and similar parcel for 2h Jun delivery at FEI bid at flat vs offer at $4.5, reflecting the front tightness caused by the Panama congestion delays. text: AMERICAS Domestic US propane demand has naturally tapered as the winter requirements have subsided, but export volumes are now regularly at record-level, whether overland (rail, truck and pipe) or – overwhelmingly - by oceangoing vessel.  In spite of that, however, propane inventory levels rose sharply over the week ending 21 April, having been recorded by the EIA at 58.9mmbbls, up from 55.5mmbbls the week prior.  A build of that size might lead to the expectation of a lower pricing structure, but non-TET propane at Mont Belvieu has so far hardly budged from its 77cpg perch.   With regards terminal fees, there was earlier in the month a flurry of activity but things have slowed considerably as freight costs have risen and – rather correspondingly – terminal fees have softened to near-cancellation levels.  Presently offers are seen in the 5cpg range, but bidders are increasingly scarce and priced at least a penny less.     Latin American demand should begin to see some improvements relatively soon as Southern Hemisphere winter demand is poised to increase in the coming weeks and months.  NWE  The region continues to receive a large volume of US imports arriving in the end April timeframe with some cargoes slipping into early May timeframe. This volume is additional to term deliveries and is keeping the region well supplied, with cargoes waiting to discharge into petchem importers. So even with the pro/nap at $153/MT for May we do not see any additional prompt demand. The is hope the larger than expected US stock build will improve the arb to Europe, and whilst the East vs West spread is at $77/MT in May the West will have to close that gap before attracting further spot tons. A large butane volume is set to be exported from Marcus Hook in May. Butane value in Europe is 76% April Naphtha, that said, large cargo lots have not been actively traded and few importers are looking for additional volume.   MED The region continues to see offers of trans-Atlantic tons. Which has kept open discussions quiet.

Market participants have slowly returned from holidays, but although this might have triggered more activity in the past the LNG market has remained stubbornly stable this past week. The majority of spot activity revolved around FOB cargo tenders, with limited new firm requirements seen in either basin and thus spot rates have remained broadly unchanged. The term market has been busier but not exactly surging, though with limited independent owner availability and and expectation of growing sentiment in the coming months, we may start to see some more activity picking up towards the end of Q2. In the newbuilding market, prices keep firming. NYK was reported securing four vessels at Hyundai Heavy Industries delivering 2026-2027 for EnBW.

text: AMERICAS Having reached over 83cts/gal at mid-month, propane values at Mont Belvieu have receded to 80.50cpg as of this writing.  Recent crude declines from the mid-$82/bbl levels to the low $77/bbl levels now have not offered support, and – curiously - neither has the most recent EIA data which revealed a 700,000bbl reduction in stock levels.   As of 14 April US propane stock levels were recorded by the EIA at 55.50mmbbls, down from 56.20mmbbls after record-level export volumes were made known.  On that note, exports from the US were reported at 2.511mmbbls/day this week, up from 2.395mmbbls/day last week.  For reference, at the same time last year exports were listed at 2.428mmbbls/day.  Propane inventories are now 150% of the levels reported in mid-April last year, and 137% of two years ago at the same time.   Meanwhile, terminal fees on the Gulf Coast have relaxed and for a full propane cargo talk now is centered in the mid-single digits mark.  Mixed-ratio opportunities are available below that, but little is being accomplished.  Latin American demand is presently satisfied, with no known requirements as contractual volumes are considered sufficient and Southern Hemisphere winter-related demand has not yet begun to surface.  NWE  An early May TOT offer in the window at a small discount reflects the CIF ARA April/May contango. Adding weight to the discount is the import program for April, with 250,000MT concentrated in the last decade. Propane naphtha spread has come in slightly but at $154/MT petrochemical buying will continue to drive demand through the summer. With US exports at record levels importers in Europe are not concerned about supply this summer. With the arb open further down the curve, some looking to lock in tons at attractive levels and hedge. Butane remains long in the region, with values directly tracking April naphtha downward  at 78.5%.  MED  The butane lull is keeping activity low as US tons continue to be offered into the region. North west Europe is experiencing C4 length though strong frieght rates are keeping the product in the region. French refinery strikes continue to hamper operations at Lavera.

text: MEG Saudi released the May acceptance with most reflected as per nominated, and limited impact was seen on Opec cuts for now. It is not to say that smaller tonnage is irrelevant, but its marketability needs careful consideration in the Atlantic whilst in the Pacific, owners are offered more relief due to a greater variance in parcel sizes.   The newbuilding price sees another small increase, yet no new buildings were reported this week.

More activity from the Atlantic, stronger rates from USG, also from South Atlantic. Ultra from USG was fixed to Far East with petcoke run around USD 27,000. Ultra from ECSA to China fixed around USD 15,570 plus USD 575,000 ballast bonus.  Supramax for trip with del ARA to Med was done around USD 16,000 for a usual scrap stem.    From the East, more fresh cargoes appearing. Indo China round were fixed at USD 10,000.  Indo India rounds covered at similar levels.

Still some holidays around which have resulted in slightly less activity. Tonnage is in excess, and rates are coming off after a relatively long period of values keeping flat. C5 is below USD 8 pmt now and c3 approaching USD 20. The average BCI is presently just below USD 14,000.

From Asia, on early trade there was some talk of some fresh tender cargoes ex Australia for May arrival dates, but this had yet to provoke any positive reaction to rates with charterers happy to stand back and assess.

Fixing first decade May in US seems to be spoken for as we no longer see any vessels left open this period. For the second decade we see two ships in the back, while last decade May currently have 4-5 vessels left and the majority of them are in control of one big owner. So far we have seen 21 spot fixtures in May out of the USG and only 6 of them have been done in 2H May - for reference the monthly average so far this year has been 31-32 spot fixtures. The West is currently trading at a discount of approximately 5 dollars the East.

Yesterday saw an influx of quoted cargoes and the arrow was pointing to mid WS 70’s MEG/East but failed to gain proper traction as owners settled for last done levels or a smidgeon more. On paper still a few MEG cargoes left to be covered for the first week of May, however, further investigation may very well find that the long list of ships on subs with no details attached will marry up with the “public” requirements. Nevertheless, downside firmly capped short term.

The downward pressure also increased with Suezmaxes absorbing significant volumes for local runs. It feels that market has reached the bottom for now, however any upside potential is not in the cards before May dates kick in and activity again could improve. We don’t expect rates to improve massively in the short fixture but if charterers rush to secure tonnage at present levels, owners might be able to slightly push for more. text: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane values have risen over the past couple of weeks from a low point of 70cts/gal to current market values which have well eclipsed 83cts/gal.  This is due to the combination of inventory drawdowns at MB and the recent surprise announcement that OPEC will cut production by up to one million bbls/day.  That news led to a $5/bbl increase in the WTI price which, in turn, gave lift to the MB pricing structure.  That buoyancy remains intact as propane closed most recently at 83.625cpg.  Going forward, domestic US liquids production is expected to outstrip demand (which – as evidenced by the half-million barrel inventory build yesterday - is clearly beyond the winter boundary by now), and inventory levels have now begun to build.  The strength and rate of stock growth, though, is contingent upon exports remaining true to the forecast that they will continue to be robust.  Terminal fees dropped from early March when values in the low teens were being seen, and bottomed out in the mid single-digit range before beginning to recover.  Current terminal fees for May are focused around the 6cts/gal level for a full propane cargo, while 2H 2023 values are pegged at/above 7cts/gal.  NWE April CIF ARA propane has continued to strengthen throughout the week with a late April TOT bid going unanswered. This prompt demand surprised the market as an 8 month high of 560,000MT will be imported in April. This strength has been largely due to maximum petrochemical demand with will continue as long at the propane naphtha spread remains wide, -$188/MT in April. Natural Gas prices remain low so we expect to see an increase in the region’s production which has been ramping up since March. Butane has been weak since the end of blending season with netbacks values for US C4 in around Mt Belvieu flat.  MED Little activity has been heard in the region, with the market quiet during Ramadan. Traders are looking to place large cargo buatne in the region as C4 remains weak in both northwest Europe and Asia, while the US arb is open.

After a week in which much of the world enjoyed a long festive break, LNG players were “welcomed” back with muted market activity and some lacklustre macroeconomic news. The LNG sector itself remains flat, with delivered prices in both basins showing little sign of recovery through the rest of the quarter; nor is there even the hint of an arbitrage opening up in the near-term. The impact on prompt shipping has been predictable, and in fact the renewed competition among disponent owners East of Suez reduced the regional disparity in rates. It’s not all doom and gloom though: this week saw several term fixtures concluded at strong levels, implying a degree of confidence in the second half of the year and beyond. However, away from LNG the IMF has lowered their projections for global growth in 2023, especially for advanced economies, and this may impact demand for LNG. If we’re again looking for a silver lining, then slower growth across the globe may lead to a lowering of interest rates and thus an improvement in the financing terms for shipowners and project developers. Good timing, as we await another round of FIDs.

It’s been an uneventful week with holidays occupying most of the trading days. However, as it often does, market soften a bit before the holidays as activity slowed down. The downwards trend continued the first trading day as a cyclone towards west Australia halted miners’ program. That we currently see a change in sentiment and except the spot dates from west Australia to China, the other basins and especially south Atlantic is looking very healthy, and we do expect better levels the week to come.

EAST ADNOC was released earlier this week as expected and we saw some activity for end April dates, but also for early May. At the time of writing, we count 2 spot fixtures out of the Middle East Gulf with last done concluded at around mid USD 70s RT/C. April fixing looks to soon come to an end as we only see 1-2 available ships left this period. So far, the positions for 1H May in MEG looks balanced unless more ships will ballast to the Unites States.  WEST With the West back from Easter holidays we are seeing some fixing activity in the US Gulf again. A couple vessels have been fixed at high 110s H/C and with them taken into consideration we are counting 16-17 spot fixtures (12 first decade) so far in May ex USG/USEC. With only a few spot fixtures done in second decade May there should be room for more, although we at the time of writing only see a couple open positions this period, but we can expect a couple additions coming back from discharge in the West. Vessel supply in the last decade also looking tight, and freight rates is set to maintain as we still see the West trade at a pretty big discount compared to the East.

Rates in the NSea moved sideways last week as tonnage list remains balanced and cargo activity is moderate. Most of the owners were happy to repeat last done numbers and moved to the next fixing window while surrounding markets don’t offer great alternatives. Moving forward, we expect market to remain flat with no big surprises. On the other side, local Med runs were fixed at lower levels as the slow activity and vessels pilling up in the list gave the opportunity to charterers to fix lower. However, owners still enjoy healthy returns for the non-premium CPC-Med runs despite Turkish Strait delays being at minimum. We don’t foresee any significant change for April laycans, but rates might be under further downward pressure if activity remains weak.

On paper, the MEG April stems seem far from finished. 20 cargoes remain? 30 cargoes? With many ships on subs, no details becoming a daily occurrence, an accurate picture can be hard to ascertain. Many charterers now increasing the way information is leaked, often when/if it suits their next cargo is a clever tactic. However, April is far from finished and the position list for the balance of the month is tightening. A couple of deals reported at WS 70+ MEG/East and owners have regained some lost confidence and showing resistance. Also, April also being the last month before OPEC+ put the squeeze on supply so some may try to maximize what the month has on offer.  A busier Atlantic will assist owners resolve as Wafr/East back to life at the WS 70 level and USG/East rates above USD 10m. Steady to a touch firmer in the short term.

Over the past few weeks, there has been a noticeable lack of activity for Suezmaxes in the Wafr and USG regions, and the situation hasn't changed at the beginning of this week. During the Easter holiday, the number of ships available has been increasing, and when charterers finally decided to take action, a downward correction in rates was inevitable. As of now, TD20 rates have dropped to WS 115, while USG/TA pays about WS 65. Although we are approaching the bottom of the market for this period, owners seem to have lost confidence, and unless there is an increase in volumes, rates may continue to decline. While activity remains relatively stable in the East, rates have softened somewhat due to the situation in the West. Looking ahead, it is expected that the market will reach a new bottom this week.

The cargo volume has been slow to surface, but tonnage count is still tight in North Atlantic, giving a balanced feel to the market. Further south has also been quieter, and with softer FFA, the charterers are holding back or rating less vs owners' last done. Seems toppy market with adjustment on routes this week.

The effect of the Easter holidays kept markets at low activities. Main loading areas in the Atlantic basin such as USG and ECSA are well balanced with sufficient cargo flow to maintain healthy levels. Tess 58 fixed USD 17,500 pd basis delivery in Santos, Brazil, for a trip to Italy. Another Supra 56’ dwt fixed delivery ECSA for trips with grains at USD 15,000 pd + 450,000 GBB to China. TA from USG to Cont/Med reported fixing at USD 17,000 pd, and trips to Singapore-Japan paying just a bit more premium. The Supras in the Black Sea market were remarkably quiet due to a lack of fresh cargo and supply of prompt tonnage. Trips to Asia fell to USD 15,000 pd and trips to USG/ECSA at very low USD 10,000 pd. The Far East market still lacks optimism, and rates remain negative. Backhaul cargoes to the Atlantic pay around USD 10,000 pd, and coal trips to China around low USD 10,000 pd for Pacific RV.

Signs of spring are appearing and seasonal national holidays creep nearer, yet the LNG and freight markets continue to trudge through a period of low activity. The spot market still suffers from an excess of availability and a lack of prompt cargoes, yet this week has seen a few requirements being worked and some very small revs of the engine. Although fixing levels have been dipping marginally lower than last done, some indications are holding firm or are at higher levels – perhaps this signals that the bottom of the shoulder months has been reached? A pause for the Easter holidays is unlikely to change the dial though, and the next few months could continue down a mildly-bumpy road without major risks to the upside or downside. In the term market, sentiment for prompt delivery was softening on the back of falling spot rates; however, new price points imply that levels remain supported by the slim list of modern tonnage available. As we inch towards a modest summer, there is clearly a view that another strong winter and beyond lies ahead.    On the newbuilding front, it is reported that K-Line have secured two SHI slots with delivery November 2026 at ~$258.5M a piece.

text: AMERICAS  Export volumes of 1.8mmbbls/day are the primary cause of this week’s reported 2.5mmbbl propane inventory decline, well beyond the average 5-year end-March draw of 514,00bbls, but directionally anticipated and surprising only because of the volume.  Current stock levels of propane in the U.S. stand at 56.2mmbbls, or 3.2mmbbls under the 5-year high of 59.424mmbbls, and more than 23.5mmbbls above the 5-year low of 32.671mmbbls.   Despite this, however, Mont Belvieu propane prices have risen with crude oil gains and are presently marked at (or above) 80cpg, which represents the peak of a two-week bull cycle.  The relationship between WTI and propane remains effectively static, however, as prices of each have recently moved in tandem, averaging ~45% on a YTD basis and presently pegged at ~46%.   Terminal fees have been challenging to accurately assess due to the recent conference and seminar schedule – which resulted in an overall lack of activity - but for 2H April have been established in the low/mid 5cpg range.  May is notionally around the 6cpg level, with June mildly higher, still.  NWE The TOT window continues to be offered, with large cargo physical values at April CIF ARA +$1/MT. Europe is importing a large volume of US LPG with 7 VLGC scheduled to arrive in the first half of April. The wide April propane naphtha spread of minus $166/MT is keeping petchem demand high and with crude oil values increasing the spread will remain wide. The downward VLGC freight correction seen this week will take some time to have an effect on the European market as much of the supply is imported on TC vessels. Additionally a large proportion of Europe’s trades are supplied on MGCs and smaller vessels, these spot markets are tight and have more resilient freight rates. This freight resilience could see the East West spread, today at minus $60pmt narrow and see further US volumes imported to Europe. Butane in Europe continues to be weak with few signs of additional demand.   MED Refinery strikes in Fance continue to disrupt opertations at Lavera. March export volume was half of the 40,000MT exported in February which was down from 70,000MT in Janaury. Length in northwest Europe in March has picked up the slack in local supply.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Apr CP at $555 for C3, down by $165; and $545 for C4 respectively, down by $195, which is in line with expectation. Qatar Petroleum issued tender to sell 10-20th May lifting evenly split cargo, whose last tender for similar ratio was awarded at May CP minus teens for end Apr lifting. And apart from producers, several lifters with AG length were also looking to resell their FOBs instead of lifting it themselves.  FAR EAST Cash premium for May delivered cargos weakened especially when deals into China traded at discounted value to curve value plus deviation. In window, 23kt propane parcel for 1h May delivery was bid at May FEI plus low single digit, and 46kt parcel for end Apr early May delivery into Ningbo was bid at May FEI plus mid single digit. However, both yet to entice seller interest yet.   Seeing the decline on feedstock flat price, coupled with the termination of maintenance in May, several petchem players have emerged this week to secure end Apr to 1h May delivery propane. Two 46kt propane parcels for 1h May delivery into East China were traded at May FEI plus mid single digit, and a couple of 23kt propane parcels for similar period were sold at May FEI plus low teens or CP plus 20ish. PDH operating rates increased this week with improved margins and we are expecting more players coming out to cover their rigid feedstock demand.

The North Sea Aframax market seem to have bottomed out at WS 180 for the time being and the tonnage list still looks tight in the front end, but then fairly balanced up to mid-month with a mix of oil company relets and independent owners in position. We have seen quite a few owners ballast away to fix in other load areas outside the North Sea basin. However, going forward we expect the market to remain around current levels depending on dates. It’s been a roller coaster week in the Med/Blsea area. The positive momentum took a U-turn end of last week following into this week. Charterers took a step back and managed to find alternatives offering them an escape. Even though the market has cooled off somewhat, owners still seeing nice returns on cross Med voyages. We foresee a soft undertone for the balance of the week.

The trend across all markets remain flat and lacking more boost. USG and ECSA gained some steam to get owners hope to rise higher.  The Continent market remains firm and Far East direction was not preferred, as owners prefer to stay in Atlantic in view of Far East market softening.  Ultra 63,000 dwt was fixed from Baltic to East Africa at USD 18,600 pd, and Supra 55’ dwt fixing delivery Continent for Med direction around USD 15,000 pd.  Black Sea and Mediterranean markets see good demand for tonnage, and rates shooting up. Owners asking a premium to go East. Trips from Med to West Africa paying USD 20,000 pd, and to China direction close to mid USD 20,000 pd. The market in the Pacific basin slides somewhat downwards and mixed rates created confusion of real demand. Ultramax 60’ dwt with delivery SE Asia fixed at USD 17,000 pd for a trip via Indo to Japan, and a Supra 58’ dwt open North China was rumored fixing low USD 10,000 pd for a trip via Indo to China.

Given activity in recent days it was no great surprise that we ended the week on a quieter note. Limited talk in the Atlantic, but some sources felt optimistic leading into next week with slightly better bids seen for transatlantic trades, but still very limited. Asia again returned a very confusing story, despite much talk of fresh demand entering the market charterers bids remained very low still consequently little happened as we end the week with a wide bid/offer gap ensuing.

It says a lot about the psychology of this market, that despite no real support from either the US Gulf or Mediterranean, West Africa has managed to bottom at a very healthy mid/high WS 130's/TD20. Participants, namely charterers, have been burnt by the bounce so many times that they are the ones ironically applying the handbrake, which is preventing further falls. The West African fixing window is firmly focused on 15-20/4, and we count max 2-4 stems left before charterers start sniffing about for early third decade. The list remains tight, and we all know how this algorithm tends to play out. In the East, TD23 has twice traded WS 70, which is a fair reflection of the list and sentiment for that run. MEG/China on modern needs a test but it should find a home at circa WS 150 levels.

Bumpy road for the biggies as long-awaited spring improvement doesn't just come as a straight line. Surprisingly low inter-pacific coal and iron ore flows combined with fast turnaround in Chinese ports pushing average daily earnings for Far East rounds down 25 pct w-o-w to USD 12,500, spot in general down a moderate 5 pct in value to just south of USD 14k/day. Atlantic seeing a healthier development as we speak, with in particular substantial mineral volumes to be moved ex West Africa. North Atlantic is thin on tonnage for April and list of ballasters not scary. Numerous traders, operators, and end-users out to lock in quality period units but bids not matching expectations - recent conclusions limited to indexed structures, exemplified by 181,000 dwt, built 2009, done for about 12 months at BCI AVE5TC + 7 pct.

With sentiment in the tanker charter market looking flat, the S&P sector, despite the overall strong market, did little to provide a significant headline. Surprisingly, a 1999 blt Suezmax made the most noise, as WHITE TRADER (150K DWT 1999 NKK) was sold for USD 27M, representing almost double the price the unit would fetch at demolition. Elsewhere, in the very popular MR sector, Parakou sold MR PTI DANUBE (50K DWT 2017 SPP) at USD 41M, a price that initially seemed elevated when the ship reached the market but has quickly been realised as value. Viken sold the last of their HMD Handytankers, with NORVIKEN (37K DWT 2010 HMD) changing hands for USD 23M.  Activity continues to increase in the dry sector with a total of 18 ships having been reported sold this week. JP Morgan purchased Handy trio of ERISORT/ERRADALE/WULIN (39K DWT 2014 CHENGXI) from Swire at USD 20.5M per unit, with MUR to manage the vessels going forward. In the Capesize sector, ROSEBANK (177K DWT 2010 NEW TIMES) was sold for USD 23M and MULAN (176K DWT 2005 TSUNEISHI) transacted for USD 16.25M, sales which will help price the spread of older units at this end of the size curve. Wisdom Marine sold Tess 58 Supramax AMIS ORCHID (58K DWT 2012 TSUNEISHI CEBU) for 18.7M, as Supramax values continue to be squeezed upwards.

Not a busy week on the open market, but ships continue to fix quietly with minimal fuss. As such, charterers have efficiently cleared the first half of April, as rates for Modern vessels MEG/China over the last week have fallen from the mid WS 90’s to the mid/high WS 80’s (to test) and many vessels fixed with no details will not add to any firmer feel. The current market direction will hinge on owners’ patience and ability to hold the line in the face of low surface volumes. The LNG shipping market continues to soften this week as we slide further down the shoulder months of 2023. The lack of prompt requirements in both basins has resulted in an eerily quiet week across the market thus far and has been made more apparent when reviewing the Fearnley LNG Availability Report. The number of available vessels in the Atlantic remains high, with Owners of modern tonnage struggling to find the prompt employment while tonnage East of Suez also appears to be stacking up. Consequently, we have lowered our spot rate assessments to reflect the softening market sentiment and surplus of tonnage which corresponds to the backwardation seen on the LNG product side going forward. On the term side of equation, the current lull in spot rates has translated into reduced short-term rates of 1-3 years, however, we expect this to correct upwards and remain bullish as we inch towards winter. For now, heads turn to the fiercely contested EGAS spot tender for which bids are due by 30th March.   On the newbuilding front, prices remain firm with reports this week that Taiping & Sinopec Financial Leasing placed orders for two 175,000m3 LNG carriers with China’s Jiangnan Shipyard while Capital Gas were reported to be identified as Owner of two LNGCs ordered with Hyundai Samho Heavy Industries for delivery by March 2027.

EAST Baltic keeps dropping across the board on the back of a weaker product market coupled with a lack of firm shipping requirements. So far we have seen 11 spot deals concluded in April in the Middle East (6 in first decade and 5 in the second) and it remains to be seen how many cargoes will be available until the last decade of April. Some of the early April positions are expected to head West, but with an equally slow market in this region little help is found to shorten the list in the East so far.  WEST With well over a week without any spot fixtures in the West and freight rates dropping fast, we are now finally seeing willingness to fix after an Indonesian spot tender came out in the market for early May dates in USG. We now see a handful of uncovered cargoes out there for end April/early May with freight ideas around USD 110 H/C, which is a huge discount compared to the East. The position list still shows 8-9 ships left in April and it remains to be seen if there are enough cargoes to cover them all or if some of them will roll over to early May dates.

Tanker Snp markets were relatively subdued with only a handful of transactions to report this week. Older tonnage is still fetching significant premiums with the Suezmax EUROVOYAGER (159K DWT DAEWOO 2005) reported sold at USD 38M and LR2 STAR PROSPERITY (115K DWT SASEBO 2009) was sold for USD 41M. While interest remains high in the MR space, only one transaction was registered this week as OCEAN III (45K DWT BOHAI 2007) was sold for USD 21.5M.  A busy week in the dry sector sees transactions taking place all across the size and age curve. Tomini splashed out on 2x scrubberfitted Newcastlemax units MP THE BRUSCHI/MP THE VRABEL (208K DWT JIANGSU NEWYANGZI 2020/2021) for a total of USD 121M. They weren’t the only ones to pick up large tonnage as Norden affirmed their commitment to Capesizes with the acquisition of AQUAHAHA/AQUATONKA (179K DWT HHIC 2012) for USD 28M each. Scrubber fitted Capesize MOUNT FABER (176K DWT NAMURA 2008) was sold at USD 22.7M, providing valuable insight to those after a potential asset play at the higher end of the age curve. Despite soaring demand in the Supramax sector, only one transaction was regsitered this week with GF ORIENT (57K DWT STX DALIAN 2011) bought by Chinese buyers for USD 13.5M.

With quite a few owners ballasting away from the Aframax market in the North Sea basin due to better alternatives in other load areas, we expect the market to firm due to shortage of Aframax tonnage going forward. Watch this space. In the Med/Blsea we seen a solid upward correction the last week, with benchmark routes jumping WS 100+ points. Cargo activity been healthy as charterers now started fixing into 1 decade April. Owners currently enjoying attractive alternatives across the board in the western markets. We foresee the Mediterranean to remain firm for the balance of the week.

Sentiment has changed a bit over the last week as cargo count in the north and south Atlantic has calmed down a fair bit. Hence, we are down 17% week on week. The next week looks a bit sluggish looking at the cargo list, however that could change quickly and the list of ships on its way to Brazil is not very significant, so sentiment can change over night.

The Atlantic outperforming the Pacific, especially more action from USG and East Mediterranean. Fronthaul from the USG to the Far East trading around USD 20,000. Trip from Mediterranean to Far East similar levels about USD 19,000.  TA now around USD 13,000.  Wafr to North China now around USD 18,000 levels. Less activity from the East though, where coal round via Indo to India done now at USD 15,000.
