A trickle of MEG fuel oil tenders has kept the early side of the list honest whilst TD23 is likely to trade at circa WS 80 levels. A MEG/China run won't give much change from WS 160 and might possibly trade a tad more for prompt dates. In the Atlantic, there is a modicum of disappointment from owners who had expected USG lightering volumes to be higher, but nonetheless, there are still some meaty rates to be had with USG/TA last trading 145KT x WS 125, with no evident downside. TD20 should be nearly done for first decade April but with the list displaying a limited number of vessels for this window, freight is likely to price circa WS 150.

Timing is everything, as they say, and there’s no escaping the fact that we’ve run headfirst into the shoulder months once again. And as usual, this has caused a pile-up of tonnage that begets a natural rate correction. What is significant, historically speaking, is the location of this fleet build-up, however. This year it’s in the West rather than the East, which of course explains the premium that Pacific vessels are earning over their Atlantic counterparts. The size of the East-West delta is also noteworthy ($30k pdpr for a TFDE as we go to print this week) owing to the magnifying effect of fewer ships in Asia leading to more Eastern spot requirements. Whilst this will provide some comfort to owners delivering and /or redelivering into JKTC, there is still a rate reduction along the curve and accordingly term rates (for prompt delivery) have softened also. Ultimately, this may all be short lived as two regularly recurring themes of the last few years have been volatility and uncertainty. Nonetheless, based on the current outlook, one would expect this to remain a charter’s market until the middle of the year when the contango into winter should firm up and then the pre-Christmas rush can begin in earnest.    Whilst we don’t have any Newbuild orders to mention this week, we can congratulate Sempra on a new FID (their Port Arthur project) and CoolCo on their New York Stock Exchange listing. At the other end of the spectrum, there has been a solitary vessel scrapping (Sinokor’s 127k ST, Grace Energy) which brings the total number of demolitions for this year to three.

The Panamax market appeared a little listless and languid this week. Minimal fresh demand seen again today in the Atlantic with little exchanged, sources said, but tonnage count seemed well balanced. Asia somewhat impacted by holidays in Japan lacked any cohesion with a stand-off between owners and charterers ensuing, but despite not a lot of activity of note many felt owners who wished to cover would have to likely to concede lower numbers in order to get fixed. Limited period activity this week.

“Great expectations” – not materializing. Logic dictated that a well-stocked cargo list and correspondingly balanced position lists would result in a rate hike this week. However, charters kept their powder dry, patiently waiting, and when an oil company relet fixed a Brazil/East export cargo at WS 85 the upward sentiment reversed which was then followed by MEG/East rates sliding into low WS 90’s. That said, the downside appears capped short term and owners in general are so far trying to add a point or two to last done levels. The Atlantic market has calmed down a bit after the recent USG export fixing frenzy, but a trickle of cargoes is keeping the light burning. Steady as she goes.

text: MEG Apr Propane CP rebounded to $560 and Butane at nearly $10 cheaper, reflecting the front lengthy supply on butane. Apr/May was traded at $15 backwardation.  Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their tender to sell a late Apr evenly split cargo at May CP minus teens.   FAR EAST Despite players are away for China Conference, we’ve still seen some activities in and off window. 23kt propane for 1h Apr delivery was bid at Apr FEI plus low teens but no sellers seen, which appears prompt and believed sellers already finished program for this period. However same parcel for 2h Apr delivery was offered at Apr FEI plus mid single digit yet to entice buyer appetite. There is also a bid for 46kt propane parcel for 2h Apr delivery basis Ningbo at Apr CP plus $2 for non-Us origin, which equates to Apr FEI plus mid/high single digit.  Off window one AG producer was reported to have some heavy butane cargo for Apr delivery available, which suppressed the discussing level. Other than such, there are still a few tenders ongoing. One Chinese player was reported to procure a 11/11 parcel into Qinzhou at Apr CP link price. Another European petchem player also tendered to buy 23kt butane for 2h May delivery into Caojing. Taiwan FPCC issued tender to procure 23kt to 46kt LPG at flexible ratio for May delivery.

EAST Despite Japan having a day off on Tuesday and the Chinese LPG Conference keeping a big chunk of the industry away from their desks we have seen a good handful of fixtures concluded this week. First decade April in the Middle East is getting quite thin with just a couple of potential open vessels remaining. The fixing window is now focused around second decade of April dates where a third deal was concluded in the MEG on Tuesday and a fourth one from Indians on Thursday. Freight have maintained relatively stable throughout the week although it now looks to be softening.  WEST Having seen 6-7 spot fixtures in the West last week we have only registered one so far this week. The position list remains relatively unchanged apart from a few additions. We are now seeing one potential relet for very end first decade in April and only one ship left for mid-month dates. End April currently showing 8-9 open positions and 3 of them are relets, but some still considering going to the Middle East as we see the BLPG3 route trading at a discount of approximately 6,000 USD pd to BLPG1, using latest Baltic print.

text: AMERICAS Were it not for the fireworks following the weekly EIA data releases, the market would otherwise be mostly eventless.  A handful of seminars, conferences, meetings, travel and Spring Break have left many away from their desks and conspired to limit activity levels in what has become a generally dull market.  The EIA, however, posted a rather unexpected propane inventory build last week, followed this week by a surprisingly robust draw of 2.3mmbbls for the week ending 17 March.  That decline brought overall total US stock levels from 61mmbbls last week to current levels of 58.7mmbbls – though even so, present inventory levels are 174% of last year and 142% of two years ago.  In spite of the fact that stock levels are very near to 5-year high’s, the draw yesterday might lead one to anticipate that prices might increase – particularly as crude values have increased from below $67/bbl last week to over $71/bbl currently.  And it did.  Non-TET Mont Belvieu propane last week was marked at 69.75cpg where values last night concluded at 74.50cpg.  Terminal fees on the Gulf Coast are known to have been fixed for April at between mid-6 and low 8cpg.  May is at this point likely within a similar range but little talk has yet been heard for the forward market.  A series of Mexican tenders have been issued and awarded, with one West Coast requirement presently outstanding.  Likewise, pre-winter South American demand was recently covered on a spot basis as at least one – but perhaps two – spot cargoes were reported fixed for April lifting.  NWE The TOT window continues to see activity from petrochemical traders, and the general mood is that CIF ARA flat is fair value. Sellers have been popping up at premiums to April CIF ARA, buyers at discounts. Nothing has come together in the middle yet for April cargoes. CIF ARA propane values rose as crude saw a recovery. Over 340,000MT of US LPG is expected to find it’s way to Europe in March partly due to the arb opening in February and partly due to the huge export volumes form the US. Butane has dipped to below 80% March naphtha as a large cargo offer continues to be seen.  MED  France’s refinery strike continues to reduce demand with almost 60% of it’s 1.15 mn b/d of refining capacity offline. That has not stopped two US MGC cargoes heading to the region for early April arrival.

Following last weeks momentum the tanker charter markets levelled as global financial and oil markets were shaken on news of potential banking crisis. In the S&P space, older units continue to receive healthy premiums with VLCCs KASSOS I (319K DWT 2007 HYUNDAI SAMHO) commanding USD 61M and VLCC YUFUSAN (311K DWT 2005 MITSUI) selling for USD 52.3M. Offers were invited on SUEZMAX LILA HONG KONG (159K DWT 2003 BOHAI), eventually seeing Chinese buyers secure the unit for USD 31M. Interest remains high in the MR sector, with rates displaying significant volatility particularly in the Atlantic. Only one transaction though was registered in this sector this week, with MRK Shipmanagement picking up SAFESEA NEHA III (46K DWT 2003 SHIN KURUSHIMA) for USD 13.75M.  Increased activity in the dry S&P market is providing is providing little relief for the ever-swelling number of purchase enquiries in the sector. Seen as the next potential asset play, and an outlet for tanker owners’ increased cash supplies, the demand for dry ships is beginning to push asset values perhaps north of where recent market returns would usually denote. In the headline size category, CAPESIZE pair GOLDEN FENG/SHUI (169K DWT 2009 DAEHAN) were snapped up for USD 23M each by Greek buyers. Elsewhere, another Chinese Ultra sale in the form of ULTRAMAX SOHO PRINCIPAL (63K DWT 2016 YANGZHOU DAYANG), going for USD 26.5M.

Presently, we sit in the gap between the March and April stems in the MEG. Charterers will be patiently waiting for stem dates with a cautious eye on the tonnage list. The Basrah dates are out however, and Smaxes actively working, providing plenty of support from below with bigger numbers reported (130 x w175 on subs). Saudi stems expected tomorrow, and there is potential for charterers to play it wrong, falling on top of each other, and we move to three figures MEG/China. However, picking softer candidates from the shadows may be the best tactic, as by the 3rd - 4th April, the MEG list opens out, the other side of this end March bottleneck.   The Atlantic continues to fix at higher levels – USD 11.4m latest USG/East and these decent levels will be needed to continue to tempt ballasters and Wafr remains quiet to test.

text: MEG Unexpected crude drop and ample AG supply, Apr Propane CP was slashed to $544 and Butane at flattish or slightly less, down by $90 compared to last week. Apr/May was traded at $20 backwardation.  Evenly split cargo was offered in window at cp minus mid 20s but yet to entice buying interest. And several late Mar lifting cargos popped up from producer, which exerted further pressure on discounted market. Adnoc released their Apr acceptance with major delays reported.    FAR EAST Cash premium weakened this week under lengthy supply, with offers seen at Apr FEI plus high single for for 23/0 2h Apr delivery basis chiba.  PDH margin slightly improved with declined flat price and softened premium, and we’ve seen a couple of PDH emerged for Apr propane cargo inquiries. One PDH was reported to procure some 46/0 parcel for 2h Apr delivery at FEI plus teens level, which equates to Cp plus single digit only.

We had a temporarily dip in Aframax rates in the Nsea this week on the back of lower activity. At the time of writing, we see rates ex West coast Norway pick up fixing at WS 170 levels. Owners will still be very competitive for any TA cargoes from the Cont. We expect the activity to remain healthy for the remainder of the month and rates moving sideways, unless we see more ships ballast or fixed out of the area. Med/BSea bottomed at the start of last week as charterers pushed for lower rates on the back of a longer list mainly consisting of ballasters from the East. Activity was steady, and as a result owners managed to push rates higher again. Market instability persists for another week West of Suez, with the main driver still being the USG market. We expect the Med/BSea to find a new equilibrium around current levels.

A deluge of enquiry blankets the Suezmax market with a firmer outlook in all load-zones. West Africa has displayed massive volatility with the region failing to establish a benchmark for more than a couple of days at most. After bottoming at WS 115, TD20 last traded end March dates at WS 117.5, but those rates are likely to ebb from charterers very quickly with WS 120 on the cards. Across the pond, we have seen enquiry levels tick up and with that so should rates. Lightering continues to thin out the list with evident upside. In the East, WS 70+ been logged for MEG/UKCM, albeit on option cargoes, but with the list of 20T crane vessels thinning out on the early side, a straight run might price close to these numbers before the week has finished. Strong VLCC market also adds an element of psychological support.

A week of significant gains for the Panamax market with all markets returning improved rates. The North Atlantic was said by numerous sources to appear tonnage tight with healthy demand driving rates, and with EC South America beginning to push too, these same sources felt further gains to come. Asia, despite being relatively slow in comparison but on reflection appeared well supported with Indonesia coal trips paying better levels even for the smaller and older LME types, coupled with this latest rally ex EC South America the market feels in very bullish mode. Unsurprisingly, some healthy period activity.

The trend across all markets remains positive despite some areas such as USG and North Atlantic could see softer rates as the number of ships is greater than the number of new requirements.    Rates paid for trips to Far East were achieving close to USD 20,000 pd, and trips within the Atlantic improved from low USD 10,000 pd to mid USD 10,000 pd.   Black Sea and Mediterranean markets see a sharp shortage of tonnage and rates improving substantially. Owners demanding a premium to go East. Rates from Med to West Africa directions reaching USD 20,000 pd.  A lack of tonnages in Indian Ocean pushed charterers to pay higher levels. A Supra open WC India was fixed at USD 18,000 pd for EC India range, while Ultramax open WC India was fixed around USD 20,000 pd.   The market in the Pacific basin remained stable with potential upside due to coal imports to China.   Supra fixed dely Spore at USD 16,000 pd for a trip to China.

EAST After a few quiet weeks we are starting to see a bit more activity in the East. A couple of cargoes are being circulated and a late running ship required some puzzle solving in order to free up a replacement. Tonnage supply is still looking quite sufficient in the East, especially for cargoes with laycans at the end of first decade April and onwards. Reports of less cargoes from both Aramco and Adnoc in April further emphasizes the current downward trend for East spot freight.  WEST With a small handful of spot fixtures this week we are now counting a total of 24 for April out of the USG/USEC (7 first decade, 12 second decade and 5 last decade). At this moment we only see a couple open vessels left for mid April laycans while last decade have about 5-6 open positions before we move over to the month of May which currently is looking very tight in the front. Using latest Baltic print we get a 12-dollar discount in the West before waiting in the Panama Canal. With that being said, we believe today’s freight rates at around mid 140s H/C and low 80s H/F to stay put, unless the arb dictates otherwise.

The spot LNG shipping market has remained stagnant, with limited activity reported. While there are a few pending requirements, most of them are within the East of Suez and are more than 6 weeks out. Presently, there is a surplus of prompt vessel availability compared to the requirements in the market, with vessels opening in the Atlantic still commanding lower spot rates than those in the Pacific.  A potential window of opportunity for the East – West Arbitrage could arise as the spread between TTF and JKM spot prices shows signs of reversal, with JKM now commanding a marginal premium to TTF. In the term market, charterers remain focused on securing tonnage for winter coverage, and there is continued interest in long-term charters. On newbuildings, Maran Gas has reportedly ordered two 174,000 cbm LNG carriers at the DSME yard, with delivery expected around mid-2027.

text: AMERICAS  The historically improbable propane inventory build of 900,000bbls recorded yesterday by the EIA puts overall stocks at 61mmbbls as of 10 March, surprising the majority of market participants.  Current stocks are 183% of last year, and 148% of two years ago and are now effectively equivalent to the highest second-week-of-March stock level since 2015.  Since then there have been only two occasions when U.S. propane inventories have built – the other being around half of yesterday’s increase.   Propane stocks for the period from 2015-2023, when plotted, reveal a high, a low and a 5-year average, and current stock levels are now on par with the highest part of the range.  With no support from falling crude oil prices – and the fact that winter-related demand has by now subsided – Mont Belvieu propane values have sharply declined from the 90cpg levels seen in early March to today’s 68cpg, which continues to decline.   As for terminal fees, a rather wide range was established this week for April cargoes, with a 6.50cpg deal being transacted, but also an 8.25cpg deal.  Latin American demand was covered via both spot purchase and tenders this week, one of which was recorded as a typical spot purchase, the others via tender, which were awarded both for a one-off parcel as well as a term contract.  NWE Credit Suisse needing a $54 billion dollar loan from the Swiss Central Bank shook the LPG market. As many LPG trader’s LCs are issued by the bank. With the prompt market well supplied traders in the region are happy to sit back and watch CIF ARA track crude oil values. Leaving the majority of US cargoes, even US East Coast VLGC exports, heading East. Further down the curve the arb looks healthy and workable, and many are questioning what the LPG and Gas markets in Europe will look like later this year? As the conflict in the Ukraine looks no closer to resolution. Butane in the region had not been bid or offered for some time, and an offer in the window correct butane values from 95% March Naphtha down to 88%.  MED The region is well supplied for the last vestiges of winter, though if butane weakness in NorthWest Europe continues it is likely those tons will find a home in the West Med. The East Med has been active as Turkey continues to see higher LPG demand as it recovers from the devastating earthquake coupled with cold temperatures.

We had a temporarily dip in Aframax rates in the Nsea this week on the back of lower activity. At the time of writing, we see rates ex West coast Norway pick up fixing at WS 170 levels. Owners will still be very competitive for any TA cargoes from the Cont. We expect the activity to remain healthy for the remainder of the month and rates moving sideways, unless we see more ships ballast or fixed out of the area. Med/BSea bottomed at the start of last week as charterers pushed for lower rates on the back of a longer list mainly consisting of ballasters from the East. Activity was steady, and as a result owners managed to push rates higher again. Market instability persists for another week West of Suez, with the main driver still being the USG market. We expect the Med/BSea to find a new equilibrium around current levels.

What a week for the big ships! After a slow start to the year, activity has really picked up and Capes are in demand. The average index rate is up USD 5,000 from last week, and the C5 is presently priced just excess USD 9 which is up USD 1 from last week. C3 has seen increased activity, and is priced up USD 2 from last week, close to USD 21.50. As a consequence, interest in period tonnage is changed, and more players are now looking to take cover.

A deluge of enquiry blankets the Suezmax market with a firmer outlook in all load-zones. West Africa has displayed massive volatility with the region failing to establish a benchmark for more than a couple of days at most. After bottoming at WS 115, TD20 last traded end March dates at WS 117.5, but those rates are likely to ebb from charterers very quickly with WS 120 on the cards. Across the pond, we have seen enquiry levels tick up and with that so should rates. Lightering continues to thin out the list with evident upside. In the East, WS 70+ been logged for MEG/UKCM, albeit on option cargoes, but with the list of 20T crane vessels thinning out on the early side, a straight run might price close to these numbers before the week has finished. Strong VLCC market also adds an element of psychological support.

The West African Suezmax market has been volatile to say the least. TD20 peaked in the WS 140s last week with last done Kribi/UKCM now reported on subjects today at WS 132.5 (albeit not technically a TD20 run, it’s a bellwether for direction). Steep/deep downside is possibly capped by firmer VLCC/AFRAMAX, but rate wise, this could easily fall to WS 117.5-125/TD20 before this cap kicks in. The Black Sea is offering little in the way of support and with northbound Turkish straits delays collapsing to 2-3 days we expect TD6 to correct downwards into the WS 150s, reflecting general sentiment and tonnage availability. In the East, firmer VLCCs should maintain a degree of stability with MEG/East Suezmax trading WS 135-140 on modern and TD23 requiring a test but we are freighting it WS 60s.

Frenzied activity at the start of the week and continuing to the time of writing. The Atlantic set the mood, with multiple cargoes ex USG pushing rates to Ningbo close to the USD 11m level. As such, owners with the option at Galle headed West to benefit from the improved TCE’s. However, not to be outdone, the MEG list, stripped of a number of modern units began to look a little threadbare. With a lot of ships picked off market in both the East and West, charterers coming to the market were left with fewer options. TD3C now sits in the WS 80’s with likelihood of higher numbers imminent, as March still has 20-25 cargoes to come. However, the current heat in the market is encouraging some to work earlier than they may otherwise do. So, that quiet zone between March and April dates may stretch longer and test owners resolve.

As the spot market continues gaining momentum, we’re seeing a focus back in the Atlantic. The long list of available prompt tonnage maintains pressure on rates in the basin, but most of these ships only have short windows of availability. The news of strikes at LNG terminals in France could have some impact as most requirements from the US Gulf had Europe in their sights. Combine this with European LNG prices recently falling to a near 20-month low, we could start to see Charterers look for alternative destinations for their cargo as more demand from the Middle East and India emerges. It is still tight if you need to find a vessel in the Pacific, especially if it needs to be cold and modern. We’re also seeing the fixing window stretch out to May, and rates within the basin remain firm but are likely to increase if we see more enquiry. Disparity on fixing levels between basins remains. Term discussions are ongoing with short bursts of activity on multi-month and multi-year, and we do anticipate rates maintaining. On Newbuild activity, NYK was reported to have ordered three 174,000cbm vessels to be built at HSHI. The price is reported at $255m per vessel with delivery in late 2026 & 2027. Today we also wish a happy International Woman's Day to all our colleagues, customers, and all women in the industry.

The Aframax list in the North Sea is thinning out as more owners ballast or fix away from the area. This could eventually put an upward pressure on rates in the North Sea unless Suezmax vessels start interfering lifting Aframax stems for the next fixing window 16th March onwards. Also, we have seen less activity in the area which could entice some owners to do less than last done for the right dates and the right voyage. So, sentiments are a bit mixed at the time of writing. CPC-Med rates decreased last week, delays in the straits were at a minimum and charterers’ relets were fixed out/programmed. Cross Med gained some strength on the back of replacement jobs and lack of natural candidates. Some momentum built as USG market remains firm and owners trying to push surrounding markets higher, upside potential might be limited.

text: AMERICAS  The trio of conferences scheduled for both this week and last has left the market dismally quiet with little to report other than a relatively small draw as calculated by the EIA.    Stock levels last week were recorded at 60.6mmbbls, where this week – the week ending 03 March - the overall total now stands at 60.1mmbbls, a decline of a half-million barrels where a minimum draw of 750,000bbls to as much as 2.3mmbbls was being forecast.  This puts inventories for the first week of March at 169% of last year and 145% of two years ago.  The 5-year average draw for this week – the 8th of the year – is 1.648mmbbls while the 5-year average stock level for the same period is 44.175mmbbls.   Terminal fees topped out in the low ‘teens’ for March and are backwardated well into the summer months, with April talked at 7cts, May just a bit lower, still, and June currently presumed in the mid-single digits.     NWE The market seems to have decided winter is over! March/April backwardation narrowed from $52/MT Friday to $35/MT at the close Wednesday, showing the a relaxing of the prompt tightness. This was coupled with the oturight drop in propane value in the region by 10% this week to below $600pmt. Though this may show more of the underlying market conditions as crude oil lost value early week. Additionallly over 300,000MT of US LPG is set to land in the region in March, as the end February and early March tightness pushed CIF ARA to a better netback than FEI. The propane nahptha spread remains favourable for propane at -$120/MT and with crude oil bouncing back today propane will remain preferable to naphtha. The TOT offer shown in the window was not renewed and the large cargo physical premium is assessed at March CIF ARA +$12.5/MT.   MED The region haas been quiet as North African butane stocks look to be enough to get through the remainder of winter. The large NorthWest European imports couple with North Sea production increasing has Medittareanean impoters waiting for offers rather than searching for cargoes.

text: MEG At the time of writing, Apr C3 Cp was traded at $636 and C4 at $3 higher only, with expectation on ample supply for butane after producers’ maintenance completion. Apr/May was traded at $40 backwardation.  FEA Window was quiet as most players travelling for Japan conference. Till Thursday we see two buyers bid for 23kt propane parcel for 1h And 2h Apr delivery with idea at FEI plus Low 20s.  Off window a handful of buy tenders from China petchem users emerged this week.  One EChina cracker user procured a 23kt propane for 1H Apr delivery into Ningbo at Apr FEI plus Low mid 30s reportedly. One SChina PDH user tendered to buy 10-25th Apr delivered 23kt or 46kt propane into Qinzhou and was reported awarded at Apr Cp plus Low mid 20. Another EChina PDH also tendered to buy similar cargo but for delivery into Ningbo in 2h Apr.

A slower week for the Panamax market with no real clear sign nor direction in market, the trend seemed positive in start of week to sideways at best. In the Atlantic, limited transatlantic trade, whilst in the South end March arrival window ex South America offers remained discounted to index but little action of note for index dates. Asia appeared mixed in places however the overriding sentiment remained positive, both routes P3A and P5 making modest.

Supramax and Ultramax markets in the Atlantic gave good encouragement to the firming market. FFA is back in the game pushing the forward curve up. A good number of fresh inquiries in most loading areas, supporting higher rates. TA RV from USG and ECSA fixing around USD 15,000 pd on Tess 58 and fronthaul at low USD 20,000 pd. North Atlantic sees more cargo flow with rates increased by USD 3,000 pd in a week’s time. Several stems with scrap from the Continent to Turkey surfaced in the market for March dates, and the last done was USD 13,000 pd. The Black Sea market started the week with a strong push for all sizes and keeps pushing further up. We see fixtures done close to USD 20,000 pd for Supramax and charterers willing to pay more for Ultramax. The Pacific market keeps increasing with charterers chasing owners to repeat last done. A 63,000 dwt with delivery China was reported at USD 13,500 pd for a trip via Indonesia to China, while similar trips but delivery Southeast Asia paid USD 20,000 pd.

EAST With many players attending the Tokyo LPG conference the week got off to a slow start in both the East and the West. At the time of writing, we have seen a couple of spot fixtures in the Middle East with last done concluded at high 90s RT/C. Although April fixing in the East is already well underway, we still find a few open ships that can make end March laycans, but some of them might end up ballasting to the West. Currently the vessel supply in early April is looking tight, but it is likely we will see more ships appearing as discharge schedules are still not confirmed.    WEST The position list is looking tight at the front of April, but further into mid and end April there are more ships from both the Owners and the Traders. In total we have seen 18 spot fixtures concluded so far in April ex USG/USEC (6 first decade, 10 second decade and 2 last decade). For reference the monthly average for spot fixtures has been 28-29 the last three months. Using latest Baltic print we get a 15 dollar discount in the West before waiting in the Panama Canal which now is showing 18 days northbound for Neo-VLGCs. Last deal done ex USG concluded at around mid-140 H/C.

Big gains, admittedly from very poor levels, for the big ships. Volumes of major commodities iron ore, coal, and bauxite significantly up on most relevant routes, jacking average daily earnings for standard units up 67 pct w-o-w to come in at a still modest USD 13k. Particular interest is on (north) Atlantic, seeing the most expressed recovery on the back of a dramatically improved supply/demand ratio. Further steady climbs expected as positive macro-economical projections combine with tight tonnage supply across the board. Period interest very high but fixing activity still limited as both sides await strike prices to match justifiable levels and forward expectations/FFA values.

The tanker charter market roared back into life this week with the biggest intraday rate jump in recent memory seen yesterday. In the S&P space, healthy MR TC returns are proving too alluring to resist, with market players flocking to snap up units all along the age curve. MTM shed 3 units, MTM MANILA/YANGON/MUMBAI (46K DWT 2003 HMD) to Chinese buyers, while Norden and Ridgebury both offloaded one unit respectively in the form of scrubber fitted NORD SKATE (51K DWT 2009 STX) for USD 24.25M and RIDGEBURY MERCURY (46K DWT 2008 HMD) for USD 21M. Price ideas, particularly for late 2000s units are on the rise, with some prospective buyers beginning to rethink their intentions. In the larger sizes, all over the age curve, prices continue to rise with USD 35M now needed to purchase a 2004 blt Suezmax, seen in the form of KRITI DIAMOND (166K DWT 2004 BRODOSPLIT) to undisclosed buyers.  Elevated activity levels in the dry market have seemingly put the recent market misfortunes firmly in the rear-view mirror, as sentiment and momentum build. Quality designs and yards are in demand with Supramax IVS Pinehurst (58K DWT 2015 TSUNEISHI CEBU) being sold for USD 23.5M by Grindrod to Greek buyers, and Supramax IGNAZIO (58K DWT 2010 TSUNEISHI CEBU) being sold for USD 15M. Last week’s reported sale of Supramax SUPRA ONIKI (57K DWT 2010 QINGSHAN), has since failed at USD 13M, with increased levels likely to be required to develop a new transaction. Oldendorff made headlines on the sales of 4 modern Chinese built scrubber-fitted Ultramax units JAN/JONAS/JENS/JACOB OLDENDORFF (61K DWT 2019 NACKS/DACKS) at USD 32M per unit, market players are sure to be taking note of this in what is a very popular sub sector.

The Suezmax market has been nothing but volatile over the last eight months and will continue in this vein for the foreseeable future. This week highlighted how quickly the Atlantic can swing from a flat to firm trend in the blink of an eye. It commenced with a handful of TD20 cargoes hunting down the few FOC ships that were available in the 17-21/3 window, with rates swiftly firming to WS 140.  Owners will likely be holding for a lot more today as there is palpable, upward momentum. The US Gulf continues to export massive quantities of oil and with that comes increased lighterage requirements which should tie up ever increasing volumes of Suezmax and Aframax tonnage with an obvious impact on regional freight rates. In the East, BOT/East should trade in the WS 140's whilst TD23 will find a home in the WS 60's.

For the week to come we expect a further increase, but hard to imagine it without some kind of breather.

Solid demand ex EC South America for March and April arrivals continued to lend support to much of the market in stark contrast to the North Atlantic where demand remains thin and early ballaster ships under pinned trades here. Asia again appeared well supported particularly ex Indonesia with strong demand for the smaller Panamax types, perhaps a reflection of a firming Supra/Ultramax market with Panamax tonnage making more commercial sense for now. Period news included the CL Mona (81,504/2013) Zhoushan 1 March fixed basis 6/8 months at USD 16,000 with Solebay.

Supramax pair PACIFIC VISION/DREAM (56K DWT 2013 JIANGSU HANTONG) fetched USD 15.5M per unit, a transaction that should help price a number of similar units in the market. text: AMERICAS After a flurry of activity during 1H February, the current and pending conference/seminar schedule has dampened enthusiasm - and activity levels.  IE Week in London this week has taken many of the regular participants out of the market, and the combination of the Japan Conference in Tokyo and an OPIS Seminar in San Diego next week – each of which is expected to be well attended - should lead to yet further quietness.  Trading during 1H Feb for the March market, however, increased drastically from February and was based on the widely opened arb to both the West and – more so – to the East.  That, in turn, was the result of positive economic news related to the Chinese economy and, at the time, weather-related demand in (mostly) Eastern Europe.  The resulting rise in both terminal fees and big-ship freight rates began a sort of tug-of-war where re-sellers on the Gulf Coast began to escalate their asking prices and with each passing transaction higher levels were achieved.  Meanwhile, to capitalize, shipowners sharply hiked freight rates, as well.    Where terminal fees for March were seen within a range of 9-15cts/gal, April is presently talked in the upper single digits, May at just below that, and June slightly lower, still.

EAST QP acceptances was released last night which could trigger some activity out of the Middle East for April dates, but we expect there is more to be done in last decade of March before focus shifts towards April. We count 24 spot fixtures (9 first decade, 9 second decade, and 6 last decade) so far for March, and have only seen one spot deal from the Indian PSUs for the whole month. Freight is relatively stable still with questions being asked of how many spot cargoes there is left on March dates.   WEST With much of the industry gathered in London for IE Week, the Western freight market has been fairly quiet. We have registered a couple fixtures so far this week and with that said we count 14 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC for April dates with last done concluded at high 150s H/C and 90 H/F. Currently we see no open positions left for early April dates, but that could change as some vessels still can come open from discharging in NWE/Med/WAF. Further into second and last decade the position list is looking tight and the waiting time in the Neo Panama Canal have increased to 11 days northbound and 15 days south.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco set Mar CP at $720 for C3 and $740 for C4, declined by $70 and $50, respectively. C3 was almost in line with expectation but C4 is slightly higher than recommended. Evenly split cargo discussions quiet down with few inquiries into India, and value for Apr loaders was expected at double digit discounts to Apr CP.  Qatar Petroleum released their Apr term lifting acceptances with some delays reported, as some players nominated early dates to avoid backwardations for 40$ into May.   FAR EAST Lack of activities in window this week as players away for IE week in London. Off window some sellers are still reported to have unsold Mar delivery tons, perhaps will roll into Apr delivery instead. One AG producer was reported to offer two 2h Mar lifting evenly split cargos for Apr delivery. Another evenly split cargo for 4-5th Apr lifting ex Darwin was also offered via tender.   Despite weakening sentiment this week, we’ve seen a handful of buy tenders for petchem use. One EChina cracker user procured 23kt propane for 1-10th Apr delivery at Apr FEI plus high 30s. Another EChina PDH user also issued buy tender to secure 3 lots of 23kt propane for Apr and May delivery. Taiwan FPCC also tendered to procure flexible ratio LPG for any Apr delivery.

Activity in the Bulker segment was muted this week in comparison to the recent acquisition of a sextet of H Line Newcastlemaxes by Golden Ocean for USD 291M. The vessels will be chartered back to H Line for 36 months at USD 21kpd. Elsewhere in the market, Winning bought Capesize OCEAN CAESAR (180K DWT IMABARI 2008) for USD 20.2M, and Supramax SUN GLOBE (58K DWT TSUNEISHI HI CEBU 2007) sold for USD 14.2M, once again showing that values in the dry sector have managed to hold despite recent negative sentiment. This will be welcome news to those dry sellers who have fended off opportunistic bids in hope for better prices.    The Tanker market continues to read from the same script with premiums being paid for Ice Class units and vessels that would have been scrap candidates only a short while ago. Ridgebury Tankers, who have been proven sellers in this market, sold scrubber-fitted Suezmax RIDGEBURY JUDITH (150K DWT UNIVERSAL 2008) for USD 39.5M. They also sold MR RIDGEBURY KATHERINE Z (50K DWT SPP 2009) at USD 24.8M, into an MR market which seems to be bubbling as players eye healthy returns. Elsewhere, Euronav offloaded ice class 1C Suezmax CAP CHARLES (158K DWT SAMSUNG 2006) for USD 41.5M to Gardsea.

Early in the week FFA push could perhaps be accountable for turnaround in sentiment in both basins. The North Atlantic appeared mostly unchanged and concerns with little fresh demand and further ships adding to the count, early and committed tonnage still forced to concede APS levels at softer levels. Further south, there appeared some support with better bids heard for second half March and healthier levels starting to be agreed. Asia saw a minor upturn, primarily led by some support ex NoPac and Indonesia which saw better demand, but views remained fairly mixed on whether this was a minor rally or something more fundamental.  A week with little activity of note, thus a clear direction was hard to call and yet to be found. Market continuing to be depressed with little signs of recovery at the moment.

Despite some replacement jobs and a tight position list in the Nsea, Aframax rates moved sideways last week. Owners did have the chance to push for higher rates, but they were left with the attempt. Unless more owners decide to ballast away, we could face a tighter market. But with moderate activity combined with a populated position list, mainly with oil company and other relets being used for internal cargoes, we expect rates to move sideways. In the Med/BSea, market lost some ground as activity was slow and tonnage list quite long giving charterers the opportunity to push for lower. Another negative factor this week was also Suezmaxes taking out some of the Aframax stems. Moving forward, we expect market to move sideways with a soft touch as stem lists for the 1st half of March don’t look that promising.

The global Suezmax market has enjoyed steady gains over the last week with the Atlantic leading the way. The US Gulf list is extremely tight, and  has acted as the main driver, sucking in ships from across the pond. This has had a knock-on effect on West Africa with West Med' and Cont' weighted tonnage having the luxury of multiple firm markets in their cross-hairs. Td20 is minimum WS 130, but there is likely further upside with the possibility we might conclude the week a couple of points higher, given the strong fundamentals. In the East, steady enquiry has kept the early side of the list very tight on 20 tonne crane requirements with MEG/China on modern in the WS 130's, whilst TD23 has traded WS 60 off early March dates, with it remaining to be seen if owners can carry these gains into the natural window.

Sentiment on Supra and Ultra pushed rates up and was well supported by spot-fixing.  In the Atlantic, from the main loading areas such as US Gulf and ECSA owners saw a good number of fresh requirements which added to pressure for March loaders.  South America as well enjoyed better demand with charterers chasing owners for offers. Owners are increasing their rates and prefer to keep their tonnage in Atlantic. FH cargoes paying good premiums to last done. Supramax is rating USD 14,500 for TA delivery Brazil for TCT to Med. So far little info with fixtures surfacing, though we expect a good rise in the rates.   Asia saw the same upturn with more fresh inquiries and good demand for prompt tonnage. CP Nanjing (63,526/2017) was reported fixed basis delivery passing Singapore for a trip via Indonesia redelivery Thailand at USD 14,500.   Supra was fixing in the low USD 10, 000 pd for SE Asia RV which is about USD 5,000 higher than a week ago.  Charterers chasing period deals and are willing to pay a premium. Ultramax asking low USD 16,000 for a medium-short period.   We expect the market to continue to rise.

A busy week, with positive moves in the Atlantic, but the MEG was suffering under the paralysis of one particular China discharge cargo. Market speculators held differing views on the outcome, with owners holding for WS 70+, but given the lack of alternative options, WS 66.5 finally on subs this morning. Likely this will unleash the remainder of the first decade stems (another 5-10), as those charterers holding off will come into work. Worth noting the MEG tonnage supply remains healthy for early-mid March. The Atlantic will be key to where the market moves now, where successively higher numbers for USG/East, up to USD 9.25m. A tight USG list for March, but ballasters will certainly dilute off later dates if the MEG softens. IOC working, collecting 5 offers from vessels committed or located West, will test owners resolve.

After some weeks with depressing rates, there is finally a small improvement for the big ships and the index is finally showing green numbers again! The c5 route has been concluded at USD 6.35 pmt up from very low USD 6s. Overall average 5 TC is up from USD 2,600 last week to USD 3,250 this week. There is still a good number of owners who prefer to let their ships wait and their persistence will be a key factor in getting returns further up.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Though the March FOB market is largely concluded at this point, there were some exciting moments as prices first remarkable saw gains, but later in the month relaxed.  April terminal fee values are now being discussed in the upper single-digit levels, with May at a range just slightly below.     The arb remains open to both the West and the East, though the number days-delay at the Panama Canal have begun to swell again, thus allowing freight rates to rise and take a greater share of the profits.  Average expectations related to the EIA propane inventories this week were in the -2.1mmbbl range, with outliers as wide as -3.25 and -1.10mmbbls.  Ultimately the EIA revealed a 3.00mmbbl decline from 66.30mmbbls last week to 63.30mmbbls as of 17 Feb.  That puts current levels at 166% of last year and 145% of two years ago.  Meanwhile, talk of containment issues in the coming summer months has been muted.  NWE CIF ARA values dropping with crude oil values this week, though not directly correlated, with CIF ARA propane showing some strength. The tight physical market has pushed early March deliveries to the highest premiums to paper seen since 2012 at +$60/MT. CIF ARA backwardation remains very steep, Feb/Mar $54/MT and Mar/Apr $37/MT showing how tight the prompt market is in Europe. March propane naphtha spread widened to -$124/MT, keeping propane favourable to Naphtha for petrochemical companies. With natural gas values falling in the region it is expected that refineries will sell more propane to the market. Though this additional production will take a few weeks to hit or have any impact on the market. Butane market has been quiet with value relative to February naphtha steady at 99%.  MED  Activity in the region has been subdued, as Far East and CIF ARA values fall. The product market is tight and the fall in value of other regions could see traders offering more aggressively into the Mediterranean.

The LNG shipping market in the East has seen a uptick in demand for vessels for March loadings, resulting in a shortage of available vessels in the spot market. Last week ended with a surge in fixtures, with almost all available vessels in the Pacific being chartered. This sudden spot demand has caused daily rates in the East to firm.   This firmer trend is expected to continue this week, as the prompt availability of vessels in the Asian spot market remains limited for March and into April loadings.   In the West, sentiment is more steady and ship availability is sufficient to cover demand.    There were no orders for large LNG newbuildings made this week, however shipyard slots remain generally tight and orders from other segments continues to fill up any extra yard capacity.

EAST There’s still a good handful of uncovered requirements ex Middle East around second decade March dates. Some vessels are held back due to uncertainties with itineraries or for own program making actual count of vessels ready to work firm in this window very slim. We have only registered one confirmed spot fixtures into third decade March so far, and with second decade still very much alive and some vessels being swooped up for US cargos, freight is remaining firm. Last done around 100 RT/C.   WEST With over a Baltic LPG3 index route jumping over 20 dollars this week we are seeing the discount in the West shrink, but it is still a small premium in the East. In total we have now seen 14 spot fixtures (7 first decade and 7 second decade) out of the USG/USEC in April and there are only a couple open positions left for early dates and a small handful for mid dates, but there could appear a few more as current fixing window is still far ahead. At the time of writing we still see some uncovered cargoes out there for ely and mid April and some are already starting to look for end dates. Last done fixture concluded at very high 150s H/C and 90 H/F.

text: MEG 1st round CP idea was recommended at the range from $705 to $730 for C3, and C4 at flattish or $5 higher to C3. Expecting export volume resumed from maintenance, and the crude drop, Mar C3 CP fell to $697 and C4 at $707. Butane was reckoned at higher value with front prompt demand into SEA, also higher butane price from other origins.  Qatar Petroleum issued tender to sell late Mar lifting flexible ratio cargo and was reported to sell one evenly split cargo and one full propane cargo reportedly.  FAR EAST Premium for Apr arrival cargos softened as of the end of winter season, together with the refrained buying for PDHs due to the bad margins from downstream products. A handful of PDH units planed scheduled turnarounds in Mar or extend their turnaround from Feb to Mar or maintain low running rates. Buy or sale ideas varied widely, we’ve seen 46kt propane for 2h Mar delivery was bid at Mar FEI plus $5, but offered at Mar CP minus $15, which equates to Mar FEI plus $50.   The decline in flat price however attracts cracking buying demand, with better economy for feedstock. One Korean importer issued buy tender for 23kt propane delivered during 8 to 14th Apr delivery into Daesan. Previously they have procured similar cargo for end Mar to early Apr delivery at Apr FEI plus $90s reportedly. Another cracker user located in Ningbo, EChina also reported to cover a 23kt propane parcel for end Mar/early Apr delivery at Mar FEI plus mid-20s, which equated to Apr FEI plus 60s by then. Following this, one PDH user covered their demand for 46kt propane delivered into Qinzhou, SChina in 1h Apr delivery, which was reported done at Apr CP plus $40. We are expecting some more inquires for Apr delivered propane will surge after CP set, however most likely for 2h Apr instead of early deliveries, depending on the margins.   Apart from such, one 5-6 Mar lifting ex Australia evenly split cargo was sold via tender to a SEA importer reportedly.

As interesting a market as we have seen in a while. With a bumper February in the MEG (150 cargoes in a 28-day month), we are moving into the early March stems at the time of writing. Two schools of thought persist on where we go from here, but both have limited downside. Current levels for MEG/China sit around the WS 65 level, and owners could try to hold back, harness the sentiment and drive rates up through the WS 60’s. However, the alternative is for charterers to play it well from the shadows and owners to ‘profit take’ on cargoes off their dates. Either way, any imminent downside in the market remains unlikely.   The Atlantic cargoes continue, with a fresh Petrobras quote at the time of writing. Some recent deals not quite the jumps owners will have hoped for, but TD15 stands around WS 62.5 and rates Wafr/UKC at WS 72.

Aframax rates in the Nsea market dropped a few points as activity slowed down and most cargoes been taken out on relets in the current fixing window. The USG market is the most interesting right now in the Western hemisphere, and we might see ballasters from the Nsea and Wmed turning their bow in that direction and ballasting transatlantic. We expect the market to move sideways with a softish feel to it. In the Med/BSea rates dropped by 30 points for local runs even though earthquake didn’t affect loadings in Ceyhan that much. Tonnage list had built up the last 10 days as there wasn’t enough activity to absorb sufficient number of vessels and inevitably charterers managed to push rates lower. We except market to remain weak for the rest of the month unless firming USG market will attract more ballasters from Europe.

In the East, vessel spot requirements kept flowing with a long list of counterparties seeking tonnage for laycans throughout March. Focus remains to secure TFDEs and modern 2-stroke vessels, but looking at the limited availability in the region, a rate upturn looks inevitable. In the West, there was limited spot activity as market participants monitor the Freeport progress. Vessel availability has basically been “on hold” until the uncertainty around start-up is cleared up, however there seem to be enough tonnage to cover any open spot requirements in this basin.  Looking at the term market, Charterers still focusing on finding tonnage for winter cover as their priority, but we also see interest for longer/long term charters.  On the Newbuilding front, there has been an order recorded this week reportedly by MOL at DSME yard. Vessel is set for delivery during Q1 2027.

EAST With Saudi acceptances released last night we may see increased fixing activity next week in the East. Freight remains relatively strong and vessel availability in the Middle East for March dates could quickly tighten. Talks of some potential Indian PSU cargos in the early part of March will be expected to pick up healthy premiums. Currently we are counting 13 spot deals on March dates and while first decade availability is getting quite slim with just 2 vessels left, second decade looks more open with about 8 vessels available. In the last decade so far we see around 7 ships open, but there could be some additional ships appearing after the last round of acceptances are firmed up.   WEST Fixing activity in the West has been quite similar to last week seeing a small handful of spot fixtures out of the United States. With that said we count 35 spot deals out of the USG/USEC for March dates and we now only see 1-2 open positions left this period. Focus will soon fully shift towards April, once the last vessels in March is absorbed, and we are currently seeing a balanced to tight position list for the ten first days in Apr. Last done fixture concluded at mid 130s H/C.

Supramax and Ultramax market in the Atlantic was not giving any encouragement to owners despite FFA market pushing the forward curve up. Due to a lack of fresh inquiries, the rates in the main loading area remained flat.  TA RV from USG and ECSA was at the lowest level fixing sub USD 10,000 pd and fronthaul at low USD 10,000 pd.  North Atlantic was very quiet despite scrap prices being stable and several stems with scrap from the Continent to Turkey were concluded. For this, charterers paid USD 9,000 pd on Supra 56’ dwt.  Last week we reported the Pacific market recovery, and however, it didn’t last. The support for the market recovery in Asia was limited.  Ultramax delivery Indonesia fixed at USD 11,000 pd for a trip via Australia to South Asia. Another smaller Ultra was fixed at USD 9,000 pd delivery China for a trip via NoPac to SE Asia.

Biggies keep burning cash in heavy seasonal downturn, and with new environmental rating regime idling is not an attractive alternative. Already miserable average daily earnings down some 30 pct w-o-w to come in at a tragic USD 2,600, close to USD 5k below running cost. Whilst Pacific just keeps on scraping bottom, lately Atlantic has followed suit as demand dwindles further. Volume on the West Australia/China conference trade is fair but far from sufficient to absorb spot supply - and iron ore + bauxite + coal fronthaul/transatlantic trades not by far matching amount of tonnage ballasting or present in western hemisphere. Period interest nevertheless remains high in anticipation of better times to come, focus however on indexed structures - recent fixtures include 171,000 dwt, built 2004, done for about a year at 94 pct, 180,000 dwt, built 2011, at 103 pct, and 179,000 dwt, built 2016, at 132 pct of BCI AVE5TC.

text: AMERICAS Market levels in March have remained robust, particularly for the first half of the month, but begin to taper by the second.  April, as well, softens and beyond that May, as well, dropping as far as the mid single-digits by June.  As yet, however, only limited activity is being noted due to the backwardation that exists, the downward curve preventing much enthusiasm in the out months.  The arb both to the East and the West remains open – and widely – despite the weak PDH margins in the East and the nearing conclusion of winter in the West. The EIA yesterday reported a draw of 2.6mmbbls, mildly more than the anticipated 2.25mmbbl – the average that the industry at large had predicted.  Still, though, stock levels remain nearer to the 5-year highs, than the averages, so even with a relatively large draw there remain sufficient stocks.  Talk of summertime brine containment persists. LatAm demand has been noted but transactions at this point have not been confirmed.  Southern hemisphere winter demand should, however, begin to appear shortly.  NWE The staggering large cargo premiums seen in January on the back of resurgent petrochemical demand and competition from the East’s re-emerging appetite for LPG are now ancient history. Premiums have plummeted from +$50/ton in January, to premiums in the mid-teens now in Feb. The cause? Propane has maintained its strength in relation to naphtha thus disincentivizing consumption at crackers, along with continued mild weather throughout the region. Further still, Its estimated Europe will import approximately 320,000 tons this month of LPG -from both the North Sea and the US, leaving the continent very well supplied and subsequently pressuring prices to the downside.   MED The Mediterranean region is focused entirely on the search, rescue, and aid of those affected by the recent earthquake. With that said, the LPG import terminal in southwest turkey has seen 2 LGC’s discharged since the disaster, leaving the region comfortably supplied for the time being.

A key feature of this Suezmax market is "volatility" in which the main protagonist has been the been the Atlantic. Markets tend to adjust to change (Ukraine) after a period of bedding in, but these recent market nuances have undeniably left an indelible mark on charterers psyche. West Africa, and more precisely, TD20 end/early February/March dates, should have traded with minimal upside but charterers dispensed with the tried and tested method of chronological fixing and piled in on top of each which sent very positive signals to owners, and with that, firmer rates. Now the froth has settled the region is looking moderately overpriced and with V's munching on second decade positions rates are beginning to look toppy: WS 110's. MEG/East remains tight for 20T cranes and trades WS 130 whilst TD23 trades mid/high WS 50's.

text: MEG Mar C3 CP surged up to $734 and C4 assessed at flattish to C3. Mar/Apr CP backwardation widen further to $85, from last week’s $75.  FOB discussion interests appear thin  this week as demands out of India fall below expectation. However, we’ve still see Indonesia PERTAMINA out to buy one evenly split cargo for 15/23 Mar lifting, or can consider buy on CFR basis alternatively. Evenly split cargo for Mar lifting are offered at minus mid single digit discount to Mar CP but yet to entice buyer’s interest in view of the huge backwardation.    FAR EAST Discussions for 2h Mar arrival cargos quieted down after the deal on Tue for one 46kt propane parcel traded at Bal Feb FEI plus $7 which equates to Mar FEI plus $75. Bids for 1h Apr delivery propane softened at Apr FEI plus $50s in the window, whereas one 46kt parcel for same period sold at Apr FEI plus 70ish outside window.  Despite the current eroding petchem margins, we expect strong demand in Apr as of the decline in flat price and low feedstock inventory, together with the potential economic alternative over napatha.   Two Korean importer tender to buy LPG, with one asking for 2/2 and/or 3/1 and/or 0/23 for 1h Apr delivery and the other for 23/0 delivered in end Mar/early Apr. One Chinese Major managed to procure two propane cargos delivered in Apr and Jun respectively for their new PDH. Another NChina PDH user also issued tender to buy 46kt propane for 1st decade Apr delivery.

text: MEG Mar C3 CP was traded at $709, rallied up again with the front robust demand. Mar C4 was traded at parity to C3. However, Apr C3 was traded at wider backwardation at $65 to Mar CP. Market players are waiting for Adnoc and Saudi Aramco acceptance with expectations on cuts from Adnoc. Evenly split cargo for Mar lifting was traded at Mar CP minus mid-single digit and seller are asking small premium this week.   FAR EAST A handful of propane for 2h Mar delivery were changed hand and mostly placed into Japan at Feb FEI plus teens or Mar FEI plus 80s range. Supply looks tighter with most cargos are absorbed into far east and there are only bids seen in window for 2h Mar delivery parcels.   One evenly split cargo for early Mar lifting ex Australia was placed into SChina at Mar FEI plus 80s basis Chiba equivalence. Another oil Major was also reported to have procured a 11/11 parcel for 2h Feb to 1h Mar delivery into Malaysia via tender. Taiwan CPC also tendered to buy 22-31st Mar delivered 11/11 parcel.   Despite the poor margins, China petchem players, including both PDH and cracker users are inquiring propane for Mar delivery. 23kt propane for 1h Mar delivery was traded into EChina at Mar FEI plus over $110 and 46kt parcel for 2h Mar delivery into Ningbo was concluded at Mar FEI plus high 90s reportedly. However, another two EChina based PDH users cancelled their buy tender for Mar arrival propane due to the high offers.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Netbacks remain robust - particularly from Asia - and have well supported strong activity levels.  There is rising concern, however, that the combination of winter’s end and the virtual armada of LPG vessels currently headed East that the hurried pace seen so far this year could begin to falter.    The most recent transactions have been seen as low as 9cpg and as high as 14cpg, with current bid/ask levels ranging approximately from 11-14cpg, depending on timing, location, ratio, etc.  The bulk of March trades have likely been concluded, though a couple of interested parties remain.  The EIA this week revealed a 4.3mmbbl draw in propane stocks, down from 73.20mmbbls last week to an overall total on 3 Feb of 68.90mmbbls.  Current stocks are 144% of last year, and 134% of two years ago, giving cause for talk of historical high inventory levels.  In the first week of Feb 2020 stocks were 4% higher than now at 71.82mmbbls, and likewise, early Feb 2016 totals were also 4% higher, which somewhat alleviates what are likely premature concerns as to brine containment later in the season.  Those issues have arisen in light of strong domestic US production levels which are expected to continue for the foreseeable.  NWE Weakness dominated CIF ARA last week, but that all changed this week after larger than expected US inventory draw saw Mt Belvieu and in turn CIF ARA spring back to life. The bid/offer spread in the TOT window was very wide, the bid equating to a flat price of $602pmt and an offer for the same dates at $800pmt. Unlikely to come together, even using Fearnleys! Trans-Atlantic cargo flows continue though the majority are term deliveries as any US spot cargoes in February and March cargoes have been snapped up to head East. The recent fall of European natural gas prices, as stocks remain high and winter cold but not extreme, will lead to an increase in LPG production from the North Sea. LPG production was reduced by around 35% when LPG was being spiked into natural gas. Butane remains assessed at 97.5% February Naphtha, with no window activity.  MED The arb to the region from the US is attractive, though no prompt cargoes are available to make the most of this opportunity. Dortyol down in the East Med reduces demand by a 2+2 VLGC every 10 days, though is not expected to remain down for long.

Market activity in the Nsea has been rather limited as we have seen relets being fixed between oil companies or being programmed for own cargoes. However, rates this week have been maintained at similar levels as last week. Going forward we expect rates to move sideways as the tonnage list looks rather balanced compared to the expected cargo volume for second half of February.   Last week, activity slowed down in the Med and as a result rates for local runs lost some more ground while the rates for CPC-Med runs also moved lower despite the long waiting days in Turkish Straits. Liftings of Azeri crude are uncertain now after the earthquake in South Turkey, something that could put rates under further downward pressure moving forward.

Since the beginning of the Ukraine war the Suezmax market has become hardwired to extreme volatility, with buy-in on both side of the phone (charterers and owners), and when there's buy-in from both parties, events usually become self-fulfilling. On that note, West Africa appears to have bottomed and with the prospect of a firmer VLCC market, there's also a psychological comfort blanket. TD20 is reported on subjects at between WS 105-110, suggesting that the Atlantic market has bottomed with probable upside in the offing. In the East, moderately firmer VLCCs will likely prevent further cannibalization of Suezmax stems. MEG/China on modern should trade 130KT x WS 130's whilst TD23 should keep its head above WS 50 with possible upside.

The recent declines in the market failed to diminish again this week with further cheaper rates reported trading and fixed. This said, in some quarters came talk that owners’ resistance appeared a tick more resolute with hopes for some of a floor being found in the market, but evidence was in short supply with both basins losing further ground.

We are entering another familiar cycle in the VL market, a pattern seen a number of times in 2022. The Atlantic (mainly USG) activity picks ups, rates jump, and the rest of the market is dragged along with it. The price for a VLCC USG/Ningbo has climbed USD 100k on successive fixtures, currently sitting at USD 8.4m. With West Africa/East also positive at the WS 60 level, modern vessels will ballast West purely for the richer hunting grounds not found in a lagging MEG market. As always however, the risk of dilution remains.  East of Suez (TD3C) rates creeping up in the low WS 50’s, and owners will be hoping for a pop in rates to match Western returns, but the February MEG program is close to completion and it's a short month also. However, the position list looks more balanced than for some time, as many ships turn left at Rondo.

The Capesize market is extremely quiet as activity in both basins has slowed down dramatically. Though we see tonnage building up, the rates have stabilized as owners now facing close to zero return. Going forward it’s hard to see rates going further south, but with more available tonnage building up we don’t see a massive uptick “overnight”.

The ageing tanker selloff continued this week with MARAN AQUARIUS (320K DWT 2005 DSME) and SEAHERO (306K DWT 2006 DSME) each fetching over USD 50M. It is easy to see why, when ships of this size and age have almost doubled in value over the last eighteen months. Clear premiums for Ice class units are still very visible in the market with the sale of scrubber-fitted Ice 1A LORELEI (73K DWT 2007 STX JINHAE) for USD 33.5M, compared to both HAFNIA COLUMBIA/KRONBORG (76K/74K DWT 2007 DALIAN/NEW CENTURY) each selling for USD 22M.    Meanwhile in the dry market, timing appears to be key as market players look to position themselves as values seem to be bottoming out. China’s post CNY recovery has been slower than usual, in part to people enjoying their first in person CNY since the pandemic began, but also due to decreased liquidity. This will likely be remedied by additional stimulus in March, which could lead buyers into action. In the highly competitive Japanese Ultramax space, scrubber-fitted NORD POTOMAC (63K DWT I-S SHIPYARD 2016) sold for USD 27.75M setting well needed benchmark in the segment with the most buying enquiries. Over in the Supramax sector, MILOS (56K DWT 2010 COSCO Zhoushan) sold in the high 13s, and Navios unloaded the SERENITAS N (56K DWT 2011 YANGZHOU GUOYU) for USD 12.5m.

Market activity in the Nsea has been rather limited as we have seen relets being fixed between oil companies or being programmed for own cargoes. However, rates this week have been maintained at similar levels as last week. Going forward we expect rates to move sideways as the tonnage list looks rather balanced compared to the expected cargo volume for second half of February.   Last week, activity slowed down in the Med and as a result rates for local runs lost some more ground while the rates for CPC-Med runs also moved lower despite the long waiting days in Turkish Straits. Liftings of Azeri crude are uncertain now after the earthquake in South Turkey, something that could put rates under further downward pressure moving forward.

Since the beginning of the Ukraine war the Suezmax market has become hardwired to extreme volatility, with buy-in on both side of the phone (charterers and owners), and when there's buy-in from both parties, events usually become self-fulfilling. On that note, West Africa appears to have bottomed and with the prospect of a firmer VLCC market, there's also a psychological comfort blanket. TD20 is reported on subjects at between WS 105-110, suggesting that the Atlantic market has bottomed with probable upside in the offing. In the East, moderately firmer VLCCs will likely prevent further cannibalization of Suezmax stems. MEG/China on modern should trade 130KT x WS 130's whilst TD23 should keep its head above WS 50 with possible upside.

The Supramax market is still a bit muted post CNY.  Further decline within the Atlantic as lack of fresh enquiries and very little reported. Petcoke run from USG to Far East fixed around USD 12,000 on a 56,000 dwt.  From the East, NoPac seem to find the ground. Supramax from Singapore was fixed from Indo China round at USD 7,000, same round done on Ultramax open Philippines at USD 8,000. Ultramax open Mumbai fixed around USD 13,000 for del Kandla redel Far East.

We are entering another familiar cycle in the VL market, a pattern seen a number of times in 2022. The Atlantic (mainly USG) activity picks ups, rates jump, and the rest of the market is dragged along with it. The price for a VLCC USG/Ningbo has climbed USD 100k on successive fixtures, currently sitting at USD 8.4m. With West Africa/East also positive at the WS 60 level, modern vessels will ballast West purely for the richer hunting grounds not found in a lagging MEG market. As always however, the risk of dilution remains.  East of Suez (TD3C) rates creeping up in the low WS 50’s, and owners will be hoping for a pop in rates to match Western returns, but the February MEG program is close to completion and it's a short month also. However, the position list looks more balanced than for some time, as many ships turn left at Rondo.

EAST Even with two more rounds of acceptances to go we have had quite a few cargoes already fixed on March dates in the Middle East. At the same time, we have seen some East candidate vessels fixed for cargoes in the West finally making the very front of March rather tight. A bit further into March there is at the time of writing more tonnage to choose from. Looking at the cargo side, maintenance at Ruwais is expected to last during the whole of March, actual impact in terms of decreased volumes remain speculative. Ras Tanura volumes are reported to come back to pre-maintenance levels while Yanbu is expected to remain less active for now.  WEST So far this week 5-6 spot fixtures done in the Western market. At the time of writing, we count a total of 31 spot fixtures (9 first decade, 16 second decade, 6 last decade) out of the USG/USEC in March. There are currently 7-8 ships (4 relets) left in USG for end March, and there could still be a couple more appearing on the list as some ships with February laycans loading in USG/USEC might discharge in the NWE/Med/Waf. Last done concluded at high USD 130s H/C.

Last week the spot market lacked activity as the market returned from Chinese New Year, thankfully, this week has kicked into action with multiple vessels being chartered in both basins and more requirements continue to flow in. The East in particular has seen activity pick up and March is starting to stack up with laycans offering owners a selection of requirements to work on.  Freeport remains a question mark and tonnage remains on standby. In the meantime, Egas tenders continue to be the focus of those mostly affected by the reduced Freeport production as they seek to source replacement volumes and the portfolio disruption adds to chartering activity in the Atlantic.   Multimonth demand continues to attract attention as further sublets seek interest through summer with some success, whilst those offering winter coverage find new homes through competitive bidding processes as Charterers who had been holding off as sentiment softened become keen bidders. As highlighted last week, the focus remains on vessels that can be worked through winter, and the yearly rates have started to rise accordingly.   For another week, there hasn’t been reports of any newbuilding orders but prices remain firm.

Despite a lack of headline grabbing transactions this week, the tanker market fundamentals remain consistent. Spot market players would likely disagree, as sentiment wobbled on the back of Chinese New Year festivities. Ice class 1C Aframax MARATHON (105K DWT 2005 HHI) sold for USD 32M, with premiums for ice class tonnage still being realised by sellers. In keeping with the norm of the last few months, Aframax LILA FUJAIRAH (113K DWT 2007 DSME) was bought by Middle Eastern buyers for USD 37M.  Navios made for the bulk of the story in the dry market, shedding three of their older units; Panamax NAVIOS LIBERTAS/PROSPERITY I (75K DWT 2007 STX JINHAE) and Supramax NAVIOS AMARYLLIS (58K DWT 2008 TSUNEISHI ZHOUSHAN). The sale of Tess 58 BONITA (58K DWT 2008 TSUNEISHI ZHOUSHAN) at USD 15.8M shows that despite widely reported hammering of values, there is still money in well regarded yards and designs. As the Dry purchase enquiries continue to mount up, some owners are revaluating their selling positions and putting previously circulated candidates on the backburner, holding out for brighter days ahead.

Despite a couple of vessels ballasting away from the area, NSea rates moved sideways last week as market activity wasn’t as strong as expected. Bad weather in the area caused delays which led to vessels being replaced, however rates were repeated even on these fixtures. Moving forward we expect market to remain balanced. In the Med/BSea market, rates took hit a last week as ballasters from surrounding markets added downward pressure. Activity was strong but not enough to absorb the long supply of vessels. Rates seem to have reached bottom right now and if activity continues being strong, we might see owners gaining momentum and pushing for more on the next fixing window.

The lull in spot activity during Chinese New Year was more than offset by a surge in multimonth business. Charterers who had been holding off as sentiment softened suddenly pounced, and a feedback loop from the noise this generated has led to further vessels being shown through summer, and to more fixtures. The most interest though remains on vessels that can be worked through winter, and the premium they command reflects both the stronger winter sentiment and, more to the point, their scarcity; we don’t expect to see much structural length in the second half of the year. Returning to the spot market, there have been dalliances with an arbitrage and some reloads, but the main driver in the West will be Freeport start up and the pull-back of tonnage.

Fortunately for owners, there has been continual drip feed of fuel oil tender barrels that keep nipping away at the early side of the list, which should prevent a steep/deep rate-collapse. MEG/China trades WS 130's on modern whilst TD23 will trade WS 50’s. Across the pond, TD20 trades WS 115 for now but with the fixing window soon moving on to early third decade, this might represent the top of the market with a softer outlook for the remainder of the week. TD6 trades WS 170's after a market cargo tested owners resolve (down 20pts).

In other words, it is the TC routes being corrected. Owners are letting their ships wait for better rates, in line with predictions that rates are expected to pick up soon.

The Atlantic market was described as sideways at best with limited activity surfacing. Certainly, sentiment appeared weaker still, despite some talk of off market business being banded around, and rates softened again. Asia by contrast came into its own with several better deals reported ex NoPac and Australia, whilst further South ex Indonesia sources spoke of better demand today, but trading appeared cautious so far with a wide bid/offer spread appearing.

A steady week with small movements up in the East and down in the West, so a bit of a dichotomy. MEG has the potential for improvement, more through resistance than enquiry, as rates for MEG/China inching up to the WS 50 level and as VLCCs stamp all over the Suezmax market. Some additional questions from the MEG at the time of writing, as charterers close out a subdued 10-20 window. Still, owners are realizing Eastern enquiry outweighing a quiet and gently softening Atlantic market (USG/China down to USD 7.2m), so we see some owners previously willing West having a change of heart.   Across all load areas this week, the usual pattern of ships on subs with a scarcity of details. Over 25 vessels fixed away and the market none the wiser. And there lies why any market swings will remain a point or so either side of last done.

USG and ECSA lack cargo supply and tonnage building up due to the ballasters from other areas.  TA on Supra fixing USD 8,000-9,000 pd and fronthaul at USD 13,000-15,000 pd. Pacific RV at USD 9,000-10,000 pd and a backhaul to Atlantic getting close to USD 8,500 pd.
