text: AMERICAS The domestic U.S. market seems to have come to the realization that at nearly 150% of last year’s end-Jan propane stock level, 73mmbbls as of 27 Jan is simply too much inventory.  As such, propane prices at Mont Belvieu have declined by more than a nickel over the course of this week and appear poised for further losses.    It is noteworthy that crude values have also declined over the period, but talk of summertime brine containment issues at Mont Belvieu has now also been raised.  Fundamentally, the declining PDH margins in the East are also at the root of the issue, as buyers there returned from holiday and found that a large number of cargoes are scheduled to arrive while – at the same time – downstream petchem margins in the East have been shrinking.  Meanwhile, spot FOB Gulf Coast terminal fees – recently touted in the mid-teens – have simultaneously been softening in the wake of recently robust freight values.  Asking levels last week were in the 12cpg range (some notably higher, but also attached to a freight component), but then 11cpg was seen, followed by 10cpg, and now – most recently – talk of 9cpg has been circulating, all for March.  There was this week a rather impromptu spot FOB tender conducted for late-Feb which was reportedly fixed in the low/mid teens.  LatAm demand continues sporadically, though a recent two-cargo propane tender was confirmed as not awarded.  Whether any additional requirements will surface publicly remains to be seen  NWE The TOT window has been very active this week, with some Monday night madness as physical window bids reached February CIF ARA +$47.5pmt. Since global propane values have seen a rapid decline in value, and the TOT window has seen a $30pmt drop to February CIF ARA +$17.5pmt. CIF ARA had been keeping up with FEI Market values, and as soon as a sign of weakness was seen, it followed suit. This has shifted the propane naphtha spread in the region from a meagre minus $30pmt to minus $101pmt and widening. Four VLGCs are heading to North West Europe from the US by mid-February, which has calmed the market. Butane has been relatively quiet compared with the propane market and values lie at 90% February Naphtha.   MED A 4KT butane offer FOB Algeciras failed to find interest, and leaves butane in the region at $800MT. indicating low demand from Morocco, the obvious home for the cargo.

EAST The East of Suez fixing activity has been fairly inactive so far this week despite a few players having tested freight levels on both end February and early March laycans ex MEG. Focus is gradually shifting to March, and it seems February is more or less done once the Indian cargo is concluded. The QP acceptances for March could and should trigger some fixing activity. Freight rates should be stabilizing and finding its feet once activity resumes despite there being some gap between bids and offers at the moment. Early March availability ex MEG could end up looking rather tight, and it may happen fairly quickly as the owners or trader relets are also still left with the possibility to go West where one can secure healthy earnings on longer voyages.  WEST March fixing remains lively in the West, albeit it has to slow down somewhat from last week’s flurry of fixtures because we are looking at laycans’ one and a half month or more, ahead. At the time of writing, we count 26 spot fixtures (nine during 1st/thirteen during 2nd and four during 3rd decade) out of the USG/USEC for March dates. There are currently 9-10 available VLGCs for March, however, it is likely that we will see a handful more vessels on the position list as some vessels scheduled for loading during February ex USG/USEC will be heading West to discharge.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco set Feb CP at $790 for both C3 and C4, hiked up by $200 for C3 and $185 for C4, respectively. Such increment was resulted by the supply cuts due to port maintenance and the delays caused by fog weather in US, together with the robust buying for Feb arrival volumes driven mainly from petchem.   Swap collapsed after the Feb CP rally, and Mar CP was traded at $673 for C3 and C4 at $10 less. Spot discussions for evenly split cargos remained active as traders need to cover shorts into India/SEA and currently bids for Mar loaders were reported at minus mid high single digit to double digits discounts, while offers heard at small discounts or even small premium over CP.    FAR EAST Strong bids for propane delivered in 1h Mar this week as of limited supply. Till Thurs, 46kt propane parcel was still bid at Mar FEI plus 90ish but offers yet to see. Off window such parcel was reported concluded at Feb FEI plus 40s which equated to Mar FEI plus 130s level by then. Premium for 2h Mar softened, as offer shown at Mar CP plus mid 50s equating to Mar FEI plus 90s. A couple of 46kt propane for 2h Mar delivery were changed hand at Feb FEI plus teens reportedly.   Due to the negative margins, PDHs in China started to cut rates or advanced their scheduled maintenance to avoid the costly feedstock purchase, and we expected a min 200kt loss in propane demand. However, shall the flat price come off more to generate marginal profits, PDHs might improve their run rate afterwards accordingly, especially with the expectation of economic recovery from post-Covid. One EChina PDH user cancelled buy tender for a 1st decade Mar delivery propane into Ningbo due to high offer. Another Chinese also tendered to buy a 15-28th Mar delivered 22kt propane parcel into Taixing which due next week.

There has been some eager fixing East of Suez, with one particular Suezmax charterer out of the blocks very early on Monday, which essentially sealed the fate of the market by keeping MEG/East firmly in the WS 140's. With Chinese New Year in full swing, you would have thought there would be a lull in proceedings, but it was the exact opposite, with last done Basrah/East trading at WS 147.5 on a modern unit. In the Atlantic, there has been a degree of stability in the Black Sea with TD6 trading conference WS 202.5-205 on the back of northbound Turkish straits delays hovering around 10 days.  TD20 suffered a setback with WS 125 being repeated a couple of times (despite a tight list). For any cargo prior to 10th February there is possible upside (if one happens to look at lists). USG/UKCM is conference at low WS 90'S.

First decade Feb is over and TD3 remains at the WS 47 level, and it is likely charterers will drip-feed the mid-month cargoes in the next week or so. The MEG list, certainly for the older ladies, remains lengthy despite 12 or so modern ships turning left at Rondo and ballasting West. There are positives - the 10-20 window yet to be explored, Far Eastern festivities over, the Baltic numbers in the East are green, and the overall tonnage lists down 10% or so since the peak of a few weeks back. However, the overall feel remains flat with slightly negative undertones. The Atlantic remains light on working cargoes, but reports of a few questions in the USG, with a replacement deal just done USD 8.15m very prompt dates USG/Ningbo.

The North Atlantic appeared mostly unchanged and concerns with little fresh demand. The NCSA has been active for fronthaul with bids in line at current index level, but USG with minimum inquires. Prompt tonnage in Far East falling over each other paying the cost of buying time doing 30-40-day rounds, earning less than half of operating costs. Ballasters in regret only making marginally better, non-scrubber units from Pacific suffering at around USD 4k/day for 100-day Brazil- or West Africa rounds. Another SnP week dominated by tanker activity with headlines stolen by Torm’s acquisition of a total of seven LR1s. The transaction confirmed on Thursday doubles Torm LR1 fleet with 4 vessels bought from Jo Invest AS and a further 3 units from ST Shipping & Transport. Total price tag for the tally stands at Usd 233m marking the substantial appreciation in values we continue to see in the broader tanker space but more particularly on the product front.  Elsewhere in the tanker space the theme of the last few quarters remains unchanged with ice class units and older large tankers finding buyers at hefty premiums.   The limited number of reported sales in the Dry market is not necessarily reflective of the activity brewing under the surface. Buying enquiries are increasing week after week with a number of market players calling the bottom with bids in line with last done. A level of enquiry that up until now has not yet been met with expected flow of market candidates with potential sellers still deliberating their timing. Saying that, this heighten competition and lack of available tonnage is driving certain buyers to offer premiums in order to dig out the right candidate which should lead to more transactions in the near future.

With Chinese Holidays this week, there is very limited activity in the market. Flat rates across all basins with negative sentiment. USG and ECSA remain under pressure. Tess 58 reported to be on subs for a trip to Italy with grains at USD 11,000 pd.  An Ultra 61,000 deliver APS Houston was reported at USD 17,000 pd for trip to India with pet coke. Rates in Continent was sliding down breaking 4-digit numbers.  Supramax was fixed on subject trip to Med USD 15,000 pd and another fixture surfaced at Cont-Far East around USD 13,000 pd. Without further details.  Ultramax fixed Olam grain cargo to Nigeria APS Poland USD 12,000 pd.  Good activity out of South Africa, with an Ultramax able to gain USD 14,000 pd + 140,000 bb delivery Durban trip to India with China option.  The Pacific market though very quiet seems more stable. Supra 56,000 dwt delivery Indonesia was fixed at USD 8,500 pd for a trip to China. Nopac and Aussie RV paying around USD 7,500 pd.

As we hop into the first days of the Year of the Rabbit, the LNG spot market continues to soften in both basins on ample prompt vessel availability and lack of near-term requirements. However, with fresh speculation and abuzz of Freeport finally coming back online, and with vessels lining up outside the Terminal as of late, a plateau in rates could be found in the coming weeks should a start-up be confirmed… so, either the rabbit will come out of the hat, or we go deeper into the hole! On the Term side of the equation, rates similarly continue to lull alongside spot, but activity does not. With the prevailing rate environment conducive in its weakened state, Traders and Majors alike are now back on the “bid” and reported to have conclude some 1-Year and multi-month fixtures in the last week. That said, as we work our way towards Q2 and vessels continue to get picked off, we expect the seasonal firming on term rates to take hold and liquidity to slowly bubble away. On the newbuilding front, all eyes are hungrily affixed on the remaining open NB availability through to 2027, with no long-term fixtures reported this week. Similarly, no new orders have been reported this week as well.  In the meantime, to all our friends and colleagues having celebrated the Lunar New Year, best wishes and Gong Xi Fa Cai!

text: AMERICAS The domestic US market has seen a series of factors enter over the past week or so which have collectively changed the shape of things.  Propane prices themselves have been influenced upwards by the rising crude market, which bodes well for the overall economic outlook, as well, and helps things along.  Additionally, terminal fees last week saw a sharp spike up to the low teens for Feb and to some degree Mar – but then the freight market took a sharp upturn thus putting pressure on fees and allowing them to relax to current levels of around 8.5 – 10.0 cpg for March.    All the while the EIA inventory data for propane was released this week and showed a 1mmbbl decline to an overall total of 75.6mmbbls – still 130% and 140% more than the last two comparative years.  The surprise, however, was in that the data revealed a 100,000bbl build on the Gulf Coast (PADD III) and simultaneously a 900,000bbl draw in the Midwest (PADD II).  This has given cause for speculation that next week’s data might contain corrective data, though it might then be obfuscated by the combination of currently milder weather, as well as the expectation that a pair of cold-fronts are expected to reach down from the Arctic during Feb.   Latin American demand levels have improved through the first half of the winter and formally issued tenders have recently been seen as a result.  This is very likely due to the recent cold fronts which have penetrated to the south.  NWE February CIF ARA propane values continue to strengthen through weak Brent and bearish US inventory figures. Two TOT window bids have been constant this week for 4-8 February deliveries. Which has kept the physical window trading at a +$3pmt premium to February CIF ARA. Though CIF ARA strengthened by $16.50pmt by close of business Wednesday, it will have to do more to tempt US cargoes away from the Asian market, which continues to be strong since reopening from its New Year holidays. Butane in the region has been weak and lacked large cargo discussions. Naphtha has been weak and butane remains assessed at 87.5% February naphtha, although when buyside interest arises this level is likely to increase rapidly.  MED The region has been quiet this week. Refinery workers strikes in France would usually hamper exports, for almost a year now refineries have been consuming most of their LPG for power generation.

EAST With reports of substantial cuts in February Middle East volumes many have been expecting freight to stay weak East of Suez. Following a rush of fixtures in the West and increased demand for volumes in Far East Asia, the sentiment has shifted also in the Eastern loading region. Reports of a couple of deals in the 70s rt/c are already being circulated, and although second half February positions still looks lengthy – the option of sailing West into a hot freight market will push the floor upwards in the East despite the expected shortage in volumes.  WEST After having seen a handful of spot fixtures getting done a couple days ago at low 100s H/C out of the USG we are now seeing last done concluded at high 120s H/C. In total we count a dozen spot fixtures in the west this week for March dates. At the time of writing it seems difficult finding an open position in ely March, but there could still be a couple more appearing as we await full discharge rotation.

text: Nothing to report from the eastern market due to Lunar New Year.

The beginning of Chinese New Year looks to prolong the Tanker charter market’s subdued sentiment, while activity on S&P remains high. No changes from the theme of the last few quarters as ice class units and older large tankers remain the darlings of the S&P market, seen in Ice class 1A Aframax SEAMAGIC (116K DWT 2007 HHI) sold for a hearty USD 47M, and scrubber fitted VLCC FPMC C HONOR (298K DWT 2008 UNIVERSAL) changing hands for USD 55M. In further Aframax activity, KYTHIRA WARRIOR (115K DWT 2006 SANOYAS) and KRITI GALAXY (110K DWT 2006 MITSUI) sold for USD 38M each, showing that even non-Ice class tonnage can benefit from this rising tide.  The Dry market too will be impacted by CNY festivities, but this did not stop Pacific Basin from dominating the headlines this week as they spent USD 125M on 6x Ultrabulk units (4x Japanese blt Ultramaxes, 1x Tsuneishi Cebu Supramax and 1x Imabari blt Handysize). Taking advantage of the recent value correction in c.10 yo Ultra/Supramax units, they have taken position at a time where others are still sat debating whether the bottom of the market has been reached or not. Elsewhere, Greek buyers have seen opportunity in PPMAX AM LIBERIA (  98K DWT 2013 TSUNEISHI ZHOUSHAN), swooping in at USD 20.50M.

Rates for Aframaxes trading in the North Sea have stabilized around WS 160 level for the last week, give or take a few points depending on the trade route. We might see some owners ballast their vessels to other areas in order to capitalize on possible higher returns compared to the North Sea. Till we see ships ballast way, the list looks balanced and rates will continue to move sideways. In the Med, despite TD19 losing some points over the course of last week, there was no actual fixture being done at lower than last done levels. Market activity was steady, and owners managed to push rates higher for CPC loadings while local xMed runs were steady/firm. Moving forward, we expect rates to continue moving sideways, however ballasters from surrounding areas and relets might add some downward pressure.

Just over a week ago the naysayers were claiming that any Suezmax recovery would be quickly clipped by VLCCs, meanwhile, TD20 paid lip-service to those noises and managed to jump circa 30 percent, which is a fat return in any market.  Whilst VLCCs have indeed started to take out a number of first decade WAFR stems, owners will satisfy themselves with rates in the WS 140's with a fairly stable outlook for the remainder of the week. A firm Med'/Black Sea Aframax market continues to gorge on Suezmax which has further tightened tonnage availability, not only for this region but by dint of this, also WAFR. In the East, a procession of Pengerang, Kaz, and Kuwait tenders keep things ticking over for now. MEG/China trades max' WS 145.

From the East, bhaul to USG was linked to USD 4,000. Steel run via Japan redel Vietnam being fixed around USD 4,500. Supramax bss CJK covered around USD 2,000 for a trip via Indonesia to China on 57,000 dwt.

Steady, with a gentle uptick is the overriding feel, as fixing for the MEG moved in to the first week of Feb (we count just over 20 fixtures for the month so far). Plenty remains off market as charterers finding their targets a little softer from the shadows. Exxon fixing a fresh deal at WS 46.5, albeit 3-4 load ports and earlier dates. Wafr/East now at the WS 50 level and USG/Ningbo paid USD 8.2m twice overnight, but activity could push rates north in the short term. However, worth noting many owners with Eastern ships now heading for the Cape. Any improvements in the MEG, may dissuade a few.

After CNY, however, we are positive to increased activity and improving levels.

Capital has also secured a further two slots for 174,000cbm MEGA vessel for delivery in Q3 2026.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS In spite of a recent warming trend across most of the U.S., demand levels from both the domestic and offshore markets have given cause for propane inventory levels to decline steadily for over a month, beginning in the 2nd week of December at 90.3mmbbls and concluding the 2nd week of Jan at 76.6mmbbls, according to the most recently issued EIA data.  A decline of 2mmbbls was recorded for the period from 6th to 13th Jan, where most had been expecting a draw of around a million barrels (or so).  Stocks now are over 130% of last year, and more than 128% of two years ago.  There is at this point little threat that stocks will be depleted over the balance of the winter period – rather, there have been recent questions related to potential containment issues later in the summer.  Meanwhile, the overarching trend seems poised to continue as forecasts are now calling for a mass of cold air from the Arctic to envelope most of the U.S. at end-Jan / early-Feb and, furthermore, demand for cargoes in Feb (and in Mar) has been strong.    Terminal fees have spiked sharply and for Feb transactions jumped from ~6cts/gal earlier in the year to the low/mid-teens at present.  March is divided due to backwardation, but asking levels are fully double-digits in 1H March, and firmly in the upper single-digits for 2H March.  LatAm demand has been seen improving, as the aforementioned cold weather has infiltrated to the South, giving cause for increased consumption levels and, thus, higher demand.  NWE The February/March backwardation continues to steepen hitting -$42pmt at the close Wednesday with the outright January CIF ARA price the highest since August 31st. Imports to the region in January are expected to be around 650,000MT. The majority of this volume has come from the US where fog delays and a large draw and strong Eastern demand, are contributing to the strength in European values. Sustained cold weather is being felt in Europe, adding to demand. Butane is another story as a CIF ARA butane sits at 85% balance January Naphtha and few demand signals are being seen.   MED Activity in the region has been subdued as local demand remains low. There have been some recent delays to loadings in Algeria due to storms, causing minimal additional buying as the catch up is set to be quick.

text: MEG ADNOC and Saudi have announced their Feb lifting acceptance with some cuts in exports reportedly due to the planned maintenance. As of the decline on MEG supply, the Feb C3 CP surged up to $688 with C4 traded at $5 higher. Feb/Mar CP backwardation also enlarged further to $41. Last but not least, Feb CP/FEI widened from last week’s minus $3.5 to minus $17 at the time of writing. Freight have dropped significantly with less liftings ex MEG and more fleets available to relet.   FAR EAST Concerning the delays on Feb arrival cargos, caused by the unpredicted fog, sentiment in window remain strong, especially traders bidding up to cover positions. 23kt propane for 2h Feb delivery was bid at Feb FEI plus $75 and similar parcel for 1h Mar delivery was at Mar FEI plus $50.   As lunar new year holiday coming near, activities are scarce except a few tenders running in the market. Off window one Malaysia producer was reported to award their sale tender for a evenly split cargo for 21-23th Feb lifting ex Tanjung Sulong. And one NChina PDH issued buy tender to secure a propane cargo for Mar delivery.

EAST Freight has been coming off substantially on the back of a lengthy positions list in the Middle East. We gradually shift focus towards second decade February fixing with 6 deals concluded off the first 10 days so far. Next decade still looks long shipping and we see some downside left in the market.  WEST After having seen two very active weeks to the start of 2023 it seems the Western freight market has taken a small breather. Currently we count 30 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC so far in February - 15 early, 7 mid, and 8 for end Feb dates. On the position list we still see up to 6 ships available for the month with half of them being relets, but some of them could still end up in MEG. Charterers currently seem comfortable waiting as sentiment softening.

It seems premature to declare that winter is over, so we definitely won’t do that. It is hard to ignore the traffic jam of tonnage that’s worked its way onto the availability list this past week, though. The net result is a sizeable correction on spot rates and given that sentiment drives all markets, there has been a softening in the term numbers too. Available Newbuilds remain stubbornly impervious to the warm European winter, however, with one Owner reportedly securing a brace of fixtures at record levels (on Subs) to an Atlantic project for mid-2024 delivery. Returning to the here and now, there’s a spate of tenders and bilateral discussions to keep the prompt market turning but with an increasing number of relets competing for each cargo, this is looking more like a Charterer’s market. At least for now. A cold snap (like the one forecast for late January in NE Asia) or a post “zero covid” demand surge in China or indeed any hint of European reinjections failing to keep pace with the level required, will change the mood again. In fact, this is likely the new normal that we contend with this year (and beyond?) - increased volatility borne out of a hypersensitive market that has re-learned the hard way that LNG is first and foremost about security of supply. This rings true for the ships as much as it does for the molecules. If you don’t have a vessel, you can’t get the product to where it needs to go and whilst the availability list currently provides charterers with some degree of comfort, in a relet dominated market it doesn’t take much of a nudge for portfolios to reabsorb this length.   No Newbuild orders to report this week but prices continue their ascent as demand remains strong.

A flurry of activity in the Dry market this week, as players tie up loose ends from the winter break and execute before the inevitable slowdown in S&P activity over the Chinese New Year period. The market will be paying keen attention to the fallout from the first CNY under China’s more relaxed COVID stance, hopeful there is no U turn in policy after the festivities which pre covid represented the biggest migration of people on earth. Transactions of note include Capes AQUANAVIGATOR & AQUASALWADOR (ABT 180K DWT 2011/12 DAEHAN) at USD 25m and USD 27m respectively, widely reported to have been snapped up by Greek interests, a transaction that could indicate a floor has been reached on dry bringing additional comfort to market players that have been patiently timing their next move in the space. Elsewhere the tier II Supramax SUNRISE RAINBOW (ABT 56K DWT 2012 JIANGSU HANTONG) sold for USD 15.25m, piling pressure on the many Supramax sellers in the market.   A lacklustre Tanker charter market hasn’t discouraged the S&P space, as asset values continue to rise. Those with an Ice class notation remain the key beneficiaries, shown in the USD 47.5m received for Suezmax ICE TRANSPORTER (ABT 146K DWT 2006 UNIVERSAL). VLCC COSGREAT LAKE (ABT 298K DWT 2002 NACKS) sold to Middle Eastern buyers for an eyewatering USD 39m, showing the run for older large tankers is not yet done. In the MR space TEN unloaded 6 Ice class 1A units APOLLON/ARIS/AJAX/AFRODITE/ARTEMIS/ARIADNE (ABT 53K DWT 2005 HYUNDAI MIPO) for a price in the region of  USD 21m each.

The softening trend continued for the VL’s this past week. However, as we have seen multiple times in 2022, the Atlantic has the power to turn direction and drive rates upwards and there are some green shoots of recovery. USG Afras busy, Smaxes tighter in Wafr and USG VL activity is flowing with multiple vessels on subs, no details. Rates for USG/Ningbo were fixing at USD 8.35m, but charterers will find for prompter laycans, it is a much shorter list. For later dates, Eastern ballasters come in to play as the MEG list remains well populated. 120 or so MEG cargoes fixed for January, so there remains 15-20 to do, but there remains twice as many ships jostling to provide transport. Rates now slowly moving towards 2023 worldscale, and TD3 sits below the WS 50 level. If we are not at the bottom, it is likely around the corner.

As expected, activity on Aframaxes in the Nsea was slow last week and rates moved sideways. Charterers took advantage of the weak Suezmax market and combined stems into bigger size vessels for local runs. Surrounding areas are firming and with owners considering ballasting away to achieve better returns we might have seen the bottom of this market before rates move north again. Different picture in the Med with activity picking up, delays in the Turkish Straits increasing, and list suddenly becoming very short. All these led to rates jumping more than 50p and owners trying to push for more on a every cargo. Moving forward we expect rates to remain firm but further upside potential could be limited.

Decent amount of cargo in the market as people seek to cover prior Chinese New Year, very much like what we saw prior Christmas. That said, the activity is expected to be short lived and slow down dramatically during the holidays. This together with the upcoming rain season in Brazil, the confidence to push the market is lacking. Hence levels are not really improving on the current activity, and in fact slightly down week on week.

The global Suezmax market looks to have bottomed and is now exhibiting modest upside in most load-zones. In the East, a continual flow of prompt Fuel Oil tenders continues to trim the early side of the list with rumours of one such fixture attaining WS 180 (2022) for an East run. Conversely, the natural window is not so generous as there has been some partial cannibalization of rates from VLCCs on short-voyage India deals, which leaves a long East in need of a proper test. In the West, firmer Aframax markets in the Mediterranean and USG have added some much needed support with TD6 likely to trade WS 170's, purely on the back its smaller relatives success. TD20 has been caught in the middle of the Med' Afra' crossfire and a number of Suezmax have been taken on part cargo which has significantly tightened the WAFR list.

Similar trend as across other segments. Tonnage building up against limited fresh cargoes/enquiries.  Supramax from USG to Far East done sub USD 20,000. Ultramax with grains from Gdansk to Nigeria was fixed around mid-12,000 USD. Ultramax bss del Port Elizabeth for a trip to China was employed at USD 17,000 + USD 170,000 ballast bonus. Pacific round voyage was executed around USD 4,000 this week.  Very limited talks on period.

text: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane market levels have bounced around since the start of the New Year when Non-LST barrels finished at just over 77cpg.  Current price levels are mildly under 80cpg so overall in 1H Jan there’s been a bit of an uptick.  The earlier detachment from crude seems to have reattached as WTI has seen a resurgence of late, having moved from  $76.93/bbl on the 3rd of Jan to $78.69/bbl at present.  Meanwhile, the relationship between propane and crude is effectively static at just over 42%. Terminal fees have seen some buoyancy this year and fixtures at 8cpg were noted on a couple of occasions.  Asking prices have risen, as well, and offers are seen now as high as 10cpg for Feb, where buy-side interest presently exceeds availability. As for the inventories, the EIA this week revealed another large draw but the data is largely believed to contain corrective data, if only because of the recent holidays.  As of 6th Jan total stocks declined by 2.1mmbbls to an overall 78.6mmbbls – which is 126% of last year and 119% of two years ago at the same time.  With North American weather now trending warmer, early expectations include the possibility of a build, since production has resumed after reductions which were due to the recent storms and subsequent cold weather.  NWE Propane has rebounded in the second of the week on the back of firmer stronger crude and a bullish sentiment looking out to 2023. The front month propane price in Northwest Europe rebounded, shooting up $25/ and now stands at around $560/pmt. Freight has continued to free fall, causing some of the early stage volatility seen throughout the European LPG market, however the volatility is also playing out in some more fundamental ways. Propane remains the more attractive feedstock, versus naphta, which theoretically would spur on European buying, however, petrochemical margins are still weak, temperatures remain mild, and Europe remains well supplied-as reflected in inventories. That said, its theorized that Europe’s ability to land US tons could be quelled by the thunderous reemergence of Chinese LPG buying, seen over the past week. A sentiment compounded by expected Middle East gulf maintenance

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Feb C3 CP surged up to $627 and C4 was traded at $15 higher, reflecting the front strength, partially resulted by some reported maintenance plans from Yanbu and ADNOC terminals. Feb/Mar was traded at $37 backwardation.  Spot discounts for Feb lifting evenly split cargo was traded at minus $13 recently.  Qatar Petroleum tendered to sell one cargo for 20-23rd Feb lifting in either 4/0 or 3/1 or 2/2 ratio.    FAR EAST Several 23kt propane parcels for 2h Feb delivery were actively traded, with one reported concluded at FEI plus $33 earlier this week. Similar bids were shown in window but offers unseen. Supply for 1h Feb delivery appeared tight and 1h/2h Feb spread was assessed at $20 backwardation.  After last week’s tender fiesta, this week the premium continued to soar up as of another flurry of tenders emerging. Unfortunately, cargos for 1h Feb delivery were relatively tight and three PDH buy tenders seeking 1h Feb volumes were reported cancelled. Only one N.China PDH user was reported to buy outside tender for a 23kt propane parcel for 1h Feb delivery at Feb FEI or CP plus 80s or 90s level. And one Vietnam-based importer managed to secure 46kt propane for end Jan to 1h Feb delivery into Vung Tau reportedly.  One EChina PDH user was reported to procure one 46kt propane parcel for 2h Feb delivery at Feb CP plus 50-60s. One NChina petchem user tendered to buy flexible ratio for Feb delivery. Another EChina Cracker also tendered out to buy one to two lots of 46kt LPG for Feb delivery. Additionally, Taiwan CPC tendered to buy 11/11 for 19-28th Feb delivery, which still in validity. Apart from spot, one NChina PDH user also secured a mini term for 46kt propane monthly from Feb to Apr delivery via tender.

EAST February fixing in the Middle East is underway and we have seen 4 deals concluded, 2 in end Jan and 2 in early Feb, so far this week all done above 80 RT/C. There is also a firm cargo from an Indian major and a tender in play. We anticipate more activity to come as we are still waiting for the Aramco acceptances. The overall export volumes from the Middle East in February are however expected to be down due to planned maintenances in the region, but it remains to see how this will affect shipping market.    WEST Since the beginning of last week until today we have seen approximately 30 spot fixtures concluded in the West. At the time of writing we count 27 spot fixtures (15 ely, 6 mid, 6 end) in February out of the USG. There should still be room for more fixing in the second half of Feb as only 8 out of 27 spot deals have been done this period and there are currently some uncovered cargoes out there. Looking at the position list for the rest of February we see 4 vessels left for mid month dates and 4 in the end. Last done fixture concluded at mid/high 120s H/C.

Happy New Year to all our friends and colleagues! As we return to the office after a quiet holiday season, there has been an increase in activity and inquiries in the market. Several disponent owners are declaring their available vessels for subletting, while charterers are issuing potential charter inquiries, which is a positive sign for spot fixtures. The demand for LNG vessels remain firm, with long-term charters being secured in anticipation of increased energy demand amid geopolitical tensions around the world.  On the newbuild front, it has been reported orders for four firm 180,000m3 LNG vessels from China Merchants Heavy Industry (CMHI), with options for an additional four. With these orders, yet another yard in China, CMHI has entered the conventional-sized LNG newbuilding segment. With a string of SPAs announced at the tail end of 2022, we can only comment that 2023 promises to be yet another interesting LNG year, following the events of 2022.

It's normal for market activity to be slower after holidays, as many people are returning to work and may not be fully back in the swing of things yet. First index day 3 of January is showing a negative market with little activity.

This week the Suezmax market has been a tale of two hemispheres. In the East, rates have rebounded on the back of a very busy first decade for 20-ton crane requirement which has considerably trimmed the early side of the list for the second decade meaning that MEG/China is likely to trade around the WS 190 level whist TD23 is WS 90 with a firmer feel. The Atlantic basin is proving not to be as fruitful with lists well stocked for all load-zones against a backdrop of very little surface activity. TD20 is in danger of slipping into WS 120's territory unless we see an influx of sustained activity today. The one silver lining is the Med' Aframax market which is beginning to take a bite at Suezmax tonnage, but this is unlikely to yield bumper returns for owners, but it may stop the rot. All rates basis 2022 WS.

After a relatively inactive Christmas period in terms of fixing activity, the year starts off with rates coming off; for the c5 West Australia route, levels are in the low 7s and c3 well below the 20 mark. Average Cape index is presently 12,500, more or less as expected. We are looking forward to a new year, where expectations to the first part are rather low, whilst the general sentiment is rather positive to the second half of the year.

Aframax rates in the Nsea have been under constantly downward pressure over xmas and at the start of the new year due as a lot of cargoes been covered on own relets. Going forward we expect rates to continue sideways, but with a softish undertone as charterers could combine Nsea stems by lifting cargoes on either Suezmax or VLCCs. In the Med/Bsea, rates seem to have hit the bottom after losing about 200 points during the last two weeks. Charterers fixing forward, vessels ballasting away and being fixed for long-haul runs have shrunk the tonnage list for normal fixing window. We expect rates to move sideways with a positive note for next week, however Suezmax could possibly limit any upward pressure by capping Afras and fixing part cargoes.

It’s been a lackluster start to the New Year in the VLCC segment and lack of fresh enquiries and transparency is weighing on the sentiment. The change in WS flat rates, considerably up from last year, is exacerbating the picture rather than improving in it. However, daily earnings are still ranging from low USD 30’s and into the USD 40’s/day for the most modern scrubber fitted units. TD3C is probably not more than WS 65-67.5 in 2022 “money” at the writing moment and will be further tested. But, although further downwards pressure persists owners will likely resist dragging things down to last year’s lows.

text: AMERICAS The Mont Belvieu propane market was in 2H 2022 detached from crude, the percentage to which fell to the upper 30 range. At the start of 2023 the relationship improved and presently equates to the low/mid 40% level. Propane inventories are a component of that as prices in the US have been reacting to the declines in stock levels. Today’s EIA data revealed an unexpectedly large 3.7mmbbl decline from 84.4mmbbls to a 30th Dec overall total inventory level of 80.70mmbbls. The market had been anticipating a decline of as much as 3.1mmmbbls, though the averages estimates were in the -2.8mmbbl range.   Meanwhile, terminal fees have improved significantly in 2023, having been heard/reported twice so far this year in the 8cpg range. This is very likely due to the precipitous declines in the freight arena, which have declined by 14% from the end of Dec, and 44% since mid-Dec. That market, in turn, is being affected by the improved rates of passage at the Panama Canal, which today stands at 2 days (North) and 2 days (South). Latin American demand has been seen improving as the recent winter weather system which enveloped the U.S. has made its way south, prompting higher propane consumption levels  NWE Considerable European imports from the US and North Sea have exceeded the unseasonably warm continent’s demand, positioning propane as the favorable choice for the European Crackers. In the first 15 days of the New Year alone, and estimated 360,000 tons of LPG is slated to discharge in Northwest Europe, a level but 10,000 metric tons below December total import volume. Spot freight on a Houston/ Flushing basis has been cut in half month on month, where it’s now being worked around $68.50/t (down from the low 130’s realized in December) allowing for more aggressive bids for US FOB propane cargos. The same cannot be said for butane, following an upswing in US Butane prices that effectively closed the arbitrage. Traders continue to bid for Handy and MGC cargos to take to NWE in January, However February large Cargos are now front of mind, with the expectation for more typically seen seasonal temperatures yet to come.

text: The week between Christmas and New year is traditionally quiet and the trend, thus far at least, is going to form. This is however not compensated by all major Far East miners + mills being constantly present, although with moderate amounts of business, covering West Australia/Far East lots for early/mid January positions. Limited activity as many players off for holidays but in general sentiment remaining negative. Very few fresh enquirers on both basins and in general feeling is to just watch and see where the direction will be taken after the seasonal break.

As the year draws to an end, we look back and reflect on another rollercoaster year for the spot market. 2022 has been a year of highs and lows; rate and commodity price records, geopolitics & diversification adding yet another layer of complexity and a newbuild market so active, the yards had to slow down order intake and take a breather.  Market dynamics are often unpredictable in LNG, but it has once again highlighted the importance of the commodity in the global energy mix, cementing its role as we continue moving towards a “greener” future. In shipping, we also have to consider new regulations coming into force from the IMO, and how these will affect our markets over the next 12 months. As expected, the short term market was mainly wrapped up in the lead up to the end of the year, so activity has been limited over the past days and rates remain at similar levels last seen for both spot and term. Activity will likely resume over the next few weeks as many return to desks, it’s still winter and pre-holiday conversations will re-ignite.  After a record-breaking year at the yards, another 2 newbuilds were added to the tally late December with Oman LNG securing slots at KSOE. We also saw ENI place an order at Wison Heavy Industries for a 2.4MTPA FLNG unit which is planned to be deployed in the Republic of the Congo. From all of us here at Fearnley LNG, thank you for all your support over the last 12 months and we look forward to another exciting year 2023.

As the year draws to a close, market has been quiet this week and there is not much activity to report East or West. Sentiment has softened recently in both markets with last done deals concluded around mid/low USD 110s RT/C and low USD 150s H/C.

The Nsea Aframax market slowed down on the back of increased Suezmax and VLCC tonnage fixing stems ex East Coast UK and West Coast Norway leaving less volumes to lift for their smaller siblings. Rates have started to come off and we expect this soft sentiment to continue into the new year fixing window. More of the same in the Med/BSea market as a mix of Suezmaxes fixing Aframax stems, oversupply of Afras, and slower activity cut around 100 WS points for local runs. Owners accepted their fate and fixed lower, however they still earn decent returns. Last week of the year might be busy with charterers reaching forward and owners having the chance to prevail rates from losing more ground.

As often seen before the market is pushing before the holidays as owners already covered themselves in a typical healthy Q4 and charterers seeking to cover as most of the market participants take a week off. Week on week the market has gained a significant amount of USD 8904 (62%), and there is still a lot of prompt cargo around to be covered. That said, forward predictions are still very limited compared to index, and we do see a strong interest from ships with slightly forward dates trying to take advantage of the spike. Hence it’s hard to see that the current levels will maintain for a longer time.

The Suezmax market has seen significant downward corrections in the Atlantic basin with most notably TD20 now trading at WS 147.5. Further softening is possibly on the cards as several vessels are on the verge of missing the fixing window with owners unlikely to want FOC vessels languishing over the festive period. The USG looks to have bottomed as a number of TA deals concluded in and around WS 145 x WS 130's with some potential upside in the offing. TD6 is all but done for the year with charterers bizarrely not willing to test the market despite the enormous differential with neighboring markets. In the East, it's worth noting that the list is deceptively tight on the early side for modern tonnage, which possibly puts a floor under MEG/China at WS 170 and a TD23 run not leaving much change from WS 85.

A negative swing for VLCC owners this past week, as rates have taken a 10-point dive across the board. A couple of deals done on ships that only have to calculate one leg (i.e., sold and delivered at the completion of discharge). Nonetheless, each enquiry received a dozen offers, and therefore each fixture will have 11 or so disappointed candidates. "Special reasons" or not the market is now set in the low-mid WS 70's for MEG/East. Charterers' current tactics of sitting on hands and drip-feeding cargoes is working in their favour, hoping for someone to break ranks yet again as Christmas moves closer. However, judging from the January fixture count, and moving closer on the curve laycan wise, charterers could be creating a bottleneck for themselves with enquiry shoe-horned into the days between Christmas and New Year.

A softer undertone continued across all basins in the Supramax market, with few fresh inquiries and Christmas holidays approaching. The Atlantic is still much more active compared to the Pacific, where rates dropped in average USD 8,000 pd. The USG market paying TA trading with rates around USD 25,000 pd for Supramax and around USD 29,000 for TCT to China on Ultramax. ECSA TA fixing on Ultramax close to USD 28,000 pd. Far East markets slowed down even further, and rates keep dropping. text: AMERICAS Its been a week of mixed signals and uncertainty in the US LPG market. On Wednesday, the EIA reported another week of record production US (2.626 million b/d), along with a 3-million-barrel inventory draw that definitively exceeded the expectations of market participants. Unsurprisingly, the Mont Belvieu propane traded up an average of 4% across the locations, further hampering the sparse speculative trading at present. That said, most recent draw included, US propane stocks stand at approximately 87 million barrels- the highest mid-December levels seen in nearly seven years. Crude also saw a substantial uptick, maintaining propane’s weakness to WTI – which now stands at 36 percent- compared to the 5 year average of 52% of WTI. Each market participants Christmas list is slightly different. Panama delays have quelled some, and now stand at 5 and 10 days delay for north and south respectively- while remaining high on the radars of traders. Some are hoping for continued resurgence of Chinese demand with the sustained walk back of their zero covid policy- While others expect the ease of freight costs with the arrivals of newbuilds in the first quarter of 2023 coupled with the near perennially Q1 slump in rates.  NWE The TOT window has been active this week and bids have risen from January CIF ARA +$5.5/MT early this week to January CIF ARA +$10/MT. On top of the physical premiums,  January CIF ARA flat price jumped up $12 partly as a reaction to the larger than expected draw in US inventories and firming crude values. It is looking difficult for European importers to secure US volumes, more due to tight freight that the draw of the Eastern market. So far 90,000 MT are heading to the region from the US for 1H January arrival. A low volume when 480,000MT was imported in December and 520,000MT in November. Large cargo butane values are assessed at 92% December Naphtha though this should be taken with a pinch of salt due to the lack of recent activity.  MED The cold spell which passed through North-West-Europe never made it as far South as the Mediterranean. This has left term supplies accounting for the majority of the demand in North Africa. The East Med has taken a VLGC into Kalamata, Greece, in early January. While Turkey is also expected to receive a 1st half January VLGC from the US.

Nsea rates moved sideways last week as activity was healthy and the list still is very thin. Despite a slight cooling in the tanker charter space, appetite for second hand units continues to grow as players fight to take up position in a historically strong market. In the standout transaction of the week, Latsco sold their seven year old Aframax FOS ATHENS (105K DWT 2015 HHI) to Turkish buyers for USD 50m. Singapore based Stamford Shipping cashed out of their Aframax exposure, with the sale of GULLIT (108K DWT 2008 SWS) for USD 34m.   In the dry market, the Ultramax sector took centre-stage with the sale of two units - DELSA (63K DWT 2015 ZHEJIANG) and STONY STREAM (64K DWT 2015 CHENGXI), with both vessels fetching USD 24m each. Market players will certainly take note as interest in this size and vintage will only increase further, with many pondering an opportunistic entry into this space over the next few months. Elsewhere, Navios picked up Kamsarmax RICH RAINFOREST (82K DWT 2022 JIANGSU YANGZI-MITSUI) for USD 34.5m.

No excitement, and very mixed picture, but overall slightly improving for the big ships - average daily spot earnings up 5 pct w-o-w to come in at some USD 14,500. Atlantic is the bright spot, where in particular West Africa/Far East bauxite trades show promise and push the fronthaul route up a nudge to USD 32k/day and climbing further. Period activity negligible as 2023 FFA's still only support hire levels not considered by most tonnage providers - expectations for Q1 remains one of caution.

Jan FEI/CP widened to nearly $50 compared to last week’s $32 though, partially due to the solid freight rate and spot availability out of AG.  A couple of 46kt propane for Jan delivery were concluded, with one reported sold into Japan and the rest for trader shorts. Additionally, as petchem margins improved slightly on declining feedstock price, some plants users emerged with tenders. One EChina PDH user covered a 5-15th Jan delivered 23kt propane into Ningbo at Jan CP plus 80s, while the other EChina player covered 1h Jan delivered 46kt propane into Lianyungang at Jan FEI plus low 30s. Comparatively, buying inquiries for 2h Jan delivery into China was slim due to the CNY holiday.

The headlines this week have been all about the cold weather that has persisted in the Northern Hemisphere, corresponding to the draw down in LNG stocks especially in Europe. It has been a good reminder that Mother Nature tends to switch the thermostat rather quickly and although most of the countries have been prepared for this, it has still caused sudden spikes especially on electricity prices across the old continent. This has in turn killed the LNG arbitrage for now, but at least the contango is looking rather firm into Q1 2023. On the LNG shipping side, most of the subletters that have tonnage have been carefully assessing the situation during the last few days, and consequently the spot market looks rather balanced, although it is to be said that all the spot opportunities are now for loadings past the new year. On the other hand, the term market seems to be holding firm with further reports emerging on term fixtures concluded with deliveries as far as Q3 next year. On the newbuilding side, it was a quiet week with no new orders confirmed, but the yards report tender activity and continue to be comfortable with the current orderbooks and future outlook.

text: AMERICAS  Terminal fees for Jan cargoes are now priced across a wide spectrum, from as little as buy-side interest in the low 4s to offers of around the 6ct/gal mark.  A couple of transactions are believed to have occurred in the mid-4s this week.  Otherwise, little is being accomplished as demand levels remain muted.  Term business was recently discussed as low as the 5s but not concluded, with a more likely transaction to occur in the upper 6s.   The EIA propane inventory data continues to surprise, as yet another practically unheard-of December build was recorded this week.  Overall stock levels are 90.30mmbbls as of 9th Dec, or 127% of last year and 107% of two years ago.  The ongoing build in PADD III continues to impress due mostly to robust production levels but aided by both Panama Canal-related shipping delays as well as a recent bout of fog- delays on the Houston Ship Channel.   In any event there has so far been only limited cold weather demand across the U.S., but now a couple of prominent forecasters are calling for a series of Arctic fronts to sweep across the nation over the Christmas and New Year period, perhaps marking the beginnings of the traditional demand season which will likely be viewed in a “better late than never” context.  NWE The TOT Window continues to be well bid for end dec and early Jan deliveries into Europe. The region has been experiencing a continued spell of cold weather keeping demand firm and the December/January backwardation wide at -$13/MT. Inland demand is increasing, demand for railcars is up and European storages are drawing down. US tons continue to find their way to Europe, though with the East/West spread at $84/MT and reduced Panama Canal delays some cargoes may decide to go East. Naphtha weakened in the region which has pulled butane down with it as it remains at 91.5% December Naphtha. The butane window has been quiet for some time, and little to no butane deals have been heard in the region.   MED The region is set to import 600,000MT of US LPG in December, close to all time highs. This has been due to early cold weather in the region and the US tons replacing imports from other regions such as WAF and local production.

EAST December fixing is seemingly coming to an end as we only see a couple of vessels left this period. At the time of writing, we count just over 30 spot fixtures out of the Middle East for December. January fixing is finally underway with last done concluded at mid-high USD 130s early Jan out of the MEG. Charterers being more reluctant to move early might signal a weakening sentiment on freight, but it still remains to be seen how many firm cargoes there are to be worked, which could be clearer post Saudi acceptances.  WEST Only 4 of the 21 spot fixtures concluded in January out of the USG are done in 2H Jan, and with only 1-2 vessels left open for 1H Jan we soon expect fixing to fully shift into the last half of January as we move closer to Christmas. The position list for the rest of Jan is looking tight and it is currently dominated by pure shipowners as we only see a couple trader relets available. Although the arb has narrowed lately and Panama waiting down, we still find owners freight ideas around the 200-dollar mark.

As the tanker charter market adjusts to new Russian crude regulations, the S&P space remains strong. VLCC SEAKING (318K DWT 2005 HHI) was sold by Thenamaris for USD 51.5m, proving there is still no shortage of suitors for ageing large tankers. Modern scrubber fitted Aframax SOUTHERN ROUSE (108K DWT 2018 TSUNEISHI) sold for USD 62m, having invited offers at the end of November, which should help price the number of Aframax units in the market.   Timing will be crucial in the dry market as players expect a run in Q1/Q2, but also debate on the impact of new regulations, and the reliability of China easing their COVID restrictions. This week’s S&P activity shows that owners must be busy pondering their options as only a handful of sales were seen. Open Hatch Supramax RIO CHOAPA (50K DWT 2012 OSHIMA) sold for USD 16.5m which is basis SS due. Kamsarmax NORD POLLUX (81K DWT 2016 TSUNEISHI CEBU) sold for USD 25.2m which we understand reflects delivery in the Sellers' option until May 2023.

The London party week in full swing, but the VLCC market not seeing much festive spirit. Rates for MEG/East dropping through the WS 70’s as owners look to draw a new defensive line. It was a rapid retreat, but to some extent owners have slowed what was a frantic slide. Support from the Suezmaxes showing steady strength (for now), and therefore opportunities open for VLCC ‘toe stepping’ on their smaller sisters, as 1mb stems prove financially attractive in both the MEG and Wafr. TD3 sits at WS 73.5 levels at the time of writing, but charterers will look to chisel away. TD15 WS 70 to test, with 130kt stems touted and a quiet USG. A softer feel ahead, but with calmer waters. Third decade MEG stems yet to hit the market and this could give owners some stimulus.

Cold weather conditions have boosted demand for heating in North Europe as well as China, but European LNG prices have kept their premium to JKM this week. In shipping, more vessels are opening up after discharge in Europe as storage capacity is being depleted. These, coupled with the available tonnage in the Atlantic from the Freeport outtage, have resulted in excess prompt availability and a further drop in spot rates. Looking out into next month, spot rates for 2-strokes are holding higher given the uncertainty around Freeport delays, while more requirements are emerging and there are a steady flow of Egas cargo tenders into the market. On the other hand, the term market remains disconnected from the recent drop in spot rates, and activity and rates remains high. In the Newbuilding market, China Merchants has order 2 x 175,000 LNGCs at Dalian Shipyard, bringing the number of units ordered for the Owner to 10 in total.

The Nsea market remained steady last week. Activity slowed down a bit as relets were used for own cargoes by charterers, but the thin position list preserved rates from falling. We expect market to remain strong moving forward in December and rates to move sideways. In the Med/BSea we saw high volatility on the rates last week as owners fixed well-below last done early in the week but managed to push back again. Market seems to be slightly oversupplied but healthy activity and a bunch of laden vessels stuck in the Turkish straits due to the P&I letter will help rates remain strong.

Not the all-out capitulation that some thought was inevitable with the East market holding up remarkably well. Tupras were forced to take a ship that has yet to go through west coast India and managed WS 95 for a TD23, suggesting a degree of resistance. Conversely, any further upside is ultimately capped by VLCCs. Ex Wafr, the front end of the list remains fairly tight but similarly, VLCCs provide a cap. The Black Sea has an increasing number of vessels unable to transit southbound Bosphorus with P&I clubs unwilling and practically, unable to provide the assurance requested by the Turkish government. This will have to be sorted out at government to government level with TD6 trading WS 295 + protective clause. USG is dead and needs further enquiry.

Asia saw a large bid/offer spread but on the whole saw firmer rates traded on most routes with increased demand dictating proceedings.

Ultramax open Douala 10 December was fixed at USD 22,500 bss del Rio Grande for a trip to Med.  Another Ultramax was booked bss Damietta for a trip with clinker redelivery West Africa around USD 17,000. Scrap run from Baltic to Turkey was done at USD 6,000. From the East, Supramax fixed around USD 13,000 for trip via Indo to China.

The spot in the Pacific has recently been showing some positive signs and c5 is up from 8.6 last week to present USD 8.8 level, expected to increase further throughout this week. C3 on the other hand is still under pressure with market level around USD 19 level, down from upper USD 19s one week back. Year-end is approaching and everyone is adjusting to next year realities; hoping for an end of the corona in China, higher exports from Vale, and a solution to the CII imposed by Bimco.

EAST Close to 30 spot fixtures have been done in December out of the Middle East, and with first round of January acceptances published last week the fixing window is gradually shifting to next month. We are still left with a fair number of open ships around end December, some of which may consider going West unless willing to accept waiting time for January cargoes. Some charterers are holding back their relets unless substantially higher than last done freight is obtained. The East premium is currently benchmarked at almost a 10-dollar premium above the West before waiting in the Panama Canal. Now seeing crude coming off, canal waiting decreasing and freight in the US seemingly easing, we are strongly dependent on a healthy volumes early January ex Middle East to support current levels.  WEST With only a couple ships left for 1H January dates in USG we expect fixing focus to soon shift to 2H Jan. In total, we have seen 17 spot fixtures for January out of the USG with last done concluded at low USD 200 H/C. Vessel supply for the rest of January still looks tight but with some players looking to secure a long voyage, ballasting via Suez/Cape, while the market is still hot is making the position list potentially longer. This, in addition to a fall in estimated waiting time in Panama down to 19 days northbound and 5 days southbound, is softening sentiment a bit.

text: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane prices overall been soft since the end of the first quarter of 2022, though through the summer months that is generally the expected trajectory.  Since the start of Q4, however – and presumably at the start of the winter season - the direction has not changed.  This is likely due to the ongoing robust production levels in the U.S. which has resulted in much higher than anticipated inventory levels.   And while this week’s EIA report showed a 900,000bbl decline, stocks are still – as of 02 Dec – at a total of 89.70mmbbls, or 122% of last year and 103% of two years ago.  The market had been anticipating yet another build as weather-related demand has yet to fully commence.   On the export front, lifting delays have been occurring due to a combination of Panama Canal congestion and, more recently, fog on the Houston Ship Channel which has been rather persistent in recent days. Terminal fees have been relatively well maintained through it all, with offers seen at nearly 6cpg and interest levels mostly in the 5cpg range.  NWE No TOT window action has been seen since Monday. The January East/West spread has widened to $106pmt, with both strong FEI and CIF ARA values. Northerly Arctic winds hit Europe this week rapidly dropping temperatures across the region, now consistently below freezing nightly, winter has arrived! This has pushed Dutch TTF values up to $43.40/MMbtu, up by $4/MMbtu on the day. Relative CIF ARA LPG valeus are, Propane $11.60/MMbtu, Butane $11.80/MMbtu. The draw in US inventories also supported global propane values. The drop in crude oil has dragged European naphtha values with it leave Dec propane/naphtha at -49USD down 12USD from the start of the week. Butane values remain 91.5% December Naphtha, down relative to propane.   MED The region is slowly starting to see an increase in demand and 400,000MT of US LPG will be landing in December. Around 40% of those imports are headed for Turkey, 30% to Morocco and 20% to France. This December volume is likely to increase, bolstered by spot cargoes as temperatures drop.

Tanker market players must be running out of superlatives to describe the market, as another bullish week comes to a close. Ice class 1A Aframaxes SAMRAA ALKHALEEJ & ALHANI (114K DWT 2006/07 SAMSUNG HI) sold for USD 86m enbloc, representing an over 30% jump in price compared to the last done back in October (PAROSEA/BLUESEA 113K DWT 2006 SAMSUNG HI FOR USD 62.5m enbloc). Market players seem to be recognising the inflated price environment, as Marinakis’ Capital ship management penned orders at New Times for 2x 115K DWT LR2 Tankers at USD 60m each. Elsewhere, MR GWN2 (50K DWT 2020 SAMSUNG HI) sold for USD 38.5m to Japanese buyers in an internal sale.   The dry market will be buoyed by the news China are soon to be easing their long standing COVID restrictions, however, such effects from this easing will take time before reflecting in rates and values. More market jostling this week saw 2 transactions in the Kamsarmax sector LOWLANDS COMFORT (81K DWT 2016 TSUNEISHI CEBU) and DL CARNATION (81K DWT 2014 JIANGSU EASTERN HI), sold for USD 26.4m and USD 18.8m respectively.  In the modern Ultramax space, ITALIAN BULKER (63K DWT 2017 SHIN KASADO) was sold for USD 26m.

text: AMERICAS There exists at present contradictory factors in the domestic US market whereby rising crude values are having an upward impact on the pricing structure while simultaneously the weight of the now heightened inventory levels is having a downward effect.  At ~40% of crude (and barely that), propane prices should theoretically be poised to increase, but current stock levels weigh heavily, particularly since there has yet been little weather-related demand across North America.  The EIA on Wednesday released its findings for the week ending 25 Nov and showed a 1.6mmbbl increase from 89mmbbls in the week prior to current levels of 90.6mmbbls.  This puts current stocks at nearly 125% of last year and just under 100% of two years ago - and pushing well past the 5-year average of 80.30mmbls.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, saw a short-lived increase but have begun to relax again as a host of sellers have emerged.  Current FOB USGC offerings can be found in the low 5s, with room to improve.  Interest, however, is a bit muted – mostly due to the lack of weather-related demand and poor petchem economics.  NWE Many European traders discussed the state of the market heading into winter at a very well attended Christmas party in London last night. One of the major concerns were if US East Coast export volumes would be enough to substitute Russian LPG export volumes unavailable due to sanctions. For the time being US cargoes continue to be offered into the region as traders look to place their cargoes avoiding the Panama canal. Although with the December East / West spread at $100 most cargoes will continue heading East. The propane / Naphtha spread in the region was bolstered by a recovery in crude oil values. Which also strengthened butane which remains 91.5% December Naphtha. Demand in the region does not look set to jump just yet and is covered by term deliveries. The main concern is if demand jumps unexpectedly would European traders be able to find freight at the last minute to cover prompt shorts?  MED Sonatrach prices set at $580 for propane and $600 for butane a rise from November. Action in the region was quiet as traders assessed these posted prices before any cold weather-related demand has hit the region.

Not too much to brag, no real support on fresh inquiries. USG picking slightly up with improved levels, where fhaul on Ultramax was discussed at USD 30,000. From the Continent, Supramax was fixed at USD 18,500 with scrap to India. From the East, Indo China round was done at USD 10,500. On the period front, Ultramax open in North China was fixed at USD 11,500 for short period.

Last week we commented “It’s long been understood that what goes up must eventually come down, and the question for the spot LNG shipping market has been when and by how much”. Well, it has impacted with gusto this week as interruptions continue to occur at Freeport and  Calcasieu Pass LNG production facilities and storage in Europe remains high. Predicted colder weather is likely to bring to an end to the winter preparations as floating cargoes commence their discharges. There is an outside chance that the colder weather will significantly reduce gas reserves, yet this should be treated with some trepidation as the contango remains narrow despite the weather getting colder on the prompt. The result is tonnage is opening up for portfolio needs and reducing the demands of the large portfolio players that have been so active over the last few weeks and months. Again, as commented last week, without an arbitrage to pull cargoes East this will put downward pressure on spot rates and we don’t foresee this changing anytime  soon given the restrictions in China due to increased covid cases. The term market continues to invite interest and with CWC conference in Athens this week, we expect some renewed demand for freight to approach market in due course. In the newbuilding market we welcome the 14th Celsius vessel to the market with a 2026 delivery at levels close to last done, albeit for a 180,000m3 with top of the market spec.

Market extremely volatile and nervous with rates going up and down as a rollercoaster. The underlying sentiment is very poor, but the fact is that there is a shortage of spot ships, and the prompt dates are being paid well and the average of all routes are up by 35% week on week. However, there is not a lot of excitement as the tonnage shortage is mainly driven by ships stuck due to bad weather and that the same ships will come back to the market as soon as weather improves, and probably by a decent number.

In the Pacific, there has been some fresh orders in past few days giving a positional gain to the market, but we are still seeing a build of tonnage going to be open next week. The South Pacific however is struggling to find support with aggressive levels concluded particularly for short round voyages. In the Atlantic, the market has been firm, and levels are reaching to mid-teens for transatlantic and low 20s for fronthaul - this is due flow of both grain and mineral combined with lack of prompt tonnage. The ECSA has been stable so far, but due to weaker Pacific particularly in South for past two weeks, we are seeing more tonnage coming open in Singapore/India range next two weeks, therefore we don’t see changes to that area. The Ukraine grain flow has been down considerably after renewed safe passage agreement due to increasing congestion and inspection delay, but we are still optimistic for December shipment.

EAST We have seen 5 spot fixtures so far this week in MEG in addition to two Indian sub-fixtures still working. Last done deals done around mid-high USD 130s RT/C and most owners’ ideas now climbing towards USD 140 RT/C. We currently count 26 spot deals done for December in the Middle East compared to an average of about 30 deals per month for the last 4 months. With uncovered cargoes still in play, both in mid and end Dec, we expect freight rates to remain firm.   WEST At the time of writing we count 11 spot fixtures out of the USG for January with over half of them done this week. Freight continues looking very tight for early Jan and further into mid-month dates. We see the current US-position list being dominated by Panamaxes and vessels coming via Suez/Cape in 1H Jan as the Neo-canal still causing delays which is forcing some players to pay up big money in the auction to reach their laycans. Currently the projected waiting are 20 days northbound and 23 days southbound in the Neo Panama Canal for non-booked vessels. The last fixture concluded ex USG done at mid USD 200s H/C and we expect this to maintain.

North Sea Aframax rates hit all-time high levels last week as owners did their best to push for higher rates on the back of surrounding alternatives paying significantly better. Supply of vessels in the area is very thin in the current fixing window. Moving forward we expect rates to remain firm. However, the possibility of Suezmaxes being booked for local runs could cool off the Aframax market slightly. On the other side, Med-BSea market took a step back, seeing a downward correction, but still owners are enjoying hefty returns. Charterers managed to cool off the market a bit by using own tonnage for their cargoes and at the same time cargo programs aren’t that busy for 1st decade December. We will possibly see rates coming off a bit more next week, but overall market fundamentals don’t indicate a freefall of the rates.

It’s been a sluggish week for VLCC owners as November draws to an end, with MEG/East rates now dipped well below the psychologically important WS 100 barrier courtesy of a MEG/Korea fixture concluded at WS 91.5. Charterers have shown great restraint, just drip feeding the odd cargo into the market and chipping away on owner’s confidence. The Atlantic basin - having previously underpinned other areas - has seen more failures than fixtures over the past few days adding insult to injury. That said, returns are still healthy with T/C equivalents ranging from USD 60-70k/day pending on propulsion and the voyage in question. Alas, that also means owners have more to lose than gain by digging their heals in. Time to “get out of Dodge” for those who can and do not have multiple ships coming up behind.

A slight cooling in the charter market was duly ignored this week as S&P activity ramped up in the tanker market. The first VLCC transaction of a 10 year old unit since Q1 was registered in the form of the C. PASSION blt 2013 HHI which was sold for USD 66m to European buyers. If viewed in regard to the old valuation adage that a 10 year old ship is worth roughly half a newbuild, this transaction will put a smile on the faces owners of modern VLCC tonnage – not that they need any excuse. MR owners should be advised not to get carried away by the sale of ATHLOS blt 2016 Samsung HI Ningbo for USD 41m, which was bought at a significant premium for US Naval purposes. Elsewhere, Pareto purchased LR1 Sisters CAPE TEMPEST/TAMPA blt 2007/08 New Times en bloc for USD 34m.   Uncertainty continues to govern sentiment in the dry space, with market players watching the worsening COVID-19 situation in China with trepidation. A transaction of note was the sale of Newcastlemax sisters CHINA STEEL TEAM/ENTREPRENEUR blt 2006/07 China Shipbld en bloc for USD 35m to Greek buyers. Elsewhere down the size curve, there were a number of handy transactions including SEASTAR HARRIER blt 2022 Hakodate for USD 30.9m and TS Bravo blt 2015 Shanhaiguan for USD 16.75m.

There are presently some improvements in the spot market, although overall average is down USD 1000 from last week. C5 is down from USD 8.375 to USD 7.7 whilst c3 moved from 18.9 to 17.4 at present. 2023 is approaching fast, with Q1 values in the low USD 6000s and generally low expectations for the beginning of the new year. On top, number of Covid cases are increasing in the Far East, with concerns this will have negative impacts on the Chinese economy.

The global Suezmax market continues to benefit from a mixture of sustained enquiry levels and regional anomalies, which have combined to deliver a very stable/firm market. In the East, there has been huge volatility with TD23 trading at WS 130 off ultra-prompt dates, whilst natural dates hover around WS 115-117.5 with upside bias (this is mainly down to tighter 2x20 ton crane availability up to 10'Dec'). Med and USG Aframax cargoes continue to take out early Suezmax tonnage which, for now, will continue to provide solid support.

With the negative sentiment carrying over from the last week there was little positive news so far with both charterers and owners yet to show their hands, but the immediate outlook looked more in charterers favor so far, market negative across the board.

Rates in all three West of Suez markets have surged last week, hitting all-time highs on the back of busy activity that inevitably made the whole supply of vessels tight. Nsea was fixed as high as WS 295 with most of owners refusing to offer as surrounding areas paying much better. Moving forward we expect owners to try to maintain stand then push for more as the list is tight. Question remains on Russian liftings after 5th of December, that will make more tonnage available for non-premium business. In the Med, rates reached levels above WS 400 ex Libya and well above WS 500 ex CPC as owners were trying to push for higher after every fixture. Market might cool off at some point if any of the surrounding areas takes a step back as well, but for the time being we don’t expect a big drop in the rates.

It’s long been understood that what goes up must eventually come down, and the question for the spot LNG shipping market has been when and by how much. Well, as the World Cup kicks off and much of the wider world looks to Qatar with nervous excitement, those of us in the LNG world are looking at the floating situation in Europe with nervous…ness. As the contango narrows and the weather gets colder, floating vessels will start to head in for discharge and the resulting tonnage will either be cycled back into charterer’s schedules or else offered to the market. Either way, without an arbitrage to pull cargoes East this will put downward pressure on spot rates. In contrast, there are few signs of the term market slowing down: there are very few vessel coming open next year under independent owner’s control, and given relatively high LNG price forecasts and demand expectations shipping balances are being maintained with some additional length. There were also five further newbuilds reported this week: Seapeak are reported to have confirmed the 174,000cbm MEGA vessels for delivery in 2027.

text: AMERICAS Happy Thanksgiving!   NWE  US imports to Europe continue at high monthly volumes as North Sea production remains low. The European window has been active for the last week and is assessed at December CIF ARA +$11pmt. The large unexpected build in US inventories could see more volume exported from Marcus Hook, the majority of these tons find their way to European shorts. With the East market softening slightly, traders could once again try to place their cargoes into European shorts particularly if they need a vessel back promptly. Cold weather is starting to creep into the region which will soon start increasing demand, for now stocks are high. Butane demand in the region has calmed slightly and values have come off to 92.5% Naphtha which has taken a dive related to the drop in crude oil values.
