text: AMERICAS As of the first week of Nov US propane inventories had eclipsed the 5-year average by some 5mmbbls and reached an overall total of 87.7mmbbls.  Last week saw a modest 400,000bbl draw, but this week – which was anticipated to realize a draw of around a million barrels – saw a build of 100,000bbls.  In effect, the market is in the ‘shoulder’ period, late though it may be. In short, as of 11 Nov the US inventories stand at 87.8mmbbls, or 118% of last year and 94% of two years ago.  This propels the current stock level to around 5mmbbls above the 5-year average (82.6mmbbls).   The immediate explanation as to why stocks increased this week is that (for starters) winter is later to commence than usual, but also includes missed laycans due to shipping delays as well as reduced load rates over the past couple of weeks at one of the Gulf Coast terminals; the combined impact being the modest build.  Spot terminal fees now range rather widely, from the upper 5cpg level to over 7cpg, depending on timing / ratio / location, etc., but little is being accomplished due to shipping-related anomalies which stem from the fantastic delays presently being seen at the Panama Canal as well as the general lack of weather-related demand so far this season.  NWE The physical window has calmed down after early week excitement due to reported LPG production curbs at Kollsnes in the North Sea. Since the arb has not seen any marked change, though buying interest has come off. Attributed to the continued mild winter and unchanged petchem demand. The East / West spread remains near $110pmt for propane, so unsold US Gulf Coast loading in 2nd half November and 1st half December are not considering selling in the West. Butane demand remains strong primarily for blending and lies 94% naphtha.   MED The mild weather continues to keep demand in the region well supplied by term deliveries.

text: MEG Dec C3 CP was traded at $640 and C4 at $5 less. Dec/Jan was traded at about $10 backwardation, reflecting the strong front market. Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their sale tender to a Chinese Major for 2-9th Dec lifting 3/1 cargo at Dec CP minus 20s. And ADNOC was said have rich inventory and have advanced some nominations for term liftings in Dec.   FAR EAST Cash premium for propane delivered in Dec strengthened this week, as supply especially for 1h Dec delivery looks tight when sellers are unable to firm up their delivery schedule unless transit slots booked. Earlier this week, 23kt propane parcel for 2h Dec delivery was traded at Dec FEI plus very low teens. And subsequently, similar cargo for 2h Dec delivery was bid at Dec FEI plus mid-teens but no offers seen on Thurs.   Off window, several spot buy tenders were discussing. One Vietnam based PDH user issued tender to buy heavy propane cargo for 2h Dec delivery into Vung Tau. And Taiwan CPC issued tender to buy 11/11 for last decade Dec delivery.    Other than spot tenders, focus of the week is still the term negotiation for next year into China. Two SChina traditional importers are reported to secure monthly 11/11 at CP plus nearly $40 and some portion using FEI link. One NChina PDH user also secured several propane cargoes for delivery in mainly 2H of the year at FEI plus low mid-single digit and partially CP link price. Another EChina petchem player also said to award their monthly 46kt propane buy tender at FEI plus mid-single digit and CP at low 40s. Last but not least, another two EChina PDHs are negotiating for monthly 23kt or 46kt propane, respectively.  And we are still expecting a few more petchem players to term up for next year.

EAST Market expect Aramco acceptances to be released later today after which more 1H December cargos should appear. Any early cargos ex Saudi could potentially put further fuel to the already burning hot market. Last done ex Middle East is at 145, but most Owners holding for closer to 150. Once the full December program is known some additional relets could potentially be made available, but comparing the availability for December with expected spot volumes freight remains tight and is expected to remain strong.   WEST Latest Baltic print is now showing close to a 20 dollar discount in the West before waiting in Panama as we see the Eastern freight rates climb even further. Three vessels have been put on subs so far this week with last done out of the USG concluded at around USD 200 H/C. In total we have seen a 21 spot fixtures so far for December ex USG, 7 of them in the first half and 14 in the second. There are 6-7 vessels left in USG in Dec and half of them might end up in MEG as Owners could catch a big East premium while also avoiding the heavily congested Panama Canal. Vessel supply for 2H December is looking tight.

Compared to recent activity, the tanker market had a rather subdued week on the S&P front. However, this is not to be mistaken for a cooling market, quite the opposite. There seems to be no foreseeable end to the tanker bull run with charter markets and asset values remaining red hot, often leaving last done in the rear-view mirror. This is shown in Performance Shipping paying USD 44m for DPP trading LR2 FOS HAMILTON blt 2013 HHI, compared to recent comparable transaction RAFFLES HARMONY blt 2013 HHI which sold for USD 41.80m in October.   Values in the dry space continue to feel downward pressure, following a notable squeeze in earning sentiment. Scrubber fitted Capesize HL SHINBORYEONG blt 2010 SAMHO HI was bought by Stealth Maritime for USD 23.8m, having invited offers across the market and following a number of recent Capesize transactions. In the Supra/Ultra sector, some rates are being reported at below OPEX levels in places indicating it could be a tough winter to come for market players. In an area of the size curve which will be carefully watched as the values correct, Ultramax ACHILLEAS blt 2012 Yangzhou Dayang sold for USD 22.30m to Eastern buyers basis ss/dd freshly passed and BWTS installed.

A ground-breaking week for tanker asset values, with Bahri paying USD 112m each for 2 x 2020 built VLCC’s from Vitol which in our book translates to about USD 120m for a brand-new Korean built vessel with scrubber. This is up about 16% from mid this year.  Vitol also reported to be selling a resale LR2 delivering 2023 which we understand comes with a three-year TC back.  Another flurry of transactions across the dry cargo segments which are illustrating the underlying market correction experienced over the recent weeks. Notably the Japanese controlled Capesize NAVIOS OBELIKS built 2012 Koyo which has been sold to Synergy at USD 29m, this follows the two vessels sold by JP Morgan last week. The Supramax segment continues to feel the downwards pressure with a number of sellers in the market looking to catch an ever sharper falling knife. Tess-58 BULK CARINA 2016 Cebu was reported sold at USD 22m, while lower down the age curve the AZZURA built 2004 IHI sold at USD 13m. There is an ever-increasing number of vessels for sale within the Supramax sector, with owners and opportunists making plans to take advantage of the potential bargains to be had.

Normally when we talk about a market being “quiet”, it is synonymous with being in the doldrums – not so this market. A complete lack of liquidity has led to spot rate inertia but somewhat paradoxically, the levels seem paralysed at historical highs. Requirements remain uncovered due to an inability to find suitable tonnage, rather than any unbridgeable bid-ask spread. Past experience suggests that this situation can’t last but then again, past experience has oft proved irrelevant this year. Looking beyond this winter (odd to be writing this before thermostats have even marked its commencement) and the tightness in 2023 now seems to be written in ink. Charterers have been working their way through the term tonnage availability lists at such a rate that one wonders whether independent owners will have anything left to do next year? In summary, we see continuing demand for term shipping and no cause to moderate spot rates. And the sentiment has clearly flowed over to the Newbuild market; we raise our price estimates here once again on reports this week of a $252 Million order at DSME.

text: AMERICAS An eventful week across the board as a number of market participants ascended on Miami as the year comes to a close, for a discussion on what to expect in the coming months. The answer. Uncertainty. While optimistic regarding recovering global demand, the timeline is very much up for debate. Freight too, has been the topic of uncertainty,  as traders try to find direction while weighing the near 50 new builds coming to market during 2023, with growing exports and operational delays, that cut into availability. In the spot market, December FEI/LST arbitrage traded as wide as $231.00/ton on Thursday,  but higher freight costs and Panama Canal delays have taken away the margins keeping speculative buying at bay. Presently, buyers' indications are in the mid 5cpg range, and a bit higher at Marcus Hook, while sellers are offering closer to 6.5cpg for December cargos.   In Panama, delays stand at 10 days for southbound travel, and 19 north, which coupled with sky high freight can prove exceptionally costly for traders.  On a Houston/ Chiba basis, freight was heard done as high as 192pmt earlier in the week but has since stabilized in mid to high 180's. On Wednesday, the EIA reported the first inventory draw of the season- showing stocks down approx. 300,000 barrels, where they now stand at 87 million barrels. The US Gulf accounted for the majority of the draw, 653,000 barrels, Conjoining with a draw of 404,000 barrels in the US East Coast (PADD1) . However, a large build in the midcontinent of 700,000 barrels mitigated a greater strain on stored barrels. The attitude around inventories is relaxed as the Gulf Coast levels are still 35 percent higher compared to this time last year. Exports were more or less flat week on week, totaling  1.4million barrels / day. While production saw a marginal decrease to about 2.5million barrels/ day. The draw, though surprising to the market, did little on the price of propane at Mt.Beliveu, which ended the session up only 0.25cpg on the day. That said, a forecast of Cold weather,  not yet seen, in coming weeks, could kick off the price activity more typically related with winter in the US.  NWE Multiple physical window bids and offers have been shown this week both on propane and butane. This pushed propane values to November CIF ARA +$6pmt, the strongest values since mid-July. Strong butane demand for blending is being seen in the region. With butane values at 94.25% November Naphtha, naphtha also being strong. The arb from the US has been improving, but with December East / West spread at +$97pmt all tons should go East. Although the potential of long waiting times at the Panama Canal or expensive auction fee to get through with reduced waiting has some traders looking to the West to stop their vessels being tied up for too long. The CFR market is active and will continue to be as freight is expensive and scarce making harder for traders to look FOB from the US and find freight.  MED Butane demand in the region is rising, though more to compete with demand from Northern Europe. As wintery weather is yet to be seen.

Active bids for 1h dec delivery parcels were shown but no offers seen. Several parcels for 46kt propane were also changed hand, for both 1h and 2h dec delivery, being placed into China at Dec FEI plus low teens range basis E/NChina reportedly. Suezmaxes in the Atlantic came off last week, as activity slowed down in most areas. Charterers took their chance to sit on cargoes as some of the higher fixtures failed, and took some air out of the balloon. The dip was expected, but owners remained confident in the market as most of third decade in Wafr remained uncovered. Yesterday we saw those dates come in to play and with 6 cargoes trading in the same window, combined with a thin frontside of the tonnage list, rates are recovering to WS 190's on TD20. We have seen same in USG and in Med and Bsea. The East market on the other hand has less activity. Rates holding up well on the short MEG/India runs, while we are lacking MEG/East activity. But, with the V's still looking strong we hope to see more long east cargoes going forward.

The Atlantic again lacked fresh activity, with both the transatlantic and fronthaul markets consolidated as APS markets. Some weaker voyage rates came to light for transatlantic equating to below index timecharter equivalents, as tonnage continues to build. Asia appeared largely Indonesia centric with the short round trips dominating activity and reports with rates easing a little on previous done. Some period activity of note including talk of the Amphitrite (98,697 2012) Japan 19/20 November fixing for 13/15 months at USD 14,250 with Cobelfret, whilst Oldendorff were linked to the Xing De Hai (82,204 2017) ex dry dock Zhoushan 11-13 November fixed for short period at a rumoured USD 17,000, but further details were less forthcoming.

The Nsea Aframax market ticked a few points in upward direction, but would be considered a bit undervalued by owners who has got better alternatives in other load areas like the Mediterranean or the USG if they are willing to ballast. The tonnage list is still looking tight for any cargoes loading in the 2nd decade of November, and some bad weather in the area is also causing delays. In the Mediterranean, owners seen freight levels move in their favor over the last week. A steady flow of spot enquiries and with charterers searching for alternatives due delays in certain main hubs have continued to put an upward pressure on rates. Suezmax owners have also been in play this week, picking of Afra stems – though predominantly Blsea stems ex CPC. We expect the area to remain attractive in the near term.

The Atlantic still looks much better compared to Pacific where rates dropped below USD 10,000. Activity in main load areas in Atlantic slowed down. USG trading was slow with rates around USD 17,000 for Supramax TA and around USD 24,000 for TCT to China on Ultramax. ECSA remains stable with 61,000 dwt fixed basis delivery West Africa TCT via ECSA to Spore/Japan with grains at USD 24,000 pd. And TA on Ultramax kept falling, losing some USD 3,000/pd from the previous week on most routes. A 56,000 dwt dely Thailand was reported fixed at USD 8,000/pd for a trip via Indonesia to China, a 57,000 dwt dely Indonesia was done at USD 9,000/pd for a trip via Indonesia to Philippines, a 55,000 dwt dely mid-China took USD 7,500/pd for a trip via delivery Brazil redly Italy.

Still no autumn rally - but at least significant improvements for the big ships. Main drivers being operational delays (and consequent congestion) at Far Eastern ports plus modestly increasing minerals output from main exporting areas Australia, South Africa, and Brazil. Average daily spot earnings up some 30 pct - from admittedly poor levels - w-o-w to come in at touch below USD 14k and set to climb further. Inter-pacific with its 50 pct rise, and transatlantic healthy despite small volume, showing most promise, whilst concern is for the long-duration China-Brazil-China round still trading at a grim and worrying discount to other routes. Worthy of notion that several industrial players find time right to try to take cargo cover for 2023. Less ugly FFA's give room for more period discussions - recent fixtures include 181,000 dwt, built 2017, done for 9-12 months at USD 14,500, similar unit already priced close to USD 2k up.

Yet again, another firm week for owners, with rates hitting WS 112 for an MEG/Korea run. This places a China discharge (TD3C) at close to the WS 115 level. With November MEG volume reaching 150, there remains 10-15 cargoes still requiring transport and those owners with available tonnage will be licking their lips. With expensive waiting days, owners can be forgiven for profit taking on stems off their dates, but at the time of writing, appetite to continue into firmer territory remain.  The Atlantic market saw a replacement deal Wafr/Thailand paying up WS 7.5 points (from the same owner) at WS 115. USG cargoes continue to flow, despite the SPR release downturn and owners eye rates above USD 13m to China. Short-term outlook remains strong across the market, and current levels unlikely to subside much this side of the New Year.

Suezmaxes in the Atlantic came off last week, as activity slowed down in most areas. Charterers took their chance to sit on cargoes as some of the higher fixtures failed, and took some air out of the balloon. The dip was expected, but owners remained confident in the market as most of third decade in Wafr remained uncovered. Yesterday we saw those dates come in to play and with 6 cargoes trading in the same window, combined with a thin frontside of the tonnage list, rates are recovering to WS 190's on TD20. We have seen same in USG and in Med and Bsea. The East market on the other hand has less activity. Rates holding up well on the short MEG/India runs, while we are lacking MEG/East activity. But, with the V's still looking strong we hope to see more long east cargoes going forward.

EAST Owners fixing ideas remain strong on the back of a tight East market. There are still some potential November cargoes and offers are few and far between. Looking further out into December there might be more vessels appearing on the East position list as routing via Suez is getting more attractive in tandem with the ever congested Panama Canal. Last done concluded at $130 RT/C.   WEST So far this week we have seen a handful of vessels been put on subs for mainly 2H December dates at freight levels from around $180 H/C to low $190s H/C and mid $90s H/F. Currently we only see one ship left in early Dec, two in mid Dec and 7-8 vessels in end Dec. The three first available positions in the USG are relets and the first open ship from a pure shipowner we find around 20 Dec onwards. With 18 spot fixtures so far in December we should expect 10 more deals to be done that month. Looking at a tight position list with few vessels having a firm itinerary and the arb widening a bit again sentiment continue looking strong.

The Nsea market moved more or less sideways again in the last week with earnings yielding around USD 55k pd for a regular Nsea voyage. Going forward we expect rates to firm a bit as quite a few ships have ballasted away from the area and not many regular Nsea players left for the natural fixing window. The Mediterranean market moved sideways over the last week, though a slightly softer undertone in the area beginning this week with regular cross-med routes correcting somewhat down, but again still offering respectable returns. We don’t expect any drastic changes in the current fixing window as long as the cargo activity remains as healthy as we have seen over the last few weeks - offering both short and long-haul opportunities for owners.

A busy few days with increasing sentiment on the owners side at the time of writing. Rates for MEG/East ticking back up past the WS 100 level as the 3rd decade November stems come into the market and with plenty of support from smaller sizes, the VL market shows no sign of any immediate softening. As in previous months, the Atlantic has driven the increase, as a busy USG has seen rates climb over the USD 12m level for the benchmark Ningbo route and West Africa/East needs a test in the WS 100's. A typhoon currently hitting the Philippines may also slow ballasters. The market today seems like a bear pit, with charterers asking questions and owners playing hard to get. Profit taking is possible, with strong TCE's, modern vessels may prefer to head for the Cape at Rondo, locking in length rather than shorter term gain.

Not the most active week on the surface but there's a steady/poised feel to the global Suezmax market. In the East, short-haul MEG/WCI cargoes are firm at WS 200 whilst we're pegging a TD23 run at WS 100. MEG/China today on modern tonnage is likely to trade WS 180's but needs testing. The Atlantic continues on a firm footing with a TD20 cargo on subs at WS 190, albeit on a vessel that is expected open Lome 12th and ex CPP to boot. The Black Sea retains its crown as the king of opaque markets with very little information filtering through but we peg a third decade TD6 loader at WS 205-210 and a CPC/ROK run unlikely to give much change from USD 7.5m. The USG continues to be the benefactor of a very strong Aframax market with USG/TA trading minimum 145KT x WS 157.5-160.

The LNG freight market continues to hold firm this week as we see an uptick of activity from cargo owners seeking prompt shipping in both basins coupled with various term opportunities that have come to market, sustaining the demand for term tonnage both prompt and as far out as 2026. Despite fluctuating LNG prices and the continued absence of a West-to-East arbitrage, the appetite for spot shipping remains strong and there is still a lack of vessels being shown from subletters holding on to their winter tonnage. As such, when availability does appear rates remain high and command three-way economics. Such an environment has prompted the question amongst market participants of whether freight rates have reached a zenith? The answer is not yet clear, with the potential for floating plays to unwind on the one hand, set against the potential for colder weather or the emergence of an inter-basin arbitrage on the other hand. On the Newbuild front, there is continuing interest in ordering at both Chinese and Korean yards with at least 3 more orders placed since our last report.

The average BCI index lost some USD 5000 daily from last week, to present average just above USD 10,000. C5 dropped one USD to current USD 8 level an c3 is priced sub USD 20 with potential for further drops in the near future, hand in hand with weak fundamentals. China is establishing a team planning to reopen the country by March next year and the forthcoming updated covid guidelines are expected to be good news.

Another muted week with little excitement as sentiment remained negative in most areas. Whilst weather issues in South Asia were causing some delays, there was still a ready supply of tonnage. The Atlantic remained subdued with little cargo interest entering the market.

As speculated last week, the market did indeed break below the USD 16,000-20,000 pd range seen for three months. Vessels heading to the major loading countries in Asia have dropped slightly, whereas the others are basically unchanged. The ballaster/laden vessel ratio still hovers around 75%, compared to the 70% seen last year. Negative sentiment was sensed across all routes. Little activity from USG mainly due to low water levels in the Mississippi River. Similar story with ECSA.   Tick more activity from the Pacific. Indonesia-India coal run being done at USD 14,000. Indo China rounds were done around USD 8,000. A backhaul with del N China redel Med was fixed around USD 13,500.

text: AMERICAS Overall U.S. propane inventory levels reached 88.10mmbbls as of 28 October, having increased by 1.3mmbbls WoW, which is again viewed as a rather surprising high weekly build.  Current stocks exceed the end-Oct average of 84.478 by 3.62mmbbls. In looking closely at the data, most appears in line except for PADD I (the East Coast) where an increase of 600,000bbls was recorded by the EIA.  That level of build normally indicates the arrival of a seaborn import, but no imports occurred, which has now led to speculation that next week’s report may contain corrective data. Still, with robust production levels and very little weather-related demand in North America, it is quite possible that yet another build – though modest – will be reported next week. Terminal fees have meanwhile found life, and for Dec volumes now range on the buy-side in the 6cpg level to the sell-side of as much as 8cpg.  NWE  The arb from the US has been wide open for some time, but a double figure USD drop in arb values today, Thursday, has put trade discussions on hold. Spiking freight rates and the East West spread, trading above $100pmt, had pushed CIF ARA up to fight with the East for winter tons. With propane values in the region seemingly more closely correlated to Naphtha and Brent values than the Natural gas prices. Ethane and Natural gas values continue to be depressed in Europe as supplies from the US continue to surge. The physical propane window is assessed at November CIF ARA +$1pmt. A strong large cargo butane bid was seen at 92.5% of Naphtha which has been strengthening in tandem with stronger Brent.     MED The lack of cold weather continues to keep the region subdued. Spiking freight rates and a wide arb from the US, usually factors which get the market moving, has had the opposite effect as no winter demand has been seen yet this year. That said Marcus Hook cargoes continue to find their ways to the West Med.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco announced Nov CP to $610 for both C3 and C4, whose propane was within expectation, but butane was surprised to be set at parity. And it’s been a rollercoaster ride for swap number this week. Dec CP was traded high to $636 on Wed from Monday’s $604 and plunged to $609 at the time of writing. With additional spot demand from Indonesia, discussions for evenly split cargo have improved, and one end Nov lifting cargo was traded at Dec CP minus single digit.   FAR EAST Cash premium improved considerably with worry of tightness on front market, as of rising freight and Panama delays. Bid for 23kt propane parcel for 1h Dec delivery was at Dec FEI plus $7 and for 2h Dec slightly less. Off window several Chinese petchem players are in the market tendered for Dec delivered propane, with only two managed to award one full propane cargo each, at FEI plus mid low teens into Ningbo and plus nearly $20 into Panjin. While the other PDH user based in Qingdao didn’t award their buy tender for similar volume as eroding margins against soaring costs. Also another Schina PDH is also reckoned that might not award their buy tender for half cargo propane for 1h Dec arrival for regular origins. Price for evenly split cargo was also on the fly. One SChina traditional importer was said to award their buy tender for a mid dec delivered 11/11 parcel at Dec CP plus freight which reckoned at 70s min in view of current Baltic. And another similar parcel for 1h Dec delivery was also reported concluded at 70s to CP into SEA delivery. Pertamina also called another spot tender to procure upto 69kt evenly split cargo for end Nov lifting AG or early dec delivery. Meanwhile, they’ve also called a term tender to secure a min 24 evenly split cargo for 2023 delivery.

EAST With last done deal ex MEG at mid/high $110 RT/C the East market maintains an upward sentiment.  As we are now in November, the QP and KPC acceptances for next month got published earlier this week. Considering the tight market; we may see players in the market for early December cargos soon, but whether the last decade of November has been finished remains a question mark.  The Panama canal continues being very congested and hearing latest auction price at 1.4 million dollars. If this encourages more Owners to ballast the ships from FEA towards Singapore/Suez remains to be seen.  WEST Entering this week we had not yet seen a December fixture out of the USG. At the time of writing we count approximately 10 spot deals ex USG with last done concluded at low $190s H/C and mid $100s H/F which accounts for well over $100k per day in TCE. There are still a good amount of uncovered cargoes out there for the whole of December, but there are currently not enough vessels with firm itinerary to cover them all. We have already seen fixing in mid+end December where vessel supply looks to be more healthy than what we witnessed in the first decade. We could still see a couple more vessels coming open in early Dec as we await discharge schedules. The arb has narrowed a bit lately but as mentioned earlier the Panama canal keeps making scheduling uncertain and we therefore expect the recently strong freight market to maintain in the short term as Owners ideas hovers around $190 H/C.

Charter market volatility has not deterred dry market S&P players, with a number of transactions being registered this week. JP Morgan invited offers on its Capesize TRUE PATRIOT built 2016 Imabari which was sold for USD 38m, and AQUAFORTUNE built 2011 Namura which sold for USD 26.5m. In the Ultramax space, a segment which will be sure to garner a lot of attention over the looming market correction, CARO PADRE built 2012 Yangzhou Dayang sold for USD 21.0m, levels that are still showing relative degree of resilience despite an increased downward pressure coming from chartering front.  Although older tankers continue to attract most of the attention with CITY OF TOKYO built 2004 Universal selling for USD 49m, a more significant transaction is the brand new, scrubber fitted LR2 ALTHEA built 2022 Daehan which was sold for USD 72.5m, showing that regardless of the rising values, market players see sense in positioning themselves for the long term. Tonnage is available for those looking to enter the market, but buyers will need to take a leap of faith and match the bullish sentiment.

Another busy week in the tanker SnP market with vessels across the age curve transacted. Sentek Marine offloaded NEPTUNE M & PACIFIC M, 2019 HHI for Usd 90m each to HMM. The price reflects a below-market charter attached. Older VLCC tonnage continues to make strong gains as demonstrated by the sale of BRILLIANT JEWEL, 2002 DSME for a whopping Usd 40m to Chinese buyers. Two interesting Suezmax sales as well, both at prices slightly above our reference values.    The dry market is beginning to feel the widely anticipated downward pressure in earnings, with some chartering managers seeing rates as low as Usd 6k/day for Supramax tonnage in the Far East. This has resulted in a somewhat quieter week on the sale and purchase front. There is no sense of urgency to move for sales candidates and buyers are as such increasingly adopting a wait and see attitude. In a notable transaction GREAT GLEN and GREAT AMBITION, 93K DWT 2010/2011 JIANGSU JINLING were sold en bloc for Usd 37m by Sinotrans.

text: AMERICAS The US market was mildly surprised by this week’s EIA data which revealed an 800,000bbl build which occurred over the week ending 21 Oct and propelled overall total inventories to 86.8mmbbls. Above-normal temperatures are being forecast across the Eastern half of the US through mid-Nov, and production levels at/near record levels.   Further, and with respect to a modest hiccup in Gulf Coast export volumes, it stands to reason that additional low-impact inventory builds are being anticipated over the coming weeks. The weight of the additional inventories should further help the arb which has improved significantly over the course of October, though freight levels and canal delays will no doubt play a significant role. Terminal fees have all the while been seen improving and though the buy-sell range remains wide, buy-side interest starts in the low 5cpg range with selling interest – depending on timing/location – exists at or above the 6cpg range.  NWE The window continues to see both bids and offers, and is gaining value vs CIF ARA. This has pushed assessed window values to November CIF ARA plus a small premium for a TOT delivery. This accompanies CIF ARA’s rise in relative values vs Mt Belvieu, that arb increasing from high $110s to low $120s, a $5pmt improvement. Traders continue to look to place cargoes in the region due to the potential delays in the Panama Canal, and to optimize their vessels for future FOB loadings rather than having to consider spot freight. The the East/ West spread  for large cargo butane has been quiet and lack of activity means butane in the region has not tracked rising crude values, moving from 93.5% to 90.5% with no recent action.   MED The region is seeing imports from the US arriving to balance the market. The mild start to winter means term contract deliveries are satisfying demand.

text: MEG 1st round Nov CP idea was recommended at $590 for C3 and $580-585 for C4. At the time of writing, Nov C3 CP was traded at $603 and C4 at $598. Nov/Dec C3 was traded at $10 contango. Discussions for evenly split cargo has improved from mid high teens to low mid teens to CP, with Indian and Indonesia players out for spot cargos. Qatar Petroleum was reported to sell a mid Nov lifting evenly split cargo at 50% FEI 50% CP link price to a Chinese major.  FAR EAST Cash premium for prompt delivery market improved further this week with prompt buying demand emerging. 23kt propane for 2h Nov delivery was changed hand at flattish level to Nov FEI. And similar parcel for 1h Dec delivery was bid at Dec FEI plus $6 while offer heard at plus high single digit.  PERTAMINA tendered to buy two evenly split cargo for Dec delivery, in either FOB AG or CFR basis. IOC was reported to buy two similar cargos for Nov and Dec liftings ex AG. Chinese players are also actively seeking cargos for Nov and Dec delivery. One EChina PDH player issued prompt tender to secure a late Nov delivered 23kt propane, which was reported concluded at Nov CP plus 50s. One NChina PDH user was said to cover a 46kt propane for 2h Nov delivery at similar price. One new PDH player in Schina purchased a 10-25th Dec delivery 46kt propane at Dec CP plus 50s reportedly. Another EChina cracker issued tender to procure a 1h Dec delivered 46kt propane into Ningbo.   Apart from spot discussion, negotiations for term 2023 are ongoing. We shall expect more players petchem users call term tenders to secure next year supply, especially for heavy propane feedstock.

Last week we saw the Atlantic market dominating with good cargo flow, now it’s a very positional market. Base trading with Russian and Ukrainian commodities pays a premium. The Continent slid slowly down. Ultramax fixed with grain cargo delivery from Antwerp to Egypt at USD 23,500.  Grains from main loading areas missing volumes and prompt tonnage building up. MV Gant Muse 56‘ dwt open USG fixed USD 25,000 for a trip to China.  Supply from Asia remains subdued with the limited fresh inquiry.

Week started with holidays in parts of Asia. Minimal activity emerged most of the week.  More tonnage in North Atlantic with few on ballasters combined with low volume of cargo, giving a softer tone to the ailing market as rates continue to slide below last done.  The prompter committed tonnage in USG have suffered due to lack of prompt cargo, fixing with way below market to take cover. Mineral volume is low/handful which does not help.  The tonnage in East Med finds it difficult to find cover due to current situation in Black sea with only ballast option towards Gib.  The ECSA has also dropping due to lengthy tonnage and lack of cargo.     Market is sliding.

Still no seasonal rally in sight for the big units, and speculations on possible recession do little to fire up a segment which is presently characterized as dull and without direction. Daily average earnings down 15 pct w-o-w to come in at below USD 16k. Milk route Brazil/Far East remains the one trade most clearly not living up to expectations, as major iron ore miners' spot output keep falling below predictions - subsequently forcing also value for ballasters doing China-Brazil-China well below USD 10k/day. Resultant Pacific supply surplus has so far not pressed levels on the healthier West Australia/China conference ore trade significantly, and Pacific rounds are only marginally down to a still uninspiring USD 12-13k/day. Period activity negligible, as forward-looking values offer little or no premium to spot - and far below levels required by owners to consider.

Although opportunities in the spot freight market are only trickling through, giving a sense of a slowing this week, this is driven more by the lack of availability rather than demand for vessels. This illiquidity, a persist characteristic of 2022, means vessels that do open for charter continue to set record highs: since our last weekly report, new watermarks for both spot and multi-year have been concluded on modern tonnage leading to almost zero 2-stroke vessels being available from independent Owners from now until 2024. 170,000m3 plus vessels with substantial availability remain a “Unicorn” these days, and we can almost say the same for TFDE vessels, leaving steam ships attracting lots of attention and successfully fixing. Open tenders for vessels continue to hit the market  for short and mid-term durations. With more Charterers looking for delivery beyond 2022, some are having to adapt their strategies to expediate the process. In previous years, it has been deemed slightly early to seek tonnage for next year during winter, yet the priority to secure shipping remains strong for many thus bringing forward many procurement needs. Yangzijiang Shipbuilding have made their debut in the large LNG newbuilding sector with two orders for 175,000 cbm vessels delivering between 2025 to 2026 and we kept LNG newbuilding prices stable this week despite shipyards continuously reporting good interest for LNG slots.

Within the space of just eight months, the New Atlantic Market has evolved into a beast, creating new trading patterns that apply stresses to the tonnage list that have seldom, if ever, been witnessed before. Each sub-region/load zone starts out devouring its own natural tonnage before turning its attention to ballasters (same algorithm every time). With this in mind, the market continues on a firm footing with West Africa and the Black Sea competing for the same ships with TD20 and TD6 likely to finish off the week at circa WS 190's and WS 210's respectively. The fixing window for both regions is focused on second decade November. The East is quiet but don't get lulled into thinking that it has down side, because unless charterers stump up WS 180's for a MEG/East run, owners will simply ballast to the Atlantic.

VLCC rates took a hit this week but only in relative terms, as it is difficult to call making upwards to USD 100k/day weakening. Rates on Monday in the WS 105-110 window before KPC set the tone with a WS 100 fixture, followed by NSRP doing WS 98 for Vietnam, both on modern vessels. Valid reasons for the owner to consider sub WS 100 however, with a short ballast from India, 9 other vessels in the trade, a named voyage 1:1 and most importantly an attractive TCE. This puts an MEG/China run close to the WS 100 mark - which side of that mark depends on where you sit. Current active cargoes aiming double digits, but worth noting near 60 MEG deals and the 2nd decade yet to fly, plenty to come.   The Atlantic a little quieter. A few USG cargoes wdwf but deals Brazil/East up to WS 107.5, albeit prompt dates. It's a tricky market to call.

We do see more owners, who earlier was only concentrating on Russian cargoes, now also looking at loading non-Russian North Sea grades. How this will affect rates remain to be seen. However, we expect the market to remain at current levels as the supply and demand scenario looks fairly balanced at the time of writing. Returns on a cross-Med run right now are even better than voyages ex CPC with owners trying to earn a tad more on each fixture. 1st decade of November might be a bit slower later this week, but overall, we expect rates to remain strong as supply of vessels is very balanced due to surrounding areas offering good opportunities as well.

The Eastern market has now moved on to mid November dates as we see last done at low USD 100s RT/C in MEG. A strong East premium could be a sign we are reaching a peak in freight rates, however the count of available vessels for the remaining of November does not cause any immediate concern. Some delays may continue in India/China due to port congestion and bad weather.  WEST When entering this week there were 6 available vessels left in November seeking employment opportunities. At the time of writing there are no vessels November dates as all have been programmed. With latest sub fixtures considered we count 30 spot fixtures in total out of the USG/USEC for November which is what the average have been for a calendar month so far this year in the US. Last fixture concluded in the West is done at mid/high USD 140s H/C which is a big discount compared to last done in the East. First decade December is already in play and market this period looks very tight as congestions in Panama is making scheduling uncertain. Having a firm itinerary is therefore a key advantage going forward.

Suezmax's continue to benefit psychologically from a strong VLCC market. In the East, cargoes are working on a very prompt basis which has maintained momentum with owners. TD23 has been particularly busy with WS 95 reported on subjects whilst NPI has fixed 130KT x 160's for their MEG/Yingkou 1-4/11. In the Atlantic, West Africa has taken a backward step with Saras reported on subjects 130KT x WS 147.5 for a Dalia load, which is likely to price TD20 in the WS 150'S for the remainder of the week. In the Black Sea, the fixing window is firmly focused on the second decade where TD6 has twice been booked at WS 190, but those numbers are likely to ebb away as the weaker links have been taken out. USG/TA is firm with strong Aframax support.

A strong week for owners, with rates in the MEG climbing over WS 20 points as the first November cargoes found coverage. Little hangover from a busy October meant the list was already tight and currently levels around WS 110 is the market for modern MEG/China. Decent TCE’s will bring in to question the owners appetite to keep pushing for higher numbers, as dates are important, any waiting is costly, and who wants to miss the crest of a wave? However, plenty remains for the first decade (25 or so done for Nov so far), so unlikely we see much softening in the short term.   In the Atlantic, rumours of USD 12m paid USG/Ningbo, and reports of the US plans to release more barrels from the SPR, will help further, at least in the short term. Plenty of cargoes in the USG & limited ships prior to mid-November, it's tight out there.

The Aframax tonnage list in the North Sea is looking very tight for end month October liftings. There are some delays in certain strategic discharge ports in the Nsea and Baltic due to no ullage for specific grades. And with other loading areas outside the North Sea basin offering an alternative to owners, we expect the current firm momentum to continue for the month of October. Same picture in the Med/BSea market with delays in some ports and charterers fixing tight itineraries to secure the best possible rates. CPC is slowly coming back into play and that could possibly push rates even higher. As all other areas West of Suez are providing very strong returns, we don’t expect any downside risk moving forward with owners being on the driving seat.

Michael Schumacher said “records are there to be broken” and those words continue to describe the freight market week on week. As expected, the number of spot fixtures being concluded is less than usual going into winter, but the lack of tonnage available to those entering LNG’s busiest season short is warranting a huge premium. With force majeure declared at Bonny and Freeport still inactive, there is some theoretical potential to squeeze out some sublets; however, given the uncertainty within the markets and a contango in the LNG curve that is encouraging floating plays, in practice sublets are few and far between and in case are quite restricted in charter period. With such a tight tonnage situation in the foreseeable future, were now seeing discussions on both spot and term well into 2023 with prices remaining firm on both and all the signs of a high freight environment as we look ahead. No newbuild transactions have been recorded this week.

Since last week there has been a drop in the number of vessels heading to the North Atlantic/Continent.  Vessels heading to the major loading countries in Asia seems like reached a peak. Not much change in vessels heading to the Med/Black Sea or the South Atlantic. Nothing clear and obvious on near-term direction in other words. Looking at macro-factors it is hard to see how demand growth is going to push upwards enough to lift the market above the USD 17,000-20,000 pd range. We believe the risk is clearly to the downside.

The market been stable over the last week, and for once we can’t really report a significant change in rates. However, we can recap that the Far East been fairly quiet, but bad weather in China has limit the new tonnage hence freight at status quo. South Atlantic sliding on slow activity while north is holding, and we do see more cargoes in the segment however it is expected to be short lived. For the weeks to come it feels like we are going back to a more bearish environment as the confidence that levels will hold or go further up is very limited.

A slow but steady week in the Atlantic basin, fresh cargoes hitting the market with an underlying demand off market too helping to keep rates steady and firm for both the transatlantic and fronthaul trips. Asia returned once more something of a two-tier market according to some sources, the North still seeing strong demand ex NoPac with firmer rates being concluded, but again there lacked any tangible mineral demand from Australia which on some positions has kept a lid on rates for now.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco released Nov acceptance with some advancements reported, which could be resulted by nomination from lifters for late month loading, in view of contango structure and soaring freight. And with Oil production cuts in Nov, we believe producers shall have less spot avails compared to previous months. Evenly split cargo for Nov lifting was reported done at CP minus mid high teens. Qatar Petroleum was reported to sell a mid Nov lifting propane. Nov C3 CP rebounded to $578 from $550 earlier this week, and C3/C4 narrowed down to $10. And Nov/Dec C3 was traded at $3 contango.   FAR EAST Cash premiums have improved with a bunch of buying inquiries surging. A couple of 23/0 for 2h Nov delivery was changed hand at FEI minus $1.5 to $2.5. Meanwhile, there are some talks on disruptions on Iran supply for Nov arrival cargoes due to maintenance and strikes, hence lending supports to the front market. A couple of cargoes in heavy propane or evenly split ratio for Nov delivery were reported placed into China at Nov CP plus 40ish.   Off window, it’s another hectic week with a handful of tenders. One Korean importer was reported to award their buy tender for 23/0 during 19-23th Nov delivery at Nov FEI minus small digit. Another Korean petchem player also tendered to procure 11kt butane for 2h Nov delivery. One SChina PDH user issued buy tender for two 23/0 parcels on Nov and Dec delivery each. Another EChina PDH also issued similar tender to secure a 23/0 for early Nov prompt delivery. One SChina traditional importer canceled its buy tender for late Nov delivered 11/11 parcel as offers are higher than expectation. One Vietnam PDH player tendered to buy 23/0 or 46/0 for 10-30th Nov delivery. Apart from spot tender, one NChina PDH importer issued tender to buy monthly 46kt propane for next year delivery.

With the tanker market taking the majority of recent headlines, dry market players enacted a flurry of transactions this week. Within the much sought after modern Japanese ultramax tonnage space, scrubber fitted NORD BISCAY (62K DWT 2019 OSHIMA) sold for USD 32.5m. Another sale to note from this sector was Pacific Basin picking up ULTRA WOLLONGONG (61K DWT 2011 OSHIMA) for USD 22m. A total of 15 sales were concluded across the board. This increased activity is dividing opinions with one hand believing a relative bottom has been been reached while the other see it as a signal that a broader sell off is around the corner.  Extensive demand and firm prices in older tonnage such as the EUROGLORY  (166 DWT 2005 BRODOSPLIT) USD 26m reassures market players that the tanker market ascent shows no signs of letting off. Ice class Suezmax vessels are commanding a particular premium seen in the CAP PHILIPPE (158 DWT 2006 SAMSUNG HI) changing hands for USD 32 m. In what is regarded by some as a significant, sentiment assuring transaction, AQUAVIRTUE (156 DWT 2022 SAMSUNG HI) was bought by Thenamaris at USD 76m.

text: AMERICAS  U.S. propane inventories are reported by the EIA to have risen by a half-million barrels during the week ending 14 Oct and are now pegged at an overall total of 86mmbbls, which is roughly 9mmbbls above earlier forecasts and 117% of last year’s total.  The data from yesterday shows that there was a draw in the Midwest (PADD II) of 300,000bbls and on the East Coast (PADD 1C), but that the Gulf Coast (PADD III) stocks increased by 400,000bbls.  Weather-related demand in the U.S. has been limited so far, though the draws described above point towards the beginnings of the winter season.  However, current forecasts are calling for a warming trend over the balance of October (per NOAA), and thus either small builds or small draws can be anticipated as the seasons shift. Terminal fees have recently begun showing signs of life and levels have moved up amid open arbs to present ideas ranging from the low 4cpg range to a high point of around the 6 cpg level.  NWE North Sea availabilities of propane and butane have fallen roughly 30% per month due to the re-injection of a portion of the LPG into the skyrocketing natural gas stream. However, a price spike and the need for additional tons has for now been mitigated, by the steady flow of US Origin VLGC's arriving in NWE.  The Propane price has gained ground in relation to Naphta- which fell more in parity with crude in the first few weeks of October.  But the focal point throughout the world of LPG this past week has been the emergence of some bullish indicators recognized throughout the market. Chinese run rates at cracking facilities have increased (and thus demand) on back of stronger margins, a curtailed Middle Eastern export program, and the theory that domestic retailers across the US will need to continue buying more product to cover for winter demand, as they elected not to do so earlier in the year due to sky high propane prices. The domino effect of the preceding could quickly matriculate into the European market,  making it difficult to attract tons from the US East Coast, where volumes- to-export perennially dwindle. The former, along with the unrealized probability of cold temperatures, has many market participants watching for a sharp increase in European LPG values on the horizon.  MED The large cargo market has been quiet as temperatures remain above average for the time of year. The butane arb from the US is closed. So, until the weather changes, term supply will be sufficient to maintain a balanced market.

EAST After QP and Petco product tenders were awarded the activity on freight has calmed down in the East. We currently count 11 fixtures concluded ex Middle East in November, whereas 8 deals done for 1st decade and 3 deals done for 2nd decade. We expect to see more demand for ships from mid-2H November, but as most ships for this window are still waiting on discharge orders for current voyages there are few ships with clear itinerary as of today. East Baltic is currently at a 6-7 dollar premium to West. One could expect that East market is about to top out unless there are cargos on the front that needs to be covered last minute.   WEST While seeing the East moving fast and the premium growing bigger the West is currently not keeping the same pace. So far for November we have seen 27 spot fixtures out of USG/USEC and there should still be a handful of more deals to be done for 2H Nov. This period is looking very tight as we only see a couple trader relets available and with the arb still wide we should expect today's strong freight rates to maintain going forward.

A busy week in the dry market saw a rare sale of a modern asset, in the form of Ultramax BERGE TRONADOR 2020 DACKS built sold for USD 32.8m. Elsewhere, Post-Panamax D SKALKEAS 2011 Newyangzi sold for USD 19.0m to Hong Kong interests. Panamaxes AGRI KINSALE / AGRI QUEEN 2009 Oshima built were sold at auction for USD 16.0m each. Many units remain in the market across the size curve, and players are braced for an interesting Q4 as they jostle for market position.   The tanker market shows no signs of cooling off as VLCC PRINCESS MARY 2004 Mitsubishi built sold for a huge USD 48.0m, granted she is SS freshly passed and BWTS fitted, but this total is well over previous market estimates. In the smaller sizes however, the S&P market is beginning to look crowded with a rumoured 50 plus MRs currently seeking new ownership. This is likely to apply pressure to values across in this sector, which saw 5 transactions this week. The pick of the sales were ENERGY PUMA / ENERGY PROGRESS 2008 Sungdong built, sold to Middle Eastern buyers at USD 20.0m each.

Same story in the Nsea market last week as rates moved sideways with Charterers fixing tight to repeat last done levels. There are still delays in some strategic discharge ports limiting the options for Charterers while most of the Owners in position are focusing solely on Russian business. We don’t foresee any downside risk moving forward and we might see rates moving even higher.Little change in the Med market last week with Owners keeping the momentum alive as market remained busy for another week. Charterers have found it hard to bring rates lower as tight/balanced supply of vessels persists in whole West of Suez market and activity is healthy. As we move closer to end-month fixing window and with CPC loadings for Aframaxes coming back for November we anticipate rates to continue improving.

text: AMERICAS U.S. propane inventory levels this week increased by 1.1mmbbls for an overall total of 85.50mmbbls as of 07 Oct and pushing stocks to nearly 120% of last year, per the EIA.  There are quite clearly sufficient volumes in tank to pose little threat to any domestic weather-related requirements this winter and to keep the exports rolling. Meanwhile, in the face of healthy freight rates terminal fees have seen an uplift and where before the bottom end of the range was in the 3cpg range, now the lower end of the range is in the 4cpg range.  Sellers, meanwhile, have adjusted their ideas from the low/mid 4s to the 5 cpg range. Through it all, activity levels are still subdued but sentiment seems to be improving despite only modest temperature declines and very little crop drying demand. A Chilean tender was released overnight which calls for a propane-only LGC or a VLGC to be delivered from 5-12 December, perhaps on a 2-disport basis.  Offers are due by 1pm CST on 13 Oct with the results anticipated by 10am CST Friday 14 Oct.  NWE A deal in the TOT window was booked Wednesday setting the end October and early November levels at CIF ARA minus $2pmt. This was the third TOT deal in as many weeks, and we do not expect the market to slow down. Netback values west are at parity with the East, and with the Panama canal delays lengthening to 10 North and 9 days Southbound the additional cost with going East has many traders looking to place their cargoes in the West. Importers have been waiting to see clear signs of additional European demand, or to be offered something which fits their needs. So the arb is wide open and the market looks tight, but counterintuitively, it is a buyers’ market. European naphtha has taken a hit which has pushed the Propane / Naphtha spread to $93pmt down from above $100pmt earlier in the week. Large cargo butane remains at a strong 93.5% of October Naphtha, though French refinery strikes are likely to weaken these levels.   MED French strikes have dampened the mood in the West Med. The effects of these on the waterborne LPG market are yet to be seen on the market, as a butane offer from Lavera was withdrawn and no other bids or offers have been seen. The East Med remains quiet as additional winter demand is yet to be seen.

text: MEG ADNOC released their Nov lifting acceptance with some advancement up to 5-7 days reported. KPC refinery production was suspended unexpectedly but was reported at a limit impact to exports. Swap market experienced a volatile week with Nov C3 CP once soared up to $600 and declined to $577 at the time of writing, C4 CP was assessed at $22 less. Nov/Dec was traded at 6-7$ contango.   FAR EAST Active market with a handful of deals were concluded this week. 23kt propane for 2h Nov delivery was changed hand at Nov FEI minus $2/2.5 during mid-week but softened on Thurs with bids for similar cargo show at minus $5.88 while offer at Flat to FEI.  Off window a flurry of tenders is in the market, especially from importers’ feedstock procurement tender on term basis for next year. Two Chinese petchem users issued propane or heavy propane buy term tender for next year delivery. Taiwan CPC also issued a swap tender to sell their Saudi FOB for monthly 11/11 and buy back 8-12 cargos on des basis at similar grades. One Korean importer also issue two term tenders to secure monthly 23kt butane in different lots for cracking and was reported to award only one. One EChina PDH procured a Nov delivered 46kt propane via tender at 50% Nov FEI minus low-mid single digit and 50% Nov CP plus low 40s reportedly. Another EChina cracker also issued buy tender to secure 23kt to 46kt propane for 2h Nov delivery.

The average 5 tc cape rate was USD 21,000 last week compared to present average USD 18,250. The c5 route is marked 9,2 down from 9,6 pmt last week. Ie it is the fronthaul trade being the most volatile route, with rates coming off from 44,000 to 38,000 over the last week. The c3 rate is more or less unchanged. Period rate is steady, but mainly for index linked deals.

BSI keeps good resistance with little change on the value of 1708 closing today. With the Asian market coming back after Golden week, we see more activity though rates remain flat.  Atlantic keeps positive momentum with good demand in key areas such as ECSA and USG. The cargoes from the Mediterranean and Black pushed rates to a higher level. US Gulf has good volume and keeps charterers busy finding prompt tonnage. We expect the market to be flat for the next week with better value in the Atlantic basin.

The Panamax market yielded a further week of losses as the market in the Atlantic appeared to idle, with little activity of note. Some spoke of certain grain trips paying a premium over mineral trades, but a wide bid/offer gap curtailed any decent activity. Conversely Asia witnessed minor gains primarily on the back of the NoPac trade but overall a week of minimal action despite an influx of Indonesian coal demand further south.

The Atlantic continues to see scores of ships disappear off market as most Charterers try to keep everything low-key rather than risk a cargo out in the open . This quickly became apparent to one unlucky Charterer who obviously hadn't read the memo and duly paid up at W145 for a Td20 run. Opaque markets normally have an adverse impact on rates, but not this time, as it appears Owners are openly trumpeting the fact when their ships are on subjects and/or fully fixed, which has fed into the present market momentum in a positive manner. Black Sea is done for the month and with CPC/ROK last trading at USD 6M we wouldn't be surprised if Charterers take a peak at early November dates. The East market has slowed down after a previously busy week but Owners still looking circa WS140's for a China run on modern tonnage.

The VLCC market has been hovering each side of the W80 mark MEG/east in the week gone by, depending on destination and the vessel’s trading background. Much of the fixing activity has been conducted under the radar and charterers have manged to keep a lid on things. However, at the writing moment "panic" has started to set in and cargoes have been toppling into the marketplace on top of each other for the last week of October loading. Adding to that some prompt-ish replacement jobs for ships failing to clear and the owning community is yet again “smelling blood”. By all accounts we will go into the November MEG program with a miniscule overhang, signalling a continued upward bias. Owners’ confidence has been further supported by a number of USG export cargoes paying $10+mill for the benchmark Ningbo discharge.

Whilst LNG prices have continued their correction this week, it appears that the only thing preventing rates firming further is a lack of available ships to be fixed. With a number of uncovered cargoes in the East, it’s not surprising to see projects selling their upside cargoes FOB. And herein lies the paradox of this market - there are ships that could lift all these cargoes, but for any number of reasons they aren’t being released. It’s a classic Prisoner Dilemma whereby portfolios are keeping their length in order to respond to Freeport’s potential restart or to capitalise on distressed cargo sales. No charterer wants to fix out in October for $500k pdpr if they have to give twice that amount back a month later to cover an unexpected short. Ultimately, it’s therefore no surprise that we now see Charterers in the market for 2023 tonnage because whilst current sentiment is keeping next year’s rates high, this year has taught us that the most expensive shipping is in fact no shipping.  On newbuilds, there’s been talk of one new order this week in Korea.

EAST Adnoc dates were published earlier this week with reports of some lifters getting advanced. Fixing activity for 1H Nov has been minimal so far but we have seen a couple deals concluded at high $80s RT/C. With some more delays in India and China the position list looks tight for first half Nov in East. How much OPEC+ oil cut from Nov onward would impact to the LPG production in MEG remain to be seen, but the sentiment in the East remains stable/strong so far.  WEST The Western freight market also continues being strong now trading at parity with the East. At the time of writing we count approximately 25 spot fixtures out of the USG so far for November with last done deal concluded at high $130s Houston/Chiba and mid $70s H/F. The last remaining vessels for early Nov have been programmed and focus is now fully on mid and end month dates. Vessel availability this period is tight, especially 10-20 Nov range, and with the arb widening in addition to an increase in waiting days in the Panama Canal we remain bullish.

The dry market had a bumper week in transactions, despite the overall uncertain sentiment that has been shared by most market players over the past few weeks. On the Supramax front, sisters GENCO BOURGOGNE & TERESE OETKER 2010 YANGZHOU DAYANG were sold at USD 15.75m and USD 16.1m respectively. Benchmarks which will be most welcome in a market that is seeing an increasing amount of similar tonnage been placed for sale. Capesize SHINYO GUARDIAN 2005 NAMURA was bought by Turkish buyers for USD 17.25m which also marks a new, lower benchmark for this vintage Capesize.  The tanker markets were relatively subdued in terms of completed transactions with product tankers capturing most of the activity this week. The standout deal in this space was UOG picking up the DEE4 FIG 2011 ONOMICHI for USD 26.5m. To put this in perspective, the vessel was purchased by DEE4 in August 2020 for USD 16m. Performance Shipping added another Aframax unit to its fleet with the purchase of PHOENIX BEACON 2011 HHI for USD 35.0m.

Rates in the NSea moved sideways early this week as Charterers were fixing tight to secure last-done levels and using their relets for own program. However, the list is still tight in the normal fixing window due to a combination of delays in strategic ports and bad weather, Charterers paid higher or fixed afra stems on bigger sizes to secure tonnage. Moving forward we expect tightness of supply to persist and rates to remain healthy as many Owners still focus solely on Russian business for as long as they can.Same trend in the Med/BSea market which continued climbing even if CPC program doesn’t contain any afra stems for Oktober.Delays in some strategic ports and Owners ballasting away resulting in tight supply as well. We don’t see any downward potential in this market especially when Afra stems will be back ex CPC.

It’s been a week where the pendulum swung firmly in Charterers favour. Perhaps the size of the swing taking some by surprise. Charterers have played it well, albeit helped by the lack of 10-20 Oct Meg enquiry (sub 40 fixtures, 10 fewer than Sept). But, with active cargoes obtaining multiple offers, Owners are grabbing a number and running for the hills. However, even with the recent decline, daily earnings remain at a healthy level - High $50's on all bells and whistles, and still approx. $35k on a non scrubber - a world away from close to $0 earlier this year. It seems there is a dichotomy in the markets, with a softening AG, but a USG & Brazil that has re-ignited. Plenty of Atlantic enquiry and Owners will be hoping , as per the past few months, it is the West that arrests the slide and drives the market upwards.

This week started where last week ended, those Charterers that still find themselves short continue to scramble for whatever tonnage is left. It goes without saying that any available (or even potentially attainable) modern tonnage has received the most attention, but the lack thereof has resulted in some surprise fixtures on the older, and smaller, steam turbine fleet. In tandem with the firm spot market, the term market has also stayed active, as multiple charterers are looking for term coverage down the curve. And next week, after the Golden Week holidays end, our friends in China may re-enter the market again!  On the newbuilding front, Excelerate Energy announced that it has ordered a 170,000m3 FSRU from HHI for June 2026 delivery which is the first FSRU newbuilding order in many years. Furthermore, it was reported that ExxonMobil has confirmed another 7 newbuilding berth slots at SHI, adding to their existing orderbook and firmly reasserting their commitment to this segment. Newbuilding prices remain firm.

The Atlantic market is improving, while the Pacific is easing off considering Golden week holidays in Asian countries.  A Supramax open Germany was rumored to be fixed TCT to USG $20,000pd. Scrap is paying similarly but Owners resist and demand a premium.  The Mediterranean market shows good resistance due to grain exports increasing from Ukraine and Russia. Owners asking above $20,000pd for TCT to West Africa. The tonnage list for vessels open in the Mediterranean is short thus giving owners the opportunity to obtain better levels.   ECSA and USG have good activity levels and rates keep climbing North. FH from USG paying $27,000pd and TA trips $25,000pd

Don't confuse a lack of noise in the market with inactivity .  This week has witnessed a chunk of East ships fix off market with the early side of the MEG list extremely tight on modern, well approved units. Whilst the list does even out towards the back end of the second decade, there does appear to be a degree of stability. In the Atlantic, Td20 appears to be defying the fundamentals as Exxon is reported on subjects 130KT X WS127.5 on a 2007blt unit against a fairly healthy list. In the Mediterranean, some Aframax cargoes have been catching a ride on Suezmax, which may cap that market but it will offer a reprieve to the odd Suezmax that has missed the natural fixing window. USG/TA trades 145KT X WS115-120

A two-tiered basin again for the Panamax market with the Atlantic building up a head of steam particularly for the front haul trips with improved demand seen in the market. The trans-Atlantic saw less activity however rates were now getting impacted as tonnage appeared tighter on a Cont/Mediterranean delivery with rates seemingly following suit. Golden Week holidays again impacted trade with a slow market this week

Big ships enjoying better times on limited prompt supply and somewhat healthier demand – daily spot earnings up some 25 pct w-o-w to come in at usd 21k, and expected to continue the climb. Atlantic, although close to negligible in volume, keeps standing out as the hotspot with miners, steel mills, utilities, traders and operators absorbing most early units as they open. With transatlantic paying usd 26k/day,  almost usd 11k better than Far East rounds, indications are of further upward pressure also for the West Australia/China milk route – so far up only 10 pct in value last 5 trading days. No fronthaul autumn rally yet to be seen, although both predictions for Brazilian iron ore export targets and Chinese financial measures are expected to translate into higher volumes + levels.

It’s been a week where the pendulum swung firmly in Charterers favour. Perhaps the size of the swing taking some by surprise. Charterers have played it well, albeit helped by the lack of 10-20 Oct Meg enquiry (sub 40 fixtures, 10 fewer than Sept). But, with active cargoes obtaining multiple offers, Owners are grabbing a number and running for the hills. However, even with the recent decline, daily earnings remain at a healthy level - High $50's on all bells and whistles, and still approx. $35k on a non scrubber - a world away from close to $0 earlier this year. It seems there is a dichotomy in the markets, with a softening AG, but a USG & Brazil that has re-ignited. Plenty of Atlantic enquiry and Owners will be hoping , as per the past few months, it is the West that arrests the slide and drives the market upwards.

EAST East fixing has taken a breather so far this week but we expect to see more activity from Indian Charterers end October, and potentially a handful of cargos from other Charterers before November fixing begins. With less waiting time in Panama, a widening arb, and a current 6 dollar West premium – we don’t expect East market to come off in the near future. Freight rates have stabilized around the $80 RT/C mark with last done deals concluded at $80 and $81 respectively.  WEST Much of the same story goes for the Western freight market as we have only seen a couple of fixtures so far this week in the USG. Rates however are remaining strong as we have seen mid $130s H/C been fixed lately and around $70s H/F. In total we have seen over 15 spot fixtures so far for November and close to all of them have been fixed in 1-10 November range. Fixing focus is now set to shift towards a tight mid-month, although some still looking early Nov dates, and with a supporting arb we expect today’s strong rates to maintain going forward.

text: AMERICAS The U.S. propane market seems to have settled into a lull as we are presently between seasons and at a time when domestic inventories are well stocked but weather-related demand has yet to commence.   It is neither warm nor cold over most of the U.S., and things are presently calm.  Export volumes are anticipated to increase in Oct.  The EIA propane stock data was released and as of Sep 20 inventories reached an overall total of 84.4mmbbls, an increase of 1.6mmbbls over the previous week.  The latest intel puts U.S. propane stocks at 117% of last year and 81% of two years ago.  Nonetheless, as there is only limited demand at present there are likely to be additional – though modest – builds going forward, and as such even the current totals are considered sufficient to simultaneously accommodate both export requirements and weather-related demand.  US terminal fees remain generally depressed, with buy-side interest most often found in the upper 3cts/gal range, with sellers looking for anything above the 4cts/gal level.  In the meantime, very little is actually being accomplished and the market is in respite.   Going forward, one factor to keep in mind is OPEC cuts combined with higher Crude prices, should open the door for increased US production, leading to increased propane production and lower propane to WTI ratio.  NWE After an active start to the week in the European window propane discussions have quietened down. Leaving end October TOT cargoes values at October CIF ARA flat and 1H November cargoes valued November CIF ARA minus $2pmt. Although October propane naphtha spread in the region is -$109pmt, we are yet to see a rise in petchem demand. This low demand environment and, the lack of cold weather, is likely to have unsold November arrival cargoes look for a home in the East market instead of the West. The butane market remains active, with an open arb form the US. Though the one bid in the window at 89.5% October Naphtha for very early November arrival was well below the 98% bid seen earlier in the week.   MED The region has seen recent butane demand rise opening the arb from northwest Europe to Lavera. With northwest Europe also tight, US LPG is being imported to the region as the arb opens. A VLGC heading for Tangiers and a MGC into Sines in October, causing bids to disappear from the window.

text: MEG Following the crude rally, Nov Propane CP was traded at $600 and Butane at $582. Nov/Dec CP was traded at $7 contango as entering winter. However front supply appears long and discussions for evenly split cargo on Nov lifting are still at teens discounts to CP. QP also issued tender to sell a early Nov lifting full propane cargo.   FAR EAST 23kt propane for 1h Nov delivery was changed hand at Nov FEI minus 8ish reportedly. Similar cargo was offered in window at FEI minus $6 for 1h Nov delivery, whereas bid for 2h Nov delivery cargo is at FEI minus $6.5, in view of slight contango on 1h/2h Nov. Off window, a handful of buy tenders emerging, especially for petchem use. One Chinese cracker user tendered to procure a 46kt propane for 1H Nov delivery into Ningbo. Taiwan FPCC awarded their buy tender for 1h Nov delivered 46kt propane at Nov MOPJ minus mid high 60s reportedly. One Korean importer issued term tender to secure monthly 23kt butane for 6 to 12 lots in 2023. HTC also tendered to buy a 23kt propane parcel for 6-12 Nov delivery into Daesan. And we are expecting more demand coming out next week when China back from holidays.

Seemingly the Atlantic saw something of a revival this week with some decent levels of activity in the North. Primarily there remained some disparity between the grain and mineral trades with the former still paying a premium with improved levels concluded and sentiment turned a little on the back of some further better deals. The Asian market appeared under pressure from the get-go, with both the Indonesia and NoPac round trips losing further ground as supply/demand fundamentals played out.

Last week ended positive as all segments improved with all the west Australian miners being present, south Brazil pushing with Vale covering several liftings and spot tonnage in the north being covered. However, the positiveness disappeared this week as Pacific went from being very busy last week to very quiet this week. Hence, we see a 27% decline in time charter hire week on week for the west Australia to China round trip. Though Pacific has been disappointing so far this week, and general sentiment is weaker, the north Atlantic still holding and Vale still being fairly active thus we see the market holding.

A couple of quiet days and the tide can turn. However, owners can not be blamed for profit taking, when seeing TCE returns in the USD 80’s per day. Decreasing bunker costs coupled with a quiet cargo list, owners are checking out at numbers lower than last done (mid WS 90's MEG/East, sub USD 10m USG-China). October is looking a lighter month, perhaps unsurprising after a near record cargo count in September for overall VLCC fixings driven by the MEG and USG. However, recession fears in the West and inevitable decreases in US SPR releases, will mean less USG exports going forward. With the OPEC+ 'threatening' to cut production to support oil prices, we may be close to peak VLCC volumes for now. Also worth noting, hurricane Ian may shut in up to 2 mbpd in the Gulf of Mexico and causing delay potential.

End of last week the Nsea Aframax market gained some momentum as charterers showed their cards and owners seized the opportunity to dig their heels in and ask for higher rates than last done. This week rates have continued to firm on the back of increased activity. Unless bigger sizes come into play, we expect rates to remain firm as the tonnage list is looking quite thin in the area for any cargoes loading up to 10th October. The Med market moved sideways last week as activity remained firm and some ships ballasted away from the area seeking business elsewhere. The position list looks tight in the front end, but with dates moving forward and some more ballasters ex East the current upside potential could be dampened a bit. However, if the activity continues, we expect the market to remain healthy.

The main support mechanism for the global Suezmax market right now is VLCC sentiment, and without this very tenuous link the pure fundamentals of this market, at least in the ultra-short term, are weaker. Let’s start off with the Black Sea which had a very industrious first decade but has now slowed to a whimper for the second, as a mixture of TC/OP listings have taken momentum away from that region. This has left us with a chunk of prompt vessels (or close to being prompt) in this region now missing the Black Sea/Med fixing window, who will now have to gamble on prompter Med cargoes popping out, or, as will most likely be the case, force the majority into entertaining West Africa at lower levels. The East is similarly fundamentally weak and in need of further enquiry to maintain present levels.

General situation remains across the Supra desk that demand growth is 0% whereas fleet growth keeps ticking upwards. Discharge waiting times are also down on last year, causing further downward pressure on markets.  Tick downturn on the last weeks activity from the USG, where fhauls were discussed at around USD 23,000. Trip from Cont to USG being concluded about USD 18,000 on Supramax. Bhaul from CJK to Cont were done at USD 20,000. Nopac round on Ultramax being fixed around USD 19,500. Supra from Indonesia with coal run to India concluded around USD 21,750.  Tick more period activity but not at the improved levels though. Ultramax was covered for 3-4 mos at 20k with delivery Atlantic and redelivery ww, another Ultra open in Far East was fixed in the low USD 18,000 for one year.
