LNG prices remain high as continuing uncertainties over gas supplies in Europe put further pressure on markets. Charterers still have a close eye on the contango into December and January, hence interest on tonnage that can cover winter months remains strong, thereby elevating the forecast rates further. There has been some more sublet length shown this week but almost all have restrictions on periods. In the West shippers have their focus on 2 strokes but these availabilities are almost non-existent, especially while market players awaiting further updates on Freeport hide their length. In the East, steamers are having considerable interest for spot or longer (!) as available modern tonnage is limited in the region. With Requirements popping up in both basins and with availability proving challenging we do expect rates to increase. On the NewBuilding market, China Merchants have exercised options on two additional vessels and signed an LOI for four vessels with Dalian Shipyard.

EAST After last week’s fixing frenzy and this week’s APPEC conference in Singapore, activity has comparably slowed down. We have seen about 20 spot fixtures concluded from the Middle East in October, but still expect to see a handful of remaining cargoes before focus shifts to November. Freight ideas remain firm with most owners’ ideas now in the USD 80s RT/C for next Eastern business.  WEST After having seen a lot of fixing in the West the last 4-5 weeks, we are now witnessing a more quiet week. It looks like October-fixing is currently over as the last remaining ships this period have been programmed. Trader relets are currently dominating a very tight position list while the big shipowners seemingly are sold out until the middle of November.   We have seen a dozen November deals in the USG so far, with last done at USD 130 H/C and 70 H/F, and there is a lot more to be done going forward.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco cut Oct propane CP by $60 to $590 and butane CP by $70 to $560, which is higher than swap value but amid the recommendation range. Given ample supply against limited demand especially for butane heavy cargos, Nov C3 CP was traded at $585. But some players believe that the flat price will rebound later with the winter demand anticipation, and slightly fewer spots available from middle east producers for Oct liftings.   FAR EAST With the APPEC in SG, activities are limited this week. 23kt propane for 2h Oct delivery was changed hand at Oct FEI minus mid-single digit, and similar cargo for 1h Nov delivery was bid at Nov FEI minus high single digit. Outside window a couple of 1h Nov delivered 46kt propane cargos were traded at Nov FEI minus low-mid teens.  PDH margins improved as of the decline in feedstock costs, however downstream propylene and PP price remained steady or weakened a bit. Several PDHs, which are off for maintenance earlier, have resumed operation from last week. Hence the feedstock demand for Nov delivery are expected to increase significantly. One NChina PDH user was said to procure a propane parcel for 2h Oct to 1h Nov delivery. Two other Chinese PDH players have also tendered to buy similar parcel for 1h Nov and mid Nov delivery respectively.

text: AMERICAS Activity levels in the domestic US market have been limited recently as most are eyeing the rising inventories and corresponding pricing structure declines.  The EIA data this week showed yet another build, this time a ‘middle of the road’ 1.6mmbbl improvement to an overall total of 82.8mmbbls.  The increase is the result of modestly reduced export volumes as well as stout production levels.  Inventory expectations earlier in the year were aimed at the mid/upper 70mmbbl level which while sufficient has been well eclipsed and has shifted the market to a lengthier – and perhaps more comfortable - position.  Terminal fees remain weak, with buy-side interest in the 3cpg range and sellers’ initial offers starting in the mid 4cpg.  September export volumes have been muted, but sentiment is calling for October exports to be more robust.  As winter nears and temperatures begin to subside, propane demand levels should commensurately improve, particularly with support from the crude arena if WTI continues its recent about-face.  NWE  A window deal was done Wednesday, pegging the TOT market at October CIF ARA +$2mpt. European netbacks are favourable to heading East from the US as the East West spread of +$54pmt is around $10pmt below the freight differential between the East and West routes. The difficulty for European shorts is finding vessels which can reach the region in time in this tight VLGC market. The window deal done was for delivery around October 20th, while VLGCs are being fixed for November 10th FOBs, which would be end November arrival in Europe. European butane has been depressed recently by the rumour of a full butane VLGC cargo heading to the region, pushing values from 94% October Naphtha down to 92%.  MED Refinery production continues to be reduced in the region as LPG is used for power during the continued high natural gas price environment. US volumes have been pushed into the Med calming any potential tightness, before the first signs of any winter demand

As widely anticipated, the dry cargo markets have witnessed a number of corrective sales this week. Navios have sold the Supramax NAVIOS ULYSSES 2007 Oshima at a price of USD 14.5m providing a much needed benchmark for a market that is seeing a number of similar candidates being placed for sale. What remains to be seen is whether this will spur on the number of transactions or encourage scepticism as we head into a potentially challenging Q4. More modern tonnage is proving desirable, with scrubber-fitted Ultramax NORD BARENTS 2019 Oshima selling at USD 33.3m.  The tanker market is alive with excitement and rumour, leaving market players wondering whether this buoyant sentiment can translate into previously unthinkable asset prices. Sales of older ships at firm levels such as VLCC VIKI 2000 Samsung HI at USD 29.5m are causing a conundrum as assets further up the age curve fail to entice buyers into chasing owner’s price ideas. Ridgebury Tankers though, have cashed in with 3 sales concluding this week MRs RIDGEBURY BIRCH & ACACIA 2006 Shin Kurushima at USD 17.5m each, and RIDGEBURY VOYAGER 2008 HMD at USD 19.5m.

A relatively quiet week in the dry market as sentiment remains largely unchanged, even with the sale of Capesize FRONTIER TRIUMPH 2012 Imabari at USD 30.0m to Chinese interests. Players in smaller segments are patiently waiting for a corrective sale, which would help price the increasing number of candidates being placed in the market. That said, owners are still enjoying a bump in earnings, so are in no rush to sell themselves short. The sale of Kamsarmax NORD CORONA 2019 Hantong for USD 29.0m will not go unnoticed, setting a renewed benchmark in the sector.  Tanker owners are still very much enjoying the upward momentum, particularly by those who perhaps took a position a few years ago at what is now considered a very attractive entry point on the price curve. More modern tonnage is attracting attention too with some owners entertaining the idea of a potential sale at substantially higher targets. A revision that is not yet met by buyers who are yet to feel comfortable with these fast-moving levels.

The average index is trading still in the high of USD 10,000, with little gains from last week and closing yesterday at USD 17,382.  Atlantic is being under pressure, while the Pacific market is more stable with rates maintaining a range of mid to high USD 10,000 pd.  Transatlantic round voyages paying just a bit more than USD 15,000 pd.  USG numbers seem to be flat without any significant changes in fresh inquiries. ECSA is stable with little to report. Tess 58 fixed USD 26,000 pd for TCT with grains from Argentina to the Continent.  Ultramax asking USD 20,000 pd del West Africa for a trip to the Continent including the UK.  The Continent market describes as a horror room without any lives. Vessels ballasting from Continent towards USEC to find employment.  The Black Sea and the Mediterranean markets remain volatile driven by Ukraine and Russian exports. The coal cargoes from Russia still pay a big premium, while Ukrainian grains struggle to find suitable tonnage due to the HRA involved. Trips to the Far East paying around USD 18,000 pd.

Following on from the UK holiday on Monday, the market saw an active week with the bullish sentiment returning in some parts. This change in fortunes perhaps could be afforded to a fervent FFA market, as sources spoke of a lack of a transatlantic market all in all, however solid demand ex EC South America continued to be a large component in the market as Gibraltar/western Mediterranean positions competed with EC South America ballaster tonnage on the front haul trips. Asia too returned a firmer with activity ex NoPac and Australia again the main drivers with better than last done levels being achieved on decent positioned tonnage.

Capesizes continue the positive trend from last week, on average up USD 4000 from last week. C5 is presently just excess USD 10 pmt and c3 is up from last week’s USD 22 to present upper USD 23s with Vale still present. Period tonnage is more in demand and levels are more interesting in order to accommodate more period fixtures.

Ships continue to disappear in the Atlantic basin with no details so we can construe that charterers are wary of making noise and are content with last done levels. With this in mind, we feel TD20 might creep up to WS 140's before the weekend. The US Gulf is gently ticking over with charterers being forced to reach on dates and fix ships not yet free of cargo, which will lead to inevitable mishaps with rates likely to uptick into mid/high WS 120's. For TD6, we are maintaining our numbers simply down to decent tonnage supply and present levels representing a fair deal for both sides of the phone: WS 180’s and USD 5.8-5.9 for CPC/S.Korea. In the East, firm numbers have been paid on a short run with Fateh/Mangalore on subjects at WS 165 which possibly prices a China run in the WS 140'S.

It is not often we report gains of WS 20 points within a week. However, in a similar pattern to last month the Atlantic set the wheels in motion and drove the market upwards, as increased activity and a limited number of ballasters saw rates for USG/Ningbo climb to the USD 9.6m level. East of Suez, a lack of MEG Chinese vessels meant Unipec required significant additional market tonnage and astutely covered requirements on multiple vessels with a minimal uptick in rates. Once the dust settled, other charterers looking at the 1-10 window faced a depleted list, coupled with ships delaying due to Eastern typhoons. At the time of writing, we are north of WS 100 for TD3C and for owners to build on these gains, the 10-20 MEG enquiry coupled with a reignition of what has been quiet Atlantic business will be key.

Nsea/Baltic market remained flat last week with charterers repeating last done levels without much hustle. Activity was moderate and some of the cargoes were covered on relets, preventing the rates from moving higher. Moving forward in October dates we expect market to improve on the back of healthier activity and tight position list. On the other side, despite activity ex CPC being very low, Med market jumped around 40p on the back of hefty cargo program, delays in strategic disports and vessels ballasting to the USG. Owners seem to have the momentum for now so market is expected to be steady in the short term as long as activity remains healthy.

text: AMERICAS The US showed another large build of 3.3 million barrels in the weekly propane inventories putting the total above 80 million barrels for the first time this year. The 81.1 million barrels now in inventories should end any concern of having enough product to cover the upcoming winter demand. Unfortunately for US exporters the big price drop went hand in hand with NWE and Asian prices,  keeping the export market pegged to the 4 cent per gallon level for October. Going forward the ever increasing freight market combined with the lack luster Chinese market is keeping a floor on terminaling fees. In South America, Gasmar covered their November CFR requirement from a Turkish Trader at what was labeled “A very competitive offer.”  NWE  The sentiment in the NWE large cargo market has tightened some in the last week and many traders anticipate more is to come - sighting petrochemical demand and colder weather.  The increased demand has allowed European arb economics to beat levels shown by far east participants- as Asian PDH margins continue to flounder. The Butane price in Northwest Europe still sits at 100 percent of Naphtha- but has softened some week on week as Mediterranean buyers ( present in the market last week) have gone away.  MED October interest in them med has picked up steam- at least directionally- as Europe's limited refinery supplies will likely not be enough to satisfy all around demand as winter looms. However, it's understood that if and when the region does tighten up- US origin VLGC's will quickly fill the void, limiting how tight the market can really get.

LNG prices remain elevated on the prompt but further down the curve, the contango rewards those with sufficient length (and appropriate tonnage) to float, whilst those without such length are left wondering how to obtain it! In the Atlantic, a couple of 2-strokes were hotly contested. Whatever transpires over the next week, it is clear that in the West, both size and boil off management capability really matters. In the Pacific, availability has taken a hit this week on the back of some frantic chartering activity. Most fixtures have been on 155,000m3 vessels and below, primarily because this is the only fit for purpose tonnage in the region (other than the occasional large vessel with truncated availability). Cold vessels remain scarce and vessels that were previously topping up the availability list are now propping up the availability list. As a consequence of all the activity, the number of uncovered cargos has reduced significantly, but with more cargoes anticipated over the next couple of weeks, there may be some very interesting fixtures just around the corner. Newbuilding activity remains muted, with the last announcement relating to Qatari business yet with so many new projects in the US anticipated, this segment remains healthy.

EAST The Indian majors have been at the center of activity so far this week, but we are now seeing several other players moving on freight for dates further into both mid and end October on the back of rising freight rates. With last non-Indian deal done at mid/high-70s RT/C we are at the time of writing approximately 15 spot fixtures concluded for October dates. We expect Eastern freight rates to remain strong.   WEST This week we have seen freight rates continue to push upwards with last done deal concluded at mid 120 H/C and high 60s H/F for early November dates. Although focus have shifted towards this period there are still a few vessels left open in October as we have seen close to 40 spot fixtures for that month.    Going forward, vessel supply looks very tight and with bad weather both sides of US, in addition to Panama congestions increasing, it will make scheduling more difficult.

text: MEG Despite the crude rise, Oct C3 CP slumped to $602 and C4 at $569 at the time of writing. Oct C3/C4 narrowed down from last week’s close to $40 to low $30s this week. However, evenly split cargo is still oversupplied, especially we’ve seen a handful of spot cargos available from middle east producers.   FAR EAST Cash premium for Oct delivered have continuously improved for propane parcels. Several cargos for 2h Oct delivery were changed hand, with full cargo lot of 46kt traded at Oct FEI minus mid-teens, or Oct FEI minus mid high single digit into Echina, and half cargo lot of 23kt at Oct FEI minus $8ish. Subsequently, 23kt propane for 2h Oct delivery was offered at FEI minus $4. Nevertheless, butane cargos are less favored. We’ve seen trader offering 23kt butane for 2h Oct at Oct FEI minus high 30s in the window, and several Oct delivered evenly split cargos are struggling to find home into EAST.   Off window still quite active with several tenders been awarded. Taiwan CPC was reported to buy the last decade Oct delivered 11/11 parcel from a Chinese Major at Oct CP plus low 40s via tender. And one Vietnam PDH user was said to procure an Oct delivered full propane cargo from another Chinese Major at CP plus 30s. One NChina importer didn’t award their buy tender for 46kt propane for 10-31st Oct delivery reportedly. One European trader just tendered to buy a evenly split cargo for 2h Oct delivery into India. And outside tender, we’ve hearing another EChina importer are inquired privately for a 23kt propane for 2h Oct delivery.

The dry market remains delicately poised as players align themselves with lowering asset values, despite a brief jolt in earnings. Capesize FRONTIER TRIUMPH 2012 Imabari is rumoured to have had over 10 suitors, showing that the appetite is very much present on the buying side despite variable market conditions. A notable sale this week is HANTON TRADER I (2014/Jiangsu/63k dwt) to Jinhui for USD 25.4m. The northern hemisphere summer may now be officially over: there’s a chill in the air, the rains falling and…LNGC spot rates are surging. There though, the similarity to previous cycles ends. Global gas and LNG markets are now front-page news on a weekly basis, yet despite the added scrutiny the various supply and demand levers are aligned in a completely novel way and are a direct challenge to those trying to predict what will happen next. What we can say with confidence is that gas storage levels in Europe are higher than anticipated, despite the low- and no-flow through Nord Stream 1, and forward curves look less intimidating for buyers. Much will now depend on the weather in the East and West as to how much demand there is for winter heating, but this is only one factor for the freight market. Perhaps of greater impact will be the behaviour of potential subletters in control of marginal shipping: the risks of missing a scheduled loading set against the returns of a neat sublet are skewed heavily against the latter. Without a seismic change in the LNG market, we may expect to see far fewer fixtures but record-breaking levels. text: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane market levels began September at nearly $1.09/gal but have softened to current levels at around $1.03/gal.  Typically, this is the time of year when winter demand begins to reveal itself and prices historically have begun to rise. However, end August propane stocks concluded at 72.2mmbbls only to rise to current levels of 77.9mmbbls, or 5.7mmbbls, in the space of two weeks when the 5-year average build for 1H Sep is 1.42mmbbls per week.  2H Sep build rate averages are roughly half that at 707,000bbls per week, which from a starting point of 77.9mmbbls – and with three weeks remaining – should allow stock levels to easily eclipse the 80mmbbl mark.  Just a month ago this was not being widely forecast, and as such the propane inventory gains explain the weakness in the domestic pricing structure.  US propane stock levels are presently 10% higher than last year, and 77% of two years ago. Meanwhile, with big ship freight rates continuing to march upwards, terminal fees have correspondingly been undermined with buy-side interest limited and well below 4cpg.  Sell-side interest is presently at/above 4cpg depending on timing/location/grade, etc, and the number of cargoes being offered continues to rise. LatAm demand was punctuated this week with a CFR supply tender issued by a Chilean importer, while Mexican demand is anticipated to increase as Q4 nears, temperatures decline, and demand begins to improve.  NWE The anticipation of increased demand is starting to be seen as traders start to bid in the window. This has pushed the physical window to a +$3pmt premium to October CIF ARA. The transatlantic flow of VLGCs has been restricted to term commitments during the summer. Spot interest into the region is picking up since US inventories look set to be able to sustain exports this winter. CIF ARA propane has returned to a discount to naphtha which has been welcomed by pethcems, but at -$9pmt we are not about to see run-rates increase from the 70% capacity they were reduced to. The two factors keeping the run rates low are low demand for finished products and high energy costs to produce them, an unwelcome double whammy. As the weather cools and inland demand picks up, European traders are cautiously making plans to import more cargoes. Butane has remained firm at 95% September Naphtha, though no public trades have been seen recently.    MED Butane in the region is a buyers’ market, with both regional producers and US exporters looking to find a home for C4 in the region. Propane demand has increased as traders look to fill storages before winter. Not due to forecasts of cold weather, more due to supply uncertainties which could cause price spikes.

text: AMERICAS Poor economics continue to plague the US export market amid unattractive arbs.  As such, and alongside swelling freight rates, terminal fees remain depressed with buy-side interest in the 3cpg range and sellers offering at around 4cpg; hovering just at/above cancellation economics.  At least four cargoes are believed cancelled for Sep, with potentially more on the horizon due to persistently limited demand – particularly in Asia and Europe. There is, however, potential demand from LatAm as winter nears end and consumption increases. The EIA today released its findings for the week ending 02 Sep 2022 amid a wide range of expectations which spanned from 1mmbbls to as much as 3mmbbls, effectively revealing the uncertainty in the market.  The data showed a 1.9mmbbl build for an overall total of 74.1mmbbls, or 106% of the same time last year but just 74% of two years ago.  This effectively propels expectations for end-Sep stocks to exceed earlier expectations and broach the 80mmbbl mark.  NWE A drop in Brent Crude pulled European Naphtha values down with it. This has pushed the September Propane / Naphtha spread in the region to +$27pmt, which is likely to further reduce petchem run rates in the region. Margins for Spot ethylene is now as low as a  25% discount to the monthly term price in August and spot propylene reached a discount of 30% to the monthly term price, Imports have slowed to the region, though planned maintenance at Karsto and Kollsnes could push up the need for imports as LPG production decreases by about a third during this time. To meet the expected maintenence demand, the number of US Origin propane cargos has continued to climb from already record levels. In Poland, an interesting supply demand dynamic is playing out as LPG demand for autogas has surged, against the restriction in accepting russian Product. Poland has sourced 50 percent less LPG from Russia and has looked to Norway and Sweden along with other sources to fill the requirment. Butane remains at 94% September Naphtha, though the C4 market has not seen activity in some time.   MED Vitol returned to the window to bid for 6KT butane FOB Lavera, September 14-16, which went unmet at a final bid of $605pmt. A butane heavy VLGC cargo loading STS off Estonia is expected to be discharged in Morocco in September.

text: MEG KPC sold a 1-8th Oct lifting evenly split cargo at CP minus mid high teens reportedly. There are other buyers exploring similar cargo but targeted at close to $20 discount to CP. Off window some 46kt propane for 1h Oct delivery was changed hand at FEI minus high teens. Product tanker values are continuing their gradual climb with each reported sale exceeding their relative last done. Celsius Shipping has disposed of its older BWTS fitted LR2 tankers -  “CELSIUS ESBERG” & “CELSIUS EVERETT”  built 2009 and 2008 at New Times – respectively achieving Usd 33m and Usd 31m. The sale is marking yet another substantial jump considering that the last comparable sale of a Chinese built unit was that of the 2006 Dalian built “JAG LYALL” which was sold at Usd 26.2m end of July this year. This momentum is partly shared by crude segments, where the overall trend in values remains positive with DHT Tankers selling their 2008 built VLCC “DHT EDELWEISS” at Usd 37m, despite some fragility seen in earnings. The vessel was sold basis survey due with BWTS to be fitted at next docking. Despite having no sales to report on the MR front this week, activity remains high with signs of a number of negotiations suggesting further sales in the near future.   Following a relative show of resistance from Dry cargo sellers we are definitely witnessing a number of owners caving to the ever lower bids shown by buyers who are looking to capitalise on the most recent correction. With every new deal reaffirming this downward trend, we expect an increased amount of sellers opting to pull the trigger sooner rather than later in hope to achieve what is still broadly considered as a high price point on the curve. A sentiment well illustrated by the sale of the 2010 Hyundai Vinashin built “CLARKE QUAY” which achieved Usd 17m.

text: AMERICAS The domestic U.S. propane market was described as dangerously directionless which has given cause for many to retreat for the sidelines; the winning strategy being to do nothing, avoid any pitfalls and reduce the chances of making mistakes. Stock levels of propane in the U.S. rose by 4.2mmbbls to 72.20mmbbls, per the EIA report for the week ending 26 Aug.  It is widely believed that over the course of September there should be very little problem in reaching sufficient pre-winter inventory levels and will likely end the month at 76-78mmbbls. Terminal fee levels have softened and the limited buy-side interest that does exist now starts in the 3cpg range.  Sellers ideas, while earlier commencing with a 5-handle, are now encroaching upon cancellation economics. The U.S. Labor Day holiday will be observed on this next Monday, and as a result very little is expected to occur in the coming days.  NWE The September Propane / Naphtha spread has flipped into positive territory, now at +$10pmt. So far there has not been any talk by petchems of switching feedstocks. Rather reducing run rates, with most European petchems having already reduced propylene output to 70% of capacity or less. So far now petchem traders have resold any volume in the window. There is disruption in North Sea supply and this could lead to higher import demand. It may have been a summer of discontent for most other things, but not for tankers. There is currently a bit of a downward pressure in the VLCC market, and a couple of points were chopped off from last done yesterday, but if anyone had predicted that MEG/East would be trading in the mid-high WS 70's only a few months ago few would have believed it - May closed out with rates trading in the very low WS 40's. We could probably still see a point or two off still, as things become more of a date- than a rate game, but we do not believe that the bottom will fall out, by any means - sentiment is just too strong.

WEST A bank holiday in London on Monday did not stop players from making a move in the Western market with three fixtures concluded in the USG - two of which from a big shipowner. The same tempo has continued further into the week, and we have seen a handful of fixtures so far with last done at around USD mid/high 100s H/C and high 50s H/F. Focus has now completely shifted towards early October dates and fixing is already well underway as charterers seem keen to secure a ship before it gets tighter.

Spot and multi year charter rates continue to move upwards this week in line with a further tightening shipping market. Further to last week, spot requirements remain plentiful in both basins however, the east maintains a majority of those, along with considerable vessel availability keeping the discount to the west intact. On term, modern tonnage is becoming increasingly scarce as market participants hold on to the highly sought-after low BOG vessels that they have managed to secure over winter and beyond. The current market environment indicates that it is only matter of time before Charterers will look to older and smaller ships to accommodate their impending requirements, although at a costly expense given the relative boil off capabilities of such vessels and the high price of LNG. No orders have been reported in the market this week, however, newbuilding prices continue to firm as demand shows no signs of slowing. For those of you who will be attending Gastech next week, we look forward to seeing you in Milan.

Performance Shipping has confirmed its purchase of the “ALPINE AMALIA” (Abt 105k dwt built 2010 HHI). Notable transaction this week being the sale of the sisterships “ALAKIOS” & “ARCHON” (Abt 50k dwt built 2016 Sasmung Ningbo). They achieved a price of Usd 36.5m each reinforcing the positive trend witnessed in the segment. A trend that becomes particularly apparent when compared to the sale of 2016 SPP built LARGO SUN which only last month was sold at Usd 35m. As we’ve watched LNG prices rise to previously unimaginable levels this week, someone reminded us that in April 2020, JKM was trading at US$1.83. Watching JKM breach the $55 mark this week serves as an expensive reminder of how much has changed in this period, but it’s worth noting that not everything is more expensive. In fact, shipping is relatively inexpensive at present. In April 2020, a spot cargo from Australia to JKTC would have cost about 25 cents in shipping which equated to approximately 13.5% of the total cargo cost. At present, and basis our rates this week, the Unit Freight Cost is $1.50 which means that shipping accounts for less than 3% of the total cargo price; a 500% decrease since April 2020 if you will. The purpose here isn’t to agitate for a rise in rates of course, rather it’s to point out the dilemma that the market faces in that almost all tonnage is controlled by Charterers yet their risk vs reward ratio for chartering out has never been less attractive. Freeport LNG’s announcement of a small delay to their restart should free up some October intra-basin tonnage, but with big ships proving harder to secure than a cargo slot into Europe, the question now is, how long until the bidding wars for the ST ships begin? No new orders again this week but then perhaps we will see a Gastech inspired flurry in a few weeks’ time.

text: AMERICAS Per the latest EIA report, the U.S. propane stocks saw no changes, which remain at 68.00mmbbls.  This equates to 99% of last year and 75% of two years ago.  Robust export volumes over the previous week are the primary cause.  The market had been anticipating something on the order of a 1.6-1.7mmbbl build.  Still more surprising - is the fact that after the stock levels were revealed Mont Belvieu propane values saw a modest decline over the course of the day.  Current prices are just below 50% of crude at ~$1.1225/gal. Terminal fees remain subdued, with bids in the 4cpg range and offers in the upper 4cpg level.  As yet there are not known to have been any ‘buybacks’, and for September the number of cancellations is thought to be only a couple so far. It is anticipated that LatAm demand – specifically in Mexico - should begin to improve as Q4 nears and winter-related demand begins to appear.  NWE The region looks balanced to short, and CIF ARA has been strengthening this week, kept strong by the dual push of firming crude and disappointing unchanged US inventories. There is interest from Eastern traders to place cargoes in Europe, at this time European traders are managing term deliveries, and feel one extra VLGC heading into the region could tip the market to long. Petchem margins in the region are not looking good, but we are yet to see a serious reduction in demand. September Propane / Naphtha spread at a measly minus $4pmt, with October and November at minus $1pmt. Butane has been firm in anticipation on blending season, and is 92.5% August Naphtha, although open buying interest for October arrival is yet to be seen. The Rhine water levels have risen to 120cm at Kaub allowing some normality to barge market and propane to reach upstream demand.   MED Petroineos sold a 4KT C4 lot to Trafigura on Monday ex-Lavera, since then the market has been quiet. The expectation that Turkey would continue to import cargoes loaded in Ust-Luga was incorrect. We continue to see those handy vessels STS-ing into VLGCs and going East, with 2 VLGCs completing this operation in August.

Tankers in all asset classes remain in hot pursuit and sellers are clearly gaining the upper hand. SFL Corp swooped for four modern Suezmax tankers from Ciner. The vessels were on TC to Kock with one year left which have been cancelled in exchange for new 6 years TC contracts to Koch, adding approximately Usd 250 million to SFL’s fixed-rate backlog. The 2019 DSME built VLCC “C.GUARDIAN” invited offers this week with 7 buyers understood to having shown their cards and the vessel is now reported sold for Usd 98 mill. Last comparable sale was Hunter’s 2020 DSME built VLCC’s at Usd 96 mill. This week’s sale represents as such about 6% increase and the implied value for resale/2022 VLCC is now Usd 110 mill. Aframax/LR2 built 2009-2011 is a sweet-spot for many buyers with several deals expected to materialize soon. The same goes for MR where UOG this week added another two 2011 built units to its fleet. Suezmax tankers with ice class 1A are few and far between which, together with the vessels having open loop scrubbers, goes a long way in explaining the firm price Ridgebury achieved for its 2006 and 2007 built vessels.  Dry asset values are under pressure. SNP volumes are low with buyers increasingly applying a wait-and-see attitude. Sellers will have to readjust price expectations or take cover for a while. Latter being the case for two 2015 JMU built Kamsarmaxes which have been withdrawn from the market as best on offer was region Usd 31.5 mill. In May, two 2015 sister vessels were sold for Usd 35.5 mill.

All eyes on VLCCs in the East which are nearing crossover levels with Suezmax. MEG/East has been a desert for Suezmaxes during the last six months, but potential splits could impact markets not only in the East, but also the Atlantic. The new Atlantic market has grown used to an abundance of ships coming round the corner from the East, but Td3c splits could drastically reduce availability and increase the likelihood of further volatility in all regions. MEG/China on modern today will trade min WS 130's whilst Td23 will likely firm up again into the high WS 70's. Owners in the Atlantic will be keeping a keen eye on the East which will ensure a firm outlook to proceedings. It's not going down and it could quite easily take another jump north.

A week of red has passed and with the exception of Indo coal there is no immediate sign of a floor being found. In The Atlantic, the tonnage list is not overwhelming, but a general lack of cargoes sends for most trades keeps the market falling.   In the Pacific, the Indonesian coal market is active with rates slightly up the last few days, however for Nopac and Aussie the levels are still under pressure. A limited supply of EC South America cargoes is also a negative factor. A few period fixtures have been reported but it seems most owners holding back from period fixing at the moment.

text: AMERICAS LPG market activity levels in the U.S. ground practically to a halt early this week with very little accomplished by a largely complacent and mostly disinterested trading community. The EIA data release on Wednesday appears to have spurred interest as a larger-than-expected build of 2.3mmbbls was reported and brought overall stocks to nearly 102% of last year at an overall total of 68 mmbbls.  Unless the newly released forecasts for a cold winter turn out to be incorrect, this should effectively set aside concerns that stocks might be insufficient as crop drying is likely going to be limited.  That, in turn, is due to poor crop yield and oppressively hot and dry growing conditions over the summer. Meanwhile, poor arb conditions, softening freight rates and limited end-user demand have kept pressure on terminal fees, which were this week quoted for 1H Sep at between 4cpg and  NWE The market continues to be well supplied with record US arrivals continuing and covering all demand. However, the market has begun to show signs of demand recovery with petchems and end users beginning to review their 4th quarter demand. Recent rains in Germany and Switzerland have given hope that Rhine levels will start to recover.   MED Lackluster market continues.  Algerian exports continuing to look East,  to take the place of Med demand,  until the market recovers.

EAST Shipping ex Middle East was moving slow until the release of Aramco acceptances on Tuesday. Several fixtures are on subs or concluded for end August and beginning September laycans at freight rates hovering around USD mid 50s RT/C per ton, and there are reports of more still uncovered in and around the first half of September. Looking ahead it should not be surprising that some owners already aim higher than last done numbers and that we'll see the market coming up slowly but surely.  WEST This week we have seen approximately five deals done in the Western market, both for August and September dates at levels around low 90s H/C and 50 H/F. We saw the first August fixture over 50 days ago and with just a notch above 20 spot fixtures for the month August fixing finally looks to have come to an end as the last remaining ships have been absorbed. Moving into September we expect an uptick in both exports and spot activity as July and August have not been the strongest.

As we slowly make our way towards the end of the summer season, the market continues to apprehensively bubble and churn out a slew of spot and multi-month requirements, predominantly from the East, ahead of everyone’s return to desk. In tandem, this week a small but consistent arbitrage window has opened up off the back of a strengthening JKM (at mid-high $50’s) while a steepening discount to TTF (at high $60’s) prevails, further hinting at an anticipated pickup in activity in the coming weeks. With cool down slots still hard to come by and Charterers holding firm in their demands for cold ships, with the number of them relatively few and far between, we’ve come to a stand-off of sorts between Owners and Charterers. However, as LNG prices mount ever-higher, availability of cold vessels begin to deplete and perhaps even the prospect of a wider arb looms, the creeping pressure to fix might just have Charterers give way and take the best of what they can get while the gettings good. Otherwise, no newbuilding orders reported this week.

It has been a quiet week on the surface for Aframax owners trading in the Nsea. text: AMERICAS The domestic U.S. market has gone very quiet with activity levels almost nil. NWE                                                 A window bid pushed the large cargo market into a premium to spot  CIF ARA price  (+$2.5/t) for the first time since July. The downward pressure in the recent weeks was a result of a handful of factors- notably, record imports from the US, compounded by very low water levels in the Rhine, not allowing for inland distribution and thus leaving the ARA hub considerably long. Macro discussions around the region have been centered around how LPG's will be utilize this winter amid the ongoing Russia/ Ukranian conflict. Some participants believe the gas shortage will induce a migration over to LPG, bolstering demand and subsequently bulling up price, while others remain convinced that the infrastructure to move from gas to LPG's in a meaningful way is not in place, and would take time and considerable investment. This is not to suggest European prices will not rise this winter,  but that they'd do so  inline with typical, seasonal-related patterns as opposed to the Russian gas supply shock. text: AMERICAS Arbs have suffered in recent weeks, primarily due to the influence on the LPG pricing structure by the declining crude market, and where at the start of July WTI was over $108/bbl it is now below $90/bbl and still volatile.  Propane values, meanwhile, have fallen from $1.21/gal to $1.09/gal over the same period. Relatively strong inventory gains have also been a factor in that propane stocks have risen to 63.6mmbbls as of end July, or 96% of last year’s level.  However, current stocks are notably just 71% of the 86.7mmbbl inventory level achieved two years ago.  Given the heat and dry climate across North America, crop drying should not be much of a factor which should then, in turn, allow stock levels to gain a bit more traction. With the inventory goal being somewhere near the 80mmbbl range, there is a 16.4mmbbl deficit at present, and to reach that target level a weekly build of 1.82mmbbls over the next 9 weeks will be required.  If the timeline is shifted to mid-Oct, then a 1.49mmbbl weekly build would suffice, and for an end-Oct deadline a 1.26mmbbl weekly increase would be needed. The August lifting roster is nearly complete with only a small number of potential cargo slots remaining.  Sep, however, is beginning to emerge and where the Aug terminal fee values are placed at/below 5cpg, Sep is perhaps at/above 5cts, at least for the first half of the month.  2H Sep is pegged in the mid 5s at present.  Q4 strips were talked in the 6cpg range. A full propane VL tender was issued last week for 2H Sep CFR Chile and was awarded at a price deemed to be ‘well below’ last year’s level.  NWE The TOT window in Europe has been quiet recently, without any bids or offers. August import volume is increasing, with term volumes starting to trickle in from the US. Netback values from the US for August are still in cancellation territory, and well below value to Asia. This is keeping August imports quiet in this period of low demand. Additionally export has resumed out of Mongstad and were around 70 KT in July, adding local supply. Baltic production exported from Ust-Luga continues to be STS-ed onto VLGC in the ARA region and head East. Until clear demand signs are seen traders in the region are happy to work on a more prompt basis, waiting for offers to be shown to them rather than going out searching for cargoes, in this well supplied low demand environment. Butane has continuously firmed up and is now 86% August Naphtha.   MED The summer market in the West of the region has ample supply from term contracts. The East Med is well offered, as traders with split ratio  US cargoes look for a home for their tons.

With TTF sitting comfortably above $60/MMBtu, it’s not surprising to see Charterers paying up for 2-Strokes. But with spot loadings fixing at a fraction of the Term rates, there’s a big spread to be bridged between now and Winter. Of course, geopolitical uncertainty is high and given the dollars at stake with every cargo, it’s arguably sound risk management to go into Q4 comfortably long. For those Owners who can monetise their length, however, recent reports of $200k pdpr deals in the 2-Stroke segment should provide the necessary incentive to optimise. Speaking of which, optimisation on the prompt is alive and well with an interesting development this past week being the emergence of very prompt cargoes in both basins. This has provided some excellent “keep cool” voyages for owners but also suggests that: i. projects are trying to squeeze out additional cargoes, and ii. portfolio players see real value in fine-tuning their schedules. If we see enough of these cargoes emerge, spot rates will firm again but for now, the only guaranteed strengthening comes from the yards, with Newbuild prices up again this week.

With the summer holiday period in full flow across most of Europe, spot shipping activity has remained light with a focus still towards multi-month business, as indicated by a growth of requirements from off takers seeking coverage across the upcoming winter period and the front months of 2023. Consequently, spot rates continue to stagnate and there has not been a material shift in the number of available vessels in either basin as various subletters seek employment in the near term. With the divergence between spot and multi-month interest, there continues to be a disconnect between spot and terms rates, as has been the theme for much of this year. It was announced this week that two 174,000 m3 were ordered at DSME shipyard, as newbuild prices continue to firm up.

Clear evidence over the past few days that around WS 60 MEG/East seems to be the level at which owners (scrubbers attached of course) are willing to profit take and fix away. Certainly, led by the relets, the MEG market has wobbled over the last few days, down to WS 57.5 MEG/Korea, despite continued enquiry and no real change in the fundamentals (apart from some cheaper bunkers). At the time of writing, there are a couple of cargoes working MEG/East, and we still have seen only 10 or so cargoes done in the 10-20 window. Owners should not panic.  The US Gulf has seen successive deals higher than last done, up to USD 7.5m to Ningbo. However, West Africa has remained light on volume and Smaxes are also running out of steam. Without late August Wafr enquiry, or fresh September USG stems, owners will have to fight to hold recent gains.

text: AMERICAS As of the middle part of this week, few deals have been done in the US Gulf FOB market attributed to unpredictable, sharp crude swings along with a general summer holiday market. Numbers in line with netback levels to the East, but failing to account for costs canal delays etc. The stagnant resale market has left freight feeling long, and predictably lead to notable drops (close to 5 bucks in past couple days)  in freight rates on a Houston/Chiba basis. As of today, the Baltic assessed Houston/Chiba freight at $92 pmt. On Wednesday, the EIA showed a larger than anticipated build of 2.4 million barrels for the week ending 22nd of July. As it stands total stocks now sit at 62 million barrels, (4 percent lower than the same period last year) Though propane exports increased week on week, so has propane production- which now sits at roughly 2.37 million barrels per day.  NWE  Propane market feels particularly week at the moment, following a record month of US origin cargos arriving in the region. The total imported volume exceeded storage capabilities alluding to the high run rates at flexible steam crackers both in and out of the ARA.  In eastern Europe, the ban on Russian origin LPG cargos has been lifted into Poland, however, there have yet to be deals done as supply current supply seems adequate to meet summer demand.   MED In the med, the spot market has continued to sit idle as demand has been more than adequately fulfilled by term contracts. Very dead summer market.

The Supra and Ultra Atlantic market remain pretty much unchanged from previous July weeks. Though we can notice ECSA market was a bit more active compared to previous week, though levels remained unchanged. Supra 56,000 dwt was fixed at USD 30,000 pd delivery N Brazil to Atlantic Colombia. text: MEG Aug C3 CP was traded at $690 and C4 at $678, up by $20 from last week as crude rebounded. Aug/Sep C3 CP was traded at flattish or slight backwardation as front CP surged up. 1st round CP idea ranged from $670-685 for C3 and $660-670 for C4. However, 2nd round recommendation is expected to be refreshed higher as oil extended gains.  KPC issued tender to sell a 2-3 Sep lifting evenly split cargo.   FAR EAST Window activities are muted, only earlier this week one 23kt propane parcel for 2h Aug delivery sold at Aug FEI minus $3.5. Off window several similar parcels were traded at Aug FEI minus $3-4. Meanwhile, a couple of full propane cargos for 1h Sep delivery were changed hand at equivalence to Sep FEI minus high single to low teens.  Due to squeezed margin in, several PDHs in East and North China are having turnrounds or cutting down rates, refraining from spot purchase.  Indian IOC issued term tender to secure one evenly split cargo monthly in Q1 2023 and believe the remaining demand for Q2-Q4 will come out consecutively. Earlier BPCL also tendered to procure in total 1.7 mmt LPG for 2023 delivery, which is still in validity but offers with good discount to CP heard. Indonesia PERTAMINA also issued spot tender to buy one evenly split cargo for late Aug lifting ex AG or mid Sep delivery.

North Sea/Baltic took a step back this week on the back of weak cargo activity in the area. A few vessels ballasted out of the area to seek better alternatives but still this didn’t help the rates to improve. We expect rates to move sideways in the short term before we see some improvement later in August. Med/Bsea rates kept climbing for another week as Libya is back fully operational with a lot of prompt requirements. Supply of vessels in the area is still tight for cross-Mediterranean runs but also for CPC-approved vessels which helps owners to earn. Sentiment in the area is strong and we expect rates to remain steady for the week to come.

East and West Suezmax markets have seen rates stall over the last week as open market enquiry levels fizzled out. Off market enquiries have evidently been able to fix at last done levels without being smoked into the open market and as a result there's a softer feel to proceedings today. With Vlcc's feeling capped there is no upside for Suezmax's in the East where MEG/East probably trades maximum 130kt x WS127.5-130 whilst TD23 will do well to stay out of WS70's territory. In the West there's a little more optimism with firm Med' Aframax's well into crossover levels and as such this will hold a number of Suezmax's in that region and away from wafr. Notionally, TD20 has a notional floor and trades mid W130's with further enquiry needed to maintain these levels. Td6 is following Afra's at about WS110

After the Panamax market levelled out and turned positive last week, this week has been more mixed. The FFA drop on Monday caused a pull back from the charterers to re-evaluate levels and market direction. In the Pacific, market felt under pressure with low volume of cargo and increased tonnage counts so rates dropped below last done. In the Atlantic, despite of low activities, the cargo volume and tonnage list are more or less balanced, and levels concluded at last done.  The tonnage count in Atlantic is reduced and low for next two weeks, therefore we reckon Atlantic market may be stable this week. ECSA is flat and tick below last done, therefore we need a clearing out current vessels before seeing any improvement. There is still very limited period business being reported.

As opposed to July last year, the market is slow and lacking requirements. Rates are consequently coming off and c5 is presently in the very low 10s, compared to upper 10s same time last week. A bigger drop on the c3 route, presently marked at USD low 28s compared to mid 31 last week. And even a bigger drop seen on the c17 route, marked at USD 22 last week and presently real value sub USD 19.

Clear evidence over the past few days that around WS 60 MEG/East seems to be the level at which owners (scrubbers attached of course) are willing to profit take and fix away. Certainly, led by the relets, the MEG market has wobbled over the last few days, down to WS 57.5 MEG/Korea, despite continued enquiry and no real change in the fundamentals (apart from some cheaper bunkers). At the time of writing, there are a couple of cargoes working MEG/East, and we still have seen only 10 or so cargoes done in the 10-20 window. Owners should not panic.  The US Gulf has seen successive deals higher than last done, up to USD 7.5m to Ningbo. However, West Africa has remained light on volume and Smaxes are also running out of steam. Without late August Wafr enquiry, or fresh September USG stems, owners will have to fight to hold recent gains.

EAST The fixing window has shifted to mid-2H August in the MEG. After seeing several deals concluded last week the market has calmed down, and there has not been too much to report thus far. A couple of Indian Majors have tested the market, but as the lineup of ships looks well supplied we don’t expect charterers to rush in for uncovered cargos. East freight is still trading at a premium to West, but we expect this gap to be further narrowed in the days to come.  WEST This week we have seen deals done both in the USG and West Africa, but fixing activity still remains slow in the West. Last done deal is now concluded at USD mid/low 90s Houston/Chiba range, but it is likely freight has to drop even more before we see an uptick in activity unless the arb soon gives some support. If neither of this happens it is a possibility we soon will see prompt open ships in the USG as the month of August are just a few days away.

All eyes on a tanker market that seems to be going from strength to strength as demonstrated by this week’s reported transactions. The product markets as expected have drawn most of the interest, leading to substantial drive in values with new benchmarks being set across several vintages. The Japanese controlled “CHALLENGE PHOENIX” invited offers on Tuesday after having up to a dozen buyers registering interest; the vessel is now sold at a price in the region of USD 18m to Greek buyers. A jump in pricing which becomes particularly apparent when compared to last months sale of the “ENERGY PANTHER” (47k dwt 2008 Sungdong) which achieved Usd 16.1m.  Similar dynamics on the more modern front with JP Morgan achieving Usd 35m for their 2016 SPP built unit “LARGO SUN”.  A comparatively subdued Dry SnP market with the most recent market slow down gradually taking hold on the SnP front. We are indeed witnessing a weakening bid with buyers now looking to secure tonnage at levels below last done. We therefore expect a relative correction in values despite the resilience shown by potential sellers who would rather wait over these summer months rather than pulling the trigger at these lower levels.

The BSI-58 10 T/C route kept southbound direction for some time and seems still not much ground to turn that direction. Due to the holiday seasons in Europe, we see very limited activity across all markets. The average index trading in very low USD 20,000 pd.  Atlantic is being under pressure; while Pacific market is more stable with rates maintaining at very low to mid USD 20,000 pd, transatlantic round voyages paying just a bit more than USD 15,000 pd. USG numbers seems to be under pressure and ECSA describes as lacking fresh enquiries.   Ultramax asking USD 20,000 pd del West Africa via ECSA for TCT to Singapore-Japan.   Fronthaul from Continent and Mediterranean pays around USD 20,000 pd. Similar level fixing for trip from West Africa to China.  Far East market is more active and keeps balanced out. Supra open Gresik end July was fixed for a trip from Indonesia to China at USD 23,000. The Ultramax mv Pacific Activity, 63,000 dwt, fixed for trip with coal delivery Samarinda to China at USD 29,000. Backhaul trips also lost value from previous month. Supra 56,000 dwt open CJK was fixed for a trip to EC South America at USD 26,000. We expect market remains flat and quiet for upcoming week.

Rates appear to be capped in the East, at least for today, as owners start cashing in at current levels. Looking at where the VLCCs are and comparing against general sentiment, we will probably see MEG/East trade about 130KT X WS 130. TD23 remains active with the general consensus suggesting WS 85 is repeatable. The Atlantic is more volatile, driven in part by a very firm Med' Aframax/Suezmax crossover-market. West Med'/UKC Suezmax positions should be running and comparing their td20 numbers against Crbs/TA which suggests there is some more upside in the region. For now, we are pricing td20 at about WS 140-142.5 whilst td6 should trade WS 190’s (natural)-WS 200/210 (prompt) subject to dates.

The Nsea/Baltic Aframax market started on a quiet note this week with very few fixtures reported. However, surrounding markets are looking very firm providing owners with an alternative. Going forward we expect rates to stay around current levels till activity in this area increases again.    Med/Bsea market saw a significant improvement last week on the back of prompt requirements ex Libya and tight supply of CPC-approved vessels. Owners’ sentiment is building up as overall supply of vessels in the West is tight and activity is expected to remain healthy. We expect rates to remain healthy and volatile at the same time.

Moderately up for the big ships as Atlantic showing more promise - average daily earnings improving some 15 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 22,500. European coal demand set to increase significantly for geopolitical reasons, outlook positive for fronthaul trades of different nature, and major Brazilian miner's production guidance meeting expectations of only a modest reduction. Mediocre interpacific volumes, combined with owners anticipating better times, further widen value spread between the 35-day China-Australia-China round (paying USD 12,500/day) and the 100-day China-Brazil-China round (USD 19k/day) for non-scrubbers. Forward values again not supporting significant period activity, thus recent conclusions limited to tonnage providers obtaining no more than USD 20,500/day for 177,000 dwt, built 2007, basis only 8-10 months.

Better rates across the board allowing owners TCE’s continue further into the positive, even for those burning the low sulphur fuel. Rates have moved up through the high WS 50’s and Tuesday saw the WS 60 glass ceiling broken. However, given the activity, charterers have played it well. We've had consecutive months of 150+ deals out of the MEG, and despite the resulting dwindling position list, charterers have worked off market, picking targets quietly which has prevented the market running away in owner's favour.   In the West, strong returns continue on the smaller sizes and this reflecting on the VL’s. WS 62 on subs for Wafr/China and continued activity today should encourage rates further upward. USG/China now USD 7.25m and the USG/UKC trade shows no signs of slowing, with more ships rptd on subs this morning.

The Panamax market finally found a floor and turned positive yesterday after a long and continues drop. The drop has been USD 8000 loss on average since June 21st, 2022. This has been biggest drop since beginning of the year. In the Pacific, a healthy cargo inquiry via Indonesia and Australia to different destinations, particularly India and Continent, has given the much-needed support with rates increasing to over USD 16,000 at the time of this report. The Nopac stays on the sideline with minimal cargo volume being reported.  In the Atlantic, rates have also slightly turned up with reports that TA is close to 17,000 and fronthaul at USD 26,000 daily on back of mineral inquiries and reduced tonnage count on the Continent. The market remains supported for both basins, but it is missing expected spark to guide rates to next level, therefore we need to see a continued flow of cargo moving forward. ECSA rather quieter for end July and/or mid-August loaders, with tonnage counts still high as weeks of low Pacific market forced the owners to ballast south towards Singapore, therefore rates remain at best flat hovering around USD 18,000 daily.

As the UK and Europe battle all that these current record temperatures are bringing, there’s no need to remind our Northern Hemisphere readers that we’re in the midst of Summer. Liquidity has dried up and the holiday season continues unabated. Nonetheless, there is definitely an undercurrent of repressed uncertainty about what might be in store when everyone gets back to their desk. NS1’s impending restart marks the first time many of us have read about the travel plans of a broken Turbine in the trade press but come tomorrow, all eyes will certainly be on East to West gas flows. Given that European volumes used for winter are currently being drawn down in some countries, the race to refill before the heating is turned on just got a little more intense. The Atlantic shipping market is displaying similar behaviours as protagonists weigh the weakness on the prompt with the need to ensure security of supply (i.e., tonnage) over winter. To this end, we see a massive disconnect between spot and term rates which makes life tricky for both Owners and Charterers at this exact time. In the East, we’ve seen a few requirements emerge this week which, as part of the usual churn of activity, sees the Pacific market retain its premium to the West. No Newbuildings to report this week (which is itself newsworthy) but as prices continue their ascent, there’s no sign of demand easing up in this segment yet.

text: MEG A week of volatile swap market as Crude fell drastically. Aug C3 CP was traded at $672 and C4 was at $9 less. Aug/Sep was traded at small contango of $2 and likewise in forward months. Saudi released their Aug acceptance with some advancement reported and was reckoned to have spot avails for sale.  FAR EAST After last week’s hectic movement with handfuls of tenders, this week trading interests appear thin comparatively. Cash premium for 2h Aug propane parcels softened as more hidden sellers emerged. Earlier this week one 23kt propane parcel for 2h Aug delivery was traded at Aug FEI minus $1. And similar cargo was bid at minus $2 while offer at plus $1 to FEI on Thursday window. Spot discussions into China quieted down. One trader was also reported to cover a half or full propane parcel for 2h Aug delivery into Tianjin. However, several PDHs and crackers are reported to lower down rates or to shut down for unscheduled maintenance due to squeezed margins and high inventory on products.

EAST It’s been a busier week in the East with several cargos quoted for 1H August load in the Middle East. Last done deal was concluded in the low-mid $70s Baltic (compared to mid-high $60s from the week before), and we have certainly reached a turning point in freight ideas. Time of writing we have seen about 11 deals done in August, but there are still other cargos in play within 1H August. We expect freight ideas to remain firm in the coming weeks as the fixing window gradually shifts towards 2H August.  WEST Last week we only saw two fixtures concluded in the Western market. The same tempo has continued into this week and we have only seen a couple deals done at freight levels around USD low 100s Houston/Chiba and low 60s H/F. The position list continues to grow and the front of August looks long. At the time of writing there is still one ship left in July and we are soon entering the last week of the month. It will not come as a big surprise if the next fixture gets done below the 100 dollar mark.

text: AMERICAS Volatility in the crude arena has allowed WTI prices over the past week to range from $96.30/bbl to $104.22/bbl, only to trade presently at $95.87/bbl as of this writing.  That has translated to volatility in the domestic U.S. propane market where prices have ranged from over $1.14/gal down to just over $1.10/gal and now to current values just over $1.12/gal.  The less-than-robust EIA report this week has allowed propane to retain some of its value as the stock data this week revealed a build of just 1.4mmbbls where the market was anticipating something above 2.25mmbbls.  Current inventory levels are 94% of the same time last year, but just 70% of those recorded two years ago.  Sentiment is that inventories are veering towards being insufficient for the winter. Terminal fees have shown modest buoyancy and asking prices for Aug are in the upper 4s, perhaps 5cpg.  Buy-side interest, though, remains subdued.  2H 2022 is being talked in the 6cpg range. LatAm demand remains generally flat, though it is anticipated that modest volumes of spot demand may emerge for Sep.  NWE The run of record LPG import months look like they will come to an end in August. The region is well supplied and demand remains low as expected in summer. The buyers with large storages could be incentivised to buy if they have the capacity take more product, to take advantage of the CIF ARA contango. August/September CIF ARA at -$5pmt and September/October CIF ARA-$6pmt. The July East West spread is +$62pmt, so all spot cargoes should be heading East, although term volumes continue to flow to Europe. The butane market in the region has been very quiet since being well offered for end July and early August arrival. Butane value notionally 82% Naphtha, this value is firming up as the butane product overhang is being worked through.   MED The summer continues to progress in the region without much activity. Although a VLGC loaded in the US is heading to Dortyol for an early August arrival.

The positive momentum experienced over the past couple of weeks in the tanker snp markets continue to drive activity in most sectors with a number of sales to report this week. As expected, the product markets are leading the charge with values reflecting the healthy earning which has gradually been taking hold over the past couple of months.  A trend in pricing particularly apparent on the MR front which has seen a higher volume of transactions setting improved benchmarks across most vintages. Elsewhere we continue to see a drive on Aframax values with a strong buying enquiry competing over a limited supply of sale candidates. Saying that we expect a number of potential sellers to come meet this renewed interest in hope to capture the value offered by the most recent appreciation in values. A jump well illustrated by the sale of the “ELANDRA ANGEL” (115k dwt 2009 Samsung) which was sold by Vitol at Usd 32m. Important to note that the vessel is scrubber fitted which would condone a notable premium against a comparable non scrubber fitted vessel.  With most headlines stolen by Tanker activity dry SnP markets remain relatively uneventful with values still showing resilience against a certain degree of uncertainty that seems to be settling in. A flat pricing curve that is as usual well supported in the Supramax market with units such as the “NEUTRINO” (58k dwt 2012 Kawasaki) still achieving levels in line with their relative last done.

EAST A substantial part of the East market started their week only on Tuesday due to holidays across the region. Adnoc acceptances was also slightly delayed, reportedly due to some IT issues. As the week finally has started to gain some traction, we have seen a couple of deals concluded on end July dates. One of which was to substitute a ship running late due to delays in India. Looking into August, positions are looking increasingly tight especially in the first 5 days of the month and depending on cargo allocations, we expect freight to have more upside than downside in the very near term.  WEST After a busy last week with a handful of US-fixtures and shipping tenders out of West- and North Africa we have not seen the same rate of activity continue into 28th week of the year. There has only been one fixture concluded this week in the United States and with that said we only see a couple of available vessels left in July that we expect to soon get absorbed. The position list until the middle of August looks relatively tight and in control of two large, pure shipowners. We finally saw a big build again this on Wednesday helping the arb widen a bit, but not enough to help increase activity.

Still uninspiring and not living up to expectations for the big ships - but with some promise for the immediate future, with in particular transatlantic and fronthaul trades to lead. Brazilian miners quietly but actively picking early ships, pretty much clearing out July arrivals for C3 loading. This, combined with limited supply and what seems a substantial August programme, is subsequently pushing China-Brazil-China round values up 50 pct to USD 15k/day w-o-w and counting. The West Australia/China conference trade remains limited in volume and Pacific rounds stuck in a USD 9-12k interval, whilst overall average daily earnings up some 10 pct to come in at USD mid 19k's. Spot appearing more balanced, whilst forward values at time of writing give little support for significant period activity.

The MEG July volume has finished off with 140 or so fixtures for the month, continuing the trend of healthy activity. This week the Eid holidays coupled with falling in the twilight zone between July and August stems has meant a quieter few days, but rates continue to improve for owners with each successive fixture. MEG/China sits a little under WS 60, but consensus is that once the August stems kick in, passing WS 60 is likely.   The smaller sizes continue their firm trend, certainly in the Atlantic, so strong upward pressure on VL rates from below. West Africa/China rates sit at WS 58.5, and stronger numbers in the USG, with USD 7.2m fixed STS USG/China (albeit off prompter dates), and a couple of unfixed Vitol stems to the UKC reported at the time of writing. No downside for the VLCC’s in the short term.

text: AMERICAS Crude oil peaked in the first week June at just over $122/bbl but has softened rather dramatically over the last month and is presently trading in the ~$93/bbl range, though with quite a lot of inter-day volatility.  This is causing volatility in the LPG space, as well, with propane having declined from $1.24/gal the first week of June to $1.10/gal in robust trading sessions.  Butane length in the U.S. continues to play a role and RVP waivers are being sought to alleviate the surplus, though this was considered a bit of a long-shot. The EIA data on Wednesday showed a build of 2.9mmbbls to an overall total of 57.8mmbbls as of 8 July, or about 97% of last year but just ~68% of two years ago.  The market had been anticipating a build of between about 750,000bbls and 1.9mmbbls, and as such the healthy growth was welcome and well received. Terminal fees remain subdued, with buy-side interest at/below 4cpg, but sellers seem anxious to commence talks nearer to 5cpg.  Little is known to have been fixed, but at this point there seem to be more sellers than buyers.  2H 2022 values, however, are healthier and were seen worked at/above 6cpg.  NWE The European propane market sprung to life for end June/early July TOT cargoes, with two bids bringing assessed values up to a $2.75pmt premium to July CIF ARA. Surprising as July imports from the US are set to be 800,000MT smashing the previous monthly record of 700,000MT. The butane market in the region remains long and stocks high. The steepening contango could temp some traders to look at storing tons. The netback values form the US are not as attractive, the August East / West spread $59pmt, though many European traders have TC vessels and European systems, skewing spot cargo netbacks. The huge trans-Atlantic volume continues to flow!  MED Has been quiet as movements in other markets take front and centre in this low demand period of the year. The region remains long butane as Northwest European traders continue to try to place tons in the region.

MEG has experienced sustained enquiry levels this week which brought some much-needed balance to the global Suezmax market and provides a strong support mechanism to an already firmer Atlantic market (holding some ships in the East). Td23 is presently WS 70 with upward bias and if present enquiry levels persist, this could easily jump 5-10 points in a blink. MEG/China will trade min WS 115-120 on modern but is susceptible to further upside. Rumors persist of an early August Td20 cargo working off market, which creates its own self-fulfilling scenario. Td20 is minimum WS 117.5-120 but has potential to firm quickly as owners should be comparing numbers against a Guyana/TA run etc. The USG is the key component to the Atlantic market, and we expect this region to remain firm.

The MEG July volume has finished off with 140 or so fixtures for the month, continuing the trend of healthy activity. This week the Eid holidays coupled with falling in the twilight zone between July and August stems has meant a quieter few days, but rates continue to improve for owners with each successive fixture. MEG/China sits a little under WS 60, but consensus is that once the August stems kick in, passing WS 60 is likely.   The smaller sizes continue their firm trend, certainly in the Atlantic, so strong upward pressure on VL rates from below. West Africa/China rates sit at WS 58.5, and stronger numbers in the USG, with USD 7.2m fixed STS USG/China (albeit off prompter dates), and a couple of unfixed Vitol stems to the UKC reported at the time of writing. No downside for the VLCC’s in the short term.

Last week the Aframax market in the North Sea took a very positive turn. Rates got fixed at above WS 200 levels yielding TC earnings at about USD 70k. This week started on a quiet note, but surrounding markets is still offering an alternative for those owners willing to ballast away. Going forward we expect spot earnings to stay healthy. However, some charterers could try and take advantage of a quiet market and challenge the current fixing levels which owners are asking for. In the Mediterranean and the Black Sea area we have seen some slightly improvement in rates. With some anticipation that we will see further liftings of force majeure on more ports in Libya, charterers have reached out to owners aiming to cover on forward dates. With more Libyan cargos coming into the market, rates will continue to firm.

We have seen another week with limited supply of new cargoes in both hemispheres. It seems an old fashioned “summer market” is creeping in on us with both physical and paper finding little support. In the Atlantic, despite of low tonnage supply, levels continue to drop on back of thin volume of cargoes. However, the North Atlantic seems to be finding some sort of support as longer delays in N. Continent ports keeping a lid on vessels output. ECSA has also followed the same suit with levels sub 20k for August loaders. Transatlantic trips have dipped well into the teens and fronthauls are being concluded in the high USD 20,000’s. The Pacific market held up a bit better than the Atlantic at the start of the week, but trend is weaker for the past few days. Pacific rounds are concluded close to USD 15k and P6 are now below USD 20k. There has been very limited period fixture reported.

It has been another lacklustre week for the spot shipping market. Despite the slight drop in vessel availability, spot rates remain soft as limited requirements were seen in both basins. LNG pricing is at historic highs yet the west to east arbitrage remains firmly shut and has also led to a lack of opportunities for shipping and rather, more sublets available and keen to compete for businesses within their respective regions. While the current situation is challenging on the spot market, demand for multi months to long term remain stable with a handful of charterers still looking for coverage for this winter and beyond. There are no newbuilding orders or ship sales reported this week.

Steady activity in the Dry Cargo sectors with healthy amount of transactions despite a relative weakening in sentiment. The Kamsarmax sector has seen a handful of vessels changing hands with values continuing to show resilience against an increasingly challenging environment. As mentioned in last week's wrap up, pressure on values seems to be most felt on the Supramax front. A correction partly due to the heighten liquidity usually seen in the sector which makes this specific asset class more reactive to price volatility. Notable pick up in buying enquiry on the Capesize front where we expect further activity in the near future.  Despite the limited amount of sales to report on the Tanker front, this week continue to see positive momentum driven by increased levels of buying enquiry. We are indeed witnessing a strong buying appetite with signs of a number of ongoing negotiations; an appetite however that is met with a fast-moving target by sellers who have been long awaiting for market rebound and who are now revising their ideas upwards in light of what seems to be an unanimous consensus of even better days to come.

NSea market rebounded this week on the back of tighter supply of vessels and main oil fields returning from maintenance. Baltic rates are moving sideways as charterers trying to secure vessels even for 3rd decade dates mainly for Eastbound voyages. Moving forward we might see rates climbing up further if activity remains strong and bigger sizes are not there to undercut Aframaxes. In the Med/BSea we have seen rates soften this last week. Lack of cargo activity and Status Quo in Libya have led charterers to pick off that tonnage list in a quiet manner. Though there have been more fuel/long haul enquiries this week offering owners an escape from the area. There is a soft undertone for the balance of the week, and one to watch is possible disruptions and shut down of the Caspian Pipeline supplying crude via CPC (Novorossiysk).

Thus far, it's been a fairly active week which hopefully bodes well for the remainder of the third decade. The Atlantic is beginning to find sustained support from MEG/West enquiry which should reduce supply of ships ballasting straight to West Africa from the East. Russian suitable tonnage is also having a positive impact as most of these owners forego back-haul opportunities as their time is better spent ballasting straight back to Russia. This increases tonne miles and stresses the fleet to some degree. Whilst most regions have traded flat this week, it won't take much for TD20 to firm 2.5-5 points whilst in the East, TD23 will see out the remainder of the week trading in the WS 50's. MEG/China needs testing on modern tonnage but should find a home between WS 107-110.
