This has impacted the general sentiment, but not to same extend as there is some signs of improvement in the South Atlantic and South Africa segment. The Pacific still look gloomy as there is available tonnage around for the expected program, however the rates itself is poor which gives support. In other words, with the Pacific now holding and activity in the West improving you could expect a better week to come.

NSea market rebounded this week on the back of tighter supply of vessels and main oil fields returning from maintenance. Baltic rates are moving sideways as charterers trying to secure vessels even for 3rd decade dates mainly for Eastbound voyages. Moving forward we might see rates climbing up further if activity remains strong and bigger sizes are not there to undercut Aframaxes. In the Med/BSea we have seen rates soften this last week. Lack of cargo activity and Status Quo in Libya have led charterers to pick off that tonnage list in a quiet manner. Though there have been more fuel/long haul enquiries this week offering owners an escape from the area. There is a soft undertone for the balance of the week, and one to watch is possible disruptions and shut down of the Caspian Pipeline supplying crude via CPC (Novorossiysk).

Rates continue to climb across the board, as strong enquiry and a tightening list is firming owner’s sentiment. MEG/East is moving up through the WS 50’s with WS 57.5 paid on a Vietnam run, albeit promptish dates and a higher speed. In the Atlantic, similar rate increases with Wafr/East now paying WS 57.5 and plenty of USG cargoes on the board at the time of writing.   However, the disparity between the scrubbered and unscrubbered vessels is stark. With a price differential close to double, an owner able to burn the high sulphur can look to the region of USD 26-27k/day at present levels for a MEG/China run. However, for the non eco, non scrubbered vessels, on the same voyage, TCE returns are still struggling to break even. Many will be eyeing the next dry dock as an opportunity to fit a scrubber and level the playing field.

Prompt demand from Japan for LNG cargoes continues, as the nation is looking at restocking inventories after the heatwave of last week. Importers from Europe and Asia keep battling for cargoes amidst the global natural gas supply shortage, but current record high seasonal prices have deterred some buyers. The West to East arbitrage is still closed, hence there are few signs of reduction of the sublet tonnage oversupply in the near future.  Spot market activity in Atlantic remains subdued, as portfolio players with tonnage keep winning prompt cargo tenders. In the East, there has been some more activity but interest has mainly been focusing on smaller Steam Turbine tonnage putting further pressure on rates. Looking further ahead, the Freeport outage continues to be a concern over the next months, but for the time being most subletters are reluctant to release any modern tonnage over winter in anticipation of potential cargo opportunities or arbitrage openings. There have been no new NBs orders reported so far this week, however both NB and SnP markets remain active with prices firming.

EAST  The Middle East Gulf position list has been looking a bit lengthy lately which has resulted in freight coming off little by little. Indian inventories are also currently on the rise which could cause some delays in ports and consequently more spot requirements from Indian PSUs. text: AMERICAS Volatility has overtaken the crude oil markets which have been reeling from fears of a deepening global economic recession (not to mention a strengthening U.S. Dollar), the former causing governments to sharply raise interest rates in a bid to slow the economy.  As such, WTI saw highs of over $122/bbl in June, but new lows were posted this week at $98.53/bbl.   Correspondingly, the MB propane market has reacted, not only in terms of the flat price but as it relates to WTI on a percentage basis.  Propane at Mont Belvieu is currently valued at ~$1.14/gal, or about 48% of WTI, where at one point the relationship had dipped in to the low 40 percent range. The EIA today released its findings on US propane stocks which, for the first time in some weeks, was expected to reveal a more accurate set of data.  Most in the market were expecting a build but expectations ranged widely from under 1mmbbls to over 3mmbbls.  As of 01 July 2022, however, the Overall Total propane stock level in the US is 54.9mmbbls, or 95% of last year, but 70% of two years ago. Terminal fees were earlier in June seen fixed in the upper 5cpg range, but buyers retreated to the low 4s until recently when the market turned and two separate transactions are widely believed to have been fixed for August at 5cpg.  2H 2022 values are at/above 6cpg.  NWE Butane Storages in the region remains full and multiple cargoes are looking for homes with no luck so far. In the propane markets, Europe is on track to import close to 625,000 tons In July, (a new record  high) , prompting a handful of unmet window offers, and a decidedly weak market sentiment to begin the short week. That said, LPG Avails from the North Sea will likely tighten further still, as liquids continue to be re-injected into the Nat Gas stream.   MED Butane is long in the region as traders look to the region to release some of the North West European butane pressure. Propane in the med appears long for the time being, as demand has quelled per usual at this point in the year. Sonatrach postings for July of $700 propane and $650 butane, will have done little to spur demand in the region. Demand above term supplies is not being seen.

As anticipated, this week has seen a number of vessels changing hands on the tanker front with new benchmarks being set across most sectors. Transactions that are indeed validating the positive trend witnessed over the past couple of weeks with values gradually catching up with this shared positive sentiment. An appreciation particularly felt on the product front with 8 units being sold this week. The 2005 built MT “EXPLORER II” (47k dwt built Onomichi) achieved Usd 13.3m basis surveys and BWTS due. To put levels in perspective the MT “ANGEL NO. 6" (45k dwt, 2005, Shin Kurushima) was sold earlier this month at Usd 9.4m representing an approximate 40% jump in values between these two comparable sales. Other notable increase on the Aframax front with the sisters “TARTAN” & “FORTIES” (113k dwt, 2005, Samsung – Ice 1A) being sold at Usd 22.5m each. Similarly the last comparable sale is this of the “SOPHIE SCHULTE” (115k dwt, 2005, Sanoyas) which was sold at Usd 19.5m beginning of June this year. Worth noting that the Tartan and sister are both holding an Ice class notification 1A which is understood to have had a positive impact on the levels achieved.  Dry SnP markets have seemingly rebounded from last weeks relative dip in activity with about 15 vessels being sold this week. While most values remain relatively flat, there are signs of weakening on certain fronts which have seen a relative loss of momentum. The SDARI 64 ultramax  “WESTERN SANTOS” (64k dwt, 2014, Hantong) was sold at Usd 26.3m which could be construed as a slight correction against last month’s sale of the one-year younger sister “BELPAREIL” (64k dwt, 2015, Hantong) which achieved Usd 29.5m. Saying that, levels continue to be well supported by high levels of liquidity in most sectors which is expected to continue to keep values in line with most recent concluded business.

Concentric tonnage flows have become the "new normal" in the Atlantic which should eventually result in the term "back-haul", becoming redundant, at least for the foreseeable future. Suezmax rates appears to be coming off a touch, whilst conversely, VLCCs appear to be adding a little bit of weight. A glance at available tonnage for TD20 suggests that rates shouldn't drop too much in the present fixing window as on the early side it still looks fairly tight. The USG also looks like it should trade flat/firm, and from what we have seen during the last few months, it just needs an ounce of resistance on Aframax's for rates to feed through to the larger segments. In the East, TD23 should trade in the WS 50's with some slack in the list whilst a MEG/China run will set charterers back about WS 105-110.

A week of decent gains for owners, as each quarter point is fought over. MEG volumes are assisting owners’ rate pushes, as we saw over 150 cargoes for June; the highest since April 2020. July also looking decent with mid-month MEG/China cargoes now fixing at the WS 52 level, up six points from the same time last week. At the time of writing in the Atlantic, four or five enquiries in West Africa suggests further upward movement and with Smaxes holding their ground, it is likely further increases imminent.  A quick note on the difference a scrubber makes – with a price differential where 380 is 45% cheaper in Singapore right now, paying almost double the price for your bunkers, the effect on the bottom line is huge. Non-scrubbered owners will not be getting carried away by the current levels, but at least are in the positive.

One of the slowest weeks this year in the Nsea/Baltic with limited cargoes in the market as main Nsea fields are expected to return from maintenance. Owners managed to push rates higher in the end of last week for Nsea runs, however market seems softer right now. Tight supply of Baltic candidates also pushed rates higher in this area. We expect rates to cool off a bit in the short term but moving forward into July rates might hike again. The Med/Blsea market has continued its softening trend from last week with lack of cargo activity. We have seen regular cross Mediterranean routes dropping 25 worldscale points give or take. With Force Majeure still prevailing in some of the Libyan ports, we expect the area to remain soft in the short run.

text: AMERICAS The EIA’s propane inventory report yesterday was viewed with skepticism, if only because of the technical-related hiatus the bureau took in the week prior.   For the week ending 25 Jun the 5-year average build has been 2.85mmbbls, where the two week span from the last EIA report to the most current showed a build from 51.8mmbbls on 10 June to 54mmbbls on 24 June, or a 2.2mmbbl increase.  In other words – on average – a 1.1mmbbl weekly build, which was viewed as weak, thus causing the market to resign itself to wait until next week’s data, which is hoped to provide a clearer view of stock levels. That said, at 54.00mmbbls as of 24 Jun 2022, propane stocks in the U.S. are 94% of last year, 72% of two years ago, 76% of three-years ago, 97% of four years ago, and 97% of five years ago. With regards current market rates, spot terminal fees were earlier fixed at as high as 6.50cpg, but have softened at present.  Spot FOB offers are presently seen at 6.00cpg, but depending on timing/ratio there is some room to the downside.  A recent four cargo tender to supply Mexico was awarded to a trader who will deliver 30,000mt propane parcels: Two in July and two in August, reportedly at 5cpg FOB. Brasil and Chile also remain active covering their winter demand.  NWE The butane bloodbath has been the main talking point in the region this week. Storages for butane in the region are full and multiple cargoes are looking for homes with no luck so far. Window offers for butane have fallen from 87% to 84% July Naphtha this week and are yet to find buying interest. The European propane market has taken a backseat and has been relatively quiet. It is clear that the market is not short propane, netbacks from the US for July and August are deep in cancellation territory. We are approaching the seasonal demand lows for the region at the same time as seeing some North Sea LPG production increases, and this increased supply and reduced demand has caused the market to go quiet.  MED Butane is long in the region as traders look to the region to release some of the North West European butane pressure. Sonatrach postings for July of $700 propane and $650 butane, will have done little to spur demand in the region. Demand above term supplies is not being seen.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco cut Jul CP to $725 for both propane and butane, each down by $25 from Jun. It is in line with 2nd round recommendation, however some players reckon it lower than expectation as seeing less Jul spot availability from producers compared to Jun. Aug C3 CP was traded at $729 and C3/C4 traded at flat.   FAR EAST A couple of deals were concluded in window this week. 23kt propane for 2h Aug delivery was traded at Jul and Aug FEI flat. Similar cargo for 1h Aug delivery was offered at Aug FEI plus $4, while bid at Jul FEI minus $1, which equates to Aug FEI minus $1. Off window 23kt parcel for 1h Aug delivery was traded at FEI plus small premium and 46kt parcel was changed hand at Aug FEI minus small digit reportedly.  Two Chinese EChina based importers tendered to buy propane for late Jul/10th Aug delivery. One is reported to procure one or two lots of 23kt propane for Jul delivery at FEI plus mid-single digit. Another one is still within validity at the time of writing.

Record temperatures in Tokyo has seen an increase in cooling demand in Japan and with it the emergence of long needed Eastern demand as LNG reserves at power stations has fallen over the past two weeks. It is reported that there is some resistance from some smaller Japanese utilities to purchase LNG as LNG prices remain close to record highs for the time of year as supply disruption continues to persist. Instead there is a push to curb demand but despite these efforts additional LNG cargoes will be required and it can be anticipated that more ton-time should help alleviate the oversupply of tonnage in the Atlantic through Q3 as vessels head East.    Fixing activity remains muted in the Atlantic with FOB cargo tenders being awarded to entities with their own tonnage. Yet in the Pacific, on the back of a couple of fixtures, rates have stabilised following a couple of consecutive weekly falls and sees owners returns in the Pacific usurp the Atlantic.     In the newbuilding market, Knutsen was awarded by Qatar Energy eight LNG carriers taking their total to ten LNGC in the Qatar Energy process. In addition, NYK was awarded seven LNGC by Qatar Energy, both the Knutsen and NYK vessels will be built at HHI.

A slow week trading across the board, with the negative market showing no signs of abating with little fresh demand surfacing. In the Atlantic, sources spoke of a regurgitation of the same tonnage along with a growing list of ballasters rearing their heads only adding to the soft sentiment already in existence. Similarly, Asia continued to lack any support despite several fresh enquiries’ ex Indonesia, but versus an ever-growing list these were being easily absorbed.  Some representative fixtures this week:  Shun Tong (81,603/2019) Sunda Straight 21 Jun tct via ECSA redel SE Asia $24,000 – Norden  Golden Ioanari (81,827/2011) Taichung 6/10 Jul tct via Australia redel SE Asia $22,500 - cnr   MBA Giovanni (93,352/2010) psg Taiwan 28 Jun tct via Indonesia redel Malaysia $15,000 – SINMAL  Rui Ning 21 (75,476/2014) Sual 28/29 Jun tct via Indonesia redel S China $24,000 – cnr  South Ocean covered USG/China mid Jul dates Cargill TBN some said approx. $32,000 + $1.0 mio bb others mentioned $30,000 + $1,0 mio bb nfd  Astraea SB (82,553/2019) Sepetiba 8-9 Jul fxd subs tct via Santos redel Spain $26,000 + $590k bb – ETG

Average TC rate remains below the USD 20,000 mark, with a drop of 1k from last week. The c5 route has been volatile over the last week but is presently more or less at the same value from last week in the low 11s. There has been some concluded c3 fixtures in the lower 30s over the last week, but index is still under pressure and presently at 29.6 pmt. Period tonnage is still in demand and index ships are still achieving decent margins.

EAST East freight is descending, and we note a couple of India deals concluded just below the 70 mark. With freight softening and fixing window being more than two weeks out in time, it seems like charterers with uncovered July cargoes remain relaxed for now. We expect a handful of unfinished spot business remaining on July dates, mainly for the last decade, to be worked later this week or beginning of next before we shift focus onto August.  WEST As we have experienced as of late, volatility in both freight rates and activity is no stranger to VLGC West market. A sudden change of pace led to several vessel enquiries both ex the US and Africa. Freight remains resilient (almost) regardless of loading dates being first or second half July, or even early August. Offers are around USD mid 100s Houston/Chiba and mid 60s Houston/Flushing. The H/F premium is growing and currently trades at USD 20,000 pd higher than H/C. Going forward, we expect the market to stay balanced to tight and in the hands of relatively few players.

Supramax market yet took more beating for another week. The negative trend spreading across all basins and owners seeking to reposition the tonnage in better areas, like loading in ECSA with better rates compared to USG. It was rumored ADM fixed one Ultra ballasting from Continent at USD 40,000 pd delivery APS Argentina with grain to Continent. Another Ultra was reported dely aps Recalada for TCT to Singapore-Japan at USD 22,500/pd plus USD 1.25 mil GBB. In Baltic and Continent market became more stable during the week and one can say, it bottomed out. More cargo appeared on the market with many scrap player to sell the commodity on spot basis. The rates did not have much impact due to the surplus of tonnage available in the area. Levels for scrap cargo to Med and grain cargoes to West Africa for June dates fining in the USD 15,000-18,000 pd, depends on delivery. Med and Black Sea market very similar to Continent, the rates are fixing around USD 20,000-22,000 pd for USG/ECSA/West Africa direction. It’s not great. Market in Far East and Indian Ocean were more stable, and rates are flat, perhaps with very small premium from last week. Ultramax 63,000 dwt delivering North China was fixed at USD 37,000 pd for a trip via Indonesia to WCI. And Supramax delivering Thailand was done at USD 32,000/pd for a trip via Indonesia to India.

Markets are shaking as the fear of recession is increasing, which is also making a big impact on Capesize expectation as steel and iron ore prices are dropping. We see freight for West Australia-China, which is the biggest flow for seaborn iron ore, is down by 16% in two trading days and the average of all routs down 23%. It’s also interesting to note that forward expectations of hire is down from 27,500 last week to 22,500 now.

Continued last week bearish sentiment and the pressure on cargo supply from Black Sea and Baltic, resulting Atlantic market falling further down. ECSA and USG after many believed to be finding ground unfortunately didn’t prove to be correct assessment. Many ships and lack of fresh inquires kept rates sliding downwards. The Continent and Mediterranean markets exposed to brutal reality with no cargos from main loading areas in Baltic and Black Sea. The Pacific market started to see signs of improvement after last week’s negative segment. Today's levels are in the mid USD 20,000 pd for Atlantic RV on Supra with premium for Ultras. Pacific RV are trading in the high USD 20,000 pd. Fronthaul from the Atlantic to the Pacific stable, but poor levels of low USD 20,000 pd.

In the Atlantic, Aframaxes continue to lend physical/psychological support to Suezmaxes whilst VLCCs could, conversely, cap proceedings. For now, the bulls are winning as it's moving in the right direction with TD20 poised to make further gains. Another support mechanism for the Atlantic comes in the form of charterers choosing to pothole the market with multiple laycans being spread out over a wide date-range. This allows momentum to build and imbues owners with confidence to ask for more. In the East, MEG/West trade flows continue to increase which has naturally benefited freight rates, particularly as both 15 and 20 tonne crane vessels are in demand which helps thin the list for eastbound requirements. TD23 is likely to hit WS 70's whilst a China run won't give you much change from WS 102.5-107.5 on a modern ship.

The Jekyl and Hyde nature of the market in the wake of the Freeport outtage has continued this week. A jump in prompt availability has depressed spot rates in both basins; yet further out towards winter and beyond, levels remain strong with more risk to the upside. In fact, many signals such as reduced production and higher demand for LNG in Europe are bearish for shipping on paper but very bullish for LNG pricing. The old adage "cargo is king" may come to define the coming years, and access to reliable shipping  is clearly supporting multimonth and multiyear rates. That aside, the prompt months may be a challenge for those with excess tonnage.  There were two newbuildings ordered last week.

A few Aframax owners, who aim to fix premium business ex Baltic, are also considering fixing cross Nsea cargos as a time filler. Despite this, the current Nsea market is looking very tight for end month loadings. Owners are with workable tonnage in position is rightfully asking for higher than last done rates. We see this firm Nsea/Baltic market trend continue going forward. The Med/Blsea market was active throughout last week with rates correcting up as charterers trying secure prompt tonnage to cover 3rd decade June/1st decade July requirements. Slightly different story this week as charterers been holding back and with lower cargo activity the lists now looking healthier, resulting in rates coming off again. We foresee a softer/stable market for the balance of the week.

Quite a turn around this week. Owners have the bit between their teeth and are looking to continue market gains over the last week or so. Driven by an active Atlantic market, with rates creeping up USD 200k for USG/East on Monday, it set the tone and the West Africa market followed suit (jumping to WS 50 Wafr/China), as only modern approved tonnage would fit the requirements. What had been a sluggish MEG market burst into life Tuesday, with Unipec grabbing what they could at the WS 45-46 level, leaving other charterers entering the market and owners looking to push (at the time of writing owners talking the WS 50’s). Those charterers that can escape on handicapped/old can do so, but it remains only a few points discount. Plenty of cargoes still to work, so it remains all to play for during the remainder of the week.

Quite a turn around this week. Owners have the bit between their teeth and are looking to continue market gains over the last week or so. Driven by an active Atlantic market, with rates creeping up USD 200k for USG/East on Monday, it set the tone and the West Africa market followed suit (jumping to WS 50 Wafr/China), as only modern approved tonnage would fit the requirements. What had been a sluggish MEG market burst into life Tuesday, with Unipec grabbing what they could at the WS 45-46 level, leaving other charterers entering the market and owners looking to push (at the time of writing owners talking the WS 50’s). Those charterers that can escape on handicapped/old can do so, but it remains only a few points discount. Plenty of cargoes still to work, so it remains all to play for during the remainder of the week.

A few Aframax owners, who aim to fix premium business ex Baltic, are also considering fixing cross Nsea cargos as a time filler. Despite this, the current Nsea market is looking very tight for end month loadings. Owners are with workable tonnage in position is rightfully asking for higher than last done rates. We see this firm Nsea/Baltic market trend continue going forward. The Med/Blsea market was active throughout last week with rates correcting up as charterers trying secure prompt tonnage to cover 3rd decade June/1st decade July requirements. Slightly different story this week as charterers been holding back and with lower cargo activity the lists now looking healthier, resulting in rates coming off again. We foresee a softer/stable market for the balance of the week.

The market began slowly entering a new week, no holidays of note but the market had yet to find a clear direction with a mixture of views for next done deals. However, the majority felt rates in the Atlantic appeared relatively healthy so far with fundamentals largely unchanged from the end of last week. The market in Asia appeared at first sight a little sloppy, but yet again market players had yet to show their hands so a little too early to call the market. Last done for non-India discharge is being reported in the mid-high 70s, while last done deals to the Indian majors have been concluded in the mid-high 80s. With the latest activity considered we expect freight to remain firm.  WEST The western freight rates are on the rise again and we are starting to see freight enquiries for August dates. We have seen over 20 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC so far in July and owners are now aiming around USD 110 Houston/Chiba and high 60s Houston/Flushing. With a handful of uncovered July and early August cargoes out there and the position list in the hands of few players in addition to the arb supporting today’s freight we expect rates to at least maintain.

text: AMERICAS Fears of recession and US governmental fuel-tax relief ambitions have caused crude to tumble, though propane has yet to react at corresponding rates.  As such, the propane-to-crude ratio has increased from the low/mid 40-percentile range to 47% at present.  Current Mont Belvieu propane for July is pegged at 120.25cpg while WTI is off by $2.25/bbl at $103.80/bbl.  Wednesday’s WTI market closed at $106.19/bbl. Propane arbs, meanwhile, heavily favor the Asian markets, but buy-side interest does not appear to have fully materialized as Middle East export volumes appear to be satisfying demand levels there. The EIA propane inventory data was expected to have been released today (having been delayed due to the newly established “Juneteenth” holiday which was observed on Monday) but a systems issue has reportedly caused the EIA to postpone until next week at the usual Wednesday 9.30am CST time. Lastly, terminal fees crested earlier in the month in the low/mid 6s for July business but have receded for late-July / early August transactions to the mid 4cpg range.  NWE Record imports to the region has closed the trans-Atlantic arb. With butane storages full and looking long in the region. Propane is looking long, with early July being offered in the window with any bids being shown in reply. Retail demand for LPG is low as to be expected with much of Europe experiencing temperatures of over 30 degrees. The petchem sector looks well supplied through 1H July and opportunistic sellers hoping to place spot tons in the market are getting worried, as record imports coincide with seasonally lower demand.   MED The East Med is long due to Yanbu butane coming into the region. While the west Med has been well supplied from the US, during this period of low seasonal demand. Additionally weakness in physical naphtha is further reducing butane value.

text: MEG Oil tumbled amid fears over recession and swap market is full of uncertainties. Both Jul C3 and C4 were traded below $700 but rebounded on Thurs at $707. One trader is bidding last decade Jul lifting evenly split cargo at Jul CP minus $15 but no offers in window. 1st round CP idea for C3 ranged from $695 to $710, and C4 at $5-10 differentials to C3.   FAR EAST Cash premium strengthened this week as less sellers outstanding. 23kt propane for 2h Jul delivery was traded from Jul FEI flat to plus $4. And similar cargo for 1h Aug delivery was offered at Aug FEI plus $5 and 2h Aug at flat.  Off window a handful of cargos been placed and sentiment improved despite the volatility in swap market. At least one 23/23 cargo for 2h Jul delivery were changed hand between traders, likely into NEA market. One 9-13th Jul lifting ex Australia, heavy butane cargo was placed into Japan and Korea reportedly. One SEA importer was said to purchase a heavy propane cargo for 2h Jul delivery, and it was said to have bought one heavy butane cargo previously for late Jun/early Jul arrival. One Korean trader procured a 16-25th Jul delivered 23kt propane at Jul FEI plus low mid single digit via tender reportedly. And one NChina PDH issued private tender to buy a July arrival full cargo propane, and the result is yet to know at the time of writing.

A relatively quieter week for Dry cargo SnP markets that have got us used to exceptional volumes of weekly transactions throughout the year. The four vessels changing hands this week are all Supramax, which continues to draw most of the buying enquiry; saying that there has been a relative shift in sentiment with the number of potential buyers thinning down and adopting a standby approach to a market that appears to show signs of weakening. Nevertheless values remain flat for the time being with the 2009 built Tess 58 MV “SAGARJEET” achieving USD 18.4m.   Slightly opposite momentum on the tanker front despite the limited amount of reported sales this week. We are witnessing a strong Buying appetite with signs of a number of ongoing negotiations; an appetite however that is met with a fast-moving target by Sellers who have been long awaiting for a market rebound and who are now revising their ideas upwards in light of what seems to be an unanimous consensus of even better days to come.

Dry cargo markets continue to capture most of the SnP activity with vessels changing hands across all segments. The sisterships “DARYA JYOTI & DARYA MOTI (2010/STX/80k dwt)”, have been sold to Greek buyers at USD 24m each representing a tick up in values for 1st generation Kamsarmax units of Korean design. Notable pick up in activity in the Panamax front with four mid 2000 built units changing hands; prices achieved continue to fall in line with most recent transactions. Buying enquiry remains particularly strong in the Ultramax segment where a number of vessels are being placed on the market for sale suggesting further activity in the near future.   It has been a subdued week in terms of concluded business for Tanker markets which is however not particularly reflective of the buying appetite witnessed in most segments. A momentum in values seems to be getting hold with signs of ongoing negotiations suggesting a tick up in levels put on the table by potential buyers. Increased levels that should soon be supported by a higher volume of vessels changing hands providing consolidated benchmarks for future transactions.

With the dust settled after another Posidonia, we catch up on deals done during the week. Plenty of AG ships on subs no details as rates struggle to make any headway, despite increasing fuel costs. AG/Korea sits at the ws43.5 level, a couple of points discount if you find yourself handicapped in any way. With June closing around 140 fixtures, volume is decent and Unipec already exploring July dates. Other sizes showing improvement, albeit heavily Atlantic driven, VL’s may follow suit, as a number plucked from the list in Rotterdam, Cape of Good Hope etc, with no details attached. Therefore a Charterer may find that as they go to the list for a ship, it will likely be thinner than it first appears. USG/Korea has edged up to $5.675m. With a tighter list, higher bunkers and firmer Smaxes, further Atlantic firming likely.

There is still a great demand from specific charterers for any vessels willing to load ex Russian ports. Despite some maintenance scheduled for some strategic export ports in the Nsea basin there is sufficient activity for both fuel and crude leaving other Owners in a position to push for a bit more than last done. Market looking a bit firmer.In the Med/Blsea we have seen a firming trend this last week with benchmark routes moving as much as +WS50-60 points w.o.w.With surrounding markets offering attractive alternatives and with charterers reaching and with long hauls in the mix - we expect the natural window to remain firm as lists looking tighter.

With the buzz of Posidonia behind us, we are rattled back to reality by the recent Freeport LNG explosion and a 40% cutback of LNG flows from NordStream 1, due to technical issues, further tightening an already stretched LNG market and releasing a flurry of prompt LNG vessels, many only until recently committed, back unto the market. In turn, while LNG prices across the forward curves of Asian and European indexes rise in the wake of these events, vessels’ spot rates across both basins plummet, bringing us back to levels not seen for some weeks. However, with a fair few requirements still out there in the Atlantic and Pacific, and in anticipation of increasing demand from the East as we inch towards winter, we can expect spot rates to maintain some level of support and buoyancy going forward. On the term side of the equation, a similar story can be told as 1-Year term rates soften off the back of current events. That said, this is driven by prompt availability discounting the coming weeks. Subject to Freeport start-up, the market remains structurally tight and the prompt discount vanishes for later deliveries.  On newbuildings, two new orders have been reported this week from a Greek Head Owner as vessel prices continue to tick upwards, and with the rise in US interest rates the impact on newbuild charter rates is likely to be significant.

Recent changes in the behaviour of the Atlantic crude oil trade has created it's own algorithm, with peaks and troughs revealing themselves to the market well in advance of them occurring. This algorithm comes with a caveat; as long as the East is quiet and keeps throwing ships back onto the Atlantic list, participants will have a degree of forewarning. We're in the middle of one of those upward trends now with Td20 trading at about W110-115 whilst the USG and Americas in general still look very interesting with Owners likely to make further gains. Vlcc's may provide a cap of sorts in the Atlantic but that segment may be tighter than anticipated. This optimism falls flat in the East where only Td23 provides sufficient enquiry to actually call itself a market. That route trades in the WS50's with further upside.

text: AMERICAS The EIA report on Wednesday showed a modest build of just 1.6mmbbls for an overall propane stock total of 51.8mmbbls as of 10 June 2022, which is about 94% of last year’s total and 73% of the total achieved two years ago.  It’s also well below the average for the second week of June, which is +2.12mmbbls.  The market had been expecting something between 2.8-3.2mmbbls (with a couple of noteworthy outliers who were calling for a “flat” or “minimal” builds).   On the whole, propane values over the last week have declined from 124.50cts/gal to current levels around 118.00cts/gal.  All the while, netbacks were seen in decline as re-sale terminal fees have shrunk to ~4cts/gal.  However, by the close of business on Wednesday there appeared promise as the arb showed signs of improving – opening, even.  Furthermore, a series of offers appeared this week and supplies seem plentiful despite the three known July cancellations on the Gulf Coast. Meanwhile, demand in Latin America appears to have been satisfied via a spot sale and a tender award, though the re-opening of storage caverns near Pajaritos in Mexico may allow for some volumes to move in that direction.  Current consumer demand levels in Mexico are seasonally limited, however.  NWE  An end June propane bid continues to be show in the TOT window, supporting the market. The value was equal to July CIF ARA +$7.5pmt. With the increased Marcus Hook exports and the majority of these tons flowing to Europe, it was expected this bid would have been hit rapidly. The summer mood continues in region as storages begin to fill up. Butane in particular is long with storages full at all major demand centres. Term supply and European traders picking up Marcus Hook tons has blocked the hopes of Eastern placing some of their length in Europe. The July Propane Naphtha spread in Europe is at $98pmt and demand from petchems remains good. The East/West spread is $56pmt in July and it is likely that July USGC cargoes which were not cancelled will try to find homes in the East rather than looking to the West.   MED The region is quiet with the mood dominated by butane length and Eastern traders trying to find homes for US split ratio cargoes. Low demand and heatwaves make for a soporific market.

Stable or tiny tick up at still mediocre and lower-than-expected levels for the big ships. Whilst the Brazil/China conference trade continues to disappoint in volume, transatlantic is showing signs of promise - average daily earnings for typically t/a coal up more than 20 pct to stand at usd 24k. India continues to be insatiable for indonesian coal, partly compensating for a slow West Australia/China iron ore trade not pushing capacity - value for pacific rounds stuck in usd 18-19k/day-territory. Slight improvements on other trades contribute to overall daily earnings putting on 5 pct to come in at just above usd 21k. Short-term forward values still in contango, and period capes much in demand - representative recent fixtures include 181000 dwt built 2014 done for 4-6 months at usd 35k.

EAST The BLPG1 index continue to come off, and as a result nobody seems to be in a rush to move on upcoming shipping requirements.  The only players that have tested freight since last week has been a handful of Indian majors, but each of these deals have all been concluded at a discount to the previous deal.  We are however seeing stronger upstream production, and many of the Middle Eastern suppliers are dealing with higher inventory of LPG. We therefore expect to see more spot fob cargos in the market over the coming weeks.  WEST We have seen the same for the West market. BLPG2 and 3 have been coming off rapidly and we had to enter double digits before freight resumed. We have seen a good handful of fixtures at the end of this week with last done concluded at USD mid 100s Houston/Chiba and low 60s Houston/Flushing. With the latest activity we count approximately 15 spot fixtures out of the USG/USEC so far in July. As the market finally seems to have found a floor and with several uncovered cargoes out there is plenty of room for more spot activity, albeit at rates somewhere in between capex and opex.

Currently it seems the market will be in for a rebound, but there is no change to the fundamental story that demand growth remains below the rate of supply growth. The market usually climbs at this time of year, so the last couple of weeks’ drop should serve as a clear sign and warning that fundamentals are headed in the wrong direction for owners. The macro-picture is too weak. Just skim through the last months’ manufacturing and steel PMI readings across all major countries/regions and it seems very unlikely that demand will rise in the coming months. USG remained flat with little fresh reported. Supramax Dafeng was covered for a trip to South East Asia in the low usd 20,000s. Ultramax open Chitta was fixed for trip via Indonesia to China at usd 18,000.

The Posidonia festivities are well under way whilst general activity remains sluggish, even quiet. We have some 110 deals done ex MEG for June which should leave, hopefully, another 25-30. Rates for benchmark routes MEG/East remains in minus double digits for those without scrubber mainly due to soaring bunker prices. The West/East market remains docile as well and rates basically flat, with tonnage list ex East just building again. A hope in the near term that WS-rates should increase simply to cover the latest increase in bunker prices should be in the cards. Not much of a hope but earnings like the present, can they really remain so low for so long? Well, we hope not!

Posidonia traditionally keeps principles bogged down in meetings all week which ironically hampers information flows. Despite this, the Atlantic market is fairly busy especially with replacements, but by the time this prime information hits the wider market, there is little to no impact. Bunker prices continue to put a notional floor under rates with potential upside in the Americas where lists are tight and likely to add some weight (once various participants return from Posidonia). For now, TD20 trades WS 92.5 but is likely to uptick whilst MEG/East remains bereft of meaningful business and needs testing. It probably trades about WS 100 for modern/fully approved tonnage whilst TD23 is the sole busy market in the East and should trade WS 50 (+/- 2.5).

text: AMERICAS Propane market levels at Mont Belvieu continue to drift, though rather inconsistently, having peaked in the second week of March at 163.75cpg, and closing most recently at ~123.00cpg.  Conversely, WTI has been trending up since early December and overwater LPG exports remain robust – the combination of which might normally lead to a firm pricing structure.  The conclusion of winter demand and rising stock levels, though, have colluded and allowed values to decline.  Meanwhile, propane as a percentage of crude has been drifting, as well, as Q4 2021 levels were in the 80-percentile range but this week are flirting in the low 40% range. LatAm demand was revealed this week as a primary buyer issued a tender for 33-44,000mt for delivery from 3-9 August.  Offers are expected by 1pm on Thursday 9 June and are to remain valid until Noon EST on Friday 10 June. Terminal fees have reached a plateu of sorts, with buyers and sellers at/above 6cpg, though out-month 2022 transactions are known to have occurred at 6.00cpg, 6.25cpg and 6.50cpg. The EIA this week showed a 600,000bbl build to a total of 50.20mmbbls, or over 93% of last year’s total.  Expectations ranged from 2.75-3.25mmbbls, so the weak build was seen as disappointing – and at least mildly bullish on a short-term basis.  NWE The region looks well supplied with a large volume of trans-Atlantic cargoes arriving in the second half of June. Counter intuitively the TOT window premiums remain for 2H June delivery at June CIF ARA +$5pmt. A stronger premium than the June / July backwardation of $2pmt. Crude continuing to climb has kept the propane / Naphtha spread above $120pmt, supporting industrial propane demand in the region. The majority of US East Coast exports continue to come to Europe, and these exports are growing rapidly. Butane has been steady at 91% Naphtha, though this level has not been tested recently in a fairly stagnant Northwest European butane market.   MED The region is well supplied through term contracts and no additional demand has been seen. Although a fire at Fawley refinery in the UK is expected to tighten butane supply to the Med.

Crude asset values are stabilizing at newfound higher levels, except for modern Aframax where the sale of RUMFORD (107k 2012 Tsuneishi) at Usd 32.8 mill represents another uptick. The vessel has SS passed and BWTS fitted. Certainly more buyers than sellers around with the sweet spot being Aframax/LR2 and MR built 2007-2012. A steady trickle of VLCC transactions and MOL's sale of DUQM (310k 2008 Imabari) at Usd 39 mill is broadly in line with recent transactions.  Dry asset values are moving sideways except for Supramax where values continue to gain. Handysize are still a favorite with buyers whereas Capesize deals are few and far between.

A week with a muted start but the Panamax market continued to hold a cloud of vulnerability as further weakening of rates continued. Little positive news surfacing.  Some representative fixtures this week:  Guo Yuan 16 (75,915/2012) Vizag 2/7 Jun tct via ECSA redel Spore-Japan USD 26,000 – Cargill.  Magic Twilight (80,283/2010) (ST Shipping) Amsterdam 1 Jun fxd nfd.   TBN 70,000/10 coal Bolivar/Tarragona 20/29 Jun SC/25,000SC USD 24.40 fio – Enel.  Marco (81,393/2009) Yeosu 29 May tct via NoPac redel Spore-Japan USD 22,000 – cnr.  Sirocco (81,610/2014) Taiwan tct via Indonesia redel Malaysia USD 20,000 – cnr.

Last week, TD20 had the look and feel of a market that could trade well past WS 100, but by the time Monday rolled around there was a hint of a stall. A number of Wafr/long Mediterranean voyages traded up in dollar per day terms (over a TD20 run), but the market tends not to focus on numbers/maths and it was the lower WS rates that grabbed the headlines, ultimately forging market direction. The US Gulf remains the prime driver behind Atlantic rates and as long as cargoes and ships continue to trade in a concentric Atlantic-manner, we will continue to see further volatility. The East remains poor hunting ground for this segment, save for TD23, which provides a free ticket back to the Med perfectly positioning those owners who trade the Russian market. MEG/East needs testing but should trade circa WS 100.

With a holiday in the US yesterday and London off Thursday and Friday for the Golden jubilee, expectations were for a busier period ahead of the Posidonia event that begins next week. While activity has been on the rise and bunkers have continued to firm, any resultant uptick in Worldscale rates has been somewhat subdued, as charterers fight for every quarter point over last done. Therefore, the result barely covers the higher bunkers costs to owners, and contributing to an overall negative on a TCE basis at the time of writing.  With some added political tensions in the Middle East (Iranian seizure of two Greek vessels) and a shortened work week ahead of a week that has many travelling, the question is will we see some further upward pressure develop, despite sufficient supply to cover demand?

A sharp drop in rates over the last week, with average 5 tc presently at 22,000 being down from 33,000 in one week. C5 is down from USD 14 to USD 12.50 and c3 is down from USD 36 to USD 31.50 pmt in this period. However, rates are on the rise again from earlier this week when c5 was concluded in the 11s. This may imply rates came off too much too quick. At the same time, forward values are keeping fairly stable with second half of the year still in the mid 30,000s.

Short week starting and ending with holidays around the world. Very little being reported. A Supramax was fixed from North coast South America to Turkey at USD 40,000.    Weaker sentiment from the East, Indo-India and Indo-China rounds losing the ground most. A Supramax from CJK was fixed for a trip to Bangladesh at very low USD 30,000.  From the period front, an Ultramax was fixed for 4 to 6 months trading at high USD 30,000 with scrubber benefit for charterer's account.

EAST One producer has been driving much of the activity in the Middle East lately, and they still keep active into the beginning of this week. After a rapid increase in freight rates recently we sooner or later had to see a correction, and that we got as the Baltic index dropped over USD 9 in a day. But there is still a small East premium at around USD 5,000 per day in market earnings compared to the West. Last done deal concluded out of the AG is around mid 90s Ras Tanura/Chiba.  WEST The shipping balance in the West remains relatively tight and in control of few players and this is likely to continue as July fixing moves on. With the observance of a US holiday at the start of this week and UK off on Thursday and Friday the recent fixing rush has slowed down, but we expect it to pick up its pace again next week when all market players are back. There are still some uncovered cargoes left 1H July and it is expected that the players in need for shipping coverage this period will bring some further action to an already hot market. At the end of last week we saw deals done at USD 140 Houston/Chiba and around USD 80 Houston/Flushing, but this week we are closer to USD mid 130s H/C.

Over the last few weeks, the LNG shipping market have seen consistent gains.  Firm sentiments and rate ideas were predominately driven by the West of Suez as more requirements were seen for delivery into Europe.  Lack of vessel availability for June to 1H July in the Atlantic have spurred spot rates to break the six-figure barrier for the larger vessel sizes, which are highly sought after.   The growing demand for modern tonnage is holding sturdy and anticipated to continue for the remaining of the year as US exports increases.   Charterers with limited flexibility on their requirement have seen fewer options and often with a significant premium attached.  Discussion on longer term charters are ever-present as offtake agreements especially from the US are being secured.  With the ongoing geopolitical issues and gas supply disruptions, FSRU/ FSU related LNG projects have also gain traction with more engagements than previous years as Utilities, National Oil companies and governments prioritize energy security.  There are no new orders reported this week, nevertheless, shipyard capacity continue to diminish as demand for Newbuilds from all other shipping sectors continue to push LNGC newbuild deliveries further into the backend of 2026.  One LNG vessel arrived for recycling this week, which is the first for the year 2022. In 2021, 7 units were recycled.

European Union leaders agreed in principle on a sixth package of sanctions against Russia preparing to finalize a ban on almost 90% of all Russian oil imports by the end of the year. This means refineries on the Continent will have to source oil in an even greater extent than before. As such we could see more intra-regional trade on some of the Nsea grades as more of the Urals could be shipped for East destinations. So far, the Aframax market across Europe is moving sideways and with some of the strategic export ports scheduled for maintenance we would need to see more volume before the market will improve.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The EIA data for the week ending 27 May was revealed today and showed a 3.3mmbbl increase over the week prior.  Current overall stocks stand at 49.6mmbbls, which is nearly 103% of last year and just under 70% of two years ago.  Concerns as to stock levels at the conclusion of the summer are beginning to dissipate, though any forecast at this point would likely be premature. Meanwhile, propane values – as a result of the larger-than-anticipated inventory increase – are trending down, having peaked before the end of May at $1.25/gal and now posting at below $1.22/gal.  At present propane is 45% of WTI, having been in decline against crude almost consistently since Q4 2021. Terminal fees in the near-term have softened, with buyers clustered around the 5cpg level but sellers holding on for values nearer to 6cpg.  The second-half of 2022 has been more healthy, with a slew of transactions occurring at between 6.00 and 6.50cpg.  NWE The June CIF ARA propane price came off 11 dollars prior to the holiday closure, and presently sits at $744/t. A tug of war persists as North Sea product remains tight, however ample exports from the US have kept demand satisfied and the muted window activity illustrates the regions balance, and  it is unlikely many new spot purchases will be made to meet new spot demand. Looking farther down the calendar, the ongoing Ukrainian conflict has some participants concerned regarding supply shocks in the coming winter. Natural gas continues to trade at premiums to  LPG, incentivizing its utilization as an alternative fuel source when/ where logistically feasible- But for now, given that it is summer, exports from the US East Coast, coupled with sparce supply available from the North Sea are proving sufficient.    MED The region has been well supplied by US cargoes in the past month due to the open butane arb. Supply to the region has been satisfied through the end of the month, with the only bright spot for demand being Turkey due to the high LPG vs Gasoline spread for autogas.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco cut Jun CP to $750 for both grades, down by $100 for C3 and $110 for C4 respectively. The price was slightly lower than market anticipations. Lukewarm demand from traditional heating segment into summer season and soaring freight dampened the buying interest. Cash differentials for July FOBs still remained in negative territory, with one evenly split cargo for 1h Jul lifting was reported done at CP minus mid-teens level. Jul CP was traded at $735 at the time of writing.  FAR EAST Cash premium for Jul cargos softened this week. 23kt propane for 1h Jul delivery was bid at Jul FEI minus $3 while offer at flattish level. Similar cargo for 2h Jul delivery was offered at FEI plus $2. Several 46kt propane for 1h Jul arrival were changing hand outside window. One SEA importer was reported to buy a end Jun/early Jul delivered evenly split cargo at CP plus 40ish. One EChina cracker user awarded its buy tender for 23kt propane delivered during 5-15th Jul into Ningbo reportedly. Another EChina based refinery was also reported to procure one or two 1h Jul delivered 46kt propane cargo for cracking use.

A number of Wafr/long Mediterranean voyages traded up in dollar per day terms (over a TD20 run), but the market tends not to focus on numbers/maths and it was the lower WS rates that grabbed the headlines, ultimately forging market direction. The US Gulf remains the prime driver behind Atlantic rates and as long as cargoes and ships continue to trade in a concentric Atlantic-manner, we will continue to see further volatility. The East remains poor hunting ground for this segment, save for TD23, which provides a free ticket back to the Med perfectly positioning those owners who trade the Russian market. MEG/East needs testing but should trade circa WS 100.

A flurry of activity in the dry cargo markets with up to 20 vessels changing hands this week. From handysize to capesize the dry SnP space is joying of sustained liquidity providing great transparency on values which in turn facilitate further transactions. A dynamic that becomes particularly well illustrated by the ultramax/supramax sector which sees a consistent amount of units changing hands over the weeks, keeping levels in line with relative last done. This week the “FORTUNE BELL” (Abt 61k dwt built 2020 Shin Kurushima) has been sold at Usd 39m in line with last months sale of the “ULTRA INITIATOR” (abt 62k built 2019 Oshima) at Usd 37.5m while the “OSIOS DAVID” (Abt 55k dwt built 2012 IHI) achieved a price of Usd 22.5m paving the way for the several sisterships that are currently in the market solicitating interest. A pickup in activity in the handysize segment this with 7 vessels being sold this week.    On the tanker front Sinokor continues this year’s shopping spree with the acquisition of the two VLCCs  “NUCLEUS” & “NEPTUN” (Abt 300k dwt built 2007 Dalian) at a price of Usd 30.8m each. Notable activity continuing to take place in the Aframax sector with a number of region 10 year old units being under discussions – as previously reported the long standing bid/ask spread seems to be slowly closing up spurring potential buyers into action. A dynamic that we expect to hold in the near future translating into heightened liquidity and an appreciation in asset values. Similar activity witnessed in the product markets where the strong rate environment continues to drive interest upwards.

The spot market remains firm this week with a steady amount of fixtures concluded. Rates continue to hold at relatively ”healthy” levels for spot voyages, with a lack of prompt vessels both East and West of Suez. Availability further out in the Pacific remains high but the fixture window is extending closer to these vessels. This tonnage is unlikely to be open for long as the majority of sublets have a backstop and may be needed internally.  European LNG storage levels remain high and we may see more vessels head East if discharge slots can’t be secured in Europe. Along with an active spot market, the term shipping market also remains on the gas (excuse the pun) with plenty of interested parties still in or coming to seeking tonnage, and term rates are firming as a consequence. Tonnage from head owners for term requirements still remains elusive. Security of tonnage for the future, predominantly modern tonnage, remains at the forefront of term discussions. Newbuild activity remains high, 6 more orders placed this week and newbuild prices may continue to increase. The first larger LNG event since Covid restrictions were lifted is currently underway as the World Gas Conference in Korea kicked off this week, drawing in crowds from across the industry. For those attending the event in Daegu we hope it has been a great success.

A weaker and softer tone engulfed the Panamax market this week, with a distinct lack of fresh demand impacting market sources said. The Atlantic was said to be lacking any substantial transatlantic activity, consequently tonnage began to show signs of building up resulting in weaker bids as charterers appeared to hold the upper hand. Asia returned something of a stand-off with a wide bid/offer spread, neither owners nor charterers willing to concede culminating in a slow and inactive days trading with little reported.   Some representative fixtures this week:  Shandong Fu Hui (81,782/2017) Algeciras 5-10 June was rumored to have fixed for a trip via US Gulf option NC South America redelivery Far East at $40,000 with ADMI.  Cape Akamas (79,454/2010) Masinloc 26 May fixed for a trip via Indonesia redelivery Taiwan at $26,000 + $80,000 ballast bonus, but further details were lacking.  Ettys Perfection (76,635/2007) Spore 8 May TCT via ECSA redel Spore-Japan $24,000 – COFCO.  Ocean Thyme (82,306/2014) Gib 4 Jun TCT via NCSA redel Skaw-Gib $29,500 – ULTRABULK.   TBN 75,000/5 coal Newport News/Vizag 21/30 Jun 40,000/25,000 SSHEX bends $53.15 FIO – SAIL.

Slight turbulence at healthy levels for the big units, with most concern being on inter-pacific volumes/activity and consensus hovering around USD 33k/day. The West Australia/China iron ore conference trade remains the fundament, but with a sudden appearance of early ships the value for Pacific rounds has slid more than 20 pct the last 5 trading days to stand at USD 31k. Transatlantic trades better in comparison, with limited tonnage supply combined with substantial base commodity volumes to move, pushing daily earnings up some 15 pct to approach USD 29k. Fronthaul iron ore trades still delivers well below expectations. Substantial focus on period amongst major takers, with forward expectations being contango or close - representative fixtures include 179,000 dwt, built 2013, done for almost 2 years at USD 31k, also 181,000 dwt, built 2016, fetching USD 26k basis about 5 years.

The BSI-58 10 T/C route is volatile on week-to-week basis, however the average index remain on similar levels above USD 30,000 pd.  Supramax market continues its positive tone and once again we can experience sustainable market despite all the distractions from global perspective of view. The Pacific market is stable with rates maintaining at very high USD 20,000 pd, while transatlantic round voyages paying just a bit more than USD 30,000 pd. USG numbers seems to be under pressure and ECSA describes as firm and stable. Ultramax asking USD 25,000 pd plus USD 1.5M gross BB delivery Santos for TCT to Singapore- Japan. Ultramax 63’ DWT delivery Argentina rumored to be fixed at USD 50,000 pd for trip with grains to WCSA. Fronthaul from the Continent and Mediterranean pays around USD 25,000 pd, while backhauls USD 35,000 pd. We expect the market to be firm with high volatility next coming weeks.

EAST The MEG market has been quite active lately and during the course of this and last week, rates have increased from mid USD 70's to above USD 100 on Ras Tanura/Chiba basis. This brings the East market earnings approximately USD 15,000 per day higher than the West market earnings for a conventional vessel running VLSFO. As a consequence, more owners are considering to ballast towards Singapore instead of going straight to Balboa after Far East discharge, which has been the name of the game for the last couple of months this year. A good amount of spot FOB sales and some distressed cargoes has contributed to lifting the sentiment, however, the question remains for how long this will last.  WEST Although we have not seen the same activity this week as the previous one the western freight market continues to be strong with last done deal concluded at mid 130s Houston/Chiba and mid-high 70s Houston/Flushing range. At the time of writing there are still a handful of vessels left in end June, but with as much as 35 spot fixtures so far in June it is likely that we will see couple of them be pushed over to July which is where focus now has shifted towards. With a handful of uncovered cargoes, a tight position list and upcoming bank holidays we can expect a busy next week in terms of fixing.

Yet another lackluster week for Aframax owners trading in the North Sea and Baltic area with rates moving sideways. The tonnage list might be looking tighter as ships will ballast away from the area turning their bows to cross the Atlantic where the market is currently looking more favorable. However, we still need the volume to support any uptick in rates, and with maintenance expected for a couple strategic ports in the Nsea for June we might see the market continue to move sideways going forward.   The Med/Bsea continued sideways last week, even dropping a few points as charterers can pick and choose among the many spot ships in the area. We now see a few of them ballasting their ships TA to take part in a stronger US-market. We are not expecting the market to firm up sufficiently in the short run.

It's a game of two hemispheres this week, with all the action confined to the West. The tight US Gulf is the key factor as charterers scramble to find the cheapest vessel DPT (Suezmax, Aframax,VLCC), which in itself only adds to owner sentiment. Td20 in isolation should, if supply/demand models were the only variable to consider, trade moderately up, but there is now momentum in the market and more cargoes are being forced to work in the open market which will see rates push through the WS 100 mark. The East is relatively quiet, save for MEG back haul enquiry, which may just prevent Wafr from taking a really purposeful rate jump. TD23 trades in the mid/high WS 40's whilst a China run needs testing, but owners will be looking for something starting with at least a 9. VLCC's are inevitably the cap.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Jun Propane CP swap fell at $736 and Butane was traded at flattish level. Meanwhile, Jun/Jul CP was traded at $15 contango, reflecting the front length. Qatar Petroleum was reported to sell two 22-24th June lifting FOBs at CP minus 20s level. Discounts deepened as of weaken summer demand against the soaring freight.   1st round June CP recommendation ranged from $725 to $770 for C3 and C4 was recommended at $5 less to flattish to C3.   FAR EAST Cash premium edged up slightly this week. 23kt propane for 2h Jun delivery was concluded over window at FEI plus $9. And similar cargo for 1h Jul delivery was bid at Jul FEI plus mid-single digit.  Off window a handful of buying tenders floating in the market, mainly driving by the petchem. Taiwan FPCC tendered to buy last decade Jun delivered 23kt to 46kt LPG at flex ratio, and awarded one 23/23 cargo at Jun MOPJ minus high 70s. Two Korean importers also issued buy tender to secure 23/0 and 0/23 for Jul delivery respectively, with one reported to secure 23kt propane for 1-5 Jul delivery at Jul FEI plus mid high single digit into Daesan. Apart from such, one European trader issued tender to buy 23kt or 46kt evenly split cargo for Jun to 1st decade Jul delivery into Malaysia, and it was reported to award one 23/23 at CP plus 20ish.

If the plan works, why change it? Charterers working from the shadows, picking a target and keeping quiet on the details is holding the current market at the status quo. This week we have counted over 20 vessels tucked away on business with no details attached. So it stands to reason that had these cargoes worked openly, we would be in a different world (or at least a few points more). Still, ships disappearing off the position list can’t be ignored and bunkers ramping up close to USD 1000/mt, owners are starting to push back. MEG/East is trickling up through the very low WS 40’s, depending on age/quality required. The Atlantic is feeding off Suez & Afra markets which are showing some heat. At the time of writing, only 10-15 VLCC’s in the West (or heading West) available to work. Tighter and firmer in the short term likely.

text: AMERICAS A week-over-week propane stock build of 1.8mmbbls was recorded by the EIA as of 20 May, which puts this year’s inventory levels at 105% of the same time last year – though they remain below 70% of May 2020.  The build was smaller than anticipated, but easily explained by the robust 1.6mmbbls/day export levels. Most are now anticipating that domestic US propane stock levels will reach “acceptable” levels by end Sep, and likely continue to build well into Oct.  The NOAA, however, just issued its 2022 Hurricane Season forecast and is calling for 21 named storms and up to six major hurricanes this season.  A typical year sees around 14 named storms and up to 3 major hurricanes.  Depending on how things ultimately develop, both domestic production levels and export volumes could potentially be impacted, which would then affect overall stock levels. Meanwhile, terminal fees now seem a bit more fragile than in 1H May when levels of up to the mid 6cpg range were achieved.  At present there have just emerged early signs of retreat, particularly from the buy-side, which was talking 5s for near-term business.  NWE As it stands, June CIF ARA propane sits at $722/t, marking a negligible uptick on the day on the back of upstream brent utilization for diesel. However, the region appears balanced, rather than tight, and it is unlikely many new spot purchases will be made to meet new demand. While natural gas' premium over LPG would suggest an incentive to source it as an alternative fuel , the unwinding of seasonal demand and adequate refinery runs, coupled with healthy liftings from Marcus Hook, make for an agnostic attitude for NWE LPG end users. Sentiment in the tanker sectors continue to show encouraging signs with a strengthening buying enquiry leading to increased SnP liquidity in most segments. Product sectors draw strong levels of interest however this week has seen a greater number of crude carriers changing hands with 5 units sold. Notable transactions in the VLCC sector where MT “LEONIDAS” (Abt 320k dwt built 2009 HHI) was sold at Usd 42m while the Chinese built “NEW TALISMAN” (Abt 300k dwt built 2009 Bohai) achieved Usd 38.2m from UAE based Buyers. Levels that remain surprisingly in line with most recently concluded business but which however are not necessarily reflective of the current buying appetite which should apply upward pressure on values going forward. Elsewhere the 2007 built Aframax “ALMI SPIRIT “ was sold at USd 20m basis surveys due providing clear direction for the several other similar candidates that are currently in the market for sale. Candidates that were struggling to transact due to a rather stubborn bid/offer spread that seems to finally tighten.  Steady activity in the dry cargo sectors with healthy amount of transactions and ongoing negotiation in most segments; notable pick up for Capesize which are seeing  an increasing number of  buyers entering the market. Elsewhere the Chinese built Ultramax “YANGZHOU CONFIDENCE” (Abt 63k dwt built 2017 Dayang) has now been sold basis SS Passed and BWTS fitted. Indicative of the current appetite, it is understood that the vessel drew up to 10 potential buyers with SUMEC inviting offers on the 17th of May which saw the vessel being sold at price of Usd 31.3m

Week started off first with holidays in Asia and in addition shipping event in Denmark slowing down activity on all fronts. USG remained flat with lack of fresh enquiries. 57,000 dwt seemed to be covered for US Gulf round trip in the higher USD 30,000’s. Ultramax was fixed basis delivery Turkey 15/20 May for 11/12 months trading at USD 29,000. Seemed it appeared less tonnage from East Coast South America. From the East, some more activity on Indonesian coal although not too much reported. Utramax open Lanshan was fixed for a nickel ore run from Philippines to China at USD 30,000 but no further details came to light. 52,000 dwt was fixed basis delivery Jakarta via Indonesia redelivery China at USD 29,000.

A further low-key week for the Panamaxes with the Atlantic showing further signs of easing with a distinct lack of transatlantic mineral demand piling pressure on the nearby positions. This despite decent numbers being achieved for the grain round trips. Asia witnessed a further slow week and lacking any real momentum especially in the South with Indonesia yet to show its hand this week.  Some representative fixtures this week:  The BBG Fangcheng (81,629/2019) Gibraltar 21 May fixed for a grain fronthaul trip at USD 41,000 with the rumor a grain house, but precise details remained under wraps.    The scrubber fitted Ultra Margay (81,921/2020) Gibraltar prompt fixed for a trip via US East Coast redelivery Gibraltar-Skaw at USD 34,000 with Oldendorff, with the scrubber benefit for charterers.   The scrubber fitted Darya Preeti (81,981/2019) Nansha 19-21 May was placed on subjects for a trip via Indonesia redelivery India at USD 31,000 with Norvic Bulk India.

This week has delivered on the premise that the shipping market is indeed strengthening, for which the signs were already starting to be visible a few weeks back. The latest levels for concluded spot fixtures have not only made us increase the headline rates across the board, but also required a notch-up on our Ballast Bonus sentiment, since charterers might now have to absorb more idle time to secure vessels unless one manages to find a perfect matching delivery/redelivery dates and location. Modern vessel availability also continues to slim down, although it is to be noted that many of the recent spot fixtures are for relatively short single voyages, meaning that the forward availability still have some length. Term markets have also been active, as new modern vessel positions are met with considerable interest, although term levels seem to be more stable, with slight upward pressure. Last but not least, the general newbuilding market remains red hot with ordering interest from several shipping segments. Newbuild prices remain firm and shipyards are receiving interest on their next available slots, even if it’s getting bit far out in time.

Market continues to firm as the appetite for vessels in the Far East continues. The fact that both West Australia and Indonesia have been very active over the last weeks is now making an impact on the nearby laycans out of South Africa which see limited amount of tonnage available. This together with improvements in the Atlantic indicates that market levels will go higher for the next week to come.

The NSea took another hit last week as the market is dominated by relets and Suezmaxes for local runs. Supply of vessels is sufficient for the time being and with Baltic loadings becoming more complex owners are on the look for alternatives. Ultimately crude oil softness did allow propane to weaken, closing the day at $1.20/gal, off by nearly 2cts/gal from the day prior.  At this point propane has fallen to 47% of WTI, having been sliding since Oct 2021. Terminal fees in the U.S. have been slowly rising, having been in the low 4cpg range only a couple of weeks ago and in the upper 4s/lower 5s range last week, only to eclipse the 6cpg level this week.  Asking levels are now at least 6.5cpg, with some priced even higher, still.  NWE The European prices lost ground after crude slid this week, this coupled with the less than inspiring US inventory build has narrowed the arb and hurt netbacks in this strong freight environment. So far none of these trades have been heard done and without window deals the levels have not seen a correction. For the time being Europe is seeing good demand and though much of the prompt looks to be accounted for, we expect to see European petchems looking to buy CFR cargoes for June arrival.    MED There is a distinctly summer market feel in the region. With no new demand being shown the market is subdued although the arb is open. Much of the spot demand has been filled by US cargoes. LPG – Gasoline arb is making Autogas favorable in the East Med.
