text: AMERICAS The market was taken aback by the large inventory build reported by the EIA on Wednesday, which showed a build of 3.4mmbbls on a week-over-week basis and which now stand at 44.2mmbbls, or just over 100% of last year.  Notably, however, current propane inventories are just 66% of two years ago. The market had been anticipating a build of between 1.25-2.25mmbbls, with most centered around the +1.75mmbbl level.  To then realize a build of nearly double was surprising, but that soon gave way to a sense of skepticism, mostly related to the PADD III build of 3.8mmbbls, which suggests that either production levels have grown dramatically, or waterborne exports have declined – or both.  But neither seems plausible and hence the doubt.  As such, observers and participants alike are now expecting a set of corrected numbers in the forthcoming data. Terminal fees remain under pressure, though very little has been accomplished this week.  The last known June transactions were fixed on either side of 5cpg, with 2H 2022 strip interest generally talked on either side of around the 6cpg level by both buyers and re-sellers.  NWE The end-May TOT buying interest in the window from BASF was hit by Vitol at 84.75% May Naphtha. Total, the other sellers disappeared. That deal was the last expected to be done for May. The European market is now focused on June and with crackers expected to come out of spring maintenance mid-May through mid-June and the market is showing strength in anticipation of this rise in demand. This weeks rise in Brent coupled with a large build in US inventories has propane at a slightly better than $160pmt discount to Naphtha and netback values form the US above 5cpg. Workable once again! Freight has continued to rise, taking a large chunk of the wider arb particularly to Europe as owners set a premium for US to Europe voyages in the hope of fixing longer voyages East at today’s high rates. Spot butane deals have not been seen in the market for some time and any new deal would set market levels.  CIF ARA Butane values have come off as US supply heads to the region. Value now assessed at 98% May Naphtha, relative to propane this is strong with the rise in crude pushing up May Naphtha values.   MED As other regions the local LPG prices have risen with crude oil values. May is more or less covered through term deliveries, with traders looking into June.

Rates continue their upward trajectory and owners are increasingly including positioning payments in their offers. This is not to say that winter has arrived, rather the market is wrestling with the innate inefficiencies of Europe being the premium market for the 6th month in a row. Conventional metrics for assessing utilisation are no longer relevant as tonne-time has soared in the battle to secure slots into NWE (with the DES LNG discount to TTF reported at around $10/MMbtu yesterday). Portfolio tonnage is increasingly tied up in operational storage (i.e., seeking a home) meaning that a handful of new shorts have emerged both sides of Suez. These spot requirements have added to the already firm term market which has in turn dragged up short-term rates (in the Pacific especially). Charterers who were originally targeting cold 2-strokes are now more willing to accommodate older and warmer tonnage, as the list of available vessels to meet a growing number of laycans diminishes. This will be welcome news to “owners” of older tonnage who should be increasingly popular in this age of energy and shipping security.    Turning to Newbuilds, it’s been a quiet week for new orders, but prices continue their ascent.

Dry cargo markets continue to see a flurry of transactions with north of twenty vessels changing hands across all segments. With strong level of enquiries being met by steady stream of sale candidates, values remain relatively flat and pricings fall in line with last done. Notable activity in the Capesize sector where Synergy has bought the 2010 Koyo built MINERAL HAIKU at Usd 34m providing further benchmarks for Japanese designed vessels of similar vintage. Panamax and Kamsarmax segments have also joyed of a pick up of activity with 6 units being sold this week, mostly driven by Chinese built vessels with pricing at relative highs for sellers but at levels that remain attractive for buyers weighing Chinese designs against their Japanese counterparts.  Tanker sale and purchase markets seem to have lost steam again off the back of a relative softening on the chartering front. A freight volatility that continues to feed into a widening bid offer spread on the snp front with most potential sellers holding off for levels reflecting a largely expected recovery. As a result only four sales to report this week with most buying enquiries falling in the Aframax space where a number of discussions taking place which may translate into further sales in the near future.

Market activity is relatively muted as participants are enjoying various celebrations around the world. LNG prices have shown a slight drop as Asian demand remains weak due to Covid restrictions predominantly in China, while in the West there is also a softening due to gas supplies currently meeting demand in Europe and prompt DES pricing is now at a significant discount to TTF. In a boost to those markets that will be seeking to refill storages, Hammerfest may restart operations by the end of the month. In the spot market, most requirements still appear primarily in the East, likely in response to South Asian buyers looking at spot cargoes. Spot availability remains ample at both basins, but with markets opening up next week and activity picking up, we may see some reshuffling in portfolios and a subsequent decrease especially in modern tonnage. Term activity remains of focus as sentiments and rate levels keep rising. There has been no New Building orders reported so far this week but prices are steadily increasing. To those celebrating in the Middle East we are wishing Eid Mubarak and to those in the East, we hope everyone is having an enjoyable Golden Week!

The Aframax market in the North Sea and Baltic started on a quiet note this week with more tonnage piling up due to less cargo activity. Going forward we expect rates to be under downward pressure. We might see some owners ballast away heading towards the Mediterranean which are showing some more promising trends compared to its neighboring North Sea market.   The Med/Bsea market has moved more or less sideways for most of the week with ships being fixed at repeat levels. However, as talks of FM being lifted in Libyan ports is flourishing this week there is a firm undertone among owners. At the same time we have seen a few stems being worked ex Bsea now, and we expect the firm trend to continue into next week.

text: MEG Following the crude rebound, June propane CP was traded higher at $815 and butane at $825. June/Jul CP was traded at $10ish backwardation. Spot discounts for early June lifting FOB was assessed at minus high single digit, however some buyer asking double digits discounts or more, in view of weak cash premium on delivered basis against firm freight rates.   FAR EAST Activities were muted earlier this week as of holiday. In window 23kt propane for 1h June delivery was offered at Jun FEI plus low teens and barely see bid interests, while parcel for 2h June was assessed slightly lower. Off window a handful of tenders are floating in the market from Thursday. Taiwan FPCC issued buy tender to secure 23kt or upto 46kt LPG for 1h Jun delivery. One Korean importer also tendered to buy 1-9th June delivered 23kt propane or evenly split cargo. Another Korean petchem importer tendered to procure monthly 3 lots of 23kt propane from Jul 2022 to June 2023 delivery, whom recent was reported to secure a 23kt butane for mid June delivery at mopj minus 30s.

Players back from holidays and activity up for the big ships - resultant average daily spot earnings improving slightly w-o-w to come in at tick over USD 19k. Fronthaul and transatlantic volumes plus levels, with only a few well-paying "exotic" exceptions, keep disappointing, with the describing TC-value Cont-Med to Far East being stuck at below USD 35k/day. The West Australia/China iron ore conference trade is stable/moderate in comparison, reflected by values for Pacific rounds standing just about still at USD 24k/day. Bright spot being coal trades and particularly anything related to India - tenfolds of Capes done during last few trading days for Indonesia/India alone. Period interest remain significant, with derivative values giving part support - representative fixtures include 180,000 dwt built 2016 done for a year BCI ave5tc + 22 pct, 180,000 dwt built 2015 fixed for a year at USD 31k, and 182,000 dwt built 2015 for 5 years at a reported USD 25,500/day.

Despite the big pressure on cargo supply from the Black Sea and Baltic, the market keeps firm sentiment. ECSA and USG pushing rates up even with the ships ballasting from the Continent and Med does not change strong demand in those markets. Stable Pacific market supporting good levels that owners asking. Today's levels are in the low USD 30,000 pd for Atlantic RV on Supra with premium for Ultras. Pacific RV are trading in the high USD 20,000 pd. Fronthaul Black Sea to Far East is like Continent to Far East fixing in the low/mid USD 20,000 pd on Tess 58.

The week gone by has been a sluggish one with VLCC rates continuing to slide in all areas, now well established just north of WS 45 from both MEG and Wafr. Arguably major trading hubs have been off on holiday, with China and Japan only back tomorrow, but a well-stocked position list will not scare charterers as they resume fixing the remainder of the April MEG program. text: AMERICAS The EIA reported a 1.6mmbbl week-over-week increase in domestic US propane stocks for the reporting period ending 29 April.  This brings the overall total stock level to 40.8mmbbls, or 98% of last year’s total and 66% of the total achieved in 2020. In order for inventories to reach the desired 80mmbbl level by end Oct 2022, and with 26 weeks remaining in the traditional ‘build’ period, an average weekly improvement of 1.51mmbbls will be required.  For the past five years, and for the period from May through Oct, the weekly build rate has averaged 2.064mmbbls.  Therefore, the desired level of approximately 80mmbbls should be achieved with relative ease.  This is in spite of generally robust export volumes but because of the rising production levels. Meanwhile, current terminal fee market levels for June range from around 5cpg to 6cpg, depending on timing, grade(s) and level of desire (from both sides).  A number of offers – particularly 50/50 parcels - have recently populated the market, but buyers note the ongoing backwardation and remain cautious.  NWE The spot market in the region has been active, and is trading end May. The bid/offer level in the TOT window has been wide, with many bidders today seeing an inflated market value in the window. Today the bottom line is that the arb from the US is closed and that production in Europe remains 30-40% below usual. Some spring maintenance is being carried out by petchems reducing demand at the same time as mild weather in the region further reducing demand. Cargoes remain well bid and offered, and physical value we assess at a small premium to May CIF ARA. That said cargoes continue to flow to the region from the US and find homes at premiums to CIF ARA outside of the window. So it looks like netback values are not painting the whole picture.   MED Traders in much of the region are off this week due to Eid holidays. The market has been subdued recently without many spot deals heard done to set market value

The week gone by has been a sluggish one with VLCC rates continuing to slide in all areas, now well established just north of WS 45 from both MEG and Wafr. Arguably major trading hubs have been off on holiday, with China and Japan only back tomorrow, but a well-stocked position list will not scare charterers as they resume fixing the remainder of the April MEG program. The armada of ships ballasting West on spec when things were looking brighter has similarly tilted things in favour of charterers with Atlantic cargo to cover. All in all, bleak prospects short term.

Deal of the week being Delta Tankers’ purchase of Suezmax STENA SUPREME built 2012 Samsung at Usd 37.5 mill basis prompt delivery FE with SS and BWTS due by the end of June. Last comparable sale was in March when DENSA ORCA also built 2012 Samsung was sold for Usd 32.5 mill with her SS imminently due as well. Even allowing for the fact that the Stena vessel has electronic main engine, this represents a hike of 12-14% in a short time. Aframax, Suezmax and MR are all hot commodity and VLCC values will also be following suit. Last done prices are becoming less relevant with sellers gaining the upper hand.  Euronav has confirmed the acquisition of two VLCC's from Hartree, both scrubber fitted DSME units - GHILLIE built in 2019 and CHELSEA in 2020 and the en-bloc price is Usd 179 mill; a tick down compared to what has been speculated in advance. Euronav also confirmed the sale of four non eco VLCCs built 2011 and 2012 for an en-bloc price of Usd 198 mill. The confirmed price is in line with what we reported as being done to Sinokor in March.  Transactions in the 33k dwt stainless steel segment are rare indeed but Stolt Tankers is now reported have acquired three such vessels from K-Line built 2012 and 2013 at an en-bloc price of Usd 76 mill. The last deal in this segment was in early 2021 when EGD Shipholding bought two vessels built 2009.   Bulkers continue to change hands across all segments. Values are moving sideways with continued focus on the smaller sizes. However two Capesize sales to report this week. The limited supply of modern Capesize for sale and sellers unwilling to reduce asking levels, bode for new higher benchmark deals in the near future. To date, the last modern Capesize deal was in April for RED SAGE 2015 JMU built at Usd 47.5.

Aframax spot earnings in the Baltic were reduced significantly on the back of a greater tonnage supply despite expected tougher EU sanctions over imports of Russian Oil and gas from May 15. In the North Sea we expect rates to continue to move sideways with a slight downward pressure due to lack of cargo activity in the first decade of May. But once the SPR exports from the USG kicks in, which could favor Aframax, we might see rates firm again.  The Med/Bsea market took a solid downward correction this week much due to the FM in Libya resulting in lack of cargo activity. TD19 has taken a 60-70 point drop since last week. We foresee a continued soft Aframax segment in the week to come. One to watch is revival of Libyan ports.

To the casual observer, the VLCC market may look quiet and uninteresting this week. But, (and it's a big 'but') there is a long list of ships on subs/fully fixed with no details. Charterers successfully working from the shadows, leaving an impression of a quiet market with little or no traction, when in fact the opposite seems to be true. S-Oil fixed and lowered MEG/S.Korea to the mid 40’s yesterday, but on their favorable terms. TD3c is a little higher around WS 47.5 level for MEG/China. However, owners with modern, sired vessels could try to push this upwards, as they become more of a rarity on the position list and at the time of writing, a couple of market quotes in fresh. With Suezmaxes cooling, VLCC opportunities in the Atlantic are becoming a little rarer, and there is a flotilla heading that way. But hope remains.

Whilst the downward correction was faster than most had predicted, a slide, nonetheless, was inevitable.  No change in the dynamics and fundamentals this week with too many ballasters heading into the Atlantic and a similar scenario impacting rates for Russia loads (albeit, not to the same degree of course).  Second decade TD20 is fixing up to mid-month, suggesting a chunk of cargoes have already covered, therefore we expect rates to threaten the WS 90 mark with an East run trading around WS 100. MEG/East will follow the same trend. Td23 looks consigned to the WS 40's unless we see a drastic uptick of inquiry. It's not all doom and gloom and we expect this market remain volatile in the short/medium term.

text: AMERICAS  Pricing volatility is the key factor in the domestic U.S. propane market, as Mont Belvieu values have declined over the course of April but seen vast pricing swings in the meanwhile.  The combination of reactive crude and natural gas prices - which are tightly linked to both the lingering Covid-related issues in the East and the war in Ukraine – has allowed April MB propane to conclude in the high $1.20’s/gal. According to the EIA, US propane inventory levels as of 22 April increased by 2.2mmbbls from the previous week, though some observers cast doubt on the accuracy of the data and are already anticipating a set of corrective data in the weeks to come.  The build was larger than expected but the market nonetheless gained a penny on the day, confounding many. Domestic production levels reached their highest levels ever, but robust exports in April (and going forward) have left the impression that a series of pushes and pulls – a ‘tug of war’, in essence - will be seen through the summer in a battle pitting production levels versus export volumes.  NWE May CIF ARA propane was last marked at $752/t (up by $4/t) as the European market looked to buy May propane and butane due to multi-dimensional supply constraints in the North Sea. The first due to lagging output in Norway due to maintenance at gas processing centers, in addition to notable decrease in exports availability pertaining to disruption in Russian product. OPIS reported a decrease nearing 35% in April exports compared to the same period last year. That said,  propane has continued its weakness in relation to naphtha- The spread has averaged -$136/t in April, compared to -$78/t same time last year, and presently sits at  -$138/t. For this reason, LPG cargos loading from US East Coast, continue to garner heavy interest as European buyers look to maintain equilibrium due to the aforementioned supply disruptions in the North Sea.  MED The Med continues to be tight, butane which has been hard to find in the region allowing the arb from the US to the Med to widen- acting as a valve to mitigate supply pressure -as vessels STS into coasters in the region. Continued maintenance on a pair of West-Med crackers has been extended slightly, however the news did little to exacerbate current tightness.

EAST The momentum on freight seen in the East in recent weeks has come to a halt. Last done deal for Singapore-Japan range was done around USD 70 Baltic, but with the current length that we are seeing on freight bss 1H May MEG, we expect next deal do be done sub USD 70. At the time of writing, one Indian major is trying to defer loading dates for a Red Sea lifting, and meanwhile we are waiting for more market requirements before ‘Golden Week’ kicks in from next week.  WEST It seems like the market has taken a bit of breather, but with “Golden Week” coming up one should expect more fixing to be done this week as the western market still remains fairly strong. Only three spot fixtures concluded so far this week with last done at mid/high USD 120s Houston/Chiba range and low USD 70s Houston/Flushing. We have so far seen about 30 spot fixtures in May and expect the last few remaining vessels left in end May to soon find suitable cargos before focus shifts entirely to June and the summer months. Vessel supply looks tight, and with Panama waiting up to 9 days North- and 11 Southbound, it should add even more tightness to the market.

The market is improving towards the end of the week, ahead of the holidays coming up Monday and Tuesday. C5 being the most active route, with freight rates in the low USD 12s pmt being concluded. All the miners are active. Another active route is Indo/India, whilst Brazilian iron ore still more or less absent, also reflected by the negative trend on the c3 route. However, the average index is at USD 18,500, and still improving.

The Supra market in the Atlantic remains strong across all main routes. USG and ECSA are most lucrative areas with strong demand for Far East as well as across Atlantic trips.   Ultramax was reported fixing USD 33,000 pd deliver Miss River for a trip with grains Singapore-Japan. ECSA continued with good activities during Easter holidays, though very little was reported. The Supramax rumored to fix basis dely Brazil at USD 50,000 pd for TCT to Mediterranean Sea with grains. Furthermore, an Ultramax, 63’ dwt, delivery Chile for loading in Argentina at USD 40,000 pd for trip with grains to Morocco.   North Atlantic and Med markets followed similar trend with good activities, and we experienced a strong push on rates on certain trades. Trips from Continent to Med with scrap fixing in very high 20's dop on modern Supramax. The owners who are willing and able to do Russian ports is getting up to 3 times premium, reaching USD 80,000 pd for delivering Baltic for any direction within Atlantic.  Indian Ocean South Africa markets are stable with rates remaining strong both for backhauls and fronthaul trips. Supramax 58’ dwt open WCI was fixed at USD 27,000 pd for trip to Bangladesh with aggregates.  A few Ultras were heard to be fixed around low USD 35,000 dop WCI with redely Far East. Far Eastern market were slow with noticeable rate reduction, for Tess 58 delivery China via Australia redly China, owners were accepting around USD 25,000 pd.

An inauspicious start for the Panamax market following the holidays, the market was slow to get started according to sources. Asia appeared poised for a further push as sentiment remained positive with some seeing better bids but fixing activity had yet to get going thus far.   A distinct lack of fixing and activity to report on but the market seemed steady according to most sources. On the surface demand ex EC South America still appeared healthy and with a decent amount of mineral demand too, the early feelings were largely confident of a push.  Some representative fixtures this week: Bahri Grain (81,855/2014) Dammam 21 April fixing basis 4/6 months at USD 31,200 to ST Shipping. Orion III (76,602/2005) CJK 20/30 April going to Ming Wah basis 4/6 months at USD 22,000.

The April MEG program closed out with a healthy 140+ fixtures, so we watch to see what May has to offer. There is only 10 days left of the current month, so May should be gathering speed. As such, plenty of ships on subs, with no details attached as charterers seek to work from the shadows to keep activity private. The position list remains well stocked, and as a result, owners are struggling to keep hold of the pre-Easter gains, with rates slipping to the WS 50 level for modern well badged MEG/China.  Activity remains in the Atlantic with a number of cargoes looking ex USG at the time of writing. However, Suezmaxes are wobbling a bit as VLCC’s have been stepping on their toes for West Africa runs. With an armada of modern units ballasting west to seek their fortune, logic dictates that rates are capped in the short term.

Baltic rates ex Russian ports is also under downward pressure as more tonnage willing to call Russian ports are emerging while awaiting further news about any possible further sanctions on Russian oil. Going forward we expect the market to move sideways with a softer undertone if we don’t see an uptick in activity. As expected, tonnage is also building up in the area and we have seen a downwards correction in rates. We expect the market to remain soft in the natural fixing window.

Suezmax STENA SUPREME 2012 SHI invited offers yesterday. The vessel is expected to be sold next week and price to be north of USD 35 mill. text: AMERICAS  Bouyancy in the crude arena continues supporting LPG markets and propane values at Mont Belvieu remain above $1.30/gal for May.  WTI as of this writing is up 2.5% at $104.63/bbl but largely dependent upon both the events related to the Russia/Ukraine war, but also Covid-related shutdowns, particularly in China. From the domestic US perspective, the EIA data released yesterday showed a build of 1.6mmbbls – just a bit more than anticipated – to an overall total of 37mmbbls, which is 91% of last year but 62% of two years ago.  Stocks built on the Gulf Coast (PADD III) but showed a decline in both the East Coast and Midwest regions (PADDs I and II). Due to the lack of cancellations and ‘buyback’ cargoes, ongoing and robust export volumes in April were expected to have limited the build in Gulf Coast stocks, but instead the decline in domestic demand is being cited as the explanation.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, range rather widely as buy-side ideas remain in the 4cpg area but sellers seem to content in the 6 cpg range.  Reduced arbs and higher freight rates are contributing factors, as well.  NWE The arb to the region has narrowed bringing trans-Atlantic netbacks into the high 3cpgs or low 4cpgs. The build in US inventories did not have an immediate bearish effect on MT Belvieu values and any moves were negated by strong freight. Houston-Flushing is now heard to be nearing $70pmts with no sign of coming off for May loadings. Propane vs Naphtha in the region continues to heavily favour propane with April, May and June Pro/Nap in the $140pmts. Though this figure has to be taken in context, with Natural Gas at $25mmBTU, making power expensive, and reduced demand for manufacturing due to supply chain issues clouding the picture. The spring weather in Europe has been very pleasant this year, so any additional inland demand has been due to larger geopolitical issues and crude oil price moves. Demand in the region remains and though urgent buying has not been seen since returning from Easter holidays.  MED The Med continues to be tight, butane in particular hard to find in the region. The arb from the US to the Med is open which will release some supply pressure as vessels STS into coasters in the region.

The spot market again saw quite a lot of activity, with a number of ships fixed in both basins. The disparity that has been seen in recent weeks between the softer market for loadings East of Suez versus those loading West of Suez does still remain, but has narrowed due to steady gains in the Pacific. Otherwise, it has been a familiar pattern of sublet vessels being marketed for relatively narrow pockets of availability, and either fixing or being withdrawn for internal use. Thus, the churn within the availability list is still outpacing the number of enquires to be worked. Term business continues to attract the few independent owners with tonnage remaining, as well as those charterers with enough length to play with. Stepping back from the microcosm of the LNG shipping market, the ongoing consequences from the terrible situation in Ukraine is behind a renewed attention on energy supply and security. The LNG markets will come into sharp geopolitical focus and although the implications are yet to be fully understood, we anticipate a lot of activity on LNG import and export projects.      In the newbuilding front, there were six orders at Hudong, placed as one order by COSCO for Sinopec needs.

A week where the pendulum has swung firmly in owners’ favour. The Afra and Suez market had been enjoying a bump for some time, but the trickle up has finally reached VL owners’ pockets as economy of scale kicked in. The Atlantic has shot up and realistically Wafr/East now starts with a 6. The VL’s have even been dining at the Smax table for runs to the UKCM, without so much as denting the latter. Add to that continued demand from the Americas and we have the makings of a perfect storm. With the change in trading patterns and increased ton-mile, it's starting to look like a paradigm shift. The MEG has followed suit, WS 50 mark for eastbound voyages on modern, but the tonnage list there remains populated with ships committed to the MEG due to age, background, and capping procedures, so cheaper alternatives are available.

Aframax rates in the West have pushed up quite significantly over the past couple of days. Owners in the North Sea and Mediterranean have reassessed their rate ideas on the back of surrounding market in the Mediterranean and USG/Caribs offering an alternative. Going forward we expect a firm market with upward pressure on the rates as the tonnage list is looking tighter for the next loading window.

Levels for the big ships dipping further as slow port turnaround/increased congestion remains insufficient to compensate for markedly lower mineral volumes traded compared to same period last year. Daily average earnings down 10 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 12k. Pain most acutely felt in Pacific, where values for rounds have fallen by 45 pct over last 5 trading days as fresh coal and in particular iron ore activity has been uninspiring. Transatlantic rates are steady in comparison, but with relevant quantities too insignificant to make much difference. Fronthaul trades remain a reflection of main Brazilian miners being far behind production and export guidance. Market generally (still) very much in contango, with keen interest in period candidates of virtually all size and colour - exemplified by vintage unit 171,000 dwt, built 2003, recently done for rest of 2022 at USD 25k.

Suezmax rates in the Atlantic continue an upward trajectory. But lest we forget the backstory, we need to look back to where this market really began to take on a life all of its own, and it commenced with that hugely impactful Wafr Petrogal fixture at WS 140 (last week). Whilst it's too early to call a cap to proceedings, the key indicator to a potential ceiling lies in the East, and namely the acute lack of MEG/East stems. This suggests that a large number of Eastern ballasters will set a course Wafr if the East doesn't pick up this side of the weekend. So, let's put a number on proceedings. You won't get much change from WS 180 for TD20 today whilst in the East modern units will be looking WS 60's for TD23. MEG/East needs testing but modern ships are talking WS 110'ish today with further firming potential.

With bigger uncertainty on the Russian coal ban and further sanctions it’s hard to say what direction the market will take – but would say market will remain strong with a slight drop over the easter. Owners willing to call Russian ports still seeing huge premiums at rates around 70-80,000.    FFA kept falling all week whilst South America FH remains thick firmer. It’s basically been a drop all over further markets and the gap between the bid/offer keeps spreading. Period market have also seen a heavy correction and is more or less not even present on the longer ones. Rate wise Continent front haul was fixed at lower 20s on a Supramax – from USG similar vessel where fixed low 30k.

A weaker Panamax index overall but according to some sources some signs of green shoots of recovery for the longer grain front haul trips especially for earlier than index dates, so this brought into play some of the Continent/Mediterranean positions which had been pegged back of late. Despite holidays in some parts, activity in Asia remained healthy, and sources felt some of the early ships had been shifted in the North and the focus for some of the tonnage here was to consider the ballast South. In the South, some tonnage with limited options or with specific trade in mind conceded cheaper rates with charterers holding the upper hand.  Some representative fixtures this week:  Peney (81,886/2016) was sourced by Cargill basis delivery aps EC South America 25 April for a trip redelivery Far East at USD 27,000 + USD 1,700,000 ballast bonus.  The Shun Chang (93,322/2010) Xingang 31 March fixed for round trip via Australia at USD 18,000 but details remained scarce.    Ultra Lynx (81,607/2018) Brake 2/4 April fixed for a trip via NC South America redelivery Skaw-Gibraltar at USD 28,000 to Norden.  The Jia Foison (75,535/2010) Qingdao 2 April was said to have fixed for a trip via EC Australia redelivery Southeast Asia with coal at USD 19,000 to Panocean.   The scrubber fitted Majorca (74,333/2005) was secured by Oldendorff basis retro sailing Qingdao 30 March was fixed for a trip via NoPac redelivery China with grains at USD 22,750 redelivery not north of CJK and USD 22,000 redelivery south of CJK basis scrubber benefit to going to owners.

Aframax rates in the West have pushed up quite significantly over the past couple of days. Owners in the North Sea and Mediterranean have reassessed their rate ideas on the back of surrounding market in the Mediterranean and USG/Caribs offering an alternative. Going forward we expect a firm market with upward pressure on the rates as the tonnage list is looking tighter for the next loading window.

A week where the pendulum has swung firmly in owners’ favour. The Afra and Suez market had been enjoying a bump for some time, but the trickle up has finally reached VL owners’ pockets as economy of scale kicked in. The Atlantic has shot up and realistically Wafr/East now starts with a 6. The VL’s have even been dining at the Smax table for runs to the UKCM, without so much as denting the latter. Add to that continued demand from the Americas and we have the makings of a perfect storm. With the change in trading patterns and increased ton-mile, it's starting to look like a paradigm shift. The MEG has followed suit, WS 50 mark for eastbound voyages on modern, but the tonnage list there remains populated with ships committed to the MEG due to age, background, and capping procedures, so cheaper alternatives are available.

Suezmax rates in the Atlantic continue an upward trajectory. But lest we forget the backstory, we need to look back to where this market really began to take on a life all of its own, and it commenced with that hugely impactful Wafr Petrogal fixture at WS 140 (last week). Whilst it's too early to call a cap to proceedings, the key indicator to a potential ceiling lies in the East, and namely the acute lack of MEG/East stems. This suggests that a large number of Eastern ballasters will set a course Wafr if the East doesn't pick up this side of the weekend. So, let's put a number on proceedings. You won't get much change from WS 180 for TD20 today whilst in the East modern units will be looking WS 60's for TD23. MEG/East needs testing but modern ships are talking WS 110'ish today with further firming potential.

Over the last week we’ve seen a steady flow of spot shipping requirements coming to the market with a shift of availability, neatly matching the new requirements. The overall activity has left the spot rates unchanged. Overarching all spot discussions is the term availability of + 170k CBM vessels and remaining and/or pending requirements to be filled until the end of 2023. The overall availability is apparently scarce, with some occasional subletters making a short appearance before their tonnage is either fixed or withdrawn. We believe that the overall focus on term coverage will persist as the market adopts to the new normal. NB prices continues to increase and does the activity at Yard’s where we’ve recorded 3 NB’s booked this week.

text: MEG May C3 CP dropped to $808 as oil slumps to three-week low, and C4 CP was at $15 higher than C3 as butane more favourable into summer season. May/Jun C3 CP was traded at $30 backwardation. Two evenly split cargos for May lifting changed hand at CP minus 10 level reportedly.  FAR EAST This week in window 23kt propane for 1h May delivery was traded at May FEI plus $35, while similar cargo for 2h May delivery was offered from mid 30s to high 20s on FEI link. Off window one Korean importer was reported to buy 23kt propane for 15-21 May delivery into Dasean at May FEI plus 20s. One EChina PDH issued tender to buy 23kt or 46kt propane for May delivery, and 23kt propane monthly from Jun to Dec delivery. Another EChina PDH also covered 23kt propane for May delivery reportedly.  Despite the recent decline in cost, PDH margins are still not healthy and two EChina PDHs, each with 600kt/y capacity, are reported to have turnround plan for 30-40 days from 2h Apr and May respectively.

A week dominated by a tanker market that seem to have finally caught up with the long drawn expectations of a market upturn. We have witnessed rates going from strength to strength in all major sectors establishing a positive sentiment across the board. A sentiment supported by news of further consolidation with the announcement of the merger between Frontline and Euronav creating the largest tanker owning company in the market comprising of 69 VLCCs and 57 Suezmax. A move that seems to have been mostly welcome by most as a sign of great commitment by some of the market leaders. This week also comes to a close with a number of units changing hands, notable activity in the Aframax market that has seen GNTMC acquire the two sisterships from Atlas Maritime built at Daehan with delivery in 2022 at a price of Usd 61m each. A price reflective of current NB environment considering that these contracts were placed in the mid 40s in 2020. We expect further activity in the sector as exhibited by a growing buying enquiry with strengthening bids trying to go meet an offer that is now firmly into a sellers market.

EAST A couple of vessels were taken out in the East at the very end of last week in the mid $60s. Positions did slim down as a result, and with potentially a few late quotes from Indians or some ships running late - next deals could quickly climb toward high $60s in the East. However, this has yet to materialize. When comparing some 18 concluded spot fixtures for April with an average month, it is fair to say that the East market is currently looking well balanced as we gradually look towards May and the next round of acceptances.  WEST With Easter just around the corner the US market has in the span of just two days seen more than a dozen cargoes quoted and above half of these already placed on subs. Most of the fixing is now focused in and around the second decade of May and we expect most market players would be counting on sorting their programs up until the beginning of third decade prior Easter. Freight levels in the first round of fixing this week has been largely hovering around 112 H/C and low 60 H/F. Owners ideas for fixing today, from those willing to show ideas, are at the time of writing being bumped up by at least 2-3 dollars on top of last done. Time will tell if the market is currently a bit overheated or if it’s a bad idea to gamble for the dust to settle.

text: AMERICAS  Since the end of March the Mont Belvieu propane market has seen intermittent declines which have been interrupted by small spurts of buoyancy, though all told the market has seen more softness than not.  This is owing to the combination of declines in winter-related demand and that crude oil has been coming off in recent days. Inventory levels in the U.S. have for two consecutive weeks risen, though rather modestly. Current stocks are posted by the EIA at 34.4mmbbls, or about 86% of last year and 57% of two years ago.  The market is beginning to think about how robust exports over the summer will match against slowly rising production levels, and calculating a required average build of 2mmbbls over the coming 5 or 6 months in order to reach ~80mmbbls by end-Sep / early Oct.  Convention wisdom is calling for a traditional tug of war between the two factors, and through the duration of the coming summer. Terminal fees on the Gulf Coast, meanwhile, are presently seen on offer at 6.00-6.50cpg, though a more enthusiastic seller was seen in the upper 5cpg range.  Buyers, however, have generally retreated to sub-5cpg levels unless a cargo is in need of being fixed immediately.    A spate of fixtures was reportedly accomplished over the past few days, and market intel indicates those parcels were concluded with a 6-handle.  NWE US crude oil inventories, rather than LPG publishing a big build caused a rapid drop in global crude oil values. This kept traders out of the TOT window and pushed outright CIF ARA values down over $30pmt. The transatlantic netbacks have been squeezed all week. Weakness in the European market has been partly attributed to the shift to the summer market and partly due to industrial demand expected to be reduced by planned maintenances. Production in the region has not increased as LPG continues to be spiked into the natural gas stream where possible. The continued question over whether European countries will put sanctions on Russian Energy, which would turn the market on it’s head. For the time being the crude moves and warmer temperatures coming in are keeping the market fairly quiet.  MED The Med remains tight, particularly propane, as strong winds hamper Algerian loadings. The commencement of Ramadan will keep the market quiet in the near future.

Rates in the Nsea and Baltic are firming on the back of continued activity ex Baltic where tonnage supply is minimal for any cargoes being lifted ex Russian ports. Rates in the Nsea are also under upward pressure for those looking for coverage for a lay can up to the 8th of April. Going forward, we expect the market to remain firm as we still expect more enquiries in the current fixing window.  From a slight softening trend in the Med/Bsea last week, we have seen rates pick up again on the back of a tighter tonnage list. Increased cargo activity also supporting same. CPC outage still lagging, and quite a few owners still reluctant to entertain Bsea business. We expect the market to remain steady/firm in the short run.

The market has gone from bad to worse as activity in the East has slowed down and the Atlantic tonnage list are building up. The increasing volumes out of Brazil is helping, but still not sufficient to give enough support to change sentiment. The war is still making a huge impact for the segment and the Atlantic is suffering down 38% w-o-w compared to “only” down by 17% in the Pacific. On a more positive note, we do expect more iron ore cargoes out of Brazil for April, thus we are slightly positive for the week to come.

A two-tier market (Russia and the rest) still persists but that doesn't mean all other markets are dull. Far from it. The Atlantic, and in particular the US Gulf, continues to spew out transatlantic enquiry with rates trading at a minimum 145kt x WS 95+. A tight natural list coupled with steady Wafr enquiry is applying further pressure to TD20 which looks like it will touch high WS 90's before too long. In the East, Kozmino has become the latest Suezmax hotspot with a number of ships being held in the East by this type of short haul business. A north China run trades about USD 950k, but further cannibalizations is expected and may touch USD 900k by next week. MEG/East is the enigma. It's been deathly quiet with very little enquiry working in the open market. MEG/China trades WS 90 flat.

Supramax and Ultramax are losing grounds across the board. We could see the shift in rates from strong Pacific to weaker Atlantic. The Pacific market has dropped quite substantially. Last week fixtures were reported for 63,000 dwt delivering SE Asia at USD 43,000 pd for a trip via Indonesia to South China, and smaller Supra of 56,000 dwt delivering Singapore was done at USD 44,000 pd. This week charterers rating tonnage in the low/mid USD 30,000 pd for Pacific trips. Trip from China to Atlantic still paying premium in the USD 40,000 pd. The Atlantic is improving, mainly due to ECSA and USG cargos inquiry increased. We see rates reported delivery ECSA for TCT to Mediterranean USD 58,000 pd, while USEC is paying much less. Ultramax ballast from Continent fixed USD 38,000 pd APS Baltimore for trip to Med. Scrap cargo from Continent increased to USD 25,000 pd from high USD 10,000 pd. Front haul from Black Sea and Continent around USD 30,000 pd on Supra with small premium for Ultramax.

The week was a week of red ink for the Panamax market as markets continued to ease with all routes seemingly under pressure. Asia was said by some to be softening on the longer round trips rather than free falling, whereas the short Indonesian round trips remained well gapped on the bid/offer spread. The Atlantic was a mixed bag of rates on fixtures reported but overall, the tone was weaker. The Evomarine controlled CL Geneva (85,228/2021) Flushing early April was rumoured placed on subjects for a transatlantic round at a rate close to USD 29/30,000 but little else emerged.  Despina V (80,734/2018) Jorf Lasfar prompt for a trip via NC South America redelivery Gibraltar-Skaw range at USD 32,500.  Klaveness secured on subjects the Yarra Star (82,624/2008) retro sailing Haldia 11 March for a trip via EC South America redelivery Indonesia at USD 28,000.  The Indus Victory (92,871/2013) Lanshan 29 March fixed with unnamed Japanese charterers for a trip via North China redelivery Japan at USD 28,000.   Cemtex Sincerity (82,200/2018) Onahama prompt agreed a rate of USD 30,500 for a trip via EC Australia redelivery India with Bainbridge Navigation.

Working the VLCC market at present, can seem like being uninvited to a party and resorting to looking through the windows. While other markets ebb and flow, ours remain somewhat subdued. However, for owners, some optimism should remain. At the time of writing, there are plenty of cargoes looking for transport. A pickup in activity (72 MEG cargoes, and we only fixing mid-month laycans) and many owners slow steaming is thinning the position list in both Atlantic and Fuj, (albeit mainly the modern-Approved-scrubbered vessels). text: AMERICAS  Crude oil market volatility, driven by headlines related to both Covid-19 issues in China and, separately, the war in Ukraine, has pushed most participants to the sidelines as the two issues have created opposing forces which – on alternating days – has caused WTI and Brent values to rise and fall at significant rates. Mont Belvieu propane, meanwhile, continues to ebb and flow consequently, having peaked on 08 Mar at $1.63/gal, only then to fall sharply to $1.22/gal by the 15th of the month.  That’s when an upward trajectory was resumed and a peak of $1.47/gal was seen, only then to fall again to $1.395/gal at present. The arbs have remained positive, however, as offshore values have mostly kept track all the while, though at present arbs have narrowed. Terminal fees, meanwhile, are loosely in the 6-7cpg range, depending on timing/ratio, etc., with a couple of outliers on either side.  One transaction to an end-user was reported for a late April 4:0 in the upper 6’s, another mixed-ratio parcel for April was said placed in the low/mid 6s.  NWE Competing macro factors in the oil market have made for a volatile week in Europe. NWE LPG prices came off considerably (11 dollars / ton) on back of Brent weakness, and large cargo activity was fairly quiet. That said, insecurity of supply surrounding the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, along with considerably cold temperatures across the region would theoretically stoke demand- however, its assumed that scheduled arrival of 1h April propane cargoes will sufficiently absorb the additional demand. The lack of strength of NWE price could also be attributed to the maintenance on as many as 5 steam crackers- that would otherwise be favoring propane- given the current discounts to naphtha.   MED Very little activity in Med LPG trade as the market mostly assessed the newly posted Sonatrach prices, that came in at an 8 year high following the strong ramp up in crude prices this month. Sonatrach posted prices of $870/ton $930/ton for propane and butane respectively.

EAST We continue to see activity on shipping in the East and the fixing window has shifted to last decade April basis MEG. Freight rates remain firm with last done reported around $65 baltic, and Owners targeting $65+ for next deals. There is still interest for shipping from outside regions such as WAF and USG, and as such we expect the current momentum seen on freight to continue.  WEST The West market is alive, it’s firm and it will be for the foreseeable future. We are counting between 35 to 40 odd spot fixtures for April and what were seemingly potential April hangover positions last week, have basically all been wiped out. Fixing focus is on first half May where there are already a handful of deals done in the USD 105-110 range Houston/Chiba basis and mid to high USD 50s Houston/Flushing basis. Northwest Europe has seen some twelve VLGC cargoes imported in March and in all likelihood, it is expected that a similar number of vessels will be heading to the region during April. Under normal circumstances, that many vessels heading to NWE during a single month could imply that freight may be taking a hit, however, as long as the same amount of cargoes are imported on VLGCs to NWE, it will keep the market on a leash.

text: MEG Following the oil price hike, Saudi raised Apr C3 CP at $940 and C4 CP at $960, up by $45 and $40 respectively, which is slightly higher than swap level but within expectations. Backwardation into May enlarged further, and May C3 CP was traded at $867.   FAR EAST 23kt propane for 2h Apr arrival was traded at Apr FEI plus $39 and $44 this week, and similar cargo for 1h May arrival at May FEI plus $48. Off window a couple of 2h May delivered propane was traded at Apr FEI minus small digits.  Main activities this week are still buy tenders from petchem users. One EChina PDH was reported to cover two propane cargo for May delivery at May FEI plus 30s. The PDH was said to resell their Apr term cargos due to ongoing turnaround program. Another EChina PDH also issued tender to secured 23kt propane parcel for end Apr/early May delivery. One Ningbo-based cracker procured a 1h May delivered 46kt propane reportedly at May FEI plus high 40s via tender. Other PDHs are keeping lower rates mostly, and one 600kt/y PDH in EChina is planning one-month turnround as of eroding margins. One Vietnam importer issued tender to buy 1-17th May delivered 3/1 or 2/2 ratio cargo.  One Australian origin evenly split cargo for late May early Apr arrival is available in the market.

With a market still trying to find its bearings in light of an ever-changing geopolitical situation and a week that is cut short by several national holidays, we close this Friday with a relatively subdued snp sentiment. Despite already closing one month into the conflict, the situation as expected remains highly volatile with sanctions and their impact on global trade representing a constant moving target for market players trying to identify alternative trading patterns. An uncertainty that is as usual felt the most in the SnP markets where potential buyers and sellers prefer to apply a wait and see approach before committing to any long-term decisions. This becomes particularly apparent in the tanker space where the gradual rate recovery should in essence provide enough support for buyers to start meeting the offers at hand but where we are still experiencing some reserve as to whether this gradual "recovery" has legs.  Dry markets continue to see very high levels of enquiry and as such liquidity remains relatively high in most sectors with Supramax and Ultramax leading the charge with a handful of vessels changing hands and signs of a number of ongoing negotiations. Levels are therefore well supported across the board with some segments seeing an appreciation in values, a trend that should be set for the foreseeable future.

A general easing of bunker prices should have helped owners’ bottom lines over the last week, down close to USD 825/mt for VLSFO in Spore. However, any savings were quickly transferred to the charterers pocket as rates have dropped in accordance. Voyages MEG to the East sit in the mid 30s depending on route/quality of ship. Hats off to charterers who have gone into stealth mode and playing the “fear-card” to perfection, picking ships off left, right and centre under the radar and leaving an impression of an inactive market when the opposite appears to be true, as charterers plow into their April stems. West Africa, clearly influenced by tonnage from the East as rates to China down to a last done of WS 37. Elsewhere in the Atlantic there is some hope, as prompter dates in the USG provide small gains, up to USD 5.4m to Ningbo.

Black Sea Suezmax rates have been one of the few shining lights in an otherwise flaccid market, and for obvious reasons. Therefore, when news started to filter through that the CPC SPM's had suffered serious “storm damage”, possibly hampering exports for number of weeks, a sharp intake of breath was likely taken by most Black Sea players. The good news is that only one SPMS is temporarily out of action whilst the remaining SPM is working normally. In the wider market, rates appear to be a little firmer in West Africa where an East run will trade WS 90's with TD20 trading mid WS 80'S. BOT/East is holding onto WS 90 by its fingertips whilst TD23 has done very well to hold onto WS 40's for a straight run. Kozmino/North China has seen a number of Suezmax's drawn into the mix as freights trade circa USD 1m.

Continued strong demand for minor bulks, as preliminary estimates for this month shows record high loadings. Demand remained strong from East Coast South America for TA. Ultramax was covered from Recalada to Algeria at about USD 49,000. Clinker round from Egypt to Monrovia were fixed close to USD 30,000.  Touch more reported from the Pacific basin. 57,000 dwt open Chittagong took USD 27,000 for a trip from EC India to China. Another 53,000 dwt open in Singapore was covered around USD 45,000 for a trip via Indonesia to China. From the North, 56,000 dwt open Bayuquan was finalized for a CIS Pacific round at USD 70,000. Some steels to USG from India paid owners USD 43,000 for a 58,000 dwt vessel open Haldia. Also a 52,000 dwt ship concluded business for trip via Thailand redel Haldia at USD 34,000 basis del Singapore.

Rates for the Nsea/Baltic Aframax market came off on the back of less activity. We still see quite high premiums for Russian trade despite a downward correction in rates. Some owners are not willing to fix current levels as the exposure for high bunker prices due to an unstable oil market is too high. Greater activity and firming rates in the USG/Caribs and the Euromed market might offer an alternative for those owners sitting with idle vessels on the Cont. Going forward we might see rates firm a bit.  Med/Bsea: Over the course of the last week we have seen healthy cargo activity push the rates up about 20 points before it all slowed down again, and rates have come back down to where they were prior to the weekend. One to watch going into next week is further developments concerning Novo port and the CPC pipeline.

Much of the activity and focus was grain led ex EC and NC South America with options to ex US Gulf and with bids further increasing against a tighter looking tonnage count, the front haul trip appeared to be impacted to this despite a lack of fixing. Asia continued to be reserved by comparison and largely flat aside from limited action ex NoPac with rates improving slightly over last done. YM Opus (81,863/2015) retro sailing Stade 19 March fixing for a trip via US Gulf option NC South America redelivery Skaw-Gibraltar range at USD 28,500 with Cargill. Navios Felicity I (81,962/2020) delivery aps EC South America 10 April was heard fixed for a trip redelivery Skaw-Gibraltar at USD 50,000. Frontier Leader (81,383/2013) retro sailing Hong Kong 21 March was placed on subjects for a trip via EC Australia redelivery India at USD 27,000. Amoy Sunny (76,598/2006) CJK end March secured by NS United for a trip via NoPac redelivery Japan at USD 26,500. Perseus (82,165/2013) Toyohashi prompt placed on subjects for a trip via NoPac redelivery Singapore-Japan with intention grains at a rate tick below USD 30,000. Boyang Garnet (75,764/2007) Rotterdam 23 March was fixed for a trip via NC South America redelivery Skaw-Gibraltar at USD 24,500 with Louis Dreyfus.

Slowdown for the big ships on key routes, consequent average daily earnings losing 20 pct w-o-w to come in at bit over USD 17k. World steel production lower than for same period last year - and dominating West Australia/China and Brazil/Feast trades both remain at far from full speed. A Europe in need for substantial long haul coal volumes to fill the void of Russian material only partly compensates, mildening a soft tendency by taking ship capacity out of the ordinary Pacific and front haul trades. Growing concern over Mediterranean tonnage build-up as Black Sea exports, normally absorbing some 10 units/month, have come to a complete stop - transatlantic market in deep need of increased mineral volumes to maintain levels. Forward expectations and thus period interest nevertheless remain positive and far above spot - representative fixtures include 180,000 dwt, built 2015, done for close to 2 years at a handsome USD 32k.

The trend in the charter market is set to continue from the previous weeks where demand for LNG vessels for a term charter has increased with various charterers issuing requirements seeking to secure tonnage over a period. The driver has certainly been security of LNG supply, given the recent geopolitical situation, however vessels are still expected to be in demand by charterers in anticipation of this year’s trading for winter, regardless of the ongoing events in Europe. These recent events have only added further demand to the already short tonnage situation for LNG vessels. As more vessels are secured by charterers on multi-year periods, the list of available modern vessels with length are diminishing over time, increasing owner’s expectations on the term charter rates. Meanwhile the spot market is relatively long with available vessels in both basins. Shipowners and subletters have been quite willing to propose competitive terms to secure spot charters during these “shoulder months” of April and May.   On newbuildings, an order has been reported at Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering (DSME) with two (2) ME-GI propelled vessels, with specifications including reliquefaction unit, air lubrication system and shaft generators. These vessels are expected to be delivered at the very end of 2025.

In the wider market, rates appear to be a little firmer in West Africa where an East run will trade WS 90's with TD20 trading mid WS 80'S. BOT/East is holding onto WS 90 by its fingertips whilst TD23 has done very well to hold onto WS 40's for a straight run. Kozmino/North China has seen a number of Suezmax's drawn into the mix as freights trade circa USD 1m.

A general easing of bunker prices should have helped owners’ bottom lines over the last week, down close to USD 825/mt for VLSFO in Spore. However, any savings were quickly transferred to the charterers pocket as rates have dropped in accordance. Voyages MEG to the East sit in the mid 30s depending on route/quality of ship. Hats off to charterers who have gone into stealth mode and playing the “fear-card” to perfection, picking ships off left, right and centre under the radar and leaving an impression of an inactive market when the opposite appears to be true, as charterers plow into their April stems. West Africa, clearly influenced by tonnage from the East as rates to China down to a last done of WS 37. Elsewhere in the Atlantic there is some hope, as prompter dates in the USG provide small gains, up to USD 5.4m to Ningbo.

text: AMERICAS Having risen with crude, which was following the unfolding news of the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the MB propane market reached a peak of $1.63/gal on 8th March, only to then sink to the low $1.20’s/gal by mid-month.  At that point the market turned again to the upside and was trading on an upwards trajectory towards $1.48/gal, only to reverse course today to current levels of $1.45/gal. In the background the EIA report for the week ending 18 March showed a modest build of 300,000bbls for an overall total of 33.6mmbbls (thus signaling the conclusion of winter), and which is 81% of the total achieved last year, and 56% of the total recorded two years ago.  The small rise in stock levels is attributed to three factors:  The decline of weather-related demand in North America, cargo buy-backs in March, and cargo cancellations in March (which when combined are reckoned at around a dozen or more cargoes). Domestic U.S. production, though healthy at 2.36mmbbls/day, is effectively flat on a week-over-week basis, but as well on a year-over-year basis. As to the trade, the steep backwardation continues well in to Q2.  While March is effectively concluded, April European netbacks are more than $20/mt below March, and May is at least $10/mt below that.  Thereon, the summertime netbacks flatten out, but as with all things LPG, crude is the ultimate driver and at this moment the headlines are the primary influence. Buy/sell terminal fee ideas, meanwhile, had at one point widened from the low/mid 5cpg range to as much as 12cpg during the height of the recent volatility, but have for now settled in a more modest range of 6-8cpg, generally speaking.  NWE April CIF ARA is showing strength as the March/April backwardation comes out of the market slightly. A bid in the TOT window also increased the physical premium assessed at April CIF ARA +$33pmt. Though this is for very early April arrival rather than whole month. The arb from the US remains open and if you take into account the physical premium Northwest Europe should be drawing tons from the US. A sever with the European market the worry is that multiple cargoes will head to the region and very quickly shift the tight market into an oversupplied one. The issue has been finding US cargoes in the second half of March for arrival in early April. These cargoes were worked well ahead of time and to draw them to the region now would need them to be redirected from heading East, not impossible with the East not showing much strength. April butane also remains valued at a high level at 92% April Naphtha, though this is approached with caution due to lack of April butane activity so far.   MED The expected ramp up of buying pre-Ramadan has not materialised. VLGCs have been stuck in Moroccan ports causing delays since early March. The Chinook is now discharging C4 having arrived at Mohammedia on February 27th. This is now starting to affect coaster discharges into Morocco and is keeping the butane market in the region subdued.

EAST There’s been a handful of deals concluded or placed on subs for Middle East second decade April cargos this week, mostly in the high 50s freight range. East/West freight differential is again pointing in favor of the West and with less waiting in Panama (latest at 4 days both North and South bound). This will attract more ships away from the East. Foreseeing less vessels available coupled with VLSFO bunkers increasing some 6-7% since last Friday on the back of again rising crude - we expect freight to move back above the 60-dollar mark from here.  WEST This week has already seen over twice as many fixtures compared to last week and the position list is now mainly dominated by pure shipowners. April cargoes are still in play and slowly but surely, early May is coming within fixing range. Although there have been over 30 spot fixtures for April thus far, we expect the last remaining handful of end April vessels to soon find suitable cargos. The last done deals ex USG/USEC were concluded at USD low 100s H/C and low USD 50 H/F, and owners are attempting to pull freight upwards from here. Time being, the arb is widening and vessels supply looks relatively tight and in control of a few owners for the front of May and it seems freight will increase gradually as time progresses.

Despite the War in Ukraine continuing for the third week, the shipping industry are fighting to get grips with the situation. The Supramax market showed some good resistance, strong demand in the Pacific made many owners leave Emed and ballast towards Suez to obtain better rates loading in MEG, India, and Southeast Asia. USG and ECSA pushed rates further up. In Asia, the demand/supply was more balanced. The period activity decreased, with big gap between owners and charterers ideas, which are about a few thousands. The BSI-58 10T/C route closing yesterday just USD 100 below USD 32,000/day. South China trip via Indonesia, E.C.India is up by, with fixure reported close to USD 40,000/day, W.Africa trip via ECSA to N.China is USD 30,000/day, lower rates from Mediterranean  to China/S.Korea is softer at USD 20,000/day. The big difference between the Atlantic average USD 15,000/day, while the Pacific round voyages and back haul paus as much as USD 40,000/day.

A softer week encompassed the Panamax market with little good cheer for owners to grab a hold of. Negative bids and tones across the board.  Negative news and indexes have been the story of the whole week.    Some representative fixtures this week: YM Pacifico (81,812/2015) sailed Hamburg 12 March was rumoured fixed for a trip via US East coast redelivery China with an intended cargo of petcoke at a rate in the region of mid USD 30,000’s with charterers Uniper.  Star Amethyst (82,123/2009) retro sailing Haldia 3 March was fixed for a trip via EC South America redelivery Southeast Asia USD 26,750 to Omegra. The Doric Armour (81,800/2018) Huangpu 15 March was placed on subjects by Messrs Cobelfret for a trip via Bunbury redelivery Continent at USD 30,000.  MBA Future (82,181/2009) Nagoya prompt was said to have fixed for a trip via NoPac with petcoke redelivery Japan at USD 30,000, but little else emerged. W-Original (81,874/2012) Yantai 12-17 March was heard to have fixed for a trip via NoPac redelivery Singapore-Japan at USD 30,000.

High level of activity in the term LNG shipping market continues, as the week brought a number of fresh new period requirements for Owners to consider. Although most of these requirements are still ongoing, the early onset of provided levels suggest a new anchor point for especially 1-year term rates going forward. In all term charter markets, the story is more or less unchanged, as more modern (and lower boil-off rate) vessels command a hefty premium, due to a predicted strong LNG price environment for the foreseeable future, although on a week-to-week basis, the prices for LNG and oil have come down from their recent highs, mainly due to the increased concern of extended lockdowns in China caused by the reappearance of COVID-19, and potential return of Iranian oil to markets. However, the narrative is a bit more complicated in the spot market, as the wide array of spot requirements have shown that despite the fact that the current LNG prices – at least in theory - create a massive disparity between the various vessel types, in reality not all requirements are equal, and many of them have factors and/or limitations that could, for example, favor smaller vessels in this type of commodity price environment. This has in turn created quite a mixed bag of fixture levels seen in the spot market and thus finding a fitting rate for each vessel type really depends on the requirement itself. However, generally speaking, the spot market has stayed relatively flat, since added availability has been matched with new emerging spot requirements. In the newbuilding market, we did not record new orders for this week, but the market is anticipating that QatarEnergy will announce further new orders any time soon.

There is a large degree of uncertainty around the world, but all in all dry bulk rates have remained fairly stable; rates went from USD 18,900 on average to USD 21,800 from last week. C5 went from USD 12 to 12,3 on index, despite talks about USD 12,6 being concluded. The Brazil/ China round has been kept around USD 30 pmt level for some time (index value USD 30,5 one week back) and is presently at USD 27 pmt, also being last done by Vale who have been active in taking ships recently.

We still see large premiums being paid for Russian port calls despite less reported activity over the last couple of days. Everyone is waiting to see if any stems get cancelled and how this will affect the export program for both March and April. North Sea crude spot earnings came off significantly last week and have been hovering around WS 120 levels due to erratic bunker prices. Going forward we might see rates in the North Sea improve as we expect even more VLCC stems ex WCN being lifted on Aframaxes.  Although the rates ex Bsea have come off this last week, voyages ex Russian ports are still giving owners a healthy return. In the Mediterranean, we have seen the market soften further and we expect this to continue going into the weekend.

This is partly due to less activity and more trader relets appearing in market for 1H April, but also due to bunker prices seemingly finding some ‘stability’ compared to previous weeks. As a result of more upstream production, we have also seen a couple of spot fob cargos for sale from Middle Eastern suppliers. But so far this has not triggered any significant activity on shipping yet, and we are (time of writing) still waiting for the Saudi acceptances for April.  WEST A couple of leftover March vessels are being targeted for some final attempts to secure March FOB loaders at freight rates in the low USD 100’s Houston/Chiba and mid USD 50’s Houston/Flushing. First half April seems more or less done in terms of spot activity and all eyes are on second half April where there is a vessel requirement and FOB/CFR tender from an Indonesian major. Under the current environment, Houston/Flushing is trading at a mere USD 6,500 premium to that of Houston/Chiba and thus far in March there are six vessels already on the way towards North West Europe and it will continue to rise – that’s about the same number of VLGC liftings ex USG+USEC to NWE seen on average over the past three months. Although activity isn’t booming so far this week, we think there is definitely more to come.

With oil prices up, then down, it’s been a week where the bunkers dominate in determining the market levels, as opposed to any sentiment or supply and demand pressures. As owners refuel at the pumps, the calculated returns can dip dramatically after the (relatively) cheaper onboard bunkers are used up. But, as we see the bunker prices decrease, so does the rate. As for supply, by our count 180 vessels arriving Fuj in the next 30 days, speaks for itself, and with quoted MEG cargoes entertaining 15+ offers, owner’s sentiment will suffer. The Atlantic, only really the USG providing much nourishment for the VLCCs.  On the flip side, OECD inventories at close to their lowest for the last 10 years, these will need replenishing, once OPEC are able/willing to lift production. It is up to Western leaders to convince them to do so.

Russian grades continue to command a premium over the regular market ex Baltic and Black Sea with the curious exception of ESPO loadings from Kozmino. The wider market is still battling rising bunkers and falling freight with few signs of resistance other than some Indian market cargoes that have recently traded Wafr/India at circa 130kt x WS 88-90. Those with scrubbers have committed the dirty deed and allowed their consumption-advantage to be traded against them with Wafr/long East trading at WS 77.5-80. MEG/India enquiry has been particularly active, whilst conversely, long haul from this region has been quiet, allowing ships to recycle back onto the list quickly. MEG/East will trade WS 87.5-90 on modern whilst TD23 may start to threaten WS 30's if low cargo volumes persist.

Dry cargo markets continue to see a flurry of SnP activity with up to 15 vessels changing hands this week. Notable developments on the Kamsarmax front where new benchmarks are being set.  The 2007 built “OCEANIC” (Abt 82k Tsuneishi Fukuyama) was sold at Usd 21m while the 2010 built “MBA LIBERTY” (Abt 82k dwt built Tsuneishi Zhoushan) achieved Usd 22m.  A comparison highlighting the relative discount carried by the Tess 82 built at the Zhoushan facility against a straight Japanese built unit. A discount however that remains minor compared to straight Chinese designs with the  2 year younger “YANGTZE XING HUA” (Abt 82k  built Guangzhou Longxue 2012) also achieving Usd 22m. Elsewhere the Supramax market continues to joy high liquidity with strong levels of enquiry being met with a steady stream of sale candidates.   Following the most recent pick up in activity it has been a quieter week in the tanker sector with most of the activity captured by the product sector. With strengthening chartering markets we expect a number of Buyers to come out the wood work in an effort to secure additional tonnage. It will be no easy feat though, with sellers expecting this gradual rate recovery to translate into higher asset values in the near future.
