text: AMERICAS Per the EIA propane inventory report for the week ending 11 Mar 2022, overall US stocks declined by 2.2mmbbls to a total of 35.5mmbbls, which is 81% of last year’s total, and just under 58% of two years ago.  Current stock levels remain below the 5-year average. Although the draw was larger than some had anticipated, it was within the generally expected range.  The areas where there has been lingering cold weather (PADDs I and II) saw draws of 100,000 and 900,000bbls (respectively), but the significant component showed a 1.1mmbbl draw on the Gulf Coast.  At 19.156 mmbbls, overall PADD III stocks are now 25% less than last year’s level of 25.920mmbbls. With regards terminal fees, there remains but one large unsold cargo in March, which at one point commanded double-digits.  Because of the backwardation, though, April avails are priced more moderately at between 6 and 7cpg, depending on the timing and grade(s).  Talk for May is slow just yet, but initial asking levels start with a 7. The volatility seen earlier in the month has subsided and the netback levels have come in a bit but remain positive for the time being.  Crude values – $102.50 for WTI and $106..00 for Brent  – will have a deciding hand.  NWE The physical TOT window premiums stand at April CIF ARA +$25pmt. Showing the tightness of the April market. The arb from the US is open and although Mt Belvieu has again strengthened the European market is expected to draw imports. The problem for Europe is that US East Coast exports have been reduced by the hefty draws and cold weather seen this winter, so traders have to look for cargoes from the Gulf Coast and compete with the East market, a higher netbacks by $10pmt. Petrochemical buying should still be at maximum with high Crude oil and propane vs naphtha in April above $140pmt. A full propane VLGC offered in the window pm a naphtha related price is not drawing any interest, due to the naphtha price swings. These swings continue to keep the NWE butane market quiet, and butane remains valued at 92% March naphtha.                                           MED With Ramadan less than 3 weeks away buying activity was expected to pick up. So far this has not yet materialized and the market remains subdued. Vessels discharging in Western Morocco have been stranded in port due to bad weather, the VLGC Chinook in Mohammedia since the beginning of them month.

It’s been an extreme week as oil and bunkers been tossing voyage numbers left, right, and centre, hour to hour, minute to minute. The North Atlantic has been suffering as the Russian invasion of Ukraine has taken out loading areas either directly caused by war or by self-sanctions. Further linked to the war we see much more coal heading towards Europe from destinations which is atypical - replacing Russian coal.  In other news, though voyage rates mostly are up due to bunkers, we see hire rates improving as well as we are heading towards a more active season out of Brazil.

The Supra market continue to surge despite changing and challenging environment. Owners remain cautious reg trading CIS. However, there were talks about Ultra fixing CIS China coal round at USD 80,000. From the Atlantic, 55,000 dwt was covered for Med to Conakry at USD 16,000. 60,000 dwt open Vera Cruz concluded a trip from SW Pass redelivery Rotterdam with grains at USD 31,000. Clinker run to West Africa were done at USD 27,000 levels. From the Pacific, Ultramax open at Yosu was covered for trip via Indonesia redelivery West Coast India at USD 42,000. Other Ultramax open Gresik covered Indonesia to Thailand at USD 50,000.  Still active talks around period; 57,000 dwt open East Med was fixed for sp at USD 24,000. 1-year for 58,000 dwt were discussed at high 20s.

Global energy prices have once again been at the beginning of most conversations this week with record levels seen for both oil and gas. Energy supply concerns, along with uncertainty and a genuine lack of tonnage available for term, sent that particular part of the market into overdrive. Term rates increased across the market with a scramble to secure modern tonnage at the back end of last week and continuing through this one. With TTF pricing where they are and more cargoes headed into Europe, tonne miles will be reduced, but tonne time may increase. However, tonnage availability may increase around the Atlantic basin. This could soften the Atlantic regions spot market in the near future despite the upward trend we are currently seeing on term rates. That being said, ships that are being taken in for term have reduced availability for the remaining enquiries now being discussed. The newbuild market remains active with another 3 new vessels ordered for delivery in 2025 from Hyundai. These vessels will be fitted with the ME-GA engine with a cargo capacity of 200,00cbm. We may also welcome another yard to the list of LNG shipbuilders as it looks like Jiangnan in China are working towards their first large LNG vessel orders.

In a market and world with a lot of a lot of uncertainty we saw this week further day of gains for the Panamax market with all routes yielding considerable returns. North appeared well supported with improved numbers reported especially for the shorter duration trips, further South something of a slower day but with SE Asia rates seeing sizeable jumps owners’ offers were said to be difficult to nail down. Further North in the Pacific, talk of some strong numbers being concluded on the NoPac runs for well described tonnage on good delivery positions, continued to improve sentiment and feeling here.   Some representative fixtures this week: The Navios Southern Star (82,224/2013) Rotterdam 10/11 March was heard fixing for a transatlantic trip via US Gulf redelivery Skaw-Gibraltar at USD 21,500.  Nan Xin 27 (74,483/2006) was heard fixing a trip via EC South America redelivery Skaw-Passero option 4-6 months at USD 35,000 basis delivery APS EC South America 17 March alternatively USD 24,750 basis retro sailing Sunda 15 February. Yasa H Mulla (83,482/2011) Gibraltar 8 March fixed clean, delivery aps NC South America redelivery Far East at USD 27,000 + USD 1.4mio ballast bonus with Norden. The Ocean Legend (78,208/2020) Cai Mep 13-14 March was rumored fixed for a trip via Indonesia redelivery Japan at USD 45,000. Last Friday K Line secured the CSK Unity (77,105/2015) Manila 11/13 March for a trip via Indonesia redelivery Japan at USD 40,000.

As the saying goes "a week is a long time in politics" and the same can be said of the Suezmax market. Healthy premiums are still being paid for Russian Baltic and Black Sea cargoes with a noticeable drop off in non-Russian rates, where skyrocketing bunker prices are savagely wiping out any profits. Attempts by America to lead an all-out ban on Russian crude may have fallen on deaf ears as the EU will take some time to be weaned of its Russian dependence. This oil will continue to flow, both short and long haul and if there's an example of cheap oil that doesn't find a home, we would love to be enlightened. TD20 appears susceptible to further falls and may test low WS 80s whilst MEG/East will hover in the mid/high WS 80s for 15T crane requirements. Td23 may start to come off a little and trade in the WS 40s.

With the current global events taking centre stage and infiltrating our daily lives, it is no different for the VLCC market, as unprecedented bunker prices bite hard on owners returns. As other sizes benefit from a little more Russian exposure on specific routes, VL’s remain soft across the globe. With the current (relatively) cheaper bunkers on board, the bump in rates up to the WS 50s was a pleasant shift away from the monotonous negativity. However, it is when owners need to refill, and the replacement cost is calculated into the return, they will have to endeavor to push rates to reflect that. On a TCE basis, we are essentially back in the pre-invasion low WS 30s. Bumping along the bottom. Sentiment played its part at the beginning, driving rates upwards, but now, reality bites.

Liquidity in the dry SnP markets is back at levels witnessed through most of last year with twenty-five units changing hands this week. The underlying macro environment is providing a relative degree of support on the freight side as mentioned last week. Rates that are driving buyers to increase their bids in order to secure additional tonnage. Most of that activity is captured by the Kamsarmax/Panamax and the Utramax/Supramax markets with seven and eight vessels being sold in those respective segments. Worth noting that sellers of Chinese built candidates are the ones more willing to transact with prices deemed to have reach relative heights while potential sellers of Japanese designed vessels are counting on the sharper drive in values usually experienced for quality designs in such rising markets.  Pick up in activity in the tanker space as well, with most market players expecting values to take turn off the back of the recent relative increase in rates. Although earnings remain limited in most sectors due to increased bunker costs, buyers are still willing to go meet the offer, expecting the current situation to have further positive impact on rates which will translate in higher second-hand values. The VLCC sector continues to see a number of units changing hands with a number of ongoing negotiations suggesting even further activity in the near future.

With most Aframax owners not willing to call Russian ports as the geopolitical situation is still very volatile, we have a two-tier market in the Nsea/Baltic area. The owners fixing out of Russian ports fix these cargoes at a very high premium compared to other areas in the North Sea. As more owners who normally would be fixing out of the Baltic market is looking at Nsea cargoes, this market came under downward pressure and rates have come off significantly. Bunker prices are still extremely high due to the current oil price, so we expect the market to stay around current levels for the time being. Much the same can be said about the Med/Bsea market with Bsea deals receiving a healthy premium vs cross-Med fixtures where the trend is softening by the day. We are expecting more of the same in the week to come.

After a sudden rush of fixing, in addition to the crude rally, the freight market made a huge jump with the last done deal concluded at USD 105 H/C. At the time of writing, we count 16 spot fixtures for April, and mid-month fixing is well underway. Having said that, there is still some leftover vessels in March and early April, which may have to absorb some costly waiting time. Firm vessel itinerary is key when fixing and not being able to book Neo Panama slots well in advance, makes some would-be charterers hesitant to make a move for such non-booked vessels. Thus, there are several cargoes uncovered in April still and many deals to be done.

text: MEG  A week of volatility with CP swings from $880 to $1000, along with the wild Oil. At the time of writing, Apr C3 CP was traded at $916 and C4 at $20 higher. Apr/May C3 CP was traded at $30 backwardation.  Saudi Aramco was reported to sell two heavy propane cargos for late Mar lifting at fixed price. And Qatar Petroleum tendered to sell 19-29th Apr lifting 3/1 or 4/0 cargo.   FAR EAST  Slow start this week and window appears thin, as 23kt propane was bid at Apr FEI plus $40 while seller asking plus $60s for a 46kt parcel. Outside window, tenders swarmed up especially after the dramatic drop on Wednesday.  Japanese and Korea importers are actively buying cargos, with two Canada origin propane cargos delivered in Apr and May respectively reported sold into Japan, and one Ferndale origin evenly split cargo into Korea for May delivery. Another two Korean importers issued tender to buy in total 69kt LPG for Apr delivery into Petchem segments. One Ningbo-based cracker user tendered to buy 23kt or 46kt propane parcel for 2h Apr delivery. Taiwan FPC withdrew their buy tender for 2h Apr arrival 46kt LPG at flexible ratio due to unattractive price as overnight FEI/MOPJ spread shrank. Indonesia PERTAMINA issued two swap tenders this week to sell their 3-4 Apr and 12-13 Apr US FOB 2/2 parcels and buy back same volumes for 11-15 May and 22-24 May delivery. Apart from tenders, several buyers are exploring Apr delivered evenly split parcel into SEA or Schina.

Cargo prices continue their rally with TTF hitting $50/MMBtu as uncertainties over gas supplies continue. Arbitrage is currently shut with all cargoes pointing to Europe.  There are several factors contributing in the shipping market turning towards either direction in the long run, however on the prompt, we are witnessing an upward trend on levels both in the spot and in the term market.  It is very uncertain yet what the full repercussions of the global situation will be as market participants remain on hold before any drastic movements are taken that could have an impact in the long run.  There have been no new building orders this week but prices keep increasing.

Some participants have been slow to react to fast changing developments in the Suezmax market and were caught up in a "last done" mind set which has proved costly on some deals as the market sped passed them. With the risk of stating the obvious, we have seen non-Urals freights increasing by over a third on TD20, whilst cross-Med rates have nearly tripled. Kozmino Aframax cargoes continue to fix with little to no issues on the selling side, suggesting urals West of Suez will soon find ways to market. Cheap crude always moves, no matter what the perceived risks are. At the time of going to print, we may see some profit taking from some early ships, but next done is more likely to be in excess of last. MEG/East will trade somewhere in low WS 100's whilst TD20 will share the same price point.

Following the tearful events in Ukraine the uncertainty over Russian oil exports is the main driver for both the Nsea and Baltic market. The rates have reached the highest ever levels for a Baltic-UKC run as only a handful of owners are willing to call Russian ports. Freight rates for cross-Nsea voyages have increased significantly as some Nsea grades are preferred as a substitute to Russian crude.  Moving forward, rates might move unpredictably as further sanctions could arise and change the current market situation. The same can be said about the Med/Bsea market where rates ex Bsea have taken an enormous jump for those owners willing to call Russian ports. The ongoing events have also affected cross-Med voyages where we have seen rates more than double on WS-points since this time last week.

Although VLCC rates have all but doubled in the week gone by the MEG position list is still in need of thinning for the market to move on from pure sentiment to a fundamental change. Baltic and Black Sea aside, rates in general have gone up because owners have been unwilling to fix and sitting on their hands. With galloping bunker prices earnings are still a far cry from any return on capital, but at the same time also a far cry from not even covering voyage related cost, which has been the norm for some time. Owners are not going to give up hard fought gains without a fight, but “last done” could become more tempting at some stage when the dust settle.

text: MEG Apr CP reach a multiple year high at $940 for C3 and $944 for C4 respectively, along with the surge in crude. Apr/May was traded at nearly $50 backwardation. Qatar Petroleum released their Apr loading acceptance with minor delays heard. Players are waiting for other producers’ acceptances and availabilities in spot sales. And this week Saudi Aramco was reported to sell one late Mar lifting heavy propane cargo at fixed price.  FAR EAST Cash premium keep soaring up as only bids seen in window. 23kt propane for 1h Apr delivery was bid at Apr FEI plus mid 50s on Thursday. Outside window seller for such parcels is heard asking at Mar FEI plus 50s range, whereas Mar/Apr FEI traded at high $40s range.  One EChina cracker was reported that they didn’t award their buy tender, which asked for two parcels of 23kt or 46kt propane during late Mar-1h Apr delivery into Ningbo. Another PDH user also tendered to buy 23kt propane for similar delivery range. PDH users are planning for turnarounds or rate cuts due to the negative margins, as some which under turnaround at the moment is reselling propane stock to capture the profits in residential sector, and some is purchasing propylene to offset the less output from own units.

An unsurprising slow start this week given world tensions and the uncertainty created by it all. The Atlantic proved to be the most affected by it all with sizeable corrections on routes P1A and P2A. Asia saw a lethargic opening too; despite a healthy-looking demand book most players appear to be in watch and wait mode with little activity reported so far. Some positive signs on FFA during the end of the week.  Some representative fixtures this week: The Sea Commander (81,856/2018) Klaipeda spot was said to have fixed for a trip via Murmansk redelivery Continent with rates of USD 20,000 and USD 24,000 rumoured with Suek. The Athinoula (82,177/2012) Singapore prompt was rumoured fixed for a trip via EC South America redelivery Far East at USD 24,000 to Bunge. Tina IV (75,187/2009) Machong 1 March fixed and failed on subjects for a trip via Indonesia redelivery Japan at USD 24,500.

EAST With East previously trading at a large discount to the West - spot fixing for the first half of March ended up being active in the Middle East. The West premium has now fallen down to just a few dollars, and we expect the second half of March will be slightly less busy. Having said that, we have seen a good amount of inquires this week both out of Australia and Middle Eastern ports. With freight in dollar per ton terms looking to find a floor around 42-43 levels the TCE levels keeps dropping due to the seemingly ever increasing bunker prices.  WEST Lack of March cargoes and subsequent waiting time, increasing bunker prices and prompt vessels in the USG seems to be a thing of the moment. Finally though, there are currently several freight enquiries both end March and first decade April ex the US, which hopefully reduces some of the March left-over’s rather quickly. Having said that, it remains to be seen if there are enough uncovered cargoes left for the balance of March to absorb all of this length and cure the ‘hangover’ without too much waiting time imposed on those left open. First half April fixing will soon be well under way, and we expect the next couple of weeks to see gradually increasing activity and rates.

text: AMERICAS  Volatility has been the primary characteristic of the domestic energy markets this week, having been spurred on by events in eastern Europe, rising crude values, softening freight and widening arbs to both the East and the West.  The result is that propane prices at Mont Belvieu rose by more than 12cts/gal over just this week to $1.53/gal.  There remains, however, quite steep backwardation which extends well in to 2H 2022 and then in to the upper $1.20’s/gal. Meanwhile, terminal fees this week spiked hard and the few remaining March cargoes are known to have been fixed in the double-digits.  Motivated buyers, sensing stronger demand in Europe because of the Russian advancements into Ukraine, emerged for March and 1H Apr volumes.  It is anticipated that around 175,000mt per month of LPG formerly supplied by Russia requires replacement, and hence the enthusiasm. With regards the inventory levels of propane in the U.S., the EIA revealed an 800,000bbl overall weekly reduction which brought stock levels to 37.2mmbbls.  The market took that in stride and essentially shrugged off the large decline in PADD 2 but pointed to the week-over-week increase in PADD III, the Gulf Coast, which saw a build of 900,000bbls.  Cynics were prepared to wait for next week’s release for a ‘truer’ stock picture, as many believe there have been data errors in recent reports.  NWE As the European LPG market tries to come to grips with the effects of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, supply concerns have come to the fore in an already tight market. This led to a scramble from European traders to find US FOBs as transatlantic March imports were expected to be around 120,000MT far below the 460,000MT imported in February. With FOB US bids rising on European trader interest March cargoes surfaced and most believe these additional exports were only made possible by the lower than expected draw in US inventories. At least 3 additional VLGCs were purchased for the European market which will calm some traders for end March and 1H April. The prompt market is short with the TOT window premium valued at March CIF ARA +$18pmt. The butane market is valued at 97% March Naphtha which is a strong value in this market and only for March tons, as the end of the month ends the gasoline blending season.  MED Butane values have hit eight-year highs, though offers are seen in the market but no bids. A butane heavy cargo from North West Europe is signalling arrival in Egypt in April. This week mixed ratio VLGC left the USGC bound for Turkey. Imports or high prices keeping bidders quiet.

Whilst the horrible actions taking place in Ukraine, the market first responded negative as rates were coming off. Later in the week however, rates were up to present average of USD 15,300. Dry shares have been increasing, with expectations linked to coal possibly will replace some of the gas demand.   The number of ships sailing towards Brazil is relatively low, at the same time as Vale is start fixing ships after a rather long inactive period from their side. This may suggest a further increase on the Brazil/ China route. Period ships are still in demand and there is a steady flow of period fixtures.

As we end another week of escalating conflicts in Eastern Europe and as sanctions on Russian interests unravel, we continue to feel its effect on all shipping markets. Confusion around which specific entities are being sanctioned has paved the way for a number of tanker owners to proceed with Baltic and BSea voyages offering substantial risk premiums for Russian liftings. The majority of players however are opting for a "self-sanctioning" approach with refiners and traders shying away from Russian product. Should the situation remain or worsen we expect these soaring regional rates to continue their climb and provide wider support for freight across all geographies. The sale and purchase markets have seen a pick-up in activity in the VLCC sector with 5 units changing hands this week, breaking an extensive stretch of inactivity in the segment. A strengthening buying interest that is driving buyers to re-evaluate their bids to go meet a thinning list of available candidates in hope to capture the gains that are currently witnessed in the chartering markets.  In a relative contrast to the volatility experienced by Tanker players, the Dry sectors are continuing to joy of steadily strengthening markets. A strength that can be felt through the most recent SnP transactions that have seen vessels achieve levels in excess of last dones. A dynamic that is particularly well illustrated by the sale of the 2012 Mitsui built MV "ORCHID" which achieved Usd 22.6m.

The overall market trended sideways whilst although it firmed in South America. The Mediterranean is soft and many owners refuse to trade Black Sea.   On the other side. Paper went up 1500 on Q2 and people are still optimistic even if paper went down heavily yesterday. The workhorse of the market is still the Pacific where market went up today.

NSea/Baltic market showed signs of improvement this week mainly on the back of tightening supply of vessels. February dates are all covered, and March lifting programs suggest increased activity – especially for urals. The x-factor of the market is possible sanctions against Russian entities but overall sentiment has changed and market will be steady/firm moving forward. In the Med/Blsea we have seen an uptick in freight levels over the past week with tighter lists on the back of weather disruptions as well as a busy 2nd decade Blsea. All eyes these days on the escalating and uncertain situation unfolding in the Ukraine - expecting market to remain steady/firm for the balance of the week.

At the time of going to press, Russian crude is trading at a substantial discount to Brent which will draw in more Eastern buyers as a more cautious approach appears to be taken by receivers in the West. Suezmax owners will also be keeping one eye on their larger sibling, VLCC's, as firming rates in that segment are likely to have a knock on impact at some stage. For now, lists in the East and West have a fair degree of slack, but with simmering political tensions, firmer VLCC's, and a rising oil price, there is a real chance that rates may start to nudge up over the next few days. For now, MEG/East trades just below WS 60 on plus 15YR tonnage and low WS 60's for modern units. TD23 is likely to trade about WS 30 with some potential to tick.

Bull mood again taking over for the big ships, despite alarming developments in Russia/Ukraine resembling what seen done by others back in 1939. Average daily spot earnings up almost 50 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 18k. Australian miners busy loading + booking whatever available tonnage for the West Australia/China iron ore conference trade, and with assistance of healthy inter-pacific coal volumes, value of Pacific round voyages almost tripling to USD 19k/day over last 5 trading days. Fronthaul trade improvement so far moderate in comparison, as Brazil iron ore exports still not back to normal volumes after a troublesome/wet period and the West Africa/Far East minerals trade not being sufficient to compensate – limited number of ballasters could however change this situation quickly. North Atlantic seeing a small boost as both inter-atlantic and export volumes of coal + iron ore destined for Far East and India increase significantly. “Almost ALL” relevant players on lookout for period candidates as timing being considered right – representative fixtures include 208,000 dwt, built 2017, done for 12-15 months at USD 30,500, also 180,000 dwt, built 2012, fetching USD 27,300 basis 9-13 months.

Further sizeable gains for the Panamax and in particular the Atlantic market with talk of fresh mineral demand in the North to add to a well-supported grain market. Asia too saw decent levels of enquiry both ex NoPac and Australia in turn improving levels and sentiment. Period activity remained active.   Some representative fixtures this week: The scrubber fitted JY Lake (81,176/2019) San Ciprian 22 February was alleged fixed for a coal trip via US Gulf redelivery Continent USD 25,000 with Viterra, the Scrubber benefit going to charterers. From the South came rumours of the Attalia (82,171/2010) delivery Aps EC South America 6/10 March fixing for a trip redelivery Singapore-Japan at USD 23,000 + USD 1,250,000 bb, and the Astrea (81,838/2015) delivery Aps Santos 18 March secured on subjects for the same trip at USD 26,500 + USD 1,350,000 bb. In the Atlantic, a 57k where fixed 25k for a trip to Mediterranean with petcoke. Last week we noted considerable uncertainty and no reason to have a different view this week, geopolitical news needs to be under constant watch, not that this is particularly profound but now is a particularly sensitive time. On top of this backdrop, spot cargoes prices rose due to weather driven eastern demand amid colder weather in China and intensified competition with Europe for cargoes, something that could very easily continue unabated. This view could explain the rise in share prices of Asian shipbuilders and shipping firms which rallied, likely on the expectations that European countries may seek more seaborne energy sources on news that Russia’s Nord Stream 2 pipeline’s approval process has been halted.   On the prompt, tonnage remains abundant as a high percentage of vessels remain contained in their respective basin leading to persistent lower than average voyage distance and thus additional capacity remains plentiful. Multi-month activity remains active with several live tenders being worked and bidding interest in vessels remains. This week we increase the multi-year levels supported by a few fixtures yet despite this rise, the bid/ask spread oscillates depending on vessel type and delivery timings, plenty of nuances that need to be understood yet clarity should start to reduce these as we get closer to Q3 and charterer preferred delivery timings near.   In the new build market, one reported transaction this week with Hyundai Glovis booking a 2H2024 slot that is rumoured to be on the back of a charter. 2024 is all but sold out whilst 2025 follows suit with all slots reserved and as such the newbuilding price continues its ascent.

Following weeks of escalation - the growing fears shared by most over the past few weeks have unfortunately become a reality with Russia’s military operations currently underway in Ukraine. A volatile geopolitical environment with undeniable ramifications across all markets which have met Russia’s aggression with large scale economic sanctions. Measures that have yet to be fully announced and which implications remain to be seen; an uncertainty that has left the tanker markets with an already tighter list of available tonnage. Adding to an already skewed fleet positioning east of Suez leading to rate gains in the Atlantic. Baltic Aframax rates have also surged with most owners deciding to hold back unless they see a considerable premium from charterers. We expect these firming chartering markets to soon translate into a pick in SnP activity with potential buyers finding enough support from these improved rates to pull the trigger on future acquisitions.  Dry cargo players are of course also endeavouring to digest the effect that these recent events will have on their market; direct impact is as expected felt in the Black Sea where Ukraine has officially halted its operations in several of its ports including from Yuznhy where force majeure has been declared. A disruption in exports for several key commodities coming out of the Black Sea that will have to be substituted should the situation persists. The tonnage list in the region is of course following suit with owners shying away from Black Sea fixtures. Similarly, we expect this tension on rates to provided support to an already steady value environment which could be mean further gains for Dry cargo assets across all segments.

text: AMERICAS Continued cold weather and increased exports are finally taking their toll on US inventories. Since last Summer, many warned that US inventories could not support exports and cold weather,  and now those forecasts seem to be coming true. This week’s inventory report showed a draw of 3.9 million barrels bringing the two week total draw to almost 10 million barrels. Another large draw next week will really get alarm bells ringing. A large gathering of the domestic players met in San Diego this week for the OPIS Conference and whereby most agreed propane production was increasing, the amount was a matter of debate. We expect propane production to increase by 170,000 barrels however there are many expecting the number to be closer to 100,000 barrels per day.  NWE The market is dominated by uncertainty and news of the Russian invasion. The European market is tight, but the arb remains closed from the US, and TOT window premiums are at $18.50pmt but so far have only sufficient to draw on cargo across the Atlantic in March. Europe will need to draw US cargoes destined for the Far East if the market is going to be able to fill current demand. With the March East vs West spread at +$53pmt this is not impossible. March/April backwardation stands at +$32pmt and prompt tightness has traders doing all they can to find March arrivals cargoes, both full propane and mixed ratio. Butane values have come off from 100% Naphtha to the mid high 90%s and is expected to continue to do so as naphtha surges with crude.   MED Butane demand in North West Europe is stopping the North South Mediterranean trade. An Algerian export cargo headed to US northeast which will help alleviate tightness in the region.

EAST The focus on shipping this week has mainly been on two Australian cargos for 2H March, where one ship is reported on subs at around USD 44 Baltic. We have seen a total of 13 deals concluded in 1H March from the Middle East so far, and expect more activity to come for 2H March. But with freight still long no one seems to be in a rush to cover their next positions, yet.  WEST Western freight markets continue to slide on the back of a narrow arbitrage. The annual IP week in London and Presidents’ Day in US on Monday caused a slow start to the week and we have at time of writing only heard of one fixture concluded for early March dates in the USG. Freight rates for West loadings looks to be heading for USD 80 pmt rather quickly, a significant drop from last done at USD 93 pmt. As the freight pmt keeps falling, the tensions between Russia and Ukraine are causing crude to edge closer to USD 100/bbl and skyrocketing bunker prices.

This week continues to see a climb in dry cargo snp activity with up to 20 vessels changing hands. As mentioned in our last report, potential buyers have re-entered the market supported by clear benchmarks being set by recent transactions taking place in all sectors. Levels that broadly remain in line with the relative highs achieved over the past quarter making it easier for sellers to trigger a sale. The Ultramax and Supramax sectors are once again capturing most of the activity with a steady stream of candidates being placed on the market to meet those increased levels of buying enquiry.  A rather more subdued sentiment in the Tanker space where values are continuing their corrections, lead by sellers who are gradually deciding to give in a market that is showing no signs of bouncing back. The mid 2000 crude carriers seem to be the first to take the hit with a number of units being sold. The Product sector is showing more resiliance with sellers keeping units out of the market or continuing to hold for levels in line with last done.

Sentiment and overall views of the market in the Atlantic continued to be a little mixed this week when writing.  APS fixtures surfacing for the early tonnage undermining the bears view who reckoned there were some better numbers. Asia by contrast continued to hold steady with solid demand and little change in numbers exchanged.   Some representative fixtures this week: Min Sheng I (81,659/2012) Gibraltar 22 February for a Kamsar round voyage at USD 19,000 Oldendorff. The scrubber fitted Ultra Serval (81,606/2020) San Ciprian 17/19 February for a trip via Kamsar redelivery Skaw-Gibraltar at USD 22,500 with the scrubber benefit going to charterers.  RB Jordana (81,301/2016) retro sailing La Coruna 10 February was heard to have fixed a trip via NC South America option US Gulf redelivery Far East at USD 29,500 to unnamed Chinese charterers.  TBN was said to have fixed a 70,000/10 coal lift ex Hay Point to Praia Mole 1/10 March shipment dates at approximately USD 23.50 fio with ArcelorMittal.

Winter doldrums not yet over for the big ships, and spot values presently stuck at close to half that of Supras/Panamaxes. Average daily earnings flat w-o-w at USD low 12k's as both major-volume trades West Australia/China and Brazil/Feast fail to meet expectations. Brazilian miners still battling weather-related production- and shipping delays, causing concern for a growing number of ballasters looking for March fronthaul alternatives - and owners discounting heavily quick Far East rounds in anticipation of better times to come. Only bright spot being the West Africa/Far East trades, compensating for part of the missing Atlantic commodity flows. Period interest and activity lives its own life as most experienced takers well aware this is the time of year when bargains are secured. Levels reflect present forward views, and representative fixtures include 180,000 dwt, built 2012, fetching USD 27,300 basis 9-13 months and 179,000 dwt, built 2011, done for 19-22 months at USD 26,500.

As the tension further escalated between Russia and Ukraine, the market reacts with intense volatility. Though strong demand for coal shipments on Indonesia-India routes pushes Asian market with high speed. Atlantic market has also shown improvement in main loading areas and pushed rates up between USD 3,000-5,000 pd from a week ago. Today's levels are in the low USD 20,000 pd for TARV on Supra and with few thousand premium for Ultras. Black Sea to Far East fixing in the low USD 30,000 pd on Tess 58. We see good number of fresh order out of ECSA with fixtures been reported Supra USD 30,000 pd loading in Brazil for one trip with grains in the Cont/Med range. Trips from ECSA to EC India-China range fixed around low USD 20,000 pd plus USD 900,000 GBB. We expect and foresee a further improvement in Atlantic Basin.

text: MEG A week of volatility as oil is on a roller coaster. Mar C3 CP followed the trajectory and traded at $784 at the time of writing. Interestingly Mar C4 was traded $10 higher than C3, due to the improved butane demand as traders bidding to cover shorts into India and SEA region against a tightness in butane supply in front market.  Saudi Aramco released their Mar lifting with no plus tolerance for butane. Additionally, both KPC and QP was reported to sell evenly split FOB cargos, one for mid Mar lifting and the other for end Mar lifting.    FAR EAST Cash premium softened this week, with 23kt parcel for 2h Mar delivery bid at Mar FEI plus mid high teens only while offers hover at plus mid-20s.  Off window a handful of tenders are floating in the market. Two Korean players issued buy tenders to secure upto 92kt LPG for 2h Mar and 1H Apr delivery for petchem use. One EChina cracker was reported to cover a 2h Mar delivered 46kt propane at Mar FEI plus mid 20s only. Another EChina PDH user issued tender to buy 1 upto 5 parcels of 23kt propane monthly from Mar to Jul delivery. One Schina traditional importer also called a buy tender for monthly 6kt or 12kt butane from Apr to Dec delivery. One Taiwan Petchem plant was also reported to buy a 2h Mar delivered propane cargo at Mar MOPJ minus high 30s for cracking feedstock.

EAST After a slower than usual month for February fixing with ‘only’ 13 deals concluded in the MEG, March has gotten off to a hot start and we currently count a dozen deals fixed (or still on subs) for 1st decade March loading. Nevertheless, last done rates still remain in the mid USD 40s Baltic region, as we are still left with a good variety of owners and traders relets even after more activity in market. Going forward the focus will be on the pending Saudi acceptances, and there are also a couple of fob tenders from Middle Eastern suppliers for mid and end March.  WEST With freight rates seemingly stable for now we find the West premium comfortably around USD 10 pmt before waiting in the Panama Canal and last done fixture concluded at USD mid/low 90s Houston/Chiba range. It seems that February and first decade March enquiries ex USG is more or less spoken for, and for the first time in ages there is a prompt open vessel available in the US Gulf. With that said, it remains to be seen if there are enough cargos for the vessels coming open first half March in the USG.

Yet another week in the Nsea/Baltic market without any positive changes to write home about. Some owners are desperately putting up some resistance, but slow activity and an abundant tonnage list neutralizes any attempts to push rates. However, a firm USG/Caribs market is offering an alternative for those owners willing to ballast. This might have a positive effect on the Nsea/Baltic market. Till then, rates are expected to move sideways moving into the next week. Much of the same can be said about the Med/Bsea market where there are enough prompt ships around to repeat the rate levels we have seen since last week. Any attempt from owners’ side to hold back on rates is replied by charterers taking ships out quietly off the market. Also, in the Med/Bsea we expect rates to move sideways in the short term.

An interesting week on the front pages of the newspapers, but in the VLCC world, has been more of the same. The MEG market has sat in the void between February and March laycans, but even if cargoes were there to work, the sheer volume of ships waiting to take them out remains a concern. New lows, with a fixture at WS 32-32.5 for MEG/China, after the charterer received 13 offers. If you have a scrubber these returns are not good. Without a scrubber, they don’t bear thinking about. The Atlantic remains a little more interesting, with West Africa working mid-month and a 10-point premium achieved on a prompter laycan for Indonesia, but unreflective of any market swing, however. The USG has ticked up by a USD 100k or so per successive fixture, but with bunker prices where they are, it’s the smallest of solaces for owners.

There is considerable uncertainty in the days and weeks ahead, but while the global LNG market and associated forward curves remain at historically high levels the freight market continues to bump along the seabed. Strong LNG prices particularly into Europe are providing profitable trading opportunities for those with flexible cargoes, but these routes are limiting the rates achievable by owners and subletters as the lower average voyage distance is dragging down tonne-mile demand and freeing up additional capacity. There are few signs of this dynamic changing in the near-future, although a flutter of life in the west-to-east arbitrage may be encouraging and the combination of political and economic stresses coupled with the balance of available vessels being under the control of portfolios and traders should be a warning against complacency. The multimonth market is a little more active, with several charterers interested in summer coverage, and beyond in some cases. Overall though, it does still appear to be a little bit “wait and see” from several market participants. On the newbuilding front, there were ten orders in the past week including four slots firmed up by Qatar Energies, four orders by H Line and two orders by Bono Energy.

Curiously, just as the situation in Ukraine looks like it’s slowly diffusing, the Joint War Committee has decided to add the Black Sea to their list of High Risk Areas. A few weeks too late maybe? Bizarrely, Black Sea rates have traded fairly flat during this period, which makes shipping the sole outlier, in global markets, not to have reacted to the threat of conflict. Elsewhere, US Gulf /TA has traded 145kt x WS 65 which underlines that the Atlantic market doesn't have a backhaul trade anymore as everything has become fronthaul. In the East, there's a fairly steady feel as TD23 is likely to repeat last done levels as fixing dates move into first decade March. MEG/East is still at the mercy of a very long list where rates will remain around the WS 60-62.5 mark for the balance of the week.

text: AMERICAS The market was taken aback by the surprisingly large inventory draw posted by the EIA, which reflected a 5.9mmbbl decline in weekly stock levels to 41.9mmbbls.  This compares to the overall total of 48.6mmbbls and 68.7mmbbls recorded over the last two years.  In other words, 1H Feb propane inventories in North America are 86% and 70% of the previous two years, respectively.  The market had generally anticipated an approximate 3mmbbl decline from the 4th to the 11th of February 2022. February price levels almost immediately spiked by over 5cts/gal, but March values were slower to respond, perhaps because the market is aware of around a half-dozen ‘buyback’ cargoes in March as well as the half-dozen (or so) cancellations which have been reported.  Furthermore, recently rising crude values are believed to have likely improved field production, all of which appear to have conspired to limit the immediate upside – at least for the moment. To that, the North American weather patterns will continue to play a role, as there remain a couple of forecasted storms over the next 10-14 days which are meant to allow temperatures (and snow) to drop once again.  That should likely, then, translate to additional demand pulls.   The general sentiment, however, is that this week’s EIA data likely included corrective data (from previous reports) but that this week’s report overreached, in which case next week’s data could quite likely also contain additional corrective figures.  NWE CIF ARA reacted strongly to the big draws in US inventories. The March price rose $27pmt on the day, most of that from when the draw was announced to close of European trading. Two bids were seen in the window with the high bid assessed a CIF ARA March +$10pmt. The European market is tight prompt all the way through 1H March, the February March backwardation widening to +$15pmt. The March East West spread has come in to +$54.5pmt and Eastern traders continue to look for homes for their cargoes in Europe. February Propane Naphtha spread is at $130pmt and continues to incentivise maximum petchem demand. Butane at 100% February naphtha with naphtha at 7-year highs. European traders are primarily interested 1H month US FOB cargoes, which can arrive in Europe in the same month as that of loading. For these they are the best FOB bidders in the market today.  MED Tight freight on larger pressurized vessels is hampering North South butane trade in the region. March trade discussions are yet to get going.

After a drop end of last week, which was mostly due to lack of activity, this week has started much healthier. Most of the prompt tonnage that been heading towards the South Atlantic is now covered. This together with more fresh cargo has changed the sentiment and boost the indexed. However, the most interesting this week has been the significant increase in period demand and the willingness to pay up. For the coming week it looks very promising, however there is always a risk expectations are a bit too high and a bit too early.

The current spot LNG shipping market continues its soft trend from last week.  The present lack of requirement and limited arbitrage opportunities have further increased the vessel availability list, putting spot rates under pressure. There seem to be no shortage of ships for February – March delivery and although a couple of spot fixtures were recently concluded, we do not anticipate any significant or positive changes to the current levels.   Due to a quieter spot market, rate ideas for multi months and up to one year term periods with early start-up have also softened.  Despite the recent bearish sentiments, there are still potential inquires for multi months and term charters being discussed.   In the newbuilding market, it was reported that Venture Global LNG is linked to a 3+3 potential LNG Carriers orders at DSME for delivery in 2025/2026. Maran Gas have also increased their orders at DSME for 2025 deliveries.

This week comes to a close with both sectors joying of an increased amount of sales; a liquidity however that reflects two very different underlying market sentiment. The long awaited tanker recovery seems to have become a long distant memory with a number of potential sellers now taking the decision to pull the trigger and dispose of assets that they have for so long resisted to sell at substantially corrected levels. A dynamic particularly well illustrated in the mid 2000 built Aframax front which has seen a great number of potential candidates being marketed over the past months, but by sellers hoping to capture the anticipation of a market rebound. Same sellers who have now decided to go meet the bid setting new benchmarks for other owners looking to catch the falling knife.   Dry cargo snp markets seem to also have set its direction seeing buying interest strengthening amongst all sectors with buyers willing to now pay levels in line with last done, in order to secure the right candidates. Values therefore remain particularly well supported both by a strong level of buying interest but also by a pool of sellers confident in the longevity of this market.

A more positive sentiment as was expected. Ultramax open Dakar fixed trip via East Africa to China around USD 27,000. Clinker run from Med to West Africa was done around USD 23,000 on bigger Supramax. 56k dwt open in USG was fixed to WC South America around USD 32,000. Usual scrap runs from Baltic to Med were concluded at USD 15,000 and to Far East at USD 26,000. Indo-China rounds were done at USD 24,000. Scrubber fitted Ultramax was confirmed at USD 20,000 for a trip with rice from North China to Med. From the period front, 58k dwt open Skaw was fixed for 4 to 6 mos redel Atlantic at USD 20,750. 56k dwt open Diliskelesi was fixed min 5 to about 7 months trading redelivery Atlantic at USD 25,000.

The Panamax began the week with some improved enthusiasm, especially in the Atlantic with the resultant BPI5TC index rising. Talk of several vessels being cleared out end of last week, has paved the way for some better bids seen according to some, with EC South America seeming the driving factor with tonnage open in the North being bid for same. Asia commenced the week more cautiously with minimal activity reported, the typical wait and watch approach with no doubt one eye on this sudden activeness from South America.  Some representative fixtures this week: Figalia Navigator (81,480/2012) aps EC South America end February was linked to Olam for a trip redelivery Singapore-Japan at USD 21,000 + USD 1,100,000 ballast bonus. Cofco China were rumoured to have secured 2-3 ships for the same trips with rumours of the Seabiscuit (82,624/2014) around the USD 21,500 + USD 1,500,000 mark delivery Aps, the Pella (82,163/2010) at a rate in the upper USD 21,000’s + USD 1,750,000 bb, and the Danae (75,349/2005) retro sailing Singapore 31 January at USD 18,500 levels.  The Andria (75,375/2006) retro sailing Singapore 31 January was said to have agreed a rate of USD 19,000 for a trip via EC South Atlantic with Polaris. In the North, came reports of the Apollon (82,083/2018) Dublin 11/13 February placed on subjects for a trip via NC South America redelivery Far East at USD 27,000 to Panocean.  The Gleamstar (75,491/2011) Hong Kong prompt was rumoured fixed for a trip via Indonesia redelivery Malaysia at USD 14,500, whilst the Atlantic legend (83,685/2009) Manila prompt was said to have fixed for the same trip, but further details were yet to come to light. The Integrale (78,162/2014) sailed Rizhao 5 February was alleged placed on subjects for a trip via CIS Pacific redelivery South China with Atlantic Coal & Bulk but little else emerged.

Last week provided little cheer for owners, but what little there was, ebbed further away this week. Lows of WS 16 for MEG/West and low WS 30’s for East doesn’t make for healthy returns. A glance down the position list shows the scrubber/eco vessels taking most of the available cargoes, as simply making more sense of the returns. Meanwhile, the older (although under 15 years) unscrubbered ships are building up. For these vessels to make the same returns, it would need a 10 point ish swing in their favour, which in the short term remains unlikely. However, with the US attitude to Iran warming, albeit more to do with angry voters at the petrol pump, we could see a shift in the VL market as we know it. Also, with Chevron proposing Venezuelan possibilities, it could be time for the shadow market to come in to the light.

text: AMERICAS  Mont Belvieu propane prices softened earlier this week and interest levels were renewed as both buyers and sellers emerged for Feb and Mar when netbacks improved significantly.  Prior to that the market seemed to have begun to resign itself to waiting for the conclusion of the Olympics, the Chinese New Year, and, perhaps, some encouraging news on the Covid front. With the renewed interest levels terminal fees were buoyed from the lows seen at the front of Feb to a current bid/ask range of around 6.00-6.50cpg, depending on timing and location, etc.  Meanwhile, the EIA report for the week ending 04 Feb shows the U.S. to have consumed a ‘net’ 2mmbbls from the previous week and putting the overall U.S. propane stock total at 47.8mmbbls, or about 93% of last year.  The market, however, based its expectations off of cold weather and heavy exports, and was predicting a draw of around 3.8-4.0mmbbls.   The difference has now given cause for speculation as to whether next week’s number will include corrective data.  NWE Crude rises again! With CIF ARA lagging leaving the propane naphtha spread at $117pmt in Feb and widening, heavily favouring propane as a petchem feedstock.  A physical propane deal was done for end Feb at February CIF ARA -$7pmt, seen as low by the market. The regions production continues to be reduced due to LPG spiking into the natural gas stream. Which has lead to a large, 430,000MT being imported to the region in February, and these large monthly import volumes are expected to continue. The strength of the European demand has been keeping the arb form the US open. Drawing US volume form the Gulf Coast. The reduced US East Coast supply due to the cold weather in the region, and the reduced February export volume from the USGC forced European traders to pay-up and buy FOB cargoes from US terminals direct this week. As the market flipped from heading for cancellation to 6-7cpg FOB, for cargoes which will be 1H March arrivals in NWE. Butane is at 99% naphtha and with naphtha strengthening in line with crude this has opened the butane arb from the US.   MED There has been some action in the Med this week with Cepsa offer 4KT butane FOB Huelva $931pmt. The market weakened in reaction to this offer, the North Sea Mediterranean butane arb lost $19pmt on the day. Morocco’s butane demand looks well supplied through February.

Last week provided little cheer for owners, but what little there was, ebbed further away this week. Lows of WS 16 for MEG/West and low WS 30’s for East doesn’t make for healthy returns. A glance down the position list shows the scrubber/eco vessels taking most of the available cargoes, as simply making more sense of the returns. Meanwhile, the older (although under 15 years) unscrubbered ships are building up. For these vessels to make the same returns, it would need a 10 point ish swing in their favour, which in the short term remains unlikely. However, with the US attitude to Iran warming, albeit more to do with angry voters at the petrol pump, we could see a shift in the VL market as we know it. Also, with Chevron proposing Venezuelan possibilities, it could be time for the shadow market to come in to the light.

EAST With market players back from CNY festivities we were hoping for more action on shipping in the East, but so far the only deal reported done was to replace a late running ship. The MEG positions list remain long with a variety of owner and trader relets, and even if a big majority of these are ultimately sent West, we still need to see more cargos in play for the Eastern market to recover. So far we have seen 13 spot deals done in February (compared to an average of about 20 deals per month for last 6 months), and owners remain hopeful that there will be some last minute February requirements before focus shifts to next month.  WEST After several weeks of unfavorable arbitrage, we are seeing an uptick in activity. February is more or less sorted on freight and product with only two vessels left open. First half March has seen several fixtures and sub-fixtures at rates in the mid USD 90's Houston/Chiba and low USD 50's Houston/Flushing. Panama Canal waiting time continues to cause uncertainty for traders in a backwardated product market and limits the amount of deals concluded. It remains to be seen if we see enough deals concluded to push a positive momentum on freight rates.

text: MEG Mar CP edged up this week and traded at $782 at the time of writing, and C3/C4 was traded at flattish level. Backwardation into Apr narrow down to $32.  A few FOB AG cargoes were changing hand recently. One evenly split cargo for late Feb/early Mar lifting was sold at Mar CP minus mid-teens reportedly. One end Feb lifting full propane cargo was reported to sell at CP minus high single digit.   FAR EAST Cash premium improved slightly this week. 23kt propane parcel for 2h Mar arrival was reported traded at FEI plus mid-20s. And 1h Mar value were assessed higher due to the previous delays caused by fog and Panama congestion. However petchem demand are not very satisfying. PDH margins eroded as end products failing to catch up the rise on the costs. Several PDH was said to delay restart after TAR or lower down run rates to cut loss. One SChina PDH was reported to shut down for one month maintenance due to glitch. This week only one NChina PDH user secured 46kt C3 for Mar delivery reportedly. Another EChina PDH user is exploring 23kt propane parcel.  Taiwan FPCC issued buy tender to purchase flexible ratio for 23kt or 46kt LPG for 2h Mar delivery.

Another week of poor returns for owners in the Nsea/Baltic as rates were moving sideways. Some of the owners have already ballasted to USG where the market is firming, and if this trend continues it could be a positive development for the local market. Moving into the next week, we expect market to remain flat for cross-continent voyages and Baltic to be under downward pressure as ice class tonnage is pilling up.  The Med/Bsea market has traded sideways all week with ships being taken out one by one at repeat levels. TCE on TD19 is still giving owners returns way below OPEX. Some owners have been looking to send their ships TA to take part in the firming market there. As surrounding markets are currently improving, owners will be optimistic to see if the Med/Bsea market follows suit in the week to come.

Whilst the vast majority of the Suezmax market continues in a mundane manner, certain load zones can occasionally provide pockets of modest resistance. One such area is the US Gulf, where a prompt fixing window, combined with a diminishing list of safe ships, could see rates pick up, at least in the short term.  In load zones that have the luxury of enticing ballasters off forward laycans, flat/soft rates are likely to persist. With West Africa/East hovering around the WS 65 level, TD20 is likely to flirt with WS 60 unless we see a sudden deluge of enquiry, which is unlikely to happen this side of the weekend. In the East, TD23 has repeated WS 29.5 a number of times, although with rising bunker prices, repeating this number may not so easy. MEG/East will price WS 60-62.5 on modern tonnage.

With the Lunar New Year upon us, activity across basins has remained limited this week, maintaining high levels of global vessel availability amongst Subletters and applying sustained downward pressure on spot rates. JKM & TTF LNG prices continue to be in flux however spreads between indexes have been diminishing towards parity in recent days. This has partly been a result of Lunar New Year but also due to milder European winter weather and increased gas flows from Russia, levelling off European gas prices to almost match those of Asia. That said, with geopolitical tensions remaining elevated in the region and Asia coming back online later this week, the window to opportunity remains ajar for now. Term shipping activity has similarly slowed however rates continue to be in markedly healthy condition and relatively unchanged in anticipation of business-as-usual later this week.   On the newbuilding front, TotalEnergies’ announcement to restart Mozambique LNG within 2022 has more or less mopped up any remaining LNG berth availability at shipyards through to 2027, further tightening an already tight LNG newbuilding market. Requests for earlier slots have been heard quoted at considerable premiums while anything thereafter, from 2027 onwards, have been marked up accordingly. No new orders have been reported this week.

A floor was eventually found beginning of this period, as index was turning from red to green on Thursday last week. Over the week, the average TC rate almost doubled, from upper 5,000s to upper 10,000s. Australia to China has been the most active route, and there are also signs of a more active Brazilian market with c3 freight again excess of USD 20 pmt. Obviously the Chinese New Year and the celebration of the Tiger has put a lid on activity levels, but expectations are positive for the near future when the holiday comes to an end.

Increased sale and purchase activity on the dry cargo front where the supramax segment has been capturing most of the buying enquiry with 6 units changing hands this week. A pick up in liquidity pointing to a relative correction in values with new targets being set. A dynamic led by Chinese and Korean designed vessels which in typical fashion are the first to dip with sellers more willing to catch a falling knife by showing less resistance against a bid at less than last done. Elsewhere the Japanese controlled Kamsarmax “ENERGY TRITON” (82k built Tsuneishi 2012) achieved Usd 25m which similarly sets a well needed benchmark in a market that has started the year with a degree of hesitancy as to where the asset values are heading. Signs of ongoing negotiations and inspections suggest further sales in the near future.   The tanker market remains extremely subdued in terms of S&P with an underlying chartering market that offers no signs of respite. Noteworthy activity this week is the sale of the VLCC “ATHENIAN SUCCESS” which was sold to Sinokor at USd 42.5m. Levels that remain unsurprisingly flat with same owners having sold the exact sister “ ATHENIAN HARMONY” in December last year at Usd 42m.

Gong xi fa cai - “Congratulations and may you be prosperous.” Year of the Tiger   The week started with further losses seen on the BPI 5TC average as holidays in Asia as well as spot/prompt tonnage continued to impact market. The north Atlantic continued to appear still extremely underwhelming with pressure continuing to apply on the ballaster and committed tonnage, whilst in Asia, despite holidays some talk of a bottom to the market being found but with so little information or activity it was hard to gauge precisely. Some representative fixtures this week: Uniper controlled Golden Brilliant (74,232/2013) was reported fixing a 75,000/10 coal lift ex Ventspils to Amsterdam at USD 6.50 fio with Jera.  Navios Libertas (75,511/2007) was heard fixing delivery Aps US Gulf 17/20 February for a trip redelivery dop Egypt at USD 17,500 with Louis Dreyfus.  Junior (92,995/2012) delivery aps ECSA 15/20 February was rumored fixed for a trip redelivery SE Asia at USD 19,000+USD 900,000.  My Vision (81,502/2015) Xinsha 1 February was alleged fixed for a trip via Australia redelivery India at USD 19,000 but further details had yet to come to light.

As the bigger sizes the Supramax/Ultramax size segment is continued to be bearish, with the BSI finishing at USD 17,354 losing USD 100 pd on a daily basis. Atlantic experiencing more the downward pressure, while some may notice a marginal improvement in Asian markets despite the CNY holidays. The fact of seasonal market development can suggest that we will soon see the recovery in the Atlantic. The period market and fixtures reporting are quite limited, Norden fixed Tess 58 delivery East Med just below USD 25,000 pd for 1-year charter and Ultramax for 2-years period was fixed to Grain House at USD 21,400 pd. USG and ECSA are lacking fresh orders which reflecting in slow pace and subdued rates. Elsewhere in the Atlantic we see prompt tonnage building up. MV Pan Spirit (56,891/2011) on subs for Black Sea trip Egypt spot USD 13,500. MV Aphros (56,108/2013) open Black Sea heard on subs USD 15,000 dop to Israel.

Despite extremely adverse weather conditions we have had another lacklustre week in the Nsea/Baltic market with rates hovering around bottom levels. Some owners are trying to find an ‘escape’ card as the weak cargo program in the Nsea for the month of February doesn’t really give owners any encouragement to push for higher rates in the current fixing window. Also, the current ice class tonnage availability gives charterers plenty of options to choose from. We expect rates to move sideways for the next week.  In the Med/Bsea the few cargoes coming into the market are taking out the prompt ships on the tonnage list, resulting in a balanced market where the rates are moving sideways. One to keep an eye on is the weather in the area the next couple of days, where rough weather may lead to delays and replacement jobs.

Just when you thought a positive news story was in the offing, along comes a relet to ruin the ending. A Wafr/East cargo managed to pay five points less than a TD20 run last night, which defies the commonly held belief that it pays a premium over TD20. Whether regular owners bite on this as a "next done" rate, remains to be seen. Suezmax owners also have VLCC's to contend with as crossover levels in the Atlantic bring Suezmax stems within their crosshairs. Elsewhere, the East market remains quiet with CNY in full swing and likely to remain fairly unremarkable for the remainder of the week MEG/East should trade WS 62.5-65 on modern whilst TD23 hovers around the WS 30 mark.

With Chinese New Year celebrations in full swing, unsurprisingly the VLCC market has not been firing on all cylinders. The MEG market remains flat, and uninspiring, with rates mired in the mid WS 30’s for MEG/China runs. West Africa/East has also come down in parity. With Suezmaxes showing a little more fight (relets aside) for TD20, there is a danger the VLCC’s may start raining on their smaller sister’s parade, as co-load opportunities present themselves. Still, with a healthy number of deals ex MEG for the last 6 months or so and a busier Atlantic, the volume is there. It is more likely a combination of owners lacking the fight, as sentiment remains as low as it can get, coupled with the abundance of relets - the charterers Trojan horse. More of the same in the short term.

It is more likely a combination of owners lacking the fight, as sentiment remains as low as it can get, coupled with the abundance of relets - the charterers Trojan horse. More of the same in the short term.

Just when you thought a positive news story was in the offing, along comes a relet to ruin the ending. A Wafr/East cargo managed to pay five points less than a TD20 run last night, which defies the commonly held belief that it pays a premium over TD20. Whether regular owners bite on this as a "next done" rate, remains to be seen. Suezmax owners also have VLCC's to contend with as crossover levels in the Atlantic bring Suezmax stems within their crosshairs. Elsewhere, the East market remains quiet with CNY in full swing and likely to remain fairly unremarkable for the remainder of the week MEG/East should trade WS 62.5-65 on modern whilst TD23 hovers around the WS 30 mark.

Despite extremely adverse weather conditions we have had another lacklustre week in the Nsea/Baltic market with rates hovering around bottom levels. Some owners are trying to find an ‘escape’ card as the weak cargo program in the Nsea for the month of February doesn’t really give owners any encouragement to push for higher rates in the current fixing window. Also, the current ice class tonnage availability gives charterers plenty of options to choose from. We expect rates to move sideways for the next week.  In the Med/Bsea the few cargoes coming into the market are taking out the prompt ships on the tonnage list, resulting in a balanced market where the rates are moving sideways. One to keep an eye on is the weather in the area the next couple of days, where rough weather may lead to delays and replacement jobs.

EAST The Eastern freight rate has taken quite a big hit with the last done India fixture below USD 50 Baltic equivalent while the Chinese New Year festivities keeps being the main focus. As much of the Asian countries slowly return from Spring Festival celebrations, more spot activity is eventually expected. Freight in the East is getting very close to breakeven levels for most Owners, typically this could lead to more resistance towards further downside on freight rates. That put aside, the Middle East Gulf had a very strong month in January lifting-wise with over 60 liftings. Compared to recent months this is the highest number with a good margin. Approximately 70% of the liftings is heading to either China or India. A third of the liftings in January are spot fixtures. At the time of writing we count 11 spot fixtures out of the MEG in February.  WEST The US continues to see healthy exports with 85 liftings in January, seven of them LGCs. This is the second strongest month compared to the last four, only behind November which saw 91 liftings in total. In January, 67% of the liftings sailed East and 33% sailed West – the lowest East percentage compared to the previous 4 months. A strong crude price is usually affecting the arbitrage in a positive way, but with the current cold weather in the US and draws on inventories, propane and natural gas prices are being pushed higher and effectively limiting arb trades. This means there is very little interest in discussing shipping at current freight rates of around $100 east. Shipping has so far come off around $20 for a US/East voyage, but at the same time shipping is also being hit by rising bunker costs and waiting time in the Panama Canal makes scheduling, causing more ships to run late for laycans.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco set Feb Propane and Butane CP both at $775, up by $35 and $65 from Jan respectively, which fell within market’s expectation. However, some petchem players are worrying that downstream products value failed to catch up the rise, and squeezed or even negative margin might lead to the operation deratings. Mar CP was traded at $774 at the time of writing and Mar/Apr CP backwardation deepened to nearly $40.   FAR EAST Market is quiet this week as of lunar new year holiday. 23kt propane parcel for 1h Mar arrival was bid in window at Mar FEI plus $18 while no offers seen. Off window discussions are also muted but we expect more buying inquires for 2h Mar arrival will emerge once players returns.  Despite the thin activities, front Mar FEI has maintained the strength at $770 and Mar/Apr FEI was traded at $30, due to a combination of unexpected coldness, delays caused by Panama congestion and fog, together with the 4.3mil big draw in US propane inventory.
