Last week’s market took a breather and some market participants suggested this was it before we head downwards towards Q1. However, the fundamentals still prevail, and the fact is that there is a very limited amount of available tonnage in all basins and the demand still very healthy. The biggest increase we see is in the Atlantic with the round voyage fixing 23% higher than last week. But all other segments also up and the average of all routs is up by 16%. Though we are approaching holiday season and can sense owners’ willingness to cover it still seems too tight for this market to have seen its peak just yet, thus we expect a further increase in levels for the week to come.

We have experienced firming rates for a couple of weeks now and also into this week. However, mid-week there seems to be a bit of toppish feeling. TA’s are currently trading in region of USD 38,000.  There is good activity out of ECSA, and owners are now starting to ballast for same. In the Pacific there has been good activity for SE Asia round and a bit slower for the NoPac rounds.

Market participants with shipping length were hoping that the shipping activity would pick up on the back end of the CWC Rome conference. However, the week has so far been quiet. The arbitrage has fluctuated around the turning point to support inter basin trades, but the underlying story of the year 2021 (limited cargo availability) has put some restraints on the activity. The shipping rates came off a touch due to the lack of cargo activity and a slight increase in sublet shipping availability.  Yard activity in terms of enquiries and orders is high and this week we’ve logged 1xCelsius and 2xJPM. Newbuilding prices are in general firming with limited slot availability.

Market enjoyed further push confirming expectations of last week. The BSI figures were all in green reaching yesterday closing USD 27,300 pd about USD 1,000 pd higher from a week ago.  Strong demand in Atlantic for loaders in USG and ECSA pushed rates further up. In Asia, the demand/supply was more balanced. The period activity increased, with rates improving across the borders.  Trips from Continent to USG/ECSA reporting to fix around USD 30,000 pd, like the rates from Black Sea-Med to USG. Ultramax delivering USG fixing above USD 50,000 pd. ECSA seeing strong USD 25,000 pd plus approximately USD 1.5 mill for trips to Asia.  In the East, Supramax delivering North China fixed at USD 25,000 pd for a trip via the Russian Pacific port to China-Korea. Australian trip paying low/mid USD 20,000 pd depends on vessels’ s delivery.

text: AMERICAS Contrary to expectations, the EIA propane inventory for the week ending 3 Dec revealed a 600,000bbl increase to an overall total of 73.3mmbbls, or nearly 84% of last year at the same time.  As such, it remains to be seen as to whether a corrected set of data might be released in the coming weeks. The market this week had been predicting a draw of ~1.25mmbbls, the difference thus leading to even closer scrutiny of the data.  Overall export volumes are off the high’s seen earlier in the summer, and the buyback scheme at Enterprise remains underway so the 900,000bbl build in PADD III (the Gulf Coast) can generally be rationalized once higher production levels are additionally considered. Meanwhile, the pricing structure appears – for the moment at least – to have settled at around the $1.00/gal level, having fallen rather steadily from the $1.52/gal seen during the first week of Oct.  Terminal fees have softened, as well, and now range from a low just under 5cts/gal to a high of just over 7cts/gal for spot business. As it remains generally warm across North America, the market seems increasingly dependent upon two factors:  Weather (or the lack thereof) and petrochemical consumption rates – both in the US and abroad.  NWE The TOT window continues to be assessed at a small discount to December, with late December and early January looking well supplied. Through the recent global price swings the arb to Europe has remained robust. The only weakness in the market was caused by disrupted operations at Terneuzen, which continues to undergo maintenance to try to fix the issue. With December pro/nap now -$63pmt petchem demand will remain high and we expect the Terneuzen cracker to come back online as quickly as possible. Weather related demand has been rising and cold temperatures across much of the region are keep railcar demand high, as well as retail sector demand. The arb to Europe has been competitive with the East market for a month now, though FEI strengthening is causing traders wait and see if CIF ARA strengthens in line and continues to draw US imports.   MED The market looks balanced and winter demand has not exceeded tons already programmed to arrive in the region. Colder than average seasonal temperatures are yet to spread further south, and prompt demand lacking.

A relative busy week in the Dry snp markets in this end of year with about 15 vessels changing hands and a number of buyers re-entering the market in light of the most recent correction in values. Having taken a step back following a string of acquisitions, Costamare are back in the market having purchased the “EGYPTIAN MIKE” & “GEORGE P” (82k dwt built Guangzhou Longxue 2011 & 2012). The sister vessels were sold at an enbloc price of Usd 39m illustrating the abovementioned correction particularly well, especially when compared to last month’s sale of the “SM AURORA” (82k built Jiangsu Eastern 2012) which achieved Usd 21m. The same dynamic is witnessed across most dry segments with Supramax values also settling at levels which are about 15% lower than the recent peak. Notable transactions are those of Chinese design vessels which had greatly benefited of the recent rally with values soaring but which are similarly the most vulnerable to downward pressure.  A sense of delusion seems to have creeped in the Tanker markets off the back of the most recent spike in Covid cases pointing to yet another wave of restrictions across most western economies. As such most players seem be losing faith in the highly coveted market recovery resulting in very subdued activity. Therefore only four sales to report this week which once again took place in the product sector.

text: MEG Following the crude, Jan C3 CP rebounded to $688 and C3/C4 spread widened to $30 at the time of writing. Jan/Feb CP was traded at over $20 backwardation.  Qatar Petroleum issued a tender to sell 45kt propane for 14 to 26th Jan lifting and can consider sell on CFR basis.   FAR EAST Far East market is full of volatility and vitality this week, and most significant cash differentials improved healthy from negative to positive territory on FEI link price. 23kt propane for 1h Jan delivery was traded at Jan FEI plus mid-single digit. Similar cargo for 2h Jan delivery was bid at FEI plus mid-single range while offer at plus low teens. Outside window a plenty of tenders are floating in the market, except that Chinese buyers have concerns on subdued consumption for end Jan/1h Feb CNY period. Two Australia suppliers tendered to sell one evenly split and one heavy propane cargo for 2h Jan to 1st decade Feb arrival. One Korean Importer secured 23kt butane for 2h Jan delivery for cracking via tender, and another Korean importer also issued tender to procure similar cargo for Jan delivery. One Vietnam-based PDH user tendered to buy 46kt propane from 25th Dec to 25th Jan delivery. One Indian PSU was said to explore monthly one evenly split cargo for Jan and Feb delivery.

EAST Still some uncovered cargoes remaining on December dates in the East before we soon expect January to kick off after the last round of acceptances next week. We are seeing a tendency of less vessels sailing via Cape/Suez as the waiting time in Panama North bound has been decreasing lately potentially reducing the theoretical availability in the East. Freight ideas has been upped slightly the past couple of days as we are about to be closing December fixing and availability for actual East vessel slimming.  WEST Some early signs of increased activity have surfaced this week. A handful of first half January cargoes are being worked or at least within striking range and at the same time there were two FOB/CFR tenders in the market requiring shipping this week (of which one has been concluded already). It seems the product and freight market are finding its feet around the USD 110-112 mark and will probably hoover this range for the next handful of deals if the arbitrage sustains. As we are getting closer to January and most vessels still open during first half January are coming from the West or via Cape/Suez, the true effect of not being able to prebook northbound Panama is yet to be seen.

The Panamax market has gained values the last week, especially in the Atlantic. TA’s are now paying mid 30’s level which is about 10k up from last week. In the Pacific we also see rates firming, however not at the same pace. Pacific rounds are currently yielding 20k, up from about 18k last week. The period market has not been as active as recent weeks.

The VLCC segment has been in a slow decline in the week gone by, as players are digesting the effects of the latest Covid variant. Falling bunker prices have eased the drop in TCE’s, but fundamentals remain bearish with more than ample supply to cover demand. Several deciding factors are in play, amongst them OPEC+ upcoming decision for January production quotas and ongoing talks for revival of the Iran nuclear deal. In the meantime, charterers and traders are sitting on their hands and keeping activity to a minimum.

There is strong activity from all the major loading regions, with a notable uptick in vessels heading to the North Atlantic, South Atlantic, Black Sea/Mediterranean, and the largest loading countries in Asia. Stronger rates discussed from the USG, where trip to Far East was done around USD 47,000. Ultramax from ECSA to China was covered at USD 32,000 + 1.4 mill bb. From the period front, Supra open USG was fixed at USD 30,000 redel the Atlantic. More reporting from the East; Indo/China rounds on Supra concluded around USD 27,000. Nopac rounds done at USD 25,000. The seasonal average market development points to a continued upturn the next weeks.

Although delays in the straits continue, and a number of stems are expected to come out of Bsea end December, we do not expect an upward pressure on rates until the tonnage list tightens.

Protective control measures that have been implemented by certain countries are possibly kneejerk and we may see a return looser controls over the coming weeks (here's hoping). The East list continues to supply the Mediterranean and West Africa with ships on demand, and until we see VLCC/Suezmax cross over in the East, this scenario is likely to persist. TD20 trades mid/high WS 50's flat whilst MEG/China is WS 65 on modern tonnage. TD23 last openly traded at WS 35, but the list suggest this could come under marginal downward pressure again.

Following a flurry of sublet activity and market volatility in LNG these past couple of months, it appears we may finally be peaking and on trajectory to softer markets. Although Asian LNG prices remain relatively elevated in recent days off the back of stronger than usual European gas, it seems shipping rates have plateaued in part due to growing spot availability from subletters keen to get a taste for record high shipping rates. Optimization has surely been key to lucrative trading reported, with most sublets seen from portfolio players and traders dominating the vessel list. On term shipping, given a fair few vessel redeliveries to Head Owners are expected within Q1 of 2022, several multi-month and short term enquiries appear to be on hold with Owners and Charterers as they evaluate the market and consider their approach. That said, we still do see and expect continued activity on the term market as Charterers seek coverage through 2022, with some even issuing requirements earlier than expected.  On the newbuilding front, it was an active week with Qatari, Asian and Greek Owners all adding to their newbuilding orderbook in Korea.

We continue to see the Dry snp markets gradually adjust to the corrected rates we have seen settle throughout these past weeks. A correction in values that becomes particularly apparent for tonnage that is 5 years and older where levels achieved are 10 to 15% lower than most recent transactions. Modern units are showing more resistance being supported by high newbuilding prices which allow sellers to maintain their targets which remain, in comparison to NB, a more enticing offer. A dynamic that is particularly well illustrated by the resale of a Japanese controlled  Capesize which was sold to Diana Shipping at Usd 60m. The vessel is being built at Namura Shipyard and is scheduled for delivery in April 2022. Similarly in the Ultramax front where a resale delivering in 2023 from Tsuneishi Zhoushan achieved USD 34.5m. With forward curves showing signs of levelling off we expect values to move sideways in this end of year with lower volumes of transactions.  Uneventful close of the week on the Tanker front with very little change from our last report. Most of the activity continues to be captured by the Product sector with a number of mid 2000 built MRs changing hands. Values remain flat in a market where this renewed buying interest is met with a steady flow of sales candidates. Worth noting that offers were invited on two 10 year old Aframax units; understand that up to 10 outright bids were collected which is tribute to the positive underlying sentiment witnessed in the Tanker space.

EAST After an active last week in the East, the pace of fixing has naturally slowed down. Reports from India suggests a couple of PSU cargoes remaining on December laycans and one is already being worked at the time of writing. While there still remain a few potential December vessels in the East, those not finding suitable cargoes there, are likely to continue sailing towards US or other load regions. As such, not any noteworthy overhang is expected into January.  WEST The West freight market has taken a downturn since last time of writing. From last week’s high of USD 118 Houston/Chiba via Panama and low/mid USD 60 Houston/Flushing, the latest deal done is now some three to four dollars below on both routes.  Just three weeks ago, the fixing window was focused on laycans up to 40-50 days ahead whereas the current fixing window has been reduced to about 30-40 days ahead. At the time of writing, there are seemingly more relets than owner-controlled vessels open during end December and first decade January combined, however, the fact is that the balance of open vessels hasn’t changed much and we are likely to see a range of fixing activity once the product market finds its feet.

text: AMERICAS The sky is probably NOT falling but it sure feels like it. Lack of weather across the US has caused propane prices to crash from a 1.41 per gallon a month ago to 97 cents per gallon today.  The inventory situation, which a month ago looked as though the US would not have enough product to cover first quarter export demand,  is no longer an issue. Talk of 10 percent production growth, the lack of weather and falling Asian demand,  have all contributed,  but the bottom line is, we are not running out of product. The weekly number showed a draw of 1 million barrels which had little effect on the market.  Terminal  fees have continued to fall with Jan cargos bid at 4.50 cpg and sellers at just under 6.  NWE  The European market seems to be the only one which knows what winter is! CIF ARA continues to show relative strength in the context of FEI losing over $50pmt today and Mt Belvieu propane dipping under the dollar mark for the first time in months. Europe is feeling winter weather already and is forecast to have coldest winter in 30 years. But that is not the whole story as PDHs started buying again in December and January, ramping up imports from the US. And local supply continues to be around 36% less than usual as LPG is spiked into the natural gas stream. The arb East coming in has the December East/West spread at +$32 and more US loading VLGCs looking to come to the region. A seen by today’s window offer of a full propane VLGC cargo for end December arrival at December CIF ARA flat. This offer was basis 1 port with EU qualifications for buyer and equivalent to an offer of CIF ARA +$5pmt for a TOT stem.   MED The market is calm in the region and it seems buyers are waiting to see offers before showing their hand. Cold weather is being felt and demand is increasing, although this is yet to translate to action in the market.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco set Dec CP at $795 for Propane and $750 for Butane, down by $75 and $80 respectively compared to Nov. Previously in 1st and 2nd recommendation, some term lifters have recommended at above $800 for both grades. Jan CP for propane tumbled to $630 and C3/C4 narrowed down to $5-10, partly caused by the volatile crude over uncertain impacts by the new variant.  Qatar Petroleum announced their Jan acceptance with some delays reported.   FAR EAST A handful of deals been concluded in window this week, but cash differentials weakened in Jan delivered market. 23kt propane for 2h Jan delivery was traded from Jan FEI plus $4 to minus $2, reflecting the bearish sentiment amid high volatility.   Outside window, One Korean petchem player tendered to buy 23/23 or 23/0 or 0/23 parcel for mid Jan delivery into Daesan and awarded for 23/0 parcel at FEI plus single digit premium. Another Korean importer also tendered to buy 23kt propane for 6-10 Jan delivery into Daesan which is due on Friday. One EChina petchem plant issued buy tender to secure in total 46kt propane for 1h/Mid Jan delivery for cracking use.

The LNG market continued to build on last weeks gains, predominantly driven by the East with robust spot LNG prices delivered into Asia and the availability of shipping to fit enquiry still lacking. The emergence of new requirement seen last week saw high level discussions firm into sub-fixtures quickly as rates showed no sign of retreat. Expected tender news for demand in Asia will give more direction to the commodity market moving forward, but with availability of vessels currently light this is unlikely to have any effect on shipping rates in the spot market. The surfacing of more sublet availability probing for enquiry into January hasn’t put the dampeners on the market further out either, and as the fixing window stretches well into 2022, rates are maintained. The regional imbalance continues as rates in the Pacific remain at levels not yet achieved in the Atlantic. Though with so few ships in the basin, and the possibility for more volume to have to remain within the Atlantic, we could see this flip/reverse at any time. The potential for a prolonged Winter, Owners continue to ride the wave, with no signs of a change on the horizon.    Despite no newbuild orders being placed this week, prices remain firm and yards remain busy with plenty of enquiry and interest being recorded.

The Aframax market in the Nsea/Baltic took another hit this week as activity calmed down. There will be some maintenance work at the Primorsk load terminal before the winter season starts. This will reduce the export volume for the first decade of December. The market is looking utterly deflating, but there are some positive indicators that we are on the cusp of better times going forward. But the current trend is soft. In the Med/Bsea we have seen a solid downward correction this week with rates on benchmark routes dropping 20 points or so. Seeing that the list of prompt open ships is so long now, ships are simply being taken out of the market to cover the few cargoes being worked. We need to see a lot of the ships in the area being fixed until we can see the market firming again.

The VLCC market continues at a sluggish pace, with rates yet again under pressure. First decade of December MEG stems seems all but a wrap, leaving behind a number of ships seeking employment. The Atlantic has yielded little to help out, with only a few US export cargoes to show for it and Wafr cargoes all but absent. Daily earnings are yet again below OPEX even for the best of them. The US have said it intends release millions of barrels of oil from strategic reserves in coordination with China, India, South Korea, Japan, and Britain, to try to cool crude prices after OPEC+ repeatedly ignored calls for more crude, which doesn’t bode well of an increase in ocean going freight short term. However, longer term same reserves have to be replenished, showing a glimmer of light at the end of the tunnel.

We have experienced a sliding market the last couple of weeks, but this week we see a bit more optimism from owners’ point of view. Rates are slowly picking up and P1A is currently yielding 25k. In the eastern hemisphere we also see rates picking up, however at a slower pace. NoPac rounds are being fixed in region of 18k. Some period fixtures have also been reported after the FFA’s stabilized and gained some value.

The positive sentiment witnessed in the tanker markets over the past couple of weeks is starting to translate into transactions with a number of buyers picking up tonnage. This dynamic is led by the product sector which has seen eight vessels changing hands across an array of vintages. This pick up in activity doesn’t however mean that buyers go meet higher price expectations but rather sellers taking advantage of an increased buying pool to dispose of vessels that have failed to attract any interest throughout these subdued markets. This is particularly apparent for vessels that are 10 years and older which are seeing a notable pick up in buying enquiry. We therefore expect values to continue to move sideways with a number of similar vessels being placed for sale.  Dry cargo continues to see a slowdown in activity with bids coming at levels below last done In hope to capture the value offered by the recent correction. Corrected values that also put pressure on transaction already in places with signs of a number of deals failing to materialize.

Bumpy ride to recovery for the big ships as spot remains nervous and daily fluctuation considerable. Generally healthy Far East volumes push overall average earnings up almost 25 pct w-o-w, to come in at close to USD 32k/day. Iron ore price developments support a positive view, despite major ship-day-consuming fronthaul Brazil/China trade volumes continue to disappoint. This could dramatically change due to low number of ballasters - again a consequence of spread in value between Pacific- vs China-Brazil-China round more than doubling during last 5 trading days to stand at USD 7k. Atlantic remains quite tight on tonnage, and could react very strongly to even minor demand variations. Coal news also fuelling speculations of an end-year rally to still happen. Period activity fair, representative fixtures including 179,000 dwt/built 2014 done for 11-13 months at USD 22,750, 174,000 dwt/built 2007 for 20-23 months at USD 19,700 and 181,000 dwt/built 2012 for 9-12 months at 105 pct of BCI ave5tc.

The outlook for the Suezmax market remains unchanged with all load zones trading flat/soft. With VLCCs fighting to hold onto every point, the chances of a mid-winter Suezmax revival appear dim. Western charterers have become spoiled when it comes to the sheer choice of vessel for their long-haul cargoes. A quiet Eastern market has supplied them with a well-stocked menu of ballasters that have kept rates pinned to the floor. A bizarre anomaly of this market is that owners are willing to lock their fleets in at terrible rates on long haul despite consecutive short haul Western cargoes paying slightly more. Bot/East trades WS 70 for now, but if enquiry levels persist as they are, expect further softening. Next stop for TD23 is WS 30 and TD20 will struggle to stay out of mid WS 50s territory.

Given the above, the question is rather how high the market rises the next weeks rather than if it will rise.

EAST Since our last weekly update, we have seen several spot deals concluded in the Middle East throughout December. With new rules for Panama transits coming into effect shortly we expect this trend to continue, and this ultimately means that more ships will be positioned for Eastern business potentially creating more competition.  WEST Fixing focus is slowly but surely shifting to first decade January as the number of December cargoes in need for shipping diminishes. Owners’ freight target has been relatively persistent at, or around, the USD 120 per ton mark, however, a handful of relets seems content with somewhat lower rates than that. We expect activity to resume relatively soon and that the market tightness will persist well into first quarter next year. Although the product market is indeed a large decision maker for the market direction and activity level, the inefficiencies in discharge ports and Panama will contribute to an exciting start to the next year.

text: NWE The TOT window saw a propane deal done at strong levels as a trader purchased a 1H Dec delivered cargo at a fixed price equivalent to December CIF ARA +$34pmt. Multiple VLGCs are set to arrive in the region at the end of December and early January. As was seen by an oil major offering 15-20 December arrival VLGC in the window. The region has absorbed all of the arb cargoes headed to the region and that looks set to continue with the window trading at hefty premiums for prompt cargoes and small premiums for January arrivals. The region has seen imports from the US which has covered the most urgent demand.   USA HAPPY THANKSGIVING!

text: MEG Following the crude, Dec C3 CP was tumbled to $770 earlier and rebounded to $810 later this week. Dec C3/C4 maintained at $33, despite that a couple of evenly split cargos have been consumed and placed into India this week.  1st round CP recommendation ideas vary widely from lowest $740 to highest $830 for Dec C3 reportedly, while C4 at $30-40 less. Dec/Jan CP still traded at over $30 backwardation structure, regardless of the forthcoming winter demand.   FAR EAST Cash differentials weakens further, seeing 23kt propane for 2h dec delivery was traded from flattish to minus 3.5$ on Dec FEI link. 46kt propane parcel for 1h Jan delivery was offered at Jan FEI plus $8.8 while half cargo was offered at Dec FEI plus $2. Paper market is full of volatility this week. Dec FEI fluctuates from $20 to $50 daily, shadowing the movement on MB export price. Off window discussions are slow as of holiday timing and players are waiting for CP announcement.  One Korean Importer issued buy tender to secure monthly 23kt butane from Jun to Dec delivery in 2022, in order to capture the good discounts for cracking butane to Napatha. One EChina PDH user didn’t award their buy tender for monthly 23kt propane from Dec to Mar delivery into Ningbo. Another EChina PDH was exploring only 23kt propane for Dec delivery. Due to the squeezed margin, 5 or 6 PDHs in China are reported to schedule or advance their turnarounds to Dec and Jan, and we expect a minimum loss of 190kt propane for feedstock demand.

Aframax activity in the North Sea and Baltic came to a halt this week. Inevitably rates came off on the back of a longer tonnage list and less cargoes quoted in the market. Going forward we expect the market to remain soft, and we could also see a further decrease in rates.  Much of the same can be said about the Mediterranean/Black Sea market where rates have come off due to there are not being enough cargoes to satisfy the tonnage build up which is currently keeping the rates in favor of charterers. Neither in the Mediterranean/Black Sea we expect rates to firm in the short run.

Much of the recent news about oil production and consumption remains very up-beat, barring the odd Covid hiccup. However, inside of our VLCC market bubble, the positivity is yet to spill in to owners’ daily returns. As the week has progressed, rates have been steady and soft, with charterers able to pull a point or so from the MEG/East rates (down to WS 42.5 for TD3C), helped by the lull prior to the December stem date release. The Atlantic has promised much, yet stuttered and failed to spring to life (Wafr/East to test in the mid WS 40's). Some owners are ballasting modern vessels in that direction on speculation of an improvement.  December usually heralds better returns, but nothing has been close to normal in the last few years. Charterers need to keep what they are doing, and owners need to keep the faith.

Supramax spot remains down from previous week with rate reductions as much as 25% in the Atlantic and more than 50% in the Far East. The period activity is close to zero as both owners and charterers waiting to see where this market will land. Rates from the Med and Black Sea was falling with less activity as one would expect during this season. The Continent seems more balanced, and rates are still at reasonable levels. Scrap cargo to the Med paying USD 38k pd, trips to USG/ECSA in the mid USD 30k pd, and front haul, which is not a lot, still paying above USD 40k pd. USG and ECSA have been more active and indexes climbing up slightly. Levels are stable with some premium been paid for front hauls. Fixtures reported high USD 40k pd going East and mid USD 30k for Atlantic round voyages. The Indian Ocean has been under pressure, however rates were more stable compared to the Far Eastern markets. Trips from MEG to China paid USD 25k pd on Supra. The Pacific market feared worst, and there were rumours that Supra fixing below USD 15k pd.

The fourth quarter is failing to deliver and it all feels very bleak. Owners haven't helped their cause by maintaining a code of silence, despite a large tranche of vessels going on subjects in the last twenty four hours. OTC markets thrive on loose tongues otherwise the benchmarking process of the underlying spot market is significantly compromised. Additionally, VLCCs have only the feintest of pulses, and without the threat of "rate-crossover" East Suezmax markets have no short-term chance of sparking into life. Lists remain long in all regions and rates could take a further dive if present enquiry levels persist. Td20 is fighting to hang onto high WS 60's whilst Wafr/East will do well to stay above WS 70. Td23 trades about the WS 30 mark and MEG/East is showing signs of weakness in the mid/high WS 60's range.

Much of the recent news about oil production and consumption remains very up-beat, barring the odd Covid hiccup. However, inside of our VLCC market bubble, the positivity is yet to spill in to owners’ daily returns. As the week has progressed, rates have been steady and soft, with charterers able to pull a point or so from the MEG/East rates (down to WS 42.5 for TD3C), helped by the lull prior to the December stem date release. The Atlantic has promised much, yet stuttered and failed to spring to life (Wafr/East to test in the mid WS 40's). Some owners are ballasting modern vessels in that direction on speculation of an improvement.  December usually heralds better returns, but nothing has been close to normal in the last few years. Charterers need to keep what they are doing, and owners need to keep the faith.

Aframax activity in the North Sea and Baltic came to a halt this week. Inevitably rates came off on the back of a longer tonnage list and less cargoes quoted in the market. Going forward we expect the market to remain soft, and we could also see a further decrease in rates.  Much of the same can be said about the Mediterranean/Black Sea market where rates have come off due to there are not being enough cargoes to satisfy the tonnage build up which is currently keeping the rates in favor of charterers. Neither in the Mediterranean/Black Sea we expect rates to firm in the short run.

From believing to have found a logical bottom last week, the Panamax market has continued to slide into this week. Even though we see more demand in the North Atlantic, it is not enough to absorb the growing tonnage list. P1A is currently priced in the mid 20’s. Shorter Murmansk rounds have although been concluded in the low 30’s. The Pacific has taken a beating this week, especially the Aussie rounds. The Pacific rounds are currently priced around 20k.

It has been a volatile week since our last report. In the East, stronger buying interest from end-users has prompted moderate gains while in the West, these gains have been outstripped on news of NS2 pipeline delays due to regulatory approvals, firmly slamming shut the window to any arbitrage opportunities. Although the ramifications of headline pipeline delays has yet to be uncovered fundamentally, the matter of fact is that the LNG shipping market continues to stay very tight. If last week appeared to be the calm before the storm, this week we may’ve just started to feel the breeze picking up. In recent days this has been made clear by an emergence of new requirements issued in advance from apprehensive end-users seeking coverage for their peak winter cargoes, aware that shipping availability over the coming period to be sparce. To this end, with many subletters holding tight onto their dear tonnage and most independent owners sold out, Charterers may have few other options than to pay up, and more often than not, also absorb hefty idle time costs in order to secure a vessel.  The newbuilding market also remains firm with another week of new and confirmed orders, this time by Maran Gas Maritime with DSME and Celsius Tankers with SHI for a pair of newbuilds each. Besides attending signing ceremonies, yards have their hands busy with multiple ongoing newbuilding enquiries.

After last week's positive start sentiment changed as more available tonnage came into the market with owners chasing charterers' attention with lower and lower freight. The iron ore route from West Australia to China is down by 17% and iron ore from Brazil to China down 8%. The combination of all time charter routes down USD 6693. On a positive note, we see there is very few ballasters left for Brazil and a very healthy list of vessels preforming West Australia to China. This indicates that the massive amount of vessels that came open after the congestion drop now is employed.

As expected, we are indeed experiencing a relative slowdown in terms of volumes of sale on the Dry cargo fronts. However, with the weekly liquidity that we have been accustomed to over the past months, this slight loss of momentum is far from a complete halt in SnP activity with north of a dozen vessels changing hands this week. Values as a whole are shifting sideways for the time being despite the adjusted bids seen from buyers looking to take advantage of the dip in rates, to secure tonnage at less than last done. Signs of which can be seen in the more liquid of segments such as Supramax units that are seeing levels which are on average 10% lower than the most recent completed sales.  Tanker markets continue to show growing signs of anticipation for a healthier rates environment. Buying enquiry is steadily rising along the recovering sentiment with product sector leading the charge showing a great number of enquiries for MRs and LR2. Well needed benchmark being set in the crude sector which has seen the Aframax “Antonis” (113k dwt, 2017 built Daehan) sold at Usd 45m. A sale that draws direction in a market that has strong levels of buying interest for units of such vintage, but which has seen no sales to provide some additional support for potential buyers to come forward with their bids.

text: MEG Swap price has been on a roller coaster this week. At the start Dec CP plunged to $800 from last week’s $860 and rebounded to $820ish during mid-week, but quickly retreated below $800 as crude declined below $80. Dec C3/C4 spread furthered widened to $33, as a plenty of butane available in the front market against lukewarm demand. Dec/Jan CP still traded at $30 backwardation. Saudi Aramco released their Dec acceptance, and majority received in line with their nominations. It is expected to export at 700kt in Dec, similar to Nov exports. Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their sale tender of 15-24th Dec lifting full propane to one Chinese player at FEI netback link.  FAR EAST Cash premium weakens this week as buying inquires subdued, together with easing congestion in Panama . 23kt propane parcel for 2h Dec delivery was offered at Dec FEI plus $3.5 while bided at plus $1. 23kt butane was offered at fixed price $762 on Thursday, yet to entice interests.  Off window a few tenders are running. One Korean petchem user issued buy tender to secure an evenly split cargo for 1-7th Jan delivery into Daesan for cracking. One EChina PDH user issued buy tender for monthly 23kt propane from Dec to Mar delivery.

EAST Saudi acceptances were released on Tuesday with no cuts being reported. We are starting to see some additional relets emerging on the East position lists, which for the short term could soften the recent increase in freight rates. That said, we are entering the winter period where we typically face more delays and inefficiencies, much of which we indeed already start to take note of.  WEST As we are over halfway through November it seems like the last uncovered cargoes mid December have been absorbed. At the same time last decade December fixing is well underway. We only see a couple of relets left this period while most of the available ships are owner controlled. The freight rates continue to increase with last concluded fixture done at USD low 110s and USD 115 Houston/Chiba on subs. Congestions in the neo-Panama Canal is finally decreasing a bit to thirteen days Northbound and twelve days Southbound after seeing as much as nineteen days last week, but there is still an uncertainty for vessels without a pre booked slot.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Massive volatility has overwhelmed the market this week, both prior to and after the EIA inventory numbers were released on Wednesday.  Mont Belvieu propane closed Monday at $1.22/gal, saw massive inter-day price swings all day Tuesday and closed at $1.21/gal, then finally went a bit calm prior to the stock data Wednesday morning but then fell sharply in afternoon trade, only to rebound again and close at $1.19/gal.  By Thursday morning $1.10/gal was seen in early activity, but then rebounded to $1.14/gal as of this writing. As of 12 Nov 2021 overall US propane stock levels were listed at 74.6mmbbls by the EIA, down by 200,000bbls from the week prior.  This took some by surprise as a decline of some 1.0-1.5mmbbls was generally anticipated.  PADD I built by a half-million barrels while Gulf coast stocks fell by 400,000bbls – not altogether surprising since export volumes are believed to be back at robust levels.  Propane inventories in the US are now 80+% of last year and nearly 84% of two-years ago.   All the while, US terminal fees have seen their fair share of volatility, though there remains a multi-tiered structure where the terminals themselves have purposefully priced themselves out.  Re-sellers have been seen offering various ratio cargoes at between 7cts and 9cts/gal, though availability is becoming thinner through the balance of 2021.  NWE The bids in the TOT window are not being hit, even it is thought 4 VLGCs 2 LGCs and an MG are expected to arrive in the region between end of November and early December. The bids have been shown at a premium to Naphtha values or at fixed prices. This week’s price swings have led to caution form traders and a fixed price is seen as an easier risk to manage. It is possible that VLGCs could consider re-routing to Asia if the East/West spread continues to widen from December +$61pmt. This uncertainty is keeping the arb to the region wide and the netback competitive. The Propane Naphtha spread has come in this week leading some traders to expect PDH buying to pick up and dramatically increase the regions demand. A butane offer in the window for early December jolted the quiet market and has just pushed values down from 110% to 105% Naphtha today on the lack of buying interest.   MED A full propane VLGC loaded Houston is heading to the region. The Butane arb from the US is open though no new cargoes have been heard making this trade. Morocco is yet to show additional demand above their existing term contracts. Though the arb is wide milder weather is yet to kickstart the Mediterranean market.

Still a bumpy road in the tanker space and somewhat lack of clear direction. We see signs and growing interest, but the market is still in need for more steady guidance. Hafnia (BW) has again proved their strong belief in consolidation and enjoyed the headlines this week with their massive acquisition of the Oaktree controlled Chemical Tankers Inc (CTI) fleet. The transaction adds 32 modern, Eco, IMO II vessels and consist of 6 MRs, 18 Handies and 8 x 25k stainless steel tankers – all Korean/Japanese built. The equity portion was funded through issuance of new shares on a NAV-for-NAV basis and leaves Hafnia the largest operator in the segment and Oaktree as the 2nd largest shareholder at approx. 20% of Hafnia (Oaktree controlled ca 95% of CTI). Fearnley Securities is acting as financial advisors to CTI in the transaction as announced on 11th November 2021. On the crude side, we have seen a new sale in the Suezmax segment with M/T Densa Whale (158k dwt, blt 2012 Hyundai) sold for Usd 32-32.5 m to Greek buyers. There are limited references in this age, but we would say the price is somewhat lower than what we would expect. More in line with expectations was the sale of M/T Astro Perseus (159k dwt, blt 2004 Hyundai) at Usd 18.5 m. More interest also piling up on older Aframaxes and we expect transaction numbers to pick up.  Subdued Dry cargo rates and uncertainty stemming from falling forward freight agreements translate in a softening of buying interest. At least relative to the unhindered wave of buyers that the markets were so accustomed to. Sellers seem to have taken a standby approach rather than going to meet testing bids at levels lower than last done - saying that we do expect the odd correction that would traditionally come from Japanese sellers transacting at best.

The Capesizes finally found a floor and the West Australia route was concluded excess mid 12 levels, expected to improve further later this week. C3 is still not being very active, with Vale running the show more or less alone, but now signs of stronger fixtures done excess index levels. Period activity remains slow, illustrating the firm sentiment and great expectations for next year.

The increasing concerns over the recent market development continues to dominate owners' minds. The fact of slower demand of the key commodities such as iron ore, coal together with strict environmental measurements in China added to the deepest index dive during the last 9 months. The period market took a complete break as we saw the decrease from the highest rates paid on Tess 58 of USD 30,000 pd for 1 year charter to the USD 19,000 pd that rumoured was fixed this week.  The most suffered market appears to be in the East where we saw drop from solid USD 35,000 pd in most of the trading routes to below USD 20,000 pd on Supra as recently reported. BSI dropped over 20% last week, which is still understating the actual market drop as per done fixtures. The Atlantic market compared to Asian markets fell as well but not as hard. USG and ECSA are still paying above USD 30,000 pd for TA destination and front hauls are around low/mid USD 40,000 pd.

Mid-week it seems that we have hit the bottom of this time’s downturn. Atlantic is trading slightly up, especially in the North Atlantic with higher than last done on rounds. P1A is currently priced at high 30k. In the eastern hemisphere we have seen more activity for NoPac rounds and Indo coal cargos. Pacific rounds being concluded in the 23/24k region. The period market has been very shaky the last week where FFA values have been plummeting and takers withdrawing until beginning this week. A Kamsarmax was concluded at 22k for 12/14 mos with Far East delivery.

text: MEG Following the crude, Dec C3 CP was retreated to $865 at the time of writing, from highest at $887 earlier this week. Dec C3/C4 spread widened to $40 as weaker seasonal demand on butane. Dec/Jan backwardation also enlarged further to $30 from last week’s $20, reflecting the front strength, partly caused by US cargos delays due to Panama congestion. Saudi Aramco was said to have one end Nov lifting heavy butane cargo available to sell. Qatar Petroleum also issued tender to sell one 45kt propane for 15-24th Dec lifting. And similar cargo for 2h Dec was concluded at $890 on Thursday.  Outside window plenty of tenders are running this week.  Indonesia PERTAMINA was reported to buy one evenly split cargo for Nov delivery at Nov CP plus high 30s via tender, but did not award their latest buy tender for Jan delivery.  One SChina PDH user didn’t award its buy tender for 66kt propane on dec delivery but was said to cover some volumes outside tender. One EChina petchem user secured 23kt propane for 2h Dec delivery into Ningbo at Dec FEI plus mid-high single digit. Similarly, another EChina PDH buyer award their buy tender for 46kt propane on Dec delivery at Dec FEI plus low single digit.  Other than spot tenders, One new PDH user located in Lianyungang was reported to award their term buy tender for monthly 23/0 at CP plus less $40. Another SChina traditional importer was said to award their term tender for monthly 11/11 parcel at CP plus less/around $40 and FEI plus less/around $10.

EAST One trader fixed a ship early December MEG in the high 50s, but apart from this deal we are still waiting for more charterers to move for December laycans. This is partly due to some of the acceptance dates for next month not being out yet, and with Adnoc dates around the corner we expect to see more activity soon. With continuous delays in some of the major ports in China, shipping availability remains tight in the Middle East from early December, and most of the owners are aiming for 60s Baltic for next deals.  WEST One of the big talking points in the VLGC market nowadays is the ‘substantial’ delays for non-booked transits via the neo–Panama Canal. Current projected waiting time is 18 days either way. These delays coupled with congested or slow turnaround time in Far Eastern discharge ports means that the vessel availability in the USG and USEC is uncertain for vessels that have not prebooked their transit. And this uncertainty is adding to the bullish sentiment. At the time of writing, there are vessels on subs during mid/second half December at USD 105-110 pmt range, however, the last concluded fixture was done during 20-25 Dec at low USD 100s. The tight vessel supply is expected to persist throughout December and as long as steaming in ballast via Cape of Good Hope is not really an economically viable option, it seems the upside is bigger than the downside when looking at the shipping market. Parallel to the product market we are yet again facing a situation where something has to give and it seems it won’t be freight, simply due to the low availability.

text: AMERICAS Flat price Mt Belvieu propane has come off considerably this week and we are not entirely sure why. Have the traders given up on winter already, are trader’s being stopped out.  Time will clarify,  but for us it seems a bit early to be giving up on Winter.  Terminal fees in the U.S. remain buoyant, and simultaneously continue to be multi-tiered.  The terminals – if there is product and dock space remaining – are able to offer product from between the low 9cts/gal up to the low 10cts/gal range.  The ongoing differential between ethane and propane values is believed to still be much of the cause.   Re-sellers, meanwhile, are offering at levels just below that, but product is somewhat limited.  On the other hand, Enterprise continue in their efforts to buy back cargoes (at its own facility) and are expected to be able to bid in the mid 5cts/gal range. Yesterday’s EIA propane inventory report for the US showed a decline of 1.3mmbbls as of the week ending 05 November, to an overall total of 74.8mmbbls – or 79% of last year and 82% of the total from two years ago.  The breakdown shows that PADD I (the East Coast) drew down by 1.1mmbbls, primarily because of cooler temperatures in the region.  PADD III, however, built by 200,000bbls, confounding many because export volumes for the week were robust.  NWE The December window in Europe opened trading with a bang as a bid at +$21pmt to balance November CIF ARA quotes for 1-5 Dec. Showing that the physical market is tight and supporting the wide arb from the US. With the December East/West spread at +$72pmt it seems strong bids are needed to attract tons to the region. This could also tempt traders to look at selling in the region rather than risk waiting time at the Panama Canal. With propane/naphtha spread at +$73 it seems winter demand is beginning to drive the market. The butane market saw some action early in the week and remains tight and at 110% Naphtha.   MED Weather in the region has been mild and spot trading activity quiet. The market remains on the tight side and the arb from the US is wide open as well as from Northwest Europe. So far no spot cargoes are headed to the region. As the weather gets colder imports will be needed for the increased demand.

The sentiment has been waning in the VLCC segment in the week gone by. Rates have come under pressure as activity has gone quiet or under the radar, and MEG/Eastbound rates have been pushed below WS 45 for the best of them, with rebates to be had for tonnage not ticking all boxes. The Atlantic has fared a tad better, trading slightly north of the WS 45 mark for the benchmark Wafr/China route. The USG export sector has been off to a slow start for December with only a handful reported fixtures for the region. With worldwide crude demand almost back to pre-Covid levels longer term optimism remains strong, but short-term prospects are on the wobbly side, although the downside appears limited.

As we cautioned last week, all load zones needed to see sustained enquiry, otherwise rates were in danger of softening. Unfortunately, the cavalry failed to arrive in time and Td23 crashed down to WS 37.5, suggesting MEG/East might now threaten the low WS 70's mark. The East list is the real bane of the market, as insufficient MEG enquiry has allowed tonnage to build and now many of these early ships, having missed their natural dates locally, have commenced ballasting to Wafr on spec'. This could see TD20 trade down to low WS 70's and in turn drag Wafr/East into high WS 70's territory. It's not all doom and gloom. Delays in the Turkish straights are climbing towards ten days north bound and Aframaxes may yet spring a few winter surprises, potentially dragging Suezmaxes into play.

We are witnessing a sentiment shift this week in the SnP markets with a loss of momentum in Dry cargo following a substantial correction in rates which resulted in an immediate weakening of buying interest. A loss of momentum which is particularly apparent in the volume of reported sales, but which has yet to transcribe into lower values. A resilience in pricing that can be attributed to sellers choosing to show composure in what many consider to be a temporary dip. Therefore, this week comes to a close with eight vessels changing hands at levels in line with their respective "last dones".  A stark contrast to the Tanker markets where the growing anticipation of a market upturn is leading an increase in buying enquiry. Norden have committed their scrubber fitted  "NORD SKATE" and "NORD STINGRAY" (51K DWT 2009 STX) at Usd 17m each. A sale falling in line with Norden's effort to renew its MR fleet considering that earlier this month they acquired the two modern sisterships ECO LOS ANGELES and ECO CITY OF ANGELS (50K DWT HMD 2020) at Usd 36.5m each.

Demand is disappearing, congestions easing off, coal shipments from Indo reducing dramatically it’s all added pressure on spot trading as well as period market vanished away. Not much more to add except that we perhaps see the overreaction on the market due to the latest FFA development rather the fundamental grounds. Rates in the Pacific trading around low/mid USD 20,000 pd, and low/mid USD 30,000 pd in the Atlantic. End last week FH rates from ECSA was reported on Ultra USD 28,000 pd plus USD 1.7 mill GBB. This week not much surfaced to report.

P1A is currently trading around 32k from last week’s 36k. In the Pacific, rounds are being concluded at around USD 25k which is down from last week’s 37/38k. All this is caused by lack of demand, but we do believe we will find a logical bottom very soon. The period market has taken a massive beating this week, also with the effect from the downward curve in FFA’s.

Market not yet fully done adjusting from October's somewhat overheated sentiment for the big ships, although last 3 weeks have looked much like a landslide. With sentiment nervous and paper players leading the way, average daily earnings shredded by another USD 13k w-o-w to come in at USD 27k. Pain is particularly felt on the Brazil/China fronthaul run, where adjusted iron ore demand prospects and lack of spot activity have knocked the 100-days China-Brazil-China round voyage value down by another 27 pct to USD 22k. Inter-Pacific spot demand is healthy and stable in comparison, but Pacific traders have nevertheless seen it coming off close to 30 pct over last 5 trading days to stand at USD 23k. Considerable period interest, but little or nothing presently being concluded as eroding spot and paper values translates into justified target levels constantly sliding.

text: AMERICAS The month of October – historically considered the conclusion of the inventory ‘build’ season and the simultaneous commencement of the winter consumption period – has seen a series of surprises.  Stocks are now 79% of the total achieved last year, and 79% of the total recorded two years ago.  Wednesday’s build of 400,000bbls is being viewed as sentimentally bullish, as the Gulf Coast drew by 600,00bbls on the back of Enterprise buybacks and reduced rates in October at Targa’s Galena Park facility (which have been solved by now but were related to onshore hydrate issues).  But reduced market values yesterday afternoon paint a different story as MB Non-TET propane values fell below $1.39/gal however most believe the drop was more related to ZWTIs fall than propane directly.  As for the near-term prospects, most of it will depend on the weather, and then where that weather occurs, and when.  For the moment forecasts are calling for a cold and wet Thanksgiving which should propel the market in a bullish direction.   Terminal fees on the Gulf Coast remain tiered and based on whether the seller is a terminal owner or a reseller.  Bids and offers are nonetheless occurring on a resale basis on either side of 6cts/gal for Dec.  NWE The region is tight prompt propane tons. ToT window bid for 14-18 November delivery has been pushing up window premiums. The bid is equivalent to November CIF ARA +$4.5pmt, and it seems sellers are testing how badly the cargo is needed with window offers some way off at +$8pmt for Novmeber 23-27 and +$11pmt for November 20-24. With netback values from the US supporting trans-Atlantic trade late November is seen as balanced in the region. The East / West spread in November is at +$50pmt but this does not tell the whole story. With Panama Canal delays at expensive freight rates traders are factoring in around $8pmt in waiting time. US imports to the region will undoubtedly be higher than in October. The question is how much volume can the market take before coming off?  MED Temperatures are falling in the region and heating demand is increasing. There are two VLGC heading to Gibraltar from the US keeping traders from showing bids before tons arrive in the market. Though the more likely explanation is that these vessels are headed to the Suez Canal to go East. Cutting out waiting time in Panama. That said if the price is right traders could decide to sell cargoes in the region.

As we cautioned last week, there were likely to be regrets from owners who threw in the towel too early in West Africa, and this proved to be correct. Despite a relatively quiet week in most load zones, Suezmax owners managed to reverse losses in West Africa with Td20 climbing back up WS 77.5. This unfortunately comes with an obvious caveat; rates might be tested marginally downwards unless we see a marked increase in global cargo volumes, and it needs to happen this side of the weekend. With Black Sea delays hovering around 8 days north bound, charterers are now fixing Td6 deep into the third decade with owners eyeing this as a demurrage trade rather than an opportunity to push rates up. MEG/East is likely to trade mid WS 70's on modern whilst Td23 has a long list of ships to choose from and may threaten mid WS 40's.

EAST The bullish sentiment on freight has continued in the East this week, and another 3-4 deals were fixed on subs from the Middle East and Australia. Last done range from USD 56-58 Baltic eqv, and the East is currently trading close to parity compared to the West (if excluding waiting time for Panama transit). There are still reports of some uncovered cargos during November, and as open ships with firm itineraries are now few, we do not expect rates to come off anytime soon. The QP acceptances for December were published beginning of this week, but we have yet to see any companies starting to look at December laycans for now.  WEST This week the West has calmed down a bit after some very busy days last week. First decade December looks to be fully covered as most now focusing on 2nd decade onwards. We only see a couple of relets this period while the majority of the available vessels is owner controlled. The freight rates are stabilizing at USD mid/high 90s after the jump last week. At the same time the congestions in the Panama Canal are still increasing, estimated waiting time is 14 days Northbound in the Neo Canal.

Aframax rates in the North Sea/Baltic increased slightly on the back of a tighter tonnage list as charterers covered their cargoes up to mid-month November. Going forward we expect the market sentiment to remain firm. In the Mediterranean/Black Sea, we have seen the market continue to firm and pick up a few more points since last week. Although charterers have held back somewhat on the cargo side this week, owners will see the delays in the Straits along with an active Suez market as positives. Activity under the radar is still very much alive, and we expect the market to be stable with a firm potential in the week to come.

Sentiment is somewhat undecided in the VLCC market, and rates have flatlined in the mid WS 40’s for MEG/Eastbound voyagers. A quieter Atlantic Basin has also limited alternative opportunities. Chinese charterers have been busy scheduling more or less the entire domestic fleet for voyages back to the homeland, in addition to fixing “third party” tonnage. However, most of which have been done on the quiet, and the owning community has been caught slightly off guard with volumes slipping through their fingers. Although treading water, the downside appears limited short term.

Stepping into the new month, brisk November weather in tandem with an absence of prompt tonnage in the Pacific has burgeoned rates further. Cargo market volatility continues to be present and this week the arb has narrowed as LNG prices retract from recent highs. Of late, Charterers have stretched their reach in an attempt to cover winter laycans ahead of seasonal rate increases, as a consequence we witness a lack of November laycans and the focus is concentrated on December and early January.  Activity remains strong with multiple fixtures occurring the past week with last done repeatedly being usurped. Vessel availability remains tight, particularly in the Pacific. In the Atlantic, the situation remains slightly muted as pockets of sublet availability offer refuge to a charterer with timely and specific needs. In addition, project tonnage continues to be offered to market and when combined with these pockets of availability, the rate levels remain below those being achieved in the Pacific. This could, however, alter very quickly as projects require the use of their fleet and/or more tonnage is directed East due to cargo demand. For those celebrating tomorrow, we wish you a happy Diwali.

text: MEG Despite the increased supply in Nov, Saudi Aramco raised up their Nov Propane CP by $70 to $870, and Butane by $35 to $830. This is much higher than most players’ expectations and the swap value traded previously. Dec Propane CP was traded at $850ish and Butane at $20 cheaper during the mid week, amidst uncertainties over crude and lukewarm demand for the front.   FAR EAST  Cash differentials weakens this week in lack of buying interests. Off window 23kt propane parcel for 1h Dec delivery was traded at Dec FEI minus low single digit reportedly. Similar cargo was offered on Wed window at FEI flat but was bid at FEI minus $6. Regardless of the delays caused by Panama waiting, Dec supply still appears ample as a couple of unsold cargos rolled from Nov into 1h Dec. FEI swaps still under downward pressure as Chinese DCE-PG continued a slump this week. However, despite the eroding PDH margins, one SChina PDH plant issued spot tender to purchase in total 66kt propane for Dec delivery into Dongguan but requested for Jan or Feb CP link pricing. Indonesia PERTAMINA also tendered to buy one evenly split cargo for either on CFR basis for late Nov-early Dec delivery or on FOB for mid Nov loading ex AG.

No major developments this week with unchanged sentiment across both sectors. The dry markets continue to see sustained liquidity with numerous deals to report each week and a steady stream of fresh sale candidates being placed in the market. This week has seen a particular pick up in activity on the modern front with a number of buyers now aiming for younger units. On the kamsarmax front, we have seen the Oshima built resale MV “RAMANA ROSE” being sold to Greek buyers at Usd 44m basis a prompt delivery from the yard while the Chinese built “SEACON SHANGHAI” (82k dwt 2019 Huangpu Wenchong) was sold at Usd 38m. A relative push in values for the modern units which becomes particularly apparent when compared against this weeks sale of the ten year old “KEY DISCOVERY” (82k dwt 2012 Tsuneishi Fukuyama) which achieved Usd 24m.  The product space has captured all of this weeks tanker activity with 5 MR units changing hands. Similarly we have seen notable movement on the modern front with two resales being sold at Usd 37.8m. The vessels are currently being built at the ex STX facilities now operating under the name K Shipbuilding – both units are due for delivery in 2022. A transaction that offers a well needed benchmark in a pricing environment that has been hostage to soaring NB prices. Values on the older vessels remain under pressure despite the relative pick up in liquidity – a sentiment well illustrated by the sale of the D'Amico controlled “High Venture” (51k dwt 2006 STX) which was sold at Usd 10.7m with DD freshly passed and BWTS installed.

It has been a couple of weeks with steady increase in rates for the VLCCs. Driven initially by an active West market where charterers with long haul voyages to cover tapping up eastern ballasters, with ships open in the Atlantic hard to come by. East of Suez also busy but with a position list filled with vintage ships or ex dd, the rates are not going through the roof quite yet. However, with owners’ sentiment strong, the rates are expected to increase as we move further into mid November laycan ex MEG. With the count now up to 50+ deals done, there is a lot of wood left to chop before we reach December, so upside potential in the days ahead.

The Aframax market in the Nsea/Baltic area finally ticked up a few points on the back of increased fuel enquiry coupled with a healthier Baltic crude export program. Going forward, we expect rates to firm further supported by surrounding markets offering an alternative for those owners willing to ballast out of the area. Owners with ships in the Med/Bsea finally have a market to get excited about as rates pick up at 25-30 points across the board over the course of the week. This is due to several reasons, but mainly because cargo activity has been healthy and at the same time delays are increasing in Turkish Straits. In the week the come we expect this firm trend to continue.

Regardless of the perceived backward steps in Wafr, the key indicator to observe is the gentle momentum in the VLCC market, meaning that owners who fixed Td20 at a discount to last done are, perhaps, short-changing themselves. Furthermore, second decade Wafr should still have a solid chunk of enquiry to come, and that despite some softer fixing, this market should push on again. Td20 has added circa 30 points in the last 3 weeks alone, suggesting it would be a brave punter who bets against this same scenario being replicated three weeks from now. Black Sea delays are up to 8 days north bound, and as we head into November this is likely to increase which will see risk-averse charterers demanding Canakkale cancelling 10-12 days prior to laycan. Td23 trades minimum WS 47.5-50 whilst MEG/East is WS 77.5-80 with a flat feel.

LNG freight levels continue their rally as we move further into the winter season. There are a handful of requirements targeting December and January laycans as Charterers have started hitting the market for tonnage much earlier than in the past. As a result, we see rate levels aligning in both basins, in contrast to the disconnection seen in recent weeks. On the vessel supply side, availability remains very tight with most independent tonnage being sold out and portfolio tonnage remains subject to uncertainties around scheduling or are restricted on period. Those willing to take the risk are seeking higher levels of compensation, thus pushing the market higher. The term market also remains busy with Charterers focusing on securing coverage for 2022 and beyond. text: AMERICAS The overall U.S. propane inventory build of 2.1mmbbls as reported by the EIA Wednesday for the week ending 22 Oct was welcome news and appears to have had the anticipated impact, at least sentimentally.    The increase pushes stock levels to 75.7mmbbls, or nearly 77% of the levels achieved last year.  The bulk of the build occurred in PADD III (Gulf Coast) where export volumes primarily occur.  A typical month generally sees approximately 90 liftings, but total Oct volumes are expected to be down to around 75 liftings due to a host of buybacks, fog, and perhaps a bit more butane liftings (versus full-propane liftings).  Meanwhile, as winter begins to approach, terminal fees have seen a bit of buoyancy as Nov and Dec resellers are seen at just above the 6cts/gal mark.   The terminals themselves are around a penny above that, while Enterprise continues with its buyback scheme into Nov and Dec.   Mont Belvieu propane values have steadily relaxed over the previous 10 days, having moved from  1.49/gal on 18 Oct to a current value of 1.36/gal today.  NWE The TOT window went quiet Wednesday. After another build in Mt Belvieu inventories signalled to traders that there will be enough product to supply the North West European market in November. The VLGC being offered in the window was also withdrawn. No surprise with the East / West spread at +$51pmt. CIF AFA tracked the drop in Brent crude, leaving the propane naphtha spread at +$38/mt for November. The pro/nap spread remains in positive territory for Q1 2022. This combined with expensive natural gas for petchem’s power generation has traders questioning when demand from the sector will pick up. The inland propane market is picking up with trades for railcars occurring at strong premiums. Winter weather in the region is yet to bear it’s teeth, and the builds in Mt Belvieu have had a calming effect on the European market.   MED The coaster market in November was busy this week strong buying interest. This did not affect butane values in the region which slid lower with crude and naphtha. Large cargo discussions have moved on to December arrivals.

Both physical and FFA followed the larger sizes south. Biggest fall in USG where less fresh orders and some reassessing of levels. ECSA balanced, where sugar runs to Indo around 45+500bb. From Continent to Mediterranean usual scrap runs fixed around USD 36,000. Trips to USG with steels around USD 40,000. Far East big drop in Indo India rounds now flying around USD 30,000. On the period front, the Bulk Manara (55,692/2010) open Koh Sichang 3 November was fixed for minimum 3 months trading at high USD 30,000s. If the average seasonal pattern repeats perfectly towards year-end, average earnings will correct to the low 30,000s per day before rebounding slightly until year-end.

The market has fallen sharply the last week as the amount of available tonnage in the East has increased and charterers holding back taking advantage of the negative sentiment. The West Australia rout with iron ore to China is down by 28%, now giving owners a time charter hire of 31,850 per day. The iron ore rout from Brazil to China is down by 26%. The overall basket is down by 34% indicating that the more illiquid routs has come off harder than where there is a more constant flow of cargo. This might indicate that there have been a lot of panic in the Capesize segment, and time of writing there is some signs of support, though still very nervous.

EAST With Diwali coming up next Thursday, Indian PSUs seemingly have been keen to sort out most of their November programs in advance of the festivities, and 6 out of the 9 spot fixtures for November so far has been Indian fixtures. As freight ideas in the West approaching mid 90s on the back of a flurry of fixtures ex US last night the East/West diff is widening. East freight should eventually also see the effects of a tightening market West of Suez as those owners who have the option to seek cargoes in US are more likely to do so now. A theoretical 50 RT/C (almost 3 dollars above last Baltic) versus a 95 H/C still results in a more than 6 dollar West premium before factoring in Panama waiting.  WEST The West VLGC market has been very active so far this week, and first decade December fixing is well underway with still uncovered cargoes early in the month.  End November only has a couple of vessels left open, and in all likelihood, these will be absorbed rather soon. Early December is tight!  Freight rates are steadily increasing from mid/high USD 80’s and up towards mid USD 90’s if all sub-fixtures are confirmed. Yet again and for the market to sustain, we are reliant upon not overcooking the goose.

text: MEG Nov C3 swap value dropped heavily to $830 on the time of writing, down by nearly $30 compared to last week, trigged by the decline in crude and the plunge in China DCE-LPG market.  1st round CP idea ranged widely from lowest to $835 to highest $860 for C3, and C3/C4 spread was recommended from flattish to $20.   FAR EAST A flurry of deals was concluded in the window this week, with majority for 2h Nov deliveries. 23kt propane for this period was traded at Nov FEI minus mid-single digit, or at flat price $845 on Thursday, and similar cargo for 1h Dec delivery was at $844 on the same day.  Three Chinese importers were reported to award some term volumes for next year feedstock use, with 23kt parcel reported done at CP plus low mid 40s into SChina, and 46kt parcel reported at partial FEI plus near $10 and partial CP at 30ish into NChina, which to be confirmed.   Another two Chinese importers also issued term tenders to secure next year supply. One SChina traditional importer tendered to buy 11/11 split monthly from Jan to Dec, the other EChina-Based new petchem player tendered to buy 9 to 10 parcels of 23kt propane monthly from Mar/Apr to Dec.   One Australia stem were reported to split into two 11/11 parcels and sold into Japan at a discount to Dec FEI for mid/2h Dec delivery.

Another week that has seen a series of dry cargo vessels being transacted at higher levels than their respective last done. Although this high weekly liquidity provides clear benchmarks for both parties to transact it can also become a moving target for buyers looking to meet the sellers’ fast changing expectations. The Supramax market has yet again seen a notable appreciation with the IKAN SELAYANG (56K DWT MITSUI 2013) being sold at Usd 26.5m. A comparable sale would be this of the sistership  “MEDI OKINAWA” (56K DWT MITSUI 2011) which was sold earlier this month at low Usd 23m. A notable dynamic remains the substantial ground gained by Japanese built vessels against alternative designs - this is particularly well illustrated by this weeks sale at Usd 21.75m of the WP BRAVE (58K DWT SPP 2012) which when compared to the sale of the Mitsui 56 highlight this growing rift.  Volume in the Tanker snp markets remains subdued with buyers remaining cautious by taking what seems to be a standby approach by waiting for a pick up in liquidity before considering meeting the current offer. Headline transaction this week is that of the 2 x LR2s sold by Navig8 to JP Morgan. The vessels were both built in 2018 at New Times, scrubberfitted and each achieved a price Usd 48m.

Capesizes slowly improving again after a big correction over the last week. C5 found support in the low 16s and is now getting closer to USD 17 pmt. C3 is trading on thin volume and is marked at USD 39 whilst value for more prompt ships is in the low to mid 40s. The average TC is at 60,000 which is still a solid number, but certainly expected higher.

There is a palpable feel in the VLCC market that we are heading in to a firmer winter market, as sentiment amongst owners continues to build. So far, no major jumps, as the MEG has continued in the same vein, despite other areas pushing an upward trend. So far charterers have been able to find an alternative, be it an ex dd, or a vintage vessel etc. But, we have had 2 months of 120+ fixtures and November looks healthy. Still, the Atlantic is leading the charge. On the UKC, traders chasing bbls off ppt-ish dates (VL’s working same dates as Afra’s). If no VL’s are there at the right price, we could see Afra/Suez rates jump further as stems are split. More Atlantic volume will encourage modern ships to ballast from the East on speculation, giving the MEG a tighter feel it has not had in a while. An interesting week ahead.

All load zones are set for further rates rises this week due to a combination of circumstances that will catch some participants off guard. We are seeing Black Sea and Td20 laycans converging, which is nothing out of the ordinary during the Northern Summer months, but at this time of year, it has traditionally been a bellwether of volatility, especially when combined with delays in the straits. This forces charterers to pick from the same pool of FOC ships which can easily stress the list. The East is also offering up similar distractions for owners, as a firmer outlook may well hold Eastern tonnage away from West Africa, to some degree at least. With VLCCs and Aframaxes also looking firmer, this market is exhibiting all the signs of further volatility and next done is likely to be higher than last done.

Global congestion levels have continued to drop slightly over the previous weeks but remains as a very high level. USG still trading firm with limited supply of tonnage. Supra from USG was covered around 65k for trip to WCCA with grains. Fhaul with grains to Far East covered around 60k, tick higher levels for petcoke to India. Sugar runs from ECSA to SE Asia fixed around 30k + 1.6 m bb. Scrap runs from Baltic to Med fixed around 40k. From Pacific basin, trip via Indo to South China covered at USD 41,500. Trip from Indonesia to MEG around 40k. From period side, Supra for 1 year was discussed around high 20s. Forward looking the last few years, November has either gone sideways or down compared to October. This year, we believe November will end at a similar spot market average as October.

Overall activity is looking healthier and Russian exports for November are expected to be at the highest since the start of the pandemic. Moving forward a step back is not expected for this market but rather an upward correction in rates as we move into November dates. The LNG market remains at historically high levels while the freight market continues to climb in fits and starts, with a definite break now appearing between the higher levels seen in the Pacific basin and lower levels in the Atlantic. This is an unusual situation heading into winter, and may be the result of fewer ships travelling on the West-to-East conveyor belt when Europe fought for USG cargoes. There are relatively few firm requirements for this time of year and not many vessels being actively marketed, and combined with fewer clean fixtures there is some uncertainty as to where rate levels will go from here. On paper at least, charter rates and TCEs could top the record levels seen last winter; however, it only takes one sublet with just the right availability seeking to mitigate idle time and costly boil-off for those theoretical returns to take a big hit. On the longer term, several charterers are already making a move for 2022 tonnage. Again, this is unprecedented for this time of year and all points to a very tight market in the coming years. There have been no newbuilding orders this week, however yard slots are few and far between due to activity in other shipping segments.

The P1A has gained about USD 5k w-o-w and now trading in the mid 30’s region. In the Pacific, Nopac rounds are being concluded at above 40k basis North China delivery.
