text: AMERICAS A primary U.S. propane inventory increase of 1.9mmbbls was recorded by the EIA for the week ending 15 Oct, surprising most of the market which had been anticipating either a modest draw or a small build.  Total stocks have reached 73.6mmbbls, or 75% of both last year and two years ago.   On a Days of Supply basis, there continues to be a deficit against last year, and stocks on that basis are still below the range of the last 5 years, hence the ongoing concerned focus related to the winter demand period as it relates to the continuing robust export volumes.  Although there has begun to be cooler weather in North America, there have yet to be any real storm systems which might mark the true commencement of winter.   Cargo availability continues to be split, with offers being seen from the trading community, while still being limited from the terminals themselves.  Terminal fees reflect this and for Nov spot trade is presently focused at just under 6cts/gal.  NWE The well documented news that LPG is being spiked into the LNG stream by producers has rapidly improved CIFA ARA values. Though TOT window offers have been generating the most discussions. Dow and Vilma both offering in the window was seen as bearish. Dow is expected to receive term tons and is not running at 100% so are looking to make an achievable profit on tons they have in the region today. For traders the arb is wide open, netback values from the US are around 9cpg for November for US liftings arriving in North West Europe in the same month. Raising the question whether selling in the TOT window can make more sense than waiting in the Panama canal to sell at a discount in the East. The question is whether these offers will push the window into a discount, or if the European market with less locally produced tons, can absorb the offered tons and more heading into this winter market?   MED The quiet market and prevailing tight supply environment continues. Moroccan public holidays adding to the lack of trade discussions. No winter weather in the Mediterranean region aiding the wait and see trader attitude.

EAST With the final round of acceptances being published at the start of the week November fixing has kicked off in due course. So far, the activity has mainly been focused around Indian PSUs who’s already quoted a handful of cargoes for the early part of the month. Freight has steadily been increasing in the East and while the West, so far, has been more flattish, West premium has diminished leading a few more vessels towards the East. It remains to be seen how long this will last as rate ideas in the West now is starting to increase.   WEST As we are over halfway through October, fixing window is mainly 3rd decade November in the US. Relets are disappearing quickly and more than a handful owner controlled ships are fixed or on subs. The freight rates have been stable around mid/low USD 80s for some time, with last done fixtures in the mid/high USD 80s. The congestions in the Panama Canal are on the rise, but the current arbs are supporting freight levels at time of writing.

Similar cargo for 1h Dec delivery was bid at Nov FEI minus $1 while offer at plus $1.88. Following a series of headline announcements this week, the tanker space has for once joyed of most of the limelight and as such we thought we will give tankers the center stage of this weekly digest after being overshadowed by overwhelmingly active dry cargo markets. On Monday, Euronav publicly announced the acquisition of 5.5% of its stock by Fredriksen controlled entities. SEC filings have indeed confirmed that the Cyprus based Famatown Finance, a company beneficially owned by Mr. Fredriksen, has now increased its shareholding stake to 9.8% in the Belgian stock-listed owner Euronav. The move seems to be a welcomed sign for most tanker players as it firmly consolidates the current growing anticipation for a substantial market upturn. As mentioned throughout these previous weeks this growing sentiment was often made apparent by an ever increasing level of buying enquiry with owners struggling to acquire additional tonnage from a continuously thinning supply of sales candidates. In any case we expect this renewed momentum to spur several other parties into action which should see a strengthening of bids across the board in an effort to go meet the rising expectations of any potential seller. Other notable news in the product sector, is the sale of the two modern sisterships ECO LOS ANGELES & ECO CITY OF ANGELS (50K DWT HMD 2020) which were bought by Norden at Usd 36.5m each. The sale was made with the balance of the current charter to Trafigura attached, details of which remain undisclosed at this stage.  Volume of transactions in the dry snp markets remains unhindered with 20 reported sales this week. The larger segments have seen a rise in activity with two modern VLOC being sold to Eastern Pacific shipping, namely the STELLA BELLA & STELLA IVY (250k dwt, Qingdao Beihai, 2016 & 2015) which have respectively achieved Usd 60m and Usd 58m basis a 5 years charter attached to BHP. Another three Capesizes built from early to late 2000s have changed hands providing additional support and benchmark for future transactions in the space.

It has been a busy week in the Nsea/Baltic market with rates climbing to the highest level since May. The split of VL and Suez stems into Aframax size increased the demand for vessels and the owners showed the necessary resistance in order to push for more. For the time being, market looks steady and moving forward we expect rates to remain under upward pressure as sentiment is high and cargo programs are healthy enough to support this.  Following last week’s excitement in the Med/Bsea with enough activity to see a pick-up in rates, charterers started holding back on cargoes prior to the weekend and as a result the list is getting longer and rates have come off a tad again. In wait for further activity we expect the market to remain steady at current rate levels, if anything with a softening potential.

We’ve seen yet another week with gains on LNG Spot rates, confirming the trend over the last few weeks. That said, it’s on a small trading volume and in such an illiquid market there is considerable uncertainty and volatility. There are relatively few spot cargoes requiring shipping as compared to previous years, and most of the independent tonnage is sold out. Current availability is controlled by subletters, and those can and does disappear quickly as schedules change so it is a risk going short shipping right now. Furthermore, most of these sublets are restricted on period as they have their own scheduled cargoes further down the line. We are certainly set up for a very interesting winter! This week we’ve added the four Qatar Gas ordered ME-GA’s at Hudong.

A deluge of Atlantic basin VLCC enquiry, coupled with a very interesting USG Aframax market, has created a potentially volatile road map for Suezmaxes. A key factor in assessing market trajectory, is the time it takes to fix a cargo, with one particular Black Sea stem reportedly still there after five days. Slow trading has been the order of the day with last done rates being rather difficult for charterers to attain, hence why we will soon see Td6 flirt with WS 80's levels.  USG-ECM/TA is no longer back haul business and is 145KT x WS 57.5 with a firm outlook, which logically dictates that Td20 which will soon challenge the WS 70+ mark and likely to push on. In the East, rates have been moving at a slower pace, but there is room for further optimism with Td23 last done at WS 40 and MEG/East threatening WS 70.

The VLCC market has been threatening to improve for the past month or so, but with a number of false dawns so far. Charterers have found a cheaper vessel, a relet, or a date re-arrangement and the market has continued sideways. At the time of writing, we are seeing quite a build up of Atlantic cargoes. Some may be tender business or rumour, but there is no smoke without fire. The MEG, quieter by comparison, is still unfinished for October and we are closing in on a healthy 120 cargoes for the month. We understand 8 offers in to a Formosa cargo, but modern 'unhandicapped' vessels are likely to steer well clear. With bunkers heading North of USD 600/mt, owners will need to push the market just to maintain current TCE’s. Higher numbers look likely in the near term, but charterers will be using all the tricks in their armoury.

Slight uptick in vessels heading to the major loading countries in Asia. We could see this increase further going forward due to the desperate need for coal. In the Atlantic, sentiment remaining strong from USG. Grains from USG to Far East were fixed closer to USD 55,000 and trips to the Continent covered around mid 40s. Ultramax for Continent round was fixed at USD 43,000. Bauxite run from Kamsar to North Continent at USD 34,000. From the East, more Indonesian coal coming into market. A Supramax open Bohai Bay was rumoured fixed in the low USD 30,000s for trip to SE Asia. Bigger Handy was covered around USD 43,000 for Indo/China round. On the period front, Ultramaxes were discussed at low USD 30,000 for 1 year and low 40s for 4-6 months.

Fundamentals generally unchanged whilst spot rates adjust - average daily earnings down 15 pct w-o-w to come in at a still very healthy USD 75k. Chinese, Indian, and partly European energy crisis with consequent desperate need for coal at moment not sufficient to compensate for a sudden drop in prompt iron ore volumes. Only one major miner active on key route West Australia/China, with value for Pacific rounds in turn losing almost 20 pct to stand at USD 65k. Similarly, but slightly less dramatic for the Brazil/China conference trade, where transactions few and far between. Congestion, however, remains significant - and number of ballasters at a historical low, leaving a delicate supply/demand balance where tonnage actually workable keeps being very limited. Operators remain very keen on any available period candidate, last representative fixtures include 176,000 dwt, built 2010, done for about 12 months at USD 33k.

After last week’s softening in rates for the P1A it seems to have bottomed out this week. A clear out of prompt positions much helped by Cape splits the supply/demand seems more balanced for now.  TA’s are currently trading around USD 30k. In the Pacific, the market has been more stable and now strengthening WOW with Pacific rounds priced at 38/39k level.

text: AMERICAS Despite ongoing gains in the crude arena which have brought Brent to $84.06/bbl and WTI to $81.31/bbl, MB propane values earlier this week seemed relaxed to around $1.42/gal, only to rise again prior to the release of the EIA to current levels of $145.00/gal which was fixed just before the inventory data release.    Expectations for this week’s inventory report – which was delayed by a US holiday on Monday – again ranged widely (and revealing ongoing uncertainty), from a draw of around a million barrels to a build of over a million barrels.    Given the strong export volumes and pending winter demand season, the prospect of a draw seemed the more likely, and that turned out to be the case.  For the week ending 8 Oct 2021, the EIA reported overall propane stock levels in the U.S. at 71.7mmbbls, which represents a draw of 600,000bbls.  The components to that include a draw of 800,000bbls in PADD I and the build in PADD III of 300,000bbls.  As there is little in the cold weather and ongoing strength in the export market this was eyed with some level of surprise.  Terminal fees, meanwhile, though still generally range-bound, have inched up and offers for 2H November 4:0 cargoes are seen at 6cts/gal – December at the same.  Buy-side interest remains limited.  NWE The VLGC cargoes which were slated for the region have redirected East. Buying interest in the window did compete with the seller’s netback taking the cargo East. The window bid seen this week has pushed up physical propane value to November CIF ARA +$5. Although the European market is tight the news did not affect CIF ARA which fell this week in line with other commodities. Though inland demand has been picking up, cold temperatures are yet to hit the region. The volume of propane set to be exported in October and November from the US East Coast is down on September due to regional demand. These volumes usually find their way to the European market, further tightening the NWE outlook in Q4. Butane has been directly correlated to naphtha at 105% October.  MED The Tunisia supply tender for 2022 was reportedly won by Petroineos. Tunisia’s 628,000MT demand comes from it’s domestic heating and cooking markets. This less local refinery production 185,000MT in the country leaves a required estimated import volume of 443,000MT.

EAST Since our Shipping Weekly report last Wednesday, the RT/C Baltic benchmark has climbed just a few cents shy of three dollars. Although there has been lots of chatter and various traders looking to buy spot FOBs, market has mostly been focused on end October Indian PSU cargoes which has been paying hefty premiums to the Baltic. Last round of acceptances for November is expected to be published on Sunday or early next week. In view of steadily increasing freight ideas from those controlling open vessels in the first half of November, we would not be surprised to see some November fixing kicking off already this week.  WEST With first half of November largely covered on freight, there are still more than a handful relets available within 2nd decade November. The freight market is showing signs of being long as freight rates essentially gone from USD 86-87 last week to USD 84-85. At the same time as we are seeing a small decrease in freight rates, it’s not helping owners’ earning levels as bunker prices keeps increasing in tandem with crude. Neo Panama Canal is currently not experiencing anything near the amount of congestion we saw last year this time. It is however too early to conclude that we won’t have congestion increasing for the VLGC’s as we come closer to Christmas and container ships starts claiming their space through the canal.

text: MEG Another week of volatility. Nov Propane swap retreated to $810ish in the mid-week from previous $850ish, but rebounded to $840ish at the time of writing. Nov Propane/Butane spread was narrowed to $26 from last week’s $38 as more inquiries on evenly split cargo emerged. Nov/Dec CP was traded at $2 contango only.   FAR EAST Cash premium for Nov delivered parcels improved amid active trades this week. 23kt propane for 1h Nov delivery in window were traded at FEI minus $18 earlier this week, while bids for similar cargo on 2h Nov delivery improved to minus $10 from previous minus mid-teens range. Full cargo for such period was bid at FEI minus $12 while offer at minus $8.  Off window a plenty of tenders were floating in the market. On inquiry for propane, three PDH users in China issued buy tenders and secured in total 92kt propane for Nov delivery, with some reported done at FEI minus low-mid teens. One Vietnam PDH also purchased 46kt propane for Nov delivery at Nov CP plus mid 20s reportedly. On evenly split cargo, two Indian PSUs issued buy tenders for one 22/22 cargo for Dec delivery each. One SChina importer also tendered to buy a 11/11 parcel for 2h Nov to 1h Dec delivery.

The LNG spot shipping market has exceeded expectations this week. The lack of workable vessels available and a couple of uncovered requirements, predominately within the East of Suez have firmed up “Owners” sentiments going into winter.  The strong product prices driven by the lack of supply and competition for LNG cargoes between both basins have also given more room and margins for freight.   History have shown how illiquid and volatile the LNG shipping market is and although most Charterers have taken measures earlier this year to cover shipping, an open West-East Arbitrage, continuous rally of spot LNG prices and potential Panama canal delays can trigger more appetite for spot tonnage. With the current cargo prices, being long shipping may be a preferred position.   We recorded another 4+2 new building orders this week and the total tally for the year is now at 52 large LNG vessels.

Slow start to the week and limited fresh orders in light of Golden Week in China. Index losing ground from Asia routes, while in the Atlantic USG making most of the gains. From the paper side, Supra FFAs joined the larger sizes in making decent gains, especially for Cal 22. From the Atlantic, the Mediterranean remained balanced where inter Med trips were covered at USD 40,000. Grains from the Black Sea to the Continent were fixed at USD 39,000 and to the Far East around USD 52,000. Fertz from the Continent to the USG covered around USD 40,000. More push from the USG with several fixtures this week. Coal run from Mississippi River to the West Med was concluded around USD 45,000. From similar position to ECSA, an Ultramax was paid USD 47,000 levels. Grain runs to China settled around USD 53,000. Little activity from the Pacific Basin. Indo/China runs fixed around USD 45,000. The Pacific RV close to USD 40,000. Ultra from WCI via MEG to Bangla with aggregates got fixed around USD 51,000.

With Golden Week in China and despite the rush in Capesize rates, this week has been very slow. In the Atlantic we see less demand and P1A has seen steady declines every day - currently priced at around USD 30k. In the eastern hemisphere rates are also slipping, although not to the same extent as in the Atlantic. Pacific rounds are currently fixing in the 36/37k level. The paper market is still strong and giving support to the period market. Kamsarmaxes are being fixed at 32k with Far East delivery for 1-year trading.

The Suezmax market looks to have found a firmer footing with most load zones experiencing solid chunks of enquiry for the first time in well over a year.  MEG enquiry, and most notably Basrah, looks to have gone into overdrive with Bot/West firming significantly. Last done Td23 jumped five points to WS 35 with owners so bullish it would be unwise to bet against rates pushing on again. The key factor that has helped balance out supply and demand has been the Atlantic where significant gains have been made in the Caribbean and West Africa with Td20 now comfortably in the low WS 60's and likely to add further weight. It now remains to be seen if NWE and the Mediterranean will have a further injection of Aframax/Suezmax interplay which could fuel further volatility. Outlook is firm in all regions.

A busy week on the whole, but VLCC rates very much like an arm wrestle, edging to the owners’ side bit by bit as charterers fight for every inch. Most rate increases driven by the busier Atlantic market, as we have drifted firmly north of USD 5m in the USG to Ningbo and the latest West Africa deal able to squeeze a half point above last done to the WS 43 level. Similar in the MEG, as fractions of points are achieved on successive fixtures. No major swing just yet however and charterers may try to keep things under the radar, or hold off to keep a lid on things, but with 85 or so cargoes for MEG, still plenty to come 3rd decade. Worth noting some Japanese and Indian power utilities have boosted operating rates at their oil-fired units enabling them to limit the reliance on gas power generation and slow LNG-inventories.

This week comes to a close with a number of fresh sales candidates being placed in the market continuing to drive liquidity across all dry segments. In terms of concluded business, the JP Morgan controlled capesize “TRUE ENDURANCE” (180K DWT HHI 2012) has now been sold to Turkish buyers at Usd 32.5m. The levels achieved fall in line with expectation as the last done in the sector is the “PROSPEROUS” (180K DWT SUNGDONG 2011) which was sold at Usd 31m last month. As expected from last week's negotiations, new supramax benchmarks have now been set with Japanese sellers committing the “MEDI OKINAWA” (56K DWT MITSUI 2011) at Usd 22.5m while the 2014 built Dolphin 57 “HTC CHARLIE” was sold at Usd 20.5m. The sale is pointing at a relative narrowing of the spread in value between Japanese and Chinese design which has recently been accentuated by the high volume of Japanese vessels changing hands.  Growing anticipation is definitely the name of the game in the Tanker segments where a strengthening buying enquiry is becoming ever so apparent. Signs of increased bids suggest that buyers are gradually moving upwards in an effort to drive potential sellers to transact and secure tonnage from a very thin supply of sales candidates. The product sector has seen the sale of the “IVY EXPRESS” (50K DWT STX 2009) which was sold to Greek buyers at Usd 15m setting a well needed target for potential MR players looking to transact units of similar vintage. Elsewhere, Xihe holdings finalised the sale of the VLCC “E MEI SAN” (317K DWT SWS 2010) which achieved Usd 39m by Far Eastern buyers.

The Nsea/Baltic market fulfilled the expectations of last week and continued firming up. Current window proved to be tighter than expected as charterers took out many ships quietly, and as a result there was a significant improvement especially for the Baltic runs on the back of healthy activity on both crude and fuel oil. As all three Western markets are simultaneously improving for the first time this year, we expect rates to remain steady with some more upward potential. The activity in the Med/Bsea has continued this week and rates have picked another 5-10 points. Suezmaxes taking out Afra-stems have not capped the market just yet. We are now in a health 3rd decade October fixing window ex Bsea, and combined with the current cargo activity out of Libya, we expect the market to remain firm going into next week.

Another amazing week for the Capesize market. The average of all basket is up by 16% adding another USD 11,994 per day to the daily average, now at USD 86,870 per day. The massive push has come from an impressive increase in the Atlantic basin and backhaul segment. This is highly correlated with the massive backwardation in ffa curve encouraging owners to seek longer duration as the forward market is showing a lack of confident. That said there is also an increasing amount of charters, and cargo owners looking to cover forward freight exposure, hence period market being paid up.

text: AMERICAS  Volatility is the keyword in the Mont Belvieu LPG market this week.  Intra-day price swings of up to a nickel have been recorded, leaving many on the sidelines.  Crude and natural gas strength have led the way, pausing only for profit taking. Propane stock levels in the U.S. continue to be the primary focus, though there remains a steady eye on both export volumes and ‘buyback’ numbers at EPD, of which there have been a solid 7 (if not 8) for Oct. Total inventory levels as of Oct 1 2021 were recorded by the EIA at 72.3mmbbls, down by 600,000bbls from the previous week – and 71% of the total achieved in 2020.  Weather-related demand in North America will no doubt compete with export volumes over the Q4 ’21 and Q1 ’22. Spot terminal re-sale values are in the sub-6cts/gal range for full propane lots in 2H Nov.  Buy-side interest is hovering at above a nickel but uncertainty is so far keeping the two sides at odds.  NWE Two VLGCs set to arrive in the region have pushed the physical cargoes to a $4.5pmt discount to paper. The propane naphtha spread for September averaged +$45pmt. This lead petrochemical users taking in 325,000 MT, to the lowest monthly intake for 15 months. The October Pro/Nap spread stands at $119pmt today, and some petrochemical users are still taking tons. Due to it being more economical to run a minimal rates than fully shutting down. The draw in Mt Belvieu inventories will keep the arb to Europe closed and with the East/West spread at $51pmt for October and rising further down the curve we do not expect to see many more tons imported from the US in the near future. Butane in the region continues to be assessed at 105% October Naphtha, though this translated to a $15.5pmt drop in value as naphtha crashed.  MED The regions is nervous about winter supply. With production issues in Algeria reducing propane output and the arb to the US closed, traders are wondering where they will find supply this winter. For the time being the market is on the tight side and traders are being cautious not to get caught in short supply if demand picks up.

EAST A couple of Indian cargos being discussed for last decade of October, together with two Australian cargos fixed on subs for end October, sums up an otherwise muted week in the East. Public holidays in China and Korea have kept activity on the low, and most of the focus has been on the West where activity has picked up. Freight levels in the MEG seems to have stabilized around the mid USD 40s mark for now, and despite more ships being sent back West we are still left with a variety of open ships from the main owners and traders in MEG from last decade of October into early November.  WEST As October positions are wiped out from the USG position lists, all eyes are now on first half November freight. Low USD 80 was done on a handful of occasions during early November, however, the market is now established in the mid USD 80’s Houston/Chiba with even a couple of fixtures just north of this level. Second decade November freight enquiries are increasing in frequency, and if owners’ get their way, we may see rates pointing north of mid USD 80’s.

Whilst there's a general consensus that the market will continue to improve, the pace of improvement remains pedestrian and dull. The East Suezmax market is unfortunately more VLCC-sensitive  than the West,  and at the time of going to print, we are way off from seeing any meaningful interplay between the two segments . In the West, the main potential drivers are the highly nuanced regional Aframax markets that have recently been well into crossover territory, especially in the Mediterranean. This potentially holds Suezmax tonnage away from West Africa which could create more bottlenecks. Wafr/East is on subs at WS 60 showing positive market direction whilst MEG/East should challenge low WS 60's for a pure long East. Td23 is an enigma and will possibly hold at sub WS 30. A pre-Golden Week rush may yet occur!

While fundamentals remain the same in the Nsea and Baltic Aframax market, it is correct to say that it was more sentiment that pushed rates slightly higher this week. Going forward the tonnage list is looking shorter and as the October lifting program looks busier, owners will try to put some upward pressure on rates. The market is looking steady but firmer.  In the Med/Bsea we have seen a rush of cargoes enter the market this week with both cross-Med and ex-Bsea being active. Rates across the board have picked up 10 points or so, and the tonnage list is tighter than it has been in a long time. However, Suezmaxes are now coming into play, as well as Aframaxes open in the North, so it will be interesting to see how long owners in the Med can keep an upward pressure on rates.

Step by step the market moves up, with MEG-East now reportedly at the WS 42.5 level at the time of writing. West Africa also holds last done at similar levels at WS 42 to test, attracting modern ballasters around the Cape. Likewise, prompter dates in the USG/Caribs - rumours of USD 5m+ heading East. However, we are a little light on enquiry at present, and with Golden week in a few days, we will need a pre-holiday rush to keep pushing rates upwards, certainly in the MEG. And it is worth noting, as rates go up, charterers may have the tactic to let standards slip a bit. Suddenly an over 15-year vessel becomes workable, dry docks are not so offensive, and remote or bunker sires are overlooked.  It is easy to get carried away. TCE's are still awful for owners, barely covering Opex, but the improvement is certainly welcome.

P1A is currently priced in the mid 30’s while Pacific rounds are trading in region 36/37k levels. The period market has been fairly active with a Kamsarmax reported done at USD 31,500 for 10/12 mos.

New benchmarks are being set at a faster pace with heightened competition driving buyers to strike decisively in an effort to secure tonnage. Vessels able to give prompter deliveries will joy of the stronger bids with buyers scouting for any candidate able to offer them the yield offered by the chartering markets. This dynamic is particularly well illustrated in the Supramax/Ultramax sectors where the high liquidity of transactions highlights the more dramatic jump in values. Similarly on the younger end of the spectrum we witness signs of ongoing negotiations on the modern ultramax front suggesting yet another upward correction in the near future.  Against this backdrop of activity the Tanker space is eerily silent with only three sales to report. Xihe Holdings is entering its final stages of proceedings with the sale of the OCEAN VELA (2009 SWS 109kdwt LR2) which invited offers end of last week and has now been committed at Usd 18.5m after attracting about 10 buyers outright - a number of potential buyers which highlights the now settled disparity between a strong buying enquiry and an ever thinning number of available candidates.

Rates across the board have picked up 10 points or so, and the tonnage list is tighter than it has been in a long time. However, Suezmaxes are now coming into play, as well as Aframaxes open in the North, so it will be interesting to see how long owners in the Med can keep an upward pressure on rates.

Full speed ahead for the big ships as congestion keeps being a significant factor supporting already very healthy fundamentals. Spot scene hectic as Australian miners struggle to fill early slots, particularly for iron ore. Average daily earnings up 25 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 75k, a level not seen for half a generation. Atlantic spot is close to becoming short of tonnage as number of ballasters is limited and hardly enough to satisfy needs of miners, power plants and steel mills - resultant fronthaul values up to USD 100k/day, China-Brazil-China round up 30 pct to USD 65k, and pushing. Short-term outlook very bull, supported by ffa's. Considerable period interest but considerable gap in bid/offer for fixed-price deals - whilst around 10 ships taken by major players during last 5 trading days for about 12 mos duration at indexed rates.

The upward continue its rally also this week followed by big sizes, however not at the same pace.  We can describe market as well balanced with some less activity due to upcoming Golden Week in China. USG market is improving and rates slowly moving up. Supramax fixing around USD 35k pd and Ultras able to reach USD 40k pd for Atlantic trade. For trips to East, owners are able to achieve close to USD 50k pd - MV Ym Advance (63,509/2019) del USEC 1/15 Oct trip grains rdl China USD 50k. Market in ECSA is stable with limited fixing reports. Tess 58 was rumoured to fix USD 43k pd for one trip to Med. The Continent and Med market is more active this week with improved demand for scrap and clinker orders surfacing. Trip from Continent to USG/ECSA reporting to fix around USD 40k pd, while scrap paying premium around USD 42k pd. Far Eastern markets show resistance despite the pre-holiday mood, and the indexes are seeing only small gains. Supramax delivering North China fixed at USD 34k pd for a trip via the Russian Pacific port to China, while Ultramax delivering South East Asia able to obtain USD 41,500 pd for a trip via Indonesia to China. Australian trip paying low USD 40k pd on Ultramax and backhaul to the Atlantic around USD 35k pd.

Step by step the market moves up, with MEG-East now reportedly at the WS 42.5 level at the time of writing. West Africa also holds last done at similar levels at WS 42 to test, attracting modern ballasters around the Cape. Likewise, prompter dates in the USG/Caribs - rumours of USD 5m+ heading East. However, we are a little light on enquiry at present, and with Golden week in a few days, we will need a pre-holiday rush to keep pushing rates upwards, certainly in the MEG. And it is worth noting, as rates go up, charterers may have the tactic to let standards slip a bit. Suddenly an over 15-year vessel becomes workable, dry docks are not so offensive, and remote or bunker sires are overlooked.  It is easy to get carried away. TCE's are still awful for owners, barely covering Opex, but the improvement is certainly welcome.

LNG prices continue to firm as competition for cargoes globally is driving the price per MMBtu delivered into Asia above $32’s. After the recent lack of activity, business now being concluded is showing all signs of firmness, with rates increasing across most sectors. As we see the fixing window move out into November, Charterers are seeing freight for winter now being priced into these discussions. There is also a lack of visibility on winter tonnage, adding to the firmer outlook. We may see gains in rates over the next few weeks as the prompt sublet tonnage retreats back into schedules and interest for spot cargoes for late November/December mature, however Golden week in China next week might put the brakes on a little.  No newbuild orders have been recorded placed at yards this week, but market talk is around the expected Qatar orders and for how many vessels they will do in this round.

EAST The East Baltic benchmark jumped up on the back of last done ex MEG at USD 44 Ras Tanura/Chiba which was concluded earlier this week. Seeing that the 'pure' owners are inclined to send their vessels in ballast towards the West in search for higher earnings, it may have a knock-on effect on the MEG market. Of a vessel line-up consisting of about ten vessels (give or take) left open for the balance of October, about half of these are relets.   WEST In the western hemisphere, eyes are slowly but surely turning towards November enquiries and subsequently, what's in store. The typhoon currently passing the Pacific Ocean seems not to have any severe impact to the shipping supply both in the MEG and in the USG. End October has during the course of the week seen a handful of relets appearing on the horizon, however, these vessels have yet to affect the market significantly and the last concluded Houston/Chiba rate was in the very low USD 80's off early November dates. October has about six or seven vessels left and seeking employment opportunities and hopes are that after the US stats are released today, there will be an increase in activity.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco set Oct CP at $800 for propane and $795 for butane, up by $135 and $130 respectively, in view of tight gas supply against strong winter demand. This being said, the value is higher than paper swaps ever traded and beyond most players’ expectations. Nov CP was traded at $815 at the time of writing, reflecting a bullish outlook into forward markets.   Evenly split cargo for Nov lifting was traded into India at CP plus low single digit premium reportedly.  FAR EAST  A plenty of deals were concluded this week in window, trading period ranging from 2h Oct delivery into next Mar. 23kt propane for 2h Oct delivery was traded at Oct FEI minus $10 and 46kt parcel was at minus $14. 23kt lot for 1h Nov delivery was traded at Oct FEI minus $2, equates to Nov FEI minus $7. And similar parcel for 2h Mar delivery was traded at fixed price of $818, while Mar FEI was assessed at $742.5.   Off window a handful of tenders were under discussion. One EChina Petchem player awarded their buy tender and secured two parcels of 23kt propane for Nov delivery at Nov FEI minus low teens reportedly. One Korean importer was reported to buy 23kt butane for 1h Nov delivery via tender at FEI minus mid-single digit. comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane values have rocketed upwards, but appear – for the moment – to be resting at just above the $1.40/gal level, though earlier in the week trades as high as $1.47/gal were reported.  The strength in the crude market amid fears of an energy shortage are the immediate driving forces, but the entire LPG complex is being underpinned by concerns related to the domestic inventory position.   This week the EIA released its findings for the week ending 24 Sep which revealed a rather surprising 2.6mmbbl improvement in overall stock levels to 72.9mmbbls, or about 72% of the same time last year, and 73% of two years ago.   The ongoing worry is that US propane stocks will be insufficient to accommodate both winter-related domestic demand as well as the ongoing strength of the export market.  However, a bit of downtime at the Galena Park terminal combined with continuing ‘buybacks’ in Houston will likely allow total export volumes to relax in September, and perhaps increase to more comfortable levels.    This remains to be seen, however, since natural gas prices around the world have shot up, giving cause for discussions about fuel-switching in the direction of LPG.  Fuel rationing and an (at least temporary) shift to coal, however, could potentially limit demand levels from that angle.  NWE Propane market is tight, with continued buying interest in the window. The renewed 7 year value highs in CIF ARA have not been able to open the Arb from the US. With regional supply reduced due to refineries using LPG they produce instead of Natural Gas where possible. Local supply is unable to cover demand. So far that has been the only effect of the high natural gas prices in Europe on the LPG supply/demand balance. Though with natural gas in the region set to remain expensive for some time we could see LPG finding it’s way into new markets. Butane was bid at $755/t CIF Antwerp by Vitol and was booked by Equinor for 7,000t of normal butane. Whereafter Equinor offered a further 12,000t of butane at October CIF ARA +$7pmt. Equivalent to 109% of October Naphtha.  MED Sonatrach contract prices for October were set at $808pmt propane and $742pmt butane. The butane market remains tight, and the Sonatrach C4 to C3 discount was a surprise. Some traders were expecting the tons changing hands in NWE window at $755 might find their way to the Mediterranean at a premium. The worry is that a spell of cold weather will send prices, butane in particular, soaring in this tight market.

A firmer VLCC market is likely to feed into Suezmax's at some point as owners look to recoup losses and buck recent historical lows. Simply counting ships versus cargoes may catch some participants by surprise, because as we start to hunt down the fourth quarter, you have to add "expectation" into the algorithm, which hasn't necessarily formed part of the market playbook during the last year. Another vital ingredient, MEG Suezmax enquiry, has made a return, with ships disappearing in bulk and thus handing owners additional options, as opposed to default ballasting on spec' to West Africa. Td23 has fixed a wadge of relets at WS 25, but this number is likely to uptick. MEG/East will threaten the WS 60 lvl within the next week whilst Td20 owners will be pushing for mid 50's.

It has been an exciting week for the Capesize segment as there is a very limited amount of available tonnage to meet the continuing health volume of cargoes. Especially the rout from West Australia to China with iron ore has increased significantly, now 22% higher than it was a week ago. This obvious strengthened the already positive sentiment, pushing the average of all routes up by 12%, which now being almost USD 60,000 per day earnings. The coming days and weeks look to be very interesting as the Pacific seems to drain most vessels opening, meaning there is a very limited number of vessels heading for Brazil and Atlantic. That said, it’s expected to be more available tonnage going forward which probably will calm down the market a bit, but the market floor continuously increase.

Another week in the Nsea/Baltic Aframax market with rates remaining at bottom levels. Even with some prompt replacement jobs, rates didn’t move upwards as charterers had plenty of tonnage to choose from. However, with the preliminary Urals schedule for October looking a bit more promising, owners have higher expectations going forward. But we expect rates to move sideways for the current fixing window before we will get a clearer picture of the direction for the rest of October. Much the same can be said about the Med/Bsea region where we still see charterers quietly taking out ships off market at repeat levels. This will most likely continue as long as we can count a dozen or more ships prompt open and free of cargo in the area. We expect the market to continue moving sideways at these levels in the week to come.

A week with much promise for owners. Rumours and counter rumours of successive higher rates reported, but little actually confirmed at the time of writing. A busy Atlantic is attracting modern ballasters from the East and a busy looking October MEG program is encouraging many to stay in that region. Owners face the decision of fixing long and booking in much their winter market now, or staying shorter for two bites at the cherry. Most are agreed we will see higher numbers in the short term, but markets move in steps and thus far MEG/China remains in the mid-high WS 30’s with owners looking to push for WS 40. West Africa to China is already past the WS 40 level, and with more enquiry in the USG and UKC, we are likely heading up from here too. The UKC-East arb is open and there remains demand for the sweet crudes in the East.

It has been yet another week of surging gas prices both in Europe and in Asia, causing a lot of speculations around how long this gas shortage can last and what will be the ultimate ramifications out of it. Naturally, this has been the hot topic this week in Gastech, as it is the first time in a very long time since we have seen a large (physical) industry gathering! Regardless of the striking headlines that the LNG cargo market has been causing lately, it has not reflected into more LNG shipping activity. On the contrary, it has been another lackluster week in the spot market, with only a handful of fresh requirements. We can perhaps partly blame the Gastech or multiple public holidays in the Asia region for this week's quietness, but the fact is that the surprisingly high gas prices in Europe have led trade-flows to be more intra-Atlantic heavy than anticipated causing majority of industry players to have sufficient length in their current LNGC fleet. However, looking past the relative weakness of the prompt shipping market, the view of the winter market still remains tight or at least extremely volatile, with no certainty on how availability might look like during the peak winter. On the newbuilding side, market is still keeping active and shipyards have their hands full with various ongoing discussions.

With holidays in China this week, the activity has come down, but it is still a firm underlying tone in general. In the Atlantic, we still see a good demand for minerals and a well-balanced tonnage book. P1A is currently trading in the region of USD 37k.  In the eastern hemisphere, Indo rounds are being traded at similar levels i.e. 36/37k, while several candidates have been fixed retro SE Asia for trips via Black Sea or USG back to Asia.

Slow start of the week mainly due to the holidays in Asia with high volatility on FFA trading, but it all subsided to flat and unexcited market across the borders at the time of writing. Rates from Med to West Africa reaching USD 40,000 pd. Continent is tight on tonnage with grain cargo to Med paying USD 45,000 pd and slightly less on fertiliser run from Continent to ECSA. USG been lacking action with natural disaster disturbances. Building up tonnage last few weeks had a negative effect on the rates, however the situation is starting to look better and rates have improved for all directions. TA paying mid USD 30,000 pd and FH above USD 45,000 pd. ECSA is well supported rates from Santos to Far East was paid on Ultra USD 28,000 plus 1.8 mil GBB. Asia and Indian Ocean market remain stable with rates as per “last done” and some premium. Young Harmony (63,567 dwt, 2014) open Koh Sichang 24/28 Sep trip via Indonesia redel Thailand USD 41,000 pd. On period market owners asking mid/high USD 30,000 pd for 6-8 months and low USD 30,000 pd for 9-11 months.

The dry market continues on the same pace and we note another week with stronger prices paid. The kamsarmax M/V Lowlands Nello (82k dwt, blt 2015 Sanoyas) has seen USD 32,2 mill in a deal with Chronos – this compares to the M/V Peak Liberty (82k dwt, blt 2015 Tsuneishi) which was reported last week at USD 30 mill. Suitably named M/V Million Bell and M/V Glad Mark (both 58k dwt, blt 2012 Kawasaki) are concluded at USD 22 mill each – half a million below Trans Oceanic (58k dwt, blt 2012 Tsuneishi) that was reported last week, but with deliveries in Q1 2022 there should be a good few months of earnings before handing over, so in total a sweeter deal for the sellers. The handies still receive their fair share of attention as well and based on the amount of enquires in the market we could expect a further lift on values going forward.  The tanker side is still fairly quiet, but with the increased activity in the spot markets and general optimism for a recovery to take place soon, we expect more interest. It seems older vessels are now sensibly adjusting closer and more related to scrap values, which is probably a sign that the support from sanctioned cargoes is easing off. Most activity is on the product segments with MRs being the most liquid asset – in an illiquid market. Prices have no clear direction, and flat is probably the best comment to make.

text: MEG Following the crude, Oct Propane CP edged up further this week, traded at $762 at the time of writing. And Butane CP was traded at $8 less. Saudi released their acceptance with no cuts reportedly. One evenly spilt cargo for Oct lifting was reported to change hand at CP plus $2.   FAR EAST Cash premium for 2h Oct delivered propane remained at negative territory and declined further this week. We’ve seen one Chinese major sold two parcels of 23kt propane for such period delivery, at Oct FEI minus $6.5 and minus $8 respectively. Bids on the next day retreated to Oct FEI minus $10 while offers at minus $7.  In order to meet targets aimed at controlling energy use and gas emissions, some manufacturing plants in EChina have cut rates and there are concerns arising whether LPG-feed crackers and PDHs might be under impact. Consequently, LPG and PP futures on DCE are traded in volatility this week, which also partially affecting FEI swap trades by hedge funds.   Several term tenders issued last week by Chinese and SEA players are closed and under discussions. Apart from these, Indonesia PERTAMINA issued another term buy tender to purchase 11 lots of evenly split cargo for monthly CFR delivery except Feb in 2022. Their last CFR term tender was reported to award to two trading houses.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: NWE A quiet market was exacerbated by the draw in US inventories. Traders expecting a strengthening price reaction. This did not materialise immediately as the strength already priced in to the market. What this means for North West Europe is that it will be very difficult to attract imports to the region. The East West spread from the US at +$53pmt for October and widening for later months not tempting traders with the freight diff at $40pmt. Propane Naphtha spread at +$63pmt for October is keeping petchem demand at rock bottom for the time being. With weather in the region above seasonal averages it’s a gamble when weather related demand might shift the market to require imported tons. A butane deal done in the window set the C4 market at 101.75% October Naphtha.  MED The mood in the region is that the market is tight and it will only get tighter. Right now questions regarding available cargoes are being asked though firm price discussions are still lacking. The market is yet to see any winter demand though the general strength is keeping everyone on their toes.  AMERICAS The EIA this week reported that US propane stocks fell by 500,000bbls over the one-week period ending 17th September.  This compares to the 97.9 and 95.4mmbbl totals recorded during the same week last year and in 2019.  Inventories are now 71% and 74% of the levels achieved in each of the two previous years.   As regards terminal fees, there are multiple tiers which depend on the composition of a particular cargo, and whether that cargo is sourced from a re-seller or direct from one of the terminals.  The terminals themselves are offering full propane lots, but at rather steep levels: 7cts/gal in the highest case, but this underscores the ongoing issue of the Ethane/Propane pricing differential (among other factors), as well as the perceived expectation that terminal fees are being more closely managed.  Split ratio parcels are offered at progressively lower rates, some under 6cts/gal – and perhaps with some room for negotiation thereafter.    Resellers, meanwhile, do not have the same E/P pricing considerations (as they relate to the production of LEP from HD5) and can let full propane lots go at around 5cts/gal, depending on timing/location.  Buy side ideas, meanwhile, reside at (or, more likely, just under) the 4cts/gal level, but interest levels have generally been pretty sparse, particularly from end users.

EAST The East market is still lagging behind the West in terms of earnings. Activity levels is picking up however and we now start to see a few deals in the Middle East. An Indian PSU spot tender is due today and there is already some chatter about a few more similar upcoming tender quotes.  As of now, there’s ample supply of competitive relets available in the MEG and it seems like freight is set to remain at a discount to the West for time being.  WEST After last week's fixing activity ex the US, there are few owner controlled vessels left for October dates. Throughout the week we have, however, seen a handful of relets emerging within the third decade of October. In combination with a tight arb this puts a damper to any sudden increase in freight rates. A couple of deals has been concluded this week just shy of USD 85 Houston/Chiba basis. According to our data, we anticipate more than a handful deals yet to be concluded in US off October dates.

The East Suezmax market took a backward step this week when a modern ship fixed MEG/East in the low WS 50's.  It's evident, that without a firmer VLCC market, there is very little that owners can do to stop the rot. All participants need to focus on the flood of East ballasters that are vacuuming up a lot of Atlantic business, which, for the most part, will mainly discharge in the West. These ships are not being recycled back onto the East list in the same volumes as just a few months ago and this will naturally apply a cap to Atlantic rates. Conversely, at some point, this will create a bottle neck in the East and if this coincides with a firmer VLCC market in the next 3-4 weeks, then the usual Suezmax release valve will not be as easy to call upon.

We count just under 115 cargoes for the month, with expectations of a repeat of July’s 125+ fading. Owners were pushing the market up through the WS 30’s, but Friday saw CPC fixing ‘vintage’ (15+) tonnage at WS 29. For modern, the market has found equilibrium just under WS 35 for MEG/China at present. In Wafr, WS 36 achieved (up a point), but many owners reluctant to tie in for long voyages, when the prospect of improvement may be likely. Therefore, many holding off to see what the next week or so brings. We expect the recent IEA’s estimate of 3 mbpd global oil production growth from now until year-end to boost rates and sentiment, however it will take time before current overcapacity has been absorbed.

With September dates soon to be all covered and still enough vessels on the list, we expect rates to move sideways. In the Med/Bsea, we have seen the market go from soft to firming this week. This is due to a combination of things, such as ships being fixed under the radar, other ships leaving the area to try their luck in improved surrounding markets, and the fact that a healthy cargo program ex Bsea for October has emerged. Add the uncertain situation in Libya into the mix, and it will be interesting to see if these fundamentals combined are enough to finally put some upwards pressure on rates.

While cargo prices strengthened and remained strong this week, the high LNG prices have so far not translated to any strengthening of the spot charter rates - hence, the correlation between cargo price movements and charter rates is yet to be seen. However, a vast majority of the available LNG vessels for spot charters are controlled by portfolio players and traders. As sellers’ cargoes are offered with the requirement to procure spot shipping, they are more often than not, lifted by buyers with available vessels for further trading and filling up short positions given the ideal LNG trading market conditions. The market is also not flushed with a long selection of vessels as the availability list is relatively short.  Meanwhile, the term charter rates for 1 year period remain steady. Charterers’ interest in security over vessel availability for a term period continue to be a priority for various players.    Newbuilding prices continue to climb as Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) confirmed the orders for upto four (4) LNG vessels at Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering (DSME) on the back of charters with Novatek Gas & Power Asia. The 174,000m3 LNG vessels, fitted with ME-GA engines for propulsion, along with a shaft generator and an onboard reliquefaction unit, are expected to be delivered in 2024.

It is with no surprise that we are closing this week with yet another flurry of dry cargo transactions. From Handysize to Newcastlemax dry snp markets are joying of sustained liquidity, providing additional support and confidence to an ever increasing number of market players looking to acquire tonnage in view to yield the returns offered by an even more sustainable freight market. The Panamax/Kamsarmax segment seem to have captured the bulk of the enquiry this week. The sisterships “PEAK PEGASUS” & “PEAK LIBERTY” (82k dwt, 2013/2015, Tsuneishi Fukuyama) have been sold to Globus Maritime at a respective Usd 27m and Usd 30m while the 2019 Chinese built “SEACON SHANGHAI” was sold at a firm Usd 36m. The Japanese controlled “SEA VISION” (77k dwt, Imabari, 2015) invited offers on Wednesday after having north of 10 parties showing outright interest – best levels received are understood to be hovering around the Usd 29m mark, however the vessel remains in negotiation and we should be in a position to report further early next week.   A similarly unsurprising state of affairs on the tanker front but with a persistent lack of activity. These subdued SnP markets are however not necessarily reflective of the underlying sentiment which is somehow positive with a building anticipation that better days are not far off. Notable news this week is an apparent pick up in demolition with 4 VLCCs reported to have hit the beaches. Increased scrap rates have indeed been driving pockets of tanker activity with a number of overaged crude carriers also finding further trading buyers over the past few weeks. A tonnage phase out which is of course welcome in an already tight supply environment for Tankers which have seen no new order inked over the whole month of August.

The market took a turn this week and rates have been firming in both hemispheres. In the Atlantic it is getting tighter for available tonnage, and the P1A is currently priced at 33/34k while the shorter rounds are breaking the 40k mark.  In the Pacific, rounds are being fixed at similar levels as in the Atlantic. Period market has regained confidence and Kamsarmaxes being fixed at 30k for 1 year.

Big ships earning big bucks on robust fundamentals assisted by Chinese weather disruption. General spot earnings up more than 30 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 53k/day, and main drivers being iron ore miners in deep need of early tonnage from West Australia and Brazil, supported by very healthy coal volumes into India + China. The Pacific under pressure in particular, as differential China-Brazil-China vs Pacific RV has gone from par to almost USD 10k/day in favour of the latter. Short- and long-term views encouraging, period interest considerable - recent fixtures predominantly at floating rates, including 180,000 dwt/2006-built spot China done for 12-16 months at BCI 5tc index flat.

Positive start of the week across all markets. Impressive push on a FFA made optimism to return. USG and ECSA were lacking action past week, but activity returned, and we see good premium paid on prompt ships. Tess 58,000 dwt fixed around USD 40,000 pd with delivery Brazil for TCT with grains to Mediterranean. Nice Ultramax 63,000 dwt modern fixed delivery Praia Mole, Brazil, at USD 27,000 pd plus USD 1.7 mill GBB for TCT to South East Asia with grains. Rates from Med to West Africa stable at around USD 45,000 pd. Trips from Continent to ECSA paying high USD 30,000 pd with premium to USEC and USG destinations. The Pacific remains stable with Indonesian trips into China fixed around USD 35,000 pd. Nopac and Aussie RV paying slightly less. Supra 57,000 dwt fixed delivery China via Australia to discharge in Indonesia with sugar cargo at USD 34,500 pd.

EAST The Middle East shipping market is slowly coming back to life after a couple of rather quiet weeks. There are still a few theoretical September MEG positions available, some soon about to reach their deviation points for alternative West voyages and some which inevitably will slide into October, bringing an overhang of ships into next month. Aramco acceptances expected to be released today after which October fixing should be in full swing. In general, the market in the East is still looking long and we need a healthy amount of spot cargoes before an eventual shift in sentiment.  WEST Since yesterday, first half October has been more or less wiped out in terms of vessel positions. A long awaited fixing spree saw about a dousin fixtures in the Western hemishpere, not only counting ex US. Rates bottomed out at mid USD 70’s and rather quickly has stabilised around the USD 80 per ton mark and now, offers from owners for what ships’ are left, is hovering mid USD 80’s. Today has been more quiet, naturally one could argue, and players are recouperating and waiting for the dust to settle. Focus has shifted to last decade October dates now, however, as it’s still more than a month away any would-be charterers have some time on their hands. Having said that, end October doesn’t look overly long at the moment and it seems time being that the market will stabilise around mid USD 80’s per ton.

text: NWE  Rising crude is dragging CIF ARA up to seven year highs. Though CIF ARA remains in the shadows of Mt Belvieu’s strength. This keeping the arb closed, though not by much, and the trans-Atlantic trade to a bare minimum. A trading house continues to bid the window, at a small premium, failing to attract interest so far this week. Petchems in the region are cracking naphtha where possible with September pro/nap spread at +$48pmt. Natural Gas prices in the region remain high and it will be interesting to see if this pushes propane into any new markets. Refineries using propane as fuel has yet to push up the volume of imports to the region. Butane 104.5% Naphtha rising to 106.8% in November.   MED The main import countries continue to look for product. Tightness in the East Med looks less severe in October than September, with sufficient volume heading for Turkey. West Med demand is present though not urgent, with Morocco looking for small volumes of butane.  AMERICAS Propane supply is now of concern to most parties, since the EIA inventory data revealed a bullishly paltry 700,000bbl build for the week ending 10 Sep, and which brought overall total stock levels to 70.8mmbbls, or 73.6% of last year.  Naturally, the pricing structure at Mont Belvieu is responding and has moved up to over $1.30/gal.  Inventory draws were recorded in both PADD I and PADD III, indicating that export volumes – despite the recent hurricane which landed near Houston and a bit of mid-month terminal downtime – remain robust.  To further illustrate the point, Gulf Coast inventories are 33.2mmbbls, down from 54.9mmbbls last year – a nearly 40% reduction over twelve months.  The ‘bright’ side is limited to the lack of crop drying in North America, but with a La Nina climate forecast on the horizon, winter – and any corresponding demand that comes alongside– looms.  Terminal fees in the US remain tiered, with spot buy-side interest at sub-4cts/gal levels, and spot re-sellers at/below a nickel.  The terminals themselves - depending on the ratio - have a stair-stepped system ranging from the low 5ct range up to more than 6.5cts/gal.

text: MEG Oct Propane CP swap rallied up to $752, increased by nearly $60 compared to last week. However, Butane was traded at $6 cheaper to Propane, due to muted inquires in the front for evenly split cargos. Nov CP was traded at $4 contango, reflecting the good expectations on winter demand for forward months.   FAR EAST Discussion level for Oct delivered propane remained stable amid limited buying inquires. 23kt Propane parcel for 2h Oct delivery was traded at balance 16-30th Sep FEI, which equates to Oct FEI minus $5. Comparatively, paper swaps on FEI were buoyed up, following the rise in Crude, other light ends in upstream, and gained an unexpected support from Chinese funds who are hedging for domestic DCE futures.    Off window a handful of tenders are flowing in the market this week. HTC issued buy tender to secure 23kt propane for end Oct early Nov delivery. One SChina importer tendered to procure a 11/11 parcel for Nov delivery. Taiwan CPC issued buy tender for one 11/11 parcel during 2h Oct delivery. Apart from spot tenders, end users emerged with their term procurement tenders. One EChina PDH user issued annual term tender to secure monthly 23kt propane from Jan to Dec 2022 delivery. Indian IOC was reported to award their last term tenders for monthly one evenly cargo at CP minus low single digit to double digits, depending on which month loading. And they’ve again issued two more tenders to secure similar volume for Q1 and Q2 delivery. Two Philippine importers issued term tender as well, with one inquiring for monthly 30-40kt LPG and the other for monthly 40-46kt.

Volume of transactions in the dry snp markets remains unhindered week after week with 15 vessels changing hands. The buying enquiries remain spread out across sectors with active buyers bidding across all sizes. The Ultramax/Supramax front is clearly leading the charge having captured 10 out of the 15 weekly reported sales. Although we continue to experience a relative climb in prices, the stream of potential sellers entering the market alleviates the upward pressure on values by diluting competition across a number of available candidates. Saying that the trend remains very much positive with TRF selling its two Hantong ultramax sisterships built 2016 and 2015 for an enbloc price of Usd 55m while Latsco achieved Usd 20.5m on its IVY DELTA (55k dwt built IHI 2011).  Tanker SnP remains subdued in terms of market activity - headlines were however stolen by SFL announcement of its acquisition of 3 x 2019 Suezmax tankers believed to be contracted at New Times by Trafigura. The transaction combines a TC back agreement to the sellers for a minimum of 5 years.

It has been pleasing to see that spot market activity picked up this week with FOB tenders appearing alongside firm requirements. Commodity prices remain strong yet perhaps surprisingly given cargo strength and increased freight activity, freight rates struggle to interrupt the depressed trend that currently overwhelms the market. The lack of prompt cargoes sees a sizable relet fleet open and interested in short localised business. As laycans drift into Q4, late October and November in particular, rates for long-haul voyages do rise significantly and we can expect the delta between BLNG2 and BLNG3 to widen in the coming weeks as winter gets priced in. Moving East, the thirst for vessels has improved yet insufficiently to absorb all open tonnage. Modern tonnage is likely to move West on their own accord in hope for Atlantic business. Those who remain East for spot Pacific requirements still have to compete with sublet vessels with pockets of availability which are dampening freight levels. LNG shipping availability may however tighten as we look ahead with the current future arbitrage opportunities. Yard prices hold firm, yet no new newbuilding transactions have been recorded.

The MEG market remains a frustrating hunting ground for owners, as the expectation of any improvement in rates remains on the horizon. Charterers able to source tonnage at last done levels in the low WS 30's MEG/East, and avoiding any rush to fix. There remains much of the 3rd decade to cover however (25-30 cargoes?) and we already over 100 cargoes for September, so plenty of fixing to be done in the short term.  The Atlantic remains busy, but again, rates yet to move as ballasters content to escape a stagnant East market if possible. Some owners preferring to keep things short, as they realize that if you fix long now, that is your Q4. Much debate among market players as to when the much vaunted rate improvements will come, but we still a little early for that right now.

There's a perception that Suezmax's always follow "big brothers" lead as soon as V's show any signs of life. Yes, if the maths permit it, we can see interaction, but the core issue for Suezmax right now is the East. Namely, its low enquiry volumes, therefore, ballasters continue to clip out Med and Wafr stems on a daily basis. A case in point being that the majority of vessels passing Rondo now set a course directly for Wafr without even considering ballasting to deviation point Galle. The East list is so overloaded with unemployed ships that owners with larger fleets aren't even looking to maintain fleet balance. They are rolling the dice on Western markets that still have decent enquiry levels. Unfortunately, this strategy becomes a law of diminishing returns and will continue to cannibalize Atlantic basin rates.

The Nsea/Baltic Aframax market experienced yet another disappointing week. The combination of an abundance of available tonnage coupled with somewhat reduced activity, in the current fixing window, are keeping rates at bottom levels. Earnings are very close to nothing or even negative for some owners trading in this area. Unless, owners find better alternatives elsewhere, we expect the next week to remain quite similar to the previous.  The Med/Bsea market also continued trading sideways at bottom levels this week. Bad weather and potential disruptions in Libya have created a little bit of excitement, however these elements have yet to develop into firmer rates. A few owners have an optimistic eye on the cargo program out of Bsea for October, so it will be interesting to see how healthy this program is once revealed.

Vsl open in Taiwan for trip via Indonesia redel WCI covered at USD 34,000. Some fertz runs via MEG to WCI closed around USD 50,000 dop Mesaieed. text: NWE Surging Natural Gas prices have been dominating the headlines. In NWE this has led to refineries using more propane as fuel, reducing local production. CIF ARA propane and butane both reached seven year highs, the strength largely driven by CIF ARA following Mt Belvieu. The price strength has not been enough to keep trans-Atlantic cargoes flowing. With less than 100KT of imports from the US in August, the lowest volume in over a year. Propane is at an $8 premium to naphtha in September increasing to $30 in December. This is set to reduce already low petchem run rates to a minimum this winter. The low demand environment in this Autumn shoulder period is the reason a North Sea loading propane VLGC is set to be exported, a sign the supply floor has been reached. Cold weather will be the remedy to jolt the subdued NWE market into action!  MED The region remains tight in the East Med, with Turkey looking for volume and the lack of imports form the US are causing concern. The West Med has been quiet though traders are worried about buying for winter. With cold weather around the corner how expensive will the product needed for winter become.  AMERICAS The release by the EIA of propane stock levels in the US was delayed due to the American Labor Day holiday on Monday, but was eagerly awaited today as the domestic market continues to precariously hinge on inventory levels.  Prior expectations varied widely, with speculation from one perspective calling for a modest draw and from another a build of up to 2mmbbls.  Ultimately the EIA reported that an overall build of 800,000 barrels, though a draw of 100,000 draw was noted in PADD III, the Gulf Coast.  Stocks are – as of 3 Sep – 72% of the total achieved in 2020.  Ultimately the stats are considered generally bullish. Meanwhile, the pricing structure continues at elevated levels, but with winter-demand looming and propane at 71% of WTI the number of those predicting even higher levels seems to be growing.  This is based on the expectation that stock levels – such as they are – can not sustain both a cold winter and heavy export volumes.  That has led to concern as to where the low point of stocks will be next Spring, and where prices will reside at that point. Terminal fees, all the while, have been sagging and for October are now seen ranging from sub-4ct bids to the mid/upper 4s on offer.  Very little is being accomplished.

Despite Tanker chartering market seeing signs of recovery we continue to see subdued snp activity, with a growing list of buying enquiry failing to be met by any realistic sale candidates. In terms of concluded business, the M/T Starlight Venture (291k dwt, blt HHI 2004) is reported sold to Nigerian buyers at USD 30 mill. Lot of talks as well this week concerning the troubled MR M/T Marvin Independence (50k, blt Hyundai Mipo 2018). The vessel is a high spec, LNG-ready, IMO II, 20 grade MR that eventually went for auction at USD 17.1 mill to Greek buyers. We understand there are still several ongoing legal outstandings surrounding the vessel and its sale that may impact the transaction.  In the other hand, activity remains high in the Drybulk space with headlines being stolen by the Capesize sector this week which has seen Turkey’s Ciner emerge as the buyer of 3 x 2016 built units. The SWS and Dalian built vessels, M/V Stella Naomi, M/V Stella Hope and M/V Stella Nora – were sold at an enbloc price of Usd 132 mill including the balance of index-linked TCs attached. The sale provides a clear target and benchmarks for the owners that we have seen place fresh candidates in the market this week. Elsewhere, Malaysian Bulk Carriers joyed of the recent appreciation in values witnessed in the supramax front by selling its two Shin Kurushima built sisters M/V Alam Madu and M/T Alam Molek (both 58k dwt, blt 2014). The vessels were sold to Meghna of Bangladesh who is reported to have paid 26 mill each.

A strong rise on Supramax from the beginning of the week faded away due to the FFA correction and uncertainty on the bigger sizes. The BSI TCE climbing to USD 38,246 despite negative FFA forward values. Demand from ECSA and USG was slowing down resulting downwards pressure on the rates. A few Supra and Ultramaxes were fixed for FH at USD 28,000 plus USD 1,800 mil GBB, which is down from 2 mill on GBB. Same patter in USG where rates were reduced slightly.  Demand for fertilizers to ECSA from the Mediterranean and the Continent holding rates up. MV Star Cleo (56,600 2013) dop Piraeus tct w/ferts via Damietta to Argentina USD 35,000 pd. No major changes on rates/activity from last week in the Pacific and the Indian Ocean market. Period activity slowed down with charterers withdrawing their last bids again due to the negative FFA trading.

There can be no denying a little uptick in activity, with several cargoes on the open market and more vessels finding employment. Maybe some green shoots of recovery, as reports of WS34+ MEG/China are doing the rounds which is likely not too wide of the mark. Modern owners holding for mid WS30’s, leaves the older ladies to compete at the WS30+ level, for cargoes that allow. West Africa has been concluded at WS35 heading for India, in line with last done levels, and reports of multiple offers on uncovered enquiries require owners to hold their nerve. Elsewhere in the Atlantic, we've seen one fresh cargo N.Sea/Eastbound, but ships held on subs for over a week and cargoes trading and disappearing unlikely to add much strength for now. US export cargoes has been put on hold due to Hurricane Ida.

As the tonnage list remains longer than the current cargo activity can satisfy, the Nsea/Baltic market has traded sideways at bottom levels yet another week. Going forwards we expect a bit more cargo activity in the 2nd half of September, however until then we expect the market to continue trading sideways. Much the same can be said about the Med/Bsea market, where the amount of ships outbalances the weak number of cargoes. We still need to see quite a few more ships be cleared away before we see any significant improvement of rates.

As congestion in China eased over the last week with more available tonnage around, the Pacific has been under pressure. Together with a slower Brazilian program this has turned the sentiment negative. However, North Atlantic still fairly tight, while the amount of ballasters headed to Brazil nor very significant. All this mirrored in the index development over the last week with Brazil-China down 8%, Pacific round voyage down 17%, and Atlantic round voyage up 1%.

With London closed on Monday the start was very quiet, but we see a growing tonnage list in the Atlantic, and less demand.  P1A is currently trading in the 28/29k region. In the Pacific, we still see good activity and rates keeping up for now. Rounds are being concluded in the mid 30’s and period activity has been good. Mid-week we do however see some ships failing.

When the market has recently traded in such narrow parameters, there was understandably some incredulity amongst participants when Wafr/East started to trade at a discount to Td20. There was a forty eight hour period which could only be described as a disorientated market. The East Suezmax market, or lack of market, to be more precise, singlehandedly created the anomaly that lead to Wafr trading in such an odd manner. The perceived impact of unemployed Eastern ballasters heading to Wafr is the reason for its limited upside. Whether it is now at parity or has returned to its old differential, will be decided by the next pure East run. For now, we are calling both Wafr/East and Td20 in mid WS50's. MEG/China should settle at WS55 given that a short East is on subs at WS57.5, whilst Td23 trades at WS22.5-25 flat'ish.
