text: NWE The lower than anticipated US inventory build pushed up Mt Belvieu propane and as a consequence CIF ARA propane prices. This has pushed propane/naphtha in NWE from -$2pmt Tuesday to Wednesday’s close of +$20pmt. Some petchem buying interest is said to remain due to traders hedging pro/nap at a a favorable spread. That said crackers are not running at capacity at the moment. CIF ARA butane has remained steady at 106% naphtha, the market is tight but quiet. The market has not followed the usual seasonal trends, LPG has been expensive throughout the summer. Soon weather related and gasoline blending demand will start to be seen. So the question for many European traders is when to start buying for winter?   MED Maintenance at Mohammedia storage which has taken out 80KT of it’s 200KT capacity has not had an effect on VLGC imports to the region. It is yet to be seen if discharge times will increase, or if stocks can be managed effectively. The rest of the region remains tight though there is very little interest in bringing in from the US as Mt Belvieu butane saw a $50pmt increase post US inventories being posted Wednesday.  AMERICAS Mont Belvieu propane values continue to tick up on a daily basis, primarily on the back of concerns that inventory levels in the U.S. will be insufficient for the combined demand that is anticipated from the petchem sector, the winter period and – above all – overwater exports.  Current valuations for non-LST Sep propane are in the $1.17/gal range.  October bids were most recently seen at $1.20/gal.   The EIA this week reported a 600,000bbl build in overall stock levels, but a draw of the same volume occurred in PADD III, the Gulf Coast – where the bulk of the exports occur.  The overall total as of late Aug is ~73% of last year, and whether or not stock totals can make it to the desired levels is an openly discussed concern.    There remain between 4-6 weeks in the traditional ‘build’ season and so much will be determined over the next month.    Terminal fees remain tiered, with re-sellers offering at (or perhaps just below) a nickel and buyers – considering current economics – at levels well below that.  The terminal owners/operators themselves are generally at yet another, higher level – particularly for full propane cargoes.

It has been another week of relatively low spot activity in the LNG shipping market. Portfolio sublet positions keep “flooding” the market at both basins, where the ones looking at securing tonnage can find some seasonal bargains at very competitive levels; yet period flexibility and promptness of available tonnage doesn’t always necessarily allow for these deals to get concluded. Looking at the cargo market, LNG prices keep climbing due to continuous supply disruptions and uncertainties, having JKM and TTF at a constant battle.  Charterers looking for tonnage for winter opportunities seem to struggle to get much traction from the few Independent Owners with available tonnage or from subleters managing their future schedules. As a result, we are witnessing a halt in near term charter activity, but with cargo market being volatile, this could quickly turn either way. NB prices continue their ascending trend, however no new large LNG orders have been recorded this week.

EAST Slight downward pressure on freight in the East and last reported non-Indian deal in the market was fixed at a discount to Baltic. We have seen about 16 spot deals concluded from the Middle East in September thus far, but we expect there is a handful more uncovered cargos during 20-30 September before we can close the month off. Freight ideas from Owners going forward is in the mid $40s territory, however some might still be there to consider less against firm cargos.  WEST At the time of writing, there are only a couple of vessels left open for the balance of September in the USG. There is also a handful of FOBs for sale from various terminals which in theory could leave September wiped out on shipping availability, however, the mismatch between owners’ and charterers’ freight ideas and terminals’ selling ideas is strangling any momentum to get deals done. Uncertainty around Panama southbound slot delays is one of the contributing factors as to why the bids and offers doesn’t get to terms. Most deals concluded during the last week for end September and beginning October laycans have been done around mid USD 80’s Houston/Chiba basis and mid/low USD 40s Houston/Flushing basis. Freight is seemingly quite resilient at or around this level and going further into October any vessels with firm northbound Panama slot may be preferred and thus fetch a dollar or so premium to non-booked vessels. Inefficiencies are expected to prevail and may tilt the market up or down a notch depending on vessel availability on certain laycans.

Subdued freight rates in the Tanker space are keeping S&P activity limited with only a handful of deals to report this week. The Judicial Managers of Xihe Holding have sold another VLCC - namely the M/T Chang Bai San (318k dwt, blt SWS 2012)  which achieved USD 41,50 mill – USD 2,65 mill down compared to the sister M/T Qi Lian San which was sold back in late April. On the older units we have seen M/T Katsuragisan (311k dwt, blt 2005 Kawasaki) sold for USD 30.3 mill. Fairly in line with expectations given current demolition rates but substantially lower than M/T Olympic Legend (309k dwt, blt 2003 Samsung) which got USD 31,5 mill in July. The latter was seen as very strong.  Dry cargo markets continue to joy of a number of transactions with a steady flow of sale candidates being placed on the market to meet the ever-increasing demand for tonnage. Supported by the solid footing provided by the charter markets sellers are raising their price expectations driving potential buyers above last done levels in order to secure a deal. Supramax and Ultramax segments continue to capture the bulk of the enquiry with vessels across all vintages regularly changing hands.

It’s been a volatile week in the LNG market, but prices seem to have recovered to just below last weeks highs. During this period of volatility, shipping rates have held up except the West TFDE rate. Traders and Charterers are marketing sublet positions for intra Atlantic voyages at attractive rates, whiles Charterers looking for tonnage to take product out east, may struggle, pending dates.  Prompt availability is dominated by subletters, some of which have pockets of availability and others with more flexibility. The fact of the matter is that vessel availability continues to be date sensitive and limited.  In the newbuilding segment, Celsius has been linked to the two latest orders at SHI. The positions are said to have been options executed at high USD 190s mill per vessel, which is below our current price guidance for a new order placed «today».

Spot levelling out at historical highs for the big ships, as main miners try pull brakes on the crucial Brazil/China fronthaul route. Same may however be temporary, as iron ore flow prospects for both this and the West Australia/Far East trade are fundamentally strong and supply of early tonnage equally tight. Significant congestion keeps being a factor expected to maintain very robust rates.  Daily earnings coming in at touch over USD 50k, up some 11 pct w-o-w, with majority of improvement related to transatlantic and fronthaul trades. Limited period activity as pricing becoming quite punchy, representative fixtures include scrubber-fitted 177,000 dwt, built 2010, reported done for 2 years at around USD 30k.

Vessel demand from all major load regions have increased the last week, reflecting that underlying fundamentals remain very strong. However, upside could be capped as the near-term outlook for the larger segments has weakened. Asia market showing more activity with congestion being big factor. Nickel ore trip from Philippines to China USD 39,500. Trip from Indonesia to China 38k on Supra open Vietnam. Supra from Richards Bay to Pakistan 31k + 720k bb. From the Atlantic basin it was more life in the USG, where trips to Far East were covered at high USD 40,000 and trips to Skaw around USD 38,000. Usual scrap cargoes from Continent to Med were fixed around USD 38,000. Black Sea still firm where usual grain runs were covered at very high USD 50k.

The Panamax market continued its firming tendency this week with fresh demand in both hemispheres. In the Atlantic, we see mineral demand picking up, but also the tonnage list is building up – thus could be a bit toppish mid-week. In the Pacific, Indonesian rounds have picked up but also NoPac demand gives support to rates. The period demand is also active with a Kamsarmax reported at 28.5k for 9/11 months basis Far East delivery.

text: AMERICAS:  Strong US overwater export volumes in July will very likely be overshadowed by record-level volumes in Aug – despite the buyback scheme embarked upon by Enterprise earlier in the summer.  The September roster appears solid, as well, with only two cargo cancellations known.   The robust outbound volumes are the primary reason that domestic US propane stocks have been unable to rise to desired levels.  This week the EIA reported overall stock levels to be 68.7mmbbls – up by 1.9mmbbls week-over-week.  Still, this is just 75% of both last year and 2019 as domestic production simply cannot hold pace.  In 2019 production averaged 1.148mmbbls/day.  By 2020 it had risen to 1.179mmbbls/day, and on a YTD basis 2021 has so far improved to 1.235mmbbls/day – but still, exports reign and will likely continue to disallow stocks from satisfactorily improving. Crop drying expectations for this Fall, however, call for minimal demand as a lasting, dry and “scorching” Midwest heat has allowed crops to “wither” in the fields.  This should allow stock levels to build at a mildly better rate, but the hope of reaching 80+ mmbbls is fading, or perhaps already dissipated. Spot terminal fees in the US in September, while sentimentally up, remain on either side of the 5ct range for Sep, though little is being accomplished.  2022 contract terminal fee values, depending on the ratio, frequency, volume, etc., range from the upper 4cts/gal level to well over 6cts/gal.  North West Europe:  The physical market in the region is tight, window premiums assessed at September CIF ARA +$4.5pmt. Propane has once again switched back to a discount to naphtha. Though at a mere -$6pmt in September it is not nearing the -$30pmt needed to switch back to cracking propane instead of naphtha. The build in US inventories is hoped to widen the arb to NWE though, in this low demand environment it is unlikely a significant volume of US tons will find their way to the region. CIF ARA butane is at 104% naphtha showing uncharacteristic strength for the time of year.   MED: A quiet week though trends are the same. The region remains tight all grades. Butane particularly with values slightly above those in NWE at 106% naphtha.

The Nsea/Baltic market remained flat with rates at bottom level despite a few more cargo inquiries. The tonnage list in the area is still plentiful as owners pushing in order to at least secure positive returns on local voyages. Moving forward we expect rates to keep moving sideways. As expected, rates in the Med/Bsea market came off a couple of points more this week, mainly due to the lacklustre activity on the cargo side. We do not expect any significant improvement to this market in the short run, and going into next week we expect it to continue trading sideways.

EAST: We expect to see a handful of uncovered cargo enquiries remaining in the 2nd half of September out of the MEG. Having said that, one Indian PSU is likely to cover a mid September requirement on their own TC tonnage which may take away one spot cargo that was expected in the market. Many of the theoretical MEG positions can still sail West, however, we are also seeing a tendency whereby some owners choose to stay East of Suez due to less waiting time and shorter ballasts. Freight rates obtained for September loading in the MEG have been somewhat inconsistent lately as we have seen a couple of last decade September fixtures concluded lower than last done during 2nd decade of the month. Depending on spot volumes remaining for the second part of September we foresee freight rates to remain relatively flat for the time being.  WEST: 2nd half September freight is somewhat date dependant shipping-wise. Any waiting time of open vessels may; either limit the downside or favour a more pragmatic rate. The freight market looks likely to remain around mid/low USD 80s for end September and seems on paper relatively balanced between cargoes and vessels which are uncovered for September. Some talks of early October enquiries starting to surface although not in full force yet. It is again likely that we’ll see little or no overhang of ships going into October. There were a few cargoes ex West Africa in play at the time of writing, however, same has reportedly not been covered on shipping yet.

Comparing this week’s East and West Suezmax markets provides some insight into demand differences between the hemispheres. Whilst MEG VLCC cargoes have ranged from 115-130pm during the summer, Suezmax enquiry from the same region has fallen off a cliff with plenty of blank days. This compares unfavourably with a modestly optimistic Atlantic basin where not only are rates a little firmer, but most of the volume is staying in the West. Take Libyan crude as a case in point, which is no longer the darling of the long-haul market, with the majority of stems now finding a home in Europe. Td20 has gained some ground this week, but Eastern ballasters will cap it in the low WS60's whilst MEG/East rates are under downward pressure and will do well to hang on to high WS50's. Td23 is quiet and might be tested down to low WS20's.

text: MEG: Following crude's rollercoaster volatility, Sep C3 CP once dived to $650ish from last week’s $680 and now rebounded close to $670, at the time of writing. First round CP idea on Sep C3 was recommended at the range from $650 to $675, and C4 at $5 cheaper or at parity reportedly.  Qatar Petroleum was reported to sell one mid Sep lifting full propane cargo.   FAR EAST: Spot discussion for 2h Sep delivery range was mute this week. However a handful of Sep arrival cargos were reported unsold and likely to be rolled into Oct delivery, as most receivers already move into Oct program. 23kt propane parcel for 1h Oct delivery was bid at Sep FEI minus $1, yet to lure offers in the window.  Off window Japanese importers are reported to buy Oct delivered cargos for stockpiling, and one 3/1 cargo for 1h Oct delivery was said to be placed into Japan earlier this week. And one Vietnam-based PDH importer awarded their buy tender for one full propane cargo on end Sep to Oct delivery at CP plus low 20s reportedly. Additionally, HPCL issued term tender to secure 14 evenly split FOB cargos from Jan to Dec 2022. However, BPCL cancelled their buy tender to one to two evenly split cargos for Oct delivery.

Active start of the week with strong push on FFA driving the physical market higher. Positive sentiment pushed up BSI in all routes reaching above $ 34500.  Rates from Med to West Africa reaching $ 45,000 and scrap paying $ 35,000 similar from Continent to Med . USG is firm but more balanced compared to ECSA, which is lacking tonnage supply. It is also very congested with some reports suggesting waiting tie for discharge in Paranagua up to 40 days. NOPAC RV on Supra is about $ 32,000 and Backhaul Supramax paying above $,30,000 with delivery China. India Ocean is on fire and we see rates getting agreed in $ 50,000 for East direction. Period market is dominating in the area where Owners asking  $40,000 for min 6 months on Ultramax deliver PG-WC India.

Whilst the fundamentals of the market remain weak, it's worth bearing in mind that historically, the middle to end of August has  provided a degree of upside for Owners (moderate or otherwise) and therefore we need to take into consideration  a number seasonal factors that could come into play . Owners in the West are likely to look for a moderate premium (to last done) to go long-haul in order to hedge against perceived Q4 optimism in the West, whilst conversely, but inline with this theory, we may see backhaul routes, such as Td23, start to soften as Owners look to ballast back to reposition in Europe. For now, Meg/East trades W57.5-60 on modern, Td23 will struggle to stay at W27 and Td20 appears stable in the mid W50's.

Aframaxes trading in the Nsea and Baltic area experienced yet another non-encouraging week as Charterers managed to push rates down even lower from a level that was already perceived as the bottom. Unfortunately, we expect the market to move sideways with no immediate recovery in sight just yet. Much the same can be said about the Med/Bsea market where the few fixtures we have seen have been done at repeat freight levels all week. In the week to come we expect this to continue, if not a slight dip in rates.

Cape market on fire with all arrows pointing up. The average TC rate is now well excess usd 40,000, approaching usd 45,000. The C5 route is presently well in the 15s with c3 in the mid 30s and a general lack of tonnage. Sentiment remains strong also for the near future.

EAST The final acceptances for September were published on Monday and since then we have seen a handful of companies, including 3 Indian majors, checking the market for freight during 1H Sep. Prior to this the sentiment on freight was looking weaker in the AG (mainly due to a healthy supply of trader relets), but with more cargos in play we expect fixing ideas to be adjusted accordingly. Last reported deal in market (for non-India) was done in the usd low-mid 40s Baltic, and we expect next deal to be done around similar territory or higher  WEST Last week we saw freight rates strengthening on the back of an improved arb US/East causing several Charterers to enter the market for shipping at the same time. A couple deals was concluded in the mid/high $80’s at the end of the week, but the unexpected draw in US inventories caused arbs to narrow and consequently put interest for freight at a standstill. That said, on an available ships vs. reported uncovered/available cargoes basis, one could argue that the market looks fairly balanced for September liftings.

Despite a number of markets still in the midst of seasonal holidays, the dry snp market continue to draw sustained interest with a flurry of transactions to report this week. The Ultramax sector has seen three 2014 Jinling built units change hands for a price of Usd 67 m enbloc marking a further step up in values for Chinese built vessels. In comparison, the "SANTA BARBARA ( 2013, Iwagi, 61k dwt) was sold at Usd 24.5m this week underlying the premium priced in for Japanese designed units. Notable activity in the Handysize sector as well which has seen 8 vessels sold this week. With buying enquiry remaining strong and signs of ongoing negotiations across all sectors we expect the volume of transactions to remain.   Tanker markets remain subdued in terms of concluded business with pockets of activity on the vintage crude carrier front with owners driven to sell by high residual values off the back of continuous strong rate offered by cash buyers for demolition, however with expected decline going forward.

After a turn last week with fresh demand in both hemispheres, we see the same firming tendency this week. In the Atlantic we see a tight tonnage list, especially in the North Atlantic. Short Baltic rounds are achieving 38/39k while P1A is priced at ard Usd 33k. In the Pacific the steady flow of Indo coal keeps owners busy and P3A is yielding low 30’s. Period activity is also picking up supported by the FFA mrkt.

The sluggish pace continues in the VLCC segment, with limited inquiry met by sufficient tonnage supply and rates hovering. MEG/East runs are holding in the very low W30’s, and charterers have been slow to progress into next month’s loading program. Wafr/East has set at the “conference level” of W33. Eastbound enquiries from the USG have been largely non-existent, but continues to hover around the $4.0 mil level for the benchmark Ningbo-ROK run. On a positive note bunker prices are down in tandem with falling crude prices, and a growing resistance within the owning community has yielded marginal rate gains in last couple of attempts. However, the supply/demand picture is still very much askew and more demand needed for a sustainable shift in fortunes.

We pass another week with relatively few spot fixtures, and the running total for the year has now fallen some way behind the high watermark of 2020. Will the second half of the year generate enough spot activity to catch up? It’s unlikely, and in fact current trends suggest the fixture count may even slip below the 2019 tally. However, with very few ships under independent owners’ control and with the cargo market remaining buoyant, the rest of 2021 is set to be a fascinating game of chess, in which novel structures and creative deals on both cargo and freight will help charterers make the most of their tonnage - there is plenty of opportunity for win-win scenarios. The multi-month market is again more active, and the limited pool of independent owners and those charterers with enough length to sublet are being kept busy. There haven’t been any fresh newbuilding orders placed this week.

text: NWE Demand in the region has dropped off significantly now that the September propane naphtha spread is +34pmt. Reducing petchem and cracking demand. Leaving the region tight but with low demand the regional production sufficient to cover demand until winter buying picks up. With no signs of cold yet we expect the market to remain relatively tight with the CIF ARA window at a premium. Butane is at 98% August Naphtha and would need to rise to 106% to Naphtha to attract US tons. The arb from the US will most likely remain closed for the being as Mt Belvieu is forecast to remain strong.   MED The Med remains tight and searching for butane, with values now at 105.4% Naphtha. Demand has been good fro the time of year. The arb from the US remains firmly closed and leaves traders looking for tons to supply the region.  AMERICAS  U.S. propane inventory levels rose by 1.6mmbbls this week, bringing total levels to 66.761mmbbls as of 13th August.  Propane stocks are now 75% of last year, though as the weeks have progressed over this summer the level of concern has continued to grow.   The primary reason that stock build rates have been so limited is because export volumes have been so robust.  The month of August is no exception and is expected to see near record-level departures.  The buyback scheme initiated by Enterprise and the various cancellations which have been noted seem to be having little impact on the vessel tally.  Meanwhile, re-sale terminal fees have come off over the course of this week, with offers now seen at 4.25cts/gal and buy-side indications at sub-4cts/gal.  The near-term future of the domestic US propane market will be shaped by the outcome of the crop-drying season and the timing of the arrival and the ferocity of winter.  In the meantime, though, MB propane values have been on the slow, steady rise and are now marked at nearly $1.15/gal ($599/mt).

text: MEG Saudi Aramco released Sep acceptance with several cuts reportedly. This undoubtedly lent support to Sep CP, which resiliently traded at $675-680 earlier this week, but dropped towards $660 on Thursday as Crude slumped more than 3%. Discussion for equal ratio split cargos are active as Indian majors call on buy tenders one after another. And FOB netback improves to premium level for Oct liftings. Sep C3/C4 also narrowed down to $5 consequently.    FAR EAST Discussions for Sep delivery parcels were subdued this week as most players have finished their program. Cash premium sink to discount level this week with 23kt propane for 2h Sep delivery was traded at Sep FEI minus $2.  Indian IOC awarded their new tender to secure one Oct delivered evenly split cargo at CP plus 40s reportedly, right after their Sep purchase last week. HPCL tendered to buy one and half cargo for Oct delivery but result is yet to know. Similarly, BPCL issued tender to secure one to two cargos for Oct. One EChina cracker issued buy tender to procure 23k propane for 2h Sep delivery. And one Schina traditional importer tendered to buy one 11/11 parcel for end Sep to early Oct arrival. Korean HTC also procured 23kt butane for similar timing delivery via tender.

After a seasonal pause in our weekly reporting we are greeted back by promising snp markets which seem to have seen no sign of softening. Headlining the tanker space this week is the highly coveted product sector which has seen Ridgebury acquire a total of 6 vessels for an enbloc price of Usd 61m. Enquiry has indeed been high in the segment however with most players scouting for younger and scarcer sale candidates. Ridgebury therefore is offering a well needed benchmark in what has been a sustained illiquid deal environment. Elsewhere we continue to see vintage crude carriers achieving what can relatively be considered as healthy levels supported by a strong demolition market.    The dry sector has lost no steam over the summer with ten units changing hands this week. Interest remains high from a range of buyers looking to lock in the returns offered by an ever established freight market. Notable activity this week is the sale of a 2017 Hudong built Kamsarmax achieving a staggering price of Usd 31m, “TRANS AFRICA”.

A fairly quiet week for LNG shipping after the slight revival of activity last week. Those vessels that did secure business fixed at rates slightly higher than last done, predominantly East of Suez. However, the feeling is that Charterers expectations are unlikely to be met especially as the fixing window approaches September, and current indications are showing increase. The limited tonnage in both basins continues to be a cause for concern for those with requirements, sublets continue to trickle back into portfolios as winter approaches and schedules are finalised. That being said, reduced spot activity across both basins could see pockets of availability compete. Winter and 2022 coverage remains of interest for some players, and sentiment remains strong for this business as expectation for a healthy LNG market holds. No new LNG orders have been recorded this week, but levels are firming up.

Another positive week for the market with BSI pushing up. More activity from US Gulf and ECSA pushed rates up. The fixtures reported from the US Gulf higher than “last done”. TCT from Mississippi River to Med-Cont being fixed at USD 35,000 pd on Ultramax and TCT to Far East at USD 45,000. Black Sea and Mediterranean market are extremely hot, and rates are pushing as high as USD 48,000’ to West Africa, and for trips to Far East owners are asking close to USD 60,000. Continent is tight on tonnage supply and charterers paying up. Indian Ocean and MEG region remains extremely strong, with period rates being done close to USD 40,000 and trips from India to China fixing at USD 45,000. Inter- Pacific coal voyages are paying around USD 31,000-33,000.

So far this week we have seen an increase in activity in almost all areas. Both North Sea, West Africa and Brazil has been rather busy, which is much needed help for desperate owners. The Brazil export is probably the most reliable one, with Petrobras quoting a Suez cargo almost every day now. Tonnage list in the West on the other hand is still not a pretty sight for owners, but hopefully if this activity remains we can see it thinning out going into next week. In the East, we also see increasing activity, although much of the fixing is happening under the radar. Tonnage-wise it is looking somewhat balanced, and going into next week we could see some more resistance from owners.

Market has been fairly quiet over the last week as many market participants have been on holiday. That said, Brazil has been very active with miners picking vessels coming in ballast from Far East to carry their iron ore to China. We therefore see an improvement on this route of almost 7% while the overall basket is up by 2%. As of now, the number of Capes able to load Brazil for end August and September is very limited and expectations of further increase in levels is strong. While the Brazil segment sees a solid increase, the West Australia route has been slow over the last week, bottoming on Tuesday with the segment slightly up today marking w-o-w down by about 65 cents.

We remain mired, deep in the Summer doldrums. So far in the region of 90-95 fixtures reported ex MEG for August and we already nearing the end of the month laycan wise, suggests a quieter month after a relatively busy July. As such tonnage has been building up at Fuj and this coupled with many deals concluding off market, where charterers pick a victim, owners are struggling to build up any steam. With the Atlantic quiet, and those that do fix, involving tying in tonnage for lengthy trips while the hope of market improvement ever lingers, it is a quandary for owners.  Worth noting the CNBC report that The White House is calling on OPEC+ to boost oil production in an effort to combat climbing gasoline prices, as officials from the Biden Administration spoke with representatives from Saudi Arabia and others this week.

text: NWE  The Northwest European market remains tight as minimal arb cargoes have been directed to the region in August and for September. The pro/nap spread has come in to -$4pmt which is reducing petchem demand. Holiday mode in the region is not the whole story as cargoes from the US are uneconomic and the region cannot survive without imports. Leading to the TOT window premiums to cover base seasonal product needs.   MED The region remains in a tight product environment. US arb cargoes not coming ti the region has led to buyers paying up only when necessary and excess demand being talked.  AMERICAS All eyes are on US propane inventories, as the EIA yesterday surprisingly reported a draw of 700,000bbls in overall US propane stocks, notably a million barrel decline along the Gulf Coast (PADD III).  US propane stocks are now 73% of the level achieved last year at the same time (89.3mmbbls) and 80% of those from two years ago (82.6mmbbls).  Export volumes – despite the rising pricing structure – are the culprit, and as of this writing there appears little end in sight.   Mont Belvieu propane market values topped $1.00/gal in late June, having eclipsed the $0.90/gal level at the end of May.  Presently MB propane is pegged at over $1.13/gal for Sep barrels, and expectations are calling for even higher levels to be achieved as crop drying demand should soon commence, and the likelihood of realizing a comfortable inventory position prior to the onset of winter is fading.  Re-sale terminal fees are now between $5.00-5.25cts/gal, within which range the last known transaction occurred.  Meanwhile, Enterprise continues with its buyback scheme, and is offering $4.625/gal for September barrels.

text: MEG  Another volatile week with swap numbers surging up. At the time of writing, Sep Propane CP was assessed at $679, up by $25 WOW and Butane maintained at $7 cheaper. Sep/Oct CP was traded at flattish level. Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their sale tender for early Sep lifting full propane at discounts to CP, or FEI netback equivalence.   FAR EAST A handful of 2h Sep delivered propane parcels were traded this week. However the cash premium inched down to flattish level to FEI, with buyer biding at discounts whilst seller asking low-mid single digit to FEI.   Off window a plenty of tenders are floating, mainly for evenly split cargos. India IOC tendered to buy one cargo for Sep delivery, while HPCL issued similar tender to cover demand for Oct delivery. Indonesia PERTAMINA issued two term buy tenders, with one for at least one cargo for monthly delivery in 2022, and the other for at least one US lifting from Jan to June. Taiwan CPC also issued tender to buy a 11/11 parcel for 21-30th Sep delivery.   Comparatively, off window inquiries for propane parcels reduced as several PDH have scheduled maintenance during Aug into Sep, partly triggered by the eroding margins. Delays in Chinese ports due to weather factors and time consuming crew-change procedures result in less tonnage available and consequently firmer markets. West Australia c5 is up, close to USD 15s, c3 around USD 30 pmt and average 5tc is gradually approaching USD 40,000 mark! It is more tricky to get hold of period tonnage, due to the positive and firm sentiment.

The upward continue its rally also this week. Strong demand all across the borders and the BSI raising on a daily basis makes owner’s confidence to boost. Ultra was rumoured put on subs USD 30,000 pd plus USD 1.6 mil GBB for trip to Far East. We have seen a slight increase in shipping activity this week as momentum starts to build up for winter.  Movements were predominately East of Suez and a decent amount of fixtures were concluded at rates in line with recent market levels.  On the contrary, the Atlantic remains relatively subdued as the lack of cargoes and close arbitrage restrict any potential West – East trades. Nevertheless, expectations leading towards Q4 and the lack of prompt availability in the West have also seen minimum changes on the recent Atlantic rates.  Furthermore, there are still ongoing discussions between market participants interested in securing multi months for winter coverage or short term. With limited ships available from independent Owners, stronger sentiments and rates are anticipated going forward.  We have increase our newbuild prices to USD 200 million as shipyards are reporting stronger activity. In recent reports, Newbuilding options were also exercised from previous orders.

The week started off in line with last week’s uneventful trend. Little fresh demand in both hemispheres caused rates to slip further. This took a turn mid-week when several of the major charterers entered the market with bot minerals and grain cargos.  P1A is currently priced in the upper 20’s while fronthauls are being fixed in region of USD 48k. In the Pacific, the longer rounds are priced similar to P1A while Indo rounds are fetching around 32k.

Halfway into the first week of August and the summer doldrums continues – lacklustre, tonnage in abundance, and rates hovering well below OPEX even for the best of them. Although rates have shed 0.25/0.5 points a floor of sorts has been found mainly due to owners’ resistance to lock in negative returns, but fundamentals show little change, and the supply-demand equation will take a time to balance. On a positive note, bunker prices have shown a downward trend in tandem with weaker oil prices.

Activity in the area was moderate for another week as bigger sizes and relets have taken a significant amount of stems so far in August. Supply of vessels is building up, and the rates are persisting at bottom levels. Moving forward, we expect rates to remain flat as we don’t expect any fundamental changes.  In the Med/Bsea there is a drought of cargoes coming into the market as the tonnage list keeps getting longer. We have only seen one or two cargoes being dripped into the market per day this week, easily being fixed at repeat levels – if not chipping off a point or two. Benchmark voyages are giving owners a return of less than USD 1,000 pd, and we expect the market to remain soft in the week to come.

EAST We have seen close to 20 spot deals concluded from the Middle East in August which is well above the usual average seen in previous months. A majority of these deals have been done by Indian majors, but we have also seen various traders booking ships for last decade August since last week. Initially, some of these deals were done in the low 40s Baltic, but as the Western premium continue to rise on the back of a more active US market, owners are not there to consider anything less that mid-low 40s in the MEG at the moment. Time of writing there are 2 uncovered Indian cargos for end August, and meanwhile we are still waiting for further September acceptances before we can start to focus on next month’s program.  WEST In the Western hemisphere, vessel supply has cleared out for August and thus, all eyes are on September.  Freight rates are showing signs of improvement from last week’s concluded deals, albeit the September market is date dependant to some extent. Current rates are hovering around mid USD 80’s on Houston/Chiba basis and mid to mid/low USD 40s Houston/Flushing basis. Increasing waiting time for South- and Northbound transits through the Panama Canal seems to be putting a lid on freight. We are bound to see more deals concluded for September ex USG and there is potential for further increases in rates due to amongst others various inefficiencies, however, it all depends on the product market.

The Suezmax market in the West is still lacking activity. Owners want to fix short, and ships taken off the list tend to return quickly. If we look for positives, the list in the North Sea is looking tighter, but with the activity we have seen up there lately there should be enough to cover what’s there. Brazil exports also been stable at a higher level for some time now, giving owners an option other than West Africa.  In the East we are seeing some upward pressure on MEG/East rates. Several cargoes being worked in the same window, and a tighter front-end of the position list has given owners something to work with. We believe the market will keep on in the same track as we have seen going forward, with a possibility of a slight improvement in the East.

text: NWE  An offer was seen in the window which equated to September CIF ARA -$2.5pmt. This was the first bit of action seen in over a week. The offer changed the view that the market is leaning towards being balanced rather than tight. On the back of VLGCs loaded in the US heading to the region in early Sept. Butane saw a bid in the window and is at 95% September naphtha, though this is a moving target due to crude volatility. Petchem demand has come off significantly due to planned maintenances being carried out and importantly forward pro/nap values go from a meagre -$18pmt September moving to an unfavorable +$2pmt by December. The temperatures are cooler than seasonal averages though this is not expected to create enough demand to change the market outlook in the short term.  MED The region has been starved of tons with the arb from the US remaining closed. This has helped drive demand for locally sourced tons, FOB Lavera values particularly strong for summer. Both the East and West Mediterranean are tight of LPG Mix and butane.  AMERICAS  With many out of the office on holiday, the MB propane market continues to trudge along in the 1.08-1.09/gal range, though all the while the level of concern related to propane stock levels in the U.S. is increasing.   Wednesday’s EIA report showed a 1.5mmbbl build, putting overall total US propane inventories at an even 66mmbbls.   This includes, though, a 300,000bbl decline in PADD III (Gulf Coast) stocks and puts this year at 76% of the 86.7mmbbls recorded at the same time in 2020, and 81% of the 79.3mmbbls achieved in early August 2019.   There are around 10 weeks remaining in the traditional stock ‘build’ season, and to reach 80mmbbls another 14mmbbls of inventory growth is needed – or 1.4mmbbls (on average) per week.   The overarching question – and the source of the concern – is whether this will be a sufficient volume to accommodate domestic needs (crop drying + res/com + petrochemical) and overwater export requirements.   Meanwhile, terminal fees continue sitting between 5.00 and 5.25cpg, depending on location, timing, and ratio.  A host of mixed-ratio re-sellers have begun to emerge, and while there are full-propane cargoes available, the Ethane/Propane pricing differential issue continues to dissuade the terminals themselves from entering the fray at competitive price levels.

text: MEG Despite the drastic drop in oil price, Sep C3 CP was traded resiliently at $654, and C4 at $6 cheaper, reflecting the tightness in general supply, coupled by the delays caused by Panama congestion. Sep/Oct CP was traded at flattish to small contango. Qatar Petroleum issued sale tender for 1-5th Sep lifting 45k propane, which is due next week.  FAR EAST Earlier a handful of full cargo propane for 1h Sep delivery were changed hand at Sep FEI minus around $1 reportedly, while half cargo propane parcel for 2h Sep delivery was concluded at Sep FEI plus $1 at mid-week. Evenly split cargo was bid at higher premium, as 11/11 parcel was bid at Sep FEI plus $8 but yet to trigger sellers’ interests. Off window Petchem demand inquires remain robust, despite the poor margin. Several tenders were awarded reportedly for either PDH or cracking feedstock. One EChina PDH user was said to have purchased two lots of 23k propane parcels for 1h and mid Sep delivery into Ningbo at the value of CP plus low 30s. One Korean cracker user was reported to award their buy tender for 23k butane for 1h Sep delivery at Mopj plus high teens. A Vietnam based PDH user secured one full cargo propane for 11-25th Sep delivery at CP plus mid high 20s via tender reportedly.

Great Scott! It’s been 36 years since "Back to the Future" blasted into cinema theaters and became a pop culture phenomenon, and with the current tanker market continuing to trudge along at a sluggish pace we have to look back to the same era to find its equivalent. The "floor" has arguably been lifted from the year low, with the current conference rate for MEG/East runs holding either side of the ws30 mark depending on a ship’s age and trading background, but still a far cry form covering OPEX even for the best of them - and few signs of a major uptick any time soon.  As Marty Mcfly said a number of times throughout the trilogy; “This is heavy”!

It has been a slow week with less demand, especially in the Atlantic. Mid-week we see some fresh requirements, although index levels keep on sliding. P1A is currently yielding 30k while fronthauls are priced at region 49k.  In the Pacific, it has been some activity on shorter periods and also some Pacific rounds which is priced around 28k.

The Nsea/Baltic market didn’t show any signs of life last week as rates remained flat at the bottom. Activity in the area is not enough to make the tonnage list shorter and charterers still manage to fix their cargoes at very low rates. We don’t foresee any tight window soon hence we expect rates to move sideways next week. In the Med/Black Sea, owners trying to optimize, but with a slight downward correction in freight levels seen at the beginning of this week, owners currently finding themselves battling for cargo opportunities not offering much more than last done levels at best. With the prevailing tonnage availability in the area, we don’t expect to see any significant improvement in the near term.

LNG prices continue to soar higher and higher amid surprisingly strong demand, keeping everyone discussing what to expect for the winter period. Nonetheless, some recently concluded shipping deals suggest a slight softening on the prompt spot rates compared to term levels, which indicates that those who have prompt vessel availability, are willing to compromise slightly on rates in order to bridge their next position closer to the winter months. It is however important to note that not all requirements are equal, and some charterers will get luckier with their laycan dates and requested period as many of the vessels in the availability list only have specific date ranges or basins they are willing to work. With overall vessel availability staying relatively tight, we are undeniably balancing on a razor’s edge trying to gauge the next market moves on a week-by-week basis. On the newbuilding front, activity remains high for many ship types, including LNG carriers but especially for container vessels, and yard prices continue to stay under pressure due to the recent hike in steel prices.

Atlantic side tonnage vs cargo remains quite balanced and seems it will remain flat true out the week. text: NWE The arb to the US remains closed, this has limit supply to the region throughout August, and limited tons are set to flow into the region in 1H Sept. Though supply has been reduced and the NWE market remains tight CIF ARA values are not improving. Demand reduction due to petchem demand slowing down has left the market balanced though bids continue to outweigh offers. One of the reasons for the slow down is Pro/Nap margins are steeply backward, around $10pmt per month from -$46 in August to -$17pmt in November. CIF ARA backwardation is widening, showing prompt tightness. The physical window is assessed at August CIF ARA flat. The butane market has been quiet and is at 95.5% naphtha.   MED A 4KT butane offer was seen in the market and although it was discounted during the window no buyer was found. This was put down to strengthening freight in the region. The offer put downward pressure on West Med butane FOBs.  AMERICAS Per the EIA report on Wednesday, U.S. propane inventories grew last week by precisely the anticipated amount: 1.9mmbbls.  Very little reaction was immediately seen, though 24 hours later market values kicked off trading with bids at 110.50cpg but this could be in sympathy with the placement of the Aug CP, which was higher than anticipated.   As the month of August is upon us the buyback scheme embarked upon by Enterprise should very likely result in higher inventory build rates as Enterprise are believed to have purchased at least 5, if not 6 cargoes in Aug.  As of 23 July propane stocks in the U.S. are 76% of last year and 82% of those recorded two years ago.  Enterprise are known to be buyers of Sep cargoes, and should sellers accept their offer, inventories would then likely be in still better position for entry to the winter season.   Meanwhile, rumors that Targa declared Force Majeure due to a fractionator going down are unfounded.  In fact, a minor mechanical issue occurred at the terminal itself, and though a F/M was declared, the problem was very quickly resolved and loading delays of no more than a day are expected, according to Targa.   As for terminal fees, the terminal operators remain priced out due to the E/P pricing differentials while the re-sale market remains approximately on either side of 5cts/gal.

EAST Last deal in the MEG was done by an oil major whom fixed a ship in the mid-40s Baltic (inclusive of options to go to India). This deal was done last Friday but since then it has been rather muted in the East. We count approx. 15 spot deals concluded from the Middle East in August, but we do expect to see a handful more during 20-30 August before we can close the month off. Meanwhile, a more active market in the US has continued to pull further ships away from the East, and together with recent weather delays seen in around F.E.A, this has started to tighten up the vessel positions list for current fixing window.  WEST On the back of improved cargo economics together with a stronger shipping market in the East we have started to see deals into the 80s H/C this week. August fixing seems more or less settled with only a few potential vessels remaining as September deals now well underway. At the moment Panama waiting time is around 1 week which is a small improvement from same time last week, however that’s not to say schedule planning is all that straight forward with uncertainties still needing to be factored in. Typhoons and bad weather in East China could potentially also create some more disruptions in the short term.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco raised up the Aug Propane CP by $40 to $660 and Butane by $35 to $655, which is above some players’ expectations. However, it reflected the tightness in the front market, resulted by cuts from one producer’s Aug liftings against robust demand on evenly split cargos. We have seen active bids for such ratio loading during late Aug to early Sep this week. Following such, Sep Propane CP was traded at $666, and butane at $5 less at the time of writing. We believed with OPEC boosting the oil production, more LPG outputs in forward months  are expected and the tightness situation might be eased.     FAR EAST Other than bids for AG FOBs, inquires for Aug and Sep delivered Propane are less active comparatively. 23kt propane for 2h Aug delivery was bid at Aug FEI plus small premium while no offers seen. Whilst seller is offering similar cargo for 1h Sep arrival at Aug FEI plus $2.5.   Off window spot discussions are muted, but still a couple of deals were concluded, mainly through tenders. One late Aug lifting evenly split cargo ex Australia was sold via tender to one SEA importer at Sep CP plus mid 30s reportedly. And Indian BPCL was reported to secure similar cargo for Sep lifting ex AG as well.  One SChina importer was reported to sell a 11/11 parcel for 1h Sep delivery at Sep CP plus 20s. Apart from spot discussion, one Chinese Major issued a semi tender to secure monthly 46k propane from Oct to Mar delivery into Ningbo.

The week gone by has yielded little of note in the VLCC market, with rates sliding sideways and ships largely trading close to or at negative returns. The only positive news in this summer doldrum is bunker prices going down, courtesy of dropping oil prices. Barring some Chinese “scheduling”, some oil company internal programming and a tad of under the counter fixing the August MEG program has yet to kick off in earnest, but as and when it does tonnage supply is more than sufficient to cover demand. However, looking forward the uptick in volumes should continue through the year now that OPEC+ has come to an agreement on reducing production cuts, hopefully balancing the books in the not too distant future.

With news of an OPEC+ agreement there are grounds for optimism towards the end of the year, however, in the immediate short term we need to see how this impacts general sentiment and expectation levels and whether owners will wait to catch "that wave" or mount some late Northern Summer resistance. We are unlikely to see rates go much lower than they presently are with any variables firmly in the hands of those paid to make commercial decisions. Td20 is showing some sort of floor in the low/mid ws50's which may apply some upward pressure to Wafr/East which will challenge the W60 mark. In the East we have seen multiple Suezmax's fixing Afra parcels, but the list is too long for this to impact rates this side of the weekend. MEG/East trades low ws50's flat and Td23 will continue to bounce between ws25-27.5.

The Nsea/Baltic Aframax market continued to be under downward pressure. However, some owners courageously put up the necessary resistance in order to achieve higher rates on some specific voyages in order to achieve a small surplus for lifting the oil. Unfortunately, with other areas not offering any better alternatives, and August dates already being fixed on bigger sizes, we expect rates to move sideways in the week to come. As for the Med/Bsea market the summer doldrums have continued since last week and at the time of writing TD19 is trading sub-ws90 levels, leaving frustrated owners with a poor return of about USD 3,000 pd. There is some optimism the market may firm a few points in the following days, but as we have seen before this summer we are pushing close to rate levels where Suezmaxes will come into play.

Only a handful of spot LNG shipping fixtures concluded and placed on subjects last week and not enough to move the market, at least on the prompt basis. There were a few enquiries this week for possible charters subject to execution of LNG cargo trades, optimisation and tender awards. However, a relatively quiet week and not as intense as compared to the previous month. Despite July being the month of summer holidays traditionally with reduced LNG demand, fundamentally the cargo market is not weak, with firm support on LNG prices.  The list of available vessels is short with only eight open ships across the world with a few more coming open in August. Hence, the market can change in an instant, not just due to enquiries for charter-ins/outs in the upcoming weeks, but the timing of which these possible charter enquiries would be issued could be a strong catalyst. Assuming a few requirements or vessels are released at the same time (i.e. same day or a few days apart) and with similar vessel delivery terms, this could lead to a perception that the market is tighter/softer than it actually is. Charter rate levels may easily move quickly in these scenarios.   LNG vessel newbuilding prices continue the uptrend with commodity prices and currency exchange rates moving unfavourably for the shipyards. The continued high demand for newbuilding ships across all sectors add further pressure to the raising price for LNG vessel newbuilds.    We wish you a blessed Eid Al-Adha Mubarak!

Spot market for the big ships fascinatingly stable at robust levels although moderate volumes – virtually no change w-o-w as average daily earnings stand at around USD 29k. Continued high demand for iron ore remains the main driver, fleet utilization healthy. From being almost at par, gap between Pacific rounds (gaining USD 6k to come in at USD 32k/day) and the 3 times longer China-Brazil-China rounds (losing USD 1k to come in at USD 25,500/day) has again widened materially, indicating relatively less push on fronthaul. Same could be very temporary as substantial Brazil/China volumes concluded between numerous operators and main miner for q3/q4, coming in addition to what the latter will handle themselves on spot. Period activity modest as fixed-prices levels struggle to match forward expectations/FFA, but with a few index-linked ships concluded.

EAST Indian charterers have been keeping things alive in the Middle East this week, and so far 3 ships have been fixed on subs for 1H Aug loading. There is currently one more cargo in play that has not been fixed yet, and there are also talks of potentially 1-2 additional cargos that has yet been quoted to the market. As a result of all this development, freight rates for the current fixing window is on the rise again, and last done deal is reported in the mid-40s Baltic. We are however yet to see any non-Indian requirements in the market, but with several public holidays happening in Asia this week we do not expect to see much further activity until next week onwards.  WEST With an East market showing signs of recovery and the last reported waiting time in the Panama Canal at 8 days north/10 days south, the West premium is slowly diminishing. Simultaneously, there has been little fixing activity to mention so far this week out of the US and freight ideas seems stable in the mid/high 70s. A few additional Charter relets appearing around last decade August fixing window, however this has yet to put any real pressure on freight and with a strong build of 3.1 million barrel build in US inventories reported on Wednesday netbacks are on the rise which again should support the freight market going forward

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: NWE  The physical market in the region is assessed at a small discount to August CIF ARA. A bid and an offer were seen in the window, with the price difference to wide to bridge. The market is starting to settle back into a normal rhythm after the crude correction. Now that both Brent and WTI are trading above $70pmt propane/naphtha spread in August is at -$36pmt in the region. Keeping LPG demand from petrochemicals healthy. This being said the window offer was form a petchem company. The reasons for the resale is said to be receiving terminal congestion rather than demand reduction. For the time being the market remains tight with little volume set to be imported from the US in August.  MED Tightness prevails in the region. It seems like the buyers have outweighed sellers for the whole year so far. Mixed butane in the West Med is tight and at 96.6% Naphtha putting it at a premium to North West European coasters.  AMERICAS The nearly universal reaction to the news of this week’s EIA report, which showed a weekly build of 3.1mmbbls, was one of surprise.  Most had anticipated a more modest build of 1.6-1.8mmbbls.  But the Gulf Coast showed a build of 2.2mmbbls, putting the total US propane inventory level at 62.7mmbbls as of 16 July.  This compares to the 82.4mmbbls reported last year, and the 75mmbbls seen the year prior to that – and leaves current stock levels at 76% and 79% of the last two years, respectively.  The MB propane market did not immediately react to the EIA data with much enthusiasm in either direction.  Pre-EIA prices were flat at 106.00 cts/gal, and only a modest decline to 105.75cts/gal was noted in the hours after the data was released.  By Thursday morning, though, crude upticks had positively influenced the market and the prices were again above 107.00 cts/gal.  Otherwise, the buyback scheme embarked upon by Enterprise continues.  It is believed that Enterprise has bought back 5 (or maybe 6) cargoes in Aug and remain a buyer for Sep, as well.  Whether or not those same cargoes are then re-sold will then (somewhat) dictate the EIA’s inventory build rate, which will then have an impact on the pricing structure.  Terminal fee ideas from the buy-side are in the 4.50-5.00 cts/gal range, while resale market expectations are in the 5.00-5.50cts/gal range.  The terminal owners themselves, still under pressure from the E/P spread issues, have priced themselves at higher levels.

In the tanker space we have witnessed some interesting transactions just before the holiday season kicks in and we see a continued lift in values on the older and bigger tankers. Olympic managed to squeeze out an extra bonus when they sold their M/T Olympic Legend (2003, Samsung, 309k dwt) at Usd 31.5 mill. No attenuating circumstances such as BWTS or scrubber that could have condoned this higher price even more so considering that she is due for docking later this year. It’s a good Usd 2.5 mill up from Maran’s sale of similarly aged VLCC only a couple of weeks back. A continued interest for modern tankers is proven yet again by JP Morgan’s move who have confirmed this week the purchase of 2 x 114k dwt LR2 resales from CMB. Although the vessels were originally caught up in the Hanjin Subic liquidation at building stage, they were subsequently completed in South Korea and have now achieved Usd 55 mill each. A relative strong price given the original yard and history of construction but one that underlines the current newbuilding markets with yards uninterested to go meet the tanker demand having taken on a flurry of more competitive container orders on their orderbooks.  Perhaps the first week within this past month that most dry players have had the time to digest more recent activity with only a handful of sales to report. As previously reported the Cape market saw a number of units being placed for sale over the past weeks which are now changing hands. Namely the scrubber and BWTS-fitted “BULK DENMARK” (2010, Koyo, 181k dwt) which was picked up by Thenamaris at Usd 31m. JP Morgan also invited offers on their 2012 HHI built Capesize “TRUE ENDURANCE” earlier this week after having up to 10 parties registering their interest.

After a couple of relatively quiet weeks in the spot market, we are seeing more requirements for August and September laycans both East and West. Nevertheless, fixing levels have continued their slight soft trend as sublet tonnage competes for these cargoes in an effort to optimise their portfolios. Cargo market remains volatile at firm levels with European and Asian markets competing for the cargoes and destination changes coupled with some production issues out of the US may encourage more sublet opportunities on the short term. For the ones keeping an eye for term tonnage, despite the slow down in activity this week, freight levels remain robust as Independent Owners with remaining availability are weighing different opportunities. Important to note again that tonnage options are slimming as most tonnage has shifted hands and been incorporated into portfolios, which will play a key factor on how the market develops in the months to come. In the Newbuilding markets, prices keep firming for all types of tonnage, including LNG ships. For new orders, Capital Gas has exercised another option and added one more vessel to their latest pair of speculative orders a couple of weeks ago. Vessel is expected for delivery late 2023.

It would seem the “summer market” has hit both hemispheres the last week, both on physical and FFA. The slight flow of fresh requirements in the North Atlantic is also seeing competition from larger vessels cutting size, hence the positive effect of the fresh requirements seem to be minimal. In general it would appear that there is simply less demand in both the Atlantic and Pacific basins at the moment. As a consequence of this, and also the dive in FFA values, the period market has also put the brakes on, with very few vsls reported fixed for period.

Rates for the big ships not quite living up to expectations, although at very healthy levels and fair volumes. Average daily earnings pretty much unchanged w-o-w, standing at usd 29k for standard 180000 dwt units. Iron ore remains main driver. Volume shift from Australia to Brazil, as the china-brazil-china round voyage route is improving to almost close the gap and par with pacific rounds at around usd 26k/day – providing hope and promise for the weeks to come. General outlook bright, both due waust/china volumes expected to pick up after a slow period, but even more so as major miners very busy picking ships for the tonne/mile-crucial Brazil/Far East trade. Commodity prices indicate further strong demand.  Period activity moderate, with recent fixtures limited to modern standard units concluded on index-basis.

Supra slightly sliding this week. Limited fresh orders not contributing to the rates, although Atlantic still looked more balanced than Asia, where rates were more under pressure.  Supra from Cont via Ust Luga to USG was fixed at 32000 USD . Clinker run on Supramax deliver at Gibraltar for trip via South Spain to West Africa covered at usd 39000 . Med region still balanced mostly due to a seasonal support with grains from Black Sea. Fhauls from Black Sea to Far East was discussed tick over 50 000 USD. Less exciting number from the East where Supra open Japan via Australia back to Singapore-Japan range was concluded at 28000 USD. Vsl open Chittagong to China heared to fix 38-39000 usd region. Ultra with nickel ore via Pihilippines to China performed at 31000 USD. From WCI to China it was fixed at 40000 USD . Usual steel runs from China to USG payed usd 27000 USD.

The market continues its pitiably mundane run with no obvious signs of abating, at least not in the ultra short term. The East market is simply devoid of adequate cargo enquiry which means that a gushing flow of ballasters continue to cap and/or dilute rates in both the Atlantic and Mediterranean basins. With some Asian countries reexporting excess crude inventories, there are serious questions posed about when pre-pandemic demand will return to a region that is in almost full lockdown. Td20 is flirting with the ws50 mark but limited upside whilst Wafr/East is pinned down in the low/mid ws50's. As we advised last week, Td23 was looking "comparatively» overvalued and now trades mid ws20's with possible further downside.

Another week and more of the same. The MEG cargo count creeping up to the 110 level for the month of July, however, we are now heading into the twilight zone prior to the major August stem release (likely late this week, early next). Therefore, limited activity expected. At present, just an Indian cargo and a Vietnamese system cargo for early August dates and rates flattering to deceive, moving nowhere at the speed of light in the MEG. The tried and trusted tactic of underground fixing continues in charterers favor.  However, a little more movement in the Atlantic, with the slightest of upticks (a point in Wafr, albeit a Ghana load) and ws35 on an ex Brazil cargo is promising. With bunker prices creeping up (to USD 550 in Spore), there is little downside to the market, but that’s mainly because there is nowhere lower to go.

text: MEG Despite the oil price slumped, Aug C3 CP was traded stably at $652, and C4 was traded at $10 less. Aug/Sep CP was traded at $4 backwardation. Market players are waiting for Saudi’s acceptance on Aug liftings, before taking further move. Qatar Petroleum was reported to sell their 12/13th Aug lifting full propane cargo.   FAR EAST A flurry of bids for 2h Aug delivered propane are shown in window this week. One 23kt propane parcel for 1h Sep delivery was concluded at Aug FEI plus $2. Off window one 23kt propane for 2h Aug was traded at Aug FEI plus $3 reportedly, and several full cargo propane for Aug delivery were changing hands at Aug FEI minus 3-4$ for 1h delivery period, and minus around $1 for 2h period. comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: NWE The physical market is assessed at August CIF ARA + $8pmt and the CIF ARA Large butane quotes were at 95% balance July Naphtha. Both strong physical discussions due to the fact that no August arrival cargoes have been heard heading to North West Europe from the US so far. With crude oil coming off and CIF ARA tracking Brent faster than Mt Belvieu is tracking WTI this is unlikely to change in the near future as the arb narrows. August Pro/Nap spread at -$37pmt will keep petchem demand up and they will have to source the product from somewhere, which should in turn widen the arb.  MED Butane market in the region has been strong these past days. Lack of supply from the US as well as demand enquiries is fueling strength. Tightness has been the theme of the summer in the region with values doing just enough to keep supply coming but not yet breaking out.  AMERICAS The domestic US propane market received this week’s EIA inventory report with a lackluster response, as the 1.6mmbbl week-over-week build was generally in line with expectations.  As of 09 July domestic US propane stock levels were listed at 59.60mmbbls, or 74% of the levels recorded at the same time last year, 80.30mmbbls. The pricing structure did very little to react afterwards and remained at about the 1.10/gal range, but overnight trading in Europe and Asia saw values in those markets decline, and with the US propane-to-WTI percentage at 64%, expectations are for MB prices to soften, particularly since WTI is now in retreat.  Terminal fees are tiered, at this point, with a recent resale having occurred at a reported 4.625/gal for mid-Aug.  Asking levels are now in the 5cts/gal range.  The terminals themselves, however, remain at 6cts/gal (or above) as the Ethane/Propane pricing differential continues to dissuade the production of Low-Ethane propane, the export-grade product derived from the American spec, HD5, which has a higher ethane content.

EAST VLGC fixing East of Suez has picked up its pace this week with more cargoes quoted out of MEG and Australia. Still with a hefty premium in the West a good amount of ships is sailing towards this direction or planning to do so - helping the supply of available tonnage to decrease. On the back of both more activity and vessels disappearing out of the region we expect the bottom has been reached for now in the East.   WEST Activity wise so far this week US has been lagging a bit behind the East – with freight now hovering in the high 70s pmt Houston/Chiba, continued difficult arb economics and delays both North and South bound in the Panama Canal some Charterers are sitting on the fence to see the direction of the market before making their next moves.

This week comes to a close with yet another flurry of transactions in the Dry cargo markets with up to twenty sales to report. Weekly benchmarks barely have time to set before being broken by ever increasing values making any potential purchase a constant moving target for buyers eager to capture the returns offered by fruitful freight markets. The Supramax and Ultramax segments have captured the vast majority of transactions with twelve vessels changing hands this week resulting in substantial gains on asset values. Notably we have seen 2017 built SDARI 64s achieving Usd 25m while the "BULK PATAGONIA" (2012, Kawasaki, 58k dwt) was sold at a firm Usd 20.5m. Elsewhere the Greek controlled "SERENE SUSANNAH" (2010, STX Dalian, 58k dwt) was sold at Usd 15m. Worth noting in this context that the same owners sold the exact sistership "SERENE LYDIA" at Usd 8.5m in February this year. These renewed values are already on the brink of becoming a short lived history with buyers putting forward levels above last done in a bid to secure tonnage in an increasingly competitive environment.   After a spike of niche VL activity last week the tanker market has seen close to zero transactions this week; however with skyrocketing dry values we are witnessing a shift of enquiry into the tanker segments with several buyers preferring to chase tonnage in illiquid tanker market that have seen values flatten over the past weeks. Notable activity in the product sector with whispers of a number of mid 2000 built MRs in the process of being sold.

A negative week on both physical and FFA is behind us. Whereas the paper has turned up again, the physical market is still lagging. The Atlantic basin has a relatively balanced order/tonnage book now whereas we see lack of fresh inquiries in pacific and sign of increasing tonnage list there. As the rates on FFAs go back up we see owners trying to fix period out, but charterers are cautious and seek further confirmation that market has definitely turned

Last week the market dropped as cargo activity slowed down dramatically. However after a quiet Monday, the cargo list started to grow and at the end of the day sentiment turned positive. At the time of writing this report optimism is back and cargo owners are paying up on freight.

A touch more bearish outlook this week across almost all routes. Only Med showing stronger numbers with numerous of fresh orders mostly due to a seasonal support with grains from Black Sea. . Trip from Med to W Africa with clinker 40k. Fhauls from B Sea been covered at over 50000 usd. USG to Med 33k. ECSA quiet with little fresh orders.

Multi-month activity dominates the focus of most discussions which continue to successful conclude despite the lacklustre prompt market.  Yet it should be noted that freight levels remain bullish compared to historical levels so it is not surprising that a temporary correction to the downside is likely as available tonnage looks for utilisation through July and early August. Beyond is less certain, yet most views agree with a contango into September. However, views do differ on how deep winter will eventually be. Regardless of individual views most are in agreement that the lack of independent tonnage continues to be an overwhelming factor and weighs heavily on decision making. The cargo market has been volatile this week and may encourage a reorganisation of portfolios and a flurry of activity as cargo destinations are altered, something that would be welcomed by those with prompt availability. The number of desponent owners with availability on the prompt continues to increase in the east yet west remains sparse, should intra-Atlantic flow increase then this should lead a balancing of the available tonnage globally. In the new build market Owners continue to order to lock in newbuilds before prices escalate further yet it does impact the number of speculative orders available for charter from 2024.

As expected in the Nsea and Baltic market we had a downward correction as rates hit bottom level with earnings just about giving positive returns. Going forward we expect the market to continue hovering around bottom levels as the tonnage list is long and quite a few ships needs to be absorbed before we will see an uptick in rates again.  Much of the same can be said about the Med/Bsea market. There is some optimism rate levels will pick up a few point in the next couple of days since 3rd decade fixing window ex Bsea looks decent and the tonnage list has tightened somewhat, however we are very close to Suezmaxes coming into play at these levels.

EAST The few requirements that we have seen in market lately have all been from Indian Charterers, but otherwise there is not much to write home about. The current fixing window is still mainly focused around end of July in the Middle East, but we do expect focus to shift towards August after more acceptances start to come out from next week. In the meantime we are still left with a healthy amount of open tonnage, both from the traders and main Owners, and sentiment on freight continue to be under pressure in the East.  WEST Compared to the previous couple of weeks, this week have been reasonably active so far. A couple of end July cargoes have been fixed at relatively low numbers, almost clearing out the July positions, leaving only a couple of candidates left. Be it end July or 1st half August, the positions list is mainly controlled by the major VLGC owners in the market, so the August cargoes fixed this week, has been concluded at a premium of 3-4 dollar compared to the end July fixtures. And this trend is expected for the next few deals in the date range. In terms of returns, the market for the standard transpacific route have come down some 10k per day compared to last week, and ships are now trading around USD 20-22,000 per day as per time of writing. However, as indicated above, this will probably come up again in the short term.

text: NWE The first propane offer for a month was seen in the TOT window Wednesday, amid continued offers. The physical premium is $6.5pmt to July CIF ARA and the lone offer has not dampened buying interest in this tight market. Butane market in the region remains stroing at 95.5% July Naphtha. Though the arb from the US has improved significantly competition from Asia is ever present and spot fixtures to Europe are yet to be heard. The all time high outright values of LPG in Europe prompted a cargo to be sold from Stenungsund storage this week, an anomaly for the time of year. Another factor would have been the tight margins of producing Ethylene and propylene making re-exporting the cargo preferable.   MED Crude coming off has prompted an opportunistic rise in butane demand. The market in the region is bullish though not as strong as North West Europe.  AMERICAS Last week’s EIA report spawned a propane pricing surge which continued unabated through the midpoint of this week when profit-taking is reported to have allowed market values to relax.  Where a high point of $1.15/gal was reached, values just prior to this week’s EIA data release are pegged at 1.06/gal.  As might be anticipated, many have taken cover on the sidelines, but a few transactions were noted. However, the pricing differential between ethane and propane seems to be as much of a factor in the limited activity levels as anything else.  The terminals themselves can offer spot product and are clustered around asking levels of about 6ct as the cost of extracting the ethane from the propane (in order to convert HD5 propane to HD2 (or LEP) has become prohibitive. Meanwhile Enterprise, continues with its ‘buyback’ program and remains a buyer of any-date, any-ratio cargo from its terminal.  Thus far a generous handful of parcels are believed to have been sold back to Enterprise in August, and talk is now heard as to September buybacks.  Current economics favor the Eastbound trade, though in each case margins are at or below 4cts/gal, thus bringing notional terminal fees to around the 3.00 – 4.00 ct/gal range, though in one case a buyer reportedly panicked when the market spiked earlier this week and paid a significant premium.  The EIA data release today – which was delayed due to U.S. Independence Day holiday – revealed a surprisingly low 500,000 barrel build, which was immediately met with jeers and mockery, as well as the early prediction that next week will see a significantly larger build.

Clouds of uncertainty prevail as OPEC struggle to finalise any agreement. Oil prices remain high and so do the resultant bunker prices, but sentiment and the market staying the same. Savvy chartering, fixing deals off market has robbed the Owners of the ability to choose where to employ their ships. Rates remain in the low ws30’s AG/China and those ‘handicapped’ ships, be it age or ex dd have had to show numbers in the ws20’s to secure employment. In Wafr, despite signs of a stand from Owners, Charterers were able to secure ws33.5 to China. Therefore, Owners returns can only be positive on a scrubber fitted ship, but even then well below operating costs. Like a mirage in the desert, the improvement in the market seems to keep moving away from Owners. A positive OPEC decision however, and the mirage may become reality.

In what has otherwise been a very dull week there are some key indicators that reveal how Charterers are reading this market. With global rate-graphs showing a relatively flatline, save for some  small movements, Charterers are now reaching forward in order to nail down todays rates, which they perceive to be a safe bet . A case in point is a Wafr/Europe cargo that is presently working over three weeks ahead of the laycan, whereas you would normally work that route 12-16 days out this time of year. Whilst this probably heralds some sort of bottom, we aren't going to see any turnaround in rates in the short term as lists in both hemispheres are over-tonnaged with meagre pickings on the cargo side. Wafr/East trades W54 with Meg/China  struggling in the low W50's. Td23 could show further slippage into mid 20's.

As expected in the Nsea and Baltic market we had a downward correction as rates hit bottom level with earnings just about giving positive returns. Going forward we expect the market to continue hovering around bottom levels as the tonnage list is long and quite a few ships needs to be absorbed before we will see an uptick in rates again.  Much of the same can be said about the Med/Bsea market. There is some optimism rate levels will pick up a few point in the next couple of days since 3rd decade fixing window ex Bsea looks decent and the tonnage list has tightened somewhat, however we are very close to Suezmaxes coming into play at these levels.
