However, we have seen a new benchmark on modern VLCCs in a deal between two listed entities. Frontline added two more VLs with the purchase of M/T Nissos Antiparos and M/T Nissos Santorini from Okeanis Eco Tankers – both vessels are 318k dwt, built at Hyundai and with scrubbers installed. The price of USD 90 m shows a clear upturn and that there is willingness for the right ships of good specs. An obvious comparison and indicator is Hunter Group’s sale of M/T Hunter Atla (blt 2019 at DSME) back in February at USD 84.5 m.  In the Dry space, we have a new benchmark of around 10 year old Chinese Capesize with the sale of “SPRINGBANK” (2010, New Times, 177k dwt) at USD 26.5 m. Except for few auction sales recently, the most comparable one is the “PACIFIC CANOPUS” (2012, Dalian, 180k dwt), sold for USD 21 m end March. Taking the age difference into consideration, we would estimate an increase of about 50% in value the past 3 months for this vintage. The lack of modern Japanese units available along with the steep development in pricing on these units have increased the focus on Chinese built tonnage. Charter hires paid are not justifying sufficient premium for the prices asked for Japanese built tonnage lately. Same is illustrated with the sale of “ELINDA MARE” (2010, New Century, 80k dwt) at USD 18.5 m. Just a month ago, sister vessel “XIN FENG” was sold for USD 16.5 m. We expect new benchmark in the Supramax sector with the “BULK COSTA RICA” (2010, NACKS, 58k dwt) inviting offers today. Reportedly over 10 buyers have purchased the report and the expected sales price is in the very high teens.

Overall slightly upwards market development. Apart from USG, with limited fresh order, all other areas traded at strong levels ,especially Med and ECSA.  Ultra from Santos to China was covered at 29000 usd + 1.35 mil bb. Santos to Algeria with Sugar 40000 usd. Supra Black Sea to Far East  at 46000 usd.   Supra from Wafr to Cont via ECSA covered around 31500 usd. Confident that Atlantic market will have further seasonal support from Black Sea and USG grains the next months. From Pacific basin also positive sentiment appeared within all routes. Supra from Mumbai to SE Asia fixed around 39000 usd. Bhaul to Cont on Supra was covered at 30000 usd. On period front Ultra from Atl was covered at 30k. Supra 1 year period were fixed around 27000 for one year.

The market continues to see action in the multi-month-plus timeframe, and this is making up for a lack of activity in the spot market. The latest term discussions have piqued the interest of several owners and charterers, but we do see a growing reluctance from both sides to work terms that are too far away from their initial expectations. All this activity does mean the balance of availability this winter will be held by sublets rather than independent owners, and those curious to see how the peak season could play out may have been granted a glimpse in the past week: a recent spot requirement in Asia saw a number of sublets being offered and these clearly weighed on the levels achievable. Will this be the pattern for the rest of the year? Perhaps the opposite; with stronger cargo economics and longer voyages in winter, we may well see the same volatility but in entirely the opposite direction. There have been no new LNG orders to report this week as we end first half 2021. However, yard prices are firming

The Nsea and Baltic market didn’t manage to maintain the momentum from the previous week and inevitably the market experienced a downward correction. Charterers have the upper hand and Owners are bravely trying to repeat last done. However, moving into next week we expect rates to remain under downward pressure as the tonnage list is building up once again.  The excitement from last week was short lived also in the Med/Bsea market as we saw a downwards correction at the beginning of this week with rates coming back down 20 odd points on worldscale. Going forwards the Bsea program in particular looks lighter than what we have seen in previous months while the tonnage list is getting longer, and we do not expect a noteworthy firming of rates in the short run.

The week gone by has been like watching paint dry in the VLCC segment, with limited "above board" activity and rates under pressure. At current rate levels even ships fitted with scrubbers are finding it difficult to eke out positive returns, and for those dependent on compliant fuels returns are well into negative figures. The Atlantic volumes, previously offering some reprieve, remains well below average for for the year. And with that we are approaching a way point where owners have to decide whether to trade or not. Consensus among analysts suggest that OPEC+ will increase production with 500k bpd for August at their upcoming meeting tomorrow, which could serve to kickstart a change in fortunes. Until then batten down the hatches.

Towards end of last week there were some stronger fixtures for August dates in line with FFA values. This as well as firmer rates for smaller segments suggested  spot rates would improve but rather the opposite happened. West Australia rounds is presently around usd 12 pmt and Brazil around 26 level. Even though a correction of some degree now looks likely, we remain optimistic on market prospects for the coming months.

There's a familiar feel to the market this week, and it's not a good one.  After yet another another false dawn, rates remain in the doldrums. There was expectation and hope last week that crossover between Suezmax and Aframax would add a little stardust to a market starved of good news stories. This  unfortunately  failed to carry over into the wider market and the "butterfly effect" died before it had time to flap. But the stark issues facing this market aren't going away anytime soon. If demand really is returning to the oil sector in Asia, then most of it has skipped the Suezmax sector. Wafr/East east has just traded W57.5 on an options cargo but may settle at w55 on a straight run. Meg/East will price mid W50's whilst Td23 has been living in its own bubble recently but that might be set to pop to test high W20's.

The index has been lagging since end last week – however mid-week it seems to have caught up. With congestion in European ports and a scarse tonnage list, charterers has had to pay up in order to cover their requirements.  We now see low/mid 40k being fixed for P1A while the long Fhauls are being fixed in region of mid 50k. Shorter Baltic/India runs has even seen a 7 in front. In the eastern hemisphere we see Pac rounds yielding low 30k. Period market is still active backed by paper values.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco raised Jul C3 CP by $90 to $620 and C4 CP by $95 to $620, more or less in line with market expectations. Aug CP surged up on Thursday to $655, alongside the crude rise, and reflecting the overall strength. Aug C3/C4 is traded at parity and Aug/Sep CP backwardation was once narrowed down to $1 but widened to $4 at the time of writing, mirroring the front strength.  FAR EAST Foreseeing reduce on US exports incurred by closed Arb to EAST and potential cancellations, a handful of buyers are bidding actively in window this week. Earlier 23k propane for 1h Aug delivery was traded at Aug FEI plus $3. And there are still a flurry of bids for such parcel at similar level while seller hefted cash premium of their offer to plus $6. Similar cargo for 2h Aug delivery was discussed slightly cheaper or flattish level. Petchem margins have been squeezed against the soaring feedstock cost, whereas the rise of end products price are refrained due to new releasing capacities. We might expect some petchem plants lower down rates or turn into maintenance if needed. Other than this, quite a handful of tenders are floating in the market. One EChina cracker plant issued tender to buy two lots of 23k propane parcel for mid and late Aug delivery respectively into Ningbo. One Vietnam Petchem player tendered to procure one full cargo propane for late Aug to early Sep arrival for their PDH feedstock. Indonesia Pertamina issued buy tender for one evenly split ratio cargo, either on FOB for mid Aug loading ex AG or CFR for late Aug delivery.

EAST CP was announced earlier this week but we are yet to see any increase in activity on the back of it. Time of writing we have seen approx. 11-12 spot deals concluded in the East for July, so we anticipate that there is at least a handful of uncovered cargos left before we close the month off. But as options on shipping still looks pretty healthy nobody seems to be in a rush to move. One Indian major booked a relet in the high usd 40s Baltic earlier, but sentiment is expected to weaken for next deal(s) provided non India voyage.  WEST In the Western VLGC market, the slowdown in the rate increase we observed and reported last week has kept on this week and seemingly more-or-less come to an end for now. This is related to a market in which only can be described as next to inactive, whereas most negotiations, with the exception of a couple, has so far failed to materialize into any clean deals. A less than favourable trading environment on the product market combined with a growing positions list, at least for the first half of August, indicates the direction of the market may be sideways to downward. At the rates most recently concluded, VLGCs in the Western hemisphere is trading at around 30k per day for the transpacific freight route.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: NWE  The market remains tight with strong petrochemical cracking demand dominating buying. July trading has been picking up though not many cargoes are being traded in the window as they are being snapped up before making it to the market. Butane is at 92.5% of July Naphtha, very strong for the time of year particularly as naphtha and crude are strong. Mt Belvieu strength is keeping the trans Atlantic arb firmly closed for the time being. Many traders expect this to change due to the continued strong petchem demand.   MED Sonatrach posted it’s July prices at $595pmt & $605pmt for C3 & C4 respectively, surprisingly strong, but then so was CP. This was a bit of a shock in the region, though it did not dampen trade discussions as the market remains tight. With crude rising today and butane trading at 90% of Naphtha the high SH postings will be taken in the market’s stride.  AMERICAS Non-TET market values for propane have risen from 92cts/gal at the beginning of June to 114 cts/gal as of this writing – a 24% increase.  But the last 5 trading days have seen the sharpest gains, having moved up by over a dime during that time. This is because of inventory-related fears in the U.S. market, which were compounded by this week’s EIA report that revealed a one-week build of just 1.239mmbbls and brought the total overall US propane stock level to 57.479mmbbls as of 25 June.  This compares to the Year Ago level of 74.599mmbbls. The ongoing concern – both from domestic and international market participants - is that propane inventories will be insufficient to simultaneously accommodate domestic demand (including potential crop-drying requirements), petrochemical feedstock demand, and export demand.  Indeed, the Days of Supply were recorded at 66.5 on 25 June, where at the same time last year there were 80 Days of Supply in stocks.  Meanwhile, cargo cancellations for August are being talked with additional vigor, and as of today we have seen at least 4. However please keep in mind we are not quite sure how to calculate the Enterprise buybacks and will they be traded on or simply put back into the inventory.  Export cargo terminal fees, meanwhile, have crept up slowly and quietly, having now loosely congregated at around the 4.50 - 5.0cts/gal range for the US Gulf.

As expected and reflected throughout our previous reports, this week has seen an increased momentum in the capesize sector. With most fundamentals pointing towards a sustained period of increased rates the cape market is most definitely catching up in terms of SnP activity. We understand that 4 vessels have changed hands this week, partly driven by sellers looking to capture the upside on units purchased earlier in the cycle. An asset play made quite apparent by the ongoing negotiation taking place on the "CAPE LEGACY" ( 2011, Daehan, 180K dwt) purchased at USD 32.5 m in 2015 and now understood to be aiming  for numbers in xs of USD 30 m. Understand the sale is yet to be finalised however illustrates particularly well the current drive witnessed in the market. Elsewhere, Cobelfret have sold their 2011 built HHIC "LOWLANDS TENACITY" at USD 29.5 m which suggests that the abovementioned targets should be achievable in the near future.   Notable activity in the Tanker space lies on the overage front with a rise in steel prices driving the value on vintage front. Last week's reported sale of the “JUPITER" ( 2000, Daewoo, 300K dwt) is now confirmed at USD 27 m marking a substantial appreciation in value. The measure of this increase becomes particularly apparent considering that Mercuria bought the vessel in January this year for USD 19.5 m. Worth noting however, that post purchase Mercuria retrofitted the vessel for FSO activities applying a positive pressure on pricing. Nevertheless, we expect these increased scrap rates to drive the second hand value of these vintage units upwards and drive potential sellers out of the woods.

A little more was expected of this week, as the July MEG stems hit the shelves. However, under the radar and drip-feed tactics continue. OPEC+ remain in discussion for further easing on oil output cuts, as prices rise on the expectation of continued demand recovery. These price increases of course having a detrimental effect on VLCC owners bottom lines, as bunkers soared to close to the USD 540/mt level in Singapore. A grim reality is that some owners on ships lacking scrubbers can only make sense of voyages if they already have cheaper bunkers on board.  The result is perhaps a glimmer of improvement when we look at worldscale rates, as MEG/East improves a point to ws32.5, Wafr/East at the ws34 level, but the TCE’s on a particular voyage likely lower, as owners battle to keep voyage calculations in the black.

Nsea/Baltic Aframax rates increased significantly after several weeks of remaining at close to zero return levels. With some vessels floating with certain grades onboard coupled with more ships leaving the area in laden condition created a tighter position list in the current fixing window. This mixed with more cargoes that usual being quoted created a perfect momentum for the owners to capitalize on. Moving into July dates, we expect the market to stabilize around current levels, but with some downward risk as charterers trying to bring in alternative tonnage with Suezmaxes, shuttles and own relets coming into play now. Also, in the Med/Bsea activity on the cargo side combined with a tight tonnage list has resulted in a 15 ws point pick up in rates this week. However, as in the North, the Suezmaxes are a threat.

An air of moderate optimism pervades the market this week.  Neighboring vessel segments, namely Aframax and VLCCs, could potentially provide some further support. Let's be clear, the fundamentals are sketchy at best, but there has been a distinct change in sentiment and with the added impetus of a firming Mediterranean and North Sea Aframax market, trading  at well over crossover levels, there are indeed positives for owners to latch onto. This will likely hold vessels on the Continent and away from West Africa, somewhat limiting the pool of ships available to charterers. So, on the back of this Td20 could touch ws55 or possibly more this week, whilst in the East Td23 trades low ws30's with potential upside.  MEG/East will challenge high ws50's/low ws60's, but will need further cargoes to support those levels.

Although the maintenance and drydocking season is well underway it doesn’t appear to affect the shipping market much. Spot rates continue to build on the previous weeks’ gains, supported by term discussions and a strong product market due in part to warm weather across Europe and some problems with European pipeline supply. There are available vessels particularly in the east, but it must be noted that most of those offering today are subletters and the tonnage could quickly be withdrawn if the cargo market strengthens further or the East/West arbitrage increases. We’ve seen two orders for multiple newbuildings this week: one from COSCO and PCI firming up three options at Hudong-Zhonghua, and one from Capital Gas at HHI. The Cosco tonnage is due for delivery at the end of 2024 and early 2025, whiles the Capital Gas tonnage is due for delivery by the end of 2023.

EAST Currently there is a premium of about three US dollars in the western hemisphere compared to the East. It seems there are too many relets in the MEG for second half July dates, and thus the West premium will likely sustain in the short term. As the first half of July is more or less done in terms of fixing, we anticipate that focus will shift to the second half of July very soon.  WEST A handful of vessel enquiries have been worked during the end of July ex USG and the uptick in rates seen last week is continuing, albeit at a slower pace. Offers from owners are currently in the mid/high USD 80's per ton H/C basis, and it is likely that we'll see rates hovering around this level for a little while. Vessel availability seems relatively balanced throughout the first decade of August and some owners are withholding vessels from the spot market in order to meet potential COA commitments. Thus, there may be a vessel or two more, or less, than what it looks like in this time period.

After holidays in Greece and a slow Monday, the market kept similar pace to last week. It was limited fresh orders, but overall sentiment was positive still. One might see USG losing some activity. Trips from USG to Skaw were discussed around USD 34,000 on Supra. Usual scrap runs from N Continent to Med were fixed around USD 34,000. Trips from Cont to ECSA were discussed at high USD 20,000. Mediterranean was picking up pace especially with trips to W Afr, where it was said to have done around USD 50,000 levels. Supra from W Afr to Amazon with redel USG was fixed at USD 27,000.   From the East, nickel ore rounds via Philippines redel China covered at USD 31,000. Supra from India with fertz to SE Asia was employed at 44,000. Some Inter MEG business on Ultra 45k dop Damman and 46-57 for trip to India with fertz for similar position. From the period side, a Supra was fixed at 6-8 mos at 29k redel ww and Ultra for 4 mos at USD 47,000.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Jul Swap extended gains this week, following the crude. Jul C3 was traded at $625 while C4 at $627. And Jul/Aug CP was traded at $5 backwardation. 1st round C3 CP ideas ranged from $590 to $625, while C4 recommended at flattish to $10 higher. One mid-Jul loading evenly split cargo ex AG was bid at fixed price $626. And similar cargo for Aug lifting was bid at Aug CP minus $3.   FAR EAST Discussions were muted this week as most players waiting for CP. Cash premium for Jul arrival cargo softened this week. 23k propane for 2h Jul delivery was traded at Jul FEI plus small premium off window. Taiwan CPC did not award their buy tender for one late Jul delivered 11/11 parcel, as offers asking Jul CP plus high 40s reportedly. Indonesia Pertamina issued buy tender to purchase one evenly split cargo for 6 to 10th Aug delivery.

After last week push market calmed down and started to slide. Big part of the explanation is that there is currently some planned maintenance work at West Australia limiting exports and a “sudden” release of vessels from discharge ports in China and India. However, the last couple of days the North Atlantic has been much more active, and rates improved significantly. This has infected the other segments sentiment as well, thus levels seem to increase over the coming days.

The Panamax market started the week on a negative trend, and indices showed red figures in both hemispheres. Mid-week it seems that the bottom is reached and that we will see further strengthening in the days to come. FFA’s are back to levels from mid last week and period takers are back in play. The P1A is yielding 30k while P3A is priced at about the same.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: NWE Window bidding failing to find seller has raised CIF ARA paper value as well as pushed the physical window premium to near CIF ARA July +$10pmt. All tons arriving to the region are accounted for by crackers, leaving 1H July tight. The arb from the US remains unworkable as Mt Belvieu strength continues off the back of strong crude and lower than expected inventory build. So although the netback has increased and CIF ARA July is getting close to 3cpg, it is still more than 1cpg below the FEI netback. For the time being the market is set to remain tight.   MED There has been butane selling interest in the region, though buyers are keeping quiet. Petchem demand in the West Med is strong, VLGCs coming in and no surplus product being resold.  AMERICAS                                                                                                                                                                                Market values for July propane at Mont Belvieu have risen to $102.75/gal (as of this writing), riding the combined wave of support from both the crude oil sector as well as the most recent propane inventory data released by the EIA. In that report the government revealed a 1.046mmbbl increase in primary propane stocks in the U.S., bringing the overall total to 56.240mmbbls, which compares to last year’s total figure of 71.331mmbbls, or a 15.091mmbbl deficit YOY. WTI, meanwhile, was marked at $73.08/bbl for August, having been spurred by U.S. gasoline futures which – in turn – were being pushed by a bullish inventory drawdown. Terminal fees in the U.S. are presently in the 4.50-5.00cts/gal range, with offers seen on the higher end of the range and bids at the lower end, and more than a penny lower on the East Coast. Meanwhile, in an interesting turn of events not seen in well over a decade, Enterprise this week marked itself as a buyer of August Enterprise cargoes (any dates, any ratio) and is now known to have purchased a cargo from a term customer.  Additional purchases of similar variety are anticipated.

Another busy week in the Dry cargo markets which have seen a number of transactions continuing to consolidate the now well established upward trend we have been witnessing across all segments. Supramax and Ultramax  prices have seen another jump with the sale of the “NORD OLIVE” (2014, Oshima, 56k dwt) which was sold by Norden at Usd 22.5m while the Japanese controlled  “WHITE HAWK” (2012, Oshima, 61k dwt) was sold at Usd 20.9m. To put the longevity of the abovementioned trend in perspective, Norden acquired the vessel in December last year at a price of Usd 14m. Chinese designs have also followed suit with Hayfin disposing of the last of their 14 Ultramax units; namely the “GH DAWN RUN” (2018, Yangfan, 64k dwt) which was sold at Usd 23.5m to Greek buyers. Elsewhere the Cape segment also joyed of improved values with the “BULK KYUSHU” (2006, Imabari, 180k dwt) achieving Usd 20.5m whereas only last month the 2004 Koyo built “MINERAL KYOTO” was sold for Usd 15.5m.   Tanker markets remain quiet in terms of concluded transactions however some notable activity this week on the VLCC front with Athenian Tankers selling the “ATHENIAN VICTORY” (2009, HHI, 317k dwt) at Usd 42.5m. This breaks a long period of inactivity for Korean designed units of region ten years of age with most recent comparable sales being those of the Xihe Holding units, which saw a number of Chinese VLs being sold through the liquidation process undertook by the judicial managers.

Supramax Index pushing close to USD 29,000 with everyday gains of a few hundred dollars up. The Atlantic basin is stronger compared to Pacific, which is driven by the strong ECSA and USG soybean and corn export season. The Med and Continent markets with the same upward trend as other Atlantic areas.  Stronger demand in the Persian Gulf and India continues. Overall rates are strong. Pacific has also shown more resistance with prompt tonnage clearing out. Indonesian trips into India were reported at the level of USD 25,000 pd.  South African trips to the Far East were fixed around USD 20,000 pd plus ballast bonus at the USD 1 mill, which is very similar to ECSA fronthaul rates.

LNG shipping rates, especially for term, continue to firm up with week-on-week gains across both basins.  While the Pacific is fairly quiet on the spot market, demand for shipping remains high in the West with several requirements to work on.  Owners with vessel availability are still very focused on either 1-2 spot laden legs or term period very close to 1 year + but nothing in between.  Charterers, on the other hand, prefer to secure vessels up till end Q1 – early Q2 next year.   Hence, it remains challenging to bridge that gap between Charterers preference to cover winter and Owners preference to secure longer period.   Furthermore, the current spot cargo prices have also fueled strong demand for ships which in part explains Owners stance at the moment. So the question remains on everyone’s mind: To fix at the current rates and duration or take “the wait-and-see approach”?   There are no new orders reported this week and newbuilding prices remain stable, with a firm undertone.

Bull mood continues with modest but significant daily gains on very robust fundamentals and positive outlook for commodities.  Average daily earnings up some 60 pct w-o-w, coming in at tick over USD 33k/day. All areas living up to expectations, with the Atlantic being the brightest spot - transatlantic short trades approaching USD 50k/day. Brazil/China iron ore trade picking up speed, with voyage rates for July heading for USD 30 pmt and 100-days China-Brazil-China rounds improving almost 70 pct in value to stand at more than USD 32k/day. West Aussie/China volumes steady, short Pacific rounds still yielding better than general market, at USD 35-36k/day. Little done, but considerable period interest from main players, with focus on index-linked structures.

The Pananax market has experienced big gains in both hemispheres this week. P1A is currently trading at 30k+ while the Pacific rounds are being priced at 31k.  We see the period market continuing to gain, both volume- and rate wise. FFA’s are continuing to give support and we do believe this trend will continue, at least short term.

This week we had more of the same in the Nsea/Baltic markets with rates hovering around bottom levels. However, activity has picked up a bit, but the excess supply of vessels still give charterers the upper hand securing cheap freight. Although, we expect rates to move in a slightly upward direction as owners putting on some pressure as end June’s dates are being worked and July schedule still to come. The situation is rather similar in the Med/Bsea where the supply of vessels is higher than cargo activity demands. This has resulted in rates coming off again since last week as expected, and the market trend is again soft. We expect the market to continue trading sideways going into next week.

It was another quiet week on the surface, as charterers continue their clandestine approach. Mysteries remain as fixtures lacking details are reported on the market. Interestingly, we are up to 115 fixtures in the MEG for June by our count (the best month since December 2020), and when the dust settles, it may even be a little higher. However, at the time of writing we are in the twilight zone between the June and July stems, so a quieter period is expected. There remain positive noises from OPEC for increasing volumes month on month through to September, so this will bring cheer to the owning community. However, a lackluster Atlantic market remains a concern and the issue of higher oil prices and therefore refueling costs ramping up to USD 530 in Singapore, owners bottom lines will remain teetering between red and black.

It's taken weeks for the market to suss it out, but finally some participants have woken up to the fact that there is more fixing going on than meets the eye. This has not been helped of course by certain owners failing to denote if their ship is on subjects or not, which beggars belief in an OTC market, where the primary rate-mover is supply and demand. The Atlantic has a firmer feel with one charterer forced to pay ws60 for a Wafr/Oz run as owners are shunning long-haul runs unless recompensed. Firmer bunkers are also playing their part but there is general resistance. This will help imbue owners with a degree of optimism which will likely see Td20 touch ws50'ish. This has been complimented in the East where Td23 has just traded at ws30, which may nudge rates for MEG/East into the high ws50's.

This week we had more of the same in the Nsea/Baltic markets with rates hovering around bottom levels. However, activity has picked up a bit, but the excess supply of vessels still give charterers the upper hand securing cheap freight. Although, we expect rates to move in a slightly upward direction as owners putting on some pressure as end June’s dates are being worked and July schedule still to come. The situation is rather similar in the Med/Bsea where the supply of vessels is higher than cargo activity demands. This has resulted in rates coming off again since last week as expected, and the market trend is again soft. We expect the market to continue trading sideways going into next week.

It was another quiet week on the surface, as charterers continue their clandestine approach. Mysteries remain as fixtures lacking details are reported on the market. Interestingly, we are up to 115 fixtures in the MEG for June by our count (the best month since December 2020), and when the dust settles, it may even be a little higher. However, at the time of writing we are in the twilight zone between the June and July stems, so a quieter period is expected. There remain positive noises from OPEC for increasing volumes month on month through to September, so this will bring cheer to the owning community. However, a lackluster Atlantic market remains a concern and the issue of higher oil prices and therefore refueling costs ramping up to USD 530 in Singapore, owners bottom lines will remain teetering between red and black.

It's taken weeks for the market to suss it out, but finally some participants have woken up to the fact that there is more fixing going on than meets the eye. This has not been helped of course by certain owners failing to denote if their ship is on subjects or not, which beggars belief in an OTC market, where the primary rate-mover is supply and demand. The Atlantic has a firmer feel with one charterer forced to pay ws60 for a Wafr/Oz run as owners are shunning long-haul runs unless recompensed. Firmer bunkers are also playing their part but there is general resistance. This will help imbue owners with a degree of optimism which will likely see Td20 touch ws50'ish. This has been complimented in the East where Td23 has just traded at ws30, which may nudge rates for MEG/East into the high ws50's.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: NWE Both propane and butane are tight in the region due to an issue restarting Karsto after it’s planned maintenance. CIF ARA propane values have been rising have been rising though the propane / naphtha spread also widened and is at -$75pmt for July, as naphtha was dragged up by a jump in Brent. Butane lies at 86% Naphtha which is very strong for the time of year, especially with strong naphtha values. This strength has not translated to an open arb from the US which has been strong as well. TOT window has been quiet this week, though still assessed at a premium, with many traders waiting for the dust to settle after crudes moves.   MED Butane in the Med has been tracking naphtha, showing strength. Prompt strength remains for 1H July with June trading all but done. Delivered buying interest is being seen both in the East and West Med for July arrival.  AMERICAS A weekly EIA propane stock build of 1.544mmbbls was met with trepidation as the previous few weeks have been riddled with corrected data.  And while there remains the expectation that this week’s data contains yet more of the same, it was perceived as directionally accurate. There remain concerns as to the ability of US stocks to build to sufficient levels, but to move from present totals of 55mmbbls to a desired level of 75mmbbls over the space of the next 16 weeks requires a weekly average build of just 1.25mmbbls, which (from a historical perspective) is entirely achievable.   With just one exception, the mid-Jun to mid-Oct average build rate has increased each year over the past 5 years, moving up from 1.3mmbbls in 2016 to an average weekly build of nearly 1.7mmbbls last year.  Therefore, it is well within reason that US stocks will rise to sufficiently comfortable levels.   The pricing structure, meanwhile, reacted to the EIA data in a bullish manner, moving from ~95cts/gal to over 96cts/gal.  By Thursday morning the market had realized additional gains and was traded at 96.5c/gal. Terminal fees have been waffling in the low/mid single-digits, with East Coast transactions occurring just under 4 cpg , and a recent Gulf Coast deal was reported at the “low 4’s” per gallon.

EAST The focus has mainly been on the Western market this week with a few exceptions. A couple of trader relets were taken out in the AG rep low usd 40s, but since then we saw another Charterer having to pay a premium for a short t/c for Indian trade. The general feeling is that freight market may have reached a bottom, for now, as more ships are expected to be sent back West on the back of improved arb economics. But at the same time we are still seeing less exports from the Middle East, and Aramco are reported to have cut several cargos in July due to production issues. This certainly needs to improve as well going forward, in order for sentiment on freight to change in the East.  WEST The West market has been very busy since last time this report was published. Several fixtures have been concluded close to the USD 80 mark for laycans spread out during the second and third decades of July and yesterday the momentum changed a bit and rates started ticking slightly upwards. The position list for July is not really tight just yet, however, there are considerably less vessels available compared to a week ago. We expect more vessels to get tucked away during the course of this week and market to tighten accordingly.

text: MEG July swap continued to strengthen alongside the rising crude. At the time of writing, July C3 was traded at $595, and C4 was traded at $2 higher, reflecting the tightness on butane for prompt loading. Saudi Aramco was reported to have some volume cuts on their July program due to the facility issues. Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their 19/21st Jul loading full propane cargo at Jul CP minus small discounts. Whereas evenly split cargo for Jul loading was bid at Jul CP plus $8 but yet to see sellers.   FAR EAST Earlier this week, 23k propane parcel for 2h Jul delivery was traded at Jul CP plus $29. Afterwards, a similar parcel for same period delivery was bid at Jul FEI plus $5, which equates to Jul CP plus low-mid 20s only.  Off window, a handful of tenders are floating in the market. One Vietnam petchem player was reported to secure a heavy propane cargo for mid Aug delivery at Aug CP plus low-mid 30s via tender. Taiwan CPC issued buy tender to purchase one 11/11 for late July delivery but few offers received reportedly. Indian BPCL also issued buy tender to procure one evenly split cargo for 15th Jul to 15th Aug delivery. Other petchem players appear quieter this week, as margins are eroding by the rising feedstock costs against weakening end products price.

The Dry cargo markets have most definitely regained the headlines this week with freight rates continuing on their unhindered rally supported by a flurry of snp transactions who have become tribute to the overwhelming positive market consensus that these renewed rates have settled for the foreseeable future. On the Kamsarmax front, JP Morgan invited offers on the 3rd of June on their sisterships “PEAK PEGASUS” & “PEAK LIBERTY” (82k dwt, 2013 / 2015, Tsuneishi Japan). Sellers invited up to 10 outright buyers to bid and both vessels have now been committed enbloc at Usd 23.75m & Usd 26.75m respectively. To put levels in perspective, same owners disposed of the 2013 built sistership “PEAK PROTEUS” in May at a price of Usd 21.5m marking an increase of approximately 10% in less than a month. This positive trend is spreading across all sectors, even more so this week in the Supramax segment where the Japanese controlled “DONAU K” (58k dwt, 2012, Kawasaki) achieved a price of Usd 19.6m marking a substantial jump in values considering that only two weeks ago the same age sister ship “PACIFIC HERO” was sold at Usd 18m. With a buying enquiry showing no signs of slowing down and a number of underbidders left to try and secure alternative units, we expect additional tonnage being placed for sale by sellers looking to capture the ever increasing value offered by these improving markets.  Very little to report on the Tanker front this week with persistent subdued rates holding any potential buyers from going to meet the ever thinning list of potential sale candidates. Most activity being found in the mid 2000 built crude carriers where we continue to witness signs of ongoing activity suggesting further sales in the near future.

The Nsea/Baltic market remained unchanged with rates not encouraging owners to move unless you have a specific reason to perform a voyage close to zero returns. Cargo activity in the area is still restrained and we don’t see an immediate recovery for the market. However, a busier 3rd decade of Urals is approaching which might help owners to regain some confidence. Although rates in the Med/Bsea keep moving more or less sideways, there has been some optimism among owners the last few days as a hand full of cargoes enter the market while the tonnage list is looking tighter than it has been in a while. We do however believe that this is not sufficient enough for owners to put up the necessary resistance, and that the firming trend we see at the moment will turn soft as we move into next week.

With a slow start to the week and no clear direction, the Panamax market has developed into sliding rates in the Pacific and firming rates in the Atlantic. Especially the North Atlantic is seeing more demand for minerals and a tight list of available tonnage. Good demand out of North America for fronthauls is also keeping pressure to the market. In the Pacific however the exact opposite is happening. Tonnage list is growing and the wide gap between bid/offer is closing in favor of chrts. Period demand is back into play and we value a good spec Kmax at low 24k for 1-year basis PRC delivery.

The week gone by in the VLCC market will soon be forgotten. Over-supply of tonnage and sluggish demand continues to weigh on sentiment. Earnings have slipped from bad to worse with sliding rates and increased bunker prices, as owners now virtually pay for the privilege of carrying crude from A to B. Current rate level seems to have flatlined at give or take ws32.5 to- and from basically everywhere, with few if any signs of picking up any time soon.

Towards the end of last week there were some signs that rates were hitting the low for now, after weeks of coming off. This was further seen during this week with fronthaul and even c3 rates improving, as well as Pacific finding support with c5 in the mid 9s. There are currently no signs of another spike just around the corner, but it may as well happen any time.

Thus far, it's been a slow news week with nothing extraordinary to break the current trend. Unfortunately, long lists and low cargo volumes has meant charterers have come up against zero resistance in attaining last done levels, or less, and that is how the balance of the week will play out. A flicker of positivity comes in the form of the current oil price. This suggests demand is increasing which should reduce stockpiles and perhaps allow OPEC+ to free up more supply, but this is all subject to pandemic economics and the ability of countries to successfully roll out a vaccination program. Wafr/East trades low ws50's with MEG/East on modern 15T cranes unlikely to trade above low/mid ws50's. Td23 is ws23-24 max.

text: MEG Due to the unexpected supply disruption from one Middle East producer, July C3 CP soared up to $587 at the time of writing, up by nearby $50. July C3/C4 was traded at flattish, reflecting the shortage on butane supply for front prompt lifting. A couple of traders were actively exploring equal ratio cargos to cover their short, caused by the unexpected delays or cancellations on their term liftings. KPC was reported to award their tender to sell three FOB cargos for Jul to Sep lifting, two of which are heavy propane ratio, and only one evenly split ratio. Qatar Petroluem also issued tender to sell one full propane cargo for 19/21th Jul lifting.   FAR EAST Failing to catch up with strong CP, Jul FEI/CP has narrowed to $18, down by $20 compared to last week. Cash premium discussion has inched up from low single to mid single digit on FEI link for CFR 2h Jul propane parcels. On mid-week, one 23k propane for 2h Jul delivery was traded at Jul CP plus $28 in the window. And similar cargo for such period was bid up to Jul FEI plus $6.5.  Outside window, one SChina petchem importer has purchased half cargo propane parcel for 1h Jul delivery outside their tender. One Vietnam based player issued buy tender to secure a heavy propane cargo for mid Aug delivery.

Activity in the spot market remained fairly muted this week. With firm commodity prices & freight rates, discussions around ship positions, cargo trades and optimisation of both were taking place, but few deals were concluded. However, the Far East thirst for 3Q deliveries are now dragging vessels from the Pacific into the Atlantic for US-sourced cargoes back to Asia. Spot Pacific requirements, offering owners shorter charter durations, would normally warrant a premium in these circumstances, but sublet vessels with pockets of availability have dampened this effect. LNG shipping availability may however tighten as we look ahead. With the current arbitrage opportunities, there is a clear risk for more and longer voyages West to East. Scheduling may then become challenging with potential waiting time in Panama versus taking the long route via Cape.  With yard prices firming across shipping segments, the newbuild market saw 2 interesting orders being concluded. JOVO place an order for a rare mid-sized 79,800cbm vessel at Jiangnan. Over at KSOE (HHI) 4x 200,000cbm LNGC were ordered and these vessels are apparently to be fitted with the new ME-GA two-stroke engines.

text: AMERICAS The EIA posted a weekly propane build of 5.5mmbbl as of the week ending 04 May, bringing overall US stocks from 48.151mmbbls to a current level of 53.650mmbbls.  The market was very surprised, having anticipated a build of not more than about 2mmbbls – on the high side. Prices reacted almost immediately to the unexpected build and declined from the low 95cts/gal level in to the mid 93ct range, though a slow resurgence was noted in the early afternoon hours.  24 hours later the market was bid at 95cts again.  This, however, may have been because buyers stepped in during the moment of pricing weakness as well as the strong crude oil markets.   While there remains quite a lot of skepticism as to the validity of the EIA data, it is generally believed that higher-than-anticipated butane exports, previously canceled cargoes, the reclassification of Gulf Coast propane inventory and healthy production levels are the reasons behind the increase. Terminal fees, having been in the low single digit levels, have this week seen a resurgence and are now seen in the 4cts/gal range.    In South America, continued buying demand from Brasil continues to provide a floor for the FOB markets, with Petrobras buying one to two spot cargos per month.

EAST Yet another uneventful week in the East so far, and talk of production issues at Ras Tanura is certainly not helping the cause. As freight remains long for balance of June and rates continue to be under pressure, it is likely that players will continue to wait until we have more acceptances for July. One trader was marketing a relet at sub Baltic levels earlier, but no takers so far and the Baltic has dropped below USD 50 for the first time since April.  WEST The uncertainty around how resilient the freight market actually is coupled with how much more downward 'theoretical' pressure from the product market freight would sustain, has been the talk of the town for the last week or so. It seems that the build in the US stocks seen yesterday aided the trading environment enough to create some momentum whereby freight would find its feet and freight fixtures could be developed. A handful of cargoes has been fixed during the last week or so, and the hope is that there are more to come.

With the rally we are seeing both in the Dry cargo and container market, there is not much to write home about in the tanker market. The chartering market continues to struggle, with VLCC and Suezmax’s producing negative charter returns. SKS have sold their “SKS SATILLA” (2006, HHI, 158K DWT) for USD 23.25m. The price achieved falls in line with the sale of the one year younger sistership “SKS SPEY” (2007, HHI,158K DWT) which was sold for USD 24m a few weeks ago. Moreover, we understand that the LR2 “CHAMPION PLEASURE” (2008, Namura,105K DWT) has been sold in an off-market transaction to Union Maritime for USD 18.1m. The price represents a small downtick in values when comparing to the one year younger “CHAMPION PROSPERITY” (2009, Sasebo,115K DWT) which was sold end April for USD 19.7m.  Another week with activity on all dry segments except for Capesizes, which seem to be taking a breather with lack of modern candidates being marketed for sale. China Development Bank Leasing steals the headlines acquiring the ex-Hayfin / Celsius fleet of 6 x Ultramaxes and the ex-Clipper controlled 11 vessel fleet of handysizes and Supra/Ultramaxes paying about USD 270 m for the two fleets in total. Noteworthy sales include new benchmarks for 15 year old Japanese Supramaxes setting the price tag at abt USD 13 m with the sale of the Olympic Oshima and Mitsui 2006 built Supramaxes “OLYMPIC PEACE” and “OLYMPIC PRIDE” at USD 25.5 m enbloc. For reference, the previous sale of a 2006 Japanese built Supramax, “CORAL ISLAND” (2006, Oshima, 55k dwt), was end February for USD 10 m. Lastly, as we have written in the recent reports, we are seeing an increase on value of Chinese tonnage with the sale of the Dolphin 57 “OLYMPIC PEGASUS” (2011, COSCO Guangdong, 57K DWT) at USD 14.8 m. Just a month ago, the “SILVIA AMBITION” (2011, Yangfan, 57K DWT) was sold for around USD 12.5 m. Costamare has reportedly purchased the “INTERLINK COMITY” (2010, Huatai, 37K DWT) for USD 12.8 m. The sister vessel, “SREDNA GORA” was sold for USD 11.6 m just few weeks back. We expect this trend to continue with the sharp increase of price of Japanese tonnage.

With a long weekend, real action only began mid-week. USG being in the forefront where earnings still increasing due to tight supply. Trips from USG to Far East were covered around USD 33,000 and to Skaw only tick less, that is around USD 29,000. From Continent to USG, Supras were discussed at USD 23,000. Trip from Gijon via USEC to Japan was fixed around USD 33,000 on Ultramax with scrubber benefit for chrts account. Elsewhere, Supra from West Africa via South Africa was fixed at USD 26,000 with redelivery Baltic. From East, a 58,000 open South China was fixed for a trip from Indonesia to China at USD 23,000. Trips from India to China payed USD 32,000. Vessels open MEG to Bangladesh was covered at USD 37,500. Ultramaxes from WCI to Med USD 32,000. From period front, Ultramax from Red Sea got employed at low 30s for min 4 mos, where 1-year where discussed around 24k for same.

Although a slow start to the week with holidays, the Panamax market has been sort of counter cyclic compared to the other segments. While the bigger Capes and the smaller sized markets has experienced declining rates, the Panamaxes are still seeing higher rates than last done. P1A is currently achieving 21/22k and although we see less demand for fronthauls, it is priced at a healthy mid 30k level.  In the eastern hemisphere rates are slipping, but P3 is still valued at a healthy mid 20k level.

Levels have come heavily down over the last week as volumes for both basins have slowed down. The basket of all routes is down by 20% since last report; Brazil-China iron ore route down 16% and Pacific round voyage down 24%. This due to increased amount of spot vessels chasing cargo.

text: AMERICAS  The 4.1mmbbl build in propane stocks for the week ending 28 May was instantly met with both elation and contempt, and resulted in an almost immediate decline in Mont Belvieu propane values (to 89.75cts/gal for Jun), but also speculation as to whether next week’s data release would include corrected data. On the former point, and after some weeks of disappointing build levels, propane stocks in the U.S. were in rather desperate need of showing signs of improving.    In any case, at 48.2mmbbls as of the 28 May, domestic US propane stocks still pale in comparison to levels of a year ago when 67.3mmbbls were reported, a 19.1mmbbl deficit YOY.  The generally accepted comfort level for pre-winter propane stocks is in the 65-70 mmbls range, which will require an average weekly build over the next 21 weeks of sbout 1 million barrels per week which we believe is very achievable.  Meanwhile, terminal fees have been seen and reported in the 3.5-4.0 cpg range for June, with asking levels in July tentatively within the same range for the Gulf Coast and a penny cheaper for the USEC.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco announce Jun Propane CP at $530, up by $35 and Butane at $525, up by $50. Jul swap rallied up this week, following the crude rise. At the time of writing, Jul C3 CP was traded at $540 and C4 at $532. QP released their July acceptance with no cuts or cancelations reported.   FAR EAST As the Panama congestion situation eased, cash premium for Jul delivery parcels softened compared to earlier this week. 23k propane parcels for 2h Jul delivery was bid at FEI flattish to $1 in the window. Off window a couple of deals were concluded. Two parcels of 23k propane for 1h Jul delivery were traded at Jul FEI plus $3.5-4.  A flurry of cargos was placed into E.China this week via tenders. At least 92k propane for 1h Jul delivery were purchased by 3 different petchem players for feedstock use, with price ranging from Jul FEI plus high single to low teens. Another SChina PDH user also tendered to secure 22/0 delivered in 1st decade July.

EAST Rates have continued to drop in the East as we are yet to see any real activity in June, while still being left with a healthy amount of open tonnage. One trader was reported fixing a ship close to usd 50 Baltic for mid-June load, but it remains to be seen if this level will be repeated for current fixing window (last decade of June). Meanwhile we are starting to see more Indian enquiry in the market, and we also expect there to be uncovered cargos left from other players before we can close the month off. But it is still likely that some of the ships open for June will have to take waiting time and opt for July cargos after we start seeing more acceptances come out for next month.  WEST The market has continued its somewhat slow pace from last week, as the charterers have more-or-less concluded their June lifting program, and both owners and charterers are getting ready for the next fixing window. We have already seen some vague inquiries for July, but so far nothing done. A market call cargo for first decade July loading, has attracted the attention of some owners, and are currently ongoing. There are only less than a handful of ships avail for June loading, and still some uncertainties on available ships for early July, so owners’ ideas have kept rather stable. As such, and with a market somewhat in the doldrums where the arb is allowing for far lower freight rates than the owners are willing to consider, we have as usual under such circumstances seen some proposals and requests for Baltic related deals. Last done at time of writing, is an end June lifting with freight calculated at an average July Baltic average. We have had another week with a discount for the transpacific route compared to the BLPG1 route, whereas the transatlantic route, although not as liquid, is trading at a healthy premium.

It has been another slightly quieter week from LNG shipping perspective, which is somewhat surprising considering that the LNG cargo market continues to thrive as LNG prices done for deals into Europe and into the Far East elevate higher. Most of the ongoing shipping activity is now focused on July deliveries and we have witnessed a modest uptick on rates in the Atlantic basin, since some of the sublets have disappeared from the availability list. However, it has been a different story in the Pacific, as we continue to see further softening on rates, as prompt availability continues to build up and there hasn’t been enough requirements to significantly reduce this. Few of the independent Owners have noticed this as well, and have therefore decided to start ballasting their prompt tonnage towards the more promising Atlantic market. Evidently the spot market continues to stay volatile with its rather unpredictable movements from one week to another, but the big picture seems to be holding strong which is clearly illustrated by the term rates remaining firm. On the newbuilding front, it was a noticeably busier week, since amidst the strengthening yard prices, it was reported that SHI have secured an order for two modern 174,000cbm LNG carriers for an Oceanic shipowner and additionally it was also announced that DSME has signed a contract to build one 174,000cbm LNG carrier for Hyundai LNG Shipping which will go to Repsol under a long-term charter.

The Nsea/Baltic market appeared bottomed out as current levels gave negative returns on some specific routes. Owners bravely put up resistance, but had to give in as charterers managed to push rates even lower on the back of low volumes and a long tonnage list for 2nd decade loadings. Moving forward, a busier 3rd decade for the Urals could give a glimpse of hope for the owners. In the Med/Bsea we have the seen the market trade sideways all week with current levels on benchmark routes being repeated a number of times. TD19 is currently hovering around high ws80-levels, giving owners a return of around USD 3000 pd on TCE. Although owners try to hold back on rates, it seems most of them expect a flat market in the week to come.

Despite huge swathes of vessels disappearing in the East and West over the last couple of weeks, charterers have seemingly been able to pluck vessels off the list with impunity.  Unfortunately, these tighter lists have not, hitherto, been tight enough, and that is wherein the problem lies. Eastern ballasters continue their procession to the West but curiously, West/East volumes have taken a downward turn over the last couple of months and we have noted fewer vessels being recycled onto the East list. This might cause a bottleneck on the tonnage supply front in the next couple of weeks and with that, possibly firmer rates. If owners start to tune into proceedings, then perhaps there could be some positivity. MEG/East trades ws53 whilst Wafr/East  is likely to stay low ws50's this side of the weekend.

Not a week to live long in the memory, made shorter by the holiday Monday in many places. Rates remained pretty steady and credit due to owners who’ve been able to prevent further slides in the face of pretty mediocre enquiry. MEG/East has remained at the ws36 level and with the MEG volume count a little behind schedule (approx. 65 fixtures of an expected 100-110), many expected a bit of a kick up this week, that so far has failed to materialize. Little support from the Atlantic market as West Africa/East deals remain around ws36.5, and the USG cargoes only drip-feeding in. Many charterers keeping cargoes off the open market, keeping a lid on things by working in the shadows.  With bunker prices now ticking up to the USD 520 level for vlsfo in Singapore, owners returns will take a hit, so a little resistance can be expected.

Recent changes in the Chinese import policies (quotas) seems to have an effect and there is a significant drop in purchase enquiries with Chinese addresses. If this continues, we could expect an effect on the pricing of the older units, but on the other hand do strong steel prices play an important role also here, with a continued push on the demolition prices. New Shipping are reported to have sold their M/T “NEW DIAMOND” (299k dwt, 2000, Mitsui) to demo/cash buyers GMS for USD 22 m – or $564,50/ton (gross). It’s important to note that M/T ”NEW DIAMOND” and the likes are among the lightest VLCCs built in that period, and whilst these have LDT in the region 38500-39000 tons, the larger (and heavier) Koreans of same age often are in the region of 43000 tons and some pushing towards 48000 tons. To put things in context – we are approaching USD 25 m demolition prices on some VLCCs, and hopefully more will follow Mr. Polemis’ example.  We continue to see Dry bulk asset prices catching up with the chartering market. This week, Enesel Group backed Valhalla, decided to take profit on some Ultramaxes with the sale of 2 x DACKS resales being delivered 2022 for USD 29.2mil each to Genco. This sale is sure to set a new benchmark for resales on both Chinese and Japanese built Ultramaxes. Furthermore on handies, M/V “SIDER SYROS” (38k dwt, 2016, Minaminippon) was sold at firm USD 20.7 m to Orient shipping, which demonstrates the strength of the market and will set another strong benchmark for Japanese built handies.

Still correcting, arguably at high levels. Average daily earnings for the big ships down another 6 pct w-o-w, coming in at just over USD 29k. Transatlantic doldrums and fronthaul imbalance for June being mostly to blame - ballasters presently having a hard time achieving last done or close on the Brazil/China route as demand side pretty much limited to one major miner. Present gap between 100 days China-Brazil-China and 50 days Pacific round is roughly USD 10k in favour of the latter, meaning no flow of "new" ballasters as long as Pacific iron ore and coal trades keep absorbing prompt tonnage. Main players waiting for market to find a floor and again improve, as major commodities much in demand and overall fleet efficiency moderate.

Signs of life emerging in the East as the list for modern, 2x20T cranes vessels have tightened significantly for the first decade with owners pushing for more than last done levels. Hitherto, charterers have been able to fix off-market with zero noise, but now, reduced tonnage availability is likely to smoke a few more cargoes out into the open market, as the perceived bottom has been reached. MEG/East trades WS55 on modern with possible upside and Td23 looks susceptible to adding a little more weight. In the Atlantic, charterers still have the luxury of attaining in and around last done without too much trading. With V's stalling and possibly coming off a tad, support for Td20 is lacking and it's going to need a further reduction of Eastern ballasters to lift rates, should trade WS47.5 with potential 1-2 points upside.

Last week was active with rates ticking in owners’ favour, but since Monday, charterers have been able to apply the brakes; holding off when possible and concluding deals off market. This air of inactivity usually plays on owners’ minds, and as such, without further volume, it is likely we are looking at a softer numbers in the near future. We ticked up to WS37.5 for MEG/East end of last week, but despite the best efforts of owners to hold the line, reports are ships are already firm at last done levels, with charterers aiming a few points lower (although it remains to test). June was expected to post the highest volumes of the year to date, so owners should not lose hope. With Iran coming back on line at some point in the near future, and potential OPEC production increases, Q3 looks a little brighter.

It was a relatively quiet week for the North Sea/Baltic market with rates moving sideways at bottom levels. However, with quite a few vessels having left the area and net tonnage supply decreasing, the tonnage list is looking somewhat tighter for first decade loadings. Moving forward, rates could remain under upward pressure supported by a healthier Urals schedule for June. In the Mediterranean/Black Sea we have seen rate levels pick up a few points this week due to healthy activity on the cargo side combined with a tighter tonnage list. However, at the time of writing Suezmaxes are coming into play, capping the market at current levels. Due to same we do not expect a noteworthy increase in rates in the short run.

Sentiments for the spot market have certainly dropped as the recent spot fixtures were done at lower levels against the recent highs. More vessels are being shown as available to the market, following redeliveries from previous month’s string of fixtures. Players with spare tonnage capacities continue to seek opportunities for sublets in both basins, although these vessels have a limited available period of about one to three months. These sublets constitute of great proportion of the available tonnage list. Looking a little further out to July, and there are signs the current dip may be short-lived. There appear to be more requirements on the horizon especially out the US Gulf, and these may test how tight the market really is, with or without the sublets.    Despite the reduced sentiments in the spot market, the charter rate expectation for term employment, i.e. multi-months over the winter, one year and multi-year charters remain firm and intact, with little indication that rates for such a duration would soften based on the expectations from shipowners with the remaining available vessels for the period.   No orders reported this week, price indication for newbuilding LNG vessels are continuing its gradual upward trend.

This week has been influenced by holidays in most European countries beginning week, and Singapore mid-week. It is not a clear direction but rather a standoff between charterers and owners.  The firm underlying sentiment is still there and P1A is currently yielding around 20k. Grain volumes out of ECSA is certainly picking up with several June stems entering the market. On the other hand we see volumes out of USG evaporating as US grain is currently priced out. In the eastern hemisphere we see index levels come off, much lead by early positions reducing their offers in order to cover before Singapore holidays. Pacific rounds are currently priced in region of 27/28k.

Another positive week for the market with BSI routes rising up. More activity from key areas such as the US Gulf and ECSA pushed rates up. The fixtures reported from the US Gulf showed good gain in rates. TCT from Miss River to Med-Cont being fixed at USD 27,000 pd on Ultramax and TCT to Far East was fixed mv Grande Island Tess 58 at USD 31,000. Trips with clinker from Med to West Africa also showed improvement in rates by gaining USD 2,000-3,000 per day from last done. Scrap from Continent followed the same trend fixing in hi USD 20,000’. Indian Ocean and Asia remain strong with stable flow of cargoes and shortage of tonnage. A 56,000 open west coast India was fixed for a trip from Persian Gulf to Bangladesh around USD 32,000. MV Unity Discovery 60’ dwt open Pakistan rumoured to be fixed for a trip to Chittagong at USD 40,000. Inter-Pacific coal voyages paying around USD 31,000.

text: MEG An unexpected surge this week on Jun swaps. At the time of writing, June C3 CP was traded at $522 and C3/C4 at $5 differentials. Jun/Jul C3 CP entered a slight contango structure at $2-3. First round June CP recommendations ranged from $500 to 515 for propane, but we believe with the rise in paper swap, 2nd round idea will edge up accordingly. KPC awarded another tender of 33/11 cargo for end Jun lifting reportedly at June CP minus high single digit, which was also their 5th spot sales for Jun loading.   FAR EAST Far East Index spiked up with FEI/CP Jun enlarged to $43, from last week’s $27.5. There are concerns over tightness of supply in the front, due to the June cancellations ex US, together with the temporary delays from Panama congestions. One 23k propane for 2h Jun delivery was traded at Jun FEI plus $6.5 on Thursday in window.   India IOC issued buy tender to secure one evenly split cargo for 1h Jul delivery. One EChina Petchem user have secured 23k propane for late Jun delivery at Jun FEI plus low single and subsequently issued another tender to buy 46k propane for 1h Jul delivery for their cracking feedstock.

EAST With the preceding week failing to revive any real momentum this week has so far followed suit with less than a handful of fixtures so far concluded. Thus, freight has followed in a downward direction. Hopes are that with a couple of Indian cargoes together with a few more end June stems, supply/demand will be more or less in equilibrium and as such making sure the drop in freight will close and flat out from here.  WEST As we are approaching the end of May, the number of VLGC liftings in total ex US and Canada is approaching about 90 VLGC equivalents (including some LGCs loaded). June looks set to follow suit. At the time of writing there are only a handful of vessels left for the balance of June and these vessels are largely controlled by only one owner. A few fixed rate bids from potential charterers have been shown for last decade June loading ex USG, however, the tight vessel supply makes it somewhat difficult to strike due to a large difference between bids and offers. Freight for second half June will find its feet again at some point, but the list of open vessels is not getting any longer.

text: NWE  CIF ARA values have been weaker than both the Mt Belvieu and FEI price quotes, leaving the June East/West spread at +$57pmt.  Houston / Flushing freight rates have stayed strong and just a bit below the Mt Belvieu / CIF ARA arb which is now -$47 for June. this not  leave buyers/traders much margin to look at US FOB cargoes and hence the FOB values continue to fall.  North Sea maintenance is progressing on schedule with production in the region is set to ramp up from June 3rd.  MED The butane market in the region continues to look long. May butane is well offered,  though 1H June shorts in the region are yet to be covered. Meanwhile with seasonal demand for propane non existent, it is very difficult to find buyers.  AMERICAS Most of the domestic US market players and observers were calling for a small propane inventory build this week; perhaps something under a million barrels, with most generally clustered around the 650-750,000bbl range. In fact, however, the EIA data revealed a decline of nearly 400,000 bbls from 44.4mmbbls last week to 44.1 mmbbls.  PADD I stocks fell from 3.9 to 3.7mmbbls, PADD II showed an improvement from 11.2 to 11.5mmbbls, while the Gulf Coast fell from 26.3mmbbls to 25.7mmbbls – all during a time when record-level exports are believed occurring. Propane stocks in the US are now squarely at minimum tolerances, with the Days-of-Supply tally running at 18.09 days, where the previous 5-year low (which occurred in 2018) was pegged at 19.83 days.    Prices reacted immediately, moving up within minutes from ~85cts/gal at Mont Belvieu to over 87cts/gal before lunchtime.  Netbacks, meanwhile, which were already suffering to the point of cancellations – seven of which are believed to have occurred for June – may be sent over the tipping point, though no additional cancellations were immediately revealed.  Terminal fees, presently offered at 3cts/gal, reflect the difficult arbs.

Stealing the headlines this week is the transaction announced by Frontline who has confirmed the purchase of six VLCC resales currently under construction at HHI. The vessels were part of an eight ship series originally contracted by Central Shipping with deliveries ranging from Q1 2022 until Q1 2023.  The aggregate purchase price stands at Usd 565.8m setting benchmarks for resale VLCCs at Usd 94.3m per unit. Current market environment seem to be validating the deal for all parties involved with buyers achieving relatively lower levels against current newbuilding offer and sellers booking a significant upside on the original contract price which is reportedly around Usd 90m per ship. Additionally these early contracts are offering prompter deliveries in a newbuilding environment that sees both pricing on the rise and slot availability for conventional tonnage slip into 2024. Elsewhere in the Tanker space we continue to see a sustained second hand activity for units built in mid-2000 across both the product and crude sectors with a steadily increasing buying enquiry suggesting upward pressure on pricing in the short to medium term.   The Dry Cargo markets have seen a pick-up in activity on the capesize front with a number of buyers entering the market looking to secure additional tonnage. In terms on concluded business the Japanese controlled “AUSTRALIA MARU” (180k dwt, built 2012, KOYO) has been sold to Seanergy at Usd 33.5m. The vessel is both BWTS and scrubber fitted and is achieving levels in line with the upward momentum witnessed in the segment. Seanergy captured most of the snp activity on the cape front with the “AUSTRALIA MARU” being their fifth acquisition this year. Elsewhere Norden has sold their 2014 built “NORD HUDSON” built at NACKS for a price of Usd 21.1m which again represents a relative jump against last week’s comparable sales. To conclude we have witnessed some notable activity in the Handysize market with six vessels changing hands this week.

The Panamax market experienced a softer underlying tone this week. Rates have slipped in both hemispheres and FFA’s traded down until mid-week. It seems it has found a logical bottom and started to trade slightly up. The P1A is currently priced at 21/22k while the Pacific rounds are traded in the 27/28k region. It seems that the period interest is back in play, however the bid/offer gap is still wide.

After a slight improvement in rates last week, owners in the Nsea/Baltic market again had to give in for the downward pressure they faced this week. Charterers marched forward and covered quietly almost all stems for May. Moving forward, unless surrounding areas can offer an alternative, we expect rates to remain under pressure for the week to come as cargo volumes will be scarce and more ships coming back into position.  The Med/Bsea has trade sideways all week as expected. However, in the last two days we have seen the tonnage list tighten a bit, and as a result we are at the time of writing seeing rate pick up a few points. If owners are able to maintain the current pressure on rates, we expect a slightly firmer market towards the end of the week, especially with a healthy Bsea program for June.

Quiet start to the week with careful market development. Feeling of market slowing down or perhaps stabilizing is the right way to describe it. However positive sentiment and BSI in the green gives room for optimism.  Spot market in Atlantic is more quiet and lacking fresh cargo flow. Mediterranean and Continent a bit slow due to the prolonged Russian holidays from last week. Tonnage list is getting longer and cargo clearing out. Rates from Med to West Africa steady fixing in region USD 20k-23k. From Continent to East Med we have seen fixtures done around low USD 20k pd. USG is flat and well balanced. Supra was reporting loading in USG TCT to Japan USD 27k.  ECSA is active and we see more fresh grain stems appearing on the market.  Ultramax USD 20k plus USD 1 mill. GBB for trip to Spore-Japan. NOPAC RV on Ultramax is about USD 28k and backhaul Supramax paying close to USD 28k with delivery China. India Ocean is on alert due to the pandemic situation in India, however demand for tonnage remain strong. Period market is dominating in the area where owners asking USD 30k for min 6 months period on Ultramax deliver MEG-WC India.

With chatter abounding of a possible Iranian return to the open market (in the not too distant future), there is some marginal expectation that this could translate into better returns at some point. Whilst that's not going to positively impact rates this week, we have seen a moderate uptick in TD23 enquiry with ws18 reported on subs. Whilst those levels provide terrible returns, it's at least up, not down. With the risk of sounding like the most scratched record in history, the East has been too quiet and the build of tonnage at deviation point Wafr/MEG tells its own story. TD20 will remain flat for the remainder of this week as Wafr/East cargoes have failed to materialize in high enough volumes, forcing owners to take Wafr/up, or, book TD23 at negative earnings. MEG/East will trade low/mid ws50's on modern.

In the MEG, May signs off with mediocre 100 cargoes for the month. Nothing special and it has meant that the June stems were eagerly awaited. And here they are. At the time of writing, 5 fresh MEG stems hitting owners’ notepads, and we are looking at a (mini) frenzy, as owners hold off to try and get the bigger picture and not sell themselves short. It is not going to change the world, but a few extra points will help owners.  Plenty of reports Iranian crude will start exporting from Jask port in June. They are getting ready for lifting of sanctions, which does not look immediate, however. But, with Opec increasing, Indian refineries shutting for maintenance, we still awaiting the real rebound post covid, the oil has to go somewhere. Therefore quite a few questions this morning from certain parties on short term storage on VLCCs.

After the rally of chartering activity over the past couple of weeks, there are now becoming noticeable signs of softening emerging as we move into summer. Prompt interest has eased, save for optimisations or speculative opportunities. Looking a month out, ship availability is increasing, but most of the tonnage emerging is controlled by subletters. Generally, their length is too short or have limitations to accommodate fully flexible periods/trades, but they are impacting market sentiment. Term fixing activity is also slowing as Charterers pause to assess what vessels are left and how the market plays out; however, Owners stance remains unchanged - at least for now - as they weigh the cost (and potential benefit, in winter) of spot exposure versus fixing for term. On the newbuilding front, there have been no new orders recorded, however prices are steadily rising for delivery in 2024.

Some kind of floor was found in the Pacific with the c5 route up to todays' USD 12.4 pmt, still down from USD 14 one week back. The c3 route however is still dropping, with few requirements seen from Brazil. C3 is presently at 25.7, USD 3 less from previous week. There are expectations we will eventually see more demand from Brazil and consequently a correction in rates here as well, although there are no concrete signs yet.

text: MEG Despite the crude drop, Jun C3 CP stands firm and by the time of writing, it was traded at $503. June C3/C4 CP narrowed down further to $5, reflecting the improved demand on butane in summer season. Jun/Jul CP was traded at slight backwardation at $2.  Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their full propane cargo for 19/20th Jun loading at CP minus teens level. KPC tendered to sell another fob, which is heavy propane ratio for 20/21th Jun loading. This is their 4th spot sale for June lifting.   FAR EAST Active buying inquires, especially driven by petchem demand, lent support to FAR EAST price. A couple of cargos were traded in window. Full cargo propane for 2h Jun delivery was traded at Jun FEI flat and 23/0 parcel for 1h Jul delivery was done at Jun FEI plus $2.   One Korean petchem importer awarded their buy tender for one evenly split cargo of late Jun delivery at Jun FEI plus high single digit reportedly. One Indian importer was said to cancel their buy tender for one equal ratio cargo for 2h Jun delivery, due to the unfavourable price and high freight rates.   One EChina petchem user purchased a full propane cargo for mid/2H June delivery at Jun CP plus low-mid 40s. One Schina traditional importer secured a 11/11 parcel for Jul delivery at Jul CP plus high 40s reportedly. Another EChina player also tendered to buy one 23kt propane parcel for late June delivery.
