comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: NWE CIF ARA propane fell further have been falling further than crude oil values.. A cargo TOT window continues to be offered and value is now assessed at a slim premium of USD 0.5 per metric ton. The spot market has been quiet. Traders are waiting to see the full affect of the region’s supply maintenance and are well covered for the time being. CIF ARA values will have to increase if they want to continue to attract US product, as a small build in inventories on the other side of the pond resulted in Mt Belvieu strengthening vs WTI and the arb narrowing.  MED Multiple butane offers are seen in the region causing bearish sentiment and leaving mixed butane at 71.3% naphtha. Demand in the region has quiet.  AMERICAS  Following the EIA’s tepid report of a 400,000 barrel build, the propane price at Mt. Belvieu softened slightly, and then stabilized at around 82 cpg. Presently, US propane stocks sit at levels 30 percent lower than this time last year (44.4mn bl), and thus a handful of market participants foresee strong US propane price on the back of product tightness, for the balance of 2021. As of Thursday morning, the June LST/FEI arbitrage on paper is yielding netbacks definitively below cancelation economics, though no new cancellations have been reported- as the Far East continues to actively search for product on the back of petrochemical demand. Participants with product sourced from the US are opting to load cargos with the hope that the FEI spot price rises on the journey over, instead of cancelling. In June, a handful of cargos remain on offer from the gulf, though at these levels it would take a very competitive offer in order to yield a deal.  In Latin America, Brazil continues to buy to cover seasonal demand

EAST The Saudi acceptances were published over the weekend, but we are yet to see any real activity on the back of it. Meanwhile, we are still seeing some length on shipping from the traders, and as such the climb in Baltic from earlier weeks has turned (for now). We have seen a couple of cargo and freight tenders in the market for last decade of June this week, and last done deal on shipping was concluded around usd 60 baltic. We also expect to see more Indian cargos quoted in the market later for June loading, which is partly due to some of the Indian majors reported having covid related issued on their own t/c ships.  WEST In the Western hemisphere the activity level has been considerably reduced compared to the last couple of weeks, much owing to large parts of the world observing national holidays. Nevertheless, the arbitrage remains relatively stable and so does freight ideas from both relets and pure shipowners. A good old count of open/available vessels in the USG for that of June is largely in favour of the market remaining where it is for the foreseeable future. There should still be some uncovered cargoes end June ex USG, thus it is likely that we will see another example of little or no overhang going into July.  NB Another Newbuilding order emerged this week, bringing the total orderbook up to 64 ships, whereas 15 for delivery within this year, 18 next year and 31 ships in 2023.

The holidays are over in most regions, and activity is picking up again. Zodiac have scored on their 4th VLCC from Xihe, with the purchase of M/T JIN HUA SAN (317k dwt, blt 2009 SWS) at USD 36.8 mill. This is $2,5 mill up from the sister M/T TAI SAN (also SWS 2009) that was done back in October last year. Still – these forced sales are not representative for the general market, and with the growing interest we expect prices to continue climbing. As we all know, there is still not much support to get from the physical markets but increasing steel prices have an impact both on the NB prices and demolition values, and as such pulling everything up. These tendences are evidenced with two 2004 built VLCCs sold - M/T STARLIGHT VENTURE (291k, blt 2004 HHI) at USD 30.6 mill and M/T NEW CENTURY (299 dwt, blt 2004 Universal) at USD 31 mill which clearly show the trend. An easy reference here is DHT’s sale of their three 2004 models only a month ago. Despite their scrubbers and Cap 1 rating the price obtained was a fair bit lower at USD 29,6 mill (on average) each. We would guess the buyers of these could score a nice profit by flipping as the scrubbers should give a further premium compared to the most recent deals. The fuel spread seems to continue to widen. Okeanis Eco Tankers’ LR2s – all 115k, built Hyundai 2015 and with scrubbers have been widely discussed in the market. SOCAR was pointed out as the buyer, but this week it surfaced that Torm managed to pull it together at the end. A nice deal for both parties it seems, and the official price is USD 40,25 mill each. With the shipyards leaning back, and the general good interest, we expect prices to keep moving north.  Another week with dry sales of all sizes and new benchmarks set. Notable sales include the 2012 Japanese built Kamsarmaxes “SPRING AEOLIAN” and “TANGERINE ISLAND”, both sold for region USD 21m each. This compares with the 2012 Japanese built Kamsarmax “KINOURA” which was sold for USD 18m end of February, and illustrates clearly the development. With the increased prices and competition on Japanese vessels, we also witness a firming trend on the value of Chinese tonnage. Sister vessels “PEDHOULAS FARMER” and “PEDHOULAS BUILDER” (2012, Zhejiang Ouhua, 81k dwt) have been reported sold for USD 22m each. The scrubbers and BWTSs fitted on both have a clear effect, but this is still a strong substantial jump compared to the previous 2012 Chinese built Kamsarmax sold, “EVERGLORY” end February at USD 16m. We see an increased amount of interest from buyers for around 10 – 15-year-old bulkers, and with the steep increase of the demo prices along with the firm dry market, we expect a continued rise across all sectors and age in dry.

More fresh orders from South America. Supra from ECSA to Continent was covered at USD 30,000. Trips from Continent to USG were done around USD 18-19,000. Ultramax from West Africa being closed at USD 30,000 to Far East. Most gains coming from Pacific basin. Trips via Indo to SE Asia been fixed at low USD 30,000 and similar trip with redelivery China at USD 37,500. Ships from MEG to China collected high USD 20,000 for the business. Still firm numbers on period front. Supramax for 6/8 MOS being concluded at USD 25,000, whereas one-year deals still discussed around USD 17,000.

The Suezmax market remains depressed with all load-zones under downward pressure. Volumes remain so pitifully low in the East that we saw a modern unit booked at 130kt x ws52 for a MAF/Bataan run.  Had charterers stuck around and fished for a bit longer, it may even have been less. Td23 looks like the next route to lose a point or two and could touch ws15 S/S as the list of FOC ships at Galle is starting to pile up. The East list is so long and Wafr/East cargoes in such short supply, logic dictates that further falls could drag that run down to mid/high ws50's. In the West, a Libya/Ningbo cargo dragged rates to a new recent low of USD 2.25M which hopefully represent some sort of bottom. There is zero support from Aframax or VLCCs which paints a rather bleak picture for the ultra short term.

The positive sentiment from last week continued into this week, also supported by FFA values. Fixtures has been concluded at more than last done in both hemispheres. The South Atlantic is holding up and mid-week the P1A is valued around USD 25k. In the North Atlantic we feel the sentiment is a bit toppish with a longer tonnage list compared to last week. For the Pacific rounds, ships are being fixed in the 30k region.

The Nsea/Baltic Aframax rates improved slightly on the back of a heavier 3rd decade Urals loading schedule.  The tonnage list is looking somewhat tighter and owners put up a bit more resistance right now. There is a firmer undertone in the market, and we expect rates to firm in the current fixing window.  In the Med/Bsea, a decent level of activity has done its part in taking out a fair number of prompt ships the last few days. Although rates have taken a slight dip since last week and the tonnage list remains healthy, we may see a slight firming of rates in the week to come if current activity levels are maintained.

Over the last week the market been extremely volatile with big movements. On the whole we see a change in sentiment from the super positive to a (maybe) expected correction and breather for the miners and charters. The West Australia route to China with iron ore is down 9% w-o-w and the basket of all routes now being marked at USD 39,055, down almost 6,000 from last report and seemingly will erode further.

The Nsea/Baltic Aframax rates improved slightly on the back of a heavier 3rd decade Urals loading schedule.  The tonnage list is looking somewhat tighter and owners put up a bit more resistance right now. There is a firmer undertone in the market, and we expect rates to firm in the current fixing window.  In the Med/Bsea, a decent level of activity has done its part in taking out a fair number of prompt ships the last few days. Although rates have taken a slight dip since last week and the tonnage list remains healthy, we may see a slight firming of rates in the week to come if current activity levels are maintained.

Not a week that will remain long in the memory, but rates are holding. This mainly due to owners refusing to contemplate numbers lower than last done, rather than any indication of a steady/healthy cargo flow. TCE’s in the region of 0 to 10k (depending on eco, scrubbers etc) there is little fat left over. Owners can choose to hold off, as was the case with a Brazil export cargo that got only 3-4 offers, but ws33.5 still achieved by charterers. Wafr/East remains ws35 and a ws37.5 up to the UKC reported, treading on the Suezmaxes toes (which are providing very little support). In the MEG, we nearing 90 fixtures for May, and we still yet to work much of the 3rd decade, so we could see a busier month than others, but at present, very little working on the surface. On the whole, more of the same expected in the short term.

The Suezmax market remains depressed with all load-zones under downward pressure. Volumes remain so pitifully low in the East that we saw a modern unit booked at 130kt x ws52 for a MAF/Bataan run.  Had charterers stuck around and fished for a bit longer, it may even have been less. Td23 looks like the next route to lose a point or two and could touch ws15 S/S as the list of FOC ships at Galle is starting to pile up. The East list is so long and Wafr/East cargoes in such short supply, logic dictates that further falls could drag that run down to mid/high ws50's. In the West, a Libya/Ningbo cargo dragged rates to a new recent low of USD 2.25M which hopefully represent some sort of bottom. There is zero support from Aframax or VLCCs which paints a rather bleak picture for the ultra short term.

Firstly, to those celebrating Eid – Eid Mubarak. National holidays have been plentiful recently and these “interruptions” could be seen to affect the rhythm of the market, yet LNG prices continue to rise throughout the curve and point to continued improvement in the underlying market. It’s impact on freight is very noticeable, owners remaining bullish with this bullishness being built on the evidence of persistent multi-month enquiries. As mentioned last week the activity in the multi-month market is likely to reduce due to the lack of supply, unless we see a step up in levels to encourage further sublets into the market as owners. Looking at availability generally, there appears to be a systemic shortage of availability within the independent owners fleets.  Although some vessel available is starting to appear in all basins from portfolio players, the prompt available remains stable with adequate yet not overbearing availability. Looking further out to June and Q3, availability is far improved and adds pressure to rate increases. Despite this the start of Q3 looks stronger than usual for LNG Prices and shipping activity.  In the newbuild market - no new orders have been seen this week yet the newbuild price continues its steady climb.

text: MEG Swap value retreated after last surge. At the time of writing, Jun CP was traded at $496 and C3/C4 traded at $8-10. Jun/Jul CP was traded in $2 contango. KPC is reported to sell their 15/16th June lifting evenly split cargo at Jun CP minus mid/low teens. This is the 3rd spot stem they’ve marketed for June loadings. With freight soaring up, FOB netbacks are discussed at deeper discounts.   FAR EAST 23k propane for 1h Jun delivery was bid at Jun FEI plus mid-single digit, and similar parcel for 2h Jun delivery was at low-single digit. Arbitrage window is closed against rising freight and we’ve seen cancellations happening for Jun liftings. Off window a handful of cargos have been consumed, mainly by petchem players. One Korean petchem player issued term tender last Friday to secure 3 lots of 23k propane monthly from Jul 2021 to Jun 2022. Taiwan CPC issued buy tender to purchase 11/11 split for 21 to 30th Jun delivery

text: NWE CIF ARA propane was weaker than crude, pushing pro/nap higher into the $100-$110pmts. Large cargo butane value in the region was down now at 79.5% Naphtha. The region has been well covered for May demand mainly through imports from the US East Coast. Traders in the region are now monitoring the North Sea Maintenance and expect it to come back on time, June 3rd. With bank holidays in much of the region Thursday, many traders have bridged the long weekend and will reassess the market next week.  MED The butane market in the region is seen as under pressure. Due to split ratio US cargoes heading to the region to discharge their butane. The only offer seen in the window was an FOB meeting Moroccan spec which was withdrawn before the close. Both the propane and butane have lacked the strength.  AMERICAS If it’s not one thing it’s another. Asian and NWE CFR prices rose enough to what should have made cargos from the US workable, only to have freight go up further and faster, pushing the Arb back into cancellation economics.   The domestic propane inventory build of 2.5mmbbls allowed the market a sigh of relief as stocks moved up from 41.5mmbbls to 44.0mmbbls as of 7 May 2021.  The East Coast (PADD 1) saw a decline of 300,000bbls (from 3.8 to 3.5mmbbls) but given the volume of overwater exports that have been – and are still – occurring, this is not surprising.  PADD 3, however (the Gulf Coast) saw a build of 2mmbbls, from 24.8 to 26.8mmbbls.  Ostensibly this can be the result of either fantastic production levels, reduced export volumes or some combination thereof.  The EIA, however, reported that production in the first week of May declined to 635,000bbls/day, down from 1.353mmbbls/day – and neither figure seems believable, since the much-discussed cancellations did not occur in the first week of May, but are expected in 2H May.  As to June cancellations, there are believed to have been around a half-dozen, but in at least a couple of cases there were corresponding re-purchases (at lower rates), which thus allows for a modest “net” cargo cancellation total (so far) of 3.  Rumors of an additional 3-4 were noted,  but remain unsubstantiated. On the buy side, only the Brazilians seem to be continued spot buyers.   Meanwhile, terminal fees are believed to have been fixed in the low 3cts/gal range for June. As of this writing price ideas for 2H 2021 are talked above 5cts

EAST Fixing out of Middle Eastern ports saw a spike in freight over the past week as vessel availability has been scarce in the first days of June. Eastern premium is consequently now in the high single digits. Some vessels are now also looking set to run late for their laycans which could further tighten the early parts of June. Looking a bit further into the month we see a handful of potential relets and together with the usual owners positions the direction will be decided by actual volumes for the month as a whole.  WEST The market has moved on, very much in the direction as reported last week. It’s a bit of an odd one, as the arb does not support the current spot freight at all, which under “normal” circumstances would dictate cargo cancellations and drops in freight levels. But not this time around. We have only seen a handful of cancellations so far, and although we might see a few more, there are also an increasing number of cargoes coming out from the East Coast. This, in combination with dry-docking and other fundamental inefficiencies, have actually pushed freight up. We cannot say the market is active, and it’s only the ones having to lift that is actually fixing, others seem pretty happy sitting on the fence so far. Freight rates for the transpacific route currently trades in the very high 30s per day, a clear discount to the East still, which as of yesterday where traded in the mid/high 40’s per day.

Despite a week shortened by a number of national bank holidays, the markets continue to joy of healthy amount of transactions. On the tanker front, activity has picked up on the mid 2000 product carriers with three vessels changing hands this week and signs of a number of ongoing inspections and negotiations suggesting further activity in the near future. Empire Navigation have sold the Chinese built “MR ARIES” (2009, GSI, 50k dwt) at Usd 13.5m setting a benchmark for MR units of Chinese design. To put values in perspective, the last comparable sale was of a 2008 Korean built deepwell unit sold last week at xs of Usd 13m. The relative lack of  transaction in other tanker segments is not reflective of the current appetite for tonnage with buyers being met by a fading offer from sellers that are taking a standby stance in view of better days ahead.   Dry SnP markets continue to see a flurry of sales with the Supramax segment capturing most of the activity this week with 6 vessels changing hands. Dolphin 57 design units are seeing their value on the rise with Cosmoship disposing of their sisterships “LEGACY & OLYMPIC” (2011/2012, Jinling, 57k dwt) at USD 28m. Indicative of the unhindered rally in values witnessed over the past several months, these vessels were acquired by the sellers in September last year for an enbloc price of Usd 17.8m.

Owners’ optimism for improved rates on the back of a heavier Urals program was quickly curbed as some owners fixed lower than last done levels. Less fuel inquiries and an abundance of relets in the area would explain their rationale behind their decision. We expect rates to move sideways till the next possible tight window in the 3rd decade of May. Although the tonnage list remains healthy in the Mediterranean/Black Sea, we have seen rates pick up a few points during the course of the week as expected. This is mainly due to a fair amount of cargoes coming into the market. The last few days it has balanced out somewhat, also due to a quiet start of the week as a few countries had public holiday. We don’t expect any significant change in freight levels in the week to come, but if any a slight softening trend.

Big ships raking in big bucks. Capesize owners enjoying earnings not seen for many years, and fundamental factors indicate it may be a lasting trend despite some balloon signals. With commodity prices at historical levels and consequent max output of iron ore ex Brazil and West Australia in particular, average daily spot value is up 15 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 45k. Upward pressure particularly felt in Far East where miners de facto struggle to fill early slots, but signs are also that the long-duration fronthauls again may reduce the present gap in pay as forward projections are promising. Considerable congestion in certain key ports, quarantine restrictions, ongoing crewing problems and most recently a very serious India situation together add further fuel to the fire as fleet efficiency is reduced. Little period activity, mostly due to bull sentiment vs uncertainty on further potential.

The Suezmax market has been relatively slow the last week. With half of the world off at the end of last week, activity died out, and owners are still out there waiting for it to come back. So far what we are seeing is a tonnage list, both East and West, that is building up day by day. Free of cargo ships are piling up, and some serious activity in all areas is needed to get rid of this overhang. Suezmax owners were looking towards the V's at the beginning of the week, but what was a glimpse of hope was quickly taken away when Petrobras received close to a dozen offers on a Brazil/East cargo. Going forward we do not expect much to change unfortunately. Activity needs to improve drastically, and fixing last done levels is the best an owner can hope for at the moment.

A truncated week, with a day or two off around the globe has given a subdued pace to the market. We went in to the long weekend with rates slowly ticking up, driven by a firmer Atlantic and a tighter feel to the tonnage list, certainly off earlier dates. Often, however, a few days of quiet can be the enemy of the owning community, and as such, a quoted Brazil export cargo on Tuesday was met by a host of offers (reportedly 12) that dented owners’ confidence. As such, the market likely slipping to sub ws40 level for West Africa-East (Brazil-East at ws37.5). The MEG market providing few alternatives with China and Korea taking time off, and very few cargoes working. Volume was strong for early May but has tailed off and rates remaining flat to soft in the mid ws30’s. Owners will be hoping May cargoes kick on this week.

After a long weekend, market kept firming up with both physical and on paper. In the East it appeared to be firmer, where Pacific round voyages were done at USD 27-28,000. Indo-India rounds were concluded at close to USD 27,000. Bhaul from WCI to Continent were fixed at USD 25,000. South Africa to Pakistan payed USD 17,000 + 700,000 bb. In the Atlantic, USG were lacking fresh activity. From USEC to Continent it was discussed 18,000 TCE deals. Usual scrap rounds from Continent to Mediterranean were discussed at USD 19,000. On period, owners/chrts appears to be mostly on collecting mode. Supra for 1 year were discussed around USD 16,500 and Ultra repsectively USD 19,750.

The week started off with holidays in several countries which led to a slow start in both hemispheres. Tuesday showed a positive undertone but still a wide gap between bid/offer. The North Atlantic has experienced a lack of demand compared to available tonnage, and mid-week we saw some Baltic cargos entering, which got fixed immediately. We do however now see from our tonnage count that tightness have reached a level that preceeded upturns previously – thus we do expect rates to spike the next couple of weeks.

With much of the LNG world enjoying various holidays and some much needed time off over the past week, activity slowed down a little but the market has picked up right where it left off. The drive to take ships for winter coverage must surely ease up at some point, as owners with open tonnage are in no rush to fix and charterers weigh up the rising cost versus remaining uncovered. It’s a fascinating dynamic and one rarely seen ahead of summer. For those taking positions today, the lack of availability last winter and the LNG forward curve will be foremost in their minds and will justify taking on extra length. Those as-yet-uncovered may instead point to the tentative emergence of sublets as a sign that the market may yet soften, albeit such vessels are typically showing only quite narrow gaps in their schedules. Whatever happens in the coming months, we’re likely to enter winter with a lower proportion of vessels under control of head owners. It will be interesting to see how LNG shippers manage any excess length. On the newbuilding front, we note one LNGC order was reported last week. Finally, we note with sadness the re-emergence of coronavirus in some parts of the world, and as we all address the uncertainties ahead we hope all our readers and their families remain safe.

EAST We have seen a couple of ships fixed for end May load in the AG this week rep in the low to mid 50s Baltic, and the sentiment on freight continue to move upwards as we are now only left with a few ships that can safely make end May dates in the Middle East. Meanwhile, there are currently 2 freight tenders in play for end May-ely June loading, and also some chatter about other potential Charterers already fishing for freight ideas off early June. With only the Qatar acceptances published for June time of writing, one could argue that this is bullish freight for next upcoming fixing window.  WEST Arbitrage trades out of the US have been closed for some time now and remain closed, as an effect we have witnessed a handful of cancellations/deferrals. Freight rates remain stagnant around mid/high $80’s pmt and some asking $90 plus as they see shipping availability is limited for June. It does not look like it is freight that will have to give this time around. We are entering a period whereby DD schedules are expected to peak in combination with record high exports for months out of the US, so if we see arbitrage conditions improving then freight has a strong potential to increase in the months ahead.

text: NWE  The CIF ARA forward curve is as flat as a crêpe! Traders in the region wait to see the full extent of LPG volume reduction due to maintenance in the North Sea. LPG exports from Karsto could be reduced by up to 77% from 15th May - 3rd June. Most had covered shorts anticipating this local production squeeze which has led to a quiet market of late. This has also brought the TOT Window premium down to May CIF ARA +$2.5pmt. Large cargo butane is assessed at 83% May Naphtha strong as Naphtha is at 3 year highs.    MED The region has been quiet with reduced demand due to coronavirus restrictions and lockdowns. This has led to buyers keeping their cards close to their chests as they believe they will be able to find tons when demand appears.  AMERICAS  The EIA this week released its propane inventory data amid expectations of a 750,000 - 1mmbbl build, only to deliver what was seen as a disappointing half-million barrel improvement.  Overall US propane stocks as of 30 April are recorded at 41.471mmbbls, a deficit of 11.905mmbbls from the 59.376mmbbl total seen at the same time last year.  Stock levels will need to build at an average rate of 1.8mmbbls per week for the next 22 weeks – which is completely within reach- (but not with such a large export program) in order to achieve the generally established minimum of ~80mmbbls by the first week of October.   Domestic production levels are still healthy at 2.273mmbbls/day (compared to 2.046mmbbls/day last year), but export volumes – despite the reported lull this week – and res/com demand are still robust while petrochemical demand continues to slowly gain momentum.  Those factors (plus any weather-related factors) could make reaching the 80mmbbl goal a challenge.    As always, however, the price will resolve everything, and as such a handful of cargo cancellations were noted this week as cargo economics remain at touch-and-go levels.    Terminal fees have recently seen a fair amount of volatility, having ended April in the 5-6ct/gal range, commenced May with offers at below 2cts, only to see a resurgence in the first week back to the low/mid 4ct/gal range.

text: MEG June propane CP surged up to $506 following the crude rise, and C3/C4 spread narrowed down to $10 as expected. Jun/Jul CP traded flattish and forward market enters a slight contango structure. KPC sold their 12/13 Jun lifting evenly split cargo via tender reportedly.    FAR EAST Although it’s holiday week in Asian market, active bids/offers emerged in window this week. 23k propane parcel for 1h Jun delivery was bid at Jun FEI plus mid-single digit on Thursday, while earlier this week such parcel was concluded at 1-2 bucks higher. Similar cargo for 2h Jun delivery was bid at Jun FEI plus $3-4 whereas offer at $6/7, off window such was traded in between. With the return from holiday, market becomes more active from Thursday. One EChina Petchem user is reported to award its buy tender for one mid-June arrival propane cargo at Jun FEI plus high single digit. Similarly, another Schina petchem buyer also issued tender to secure 23k propane parcel for 5/15th Jun delivery.

We have seen healthy activity levels across the board as owners are looking to place their chips for the long awaited upswing in the tanker market. Ridgebury stole the headline this week and have bought 4 x 2007 and 1 x 2006 Dalian built VLCC’s at USD 120m. The vessels all have a BB attached to Euronav until 2021, giving them downside protection before the chartering market is expected to recover. Furthermore, Thenamaris bought the 2 year younger sister ship “NEW CREATION” for USD 37.5m. International Seaways have sold their CAP 1 rated “SEAWAYS TANABE” (2002, HITACHI, 300K DWT) to Chinese buyers for USD 24m, which falls in with last week’s sale of the “MARAN CARINA” (2003, DSME, 306K DWT) at USD 24m when we take survey positions into account. Liquidity in the vintage Suezmax space remains healthy and we understand that Tsakos have sold the “SILIA T” (2002, HHI, 164K DWT) for USD 15.8m. The deal falls in line with pricing achieved on the “EUROFAITH” (2004, HHI, 151K DWT) which also changed hands this week for USD 18m, once relevant discounts for age applied. In the product market, Cido are rumoured to have committed the “LR2 POSEIDON” (2009, SASEBO, 110K DWT)  and  “LR2 POLARIS & LR2 PIONEER”(2008, SASEBO, 110K DWT) on subject finance terms for low 60s enbloc to undisclosed buyers. Pricing looks attractive compared to last week’s sale of the uncoiled “CHAMPION PROSPERITY” (2009, SASEBO, 115K DWT) which achieved a price of USD 19.8m after seeing a hefty amount of interest.   With the Golden week coming up in China and the Easter holidays in Greece, we have seen good activity across all the segments in dry although expect this to come off next week. Notable sales on the dry side include the widebeam Kamsarmax resales ex-Chengxi Shipyard from Foremost Group with delivery this year to Yasa Shipping of Turkey at USD 28.5m each. With newbuilding prices at region USD 27 – 28m in China, we regard the deal as a favourable one for the buyers considering delivery in the strongest dry market we have seen in a decade. Scrubber and BWTS-fitted “EMERALD STAR” (2014, TESS CEBU, 82K DWT) have been reported sold for USD 25.1m after receiving initial offers at region 23-24m. “PACIFIC BRIGHT” (2013, Hantong, 57K DWT) sold for USD 14.8m illustrates a substantial increase (about 50%) in value of Chinese built Supramaxes comparing to same age Dolphin 57 “GLOVIS MADONNA” sold for USD 9.7 m early this year. The sale is also a good indicator for the discount to Japanese design, when comparing to the sale of “LOWLANDS PATRASCHE” (2013, TESS CEBU, 58K DWT) at USD 18.2m.

In the North Sea/Baltic market we have seen a slight improvement in rates this week. This has been mainly driven by a more balanced tonnage list coupled with the largest Urals schedule since April last year. We expect rates to stay under upward pressure, given the current activity will continue to feed owners’ optimism and while waiting for a busier 3rd decade again. Much of the same can be said about the Mediterranean/Black Sea market this week where rates have improved a tad mainly due to a healthy CPC program. Although there are still quite a few prompt ships in the area, owners have been showing some resistance. In the week to come we expect the market to move sideways with an upward potential.

As we head in to the Chinese Labour day holiday next week, it appears a lot of that business is being tidied up prior, with COA’s taking Chinese MEG tonnage up to the 20th May. The market has been on a steady climb this week and we have seen numbers for MEG/East creeping up to ws33.5 (cheaper older/handicapped tonnage are available). However, it is in the West where the majority of activity lies, with the Atlantic driving the market. Rates for West Africa coming on leaps and bounds to the ws40 level for East. The demand for modern, well approved tonnage in the USG is also drawing on the supply, meaning rates there creeping up to USD4.35m to China. There remains plenty of tonnage, but a little tightening has resulted in a firmer sentiment, and most VLCC owners are adept at driving sentiment when given the opportunity.

The term LNG charter market continues to heat up, with large week-on-week gains across all vessel types, and spot shipping rates are feeling the warmth spill over. Charterers seeking spot coverage now need to compete for Owner’s attention as Owners seems to be more interested in evaluating and securing term coverage. Availability is tight both in Atlantic and Pacific and coverage in the Atlantic have in some instances needed to source tonnage from the Pacific, which is uncommon considering that it’s still April. With more vessels chartered for term over the last few weeks, we could see more subletters showing positions for spot over the coming months.  It has been quiet on the LNG newbuilding front this week, but yard quotes on almost all vessel types are firming up.

Although general Suezmax volumes in the Atlantic basin appear down, conversely, we have seen a significant number of ships disappear over the last week, which has created almost zero noise. The net impact of limited chatter in an OTC market invariably results in flat to soft rates and this has now become self-fulfilling. Td20 will graze mid/high ws50's as there is simply inadequate MEG volumes to prevent a stream of ballasters from cannibalizing Western rates. Logically, MEG/East will struggle to stay out of high ws50's territory on modern tonnage and Td23 limps in at ws18. One positive news story is that in the last forty-eight hours, Western VLCC markets have put on a little fat which Suezmax owners will be hoping to take some positive cues from.

The softening trend from end of last week continued into this week. Rates are slipping on all trades and currently the P1A is yielding high 18s. There were some talks of more demand in SE Asia, however the standoff between owners and charterers has caused it not to affect rates. Period market has been somewhat stable so far.

Capesizes are super strong and expected to remain strong for some time. West Australia is approaching USD 13 pmt and c3 USD 30, leaving the average index at close to USD 40,000. It is expected to increase further, obviously a situation the dry bulk market is not facing very often.

Positive sentiment continues among all segments and trading areas.  Spot market in the Atlantic is more quiet than owner wish to expect. Decreased activity resulting lower rates in certain areas in the Atlantic such as the Mediterranean and the Continent. Tonnage list is getting longer and cargo clearing out. Upcoming Russia Orthodox Easter might have a role in declining activity. Rates from the Med to West Africa fall about USD 2k-3k per day compared to last week’s fixtures. NOPAC RV on Ultramax is about USD 25,000 or touch lower on Supramax delivery Japan. India Ocean remain very strong with rates achieving highest level - Supra was reported fixed basis delivery Karachi for 2 laden legs redelivery Singapore-Japan at USD 27,000.

text: NWE  The TOT window premium has been steady this week, and now lies at May CIF ARA +$11pmt. Seen as a positive sign as the curve has been flattening out, with May/June +$5pmt. Butane has been strong in the region, 82% Naphtha. The butane strength and propane premiums are not enough to attract US cargoes. Mt Belvieu strength on both C3 & C4 has stymied the trans Atlantic trade for May after a record 485,000 MT in May. These moves have overshadowed propane / naphtha spread going back out $101 per MT, which will continue to stimulate demand in the region.  MED The Sonatrach prices for May were set at $465/ $460 for propane and butane respectively. The butane market in the West Med looks long. Demand has been reduced in Morocco due to ongoing Coronavirus restrictions over Ramadan. Demand during this period has historically been high. Propane market has been quiet in the region, though assessed stronger.  AMERICAS The pace of the market has been subdued this week, though a renewed sense of negativity related to US propane inventory levels began to creep in after the EIA data release on Wednesday.  The arb has narrowed due to the recent strength in the Mont Belvieu market, and to the point where the lengthy list of cargoes presently being offered is only growing as buyers remain scarce.   As for the EIA propane inventory levels, many now openly doubt that propane stocks will be able to rise to at least the 80mmbbl mark by early October – and that doubt is causing prices to increase.  The question is whether stocks at the conclusion of the ‘build’ season will be sufficient to accommodate both exports and winter-related demand simultaneously in the U.S.   Expectations for this week’s EIA propane inventory report was again a mixed bag of predictions.  Some were calling for a small draw of around a half-million barrels, others for a build of a million barrels.  The relatively lighter export volumes but improving petchem consumption rates were considerations, but there has also been strong production levels thus far in 2021.  The half-million barrel build that was ultimately reported is surely a step in the right direction, but hardly sufficient, and prices reacted by increasing.  US terminal fees were earlier seen at ~4cts/gal for an end-May transaction, but as there were a host of sellers, the asking price is now below 4 cpg and buyers ideas well below that. Based on current econs,  we expect cancellations for both May and June.

text: FAR EAST A couple of deals were concluded in window this week. 23k propane parcel for 1h Jun delivery was traded at May FEI plus $5 earlier, and then cash premium dropped to $1. Similar cargo for 2h Jun delivery was bid at June FEI plus $1 while offer at $6. Off window a handful of tenders floating in the market. One Korean Petchem user was said to secure one 23kt C3 for 6-12 June delivery at June FEI plus low teens via tender. Another Korean Major issued term tender to secure 7 upto 12 lots of 23k butane parcel monthly from June delivery onwards. Indian IOC was reported to purchase one equal ratio split cargo on FOB scheduled for 2h June delivery at June CP minus mid-low teens. And Indonesia Pertamina reissued their term buy tender to purchase 1-2 evenly split cargos monthly from July to Dec delivery.   MEG Saudi Aramco set May Propane CP at $495, down by $65 and Butane CP at $475, down by $55. Such is more or less in line with swap value. And backwardation into June has narrowed down to almost flattish. We expect C3/C4 spread to narrow down further as better demand for butane into summer season. KPC is reported to sell their 4/5 Jun lifting equal ratio cargo.

EAST The shipping market in the East has been less active compared to the last few weeks, but we are still seeing a couple of deals concluded behind the scenes. Last done deal is being reported around low/mid 50s Baltic, and current fixing window is mainly focused on last decade of May basis MEG. Going forward we expect these sort of freight levels to maintain, and we also expect to start seeing early June cargos from next week after the acceptances start to come out.  WEST A handful of deals were concluded during the course of last week, at rates hovering in the mid-to-high USD 80's to the USD 90 per ton mark (Houston/Chiba basis) and around mid-to-high USD 40's for the Houston/Flushing route. The number of vessels still remaining for May dates is relatively low and therefore, it seems the arb will be the decisive factor, as to whether or not the overhang of ships going into June, is going to be there or not. The majority of the May lifting program is seemingly done, however, there are some spot FOBs for sale which may absorb some of the length, if the arb allows. From a pure supply/demand of ships point of view, it is likely that we will see the market remaining relatively flat unless the economics dictate otherwise. With the current freight levels, the transpacific route is currently trading at a marginal premium to the Eastern index route, whilst the transatlantic route is trading at around 15% premium.

With the intensity of the LNG shipping market last weeks, one could have perceived this to be the pre-winter months of previous years when comparing the amount of chartering enquiries, the increasing LNG prices and the firming charter rate levels. While the market corrected itself last February after a winter with high gas demand, it was expected that replenishment of LNG inventories would take place over the subsequent summer months. Hence, the market were preparing itself for maybe a more active summer. Vessels are now being fixed on term charters as a regular occurrence, not just to ensure shipment coverage over the winter of 2021, but also in anticipation of a more active summer. With this activity and LNG market setting, greatly reducing a charterers potential idle time over the next 12 months charter period, Charterers are able to justify to move quickly to secure tonnage. Available modern vessels are depleting fast in both basins as spot and term charters are being concluded.

The Capesize market is in flames! TC basket has gained 27% since last report and sentiment still very strong with all routs improving. It’s also interesting to see that even though at these historical high levels it’s not only the very profitable iron ore trade being active but also the coal segment is keeping itself busy adding gasoline to the fire.

We evidently have a firmer Caribbean/TA Aframax market where rates are presently trading at crossover levels which will now hold American seaboard tonnage away from West Africa. North West Europe is also showing signs of life which will further distract tonnage on the Continent. In the East, there's a flatter feel with a long list that will see rates trade in and around last done levels. Td23 has traded a few times at WS22.5, which now appears to be the conference rate for this week. Basrah/East trades at WS62.5 flat with owners and charterers happy to repeat.

Difficult for owners to really drive the market upwards. However, in a much promised busier 2nd half to the year, owners will hope this tactic will be harder to achieve. text: NWE May propane vs naphtha remains above $100pmt which will keep cracking demand to a maximum. The pro/nap spread remains in triple digits until August. Many of the large cargo traders in NWE are covered for May. North Sea gasfield maintenance is set to end June 3rd which would bring local production back. A number of traders are waiting for maintenance to end before buying additional tons int he hope that the CIF ARA will come off. The narrowing arb from the US is also keeping European traders quiet for the time being. This has been reflected in the TOT window which is assessed at CIF ARA +$7pmt for May, down from +$13pmt a week ago.   MED The sentiment was weaker in the West Med though butane was steady vs Naphtha. Demand levels were lower than anticipated. Though this has yet to be reflected in regional prices, butane was steady and propane showed some strength.  AMERICAS Crude oil prices were down early this week as the API were forecasting an increase in crude oil stocks, while Mont Belvieu propane values continued to drift on the belief that domestic stock levels will remain sufficient.  Looking towards the summer, the domestic US forward propane pricing curve is effectively flat through September.  This is primarily due to the belief that crude oil production will continue to be healthy and promote production levels, which will need to exceed the combined demand levels of the North American res/com market, the US petrochemical sector and – most importantly – waterborne export markets which – according to the EIA – are at well-above average rates of 1.7mmbbls/day. In fact for this month, April 2021  we expect a record of 90 vessels loading.   Meanwhile, the EIA this week were expected to report that propane stocks in the US built by something under a million barrels as of the week ending 16 April.  It reported, however, a 74,000bbl draw – which included a half-million barrel decline in PADD 3 stocks.  Total overall propane inventories as of 16 April are now 40.5mmbbls, which compares to last year’s 57.4mmbbls and the 2019 total of 51.8mmbbls.  All the while a spate of petchem-related buying in Europe has kept the US export market moving at a robust clip as US terminal fees recently dipped to levels in the low 4ct/gal range for end-May, but are sharply higher for June volumes at asking levels of 6ct/gal.

EAST Saudi acceptances for May were published over the weekend and since then we have seen another handful of fixtures concluded in the East. 1st decade of May in the AG seems pretty covered by now, and next fixing window is focused around 2nd decade of May. The last done deals have mostly been done in the high usd 40s Baltic, and it is expected that rates will stay in the 40s unless we see an improvement on Arb economics in the West (which subsequently could pull more ships back to the US Gulf). We have also seen a couple of fob tenders from Middle Eastern suppliers marketed this week for end May loading, but it remains to be seen if spot shipping will be needed for these cargos time of writing.  WEST The market in the West seems to have taken a bit of a breather this week, and it seems charterers are awaiting some clear direction before making their moves. With the sentiment from last week in mind, it was clear the owners had expected rates to come up in the 90’s this week, but it has yet to materialize for the standard transpacific route. One fixture has been done at levels very close to this, but not for the standard destination. It is not unlikely though that we’ll see an increase in rates, as the list of remaining available ships for loading May cargoes, are in-fact rather short. Although, rates may still turn out to be sliding sideways, as it remains to be seen how many cargoes we’ll have before the market start to focus on the June cargoes in a week or two. After a couple of weeks with a discounted freight in the West, the balance shifted last week, and is now established with a more “normal” western premium whereas the East trades in the low 30k’s per day and the west trades in the mid-30s.

text: MEG Flat price is volatile this week. May propane CP rebounded to $485 and butane at $20 less. Earlier this week, May/June CP spread narrowed down to $3 but quickly enlarged to $7 by the time of writing. Saudi Aramco released their May acceptance with no cuts reported, but supplier is said to have rich butane supply as previous months. KPC was reported to sell their late May lifting heavy propane cargo at Jun CP minus around $10. And following this, QP was said to award their sale tender for late May loading full propane.   FAR EAST Off window a handful of deals were concluded this week. 23kt Propane for 2h May delivery were traded actively, ranged from May FEI plus mid to high teens, and cash premium is expected to edge further high. One reason being is the prompt cracking demand due to the improved economy on FEI/MOPJ. Earlier this week it went to minus $80 and several petchem users have emerged to procure LPG for cracking feedstock. However the spread narrowed down quickly to minus low 50s afterwards. Taiwan FPCC procured one full cargo propane for late May delivery at May MOPJ minus low 50s via tender. And they’ve also issued term tender to secure seven to twelve cargos for June to Dec 2021 delivery or July 2021 to June 2022 delivery. Another Chinese Major also issued buy tender to secure 12 cargos for July 2021 to June 2022 delivery.

The negative trend in the Panamax market continued into this week – however this seems to have taken a turn mid-week. Maybe we have found a logical bottom for now.  P1A is currently priced in the mid/upper 12’s. In the eastern hemisphere we see Pacific rounds yielding 18/19k depending on delivery.

The BSI turned North for the first time in two weeks of negative movement. We see big difference in two basins where Pacific firming up and Atlantic keep dropping. Good level and healthy fixtures being concluded both on TCT and short period trading in Pacific.  Mv Hanton Trader, 63,000 dwt, open Manila, reported to be fixed 2/3 LL USD 24k to Chinese operator. Ultramax delivery China fixed TCT via Australia at USD 22k with grains to Singapore-Japan. A 55,000-dwt open Indonesia fixing a trip via Indonesia to China at healthy USD 25k. South Africa and Indian Ocean have same trend from last week, slightly under pressure due to the lack of fresh requirement and prompt ships building up.  Not many fixtures been reported but owners were able to obtain for Tess 58 type in region of USD 13k plus USD 500k GBB for trip from South Africa to Far East. Atlantic market in general under pressure and rates sliding further down. The Baltic Sea market is still going down with tonnage building up. Clinker cargo is fixing in region of USD 18k-20k basis APS load port to West Africa. Continent has the same trend to Med-Black Sea market – under pressure and rates are flat. The US Gulf is suffering most as rates dropped dramatically to all destinations.  Ultramax fixing USD 22k’s for trips to India and USD 14k with petcoke to Mediterranean. Trips from Brazil and Argentina were very inactive and little fresh inquiries lead to lower fixtures. On Supra 56,000 dwt delivery ECSA chrts offering USD 17k APS load port with grains to Continent. We expect flat market in Atlantic and firm tone in Pacific.

We are witnessing a rare scenario, as the start of Q2 2021 has been rather exciting compared to previous years.    LNG Shipping remains positive as fixing levels across both basins continues to increase day-by-day, and Owners with prompt availability in the Atlantic or those able to work 2H May US loadings are likely to see considerable interest on their ships.  The lack of availability in the West, strong gas demand and decreasing inventory levels in Europe are just a handful of reasons why sentiment is holding firm.     While the LNG market continue the steady upward trend, several Owners are still prioritizing utilization, longer period businesses instead of spot charters. This could mean more inclination from Owners to work more competitive rates at present for longer duration such as multi months to short term time charters.

Big ships doing well. Average daily earnings up 16 pct w-o-w to come in at just over USD 26k. Main driver being continued solid steel and iron ore margins, and major miners are busy covering slots by the dozen to meet industry demand. Lion’s share has been on West Australia, but Brazil again picking up speed with resultant triple contribution to tonne-mile. Coal finding new trades due to political deadlocks, substantial congestion in a number of main ports and ongoing quarantine/crew change restrictions all add to reduced fleet efficiency and upward pressure on rates. Limited period activity, as expectations seem to exceed ffa values supporting well in excess of USD 25k on model type tonnage for balance 2021.

Momentum continues to build in the tanker SnP markets with an increasing number of transactions materialising this week. The Japanese controlled LR2 “CHAMPION PROSPERITY” (115k dwt, built Sasebo, 2009, Coated) invited offers after having north of 20 buyers inspecting. The vessel is now committed at a price of Usd 19.8m to Greek buyers. The strong interest is not only a clear indicator of the growing appetite for quality tanker tonnage but when compared to the sale of the one year older “FALCON EXPRESS” (115k dwt, built Sasebo, 2009, Coated) sold last month at Usd 14.5m; the price achieved this week points to a clear upward trend in values which should remain unhindered with a number of buyers finding themselves looking for alternative opportunities in a market with a thin supply of sale candidates. Also increasing activity across most product segments as seen by East Med’s purchase of SOCATRA’s two HMD resales. Both vessels deliver in 2022, and the price is reported at Usd 35.5 mill each – presumably on novation basis. Even for LR1s which normally is a pretty illiquid class we see more deals surfacing.  The dry markets seem to have met some relative stability following the steep appreciation in values witnessed over recent weeks. Most reported transactions are now falling in line with last done, consolidating benchmarks across sectors. Saying that, buying enquiry remains strong with sign of ongoing negotiations however a constant stream of tonnage being placed for sale seems to be keeping a lid on competition and contributing to the abovementioned flattening in prices – famous last words.

The North Sea/Baltic market hit its lowest level since early month of February when we had cheaper bunker prices. Despite a few injection stems in the 3rd decade of the Baltic Urals schedule a long tonnage list coupled with less fuel enquiries put charterers in a position to test rates. No surrounding markets provide owners with any better alternatives, so we expect rates to move sideways for now. Much of the same can be said about the Mediterranean/Black Sea market where the mere amount of cargo activity is a far cry from satisfying the long list of prompt ships in the area. Rates have come off this week and we expect this to continue in the week to come, at best moving sideways.

text: MEG Flat price is weakening this week. May Propane CP plunged to $480, and Butane was traded at $25 less. Backwardation into June narrowed down to $5 from last week’s mid10s. ADNOC released their May lifting acceptance with some delays being reported. However, it doesn’t lend much support to CP value. FOB discussions of evenly split cargos are still under mid-high teens discounts. Qatar Petroleum issued tender to sell one late May lifting full propane cargo, which is due next week.   FAR EAST A handful of deals were concluded in window this week. 23k C3 parcels for 1h May delivery was traded at May FEI plus low 20s, and similar cargos for 2h May delivery was done at May CP plus $43/44. However, cash premium softens as US delay situation is getting eased. On Thursday similar cargo for 2h May delivery was bid at May FEI plus mid-teens, while offer equates to high teens level. Off window a flurry of tenders floating this week. One Korea Petchem user tendered to buy one 22/22 or 23/0 for end May early June delivery. One SChina traditional importer awarded their buy tender to secure one 11/11 parcel for 2h May into June delivery, at a mixed price of CP plus low 30s and FEI plus teens. Another SChina PDH user also procured one 23/0 parcel for 2h May delivery via tender at May CP plus mid 30s reportedly. And we are expecting more cracking demand emerge next week, as LPG economy improving as feedstock. At the time of writing, May FEI/MOPJ was traded at around minus $70.

This week has seen some surprising pockets of resistance in areas where none was expected. A Basrah/East run set the tone when it entered the market on Monday and quickly jumped on a WS62.5. This speedy fixture quite possibly puts a floor under East rates for the time being. Basrah/West has also shown some small signs of resistance, with charterers being forced to slow trade, as opposed to early last week, when owners were just looking to cover exposed positions. As the week has progressed, an improving VLCC market may lend some further psychological support to its diminutive cousin, at least in the East. However, in a tale of two hemispheres, Western markets will continue to be pinned down by a never ending conveyor belt of ballasters, with Wafr/East doomed to low/mid WS60's territory.

As April stems close out, the MEG has warmed up for modern tonnage. It may not be the green shoots of a full recovery, but welcomed by owners nonetheless. We can see the impact of an exodus West around the Cape in recent weeks as it has created a shortage of well badged ships in the MEG. As such we have seen rates move up beyond the mid 30’s for end month dates MEG/East. Anything remaining for April dates may get a little sting, as owners react to the last few deals. In the Atlantic, rates have struggled for traction given the tonnage availability, and remain flattish in the low WS30’s for Wafr/East. Worth noting that Suezmax a touch softer, certainly in the West, so little support there as we now have the quiet period before the May MEG stems start coming in. Despite this, owners will look to keep this bump rolling.

Despite a few injection stems in the 3rd decade of the Baltic Urals schedule a long tonnage list coupled with less fuel enquiries put charterers in a position to test rates. No surrounding markets provide owners with any better alternatives, so we expect rates to move sideways for now. Much of the same can be said about the Mediterranean/Black Sea market where the mere amount of cargo activity is a far cry from satisfying the long list of prompt ships in the area. Rates have come off this week and we expect this to continue in the week to come, at best moving sideways.

EAST With vessel supply in the West looking balanced to tight for that of May ex USG, we foresee the MEG market to remain relatively strong going forward as we expect owners to send the majority of their vessels back to the West. At time of writing there has already been six spot fixtures ex AG for the first decade of May and depending on the Aramco acceptances, focus might be shifting towards second decade soon. Further into May with delayed Adnoc dates we could see increased activity which should absorb most of the ships not sailing West, and we therefore expect current rates to maintain or come off slightly.  WEST The West market has been trading at a discount to the East for most of the week, but activity in the market picked up somewhat yesterday, and we are now seeing freight around mid/high USD 80 per ton Houston/Chiba basis. And with that, combined with a slight drop in the East, the market in the west is again trading at a premium. The balance of May in terms of vessel availability looks to be somewhat balanced to tight in the US Gulf and the need for ships seems to be looming. So, we don’t expect that somewhat unusual western discount  to return any time soon.

text: NWE The big story in the region is Propane Naphtha spread going out to -$105 pmt for May. The Mt Belvieu CIF ARA arb has been widening since Wednesday. Although as the arb to Europe widened by about $10pmt so too the cash premiums in the TOT window decreased by $10pmt. The wide pro/nap will keep demand in the region high. The Mt Belvieu butane arb to NWE is above that of propane, which will contribute to maximum LPG demand.  MED The Med has been quiet in the wake of global propane moves and the region remains well supplied.  AMERICAS Crude continues to march upwards, with May WTI improving this week to over $63/bbl and Brent is now approaching $67/bbl.  Conversely, however, the Mont Belvieu propane market remains in retreat as non-TET values at Mont Belvieu have been in decline for the last 10 days, having most recently reached  77.50 cents/gal.   The most recent price reduction comes on the heels of the EIA report which revealed that propane inventories in the U.S. had risen by 1.016mmbbls from the 2nd April to the 9th April to an overall US total of 40.588mmbbls.  One year ago, in the first week of April 2020, stocks were recorded at 56.780mmbbls.   Domestic production of propane rose modestly from 2.299mmbbls/day last week to 2.313mmbbls/day at present, remaining robust as compared to the year-ago rate of 2.061mmbbls/day.   Overwater exports remain healthy despite a half-dozen cancellations, and terminal fees reflect the sentiment, having moved from below 4cts/gal to current asking levels of 6cts/gal.  Improved interest from Europe on the basis of the Propane/Naphtha spread and a widening F/E arb – which is enhanced by reduced waiting times at Panama – should bolster the US-to-Asia trade and assist in maintaining healthy US waterborne trade volume.

A shift of activity this week with the tanker sector seeing an increased level of activity. Vintage crude carriers have joyed of strong buying interest with DHT reported to have disposed of three 2004 DSME built scrubber-fitted VLCC’s. The number of comparable VLCC's now sold amount to seven over the past month with Far Eastern buyers leading the charge. Notable activity in the product space with the sale of “OVERSEAS GULF COAST” (2019, HMD, 50k dwt) which was sold to Eastern Pacific Shipping at a price of Usd 32.5m. The transaction breaks a long streak of inactivity for units of such vintage considering that the last comparable sale dates back end of last year. This notable illiquidity on the modern front is particularly well illustrated by a relatively flat value curve.  We have seen a substantially lower number of dry sales compared to the frenzy witnessed over the past few weeks. Notable sale this week is “NORD STELLAR” (2016, Hudong, 82k dwt) sold for Usd 25.5m to Greek buyers. Same vessel was sold for Usd 20m early December last year, ex-name SBI Zumba.

The Nsea/Baltic market took an after Easter break with limited activity in the market. Despite a relative short tonnage list, cargo activity doesn’t seem sufficient for rates to hold and Charterers will try and push for lower than last done. Going forward we expect rates to move sideways with a slight downward pressure before we hit the 3rd decade April loading window where we expect more injection stems for the Urals program.  In the Med/Bsea we saw short lived excitement on the back of Suez Canal closing prior to the easter break. However with the reopening of the canal in combination with little cargo activity, and ballasters coming into the area we have seen the market taking a solid downward correction. We expect the market to remain soft in natural fixing window.

The long Easter weekend in Europe gave some participants a much welcome break, but it came at a heavy price. This is a momentum game and in a market that was already softening, a Meg/China cargo took full advantage of this lull and dragged this route down to W59. With a fleet of Eastern ballasters hellbent on West African loads, the prognosis in both hemispheres remains rather subdued this week. Td20 will stay bogged down in the low W60's whilst Td23 will struggle to stay out of teens territory. On the upside, but possibly a little further down the line, economic figures emanating out of China and the USA suggest that those respective economies are riding out the pandemic much better than expected, which should help sentiment in the medium term.

The overall index is up from last weeks average of usd 18,327 to this week's usd 22,468, ie up 22.6%. Present c5 level is up usd 1,50 from last week to usd 10,4 index level. The main driver for the index recently has been a couple pf strong front haul fixtures in the mid 40,000s. The atlantic is expected to improve further as well as c3 activity will pick up.

Bittersweet for owners as a positive result from the OPEC meeting a few weeks back promises a brighter future, but until that point, rates have remained under pressure. The Suez canal blockage proved a flash in the pan and with many Modern/approved Owners pointing to the Cape of Good Hope; Petrobras, Petrogal and the like received a high number of offers for their Atlantic stems. With rates dropping across the board, USG/East is down to $4.3m, and West Africa to test, but a cargo working now will be pushing mid-low ws30’s. AG/East likewise, with the astute Charterer, picking the right ship knocking on the ws30 level.  With the IMF raising 2021 global growth forecast to 6% (up from 5.5%), there remains optimism for the year ahead. As we have said before, it’s a case of riding the trough, for the crest of the wave ahead.

LNG shipping market activity has picked up right where it was before the short Easter break as new spot requirements emerged from both basins boosted by the strengthening LNG cargo prices, which are currently rendering the threat of US cargo cancellations to minimal at least in the near term. Furthermore, there are handful of ongoing term-requirements, which together with the fresh spot requirements, are giving available Owners plenty of options to choose from. Accordingly, spot rates are cautiously climbing upwards as vessel availability shortens, however the cap between spot and term rates still stays relative wide as expectations of stronger market conditions for the second half of the year persists. It definitely feels like the overall shipping market is a bit more volatile this year and this uncertainty might not disappear anytime soon. Notwithstanding the recently launched long-term tenders from a few big industry parties, there were no new LNG carrier orders placed this week.

Supras from USG to Cont discussing 15000 levels.  Continent also slowing down with fresh new cargoes.  Fhaul from Black Sea done now at 26000 level. text: MEG May CP was traded at $509, and backwardation into June was assessed at $17. May C3/C4 spread narrowed down to $17 from previous $30, as the summer demand recovering for Butane. Netbacks for May FOBs are improving due to the delays on US supply against better demand driven by petchem sector. KPC was reported to sell one 4/5 May lifting heavy propane cargo at May CP minus 10s. Previously it sold one end Apr lifting evenly split cargo to one NChina petchem importer via tender.    FAR EAST A plenty of bids in window this week has propped up the cash premium for May delivery cargos. Bids on 23k propane parcel for 1h May delivery were edging up to May FEI plus $28, however no offers seen yet. Similar cargo for 2h May delivery was bid at May CP plus $40, which equates to May FEI plus $20, and offered at May FEI plus mid-20s. 1H/2H spread is assessed at $10 or more, caused by the delays on Panama canal under foggy weather.  Off window buying sentiment is also active. One EChina petchem user managed to secure a 23k C3 parcel for later May delivery at May CP plus low 40s reportedly via tender. However, another SChina PDH user who aimed for similar cargo for early May delivery, didn’t award the tender due to high price charged for prompt delivery. Taiwan CPC also issued tender to secure one 11/11 parcel for May delivery and the result is yet to know. Other than this, Indian IOC tendered to purchase one evenly split cargo for mid/2h May delivery after quieting down for months.

text: AMERICAS At least “a few” LPG cargo cancellations are known to have occurred in April, while yet another is very likely to be cancelled prior to the conclusion of this week.  All in, perhaps 5 or even 6 VLGC’s will be removed from the April roster, which should allow up to 3mmbbls to remain in the domestic system.    Propane stocks as of the week ending 02 Apr were reported by the EIA to have increased by 325,000bbls, bringing overall US inventories to 39.572mmbbls – some 20mmbbls below the 59.027mmbbls seen at the same time last year.  The EIA also reported Wednesday that the Days of Supply of propane in the US fell from 28.9 to 26.6 days as of 2nd April, well off from the 51.5 days of supply recorded a year ago.  Meanwhile, res/com demand in the US is relatively robust at 1.46mmbbls/day as of 02 April, up from 1.356mmbbls/day at 26 March.  This compares to the April 2020 demand rate of 1.146mmbbls.   US petrochemical sector consumption of propane, though, remains below par at ~225,000bbls/day, still weak after the storm which occurred over a month ago.   Spot terminal fees have seen a bit of weakness as the arbs have closed in recent days, with talk of a deal between traders having been heard at 4cts/gal for May.  Term business, however, likely resides 2 cents above that.  NWE A Tuesday deal set the physical window premium at April CIF ARA +$13.5pmt for last decade delivery. This softened the demand for prompt propane tons and was seen by most traders in the region as the end of large cargo buying for April. Petchems and end users seen as being well covered through the month. The post Easter, pre Ramadan period which expected by some to be a time of high activity never materialized. The recent drop in Mt Belvieu did not have a marked effect on the arb to Europe as CIF ARA softened in tandem.  MED Some action was seen in the MED with 4KT butane offered in the window. Which put pressure on outright butane values. There remains very little propane demand in the region.

There remains a sense of separation in the LNG shipping market as spot remains relatively inactive, and term continues to be the main focus for many. Requirements are picking up prompt vessels though, and this is helping rates gradually increase week on week, seemingly typical of the shoulder months. Term enquiries are more abundant with plenty of charterers in the market, and there’s a definite rise in sentiment with healthy levels being discussed. LNG shipping suffered little during the Suez disruptions, as cargoes were replaced, ships diverted and panic averted, highlighting the other side to the volatility we often see within the industry. Delays for traffic already waiting in line remains to be seen, but there’s little to suggest anything other than business as usual. The current spread of prompt tonnage across the basins suggests that if vessels were needed quickly, they could be found. No conventional Newbuilding orders have been placed this week, but we continue to see prices increasing.

Whilst the Suez Canal drama has come to end, it’s worth pointing out that the origins of last weeks firmer west market  have been lost in the Suez Canal narrative. This event simply added to what was already a more confident market. Hence why some of the steep falls we’ve seen in West Africa over the last twenty four hours, appear very hasty, ignoring  an active cargo menu in neighbouring regions. Fundamentally, the Td20 list is still competing with a busy Black Sea and Libya program, whilst Aframax’s, albeit softer, remain in Suezmax owners crosshairs. For now, Wafr/Ukcm will trade circa W70 whilst a lack or enquiry in the Middle East Gulf will apply some downward pressure with an East run likely to fall back into the w60’s on modern tonnage. Td23 will look to mop up some of the slack on the list at mid/high W20’s

End of last week we experienced an extremely firming market which has faced a correction this week. The FFA market took a major hit which again has resulted in a hault for the period market. P1A is currently yielding 23k while fronthauls are priced in the mid 30k region. In the Pacific, we also see a standoff in bid/offers and there seems to be a lack of demand for prompt positions. P3 is valued in the high 20k.

The LNG shipping market remains active, primarily driven by charterers seeking term tonnage through to winter and beyond. Several fixtures have been concluded so far and with vessels disappearing, term rates have risen and are expected to strengthen further. Conversely, the spot market remains relatively flat despite a handful of fixtures during the week. Prompt vessel availability has reduced but further ahead redeliveries and sublet tonnage are adding to the position list. Whether this strong activity in the term market will last is yet to be seen, as some are taking a wait-and-see approach hoping for some softening in summer. There haven’t been any new orders on conventional tonnage recorded so far this week, however Newbuilding prices showing some small gains.

Activity in the dry snp market is sustained with sales ranging across all sectors. Compared to the substantial jumps witnessed over the past few weeks, values seem to have relatively stabilised for the time being with levels paid broadly falling in line with last done. However few particular segments such as very modern Japanese and top tier Chinese Kamsarmax/Ultramax have caught up in terms of liquidity this week resulting in values marking a more significant jump. Notably we are now seeing very modern tonnage achieving relative premiums against current newbuilding prices. With the lack of such second hand candidates being openly marketed for sale, we expect the sellers to keep the upper hand against an ever increasing buying enquiry. The recent uptick in values of Japanese handysizes seem to have changed the focus of buyers to Chinese tonnage which should trigger a narrowing of the gap currently witnessed between Chinese and Japanese built vessels.   With subdued freight rates continuing to loom across most tanker segments buyers are not yet finding the incentive to increase their bids; this against a background of sellers that share a more general consensus that a market upturn is underway for the 2nd half of this year. This trend is evident by the nature of the this week’s reported sales whereas 6 out of 11 transactions are bank driven. Values of 10 year product tankers seem to have bottomed out after a period of continuous downward correction with the sale of 2010 Iwagi built MR “NORD INSPIRATION” at a reported sales price of Usd 15.75m.

We have seen a dramatic change in sentiment from positive to negative as the smaller segments as Panamax and Supramax has lost its pace. This has put some pressure on the Capesize segment, but mainly on forward pricing and period, while an inferno in the spot market is yet to be seen. The explanation probably lies in the heavy contango, but still of an interest and maybe a sign of still healthy demand of vessels.

Positive sentiment started to vanish and market taking a dive among all segments and trading areas. Spot market in Atlantic “crashing” as some charterers suggested adding some uncertainty going forward. Decreased activity and lower rates also affecting the Pacific market. Indexes turned south for second day in a row. Grain export from USG traditionally will be slowed down during spring moths. The Black sea and Continent drastically down on fresh cargo inquiry. Rates from Med to West Africa fall about USD 5k-7k per day compared to last week’s fixtures. From the Continent to East Med we have seen fixtures done around USD 26,000 pd. Ultramax APS SW Pass fixed 27,000 TCT to Med. ECSA for time being remaining firm with fixtures reported USD 20,000 plus USD 1 mil GBB for trip to Singapore-Japan. NOPAC RV close to USD 26,000 or touch higher on Ultramax delivery Japan. Indian Ocean remain strong with rates achieving highest level - Supra was reported fixed basis delivery Karachi for 2 laden legs redelivery Singapore-Japan at USD 33,500.

A much better week for owners, as rates moved further in their favor. TCE’s are far from anything to celebrate, but coupled with slightly lower bunkers, returns are somewhat improved. In the MEG, the two tier market very evident, as older or ‘challenged’ tonnage struggle to ride the same wave as their modern equivalents. Charterers with slightly more relaxed vetting able to take ships at lower levels as was shown in Formosa taking an ‘05 built vessel at WS26.5, meanwhile the market was 6 points higher for modern. Today we are another half point up and owners will have the bit between their teeth for more. In the Atlantic, it was West Africa liftings that led the way, with rates climbing up through the WS30’s, as tonnage availability was squeezed off mid-April dates. Again, owners will be eyeing better numbers ahead.

EAST The momentum on freight from last week in the East has continued and last done deal in the market is reported around USD 40 pmt Baltic. Various fob tenders from Middle Eastern suppliers has kept market players busy, and we are also expecting more activity from Indian majors for 2H April cargos. As such, owners’ ideas are building as we continue to see more ships booked away on subs.  WEST The West market has been rather active over the last couple of days around the relatively few vessels which were still open for spot business. A handful of FOB cargoes changed hands off dates in the last decade of April and which consequently led to some ships getting fixed. There are still a few cargoes for sale in the second decade of April which are attracting some attention. Freight fixtures have been concluded at consistently increasing levels since last week and are now in the mid USD 60’s H/C and mid USD 30’s H/F. Focus is largely still on April dates, however, a handful of enquiries have surfaced for first decade May loadings.
