text: AMERICAS US propane inventory levels continue to be of strong interest among both the domestic participants as well as the foreign players.  Ultimately the Mont Belvieu propane pricing structure is dependent upon availability, and as such stock levels are a focal point.   Using the current total US propane stock level of 41.2mmbbls as a starting point, and considering the 5-year average summer build of 43.5mmbbls, it can be calculated that an end-Sep/ely-Oct 2021 propane inventory level of ~84.8mmbbls should be achieved.  Except that this is no ordinary year.     If stocks build by 10% less than average (or 39.1mmbbls), a total of ~80mmbbls will be achieved.  Likewise, if the 5-year minimum summertime build of 37.9mmbbls is seen, a total of less than 80mmbbls would be seen, thus painting a rather bullish pricing picture.    Meanwhile, domestic production levels are mostly recovered after the storm in February, but the petchem sector continues at less than full operating rates, having fallen to the low 70% utilization range.  The domestic res/com sector will likely only realize averages this year, leaving export volumes as the deciding factor, which in Q1 2021 have been light.  The combination of sub-par chemical consumption and generally minimized exports should likely allow for some of the bullishness to be tempered.   As to the current terminal fee market, rates for Apr are seen bid at 4.5, with sellers offering around 5.50.  May values are tentatively pegged at just above that range, indicating that a bit of strength has emerged.  NWE Good cracker run rates continue in the region. Butane the most favorable feedstock, is at 91.5% Naphtha and on the tight side in the region. Split ratio large cargo volumes coming to the region have not hit the resale market. The TOT window remains high single digit premium. The market is still tight though a large volume of exports are arriving int he region due to planned maintenance at local gas fields reducing production. In ARA the switch to summer gasoline spec usually has a marked bearish effect on C4 prices. Though reduced gasoline demand this year has kept butane blending demand low throughout winter.   MED The logistics issues caused by the blockage of the Suez Canal have not had a marked affect on the LPG market in the region yet. VLGCs will be affected with at least four waiting to transit in the north and two at the Southern anchorage. No discussions to place tons in the region due the canal delays have been heard. Moroccan buyers are well covered dampening butane interest in the West Med.

The Aframax market in the North Sea and Baltic looks like will face a downward adjustment, but we still need to keep an eye on the Mediterranean/Black Sea market which can offer an alternative for non-ice owners open on the Continent. The Ice season in the Baltic is slowly coming to an end and owners will try to take advantage of the last premiums paid before restrictions will be lifted.  As we are now looking at early-April fixing window, we expect rates to move sideways in for the North Sea in the week to come, with a downward pressure on rates for cargoes loading ex Baltic. In the Med/Black Sea the market has moved more or less sideways the past week. This week started with a slight upward correction, mainly due to weather delays in a few key ports causing a tighter tonnage list. We expect the market to remain steady/firm.

The Suezmax market has sparked into life this week with the Atlantic basin being the main protagonist. Mediterranean and Black Sea Aframax rates have been too tempting for owners to ignore with a Suezmax reportedly on subjects for a Black Sea/Med' Aframax parcel at the equivalent of 130KT at WS92.3. This will continue to hold vessels in the region and positively impact Td20 and Td6. Owners will be further emboldened by reports that a Guyana/Ta cargo is on subjects 130KT at WS90. In the East, VLCCs are on an upward trajectory which will support Suezmax rates in the region and possibly add some momentum. MEG/East trades 130KT X WX65-67.5 on modern tonnage whilst Td23 feels firmer at WS22.5-25. West Africa/East will likely settle at W75-77.5.

Spot earnings for the big ships flat w-o-w, stable at around USD 18k/day, but market in clear contango thus period deals discussed+done substantially higher. Representative fixtures include vintage 180,000 dwt fetching USD 20,500 for about 12 months, modern Newcastlemaxes closer to USD 25k.

Over the last week there have been some gaping opportunities for owners to push on and capitalise, but instead, they dropped the ball. They may get another bite at the cake this week as the Mediterranean Aframax market has seen a number of parcels find a home on Suezmax. With the Black Sea barely touched for April dates and the list of CPC suitable ships getting tighter, Aframax/Suezmax crossover, may yet yield some upside. The majority of Suezmax are weighted in the Western Mediterranean/UKC and ballasting in for Min flat Augusta may not be appealing at present levels.  Td20 may be a beneficiary, as this could hold vessels away from West Africa whilst Eastern ballasters, with half an eye on proceedings, may sniff out a point or two more. Td23 trades WS20-22 and MEG/East on modern is steady at WS60-62.5.

Rates increasing mainly in the Pacific, while the Atlantic appears more flat, however the trend is firm and expected to continue in this way. In the Atlantic, rates are seeing around USD 28,000 for Continent/Mediterranean and USD 26,000 for Mediterranean/West Africa and USG/Continent paying around USD 29,000. Fronthaul ex ECSA paying Ultras around USD 20,000+1mio gbb, while fronthaul ex Continent/Mediterranean fixing in the low-mid 30's. Strong numbers reported from the Indian Ocean where India/China paying high 30k and backhaul to the Continent in the mid USD 20k. Further East, SE Asia round back to China paying around USD 24,000 and USD 22-23,000 to MEG/India range.

A few more deals this week then last, but not at the volume to force any turn around in numbers. Owners can take some comfort in the fact that rates are unlikely to get much lower, certainly at the current bunker prices. But many are resigned that they are unlikely to jump up in the near future either. Plenty of optimism remains for later in the year, it is simply a case of getting there.  This week falls in the gap between March and April MEG stems, so the remainder of the week, bar a few early birds, will unlikely fire up. MEG/East remains mired in the high WS20’s with charterers trying to chip a fraction of a point from last. In the Atlantic, the longer ton-mile often requires a longer ballast, so bunker prices preventing any major drops. West Africa flatlining at the WS32 going East. Mong/Ningbo at the USD 4.125m level.

Ireland doesn’t play a significant role in LNG, yet St Patrick’s day is well known globally and the celebrations this year will be very different to the famous Guinness or two in the company of good friends. There isn’t too much for Owners to celebrate today though, with rates still languishing below breakeven. However, there is good reason to believe there’s more demand for LNGCs ahead including prompt multi-month deals that have emphasized the delta between steam propulsion, TFDE and 2-stroke. The steams are presenting good value for charterers, particularly given the tender for 24 cargoes into Argentina that can accommodate the smaller parcels sizes of most steam vessels. As a further boost, the warming weather hasn’t held back cargo pricing; LNG is strengthening to an extent that may see more Atlantic cargoes flow East, all good reason for optimism for Owners.     Although no new orders this week, newbuild prices experience a modest increase, which may prove persistent.   In short, the prompt market and into Q2 2021 may not appear too interesting, but looking further forward the market looks set to rebalance

After last week’s pause in increasing rates and activity we see a different trend this week. Rates are firming in both hemispheres. Also backhaul trades are seeing a decent increase. Period market is well back into play with a good spec Kamsarmax achieving 22k for 6/8 months with fwd delivery in June. FFA’s are also pushing up and giving support to the period market.  We see increased demand in the Atlantic and also a very active ECSA market. P1A currently yielding around the 20k mark while P3 is almost priced at 25k.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco released their Apr liftings with some cuts and shortage on propane reported. Apr C3 CP was traded at $584, while C4 CP at $25 less, reflecting the length on butane. Apr/May CP backwardation enlarged to nearly $40, foreseeing more supply out of AG onwards. Despite the Saudi’s shortage on propane, a plenty of Apr Fobs are available from other AG producers. KPC issued tender to sell its late Apr lifting 2/2 split cargo, previously it was reported to award its Q2 sale tender of three similar ratio cargos. Qatar Petroleum also issued two tenders this week to market one full propane and one evenly split cargo for Apr lifting.   FAR EAST Buying sentiments for Apr delivery slightly improved this week, amid potential delays ex US and the rebound on petchem demand. Propane parcel for 2h Apr delivery was bid at Apr FEI plus high teens. Off window several parcels was placed into Japan at similar level, and one sold into EChina at Apr plus 30s with deviation counted. However, Apr FEI/CP was still in negative territory, traded even lower this week at minus 30s, partly due to the anticipation on higher CP as of Saudi cuts.  Apart from this, several buy tenders are running this week. Taiwan FPC secured another 22kt butane at Apr MOPJ minus mid-40s via tender. One Schina PDH user also awarded their buy tender for 23k propane in May delivery into Dongguan. Another EChina PDH user issued a buy tender to purchase 23kt propane delivered into Ningbo monthly from Apr to Jun.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS  Though by now most of the problems related to the storm in February have been overcome, cargo loading issues persist on the Gulf Coast.  Delays and setbacks have beleaguered Gulf Coast terminals, with recent lifting rates having been exacerbated by fog-days – or at least fog-mornings.  Those days appear to have passed, however, as the weather along the upper Texas Gulf Coast is now clear, dry and cool.   The EIA yesterday reported that domestic US propane stocks fell by 170,000bbls as of the week ending 21 Mar, leaving an overall total of 41.029mmbbls of propane in primary storage.  This compares to the 61.379mmbbls recorded in mid-March 2020, a decline of 33%.    Notably, where stock declines were noted in both PADDs I and II, PADD III inventories rose from 25.464mmbbls to 25.920mmbbls.  This is likely due to a combination of curtailed exports and the slow return of the chemical sector.  US production figures, meanwhile, actually declined; from 1.894mmbbls/day on 5th Mar to 1.867mmbbls/day on 12 Mar.   March is all but done, but spot terminal fees for April remain the mid 5ct/gal range, with offers for May at 6cts/gal, or just below.  Corresponding bids are in the low 5cts/gal range for May.  Talk of June has yet to fully materialize, but notional rates were initially being talked at around 6cts/gal.  NWE Market has tracked crude down to some extent although this has not hampered buying interest. March Pro/Nap at -$53pmt is keeping the market supported by the petrochemical buyers. Rising imports from the US have all been snapped up and the market remains on the tight side. ToT Window premiums have come down to April CIF ARA +$5pmt. A bid for large cargo butane was seen in the region for early April delivery was seen. Lifting April  butane values to 90% Naphtha.   MED Has returned to it’s state of calm as demand in the region cools off. Increasing US tons finding their way to the Med has also helped. Moroccan demand has been off this year which has been attributed to persisting global travel restrictions depressing tourism in the country.

EAST The MEG market climbing steadily as we still await Aramco acceptances. The first decade of April has been quite active with 6 spot fixtures already concluded ex MEG. Availability remains pretty thin although some hidden relets could emerge once Saudi is out. Theoretical mid-April MEG positions would be in the US sometime in early/mid-May where many expect the market to be stronger than of current and as such, this could help the East market to firm further. Another interesting point is that we are yet to see any April requirements from Indians, this should also be a bull sign.  WEST Although the activity in the market has come down somewhat in comparison with the two past weeks, the momentum is kept, and the trend is pointing upwards. After a big change in direction, and some healthy activity to follow, it is only natural that market players are taking a step back to regroup. Although there are a few deals done this week too, the list of available ships is only marginally reduced in comparison to what we reported last week. There are still March positions that need to accept some waiting time before being fixed. Based on current freight discussions, western loaders are trading at around 15-16,000 per day for the transpacific route, and close to 20,000 per day in the Atlantic basin.   On the project and newbuilding scene, the activity has picked up quite considerably, and up to 10 newbuilding orders have emerged this week alone. Somewhat unclear about sorting facts and rumours at the moment, but combined with other orders in recent weeks, it’s clear the orderbook has grown considerably.

The week started off with a firming Pacific market much lead by ECSA and NoPac grains. This however took a turn on Tuesday when charterers and owners were uncertain on where the logical market price should be. A big bid/offer gap was evident. P3 is currently priced at around 22k. In the Atlantic, the demand has been low for some time now and the tonnage list is still growing. Mid-week we see some more demand in the North Atlantic, yet the P1A is yielding in the 17k region.

Capes saw further improvement in the Pacific with c5 route up 13% from last week. This was also resulting in less ships ballasting towards Brazil, and from Friday there were signs indicating freight rates would move up. Present c3, Tubarao to China route, is at USD 20 pmt, which is up 21% from last week. Over the past few years a c3 market excess USD 20 has been considered strong, but perhaps this will be the new normal for this year?

Sentiment remained strong and BSI continued positive while Panamax saw a smaller correction. We have seen decent period activity with Supramax delivery Far East being fixed mid 15k for a year. Furthermore, Ultramax open WC India/MEG area are seeing above 40k for a trip to Far East and mid 20s for a trip to the Atlantic. The Pacific basin seem to maintain strong while the Atlantic remains as of last week after a smaller correction. We do expect another positive week ahead with rates for 1 year + to keep climbing.

Once again, another week of higher bunker prices and ever lower Worldscale rates taking its toll on owners returns. Coupled with the disappointing outcome of last week’s decision by OPEC to essentially maintain the status quo and not inject the expected 1.5m barrels into the global supply chain, certainly compounds the misery. In a market awash with Oil Company relets, whose desire to keep the vessels moving and thus minimize losses, applies pressure on the independent owners to compete. Quiet mutterings of warm layup remain mutterings at present, but with continued current conditions, these may increase in volume. Certainly if you lack a scrubber. But we should not forget that there remains plenty of optimism for the summer and beyond, as the world (and our market) hopefully returns to a form of normality.

Whatever the underlying reason(s), the appetite for eastbound Suezmax moves continues to grow. This naturally brings increased tonne miles and rocketing bunker prices head to head.  Owners can only mitigate rising bunker levels by demanding higher freight. This is a particularly burning issue for non-scrubber vessels. Rate wise, there has been a moderate uptick in Suezmax freights over the last week or so, but unfortunately this has done very little to improve an owner’s bottom line.  USG and West Africa rates have steadily firmed with Td20 trading WS57.5 with a firm outlook. East markets have started to absorb this firmer sentiment as owners are talking low WS60's for MEG/East whilst Td23 should trade WS18-20.  Owners will continue to hedge further bunker volatility by asking for more money.

The Aframax market in the North Sea and Baltic have been firmer this week, and rates are still under upward pressure. A decent cargo volume in the North Sea for the 2nd decade coupled with a busier 3rd decade ex Baltic left owners with expectations that they could push for higher rates.  The tonnage list is already quite slim in the North Sea basin and with the Caribs and Mediterranean offering viable alternatives, we expect rates to stay firm in the week to come. In the Med/Black Sea we have seen a small downwards correction in rates over the course of the week before stabilizing at current levels. A number of West Mediterranean positions have started to ballast towards Caribs in order to take part in the firm market there, resulting in a tighter list of Black Sea players. In the week to come we expect mainly the Black Sea to be the driving force of this market.

Spring is a time of renewal, and having endured a torrid few weeks we do see some encouraging signs for LNG shipping. After falling from record highs to unsustainable lows, rates appear to have bottomed out and if anything may be starting to firm again. The main drivers are on the demand side, as a flurry of spot and term enquiries hit the market this week with more to come. The cargo market is also encouraging, with forward pricing in both Europe and Asia considerably higher than last year. Back to the shipping market though, and the supply side remains challenging due to prompt availability and a number of sublets joining the fight for spot and term business. It’s too soon to report green shoots, but owners and charterers will be watching carefully in the coming weeks. There were no newbuilding orders placed this week.

The strong physical dry bulk market has been picked up by capital market participants with rising asset values and continued strong rates translating into higher share prices and premium pricing to NAV, which in turn may tempt other listed companies to follow Belships example of raising capital for growth. We had another week where we saw the values increase across the line. Seanergy acquired Capesize BULK SWITZERLAND (2010, Imabari, 181k dwt) at Usd 25.6 mill, which is up from the sale of COLOGNY (2011, TESS CEBU, 180k dwt) at Usd 22.9 mill a month ago and will set a new benchmark for 10 year olds. Other notable sales include LADY GIOVI (2007, Mitsui, 82k dwt) reported sold for Usd 16.1 mill to Castor Maritime. For comparison the one year younger Oshima built Kamsarmax FORTUNE RAINBOW was sold for Usd 14mill three weeks back. Another interesting sale was EASTERN EDELWEISS (2012, Hantong, 57k dwt), which was liquidated in bank sale in June last year for Usd 8.1 mill, now resold for Usd 11.8 mill.   Although activity in the tanker markets remains limited in terms of completed transactions, we see an increasing number of buying enquiries seeking to take advantage of the current correction in values and position themselves for the upcoming market rebound which seems to have become the general consensus among most market players. Many buyers were in the running for ex Xihe owned VLCC CHANG BAI SAN 2012 SWS built which ended up being sold to Pantheon for Usd 44 mill. In the clean sector, the two sisterships LEOPARD SUN (2013, SPP, 50k dwt) and LEOPARD MOON (2013, SPP, 50k dwt) have now been sold at Usd 21.4 mill each setting a well needed benchmark for units of such vintage considering that the last comparable sale dates back to November. We expect volume of sale to remain limited in the short term with sellers choosing to stand their ground therefore widening the existing bid offer spread.

EAST The sentiment on freight seems about to turn in the East on the back of more requirements in the market, and subsequently less ships being available on prompt basis like before. March fixing in the AG is pretty much done, and a handful of players have already started working freight for April loading. The Adnoc acceptances were published earlier this week, and the only pending acceptances for April, being Aramco, is expected from early next week.  WEST A long-awaited activity increase has finally resurfaced in the West VLGC market, albeit the majority of vessels fixed this week were off first half April dates rather than that of March. Several vessels have been fixed at rates hovering OPEX and there are still some uncovered cargoes left for both end March and the first half of April, however, it seems inevitable that we will see a handful of vessel-overhang as March enquiries wipe out and all eyes turn to April.  In other news, this week following a newbuilding order at the end of last year, one of the largest VLGC owners in the market has declared options for three more VLGCs for delivery in 2023. That is bringing the total order book up to 44 vessels.

text: AMERICAS The last few weeks have seen US propane inventories decline at surprising rates, but the accuracy of the data has been questioned since the devastating storms, a national US holiday, intermittent fog, regional production outages, massive (but short-lived) domestic demand and petrochemical downtime have each played a part in shaping the market.  This week, though, both market sentiment and the EIA data indicate that things seem generally back on track since the government reported a week-over-week decline of just 47,000bbls – effectively an even draw – and leaving total US propane stocks at 41.199mmbbls.  Some expectations were calling for a draw of 3 (or more) million barrels, while at least one observer was calling for a 1mmbbl build. We like to remind our customers the monthly eia inventories are much more accurate than the weekly’s.  Propane values at Mont Belvieu reacted with mild weakness, not the kind that might be associated with the end of winter drawdowns, and remains in the low 90’s/gallon.  Arbitrage economics did improve, however, and while export volumes have been limited as of late, at this point the terminals are all up and running at prescribed rates.  We are calling the export market for 2 Q Bid 5.50 and offered 6 cpg.  NWE The prompt European propane market has been weak, and demand for refined products in remains low. March/April backwardation is decreasing, now at minus $25pmt down from minus $30pmt. Double digit premiums to April CIF ARA are being discussed in the TOT window. We are seeing the widest Pro/Nap spread of the year so far at March minus $52pmt. A vessel headed for Europe diverted towards Panama tightening the prompt market. Large cargo butane in the region is at 88% Naphtha.  MED Discussions picked up this week with Cepsa public offer of 4KT butane FOB Algeciras. Their best offer of $588pmt FOB, did not find a buyer.

text: MEG Apr CP has plunged to $580 from $600 earlier this week, reflecting the overlength on FOBs. FOB discussions are under heavy discounts, as limited buying interests against ample supply. KPC is reported to award its sale tender for three evenly split cargos from Apr to Jun lifting at CP minus high teens discounts. And following this, another trader tendered to resell similar cargos. Qatar Petroleum also tendered to sell one mid Apr lifting full propane, which shall attract more buying interests due to more propane outlets in the EAST for the time being.    FAR EAST Cash premiums for Apr delivery cargos slid down. Bids for 23k propane parcel of 2h Apr delivery were shown in window at Apr FEI plus low teens, while sellers’ target at high 20s. Apr FEI/CP was traded at minus 30s, which is quite frustrating for some sellers with non Us origin cargos. This being said, petchem demand slowly rebounded as players emerging to seek feedstocks either for PDH use or for replacement of Naphtha in cracking, which will relatively absorb some surplus volume. Taiwan FPCC tendered to buy flexible ratio within 46kt for Apr delivery and secured one 11/11 parcel at Apr MOPJ minus low 30s. Another NChina petchem player also issued buy tender for similar cargo with such flexibility. One SChina PDH importer tendered in advance to seek a 23/0 parcel for May delivery, and its last tender for Apr delivery did not award. Apart from these, one Korean player tendered to buy 23k C3 for 2h Apr delivery, and its last tender for 11/11 was reported not awarded either.

Another week that has seen a flurry of dry transactions with values continuing their unhindered upward drive. The Supramax/Ultramax sector has seen five vessels changing hands with the notable sale of Japanese controlled BASIC PORTLAND (61k dwt, 2016 Sanoyas) which achieved Usd 21.5m from Greek buyers. The transaction illustrates well the current momentum considering that only last week the same owners disposed of BULK HERO ( 61k dwt, 2016 Shin Kurushima) at Usd 20.5m. Signs of ever increasing buying enquiries with ongoing negotiations that clearly means that the upward trend is set to continue. On the larger segments, Panamax/Kamsarmax also joy of strong activity with four vessels being sold whereas Capesize slowly seem to follow suit with a number of candidates being placed for sale suggesting further sales in the near future. Also worth mentioning the Newcastlemax resale 2021 SWS at Usd 53m where initial expectations were region Usd 50m. Prices are clearly moving north in case anyone was in doubt.  OPEC+ rolls over current production levels into April, and Saudi Arabia will only gradually return its 1mbpd additional cut. Not exactly what tanker owners would be hoping for, and leaves downside risk for earnings the next couple of months. However our outlook for improving tanker rates in the second half of the year remains unchanged; certainly a view shared by many owners who are increasingly getting ready to move for attractive candidates. Our read being that we have passed the bottom as far as values go (save for the oldest ones) and sellers will increasingly hold the upper-hand. Exciting times ahead.

Although we’ve seen a correction in spot shipping rates over the last few weeks, we are now seeing signs of the market leveling off. However, there isn’t much activity in the spot market overall. On the term side, market participants seem to be approaching owners earlier than in previous years in trying to line up term coverage for next winter. At this stage, owners appear to be holding on to some of the gains in term rates achieved in November and December 2020. Despite vessel utilization risk in the spot market for the upcoming periods, owners looking ahead with one eye on winter past. No LNG newbuild orders recorded this week either.

In the North Sea and Baltic markets, the rates have moved sideways for the past week. Despite a break in the Baltic program in the 2nd decade of March, we see increased activity in the North Sea basin as well as some long-haul fuel enquiries. Charterers will look at other sizes as an alternative to Aframaxes, but we expect the market to remain stable with a potential for a small uptick in rates. In the Mediterranean/Black Sea the market has had a downward correction since last week, dropping about 20 points on benchmark routes. This is mainly due to a reduction in delays, and activity on the cargo side has also come off somewhat. That said, cargoes are still coming into the market at a steady pace, so it will be interesting to see if there is enough action for owners to hold rates at current levels in the week to come.

The common aim of most owners this week has been to hedge by looking to go short, and therefore repeat market, or go long and be recompensed for their efforts. Since the beginning of the downtrend, Eastern ballasters have been a key depressor of West Africa/East moves, but turbulent bunker prices have made owners question whether last done rates justify a long haul gamble.  Owners appear reluctant to forecast what their backhaul bunkers could be, and this is where a possible silver lining lies. West Africa/East was booked last night on what we believe was a no heat stem 130KT x WS63, which is up. Throw into the mix that it was a relet and we have further grounds for optimism. USG is firm with TA trading 145KT x 60 whilst MEG/East has a more sombre feel with WS53 being repeated a few times. Td23 trades WS15.

Having said that, we do not expect any significant changes to the vessel balance versus cargo inquiries ex USG for some time. A West Africa FOB tender was floated this week as well and did receive some interest from various traders.

FFA values and volumes also picked up – however in the North Atlantic the slow trend has continued. P1A is currently priced at mid/high 18k. Also expectations of an additional 1.5mbls injected in to the daily output after the OPEC+ meeting on Thursday, all point to good signs for our tanker market. text: MEG Saudi Aramco raised up Mar propane CP by $20 to $625 and Butane CP by $10 to $595, which is more or less within expectations. Apr propane CP was traded at $575, while spread to butane narrow to $20, expecting on Butane demand recovery due to summer. Evenly split cargos for Apr lifting was shown at low teens discount while buyer expects more discounts as netback into EAST market still not pleasant, and also the deep backwardation into May for around $37, despite the weakening freight.  FAR EAST A flurry of bids in the window this week. Bid idea for 1h Apr delivery was at Apr FEI plus mid 20s while offer at low 30s, and 2h Apr discussing idea at $3-4 lower. One SChina Importer awarded via tender to secure one 2h Apr delivery 11/11 split at partially Apr CP plus low teens and partially Apr FEI plus 20s. Another SChina PDH user issued tender for 23k C3 for 1-10 Apr delivery into Dongguan. And one Korean Importer also tendered to buy 11/11 split delivered into Daesan delivered in 1h Apr.

It’s another strong week for Supramaxes in all areas with slight firmer dominance in the Pacific basin. Period deals still pushing up the rates. Supras being fixed now already at high 14k and Ultramaxes at 16,000. Fronthauls from Black Sea being covered at 35,000. Continent continuing with firm pace where usual scrap runs from Continent to Mediterranean being hedged at mid 20,000. From USG, Ultramaxes cashing in around 34,000 for TA business and ECSA following with solid numbers for where Ultras were holding above 20k + 1mill for fronthauls. Besides these strong numbers some suggest there is tonnage building up in the Atlantic though. From East, a trip from MEG to Bangladesh traded off at 36,000 on an Ultramax. Supra from South Africa to China ended up fixing 16,500 + 600k bb.

text: AMERICAS The US market has rebounded quickly from the freeze that impacted many of the export terminal operations in the US Gulf. However, some reverberating effects remain. Delays have limited spot activity in March, and many of the terminals have shifted their spot focus to April- For this reason, ships are abundant and freight levels are low (around 55 pmt basis Houston/ Chiba). It has been reported that as many as 80 unladen VLGC's stand available to load in the US Gulf in the next 30 days. The good news is that fog has played less of a role than expected in the days following the storm- and the forecast looks promising for the time being. The premium that Marcus Hook cargos had commanded (in efforts to opt out of potential storm and fog delays in gulf) had reached a premium close to one cent per gallon to cargos offered in the US Gulf- but has since leveled off. At present offers for April, cargos are being discussed close to 5cpg, buyers coming from the mid 4's. Yesterday (Wednesday) the EIA reported a draw of 2.2 million barrels for the week ended February 26th on the back of seasonal heating demand-the bulk draw came from the Gulf (964,000 bl) and the Midcontinent (786,000 bl).  NWE The physical window premiums continue to strengthen in the region now assessed at CIF ARA +$12.5pmt for March. This due partly to a cold spell in Europe and partly due to the pro/nap spread remaining at -$27pmt. Keeping both heating and industrial demand high. A trend expected to continue with crude above $60bbl and forecast to remain strong. Imports from the US are being looked at with traders focusing on 1-10 April. To be sure that they arrive in the same month as loading as the April/ May backwardation remains a steep +$24pmt.   MED Values remain steady and with minimal cargo discussions occurring. An early March US Gulf loaded VLGC heading to the East Med is expected to keep the market balanced. In the West Med butane values are seen to be strengthening on sentiment, due to the lack of firm discussions.

Crude spot market remains sad and depressing, but another modern VLCC was sold this week when Hunter announced the exit of its 1,5 year old HUNTER ATLA (delivered Sept 2019). A price of USD 84.5 mill paid by ADNOC is considered firm by some market players, but in our books it is a fair level – especially in light of the recent pricing from leading shipyards. Generally speaking, there are not many sellers of modern tonnage in this space today. Still, we see an impressive number of takers for older crude tankers, and prices keep up fairly well.  Given the scrap-levels on offer, the poor earnings in the (conventional) market and the increasing bunker prices we had expected more older ships sold for demolition. There is a strong demand in the product market and both MR and LR2 tonnage in decent condition and age do get a lot of attention.  The dry markets continue to display strength. Supramax rates are up excess 40% the last week, breaking USD 20k/day on Wednesday for the first time in a decade. Even crazier, the historically less volatile handies are also on fire where the Baltic has recorded over a month of daily consecutive gains and are now at excess USD 19k/day. There are a lot of bidders on available ships for sale and we expect values to quickly follow suit. Also this week we see a lot of activity on region 10yrs old Kamsars, and again the values are increasing slightly from last week. Less transactions for the modern Eco units, but that is not due to a lack of buyers. There are many owners scavenging the market for Eco units in fear of future IMO requirements, but there is simply very few units for sale. The only one this week was the BULK HERO (61k dwt, Universal, 2016) sold at at USD 20.6mill, which will represents a new benchmark on the 5yrs old Ultramax.

Market kept the momentum from previous week. BSI raising with magnificent gain on all routes. Strong physical demand in both basins, though the feeling is toppish. Push after Chinese New Year in the Asian market seems still have some room to improve. Rates in the Atlantic reaching high USD 20k and low USD 30k, depends on origin. Supra reporting at USD 28k fixed from Cont to East Med with scrap cargo, and similar rates paid for clinker cargo from East-West Med to West Africa.  Rates in the USG for TA is getting close to FH rate USD 31k-33k for Supra-Ultra. It was rumored Ultramax fixed delivery Mobile USD 42k TCT with petcoke to India. Rates in the Indian Ocean were the “winners” of the week. Supra fixing at solid USD 20k for backhaul cargo from MEG to USG. And Ultramax reporting USD 16k plus USD 600k delivery South Africa for TCT to China.

It has been a flat week for the LNG Shipping markets. Sentiment continues to dip further with limited activity and soft demand for shipping. There were requirements to be worked, however the impact on rates remain minimal. The continuous increase in prompt availability across both basins, potential cargo cancellations from US projects, constant decline in product prices as we move closer to Q2 and a closed West – East arbitrage window did contribute to the lack of shipping opportunities. Multi month and short term inquiries seem to be put on hold as Charterers take the “wait and see” approach to further evaluate their shipping portfolio. Nonetheless, we do expect some interest in the coming weeks or months as Charterers look to take advantage of the current market conditions. Utilization is imperative and this could mean more inclination from Owners to work competitive rates now for longer duration to brace the shoulder months. On Newbuilding activities, Maran Gas seem to have added to their order tally at Samsung.

After last week’s rally in the Panamax market, this week started off with a more quiet tone. This was expected after the major increase in rates we have experienced. We are now facing a market where chrts and owners are trying to find a common ground. It has been very quiet in the North Atlantic and also in the Pacific. Volumes out of ECSA is still keeping up. P1A is currently yielding in the low/mid 20’s while P3A is priced at 20-21k.

Bottom reached for the big ships? Activity still modest as Far East players returning to the scene, with average daily earnings for typical 180,000-tonners down more than 20 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 12k. Area of most concern is fronthaul, where disappointing volumes coupled with growing number of ballasters result in China-Brazil-China value down 40 pct to par with Pacific r/v at USD 10k/day.  Far East ore and coal volumes healthy but not sufficient to absorb supply. Some support coming from smaller segments on fire, with substantial number of babycape/postpmax/kamsarmax stems now being covered on Cape tonnage. Period in doldrums, much due cocktailed mismatch spot/ffa's/general expectations.

This week has seen a number of Suezmax fix and/or appraise Aframax stems in North West Europe and the Mediterranean basin. This may hold vessels away from West Africa and provide some short-term stability.  In the pre-Covid era, any tightening of the UKC/MED list would have almost certainly firmed Td20, but slap bang in the middle of this pandemic, all it can manage to do is maintain rates. There are some positive signs in the USG where Aframax have firmed and may drag Suezmax into the game, but any benefit from these crossover scenarios is likely to remain highly regionalized. West Africa East trades 130 x WS59 with MEG/East on modern trying to move on from WS55. Td23 has shown some signs of resistance with most owners holding for WS20 S/S.

In the Nsea/Baltic market, rates have remained flat the past week. As ice restrictions are extended in the Baltic, owners are ballasting in other areas seeking for higher returns. Activity has been sluggish for the current fixing window of early March with relets putting some pressure on the rates. We expect rates to be maintained at these levels with a downside risk. The upward correction in the Med/Bsea has continued this week as increased cargo activity combined with delays in the straits keep tightening the tonnage list. As long as Suezmaxes do not come into play and cap the Aframax market we expect the market to remain firm in the week to come.

There was a slight whiff of optimism in the VLCC market at the end of last week, with emphasis on the Atlantic basin. Rates broke through the mid WS30’s for Wafr/China runs, and amid the unprecedented icy spell in the US south USG export cargoes touched USD 4.5 million for the same destination. However, many of the deals concluded last week came to nothing, with ships failing subs left right and center. The MEG market was, and still is dilapidated, kept down by a number of discounted ships with various backgrounds. Rising crude prices has brought with it a hike in bunker prices too, making it difficult to calculate home any positive voyage alternatives.

text: AMERICAS Last week’s winter storm halted hydrocarbons production in the Permian Basin of West Texas.  Simultaneously, feedstock deliveries to the chemical sector were stopped as that system shut down, as at the same time millions of barrels of Raw Make production was lost.  All that while the Houston Ship Channel was closed. The weather has now abated and the various systems are being returned to service much more quickly than anticipated.  Most are indicating that the lost time will be caught up with by the end of the month (if not sooner).     The EIA on Wednesday reported that propane stocks in the US drew by a surprisingly high 5.2mmbbls as of the week ending 19 Feb.  The market had assumed a draw of between 3.0 and 5.0mmbbls.  The prospect of fog remains a possibility, and with that comes the potential impact on LPG vessel transits which could limit export volumes and, therefore, inventory draws.  Meanwhile, WTI strength should foster production levels and allow propane stocks to begin recovery in Q2. Terminal fees are on the Gulf Coast are bid at 3.5cts/gal, with offers at/above 4cts/gal.  Meanwhile, though, an East Coast March fixture is believed to have occurred at 5.25cts/gal.  NWE Strength in the front of the market remains although CIF ARA has not tracked the rapid rise in Mt Belvieu. The cold weather in the US affected East Coast exports leading to a lower than anticipated volume of LPG finding it’s way to NWE from 1H March Marcus Hook. This in turn has pushed up the CIF ARA window premiums which are assessed at CIF ARA March +$11.5pmt for a 1H March TOT stem. March Propane/Naphta spread in the region is now -$44pmt the widest spread so far in 2021.  MED  Has been quiet of late and with the US delays having a knock on effect and causing some supply uncertainty.

This week has seen a number of Suezmax fix and/or appraise Aframax stems in North West Europe and the Mediterranean basin. This may hold vessels away from West Africa and provide some short-term stability.  In the pre-Covid era, any tightening of the UKC/MED list would have almost certainly firmed Td20, but slap bang in the middle of this pandemic, all it can manage to do is maintain rates. West Africa East trades 130 x WS59 with MEG/East on modern trying to move on from WS55. Td23 has shown some signs of resistance with most owners holding for WS20 S/S.

EAST February was overall quite dull in terms of spot activity in the MEG. With a weak start to March fixing and reportedly no Saudi cargoes nor any Indian requirements for the first 10 days of March, spot freight is still tumbling downwards. We have seen a few cargoes being mentioned for second decade March dates, but with a market getting a little bit weaker by the day and availability still remaining long, charterers seem to be in no rush for now.  WEST US Gulf is experiencing delays at the load terminals and uncertainties with more fog approaching is keeping freight markets on hold. We are fast approaching OPEX earnings for the owners, but even at these earnings, there are arguably not enough cargoes to be lifted ex-US in March to employ all the ships coming open.

There was a slight whiff of optimism in the VLCC market at the end of last week, with emphasis on the Atlantic basin. Rates broke through the mid WS30’s for Wafr/China runs, and amid the unprecedented icy spell in the US south USG export cargoes touched USD 4.5 million for the same destination. However, many of the deals concluded last week came to nothing, with ships failing subs left right and center. The MEG market was, and still is dilapidated, kept down by a number of discounted ships with various backgrounds. Rising crude prices has brought with it a hike in bunker prices too, making it difficult to calculate home any positive voyage alternatives.

Boom! A surprisingly strong dry market has caught most off guard, and we have this week seen the highest rates for both Panamax and Supramax since 2010. The surge is on back of strong demand for grains and coal in the Far East, but also a general pick up in demand all over. We continue to see a flurry of deals for region 10yrs old Kamsarmax with the KINOURA (82k dwt, Tsuneishi, 2012) sold at USD 18mill, the EVERGLORY (81.5k dwt, Qingdao Beihai, 2012) sold at USD 16mill and the GLOBE ELECTRA/DANAE (81k dwt, STX, 2010) sold at USD 15.75mill each. All in all the sales point towards rising values, with the KINOURA being an exception. The market being most bullish on the Japanese built tonnage which is expected in an upturn, and in the next phase we expect that re-pricing of the Chinese built tonnage will outperform.    Tanker sale and purchase markets remain subdued with limited liquidity. The ever deepening bid/offer spread renders transactions hard to materialize with potential sellers holding back in view of better times. Only three sales to report this week with new downward benchmarks being set in the MR sector with the sale of the Japanese controlled pump-room unit BRIGHT FORTUNE (48k dwt, Iwagi, 2020) at USD 13.75mill.

With improved vessel availability in both Basins and a quiet cargo market, rate levels discussed in the LNG shipping market soften further this week. In the Pacific, the holidays saw only a trickle of requirements which failed to support existing levels, pushing headline rates lower as vessel “Owners” continue to compete. The relatively strong earthquake in Japan caused limited impact on demand as no delays were seen and the thermal power plants that were affected restarted quickly. Some Owners are now looking west for employment opportunities, taking the ballast leg into the Atlantic basin in hope of a better market in the coming months. However, the market in the Atlantic Is also quiet/subdued. Recent loadings from the US Gulf seem to be heading into Europe for discharge, circulating tonnage back into the basin. The unexpected cold weather in the US Gulf is likely causing some disruption to loadings as terminals battle gas flow, manpower and production issues. Looking forward, its still cold in Europe and demand from China may develop as many return to work after the Spring festival. This extra demand could help reduce some of the vessel availability.  No newbuild orders for larger LNG vessels seen placed this week.

The Capesize market have seen a tremendous recovery over the last week. The two main routes with iron ore from Brazil and Australia to China is up by 23% and 46%, and the total time charter basket of all routes is up by 48%. This is backed by a very firm Panamax market and an increasingly strong belief amongst market participants in the Dry Bulk segment.

You might remember 2008, and this week has really given us the same feeling. From 50k being done for a Baltic round one day, and the next day 110k being done. It is extremely hot in the North Atlantic. In a normal market we would need ice conditions in both St. Lawrence and the Baltic to achieve some premium from the P1A. Now we experience sky high rates in a sudden for both breach of INL cgos and regular P1A. Commodity prices have risen significantly, and with cold weather hitting Europe the demand for coal has come up. It is hard to put a figure one it, but the Indices are lagging. We see 40k vs 35k on regular Atlantic trades. In the Pacific we also see rates coming up with 20k being done for a regular Pac round. The Baltic Indices have not been this high since 2010.

Sentiment remained strong and the BSI continued its positive mode during the week.  Panamaxes are rallying and although positive indexes the BSI not in same pace as PMX.  We seen decent period activity and worth mentioning the yesterdays close. Period activity was prevalent, the Star Columba (56,530 2012) open Bin Thuan 18/19 February was heard to have been fixed for period in the mid $13,000s but further terms were not disclosed. The Star Apus (63,123 2014) scrubber fitted open Fujairah was failed at $19,900 for minimum 3 months trading.  Baltic Ice market remains as its own with a 57kdwt fixed dop West Mediterranean via Baltic to India redel Port Said @ 19,500 and 100k range on the bigger sizes – further out on the week smx holding bids 25k for scrap runs from the Continent.  We expect a positive week ahead.

The Suezmax market in the West is still looking interesting. North Sea, Mediterranean/Black Sea and USG market are all looking tight-ish, making charterers in West Africa focusing mainly on eastern ballasters. This has put pressure on the West Africa market, and owners are doing their best to push rates further. We are hovering around high 50's, but with an upward potential towards the end of the week. In the East, we have had decent activity the last week. Tonnage-wise the MEG-market is well covered, but with many owners looking towards West Africa on their ships, the actual list in the East is rather balanced. One of the main factors for all markets right now, is the increasing bunker prices. There are very few ships left with cheap bunkers, and this alone will help push rates further.

Xin nian kuai le (Happy Chinese New Year). We welcome in the year of the Ox, which is meant to bring stability and calmness and it has certainly started that way. Calm, as there has been very little for owners to get their teeth into; and stable as rates have gone nowhere. It also coincides with the gap between the February and March MEG stems, which exacerbates the feeling of quiet. Chinese tonnage quickly snaring the compatriot cargoes that are available on COA, leaving others to fight over the remaining business. With the MEG so quiet (a disappointing sub 90 fixtures for February), much of the action has been in the Atlantic. Petrobras leading the charge with a couple of deals, but were able to keep rates suppressed. Alarming for owners, who given the oil price, are calculating in some bigger bills for their bunkers.

Ice conditions persist in the Baltic helping ice-class vessels to pocket 10k/day while delays in major discharge ports of North Sea, alternatives of other markets and a tight window have brought cross-North Sea runs at positive returns. As we move forward, we expect rates to be maintained at these levels but with a downside risk. Freight rates have therefore continued its downward trend, and some are worried that we might even reach closer to OPEX levels before we see the freight market turn. In terms of deals done this week, one trader took a ship on subs for a short time charter in the USD high teens per day, and one Japanese player was reported fixing a ship from North Australia in the mid/high USD 30s Baltic. text: ASIA Traders and end-users are trickling back to their desks after ushering in the year of the Ox.  Western suppliers and traders are hoping this will spark some buying,  which has been slow to materialize despite what appears to be low inventory throughout the region.  Maybe it is the high absolute levels, (although low as a percentage of Brent), or the hope of increased Middle East availability based on the Saudis recent announcement, or the belief that US Tons have nowhere else to go, but whatever the reason, the lack of buying interest has definitely caused a few sellers to reexamine their thinking. Whatever the reason what now seems clear is that exports from the US to Asia will be reduced at the current arb levels.

text: AMERICAS Its hard to stress the severity of the winter storm that has unfolded across Texas from both an energy and more importantly humanitarian standpoint. Millions of people were left without electricity and water for days on end - and as of Thursday morning, while electricity is being restored- due to infrastructure failures- water pressure has yet to return- and a boil order remains in effect. With regard to LPG, the big question is what will be impacted on a larger scale, exports or demand. The four major terminals on the US Gulf have all been impacted, all be it to different extremes. One believes that once they are operational again, they will be able to make up for lost exports in 5 days. Another hopes to be caught up by March 1st, and a third thought they would be up and running by the weekend at the earliest, and would not be fully caught up until march at the earliest, with no spot cargos until April. The last has declared a full force majeure and will have a better idea by Friday of the timeline to recovery. With regard to domestic demand, Severe winter weather has caused nearly every major chemical complex in Texas to board up the windows. Many shut over the weekend as feedstock, power, and natural gas supply has been interrupted at many locations.  All that said, cargo discussion has not been completely neglected. A couple of Marcus Hook cargos have been offered last decade march, just below 5 cents- the seller was commanding a premium to the Gulf coast FOB’s due to logistical simplicity (weather, fog, delays etc). In the US Gulf- an all-propane FOB was being discussed much closer to four cents earlier in the week. Though that has yet to change hands and now looks less likely due to the dwindling LST/FEI arbitrage. Due to the holiday weekend, the EIA’s much-anticipated inventory report came out a day late, showing an in line with expectations draw of 2.9 million barrels.

Stock-listed dry companies are wasting no time monetizing their newly repriced shares as hard cash to scale their business. Eagle Bulk has acquired three 2011 Dayang built Supramaxes at region USD 29m financed with USD 21m in cash and 329k common shares which proves its financial flexibility as a listed company. We expect more such deals to materialize as long as P/NAV pricing remains favorable. Good activity in general on the dry side with several 10yrs benchmark sales to report this week. Lemos-backed Valhal Shipping picked up the scrubber fitted Capesize COLOGNY (180k dwt, 2011, TESS CEBU) for USD 22.9m. The last benchmark sale for a 10yrs old was the scrubber fitted CAPE ISTANBUL (176k dwt, 2011, HHIC-Phil) which went for USD 19m early this year. Albeit not directly comparable, the whopping USD 4m gap undoubtedly demonstrates the positive shift in sentiment. Another benchmark deal was the KIND SALUTE (96k dwt, 2011, Imabari) at USD 16.5m with docking due May 2021. To compare, SANGEET (96k dwt, 2012, Imabari) was sold for USD 15.5m late last year. Lastly, on Ultras we saw the ULTRA WOLLONGONG (62k dwt, 2011, Oshima) exchange hands at USD 13.8m.   Four mid-2000 built Aframax have been sold this week reaffirming the downward trend in values witnessed so far this year especially for units of such vintage. Teekay has disposed of its two 2008 built sisterships EXPLORER SPIRIT & NAVIGATOR SPIRIT (105k dwt, 2008, Tsuneishi) at Usd 16m each while Castor Maritime has purchased DUBAI HOPE & DUBAI HARMONY (115k dwt, 2005, Samsung) at Usd 13.6m. The correction in values becomes particularly apparent when compared to the sale of the 2009 built STAVANGER FALCON &  STAVANGER EAGLE (105k dwt, 2009 Sumitomo) which were sold earlier this year at USD18.25m each.

LNG shipping market continues to soften this week as the nearest fixing opportunities get pushed to March and beyond. There is no hiding from the fact that the recent build up in available tonnage has caused a deep dive on the daily rates in both Atlantic and Pacific basins, as owners compete with subletters for the limited spot requirements left in the market. Furthermore, with the Lunar New Year starting this week, we don’t expect any catalyst to the current market situation in the near term especially in the East, possibly adding to the injury for those who have available tonnage in the Pacific after the winter cargoes have been discharged. All things said, it is good to remember that this ongoing correction in charter rates was anticipated, and moreover, LNG shipping market has been epitomized by high volatility and seasonality during the last few years. Thus, it is no big surprise that we see a switch in focus from spot market opportunities to term market opportunities as market participants are already starting to gauge the next winter, however there still seems to be a bit of discrepancy in the rate ideas between charterers and owners. Finally, there are no LNG newbuilding orders to report this week, but it is noteworthy that earlier in the week Qatar Petroleum reached FID on its North Field Expansion project, which may indicate a greenlight for their LNGC newbuilding programme in due course.    Wishing all our readers a Happy and Healthy Lunar New Year – Gong Xi Fa Cai!

The market is continuing its positive trend since the start of the week.  Mainly driven by South America and North Atlantic trade.  On Wednesday we had 20 vessels reported fixed for ECSA trade alone.  The North Continent is also working for full pistons and we have seen +30,000 pd for quick rounds.  It’s not only grains driving the market but also minerals have been active.  Period rates continues to push and with +500 on BPI every day it is not likely to ease off any time soon.

Different stories from the two basins this week where slowing sings in the Pacific ahead of the Lunar New Year, whereas the Atlantic basin is steaming. From the USG, Ultras fetching in the mid 20’s for TA and around USD 30,000 for FH. Backhaul rates from the Continent and East Mediterranean trading in the high teens/USD 20,000, while ECSA fronthaul is around USD 16,000+600k gbb. In the Pacific, Nopac and Aussie rounds are fixing around USD 12,000.

Chinese New Year is here, and as expected the activity is lower. This results in rates dropping further, down to present average of USD 10,750. For West Australia, the demand for tonnage has been limited for some time, and miners are presently looking at March dates, already. Out of Brazil, ships arriving end of February and up to early March dates have been fetching decent rates, USD 17 pmt and more. Whilst for index dates, the freight has been closer to USD 14 level, although there have been few fixtures for such dates.

Another week and more of the same. Rates have remained continually depressed as we build up to the Chinese New Year. The lack of enquiry ex MEG has been a constant issue and at the time of writing, no enquiry outstanding from the region. The Atlantic has been the major source of activity, but rates have flattered to deceive here also. However, we may see higher rates in the near term as the bunker prices follow the oil market upwards. Bunkers now in excess of USD 500/mt in Singapore and owners will have to take this into account. text: AMERICAS The current US propane inventory situation can be likened to travelling down the highway in a car with a flat tire, a fuel gauge nearing empty and a dirty wind screen:  Something will soon need to change. Speculation as to the US propane inventory data release this week was enthusiastic, but the matter has been settled (for now, at least) as a stock decline of 4.508mmbbls was reported by the EIA Wednesday morning and brought the total US propane inventory level to 51.545mmbbls as of 10 Feb 2021.  Last year at the same time there were 71.822mmbbls in stocks, or a 28% decline YOY.  Domestic production was off by 38,000bbls/day to 2.37mmbls/day while Res/Com demand grew by 714,000bbls/day to 2.204mmbbls/day.  It has been cold, after all, and weather forecasts over the next week or so are calling for extreme temperatures over much of the nation. Exports (both overland and waterborne) of ~1.1mmbbls/day were recorded and seem to have been negatively impacted by a recent spate of fog along the upper Texas Gulf Coast.  The weekly export average is around the 1.6mmbbl/day range. In turn, the Days of Supply has fallen by 4.5 days to 15.6 days.  This is encroaching on historical lows, where the highest level recorded was in the 60-day range.  PADD III (Gulf Coast) stock levels fell this week by 1.726mmbbls to 28.797mmbbls.  This is significant, and additional attention should be paid any time the 30mmbbl level is breached.  PADD III stocks have fallen this year by an average of 2mmbbls per week.  At that rate – and in consideration of the massively cold weather at present – it is easy to calculate that Gulf Coast inventories will in early March be at (or near) 5-year lows.  As of midday Wednesday, however, the Mont Belvieu market showed little, if any, reaction.  Belvieu yawned, in fact, making the situation uncertain and unclear. With rising bunkers and falling rates, owners will be hoping to apply the brakes at some point this week. Something surely has to give. West Africa/East has been pinned down by ballasters and is steady at WS55 and will trade out the remainder of the third decade at similar levels. In isolation, there are some regions that are more stable than others. For example, TD6 appears unlikely to trade sub mid/high WS60's for the balance of the week as the Black Sea tonnage list competes with a very busy Libya program. This in turn may provide a floor for TD20 as Eastern ballasters, who by and large, are looking for long haul, limiting options for the shorter runs into Europe. In the East, TD23 will trade WS17 for a straight run whilst MEG/East (non Basrah) will trade WS47.5-50 on modern.

EAST Adnoc acceptances were released yesterday, this has created some long-awaited vessel demand in AG. That said, most Charterers are in no rush prior to the long weekend coming up with CNY around the corner. Many of the vessels still open on Feb dates in the East are likely to go via Cape and end up in the US last decade March. The same could also be the case for those with potential early march positions, depending on demand and freight levels.  WEST Following a couple of weeks with a fair amount of activity in the West and dominantly the US, the market has taken a bit of a breather this week. A few fixtures have been done, and it seems the freight level established last week in the mid-80’s pmt for the transpacific freight route, has prevailed this week. As we see it, US cargoes for the first decade of March seem to have been covered more or less, however, the Chinese New Year’s celebration seems to halt activity so we’re in for a quiet period until next week.

With the announcement that Star Bulk acquired 3xUltramaxes and 4xKamsarmaxes from Scorpio in a cash and stocks deal and that the remaining 3xUltramaxes are rumoured to be committed, Scorpio is finally exiting the dry bulk segment. There has been rising prices throughout the sales process the last few months on the back of an increasingly bullish sentiment on dry. For comparison, the SBI ZEUS 2016/Mitsui/60kdwt was sold for Usd 18.5 mill end October while the SBI CRONOS 2015/I-S/60kdwt was sold this week for Usd 19.6 mill. This represents at least an increase of 10% in the midst of a grand sell off, which really support the dry story. The straightening of the depreciation curve is in full motion, but further big increases on values would have to come from rising resale prices. The sale of URSULA MANX 2021/TESS-Zhoushan/82kdwt this week and UNA MANX 2021/TESS Zhoushan/82kdwt reported last week at Usd 29.5 mill each demonstrate that resale prices are still hovering around newbuilding prices.    GNMTC of Libya has acquired two more scrubberfitted LR2 newbuilding resales after its recent purchase of a similar resale just delivered from a Japanese builder. The last two vessels will very soon be delivered ex Cosco Shipyard and the price of Usd 52.5 mill each is about 5% lower than the first deal which one would expect as a minimum when comparing Japan vs China yard pricing. Whilst GNMTC might be considered an “exotic” buyer we certainly subscribe to this being a market deal and underlines where ask levels are for brand new tonnage. Goal posts may quickly be moved in what is becoming a sellers’ market for brand new ships, despite the present dire state of the spot market. Values for older/vintage VLCC are still holding up nicely, but the other crude segments of this age have a more brutal reality check with the majority of enquiries being for the 8-10 year old crude and LR2 tankers. Bets will continue to be placed on a rebound of fortunes come 2nd half/end 2021 and into 2022.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco raised Feb CP at $605 for C3 and $585 for C4, up by $55 respectively. Mar C3 CP swap soared up and traded at $588 at the time of writing, and C3/C4 spread narrowed down to $7$, as more equal ratio buying interests emerged this week. Qatar Petroleum released their Mar acceptance with some minor delays reported. Despite the freight is dropping dramatically, Netback on FOBs are still discussed in heavy discounts, especially when Mar/Apr backwardation assessed at $50.  FAR EAST Less activities this week in the window. One 23kt propane for 1h Mar delivery was done at Mar FEI plus $15, and off window similar level was concluded into Japan. There are some concerns on the tighter supply for 2h Mar arrival tons as the result of Feb lifting US cancellations. Together with the coming China Lunar New Year, receivers are moving ahead of time to explore cargos for 2h Mar and even 1h Apr arrival. Hence we’ve seen a flurry of buying tenders this week. A new cracker located in Ningbo issued tender to purchase one full propane cargo for end Mar early Apr arrival. Similarly, another NChina Petchem user also tendered to secure such propane for feedstock. One SChina importer cancelled their buy tender for 1-2 lots of 11/11 delivered in Mar and Apr respectively, as offers reported at FEI plus 40s were yet to attract interests. Taiwan FPCC secured 22kt propane for 2h Mar delivery at Mar FEI plus 20 via tender, meanwhile CPC tendered to buy a parcel of 11/11 for 2h Mar to 1h Apr delivery.

Most of the Owners are willing to hold the line and put some upward pressure on the rates in order to cover opex at least. However, we expect rates to remain at bottom levels as the fundamentals are not there to support a strong bounceback yet. Following last week’s rush of cargoes in the Med/Bsea which resulted in a slight uptick in rates, the market has calmed down again somewhat this week as cargo activity has come off and tonnage builds up again. Also in the Med/Bsea we expect the market to remain at bottom levels in the short run.

The VLCC market continues at a snail’s pace. Rates are being tested in all areas, and with bunker prices on the rise it's more or less negative territory all round unless a ship is scrubber fitted. China Inc. continues to cater for their own, leaving slim pickings for 3rd party owners. The question now is “should I stay or should I go” as the song goes. With plenty of available tonnage basically spot, with the  option of heading west or sticking with the MEG, there’s currently no winners wherever you lean. If this continues the ultimate question will be “should I trade at all”. With USG export cargoes on offer now loading medio march, the commitment is well into spring for a China destination, leaving little hope of a recuperation any time soon.

An armada of Eastern ballasters appears to have sealed the fate of West Africa and the MEG, at least as far as the third decade of February is concerned . The obvious effect is that TD20 will trade down to the low W50's whilst a Wafr/East run will  be lucky to hold onto high W50's/low W60's tops. However, it's  not all doom and gloom as was highlighted in the Caribs last night. The prompt nature of the USG and Caribbean market has afforded it some insulation from the marauding ballasters. An East Coast Mexico/TA run was booked at 145kt x W50, which highlights that pockets of opportunity do remain, however bleak the macro picture looks. MEG/EAST will correct down to low/mid W50's on modern and TD23 will follow this trend finding a home at low/mid teens

The LNG market have continued with a breather following weeks of reduced intensity on LNG trading and ship chartering efforts since the heights of mid-January 2021. Cargo prices and headline shipping rates have corrected to levels of today. The shoulder months are upon us as vessel availabilities stack up from redeliveries. This week’s shipping fixtures have been reported with rate levels at five-digits and back to round-trip economics, down from the “three-way” terms which shipowners and subletters have enjoyed during the last two months. Despite the backwardation and the dwindling sentiments amongst shipowners, it is not to forget that the shoulder months of this year are still expected to be relatively healthier in terms of LNG shipping rate levels as compared to the previous years of 2019 and 2020.  This winter has been epitomised by the supply squeeze for both LNG and LNG shipping. Despite months of planning ahead by players to mitigate winter demand with additional shipping positions, it is almost certain that unpredictability remains a constant and change of sentiment can happen in an instant.  No LNG newbuilding orders to report this week.

Less excitement from market this week. With paper dropping and period market remaining rather flat.  From Atl basin most action came from USG, where fhauls were covered at USD 26000. Supra from USG to Egypt got covered at low USD 20 000. Continent remained flat . Usual scrap runs on smaller supra covered at USD 17000 and on ultramax same was paying USD 20000. Some talks about scaling down panamax cargoes to ultra/supra might add some action, but rather for breachers. From ECSA usual soyabeans runs to SE ASIA got covered at ca USD 16000 + 550k ballast bonus. Ultramax from Durban to China was covered at low USD 14000 + 400k ballast bonus for end feb dates. Indo-India rounds lost most ground , where same was paying USD 9500. On the period front a Supra was placed at USD 14000 levels for 4-6 monts and Atl trading and an Ultra got secured for 4-6 mos at high USD 15000.

EAST We have finally seen some activity on freight in the East this week with a couple of ships fixed for 2H February in the AG. These deals were all done in the high USD 40s rt/ch, and as such the Baltic index has fallen below USD 50 for the first time since July last year. The negative sentiment on freight is expected to continue as there are still far too many open ships versus outstanding shipping requirements (time of writing we do not see any uncovered cargos for the rest of February), and the focus will slowly shift to March as the cargo acceptances for next month have started to come out.  WEST After a relatively quiet period, activity finally resurrected ex US-Gulf during the course of the last week. The market has for a while been struggling to find its feet in terms of fixed rates and although a handful of vessels were fixed at rates in the mid USD 80’s per ton on a Houston/Chiba basis, the majority of the March US-Gulf deals concluded were done at Baltic average rates. There seems to be more momentum and willingness to conclude shipping deals going forward although not at any price.

text: AMERICAS A welcomed lower than expected 1.6 million barrel draw in US propane inventories. US FOB bids are beginning to rise back up to levels sellers are willing to consider. The question is, are FOB bids rising fastest to prevent any further cancellations? Our prediction. Yes!

Public-listed bellwethers continue to seize attractive buying opportunities in the crude sector. Following DHT’s well-timed acquisition of two 2016 DSME built VLCC tankers last week, Euronav came out on top in the competition for two Suezmax newbuildings at Daehan, both with delivery in January 2022. These were cancelled contracts and sold by the yard, not as resales but by entering into new contracts between the builder and Euronav with what we understand is 30% down-payment. Daehan invited offers on Tuesday and the deal was done the next day with several strong names in the running. We can confidently conclude that the bottom is behind us as far as values for very modern tankers goes. Big question now being who else will sell at these levels. As such we see an upside for the modern ones. Leading yards are also upping the prices.     The dry S&P market is powering. Whilst 2nd hand values moved sideways last year, strong demand now makes for a more dynamic pricing and values are up by abt 10% for the modern units and abt 20% for 15 year olds since Mid-December.

Chartering activities remain muted for another week in both basins, as charterers pause to assess the market on the back the strong backwardation in LNG commodity prices ahead. Global availability has increased as a handful of sublets have appeared in the Atlantic, coupled with vessels redelivering from winter charters in the Pacific. These signs point to a typical seasonal LNG cycle, and an inevitable correction on spot rates into March – yet the year-on-year average looks higher this year than last. There is a balancing point ahead: utilisation should be relatively strong as end users seek to rebuild inventories that were depleted in this winter cycle, although vessel redeliveries and the uncommitted New Buildings coming to the market in the first half of 2021 are likely to keep some pressure on term rates moving forward. In the New Building market, Cosco Shipping was reported to have ordered three LNG carriers from Daewoo shipyard in Korea to serve the Arctic LNG II project.

text: AMERICAS The story of unfavorable Arb economics continues. Strong propane prices in the US markets and falling FEI numbers have hurt the Arb and until these items reverse we do not foresee much of a change.  In Mt Belvieu pad 3 inventories are dangerously low despite a warmer than normal start to Winter. This is a result of record exports and hence is reflected in the strong Belvieu price. However, with WTI above USD 50 per barrel ($52.41) increased production might be the white knight that saves the arb,  but for now the market is looking for cancellations. If cancellations do occur the issue then becomes how can Asia survive without US product. Hence cancellations might accomplish decreasing Belvieu and increasing the Fei but this may not happen until the second quarter. Freights have come off considerably, doing its part to help the arb, and shipowners are now wondering how low they must go to get the trade going again. In Mexico, Covid is still having an effect on demand thus causing slower discharges into their ports.

EAST The Baltic has continued its decline this week despite not seeing any real activity on shipping in the East. One cargo from an Indian major is currently being worked for mid-Feb load in AG, but otherwise, there is not much else to write home about. The general sentiment on freight remains bearish, however, tonnage availability for the second half of Feb is not looking as long as it was for the first half of the month.  WEST The West VLGC market is seeing some signs of increased activity. Fixed freight rates have proved difficult to close and appetite for Baltic average rates are sought for. Focus is shifting to that of early March dates but with a number of cancellations and FOB resale candidates during last decade February, we may see some fixtures done once freight and FOB prices match again.

text: MEG Swap market experienced another week of volatility. Feb CP was assessed at $595 at the time of writing, down by $30 compared to last week. 1st round CP recommendation ideas vary widely from lowest at $580 to highest $620, and butane was advised at 15-40$ cheaper. Despite the softening curve value, some players expect CP to be set above $600. One middle East producer was reported to sell their late Feb lifting evenly split cargo at over $20 discounts to Mar CP.   FAR EAST Less activities in the window this week with the focus shifted to 1h Mar delivery. Feb FEI/CP has declined sharply into $65 this week.  Off window, some Japanese are still exploring cargos for 2h Feb delivery, concerning potential shortage due to cancellations ex US for Feb liftings. Despite this, the cash differentials for 2h Feb delivery has turned into flattish and even negative territory, as one 23kt propane parcel was reported sold at Feb FEI minus $1. In the meantime, seeing the flat price and cash premium falling, Chinese Importers are also emerging and absorbing spot cargos for 2h Feb to 1h Mar delivery. Full propane cargo for such period was placed into China at Mar FEI plus around $30. One N.China Petchem importer secured via tender one evenly split cargo and one full propane cargo for 2h Feb to 1h Mar delivery. And following this, another E.China PDH user issued buy tender to purchase two 23/0 parcels for the same periods.
