Tess 58 open feast was fixed $11,500 for 1 year charter to Fednav. The Continent and Mediterranean market saw strong demand with rates reaching $18,000 for scrap runs and $19,00 for clinker to West Africa . The flow of fertilizers from Baltic keeps a steady pace with ice possibility for loaders ex St Petersburg area paying good premium. Backhaul rates to USG and ECSA fixing around low $10,000. For Trips ex Baltic to Fareast Owners asking high $20,000 . USG and ECSA are firm with little change from the last weeks. An Ultramax was reported fixed $23,000 from Miss River to Egypt. Trips form ECSA was fixed $15, 750 plus $575,000 GBB with sugar cargo to South East Asia. Pacifc and Indian Ocean market seen good supply of fresh cargo resulting rates keep strong. NOPAC round voyage paying $13,000 and similar level for Australian grain trips.

The week started off quiet but with an underlying positive tone, continued into a bit more mixed mrkt mid week. There are still strong fixtures being done in the Atlantic and especially for the breaching cgos in Baltic. A 82k dwt was reported at USD 17k for 2llegs in the Atlantic bss delivery Immingham and the P1A is currently priced at mid16k. In the eastern hemisphere we see NoPac rounds being fixed in the low 13k for grain voyages.

As congestion have eased and some of the activity slowed down for seasonal reasons, the time charter index fell by USD 7767 during the last week. This is obviously quite dramatic, but it has also been expected by most market participants as February is usually a slower period for capes . The C3 route, which represents iron ore from Brazil to China is down by 13%, and the C5 West Australian loaded iron ore to China is down by 18%.

The writing appears to be on the wall for Suezmax's this week, especially in West Africa, where Vlcc's have swooped on a number of stems that were initially earmarked for their little sister. This release valve hasn't immediately softened rates, however there is some negative pressure in the  offing as the East list is long , especially prompt tonnage, of which a large number have missed the natural MEG window and have now committed to West Africa. Whilst moderate VLCC sentiment and high bunkers will prevent rates from falling off a cliff, Td20 is unlikely to trade above W60 as we eat into the third decade of February. Likewise, this will leave Meg/East with a similarly weakened outlook.

The Nsea and Baltic markets have remained flat around bottom levels for yet another week. Owners are bravely putting up some resistance trying to push for a few extra points for cross-continent runs in order to achieve returns which give them break-even levels instead of negative returns. Some Owners are ballasting out of the area seeking alternatives elsewhere, but the tonnage list is still in charterers favour and we expect rates to persist at current levels, give or take a few points.  In the Med/Bsea increased activity combined with delays in key ports has resulted in a tighter tonnagelist and freight levels across the board have picked up about 10 points. One to watch is if momentum can be maintained in the next few days, bearing in mind additional ships coming into the area from surrounding weaker markets.

The VLCC market has moved up a little, but only dragging rates from loss making levels to almost covering OPEX, depending on the voyage in question.  The MEG continues to be the quietest area, full of mysteries and ongoing Chinese “COA” commitments. The Atlantic has been the main focus of attention, with a stronger bias and rates currently in the mid to upper W30’s to the east. Brazil has been particularly busy, with upwards to a dozen export cargoes concluded in the week gone by. As rates for USG export cargoes have dropped to $4.2 mill lumpsum for China, the USG has seen more questions for the last decade of February, but have yet to see the same push as from Wafr and Brazil.

Whilst moderate VLCC sentiment and high bunkers will prevent rates from falling off a cliff, Td20 is unlikely to trade above W60 as we eat into the third decade of February. Likewise, this will leave Meg/East with a similarly weakened outlook.

The VLCC market has moved up a little, but only dragging rates from loss making levels to almost covering OPEX, depending on the voyage in question.  The MEG continues to be the quietest area, full of mysteries and ongoing Chinese “COA” commitments. The Atlantic has been the main focus of attention, with a stronger bias and rates currently in the mid to upper W30’s to the east. Brazil has been particularly busy, with upwards to a dozen export cargoes concluded in the week gone by. As rates for USG export cargoes have dropped to $4.2 mill lumpsum for China, the USG has seen more questions for the last decade of February, but have yet to see the same push as from Wafr and Brazil.

The Nsea and Baltic markets have remained flat around bottom levels for yet another week. Owners are bravely putting up some resistance trying to push for a few extra points for cross-continent runs in order to achieve returns which give them break-even levels instead of negative returns. Some Owners are ballasting out of the area seeking alternatives elsewhere, but the tonnage list is still in charterers favour and we expect rates to persist at current levels, give or take a few points.  In the Med/Bsea increased activity combined with delays in key ports has resulted in a tighter tonnagelist and freight levels across the board have picked up about 10 points. One to watch is if momentum can be maintained in the next few days, bearing in mind additional ships coming into the area from surrounding weaker markets.

On the tanker market we have seen notable activity with three modern VLCC’s sold this week setting some much needed benchmarks for units of similar vintage. Following its purchase in November of TRF HORTEN built 2018 at HHIC-Phil at Usd 72m, Delta Tankers of Greece has now acquired the one year older sistership HUDSON for Usd 71.5m. Both vessels were sold by TRF who is also a 50% shareholder of the sisterships ECO QUEEN and ECO FUTURE built 2016 DSME which are sold at Usd 68m each to DHT Holdings. We expect liquidity on the modern front to pick up momentum in the near future supported by an increasing amount of enquiry with a market consensus anticipating a recovery for the second half of this year. Newbuilding prices have certainly passed their bottom spurred by a combination of increased steel prices, strengthening local currencies vs USD and a strong influx of large container vessel projects.  Dry SnP markets continue to joy of high volumes of transactions with vessels changing hands across all sectors. Pricing-wise it seems that most market players are still looking to digest the recent appreciation in values that we witnessed last week with buyers looking to figure out whether this is indeed the start of a sustained upward trend in values rather than a one off glitch in what has been until now a relatively flat market.

This week has been met with slight trepidation as portfolio players and traders alike take a moment to reassess the trading patterns of their portfolios. Record-breaking LNG cargo prices have retreated from their peak yet vessel availability remains tight through February, and those with availability are holding firm against offering a discount. When reviewing March and beyond the picture changes as seasonal effects take hold, but levels remain elevated year-on-year. Panama continues to cause headaches to scheduling and at the time of writing the number of vessel trading from the Atlantic to the Pacific via Suez or the Cape instead of via Panama is markedly up. The situation in the Pacific is slightly different with the onset of increased availability starting to materialize at the back end of the availability list, but as the fixing window is far prompter the full effect of this will not be seen for some weeks! Newbuild market remains subdued with no reported newbuilds this week.

text: AMERICAS Discussions and activity on the Gulf Coast were mostly muted, in part due to fog-and in part due to the ambiguity in the freight market, where rates on a Houston/ Chiba basis, were pegged as low as USD127 per metric ton- a far cry from the 180-200 pmt discussed just a week ago. The negative propane/naphta spread in Europe has led to a handful of European players to source tons from the US,  both from Marcus Hook and US Gulf, preferably on a delivered basis, in efforts to avoid the volatile spot freight market. In Mt. Belvieu, front month propane prices have come off considerably due to warm weather and falling international prices and Propane now stands att roughly 65 percent of WTI compared to the 75 percent level seen last week. .  A handful of February and March FOB cargos are now on offer at around 4 cents, though buyers have been unwilling to achieve these levels quite yet. On paper the Feb/March stands at -115/ ton. The big question today, is the market oversold, or has the high for 2021 already been achieved. Stats delayed due to MLK Day and the inauguration will shed more light Friday.

The Panamax market cooled off end of last week for all trades except breaching Baltic cargos and ECSA grain hauls. This trend has continued into this week, and we do see owners booking forward cargos for March/April well below current spot earnings. The period market has continued to pick up thus some optimistic views are still out there. P1A is currently yielding in the low 16k while fronthauls are fixing in the 23k region basis Continent delivery. In the Eastern Hemisphere we also see a downward trend with Pacific RV’s fetching in the 12’s.

The Suezmax market have started the new year very different from where it ended 2020. Cargo activity has been higher than expected, and also worth noticing; rather steady the last couple of weeks. This has helped removing the huge overhang we had in the Atlantic, and the tonnage list in West Africa is now looking tighter, at least the front side of the list. Owners are more bullish and managing to hold back instead of jumping on every possibility out there. Still, we need to remind ourselves that TD20 is not making owners rich at the moment, with TCE's at less than USD 5k/day, but nevertheless a huge step in the right direction. The East market is also picking up, with West Africa giving owners a different alternative, but a bit more balanced tonnage list might demand more patience from owners.

Resultant value for Pacific rounds down some 35 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 17,500. Atlantic remains very strong and in need of available tonnage, value for rounds at times now exceeding USD 40k/day. Fronthaul trades characterized by low supply and great iron ore + coal expectations, China-Brazil-China rounds up almost 10 pct to USD 20,500/day. Period activity limited as discounts required to conclude long term makes enjoying spot levels more tempting for most owners.

EAST This week started off with the news of about 4-5 canceled February Aramco cargoes. As such, in an already relet-dominated market, even more, open ships started to appear, and the number of workable cargoes was at some point seemingly nowhere to be found. Freight ideas significantly lower than of last done have been circulated without much luck to be found. WEST With the exception of one very late market call for a late January loader out of the US Gulf, there has been little or no action in the region. text: MEG Very volatile on paper swaps this week. Feb Propane CP was traded from lowest at $585 to highest $625, and backwardation into Mar enlarged from last week’s $20s to nearly $50. At the time of writing, Feb C3 was traded at $600 and Mar assessed at $552 relatively. Saudi Aramco was reported to cut 4-5 cargos for Feb liftings, which alternatively lent support to Feb CP. However, with limited butane buying interest, Feb butane was valued at $40 cheaper. Qatar Petroleum still has a late Feb lifting evenly split cargo to sell.   FAR EAST  Cash premiums for both Feb and Mar arrival cargos have been traded down this week. 23k propane for 1h Mar delivery was traded at Mar FEI plus low-mid 30s only on Thursday, while earlier this week bids hover above $50 in the window. Outside window sellers with FEB arrival cargos also lowered down offers to attract buying interests, plus the freight is falling sharply as of fewer liftings due to Saudi cuts and US cancellations. One Chinese PDH secured two parcels of 23kt propane for Feb and Mar delivery respectively, which reported done at 50% FEI pricing plus the 40s and 50% CP pricing plus teens only. Another Chinese major also tendered to buy one full cargo with the flexible ratio for 2h Feb to early Mar delivery, which is due on Friday. Indonesia PERTAMINA secured one early Mar arrival evenly split cargo and following this, another SEA importer also issued buy tender to purchase similar cargo for 1h Mar delivery.

2021 has kicked off with a whisper, with reduced Middle East Gulf volumes and a tonnage build up. Rates have gone from weakness to weakness, and for the first time in years we have seen fixtures concluded yielding negative returns – in other words owners paying for the privilege – and risk – to carry crude oil from A to B. From a slim January program the tonnage overhang into next month is greater that seen for a long time, not helped by ships coming off storage and quicker turnarounds. The Atlantic has been a saving grace, in a manner of speaking, although rates for the longer haul voyages have also given way with correspondingly lower earnings, barely showing positive returns. Alas, with February being a short month, and Chinese New Year celebrations to bout, we do not foresee a pickup any time soon.

The record-breaking start to the year continues as both the LNG and shipping markets gain strength week-on-week. Availability remains tight, and our reported headline rates combined with full three-way voyage economics are pushing TCE levels above $300,000 per day for some routes. This seasonal cycle has several factors at play, from uncertainty in demand due to Covid-19 through to cold weather, but the full examination will follow in due course; for now, buyers, sellers, charterers and owners are focussed on their exposures or opportunities. There is perhaps a glance now away from “how high will it go?” towards “how long will it last and how hard will it fall?”, but while there is backwardation in the forward curve the commodity price sits materially higher through 2021 than it did just weeks ago. Rebuilding inventories and a more conservative approach to next winter should support a more stable market once the current dynamics have played out: we should see more utilisation and less volatility on the shipping side this year than last.

It has been a very strong week, illustrated by present Baltic TC average at USD 26,500 against last week’s USD 17,500. The delays in China pointed out last week is still a factor as well as some COVID-19 cases in at least one of the Chinese ports, continue to put pressure on early ships. C5 was concluded up to USD 11 level and c3 well above USD 20, a sharp improvement from last week. There are also weather delays in the Atlantic and close to none early ships available. A volatile ffa market makes period somewhat challenging right now, but there is generally a buying interest as levels are increasing.

Most of the routes gaining ground and this week’s best performers being Continent and ECSA in Atlantic basin, whereas USG cooling down. From Continent usual scrap runs getting covered at USD 17,000 and trips to USG around USD 12,000. From USG to Continent, Supras being fixed at USD 22,000 and Ultra tonnage at USD 25,000, fronthauls paying high 20s for same. More activity from ECSA where TA being covered at USD 17,000 and fronthauls at USD 15k+500bb on Ultra and 13,500+350 on Supra. Similar trend from the Black Sea where fronthauls now reported at around USD 20,000. Positive sentiment also from the East where Pacific round voyages covered at USD 10,000 this week. Trip with limestone from MEG to China done at USD 14,000. On the period front, bigger Supramaxes were covered at USD 10,500.

The firming tendency from last week continued into this week as well. In the North Atlantic we saw strong numbers being achieved on the Baltic rounds and USD 30k was reported done. It was hard to put the finger on the longer Atlantic runs but p1A is currently yielding in the 17k. Tuesday we saw some fixing and failing being done, especially out of ECSA which could reflect that some chrts feel the market is toppish, however the tonnage list for grain clean ships is still scarce. This might as well be a breather after several days with rising market. In the eastern hemisphere, we still see an active period market while the spot market is somewhat slower. P3a is currently priced in the 12-13k region depending on delivery.

text: AMERICAS Expectations that the EIA would report on Wednesday morning a draw in US propane stocks was unanimous, though the anticipated rate of decline was contested.  Some were forecasting a 2mmbbl draw, while others were predicting as much as a 6mmbbl decline.  Historically, the largest single weekly draw occurred in Jan 2017 when stocks fell by 7.188mmbbls.     The EIA yesterday reported a 6.7mmbbl draw, surprising most and prompting discussions related to minimum comfort levels of propane inventories in the US.  As of last Friday there were 66mmbbls ‘in tank’, and there are another 9 weeks of winter-related demand (with winter ending mid-March).  History shows that stocks have declined on a weekly basis from between 1.1mmbbls/day to 2.4mmbbls/day.  At 1.1mmbls day a ~10mmbbl draw can be anticipated, at which point stocks will have fallen to 56mmbbls.  If, however, stocks decline at a rate of 2.4mmbbls/day, ~22mmbbls will be removed stocks and overall stocks will have fallen to 44mmbbls.   It is when stocks dip below around 30mmbbls that inventory difficulties are typically encountered, so unless an unusual series of events occurs it seems unlikely at this point that stocks will fall to jeopardized levels – particularly if crude oil prices are on the rise which should bolster domestic production levels.  Furthermore, according to the EIA,propane production rose by 83,000bbls/day to 2.34mmbbls/day as of last week.   The issue, however, is not necessarily the condition of the overall stock levels, but those on along the US Gulf Coast – in PADD III – which includes much of the production areas, but also most of the exporting sites.  There are, as of last week, 34.96mmbbls inn PADD III, down by a significant volume of 4.279mmbbls week-over-week.   Of course the price of the molecules themselves will ultimately have a say in the matter.  Mont Belvieu propane values very quickly (and rather predictably) rose after the release of the EIA data, climbing quickly to 90cts/gal for prompt barrels.  Perhaps the weather (or lack thereof) in the US will finally have a hand in the matter, too.

EAST The acceptances from Adnoc were released over the weekend and since then we have seen a handful of deals concluded in MEG for 1st decade February loading. We have also seen some additional shipping length from traders being marketed, and as the majority of these are yet to be booked this has turned a climbing Baltic sentiment, for now. We are still also waiting for the Aramco acceptances, but it remains to be seen if these could have any significant effect on new shipping requirements as there are some talks of cuts from Saudi in February.  WEST West of Suez we saw a range of deals concluded on shipping ex USG with freight rates peaking at some USD 110k per day or very high USD 180's per ton Houston/Chiba equivalent. Fixing activity has slowed down a bit this week compared to last, however, the balance of February is still looking relatively tight due to amongst others limited northbound Panama slots being available for pre-booking. Bids from would-be charterers are currently somewhat lower than the fixtures we saw concluded as of last week, but we have yet to see such bids hit.

The sound of silence has been deafening in the VLCC market in the week gone by. Lack of MEG enquiry, a correspondingly long position list, galloping bunker prices, and charterers seeming well covered by own tonnage or COA arrangements. The Atlantic has offered a couple of opportunities, but every successive fixture has seen lower numbers concluded. All in all, a lacklustre picture, with daily returns yet again well below OPEX - and few if any signs of improvement in the short term.

After nearly a year of negative news stories, we are delighted to bring you a positive spin, well, sort of positive. Despite the best efforts of the chartering community to apply downward pressure, rates, for the most part, appear to be trading flat. Given present returns and rising bunker prices, it's no surprise that owners have tried their utmost to resist further falls. However, in a market where owners and charterers are happy to repeat last done, there is always the danger that complacency can set in and if these derisory enquiry levels persist, it is not inconceivable that rates could be traded down a few more points.

An oversupply of vessels coupled with limited activity in the North Sea area have led owners fixing cross-Continent runs on negative returns just for re-positioning matters. On the other side, as we have got colder weather and new ice forming in some strategic Baltic load ports charterers prefer to fix in ice-class vessels giving owners hope for some slightly higher returns. We expect market to remain flat in the week to come with most of January’s liftings in the Nsea already covered. In the Med/Bsea we are counting more than 30 ships prompt open free of cargo this week. The few cargoes coming into the market is a far cry from satisfying the amount of available tonnage, which in turn is reflected in TD19 showing a loss of close to USD 2,000 pd on TCE. We do not expect a significant recovery in the week to come.

text: MEG Feb CP continues to rally up this week, with the expectation on Saudi cuts on Feb liftings. At the time of writing, Feb C3 CP was traded at $620 while C3/C4 spread deepened further to $38, as of limited buying inquires for butane.  Qatar Petroleum was reported that it didn’t award its sale tender for 24/25th Feb lifting evenly split cargo. Other similar cargo for 2h Feb lifting was offered at Feb CP minus teens but yet to attract interest, especially with the prevailing high freight rates.   FAR EAST Despite active inquires in window this week, cash premium for 2h Feb delivered 23/0 has declined from high 30s to low 30s on FEI link, and full cargo lot was assessed at $10 less or even cheaper. Outside window a handful of cargos are seeking home, which exerted pressure on Feb FEI and FEI/CP narrowed down sharply from last week’s $40 to $20 accordingly. Seeing the backwardation for over $50 into Mar FEI, importers with comfortable inventory intent to defer their buying inquiries into Mar instead. Similar parcel for 23/0 delivered in 1h Mar was bid at Mar FEI plus at $53, which equates to Feb FEI plus low single, however sellers are reluctant to offer their Feb arrival tons at the time being. Other than the spot activities, Indian HPCL issued tender to buy from 6 upto 10 equal ratio cargos for Mar to Dec delivery.

It has been a strong week for dry earnings, with Capesizes pushing above USD 26k/d from last week’s level of USD 17.5k/d. However, gains have been levelling out in recent days on the back of a very volatile paper market. The S&P activity is brisk across all segments with a large number of vessels transacted. Older Capesize values are the first to benefit from the newfound optimism which is well illustrated by the sale of OCEAN COMPASS (2006/Imabari/180kdwt) which achieved a price of Usd 17.5 mill this week. This appreciation in values for older units is not only supported by a firming chartering environment but also by strengthening demolition rates which is approaching USD 500/LDT. We expect this momentum to continue with sellers starting to raise their price expectations leaving an increasing amount of buyers competing over a thinning number of available candidates.  Activity on the tanker front is limited to tonnage of around 10 year of age and older with a number of older crude carriers changing hands this week. Three sales to report in the VLCC sector where Navios Maritime has sold its NAVE CELESTE (2003/DSME/300kdwt) at Usd 25mill to Chinese buyers. Activity on the modern side remains subdued with weakening freight rates leading any potential seller to take a step back rather than face current bids by buyers looking to secure substantial discounts against last done.

An oversupply of vessels coupled with limited activity in the North Sea area have led owners fixing cross-Continent runs on negative returns just for re-positioning matters. On the other side, as we have got colder weather and new ice forming in some strategic Baltic load ports charterers prefer to fix in ice-class vessels giving owners hope for some slightly higher returns. We expect market to remain flat in the week to come with most of January’s liftings in the Nsea already covered. In the Med/Bsea we are counting more than 30 ships prompt open free of cargo this week. The few cargoes coming into the market is a far cry from satisfying the amount of available tonnage, which in turn is reflected in TD19 showing a loss of close to USD 2,000 pd on TCE. We do not expect a significant recovery in the week to come.

New lockdowns are here but so are gradually vaccines, which hopefully means we may soon apply normal forecasting parameters again. All going well we expect decent average tanker earnings in 2021 based on a return of oil production and a turnaround in sentiment in 2nd half of the year. However the near term tanker outlook remains soft and 2nd hand values will remain under pressure. On that note, the year kicks off with a notable MR deal. Top Ships is reported to have sold three scrubberfitted MR newbuildings with delivery in February and March 2021 ex HMD. The price is reported to be just below Usd 34 mill each.  It’s a promising start of the year in the dry segments and the transaction volume remains steady across all segments. Capesize values may see an uptick on the back of an unexpected strong start.

The first full week after holidays across many countries with gaps between owners’ and charterers’ expectations as the market is trying to find some common ground. From the USG strong numbers still being discussed, with TA around USD 20,000 and FH around USD 25,000. The fixing levels are under pressure from the Continent and the Mediterranean, where FH paying close to USD 20,000 ex Baltic and around USD 18,000 fm Emed, while Mediterranean to USG in the low 9k. Further East, CIS coal RV fixing in the low-mid USD 9k, while Indo coal RV to China trading in the low teens.

This year started fairly positive with a lot of new requirements in the East, and together with the bad weather currently experienced in China, delaying discharge operations, makes the demand/supply ratio for prompt tonnage very healthy. We see the West Australia to China route up from about USD 8.00 to 8.80 per metric ton week-on-week. The Brazil segment is still pretty busy, but as the prompt dates where we saw a very limited amount of tonnage now been covered, the levels are now slightly lower for index dates. That said, they are still much higher than what was expected only a couple of weeks back. The North Atlantic should also be mentioned being very tight on tonnage, however activity fairly slow so a dramatic push there is yet to be seen.

2021 kicked off with firming rates in both hemispheres. The Atlantic is leading on with fresh demand and confident owners raising their fixing ideas. Solid grain demand out of the Americas will most likely push up the Pacific as well and ballasters from Singapore are fixing in the low USD 12k basis delivery DOP for ECSA/Far east rounds. TA’s are currently yielding mid 15k. Period fixtures have also regained activity, and a modern Kmax was rumored concluded for 1 year at 13k basis SE Asia delivery.

In the first week of 2021, the LNG Shipping market picked up where it left it off at the end of 2020. The availability is tight across all basins and the tightness continues well into Feb/March for Atlantic/USG cargo loadings. The headliner rates are “stable” at very firm levels (around 150-160k/day for TFDE’s), but as most fixtures include a “3-way economics” with substantial positioning and repositioning costs, it keeps pushing up vessel “owners” TCE. The Majors and LNG Traders doesn’t appear to be to dishearten by the current shipping rate levels as they themselves are trading the JKTC market at prices we haven’t seen since Feb 2014.

There was hope in the air for the first full trading week of the New Year, with added volumes from OPEC+ and the perception that we were behind the curve on the fixture count. Alas, OPEC did a U-turn and as proceeding got going it transpired that much more had been done quietly under the radar than first thought. Like one politician ones uttered “It feels a bit like someone stole our clothes while we were enjoying a swim”. With that, rates have taken a hit in all areas and a continued downward bias is evident. Please note that new 2021 Worldscale flat rates are down 16-17% on average, thus rates are not directly comparable to last years.

EAST After a quiet Christmas the VLGC market is getting back to life in the AG with a few fixtures done both on end January and early February dates this week. January is now left with only one open vessel and availability for early Feb dates is becoming increasingly tight. It can be expected that Charterers will ask for early Feb lifting dates from their suppliers in view of the current backwardation in the FEI, potentially creating an even firmer market. Last done is now being reported around 115 and we see a clear upward trend in freight.  WEST As we embark on the new year, the West market is more or less halfway through Q1 already in terms of fixtures. Vessel availability is tight for February dates and slowly but surely the market players look set to start covering the second half of the month. Although most owners are preoccupied with making sure their commitments fixed at the end of last year for the first half of February, we have seen several deals done during the second decade at rates ranging from mid/low to mid/high USD 170's H/C basis. The fear of even the slightest delay in arriving and exiting the loadport may have severe effects and is keeping everyone on their toes. The short term market outlook is strong.

text: MEG Feb Propane CP has soared up to $596 following the crude jump, but Mar CP was traded at heavy backwardation of over $40. As Saudi pledged to cut oil output, Feb CP gained more support with expectations on potential shortage of propane. Meanwhile, Feb C3/C4 enlarged to $30, as propane is more favorable than butane in winter season. Qatar Petroleum issued tender to sell 24-25th Feb lifting equal ratio cargo.   FAR EAST This week a flurry of deals is concluded with solid heating demand in winter. Full cargo propane for 1h Feb delivery was concluded earlier in window at Jan FEI minus low teens, whilst half cargo parcels for 2h Feb delivery were traded at Feb FEI plus high 30s. Off window a handful of cargos have been placed into Japan and Korea also, with full propane for 1h Feb delivery done at Feb FEI plus around $30 and half parcel at around $40. In the North Sea and Baltic market, rates continue hovering at bottom levels. The market has been dominated by relets and vessels of bigger sizes having absorbed a big portion of the cargoes ex WCN and ECUK. Even with delays in some strategic ports we expect rates to move sideways into next week. However, some ice formation in the Baltic coupled with a busier 3rd decade could add some upward pressure. A New Year, same old market. Let's start the year off on a positive note. Various vaccines have been successfully developed and given the green light which should see this year’s Covid-19 variant brought under partial control, or at least in the countries that can afford to buy it. The downside is that a general malaise in the Suezmax market is going to persist until demand picks up towards the end of the year. It should be noted that attempted terrorist acts in the Red Sea and MEG have had zero affect on rates, which suggests owners  will adopt a reactive approach, therefore only attaching a premium to these runs if the unthinkable happens. All Suezmax markets will trade flat/soft for the remainder of the week, with Western markets looking particularly vulnerable to further falls.

Like one politician ones uttered “It feels a bit like someone stole our clothes while we were enjoying a swim”. text: AMERICAS A lesser than expected 2.4 million barrel draw occurred in US propane inventories for the week ended January 1st 2021. This was below expectations of 3 million barrels and importantly the export figure for the week was only just above 1 million barrels per day. The recent record level of LPG exports has renewed fears of insufficient domestic inventory to see out the winter. If draws averaging 3 million barrels a week occur until build season (1st week of April, 12 weeks) we will be left with 37 million barrels in inventories. Tight! This fear pushed Mt Belvieu propane up to 70% WTI before Saudi Aramco announced they would cut oil production by 1 million barrels per day from Feb 1st. Lack of VLGC availability is set to leave US export tons unsold in January. A double whammy of reducing export volumes and building inventories. The question is will Mt Belvieu propane value strengthen so much as to destroy demand, or will US inventories remain manageable  and keep propane arbs open?

We are in that strange week between Christmas and New Year, that can bring vast riches or very little at all. As it is, we are very much on the latter. With it being a short week and many out on holiday, we have seen only 29 fixtures fixed worldwide on the VLCCs over the past week, which is light by any count. Many owners will be holding on for a promising start to 2021, where there is the possibility of a catch up required across the board. Therefore, many have been keeping their powder dry by not offering in, but in fairness, there has not been a great deal to offer in to. Rates have moved very little, with MEG/East creeping up a touch (WS36.5 done on a vessel with an old sire) but the Atlantic (albeit an Eastern ballaster at WS32 Brazil/East) coming off. It very much depends on dates and sentiment at the current time.

We should start referring to the week preceding New Year as "no quibble week". As expected, the market has been quiet with charterers and owners happy to fix variations of last done.  This will continue until volumes hopefully increase next week. Above radar activity has been at a minimum, resulting in Wafr/Portugal trading at WS35 which will see Wafr/East find a home at about WS40. Bot/USG was last booked at WS17.5, albeit via Cape of Good Hope, which pitches a Suez/Suez Med run at WS10-12.5. Need to keep an eye on Td3c VLCCs as that list looks tighter for end 2nd decade dates. This should hold MEG/East Suezmax at a minimum of WS37.5 level for a modern vessel. There's very little else to say other than to wish you all a happy and prosperous 2021.

The main fixing activity out of the US is currently focused around 1H Feb dates, while the MEG market still focusing on last decade Jan. We have started to see some delays in the East where one oil major already has taken in a replacement ship on subjects at a healthy premium to last Baltic print. We would not be surprised if we were to see more delays going forward adding fuel to the already burning hot market.

The last week of 2020 and Christmas holidays last week added some rush activity from certain areas in the Atlantic, mainly USG and NCSA. The BSI maintained relatively good level and healthy period fixtures were concluded. Ultramax 60,000 dwt was able to obtain USD 11,000 for period delivery in China.  The US Gulf is the main attraction area with Ultramax fixing USD 22,000s for trips to the East Mediterranean and in the USD 28,000s for trips to China. Trips from Brazil and Argentina was active, however rates for a 61,000 dwt were reported fixed in the mid teens. The Asia market was very much positional as some owners were lucky to obtain higher rates than others.  A 55,000 dwt open Philippines fixing a trip via Indonesia redelivery China at USD 13,000, while others was fixing only in the low USD 11,000s. West coast Indian trips into China were reported at the level of USD 14,000.

Holidays are upon us, and this is clearly seen in the Panamax market. Early January positions are being circulated and activity is next to none. Charterers are bidding less than last done, but in no hurry as it seems everyone is holding back till after New Year’s before moving. This quiet tendency reflects in both hemispheres and we can only wish you all a Happy New Year!

As we look back on the LNG shipping market throughout this year, it would be fair to say that most market participants were surprised, some very pleased by the rate levels seen in the last couple of months. Going back to the first half of 2020, sentiments were certainly softer for Q4 and the majority would not have envisaged fixtures being concluded at current levels. A colder winter with increasing demand for LNG in North East Asia particularly in China and the continual strength seen on the product prices are supporting an arbitrage for West to East trades, contributing to the solid demand for shipping. Challenges to secure slots through the Panama Canal have also resulted in longer waiting times, further tightening the market. As we edge closer to 2021, the lack of tonnage and clarity on vessel availability means there are still a couple of cargoes to be work for 1H February loading. Shipping remains tight for now and with JKM rising for the forward month and owners fueled by optimism, we are anticipating levels to remain buoyant.    On recent newbuildings, both HHI and SHI were reported to have secured a total of 17 LNG carriers with four shipowners, although with some conditions on the contracts. The newbuilds were reported to be allocated to the Mozambique LNG project. 2020 will end as a very good year for shipyards with a total close to 50 conventional LNG carriers.  From everyone at Fearnley LNG, wishing you a happy, healthy and prosperous new year !

Activity fading at healthy levels towards year-end, with average spot earnings hovering around USD 15-16k for standard type tonnage. Major miners enjoy historically high iron ore prices, and keep being busy stacking up tonnage for up to mid January loading from West Australia where spot rates have at times gone in excess of USD 8.00 pmt. Similar pattern from Brazil, where a generally tight Atlantic market see anything between USD 15.00 and USD 16.00 pmt done for the Brazil/China route depending on terms and dates. This situation expected to continue into the new year. Limited period activity as ffa levels not supporting expectations – representative fixtures include mediocre 177,000 dwt/built 2010 concluded for 16-10 months at USD 14k.

In the North Sea and Baltic, we experienced a small uptick in rates mainly due to a couple of replacement jobs. However, this also added some upward pressure on rates for charterers working in the normal fixing window ex Baltic. Looking ahead the tonnage list looking a bit more balanced, and we expect rates to continue moving sideways unless we see any prompt replacement jobs. In the Med/Bsea we have seen a steady flow of activity continue this week. Rates have picked up a few points across the board, but benchmark routes are still only giving owners a few hundred dollars in returns. Albeit recent cargo activity the list of vessels FOC in the Med remains long, and we expect rates to move sideways over the holiday season.

If there was any so-called pre-Christmas rush, a lot of it was happened below the surface as ships were fixed away quietly. As a result, there was no ‘pop’, and Worldscale rates have flattered to deceive, ticking up from the mid WS30’s in the MEG, to a high of WS37.5 eastbound (so far). Hardly a huge leap, but charterers have been able to find a suitable dance partner, even if it means a slight relaxation of vetting protocols. Modern, well approved tonnage will be keeping their powder dry and will continue to push for better returns as we head on into January, as only 30 or so MEG fixtures has been logged so far, and a quiet month ex West Africa, suggests there may be a little catch up required post-Christmas.

Firm market conditions remain but with many expected to take some well-earned rest after a long year, we could see activity wane in the last two weeks of 2020. Bids continue to flood in for vessels with prompt availability and the drag from the Pacific into the Atlantic continues to be the preference for Owners. Those with Pacific requirement remain at battle against strong duration at high levels in the Atlantic. Tonnage opening in late January could be a cause of concern as current backwardation on the cargo side shortens opportunities for trade return at current freight levels. However, the prompt market is likely to continue to hold until we see the fixing window shift into play with increase of tonnage expected. Rates are likely to hover around current levels for now, but sublet availability could put a slight soft tone on rates towards end of winter period.  The newbuilding market remains active: at least four new 174,000cbm have been inked in this week, two will be built at Samsung Heavy, and two at HSHI. Despite a recent influx in orders, we are currently still down from the 19 orders placed in December last year.  For those who celebrate, a very merry Christmas from all of us here at Fearnley LNG.

We were optimistic and cheerful about the dry cargo market. How drastically that took us by surprise in March with a new phenomenon called Covid19. In January wearing a mask in a store would get you arrested, now in December it’s the new normal. Market at a glance, January vs December if you look at fuel difference 586-393=193 USD. On a transatlantic average of 700 mt x193 USD diff=135,100 USD/50 days duration=2,702 pr day difference just on fuel January vs December.  The market continued to ease as we close in on the final full working week prior to Xmas holidays. Many started the week talking of a slower market as activity levels waned. This was in fact the case as many of the operator’s books appear complete for the year. This has been adding some additional pressure and the indices appeared to reflect same with a full week of losses. All Panamax indices is red this week. The market was weaker across all regions, as a lack of activity owing in large to a lack of bids with charterers stepping back and seemingly happy to wait prior the holiday break.  Merry Christmas and happy New Year.   Please follow us on Instagram #friendsoffearnleysdry

With the miners still there to fix tonnage for January, rates are presently around USD 16 level, up USD 1 from last week. Atlantic remains firm; coal still being sold from Atlantic discharging ports to China. Period activity has been fairly active recently with tonnage being fixed for 1 year in the mid/upper 14,000s.

We think it is safe to say now that the Xmas-rush is cancelled, and owners are now focusing on getting their ships fixed before the Xmas and New Year’s festivities begins. Wafr still have a long list of ballasters coming from the East, and we expect the market to remain in the high WS30's into the new year. The MEG-market seems to remain stable in the high WS30's as well, and with up to 5 offers on market cargoes needing modern, non-ex-dd ships, we don’t see this market going anywhere. Only area that has a tight-ish tonnage list is the Nsea/Baltic, but the lack of cargoes there have made ships ballast out of the area so does not seem like we will see any obvious Xmas-gifts for owners there either.

There is some light at the end of the tunnel for tanker earnings and rates may have already bottomed for now as the delta in terms of tanker demand looks decidedly positive over the next few months. We expect a stronger rate comeback for 2nd half 2021 as the oil market is not out of the Covid woods just yet and it is likely to take some more time before oil demand recovers to levels where production may be sustainably and meaningfully increased. These expectations go a long way in explaining the lack of modern tankers changing hands for which the bid/ask spread has been consistently wide. However there are now unconfirmed reports that the Libyan state-owned company GNMTC is in the process of acquiring an Aframax newbuilding resale due for delivery ex Sumitomo in early 2021. This being a tender process we expect pricing to be firm but still it is expected to reaffirm that determined buyers of brand new tankers with a very specific buying requirement have to pay up and face sellers’ asking levels.    JP Morgan continues to be an active buyer of large bulkcarriers. Following its purchase in November of two 2016 JMU built Capesizes for Usd 38.9 mill, the company is now reported to have acquired one Capesize built 2011 and one Newcastlemax built 2017. The latter is Chinese built and scrubber fitted but in our books the price of region Usd 37.5 mill is fairly neutral as far as any scrubber premium goes. Maran is reported to have acquired a sister vessel from the same stable on similar terms. All in all, dry values are moving sideways across the board.

The LNG market continues to stay boiling hot (ironically) as the Far East and the Middle-East delivered LNG prices hit new multiyear highs almost every day now, while short coverers and end-users are scrambling to find cargoes in the region. This in turn has caused the LNG shipping market to move from high-speed to hyperdrive, as every promptly available vessel gets taken in a heartbeat causing the global vessel availability to look very scarce indeed over the next month. Naturally, this tightness of available vessels have spiked up the charter rates, which have also reached levels that were last seen only during the peak winter of 2018. Furthermore, with new vessel requirements emerging this week to cover February liftings, we do expect this tightness to drag out a bit longer than we predicted just a few months back. That said, even if the first two months of 2021 look tight, we are still holding the view that vessel supply and demand will balance out before the end of Q1. On the newbuilding front, it was reported this week that Hyundai Heavy Industries have inked another four new LNG newbuilding contracts, two with Pan Ocean, one with Knutsen OAS and one with JP Morgan. All of these newbuilds are 174,000cbm and highly-equipped with XDF propulsion systems, and will be long-term chartered by Shell. With these new contracts, Shell’s total LNGC newbuilding tally stands at 18 modern XDF vessels, all being built by HHI.

The traditional pre-Christmas rush has thus far failed to materialize. Owners will need a busy back end of the week if they are to make any headway, as hopes of an end of year bonus slip away. Furthermore, the quizzical delta, between VLCC and Suezmax rates, has failed to converge, leaving many participants scratching their heads. West Africa/East continues to be blighted by an ever ready stream of ballasters and is likely to finish the first decade January languishing in the low/mid WS40's, whilst Black Sea/East is similarly handicapped. The one possible glimmer of hope may lie in the East, which has seen sustained enquiry up to the mid-point of this week. Charterers have been aiming sub WS40's for MEG/East, but owners may be able to make some gains if they start to dig their heels in.

A quiet week on the surface so far in the VLCC segment, however, more has been happening on under the radar than meets the eye and brings with it unanswered questions. Numerically it seems the December MEG fixture count will come in 15%+ over the previous months. It begs the question of possible “stretching” of the production quotas, although it’s year end, prices have been rising and a bit of profit taking is not unsurprising. Increased volumes have so far failed to have a significant effect on rates, but bodes well for January, with a substantially less tonnage roll over, especially from the modern fraternity. Most of the Chinese fleet is also tied up well into first half of the month which dictates more need for third party tonnage. Short term demand is still blurry, but 2021 looks better rigged than for some time.

Beginning of the week, the Panamax market continued its positive trend from last week in both hemispheres. Strong numbers have been reported and especially for the shorter Baltic runs were breach of INL premium is starting to come into effect. We still see a healthy mineral demand in the North Atlantic, however the tonnage list is increasing. TA’s are currently yielding 17k, however mid-week we do feel the market is a bit “toppish”. Less activity in Asia, but still rates are somewhat holding up at time of writing. Pacific rounds are priced at 13-14k depending on delivery.

text: AMERICAS As the US market begins it wind down to the end of 2020, a number of big questions remain. First and foremost being will propane production remain at 2.3 million barrels per day as it has for most of the 4th quarter. If so, despite the huge export numbers which have become the norm,  there should be enough propane to sustain the exports, the domestic petchem market,  and the retail demand. The second big question is will freight rates remain at these near-record levels, and to this, we can answer yes. We do not see any end in sight to the Panama canal delays, the US export levels, and the intensive drydock schedule.  And finally, the last big question is will the world continue to need US exports, even at a higher price, and once again the answer is yes. Thus with positive answers to all of the above, we expect the arb to stay open and record exports to continue. In South America Brasil continues to be a regular spot buyer taking at least one spot VLGC per month, while Mexico has yet to appear as a winter buyer as we expect they will..

Over the last week the market has improved by 34% for the basket of all the routes. Especially the Brazil to China route with iron ore have recovered significant with 27% as the ballasters are fairly few and the volume not as poor as previously expected. While writing this report we see some mixed signals with slow activity on spot fixtures, but holding. This while demand for period tonnage is growing, increasing the forward expectations.

It has been a very quiet week in the North Sea and Baltic Aframax market. As there are still quite a few relets in position in the current fixing window, and not too many stems left for December to cover, we expect the market to move sideways also into next week. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea we have seen a rush of cargoes enter the market at the beginning of the week, however the rates have stayed flat due to the long list of available ships in the area. With the approaching holiday being an x-factor, we may see a small firming of rates towards the end of this week. However, we do not believe in a notable recovery of the market this side of Christmas.

As anticipated values in both the tanker and dry S&P markets have largely stabilised with a healthy and steady amount of ships being sold across most segments at prices falling in line with recent transactions. However a softer sentiment is certainly more evident for older tankers than for bulkers. Sales activity on the modern tanker side is negligible against a stream of modern bulk tonnage changing hands. Scorpio Bulkers continues unabated its selling spree of its modern fleet with the sale of SBI ZUMBA (81k DWT, 2016, Hudong) at Usd 20mill, which is in line with the sale of SBI Reggae (81k DWT, 2016, Hudong) last month. We also have a benchmark sale on Post-Panamax with the  sale of SANGEET ( 95k DWT, 2012, Imabari) at Usd 15.5mill to Polembros. The sale illustrates the decline in values since last done, which was SUNNY SMILE  (95k DWT, 2013, Imabari) sold at Usd 21.5mill to the same buyer back in the summer of 2019.

The sense of market optimism radiates throughout the world as stock markets reach “all time high” and COVID-19 vaccines are issued out to citizens of various countries, contributing to the sense of hope to get back to normal times. In parallel, the buoyancy amongst the LNG players are increasingly evident as cargo prices continues to escalate, leading to trading opportunities for LNG traders, producers and buyers alike. LNG shipowners and sub-letters are currently enjoying the relatively firm charter rate levels in the markets which may be prolonged if the relatively strong demand for LNG continues. It is not implausible to expect the arbitrage to open, to pave way for more inter-basin spot trades where increased tonne-miles would maintain the tightening of the shipping market throughout this winter.   As the year is about to end, LNG buyers and producers are now close to complete their annual delivery programme. This could further reveal potential shipping requirements and/or availability for sub-let in gas year 2021. Despite a mere three weeks to the end of 2020, most certainly the intensity of LNG and shipping trades seems not to be tapering down short term.  No new LNG vessel orders were reported this week. However, one owner may have retired the 1981-built Pacific Energy and 1984-built Atlantic Energy as these vintage vessels were reported sold for demolition after being in lay-up for some years.

If not a vaccine, the VLCC market got a vitamin shot this week and rates have inched up in all areas. In part as a result of increased bunker prices, but sheer willpower on the owners’ part has been a contributing factor. Initially led by the Atlantic basin, the MEG took up the mantle, sending eastbound rates into the WS30’s. The position list is still well stocked, but no one seems to be breaking ranks. A bit of a standoff has followed, with owners looking to push things further up, and charterers holding back and turning every stone not to. Although not spectacular, daily earnings are now covering OPEX from the MEG, and then some, and for long hauls from the Atlantic USD 4-5k more/day. Sentiment is not to be underrated, but it remains to be seen if there are enough left-over volumes to support further strength.

text: AMERICAS The FOB US Gulf Propane resale discussion remained thin for January cargos- as freight continued to eclipse the entirety of the Jan /Feb LST/FEI arb, (which now stands at $175/ton). On Wednesday the EIA reported a sizeable draw of 4.1 million barrels, exacerbating the negative pressure on the arb. An easing of propane production, coupled with another strong week of exports (1.3million barrels/ day) was the catalyst for the considerable 3 million barrel draw in padd 3. The East coast inventories drew down just shy of 1 million barrels while the midcontinent realized a small build. It’s beginning to feel a lot like Christmas.. Activity feels muted and while there are a sparse few January cargos on offer both from Marcus Hook and Houston, it will take a trader/ end user who already has a vessel if there’s to be any chance to mount a competitive bid.

EAST The shipping market has continued its momentum from recent weeks, and all deals concluded lately have mostly been done at premium levels to the last deal. Tonnage availability during 1H January in the Middle East currently looks very tight, and all players whom have been short shipping for same period have already covered their position even if we are still awaiting the Adnoc and Aramco acceptances for January. Meanwhile we continue to see strong demand for ships in other load regions such as WAF and the US, and this could potentially pull more ships back West via Cape. Needless to say, this would be bull shipping and we expect this trend to continue for at least the short term.  WEST The shipping market has continued its momentum from recent weeks, and all deals concluded lately have mostly been done at premium levels to the last deal, both East and West of Suez. Currently, fixtures are being concluded at or around USD 155 H/C, and seem there is potential for even a further increase.

text: MEG Jan Propane CP is traded at $458, ticking up by $12 this week. However, butane price is deteriorating as plenty of evenly split cargos were shown in the market this week. Qatar Petroleum is reported sold one late Jan lifting evenly split cargo, and it also tendered to sell another equal ratio cargo for mid Jan lifting. Meanwhile, one similar cargo for 10/11 Jan lifting was sold but yet to hear details.    FAR EAST  We’ve seen prompt demand for 2h Dec delivery cargos this week, and some prompt swap inquires due to the latest Panama delays. Half cargo propane for Jan delivery was discussed at Jan FEI plus teens level, but cash premiums softens a bit as foreseeing more cargos loaded ex US shall sail to east after the Panama backlog cleared.    The freight is soaring up due to short availabilities on vessels, either east or west, and Jan FEI/CP spread expands widest at $60 and now at $50, compared with last week’s 30ish range. One EChina PDH importer tender to secure one 4/0 for early Feb delivery into Ningbo. Other than this, Chinese buyers refrain from buying interests and would like to wait before taking further moves.

LNG demand for deliveries into Asia continues to firm and spot product prices got further gains this week, as supply disruptions continue both East and West. This, coupled with anticipation of lower temperatures in the northern hemisphere, have supported LNG shipping demand and rate levels for yet another week. Activity and shipping requirements remain at high levels, but lack of available shipping, especially in Atlantic, combined with Panama delays, has turned charterers enquiring for Atlantic liftings to look East of Suez for tonnage. In the East, there is a bit more availability, but enquiries and tender activity has kept the chartering markets active with good interest for all types of tonnage.  Vessel availability is expected to remain tight over the next weeks as the imbalance of availability between the basins persists, likely until the next wave of redeliveries in late January. For now, however, the current setting suggests a prolonged winter market.  One new single LNGC order at Samsung Heavy was reported this week for delivery in 2023.

A sustained amount of activity across SnP markets this week with a number of vessels changing hands. In the dry markets Scorpio Bulk has disposed of a further three units. The levels achieved on all three Ultramax vessels fall in line with last comparable transactions. With a continuous stream of sales candidates meeting the current buying enquiry we expect the values to continue moving sideways for the foreseeable future.  Tanker markets continue to see a high level of interest especially across the MR and Aframax segments which have seen the vast majority of sales. An increasing number of ten to fifteen years old MR tankers are being placed for sale suggesting values are most likely to remain under pressure. The same applies to older Aframax tankers as clearly illustrated by this week’s sales, although it should be noted that the price for the two 2003 built BAKU and AZERBAIJAN reflects that the vessels have been in lay-up for some time. Younger ones are faring better with PAMISOS (105k dwt 2011 HHI) achieving the same price as the same age sister vessel KALAMI went for in early November. Sign of ongoing inspections and negotiations suggest we will be in position to report further transactions in the near future.

For another week the North Sea/Baltic market didn’t escape its vicious cycle and kept hoovering at around bottom levels. A tight window gave owners the opportunity to ask for slightly higher rates, but the upward correction didn’t really manifest itself. For the time being, fuel oil inquiries with East options are the main driver for this market. We expect rates to drift sideways in the current fixing window, before we might see an improvement in rates moving into the 3rd decade fixing window. In the Med/Bsea, cross-Med voyages remain flat, while voyages out of the Bsea have picked up 5 points or so since last week. This is mainly due to delays in Bosporus, and it will be interesting to see if this combined with the increasing activity out of Libya can be a driving force towards a firmer market in the week to come.

As we turn the page to a new month, we are past the halfway point count wise for December already. The MEG remains quiet and with a good two weeks before we see January dates appearing, once again we don’t expect much change in fortunes short term. On paper the east-bound market remains in the upper WS 20’s for modern units, but with increased bunker prices daily earning is still well below USD 10k/day. The Atlantic has fared a little better. A combination of tighter dates/positions, longer commitments, increased bunkers and less wiggle room tonnage wise, and rates have moved up into the low-mid WS 30’s, yielding above break-even levels – if only just. That said, it is likely closer to the peak than the beginning of a continues upward trend.

Steady enquiry levels have failed to prevent further rate-slippage in the West.  TD15 should have acted as a support mechanism for TD20, at least psychologically, but it has continued to exhibit underlying weakness. Eastern ballasters remain the chief culprit in the Med-Black Sea as there seems to be no end of willing candidates. Prior to Covid-19, this would have made a significant dent in the East list, but in this pandemic scenario, the list remains long. MEG/East will trade 130 x WS 40-42.5 on modern whilst TD23 may struggle to maintain high teens. TD20 will trade mid WS 30's.

The present average index value is at USD 12,000 and there is potential as well as expectations for a further drop. After a long inactive period on the period front, there has however been some more activity recently, in line with ffa values.

text: AMERICAS A relatively small – but nonetheless generally expected - decline of 844,000bbls in domestic US propane inventories left stock levels at 91.718mmbbls overall, which compares to the late-Nov 2019 total of 86.443mmbbls, a difference of more than 5mmbbls.  Overwater exports of propane during the period were reckoned to have improved to a robust level of around 1.5mmbbls/day while production was effectively flat at 2.291mmbbls/day, according to the DOE.    Most of the terminals are running well at this point, though a day or so of fog on both the Houston Ship Channel and in Freeport was recorded this week.  And while this has left a number of vessels waiting offshore, the terminals themselves report little disruption as they’ve become adept at managing their respective facilities during the (mostly) short-lived but periodic waterway closures.  The weather in North America has heretofore been relatively mild, but a healthy dose of Arctic air has by now descended and blanketed much of the Midwest and Northeast.  Still, however, NOAA are calling for a generally mild winter overall, with better-than-average chances for above-average temperatures and below-average precipitation.  If that prediction were to be realized, then reduced weather-related demand should likely allow the rate of decline of propane stock levels to slow, the weight of which should then cause MB values to soften and – in turn – support an open arb.  Exceedingly bullish freight rates, however, will likely play a role in the outcome, however.  Petrochemical consumption of propane is reported for November to have been upwards of 300,000bbls/day, where Dec is likely to decline towards the upper 200,000bbl/day range, though expectations of even lower rates were discussed for Dec.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco raised up both Propane and Butane CP by 20$ respectively to $450 and $460. C3/C4 spread narrows down to $7 as butane are less favorable in winter season and in lack of cracking demand due to poor economy. Jan CP was traded at region of $440-449, slightly backwarded to reflect the oversupply of front market. QP issued sale tender to market one 26/27th Jan lifting equal ratio cargo.   FAR EAST The Panama congestion and HSC closure on mid-week have caused some further delays on Dec delivery and 1h Jan delivery cargos. Coupled by the soaring freight, cash premium continued its upward trajectory, with full propane for Jan delivery traded at Jan FEI plus around $10 reportedly, and half cargo basis at Jan FEI plus high teens. Despite the escalating freight and rising premium on CFR into Japan/Korea regions, cargoes into China are still traded at heavy discounts. One EChina importer was reported to cover an end Dec delivery 23/0 at 30ish on CP link. Similarly, one SChina importer secured a 11/11 parcel for late Dec to Jan delivery into Shenzhen at Jan CP plus high 30s via tender.

The creditor controlled sale of the Xihe fleet is still underway with administrators inviting offers on three VLCC’s this week. The 2013 Jiangnan built VLCC JING GANG SAN is now sold at a price of Usd 45.2mill while we understand that the two sisters HUA SAN and LU SAN  (318k DWT 2008 and 2009 SWS) are under close negotiations with price expectations in the region of Usd 30mill and Usd 33mill respectively. This downward correction in values can be witnessed across most tanker sectors which is particularly well-illustrated in the Aframax segment by the sale of the Japanese controlled LR2 unit CHAMPION PRINCE (105k dwt 2012 HHI coated) which achieved Usd 24.1mill. Only a few weeks ago same owners disposed of the the sister CHAMPION PRINCESS, also 2012 built, to GESCO for Usd 26.4mill.  Activity in the Kamsarmax segment remains high with a further two vessels changing hands this week. Namely the Japanese controlled CETUS OCEAN (83k DWT 2013 Sanoyas) sold at Usd 17.3mill and LEDA (82k DWT 2013 Tsuneishi Fukuyama) at USD 16.7mill. Worth noting that the CETUS OCEAN was sold with BWTS installed hence the mark up in pricing. Scorpio Bulk’s sell-off continues unabated with four NACKS 2015 built Ultramaxes sold to Pacific Basin. All units were scrubber fitted and the reported price of Usd 16.75mill each is therefore more or less in line with recent sales of non-scrubber fitted  comparable units.

The Suezmax market has had a very familiar stop/start feel to it this week. In the East, charterers were in a generous mood as they did their utmost to support rates by piling in on top of each, resulting in modest gains for some owners. The Mediterranean and Black Sea continue to attract eastern ballasters who have missed the MEG/East fixing window which has conversely put a ceiling on Black Sea-Med/East moves. This has naturally started to trim the East list, but not to the degree that rates are likely to runaway.  Owners will need a busy back end of the week for MEG/East to threaten the high forties mark, which should otherwise trade flat. TD20 has flattered to deceive recently and will similarly need a busy Thursday to push on.  The overarching issue of lack of oil demand continues to stymie this market.

In the North Sea/Baltic market even a tight window wasn’t enough for owners to earn some extra worldscale points. As we proceed with the loading dates of early December, we expect market to remain rather flat as cargo exports are still low to support the long tonnage list. Keep an eye at the USG though, it could be the alternative that will bring some optimism.  In the Mediterranean/Black Sea, the rates have dropped a few more points this week and TD19 is now giving negative returns. The tonnage list is currently building up again, however owners will be keen to see if the improving markets in the USG is able to attract potential ballasters away from the area and in turn reduce competition.

In the Atlantic, many owners are contemplating a direct ballast West in search of higher TCE’s but West Africa/East has not moved off the ws29 conference rate to China. Cargoes ex USG are also flat, with ex dry docker fixing at USD 4.5m to Ningbo and regular tonnage 100-200k more. The North Sea has seen activity, as charterers try to get their ducks in line. A little under USD 4.5m for Hound Point East secures tonnage.

LNG markets continue to improve with buoyant demand supporting LNG shipping. Although there has been a short plateau in rates, requirements continue to surface as vessel positions firm up and ships are fixed with little idle time. Tight availability thus persists globally and is expected to remain light, as the wave of fixtures earlier this month will see ships employed through December and into the New Year. The regional imbalance continues with very few vessels in the Atlantic, and Panama Canal delays and longer voyages delivering into the colder winter in the East exacerbating the issue. There were reports of cancellations of January cargoes loading out the US Gulf, due in part to a lack of available shipping.  Views looking further into 2021 are more pessimistic, as reflected by the difference in spot and one year levels. Owners seeking utilisation over spot exposure may move to avoid competing with uncommitted new arrivals next year and the redelivery of existing tonnage. On the new building market it has been reported that Shell is adding to it’s tally of vessels by signing up shipowners to berths is has reserved in South Korea taking the total from 14 vessels up to 18.

Positive sentiment remains across this week following last week’s rising trend. In the Pacific, China coal demand pushing rates for Indonesian coal where owners are seeing in the mid/high teens for Indo coal rounds back to China/SE Asia and around USD 12,500 to India. Nopac RVs paying around USD 10,000, while Aussie RVs closer to USD 11k. From the Indian Ocean seeing rates in the low USD 13k for WC India via MEG trip to EC India. Meantime, in the Atlantic, USG is paying around high teens to Mediterranean and FH around USD 24,000, while the Continent is still firm with scrap to Emed paying in the mid/high teens.

EAST Activity and freight levels have indeed picked up quite significantly on both sides of the Suez this week, availability is as a consequence starting to become very thin for the remainder of December in the Middle East. Baltic has jumped up more than 4 dollars from Friday, however, we continue to see the West premium remaining wide. On the back of current freight ideas from owners and last done levels, Baltic is expected to continue upwards for now.  WEST The western VLGC freight rates are currently skyrocketing on the back of tight vessel supply and plenty of cargo inquiries for both ends of December and the first half of January. Although we have seen only a handful of deals done since the end of last week, freight rates have increased from USD 110 to high USD 120’s on a Houston/Chiba basis. What is exacerbating the tight vessel supply is that owners and even traders who have potential relets are currently holding back before fixing anything further in order not to over-commit their fleet and because the current discharge schedules are not firm. The market will remain tight for the foreseeable future.

text: AMERICAS Happy Thanksgiving! A 300,000 barrel draw occurred in US inventories. Although this was lower than expected it was very much an after-thought in traders minds this week. The main focus has been finding freight to lift US FOB cargos. This has caused traders to work FOB cargos well in advance to be sure they can secure freight. With mid to late January now being discussed. US FOB sellers have had to re-assess values as popping freight has eroded January netback values. With all eyes on the arb, the question is will it widen and stimulate FOB deals while sustaining strong freight?

The week started off on a positive note with fresh mineral cargoes entering the Atlantic market. Especially the North Atlantic with Baltic rounds being concluded at higher than last done and Kmaxes achieving ard Usd 15k for a round. In the eastern hemisphere we also see rates gaining – however the bid/ask gap is big, but an underlying positive trend makes rates firming. NoPac rounds are yielding mid/high 10k. With the current soft trend for the Capesize mrkt, it will be interesting to see how long this firming Pmax market will last.

Optimistic mid-term outlook, but still drifting, dull and without much direction for the big ships. Spot values down some 15 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 11700/day. Mixed developments, with Far East pt outperforming Atlantic by a fair bit. All major miners on the west australia/china conference trade keep actively picking ships whilst Australian coal seeks others destinations following china trade ban, lifting average daily returns marginally to approach usd 14k basis 35-50 days duration. In grim comparison, the 100-day China-Brazil-China round is down 10 pct to come in at just over usd 10k/day. Fronthaul and transatlantic trades keep being an impotent mixture of limited iron ore/coal/bauxite flows ex Brazil/usec/wafr against a notable number of ballasters. With high commodity prices and closing of books, expectations are to see sharply increased demand on these routes in few weeks to come. Period activity limited as ffa fail to support, present value for very modern/eco 180000-tonners basis about 12 month estimated at usd mid 15k's. Best option for the period-minded owners not willing make such sacrifice being index-linked, for which around BCI AVE5TC + 21 pct just rumoured concluded.

The week started quietly with limited offers. By mid week almost all routes were pushing up. Especially USG in Atl, where trip to Far east was paying close to USD22,000 and to Continent direction rates were closed to USD16,000. Grain runs from Brazil to China where concluded at USD12,000 + 400k bb on Ultramax.   Ships with fertz dop Cont to USG fixed at USD11-12,000 and usual scrap round could pay USD17,000. In Pacific basin all in all not many fresh orders. Vsls from South Africa to China went at USD12,000k + 200 k bb. Trip from AG to Bangladesh at USD12,500. Business from WCI to China was paying USD11,000 and steel run from ECI to China at low USD13,000 on ultra.  Less attractive trading on the period front where supras were covered at 8700 for 11-12 mos redel ww.

EAST The Eastern market has pretty much been in waiting mode for most of the week as awaiting the Aramco acceptances which were finally announced last night. We have since then seen a couple of ships taken out on subs for 1H December load in the AG, but there has not been an abundance of activity as some Owners were hoping for. Aramco is reported to be short propane in December and a few lifters have as a result gotten their cargoes deferred to the later part of the month. Meanwhile, we are still left with a couple of open trader relets within 1H December in the AG. But some of these ships may ultimately end up being programmed elsewhere unless finding employment out here in the East, and thus we do not expect freight rates to come off over the next deals done.  WEST West of Suez the market remains tight on vessel supply apart from a couple of first half December vessels. There are still some uncovered cargoes during last decade December that are yet to be sorted shipping-wise and early January has actually come into play. We are likely to see some early January fixtures concluded within this week, however, some of the vessels which are early January lifting candidates haven’t even loaded. Last done for an East only fixture ex US is USD 107-108 and although owners trying to pull the market further up towards USD 110, the momentum is currently not there yet.

The December MEG program has kicked off with a yawn. The Chinese are “programming” Chinese ships under so called “COA” terms, so far needing little aid from third party VLCC owners. The position list, albeit well stocked, has thinned somewhat of modern unrestricted units. One owner “scored” yesterday, fixing a W28.5 for a replacement job MEG/China off a prompt laycan. Alas, it was the exception that confirms the rule, as later laycans are likely priced closer to W25 – with a couple of points off for older and/or ex d/d types. In the Atlantic our own Equinor also got a premium for one of their relets, fixing a USG/China run at $5 million lumpsum, well up from last done - but again off a  laycan where the competition was limited. Time will tell, but we doubt it is going to move the market in any significant manner.

This week has seen a flurry of transactions in the dry sale and purchase markets with vessels changing hands across all segments. The increased buying enquiry witnessed over the past weeks in the kamsarmax segment has met a flow of sales candidates with 7 units changing hands this week alone. Four of which were sold as part of Scorpios Bulks divestment programme. Off the back of this increased liquidity values remain well supported and we expect  them to remain flat as long as tonnage continues to be made available for sale.    Despite only a handful of sales to report  on the tanker front, activity remains high in the sector with a number of upcoming inspections and ongoing discussions. We expect further activity in the Aframax segment with four units inviting offers next week. This is following a number of sales which should give a clear idea of what direction values will take going forward.
