text: AMERICAS Yesterday, the EIA reported a conventional draw of 2 million barrels for the week ended 13 November, exceeding, though directionally in line with market expectations. Almost the entirety of the draw can be traced to the US Gulf coast (1.9million barrels), as exports continued to rise to 1.22mn b/day. Contrarily, the midcontinent built 180,000barrels as mild temperature persists, effectively cutting into heating demand. As it stands, the arbitrage east (lst/fei) hovers around $157/ton. A forthcoming tender for a 1h December VLGC cargo- from a US Gulf terminal will provide insight as to truth of value, but as it stands, 1h December cargos are seen offered in the low 8cpg region, while bids are in the upper 7's/ just about 8cpg, a far cry from the double-digit levels seen concluded for December cargos in the weeks prior. With that said, second half December cargos carry a premium to the earlier barrels, and remain on offer in the 9-cent region. Freight basis Houston/ Chiba which was last done at $108/ton has effectively hampered what potential lifters can pay for spot cargos.

With other surrounding markets offering a better alternative, we had quite a few ships ballasting away from the Nsea/Baltic. With less tonnage supply in the area Owners were filled with some more confidence to push for higher rates. However, this momentum didn’t last as cargo volumes weren’t great enough to support any upward pressure. Going forward, we might see some weather delays and we could see the market gain a few points on back of ships getting delayed. Activity has slowed down again in the Med/Bsea, and with a growing tonnage list we have seen a slight downwards correction in rates. Although the December cargo program out of Bsea is lighter than previous months, Libyan export activity is contributing in a positive manner. In the short run however we expect the market continue to trade at current low levels.

The LNG markets remain buoyant, with strong margins continuing to support the six-figure headline rates for prompt business we’ve seen in past weeks. Charterers enquiring for January loadings in the Atlantic are reluctant to move just yet as owners are showing no sign of softening their stance for spot business, and certainly the combination of a tight basin, delays through the Panama Canal and favourable trading economics for the first half of the month are in their favour. The situation in the East is more nuanced, as the fixing window is more prompt and limited availability is in owners’ favour today, but there are a number of vessels due to redeliver in the Pacific in December that may put pressure on levels. While owners continue to ride the winter wave, as these dynamics play out some will move away from spot business towards utilisation and we do expect more longer-term business in the weeks ahead. There have been no new orders placed at the yards this week.

Those participants who started the week with a sense of optimism may be feeling a little short changed. Td20 has spent a week flirting with W40, but attempts to push rates further have been thwarted by Charterers slow trading every cargo. Whilst the WAFR December program is fairly lean, the main physical and psychological support may yet come from the Black Sea and Libya. The December Russian Black Sea program  is noticeably bigger than November, which has encouraged Charterers to reach forward, creating date-convergence with the West African fixing window. This has held a number of  vessels on the Continent and West Mediterranean away from WAFR, creating some balance .  MEG/East has taken a breather  for now with rates likely to settle at 130KT x W45 on modern whilst Basrah/Med trades 140kt x W20-22.5.

Whilst 2nd values for the older VLCC tankers are still holding up relatively nicely, the other crude segments are faring worse. The sale of Suezmax BACALIAROS built 2003 SHI at Usd 15.3 mill represents a 30% drop in values since the peak in February when a same age Korean built Suezmax was sold for Usd 22 mill. Also pressure on Aframax values as seen by this week’s sales. Offers are invited mid next week for tranche 2 of the Xihe creditor controlled sale of three VLCC’s built 2008, 2009 and 2013 (all China). We understand the latter has by far received most attention from potential buyers.  Finally some positive Covid-19 news with effective vaccines being announced. However the near term challenges for both the oil and  tanker markets will remain unchanged. IEA revises down 2021 oil demand by 0.1 mbpd, stating that “vaccines are unlikely to significantly boost demand until well into next year”.  We still expect relatively sluggish rate development for the rest of this year and during most of the first half of next year. Given our more positive outlook for the second half of the 2021 and into 2022, however, this should give some interesting S&P opportunities going forward.  The dry sector remains active with the majority of transactions being in the 10-15 year bracket. Prices are however still best case moving sideways in the majority of sectors.  An increasing number of 5-10 year old Kamsarmax candidates are coming for sale from Japan which could set new benchmarks going forward.

This week started off on a positive note with news of a Covid-19 vaccine spurring all markets. Half a dozen VLCC cargoes hit the market from the get go, an unusual occurrence regardless of market conditions. Alas, with the recent tonnage build up, and no visible united front from the owning community, they were quickly absorbed at last done levels. Each to his own seems to be the prevailing mantra, whether an excuse on age or vetting status, or the larger outfits being awash with tonnage and mopping up. MEG/East runs remain just north of WS25, translating to TCE’s well below OPEX, and further hit by increased bunker prices. The Atlantic market is arguably a tad better, but for much longer commitments and still barely breaking even. We do not expect any significant change short term.

In the North Sea and Baltic markets, Aframax rates have been steadily fixing around bottom levels give or take a couple of WS points pending on the voyage in question. We now see more ships ballast out of the area as surrounding areas are offering a better alternative than fixing current levels in the Nsea. Going forward we expect the market ex Baltic to increase slightly, but unless we don’t see any increased activity for cross Nsea it won’t be a significant upward correction in rates.  In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, we have seen a rush of cargoes this week with activity both cross-Med and out of the Bsea. Rates across the board have picked up 5 points or so, and although the tonnage list is still looking healthy it is tighter than it has been in recent weeks. We expect the market to remain firm in the week to come.

On the surface it looks like another uneventful week in the Suezmax market, but this belies some of the more subtle cues that point to modest optimism. Anticipation of a Covid-19 vaccine has helped kickstart a raft of TC enquiries as charterers hedge 2021 and a possible return to higher oil demand. These TC moves are straight out of the Warren Buffet playbook of being "greedy when others are fearful" and will likely payoff. The spot market has finally shown signs of life as lists tighten for early third decade stems in the Mediterranean and West Africa.  A prompt WAFR/Portugal cargo clearly missed the memo and  paid WS39, pricing TD20 in the high WS30'S. TD6 will trade mid/high WS40's whilst in the East we may see rates benefit from Western sentiment but ultimately capped by VLCCs.

The week started on a slow note with little fresh business entering the market. In the Atlantic, we see less demand and a growing list of available tonnage. TA’s are currently yielding USD 11k while fronthauls basis Continent delivery are priced at a softer 18k. In the Eastern Hemisphere, we have since Tuesday seen rates gaining. We see this due to increased Aussie volumes with November cancelling and there are not many candidates available - also due to Covid measures among crew members.

From the beginning of this week indexes kept heading south. Very little activity and in general we believe the market is fading away. There are a few grain cargoes recently surfacing in the USG to Far East destinations. Rates reported in the region of USD 21,000 for Ultramax and below USD 20,000 on Supra. ECSA also losing ground and rates reported on fronthaul run in the upper USD 13,000's plus USD 375,000 ballast bonus. Scrap from the Continent to Turkey was fixing in the high USD 10,000's. Tonnage building up in East Mediterranean putting further pressure on rates. Limited fronthauls with grain ex Black Sea made owners to adjust rates downwards. The Asian market was stable, but rates was also under pressure. Nopac and Australian round voyages was reported fixing Tess 58 index type at USD 8,500's with respective ballast bonus on APS load port.

Average index TC value is presently just short of USD 13,500, down close to USD 1,000 in one week. Although there has been a negative mood across the Cape market over the last weeks, c5 has been fairly steady. However, overnight, this route dropped 40 cents to present index level of USD 6.5. C3 has over the last weeks been dominated by Vale, and consequently they have been in control of the game. Recently there was an increase in COA nominations resulting in some kind of support and balance, but now it seems Vale again is in control. Present average is just short of USD 14 and expected to come off further in the near future.  There is no period activity.

The past week saw an open Arbitrage between the East and the West, which prompted several opportunistic traders to take on tonnage for US Gulf loadings. With the Atlantic basin so tight vessels had to be taken from the East, which locked in full utilisation at round-trip economics or more for these fixtures. Such longer charters are currently attractive to owners, with the knock-on effect being an uptick in headline rates and continuing three-way economics for shorter, intra-basin business. Both owners and charterers are looking at the fundamentals carefully for directional signs in the weeks ahead, and with low prompt availability, high feed gas into the US terminals and positive developments on the Covid-19 front we do expect the current conditions to last in the short term. Further out, a number of vessels redeliver from mid-December, but coming off the West-to-East convey belt the global availability will likely remain unbalanced.

text: AMERICAS Per the EIA report of this morning (which was delayed by a day), US propane inventories fell from 95.828mmbbls at end Oct to 94.889mmbbls as of 06 Nov, a decline of 939,000bbls.  A build of 812,000bbls was achieved in PADD I (US East Coast), and an increase of 305,000bbls was seen in PADD II (Midwest).  The Gulf Coast, however, saw a draw of 2.033mmbbls, on the basis of both stronger petrochemical demand and swelling overwater export volumes.   November marks the 6th straight month of improved propane consumption, having steadily climbed from 184,000bbls/day in May to 324,000bbls/day in Nov.  Overwater exports, meanwhile, continue to dominate – with more than 4m tons of LPG’s exported from the US in Nov (3.5m tons propane and nearly 700,000mt of butane).  At present there are no signs that the trend will abate, as the December rosters are largely complete. Buyers are eager to engage as the arb to the East is open, but sellers (most of whom appear to be re-sellers), are holding at robust terminalling fee rates.   Weather-related demand in the US came early, but for the moment seems to have left early, as well.  NOAA updated its prognosis for North America which (again) shows a propensity for a warmer-than-average temperature forecast over the Nov/Dec/Jan period, which doesn’t necessarily preclude the possibility of cold spells, but indicates the likelihood of a generally warmer winter which could, in turn, lead to softer domestic values.  That, however, may be decided – at least in part, and on a short term basis – by the petchem sector and, most importantly, exports. Finally , strong demand from Mexico and Brasil is continuing and looks like that will be the case through the first quarter of 2021.

text: MEG Dec Propane CP surged up to $450 at the time of writing, gaining supports from front strong demand. Butane was traded at $10 higher. Dec/Jan CP traded at $12 backwardation, and it’s likely to enlarge further, with anticipation of forthcoming ARB volume into EAST. ADNOC released their Dec acceptances with some delays being reported, since majority tend to nominate early liftings to avoid backwardation into Jan.   KPC issued tender to sell one 11/11 loading 6/7th Dec. While QP tendered to sell one 21/25th Dec lifting 4/0 or 3/1. FOB discussions for Dec lifting equal ratio splits were at Dec CP minus around $10 while heavy propane cargo was bid at heavier discounts.   FAR EAST A flurry of bids was shown in/off window this week. Several 23kt propane parcels for 2h Dec delivery were traded Dec FEI plus $9/10. And outside window traders and importers are actively inquiring Dec delivery cargos, propane mainly. Evenly split cargos were slightly less favorable into NEA.   Other than spot discussions, intensive term negotiations are going on this week. Indian BPCL was reported to secure 90% of their term volumes at CP minus mid high single digits. One Schina traditional importer awarded their annual tender for 11/11 monthly at CP plus low 30s reportedly. Following this, another two petchem importers also issued term tender to secure heavy or full propane cargos for feedstock use.

EAST As cargo acceptances for next month gradually has started to come out, fixing focus in the East has shifted towards 1st decade December. One Oil Major did secure shipping for early December while talks of some receiving delayed ADNOC dates could mean less cargos from the supplier in the first half of December. That said, together with the release of Aramco dates which is expected early next week, the picture for next month will become more clear. Available tonnage is not in abundance, and as such we expect freight to remain stable to slightly increasing going forward.  WEST The West market continues in a similar fashion to what we have seen over the last couple of weeks; relatively tight vessel supply, a couple of owners largely in control of the majority of vessels and rates simmering somewhere between USD 103 and USD 106 per ton Houston/Chiba basis. As we are not yet done with all of the December fixing, it is likely that we are a couple of dollars away from the peak of the market.

The buying interest in VLCC tonnage remains steady and firm. Two more 2002 built are sold at prices in line with last dones. Following Hunter Groups’ recent sale of two 2019 HHI built VLCC’s at Usd 84.2 mill each, we now have another noteworthy sale. We understand TRF HORTEN built 2018 HHIC-Phil has been sold to Delta Tankers for Usd 72 mill. Adjusted for age this is some 10% down compared to the Hunter deal. The vessel is built at Hanjin’s previous Philippines facility with a retrofitted scrubber which explains part of the difference. However, in a more stable market we would expect a difference around 5% so this may arguably point to further downwards correction in values. As far as replacement cost bench-mark goes, we do not see much further downside potential in newbuilding prices from the Korean majors.  The combination of a strengthening WON vs USD and increased steel prices tells us that we are at bottom levels now. Tellingly, several VLCC contracts are in the making in Korea which may ease the pressure on the yards. With the new-found optimism in the container markets we will not be surprised also to see the Korean yards benefitting from increased ordering activity for the big sizes.   Despite the weakening freight market the dry S&P market is full of life with a large number of vessels changing hands across all sizes. There are unconfirmed reports of two 2016 JMU built scrubberfitted Capesizes being committed in the high 30’s, we expect to have more details next week.

A new week, a new month, alas the same poor VLCC market, with the coming winter looking more Game of Thrones than gain in freights. The second Covid-19 wave has hit hard, leaving little hope for oil demand, emphasized further by leading OPEC countries and Russia suggesting further production cuts – on the back of which oil prices have recouped most of last week’s losses. Adding insult to injury bunker prices have followed suit, with daily tanker earnings now into single digits per day. text: AMERICAS As the election continues oil prices have drawn back after an initial surge. Mt Belvieu propane has remained strong and lies just below 60% WTI. A larger than expected 2.6 million barrel draw in US inventories for the week ending October 30th was bullish Mt Belvieu. The draw was largely due to massive exports through October, and averaging 1.425 million barrels per day for the week. Some believe with 95.8 million barrels in domestic inventories and already well into draw season Mt Belvieu should not be at such a high % WTI. The question is, with terminal expansions and export volume records set to be broken this winter, could the inventory doubters be proved right?  Unseasonable demand from South America and prompt demand from Latin America continues to be seen.

It has been a slow week with little fresh demand, especially in the Atlantic. Rates keep on sliding and TA’s are currently yielding 12k. The shorter mineral rounds in the Baltic are being paid slightly better, with 13.5k reported done on a Kamsarmax.  In the Eastern Hemisphere we also experience a softer market with levels around 9k being achieved for rounds.

EAST The week got off to a quiet start in the East, but we are slowly starting to see a few companies looking at freight quietly for loading within 2H November. There is also an expectation of 2 possible Indian cargoes being shown to the market within this or next week. Out of a list of potentially 8-9 vessels open for the balance of November, we expect that a few of these could go back into own programs, while some Owners might also send ships West on spec. As a result the actual open tonnage for the remaining days of November may not be as long as it looks at first glance.  WEST First half December shipping availability is very much down to only a handful of vessels. Cargo enquiries for the same period are more or less done by the looks of it, however, delays in Far Eastern discharge ports is- and most likely will continue causing vessels to run late.

Sliding rates across the board with most of the areas losing ground. In the Atlantic, still seeing healthy rates from Continent although it’s not as tight as previous weeks. Owners are fetching around USD 18,000 for scrap from Continent to East Mediterranean and around USD 14-15k to USG, while from USG to Far East are trading in the low 20k's and TA in the mid teens. From the Indian Ocean, ships are covering South Africa to SE Asia around USD 11,500+150k gbb, while further East Nopac rounds fixing at around USD 10,250 and Indonesia/China coal rounds at low USD 9k basis South China delivery.

text: MEG Dec Propane CP surged up to $445, up by $30 this week, reflecting the strength in front market. Butane CP was traded at $8 higher than propane at the time of writing, slowly narrowed down as being less favorable in winter season. Dec/Jan CP spread was at $11 backwardation and might enlarge further. Qatar Petroleum released the Dec lifting with not cuts being heard. AG fobs discussions are in a stalemate as buyers exploring at double digit discounts or more, while sellers targeting at single digit only.     FAR EAST Another hectic week with active inquires for Dec delivery cargos, especially on propane. Cash premium stands firmer as better winter demand against continuous delays on US cargos via panama. A plenty of buyers are bidding propane for Dec delivery in and off window but only a few sellers emerged. Half cargo propane parcel for 2h Delivery was bid at mid-high single digit on FEI link while sellers asking at double digits premium. One full cargo propane for 2h Dec delivery was sold into E.China at Dec FEI plus teens, and half cargo was bid at Dec CP plus from 20s to 30s subject to different conditions. Other than this, a handful of tenders are running in the market. Korean HTC awarded their buy tender for 23kt propane in 1h Dec delivery at FEI plus high single digit reportedly. Taiwan FPCC was reported to secure 23kt propane for 1h Dec delivery at Nov FEI plus high single digit, while CPC’s buy tender for 11/11 last decade Dec delivery was still yet to award. CPC also issued a FOB/DES swap tender by selling 176k-264k FOBs and buying back 8 to 12 lots of 11/11 on delivery basis for next year.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco raised up Nov propane CP by $55 to $430 and butane CP by $60 to $440, which is in line with most expectations. text: AMERICAS Despite record exports from the US Gulf and East Coast, propane inventories remain very high. In fact this weeks EIA small build left inventories at 98. 4 million barrels, a number that should give comfort to even the biggest skeptics,  that there will be enough product for a cold winter and strong exports. Hurricane Zeta, has now come and gone leaving all export terminals untouched, but strong concerns over Panama Canal delays remain central in talks over exports.  Unseasonable demand from Brazil, and seasonal demand from Mexico,  are additional factors keeping export demand strong, and as a result we see no end in sight for record exports.

General levels for the big ships slightly up last 5 trading days, trying find a direction whilst navigation in a sea of overall Covid-19 related uncertainty.  Iron ore and bauxite fundamentals for the Brazil option West Africa/Far East fronthaul route look promising, giving a very healthy supply/demand ratio for remainder of year. Value for the China-Brazil-China round trip up 10 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 17k. Coal trades continue to perform below expectations as Chinese political bans still take their toll, only just partly offset by mixed fleet inefficiencies and Indian stockbuilding.  With FFA levels for 2021 standing at USD mid 13k's and thus far from matching physical expectations, period activity is limited - focus being on floating structures of which recent include 178,000/2010 reported done for around 12 months at ave5tc + 1.5 pct.

The Nsea/Baltic Afra market remains at bottom levels this week, and November lifting schedules do not indicate any upward pressure. The x-factor being the surging coronavirus cases across Europe which could possibly lead to some storage inquiries. Unless alternative markets attract ballasters away from the area, we expect rates to remain gloomy in the week to come. In the Med/Bsea however, we have seen a relatively active week for the first time in a while with the return of Libya being the main force. Owners will be excited to finally see an upward trend in freight levels, as benchmark routes have picked up close to 10 points since last week. With the Med being a bit more of an attractive area for Afras to be in now, we expect the market to remain firm in the week to come.

The November MEG program is in full swing, however rates continue on a downward trajectory. Any normal year we’d see increased demand and rates ticking up for the winter season, but Covid-19 has put a stop to any normality. MEG/East rates are drifting down through the WS20’s, and Wafr/eastbound rates have also dipped below the WS30 mark. From the USG, often an area of strength in comparison, charterers are understandably using their own vessels whenever possible. Many owners are taking the opportunity to dry dock their vessels in this depressed environment. However, upon completion these ships often become sitting ducks, given the (arguably) misplaced ‘perception’ of cargo clingage. Still, charterers have plenty to choose from, and without a viable vaccine and a big shift in global demand we expect more of the same.

EAST Although one trader relet was booked yesterday for a vessel swap, we are still left with a handful of possible open ships from traders during 2H November. There is currently not an abundance of activity going on in the East, but we do expect to see more cargos shown to the market later, and especially during last decade of November. Owners’ ideas are currently in the USD mid 60s Baltic, but some might be incentivized to do slightly less if they can book their ships close to vessel dates. On the other hand, if various parties end up moving on freight at the same time rates could jump further.  WEST West has taken a step back this week as fixing window has moved into 2nd decade December for US loadings. West and East freight rates at par at TCE around mid USD 50k's pd. October has been expected to see record exports ex US at close to 75 VLGC cargoes lifted, but with only a few days left of the month it looks like delays in loadings could cause the record from April this year to remain.

Coming into this week, Suezmax owners had a different mindset than they have had in several months. Increased activity at the end of last week, with prompt cargoes begging for offers during the weekend, made owners bullish for the first time in a while. The main factor behind this is the massive export from Libya entering the market. This activity pushed Med/East rates up USD 500k, and even TD20 was up 7.5p in a couple of hours. Owners were holding back, and market looked to be improving significantly. But as charterers managed to keep their cool, it all slowed down quickly. Tonnage list is looking healthier but still plenty of ship to fix, and owners started taking out cargoes one by one. Now we see healthier tonnage lists both in the East and Atlantic, but still prompt ships around, and we expect market to stabilize.

Majority of Supramax routes losing ground this week. Atlantic felt softer with especially USG falling farther behind. Fronthaul from USG to Far East was concluded at low 20s now. After strong period also the Continent started to drop off. Fronthauls paying at ca 23,000. Trips to USG being fixed at USD 13,000. For ECSA inbound tick less. Gloomy feelings across Asian routes as well. Ultramax was fixed for a trip from Indonesia to China at 12k.  North China to ECI was covered at 9k on Supra. Vessel open South China fixed for a trip via Indonesia to EC India at mid 8k. On the period side, Supras were fixed in the low 9s in Far East.

The Panamax market seemed to be a 2-tier market beginning week, with lower levels being achieved on voyage basis in the Atlantic. This took a turn on Tuesday where we see more activity out of North Atlantic and especially shorter round trips has inked up the index. Same goes for fronthauls where the activity out of USG to Far East has increased and ECSA being without any direction. TA’s are currently yielding mid 11’s while fronthauls are trading in the low 20’s. In the Eastern Hemisphere we see a softer tone with rates slowly sliding downwards and Pacific rounds are being fixed in the low 11’s.

No sign of any impending winter season as far as crude spot rates goes. Vintage VLCC’s continue to attract steady buying interest with another three vessels sold this week.  Price levels concluded are on par with recent transactions.  A 2011 Korean built Suezmax tanker is being offered for sale which should give good direction of where we stand on values for the semi-modern, non-eco ones.  We expect low 30’s will prove to be best case for this vessel.     Scorpio Bulkers continues its sales activity. Values are moving sideways and this will remain the case for as long as the number of ships for sale remains high.

We did see Atlantic voyage fixtures being concluded with TCE to low 9,000 already end last week, thus we do feel the index has been lagging somewhat as p1A is being priced at high 10,000 mid-week. The slow demand compared to the growing tonnage list is what we are up against. In the Pacific, there is a higher volume of concluded business, however rates are down some USD 2,000 w-o-w and currently yielding 10,000.

Slow start of the week with limited fresh inquiry and lack of market direction. Positive sentiment in Atlantic is fading away and charterers rating tonnage down USD 1-2,000 from last done, except Continent market which remains firm and very tight on tonnage supply. US Gulf and ECSA lacking fresh enquiry with prompt tonnage building up. Rates adjusting from USD 17,000 down to USD 15,000 with coal cargoes from USG to Mediterranean. Same trend we see in the Mediterranean for Clinker runs. Last week Supra was reported fix USD 21,000 delivery West Mediterranean to West Africa, whereas now charterers rating way below USD 20,000. Far Eastern market didn’t show sign of recovery after the holidays despite all expectations, thus remain weak with rates similar to last done. Supra 55’ dwt fixing around USD 9,000 for Indonesia-Thailand coal voyage.

text: MEG Nov Propane CP was traded at $430, despite the oil tumbled down. Nov/Dec swap backwardation maintains at $7. Saudi Aramco released its Nov acceptance with some liftings advanced and no cuts heard. Indian BPCL was reported to secure one Dec delivery equal ratio cargo at Dec CP plus high 20s via tender. One Chinese Major have issued term tender to secure one cargo monthly from Jan to Dec delivery 2021, ratio to be either heavy propane or evenly split.

Over the last week the market has come off by 26% for all routes, and the sentiment have been very gloomy. However, the market finally found some support and today we see better freight for both Brazil-China and West Australia-China, the two major routes for iron ore. This has turned the sentiment positive and the cargo list has increased especially in the South Atlantic region. That said, not everyone are convinced we are set for a new upturn so it’s still vessels pricing decent freight levels though at higher prices.

text: AMERICAS US propane inventories declined by 1.6mmbbls, which was slightly more than anticipated, leaving c3 stocks at 98.325mmbbls as of 16 Oct.  Last year the mid-Oct stock levels were recorded at 95.282mmbbls.  This week’s decline in stocks and the simultaneous arrival of a cold front in the US Midwest appears to mark the commencement of the winter-demand season, but MB values have nonetheless drifted because of declines in the crude arena.  US exports remain robust, with Oct anticipated to see near-record level monthly lifting volume of 74 VLGC cargos.  Shipping delays at the Sabine River on the Gulf Coast are being overcome inasmuch as there were 6 VLGC’s awaiting transit yesterday, but 4 of those ships have resumed movement as of this morning.  Meanwhile, delays at the Panama Canal are presently reported at 8 days and are occurring primarily due to C19-related safety measures (specifically social distancing efforts and minimized crew numbers), but also to fog (10 days in Sep and 8 days – so far – in Oct) and the simultaneous occurrence of higher grain and LNG vessel passages.  Big ship freight rates from the US/Asia remain in the $103-105/mt range, while to Europe rates are pegged at $53/mt which is impacting the netback levels.

Winter for the year is establishing nicely for cargo owners and shipowners alike. Activities are ramping up as LNG prices are on the rise in the Far East, in anticipation of a relatively cold winter as compared to the previous years. Charter rates have risen substantially versus levels merely a month ago, and spot fixtures are concluded basis more than the standard round-trip. There have been a string of fixtures concluded and quite a few more being worked on this week, and remaining available vessels may not be open for long. We hear that the number of shipping enquiries received by players with available tonnage have heightened considerably and this is creating interesting opportunities for fleet optimization, cargo sales and freight trading. The winter market has only started and it remains to be seen where shipping rate levels could end up to in the weeks to come.  No newbuilding orders or ship sales have been reported this week.

EAST Market expected activity East of Suez to pick up again with the release of the Aramco acceptances this week. But time of writing we are yet to see any real momentum, partly explained by more Saudi cargos allocated towards the 2nd half of the month. Based on monthly averages from previous months, there should still be a handful of 1H November cargoes out of the Middle East. While we are yet to reach 2H November fixing window, more cargoes should be coming to market.  WEST The VLGC market West of Suez has seen a couple of fixtures concluded thus far this week and there are seemingly a handful more enquiries left uncovered for end November and early December. Freight availability is relatively tight for November and when looking at the beginning of December positions there is a large chunk of vessels which haven't reached discharge ports yet. In turn, this uncertainty in discharge schedules currently creates difficulty in fixing vessels at the moment, something which will keep the market firm.

At the beginning of the week there was a palpable sense that the market was grazing the bottom with possible upside. There was sustained enquiry in both Eastern and Western Hemispheres, which had created small pockets of resistance. All was looking up, or so we thought. That quiet optimism was shattered by a Wafr/options cargo booking UKCM at WS29 which other charterers will now surely use as leverage. TD6 will trade low 40's whilst long cross-Med is stable in the mid/high WS30's.  In the East there's a balanced feel with MEG/East trading mid/high WS30's for modern. The key fundamentals of oversupplied tonnage and reduced oil output have not disappeared, meaning that if any resistance resurfaces the foundations remain soft.

We understand the VLCC’s saw a hefty amount of interest and around 8 bids where placed. The jury is still out, however early reports suggest that the vessels are closed to being committed at USD 110mill en bloc. If confirmed, it represents a solid correction in values in light of the recent sale of the “TAKAOKA” (2011/Universal/300kdwt) which was sold for USD 45m last week. Albeit a discount is expected in light of the auction process, that the vessels have been idle for some time and Chinese built. Furthermore, ADS Crude sold “ADS SERENADE” (2002/Hitachi/300kdwt) to UAE based buyers for USD 25.5m, leaving the company with only one vessel left in their fleet. The sale falls in with the sistership “ADS STRATUS” they sold in September also for USD 25,5m.   In the dry sector Nissen Kaiun have sold yet another cape this week, namely the “HUGE HAKATA” (2012/Koyo/180kdwt) for USD 21m to clients of Zodiac. Moreover, Oldendorff have sold the “TILDA OLDENDORFF” (2011/STX/180kdwt) for USD 18.7m to Alpha Bulkers.   “Scorpio Bulkers” stole the headline this week by selling 4 x Ultramax’s bringing their total sell-off to excess of 100m since the company announced their move into offshore wind. Navigare is understood to have picked up the “SBI  PHOENIX” & “SBI SAMSON” (2017/Chengxi/63kdwtI) for USD 17m each, whilst the  “SBI HERA” (2016/Mitsui/60kdwt) was sold for USD 18.5m to undisclosed buyers. Lastly, the “SBI HYPERION” (2016/Nacks/61kdwt) was sold for USD 17m. Scorpios sell-off is making them the market maker in the Ultramax segment at the moment.

It has been another busy week in the LNG shipping market as the anticipated Q4 activity is really ramping up. LNG cargo prices are on a rapid rise in the Far East as buyers have started to secure their early winter cargoes in expectation of a colder winter. This has made disponent owners to think twice before subletting their vessels out since the risk of finding yourself short, or in the mercy of tighter shipping market, has gone up. Also, the possibility of arbitrage opening between the West and the East has increased, and capturing that potentially short period might only be available to those with enough length in their shipping portfolio. Aforementioned is also reflected in the current elevated spot shipping rates, with especially the East of Suez seeing highest demand for tonnage whereas the West of Suez is tightening up quickly, but still lacking slightly behind due to a few uncertainties, such as the latest hurricane aftermath to some of the USG liquefaction plants. During these times it is however good to remember that the final quarter has been historically the most volatile period within the calendar year, and this seems to be true even in this extraordinary year of 2020, and by the looks of it, we might have very interesting weeks ahead. In the newbuilding side, it was reported that DSME has signed firm contracts to build six Arc7- ice class LNG carriers for two separate European companies with delivery expected in 2H 2023.

Rates continue further down after the Chinese are coming back from their holidays, with as much as USD 10,000 off on average from last week. Present average is just excess USD 23,000. The reason being less c3 activity demand, presently in the 18s pmt, consequently resulting in more ships for c5 and lower rates here as well. Period has continued to be difficult throughout this period as well, but with a further hit more activity can be expected here.

With China and Asia back from holidays, the week kicked off with a flurry of enquiry. However, most open market cargoes found dance partners in the high WS20’s MEG/East – although a couple of charterers were “stung” with a flat WS30. “Disadvantaged” ships remain all the rage to save a buck, albeit a risky play. One had to pay up 3.25 WS points to replace their first bargain attempt. We seem to have run out of steam come mid-week. The MEG fixture count is now in the mid 90's. Extrapolating from the previous months, people are starting to question whether the October program is a wrap. On positive note, we only count a tonnage overhang of +/- 25 ships moving into the next month. A couple more turn of the month deals are likely, and with that the supply/demand picture looks a tad more balanced than for quite some time.

The market overall remains fairly flat this week. The ECSA is showing negative signs with falling rates, where Supras has fixed around USD 13,000 for TA to Continent, while FH ex USG paying in the low 20's. The Continent on the other hand remains very firm with very limited tonnage list and still fresh cargoes coming out for end Oct dates, Ultras fixing low 20's for scrap to Emed. From the Indian Ocean, levels around 11,500+150k gbb for rv back to Pakistan/India range, while further east Indo/India is paying owners around USD 9,000 and similar level for other SE Asia destinations.

The Suezmax market seems like a never-ending story at this point. Activity is decent, but there is just way too much available tonnage, in all areas. Some positives in the West the last week though, Libya is now back on, soon at the capacity they were at prior to the shutdown. As a result of that we have had more activity in the Med/Bsea area than in a long time. In the East we are still at bottom levels, even if tonnage-list is looking slightly better than last week. With the activity we see in both East and West, we expect the market to have some potential upside, but it will take time. This week rates will remain steady, and we are not having too high hopes for next week either.

EAST Shipping activity East of Suez has been rather slow this week with most eyes on the West. However, one Indian major is still in the market for a ship off early November, and another fob tender for mid-November load in the Middle East has also received some attention. Last done deal was to a Chinese trading company reported at usd 63 baltic, but otherwise there is not much else to report. We are still waiting for next month acceptances from Aramco which will provide final clarity for the November lifting program. Meanwhile, turnaround time in some southern and northern Chinese ports are still very slow making ship schedules more uncertain, and it is expected that freight rates will remain firm for the weeks to come.  WEST After a slow start to the week owing to large parts of the US being off due to the Columbus Day, the market activity indeed picked up the pace. Uncovered cargoes versus open vessels seeking employment has been largely in favour of the latter and as such we saw rates jumping from mid/low USD 90’s H/C fixed last week to USD 103 H/C within a matter of days. The market remains tight on vessel supply for November, however, we expect chartering activity to keep going albeit at a slower pace and that owners’ and trader relets’ freight ideas will keep north of last done.

Aframax owners trading in the North Sea and Baltic market have been in dire straits for the past few weeks. Rates have been hovering around bottom levels. For some owners it makes more sense to sit idle and wait than perform a voyage with negative returns. This is also the reason why some charterers have paid a couple points more than last done levels. The Mediterranean and Black Sea market remains low and steady, as benchmark routes have been fixed at repeat (bottom) levels for more than a month now. Apart from Libyan activity slowly recovering, there is little for owners to get excited about in the short run. We expect a soft market in the week to come.

After the Chinese holidays came to an end, we have experienced a declining market – especially in the Atlantic. The rates kept falling even though the index did not pick this up until mid-week. We see chrts withdrawing from the market after owners confirming bids without any negotiations and we do expect a falling curve short term. TA’s are currently yielding USD 13.5k on the index, but the physical market is priced lower. In the Pacific we see NoPac rounds being concluded at USD 13k for modern Kmax units, while the longer rounds are being priced in the low 12k.

A number of sales to report across all sale and purchase markets with a notable pickup in activity on the tanker front.  The week began with Japanese owners inviting offers on the clean trading LR2 unit “CHAMPION PRINCESS” (Abt 105k dwt built 2012, HHI). The vessel had been inspected by up to 10 Buyers and is believed to have received up to 6 offers to finally end up in the hands of Great Eastern Shipping at a price of Usd 26.4m. The substantial buying interest can in part be explained by an extensive period of inactivity in the sector with virtually no transactions, which, coupled with a falling chartering market has lead  buyers to chase a considerable correction in asset values.  A correction that becomes particularly apparent when looking at the last comparable sale of the Aframax “NANYANG STAR” (Abt 105k dwt built 2012, Sumitomo) sold at Usd 29.8m in March this year. We expect further activity in the Aframax/LR2 sector with a number of vessels inviting offers over the coming days.  NYK has also disposed of its VLCC “TAKAOKA” (Abt 300k dwt built 2011, Universal) which was sold at Usd 45m earlier in the week. This follows the sale of “TOKITSU MARU” (Abt 300k dwt built 2011 , Mitsubishi) which was sold from the same owners at Usd 45m last week.  In the dry sector Scorpio Bulkers has sold the sisterships “SBI SOUSTA” & “SBI CONGA”(Abt 81k dwt built 2016 &2015, Hudong) for region Usd 18.5m each. This brings the tally to three vessels sold over the past two weeks and we expect the selling exercise to continue in line with the company’s strategy of shifting capital and focus to its recently announced offshore & renewable venture.

text: MEG Nov Propane CP surged up by nearly $25 to $407 this week, following the oil rebound, coupled with the active inquiries on evenly split cargoes. Sellers are targeting for premium in view of less butane available from US, while buyers bid at teens discounts. The strong Nov swap turned Nov/Dec into backwardation at $3.   FAR EAST Far East value extended gains this week, as traders covering shorts caused by previous US delays and concerning on coming Hurricane Delta. FEI Nov boosts up to $431 and FEI/CP Nov enlarged to $26 from last week’s $18. Cash premium for 1h Nov delivery propane was finally turned into positive territory, with 23k propane parcel concluded at Nov FEI plus low-mid single digit, which hasn’t been seen since this June. We believe the potential delays will still lend support to far east market, until terminals clear all the backlogs.  Despite the China holiday, a couple of Chinese importers managed to cover some parcels for Nov delivery and still explore to buy more. We expect that more buying interests will emerge once players return, and forward month FEI will continuously be traded under good liquidity, with DCE future players participating behind

EAST  With China off on longer holidays this week the market has been fairly inactive. We saw a couple of ships being fixed for October laycans at the beginning of the week, but apart from these deals there is not much to report. We are still left with some possible length from traders during end Oct/early Nov, but some of these ships might eventually be absorbed into own programs or sent back West later. However, owners and traders would be inclined to wait until the Adnoc acceptances are out from early next week before making any decisions on where to send their open ships, as these acceptances could potentially create more interest for freight from early November in the MEG.  WEST Activity has indeed been looming rather than booming this week in the West. A widening arb and healthy FOB appetite (though lack of FOB sellers right now) will in all likelihood increase activity on the shipping side sooner rather than later. Vessel availability is largely controlled by only a couple of owners and as such we expect the market to remain firm around mid/low USD 90’s Houston/Chiba before potentially even increasing again. A West Africa cargo early November and a USG cargo tender ex Nederland 6-7 Nov seems to be the talk of the town and would indeed provide a good gauge for the market.

text: AMERICAS   A draw of 100,000bbls left US propane inventories effectively flat at 101.842mmbbls.  Market participants were anticipating anywhere from a 1mmbbl draw to a 1mmbbl increase.  Domestic US propane market values moved up from a close on Monday of 50.125cts/gal, to a close of 51.333cts/gal on Tuesday and then closed Wednesday at 50.500cts/gal – leaving the pricing structure, while still mildly positive, rather unchanged as of midweek.  Export volumes are deemed to be stronger, but Hurricane Delta now threatens the US Gulf Coast and in one case a rather precautionary Force Majeure was declared for a cargo which was slated to load on the weekend.  Depending on the actual path taken by the (now Category 2) storm, a temporary closure of the Houston Ship Channel is presently unlikely.  Crude oil prices are up at present on oil shutdowns in the US Gulf, as almost 1.5mmbbls/day of production has been shuttered.  Meanwhile, arbs for Q4 have seen significant improvement as Asian values extended gains, propping up the likelihood that the West-to-East trade will be bolstered.  Spot terminal fees have adjusted as a result and have risen from a last-done level of 6.5cts/gal (for Oct) to present levels of around 9.0 cts/gal, though the results of a UGSC tender will likely set the market

Celebrations for China’s Golden Week continue, and while some may have expected a pause in the market instead, a steady flow of requirements mainly in the East has kept Owners busy and we are seeing rate levels reaching new highs this week. Availability has tightened across all basins, also in the Atlantic where activity was somewhat muted following supply disruptions from Hammerfest and possible weather related delays in US Gulf liftings due to another hurricane approaching.  Looking ahead, we see risk in potential sublet availability being withdrawn and with the expected restart of Hammerfest, US Gulf back to “normal”, we may see additional tightness in the Atlantic basin. As a consequence, Charterers may have to look at positioning tonnage from the East and coupled with a winter market approaching – it may result in further spot charter rate increases, which should not be a big surprise as it is seasonally “normal” this time of the year.  There were no new LNGC orders reported this week.

This week has been characterized by Golden Week in China. Oil giant Unipec tied up a chunk of the local fleet under so called COA terms to cater for some peace and quiet over the holidays, leaving little for third party owners to bite into. Apart from the odd Korea/Taiwan bound cargo, a few Indian ones and a smattering of Atlantic activity, it’s been very quiet. However, those charterers who did dip their feet in met some resistance from a very bored and disinterested audience. Yet biding their time, the results were in line with last done levels, or a smidgeon less. The tonnage list is like a box Liquorice allsorts, plenty to choose from no matter your taste, keeping a lid on MEG/East rates in the WS20’s - returning TCE’s below OPEX. The USG export market held steady, paying in the region of USD 4.6 mill for China.

For Aframaxes in Europe we have seen another week where the market remained flat at bottom levels. Consistent oversupply of vessels is the key factor across the board as demand is not there to absorb the available tonnage. In the Baltic/Nsea we see a small number of ships floating with cargo on board, but nothing yet supporting a contango situation which could encourage floating storage. As we reach the second half of the monthly cargo program, rates are expected to remain flat. In the Med/Bsea, a few ships have been fixed out of Libya offering some optimism although not enough to put any pressure on rates. As it stands now owners are not seeing alternative markets to flee to, hence we don’t see the fundamentals change much in favour of owners in the natural fixing window.

With the fourth quarter well underway the Suezmax market is still hampered by tonnage-oversupply and depressed cargo volumes. Whilst the majority of load zones have experienced moderate cargo enquiry this week, seasonal and physical support mechanisms that we generally associate with this time of year are blatantly missing.  In North West Europe we've seen a handful of arbitrage plays, albeit at insufficient volumes to hold most ships interest on the Continent. This will further add to freight woes in West Africa with TD20 likely to stay in the low WS30's for the remainder of the week.  Compounding this issue is a plethora of eastern ballasters that continue to cap upside for Wafr/East moves at WS40. MEG/East and Basrah/West will stay depressed for the balance of this week in the WS30's and WS10's respectively.

Continent remained firm. Usual scrap runs were discussed now closer to 20k. Black Sea seems losing some ground with many ballasters from ECI. Fhauls with grains now concluded at ca 22k. More activity from USG and ECSA remaining flat, where grain runs on Ultra were concluded at USD 15k to Continent and Supras to West Africa at USD 12k. Ships with bauxite from West Africa to Black Sea payed 11k. Ships for fhaul from Kamsar to ECI levelled at USD 17k. Pacific basin kept its slow speed due to remaining holidays in the area. Indo/India trips where covered closer to USD 9k. Ultra open Philippines via Indo to SE Asia reached USD 11k. Ultras fixed at 13k + 200k bb for trip to Far East. Trip from MEG to Bangladesh on Supra payed USD 11,600.

With the Chinese away for holidays it was expected less activity, however the volume of fixtures has increased. The TA rates increased some USD 1000 w-o-w and currently yielding in the mid 13k’s while shorter Baltic rounds are being fixed in the 14’s. In the eastern hemisphere we also see firming rates with NoPac rounds being fixed in the 14k region bss North delivery while Aussie rounds are being prized in the 12k region.

Year-high and positive Q4 expectations for the big ships despite a moderate correction taking place as we speak. General Atlantic and fronthaul iron ore volumes being the main drivers, with Brazilian miners facing a possible lack of early loaders. Far East activity is moderate in comparison, with West Australian iron ore trade making up almost all demand. Average daily earnings up more than 30 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 33,500. Market however still in need of positives to gain self-confidence, as value for long- vs short rounds have gone from premium to discount. The glaring discount also for forward values gives little room for long period fixing, with most conclusions limited to short duration - typically talk of index type tonnage done for 5-7 months at USD 20,500 and around 12 months struggling to exceed USD 16k.

In what we understand was a deal concluded a couple of months ago, Dynacom is reported to have purchased a nine year old Japanese owned/built VLCC for Usd 45 mill. This is as such the second VLCC of this age sold at more or less same levels so we can safely conclude that values have taken another tumble. Values for vintage VLCC are moving sideways with SEAWAYS MULAN built 2002 reported gone at levels in line with last week’s sale of PANTARISTE, also built 2002. We see more and more vintage available for sale with further deals expected to materialize soon. As expected, more tanker newbuilding contracts are coming to light with Atlas Maritime this week reported to have signed for two Aframax tankers at Daehan for mid Usd 40 mill. Additional Suezmax and VLCC contracts are also being done at levels in line with expectations. This, together with dismal spot rates are certainly not lending support to any positive development for crude values. Following inspections by around 10 buyers, offers are invited on Monday for LR2 tanker CHAMPION PRINCESS built 2012 which, together with the Xihe tanker sell-off, will be the ones to watch in the near future.   The increased activity out of Brazil has seen Capesize earnings skyrocketing, the BCI has more than doubled in under 3 weeks. This marks another dramatic market move in a year that has been the most volatile ever for Capes. In general, we find fundamentals to be more than sound and expect it to be so for another year and a half at least. For the smaller segments things are also moving in the right direction, albeit slower. We see demand coming back by varying degrees in all major discharge regions (Europe, Japan, Korea, India, South East Asia), whereas China remains strong notwithstanding the last month and a half’s slowdown. Fresh YTD spot market highs for Supramax are highly likely during Q4, but we are less certain of that for Kamsarmax. Vessel deliveries will fall markedly the next year and a half which, coupled with a continued economic recovery and massive stimulus measures, could make for very interesting times ahead. The renewed dry optimism is evident in the very significant number of second-hand transactions every week. Values are at a robust floor and from here any movement should be north.

As we publish the energy major Total is performing its remote investor day with a very central focus on the environment and a transition to a less carbon intensive future. At the same time prominent news stories portray that traders are also accelerating their transition to renewables.   It’s this transition that relevance to LNG really starts to take hold and should give some comfort to the average reader of this weekly publication - LNG currently has a very significant role to play. Global LNG demand might be taking a pause whilst celebrations are enjoyed for China’s Golden week but weather systems such as ‘La Nina’ are predicted to bring colder temperatures in due course adding to increasing market demand. On the flip side, supply is subject to significant interruptions across the global with the latest in Norway at the Hammerfest plant, thankfully no injuries, but production is not expected to return until November.  More specifically and to LNGC’s, interruptions, increased demand and illiquidity of vessels combines to create a very intriguing market, consequences could result in muted activity but could also cause significant opportunity for freight to rise to year highs as schedules change and ton time increases as vessel head further afield. Naysayers will point to high European storage levels and the lack of global industrial production as everyone tousles with the pandemic. It won’t change overnight and we don’t expect great changes in levels this week but next week may bring more clarity and improved owner returns. In the meantime we would like to wish all those who are celebrating Golden week a pleasant and restful break.

We see the market continuing its move upwards despite an expected quiet week with holidays in China. The Brazil to China route with iron ore is the main driver where it’s been a lot of activity with levels up 18% from last week. However, in terms of increase the north Atlantic is the most impressive with the fronthaul rate being up 50% and transatlantic up 69%. The Pacific is more stable, but still with good amount of activity is up 3%. For now, the market seems very solid and with a thin available tonnage list for Brazil it is expected to see further near-term improvement.

For Aframax owners trading in the North Sea/Baltic, even a relatively busy week with a decent amount of cargoes was not enough to push the market up higher as the tonnage list was too long. Owners are showing some resistance to fix current low levels, but again the volumes are not there to support them. Some delays in strategic load and discharge port coupled with some bad weather could possibly play their role in the short term, but we do not expect any dramatic change in the rates. Also in the Med/Bsea the low rate levels have rolled for another week. On a positive we have seen a few more inquiries from Libya as a result of the force majeure being lifted in some ports, however due to the unbalance of cargoes versus ships we do not foresee an imminent improvement in the week to come.

VLCC rates have continued to slide in the week gone by. Numerous MEG/China “COA” movements have been booked, with Chinese charterers taking care of business ahead of their holidays next week - leaving little enquiry of note for third party owners to bite into. The market remains firmly mired in the WS20’s for MEG/Eastbound cargoes, ranging from the low end for the somewhat challenged units to the upper end for modern tonnage. The Atlantic has fared somewhat better, with daily earnings twice that available from the MEG, but it’s a Hobson’s choice whether to lock in current rock bottom levels well into the new year. 一口吃不成胖子 (One meal won’t make a fat man).

It has been slow activity and with Chinese and Korean Holidays starting off today, we believe the activity will remain slow. TA’s are yielding USD low 12k while fronthauls bss Continent delivery are being fixed in region of USD low 20k. The Pacific round voyages are priced similar to the Atlantic rounds and are being fixed in the low 12k’s.

Imabari’ 63, built 2019, open China med September was fixed USD 11,100 bss 8-10 mos. Seasonal grain export from Black Sea and Continent dominating Atlantic market. EAST A handful of ships have been taken out this week in the mid usd 50s baltic range, but time being there seems to be few requirements left for October load unless ships get delayed and miss their laycans later. The market is also preparing for long holiday in China next week that will last until 8th Oct. Meanwhile we continue to see strong activity on freight for US cargos and thus we do not expect the baltic to come off anytime soon, as Owners would rather send their open ships back West unless able to program them at favorable rates in the East.  WEST Things have slowed down to some extent in the West this week compared to a busy week of fixing in the US last week. However, there are things going on, and although we have only seen one fixture done in the new fixing window so far, a couple of ships are on subs, and another few are under discussion. We are still seeing interest on freight for both October and November dates, and rate wise it seems levels in the new fixing window pretty much carry on from the last.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS A larger than expected build of 4.1 million barrels finally pushed US propane inventories above 100million barrels for the first time since 2015. With inventories at 102.0 million barrels Mt Belvieu was expected to weaken from above 50% WTI. This has not happened mainly due to the strength in international markets. This strength has partly been fueled by delays in USGC loadings caused by Tropical storm Laura and waiting time in the Panama Canal. Structural shifts in the forward curve in both NWE and FEI have strengthened prompt netback values and in turn US FOB buying ideas for November. This has caused the US FOB market to flip from well offered to well bid. Energizing FOB discussions and pushing bids up from a 5 handle to a 6 handle in a very short space of time. Going forward we believe US FOB values will continue to improve, even once the delays and bottlenecks have cleared.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG Saudi Aramco set Oct Propane CP at $375, up by $10 and Butane at $380, up by $25. Such number is in line with most recommendations. Nov and Dec CP are traded at healthy contango structure, with expectation of better winter demand.  QP sold its 24/25 lifting full propane cargo, at the level of Nov FEI minus high 40s reportedly. India BPCL is reported to purchase one Nov delivery evenly split cargo at Nov CP minus $8, much higher than other spot discussion on double digit discounts for Nov liftings.   FAR EAST Front market gains momentum due to the US cargos delays caused by panama congestion. Propane for 1h Nov delivery was bid up and one full cargo was reportedly traded at Nov FEI minus mid high single digit. One Korean petchem user secured a parcel of 23k propane for end Oct/early Nov delivery at flattish to Nov FEI.  Before the coming Golden Week and mid-autumn festival in China, importers are actively inquiring for heavy propane cargos for Nov delivery. Future players on DCE also closed their Nov contract position before holiday and some rolled positions into forward months, actively trading FEI intermonth spread simultaneously.

Last week was so quiet you could hear a pin drop in the VLCC market. However, this week kicked off in a promising manner with a handful of cargoes entering the market from the get-go on Monday morning, some of which with tight laycans and a potential for an extra point or two. Alas, the end result was a further decline, and as the week progressed the sound of rates dropping drowned the sound of the pin – culminating yesterday with a sub WS30 MEG/Eastbound for all classes. Lower bunker prices have supported daily earnings, however covering OPEX is yet again becoming a challenge. The western hemisphere has ventured slightly better, but continued downward pressure in the MEG will entice tonnage to ballast from the East on spec, and the ramification inevitable. Batten down the hatches.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The US propane supply is in very good shape heading into this Winter. In fact, with domestic storages at tank tops, if it is not a cold winter, the market will shift from comfortable to long. However,  what the traders are now concentrating on is the next winter. The generally feeling is that although this winter should be fine, the winter 2021/2022 looks very tight. International demand is growing at a rate that surpasses US production growth and in order to keep the world supplied, US exports will need to be at maximum levels. How this effects the relative price is what traders are trying to decipher but it looks certain exports will maintain at terminal capacity. In South America, the Brazilians have remained active despite their winter season winding down and we look to the other South American importers to begin contemplating the sale of their imports into the Northern Hemisphere winter markets.

WEST Freight is strong in the US and trading at closer to mid USD 90's, which is a couple USD premium to Baltic. The shipping markets are currently experiencing inefficiencies due to bad weather in the Far East, up to a week of delays in Panama and Houston is at time of writing lagging 3-4 days in loadings. In October we see quite a few uncovered cargoes for the back end of the month and we could see freight rates strengthen more in the weeks ahead, although the arb West/East so far seems to keep a ceiling on freight before we experience three digit rates concluded.  EAST We continue to see more activity on freight in the east this week. Several ships have been taken out of the market for MEG load in October, while at the same time we are awaiting the result of a few different cargo tenders that could potentially need spot shipping coverage. Last done deals have all been around the usd 53-54 baltic range (as compared to usd high 50s – low 60s baltic on some of the deals from last week to Indian Majors). But with a stronger freight market in the West we do not expect that the Baltic will continue to come off, as Owners would be more inclined to sent their open ships out West while this trend continues.

Over the last week the iron ore segment from Brazil to China has picked up, and we see freight rates up USD 2 (12%) week on week. On top of this, all the Australian miners have been fairly active pushing the West Australia to China route up 17%. In general, the mood is positive and taking into account we are head into a seasonal strong period, it’s expected that the market will continue the upwards trend.

As we leave behind a difficult summer, we move forward into an autumn showing cautious signs of the usual seasonal recovery. The shipping market is still grappling with the fallout from recent and potentially upcoming US Gulf storms and a revival of the Covid-19 threat, but the immediate impact of relets flooding the Atlantic basin has eased. Any such tonnage is only available for a limited period, so while there may be some bargains for very prompt charterers, the typical fixing window looks brighter for owners. The continuous bubbling of cargoes and requirements in the East picked up in recent weeks and is now cutting into the availability list, and rates are moving up as a result.  There were no fresh orders placed at the yards this week

The Suezmax market is still struggling at bottom levels. The start of this week was no exception - two fixtures done in West Africa, both in low WS30's. Ballasters from the East are now looking at negative returns for a normal TD20 run. Halfway through the week we see some more action in the East. Cargo activity in MEG has picked up, but with a tonnage list being the longest YTD, rates remains at the bottom. Going forward we expect the Suezmaxes to continue facing terrible earnings, at least for the short-term future. Looking further than that there are some positives. Libya have now started exporting, and it is only a matter of time until production is up and running again. This will be a very welcomed happening for what lately have been a "dead" Med-market for the Suezmaxes.

This week the Panamax market has experienced a slight uptick in rates in both hemispheres. There are however signs of slight weakening in the Pacific market the last couple of days. TA’s are currently yielding in the 10-11k region, while Pacific rounds are being fixed at 12k. We do see more demand for minerals in the North Atlantic and a quite tight tonnage list for now. This can turn quickly when available tonnage will re-appear.

Strong sentiment from the Pacific where rates pushing upwards, while sideways feeling in the Atlantic, with some pressure building up in certain areas, leading to increased expectations into the coming month. In the Far East, Aussie RV's paying around USD 11,000, while Indo/India fixing around USD 13,000. In the Atlantic, bad weather led to congestion and pressure on rates especially in the handy segment, but also limited tonnage of Supra at North Continent. FH paying in the low USD 20's ex Continent and Black Sea, while backhaul to USG around USD 13,000 ex Continent.

However, this week kicked off in a promising manner with a handful of cargoes entering the market from the get-go on Monday morning, some of which with tight laycans and a potential for an extra point or two. Alas, the end result was a further decline, and as the week progressed the sound of rates dropping drowned the sound of the pin – culminating yesterday with a sub WS30 MEG/Eastbound for all classes. Lower bunker prices have supported daily earnings, however covering OPEX is yet again becoming a challenge. The western hemisphere has ventured slightly better, but continued downward pressure in the MEG will entice tonnage to ballast from the East on spec, and the ramification inevitable. Batten down the hatches.

Another disappointing week for owners trading in the North Sea and Baltic Aframax market has passed. Some owners have put up some resistance refusing to fix at current low levels. However, there is always someone who is willing to accept rates close to breakeven levels in order to keep their ships sailing. We expect rates to stay around current low levels in the week to come. Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea market another week has passed with little excitement for owners as cargo activity stays low and the list of prompt ships in the area just keeps getting longer. It is hard to see any signs of an increase in cargo activity in the short run, and we expect rates to continue hovering around bottom levels in the week to come.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market

Newbuilding contracting is becoming an increasingly attractive option spurred by much reduced yard prices. NAT this week announced contracts for two Suezmax newbuildings at Samsung at a price believed to be in the mid 50’s. The last time NAT placed Suezmax contracts at Samsung was in October 2016 at more or less same price.  Post-Lehman these represents to date the low-points in Suezmax prices from the Korean majors. Logic dictates that Chinese prices for such tankers should now be close to Usd 50 mill. We will not be surprised to see additional tanker orders coming to light in the near to medium term. In the present earnings climate, values for modern tankers are inevitably bench-marked to replacement cost and as such we have YTD a significant drop in values. A prompt resale Suezmax tanker from Korea was for instance at the outset of the year valued at region Usd 68 mill. No longer. Rumours abound all week related to the sale of a 2011 built VLCC, it appears to be Minerva’s PANTANASSA built 2011 HHI. The reported price of Usd 46 mill reaffirms softening prices. Capesizes extended the earnings gains yesterday with rates gaining 23% to USD 22.8k/d. This should bode well for more action in the Capesize S&P market as well.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS An unexpected draw in US inventories stymied the march towards 100 million barrels in domestic propane stocks. This draw did not affect Mt Belvieu propane’s value as a percentage WTI, which remains at 53%. The US FOB market looks poised to break out of it’s summer lull. FOB trades for October have been occurring between 4.5-5.5cpg with price difference based on preferable laycan dates, and VLGC availabilities. Expected global demand ramp up in Q4 due to winter and new PDHs coming online is imminent. The question when will this strength be seen in US FOB values, as we near working November loading cargoes?

Its been a relatively quiet week in the LNG shipping markets. US cargo cancellations on the back of hurricane Laura continue to keep the spot market in check. The increase in sublet availability has put a cap on how much Owners can ask for prompt shipping opportunities in the Atlantic and at the same time uncertainty around US production puts a restriction on what such sublet vessels are able to do on periods, which may support shipping rates 4-6 weeks out. Should US production pick up quicker and earlier than anticipated, this could result in a kickstart for the LNG winter season in the Atlantic.  We have seen more activity east of Suez and vessel availability is date sensitive, but rate levels in general remain stable also there. There is limited activity at yards for many shipping segments and newbuild prices remain stable while second-hand values are soft for vintage vessels. BP’s 2020 Energy Outlook was published this week and the LNG section is worth a read.

Another week with no sale and purchase activity on modern tanker tonnage. Market players are too far apart, with buyers looking to do a good deal in the current subdued market and sellers holding on to their price ideas with the crazy ride the last 12 months fresh in mind. Owners of vintage units with SS/DD coming up is however easier to convince and the sale of KRITI SPIRIT (160kdwt/2000/DSME) and KRITI SFAKIA (160kdwt/2000/HHI) at region usd 14.5 mill each display that values have found a temporary floor in line with last done SONANGOL KIZOMBA (160kdwt/2001/DSME) at usd 16.5 mill one month ago.   Continued high snp activity on dry, but still primarily on older units. New sales candidates more than offset vessels being sold, especially on Supramaxes/Ultramaxes, which is putting a lid on values and could potentially result in values sliding should the expected uptick in rates in the 4th quarter not materialize.

text: MEG Despite the status quos of oversupply, Oct CP swap surged up surprisingly to $370 from last week’s $350, and Nov maintains at $10 contango. By the time of writing, Saudi Aramco hasn’t released its acceptance, but there is talk circulating it could have cancelled three term liftings. KPC is reported to award its 17/18th Oct lifting equal ratio cargo at Nov CP minus mid-teens level, whereas it just sold one early Oct lifting heavy butane cargo at Oct CP minus low 20s last week.     FAR EAST FAR EAST market improves this week despite that cash differentials still traded negatively on FEI basis. 23kt propane for 2h Oct delivery was traded off window at Oct FEI minus around $20, and following bids raised up to mid high teens discounts while seller asking mid low teens discounts. Comparatively, butane is still more favored in marginal regions, with one 11/11 late Oct delivery cargo was sold to Taiwan CPC at Oct CP plus mid 20s via tender reportedly. And meanwhile, IOC issued buy tender for two evenly split cargoes for 2nd and 3rd decade Nov delivery. Other than that, one heavy propane cargo for late Oct delivery was sold into China at CP minus level. Other Chinese importers appear quiet but busy with domestic distribution amidst high inventory.

The VLCC market sprung to life at the end of last week. A flurry of activity, and rates all but doubled from their record low set a couple of weeks back. Poised ahead of October MEG stem nominations the WS40 mark was within grasp from both MEG and Wafr. Owners’ confidence were further strengthened by a number of +/- 6 months period fixtures, at daily rates well in excess of spot market earnings. However, the run of T/C fixtures has now tempered, and oil demand remains weak. Another flip side to charterers now wearing an “owner’s hat” is not needing to charter in third party ships, or not being to fussed when letting their ships out - witness no less by two different oilco. relets shaving a chunk off last done levels yesterday. And, with no lack of available tonnage, we’re likely still in for a bumpy ride going forward.

The Suezmax market was looking at the activity in the VLCC sector at the end of last week, with a hope it would rub off. Coming into the office this week, that small bit of hope was crushed by tonnage-list longer than we have seen this whole year. Almost half of the Wafr-list was 'free of cargo' ships, looking for somewhere to hide. In the East, you would think that the bunch of ships ballasting from East to Wafr would make the tonnage list for MEG look better, but unfortunately for owners there are plenty left. Right now, owners have nowhere to hide, and for the weeks to come, there is not much to do other than minimize waiting, and hope for an increase in activity.
