comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Oct Propane swap fell to $350 but Butane traded at $6 higher. Contango into Nov widened to $10 from last week’s $3, due to lackluster demand for the front.  Qatar Petroleum is reported that it didn’t award sale tender for 6/7th Oct lifting propane, understanding the netback into FAR EAST market is dreadful for such ratio.  KPC issued tender to sell one early Oct lifting heavy butane cargo, which is still under validity.   FAR EAST: The oversupply situation is still not eased. Propane for 1h Oct delivery was traded under downward pressure, at high 20s to low mid 30s discounts to Oct FEI. Similar parcel for 2h Oct delivery is assessed at more than $10 contango with expectations on recovery from heating demand into winter and new petchem use.  Taiwan FPCC awarded its buy tender to secure 23k propane for end Oct delivery at MOPJ minus 30.  Discussions for other regions focus on evenly split cargo mainly. BPCL awarded its tender to purchase one cargo for Oct delivery at CP plus high 20s based on two disports. Similar cargo for 2h Oct delivery was sold into SEA at Oct CP plus teens. In addition, one China petchem importer is reported to cover such ratio for later Oct delivery but at discounts to Oct FEI.

Even though we do see more demand in the Atlantic with fresh orders out of the Baltic and USG, the rates are still sliding south. TA is currently yielding around USD low/mid 11k. ECSA grain cargoes are still at good volumes and fronthauls are being fixed in the low 20k region. In the eastern hemisphere, we see the same trend with declining rates and Pacific rounds are priced at low 12k.

The market has come off over the last week with the basket of all routes being marked down by 12% to USD 15,482. This is mostly due to slower activity from miners and tonnage being freed up after bad weather in the Far East. On a positive note we see that the coal segment starting to find the current pricing interesting and the economy of scale is making sense compared to Panamaxes.

A negative start to the week with indexes going down and the general sentiment turning negative. There are still some areas that are getting better demand than others. ECSA remains firm with solid fronthaul fixtures for Japanese Ultra about USD 15k+500k GBB for trip to Spore-Japan. USG stable with some signs of a slightly sliding market. Trip to Med/Cont fixing in range USD 15-16k pd. Continent and Mediterranean followed rest of the market with rates sliding further down and chrts fixing between USD 1-2k pd less from last done. Trips with clinker from East and West Med to West Africa fixing about USD 15k pd, while a week ago it was USD 18k for the same runs. The Pacific market is more quiet than usual, and little fresh cargoes are surfacing on the market. Pacific RV from China via Indo reported fixed USD 7k on Supra and NOPAC RV close to USD 10k. India market still seems to be holding the positive sentiment with steady flow of iron ore to China. Supra fixed from EC India to China USD 12,500 pd. We expect the market to correct downwards over the coming week.

After weeks of gradual firming rates, the LNG shipping market has taken a pause. We have seen an increase in prompt availability, predominately sublets from portfolio players and traders, emerged in the market as a result of the disruptions caused by the hurricane. Spot rates have therefore softened for the first time since mid-May this year due to a cargo overhang which has put rates under pressure.   Although the damages in the US Gulf were heard to be minimal, the uncertainty and duration taken to resume operations are threatening hopes of a quick bounce back in rates. However, if production resumes swiftly at most US terminals, resulting in sublets withdrawn from the market and an increase in LNG demand moving into Q4, we may see an improvement in rates again. Until then, the shipping market remains uncertain.   We have kept LNG newbuilding prices stable and no new orders have been reported this week.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS  The front month propane price at Mt. Belvieu softened slightly today (Thursday) following another strong US Inventory build (2.2 Million barrels) Freight remains in the 90's basis Houston/Chiba and has done little to support netbacks- however the arb has improved week on week and now stands at approx. $135/ton basis Oct/Nov LST/FEI.  Very end October cargoes are now on offer at MB+5.875cpg with buyers coming from a 4 handle. The overbought product glut in Asia is showing signs of finally dissipating and this will hopefully allow for more concrete spot discussion basis November arrival.  On the US East coast, the few remaining Butane parcels are being worked end September and 1h October before all the volume will be consumed by blending season.

EAST With an increase in activity out of West African ports coupled with a continuing strong West market taking out a few vessels from the Middle East Gulf list of positions, we have seen Baltic climbing the last couple of days. We expect activity to pick up together with the release of Adnoc and Saudi acceptances later this week and early next week respectively. Meanwhile, there are still some ongoing discussions for end September dates in the MEG.  WEST September US Gulf positions were finally absorbed during the course of the last week, and all eyes have shifted to October loadings. A large chunk of the first half October USG positions have already been cleared at rates in the mid/high 90’s Houston/Chiba, despite the product market trying to suggest otherwise. There are reportedly some FOB avails during first half October ex the US, however, opportunistic buyers seem time being to be halted by owner’s freight ideas.

The VLCC market appears to have finally found a bottom. Yesterday saw a flurry of cargoes and rates ticked up a few points in all areas. Try as you like to hold a beach ball under water, but eventually it will pop back up. But, unless you fill it with helium it is likely to bounce along the surface, where we are likely to be for some time still. Falling bunker prices is another positive for the owning community, although earnings are still barely covering OPEX. Weakening crude prices and a widening contango could become a saving grace, with charterers increasingly eyeing storage candidates, and period rates on offer are double that of current daily earnings in the spot market. Even so, most owners with modern tonnage are reluctant to tie in and forgo a potentially strong winter market. Hope springs eternal.

Rates in the Mediterranean and Black Sea moved sideways this week, while in the North Sea and Baltic they took another hit in the southward direction. Each quoted market cargo in the area attracted between 9 to 12 offers. Going forward there are still plenty of available positions and we expect rates to stay around current low levels.

The Suezmax market is still struggling, and last week was the lowest year-to-date on TD20. Some owners were willing to go as low as low WS 30's, but it quickly bounced back to WS 40 this week. Not saying that the market is looking much better, but pointing more towards the levels from last week not close to being sustainable. It has been more activity this week though, but with a tonnage-list longer than we have seen in several months, the fundamentals not there to move this market further. Same apply for the East market. With a 30-day tonnage count close to 150 ships, the market is at the bottom, and it is likely to stay there for some time.

Rates in the Mediterranean and Black Sea moved sideways this week, while in the North Sea and Baltic they took another hit in the southward direction. Each quoted market cargo in the area attracted between 9 to 12 offers. Going forward there are still plenty of available positions and we expect rates to stay around current low levels.

The VLCC market appears to have finally found a bottom. Yesterday saw a flurry of cargoes and rates ticked up a few points in all areas. Try as you like to hold a beach ball under water, but eventually it will pop back up. But, unless you fill it with helium it is likely to bounce along the surface, where we are likely to be for some time still. Falling bunker prices is another positive for the owning community, although earnings are still barely covering OPEX. Weakening crude prices and a widening contango could become a saving grace, with charterers increasingly eyeing storage candidates, and period rates on offer are double that of current daily earnings in the spot market. Even so, most owners with modern tonnage are reluctant to tie in and forgo a potentially strong winter market. Hope springs eternal.

While a few owners have been able to lock away VLCC’s for six months at rates in the low to mid 30s the spot market is at opex levels presently. It is really just a numbers game at this point, with about one of three MEG cargoes lost over the three last month’s vs same period last year.  Sale of modern conventional tankers is just not happening and the bid/ask spread is getting quite wide.  The dry story is much easier to read with a good transparency on values throughout.  Attractive vessels/designs are showing some gain as seen by the sale of Tess-82 LOWLANDS KAMSAR built 2010 at slightly above Usd 15 mill. Offers were invited on Wednesday and a sale was quickly concluded.  Expectations were that the price should end up somewhere between Usd 14-14.5 mill so we can safely concluded that this was a notch up.  The vessel has just passed the second Special Survey with BWTS fitted.

The Suezmax market is continuing down the same path as it has been the last month. Cargo-activity is slow all over, and owners are getting more and more desperate to find something for their ships. In the West, TD20 is still trading at low WS 40's, and it does not seem to move anywhere. In the East, we see more ships berthing in China, causing the list to grow even longer. Owners are fixing negative returns to get their ships West, and for a MEG/East they will do less than USD 5000/day. Going forward we do not see the East market going anywhere - we are staring at the bottom of the market and probably will be for some time.

It’s been a summer with a chronic lack of demand for crude, slowly chipping away on tanker earnings. Since the ‘short T/C frenzy’ at the end of April we have seen consecutive weeks of lower returns. There will be a bottom somewhere, and we might just be coming close this week. 'OPEX’ is at the forefront, as owners run their numbers in a state of alarm. Last 24 hours, however, has seen an uptick in inquiry and e.g. Chinese giant Unipec were able to secure a number of ships for end 2nd decade September load down to WS 25 MEG/China. West Africa is also a little busier, and cargoes remain open in the USG. Thus, there is every chance owners can squeeze a point or two more across the board. Unlikely green shoots of a recovery just yet, as all fundamentals, including a lengthy position list point to more pain before pleasure.

A very slow activity level for Aframaxes trading in the North Sea and Baltic markets add to a lacklustre week for owners. We don’t expect much change in sentiment and rates will move sideways around bottom levels in the week to come. Same can be said for the Mediterranean and Black Sea markets which has moved sideways at bottom levels all week. This is simply due to the long list of available ships in the area, compared to the poor levels of cargoes entering the market the last 7 days. Due to the sufficient amount of re-lets in the area covering own barrels, we do not expect any significant improvement in the spot market in the short run.

Initial slow start to the week, which picked up by mid-week and still Atlantic areas remaining firm. From the Black Sea, Ultras are fetching mid 20's to Far East and high 20's to India. From the Continent, Ultras are fixing scrap in the high teens to East Mediterranean, mid-high 20's to India, and mid-teens for ECSA bhaul. The South Atlantic market is strong with TA's paying USD 20,000 and fh USD 15k + 500k gbb on Ultras. From the Indian ocean, ECI/China fixing around USD 15,000 and South Africa/Far East USD 13,000 + 300k gbb. In the Pacific, nopac rounds fixing USD 11,000 on Ultras.

The list of open tonnage continues to diminish, firing the shipping market in both basins just as the fixing window approaches the fourth quarter of the year. The Pacific and Middle East continue to see more activity through a combination of bilateral discussions and tender business, while the Atlantic is seeing higher rates and longer fixtures. Despite the slight difference in trading environments, Owners will be heartened by more opportunities and improving economics in both basins. That said, there is some uncertainty in the prompt LNG market in the west as we await the full impact of the recent hurricanes that battered the US Gulf terminals; early signs are that the damage is less than was feared although there are some cargo delays and cancellations, and we wait to see how this effects the shipping market. We show further rate rises this week, but the familiar story of a relatively weak cargo market and players lifting with their own tonnage is keeping the market in check. There are flickers of a strengthening LNG market, and if that takes hold shipping will follow. The sale and purchase market remains active but transactions are limited as buyers and sellers engage in pricing discussions. There have been no newbuilding orders placed at yards this week

It was a slow start to the week with bank holiday in the UK. Tuesday got the Monday blues with little emerging. Rates however keep sliding in both hemispheres where TA’s currently yielding high 13k/low 14k depending duration and delivery. In the Pacific, we see Aussie rounds being fixed at around USD 14k. There is still some glow to the ECSA grain market where low 15k being achieved retro sailing India for trips to the Far East.

Rates softening somewhat for the big ships, despite very punchy iron ore prices and subsequent volumes. Further surprising is that the accumulated effect of close to zero fleet growth, countless ship-days lost due to crew change delays, typhoons, substantial congestion and a large number of ships waiting off China since months to discharge Australian coal has yet to turn spot sentiment positive. Average daily earnings down 7 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 17,600, the Atlantic being the area holding up best despite labour issues in major coal exporter Colombia. Going forward, optimistic projections much attributed to seasonally increasing trade flows on the Brazil/China conference route. Period activity limited as ffa's give little support for levels anticipated/asked and number of definite candidates low - only a couple of conclusions for around 12 months duration on BCI index type tonnage in the USD low 15k's recently done.

EAST We are finally starting to see more activity in the East after a couple of quiet weeks. A few more ships have been taken out in the mid usd 50s baltic for last decade September loading, and time of writing there are still some uncovered requirements for same period. There are still a couple  of traders with extra length on shipping in the East, and as the Western markets seems to be more in balance we don’t expect East rates to continue its downward trend.   WEST Hurricane Laura caused some delays for USG loading end Aug, but only Nederland loadings have been largely affected. Delays amounts to around 10 days at time of writing, there is currently 4 ships at anchorage waiting for firm berthing prospects. September looks largely covered for and 1st decade October fixing has slowly started. Freight rates for West loadings are back to trading at a couple dollars premium to Baltic. On the back of tight availability for ships in US up to mid October, it is hard to see the freight markets coming off significantly despite a challenging product market.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Saudi Aramco has maintained Sep Propane CP at $365 and raised up Butane CP by 10$ to $355, which is below most expectations, and even lower than swap value. Propane Oct CP edged up to $382 but dropped to $366 on Thursday, reflecting the length in the front market. And FOB propane netback seems miserable as delivered value is traded under heavy discounts.  Comparatively, butane is more favorable. KPC awarded its 27/28th Sep lifting equal ratio cargo tender at Oct CP minus mid-teens reportedly, which significantly improved from previous FOB sales.  QP issued sale tender to offer one 6/7th Oct lifting 45/0, which is due to close by 8th Sep.   FAR EAST: Propane for 2h Sep market appears dreadful this week, with one 2h Sep 23/0 parcel traded at Sep FEI minus $30. Similar cargo for 1h Oct delivery is offered at Oct FEI minus high teens discount but barely attract buying interests.  In contrary, butane discussion is more active. Indian IOC secured two evenly split cargos at CP plus 30s for 2nd and 3rd decade Oct delivery respectively. Similarly, BPCL issued buy tender to secure one evenly split cargo for 7-25th Oct delivery for 2 disports basis, which is yet to close. PV Gas also purchased one 11/11 parcel for early Oct delivery promptly at CP plus high 20s.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS: The weekly EIA propane inventory report  showed an unexpectedly high build of 4.389mmbbls, from 90.833mmbbls for the week ending 21 Aug 2020 to 95.222mmbbls as of 20 Aug 2020.  The data also revealed a YOY increase of 2.366mmbbls when comparing the Aug 2020 figures to the Aug 2019 data.  Most of the build occurred in PADD III (Gulf Coast) and is reckoned to be the result of lifting delays as related to the passing of Hurricane Laura.  On that, the only terminal to be directly impacted – and which continues to suffer closure – is the LoneStar facility at Nederland, TX.  Where the Houston Ship Channel and Freeport, TX terminals were temporarily closed (and briefly, at that), the Category 4 storm made landfall only slightly East of the Sabine River and caused significant damage in its wake, and left the LoneStar terminal out of commission for approximately a week.  Front-month Mont Belvieu values are presently hovering in the 49ctgs/gal range but then rise through the balance of the year, only tapering, presumably, on seasonality factors at end Q1 2021.  With US stock levels having risen so sharply at the end of August the sentiment is one of cautious optimism in that it appears at present to be sufficient volumes to satisfy both domestic res/com and petrochemical-related demand and export volumes.  But with near record-level exports seen in August, and concern of production declines, the underlying concern of insufficient stocks lingers and is thus supportive of the pricing structure for the next 4-5 months.

It has been a rather turbulent week in the LNG market, as commodity prices have seen almost roller-coasterly up and down movements, spot shipping rates have stormed upwards and last, but unfortunately not the least, there is a major hurricane (Hurricane Laura) about to make a landfall near Texas-Louisina coaster border, consequently threatening to shut down a chunk of US LNG production at least temporarily. Spot shipping market has remained active, mainly driven by multiple spot requirements from the East of Suez, resulting into a rather slim prompt tonnage availability, quite surprisingly for this time of the year. That said, the West of Suez have also had its’ fair share of interest for tonnage, but notably with delivery windows a bit further ahead, perhaps in the hopes of capturing the best potential contango window before the Northern Hemisphere winter starts. The shipping market definitely feels strongly buoyant in the near-term, but there is still some uncertainty whether this heightened sentiment can be supported over the shoulder months, which only time will tell for certain. From the newbuilding front, it has been reported that Smart LNG has finalized agreements to order additional ten Arc7 LNG carriers from Zvezda Shipbuilding Complex in Russia, for the upcoming Arctic LNG 2 project. Furthermore, there are also quite a few S&P transactions circulating in the market.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS: Discussion this week have been centred around Hurricane Laura which made landfall Wednesday evening between Texas and Louisiana. From reports this morning it seems the hurricane bypassed Houston and the ship channel. Enterprise expect 1.5 days of delay due to ship channel closures. Nederland, which was in the path of the storm has avoided major damage and, after a coast guard survey, expect 1 day of delay. We expect this news to assuage fears of long delays. The 1.5 million barrel build in US inventories has now pushed stocks up to 90.8 million barrels. With domestic production stronger than originally expected, traders believe there will be enough product to sustain winter demand and exports. The more pressing question in today’s market is when will we start to see global winter demand?

text: MEG: Sep CP inched up this week to $372 and Sep/Oct CP traded at $2 contango. Regardless the bullish expectation on Q4 demand, Q4 CP contango appears narrow and might not widen until real demand kicks in. 1st round CP have been recommended from $375 to $390 for propane, and $10 less or parity for butane. Netbacks for FOB AGs are discussed at minus 20s but is improving with the fresh Indian demand on preparation for Deepavali.   FAR EAST: A couple of propane parcels from 2h Sep to 1h Oct delivery have been traded this week.  2h Sep 23/0 was done at Sep CP minus high single digit, equates to Sep FEI minus mid high teens. And similar cargo for 1h Oct was reported done at Oct FEI minus high single digit. Despite that some US loadings are delayed due to the hurricane, FAR EAST price stabilized and even softened later this week. One of the reasons being is the overlength for 2h Sep arrival cargos, against thin buying interests due to high inventory. Indian IOC issued tender to purchase two evenly split cargos for 2nd and 3rd decade Oct delivery, which is yet to close.

In the North Sea and Baltic the Aframax owners have suffered from very few available market cargoes for end August and early September dates. Rates are hovering around bottom levels giving Owners a very low TCE just above operational expenses. Despite some bad weather in the area causing some delays we expect the market to move sideways in the first decade of September before we will see any improvement on rates.  Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea the market has continued to move sideways at levels below OPEX. Activity out of the Bsea and Emed has been healthy, however there are still too many prompt ships around to create a firming trend. Although we have reached cargo programs for September, we still expect the market to remain flat in the current fixing window.

WEST: The tug of war between Charterers and Owners has continued this week, with freight remaining high despite unfavourable arb economics. At the end of last week a couple of deals were done around Houston/Chiba USD 90 (+/-) but once those ships cleared, owners have largely been able to dictate the pace. Given that there are currently no relets to compete with, a number of ships were put on subs at mid $90s Houston/Chiba. With that said, some Charterers are still deciding whether it would be better to cancel or change the size of their liftings given the current trading environment. In addition, terminals in the US seem to be withholding FOB cargoes for sale in September until Hurricane Laura makes landfall.  Looking ahead into early October, the VLGC market in the West remains tight. However, with the West now back at a premium to the East and with the possibility that traders could cancel liftings to relet at strong levels, this could change quickly unless the arb improves.  EAST: The shipping market in the East has been fairly inactive this week. One late running ship for an Indian cargo created some attention, and there are possibly a couple of uncovered stems shown to the market for 2H September, but otherwise not much else to report. The increased activity seen ex US recently could potentially slow down a falling Baltic, as Owners are likely to direct more ships back West if this continues. But at the same time if arb economics remains poor then this shouldn’t necessarily have any added effect to the tonnage availability in the east. Going forward 1H September seems pretty much done on shipping in the Middle East, and next focus is from 2H September onwards.

The tanker market is in the August summer doldrums. Tonnage remains plentiful all over, and although some resistance is evident, rates for modern unrestricted ships are slowly sliding towards the W30 mark MEG/eastbound, with Wafr trailing closely behind. To add insult to injury bunker prices are up overnight. Despite strengthening oil prices, lack of oil demand is still noticeable. Many regular VLCC charterers are opting for smaller liftings, the likes of Suezmaxes, despite paying higher freights per barrel. An increased interest in floating storage could become a saving grace, suggesting land based storage capacity is becoming strained, although one school of thought propound it’s just a zero game with ships previously fixed at higher rates being replaced.

Another week that has seen a flurry of activity across all segment of the Dry Cargo markets with close to 20 sales reported this week. In terms of values we continue to see an increasing number of more modern units being traded, setting consolidated benchmarks for assets of all vintage. Notable transaction in the Ultramax sector being the sale of the 2019 Oshima built Ultramax "ADVENTURE III" which was sold to clients of Meghna shipping at Usd 24.25 mill setting a clear picture for modern Japanese designs. Similarly in the Kamsarmax market we have more clarity on the modern Japanese front following the sale of the 2017 Namura built “SAKUZAYA JUSTICE” sold at Usd 25 mill. Generally although buying interest remains high, the steady stream of sale candidates is diluting competition giving buyers enough options to keep values relatively flat.   Not much to report in the tanker sector except for the 2000 HHI built VLCC “BAG MEUR”, which we understand has been committed at region Usd 21.2 mill which is another confirmation of the erosion in values for vintage tankers. The same age "MARINA M" also HHI built, was in comparison sold for Usd 32 mill about 2 months ago, albeit with SS passed.

Last week we saw the Panamax market taking a turn with a slower market and less demand, especially in the Atlantic. This week the demand has picked up, but the tonnage list is increasing day by day. ECSA TA’s are being fixed on APS bss and the P1A index is currently yielding ard 15k while the shorter Baltic rounds has been fixed at low 14k bss UK delivery. For the ECSA grain run to Feast there has been talks of better bids, and currently being reported at around 14k bss delivery SE Asia. In the Pacific in general we do see a more stable market with rounds being fixed in the 13,5-14k region depending on delivery.

More or less flat from previous week, with cape rates moving from 19500 to 18900 on average. West Australia however being more positive, with c5 presently at 8,4 pmt level, up from upper 7's previous week due to tighter supply caused by another typhoon hitting as well as practical challenges related to Covid 19. Period activity is presently low.

The Suezmax market is still hoovering around the same levels as its been the last month. List of available tonnage in the west is long, and even with more activity in wafr this week, there is nothing pointing towards this market moving anywhere. If anything we could possibly see TD20 creeping down towards W40. In the east, its if possible, looking worse than it has the last weeks. We have seen older ships breaking w40 for meg/east and modern units fixing low  w40's. The east market is not moving anywhere the way its looking now, and Owners cant do much else than hope for more activity going forward.

Less activity from Atlantic where all routes lost some ground. Handful fresh orders from N Cont. Some scrap cargoes were fixed arn 15 on ultras. Grain run from B Sea to SEASIA were concluded close to 23k. From Med  to W Afr with clinker one could reach levels arn 18k.  Similar for ships open Cont- levels for USG fhaul rates where ships were covered arn 25k . USG back to Cont were done arn 16k. Still strong rates from the Indian Ocean where ships are fixing around USD 16000 to China and around USD 14000+400k gbb Safr to Feast. Further east Nopac rv fixing above 10k for nopac rv’s, while backhaul rates around half.

The recovery in the dry markets is still feeble but at least we continue to have a decent S&P volume. Last week we reported the sale of a Kamsarmax newbuilding with prompt delivery ex Oshima at Usd 30.5 mill, we now understand that this transaction has failed to materialize. Two Capesize sales are certainly on the low side – nine year old PACIFIC ENDURANCE BUILT Koyo at Usd 18 mill is well below expectations, the vessel was initially reported to be withdrawn but subsequently understood to be sold after all. Furthermore, the price for 2013 Koyo built JUBILANT EXCELLENCE gives no encouragement for an uptick in values in the near term.  It comes as no surprise that values for vintage crude tankers continue to soften, however various reports that Suezmax SONANGOL KIZOMBA built 2001 is sold in the mid Usd 12 mill is incorrect and we understand the deal was done in the mid Usd 16 mill to Dubai based buyers.

Another quiet week in the North Sea and Baltic market where the majority of available cargoes has been covered under own program or with other relets. Going forward we expect the soft trend to continue as other export areas aren’t really offering any viable alternatives for owners to ballast on spec.   A small rush of cargoes in the Mediterranean and Black Sea at the end of last week was not enough to put any significant upward pressure on rates, and the market has moved sideways yet another week. Reports that Libya will allow limited exports from blockaded oil ports to free up storage space is positive news for the shipowners, who will be keeping a close eye on any activity out of the country going forward. Nevertheless we expect the market to remain soft but stable in the week to come.

Unfortunately for the owners, the market both in the east and in the west have been flat since we last spoke. Owners lack fundamental support to take the fight to the charterers and accept variations over last done in fear of losing the cargo. The activity level, albeit for the western hemisphere, have been decent but with the eastern market being in the doldrums, the Atlantic is getting a steady supply of ballasters from the east looking for employment and ,as such, we see little chance of immediate change for the balance of this week

Charterers have been able to search for new lows this week, at least on worldscale terms, as a lack of enquiry due to a number of well documented factors takes its toll. In the Meg, Korean Charterers, albeit with favourable terms, were able to crack the ws30 level. For a China run, Owners have dug their heels in at the low ws30’s for modern, as we edge ever closer to opex costs for a VLCC. A quiet West Africa has not helped, just a few deals done at the ws38.75 level. The USG has been able to remain somewhat active in comparison, increasing the ton-mile, when we look for positives. $5.4m to Ningbo reported at the time of writing.  Those with long memories will remember we have seen worse, but if September follows August in terms of enquiry. There could be a little more pain before we see any turn-around in outlook.

Sentiments picked up over the last few days as demand and enquiries for shipping increases due to the anticipation of winter demand for gas. Despite the apparent long list of available vessels, proposals for vessels with compliant specifications and available periods come far and few in between. Portfolio players and projects are constantly having to optimise their fleet schedules in order to offer their vessels to charterers’ requirements, clearly indicating there is not many vessels to choose from which are readily available. It may not be a good time to be short shipping going forward as availabilities change on a daily basis. Both basins have seen enquiries for the months of September, October and November deliveries. Charters for inter-basin trades could be revived in the next weeks or so, which would soak up shipping even more. Charter rate ideas have generally been far apart between owners and charterers, and it may continue to be the case as shipowners stand firm on their commercial expectations.   Brace yourselves, winter is coming.

Over the last week we have seen the market push from USD 7,95per metric ton on the west Australia to China route up to 8,45, before it started to decline again and we presently trading at same level as we were 7 days ago. The South Atlantic is still unbalanced with more than enough tonnage in position thus the Brazil-China route is currently 3% lower than last week. All in all the positive sentiment linked to rising congestion in China when this report was written last week has been replaced with decreasing amount of cargo activity with owners seeking to cover against the available cargo out there

A number of Australian trips into China were reported fixed in the USD 8,000/9,000 pd range. A number of Indonesian trips into India with clinker were reported at the level of USD 6,000/7,000 pd. East Coast Indian trips into China were fixed around USD 17,000 pd. Persian Gulf trips via Black Sea into China with HBI were fixed at the level of USD 11,000 pd. South African trips into China were reported at the level of USD 12,000/13,000 pd plus ballast bonus at the USD 200K/275K. Mediterranean trips into West Africa with clinker were fixed around USD 16,000 pd. South American trips into Continent were reported at the level of USD 14,000/14,500 pd. USD 14,000 pd plus USD 500k on an Ultramax for minimum 4 months employment basis delivery in the Mediterranean.

After weeks of firming rates in both hemispheres, the Panamax market now seems to have taken a breather. Rates are slowly coming off on all trades, and p1 is currently yielding around USD 19,600. The tonnage list is still tight, but demand has come off this week. In the eastern hemisphere we see p3 fixing at 14k bss China delivery. The grain market is still active out of ECSA and Black Sea and ships are being fixed retro SE Asia at ard USD 13/14k.

WEST: Despite being increasingly prompt, there have been some discussions related to freight for stems in 1H September ex US. The first ship on western position lists comes open in only a couple of weeks, and this is evidence of the continued stand off between owners and charterers, who currently seem unable to agree on rates. At the same time, the baltic has come off this week, reducing the discount in the West which has prevailed for 3 weeks now.   Looking ahead to 2H Sep liftings, some traders worry that CFR rates in the far east will remain discounted until further into Q4. Simultaneously, the balance of freight to uncovered cargoes makes it seem that the market could be slightly long on a net basis. However, while these are factors which could mean softening sentiment, tonnage is mostly controlled by only a few owners and this might mean the market remains more resilient than some would expect  MEG: After the release of the Saudi acceptances we are yet to see any flurry of new fixtures from the Middle East that some were expecting. Most of the action so far has been centered around Indian cargoes, but there was also some interest on shipping from Chinese counterparts whom eventually ended up locking in freight in the high usd 50s Baltic. Looking ahead, first half of September is predominantly Owner controlled as some of the traders with length have decided to direct their ships West i/o keeping them East. Meanwhile, there are still a few outstanding stems from the Indian majors (with a few more requirements expected later). Ideas from most Owners remain in the low usd 60s Baltic, but with most of the deals concluded this week in the high usd 50s Baltic it will be interesting to see where freight is headed.

text: AMERICAS: The front month propane price at Mt. Belvieu was buoyed Wednesday, following the EIA's surprising flat Inventory report that effectively decreased the arb even further-to roughly $117/ton. Freight in the 90's basis Houston/Chiba has done little to support netbacks and the last concluded September cargo out of the US Gulf is said to have sold at MB+3.75cpg- reflecting the poor economics East. The overbought product glut continues to loom over Asia which in turn has led to as many as 12 September US cargos to have been cancelled, though that number remains up for debate. Despite the large number of cancelations, these cargos continue to be resold, allowing for exports to remain strong, along with a number of September cargos still up for sale from both Marcus Hook and the Gulf where buyers are said to be coming from the high 3's and sellers in the low 4's.  A number of traders seem to think the discussion for October cargoes from the US gulf will be more competitive as the east oversupply clears.

text: MEG: Sep Propane CP stands firm at $365 level, while spread against butane narrows down to $10. Saudi Aramco released their Sep acceptance as per term lifters’ nomination, except for some ratio switch to more butane. FOB discussions improved from pervious CP minus 30s to minus 20s with better netbacks from India. KPC was reported to sell its 19/20th Sep lifting 2/2 at CP minus low 20s.   FAR EAST: 1h Sep discussions are muted while 2h Sep deals are active this week. Cash differentials for 2h Sep delivery inched higher, with 23kt propane for this period traded at FEI minus $10-12.  Full propane cargo for 2h Sep arrival was placed into NChina at around CP flat, while evenly split cargo for late Sep delivery was sold at CP plus low teens. Taiwan CPC has secured one 22k butane for Sep/Oct delivery at CP plus mid 20s via tender. And similarly, one SChina importer also purchased one late Sep arrival 11/11 parcel at CP plus 20ish.

A resurgence of the coronavirus in parts of the world with associated lockdowns re-imposed is like cancer for the world economy and inevitably shipping. Whilst we continue to see a steady flow of bulkcarriers changing hands, the 2nd hand market has failed to fully ignite and caution is prevailing. That being said, dry values are well supported and both buyers and sellers should have enough transparency to transact in light of the above mentioned liquidity.  The crude tanker S&P market is more in a limbo. The brand new ships are inevitably being revalued in line with falling replacement costs and earnings are far from lending support to any significant activity nor premium above assumed replacement cost. The result is zero sales volume of very modern ships. The vintage crude tankers have a double whammy – low earnings/storage play gone and recently also much reduced demolition prices. Values are clearly adjusting downwards. Two 2001 built suezmax tankers are in play with deals expected to be concluded in the mid-teens. That leaves the semi-modern, non eco ships built say from 2008 to 2012 which is where we expect to see increased sales activity going forward. As always, it’s “just” a question of price but buyers will hold the upper hand.

Firm market across the Atlantic with activity stronger in the Bsea. Thin tonnage list on the Continent, leading to pressure on rates. The Far Eastern market is more moderate and flat. From USG fh paying mid 20's and high teens for TA. Black sea market pushing hard where backhaul to USG is paying USD 10000, Wafr trip around USD 17000 and fh roughly USD 24000. In the Indian Ocean, Safr/Feast concluding in the around USD 12500+250k gbb and WCI to Seasia via Ag, around USD 12000. In the Feast more moderate levels are discussed CIS rv back to China mid USD 6000 and Nopac rv around USD 8000.

Spot again moving north for the big ships, on a combination of commodity trading fundamentals, crewing issues related to Covid-19 and expected effects of new Chinese customs procedures. Whilst iron ore trade volumes are at year-high and import stockpile quantities drop, supply of tonnage may be reduced as crew-changing becomes an ever more complicated task. Adding to this, dramatically increased time required for Chinese customs clearance may tie up a further massive number of ships. Far East levels are marginally down as only one major miner and a handful of operators picking ships for the west Australia/China conference trade, coming in at around USD 7.90-8.20 pmt depending on age/position. Picture is rapidly changing for the Brazil/China trade, where sentiment and fundamentals have brought levels from USD low 16's to more than USD 18.00 pmt in just a few days - further improvements expected. Paper levels follow suit, and increased period activity/pay apparent.

The Panamax market is certainly firm in the Atlantic. The tonnage list is getting thinner day by day and we see higher rates for every day.  However, it’s a bit two-sided story; for the shorter runs in the North Atlantic we have seen the 20’s being done for time charter.  However, a “normal” TA run is actually being paid below the Baltic index 1a which at time of writing is at USD 19k. In the eastern hemisphere we also experience firming rates, but the trading has been slower mid week. There are still some August stems out of Aussie to be covered and rates are hovering around USD 14-15k bss China delivery.

text: AMERICAS: Domestic US propane inventories are now at 89.3 million barrels after a slightly larger than expected 2.6 million barrel build for the week ended Friday August 7th. With these high inventories, one would expect Mt Belvieu to be below 52% of WTI as it is today. The netback picture is not pretty from the US at the moment. The arb for September could support US FOB bids in the 4cpgs around cancellation levels. However the physical window discount in the East is keeping firm bids from being shown. We expect to see an improvement in netback values if any positive demand signals are seen from the East. If this occurs at the same time as a drop in Mt Belvieu and cheaper freight rates, the netback value could see a sharp rise. Let’s hope this occurs sooner rather than later.

In the west we are still seeing decent activity on Suezmax, both in Wafr and Brazil. Unfortunately for Owners the tonnage list is still growing and this week we are counting almost 140 ships in wafr next 30 days. TD20 dropped to w45, and going forward it does not look very promising. Still cargoes left for 3rd decade, but not enough to help the market. In the MEG we are seeing the same old story that has been going on for many weeks now - too many ships and too little activity. VLCC's are slow, dragging the Suezmax down with them. We expect the market to remain stable below w50 going forward.

ANNOUNCEMENT: Libra Fearnley Energy is please to announce Mr Scott Gray will join as a cargo broker starting Sept 17th,2020. After 35 years experience in the LPG market at ICIS, The Waterborne Report and most recently IHS , we are very excited to have Scott bring his extensive contacts and experience to our team. Scott will work out of our Houston office located at 1 Riverway , Suite 1810 Houston Texas 77056 and is contactable at his direct line of + 1 713 403 2547 and mobile + 1 713 824 0252.  --  WEST: Despite a fair few options with regards to spot FOB cargoes in 1H Sep, freight activity West of Suez has been relatively limited so far this week. Charterers seem to be between a rock and a hard place: on one hand, Owners’ ideas remain strong at around mid $90s Houston/Chiba. On the other, current arb economics and a persistently weak Ginga window mean September liftings are not especially appealing. This dynamic has all market participants primed for news of cancellations ex US, although so far it seems some players have preferred to defer to later in September than to cancel altogether.  EAST: The week got off to a quiet start in the East with public holidays both in Singapore and Japan on Monday. But as soon as people returned to their offices we saw increased activity on shipping for 1st decade of September, which was mainly triggered by the announcement of the Adnoc acceptances earlier. Last done levels are now around low/mid usd 60s Baltic, and the general sentiment going forward is that Baltic should come off slightly as there is currently more supply of spot open tonnages. However, we are still awaiting the acceptances from Aramco which could potentially create more demand for shipping from Indian majors (along with other lifters). If a larger part of these cargos were to be allocated towards the front end of the month that could help to maintain the levels we are seeing today.

The VLCC market, as most other segments, is rapidly moving from a market place to a "money exchange". We are up to 80 MEG fixtures plus a few mystery disappearances for August, approaching the end game by the look of things. That leaves plenty of tonnage for charterers to continue moving cautiously, testing the W30 mark on modern ships for MEG/eastbound cargoes, and yielding little leftover lolly to speak of for the owning community. Although also under pressure, the Atlantic has produced a few fixtures from both West Africa and the US at rates contributing positive returns. However, with rates barely covering OPEX in the MEG - at best - owners will naturally be eyeing the western hemisphere more intensely. Thus, as loading dates move forward, it will likely not take long before that area becomes saturated too.

Both in the North Sea/Baltic and Med/Bsea markets we have seen the trend go from flat at the end of last week to slightly firming this week. This has much to do with the increased activity out of the Baltic an Black Sea in the 3rd decade fixing window of August, which we are in at the time of writing. Fuel oil cargoes destined East of Suez have also played it’s part in putting the current upward pressure on rates. We still expect the market to pick up a few more points in the short run.

The LNG market has slowly started “getting into shape” for winter, with sentiment gradually increasing. A couple of multi-month shipping requirements have been covered and spot interest remains active,  increasing spot rates. Asia delivered LNG price has further improved, opening a handful of potential opportunities for traders and portfolio players. Availability of vessels has seen a slight decrease, yet there remains an overhang of tonnage to work through, still with Charterers’ seeking coverage for future laycans while Owner’s attention is focused on prompt. On the flip side, concerns over a second wave of coronavirus could put a halt to recent improving sentiments, as a number of countries are monitoring recent upticks in infection levels. Nevertheless, for the time being, Owners are holding a firm stance on their ideas for winter. In the Newbuilding market no new orders have been reported this week.

text: MEG: Sep Propane CP stabilized at $368 at the time of writing, and Butane traded at $13 less. CP spread from Sep to Nov is traded at nearly flattish, yet to reflect the seasonal demand changes. ADNOC released their Sep lifting acceptances with advancements reported as well. Supply ex MEG still appears long as producers reported with spot availability for 2h Sep liftings.   FAR EAST: Discussions for 1h Sep delivery propane were muted, and players attempt to swap cargo for later arrival. Propane for 2h Sep delivery was traded at FEI minus mid-teens for half parcel, and minus high teens respectively for a full lot. Despite the potential 10-11 cancellations from Aug to Sep liftings ex US, the Arb volume was not expected to decline much due to terminal resales and recording new high exports for Jul and Aug.  Taiwan FPCC issued buy tender to secure 23kt LPG for 2h Sep delivery, either 11/11 or pure propane or butane. Other East buyers are exploring cargos for similar period or end Sep/Early Oct delivery, but not rush to move with current high inventory.

In the west we are still seeing decent activity on Suezmax, both in Wafr and Brazil. Unfortunately for Owners the tonnage list is still growing and this week we are counting almost 140 ships in wafr next 30 days. TD20 dropped to w45, and going forward it does not look very promising. Still cargoes left for 3rd decade, but not enough to help the market. In the MEG we are seeing the same old story that has been going on for many weeks now - too many ships and too little activity. VLCC's are slow, dragging the Suezmax down with them. We expect the market to remain stable below w50 going forward.

The sale of fifteen year old VLCC “OTOWASAN” at Usd 26.25 mill is a reality check for vintage tankers. To compare apples with apples it should be noted that the vessel will be delivered with her third special survey due, but it’s still a far cry from the Usd 38.1 mill which Euronav achieved in April for the same age TI HELLAS with survey just passed. In a “Korea Inc” deal SK Shipping has acquired 5 brand new VLCC’s from a Korean fund with 10 year charters attached to domestic oil major GS Caltex. Suezmax “ADVANTAGE SKY” built 2010 Rongsheng was sold yesterday by online auction for Usd 25.5 mill. The vessel has been under arrest in Durban since August 2018; at the first auction in April 2020 the highest bid was Usd 18.8 mill. Crude values are softening across the board, clean values are best case moving sideways.  Euronav as always first off the block in the reporting season, its VLCC fleet averaged a stellar Usd 81500 pd in Q2 and its suezmax fleet Usd 60,000 pd.    Modern bulker sales have been few and far between YTD but this week sees the sale of two 2017 Japanese built Kamsarmax bulkcarriers at Usd 26 mill.  This underlines a firming of values – in June a 2020 Japanese newbuilding resale achieved Usd 28.5 mill.

August is here and the ‘holiday season’ feels quite different. Uncertainty of recent months has only been exacerbated by the continued worries around a potential second wave of coronavirus in Europe and the ongoing depth and breadth of the first wave in the US and this goes to reflect why activity and winter sentiment is more muted this year compared to previous ones.    Governments and advisory firms are more openly starting to question if the recovery will be a more of a ‘U’ than the ‘V’ that was touted in earlier predictions, but no one really knows, so for the time being risk by the majority is been minimized and this leaves shipping floundering. European storage inventories act as a good indicator to the glut that is upon the industry reaching 86% capacity earlier this week compared to a 5 year average of 70%, could this trigger the need for floating storage? This week North Asia prices extended their recent rally which follow similar gains in Europe and North America, so although LNG is abundant there are improving signals ahead of winter. Availability in all basins remains sufficient yet laycans remain frustratingly distant and economically undesirable for owners sitting prompt. In short, let the holiday season pass and bring on winter.   In the new building market Shell has signed separate agreements for two LNG ships each with Knutsen LNG, Korea Line and ICBC Financial Leasing and institutional investors advised by J.P. Morgan Asset Management.

text: MEG Sep Propane CP swap climbed to $367 and Butane traded at $354. With ample supply from AG and strong freight, FOB netbacks are heavily discounted. text: AMERICAS The EIA reported a build of 2.3 million barrels for the week ended July 31st all the while propane exports increased nearly 600,000 barrels on the week compared to last. The strong build atop robust strong exports further illustrates the sentiment that propane supply has been cut into disproportionately less than crude following the April crash. Physical Delivered cargoes in the east continue to trade at substantial discounts, effectively crushing the lst/fei netback and bolstering cancellation discussions. It has been reported that between 5-7 August, US Gulf origin FOB cargoes had been cancelled as well as  3 September cargoes.  In Latin America, a tender was issued for for 44,000 mts for delivery Sep 15-19 into Chile

WEST Activity has been limited in the US this week. Arb economics don’t seem to support current high freight levels, while some charterers still have time to decide whether or not to cancel US liftings if things don’t improve. Elsewhere, there was some noise around WAF, where one oil major had a freight requirement for early September and an FOB was tendered for sale for around the same dates. VLGC freight offers were too strong for the former, and as a result the cargo ended up being loaded onto a smaller ship.  Looking at the positions list for September in the US, the first half of the month remains tight with only a couple of ships available for the period. Further into September, the picture becomes less clear; it is still too far out to determine how owners will position their ships and whether or not more relets will emerge if any liftings are cancelled.  EAST Shipping market in the East has finally taken a breather after 2-3 weeks with lots of activity. The August program seems pretty covered for now (unless ships run late for their laycans later), and time of writing we are awaiting Adnoc and Aramco acceptances for September which will set the tone for next month. A couple of fob tenders from middle eastern suppliers in early September has created some attention from the Owners, but otherwise we expect the market to remain fairly quiet until the balance acceptances for September are announced.

The first half of August we have witnessed a very slow and dull Aframax market in the North Sea and Baltic. However, due to a busier Baltic program in the last decade of the month there is a bit more optimism to trace among owners. This week we will see rates move sideways, but then with a firming potential from next week. Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea market there has been little excitement for owners during the week that has passed, although they have been able to maintain the rate levels we saw last week. This is much due to the fact that TCE’s have reached bottom levels. In the week to come we expect this to continue and the market to remain soft.

In the West, the Suezmax market has been fairly busy, mainly driven by large export volumes ex Brazil and a stable West Africa market. At the moment, heading in to 3rd decade, we see increasing cargo activity in West Africa, causing TD20 to tick up a couple of points. Tonnage list is balanced, but with increasing activity, the market looks rather positive heading into next week. In the East, on the other hand, owners should not be too optimistic. We are counting approximately 140 ships the next 30 days, and with the slow activity we have seen out of MEG lately owners should be focusing on trying to fix last done, as there will be plenty of competition on every cargo out there.

Yesterday gave us a small reprieve from staring at the wall in the week gone by, with a number of cargoes emerging, the Atlantic being the centre of attention. The result, however, was more of the same; variations of USD 5.3 million USG/China, WS37.5-38 from Wafr, and MEG continuing to slip. MEG/eastbound rates have now broken the WS35 mark for modern tonnage and discounts still to be had for older units, albeit the gap has narrowed. But, after yesterday's fun and games we’re back to a very empty looking cargo-board, save a couple more USG possibilities and one outstanding cargo in the MEG that is unlikely to last long.

The Supramax market continued sideways trend, and little inspiring news appear. Oversupply of tonnage in both basins putting pressure on the spot rates. We are missing fresh inquiries in the key areas to turn the bearish trend around. Period activity is limited, and very few charterers taking long term commitments. Q1 putting pressure on forward curve. USG and ECSA remain flat. The Black Sea expecting more activity on the grain side, but same still submerged.  Fronthaul rates from the Black Sea to Far East fixing around USD 20k/day. West African trips to China with manganese ore reported at the level of low USD 20k/day. NOPAC and Aussie round trips into China vary in region 9k/11k pd range depends on delivery and vessels specs. South East Asia trips to China were reported at the level of USD 8,500/9,500 pd.  EC India remains strong and paying close to USD 15k/day on Supra and USD 17k/day on large units.

The Panamax market took a turn mid last week, and has experienced firmer rates in both hemispheres. TA’s are now paying excess 12k for the longer runs, while the shorter are being paid in the 14k’s. In the Pacific, we see Aussie rounds being fixed in the 12k’s. We do expect this firming tendency to remain short term with a short tonnage list – especially in the North Atlantic. ECSA grain cargoes are still in a roll and being fixed at around 15.5k+550k GBB, and we now also see the Black Sea grain market coming into play.

The decline in rates in all basins continued the last week. The Atlantic seemed to be “freefalling” whereas the Pacific had a more controlled decline. TA rounds took a dive from USD 13-14k to below USD 10k, and trips out came down from over USD 22k to below USD 19k. As for the Pacific, rounds have fallen some USD 1,500 from last week. However, some fresh orders may indicate that the Pacific could be bottoming out. As for the Atlantic market, there is talk of more business easing the fall, in particular from ECSAM, where rates seem to be stabilizing around USD 14k+400. The tonnage situation in North Atlantic is still, however, a reason for concern. The period market remains quiet with few fixtures reported.

After weeks of dropping rates, there are finally some resistance for the Capes. Pacific rounds improving to upper 15,000s by the middle of the week and c5 back to USD 7 pmt level, followed by Brazil with c3 paying excess of USD 17 pmt. The sentiment is positive and period interest is steady, although limited concluded period fixtures last week.

EAST As the supply and demand for spot open tonnage versus available cargoes for current fixing window are still very much in imbalance, the bull run that we have witnessed on freight during the last couple of weeks has continued, and Baltic has just breached USD 60 Ras Tanura/Chiba for the first time since April. At time of writing, there are reportedly still uncovered shipping requirements in August, while remaining available ships are few (if any at all). This will continue to add pressure on freight rates. However, as the fixing window is currently quite far ahead in time, there is also an extra risk of ships running late for their laycans due to uncertain itineraries, and we might see ships come back open again at a later stage.  WEST Freight rates have strengthened again in the West this week as the fixing window progresses further into September. However, there are questions about how much longer this trend can continue. On one hand, traders argue that arb economics are unsupportive of freight at such high levels and therefore something will have to give. On the other, shipping still seems to be in short supply when considering the balance of the fleet across East and West of Suez. Regardless, most  charterers still have some time to determine whether to cancel FOBs or fix in. Combined with the fact that Singapore is off on Friday, this could mean a quiet end to the week.

By mid-week the index continued downwards, but after a slow start some more activity came to light. From USG, vessels are getting around mid 20k to India, while from Black Sea fh is paying low 20k. On the Continent, scrap runs are fixing around 11k, while further East, Pacific round voyages are paying mid/high 9k. Period rates remained relatively stable so far.

text: AMERICAS  Although the seasonal build was predicted by majority of the market, the propane price at Mt. Belvieu continued downward following the EIA's report of a 2 million barrel inventory build. It appears  that crude production has not decreased to the degree many had originally thought and furthermore- it seems propane production is declining at a rate half as quickly as crude-hence the downward pressure on the C3 flat price. text: MEG: Saudi Aramco set Aug CP at $365 for Propane and $345 for Butane, up by $5 respectively.  Sep Propane CP swap is traded at $350 and Butane is traded at $15 lower, as of ample supply and soaring freight. Qatar Petroleum sold their mid-July lifting evenly split cargo at CP minus 30ish. KPC also tendered to sell their End Aug lifting heavy propane cargo.   FAR EAST:  Cash differentials slided further due to limited buying inquires. 23k Propane for 2h Aug delivery was traded at Sep FEI minus $24. Off window propane parcel for 1h Sep is offered at minus mid-high single digit yet to attract bids.  Indonesia PERTAMINA retendered to purchase monthly one evenly split cargo lifting ex US from Sep to Dec. One Korean Petchem user reportedly covered a 23k Butane parcel for 11-20 Sep delivery at MOPJ minus high 20s. One NChina PDH secured their term from two to three suppliers, for monthly one propane cargo at CP plus teens, delivered from Aug 2020 to Dec 2021. Another NChina importer also issued annual tender to secure one propane monthly in 2021.

Voyage economics remain broadly flat this week, but the sense of a firming shipping market is growing. Prompt business is still dominated by spot cargoes and tender-driven enquiries, and this continues to churn through the availability list without reducing it much. Looking ahead though, sublets are being withdrawn and the bid / offer spread is finally converging, giving hope to owners seeking to salvage something of the year. It's now a question of timing: the best cargo economics span roughly October to December, but owners are reluctant to risk this much idle time prior to delivery, so few multimonth fixtures have been concluded. As the weeks roll on and owners get more visibility of their fleet schedules, we expect a flurry of these fixtures. This has not been a normal year, but despite the disruption of recent months it's reassuring to see the familiar dance of owners and charterers as we look towards winter. No newbuildings reported this week and prices remain flat.

As expected, the Baltic and North Sea market has been through a downward correction the past week. Although the cargo program out of Baltic for August is a healthier one than the previous month, the tonnage list is still long enough to keep a stable pressure on rates as we approach the 2nd decade fixing window of August, and we expect a balanced market in the week to come. Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea we have seen the availability of prompt tonnage impose a declining pressure on rates, and the market has dropped close to 10 points across the board since last week. Although an increase in cargo activity out of Black Sea is forecasted for next month, we still expect the market to remain soft in the short run.

Suezmax rate-support has been underpinned by a mixture of sentiment and stresses to the list. Whilst general enquiry levels have suffered due to production constraints, resistance has been established by dint of many of the modern ships on the list being in the hands of fewer owners. When continued delays in China are added to the mix, the net affect of this owner-concentration is that they are more willing to test the market upwards and less willing to give ground when market activity subsides. This pattern is likely to be repeated as charterers bite deeper into the second decade.

Volumes are marginally up from the last couple of months, reflective of the increased production, but rates stay put. Tonnage supply remains plentiful allowing charterers ample choice, whatever their preference, and owners appear happy to fix and get out of Dodge for the summer. On the plus side it seems to be holding 'firm' around current levels, and earnings in the high teens/low USD 20's/day is currently just a dream scenario for the other smaller classes. The Atlantic has fared a tad better with West Africa/East leading the way, rates coming in around the WS 40 mark, although for a considerably longer commitment.

Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea we have seen the availability of prompt tonnage impose a declining pressure on rates, and the market has dropped close to 10 points across the board since last week. The Capesize segment seems to gradually be following suit with some owners deciding to take advantage of the buying momentum witnessed in the smaller sectors by putting a couple of units onto the market. Namely the Japanese controlled “PACIFIC ENDURANCE” (2011/Koyo/180kdwt) and the sistership “JUBILANT EXCELLENCE” (2013/Koyo/180kdwt) –  both owners are inviting inspections on their respective units and understand that 5 buyers are lined up to get onboard the 2011 built unit while the “JUBILANT EXCELLENCE”  will be made available for inspection while in DD in China beginning of August. text: MEG Aug CP has been volatile, with highest being traded to $390 earlier this week and slashed by $20 to $370 on Thursday. Hence, 1st round CP idea ranged widely from $350 to $400. With the decline on front CP, Aug/Sep turned into a slight contango.  Saudi Aramco released Aug acceptance for with some liftings being advanced. KPC awarded their CFR tender to sell one 3/1 cargo delivered during end Aug early Sep into East, at the price of Sep CP minus mid-teens reportedly.   FAR EAST  The cash discounts for Aug delivery propane has narrowed to mid low single digit to Aug FEI. One 23kt propane for 2h Aug delivery was changing hand at Aug FEI minus $3. Aug FEI/CP fluctuates wildly from -$29 to +$2.5 by the time of writing, partly back by the robust freight rate.  One Korean petchem user issued a semi tender to secure monthly 23k propane delivered from Sep to next Feb. One EChina PDH user issued annual term tender to purchase monthly 23k to 46k propane delivered into Ningbo in 2021. Indonesia PERTAMINA has issued buy tender for monthly one evenly split cargo lifting ex US from Sep to Dec, which is still in validity.

EAST A continuous introduction of more freight requirements from Indian majors has kept the owners busy this week in the East. Meanwhile, the availability of ships with firm discharge programs up until mid/second half August remains few, and hence some traders have already started to check the market for freight ideas for last decade August loading although this is more than one month ahead. Needless to say, freight rates are under pressure, and last done deal in the market was concluded at a significant premium to last posted Baltic.  WEST Much of the same story goes for West of Suez where at the time of writing there is no firm positions left on August dates, this could change depending on turnaround for vessels discharging in Europe. Some already have made moves for early September loading laycans, but most owners are comfortable waiting with giving out firm positions as right now time is on their side and scheduling is very blurry this far ahead.

text: AMERICAS The build of 2 million barrels in US inventories for the week ended July 17th firmed Mt Belvieu propane values slightly. Domestic propane production is averaging 2.223 million barrels per day. This consistent production has been higher than expectations, and should begin to restore confidence in building sufficient stocks before draw season. Exports have also been consistent averaging 1.094 million barrels per day over the past four weeks. Strengthening FEI has been improving arb while rapidly rising freight rates have been keeping netback values stable from the US. So although terminalling fees may still be in the 5-6cpg region for US August FOBs positive momentum has returned to the market.

The shipping market has seen plenty of activity this week, with Australian exports generating interest in the east and US Gulf enquiries picking up in the west. Fixing levels aren’t yet showing sharp increases while the tonnage is there to meet demand, although ships are slowly trickling into employment and sublets are being reabsorbed back into their portfolios. While most firm activity has been east of Suez, the Atlantic market is being watched carefully; after a very weak summer, expectations of an improving LNG trading environment appear to be bearing fruit as early estimates suggest September US Gulf cargo cancellations are down considerably. With players seeking winter coverage and the window for September spot chartering approaching, we could see sentiment firm up in the basin. No Newbuilds have been ordered this week but interest in projects and small scale seems to be restarting, with the Philippines moving forward with FSRU talks, Mozambique LNG project getting financed and the Qatar expansion progressing. As parts of the world re-emerge from lockdown and some limited cross-border travel returns, a sense of normality is returning. Wherever you are in the world, stay safe and we hope that your 2020 will perk up soon enough.

Despite negative developments in the bigger size segments, the Supra segment still have some resistance, and the indexes keep rising with good support of physical demand. However, the balance cargo inquiry and tonnage supply may indicate neutral market direction. Market in general lacking direction. Supramax fixed USD 15,500/day delivery ECSA for Med/Cont direction, while Ultramax close USD 20,000/day. On fronthaul, we have seen rates on Supramax at low USD 20,000/day, and on Ultramax high USD 25,000/day, which indicates quite a big spread. Fronthaul had similar levels to last week about USD 14-14,500/day + about 400,000 bb. Market was stable with a bit more optimist compared to last weeks. Tess 58,000 dwt, with delivery Singapore, was done at USD 10,500/day for a trip via Durban to China. Pacific RV for Supra was fixed at USD 8,250/day and close to USD 10,000/day on Ultra.

Levels for the big ships spiraling downwards on a combination of modest iron ore/low coal trading volumes and a derivatives market being sold by numerous players lacking faith. Fundamentals, however, remain robust in comparison, and question is when levels will again find a floor and rates again start to pick up. The queue of ballasters heading for Brazil and other Atlantic loading areas is limited, whilst major miners work under the radar and keep picking ships for fronthaul at softening levels. Period activity is limited to floating rate-discussions and a number of candidates being pulled due to recent drop in money being bid.

The last week we have seen a sliding market in both basins. In short, the amount of fresh requirements have become rather thin across the board, with quite immediate consequences for hire levels. The fall in rates in the Atlantic has been strongest for TA rounds, with levels down from USD 17-18k mid last week till USD 13-14k at the beginning of this week. The ECSAM/Feast rounds have dropped from USD 16k+600k to just over USD 14k+400k. In the Pacific, the trend is similar but less dramatic, with levels down from mid USD 12k’s to low USD 11k. The period market has been very quiet.

Aframaxes trading in the North Sea and Baltic have seen an uptick in rates since last week. This on the back of owners either being fixed or ballasting away from the area, leaving a tight tonnage list for charterers trying to cover 3rd decade stems. In the week to come, we expect to see a downward pressure on rates following the insufficient cargo activity in the area. The Mediterranean and Black Sea market have maintained in an equilibrium state the past week, with straight cross Mediterranean route (td19) trading around ws70 levels. With the current tonnage availability in the region and with a steady flow of cargoes entering the market, we foresee the market to remain stable in the natural fixing window.

The Atlantic market has taken center stage with the lion’s share of activity, as the week in the MEG has fallen between the monthly programs. We have seen the drip of early August stems entering the market when charterers deem it necessary. Unipec COA’s dominated and rates for modern tonnage remains to test. Delays out East have kept back a flood of tonnage, but current first decade looking like slim pickings will put last done to the test.  Worth noting, it has been 2 consecutive months of total monthly fixtures in the 90’s. However, had they been regular fixing months in the 130-140’s where this market would be…  Wafr/East has remained steady in the ws42-43 level, helped by a busier Suezmax sector. However, the Atlantic is not immune to the quieter MEG, and a number of ballasters have already pointed West.

Although the impact has been rather minimal, sentiments did improve as a handful of Charterers with short shipping positions during autumn-winter period were eager to secure a vessel earlier than usual.  Similarly, forward fixing levels for both Owners and Charterers are not aligned.  Ideas on floating storage plays for winter deliveries have also encouraged multi month discussions to resurfaced again as there could be some potential upside in a trade, storing now and selling into the later part of the year.   Market participants are also keenly awaiting news on the amount of US cargo cancellations for September as that would either increase or decrease demand for shipping.  Newbuilding prices remain unchanged and there were no further reports of any new large LNG carrier orders this week. With upcoming LNG projects currently in yard discussions, we could see a spur in newbuilding orders over the second half of 2020.

We have a strong start to the second half of the year for all dry segments and the bottom for period rates and asset values have likely passed for all segments and vintages. Following inspections by nine buyers, the Japanese controlled Kamsarmax KM YOKOHOMA built 2011 Sanoyas was promptly sold at region USD 15m, levels which fall in line with expectations. BW Dry’s recent deal on subjects for the sale of its three ten year old; Japanese built Kamsarmax BW ACORN, BW BARLEY and BW EINKORN failed to materialize, and they were instead quickly sold to new buyers this week. We understand Centrofin is the buyer of the latter two and Orion the buyer of BW ACORN. This vessel was in fact contracted as newbuilding by Orion and sold to BW Dry in 2018.   Any movement in dry values will be north in the near to medium term and we shall soon be seeing more modern tonnage being offered for sale.   It is time-out in the tanker S&P market. Values remain under pressure and there is no sense of urgency to acquire assets unless a particularly attractive deal comes along.

Only positive for Owners out east, is that we see quite a lot of ships ballasting towards West-Africa which could help remaining tonnage going into next week.

Belvieu propane price, and effectively widened LST/FEI arbitrage. Netbacks for August cargos are back above 4 cents and discussions in the spot market are bid at 4.5 and offered at 5.5cpg for C3 cargoes. The ramp up of US Crude and Natural Gas  production has continued its bullish momentum, as the WTI price has stabilized above $40/ barrel- allowing for a return of US East Coast exports which were cut into sharply back in April/ May as producers scaled back volume in the Marcellus/ Utica regions. It is estimated now that Marcus Hook exports are back up to the equivalent of 10/11 or so VLGC's/ month. That said, US traders are still feeling the covid induced demand lapse in Asia -however economics are decent enough to stave off any cancelation rumblings, especially when supported by large product builds and the subsequent hope of cheaper Mt. Belvieu.

Still firm in several areas and gains to the index in the beginning of the week. In the Atlantic, strong numbers seen from both Black Sea and Continent, where ultras are fetching close to mid 20’k and low 20’k respectively for fh.
