text: MEG Aug swap CP surged strongly to $372, up by $24 and backwardation into Sep enlarged to $15.  ADNOC acceptance is released with advancements reported, as lifters prefer to nominate for later month loading. KPC finally sold their 4/5 Aug lifting 3/1 cargo at Aug CP minus around $30 via tender. Netback on heavy propane FOBs are still under heavy discounts. To the contrary, equal ratio FOB discussion improves with the increasing demand on butane.   FAR EAST Asian market improved this week with far east players emerged to cover Aug demand. Earlier this week, 23kt propane parcels have been traded at Aug FEI minus mid-teens for 1h and low teens for 2h Aug delivery respectively. On Wed similar parcel for 2h Aug delivery was traded at Aug FEI minus $7 only, amid the stronger paper swap. In addition to this, several equal ratio cargos have been placed into China and some Chinese major is keen to swap by taking in heavy butane ratios. Two PDHs located in EChina with total capacity exceeding 1mmt/y propylene are under trial run. And one 1.1mmt/y ethylene cracker located in Panjin NChina is expected to come online next week, which now receiving their first VLGC cargo for feedstock.

As expected the increased level of buying enquiry in the dry sector has resulted in a notable pick up in activity with a number of inspections and negotiations taking place this week. Japanese owners invited inspection of the 2011 Sanoyas built Kamsarmax “KM YOKOHAMA” and up to 9 buyers are now outright with offers invited next week. This firm interest has inevitably driven additional sellers onto the market with new Kamsarmax units being placed for sale. We expect this increased competition to drive values upward and also activity to continue to spill over into other segments including the Supra-/Ultramax segment where we have seen 5 units change hands this week and a number of firm discussions are taking place. Although most reported sales are of more vintage units, this increased liquidity has provided extra support to values enabling potential sellers of more modern units to engage with renewed confidence.  The tanker sector remains subdued and unless sellers reduce their ideas substantially, we do not see much appetite to secure tonnage in the current market environment.

The big ships experiencing partly awaited correction after almost one month of steady/aggressive spot improvements.  Topping post-weekend, daily average earnings are down 5 pct w-o-w to come in at a still very healthy USD 29,500. Basic fundamentals remain good, with big ore volumes concluded and expected going forward on main routes. Atlantic in particular keeps being very tight on early tonnage and appears a key driver for subsequent recovery.  Period interest considerable whilst conclusions limited - most recent fixtures include 211,000 dwt, built 2016, reportedly done for 14-18 months to industrial majors at USD 19,950.

After a couple of weeks of inactivity in the VLCC market, this week kicked off with a flurry of activity, and rates have soared up some 40%. Spurred by previous weeks' decline charterers held back in order to propel things further down. However, delays in the East and increased ton-mile have taken its toll, slimming tonnage availability. When it became evident that a floor was established in the mid WS30's MEG/eastbound, charterers entered the market en masse, creating a "ketchup-effect". Owners quickly caught on and adjusted ideas upwards by the hour. All areas have contributed, and daily earnings have doubled. The jury is out whether the upward spiral will continue, some warning that Suezmaxes will come into play as an alternative soon. But the summer nevertheless looks much brighter now than it did a few days ago.

With market jumping 7.5 points late last week, and activity picking up in West Africa, we expected owners to pick up the thread Monday. The tonnage list was looking tight for dates being worked, but as many times before, oil company relets tend to spoil the fun. Rates did not move further, rather opposite, and TD20 is now looking rather stable just above WS50. In the East, it’s the same old story. Market hoovering around WS50, and seems difficult to move, especially without help from the V's. Going into next week we expect the Suezmax market to remain stable at current levels.

EAST We are experiencing a relatively flat freight market as the shipping activity in the Middle East seems to have taken a breather so far this week. The handful of ships open on July dates, some of which are likely to slide into August, might potentially look for opportunities in the West. Lay of the land for August will be a bit more clear next week when both Adnoc and Saudi acceptances are expected out. Meanwhile, talks of Indian importers being long product for August might put a dampener on the recently climbing VLGC shipping market.  WEST West of Suez, the week started off quietly following a long weekend in the US. However, things are quickly beginning to look tighter for August ex US after a handful of fixtures and increased interest in freight against various FOB transactions. Only a small proportion of uncovered cargoes in August have had ships put against them so far.  Aside from the tightening micro picture, a notable number of ships have been routing via the Cape of Good Hope in recent months while owners have upped the number of vessels they are pointing towards drydocks. Looking at both micro and macro landscapes, there is the sense that rates will begin to edge higher from here as a result, particularly as we near the autumn months for the Northern Hemisphere.

text: MEG Despite the deteriorating FOB netback, Aug CP surged up to $348, up by $14 compared to last week. C3/C4 spread has narrowed down to $10 from previous $20, due to the improving butane cracking demand. QP has released their Aug acceptance with some advancements. It is also reported to award its sale tender for 4-7th Aug lifting 3/1 cargo at Aug FEI minus mid-30s, which equates to Aug CP minus 40ish. KPC failed to award the sale tender of 1/2nd Aug lifting 3/1 and retendered to 4/5th Aug lifting, which is due by this Friday. One Chinese importer is offering a mid Aug lifting full propane at Aug CP minus high teens but yet to attract bids.   FAR EAST  Aug delivered propane value is still under heavy discounts to Aug FEI, with offers for 1h Aug parcel at minus $17 while bid at minus $20.  Off window Aug buying inquiries are quite thin this week, except for Korean cracking use. One Korean petchem user purchased a late Aug delivery 23/0 at Aug FEI minus low teens reportedly. Another Korean importer tendered to buy monthly 23kt butane delivered from Oct 2020 to Mar 2021. One NChina importer issued a mini buy tender to secure two to four full propane cargo delivered during Aug 2020 till Dec 2021.  Although US FOB netbacks are into cancellation territory, some players still rather to lift tons and sit for contango with anticipation on recovery into Sep and Q4.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS The EIA reported a build of 2.2 million barrels this week, in line with expectation- all the while exports rose to 1.33mn b/d. As it stands, the butane arb to Europe looks better than propane, (around $80/ton) while the propane arb in that direction has come off. The LST/FEI spread last showed $83 lst/fei following the build, netting back just over 4cpg (when using low 60s for freight on a houston/chiba basis) where FOB discussion for August cargos now stand. Many participants have taken the view that the catalyst for higher netback values will come in the form of Indian demand -as China, South Korea and Japanese stocks seem well built at this time. US producers, notably in the Marcellus, Utica and Permian regions have pressed onward with their volume recovery as the crude price now sits in the low 40's following the mid april crash that subsequently choked out Marcus Hook export volumes.

Over the past week we’ve seen a few signs of life in the spot market, with those vessels fixed or placed on subs being at or slightly above recent spot rates. The focus of the market continues to be winter coverage, with reports of several Charterers securing additional tonnage through the winter. These fixtures have established a forward view that is not necessarily as weak as the current sport market would have it. Furthermore, independent owners with open winter tonnage are growing increasingly selective on which opportunities they will entertain. It’s almost mythical how these things tend to come together around week 27 every year. One thing does seem certain, and that is that the market may have bottomed out…although this does not mean that we’ll see a sudden increase in spot rates this side of the summer holidays.

Another week that has seen a flurry of transactions in the dry snp markets with a number of vessels changing hands across all sectors. In the Capesize segment the Japanese controlled “GRACEFUL MADONNA” (2010 Koyo 180kdwt) has been sold to clients of Eastern Pacific at Usd 20.7m with DD passed and BWTS installed. The deal is setting a well needed benchmark for Japanese built Cape units of this vintage considering that the last comparable sale dates back to February. Elsewhere the majority of units being sold remain of early to mid-2000 built tonnage with the Handysize sector seeing increased activity on the more modern side of the spectrum.  On the tanker side activity remains subdued to say the least with only two sales to report.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS A larger than expected 3.3 million barrel build was seen in US inventories. Part of this increase was attributed to US refineries coming back online and running at 75.5% the highest since early April. Domestic production has been more resilient than initially expected and with WTI at $40 a barrel some wells are coming back online. The improved production picture will put downward pressure on Mt Belvieu as a percentage of WTI which today lies at 50%. This should in turn open the arb if we see demand recovery form the East market. These MT Belvieu price moves are strengthening US FOB bid/offer levels and keeping cancelations talks in the rear-view.

text: MEG Saudi Aramco has raised up July CP to $360 for propane and $340 for butane, up by $10 respectively. Most players reckon the number is higher than expectation. Aug CP is traded at $334 on Thurs. QP issued sale tender to market a 3/1 cargo for 4th to 7th Aug lifting, and previously it was reported to sell two end July delivery heavy propane. KPC also issued tender to sell one 1/2nd Aug lifting 3/1 yet to hear the result.   FAR EAST  LPG cracking demand continuously improved especially butane is favored by Korean petchem users. One Korean importer reportedly bought one 2/2 for 1h Aug delivery this week, and meanwhile it also issued purchasing tender for monthly 23kt butane parcels delivered from Sep onwards to Nov or next Feb. One Japanese Oil Company issued close tender to sell an Australia origin heavy propane cargo for Aug delivery.  Indonesia Pertamina issued new buy tender to secure another equal ratio cargo for Sep delivery or 24th Jul to 22th Aug lifting ex US, valid by this Friday. China May LPG import exceeded 2mmt, up by 20% from April. However, June arrival is estimated with a big draw upto 460kt due to high inventory and slow consumption. 1H 2020 import is expected to decline by 12% or 1mmt.

It is still a continuous struggle for Aframax owners trading in the North Sea and Baltic to find suitable employment for their vessels, resulting in a freight that barely cover their operation costs. Going forward, rates will continue at these bottom levels yielding minimal returns for owners which also encourages owners to sit idle instead of competing for cargoes giving negative returns. Also the Mediterranean and Black Sea market has continued to trade sideways yet another week as we are approaching the midst of summer. As in the North, TCE returns are barely in the black as cargo activity is not satisfying the supply of available tonnage in the area. We expect a continued flat market in the week to come, as there are no signs of activity picking up in the short run.

EAST As a knock-on effect to the increased activity on shipping seen in the West from last week, the Eastern VLGC market finally came back to life again as well. Several ships have been taken out for 2H July MEG load during the week, and freight rates have slowly started to climb upwards again. Owners’ ideas are now in the USD 30s Baltic (compared to low USD 20s the week before), and time being they would rather send their open ships back West on speculation unless they are able to secure voyages at these sorts of levels in the East. Meanwhile we are awaiting next month’s acceptances from the Middle Eastern suppliers, which are expected to start coming out from this and next week onwards.  WEST West of Suez, this week has been calmer than last as the market takes a breather. Less inquiries have been seen and players seem to have paused to make sure their programs are lined up properly. Although there are still a few loose ends remaining in July, fixing looks generally over with for this period. Freight has cooled off marginally as the focus turns to August. This is due to slightly more freight length and reduced interest from charterers for the time being.

The Suezmax market have had decent activity for the last couple of weeks. Going into this week, the tonnage list in the West was looking healthier, counting less than 120 ships next 30 days in West Africa. Owners have picked up on this, but unfortunately for them, we are missing the activity to tip the market in their direction. We are still looking at low WS40's for TD20, but heading into the 20-30 window, a small increase in cargo activity could have a bigger effect on the market than we have seen lately. In the East on the other hand, it’s basically status quo. Tonnage list is still looking awful in owners’ perspective, and for the time being something extraordinary will have to happen to move MEG/East anywhere close to WS50 again.

Alas, the light at the end of the tunnel is as likely to be a train coming in the opposite direction, with July volumes so far trending down from an 18-year low June. With summer holidays just around the corner most owners will sign up to the quote; “A vacation is what you take when you can no longer take what you’ve been taking.”

The Atlantic market has seen a daily increase in rates where p1A currently yields around the upper USD 12k, and a general optimistic view for further increase across the market for the coming weeks. In the Eastern hemisphere we see a slow growing list of available tonnage and lack of fresh requirements to absorbe same. text: AMERICAS: The 2.36 million barrel weekly build along with tanking crude caused the July propane price at Mt. Belvieu to drop sharply (aprox 48cpg) - However, this did little to support the dwindling arb as the FEI and NWE prices came off considerably as well. Further discussions of cancellations, (two) are being reported, though unconfirmed, for US Gulf July FOB cargos, as freight shot up basis Houston/Chiba. That being said, exports increased week on week, as US production has come back online in a big way following COVID 19 related cuts. As it stands, FOB bid side interest in the gulf has dissipated, with offers around  4.5-5cpg.  In Latin America , Gasmar tendered for their third cargo of Southern Hemisphere Winter with offers due today for 44,000 mts propane basis delivery August 13-18.

Dry markets continue to see the vast majority of sale and purchase activity with 8 sales to report this week. The panamax market have seen three 2005 built vessels change hands setting clear direction for 15 year old units, while the smaller segments have seen increased liquidity for more modern tonnage. Although new benchmarks have been set, consensus among most market players is that values are at or have passed the bottom and we should start seeing sellers showing a little more resistance by revising their expectations upwards. That being said, determined sellers now face a more receptive audience allowing an exit at numbers which was not realistic short time ago. Interesting times ahead in this sector.  Tankers are certainly not the flavor of the month and we are moving into uncertain territory for values with no transactions taking place.

text: MEG: Despite the crude rally and fall, Jul CP swap stabilized due to the coming CP announcement. Jul CP was traded at $341 but backwardation into Aug widened to $15 from previous $5. 1st round CP ideas varied widely. FAR EAST:  Residential demand is still sluggish due to summer season, whereas cracking demand slowly recovered with a couple of butane parcels have been absorbed into Korea. One Korean petchem user secured an end Jul delivered 2/2 with propane at Jul FEI minus $10 and butane at Jul Mopj minus 50s via tender reportedly. Indonesia PERTAMINA issued buy tender to purchase one equal ratio cargo for mid Jul lifting ex US or to be delivered during end Aug, which is closed by this Friday. PERTAMINA had bought one early Jul lifting US 2/2 in its last tender.

There are plenty of permutations of possible events that could greatly influence the LNG shipping market in the months to come. Vessel availability at the moment is high, as expected as per the seasonal lack of gas demand during summer months where utility players generally have pockets of availability of sublets. This, further fuelled by cargo cancellations in the United States due to the drop of LNG demand caused by COVID-19 lockdowns, led to US lifters’ vessels being available in the spot market. Longer voyages are expected by the LNG fleet dedicated to LNG exporters when long term buyers defer the receipt of cargoes to manage their inventory levels, which could absorb shipping capacities but these have not been sufficient to manage the long tonnage situation. Geo-political events could yet again be the catalyst for volatile swings in shipping rates as international disputes could lead to possible sanctions, blockades, et cetera. While further progress on treatments and vaccines for COVID-19 could lead to added confidence on lifting of lockdowns worldwide, which could lead to rise in LNG demand. These are unpredictable times but as for this week, rates and sentiments remain flat.  No newbuilding orders to report this week.

The dam has burst, and VLCC rates have taken a - overdue - nosedive. The recent lack of activity, with the June MEG fixture count at an 18-year low, and July has kicked off with a rate slide. MEG/East rates are now realistically in the WS 30’s for all classes, and West Africa/East has followed suit. Daily earnings are still in the USD 20’s, but with increased bunker prices and further downward potential OPEX levels could come under threat moving forward. By all accounts it’s going to be a hot, long summer of discontent.

After a busy last week, some owners had a slight hope that the market could have bottomed out, but boy they were wrong. After the VLCC's tanked at the beginning of the week, Suezmaxes were suddenly not the cheapest alternative anymore, and split VLCC cargoes on subs failed. Going forward this will mean more VLCC cargoes and less for Suezmaxes, and with 120+ ships on the 30-day count in West Africa, owners should be happy to get USD 10k/day on their ships. The East is still over-tonnaged, and we could see a couple of more points downside to the MEG/East market.

Aframaxes trading in the Nsea and Baltic continues to suffer from the lack of available market cargoes. This is mainly due to the production cuts especially from the strategic crude export terminals in the Baltic. Another main factor is that relets fix a huge portion of the few available cargoes on a private basis, hence leaving very little to fix for other owners. Going forward the market will move sideways around current bottom levels. Much of the same can be said for the Mediterranean and Black Sea where the market has continued to move sideways yet another week. Although little activity from charterers, rates have bottomed out at around WS60 for a straight cross-Med voyages. This gives owners a return of about USD 1,500 pd in TCE. We expect this to continue in the week to come.

text: MEG: Despite the weak sentiment on physical purchases, Jul CP rebounded to $337 this week, with the anticipation on Saudi cuts.  Aug CP is traded at $4 less, still in backwarded structure. comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS: A larger than expected build of 2.7 million barrels in US propane inventories helped improve the arb slightly Wednesday. The underlying positive note from the EIA stats was the production level. This has risen for the third week in a row to 2.142 million barrels a day. This rise in production is already having an effect as export volumes are beginning to ramp from the US East Coast. With global demand starting to recover and US production rising traders are reluctant to cancel US cargoes. Lets hope both these trends continue and keep cancellations at bay.  In South America Gasmar awarded the second tender of the season and are expected to have at least one more before their Winter ends.

Global markets have gradually started their recovery, although improvements in the LNG market are likely to lag a little as product prices and shipping rates remain flat across the board. Shipping availability is slowly building into July, and in anticipation of US cargo cancellations a rather tough environment exists in the prompt market. The current bid/ask spread remains relatively wide, making transactions challenging as Owners and Charterers expectations remain somewhat disconnected. Nevertheless, there is some optimism looking further ahead to autumn and winter. A West-to-East arbitrage and contango pricing may result in a stronger cargo market, where ship owners and players long tonnage may see some profitable opportunities.    On the Newbuilding front, again there have been no new large LNG vessel orders to report this week or this year, and we may end up with no new orders to report for first half 2020!

Positive sentiment and stronger rates discussed this week, with period rates increasing. From USG TA paying around high USD 12000 to Bsea, from Cont to Emed scrap runs in the high USD 7000 and ECSA fh trading around USD 13000 + 350k gbb. Period rates pushing over USD 11000 bss redelivery Atlantic. In the East, Aussie rv's are paying around high USD 7000 while Indonesian coal has been quiet vessels open CJK looking at around mid/high USD 6000 for Indo/China and similar level for CIS rounds. Short period rates has pushed over USD 9000.

Rates in the North Sea and Baltic have reached the bottom level with returns close to nothing. Some owners even reluctant to fix at current levels as it is nearly better to sit idle and wait. However, we don't see much upside in the short term and the market will move sideways going forward. The situation is similar in the Mediterranean and Black Sea where the market has dropped slightly further from last week. Although there is some activity from charterers, there is not enough cargoes in the market to satisfy the amount for available ships. TD19 is currently trading around WS 60 giving owners a poor return below OPEX levels. In the week to come we expect the market to remain soft here as well.

It’s been a quiet week so far in the VLCC segment. We’re up to 95 reported MEG June fixtures give or take, a modern historical low, and it looks like we’re pretty much done. We await the publication of the main MEG July programs due this week, although with the usual juggling and program sorting following their release, we may not see a lot of action before next week. A potential mass sanction over trade with Venezuela now appears unlikely, as a group of Greek-managed tankers on the OFAC list is likely to find themselves back in Washington’s good graces again, the Union of Greek Shipowners said on Tuesday, citing a US diplomat. Rates have nevertheless held on remarkably well, hovering around the W60 mark MEG/east, especially seeing the Suezmax segment trading at 2.5-5 points discount to their bigger sisters.

The dry S&P activity continues to pick up with a large number of vessels reported sold. Whilst older units still account for majority of sales we now have an interesting bench-mark set by the sale of the Japanese controlled Oshima Kamsarmax resale which was sold to Greek interests at $ 29m. Furthermore three 2010 Japan built Kamsarmaxes are also reported to be committed on subjects at region Usd 40 mill en-bloc. The buying momentum now shaping up leads us to conclude that the downside risk on values is limited. Buyers hoping for a re-run of 2016 values will wait in vain.  Tanker values are sliding and vintage vessels remain most at risk.

For the first time in many weeks the activity in the Suezmax market has picked up. Mainly driven by a busy first decade in West-Africa, but also the activity in the US gulf is looking better. Rate-wise we have seen much change yet, but the massive overhang of ppt tonnage we have had after this extremely quiet month we have been through, need to be fixed away first. In the east it is looking a bit more quiet, tonnage-list is still looking rather long, but almost 25 vessel on that list are still stuck in Chinese ports awaiting berthing prospects. Going forward we do expect some improvement in the rates, predominantly in the west - especially if this activity keeps up.

Cape rates continue to increase fast, with average index value up USD 10,000 from last week to today’s USD 19,000. The main driver is Iron ore, with both the Australian route c5 and Brazilian route c3 being strong, still expected to improve further. Period interest is increasing gradually as well with operators again being more active.

Rates in the North Sea and Baltic have reached the bottom level with returns close to nothing. Some owners even reluctant to fix at current levels as it is nearly better to sit idle and wait. However, we don't see much upside in the short term and the market will move sideways going forward. The situation is similar in the Mediterranean and Black Sea where the market has dropped slightly further from last week. Although there is some activity from charterers, there is not enough cargoes in the market to satisfy the amount for available ships. TD19 is currently trading around WS 60 giving owners a poor return below OPEX levels. In the week to come we expect the market to remain soft here as well.

After a dull last week, we have experienced more activity in the Panamax market this week. Especially the Atlantic has experienced a firming market with big gains compared to last done. TA’s are now paying excess 6k which is almost the double WoW. In the Pacific we also experience a firming market with rounds now yielding excess 8k – some Usd 1000 up from last week. The ECSA ha been the main driver this week as well, but we see increased activity in the North Atlantic for both Feast and Cont destinations.

EAST: The market in the East has remained fairly inactive this week apart from a couple of companies checking freight ideas against early July loading in the Middle East. Most players are still waiting for the announcement of Saudi July acceptances, and as freight remains long with available ships from both the main owners and the traders, the sentiment is rather weak and there is no real rush to commit on shipping just yet. We are also seeing additional delays for ships coming open ex India. This could normally lead to some tightness of the spot available fleet in the East, but with continued LPG production cuts and the current length in vessel supply elsewhere we do not expect this to have any significant impact.  WEST:  There hasn’t been much to write home about this week with regards to the VL market West of Suez. Things seem to be in a state of inertia: bunkers have been largely stable, East and West still seem broadly equivalent on a baltic basis and earnings have weakened only marginally. Positions lists remain long with a number of relets available, and as we head further into the weaker summer months it seems the market will come under some more pressure.   On the basis of a weak CFR market in the East and given the low cost of waiting time compared to the Panama Canal fee, it seems the vast majority of ships should be routing via the Cape of Good Hope. However, it is hard to say when any bullishness of the longer tonne mile will feed through to the market; sentiment is still unanimously bearish and is expected to remain so for a while longer.

This week continues to see most sale and purchase activity take place in the dry market where a number of vessels have changed hands. This increased liquidity in the sector has enabled the relative downward correction that most market players expected in light of the global disruption. However the consensus seem to be that we are near the bottom in terms of values with a relatively positive market expectation for the quarters to come. Saying that values are on average down between 15 to 20% since pre-covid transactions therefore still representing an attractive play from a buying perspective. We expect to see more deals take place in the coming weeks which should provide a clear indication as to what direction this SnP market will take.   No change in the tanker market where we witness very little activity with the few exceptions on the overaged front with sellers willing to transact. Past sellers of more modern units have now most definitely taken a step back unwilling to entertain discussions at today’s levels.

General news flows in recent weeks have had an air of pessimism but the mood may be changing, with countries reopening and an expectation that things are starting to look a little brighter and the same can be said for the LNG industry. Despite low product prices and LNGC rates, the industry continues to its forward progress. The 19.2 billion US dollar shipbuilding deal agreed last week by Qatar Petroleum with three South Korean yards offer Owners a well needed distraction from today’s spot market.  New areas and sectors of demand is also bearing fruit, with further LNG bunkering vessels being launched.  And whilst operating on the open seas has seen new challenges raised through the restrictions on movement of personal and quarantine measures, MAN dual-fuel engines passed one million operating hours this year, which reflects a level of experience and operating history that should offer improved reliability and a greater understanding of the technology meaning smoother sailing for Owners and Charterers alike. All we need next is a sustainable arbitrage to reduce what is a slightly bulging availability list.

text: AMERICAS: Following a flurry of July FOB cargo sales at the beginning of the week, the US/ Asia arbitrage narrowed Wednesday following an unseasonable draw in Inventories. The  US Gulf made up the entirety of the draw (1.3 million barrels) as the Mid continent built. As it stands, US inventories now rest at a similar level to this time last year, though the sentiment of considerable Q3 and Q4 product tightness remains throughout the market. With that said, two US producers echoed a similar feel this week in that barrels redacted last month, following cutbacks due to tanking crude prices have reappeared due to the historic May rally. A handful of July cargos remain unsold. Traders and terminals alike continue to target terminalling fee’s at or above 5cpg to move, while others hope to roll cargos back. In South America, a Tender was issued for 44,000mts of propane for an end July arrival.

The VLCC market failed to capitalize fully on the upward momentum from Friday when a W65 was logged MEG/China. Numerically activity has been healthy, but most have been Chinese “COA” liftings and a few program deals, leaving little to choose from for independent owners. The owning community’s fighting spirit still remains high, however, and a W60 concluded midweek – on an oil company relet to bout – was against the tide and shows strength. There are still discounts to be had from the vintage fraternity, but a W53.25 replacement fixture MEG/Vietnam on a ’03 built unit is not a giveaway either. Rumours of a mass US sanction listing of owners having traded from Venezuela failed to materialize, but the threat of same has cautioned players and partly aided current rate levels. Continued OPEC+ cuts through July does not indicate a turnaround any time soon, but daily VLCC earnings in the high $40k’s per day is nevertheless miles ahead of those of their smaller sisters, struggling to cover OPEX.

Aframaxes trading in the North Sea and Baltic area have seen rates hit rock bottom with earnings being close to nothing. With the current lack of activity and even oil company relets looking for employment we expect no improvements in the near future.    In the Mediterranean and Black Sea rates have slowly crumbled down another 10 points or so during the course of the week. TCE’s on benchmark routes have fallen below OPEX levels and the general consensus in the market is that we are seeing bottom levels. In the week to come we expect the market to remain at same levels as we are still seeing a long tonnage list.

It was a slow start to the week across both hemispheres with Fhauls keeping somewhat flat allthough chrts bidding lower. Both the P1A and P3A kept sliding with rounds being concluded in region USD 3,5-4k and 7,5-8k respectively. Mid week we do however experience a more positive sentiment, much led by the bigger Capes and for what could be more split cgos entering the mrkt.

Sentiment still positive as iron ore prices at multi-year highs. West Australian iron ore being pumped into the pacific and we see the hire rates on vessels shipping the commodity doubling since last week.  For Brazil there is still some prompt tonnage left keeping hire levels lower than pacific, however they are gradually taken out and we expect this continue further though Brazil is experiencing the covid-19 setback as we speak. All in all the time charter basket of all routes is up by 74% from Wednesday last week

The majority of players remain bearish with regards to freight rates, while bunkers have continued to rally some 10% at time of writing. These things together have put pressure on earnings for those with tonnage. However, there is a glimmer of hope within the product market, where netbacks are looking slightly better and there seems to be healthy interest on both the buy and sell side of FOB cargoes. In theory, this could mean greater demand for tonnage and may be the start of a shift towards a more balanced supply and demand picture on the VLs.  EAST: In Middle East the Adnoc acceptances were posted Tuesday, and in addition to their term cargoes there are talk that they may also have some spot fob availability. Meanwhile there have also been a couple of fob tenders discussed from other suppliers for loading within 1st decade July. But with ample freight availability dominated by trader relets, freight rates remain under pressure. There is an overhang of about 15 vessels from June which are likely set to take some waiting time as fixing window is now slowly moving towards July. In terms of activity thus far this week one Indian major booked a ship for end June loading, while a trader was reported fixing a ship for mid June load in the MEG.

Despite a slow start from the Monday there was heightened activity in both basins. The most strength in rates have been in USG and ECSA .  West Africa saw good demand for tonnage both for Far East and Transatlantic destinations. From the Mediterranean and  Continent activity remains low. Indian ocean and South East Asia continue last weeks trend of increasing demand.  On the period side  Mv Nikolaos A 58k dwt open Surabaya 5 June fixed min 3 abt 5 months redelivery worldwide at $9,500 p/day. Forward NB TBN (63,500 2020) dely cjk in sept clean fixed 1 year at $10,500.

The sense of urgency to buy tankers is waning and values are slowly correcting downwards. Two 2000 built VLCC’s have been sold for region Usd 24 mill each which is Usd 6 mill lower than the recent peak at Usd 30 mill for the same age LUCKY TRADER concluded at the end of April. However it should be noted that LUCKY TRADER had her Special Survey passed and gave prompt delivery. Values for vintage tankers will be most exposed going forward but across the board we see the bid/ask spread widening in line with falling newbuilding prices and expectations. Judging by history we are likely to enter a period of limited sales activity with a wait-and-see attitude prevailing.  For bulkers we see a clear buying momentum building up and we may indeed be getting closer to a more robust floor on values which should trigger increased S&P activity. Sales volume YTD has been dominated by 10 year olds and older which is where we expect such a floor first to be established.  The more modern ones should then follow suit, perhaps with another 10-15% correction downwards.

Slow start to the week with holidays in many European countries and little concluded by early mid-week. In the Atlantic USG to Feast, is paying around USD 11000, while same from ECSA is trading around USD 11000+112500 gbb. Any TA is paying owners around USD 6000, while Med fh is as well paying around USD 11000. In the Indian Ocean, for ECI/Bdesh trip to Seasia the levels is in the high USD 10k-11000. Meanwhile Indo/China is paying around USD 8000.

June is generally a happy month, and if it hadn’t been for Covid-19 we'd all be enjoying Posidonia poolside in Greece now. That said the weather in Oslo has been better than Greece in the last week, although there are now clouds on the horizon, as is the case in the VLCC market. With rates having soared in the region of 35% last week, all but a couple of points have now been negated. MEG/east is currently standing at a flat W50 MEG/East for older tonnage, and 2.5-5 points more for a modern unit. Still quite a healthy demand in the Atlantic helping to shore up rates. However, everything is interconnected and unless the rot is stopped in the MEG, then rates from the western hemisphere will inevitably follow suit. Bunker prices have also gone up on the back of soaring crude prices, denting daily earnings further - although still yielding somewhere in the $40k's/day depending on the ship's attributes and the voyage in question.

The Suezmax market is continuing the downward spiral from last week. The 30 day count in both WAFR and MEG is at the highest year to date. For Owners this means one thing - there is nowhere to hide. TD20 is closing in on $20k/day and Owners now need to focus on minimizing their waiting time and keep the ships sailing. As of now, we dont see any signs of improvement going forward either, so for this market to stop this downward spiral we would probably need rates to come down to a level where Owners would rather float than fix.

As expected we have seen rates in the North Sea and Baltic come off significantly from last done levels. Even more vessels are entering the market as there is no further incentive for storage. We also see that in some of the congested import terminals turnaround has picked up again and vessels are discharging quicker than expected. So with an abundance of available tonnage  we expect the downward pressure on rates to continue into next week. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea we have seen the market move sideways all week as little activity from Charterers side is just enough to keep the market balanced. At the time of writing a cross-Med voyage currently pays just below WS 80, while fixtures ex Bsea have been repeated several times during the course of the week at WS 90. Owners choose not to flee to surrounding markets such as USG and the North as these are coming off at the moment. As available tonnage keeps piling up in the area we expect the market to remain soft in the week to come.

As prompt LNG trading and shipping conditions continue to underwhelm, most market players are busy making the best of things today while looking ahead for hints of change. The bare facts are that LNG pricing remains low across the globe, US cargo cancellations are biting and vessel availability is creeping up. But if these pessimal conditions are the harshest for survival they’re also a great driver of ideas and innovation, and as we enter the second half of the year there are increasing signs of clever thinking and smart trades. High inventory levels and low pricing in Europe combined with fewer US cargoes is creating a novel dynamic in the north Atlantic, and demand continues to return to markets in the east as economies gain momentum emerging from lockdown. The prospect of European reloads to capture value either in localised contangoes or in inter-basin trade are encouraging for tonne-time and tonne-mile demand, and in turn ship owners are entertaining creative ideas on rates such floating structures. text: AMERICAS: A higher than expected US propane inventory build of 3.1 million barrels was the fifth straight build in inventories. Arbitrageurs hoped this would improve the curve,  however Mt Belvieu remained strong as US traders focused more on production declines than inventory builds. Current production dipped slightly to 1.989 million barrels per day and we believe the days of production over 2 million barrels per day is now a thing of the past. Netbacks remain around 4 cpg however deals continue to be done above these levels as buyers seem to be more content on moving their vessels as opposed to netback econs. Discussions on export cancellations is continuing but it seems to us the number is fewer than believed,  although the net amount of cargos from the US is dropping and this is really taking its toll on the shipping market.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Saudi Aramco raised up June CP Propane at $350 by $10 and lowered down Butane by $10 to $330, which was amongst the recommendation range. Afterwards Jul CP has rapidly surged up to $345 from last week’s $305, with the concerns over escalating China-US tensions. Qatar Petroleum has released July loading acceptance with some liftings being advanced, as lifters tend to nominate later loading to avoid cargo landing in bearish July market. It was reported that KPC failed to award their 1-2 Jul lifting 4/0 cargo with bids received at CP minus 20ish or more.   FAR EAST: Limited activities this week as in lack of buying inquiries. 23kt propane for 1h Jul delivery were traded at Jul FEI minus $5, while 2h Jul with small contango at minus $2. Asian Importers are still under high inventory and barely have appetite for 1h Jul arrival cargos. Only one EChina PDH user shows interest to take a parcel of 23kt propane for such period. One Chinese Major has sold a full cargo propane for 1h Jul into Tianjin at Jul FEI plus small digits. One SChina PDH user issued buy tender to secure 23kt propane for last decade July delivery, which is still in validity with abundant offers received. One NChina new petchem player with 1mmt/y ethylene cracker was reported to secure a 2h Jul delivery equal ratio cargo as feedstock to start up in Jul/Aug

EAST A few cargoes are being worked in MEG and some have been placed on subs so far this week. Despite some activity including FOB tenders and a few Indian bound cargoes, length remains for June positions with availability widely spread across the month. We also continue to see more owners sending ships West on speculation. Nevertheless, the question now seems to be where we will find the freight floor as earnings are about to slide below break-even levels.  WEST Freight rates West of Suez have continued to come under some pressure this week. With Houston/Chiba voyages now some $40pmt cheaper than they were a month ago, waiting time is considerably cheaper than it has been for much of the past year. This might be one factor in why owners have continued to dig their heels in and have been reluctant to be too competitive on freight in recent weeks. Consequently, it seems that traders have had more success in reducing their freight exposure in June, with owners looking longer freight as the market’s focus turns towards July. While owners’ decision to slow steam ships will help to stretch the fleet in the short term, ultimately there is still the sense that rates have further to fall. The extent to which this will happen will depend on how aggressive owners choose to be when the next round of fixing commences.

A pickup in activity this week, with a number of countries around the world returning to some form of relative normality. In the tanker space, the majority of vessels changing hands remain those of older vintage, whereas mentioned last week sellers are more lenient and willing to go meet buyers at levels below the last done that were set over the past stronger weeks. On the more modern side of the spectrum, the stand-off remains with the few remaining potential sellers still holding off for levels set at the peak of the aforementioned market.   As expected, following the recent increase of Buying enquiries, the dry SnP markets are seeing a number of transactions taking place with new benchmarks being set. A number of potential sellers have now got clearer visibility on the potential bids and are willing to test the market by making candidates available for inspections.  Although the panamax and post-panamax segments have seen a couple of units being sold this week there still is a notable lack of activity in the capesize market rendering it difficult to assess where pricing currently lies. This price dislocation being particularly well illustrated by the Taiwanese controlled MV “NEW STAGE” (176,877 dwt built 2008 Namura) which was withdrawn after seeing a top offer of Usd 14m against sellers expectation of Usd 16m.

Similar to last week, Suezmaxes are struggling all over, with no place to hide at the moment. Owners prefer to fix short voyages, or wait it out. The tonnage list in the Atlantic is long, but not hopeless. In the East on the other hand, it looks terrible. Two weeks of almost no activity has built up a list we have not seen in quite some time. A 30-day count in the MEG shows 141 ships on paper, which will make most owners give in. Until today it has been difficult to find any positive signs at all, but things have started happening with VLCC activity and rates moving in the right direction, which should spill over into the Suezmax segment. Additionally, we now see some movement in Libya as well. It remains to be seen if this is sustainable, but getting Libya barrels back in play would be a huge plus.

text: MEG: 1st round June CP recommendation ranged widely from $300-$370 for Propane with majority at $330-340, in line with swap value. Butane was recommended at parity to propane or $10-15 less. Saudi Aramco is reported to have a heavy butane spot cargo for June lifting. And other AG producers including QP and ADNOC are also said to have spots avail. This adds on more volume to an oversupplied market, which revealed a reason why June/Jul CP backwardation has enlarged from $10 to $30 now.   FAR EAST: With a bunch of June arrival cargos unabsorbed, front still appears long amid lukewarm demand and Jul price discussion is edging down. One full cargo propane for 1h Jul arrival was reported sold at Jul FEI minus $4 while another equal ratio for Jul arrival was at even lower minus $7 reportedly. Asian importers are still hesitant to move for July spot amid high inventory.  Despite the narrowing Arb, there is no June cancellations so far. And lifters are said now consider shipping cargos via CAPE instead of Houston Channel to avoid the depressed Jul market and capture the contango into Aug.

After last week’s «push», the market started to slide prior the long weekend for UK and Singapore and continued so this week. Week on week the Australia-China iron ore route is down by 10% and the average time charter route down by 4%. The Brazil-China route has been very quiet and value more or less the same as last week, however sentiment is also negative for this trade. There has been some period activity, but on index linked structures as owners hardly see it as a good timing to go for fixed priced.

In the North Sea and Baltic market, we have seen a significant downward correction on rates. Mainly due to lack of activity and even relets are now competing over the few available market cargoes. In the week to come, we expect rate levels to dip further and then hover around bottom levels in the short run with no immediate signs of recovery just yet. The Mediterranean and Black Sea market has more or less moved sideways the past week as prompt ships pile up in the area and little activity from charterers has made it difficult for owners to revive an upward pressure on rates. At the time of writing, a cross-Med voyage currently pays just above WS 80 giving owners a TCE return of around USD 15,000 per day. One to follow going forwards is if any development arises in crude oil activity from Libya.

Another positive week for the Supramax market with Baltic Index climbing slowly upwards. Though activity was somehow disrupted to the widespread holidays. South East Asia and India have seen good gains in the rates. 63,000 dwt was fixed from EC India to China with iron ore at USD 13,000 pd.  Another Ultramax delivery Vietnam was fixed at USD 9,500 pd for a trip via ECI to China. The Pacific market gained premium as well, and owners were able to obtain around USD 1,000 premium compared to last week’s rates. The Continent and Mediterranean markets was comparably quiet again due to the holidays across Europe. Owners increased their rates for FH asking USD 12,000 for trips to India and Far East.  USG still suffers lack of cargoes, and 63,000 dwt was fixed at USD 9,000 pd from USEC to China. ECSA see slightly better returns with rates about USD 11,000 pd plus USD 110,000 GBB Ultramax.

With increased demand China is sourcing more and more supply from the Atlantic to replace lost Middle East cargoes, adding to ton mile and thinning the MEG position list. Add to that a delayed start to the June program, with corresponding compressed activity, and the VLCC market was rigged for an uptick. Having bottomed out in the very high WS 40’s for the benchmark MEG/East route, rates have since shot up. Last done at time of writing is a WS 64.5 paid for a MEG/China run, and WS 62.5 from West Africa for same destination. Arguably increased bunker prices are capping some of the gains, but sentiment is a strong driver and with a number of uncovered cargoes, remaining rates could easily continue to tick up.

Similar to last week, Suezmaxes are struggling all over, with no place to hide at the moment. Owners prefer to fix short voyages, or wait it out. The tonnage list in the Atlantic is long, but not hopeless. In the East on the other hand, it looks terrible. Two weeks of almost no activity has built up a list we have not seen in quite some time. A 30-day count in the MEG shows 141 ships on paper, which will make most owners give in. Until today it has been difficult to find any positive signs at all, but things have started happening with VLCC activity and rates moving in the right direction, which should spill over into the Suezmax segment. Additionally, we now see some movement in Libya as well. It remains to be seen if this is sustainable, but getting Libya barrels back in play would be a huge plus.

In the North Sea and Baltic market, we have seen a significant downward correction on rates. Mainly due to lack of activity and even relets are now competing over the few available market cargoes. In the week to come, we expect rate levels to dip further and then hover around bottom levels in the short run with no immediate signs of recovery just yet. At the time of writing, a cross-Med voyage currently pays just above WS 80 giving owners a TCE return of around USD 15,000 per day. One to follow going forwards is if any development arises in crude oil activity from Libya.

Although we’ve seen some rate increase it is a flat tendency with more cargoes in the market, but the list of available tonnage is still outnumbering the requirements. TA’s are now fetching excess 6,000 while fronthauls are being fixed in region 11,000-12,000. In the Pacific, rounds are being fixed in region 6/7,000 depending delivery and duration.

text: AMERICAS: On Thursday, The EIA reported a 1.5 million barrel inventory build which did very little to buoy the US/FEI arb-that has come off close to $40/ton since the start of the month. If not for crashing freight rates (Houston-Chiba last done at $67/ton on Wednesday and now being discussed at USD 60/mt)  it is likely we would have seen June cargo cancellations from the US Gulf-though none have been reported as of yet. A lot of talk in the US propane market is orbiting around considerable product tightness come the end of 3q and 4q of 2020. Covid related demand lapses have led to considerable cutbacks on the part of crude producers in the Marcellus, Uttica, Permian and Midland basins. Some 600mb/d of production have been cutback this month-as producers wait for demand in Jet fuel, motor oil and other crude demand drivers to wake back up before turning the tap back on. As we are still building inventories, per usual this time of year, the propane production cutbacks are not yet felt in full force although there are certainly warning lights flashing.

Spot shipping rates are mostly unchanged from last week and sentiment remains soft. Another round of US cargo cancelations, although perhaps not as large as some participants feared, has nonetheless dampened hopes of an improved summer market. Some charterers are testing the market for opportunities to take winter coverage at reduced rates. However, as of this week, there exists a stand-off with independent owners reluctant to fix the traditionally stronger winter months in today’s soft market. While there aren’t many encouraging signs for owners in the immediate future, cautious optimism will endure as uncertainty hangs over second half of the year. Much will depend on the cargo market and in particular regional gas pricing; for example, high gas storage and low pricing in Europe may support the emergence of reloads. While this might not support the levels seen in recent winters, it would be an encouraging sign for utilisation.   Again, no large LNG newbuilding orders to report this week, but DSME did report a notable large Q-Max type FSRU by a Far East owner for German terminal project. There are also a few second-hand transactions in the pipeline.

EAST: The week got off to a quiet start with several countries on public holiday on Monday. But since then we have seen a few ships being fixed away for 2nd decade June loading in the Middle East. All of these deals have been reported in the lower USD 30s Baltic, and with a continuous lengthy list of available ships in the East, freight rates will continue to be under pressure. As this trend seem set to continue for current and next fixing window, some owners have decided to send more ships back West via Cape hoping for better freight returns there. Meanwhile, there are talks of a few more uncovered cargos from Indian majors during mid and 2nd half of June, but time of writing it remains to be seen how many of these that can actually be firmed up.  WEST: Activity at the start of this week was limited, with most of the West having a public holiday on Monday. A handful of fixtures and FOB transactions has meant that the positions list is now marginally shorter than it was. In addition, a decent build in US stats should theoretically be a supportive factor for freight rates.   However, despite the fact that fixing for June should be largely over with, freight remains on the long side with a combination of owner-controlled ships and trader relets available throughout the month. There is still a slightly bearish sentiment as a consequence, and it is difficult to come up with reasons why this would change any time soon.

It has been another monotonous week for the LNG Shipping market. Sentiments continue to dip further amid signs of limited demand in both basins. The vast number of cancellations on cargoes to be delivered in June from US projects and what seems like an unending closed arbitrage trading window have led to a lack of opportunities for shipping and rather, more sublets seen in the market. The shipping rates is still under pressure as “last done” were reportedly concluded lower week on week. Nevertheless, we do see some premium on the larger sizes, as more end users look to take advantage of the low LNG spot prices to procure larger quantities. Furthermore, there are discussions with some players interested in securing multi months at the current levels, for prompt to Q3 2020 delivery and for periods up till the end of next winter season. While the present environment is challenging, if the ongoing lock-downs and restrictions in most parts of the world eases, we could see the global energy demand pick up and LNG demand to follow. On the Newbuilding front, there hasn’t been any firm deals concluded last week and sentiment remains steady to soft.

text: MEG: Jun Propane CP swaps surged up to $340, in tandem with the crude rise. June Butane CP was assessed at $15 lower at $325.  Saudi Aramco has released acceptance for June liftings, with 9 to 10 cargos deferments/cuts reportedly and half for Indian market.  This being said, supply is still overwhelmed demand and FOBs discussed at heavy discounts. Qatar Petroleum was said to sell another late June lifting heavy propane cargo at minus 10 to Jul CP, similar price level to their last sale tender for 18/20th June lifting evenly split cargo .  Jun/Jul CP still traded at 10$ backwardation. We expect Jul CP might dive deeper after June CP set, as front length hasn’t been absorbed fully and might roll into July.    FAR EAST: Cash premium on June delivery cargos fell sharply amid bearish demand in EAST this week. 23k Propane for 2h Jun delivery was traded at June FEI plus $2 earlier this week, and on Thursday offer plunged to Jun CP minus $9, equates to Jun FEI minus $5. It’s indeed a very tempting price for North East Asian importers, seeing a delivered cargo offered at discount to CP. But majority are stuck with high inventory and expect lower import costs due to backwardation. Spot cargo for Jun arrival has been offered at CP plus teens into China but yet to hear interest either.  China import in May likely to hike up to 2mmt, up by over 30% compare to April. One EChina PDH user issued semi-term tender to secure 5 full cargo propane delivered from Jul to Dec. Undoubtedly it’s a pretty good timing to secure term amid such oversupply market.

text: AMERICAS Another good build of 1.1million barrels occurred in US inventories. There was little immediate Mt Belvieu price reaction however today propane is trading above mid-winter levels. Traders noted a second consecutive week of production around 1.935 million barrels per day and exports around 830,000 barrels per day. Production below 2 million barrels per day was expected. Exports on the other hand were surprisingly low and likely to increase. The mood regarding 2H June US FOBs being traded at the moment is that once the overhang of US cargoes loaded in May has been cleared in the East market strength will return to a market trading around cancellation levels today. Some predict it will return with a bang! Due to global waterborne LPG volume being cut to far, and demand reviving.

As we have mentioned for some weeks now, the Suezmax market has reached the top, and we have been waiting for the activity to slow down, and lists to grow. And boy, it did. Well, it’s not like this has not happened before! We are back to what we can call a normal market. Tonnage list in the East is long, and will keep growing. West is looking a bit better but with very little activity, owners will start looking for the big red panic button. The quick re-balancing in the oil market has taken most by surprise. The following price jump is a result of factories across Asia’s largest economy restarting and people return to work, with some favouring their cars over taking public transport. Crude processing at China’s independent refineries is now higher than pre-virus levels, while fuel demand is also starting to rebound in India. MEG production cuts, and corresponding price hikes, has turned Asian buyers’ attention back to the Atlantic for alternative- and for some a more favoured supply.  A couple of MEG players have dipped their feet in and had a stab the more vintage end of the market, but still facing rates in the ws50'ies - albeit at the lower end of the scale.

Owners of modern tonnage are still hopeful in achieving yesterdays benchmark rendering the bid offer spread hard to bridge, we do however see sellers of more vintage units gradually correcting their expectations in order to dispose of their older vessels in what can still be considered a relatively strong exit environment.  With an increased level of buying enquiry for dry tonnage it comes to no surprise that most transactions this week are found in the Dry SnP Markets. Some of these ships later failed subjects, but irrespective of this the sentiment on freight seem to have turned (for now) in the East. Cyclone ‘Amphan’, one of the worst storms to hit Eastern India in decades made landfall overnight. It is still unclear what impact this will have on seaborne imports of LPG into this part of India, if any, but it could potentially result in further delays for ships who are due to discharge there.

The increased activity in the Pacific helped rates rebound, coming up from their lowest market to slightly better level.  Main driving force was India and South Asia. We have witnessed good flow of fresh enquiries and rates jumped from range of USD 4-6,000 pd to USD 7-9,000 pd range. Cos Prosperity (55,676 dwt/2006) open Singapore, fixed USD 9,500 for EC India trip China. Ultramax 60’ dwt open Fangcheng for load Thailand redel China USD 7,500 pd. Fixture of mv Antakya-M (55,888 dwt/2005) with dely Chittagong trip via Richards Bay redel Vietnam USD 8,500.

The index shows around 2k for TA rounds, however the shorter Baltic rounds are also yielding around same levels.  In the Pacific, we can see some signs of improvement with bids being above last done. Momentum in the tanker markets seems to have taken a downturn this week with most players digesting weeks of high rate volatility which was mainly driven by a now fading storage play. As a result there are no new sales to report this week but quite to the contrary we are seeing a number of older transactions fall apart in light of the weaker charter markets. Notably a number of owners who had managed to take advantage of the buying appetite for vintage crude tonnage are seeing their buying counterparts unable to execute.   Buying enquiry seems to therefore gradually shift to the Dry SnP markets where the everlasting pressure on charter rates is taking its toll on values. A number of sales this week have indeed seen a relative value correction with an increased amount of sellers deciding to trigger at today's market rather than face the uncertain outlook currently shared by most market players.

text: MEG: Moves in June CP Swap market was muted earlier this week and Propane CP swung between $280 to $290. Until Thursday it surged up to $305 with the anticipation of further cuts on Saudi’s June liftings. Butane CP rebounded to $300, narrowing down the spread against propane from previous $30. Qatar petroleum was reported to award 18-20th June lifting equal ratio cargo via tender. Despite the advance on flat price, FOB netback remains at double digit discounts. Earlier this week two half cargo propane parcels were traded into China at June CP plus 30s, and Thurs one EChina PDH player was reported to award their buy tender for 23/0 delivered during end June/early Jul at CP plus 20ish. Taiwan CPC also issued buy tender to secure one 11/11 for last decade June delivery, which result is yet to know. With limited inquiries for June arrival tons, cash premium keep declining, which alternatively suppressed the FOB values and refrained trading activities. However, with the expectation on lockdown easing and slow recovery, players are still cautiously monitoring the arbitrage window and trying to move tons to EAST.

text: AMERICAS: A large build of 2.2 million barrels in US inventories was not enough to have a significant bearish effect on Mt Belvieu propane value. Strong Mt Belvieu propane and global demand destruction due to the corona virus has lead to weak FEI and CIF ARA values. Putting netback values close to cancellation levels to the East and negative to Europe. There is hope that further production cuts from the AG for June will clear some of the overhang of cargoes in the East and Indian markets, and improve the arb. No US cargo cancellations have occurred for June liftings . The question is will the arb improve rapidly enough to stimulate trades and keep cancellations to zero? Our guess is YES.

The inertia of last week’s shipping market continued at the start of this one, as a lack of fresh activity held the market in a slight limbo. The cargo market has only seen a modest improvement in Asia: Japanese inventory levels are now nearing capacity, and with plenty of cargo already on the water, we're likely to see an increase in floating activity over the next few weeks. However, with a healthy tonnage list in the Pacific well into July, rates continue to trickle off. The Atlantic is showing a softening market for intra-basin trade, with sentiment falling and uncertainty on the cargo side. Conversely, ships moving East with US Gulf spot cargoes are still fixing at last-done levels. Multi month enquiries are becoming a hot topic as some charterers look at taking coverage in this seasonally soft market. Looking ahead, there are still plenty of unanswered questions caused by the pandemic that will have an impact on LNG trades and LNG shipping for the rest of the year: dry docking schedules, SIRE inspections, crew changes to name but a few and it's not until countries and travel arrangements begin to return to the 'new normal' that these will be answered. No newbuild orders seen to be placed at Shipyards this week, despite economics in favour of the buyer. We have therefore kept newbuild prices stable.

With a large proportion of available vessels on the tonnage list in the North Sea and Baltic being relets, we had as a result less spot cargoes in the market. As activity cooled off a little rates came off accordingly down to ws105 level. This week we have seen a bit more activity and owners holding back and thoroughly calculating returns on each cargo being proposed. Sentiment has changed a bit and we could see rates firm further in the week to come.  In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, we have seen some activity this week with a healthy flow of fresh cargoes coming into the market, among them quite a few FO stems with options going East. However, the tonnage list is still long and with a number of ships available in the natural fixing window, rates have more or less remained at steady levels throughout the week.  In the week to come we expect the market to keep on moving sideways, if not a slightly softening trend.

EAST Market liquidity has been limited East of Suez this week: on the supply side, a large number of trader re-lets spread throughout May and into June has increased competition between owners. On the demand side, charterers see a falling baltic and a lengthy positions list and feel there is no pressure to fix in before it is necessary to do so.   Reduced market activity has made it difficult to say exactly how freight should be priced. However, a trader was heard to fix in a 2002-blt vessel at $45 Ras Tanura/Chiba for early June while an Indian oil major fixed in at a few dollars below that for the end of May. Although not necessarily the best benchmarks, Charterers will likely use these two things as a reference before the release of Saudi acceptances early next week.   WEST In the West, there is a gap between the expectations of charterers, who can’t justify buying spot cargoes on current netback econs, and those of Owners, who find it difficult to accept freight ideas substantially below last done. The result of this is a longer positions list with a fair share of relets and an abundance of FOB cargoes for sale throughout June in the US. There has been no news of cancellations in 1H June so far, and Owners may feel they are able to leverage that to get better rates for the earlier part of the month. However, many are of the opinion that weak product sentiment globally means that concessions will need to be made on freight. The addition of ethane carriers into the VLGC market this week will put further pressure on those with ships to be more competitive when it comes to pricing.

The Suezmax market is still trying to find its balance. The moment we think its stabilizing, the cargo activity increases, and we have another peak. This time might be different though. The list is looking fairly balanced in the West, but we will have a massive list in the East going into next week. In the West, it is the Mediterranean and Black Sea being most active, keeping the market at decent levels. North Sea has been strangely quiet, so owners opening up there, have need to ballast south for cargoes. Going forward we expect the market to remain rather stable, at least if we compare it to previous months.

The VLCC market is moving in a sideways fashion, still yielding daily earnings in the $50-60k range. However, the longer view has taken a hit after Saudi announced an additional “voluntary” output cut of 1 million bpd from June, which was quickly supported by Kuwait and UAE committing to cut an additional 80k and 100k bpd respectively.  And, needless to say, with the ongoing pandemic and surrounding restrictions, demand is unlikely to increase significantly for quite some time yet. Thus, a certain "urgency" is becoming evident, and with that more susceptible owners. As such we see little or no upside going forward, unless we get a new Contango scenario with WTI contracts due to settle next week.

From ECSA fixture was reported Tess 58 fixed USD 5,000 TCT to Mediterranean. Supra delivery Durban via PE was fixed USD 9,000 plus USD 90,000 GBB TCT to China.

In the Atlantic we see rounds still hovering around 2.5-3k, while the ECSA/Far East candidates are being paid around USD 12k + 200k GBB. In the Pacific, we see NoPac rounds being fixed at around 6-7k bss China delivery. Some period fixtures have been reported – however details are scarce.

This is still a far cry from the Usd 106 mill paid for prompt delivery VLCC newbuilding, also from DSME, in January and confirms that recent spot earnings and values for brand new ships are decoupled.  The answer is that no one believes the recent massive earnings spike is sustainable and we have indeed this week seen crude spot rates falling off. CM Lemos has booked two newbuilding Suezmax tankers at HHI for usd 59 mill each without scrubber, and as the year develops we will continue to see competitive pricing from Korean and Chinese yards.   Dry values are dropping. The sale of Supramax ROYAL EPIC built 2008 Mitsui at Usd 7.8 mill is a telling example, but mind you we are still about 20% off what was done at the recent bottom in 2016. We have yet to see any tangible modern reference sales, but buyers are increasingly getting ready to move for bulkers.  We understand the sale of Kamsarmax CERBA built 2010 STX at usd 13 mill has failed on Sellers’ subjects.

Suezmaxes have, as the V's, taken a real beating this last week. Cargo-activity has slowed down severely and with tonnage lists increasing in lenght Owners caved in eventually. Another factor here, is for every cargo traded in the market, there is always a relet available. This has put even more pressure on Owners to sharpen their pencil. The activity have picked up on the back of this rate-drop though, and we could be close to the bottom very soon. The big question is if it will be where will we go from the bottom? The cut in oil production could mean the market will have more trouble re-building this time, than it has had the last couple of months.

One sentence that could sum up 2020 is of course that at one point in recent weeks, 1 loo roll was worth more than a barrel of crude oil. But another may be that owners became too focused on oil trading, thereby over estimating the shipping market - whereas their counterpart suffered from the opposite. They should probably both have stuck to what they are good at. The softening trend from last week continued into this week. Allthough some Indian players re-entered the mrkt on Monday with coal from Sth Africa and Indonesia - it has not relieved the pressure on tonnage comitted for ECSA.  Rates keeps softening and ships are being reported fixed at ard Usd 8,5k retro Spore or ard 11,5k +150k GBB bss APS delivery. In the North Atlantic we also face fixtures at below last done, and owners tends to book the cgos in order to delay positions for short durational business.  In the Pacific we also see rates tumbling with Aussie rounds being concluded at 5,5-6k bss delivery SE Asia. With most Asian countries (except Japan) back after holidays mid week – it could lead to some more activity going forward.

Poor week across all basins with holiday disruption in Europe and Asia. We see some activity in the East and moderate activity in the Atlantic . We still see most basins with oversupply of tonnage and rates under pressure. The effect of the Covid-19 pandemic continue with consequent negative effects on demand for commodities. However, we see more inquiry / interest for period candidates but the gap between owners expectations  and Charterers seems too big to bridge. From the Atlantic via East Coast South America to Singapore-Japan range Ultras fixed at $11,500 plus $150,000 ballast bonus, unch from last week. From the same area to Mediterranean we see rates around $6,000 paid for large Ultramax units. The east Mediterranean and Continent market remained in poor condition, with lack of fresh cargo and prompt tonnage building up. It was rumoured Tess 58 fixed del Canakkale via Black Sea to China at $13,500.  Sian marker saw a mix of different rates , some suggested 55,000-dwt was fixed from Indonesia to China at $6,500s, while 57,000dwt was fixing $4,500 to Thailand.  The market in Indian Ocean , PG and South Africa have slightly more activity and we see better rates paid compared to previous weeks.  Supramax delivery PG rumoured to be on subs $7,000 to China. 63,000- dwt fixed basis delivery Richards Bay trip to south east Asia at $10,500 plus $125,000 ballast bonus.

In the last week we have seen rates in the Nsea and Baltic taken a severe hit and we are now trading at what is being perceived as bottom levels for now. We continue to see delays in ports due to no ullage or a delayed delivery window due to refineries slowing down their activities. A decent number of ships are still tied up with floating storage and with some increased activity, especially on the fuel side, we could see rates improve coming into the 3rde decade of May fixing window. Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea market the rates have taken a hit this past week. We have seen benchmark routes drop 80-90 points as activity has been slow and vessels have piled up in the area. However, at the time of writing the market has started to stabilize due to cargo activity picking up and relets and prompt ships are being taken out one by one. There is now a number of cargoes in the market yet to be fixed, therefore we expect a more balanced market in the week to come, and if fresh cargoes continue to come into the market at the current rate we may see an upward correction in the next couple of days.

Spot again nervous, negative and far below OPEX for the big ships, as underlying industrial fundamentals remain weak and in particular atlantic/fronthaul volumes nowhere near recovery. Values for the China-Brazil-China conference trade consequently chopped almost 40 pct, whilst worldwide average daily earnings down 33 pct w-o-w, coming in at a poor usd 5300. The West Australia/China ore trade is steady in volume and USD/MT pricing, but pacific nevertheless sees a 20 pct drop as coal trades slow, bunkers are up and major players on holiday. Period activity limited as most owners resist committing tonnage too much forward at poor levels, exceptions being index-linked charters where for instance 2012-built 180000 dwt recently done for upto about 12 mos at BCI AVE5TC + 4.5 pct.  Market balance improvements expected going some way forward as major brazilian miners slashing 25 vlocs presently servicing long-term coa's.

Another factor here, is for every cargo traded in the market, there is always a relet available. This has put even more pressure on Owners to sharpen their pencil. The activity have picked up on the back of this rate-drop though, and we could be close to the bottom very soon. The big question is if it will be where will we go from the bottom? text: MEG: June Propane swap is traded at $290, slightly rebounded however yet to rise further as in lack of support fundamentally. The slowdown of India and Indonesia demand has exerted pressure on butane price, which swap is traded at $35 less than propane.  Qatar Petroleum has released June lifting acceptance with no cuts but some minor delays. And they’ve issued sale tender to market one 18/20th June lifting equal ratio cargo. FOB with same ratio but for end May/early Jun lifting was offered at small discount to June CP but yet to attract bids.    FAR EAST: A slow start in Golden week holiday.   1h June arrival propane was bid at June CP plus mid low teens or June FEI plus mid-single digit, yet to entice sellers’ interests. On the contrary, a handful of equal ratio cargos including US origin which will land in June, are struggling to find home.  Chinese importers have finalized 1h June program and now exploring for 2h June arrival tons, propane heavy mainly, driven by petchem demand. One NChina PDH has restarted its unit of 600k/y capacity today, which was offline for last two weeks.  China imports has slashed by 21% in Q1 with average monthly import below 1.3 mmt. However, import in April has recovered to 1.5mmt (VLGC tracking) and May also expects with a slight increment.  With two new PDHs of total capacity over 1mmt coming online in June, we expect from June onwards there will be additional 100k feedstock demand monthly at least.
