comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS: The EIA reported PADD 3’s (US Gulf) first significant inventory build of the season on Wednesday. Despite the echo of production cutbacks, US propane output remains above 2 million barrels/day though further cuts are likely on the horizon. As it stands, the arbitrage is shut. A weeklong US crude rally, on top of a cautious supply outlook has crushed netbacks to 2.875cpg to Asia and 0.250cpg to NWE. Cancelation levels. With that said, no US cargos have been cancelled yet on the belief that the substantial Mid-East propane cutbacks, and continued strength in India will result in physical premiums upon cargos arrivals. A tender issued by a Chilean Importer was awarded on Wednesday to a competitive offer of MB +15cpg, catching the market off guard.

EAST: This week had a quiet start with several Asian countries on public holidays. Come mid-week however we saw an uptick in activity with a handful of cargoes either worked or placed on subs. Looking at the positions list, May looks tight – but on the other hand it’s not looking like there is a lot of uncovered cargoes for the rest of the month as we start to look ahead towards June dates.  WEST: Bearish sentiment continued West of Suez this week, with the threat of cancellations given poor US-Japan netbacks never far from players’ minds. While it’s unanimously agreed that freight is weaker than the 3-digit Houston/Chiba rates seen not long ago, limited liquidity has made it difficult to say exactly where the market should price tonnage. East and West have nearly been at parity for some time, which means it's also not immediately obvious which direction the fleet will sail. These uncertainties may pave the way for more deals to be done on a floating basis.   Earnings have remained strong in spite of weaker rates, but it seems as though they could come under some pressure as bunkers have ticked up with stronger crude in the last few days.  Looking into June, the positions list looks reasonably long, with a combination of Owner-controlled vessels and a handful of trader relets that are likely to be competitively priced. Although these two things together should put owners in a squeeze, it’s important to remember that a record number of liftings in the last couple of months and longer tonne-mile voyages recently may prevent freight from coming off a long way in the short term.

It has been a slightly quieter week as we have been enjoying several public holidays across the globe (namely Labour Day holidays and the Golden Week in Japan) giving the markets a short breather. Moreover, based on the news this week, the Covid19 – situation might find a bit more light at the end of the tunnel, as various countries have slowly released their plans for lifting some of the ongoing restrictions. This is cautiously positive news for the global economy and energy demand, but the road to recovery is still very uncertain. The same fundamentals apply to the world of LNG, where the supply overhang is still very much a fundamental problem causing bearish views for the rest of the year for both cargo volume and shipping. That said, we have seen a bit more interest in multimonth TC-periods as Charterers’ and Owners’ ideas on expected rate levels have narrowed. This might be more speculative than purely demand driven, but nonetheless seeing more term activity is a good sign. In the spot market, we are recording a small softening on the rate levels this week, as the ongoing charter interest, which is mainly driven by various spot cargo tenders, is not enough to compensate for the lengthy vessel availability list. Finally, there has been no new large LNGC orders reported this week (and orders for first 5 months 2020 are down by 12 units compared to 2019). With a strong US dollar, low interest rates and limited new orders from other shipping segments, there could be a risk of softening newbuilding prices.

In the north sea we still see quite a few Aframaxes floating with BFOE grades. Also, delays at strategic import terminals seems to continue into the month of May. Despite a lot of tonnage tied up, rates are under downward pressure due to lack of cargo activity and ships start piling up free of cargo looking for employment. The main reason for this is that nearly everything of oil being transported goes on own keel as both Oil companies and Oil traders have their own relets in position for own cargoes. We therefore expect a downward correction on rates in the coming week as there will be a lot of competition for any quoted cargo in the current fixing window.  In the Mediterranean and Black Sea we saw rates continue their upward trend prior to the weekend, before the market has softened at the beginning of this week. There is still a few cargoes in the market yet to be fixed, however cargo activity is not sustaining the levels of last week. On the positive side for Owners we have seen a pick-up in FO-stems going East potentially sending ships away from the area, on the negative we are expecting a cut in the cargo program for May out of Black Sea. In the week to come we expect the market to be soft.

The week gone has on the surface been a quiet-ish one for the VLCC’s, with falling oil prices, contango and period fixing stealing the limelight from the spot market. The question on everyone’s mind has been to what extent production cuts, or adherence to the agreement, would impact the May MEG program. Albeit a slower pace than usual, and Ramadan not helping to speed things up, it has so far been more or less business as usual, at least for the first half of the month. The Atlantic has been MIA, which has put further pressure on MEG rates, and recent period fixtures has thus far not resulted in a significant reduction in tonnage availability. However, rates have held up better than feared, and plummeting bunker prices have by and large compensated for sliding WS rates in terms of daily earnings.

The Supramax and Ultramax market showed resistance and rates started to increase. Increased cargo enquiries from Brazil and Argentina was the main driver in the South Atlantic market. An Ultramax del SW Pass was fixed with grain to Egypt for $7,500 pd. For trip from Miss River to Japan an Ultramax was rumoured to fix $12,000 pd. Continent and Mediterranean basins didn’t see much of obvious improvement. Clinker cargos were fixed frm Med to West Africa around  $5 – 6,000 pd level and trip from W Africa to Med/ Bsea were paid only $3- 4,000 pd. Thus average earning for Supra in Atlantic about $5-6,000 pd and somewhat more for Ultra. The market in the East flattened out and seen some premiums on the rates. We are coming from a market of  $2- 3,000 pd to a market of $4-5,000 pd. Supra fixed dely S China was at $4,000 pd for a trip via Vietnam to China .

The Suez market topped out end of last week with a number of deals done in the high W100s being failed over rate as charterers managed to regain momentum. Sentiment has taken a rather bearish turn so far this week with charterers looking to test the owners and with several FOC units in the west they might get away with it. In the east, although fundamentally better looking, it is more of the same with sentiment having a rather bearish feel to it and charterers taking their time. Itineraries still play an important role, but right now there is an overhang of ships in the west-med / GIB area that needs clearing before we can see any real movement in rates.

A very slow start to the week with an uneventful Atlantic market. Some Baltic cgos has been done at lower than last done. The same goes for the usec and usg market. In the Pacific we see the NoPac Round market hovering ard Usd 5500 bss North China delivery. The ECSA market is still in play and well spec'ed ships are still being fixed DOP or retro India-Spore rge.

An active Pacific market towards the end of the week, with more volume of West Australia iron ore and East Coast Australian coal. Although this increase in demand is not affecting rate levels much so far. West Australia round is presently marked at USD 4,1 pmt more or less similar to last weeks level. The C3 market is less active and freight is approaching USD 10 pmt. On average index is down USD 1000 from last week.

WEST: As a result of bad weather in the Pacific and delays at disports in both East and West, some of the ships which were open in the final decade of May ex US have slipped into June. While there are still a few outstanding FOBs in the US in May, we count roughly 30 fixtures having been done for the month. In addition, some fixing has already begun for June; these two things suggest that players are now mostly balanced for May.  Positions lists look reasonably long going into June, with a mixture of relets and Owner-controlled vessels, and this is likely to put some pressure on rates in the short term.   While it is very difficult to make any assertions given the amount of black swans in the market lately, it is important to remember that a large number of liftings in the US must go ahead regardless of the arb. In addition, a high number of liftings globally in the last couple of months and longer voyages to India and Indonesia may have a lagged bullish effect on rates.  EAST:  The shipping market in the East has been very uneventful this week, and only new fixture to report was on the back of a freight tender from an oil major loading Australia.    With the last rush of fixing that we saw a couple of weeks back, most market players ended up fixing ships way ahead of what’s considering the normal fixing window, and as a consequence things are expected to remain quiet for a while. One Indian major quoted the market for a cargo loading in the MEG during last decade of May, and there are talks of potentially a couple more for same period to be quoted later, but would likely need some time before the latter is firmed up. Meanwhile freight availability remains fairly balanced with more Owner controlled tonnage available for rest of May as opposed to trader relets.

“COVID-19” has been a consistent feature in our weekly reports lately, as the impact of the pandemic is evident on LNG and LNG shipping. LNG prices are undoubtedly kept at low levels due to the glut of LNG cargoes. While the summer months are traditionally with the weakest LNG demand for the year, this year comes with the added element of pandemic-induced bearishness. One may expect muted activity but this is actually far from what we observe. Vessels are being fixed in both basins, many on the back of cargo tenders or spare cargoes on offer from producers, seemingly due to cargo deferments from long term buyers. LNG prices from the long term contracts are higher priced compared to reported spot prices, providing portfolio players the opportunities to acquire FOB cargoes at low prices to fill these high-priced shorts, which is leading to vessel enquiries for optimisation.

A busy week in the tanker S&P markets with a continued string of older tankers changing hands.  We are reporting three older VLCC’s sold at storage induced prices, however we understand the sale of GRAND LADY was concluded some time ago. A large number of older Aframax and MR tankers are for sale, but transactions taking place underpin that values for same are not seeing any gain and are best case moving sideways. Not since Euronav’s acquisition of VLCC newbuilding resales at Usd 93.5 mill in early March have we seen any modern/brand new tankers being transacted.   Talk of the week has been the massive surge in the share price for NAT aka “the come-back kid”. Following an airing on CNBC a week ago by its CEO Herbjørn Hansson, a massive 110 million shares were traded on Tuesday worth about Usd 807 mill.  Its market cap broke the Usd 1 bn mark but is now at Usd 880 mill.   The dry S&P market is still kind of alive, albeit we have yet to see any noteworthy modern units being sold. Chinese Dolphin 57 Supramaxes see prices drop; AMAZONIT DOLPHIN 57k built 2011 Hantong invited offers earlier this week with best bid at low Usd 7 mill. This is in line with the sale of CONTI PERIDOT built 2011 Taizhou which this week achieved low Usd 7 mill in a bank controlled sale.

text: MEG: Saudi raised up May CP for propane by $110 to $340, and for Butane by $100 to $340, which in line with some recommendation idea. That being said, the value is higher than paper swap. June CP is traded at $277 at the time of writing, which is $63 less than May CP. Apparently the anticipation on cuts from AG exports is unable to offset concerns over demand loss.  One evenly split FOB for late May lifting ex Kuwait was offered at $336 for both propane and butane, while another June lifting ex QP was offered at $275 for propane and $245 for butane.   FAR EAST:  Earlier this week one full propane cargo for 1h June was traded at June CP plus $27. However, the premium discussing level quickly reduced to teens as of ample supply in 1h June arrival.  Despite the narrowing arbitrage, Us tons keep sailing to east, especially for equal ratio cargos.  China spot demand is mainly driven by petchem this week. One EChina PDH didn’t award its buy tender for propane delivered in 1st decade June due to program changes. Another SChina PDH purchased one 23k propane parcel for mid-June delivery at June CP plus mid low 40s via tender. One NChina PDH of 600k/y capacity is still offline till mid May and yet to purchase any June spot.  Apart from spot discussion, one China Major importer issued term tender to secure one cargo per month from July 20 to June 20, ratio to be evenly split or heavy propane.

text: AMERICAS: Widespread capex cuts were announced in quarterly earnings calls for a large number of US oil & gas companies this week. With many projects now on hold, many traders have been wondering what this means for LPG production and export volumes in 2020. Since the oil price war, propane production has remained above 2 million barrels per day. Export volumes in April have been near record levels and the May volume is expected to be similar. Inventory build season is now well underway and we have only seen one build so far. The most recent EIA report showed a 607,000 barrel draw for the week ending April 24th. This came as a surprise to many and caused them to question when we will start to see the large builds required this year to maintain these high export volumes?

text: MEG:  Saudi Aramco finally released acceptance with 7 cargos being cut for May lifting reportedly, which in line with expectation as oil cut in motion. Despite US crude turned negative during this week, May Propane CP stands firm and edges up to $320, with butane at $10 less. With front strength, May/June CP backwardation enlarged once to $40 and narrowed to mid-30s on Thursday.  June CP might experience a decline after May CP set. However, due to the volume cuts from AG producers and potential India residential demand, June CP swap shall still gain support fundamentally.   FAR EAST: Limited activities this week before May CP set.  Active bids in window but few deals are concluded. 23kt C3 for 1h June delivery were bid at June FEI plus high teens or June CP plus high 20s. This is yet to attract sellers’ interests, who are keener to ship tons into China instead.  One Korean petchem player was reported awarded their buy tender for 23kt propane delivered in end May to early June.  This week a couple of June arrival propane were placed into China at June CP plus 40s. PDHs plants still enjoy a considerable margin, but the weakening end products price VS rising costs are eroding the margins. Most plants are still operating at high rates, apart from two N.China units are offline due to glitches this week.

text: AMERICAS: On Wednesday, the EIA reported a build of 660,000 barrels, the bulk of which came from the East Coast. While exports decreased this week compared to last, it’s reported that 1.15 million barrels /day found their way to the water, furthering the notion that propane and butane has been far less susceptible to coronavirus demand interruptions than rest of the barrel. In the recent weeks, the propane price along with Spot cargo discussion has been kept afloat by considerable demand from China, Indonesia, Korea, Japan and India. Indias demand for LPG has increased as much as 20 percent, and will keep exports firm if it continues.  As it turns out, the US is no different. Argus reported that domestic propane marketers saw 10 percent increase in usage this month compared to last- contributing to balance. In the US Gulf, terminals and third party sellers are looking to market the remaining 2-3 May cargos, before looking ahead to June. As it stands levels for these cargos are being valued at 6-7  cpg , with ship availability proving the difficult variable.

After a quiet-ish end to last week the VLCC market kicked off in earnest on Monday when the May MEG stems finally came out, later than normal. Rates quickly established a platform at W157.5, courtesy of Unipec taking four units in one swoop, and then ramped up from there. Yesterday culminated at W195 for a MEG/China run, with historically high daily earnings helped further by plummeting bunker prices. However, some of the momentum seems to have gone up in smoke at the writing moment, with Suezmaxes underbidding their larger sisters by a considerable amount. That said, however, not all charterers have the luxury of splitting their cargo - and delays plus period/storage fixing has left the position list wanting. As such the downside should be capped if owners can hold their nerve, although history has shown that can be a big if.

Another week for the history books in the crude and clean markets with latter now also on fire with spot rates hitting all-time high levels.  The S&P activity is mostly unaffected, except for older VLCC's which remain hot commodity.  Four such vessels are sold this week alone of which two 2005 built at a reported Usd 38 mill each.  This is approximately Usd 5 mill more that same age YUGAWASAN fetched only three weeks ago.    The price for the LR1 tanker ETERNAL DILIGENCE built 2006 Onomichi is surprisingly low, but we expect it’s a function of few buyers having been able to inspect the vessel.

With May dates in the MEG finally coming into play, owners have enjoyed a bullish mix of VLCC cargoes splitting in two and big uncertainty in itineraries following weeks of lock-downs amid Covid-19. Ships have disappeared into TC's of various duration combined with charterers that are scrambling to secure the safe, free-of-cargo ships - a mass that is decreasing by the hour. Safe positions are like gold dust at the moment and owners will aim to make the most of it for as long as they can.

Rates in the Baltic and North Sea market bounced back this week and will continue its upward direction as we now move into the first decade of May fixing window. Increased cargo activity for both fuel and crude in the current fixing window coupled with numerous vessels that have and will leave the area for East discharge, delays in UK import terminals, and an increasing number of vessels tied up floating,  are all factors creating a tight and firm market. Watch this space.  Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea the rates have taken a strong upwards leap this week as activity has been healthy. Fuel oil cargoes East bound have taken out ships and vessels coming open West Med have opted for participating in the firming markets in the North rather than try for cargoes loading East Med or Bsea. Going into next week we expect owners to hold back as the tonnage list gets tighter and rates continue upwards.

That said, however, not all charterers have the luxury of splitting their cargo - and delays plus period/storage fixing has left the position list wanting. As such the downside should be capped if owners can hold their nerve, although history has shown that can be a big if.

EAST: Saudi dates finally came out on Tuesday night – a big portion of which to be ex Yanbu and a handful of cancelled cargos. First half May is still where the main action is happening, but we have started to see fixtures done further into the month as well which is typical for a rising market. With the Eastern market being as tight as it has been of late coupled with a strong market in the West – we expect the freight to remain strong also in the near future despite some cancellations.  WEST: On the surface, the market still looks tight in the short term, with a relatively short positions list and a handful of uncovered cargoes remaining in the US in May. However, given WTI’s unprecedented sub-zero plunge this week and an accompanying weak arb, it seems freight levels at triple digits are too expensive unless there is a change on the product side. Until now, strong demand in Asia due to low refinery throughput in India, Indonesia and elsewhere has helped to keep the VL freight market strong. However, looking ahead there are doubts as to whether demand for non-domestic product will continue at the volume we've seen recently, and this could be bearish freight rates.  With that said, it's important to remember that there was a greater number of liftings in April than in the rest of 2020 (around 10-15 more across East and West compared to March). In addition, a longer ton-mile from the recent US-India arb should stretch the fleet. These factors together could buoy freight earnings in the coming months.

Implications of Covid-19 continue to affect global markets as demand keeps plummeting worldwide. Oil is trading at remarkably low levels, and whilst the oil price contango has a positive impact on tanker rates due to storage, when it comes to LNG the scenario is different. Cargo prices have remained soft and shipping rates may see further pressure as vessel availability increases in both basins. As was widely anticipated, a significant number of cargoes for June loading in the US have been cancelled leaving excess shipping length from portfolio players, utilities and traders. In this environment we could see further rate drops as talks on potential production cuts continue. On the operational side, vessel discharges, Dry docks and quarantine restrictions have caused uncertainties in availability amongst market participants and one could argue that we might see sporadic upticks on the back of these disruptions. Only time will tell as economies start recovering, but there is no doubt we anticipate a bumpy ride in the months to come. In the Newbuilding market, it was reported today that Qatar Petroleum signed a Deed of Agreement with Chinese yard Hudong- Zhonghua to reserve yard capacity for upto 16 vessels of 174,000 cbm for delivery 2024 and 2025, and with options into 2026.

With May dates in the MEG finally coming into play, owners have enjoyed a bullish mix of VLCC cargoes splitting in two and big uncertainty in itineraries following weeks of lock-downs amid Covid-19. Ships have disappeared into TC's of various duration combined with charterers that are scrambling to secure the safe, free-of-cargo ships - a mass that is decreasing by the hour. Safe positions are like gold dust at the moment and owners will aim to make the most of it for as long as they can.

Mixed signals and slight gains for the big ships, average daily earning coming in at usd 9k which is slightly up w-o-w. Negative export updates reported by most major iron ore miners due to global economic setbacks dampening an otherwise positive spot development on in particular the Brazil/China conference trade – china-brazil-china rounds up 5 pct to stand at around usd 10k. With certain coal trades partly paralyzed and bunkers falling markedly, certain key routes like waust/china are down somewhat in terms of usd/mt but up to some usd 7k/day on standard units. Nerves and uncertainty prevailing for coming quarters, giving little support from derivatives for fixed-price period business. Recent representative fixtures include 2004-built 170000 dwt spot china done for 4-6 months at usd 11k, with more sad conclusions expected to follow shortly.

Cheap oil all around with storage play still providing impetus to buying interest for older VLCC’s in particular.  It’s all about presenting candidates at one of the very few places where inspection can be conducted and with prompt delivery on offer.  Tellingly, a 1998 built VLCC is understood to be working firm at region Usd 25 mill basis prompt delivery Singapore. The 2005 built VLCC TAKASAKI was inspected in Singapore by six buyers this week with a sale expected to be concluded in a week’s time.  There are unconfirmed reports that Middle Eastern buyers are in the process of  acquiring the three VLCC’s RENE built 2005 Imabari, MAERA built 2002 Mitsui and KELLY built 2000 Mitsui but we await further details.    Euronav announced the sale of its 2001 built Suezmax CAP DIAMANT at Usd 20.8 mill.  The deal was concluded some time back and the vessel has already been delivered to its new owner.  There are a large number of Aframax tankers for sale built early-to-late 2000 however sales activity has failed to ignite this time around.  The bid/ask spread has proved difficult to bridge with potential sellers opting to ride the wave while it lasts.  Tangible bulker deals remain few and far between but the sale of handysize IKAN LANDUK built 2013 Onomichi is a rare exception.  The price reported is very much in line with our value estimates.

text: AMERICAS: April is shaping up to be a record setting month for exports from the US. This large export program coupled with the reduced imports from Canada has extended the demand season for propane.  Normally by the end of March builds are seen in the inventories but that is not the case this year, even with daily production being sustained over the 2 million barrels per day. With the strong exports, freight has made a recovery, which is putting pressure on the arb, but strong worldwide demand seems poised to keep arb open. In the Southern hemisphere seasonal demand is coming into play with Petrobras becoming an active buyer for US cargos and other buyers preparing to do the same.

text: MEG: Despite the crude slumped this week, swap value came up drastically with anticipation on Saudi cuts for May term liftings. May Propane CP has traded at $314 at the time of writing and the spread between Butane narrowed down to flattish or $2 only. Due to front strength, May/June backwardation has enlarged to around $20.   FAR EAST: Active bids in window this week again but only one parcel of 23kt propane for 2h May delivery has been traded at May FEI plus $19. Comparatively, a flurry of deals were concluded into China this week.  One full cargo propane for 2h May delivery reported sold into China at May FEI plus 20ish. And several evenly split cargos were sold at May CP plus 40ish. Despite the premium softening to 30ish level into India and Indonesia this week, the household demands from both regions continuously lend support to the EAST market. India has announced further lockdown and players expect its June purchase requests. Indonesia Pertamina issued several tenders this week to secure evenly split cargos from End May to July delivery, with requests on fixed price for June/July tons. Taiwan CPC issued buy tender for end May/early June 11/11 but limited offers received.

Owners and charterers have had to respond quickly and aggressively in some instances to the pandemic that continues to effect the global markets. The response has varied but generally we have seen the emergence of a two-tier market over the past couple of weeks. In one camp, and reflected in the reductions in headline rate in our weekly report, are the owners and disponent owners seeking coverage and utilisation for their fleet; in the other camp are the owners who remain firmer, in anticipation of a tighter market due to the disruption to fleet schedules, delays in discharging and in project maintenance, and in quarantine measures requiring set periods between port calls. With such distinct views and limited depth to the market, there is considerable volatility at present. This may subside as the fixing period moves into June, when the possibility of cargo cancellations and the potential for vessel availability to grow could have an impact on the shipping market. On a separate note no new orders have been placed, as one would expect and new build prices take a small decline, as do second-hand prices.

Rates in the North Sea and Baltic took a hit this week due to a quiet Easter period with ships piling up in early position looking for coverage. Charterers seized this opportunity to push rates down. Rates will continue around current levels going forward. However, with some expected delays at strategic discharge ports and some ships floating with cargo onboard. This coupled with a bit more busier market in the 3rd decade of April could eventually push rates back up again for end month fixing window. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, we have seen activity roll back somewhat last week as several offices have been closed for Easter break holidays and rates have consequently taken a slight dip. Although charterers can enjoy the luxury of several prompt ships at the moment, we expect the market to firm up a bit going into next week due to a healthy cargo program in the Mediterranean as well as Black Sea, combined with the delays we are seeing in several ports at the moment.

EAST In the East this week, rates have begun to strengthen on the back of more inquiries ex MEG. One consequence of this has been the decision by some to keep vessels East in order to avoid getting caught out by a strengthening market. Looking into May, freight looks much shorter than it has done over the last couple of weeks and so it would not be unreasonable to expect more strength in the short term. With that said, the OPEC+ decision to cut a handful of cargoes in May is one factor which could put pressure on rates. Given strong Indian and Indonesian demand, it is likely this shortfall will have to be made up for with tonnes from the US, NWE and elsewhere, and this should be bullish for freight in the longer term.  WEST The West has also firmed up this week, particularly since activity in the East has removed some western candidates from position lists. Looking ahead, the West looks to remain fairly tight; ships aren’t that many in number (around 10 remain for the rest of May) and are mostly owner controlled. American producers have pushed back on Trump’s proposed cuts which should mean demand for freight is maintained at least in the near term. Finally, the West and East are broadly equal on a Baltic basis, and this should stop too many players from flooding the Western market with additional tonnage.

To paraphrase Hamlet; to cut or not to cut, that has been the prevailing question in the week gone by. We now know, and as a consequence, the VLCC community is hoping to get the last order in for that tray of shots before the bar closes. Suezmax owners have jumped the queue a bit, limiting V-owners choice of beverage, but by and large it looks like most will get served before April is over and probation kicks in. However, with oil prices continuing to fall, despite the cutback agreement – WTI currently trading at its lowest since 2002 – the contango is very much back in play, giving the owning community an extra outlet, and propping up spot rates at the same token. Reduced volumes will eventually take its toll, but the volumes to disappearing first will be the same as those which were about to disappear anyway, regardless of any OPEC+ agreement. In the meantime, there is life in the party yet.

This week the Suezmax market have one key word - itinerary. Berthing prospects is for the few lucky ones, and we see ships floating all over. This of course thins out the fleet, but also causes uncertainty which usually should benefit the owners. As of now, we still remain steady, but as more ships gets delayed and replacement jobs will pop up, we could yet again see this market move. Activity at the moment is decent at best, so with an increase here we expect this to move.

The market in the South Atlantic has improved over the last week, with the iron ore route from Brazil to China being up about 15% on voyage basis, and 40% on time charter basis. This is due to decreased congestion at load-ports and in general more activity indicating that export is picking up after the wet season. The Pacific has experienced some positiveness, however over the last 2 days it has come down to where it was the previous week, with C5 - the West Australia-China route - fixing at USD 4.40-4.45 levels. At the time of writing this report the market for Brazil is improving, but participants are far from convinced this is the beginning of a spring rally and the Pacific is a bit of a question mark.

The Supramax market kept drifting downwards from last week and the effect of the Covid-19 has added more pressure on spot market rates. Tonnage in USG was building up for prompt dates and a Supra was reported to fix in the low $8,000 for trip to Med. ECSA on the contrary we seen a bit more demand for prompt tonnage and Ultra was reported $10,000 for trip with grains to Spain.  Continent and Med markets were lacking activities with very little fresh inquiries . An Ultramax was fixed del Cont TCT to USG with fertilizers for $6,000. Tonnage in Asia was building up and rates kept sliding down. Supra fixing delivery Singapore for round trips with redelivery South East Asia around $3,000 level. NOPAC grains was fixing around $7,000 on Ultramax delivery South Korea.

With Easter Holidays coming to an end on Tuesday, it has been a slow start to the week with few deals being concluded in the North Atlantic. The ECSA grain market has however made for a steady volume of deals being concluded. LME’s are being paid in region of USD 13.5k + 350k GBB, while the ECSA/Continent trade yields around USD 10.5k bss APS delivery. It has been a fair number of deals for NoPac rounds being concluded as well, and paying around USD 7k bss delivery North China.

text: AMERICAS: Export cargos from the US continue, despite cratering worldwide oil demand. In fact we expect the exports to continue thru 2020 and April is on track to be the largest month so far this year. Ironically the falling oil demand has actually increased worldwide lpg demand due to refinery lpg being virtually eliminated. A twist few expected when the economy came to a halt a mere three weeks ago. With the demand side holding, the next question is on the supply.  Production had already decreased and many are now waiting to see if there will be a new OPEC which might include US producers. Propane inventories fell 156,000 barrels this week but still remain well above 2019 levels.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Swap values edged up this week, following the crude jump with anticipation on production cuts. May CP was traded at $260ish, however refrained gains later this week amid uncertainties. As expected, C3/C4 spread has enlarged to $20, due to the robust prompt demand from India.  FOB discussions varied widely as bid idea at small premium while seller targets at double digits. The sole support on premium lies in the consistency of India purchase, which remains a question for forwarding months.   FAR EAST:  Earlier this week 23kt propane for 1h May delivery was traded at May FEI plus $13, which equates to May CP plus $20. Despite active bids at FEI plus teens in window, sellers are keener to sell cargos into China. As FEI/CP spread narrowed down within $10 only whilst landed price into China for May arrival at May CP plus low 40ish, weakening but still more economic.   Several Indian tenders were awarded with CFR price ranging from CP plus 40s to 80s reportedly, relating on exact laycan/laytime requests and other conditions. This week BPCL issued buy tender again to secure another 90k tones for May to early June delivery. Indonesia Pertamina was reported to award one evenly split cargo for May delivery in last tender, and this week issued new tender for another cargo in June delivery.   Deals into China recently are mainly driven by petchem feedstock demand. One Schina-based PDH closed their tender to secure 23kt propane delivered in last decade May. Meanwhile, at the time of writing, two more PDH users have tendered to buy total up-to two full propane cargos from mid-May to 1h June delivery.

WEST: In the West this week, the market began fixing in for the first half of May, which cleared out much of the outstanding freight length remaining in April. Rates have remained fairly stable relative to the end of last week at around mid-to-high $80s Houston/Chiba. Despite generally stronger ideas from Owners, a couple of factors have prevented the market from running away. On one hand, more relet candidates have entered the market now that the market has shown signs of an uptick. On the other, the East has continued to come off while the West has remained stable, erasing the premium which has been seen East of Suez for a while now. Consequently, Owners are showing some bias towards sending ships West, while some traders have been heard in the market looking at fixing in in the MEG in order to relet in the West.  EAST: We have continued to see activity on shipping in the East this week, mainly on the back of Indian demand but also other requirements. Freight availability has remained long and as a consequence each deal has been done at a discount to the other. The fixing window is still very much concentrated around April dates, but as we start getting more acceptance dates for next month then discussions would move forward to May program. It is expected that Owners will direct more ships back West on the back of better freight markets there, and this could eventually turn things around on shipping here in the East as well. The product market is still in backwardation, so one can also expect to see more early month liftings in May which also positive freight.

Another week of uncertainty has passed, with various schemes and scenarios stretching out like a river delta for the coming months, and owners and charterers face decisions today armed with an incomplete picture of an unknown future. The cargo market remains soft, and following several force majeure events and high inventory levels one might fear the worst; however, trading uncertainty has led to some increased tonne-time, and travel restrictions may cause some terminal operators and ship owners to defer maintenance to later in the year. Amidst this, the cargoes have kept coming…so far. Availability has broadly kept pace with fresh requirements, so rates and voyage economics are holding firm, albeit with some froth. Further out, an array of factors muddy the pitch even more: the persistence or otherwise of COVID-19; the continued level of production out the US Gulf; the pace of demand growth as different economies begin their recoveries at different times and at different rates; rescheduled terminal maintenance hitting LNG supply as we enter winter; a possible tightening of the shipping market if a surge of vessels head in for dry dock…as we move through the year, only one thing appears certain: nobody will get every call correct. Yard activity has been quiet, with no new orders placed this week.

As evidenced by the flurry of period fixtures being reported across the board, the strong rates in the tanker markets see owners striving to lock in  tonnage on lucrative long term charters.  Activity in the S&P markets remain subdued to say the least.  Buying interest remains in principle high for older crude carriers able to offer prompt inspection and delivery, however the hurdles very much persist for any sale discussion to take off.  In terms of concluded business, following inspections by up-to eight buyers only last week the 2005 built VLCC YUGAWASAN has now been sold to Greek buyers at USD 33.3m. The vessel is SS due in August and price achieved was more or less in line with expectations.  We expect to see more activity in the sector with another Japanese controlled 2005 built unit being placed for sale this week.  Owners are inviting inspections in Singapore mid April where a similarly large number of prospective buyers is expected to inspect.  However it remains to be seen how the new raft of restrictive measures announced in Singapore today will impact inspections and whether all necessary arrangements can be taken at this vital port.  A steady trickle of bulker transactions are still being done, however until we see tangible deals for larger and more modern vessels the jury is still very much out as to where values are heading.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS: With all the changes in the world over the last fea weeks, two big questions are hanging over the US markets:  1.	Will there be enough supply to keep the mt Belvieu Price of propane and butane to support exports ? 2.	Will there be enough international demand to support the exports if the product and price maintain reasonable levels ?  We feel the answers to both are supportive for US exports. Firstly, we do not expect the cheap crude markets to maintain beyond the Summer and within this time frame,  we expect producers to maintain current production levels. Current economics will prevent growth,  but maintaining current levels , can and will support exports. As far as international pull on US product, we feel this will be there as well. Possibly for different reasons than usual but there none the less.  US inventories ended the demand season at 64 million barrels , a figure which is 21 million barrels above last year. The arb , a bit all over the place, seems to be maintaining above cancellation economics , which is certainly good news for all.

For Aframaxes in the Baltic and North Sea the spot market rates have come off a tad since last week. However the recent increase in oil supply has led to a number of Charterers focusing on taking in several ships on time charter and for storage deals. Aframax vessels are reported on subs for min 6 months at around $40,000 per day, as we wait to see how many will be concluded. As for the spot market; although at least 10 Aframaxes have been fixed ex Baltic going to China (and more expected going forward), there are still a few prompt ships that need to be fixed away before we will see the market start moving - thus we expect rates to hover around current levels until it start picking up on entering 3rd decade fixing window.  In the Mediterranean and Black Sea we have seen a steady market through the week with healthy activity both cross-Med and ex Bsea. Also among the Med players TC has been a hot topic, with Charterers also asking for storage option in D/C of spot voyages. In the week to come we expect rates to firm, a lot due to expected activity out of Sidi Kerir combined Bsea driving the market.

The VLCC market continues at full speed ahead. MEG/China now done a couple times at W210, one by a Shell relet named "Advantage Value, which couldn't be more describing in the current climate (W220 also rumoured done, but not confirmed). Red Sea runs have been repeatedly done at W250. The Atlantic has followed suit, with USG exports back in play in earnest, paying upwards toward $20 mill, in addition to plentiful Wafr- and Brazil east cargoes - and as Suezmax rates are approaching that paid to its large sisters there is nowhere to "hide". The MEG position list is tight as a ducks ass, by and large "cornered" by traders and oil companies having taken ships on period charter, inadvertently propelling rates higher by default.  Delays on the discharge end in the far east is thinning the list further. The MEG fixture count has passed 100 for April, but March ended in excess of 150 and with every man to the (oil)pumps still, there is plenty left that needs covering. So onwards and upwards still it seems.

This week we see some positive signs across both hemispheres. The sentiment is better for Pacific rounds where now Australia seems more active again and the NoPac rounds are keeping somewhat strong.  In the Atlantic we see some signs of more activity with rounds being fixed at higher than last done. Allthough the market is quite tense due to the Covid 19 virus, we see signs of improvement with TA’s paying ard 5k while the shorter Baltic rounds yields around 5,5 – 6k. The ECSA market also showing improved numbers with rounds for Pmaxes being paid abt 8k bss dely Spore-India rge. Some period fixtures has been concluded mid week with the Kmaxes getting paid ard USDd 10k for 1 year.

The volatility in energy markets around the world is keeping traders busy as they try to capitalise on an open arbitrage or other fluctuations in product prices. This is in turn leading to a “stop/start” LNG shipping market, where market participants are constantly evaluating their options to either add tonnage or sublet depending on the latest price movements and trading opportunities. The end of last week saw positive momentum in the shipping market, but as the arbitrage closed so did charterers interest in tonnage and activity quietened down again. Subsequently, rates have come off a little from last week. Charterers appear to be looking at multi-month business a little earlier this year than last, although competition between owners remain strong. No new orders or 2nd hand transactions since last report.    We hope all are in good health during this challenging time. Stay safe!

WEST:  Looking at Western positions lists, it becomes clear that different owners have taken different strategies with regards to the short term. Some have fixed out their tonnage quickly, while others have bet that there should be more uncovered cargoes in April which are waiting in the wings. The result is that tonnage is generally controlled by a smaller number of players. There is little in the way of relets. Given limited liquidity in the freight market, this has meant that rates discussions of late have been very volatile, and it is possible some of the next few fixtures could be stronger, subject to cancellations ex USG.   Looking further ahead, strong Indian demand and rumours of supply bottlenecks could mean that some US origin cargoes head towards India. This should be good for the tonne-mile and supportive of freight in the slightly longer term if so.  EAST: Short term residential demand for LPG into India remains strong, and hence we have seen more requirements on freight and delivered cargoes into India. The activity level remains on the active side with fixing mainly focused around last decade of April, but despite a healthy number of inquiries, we are still left with significant length on shipping and hence the Baltic is yet to find a floor. We expect the current Baltic premium to the West to narrow or even out and it will be interesting to keep an eye on where Owners choose to send their ships going forward.

Rates are improving with the current BCI average presently at 5899, up approximately 50 percent from last week.  There has been more activity on c3 this week, with present freight levels around 10,5 USD. The West Australia route is presently relatively active and freight rates have improved to over 5 USD per ton. For earlier positions, some owners have been gaining in the upper 5’s.  Despite these encouraging signs, uncertainty remains with regards to the durability of an eventual imminent market upturn as estimates are that 1/3 of the global population are under some degree of covid-19 induced lockdown.

Negative week for the supramax market across all regions. Demand and cargo volumes are getting thinner and owners are forced to accept lower rates for firm cargoes. A Tess 58 del Southwest Pass for a trip with petcoke to Med was fixed at $9,500. An Ultramax vessel open USEC was fixed at $8,000 redly Continent. Grain house fixed subs Japanese Ultra del Recalada tct to SE Asia at $12,000 + $200,000 .  Asia market was hit hard and lost about $ 3-4,000 pd in a week . Indonesia lacked volume, partly due to Force Majeure in Indian ports fixing in region between $ 3-6,000 depending on delivery and vessels specs.

In the week to come we expect rates to firm, a lot due to expected activity out of Sidi Kerir combined Bsea driving the market.

The market is back on the move, fueled by surging VLCC rates and floating storage / TC inquiries, rates have gained territory almost as quick as they lost it. A wide open contango structure have seen charterers scramble for tonnage also for suezmaxes with multiple deals concluded the last couple of days for 6-12 months. MEG is the driving force at the moment and charterers with cargoes to move in the Atlantic have to dig deeper in their pockets in order to attract any interest from owners. We expect rates to hold firm for the balance of the week

text: MEG: Swap prices are on a roller coaster ride this week again. Apr C3 CP has plunged to 150ish mid-week and rebounded later to $200, with C3/C4 traded flattish. Apr/May CP was once in small contango but quickly returned to backwarded structure when Apr CP surging up. 1st round CP recommended idea varied significantly, ranging from $150-$250 reportedly. Some players do not favor a super-duper cheap CP to cause huge inventory loss.   One trading house issued semi-term buy tender for one equal ratio cargo monthly from Jun to Dec lifting.   FAR EAST: Despite the bearish number and non-economic ARB, sentiment is gradually turning positive. Extra spot volumes out of AG are slowly being absorbed into East.  A handful of deals are concluded this week. 23kt propane parcels for 1h May delivery have been traded at May FEI minus $2 to $4. We think some are advance purchases with the anticipation of tighten supply in 2h May CFR market, as 8 to 10 Apr liftings ex US were reportedly cancelled.  Chinese importers are also actively buying 2H Apr to May delivered cargos lately, with some deals concluded at the premium over $40 and few equal ratio buyers remaining. One SChina PDH user issued tender to buy 22kt C3 for 8-16th May delivery. Other PDH users are also inquiring for May arrival propane for feedstocks. Taiwan CPC issued buy tender to secure one 11/11 delivered during 3st to 12rd May, and the tender is still in validity. Indonesia tendered promptly to buy one equal ratio cargo for 19-21 Apr delivery, and the result is yet to know.

text: AMERICAS: Discussions in the US Gulf today are focused around the number of cancellations which have or will occur for April loading cargoes. Understandable when Mt Belvieu propane prices have been relatively strong compared to crude (although at 20 year lows on flat price) while delivered markets weak. The seventh consecutive draw in US inventories of 1.8 million barrels was larger than expected and did not help. The effect has been USGC FOB market is cancellations. Rumoured between seven and ten VLGCs for April. The hope is that these cancellations will build inventories, bearish Mt Belvieu, widening the arb. The dampener could be new bearish propane production estimates for 2020-2021 in this new ultra-low crude price environment.  Leading to traders asking themselves if the arb will widen as hoped, and if so when?

After a rough week for the Suezmax owners, rates seem to have bottomed out. TD20 stopped at ws100, and now with activity picking up - this might be difficult to repeat. The supply of oil is still massive, and finding a home for all these cargoes could prove difficult. Covid-19 virus not only decrease demand, but turnaround in ports is also much slower. We expect more ships to be floating, and there has been an increase in TC/storage requests from charterers already. All these are pointers that the market could tick back up again, possibly already this week.

Still extremely challenging times for the big ships, and with present + expected virus-related restrictions on trades for major raw commodities, it would not be wise to expect any immediate recovery. India, South Africa, and possibly other relevant areas fully or partly shutting down their port operations, adding negativity to sentiment. The West Australia/China milk route remains healthy in volume, contributing to keep Pacific rounds for 180,000-tonners at a still miserable USD 3,500-4,000/day.  Fronthaul activity is negligible, and the Tubarao/China reference rate has fallen below USD 10/mt. With much assistance from falling bunker prices - which de facto only benefits tonnage not yet fixed - average daily income nominally up marginally to USD 4k/day and still far below OPEX. Again, the question is for how long this situation can last before casualties will occur - counterparty exposure is already amongst topics discussed. Period activity remains focused on index-linked deals, with 176,000 dwt/built 2005 done for 3-5 months at BCI AVE5TC less 2 pct concluded, exception being 179,000 dwt/built 2013 reportedly done for 13-15 months at USD 11,250.

EAST It has been a week of many moving parts in the East. Covid-19 continues to create a lot of uncertainty, such as India on lockdown and implementation of 14-day quarantine rule from departure of last port, which could potentially create havoc for MEG to India trade. We already seeing the effects of this with delays at most Indian ports.    Activity on shipping has been limited to a couple of freight tenders, surprisingly from players who are not usually active in the freight market. One of these tenders is on the back of spot fob purchase therefore taking advantage of current low prices.    Freight rates have so far been holding up for current fixing window 1H April, but moving into 2H April we feel that freight may come under pressure again. This partly due to weakening spot demand for LPG in countries like India, as industrial demand is expected to take a big hit.  WEST In the West, the general consensus this week has been that freight rates should be lower given a weaker outlook on the product front. However, a lack of liquidity has made it difficult to determine exactly where the market should be.   The number of fixtures beyond 10th of April has been few and given that we are now too late for cancellations in the second decade of the month there should still be a handful of uncovered cargoes for that period. With that said, the third decade looks a lot more sparse on inquiries since a handful of cancellations are rumoured in the market towards the end of April. As a result, it is difficult to find compelling arguments for why freight rates would be supported going into May, as charterers will seek lower rates to compensate for poor netbacks.

We expect more ships to be floating, and there has been an increase in TC/storage requests from charterers already. All these are pointers that the market could tick back up again, possibly already this week.

With port closures in India and mines closing down in both South Africa and the US, owners have struggled to fix as per last done in most areas. A positive in the otherwise weak market has been the steady fixtures at reasonable levels from East Coast South America to China. For a transatlantic trip, Kamsarmaxes (82,500 dwt) currently earn low USD 5,000 per day, while short fronthauls from the UK/Continent-region are priced at the mid USD 14,000's. From East Coast South America to China, charterers pay around USD 8,000 DOP Singapore for a roundtrip. A transpacific round voyage in the East pay shipowners around USD 5,000, and the Baltic 4TC-Index is down 166 points since last week, now at 720 points.

From wuthering highs, VLCC rates have seen a slow but steady decline in the week gone by, with more failing than fixing. It’s been more emotions than fundamentals propelling the decline, with “more to lose than to gain” being the unspoken mantra. However, at the writing moment it appears that the market has bottomed out. “Failed” cargoes have reappeared, sugared with additional requirement on top. A widening arb is spurring storage-T/C interest and adding fuel to fire. Rebated oil continues to be pumped into the market place, and although immediate demand may be dwindling, lack of on shore storage capacity dictates it has to be shipped out in one form or another. We will always have volatility, but until OPEC+ gets together and cap oil production again, we continued to see strong upside going forward.

So far, the week in the North Sea and Baltic have been rather quiet compared to previous weeks in March. The uncertainty around Covid-19 and how it will affect the markets still remain a big factor. Charterers efforts in trying to hold back has temporarily shown to work as rates now are under downward pressure. Despite some charterers taking a risk on very tight itineraries we expect short term that rates will continue to soften somewhat. But with more floating scenarios in the North Sea expected, we will see rates firm again on the back of less available tonnage and increased cargo activity. Following an active and firming market in the Mediterranean and Black Sea the last couple of weeks, we have now experienced a downward correction in most segments and areas. Also here the Covid-19 is causing uncertainties with additional delays encountered in port calls and for crew changes as certain countries and ports impose further countermeasures to try and prevent further spread of the virus. We foresee the market to remain stable at best in the area with a possible softening as tonnage is stacking up with not much alternatives provided elsewhere giving much of a joyful upside.

A week of negative sentiment brought rates sharply down. Especially with Corona Virus escalation made negative influence on spot and forward rate. Demand in ECSA was vanishing away. South Atlantic rates dropped rapidly. Supramax del South Brasil to Mediterranean was reported to fix USD 10,000, while TCT to WCSA from Argentina paid USD 12,500.  USG market also felt under pressure with tonnage building up and lack of fresh cargoes. TCT to Mediterranean with petcoke was paid around USD 16,000, however for clean cargoes such as grain, charterers were willing to pay much less. The Mediterranean and Continent market had decent activity with seasonal fertilizers export from Baltic and enough minerals from Black Sea and Medeternina. Ultramax was rumored  to fix del Canakkale to West Africa with clinker at healthy USD 13,500. The Asian basin came under pressure, and rates fall for about USD 2,000 per day from previous week. We have seen owners accepting USD 6,000 for Indo RV and slightly more for trips to China.  The Indian Ocean is under pressure and due to South Africa shutting down, there is a big concern about near future. End of last week, Ultramax was fixing delivery Richards Bay trip to Vietnam at USD 12,000 plus USD 200,000 ballast bonus.

Tanker owners continue to enjoy the ride.  Floating storage is presently the name of the game and our tanker analysts estimate fifteen to twenty VLCC's have been taken up for storage up until now.  The 2005 built VLCC YUGAWASAN was inspected this week in Singapore and upto eight prospective buyers went on-board with a sale expected soon. The three Chinese controlled VLCC's NEW CREATION built 2009 Dalian, NEW TALISMAN built 2009 Bohai and NEW CORAL built 2010 Jiangnan are reported committed on subjects at Usd 43 mill each but we await further details.  The sale of 2012 Japanese built Aframax NANYANG STAR is a bit of a cold shower for values.  After a previous deal failed to be confirmed, reports suggest the vessel has now been sold below Usd 30 mill.  Dry sales are thin on the ground and we have yet to see new benchmarks for capesize with the rumoured failure of GREAT NAVIGATOR built 2006 Universal which had been reported sold to Greece for region Usd 14 mill. Capesize NEW STAGE built 2008 Namura is reported to have been inspected by five parties this week of which four Greek and one Chinese. Buyers and Sellers are generally out of sync on pricing, but we are slowly seeing opportunistic buyers appear who are ready to take advantage of the current market downturn.

The commodity and financial markets across the globe have been nothing less than volatile, no different to what the LNG shipping markets have experienced of late. The LNG shipping spot market activities went into overdrive in the Atlantic with a series of vessel requirements issued, along with  a flurry of spot fixtures and vessel swaps, as sentiment spiked amongst the shipowners and players with relets. These are spilling over to the Pacific market where intra-Asia chartering requirements began to emerged. Vessels are available for shipowners to propose to these requirement, however with increased rate expectations as compared to just a week ago.  As many of us work from homes during these unprecedented times, the lockdowns, quarantines and border closures have proved to provide a challenge to the shipping operations and crew management efforts. We spare a thought to all seafarers who have been affected during this period.  No LNG vessel newbuild orders or 2nd hand transactions were reported last week.

Some smaller cap deals are in the making particularly in the clean sector but overall the S&P activity is very muted. Dry bulk equities had another awful week with most listed names now down more than 50 per cent y-t-d.  The escalating Covid-19 pandemic makes it increasingly difficult to transact S&P with anything resembling normality.  Pre-purchase inspections, crew changes and most legal aspects of a financial closing are severely disrupted.

Blood is still very much in the streets for the big ships, and further pandemic-related restrictions in major load- and discharge areas do little to help on the situation. That said, heavy industry in major raw materials import countries like China and South Korea on their way back to capacity, and there is a glimpse of light in the present tunnel for coal and ore trading volumes to recover.  Reflecting this, average daily spot earnings are up 40 pct w-o-w, but coming in at USD 3,500/day it is still miserable and far below operating expenses.  Far East is the only area with activity of significance, the West Australia/China conference trade being steady around USD 4.40-50 pmt and Pacific rounds paying at best USD 3,500-4,000/day. Fronthaul liquidity lacking big time, and no substantial market improvement is expected until same is back on track. Question is again for how long this can go on until prudent owners choose to idle their ships, or in worst case when will the first company casualties occur.  Fear is presently eating facts for breakfast amongst operators, and recent period activity has been centered around index-linked agreements.

In the North Sea and Baltic, rates have continued in an upwards direction this week as the availability of tonnage willing to fix intra-NWE voyages tightens. We have seen more owners looking to go long and spend more days at sea due to the current virus situation. How the week to come will look is really unknown territory, but the list looks tight and we could see higher rates get done. Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea market has picked up a further 40 points on benchmark routes this week, mainly due to high activity on the cargo side. Owners are now fixing additional 20 points premium for calling Italy due to the outbreak of coronavirus there. Since there are still many cargoes in the market yet to be covered, and on the back of the surrounding markets such as NWE and the US market picking up, we expect the market to remain firm going forwards.

WEST In the West this week, rates have gradually edged higher as we progress further into the April fixing window. At the same time, bunkers have continued their free fall and as a consequence owners’ earnings are now back around the USD 50kpd mark. With this rising market and the fact that there seems to be little value in lifting FOB cargoes, a number of players have been more vocal about potentially reletting their vessels. A consequence of this could be some downwards pressure on rates. However, it is now too late for most players to cancel term liftings, and with a large number of cargoes set to be exported from Marcus Hook from April onwards rates should remain supported for now.   Looking slightly further ahead and into May, the picture becomes markedly more bearish, with the market generally anticipating the arb to be much weaker and for cancellations to be prevalent. The obvious consequence of this is that freight may have to give way to unfavourable product conditions. With that said, the extent to which freight could weaken will be determined by whether Chinese demand picks up again and whether the Saudis make good on their word to ramp up production as much as they say they will moving forward.   EAST The momentum in the freight market has continued as we have seen increased volume ex MEG due to the extra output from Saudi Arabia. The sentiment on freight has therefore reversed its bearishness and is looking more bullish, with owners’ latest ideas being around low USD 60s Baltic. It remains to be seen if the flurry of fixtures will continue during the coming days, or if the market will start to slow down, but there is an expectation of Indian majors coming into the market for several 1H April cargos. Going forward, though there is still a healthy line up of ships for the next fixing window, so we don’t expect the market to shoot up too quickly even if the overall sentiment has changed.

With ongoing events affecting most of the global economic markets, LNG shipping firmed up this week. Rates in the Atlantic have turned and we’re now seeing an uptick, and although the Pacific didn’t see quite the gains that the Atlantic did due to prompt tonnage still lingering in the basin, fundamentals are growing stronger and the floor feels like it has been found for now. Sentiment from Owners is likely to rally off the back of stronger voyage economics, but the requirements are needed to back this up: the Atlantic was supported by a spate of enquires for US Gulf cargoes while the Pacific was a little quieter. On the cargo side, China is likely to need higher imports in the short term as the country begins its recovery, as many head back to work and industrial demand increases. This could see growth in spot opportunities over the next couple of months. One growing concern though, is that with China now appearing to recover from COVID-19, could we see the country impose restrictions on inbound trade from regions with ongoing infections? There were no newbuilding orders this week but yard prices have come down reflecting a strong US Dollar. Staying with the yards we’ve yet to see the full impact of the ongoing situation: disruption to supply chains and workplace restrictions put in place for the yard workers, there may be delays to deliveries ahead. With COVID-19 now affecting most of the globe, we hope that you and your families, and those of the seafarers we rely on across all sectors, all stay safe and healthy.

It’s been a week of frantic activity, with rates shooting up and daily earnings in the USD 100’s of thousands. However, things have calmed down in the last 24 hours, and with that we are seeing some ‘profit taking’, and the arrow is tilting slightly down. text: MEG: Another week of drastic market drop. Crude has slashed by another 20% and Apr C3 CP plunged to $207 while Butane CP maintains at $3 spread higher.  Saudi Aramco released their Apr lifting acceptance as per nomination with minor changes only, and they still have spot tons available after 5-6 cargos were sold reportedly. Qatar Petroleum was said to award their 23-25 Apr lifting 3/1 sale tender at single digit discount to Apr CP link, however some players reckon this price too aggressive as of $15 Apr/May backwardation, let alone the negative FOB netback due to weak demand amid long supply in the front.   FAR EAST: April offer stood firm earlier this week with seller asking at teens’ premium over Apr FEI. Until later this week offer dropped down to plus $5 only and bid at flat in the window, as more sellers emerged with clear shipping structure.  This week, premium for propane delivered in Apr into China has come off to 30ish level on Apr CP link. Some talk one 1h May arrival propane was also traded into China at 30s but on May CP link. China import in 2020 Q1 is expected to decrease by roughly 35% compared to last Q1 at 4.76mmt, and hopefully the volume can recover from Apr onwards. Chinese domestic PDHs has improved run rates lately as great margin to produce propylene, and Zhejiang Satellite has restarted their 450,000tonnes/y unit from maintenance.   Taiwan CPC has secured 11/11 end Apr delivery Apr CP plus 40s via tender late last week.

text: AMERICAS: In the midst of another tumultuous week in global trade the EIA reported a draw of 310,000 barrels, slightly below what was predicted. The news did little to affect the US propane market which had already plummeted in parity with international declines, on the back of crude. As it stands, the April/May arb and netbacks sit at around $112/ton and 4 cents/gallon respectively. With that said, discussion for spot cargos has not completely dissipated. Logic being that as daily life heads in the direction of normalcy in China, the demand PDH and petchem feed stock will once again require tons from the US. The discussion that many contact holders are currently having is whether the economics dictate to cancel cargos, pending agreed upon fee, and buy from the spot market. This equation has kept activity buoyed, at least for the time being.  Remarkably, Mt Belvieu Non-Tet propane stands at 61.14% WTI and has crossed the below 30cpg for the first time since Jan 17th 1999.

While the rest of the world is shutting down rapidly, the VLCC market has continued full speed ahead in the week gone by. It’s been a week of frantic activity, with rates shooting up and daily earnings in the USD 100’s of thousands. However, things have calmed down in the last 24 hours, and with that we are seeing some ‘profit taking’, and the arrow is tilting slightly down. That said, more than 2/3’s of the April MEG program remains to be done, and with the well announced production boost it’s likely to be busier than normal still. Although a correction may be in the cards, it’s also important to note that plummeting bunker prices is contributing positively. Steady as she goes.

VLCC spot rates have reached unprecedented high levels with Suezmax and Aframax following suit.  How this will impact S&P activity is hard to predict as the COVID-19 pandemic escalates, but short term we should see renewed chase for older tankers able to give prompt delivery.   Several buyers are for instance next week inspecting the Japanese controlled VLCC YUGAWASAN built 2005 Mitsubishi which is expected to be sold soon thereafter.  Reports that the 2000 built Suezmax MOGRA is sold at Usd 17 mill certainly lend support to a robust floor for the older units.  Otherwise it’s all doom and gloom.  With the world’s fourth largest COVID-19 infection rate per capita, the Norwegian government yesterday imposed the most wide-reaching restrictions ever in peace time.  Equity markets are bracing for a severe meltdown, and in the coming weeks and month’s sentiment and macro backdrops will continue to weigh on the shipping sectors.

text: AMERICAS: Mt Belvieu propane has not been falling as fast as global propane markets, or even crude oil markets for that matter. Non-TET propane now lies at 46.8% WTI. This has closed the arbs East and West, and although freight has been coming off helping netbacks slightly , we are now in cargo cancellation territory. The 2.9 million barrel draw for the week ending March 6th was the 5th consecutive draw in inventories which is not unusual for winter however in this new era of mega production we had become used to  Winter inventory builds. With the current oil price war going on there have been worries of shrinking domestic oil and gas production through 2020. US companies already in danger to survive might be forced into bankruptcy with WTI crude in the high 20’s  and Natural Gas well below 2.00 / mcf.  Many have a view that 100 million barrels in inventories by the start of the 2020 draw season (October 1,2020) are needed to sustain new export capacity and US winter demand. These factors are lending strength to the Mt Belvieu propane market, and the question is will cancellations in April be needed to weaken Mt Belvieu and reopen the arb.

In the North Sea and Baltic, increased activity in the area combined with stronger surrounding markets in the Mediterranean and USG have pushed rates up a few points. Owners have more alternatives to choose from and rightfully asking for higher rates on cargoes coming out of the North Sea/Baltic to achieve similar daily earnings as they would have got fixing out of other loading areas. Moving further into the 3rd decade loading window we expect the market to remain firm, especially due to the increased uncertainty around the current oil market. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, the market has continued its upturn this week, with rates picking up a further 20-30 ws-points across the board. We have seen a relatively active market all week, both for cargoes coming out of the Black Sea but also for cross-Mediterranean movements. Owners have made sure to take advantage of the situation keeping an upward pressure on rates, even fixing a premium for calling Italian ports due to the outbreak Coronavirus there.  Also, in the Mediterranean/Black Sea we expect a firm market in the week to come.

To yet again quote our brilliant analyst; supply trumps demand, and that’s true because supply has turned into demand big time - for oil tankers, and VLCCs in particular. Saudi Aramco have stated they will increase production to 13 mbpd, which is a 34% increase over the 9.7 mbpd they have been pumping.  ADNOC will do the same, increasing from 3 mbpd to in excess of 4 mbpd and plan to accelerate their expansion to 5 mbpd, and everyone is scrambling for tonnage. Rates have soared, with ws152.5 being last reported MEG/China, corresponding to daily returns in the USD 150k/day region, and further upward potential evident. The Atlantic basin is being dragged up as well, as its source of tonnage has dwindled considerably with the MEG absorbing most of the tonnage.

text: MEG: Oil price has slashed down by over 25% in this unprecedented oil war. Swap number fluctuates in heavy decline, as April C3 CP plummeted by more than $100 at the start of this week and at the moment traded at $255. C3/C4 spread has rapidly narrowed down from previous $45 to $10, as demand mainly driven by propane for petchem especially into China. Producers are boosting their oil production, and on mid-week Saudi Aramco was reported to sell 4-5 spot cargos loading in Later Mar and April, and still have spot volume avails.  Additionally, Qatar Petroleum also issued sale tender for one 23-25 Apr loading heavy propane or equal ratio cargo. Chinese Importers very actively purchased Apr cargos, with more than 3 full propane cargos being sold from late last week and price ranging from 40 to mid-40s on Apr CP link. Since more sellers seen this week, remaining buyers lowered down or held back bids. This being said, PDHs and crackers have seen attractive margin amid lower feedstock price than before. And it might be a good timing to stockpile before entering into contango in forward months, if with storage allowance.

Slightly stronger numbers in both basins this week, with the North Atlantic having the better uptick, and a more sliding market in the East. For a transatlantic trip, Kamsarmaxes (82,500 dwt) currently earn around USD 9,000, while short front hauls from the UK/Continent-region are priced at the high USD 18,000s. From East Coast South America to China, charterers are willing to pay around USD 11,000 DOP Singapore for a roundtrip. A transpacific round voyage in the East pay shipowners around USD 7,500, and the Baltic 4TC-Index is up 96 points since last week, now at 961 points.

After some quiet and flat weeks in the Suezmax market, the failing co-operation of the OPEC countries have increased the supply of oil dramatically. This has had a huge effect on the tanker market in general, starting with the VLCCs, continuing with Suezmax and Aframax. We already see VLCC cargoes being split in both West Africa and MEG, just adding more fuel to the fire for the Suezmaxes. West Africa/UKCM is close to three digits now, and even with sufficient amount of ships in the area, all owners are taking advantage of the situation, and putting on the breaks. We expect the peak to continue for the rest of the week, at least as long as we see this cargo activity. The only question to ask now is how far can this go?

Still very sad times for the big ships, and merit in further trading at present levels is highly debatable for most tonnage. Spot fixtures in many cases reflect zero to negative daily income, with owners even taking on contractual risks of potential further virus-related losses. This stated, the West Australia/China iron ore conference trade presently sees increased volumes. Values for Pacific rounds are nevertheless at far below operating expenses, and best case at a nominal USD 3,300/day. Period activity is moderate and interest remains cautious, with representative recent conclusions including 174,000/2006 spot China fetching USD 12,700 basis 8-9 months and 179,000/2009, also spot China, done basis BCI AVE5TC + 3 pct.
