Still very rough seas for the big ships, with the majority of the fleet trading Far East or fronthaul and consequently earning far less than the mathematical average - same being stable w-o-w at USD 9000/day. Vintage, non-eco, non-scrubber units suffering by far the most. With historically high bunker prices, scrubber-fitted ships presently earn an extra USD 8-10k/day in comparison. Far East iron ore and coal volumes are fair but not sufficient to change a nervous spot sentiment. Atlantic and fronthaul minerals outlook is better, but still remains to be seen if live up to expectations next few weeks. Healthy period interest, but actual activity limited and much focused on index-linked levels view poor spot and forward values - representative fixtures including spot 180,000 dwt, built 2010, for about 12 months at ave5tc plus 10 pct.

This week started in the red with limited activity, but picked up during the next days as usual. Positive sentiment, especially from ECSA, has turned the index green again with new cargoes entering the market mid-week. A TA round voyage pays owners around the mid USD 7,000 per day. A fronthaul from the Continent yields around the low USD 15,000's. In the Pacific basin, a round voyage pays owners around USD 4,500 per day, while a kmx fetches around 10,000 DOP Singapore for a grain run via ECSA. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 825 points, 22 up since last week.

The market flattening out and some more resistance from owners in the East, although still at low levels. Indo/China rv fixing around low/mid USD 6,000 bss aps Indo, while Cis rv to China talking around USD 4,500 aps. Nopac rv fixing around USD 7500 + 250k gbb aps nopac, while Aussie rv talking around low 6k dop China delivery. In the Atlantic, ECSA fh are paying around 13,000+300k gbb, while to TA to Med around USD 12,000. From Med to Wafr it is paying around USD 7,500, while fh ex Continent is paying around USD 20,000. There has been some period activity where Ultras covered short period around USD 9,500 in the Far East, while for longer periods close to 1 year, split rates are discussed roughly around 5,000 first 30 days and in the 8k's for the balance.

We finally have a reference sale for brand new scrubber fitted aframax tanker.  Minerva is reported to be paying region usd 55.5 mill for AQUAFREEDOM - delivered from Samsung in September 2019. This is in line with our value estimates. Rumours abound about another 2019 built VLCC being sold for region usd 107 mill but details are still sketchy. Several early 2000 built suezmaxes are in play in the usd 19-22 mill range and we expect to soon report more such sales.  Dry values are under pressure. There are many buyers waiting to strike but consensus seems to be that values have yet to reach its floor in the near to medium term. Tellingly, negotiations for the 2010 Japan built capesize CAPE AGNES was aborted as the sellers’ price idea of usd 22 mill was not met.  We understand the best bid came at region usd 19.5 mill.

text: AMERICAS: Mt Belvieu propane prices remain at 30% of WTI. This is due to global uncertainty caused to the US-Iran situation. Which meant the unexpected build of 690 000 barrel in propane inventories did not have the bearish affect on Mt Belvieu prices you would usually expect to see. US inventories are now at 88.9 million, 29% above this week last year and 17% higher than the 5 year average. We have seen Mt Belvieu Non-LST January propane discounted by 2cpg to LST January propane. This disparity has been attributed to very high production, and export capacity constraints leading to a glut of product in the caverns. The stratospheric rise US terminalling fees over the past few months, with recent January and February FOB slots being sold above 30cpg, is showing signs of slowing down for the first time. The US-FEI arb has narrowed and this coupled with rising freight rates form the region has eroded netback values.

The amazing earnings have ignited the tanker S&P market with particularly modern, scrubber fitted crude tankers hot commodity.   It comes as no surprise that sellers’ price ideas for modern/brand new tankers are finally being met.  Deal of the week being Hartree’s sale of a scrubber-fitted VLCC newbuilding with delivery ex DSME in January for usd 106 mill.  The buyer is reported to be a new joint venture between George Economou, Idan Ofer and the Norwegian investor Øystein Stray Spetalen.  One more VLCC resale is also rumoured sold by Hartree to Korean buyers at same level. The price is about 8% up on last done which was Hunter’s sale of a sister newbuilding to Korean buyers at usd 98 mill in June 2019. The last time VLCC’s were sold at similar levels was in 2014 when Gener8 acquired 4 newbuilding contracts from Scorpio at usd 105 mill each, albeit with delivery in 2016.  More deals for very modern, scrubber fitted tankers are in the making.  The dry case remains challenging and values are coming off.  Increased sales activity for supra- and panamax at lower levels with prices arguably down by usd 1-1.5 mill since December.   For capesize the present bid/ask spread is hampering sales activity.  CAPE AGNES 180k built 2010 Koyo is, for example, reported to have seen region usd 20 mill but sellers have yet to bite the bullet.

text: MEG: Swap price is riding a roller coaster, as new year starts with uncertainties between Iran and US.  Earlier this week, Feb CP spiked up to $565 but rapidly plunged to $505 on Thurs, following the crude.  Qatar Petroleum has released Feb acceptances with delays reported from 5 to 12 days. Since most lifters nominated for early Feb laycan to avoid heavy backwardations, which assessed at $50 at the time of writing. QP has tendered to sell a 24/27th Feb lifting full propane cargo, which due at 14th Jan.  Other than this, limited FOB offers were seen, as lifters concerning acceptances for Adnoc and Saudi. The FEB FOB value ranges from small discounts to teens premium, subject to the loading laycan and ratio.   FAR EAST:  A handful of propane delivered in Feb into Japan/Korea are concluded this week. Premium starts higher early this week, with deals traded at Feb FEI plus 53$ for 1H Feb and $45 for 2h Feb, later declined to $40 mid-week. Despite the softening premium, Far East market still appears strong with MB/FEI arb opens wide, which props up the discussions on terminal fee premium for US fob liftings.  Moreover, continued tightness in Non-Us origin supply has buoyed up market sentiments. Several Chinese PDHs have carried out or going to have maintenance, partly due to negative margins and partly in lack of feedstocks. Offers for equal ratio cargos during 2h Feb delivery into China were heard at Feb CP plus 90s, whilst propane offers barely seen.  Indian HPCL has a term inquiry for 6 plus 3 optional equal ratio cargoes for 2020, which is reportedly still under negotiation. BPCL has issued buy tender to secure 800kt 50/50 ratio cargos from Mar 2020 to 2021, close by 20th Jan.   Indonesia PERTAMINA issued buy tender to secure two equal ratio cargos delivered in mid FEB several times, with nothing being awarded reportedly.

In the Baltic and North Sea market we have seen a downward trend in rate levels at the beginning of the year. The decline is much due to an abundance of vessels for cargoes loading in the first half of January. However, with several vessels ballasting towards healthier markets such as the USG and Caribs, combined with bad weather in the North Sea, we expect a halt in the declining rates as we are coming into the 3rd decade fixing window – we may even see rates firm up again in this window. Also in the Mediterranean and Black Sea market the rates came off a bit at the beginning of the year, mainly due to low activity where the few charterers entering the market still benefited from the very healthy tonnage list. At the beginning of this week however, we have seen activity picking up and we do expect an upward correction in the week to come. This is also due to factors such as delays in the Bosporus, uncertainties in Libya, and vessels leaving the area and ballasting towards the USG to try their luck there.

It has been a busy start to 2020 for Suezmaxes with all areas being active giving owners plenty to choose from. West Africa, Mediterranean-Black Sea and North Sea have absorbed a lot of ships, both natural positions but also ballasters coming from the East. This in turn forces charterers with MEG loading requirements to dig deeper in their pockets for owners’ services - especially with the political unrest we are seeing in the region. West Africa and Americas have been busy competing over the same ships coupled with a lot of ships being absorbed for Black Sea loading which stretches far out in the new year with bad weather increasing the Turkish strait delays. All in all, the Suezmax market remains firm across the board.

With the heightened tension in the Middle East Gulf area it’s been a turbulent few days in the VLCC market. With the odd exception rates have for the most part remained steady around the same level as previous week, trading around the ws140 give/take for MEG/eastbound cargoes up until a day or two ago. However, the recent flare up in the region has seen rates upwards to ws150 concluded. Some of the gains have been eaten up by increased bunker prices, particularly so for non-scrubber vessel. Supply of VLSFO has also had logistical- and quality issues. At the writing moment players seem to have adopted a “wait and see” attitude, in anticipation of US reaction to last night’s rocket assault on US troops in Iraq, and as such the market hangs in a balance. That said, the fundamentals remain strong, so the question is rather how much premium charterers will face depending on further developments in the conflict between Iran and the US.

WEST  Happy New Year!   It seems market participants have returned following the Christmas break reinvigorated and ready to tie up any loose ends from before the Christmas break. As such, the VLGC market has been much more active in the West this week than it has been over the final few weeks of 2019. Much of the freight length which had been open relatively prompt in Jan has been fixed out, and owners are beginning to feel emboldened to ask for higher rates which they believe to be justified by incredibly strong netbacks and a tightening freight market.   On the other hand, an increasing number of traders are looking to relet their tonnage, and it is possible this could prevent rates from running away too quickly. In addition, some players have already indicated that they will send their vessels west on the back of turbulence in the Middle East. It’s worth noting that, although this could put pressure on western rates in the short term, it will ultimately mean a longer tonne-mile and therefore is beneficial to those who own vessels.    EAST  We have seen a couple of January cargoes fixed this week all around latest Baltic, although recent developments in the Middle East has created a lot of uncertainty for the way forward. With that said, some players with tonnage currently positioned in the east are saying it is preferable to head west given the strong premium there and the risk of escalated conflict. The QP acceptances for February were announced end of last week where mostly seeing delays, and we expect dates from Adnoc and Aramco to be out next week. So we probably will not see much fixing activity for February program until next week onwards.

The Capesize market has hit new low's in the first week of the new year, with the West Australia route being fixed at USD 6.6 being the lowest, before improving to USD 7 level towards the second half of the week. TC level is presently sub USD 5,000 for a Pacific round. The weighted average is presently USD 9,000. Period fixing is more or less none-existing at fixed levels, whilst index linked deals are considered interesting.

First week of the new year started poorly. Oversupply of tonnage in the Pacific and lack of fresh enquiry in the Atlantic add lots of pressure on current market conditions. A number of Indonesian round trips were reported at bellow USD 5,000 pd levels. Ultramax for Nopac grain loading was fixed USD 7,900 pd. USD 11,000 pd plus an USD 100,000 ballast bonus for a South African trip into India-China range.  US Gulf petcoke runs into the Continent and the Mediterranean were reported in the USD 14,000/15,000 pd range. MV Xing Shou Hai 61’ dwt fixed at USD 13,500 aps Recalada trip Black Sea. From the Mediterranean, a Supra fixed delivery Iskenderun trip to West Africa at USD 7,750.  Scrap runs from Continent to Turkey fixing USD 10,000 pd level.

Weak sentiment has put rates in both basins under constant pressure in the last weeks, with no exceptions this week. Please take note that the rates quoted will from now on be basis a Baltic type 82,000 DWT Kamsarmax. A TA round voyage pays owners around the mid USD 8.00 per day. A fronthaul from the Continent yields around the mid USD 15,000's. In the Pacific basin, a round voyage pays owners around USD 4,500 per day. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 803 points, 618 down since week 50, 2019.

It seems that the 2020 business year effectively only started this week as the majority of the market players returned to their desks from their holidays. There has been more activity in all of the basins this week, with a number of fresh spot requirements emerging together with one long-term shipping tender from a European utility. However, due to the lack of fixtures in the recent weeks, the spot rates continue to stay under pressure as the number of available tonnage have increased. Yet, if we continue to see further requirements developing, especially ahead of the impending Chinese New Year, we might see rates holding better than expected as the overall shipping length is not that drastic. Furthermore, the increasing unrest in the Middle-East is causing some concern to those who have LNG cargoes in and out from the region, and the potential ramifications to the shipping market still remains unknown. IMO2020 regulations are also now in full-force and we are already seeing the spread between low-sulphur fuel and high-sulphur fuel rise to highest levels seen in years, as quoted prices for low-sulphur fuels have soared. Albeit LNG shipping is less affected by the surge of low-sulphur fuel prices, this will definitely have an impact on ballast bonus discussions and Owners' decision on heel retention after voyages. On the newbuilding front, there were no new orders this week, although it was post reported that Hyundai Samho Heavy industries got the final LNGC newbuilding order for the calendar year 2019.

Firstly, Happy New Year! We wish everyone a prosperous 2020.   The week leading up to New Year has been quiet as LNG chartering experts (who planned ahead) took a well deserved break, the consequence has been limited vessel requirements West of Suez and the same can also be said for East of Suez.  Availability remains tight in the West with portfolio players running the show on prompt vessel tonnage, which will result in levels remaining stable. On the contrary, in the East there seems to be some added availability which is a cause for concern for ship owners.    Looking back, we can certainly say that 2019 was a year with seasonal rate fluctuations, reaching an unexpected low during Q2, to then firm up through Q3 and Q4. LNG prices were however «flattish» with limited to non existent West to East arbitrage in the main, but did see a mini-armada set sail in September for discharges in November.  LNG trading pattern - we saw more intra-basin activity as LNG stayed «local». 2019 was also a busy year for the few remaining LNG building Yards, as new orders remained robust throughout the year with a total count of 42 orders. What 2020 will bring is yet to be seen...but we at Fearnleys see another year with strong volume growth, more focus on «greener» shipping and some interesting trends worth monitoring. Hence, we are looking forward to the new opportunities of this New Decade! Once again we wishing you a Prosperous and Happy New Year!

In the Atlantic, weather has caused some disruption in South Hook and strikes have created delays in France. These have started to ease, particularly in South Hook. So as Father Christmas loads his sleigh, LNG parcels are arriving thick and fast. The arbitrage has widened as the West sees a softening at a quicker pace than in the East. A cargo tender in the Middle East has kept players working this week whilst tight availability in the West sees many checking in to assess potential needs. Turning to the availability, the market remains balanced yet with the signs of additional length starting to appear in the East. With no profitable inter-basin arbitrage and limited independent Owners in the Atlantic, levels are likely to hold despite the lack of a flurry of obvious long-haul routes. Why? Portfolio tonnage makes up the majority of the availability and while these vessels flirt with the ideas of subletting they can quickly retreat to the portfolio for internal business leaving one or two players to negotiate it out.   The New build market saw a lot of activity as the contracts for the Shell NB program firmed up this week, resulting in more orders and leaving the number of available vessels untouched. Will we run out of yard space? unlikely at this moment in time and prices remain flat. Just leaves us just to say - we wish everyone a very pleasant break during this festive period and we will leave the sentimental commentary for next week as we look back on 2019 but more importantly forward to 2020.

The tanker S&P market is pretty subdued but our read is that many buyers are on standby with a strong level of enquiries waiting to strike in the new year.  Whilst brand new ships are fully priced, we see continued upside on values for the semi-modern tonnage across the board.   The dry case has lost steam with cape earnings taking a beating. Next year will start with a large number of kamarsarmax newbuildings hitting the water and as such it’s fair to expect a challenging quarter in sight. Relevant transactions are few and we end the year with a steady and large overhang of ships for sale.  Any movement in dry values in the near future will be down.  The scrubber case is looking very promising as 2020 approaches with the compliant fuel spread now in excess of usd 300/ton.

For a week that saw relatively few fixtures and broadly static rates, there sure were enough intriguing developments to keep everyone on their toes. The Atlantic saw a combination of factors disrupt trade flows, including continuing long queues for cargoes into the UK, severe storms in the Bay of Biscay and industrial action in France impacting some discharges. The additional time on water for laden cargoes and slower ballast passages raised concerns among charterers with tight schedules, and with issues continuing through the week coupled with the first exports out of Freeport we may see an uptick in fixing levels. The Pacific hasn't seen the same excitement, but continues to tick over with a steady flow of requirements for owners to work. It hasn't all been rosy for owners though, as charterers can take comfort in the amount of interest generated by a multi month requirement from the spring. As we approach the final week before Christmas and the last fortnight of the year, we hope both owners and charterers can find some festive cheer.

text: MEG: Saudi Aramco’s Jan lifting acceptance has astonished the whole market, with cancellations/delays/cuts/grade changes happening. This being said, the front supply has tightened up further.  Due to this, swap value has shot up again this week. At the time of writing, Jan propane CP is traded at $507, $67 higher than Jan CP, and butane rose up to $531 with continuous $25 gap. Feb CP chased up, traded at $487 with $20 backwardation, and we believe the spread might narrow down further as Feb supply doesn’t look abundant either.  Qatar Petroleum was reported to award their sell tender for 27/29th lifting full C3 to one Chinese importer at CP plus high single premium.   FAR EAST: Very eventful market this week before Christmas, with various bids in/off window on either US/non-US and tenders floating.  Propane for 2h Jan delivery is bid at Jan FEI plus mid 30s or flat price $564 while no seller seen. Mid-Jan lifting equal ratio cargos is being bid at $515/545 but again nothing concluded.   Equal ratio demand appears strong with SEA inquiries. One Vietnam importer has issued buy tender to secure two parcels of equal ratio cargos delivered in 21st Dec till 1h Jan and 25th Jan to 10th Feb, and the result is yet to know. Meanwhile, Indonesia Pertamina has issued new tender to secure two evenly split cargo as well, but delivered during early and mid Feb, which valid till tomorrow.   However, demand into China is still mainly driven by propane for petchem use. One SChina Importer has bought 2h Jan arrival 23/0 at mid-80s, luckily we would say, since apart from this, still several rigid demand haven’t been covered. Despite the squeezed margins on PDHs, some plants with downstream complex still have profits and keep exploring cargos. However, several failed to award their buy tenders for propane delivered from 2h Jan till 1h Feb as in lack of offers. Some readjust the program and try deferring into Feb purchase, otherwise might need to lower down run rate before running out of feedstock.

text: AMERICAS: A larger than expected 2.5 million barrel draw in Mt Belvieu did nothing to change the slide in Mt Belvieu values vs WTI. Mt Belvieu now lies below 35% WTI and inventories remain high at 91 million barrels, which has been keeping downward pressure on Mt Belvieu propane prices. With demand ramping up in the East the arb is wide open, and some recent softness in the freight market has led to very high netback values. Due to this we have seen the 4 week average of exports climb to 1.3 million barrels of propane per day. This trend looks set to continue as FOB buying interest from the US is very strong and every ton which can be, is being exported. The question now is will recently set FOB values of 20cpg become the new normal or will FOB values continue to increase? In South America, news of the winner of the 1.3 million ton Petro Ecuador tender is keenly being awaited.

There has been a rapid drop in rates over the last week. West Australia round is presently in the low 7s and c3 still not seeing any significant change in demand, with levels presently below USD 20 pmt. Period activity remains poor but expected to pick up once we get into the new year.

Freight rates in the Baltic and North Sea market seem to have found their feet around ws235 levels in the Nsea and ws190 levels ex Baltic, depending on what discharge options one needs. Stems loading very end year are currently being fixed with quite a lot of cargo activity taking place off the market. Although certain owners have expressed their willingness to put their clean ships into dirty trade, the tonnage list remains tight, and thus we still expect a firm market going into the new year. Cargo activity has been healthy in the Mediterranean and Black Sea this week and owners are pleased to see the market bounce back. Benchmark routes both ex Bsea and cross-Med have picked up about 25 ws-points, and at the time of writing TD19 is trading just above ws200. As transits through straits keep delaying and charterers are looking to cover their stems ex Bsea for second decade January, we expect the market to remain firm in the week to come.

The spread in owners’ earnings East vs West narrowed significantly with fixtures reported in the mid 110’s for Houston-Chiba. Together with a firming eastern shipping market we were getting close to a market equilibrium between the two sides of Suez. Then Aramco acceptances for January were finally announced last night with big delays. Some of the lifters were even asked to cancel or defer their liftings mainly due to upstream oil cuts. With more shipping length building from traders in 1H Jan these delays from Middle Eastern suppliers means that freight rates may come under pressure again. Same time it seems like the list of available re-lets in the West is decreasing in size, and as such we don’t expect the western shipping market to continue tumbling downward from here but rather flat out.

In the beginning of the week, the Suezmax market world-wide looked fairly balanced, and it looked like we would have a situation where owners would be keen to fix their ships before the holidays without putting too much pressure on the charterers. After a very busy Tuesday, tables have turned, and charterers are now the ones that need to fix their cargoes in time for Xmas. The rest of the week, we could see rates moving further with tight position lists in the Atlantic as well as MEG. Still quite a lot of cargoes left uncovered, so the rest of the year is looking really interesting.

What a rollercoaster ride! As last week drew to a close VLCC rates were on a downward trajectory with MEG/East testing the ws100 mark. However, things turned on a sixpence this week as January cargoes came into play. MEG/East went from ws100 to ws110 in one jump, and panic set in. Rates have since continued to climb, with owners now eying rates above ws120. MEG rates have also been supported by an influx of USG export cargoes, currently trading close to USD 12 million for China/Korea discharge. N.Sea/East has been correspondingly active, and ships discharging in the area have all but been absorbed. Wafr/East runs, however, has been surprisingly few and far between, although we’re seeing signs of a pickup in last decade of January. With a heaving Suezmax market there are few “get out of jail cards” at present, so the run up to Christmas is looking bright for the owning community.

Negative pressure across the board as the year come in for closing. In the Atlantic, scrap cargoes Cont/Emed paying around USD 11,000, while FH ex Bsea is paying in around USD 17,500. From USG, fh yields in the very low USD 20k's while ECSA trip out is trading around USD 13,000+300k gbb. Stronger downwards pressure in the East, especially in the northern parts. Despite sustained period of healthy earnings in the tanker chartering markets, it seems the upcoming seasonal holidays are gradually slowing down potential S&P interests. The firm spot markets continue to support Sellers quest for premiums over last dones in order to conclude any potential sales. Saying that, a couple of Buyers are willing to go and meet sellers expectations in order to secure prompt spot tonnage, particularly on the region 10 year and older vintages. This is well illustrated by the sale of the Zodiac controlled JUPITER SUN (ABT 115K DWT SASEBO 2007) which was sold at USD 28.7m. This is the second vessel sold by Zodiac to this buyer, worth noting that the Jupiter Sun is scrubber-fitted hence the premium against the same age sistership Virgo Sun which was sold last month. Regardless both levels represent a significant  jump from last concluded transactions.  With signs of ongoing negotiations for tanker units of similar age we expect a number of Buyers to take positions before year end. The majority of eyes are now however, focused on 2020, patiently waiting to assess the actual impact that the new regulatory constrains will have on the markets.    New revised benchmarks are being set in the Dry SnP markets with three deals being done across segments. The Capesize GOTIA (ABT 178K DWT SHANGHAI WAIGAOQIAO 2012) was sold at Usd 23m, the Kamsarmax MENARO (ABT 81K DWT JIANGSU JINLING 2016) achieved Usd 22.75m while the Dolphin 57’ design Supramax BAOJI (ABT 56K DWT XIAMEN 2013 C4x36 T) was sold at Usd 11.6m. These levels illustrate particularly well the subdued sentiment we have been witnessing from potential Bulker Buyers which, as indicated by the abovementioned sales, has driven values down by 5 to 10% since the summer.  This negative trend can also be demonstrated by the lack of Japanese built vessels changing hands with Sellers preferring to withdraw their units rather than following this downward direction.

We are only in the second week of December but with the reduced activity it feels as though the holiday mood may have already hit the market. As overall availability has increased slightly, spot rates continue to soften from recent highs although so far both headline levels and voyage economics remain broadly positive. Therefore, the delicate market balance continues to hold, and could yet tilt further towards charterers or swing back in owners’ favour,  especially if the build-up of vessels waiting to discharge at certain terminals leads to prolonged floating storage. There is more action on the long term side, with continuing newbuild tenders for charterers looking to secure slots prior to the anticipated ordering boom for Qatari and Mozambique volume, among others.    Maran has contracted two new MEGI 174k CBM vessels at DSME for delivery in 2022.

Following a busy period, rates firmed up end of last week. This week have continued in the much same pace with healthy fixing activity in the Atlantic and in the East with rates creeping up even further - all be it in more healthy increments which bears hope for less rate volatility, which in turn can make this upturn last. Tonnage lists however look ample, so for this to last we need to see continued fixing activity in all areas.

Mid-end last week the VLCC market was searching for direction with rates all over the place, but finally found a consensus this week, climbing quickly from ws95 to ws110-112.5 for MEG/eastbound cargoes before levelling off. Current levels are yielding earnings in the USD 80k’s per day when burning the more expensive compliant 0.5% VLSFO and upwards to USD 100k per day if scrubber fitted. Waiting days are thus equally expensive, moving the focus more on loading dates than pushing rates further. The West/East trade has picked up again as well with a number of US export cargoes, spreading the fleet and in turn supporting all load areas. Short term we expect the market to move sideways, with smaller discounts possible for good dates or longer voyages. The position list is thigh in the front end, but opens up as we move into January, hence the preference for longer employment.

EAST: There has been more activity on shipping lately in the East as traders have been clearing their December positions ahead of Xmas holidays. Last done deal was done at discount to Baltic for December loading, but going into January we expect the market to slowly turn. We are however still waiting for acceptance dates from Aramco, so one might have to wait until next week before seeing players move for January cargoes. Meanwhile there are also a couple of uncovered WAF cargos during 1H Jan that will draw some attention.  WEST: A handful of ships have been fixed so far in the West this week, with the release of a few WAF cargoes and also some activity in the US. Despite this, freight availability generally looks quite long for the second and third decades of Jan, and an increasing number of traders are showing relets as well. These things together should mean rates come under pressure; we would expect fixing to continue at low 120s Houston/Chiba or possibly even dip below 120 depending on waiting time.   On the other hand, the direction of rates will ultimately depend on the intensity with which charterers come out to fix. So far early movers for second decade Jan cargoes have enjoyed quite a large degree of choice, and this has been reflected in lower rates. We anticipate that there should be a substantial number of uncovered cargoes remaining in January, and if requirements all come at once this could lead to some resistance at the lower bound of what owners are willing to fix out at.

Rates are under pressure as end of the year is approaching. From last week West Australia to China freight is down 12%, presently marked USD 9.3 pmt and Tubarao to China is down 9%, presently marked USD 20.5 pmt, both still on a negative trend. Period activity remains low, with forward values remaining disappointing.

It’s been an exciting week in the North, with freight levels taking another leap with a solid upward correction in the Baltic and North Sea basin. The tonnage list remains tight even for next 10 days with cargoes hitting the market 3rd decade. Right now, the only direction is upwards as we expect owners to continue to put further pressure on those freight levels as we are moving into the festive season. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, a downwards correction has continued this week, except the last couple days where a pickup in cargo activities has resulted in the market flattening out rate-wise. A cross-Med voyage is still gaining owners a return around USD 50,000 pd on TCE, and delays in the straights is maintaining pressure on rates for voyages ex Black Sea. In the week to come we are expecting some ships to look to the North, and if cargo activity keep up we might see the Med/Bsea market bounce back.

text: MEG: Price shoots up this week amid robust demand. Jan CP has traded at $475, up by $30 WoW and butane is traded at $25 higher.  ADNOC has announced their Jan lifting with 7-10 days delays reportedly, and some ratio being changed from equal ratio to heavy propane.  Qatar Petroleum has issued a sale tender for a full propane loading 29/31th Jan, which ratio is very attractive to Chinese Petchem buyers.   FOB discussions are active with India and Indonesia buy tenders flowing in the market. One late Jan lifting equal ratio cargo was reported traded at Jan CP minus small discount, as Jan/Feb CP falls into over $25 backwardation. Whilst other earlier liftings, which can make within Jan arrival, are assessed at the value of at least $5-10 premium.    FAR EAST: Very heated market with bullish sentiment for whatever origins.  23kt propane for 2h Jan delivery have been traded from Jan FEI plus $13 Monday, to plus $29 on Thursday, which equates to Jan CP plus around $55. And off window still many buyers exploring 2h Jan arrival tons. Non-Us origin cargoes also in strong demand from not only SEA, but also China.  India IOC has issued tender to buy two equal ratio cargoes delivered in Jan and Indonesia Pertamina has also tender to buy 29/31th Jan 22/22 CFR into Kalbut.  Chinese importers are bidding aggressively for Jan and even Feb arrival propane. Earlier this week one Chinese importer managed to secure 23kt propane for 1h Jan arrival at Jan CP plus high 60s. Another SChina Petchem buyer has just closed tender to buy 23kt propane for 16-25th Jan delivery, which still in validity. Players assessed the cash premium will easily exceed $70 as front market too tight, against too many propane inquires from petchem rigid demand. One Chinese player is reported that awarded on the latest Sonangol tender for 7/9th Jan lifting heavy propane and has placed the propane parcel into EChina.

The tanker S&P market remains somewhat subdued in terms of completed transactions despite signs of  a number of buying enquiries.  Main reasons being a resilient bid offer spread  with the bellwethers having already placed their cards and others are now preferring to see how the beginning of 2020 plays out.  In what looks to be good timing, Advantage Tankers is reported to have acquired two 2009 Chinese built VLCC’s for usd 38 mill each.  We understand this is a deal done some time back which explains the low price, even allowing for Chinese built discount.  Teekay starting to clear out its older suezmaxes with the 2003 HHI built ISKMATI SPIRIT gone for usd 19.3 mill.  This follows Teekay’s recent sale of same age ASKHINI SPIRIT to Chemnav at same level.  The LR1 GULF CASTLE built 2009 HMD is in play with offer reportedly seen in excess of usd 18 mill.    Steady flow of bulker sales with a softening undertone on values.  Chinese buyers taking advantage of the huge supply of vessels for sale.

text: MEG: Qatar Petroleum has released Jan lifting schedule with a few delays being reported, mainly due to early-month nominations.  Swap price has ridden a roller coaster this week, with Jan CP being traded from $431 in mid-week to $444 at the time of writing.  End Dec lifting FOB was traded at small premium on Jan CP, and sellers with Jan lifting Fobs also targeted at premium level, especially seeing robust demand into Asia in front amid softening freight.   FAR EAST:  1H Jan CFR Asia Market appear tight, either US or Non-Us origin.  Off window 23kt US-origin propane for 1h Jan delivery is traded at Jan FEI plus $13-14. Discussion for similar cargo delivered in 2h Jan is slightly cheaper but sellers’ ideas hover above teens on FEI link as well.  Non-US origin supply for 1h Jan arrival is short as well. One SChina PDH user has secured 23kt propane for 1h Jan delivery at Jan CP plus mid 60s via tender, while another Major also purchased a full propane for mid/2h Jan delivery at Jan CP plus 60ish.   However not every buyer is that lucky to cover their demand. Till the time of writing, Indonesia Pertamina was reported not covering the 22/22 demand for 1-6th Jan delivery; One Echina petchem user was said that not cover their prompt demand for 23kt propane delivered from 2h Dec into 1h Jan; even Taiwan CPC tender for 11/11 delivered during 1-10th Jan was not heard awarded either. Some Chinese importers has reprogramed and tried to defer their demand into 2h Jan arrival. Apart from spot inquiries, term discussion are still going on. Mid-week one Schina importer was said to cancel their term inquires for 11/11 monthly as the received offers not satisfactory.

text: AMERICAS: Winter market is here and Arb is popping. As stated before the NWE and Eastern markets have come to rely on the US as the principal supplier and as a result the Arb is, and will remain firmly open for the foreseeable future. It is even seems to have evolved in to what economist like to call a Goldy Locks scenario,  where it is neither too hot nor too cold,  but just right. With today’s economics , terminal operators are making money, ship owners are making money,  and traders seem happier than they have for a few years. These markets never seem to last but for now it is hard to see how and when it will end. In the domestic market propane inventories drew 1.7 million barrels on the week which was in line with industry expectations. There is enough propane in the US to support cold weather and strong exports and hence we do not expect prices to blow out either way.

We are in the last month of the final quarter of 2019 and what was predicted to be a robust Q4 2019 has not exceeded Owners’ expectations. Ship Owners enjoyed a mini-boom from early October, however the firm sentiment was short-lived as the market has moderated in the last few weeks. The lacklustre performance of the product market, subdued shipping demand for the winter and an increase in tonnage availability, not just from Independent Owners but also sublets, have contributed to the sentiment change.  The Atlantic Basin kept some balance with prompt cargoes and limited availability, but Owners with ships in the Pacific may feel the pinch as we see rates slip below six- to high five-digit levels due to the lack of activity and cargo demand in the region. However, it’s not all gloomy as fixing levels are still healthy and for most Owners, “in the money”. The concern is more for the post winter season next year where many, including us, anticipate a slightly more challenging environment.  Utilization is key for those months and could mean more inclination from Owners to work competitive rates now for longer duration to brace the shouldering period. That said, rate ideas would need to connect.  For the longer term charters, the future looks active for Owners as a good handful of Oil Majors, Trading Houses and Projects were seen issuing tender documents to secure vessels for delivery between 2022-2025.  On the newbuilding front, Samsung announced 8 orders - believed to be linked to Mozambique LNG - and more orders from them are expected.

The positive sentiment from the past week turned more sideways this week. We see USG – USEC still have healthy demand and ships getting paid premiums. Tess 58 mv Teal Bulker was fixed USD 25,000 Aps SW pass to WC India with petcoke. Another Supramax was rumoured to be fixed USD 23,000 to Japan. And strong USD 17,000 was paid on Ultramax fro tct from USG to Med The rest of the Atlantic were rather quiet and positive expectations from owners were fading away. Bsea and East med market didn’t provide enough demand to sustain strong rates from previous week. We have seen vessels from West Med ballasting either towards continent or USG direction.  The ECSAM market is stable except we see slightly less orders on the Far Eastern routes.  Ultramax for trips to Cont/Med went USD 14,000 level . Supramax rates for trips to Singapore/Japan to $13,000/d + $300,000 BB. India ocean and Safrica market remain calm. Supramax delivery Safrica to India was fixed USD10,500 plus 150,000 BB. The Far Eastern market remained stable with positive sentiment.

Positive sentiment all over, with especially the Atlantic strengthening. The pace was strong at the beginning of the week, but calmed down and settled at better levels mid-week. The Pacific market has also been solid, with Australian coal being the main driver behind it. A TA round voyage pays owners around USD 12,00 per day. A fronthaul from the continent yields around the USD 17,000's. In the Pacific basin, a round voyage pays owners around USD 10,000 per day. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 1326 points, 215 up since last week.

As expected rates in the Baltic and North Sea market have picked up this week with the North Sea being the main driving force for the upward pressure. This is because the tonnage list is tight for North Sea cargoes loading up to mid-month. Currently ships open in the Baltic are picking off the stems loading in the 14th - 20th December window. However, the cargo program coming out of the Baltic in the 3rd decade fixing window looks healthy, and therefore we expect the market to remain firm going forwards. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea however, we have seen a downwards correction in rates this week since cargo activity has not been strong enough to prevent tonnage building up in the area. Across the board it has been a quiet week on the cargo side, and we have seen re-lets covering the few cargoes around. In the week to come we will keep an eye on further delays in Straits, and it is expected that activity will pick up somewhat as charterers will want to cover their program through the holiday season.

Slight improvements at generally healthy levels as spot fundamentals are satisfactory for the big ships. Average daily earnings up some 11 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 25k - the main driver again being high iron ore volumes traded. The west Australia/China trade is seeing a pre-christmas boost with all miners active and subsequent pacific roundvoyage levels up 13 pct to USD 30k for standard 180000-tonners. So far more modest on the crucial Brazil/China route, where miners and operators are busy picking the very few remaining december loaders at steadily improving numbers - China-Brazil-China round value up 6 pct to come in at USD 24k/day. Bunker delivery delays and final preparations for 1 jan 2020 IMO regulations expected to add further upward pressure. Period activity picking up as spot and ffa support more forward confidence, with recent conclusions including 180000 dwt built 2013 fetching the equivalent of arnd usd 18k for abt 12 months basis Far East prompt delivery.

Earnings are still around US$70.000 a day, but with activity slowed down along with London Christmas Week, activity will have to pick up severely for owners to see a bounce back to the 3 digits. A tightening positionlist in the east, and cargo Meg count lagging might see owners turning it around next week, as more 3rd decade December cargoes will surface.

Owners are looking to make up the lost ground from earlier this year and will not settle with last done in what has become a firm market in the Atlantic.

text: MEG: Saudi Aramco has set Dec Propane CP at $440 and Butane CP at $455, up by $10 respectively, which some players reckon above expectations. Therefore, the contango structure into Jan has changed and Jan CP slides to $438. It’s still early to judge how will Jan CP turns, but we believe the Jan swap will edge up, as forthcoming winter demand will lend support fundamentally.    FAR EAST:  Front market appears to be strong this week. Off window Propane for 2h Jan delivery was reported traded at Jan FEI plus high single prem to $10. Dec FEI/CP enlarged to 50ish this week and Jan FEI/CP maintains at high 30s to $40. The unexpected explosion in Texas has roused some concerns on Jan delivery so far limited effect being shown, but players are still closely monitoring the situation.  Apart from window, market is floating with all tenders. Indonesia Pertamina was reported to award their last tender for three evenly split cargos delivered from early Jan to late Jan, price ranging from high 40s to high 50s depends on delivery date. And they’ve still inquiring via new tender for another early Jan delivery cargo, which result is yet to know.  India IOC is reported to award their buy tender for 2h Jan delivery equal ratio cargo at Jan CP plus 50ish.  Taiwan FPCC also secured an early Jan delivery full propane at Jan MOPJ minus around $40 via tender. Other Chinese importers are actively seeking supply for next year via term tender or private discussions. Cash premium negotiation is in line with freight as of non-Us origin request, but more players are keen to discussing FEI link as well, instead of 100% CP link. On spot side, importers start to explore Jan cargos especially 1h Jan arrival, with one SChina PDH user tendered to buy 6-15th Jan delivery propane.

The sales activity is dominated by older vessels, both wet and dry.  Recent bulker sales reaffirm a softening in dry values across the board and there is certainly no lack of vessels for sale.  Several bulker deals are in the making with varying reports that AZUL FORTUNA 204k dwt built 2005 Universal is close to being sold for high usd 15 mill. If confirmed, this will be a notch down from the sale of one year older sister AZUL INTEGRA a month ago at usd 16 mill.  Tanker values are in positive trajectory but we have yet to see any very modern units being transacted.  Increased buying interest now also for LR1’s with reports that GULF CASTLE 75k dwt built 2009 HMD is under negotiation after being inspected by up to 10 buyers before inviting offers earlier this week.

text: AMERICAS: Happy Thanksgiving! A lower than expected draw of 683,000 barrels was seen in US inventories for the week ended November 22nd. Although this was expected to be bearish, Mt Belvieu now lies at 41% WTI. The highest level since March of this year. This has not dampened the arb which is wide. Supported by strength in both CIF ARA and FEI. The affects of the fire at Port Neches on LPG exports from Nederland are yet to be seen. Nederland exports range between 6 and 8 VLGCs per month and for the moment the Neches river channel is closed. Any export tons lost would further support the arb. January cargoes have traded and high single digit terminalling fees. The question is was it a pre holiday rush, or are we heading back to double digit terminalling fee premiums?

WEST: The past week has been muted in the West, presumably as a consequence of players having fixed far in advance previously. With that said, some players have started to think about January fixing and could be keen to clear their requirements as the holiday season approaches. Looking ahead, some vessels are scheduled to go into dry-docking for retrofitting of scrubbers and special surveys, and this could have an influence on rates in the months to come.   EAST:  It has been another uneventful week for shipping in the East so far. We are generally seeing more open ships for next fixing window i.e. December, also from traders with extra length, and this continue to add pressure to freight rates. Last done deal in the market was done at USD 72 Baltic, and time of writing there is only one other cargo from an Indian major being worked.

The headline story this week has been the auction sale of six year old VLCC “BRIGHTOIL GEM.”  This was an online auction sale (local “Ebay”) in China and we understand only two buyers participated.    This is clearly a bargain for the buyers, our read being they are USD 10 mill in the money after DD and BWTS completed.  We fail to understand the commercial logic behind  this deal and we do not consider this a bench-mark sale due to the sales process. Most other deals coming to light this week are yesterday’s news.  The only significant deal concluded at today’s numbers is Zodiac selling aframax VIRGO SUN 115k dwt blt 2007 Sasebo at USD 26 mill.  In our book this equates to low 30’s for a suezmax of similar age.  Zodiac as always proving to be an agile player willing to take a profit when possible.  Zodiac purchased the vessel in October 2013 for low 25’s.  Dry bulk values are falling on the back of a growing pool of sales candidates. Kamsarmax KM TOKYO built 2010 Sanoyas is rumoured sold at high 15’s which is certainly on the low side of expectations.

Sentiment softened throughout the week as a lack of requirement was felt in both basins. Despite the lack of activity, the ideas being discussed suggest that expectations are being lowered in terms of what rates can be achieved.  More tonnage became available both prompt and into the New Year in the Pacific and while the Atlantic and Middle East remain tight, there’s still not enough requirement in the market to add much positivity to the rates. Unsold volume still lingers in both Basins, and with muted demand, it seems to push product prices down. That combined with an increase in tonnage availability, have reduced the Bullish sentiment the market held not too long ago. One continuing uncertainty that may support tonnage providers is the prospect of floating storage – we’ve seen more floaters discharging recently but with inventories remaining high we might not have seen the end of floating storage. That said, with the declining sentiment we’re currently being exposed to, the risk is that we may see rates softening as the fixing window moves closer and closer to the New Year, unless we see a sudden surge in requirements. Term tender activity is high, but no large LNG newbuilding orders were reported this week and prices remain stable.

VLCC rates bottomed out in the mid ws70’s middle of last week for MEG/eastbound voyages, and have not looked back since. The going rate is currently estimated in the mid ws90’s for modern ships, with normal discounts to be had for older/restricted units. The Atlantic basin is following the same pattern, with even ws100 paid for a Wafr/China voyage, albeit including a premium for North China discharge. Tonnage availability in the area is thinning, to an extent a result of IMO 2020 low sulphur requirements coming into play for those longer voyages. Bunker prices for normal 380 cts is on a downward trajectory, thereby sugaring TCE results further for those units having installed scrubber. Further upward potential is evident in all areas, with 3 digits rates more than likely within the not too distant future.

Nervous and softening, with average daily earnings down 10 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 18,500 as Brazil iron ore exports again fail to live up to expectations and Atlantic coal is in limbo. Although hardly significant in relative terms, a 25 pct drop in transatlantic earnings has considerable effect on sentiment. Fronthaul volumes however expected to increase, and with a short list of ballasters towards ECSAM there is quite some optimism amongst players. Far East volumes are stable and just enough to withstand further negativity, the Dampier/Qingdao conference trade hovering around USD 8.75 pmt and Pacific rounds for modern 180,000-tonners just a fragment down to pay a present USD 22-22,500. FFA's give little support for considerable period activity, and recent long-term conclusions appear limited to 177,000 dwt, built 2006, done for about 2 years at USD 15k or touch more.

The Suezmax market worldwide is picking up now. USG market getting more active and with not much available, safe tonnage, they would start looking at ballasters from Continent. Above 7 mill has been paid EC Mexico to Japan, which again put pressure on an already busy West Africa market. Then we have delays in the Turkish straits putting pressure on the Black Sea and Med market. In the East, we have seen a boost in activity this week, and at the moment all markets are pushing in the same direction, and we expect the market to keep improving for the rest of the week.

Last week rates in the North Sea and Baltic saw a sharp increase in rates from last done levels on a couple of fixtures. This week the market looks more balanced as there is more available tonnage for the next fixing window.  Despite a small downward correction in rates, activity is still quite good and TC earnings are about USD 70,000 pd. We could see a further downward correction on rates for the next week until if will firm again. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, we have seen the recent amount of cargoes coming into the market satisfy the relatively healthy tonnage list. Delays in the Straits combined with activity on the cargo side has given the market a boost and rates have picked up around 80 worldscale points on bench mark routes. TD19 is currently trading above ws200. As a lot of prompt ships have been taken out of play, we expect the remaining owners to take a stand in order to keep an upwards pressure on rates in the week to come, unless Suezmaxes cap the market.

Despite a slow start, demand has picked up throughout the week as it seems like the market has reached its floor. This has been especially evident from the volume of fresh requirements from USG as well as from increased demand from Australia and the North Pacific. Currently, a TA round voyage pays owners high USD 7,000 per day. A fronthaul from the Continent yields around the USD 17,000. In the Pacific, a round voyage pays owners around USD 8,000 per day. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 1,127 points, 43 down since last week.

WEST: The West has been fairly quiet this week. Some ships are beginning to run late for early Dec laycans. Going forward, it would not be unreasonable to expect further slippage given how ahead of time fixing has been happening so far. A likely consequence of this is an increased probability that players will look to optimise by way of vessel swaps where possible.   With regards to freight rates, the recent flow of ships from US to East via the Cape of Good Hope has left vessel availability relatively shorter in the West. Combined with the fact that there are a number of ships which will be retrofitting scrubbers in the next few months, rates should remain strong into the early 2020 fixing period.   EAST: In the East there were a few fixtures this week following saudi Acceptances. Rates have come off slightly, and a few additional trader relets remain. With that said, more players are looking to swap vessels with others in order to minimise expensive waiting time. In terms of delays in Eastern disports, things seem to be generally running on time at time of writing.

The Suezmax market worldwide is picking up now. USG market getting more active and with not much available, safe tonnage, they would start looking at ballasters from Continent. Then we have delays in the Turkish straits putting pressure on the Black Sea and Med market. In the East, we have seen a boost in activity this week, and at the moment all markets are pushing in the same direction, and we expect the market to keep improving for the rest of the week.

text: AMERICAS: Some bitterly cold weather in the US and  late season crop drying led to a higher than expected 3.4 million barrel draw in US inventories. This, as expected, was bullish Mt Belvieu prices which now stand at 40% WTI. Rather than closing the arb this rise in Mt Belvieu dragged FEI and CIF ARA prices up with it maintaining a healthy level. This has kept January FOB discussion active and being worked well in advance of the Christmas break. US inventories are 12.43 million barrels higher than the same week last year. Exports for the week were 1.362 million barrels per day, remain very high which points our view that the world has grown to depend on US exports and we expect this to continue at least through the Winter.

An active VLCC market last week, with most fixtures concluded under the radar as the soft trend continues. The MEG count is now moving up towards 135, and with charterers already looking early December loading. Atlantic showing signs of more activity, but at this stage it will most likely dampen the soft trend rather than it is turning around. Most of the tanker market participants are out in Dubai for Bahri Reception and we will not be surprised if by Friday more ships has disappeared under the radar at last done levels.

Following a relatively slow week in the Baltic and North Sea market, we have seen an upwards correction in rates the last few days. As the tonnage list is tightening and there still are cargoes in the market yet to be covered in the 20-25 window ex Baltic, we expect the market to stay firm in the week to come. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, the market has also bounced back this week. Much to the excitement of owners we have seen an active market with an upward trend in rate levels which has resulted in benchmark routes ex Bsea and cross-Med picking up around 20 points on worldscale. Although we still see a healthy tonnage list, we expect the market to stay firm in the week to come due to the sufficient amount of cargoes currently coming into the market.

The Atlantic Suezmax market finally hit bottom this week and even bounced back some points. Some charterers ex West Africa were holding back a bit too long and ended up being above ws100 for Wafr/UKCM. Position list in West Africa is looking short for November dates, and owners finally feeling a bit more bullish after two really slow weeks. One thing that also could help this market going forward is the fog has arrived the Turkish Straits. This, and expected increasing cargo activity, could point towards a positive market the next weeks. In the East, on the other hand, the market is looking really slow. Hopefully a bullish Wafr market could make owners ballast some ships, but until then the we expect the East-market to remain slow.

The intensity of the October market seems to have eased off as we arrive here in mid-November. New vessel availabilities have been observed, rather on regular basis in the East. Outright availability of LNG vessels in the West are still few and far between, but FOB/DES swaps seems to solve it for now. In the Pacific, there seem to be more LNG vessels available than there are spot chartering opportunities, for the moment.   We are now perceived to have come “back to normal” since the elimination of the US/China sanctions effects. However, many are of the opinion that current levels are where the market should be if the recent sanctions did not happen. This have led to speculation of a possible “double peak” as the anticipated winter activity has not gone full blown as yet, but this view have been disputed with the claim of soft demand for LNG imports in China for these upcoming months. For certain, the LNG shipping market have been more volatile recently as weather and geo-political movements or announcements could lead to tremendous shift in sentiments.   No newbuilding orders or ship sales have been reported this week. However, a few ships are being circulated in the SnP market.

A poor week across all borders, with tonnage building up and lack of fresh orders. The Baltic Supramax Index (BSI) now reaching level below 800. The period market almost disappears from the focus, as owners simply not ready to face the low rates going forward. Atlantic market was falling steady with limited amount of fresh enquiry. Ultramax loading Norway to China reported to be fixed USD 19,000, some said it was less. Ultramax loading scrap in Baltic to Turkey was fixed at USD 10,000. East Med market was under pressure with lots of prompt tonnage building up, TCT with clinker from Turkey to West Africa was trading at USD 10,000 mark. Fronthaul from Black Sea to Asia was trading close to USD 15,000 on Supramax. The market in East Coast South America followed the trend. Rates were down to USD 12,000 delivery Brazil to Med. 61,000 dwt ship was reported fixed basis delivery Santos trip redelivery Singapore-Japan range at USD 12,000 plus USD 200,000 BB.  US Gulf was slow and the gap in the rates remained wide. In Asia rates were sliding further and we see Supra fixing USD 6,000 for round voyage from China via Indonesia.

EAST This week has generally been very quiet thus far and only real activity on shipping has been from the Indian majors. The Baltic seems pretty balanced for now and last done deal reported at USD 77 pmt.  We are still awaiting the December Aramco acceptances which ultimately should set next direction on freight going forward.  WEST This week the Western market seemed to be catching its breath, with rates cooling slightly. Most likely, this is partly due to the market fixing too far ahead and partly to a weakening of netbacks relative to recent weeks. That being said, position lists now look very short for the final fixing period of 2019, with a handful of uncovered cargoes expected in the market. We anticipate West-East freight rates to strengthen again as a consequence.

On Wednesday last week, the market for the West Australia-China route c5 traded at USD 9.00, but dropped significantly on Thursday and Friday down to 8.05. However, this week the sentiment changed again and we are currently back to USD 9.00 for this route. The reason for the comeback is simply because of more West Australia activity and all the majors being present, but also due to the Brazil segment waking up picking up tonnage positioned for both basins. The future relay on continued activity from Brazil, and with a fairly low ballaster list this segment can potentially push the basket towards USD 30,000.

text: MEG: Swap market value edged up this week. Dec Propane rebounded to $415, and Dec FEI/CP spread has further enlarged from mid 30s last week to mid/high 40s. With acceptance for Dec lifting being released, players starting to engage actively in FOB discussion, but bids are at discount level as of soaring freight.   KPC issued a sale tender to offer a 14/15 Dec lifting 22/22, the result is yet to know at the time of writing.   Qatar Petroleum has officially announced a ten-year agreement with Wanhua Chemical to supply roughly 800,000 tons LPG annually. Just in last Nov, Wanhua also signed a ten-year purchase agreement to ADNOC to secure 1 million tonne LPG per year.   FAR EAST:  Front window is strengthening this week. During mid-week, 23kt Propane for 2h Dec delivery is traded at Dec FEI plus $6. As Dec FEI/CP keep widening, the US/Non-Us origin spread has rapidly narrowing down. We might soon see players deliver non Us origin into Japan/Korea range instead of swarming into China.   Spot inquiries from China remains slim, compare to recent term discussion. One EChina PDH issued a mini term tender to secure 23/0 or 46/0 in Jan and Feb but later withdrew as offers not attractive. One 11/11 for 1h delivery into Schina was reported done at Dec CP plus around $60 only.   Indonesia Pertamina was reported to awarded their tender for a equal ratio split cargo delivered mid Dec at Dec CP plus high 40s, which is roughly Dec CP flattish or small discount on FOB netback.   CPC was reported awarded their buy tender at Dec CP plus low mid 60s for the purchase of one 11/11 delivered in 2h Dec. And they’ve issued a FOB/DES term tender to swap a volume of 176k-264k AG FOB cargos for 176k cargos Des into Taiwan. Considering 20 Cal freight level, there might be limited parties can commit such.

text: AMERICAS: Cold weather coupled with strong crop drying demand has pushed up domestic propane demand, and as result weekly inventories drew 2. 5 million barrels. A rise in motor gasoline and the blending of butane into gasoline has pushed up domestic butane demand. These factors combined with strong exports have allowed domestic prices to increase substantially over the last month. Now the question is will these price increases  close the arb or will international prices keep pace. If we were asking this question in March , we might say no,  but in November our answer is we expect International prices to keep pace.

A very slow start to the week with little activity reported and a few European holidays disrupting trade to some extent. The demand-side was slow with few firm cargoes entering the market, and the market has been in the red in both hemispheres throughout the week. Fewer ECSA-ballasters than have been seen in several months may be a positive sign, but the activity has also slowed down and is expected to continue doing so going forward. Activity in the Black Sea has also dampened significantly. Currently, a TA round voyage pays owners high USD 7,000 per day, with a couple thousand in premium for short, Baltic runs. A fronthaul from the Continent yields around the high USD 17,000's. In the Pacific, a round voyage pays owners around low USD 8,000 per day, down almost 2,000 since last week. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 1170 points, 215 down since last week.

The chase is on for mid to late 2000 built aframaxes with several 2007/2008 built units rumoured being committed in the Usd 26-28 mill range. If confirmed, this is approximately a Usd 2m appreciation in value since last done. Early 2000 built Vlcc’s are still in play with clients of MMT, Singapore leading the charge with 4 vessels bought in the past couple of months all basis prompt delivery. Signs of ongoing negotiations suggest we should see further similar units change hands in the near future.   Dry s&p markets continue to be muted this week with an ever increasing uncertainty stemming from falling freight markets which coupled with an increasing number of sales candidates are making it difficult for sales to materialise. Values are therefore subject to downwards pressures.  The s&p situation for very modern both bulkers and tankers is very similar - the bid/ask spread is too wide to result in any tangible deals. The returning question is clearly which buyers shall pay up for such very modern assets. Most of the public listed companies are very vocal in that no further capex is in the cards, now it’s all about returning dividend to shareholders. Add to this that many PE funds are looking to exit, we are left with the backbone of  cash-rich private owners looking to extract value from a potential modern tonnage acquisition. However most of these have already placed their bets at prices well below today’s asking prices and are quite happy to see the market play out.

The 2007 Japanese owned VLCC “PHOENIX VANGUARD” did, as expected, receive several offers this week and was quickly sold.  The price is reported to be in the usd 41.5 – 42.5 mill range.  Whilst this is 8-10% up on the previous deal which failed, it comes in the lower end of our expectations considering the original deal was concluded back in June and the spot market has since then settled at very healthy numbers; albeit considerably less than the initial spiky ones.  Early 2000 built crude tankers remain in demand and sellers able to give prompt delivery will be able to see new higher levels.  Several such deals are in the making. However sellers should be cautioned that the number of determined buyers is fairly thin on the ground and now may prove the right window of opportunity to exit; come Q1 and Q2 the number of older sales candidates will for sure increase.  It’s all about prompt delivery and a realistic runway for buyers to make a decent return.  The dry s&p market is lacking direction with many buyers taking a wait-and-see attitude.  The freight market is not lending support to the case and buyers are gaining the upper hand.There’s a very large number of ships for sale across the board, albeit few very modern ones.

LNG rate market phrenic seems to be slowly easing, as the effect of US/China sanctions eliminates, however there are still a couple of upcoming requirements that need coverage especially in the East. Charterers looking at securing a vessel today for late November or December loadings, still have to pay six-digit figures as prompt availability remains tight. Looking at the spot availability going forward it is expected that a few vessels that caught the Oct-Nov arbitrage will start redelivering. That might put pressure on rates. However, we might see some of those vessels looking at business West of Suez as West to East arbitrage is very slowly reviving. In the Atlantic, prompt availability has dried up, however a few opportunistic sublets appear here and there from portfolio players, as FOB cargo optimisations look like a preferred option for them creating some potential length, but with limited flexibility. Despite high tender activity, newbuilding prices remain stable for now....

Another week of dropping Supramax rates across the basins. In the Pacific, Indo/China fixing around low USD 8,000 with Singapore delivery, while similar trade to WC India paying in the mid USD 8,000. From the Indian Ocean, South Africa/WC India paying around high USD 11k+180k gbb, and from MEG to WC India ships fixed around low USD 12,000. In the Atlantic, Black Sea to ECI/Bangladesh paying around USD 20,000, while trips from Continent to Brazil are fixing in the high USD 7,000. From ECSA fh's paying around 13k+300k gbb, and TA to Continent/Mediterranean paying in the low USD 12,000.

A week in the red with a rapid weakening of the BPI in both basins. Both the Atlantic and the Pacific continued to fall significantly, but the rates in the East have been slightly less affected by the softening. A TA round voyage currently pays owners around USD 9,500 per day, while a fronthaul from the Continent yields around USD 20,000. In the Pacific, a round voyage pays owners around USD 10,000 per day. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 1385 points, 189 down since last week.

In the North Sea and Baltic market, rates have come off even more from last week’s levels, and we still expect rates to soften further in the week to come. This is mainly due to a lack of cargo activity, and that most of the cargoes that are available have been covered on relets. The number of available vessels is building up, and even if activity level is increased it will take some time for the market to gain firm momentum again. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, the tonnage list is still long, and activity the last week has been insufficient in having any positive effect on rates. TD19 is currently trading sub-100 levels on world scale. Although we have seen some delays in straits, this has still not had a positive impact on freight levels just yet, and we expect the market remain soft in the week to come.

This week has been markedly more quiet than last week in the West, although there have been a handful of fixtures. Rates have come off marginally, with fixing now being done slightly below USD 130 H/C. There are a few possible reasons which could explain this cooling in rates. Among them is the emergence of more economical trader relets, netbacks coming in due to stronger Mont Belvieu pricing and fewer freight inquiries due to the fixing period in question simply being so far ahead.   In the East, things were even more quiet, although it is expected that activity will increase after the release of ADNOC acceptances early next week.

The VLCC market has been surprisingly slow this week, with only the odd cargo being drip-fed into the market - and all areas have been correspondingly inactive. As a consequence, rates have dropped, albeit less than previous in similarly quiet spells, with latest benchmark standing at ws85 for MEG/China on modern tonnage, an oil company relet at that. The third decade MEG November program has hardly been touched, so optimism persists within the owning community for another 35-40 cargoes still to be covered. Albeit widened the last few days, the position list still appears balanced when it comes to modern tonnage, although there’s an oversupply of restricted ship, old and/or ex d/d etc., hanging like a cloud over the market, as and if workable.

Spot market saw some improvements in the beginning of the week with c5 levels increasing to mid 9 pmt levels, but soon to drop back to sub 9s, more or less in line with last week’s levels. The demand from Brazil is limited, and freight rates are coming off on the c3 route accordingly. Overall, five TC average dropped 13% from last week to present USD 22,217. Forward values are taking a further hit with next year trading below USD 15,000 level at the time of writing, discouraging owners from fixing period.

text: MEG: Despite the crude rise, the Dec CP plunged to $398 at the time of writing, whilst Dec FEI/CP spread fluctuates from $29 to $36. QP has released their Dec lifting nomination with some delays by 5 days or so being reported. Baltic continues to rise until mid-week stabilizes at $75ish. This being said, few fixtures happening in MEG and the soaring freight has erodes buyer’s appetite to explore FOB spot.   FAR EAST: This week front market is weakening. Propane for 1H Dec delivery was traded at Dec FEI plus $5 and dropped further to $3 reportedly. 2h Dec also traded in similar level earlier this week, with slight backwardation only. Some importers are closely monitoring year-end stock and avoiding over purchase.   Off window there are some traders’ inquires for prompt delivery into India and Indonesia which supports butane price a bit, despite the bids are in discounts on FOB netbacks. One reason being is less butane from US available as arbitrage window closed now, therefore players has turned to explore AG origin.   Other than such, last Fri one South China PDH user has awarded their buy tender for 23/0 1st decade delivery in Dec at Dec CP plus around $60, and they’ve issued another buy tender for similar cargo delivered in mid Dec. And one more propane cargo reported sold into North China at Nov CP plus around/below $70, which equates to CP minus mid-single digit discount. Other Chinese also exploring heavy propane cargos in 2h Dec delivery. CPC issued buy tender for 11/11 or 0/11 delivered in late Dec, result is yet to know.

In the Atlantic, all markets have really taken a dive this week. Rates in West Africa is coming off in chunks as position-list has been building up for a while and cargo-activity has not picked up at all. USG exports are still quite slow and the only area with decent activity has been Med and Black Sea. Unfortunately, not even close to enough to prevent this decline. In the East, we see the same story. A long tonnage list, and not enough cargoes, and with West Africa coming off there no places to hide for owners. We expect to be close to the bottom soon, but it will take some time to turn this around.

As a consequence, rates have dropped, albeit less than previous in similarly quiet spells, with latest benchmark standing at ws85 for MEG/China on modern tonnage, an oil company relet at that. The third decade MEG November program has hardly been touched, so optimism persists within the owning community for another 35-40 cargoes still to be covered. Albeit widened the last few days, the position list still appears balanced when it comes to modern tonnage, although there’s an oversupply of restricted ship, old and/or ex d/d etc., hanging like a cloud over the market, as and if workable.

text: AMERICAS: A surprise build of 300,000 barrels was seen in US inventories. The hope that this would be bearish for Mt Belvieu prices was short-lived. Mt Belvieu continued to increase through this build due to cold weather biting on the East Coast and in the Midwest. This strength in Mt Belvieu which now lies at 38% of WTI has been steadily eroding the arb. Help will need to come from price strength in demand markets. For now FOB trades have quietened down. This is due to the shift form double digit terminalling fee discussions for full propane FOB cargoes, down to just above cancellation levels, around 6cpg. Traditionally the onset of US winter is early than in Europe and the East. Now the question is when will it get cold in those demand markets?

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Saudi Aramco has set the November Propane CP at $430 and Butane CP at $445, each up by $10 from October price.  The Propane CP is in line with latest swap value, yet some end users/importers reckon it is higher than expectation. Also, the spread between Propane and Butane is wider than latest trade which was at $10.  At the time of writing, December CP is traded at $410, $20 less than the just announced November CP. December FEI/CP spread is traded at around $35, partly driven by the sustained strong freight.  Qatar Petroleum is reported to have awarded their December lifting of a full cargo Propane at December CP plus a small digit premium to a Chinese Major.   FAR EAST: A flurry of deals was concluded in the window this week. 23kt Propane for 2h November delivery was traded at November FEI plus $14, and one equal ratio cargo for end November delivery into Chiba was done at November CP plus $77, which equates to November CP plus $5 on FOB netback.  Off window discussions on Propane for December delivery are also active with a few trades concluded at December FEI plus mid-high single digit during mid-week. However, the levels currently under discussion are weakening.  One S.China PDH operator issued a buy tender to secure a 1-10 December delivery of 23/0, the result is yet to be known by the time of writing.  Other Chinese importers are cautious and want to think twice before taking spot cargoes in December before CP is set, importers also se sluggish demand from domestic customers combined with surplus supply from refineries.  Nevertheless, importers still expect strong rising demand and are starting inquire for next year’s term supplies but some discussions are still pending with uncertainties on US-China tariffs and strong freights in 2020.
