WEST Much of this week has been fairly slow-moving, with the US out for Labour Day on Monday. In the West, there has been a relatively consistent number of relets for much of the week. These should result in some downwards pressure on Houston/Chiba rates. With that being said, position lists have begun to tighten towards the end of this week as the number of vessel inquiries for early October has risen. Given that there are severe delays in the East and limited availability for northbound Panama Canal passage, we perceive the conditions to be right for a possibly quick tightening of freight going forward.  EAST  In the East this week, the delays at disports which were a consequence of typhoons have continued, making it difficult for players to schedule their ships both in the East and the West. There were a handful of fixtures for end September which absorbed vessel relets and were most likely the basis for a falling Baltic. Following these fixtures, the bulk of vessels remain in the hands of the major owners - it will be interesting to see what effect this has on rates moving forward.   It is also worth noting that further delays in the East could be possible as eastern bunker barges are cleaned to prepare them for loading low Sulphur fuel oil ahead of IMO 2020.

Suezmaxes in the West lost some of its momentum last week. West Africa came back down to ws60, and even though its decent activity, there is still some overhang of tonnage that need to be cleared for anything to happen. On the positive side, Suezmaxes in the Med/Bsea and in the USG have been busy and could possible help owners push the market going into next week. In the East, owners still waiting for more action. The 30-day tonnage count is on average, and market seems pretty steady now after dropping some points early this week.

Ultramax was fixed to Singapore-Japan at USD 18,000 plus USD 800,000 ballast bonus. The Continent and the Mediterranean see good flow of requirements. Indo RV fixing in USD 15,000, 58,000-tonner open China fixed a trip via Indonesia, redelivery China, at USD 16,000.

text: AMERICAS: After a brief quiet spell,  demand for FOB cargos has picked up once again. For October, the 4 US Gulf terminals are sold out and any spot possibilities will have to come from the resale of third party barrels. The Enterprise expansion barrels have yet to show up and this is causing us to ask why. Is there a problem the company is not discussing or is it just taking a bit longer than expected.  In the domestic market, propane is holding up above the 30 percent versus WTI  level despite very high inventories. We believe this has to do with vast amounts of propane being bought to hedge the exports but we do not expect this to continue. With this weeks build of 2.9 million barrels, we expect propane prices to fall.

The market has been trending sideways since Monday, with a bit less activity than the end of last week. In the Atlantic, some fixtures have indicated softening rates, where a TA round voyage currently pays owners around USD 20,000 per day. A fronthaul from the Continent now pays around USD 30,000's, while the activity and rates from East Coast South America have remained at the same levels as last week, at around USD 19,000 DOP East Coast India for a trip via Brazil to China. In the East, a Pacific round voyage pays around the USD 17,000 mark. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 2261 points, up 43 points from last week.

As August comes to a close with the LNG cargo market continuing to underwhelm, owners and charterers circle the dancefloor waiting for each other to make the next move. Portfolio players and traders with length in their fleets, either through trading shorter routes or with pre-secured winter coverage, are growing reluctant to sub-let but continue to be well-placed to pick up the cargoes that do come to market. The result is a general lack of demand for independent tonnage; however, the good news for owners is that vessel availability remains tight particularly in the west, and the east is not awash with vessels despite the usual seasonal build-up. With the imminent start-up of Freeport and the approaching winter demand, the enduring strong sentiment is readily understood.    On the newbuilding front, there were two further orders last week: one fresh order placed by NYK at SHI and an option exercised by Maran Gas at DSME. This brings the YTD total for 2019 to 31 conventional LNGCs, versus 37 for the same period in 2018 and 62 for the full year.

The suezmarket is still going strong, despite less activity so far this week. Monday was bank-holiday in UK which explains some, but charterers are doing their best to hold back to kill the momentum in the market. This could backfire and we believe the activity will be strong for the rest of the week, with W70 being next done for a wafr/ukc. In the East we have the same story as last week - decent activity and the 30 day count is lower than normal which points towards a better market for the Owners going forward.

Over the last week the Capesize market got stronger as the basket of all routes increased 13%. Especially on the Brasil to China route we have seen a big improvement with USD 4 dollars per metric ton added to the freight. For this route we see significant activity with less and less early tonnage available. This tightness indicates that we are looking at further improvement in the week to come, however it mostly depends on the schedule and activity of one major freight consumer.

The Aframax market in the North Sea and Baltic has moved sideways the past week again with rate levels ex Baltic (TD17) standing steadily at WS 55. Although we have in fact seen a small rush of cargoes coming into the market the last couple of days, it has not been enough activity to satisfy the available tonnage in the area, and therefore rate levels have not picked up just yet. However, the cargo program ex Baltic looks healthier for September in the 2nd half, and it will be interesting to see if the market finally moves in the week to come. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea we have seen an upward correction this week with benchmark routes (cross-Med and Bsea-Med) picking up around 10 points over the past 7 days. TD19 currently stands at WS 85 and much to the delight of the owners there is still cargoes in the market yet to be fixed. It is expected the market will stay firm in the week to come.

Continuous push in most areas, Nopac rv fixing in the USD 14,000s while Indo coal to China is paying around USD 16,000 and Indo coal to ECI around USD 14,000. Still tight tonnage supply in the Atlantic, where bhaul business to USG or ECSA is paying around USD 15,000 while, FH ex Cont is trading close to USD 30,000.

After a couple of hectic weeks for the Vlcc’s with rates steadily climbing we have seen a few rather quiet days. Activity in general is still there but in a more measured way as charterers took a step back due to the UK holiday on Monday to see if they could ease the firm trend. For now they have managed to slow things down and shave a couple of points off the rates. The optimism for the next couple of months is far from changed among the owning community and merely seen as a ‘pit-stop’ before it all starts up again. text: MEG: Saudi Aramco today announced September Propane CP at $350, this being $20 less than August, Butane September CP came at $360, flat to August.  Paper swaps had been traded higher this week, due to prompt demand from both India and Indonesia for September liftings of equal ratio cargos.  After the September CP announcement, October CP traded at up to $357, October FEI/CP quickly narrowed to $21 from a previous $30ish.  One European trader reportedly sold a 20-25 September lifting of full cargo C3 to a Chinese importer at discount to Oct CP.    FAR EAST: A few deals were concluded in the window this week as traders had to cover shorts.  23k Propane were traded at September FEI minus $11ish. A similar cargo for 1h October delivery were offered at Oct FEI minus $16, buyers are still to come forward.   Indonesia’s Pertamina awarded an evenly split 2/2 delivery into Kalbut during 4-6th October, reportedly at October CP plus high 30s. And new tender for same ratio cargo at 8-10th October delivery into Teluk Semankga has closed but result is yet to be known. India’s HPCL also issued prompt tender for end Aug and Early Sep delivered equal ratio cargoes, which they didn’t manage to award. Later they reissued buy tender for 45kt equal ratio cargo to be delivered during 11 Sep to 5 Oct, and a 21k equal ratio cargo for 21-31 Sep delivery.   Comparatively, the Chinese market appeared quiet this week as most Buyers have already covered their September positions and waiting for September CP announcement before taking October positions. One end September/early October arrival of full Propane is reported to have been sold to China at October CP plus low mid-40s. One E.China petchem user is reported to have purchased 23kt Propane for 2h September delivery at September CP plus low 50s level.  China custom data shows August imports at close to 2mmt, which is the highest monthly import level in 2019 so far.

text: USGC: The market mostly shrugged off the 3.7 million barrel build with some assistance from crude. However we are now 23 million barrels over last year and for sure on pace to break the 100 million level. Volumes are still somewhat lack luster as it has priced most of this in and traders are still nursing summer hangovers. With three weeks of over 3 million barrels built per week in US inventories, this has become the new normal. The FOB market in the US continues to be active for end September and early October although more offers have recently been seen than bids. Despite this FOB discussions continue around the 6cpg mark.

WEST: The West VLGC market has not really seen much activity so far this week. September liftings ex USG are seemingly more or less done, and the vessel overhang going into October is rather limited with a handful of vessels available. Towards the end of this week there have been a number of tenders in WAF and Marcus Hook, offers for which are due on Friday. Indicative levels being discussed so far show a slight premium to the Baltic.  EAST: Vessels currently discharging in the Far East are being watched carefully as delays due to ullage issues have led to a backlog at disports. This could potentially leave early October vessel supply relatively tight in the USG and elsewhere. Otherwise, the AG has been relatively quiet, with a few Indian cargoes expected to be floated at the end of this week.

text: MEG: Despite the Brent stands above 60$, LPG paper values doesn’t follow anywhere near closely this week. By time of writing, Sept Propane CP traded at $338 whilst Butane is $10 higher at $348. Saudi Aramco has announced Sept lifting acceptances with some liftings reported to be deferred into 2h Sept and later month lifting, with less supply due to oil cut. Therefore supports front CP and front contango narrowed from $5 to almost flattish.  Other than this, a couple of 1st decade Sept lifting FOB spots have been traded this week at single digit discounts, against the rising freight. This week Baltic has risen amid plentiful shipping inquiries from Indian players and tight supply in 1st decade Sept.    FAR EAST: CFR prices for delivery into Korea/Japan still appears weak, as 23kt Propane for 2h Sep delivery traded at Sep FEI minus $16, which equates to a CFR price of Sep CP plus high single digit this Wednesday. Similar cargo for 1h Oct delivery is offered at Oct FEI minus $12.  With ample supply from US and limited buying interest for US origin, Sep FEI/CP has narrowed rapidly from $28 earlier this week to $20.   During the Thursday window, One Chinese major was bidding a 3/1 cargo for 2h Sep delivery at Sep CP plus $44, meanwhile they are bidding one 3/1 loading 22/23 Sep at Sep CP minus $2 and one 2/2 loading 17/18 Sep at Sep CP minus $3. Another Chinese major bids a 3/1 for Oct delivery at Oct CP plus 43$.  However such bidding ideas are yet to attract seller’s interest, considering current rising freight.  One Chinese major is reported to have covered a 33/11 Sep delivery at Sept CP plus 40ish this week. discussions from traditional importers remain tepid due to high stocks and concerns over weakening domestic prices with the possibility of cheaper Sept CP.    Pertamina issued buy tender for two equal ratio cargoes delivered into Indonesia at 4-6 Oct into Teluk Semangka and 8-10 Oct into Kalbut, FOB alternative are also considerable.

As the surrounding VLCC and Suez markets are currently picking up, the Aframax market in the Baltic and North Sea however is still hovering around bottom rate levels. Although we have seen a bit of activity the past week, such as Fuel Oil cargoes out of the area for Eastbound destination, and Baltic September dates in play, we are not expecting a noteworthy uptick in rates in the week to come. Following the flat market we have seen in the Mediterranean and Black Sea the past month or so, owners are regaining their optimism today as a spark in activity the last couple of days has resulted in a slight uptick in rates. Going forwards into September fixing dates we expect to see an upwards correction in rates as the Mediterranean and Black Sea market starts to recover.

The VLCC market has gone from strength to strength the last week, culminating at the writing moment with rates in the high W60’s from both MEG- and Wafr/east – yielding daily earning ast $40k or above. We are now at the last leg of first decade MEG cargoes, and when concluded it is not unlikely that rates will level out moving further into the month, as tonnage availability widens. The Atlantic has by and large been quiet, although Wafr stems have started to appear, whereas Brazilian export continues in an increasing tempo, keeping the firing burning I the west.

Finally we see some positivity in the Suezmax market. This market has been flat at bottom levels for some time now, but with increasing activity and bullish Owners it looks like the table has turned. In wafr we have now got rid of most of the overhang and the position list is looking really tight. Whats interesting now, is that we also have a rather short 30-day count in MEG as well, so both markets are pulling in the same direction. We dont see any reason why this should stop, as cargo activity is expected to increase and Owners are finally smelling money.

We are now at the last leg of first decade MEG cargoes, and when concluded it is not unlikely that rates will level out moving further into the month, as tonnage availability widens. The Atlantic has by and large been quiet, although Wafr stems have started to appear, whereas Brazilian export continues in an increasing tempo, keeping the firing burning I the west.

Another week with positive push on supra rates across all areas. In Pacific Indo/China rounds fixing around USD 15000 bss Spore delivery and Nopac  and Aussie rv's paying aound USD 11000, while AG to China paying in the high teens. In the Atlantic basin, TA's paying in the low 20k, while fh's ex USG around USD 30000.

A slow start to the week with few fresh fixtures reported, however the little information emerged has shown a market that remains firm in both hemispheres. Grains from East Coast South America has remained firm, as efficient 82,000dwt vessels have fixed around USD 19.000 per day, with delivery India and Singapore, or USD 19,000 + 900,000 with delivery APS. With few fixtures in the Atlantic, a Panamax which fixed a Bauxite-run from Jord Lasfar via Kamsar to Aughinish at USD 20.500 kept the market at similar levels to last week, as regular transatlantic round voyages pays owners around USD 20,000. A fronthaul from the continent now pays about USD 29,000. In the east, a Pacific round voyage pays above the USD 14,500-mark. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 2163 points, up 74 points from last week.

During the past trading week we’ve seen a firming sentiment in all basins, but this has yet to translate into firming rates. The stronger sentiment is mainly driven by a reduction in available tonnage, a number of cargoes to work/ offer on and expectations of strong winter shipping market. Sublets are however keeping the shipping market in check but only for the time being. The sublet tonnage will eventually be required back to its original intended trades which will again set the stage for the independent owners and the winter market.  In other news, Samsung has secured yet another LNGC newbuild order and Global Venture has reached FID on their 10+ MTPA Calcasieu Pass LNG project. We also congratulate Cameron LNG train 1 for starting commercial operations. Next in line may be Freeport Train 1?

After a significant push last week the market calmed down and started to slide on Friday. The West Australia to China route was down from USD 10.00 per metric tonn to USD 9.50 per metric tonn whilst presently again turning positive. The Brazil to China route has been stable in the low 20's and now showing signs of improvement as well. All in all the sentiment is positive and the capesize segment is confident and well supported.

West  This week has seen a weakening in the Western premium which built up previously. In the west, this was driven mostly by an abundancy of relets through which players looked to benefit from the higher Western rate. Despite limited vessel availability in 1H Sep, there are a larger amount of ships in the second half of the month. It will be interesting to see whether or not this leads to a further reduction of Western freight rates.   East  There were dynamic movements in the Baltic this week. It weakened quickly from $60 to low $50’s, before strengthening to $60 again. This sudden change was driven by two relets deals which pushed down the market. As those relets were gone and many vessels headed West to seek a premium, the East market turned firm again. Moreover, massive Indian demand finally returned – we expect 5-6 spot inquiries in 1H Sep, which could help tighten the Eastern vessel position list. Beside the 1H Sep market change, several Saudi FOB cuts haven't affected anything in the market yet.

Finally we see some positivity in the Suezmax market. This market has been flat at bottom levels for some time now, but with increasing activity and bullish Owners it looks like the table has turned. In wafr we have now got rid of most of the overhang and the position list is looking really tight. Whats interesting now, is that we also have a rather short 30-day count in MEG as well, so both markets are pulling in the same direction. We dont see any reason why this should stop, as cargo activity is expected to increase and Owners are finally smelling money.

text: AMERICAS US inventories grew 4 million barrels last week which was above market expectations but the market managed to not lose any further ground from prior to stats. Current inventories stand at 90.5 million barrels a large 22 million barrels over last year. This has traders looking at the weekly propane production. The 4 week average of 2.253 million barrels a day is high. This production coupled with high inventory levels has been keeping Mt Belvieu propane around 30% of WTI. Export capacity from the US has increased this year and if Mt Belvieu remains cheap we could see a large amount of that export capacity being utilised sooner than expected. Traders are wondering if we will see multiple cancellations before the end of the year. Or if the market will continue to support elevated freight rates, and FOB trades slightly above cancellation levels.

As the surrounding VLCC and Suez markets are currently picking up, the Aframax market in the Baltic and North Sea however is still hovering around bottom rate levels. Although we have seen a bit of activity the past week, such as Fuel Oil cargoes out of the area for Eastbound destination, and Baltic September dates in play, we are not expecting a noteworthy uptick in rates in the week to come. Following the flat market we have seen in the Mediterranean and Black Sea the past month or so, owners are regaining their optimism today as a spark in activity the last couple of days has resulted in a slight uptick in rates. Going forwards into September fixing dates we expect to see an upwards correction in rates as the Mediterranean and Black Sea market starts to recover.

The Aframax market in the Baltic and Continent has moved sideways all week, with benchmark routes such as TD7 and TD17 flattening out at ws 85 and ws 55 respectively. Over the week cargoes have continued to be fixed at steady rates off market,  but as we get closer to September dates we expect the window to tighten and the market to have a small upward correction. Much to owners dissatisfaction the Mediterranean and Black Sea has also seen yet another quiet week with plenty of prompt open ships waiting for employment. TD19 currently stands at ws 72.5, and has done so all week. On a positive note we have seen a slight increase of activity the last day or so, and combined with the current market levels being widely perceived as rock bottom, owners are becoming optimistic as we approach cargo programs for September.

For the suezmaxes we have had decent activity for all markets last week. The tonnage-count in the Atlantic is looking better but we still have an overhang of tonnage preventing the rates from moving anywhere. The start of this week has been slow though, and we would need some end/ely activity to put Owners in a better position going into next week. In the MEG the market remains stable. The 30 day tonnage count remains steady just above 100 ships, and Owners are still getting around $18-19k for a round-trip MEG/Spore on a modern eco-ship.

EAST: It has been a relatively quiet week in the East so far with public holidays in the Middle East, Japan and Singapore. We are still left with prompt open ships in August which continue to add pressure on rates, and more Owners have decided to ballast their ships towards Cape on the back of stronger freight markets in the West. Aramco September acceptances are also expected soon, and as per usual we expect to see more activity on freight once those dates are known.   WEST: In contrast to the last few months, this week has seen the Western VL market flip into a premium relative to the East. There have been two main drivers behind this particular market move. On one hand, a handful of fixtures in the West have absorbed much of the slack in vessel availability. On the other is the composition of ownership of the remaining open vessels, with the vast majority being controlled by the largest few shipowners. Consequently, H/C via P voyages are now being fixed at around $110pmt – some $10 higher than the equivalent Baltic. It will be interesting to see whether Western rates continue to strengthen and to what extent this might influence the balance of the fleet across East and West.

After a busy last week the VLCC activity has slowed down whilst waiting for the September MEG program to be confirmed. However, being in the twilight zone between monthly programs is unlikely to cause much suffering, with bunkers still trending down and decent TCE’s returns at $30k/day or above. There has been some evidence of “profit taking” for a date advantage, but there little change in sentiment. Where possible, charterers are still targeting the older and/or restricted class, which has settled at the very high W40’s for MEG/east cargoes, while modern ships still command rates in the low to mid W50’s.  Overall it’s a holding pattern at the moment, but we do expect charterers to get cracking on September as soon as they can. A firm foundation and a tighter than normal position list could well see further improvements once it gets going in earnest.

text: AMERICAS: The market was battered down after inventories on Wednesday after showing a higher than expected build of 3.2 million barrel build for the week ending August 9th 2019. This has left US inventories at 86.5 million barrels, 24% above the same week last year. The way US production is going has lead traders to believe US inventories will exceed 100 million barrels of propane before draw season begins. It has also lead to traders believing that draw season will begin later than the historic October 1st date. US FOB discussions are still above cancellation levels, but with delivered markets looking very weak and discounted, traders are wondering where they can place the tons. The question is if Mt Belvieu propane continues to be cheap, around or below 30% of WTI, will the good value manage to sustain 1.3 million barrels per day or above of exports from the US through winter?

For the suezmaxes we have had decent activity for all markets last week. The tonnage-count in the Atlantic is looking better but we still have an overhang of tonnage preventing the rates from moving anywhere. The start of this week has been slow though, and we would need some end/ely activity to put Owners in a better position going into next week. In the MEG the market remains stable. The 30 day tonnage count remains steady just above 100 ships, and Owners are still getting around $18-19k for a round-trip MEG/Spore on a modern eco-ship.

It’s been yet another monotonous start to the week for the LNG shipping market with limited requirements seen.  The national holiday(s) in Asia earlier this week did contribute to a slow start, however trade deals may have also not materialize due to the current softening of LNG prices. There were a few sell tenders which could have developed into shipping requirements, but again they were mostly awarded to Traders/ Portfolio player with length in shipping. The continued limited cross basin arbitrage has also decreased ton/ miles and ensure a relatively decent short-term supply of shipping as vessels fixed on spot for a single voyage are mostly trading within the basin and would return on the  availability list within the span of 2-3 weeks.  Despite this, sentiment and rate expectation remain stable as we move into September. We do feel that traders/ portfolio players are slightly cautious with regards to subletting their tonnage during this period as the majority of market participants expect rates to pick up.  As for multi month charters, we did hear favorable numbers on the last deal concluded and we still do encounter some strong multi month interest from a handful of charterers looking for coverage this winter.  On the Newbuildings, Tsakos Energy Navigation have order up to two vessels (1+1) from Hyundai Heavy industries last week.

Confidence regained for the big ships after a brief nervous period, average 180000-tonners now enjoying daily spot earnings of close to usd 28k. Considerable geographical bunker differentials and weather issues cause tonnage supply disruptions. whilst iron ore prices are up and all major miners needing/taking prompt units. The West Australia/China trade is stable in volume with resultant gains in daily earnings of 23 pct for pacific rounds, coming in at usd 27k. With assistance from increased fronthaul activity,  transatlantic levels are up 18 pct to print at usd 25k. General outlook is positive as reflected in FFA support and a hectic period ahead for extensive scrubber retrofits and IMO 2020 compliance works.

After a busy last week the VLCC activity has slowed down whilst waiting for the September MEG program to be confirmed. However, being in the twilight zone between monthly programs is unlikely to cause much suffering, with bunkers still trending down and decent TCE’s returns at $30k/day or above. There has been some evidence of “profit taking” for a date advantage, but there little change in sentiment. Where possible, charterers are still targeting the older and/or restricted class, which has settled at the very high W40’s for MEG/east cargoes, while modern ships still command rates in the low to mid W50’s.  Overall it’s a holding pattern at the moment, but we do expect charterers to get cracking on September as soon as they can. A firm foundation and a tighter than normal position list could well see further improvements once it gets going in earnest.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Despite the crude rise and fall, Propane CP has been quite stable at 340ish until Thursday, it dived to $335 at the time of writing and still traded down. Butane CP maintains $14/15 higher and it’s likely to sustain as of better demand from India. Limited lifting inquiries from last decade Aug into early Sep, amid ample shipping length, have exerted pressure on freight.  FOB discussions have been improved to smaller discounts, especially for later Sep lifting cargos, due to weakening freight and slight contango into Oct. Players are still waiting Saudi Aramco’s acceptance to reveal a clearer picture on Sep FOB market.     FAR EAST:  Market remains quiet until Thurs, a flurry of offers appear in window with delivery ranging from 1h Sep into 1h Oct. 23k propane for 1h Sep delivery is offered at Sep FEI minus $23 which equates to Sep CP plus $4! 2h Sep delivery cargo is offered at minus $16 while bid at minus $25. And sellers with 1h Oct cargo are asking Oct FEI minus $9/$10. Off window, 2h Sep propane was reported traded at Sep FEI minus $15 earlier this week. As Us arb to east is still open and weak demand from Europe, we believe lifters will continuingly bring tons and east discussion will still be heavily discounted.    Other than window, some tenders are flowing in the market.  One E.China PDH is reported to issue a buy tender for 23k propane delivered in late Sep, while another E.China petchem user is reported to issue a buy tender for 23k propane monthly delivered from Oct to Dec. There are a few more propane demand in late Sep from other petchem users, but traditional importers are cautious and hesitant to stockpile in such bearish market.  India demand is slowly recovering, with one importer have purchased 23k butane for 2h Sep delivery via tender, and some other inquiry for Sep lifting cargos emerge.

The market started on a quiet cosious mode with a firm undertone at the beginning of the week, however the signs of improvement overall became quite obvious and indexes pushed up. Atlantic basin pushing up with lots of fresh requirements in Black Sea Aran and Continent. Strong demand in ECSA adding pressure for South Atlantic loaders. Ulta fixed above $16,000 plus $650,000 BB del ECSA to Japan. Indian ocean experiences shortage of tonnage and rates pushing up, Tess 58 obtaining $ 14,000 plus $400,000 BB TCT South Africa - China.  The US Gulf improved significantly with rates for 63000DWT achieving $30,000 for FH.  Overall rates from the Pacific improved with good support of coal export from South East Asian to China and India. Supra seen $10,000 plus for Indo RV and premium paid for India discharge.

The Aframax market in the Baltic and Continent has moved sideways all week, with benchmark routes such as TD7 and TD17 flattening out at ws 85 and ws 55 respectively. Over the week cargoes have continued to be fixed at steady rates off market,  but as we get closer to September dates we expect the window to tighten and the market to have a small upward correction. Much to owners dissatisfaction the Mediterranean and Black Sea has also seen yet another quiet week with plenty of prompt open ships waiting for employment. TD19 currently stands at ws 72.5, and has done so all week. On a positive note we have seen a slight increase of activity the last day or so, and combined with the current market levels being widely perceived as rock bottom, owners are becoming optimistic as we approach cargo programs for September.

Rates have been increasing in both hemispheres for a good week by now, as we see additional cargoes constantly emerging in the market. The ECSA-market has arguably been the dominant force in pushing the rates, where we have seen LME's (around 75.000 DWT) fixing at levels above 18.000 + 800k GBB for grain-trips to the far east. A TA round voyage currently pays owners around USD 20,000 per day, while a fronthaul from the continent now pays about USD 28,000. In the east, a Pacific round voyage pays above the USD 13,500-mark. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 2089 points, up 318 points from last week.

Weak end user demand mainly coming from North East Asia has held the product price on the floor this past week with the LNG supply overhang still apparent in both basins. However, we have seen more creative chartering opportunities, as spot rates climbed despite the amount of available tonnage, especially from the Pacific. Those Charterers in Europe who are observing the forward pricing curve, are perhaps now considering to float cargoes in the area, which could tie up some tonnage in the basin as we head into the winter months. Owners still remain bullish for winter and multi-month chartering still seems to be the most attractive option for them with healthy appetite for this type of business holding rates strong. However, with the product price remaining low compared to this time last year, it may be unlikely that Charterers will be able to justify the dizzy heights gained by Owners last year if they have a say. Yard pricing remained unchanged since last week, and no new orders have been reported.

Although Aframaxes have seen another fairly quiet week in the Baltic and North Sea markets, rates have in fact picked up a tad since last week. This is mainly due to the tonnage list tightening somewhat and vessels in position taking out cargoes being fixed under the radar. Owners are still waiting in vain for the upturn which has been expected for Q3. We are expecting an upward market correction as we get closer to end month fixing window. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, we have seen the rates take a further 10 point drop on benchmark routes over the course of the week. Owners have been battling to fix the few cargoes entering the market, and as the cross-Med voyages are currently paying low ws70’s, owners are seeing a return of around USD 4,000 per day TCE; for most owners not enough to cover their OPEX.

A typical slow start to the week with bit more activity by mid-week. In the Atlantic, the feeling is market is again stabilizing where strong numbers are getting fixed in ECSA.  ECSA fronthaul paying around USD 16,000 + 600k gbb to Far East, and TA paying around USD 17,500. From USG owners are getting around mid teens for a TA. In the Indian Ocean, tonnage supply is still tight and rates moving upwards, and vessels are getting paid around USD 19,000 for MEG/ECI tct. In the Pacific, the rates are bit pushing but relatively flat by mid-week with Aussie coal rv paying around USD 10,000 back to Far East, and Indo coal around USD 12,500.

After a busy couple of weeks on a very date sensitive market, it all came to rest at the end of last week as charterers gradually fought back to gain the upper hand on the owners. Fundamentals trumped sentiment at last and rates began to slide as owners had to make a move and reposition their ships for the autumn which, historically speaking, is firmer than the summer months. Activity levels are low at the moment with VLCCs enjoying all the fun for now. There are simply too many ships out there and fundamentals are not supporting any swing in owners favor anytime soon.

Owners are still waiting in vain for the upturn which has been expected for Q3. We are expecting an upward market correction as we get closer to end month fixing window. There is still an abundance of vessels heading towards the Atlantic, which has been coupled with a significant reduction in fresh requirements the last few days. Therefore, the downwards market trend will probably continue in the near term.

After a couple of weeks of the beforehand predicted downturn, the market has cautiously started moving into the greens yet again. The week started slowly, both the east for NoPac runs and with few reported fixtures in the Atlantic hemisphere. However, reports of Increased Australian and Indonesian volumes, shortcomings of tonnage ballasting for ECSA along with few vessels available in the North Atlantic are both signs to take notice of, which has already pushed rates up somewhat. A transatlantic round voyage currently yields about USD 16,500 per day, while a fronthaul from the Continent yields around USD 25,000. In the east, a Pacific round voyage now pays around high USD 10,000's per day. The BPI 4TC-index is down 100 points week-on-week, currently at 1791 points.

It’s been close to a perfect storm in the VLCC market in the week gone by, with very strong demand in all areas, falling bunker prices and looming typhoons in the Far East. MEG eastbound rates have gained upwards to 10 points, with West Africa/East following suit, and to an extent leading the way – now firmly established in the mid ws50’s. USG export freights have similarly strengthened, now said to have reached USD 6.5 for the benchmark Koreas destination, although yet to be confirmed. The only cloud on the horizon has been a number of oil company relets boosting an otherwise thinning supply side. Although activity is expected to slow down going into next week, we see little downside risk short term. Whether this is the start of the long anticipated paradigm shift remains to be seen, but for now owners are making the most of daily earnings not seen for a long time.

WEST Following a very quiet fixing period for 1H August, and despite European and Korean/Japanese storage capacity being limited, there were a number of fixtures for the final decade of August this week. Given that the state of the product side did not seem especially conducive to lifting, it seems players either took advantage of cheaper freight which had been locked in previously or sold cargoes on a FOB basis and relet their vessels. Since this flurry of fixtures, freight has seemed slightly shorter in the West than it has been in the last couple of months. Going forward, the direction of rates will depend on 1H September cargoes and whether or not the peak of hurricane season in the USG will bring any delays.     EAST In the East this week, freight rates have remained under pressure as we move closer to the next fixing window in September. There have been few deals concluded, but each has been a couple of dollars below the last Baltic print. Given that it is unlikely there will be many more cargoes to help absorb vessel availability for the remainder of this month, it is likely further pressure will be faced in the short term.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Unexpected plunge in swap market in this week, following the crude. Thurs Sep CP is traded low at $335 only, $35 less than last Thur. Contango into Oct also shrank to $2 from previous $7.  However, butane spread against propane has improved from - $8 to $11, as of better demand and relatively long supply for propane overall. Qatar Petroleum is reported to sell an early Sep lifting full propane cargo to One Chinese buyer at Sep CP with some discounts.   FAR EAST: Very weak sentiment in the market this week. On Thursday window, propane for 1h Sep delivery is offered at Sep FEI minus $15, which equates to Sep CP plus $12, while buyer at minus $30! 2h Sep delivery is offered at $3-3.5 higher but still no buyers seen. Despite such discounts, off window some Japanese and Korean importers reflected with high stock level and they are reluctantly to do more stockpile, therefore such price still faced with downward pressures.   One N.China PDH user awarded their buy tender for 1h Sep arrival full C3 at reportedly Sep CP plus mid-60s. Nevertheless, the discussion level come off quick due to ample supply and softening freight. Bids on propane dropped to 50ish while equal ratio even cheaper as limited buyers available from China. There are some chances that less supply ex Iran might stimulate some demand for substitute cargos, however current poor margins with previous high inventory have exerted pressure and suppressed buyers’ appetites.    Whereas outside China, demand from India seems returning from previous stalemate. One Indian importer is reported seeking butane for Sep delivery, and several traders are procuring late Sep lifting equal ratio spot tons into India.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS: The US market showed weakness after a larger than expected build of 2.8 million barrels. We are now nearly 17 million barrels over last year’s inventory level. This combined with the weakness in crude has made US NGLs weaker. The bearishness in US NGLs has been mirrored by delivered East and West markets. Which carried heavy physical discounts even before the inventory stats were released and larger discounts have been heard since. The effect of this has not yet been reflected in terminalling fees due to quiet FOB discussions. There is skepticism in buying FOBs with so much product in the market. Traders see the potential downside outweighing the potential upside at the moment for spot market trades.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Saudi Aramco announced August propane CP at 370$ down by 5$ while butane CP at 360$ up by 5$, in line with market expectation. Few fobs available from producer on Aug lifting, apart from one trader is reported bought a mid Aug lifting equal ratio cargo from Saudi at Aug CP flat level, to utilize their vessel.   Paper swap is volatile after Aug CP set. Sep CP surged up to 380$ on Wed but came off quick on Thursday, traded flattish to Aug CP at 370$ only. Sep FEI/CP also narrowed down to mid-30s and still under pressure.     FAR EAST: Nothing was concluded in Window this week despite active bids/offers in window. On window 1h Sep propane seller asking Sep CP plus $29, or Aug Balance FEI minus $1, whereas buyers are not seen. 2h Sep seller offers at Sep FEI minus 7.5$ while bid at minus 11$. Off window 1h Sep was reported traded at Sep FEI minus 8.5 to 9$ mid-week. Although forward market in contango structure, abundant front length still exerts pressure on CFR value and buyers are expecting bigger discounts.   Chinese buyers have started exploring Sep delivery cargos. One Nchina PDH buyer has issued tender to secure one full propane cargo during 1h Sep delivery. At the time of writing the result is yet to know. Off window sellers is heard targeted at high 60s to 70s for such cargo.   Indonesia Pertamina is reported to have awarded their latest tender for 10-14th Sep delivered into Kalbut at Aug CP plus low 50s, which alternatively reflected less discounts on FOB netback.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: AMERICAS: Due to unprecedented delays in the US Gulf during the late Winter and Spring of this year the Arb market enjoyed a very good few months. Many traders pondered whether this was precursor to going back to the future of the export Arb or simply a short term outcome of unusual circumstance. As the market now has returned to a more normal summer market, it seems it may be more the latter.    In the US inventories built at close to the expectation of 1.4 million barrels. However this  did not stop the wacky markets between LST and Enterprise. With LST losing a substantial amount of price on the  last day of the month, they now start August at parody. We do not expect this to last but only time will tell. Ethane reached single digits on the week for the first time  but that was also just for the July barrel. In August Ethane may  test the single digits again.

The past week the North Sea and the Baltic aframax market has been quite lacklustre. At the time of writing we have more than 10 prompt ships in the area.  Too many oil-company relets in the area leaving other Owners with any viable options. As a consequence we have experienced in average 10 offers for every cargo quoted in the market.  Moving into the 2nd decade fixing window we still expect supply of both fuel and crude cargoes to be slow. This factor combined with a long tonnage list means we will have to wait a bit more till we see any improvements in rates.    The Mediterranean and Black Sea aframax market has been stuck in the doldrums for a while, and not surprisingly seeing rates taking a dip last week on the back of a healthy tonnage list and lack of activity. Alternative markets in the north and in the US-Caribbean region currently not giving owners much leeway in the search for better returns. We expect the market to remain flat in the week to come while waiting for activity levels to pick up.

The market for Supramaxes has seen weakening sentiment the last week following from the drop of the bigger sizes. The lack of  fresh interest from charterers in the Atlantic region have put some pressure on the rates in USG and East Med. ECSA is stable, with owners able to obtain good rates for direction Med USD 17,000 and FH USD 15,500 + 550,000 BB on Tess58.  PG-India, as well as Asia markets despite the negative indexes, remains active and well supported with long list of cargo orders.

A couple of charterers got caught out late last week in WAFR as dates ran away from them. Faced with a limited supply side, their only choice was to pay up and rates jumped another ten points up from last week’s update. Most other areas have been quiet on the surface with little movements in rates and now that the early dates have cleared in WAFR we expect charterers to start adding downward pressure on owners again.

The market has taken a breather in both basins, and the summer-boom has taken a rapid turn to the red. However, the sentiment in the market is still positive for the longer term, and many expect rates to continue the increase or at least stabilize going forward. A TA round voyage currently pays owners about USD 17,000 per day, while a fronthaul from the continent now pays in the middle of USD 25,000. In the east, a Pacific round voyage pays above the USD 12,000-mark. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 1891 points, down 318 points from last week.

The LNG prices, particularly the North East Asian prices have been relatively low, reportedly due to limited demand from the end-users. Despite the flat LNG prices, there has been more activity in the LNG ship chartering market. Vessels have been recently fixed for single voyages and multi-months charters for August and September deliveries. Charter rates have been relatively firm, despite owners facing stiff competition for each and every chartering requirement. All eyes are on the fixing levels for September cargoes as these are currently being negotiated. These would clearly indicate the direction the shipping market is moving as we approach Q4 where traditionally the increasing LNG demand due to winter may lead to a number of players seeking to play the contango.   Despite the strong sentiments for LNG vessel newbuilding activity recently, no new orders were reported this week. However, this year is due to be an interesting one as we expect the yard slots to be taken up in due course.

Although the long term optimism remains strong, the VLCC market has continued to tread water in the week gone by, with little or no upward traction. However, the owning community has drawn a line in the sand each side of the W40 mark Meg/ East for unrestricted tonnage, pending on the voyage in question, terms and conditions. There are of course discounts to be had, with plenty of more vintage- and/or ex d/d's or ex scrubber retrofits etc. available, but even this class has shown unwillingness to drop below the mid W30 level. Although suffering from the present malaise in the Meg, the Atlantic basin is showing upward bias potential, as activity has picked up substantially over the last day or so with a number of cargoes from both Wafr and the Americas.

Two weeks ago the 5TC index was at 33,000 USD pd. Since then it has fallen off a bit and has stayed around 27,000 USD pd the last week. As we see it the main reason for the correction is that the fleet has repositioned in a more balanced way with the Atlantic basin filling up. The amount of vessels heading to the Atlantic has resulted in a more cautious outlook amongst market players reflected by August FFA being priced at 23,500 USD pd. However, cargo volumes remain at healthy levels so it is hard to believe in a dramatic market fall the next weeks.

However, the owning community has drawn a line in the sand each side of the W40 mark Meg/ East for unrestricted tonnage, pending on the voyage in question, terms and conditions. Although suffering from the present malaise in the Meg, the Atlantic basin is showing upward bias potential, as activity has picked up substantially over the last day or so with a number of cargoes from both Wafr and the Americas.

WEST For much of this week, the prevailing sentiment was that Western VLGC freight rates were coming off; Houston/Chiba rates weakened to $105pmt, while bids were lower than that on the follow. However, an influx of 3rd decade cargoes rumoured to be in the market was used as a reason by some to offer higher rates again. There are many factors determining whether or not these will be achievable: notably, how many of these cargoes are firm and what levels owners with open vessels at the front of the month want to target compared to those with ships at the back. Arguably the most important factor, though, will be how the arb responds to US stats today.  This could be crucial in helping players decide whether to firm up freight requirements.   EAST Even though current fixing window has shifted towards 2H August in the MEG, we still see available shipping length from Owners and Traders in 1H August. This has yet again added some pressure on rates, and last done deal was reported in the mid/high usd 60s Baltic. In view of the present physical contango situation we do not expect to see any remaining cargos before 20-30 August onwards, although there were talks that some of the MEG suppliers might have spot fob tons available for sale. This is however yet to be confirmed. Going forward QP acceptances are also just around the corner which will start to set a direction for next month.

text: AMERCIAS A 1.6 million barrel build has done what it can to help a US-FEI arb. Traders feel that US product inventories will approach 1 hundred million barrels before the start of the demand season . Terminal expansion discussions continue to ramp up, but in the current market the terminalling fee discussions are edging towards cancellation levels. This may or may not be affecting the speed of potential export growth which looks to have slowed. Product traders are looking at FOB opportunities, and unless they have their own freight , the arb does not make sense. Traders are hoping for an imminent freight decline to make arb cargo trades workable.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: Despite the crude rise earlier this week and improved demand, August swaps was traded under pressure at $360, $15 less than our last report. September CP still maintains at $3-4 contango for the time being. FOB market appeared quiet this week, both for cargo and freight trades. Some players with shipping length are reportedly looking for possible spot cargoes to utilize their ships. With softening freight and improving premia in Eastern market, FOB discounts have narrowed and today one trader was seen offering their late Aug Yanbu lifting 2/2 ratio asking Aug CP plus $5 (Yanbu discount to apply), while the last deal for similar cargo was done at CP minus single digit.     FAR EAST:  Window bids/offers still roam at discount levels.  On Wednesday a 23k Propane for 2h August was traded at August FEI minus $4. A similar cargo for same period, today was offered at minus $2 and cargo for 1h Sep offers at minus $5 basis Sep FEI, yet no bids was seen.  Earlier this week, the strong MB and firm freight squeezed the arbitrage value but latest stock data with a considerable build has enable the economy to return again for Eastern trades.  Off window enquires have been rather active. One EChina PDH user awarded their buy tender for 23k Propane delivered in 2h Aug at Aug CP plus mid high $60s, in addition, an other EChina cracker user was reported to have awarded their buy tender for 22k Propane for delivery end Aug into Taixing at Aug CP plus $60s, even if their original tender demand was for upto 44k Propane.  FPCC has issued a spot tender to buy a 33/11 or 44/0 for delivery during 11-15th Sep, the result is not yet to known.  Pertamina reportedly awarded one 2/2 for their mid Sep demand into Teluk Semangka, and are still looking for one more.

The sentiment has remained the same over last 7 days , although the pace of rate increases slowed down . In the Atlantic the upward trend stopped today and USG to Continent pay again around 18500 . Back-hauls voyages to USA/SAM were slightly higher , average USD 500 more by comparison to last Wednesday levels . On the other hand North Continent /Baltic tonnage was in search of cargoes direction East Med/Black Sea , so spot cargoes to USG/SAM had to pay premium rates . Pacific rates stayed very healthy and rose last week by average of USD 1000, whilst Nopac voyages are paying now more or less USD 1000 a day more comparing to last Wednesday reports . The overall BSI index rose from  928 to 1019 , therefore all in all the bullish sentiment prevails in the market .

Aframaxes in the Baltic and Continent market, as well as in Mediterranean and Black Sea, have been trading more or less sideways over yet another uneventful week. Throughout most of the week ships have continued to pick off the stems coming into the market one by one in order to keep rates on benchmark routes unaltered, however in the last two days we have seen supply of ships surpass demand and a slight downwards correction has taken place; most routes dropping between 2.5 and 5 points. TD19 (cross-Med) currently stands at WS 85 giving owners a TCE of around USD 6750 per day.

It has been another active week on the shipping side, as we have witnessed a number of fresh requirements from both the East and the West of Suez. Various cargo tenders have been keeping Charterers and Owners busy especially in the Pacific, although these tenders usually yield only shorter one voyage spot fixtures. There are still a handful of open prompt vessels competing for the next business and thus rates have remained steady this week. Looking forward, we still see a few Charterers trying to find the perfect vessel to cover the upcoming winter period and thus multi-month rates have been holding strong but only a few deals have been concluded. On the cargo side, the aforementioned sell tenders have kept the supply high and thus LNG prices low, a tricky situation to many given the relatively firm shipping market. The uncertainty of the shipping outlook, together with the comparatively bearish cargo market, has created a lot of discussion around freight derivatives and the possibility to adopt them in wider perspective into LNG shipping – something that will be very interesting going forward. On the newbuilding front, SK Shipping has been confirmed placing an order with HHI for one 180,000cbm LNGC with planned delivery in 2021.

It has been a busy week for Suezmaxes with an Atlantic market that has had a lot of ships to absorb and with rates mostly moving sideways. Aframaxes in the Baltic and Continent market, as well as in Mediterranean and Black Sea, have been trading more or less sideways over yet another uneventful week. Throughout most of the week ships have continued to pick off the stems coming into the market one by one in order to keep rates on benchmark routes unaltered, however in the last two days we have seen supply of ships surpass demand and a slight downwards correction has taken place; most routes dropping between 2.5 and 5 points. TD19 (cross-Med) currently stands at WS 85 giving owners a TCE of around USD 6750 per day.

WEST  Most of this week has been quiet, with freight weakening. It will be interesting to see what impact US inventories will have later today.  Vessel availability has generally remained unchanged. It is a bit too late for cancellations in the first two decades in Aug, so we would expect players to need to come out to fix soon.  EAST   Baltic finally enters the stage of correction. Market decreases by about a dollar day by day, and daily TCE has decreased to lower than $60,000. Worldwide, less congestion means more vessel supply in the market, but lifting demand is limited so far. Indian demand is being sluggish from May onward and present physical contango set end month FOB lifting status. Even though freight is getting cheaper, we still see many traders relet for Aug in the Eastern market. Considering present Baltic falling speed and downward pressure from many relets, freight heads to $50,000 level as bottom line in a short term unless we see some bullish events such as Typhoon, Hurricane etc.

The VLCC market sprung to life this week and the fixture count is increasing by the hour, with ships disappearing all over, albeit more under the counter, which does little to help the market malaise. Despite thinning, the position list remains well populated. Thus, overall we still do not see any dramatic changes in fortunes for the owning community in the short term . Downside , however appears capped in low W40’s MEG/East for modern unrestricted tonnage and high W30’s for their older sisters. The Atlantic has also seen a steady flow of cargoes. However, rates have yet to gain momentum, with West Africa/East stuck in the mid W40’s and USG export cargoes in the low to mid $5 million for the benchmark Korea destination. Increased activity simultanously for all the major Vlcc routes required for rates to strenghten from present levels.

Still, fundamentals are better, and expected to improve further in the coming months. So the remainder of the year should still see rates at levels giving good returns for owners...

Suezmaxes in the MEG and East are trading fairly steady at mid-low ws70's. The ballasters from East to West Africa have not had too much effect on the MEG market, but on the other hand, created an overhang of tonnage in West Africa. This overhang is shrinking as activity has picked up this week. Rates have remained rather stable around ws60, but we now see a upward pressure, and rates should tick up by the end of the week. The Black Sea-program is done for the month, and first stems has been done for early August. Black Sea and Mediterranean seems rather stable, but could see an uptick on the back of what happening in West Africa.

We foresee a soft/steady market in the North for the rest of the week, with cargo activities and tonnage availability remaining in equilibrium. Unfortunately for owners, the market in the Mediterranean and Black Sea has seen a slow downward correction this week, as benchmark routes have dropped a few points. This is due to the simple fact that there are not many cargoes around to be fixed. Unfortunately for owners, the market is not expected to see a noteworthy pick up in the week to come. It is possible owners will reposition their ships for alternative markets, which as the USG/Caribs market which has increased a few points the last few days.

Like in all other sizes of bulk shipping last week, Supramax tonnage enjoyed the constant improvement of TC/voyage levels. This bullish sentiment was more apparent in the Atlantic, where rates on all routes went up by an average of USD 2,000 in the last 7 days. The lack of tonnage able to load still in July dates has been especially seen in the North Continent and Baltic, and resulted in high rates for any order/cargo out of those zones, regardless the final destination. Pacific rates have also been going up, but not to the same extent like in the Atlantic. The short voyages from Indonesia to China gained the most, paying USD 1,000 a day more compared to the last week fixtures. Stems from Indonesia to India raised by average USD 750, whilst Nopac voyages are now paying more or less USD 500 a day more compared to last Wednesday reports. The overall BSI-index rose from 845 to 928.

text: AMERICAS: After a 3 month run of open arbs, rising freights,  and a general good feeling, the window  has been slammed shut. For the second week in a row, the inventories in the US showed a much smaller build than the industry had expected. A week ago the US showed a small draw and this week the inventories showed a small build of 500,000 barrels. This has occurred at a time when most were expecting builds in the magnitude of around 2 million barrels a week,  and combined with these expectations,  the US market has firmed considerably. We are still believers in the  growing US production and nececessity to export,  but afor now  traders have become much more skeptical and th netbacks have fallen back to cancellation levels.

There’s been very little change in the VLCC segment over the last week. MEG rates remain stagnant, ranging in the mid ws40’s eastbound for modern unrestricted tonnage, and in the upper ws30’s to very low ws40’s for the more vintage fraternity, depending on the voyage, terms and conditions. Despite somewhat increased activity for USG export cargoes, rates remain static at USD 4.0/5.0 million for Singapore/Korea, respectively. The same picture is evident for the West Africa/East market, similarly hovering in the mid ws40’s. The only glimmer of optimism has been a couple of Brazil/East runs paying up on last done levels, but overall tonnage remains plentiful in all areas so even with the August MEG program coming into the picture, little change is expected short term.

With the rates continuing upwards, the Panamax index has climbed an additional 294 points since last Wednesday, currently at 2085 points. Vale is back in the market, and a strong iron ore price combined with high Chinese demand is giving rates a solid push. Several strong fixtures have been concluded, with Kamsarmaxes being paid over USD 30,000 for fronthauls to China, and ECSA to Far East are closing in on the USD 18,000 per day + 800,000 GBB mark for similar vessels. A transatlantic round voyage for regular Panamaxes now yields ahead of USD 20,500 per day, and a fronthaul from the Continent pays shipowners in the low USD 27,000's. In the East, a Pacific round voyage currently pays around mid USD 13,000's per day.

Suezmaxes in the MEG and East are trading fairly steady at mid-low ws70's. The ballasters from East to West Africa have not had too much effect on the MEG market, but on the other hand, created an overhang of tonnage in West Africa. This overhang is shrinking as activity has picked up this week. Rates have remained rather stable around ws60, but we now see a upward pressure, and rates should tick up by the end of the week. The Black Sea-program is done for the month, and first stems has been done for early August. Black Sea and Mediterranean seems rather stable, but could see an uptick on the back of what happening in West Africa.

Another great week in line with our predictions for the big ships, and no sign of activity to taper off or levels to be at risk for the immediate future. Whilst Pacific activity is steady but moderate, Vale's big-style comeback on the Brazil/China run combined with markedly increasing transatlantic volumes make up the main driver, and there is at moment for all practical purposes a tonnage shortage for early stems ex Brazil. With a high number of Capes, Newcastlemaxes and Valemaxes going out of service for drydock/scrubber fitting, the following weeks/months are expected to see present climate maintained and further strengthened. Average daily earnings for 180,000-tonners up almost 20 pct w-o-w to come in at USD 31k. Any owner securing fixed period levels earlier this year at levels ranging from USD 10k to USD 15k can watch with envy USD 18,500 recently done on mediocre 175,000-tonner for about 12 months, knowing next unit expected to be concluded substantially higher.

There’s been very little change in the VLCC segment over the last week. MEG rates remain stagnant, ranging in the mid ws40’s eastbound for modern unrestricted tonnage, and in the upper ws30’s to very low ws40’s for the more vintage fraternity, depending on the voyage, terms and conditions. Despite somewhat increased activity for USG export cargoes, rates remain static at USD 4.0/5.0 million for Singapore/Korea, respectively. The same picture is evident for the West Africa/East market, similarly hovering in the mid ws40’s. The only glimmer of optimism has been a couple of Brazil/East runs paying up on last done levels, but overall tonnage remains plentiful in all areas so even with the August MEG program coming into the picture, little change is expected short term.

The softening trend of recent weeks seems to be bottoming out. LNG price environment remains low, particularly JKM when compared with the 10’s seen this time last year. The spot arbitrage between European reloads and North East Asian has widened this week showing glimmers of light, yet insufficient to buck the general trend seen this year and leaving traders little margin to accommodate the demands of the recent freight levels. Looking to the East, the past week has seen a notable pick-up in activity on the spot and while the shipping market is generally bullish as shipowners look towards the winter, it is not far-fetched to suggest that the weak prompt that has been threatening to continue throughout Q3 may be coming to an end.   Tonnage for winter coverage remains the priority for many traders and portfolio players alike. The recent string of multi-months fixtures may have contributed to the recent heightened bull run which drove rates up to levels typically seen in winter months. These are fixtures meant primarily for winter cargoes and access to worldwide flexibility, suggesting that the charter rate increases are more sentiment driven rather than reflecting actual fundamentals. All eyes will be on the actual gas demand from the North East Asian importers as we inch further into Q3 which could certainly drive freight costs beyond levels the market has seen this year.

EAST We saw increased activity on shipping East of Suez end of last week/beginning of this week, and all July positions have now been cleared. This stopped a falling Baltic, for now, and the freight market seems to have stabilized itself again in the East. Aramco acceptance dates for August were announced yesterday, and market players have slowly started to move against August positions. However, we still see few traders with shipping length left for 1H August, and current fixing ideas are around mid/high USD 70s (excluding cost for awrip).   WEST A couple of fixtures were concluded towards the end of last week at sub USD 120 Houston/Chiba basis, thus resulting in a slight reduction in the number of available vessels for first half August in USG. It will be interesting to see whether this reduction in vessel availability and drop in freight level are just outliers, or if the West continues to be further discounted relative to the East in the week ahead.

text: AMERICAS: Enterprise Products issued a press release this week stating that in addition to their 175,000 barrel expansion coming on line in September of this year, they would have another expansion of 260,000 barrels per day commencing third quarter 2020. When completed this would give Enterprise a capacity to load 1.1 million barrels per day of LPG or 60 VLGC cargoes per month. It seems hard to imagine where all this product will go but one thing that seems certain in LPG is the product always seems to find a home. Closer to the present the Gulf Coast is gearing up for its first storm of the season, Current forecasts have the storm missing the Texas export Terminals and going into Louisiana but precautions are being made none the less. With Enterprise and Targa finally recovered from the winters disruption they are holding their breath and hoping this storm does not hit.

The West Africa market is still feeling the effects of the eastern ballasters, and we now see West Africa/Continent fixed below ws60. Front-end of the tonnage-list is still heavy, so no many signs of improvement this week. In the East, the 30 days tonnage-count is almost at the lowest this year, but we are still seeing ships willing around ws70 MEG/East. Cargo activity has been decent, so we could see some upward pressure in MEG the week to come.

Yet another very positive week for rates in both basins, even though the majority of the growth was seen in the Atlantic region. With both the USG and the Continent lacking spot tonnage, charterers are forced to pay more than the previous fixtures. From Brazil and Argentina, the grain market remains firm, where the last reported Kamsarmax (82kdwt, 2009-built) fixed APS USD 17,000 + 700,000 GBB for a trip East. A transatlantic round voyage currently yields about USD 18,000 per day, while a short fronthaul from the Continent yields around USD 24,000. In the East, a Pacific round voyage now pays around mid USD 11,000's per day. A backhaul fixture from China to UK/Continent is rumored fixed at USD 7,000 - significantly higher than last reported Backhaul and the Index. The BPI 4TC-index is up 358 points week-on-week, currently at 1791 points.

Fundamentals for the big ships remain robust, with all major miners back on stage, enjoying historically high iron ore prices and pushing out as much volume as possible. Spot returns have risen sharply to level out at some USD 26k, up 14 pct w-o-w. Fronthaul and transatlantic trades remain the brightest spots, where shortage of available early units have forced major Brazilian exporters to split Capesize stems destined for China into Panamax lots at high cost to secure tonnage. Reflecting this, pay for transatlantic rounds are up 20 pct to USD 30k/day, fronthaul milk trade trips are at USD 50k/day and improving, whilst the even more important long-duration China-Brazil-China route is up also 20 pct to come in at USD 24k/day. Period conclusions are limited despite keen interest from all major players - owners mostly holding back as bids on table merely in line with FFA levels, far below physical expectations.

text: MEG: There are plenty of FOB spot cargoes available from producers and traders as resales, some of which have already been concluded. text: The 4th of July traditionally marks the middle of the summer and the market seems to be reflecting this as well. Inventories are building as expected,  and with this weeks build of 1.3 million barrels it seems almost certain that inventories will peak at  over 100 million barrels when the winter season officially starts on October 1st. Production is maintaining over 2 million barrels a day and exports are maintain over 1 million barrels per day. In South America, Gasco, the owner of Gasmar, and Enlasa announced their plans for a new fully refrigerated floating storage has been approved. Construction is scheduled to start in March of 2020 and the project should be completed in the 2nd quarter 2022. The tank will be 45000 cubic meters and the imports will be handled by Gasmar.

The LNG shipping market continues to pull owners in different directions, with the soft cargo market weighing on prompt business while a flurry of term requirements maintain longer-term confidence. The week began with a slight upturn in Asia spot pricing and the prospect of an inter-basin arbitrage, but such hopes were short-lived and had little impact on shipping before margins narrowed again – prompt availability persists and may creep steadily higher over the coming month as current charters end and more sublets appear. It’s a different story on multi-year business, with several majors and portfolio players coming out for tonnage from next year leading to a surge of activity, and sentiment remains firm. Between prompt pessimism and longer-term optimism, owners and charterers face some interesting decisions over their winter strategies.   Newbuild prices remain unchanged and no further reports of any new orders this week.

text: MEG: As far as deals are concerned, it has been a quiet week in the MEG. The big news was the announcement of the Saudi Aramco Contract Price for July of USD 375/MT for Propane and USD 355/MT for the Butane. The Yanbu discount was set at USD 13 pmt, reflecting the strong VLGC freight market. Forward numbers have been dropping throughout the week, with a small rise at the end of the week, basically shadowing the Crude futures. Most MEG based producers have additional cargoes for sale, with 2 of them having floated sales tenders. One being 3 x 22+22 kt loading 30-31 July, 25-26 Aug and 15-19 Sept, respectively. The other being for 45 kt c3 loading 31 July/02 Aug. It will be interesting to the outcome of these. In addition, India based importers are trying to delay their contractual MEG FOB volumes, because of the slowing down of import requirements.   FAR EAST: It is not, nor has it been a busy week in the Eastern CFR markets. With the HK LPG conference having completed last week, there was hopes for an active return but this was quickly squashed. The petchem demand is very low with cracker turnarounds in August, so no reprieve from that side. The prices in the East continue to be under pressure, which will likely continue with Indian slowdowns, excess MEG supply and US origin cargoes still arriving at pace. Strong VLGC freight’s doesn’t make life easier for Sellers or Buyers and the tariff’s just continue the inefficiencies. Propane still enjoy strong demand from PDH operators, which is expected to continue for the near term, at least.

Supra and Ultra have found good support followed the trend by bigger sizes. Atlantic and South East Asia have made impressive gains. Indexes raised on a daily basis. USG and Black Sea was the driving force. USG to Continent pushed close to mid-teens level, and high-teens for USG to Singapore-Japan range. ECSA markets were stable with small gains. Black Sea grains pushed rates higher and charterers had to pay close to USD 20,000 pd on nice Ultra for trips East.  South Asia was busy with Indo coal rounds achieving low USD 9,000 pd for Tess 58 open in Vietnam, and USD 11,000 pd on APS Indo.

A lacklustre week in the VLCC segment with rates under pressure, especially in the MEG. With the dust having settled from the previous attacks, the trade is more or less back to normal, barring insurance premiums which by and large are picked up by charterers. High ws40’s is now the benchmark rate eastbound for unrestricted modern tonnage from all loading areas, yielding around USD 20k/day give/take in T/C equivalent. Current loading dates are behind the curve, giving some hope that activity could pick up, although a lot of “off market” fixing is clouding the supply/demand picture short term.

Another week has passed by in the Aframax segment with the North Sea and Baltic market, as well as the Mediterranean and Black Sea, moving sideways. Ships have one by one picked off the stems coming into the market frequently enough to maintain rate levels through most of the week.  However, while the Mediterranean and Black Sea market has had a slight downwards correction the last day or so, we have seen an uptick in rates ex North Sea and Baltic, as owners put up a little more resistance in a tighter window and take the opportunity to ask for a few more points. One to keep an eye on in the week to come, is a seemingly healthy cargo program ex Black Sea as we move closer to the 3rd decade fixing window.

The Capesizes are experiencing a rally this week, supported by a range of factors but increased iron ore prices being the main driver as iron ore prices have reached its highest value since 2013. Activity from Brazil and Australia is therefore healthy, and rates are increasing healthy day by day. The average index broke 20,000 at the beginning of this week and is expected to strengthen further.

A lacklustre week in the VLCC segment with rates under pressure, especially in the MEG. With the dust having settled from the previous attacks, the trade is more or less back to normal, barring insurance premiums which by and large are picked up by charterers. High ws40’s is now the benchmark rate eastbound for unrestricted modern tonnage from all loading areas, yielding around USD 20k/day give/take in T/C equivalent. Current loading dates are behind the curve, giving some hope that activity could pick up, although a lot of “off market” fixing is clouding the supply/demand picture short term.

Another week has passed by in the Aframax segment with the North Sea and Baltic market, as well as the Mediterranean and Black Sea, moving sideways. Ships have one by one picked off the stems coming into the market frequently enough to maintain rate levels through most of the week.  However, while the Mediterranean and Black Sea market has had a slight downwards correction the last day or so, we have seen an uptick in rates ex North Sea and Baltic, as owners put up a little more resistance in a tighter window and take the opportunity to ask for a few more points. One to keep an eye on in the week to come, is a seemingly healthy cargo program ex Black Sea as we move closer to the 3rd decade fixing window.

A very strong week for shipowners in the spot market, as rates in both hemispheres have surged throughout the week. Many owners are trying their best to stay in the Atlantic, awaiting the rising fronthaul-rates. A TA round voyage currently pays owners about USD 12,500 per day, while a short fronthaul from the Continent now pays USD 20,000. In the east, a Pacific round voyage pays above the USD 10,000-mark. The BPI 4TC-index is currently at 1433 points, up 242 points from last week.

Last week we saw increased activity in both West Africa and MEG. Rates have been stable in MEG since the attack, and with the 30-day tonnage count looking decent we expect rates in this area to remain stable. In West Africa we saw rates ticking up at the end of last week, but ballasters from the east is putting downward pressure on this market, pushing rates back in the mid ws60's. Going forward there is a potential for owners to get some decent rates from Black Sea, as last done to Korea is USD 3,400' - with a massive 3rd decade program to come.
