comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG: ADNOC released their May acceptances with some delays reported, this was inevitable as most lifters nominated basis preferred early month lifting because of the heavy backwardation from May to June.    Qatar Petroleum is reported to have sold a May 31 to Jun 1st lifting of 46/0 at June CP plus $11-12 to a trading house. Premium for May FOB liftings varies widely pending on the different loading laycans, from mid high teens to single digits, the latter the cheaper.  At the time of writing, May Propane CP is traded at $505 and Butane assessed $15 higher, with June Propane CP is at $29 less.  Freight market ex MEG remains tight in the front month. Baltic kept it’s upward momentum up this week, which eroded the margins on delivery basis, with lifters tending to sell FOBs at premium to cash premium instead of bringing the cargo into the East themselves, unless they have their own shorts to cover.    FAR EAST: It was another hectic week with robust buying inquires, especially so for front the market against only a few offers. Although Houston channel has resumed operation, minimum 7-10 days are still expected to clear the backlock loading at some terminals.  Therefore, the front tightness extends into 2h May or even 1h June. Off window there is talk circulating that a 23k Propane cargo for delivery during 1h May traded at May FEI plus $60, while 1h/2h May swap value is at $20. On Thursday a 22/22 cargo for 1h May delivery were bid at May FEI plus $70, and bids for 23/0 for 1h May and 2h May was at May FEI plus $55 and plus $30 respectively, no offers for 1h May delivery was seen and 2h May sellers was at 10 dollars higher.  Chinese importers are also exploring cargoes for May, however limited cargoes are shown and the few that are is asking high $60ish or even higher, this is due to the higher FOB premiums and freight.   Some importers have shifted buying requirements from 1h May into 2h May, hoping they can secure cheaper cargoes, this doesn’t look to be the case yet, especially when there are outstanding trader shorts competing for the same cargoes.  Though Propylene appears weak and has squeezed PDH margins, this is unless it is an integrated downstream units.  Compared to high premium on “regular” tons, Iranian origins appear rather attractively priced and April/May imports is expected to be maintained or exceed the March volume which was at 500k tonnes.

Both east and west of Suez the VLGC markets have rallied during the course of the last two-three weeks. The fact is, we have witnessed a ten dollar increase in the BLPG index and further jumps are looming as the May acceptances are not out yet from MEG suppliers. Early May vessel availability is seemingly tight in the MEG and as such there is a feeling of anxiety in the market in case May cargo dates are accepted in the beginning of the month.   In the Atlantic basin, there have been a number of fixtures for laycans up to fifty days ahead, something which in turn is creating challenges with regards to vessel scheduling. Actually, owners currently hold back from further fixing activity simply because there is too much uncertainty. At the time of writing there are basically only a couple of workable VLGCs available for the end of May, however, we expect more vessels available in mid/2nd half May once they have loaded and discharge ports are nominated. As the US terminals are catching up with the delays and things normalize, the inevitable question is, how long will these rates sustain.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: FOB discussions in the USGC remain thin. The fog and benzene spill caused havoc and delays which will affect USGC loadings well into May. Traders with cargoes loading from terminals on the Houston ship channel are still unsure of the exact number of days delay they will incur. Halting all FOB trade discussions in the area due to laycan uncertainty. This has led to Marcus Hook going from the ugly duckling, during the well documented ME2 commissioning problems, to the belle of the ball today. Demand for East Coast US tons is at a premium and Marcus Hook has not disappointed. Set to export 9 VLGCs in April and we believe 7 VLGCs per month onwards. Marcus Hook is having a global impact on export cargo flows. The build of 1.2 million barrels although expected surprisingly pushed MT Belvieu up to 42% WTI from 39% the week prior. Latin American demand has been strong, with 80 000 MT more imported into Mexico alone in the 1st quarter 2019 compared with 1st quarter 2018. South American incremental seasonal demand continues, a recent US VLGC tender is rumoured to be heading that way.

LNG 19 in Shanghai is well underway and there is some exciting news being released in connection with the conference. In terms of shipping, it has been announced that TMS Cardiff secured a 10yrs contract with Vitol. In the product market Shell has signed a SPA with NextDecade for 2 MTPA from the Rio Grande project and Novatek has signed preliminary supply agreements with both Vitol and Repsol for volumes from their Arctic 2 project. With a lot of the market participants in Shanghai for LNG 19 the spot market is quiet, with only sporadic requirements surfacing. Spot rates are stable from last week, but the outlook continues to look positive.

A continued strengthening of rates in the Atlantic hemisphere has resulted in yet another positive week for the BPI index, despite a slight decrease of rates in the Pacific. A transatlantic round voyage currently pays owners about USD 10,000 per day, while a short fronthaul from the Continent yields about USD 16,500. In the East, a Pacific round voyage pays around the low USD 7,000's. The BPI 4TC-index is up 71 points to 1127.

The VLCC market took a proper beating this week, trading in the mid ws30’s MEG/eastbound at the time of writing – barely covering OPEX. Although dramatic, it is not unusual for this time of year, and on a “positive” note, it probably can’t go much lower. Alas, we do not foresee a pick-up this side of the summer, although market players are full of optimism for second half 2019.

Another challenging start to the week for owners in the Suezmax market. There was false hope at the latter part of last week as some injection barrels in West Africa stimulated some firmer sentiment, but this fizzled out as reality hit home as there was little action elsewhere West of Suez to support the drive.  TD20 briefly fell back to ws50.  As third decade dates are now being shown in reasonable volume this action has reignited a firmer sentiment with TD20 threatening ws55 as we write as cargoes attract limited offers. A minor recovery beckons but this will likely be short-lived as Charterers will likely sit back after this period of action.

Still short-term doom and gloom for the big ships, as market is only slowly absorbing an abundance of prompt units left without employment following some 8 mio tons of West Australia iron ore exports falling out due to cyclone.  Apart from certain bright spots on fronthaul, spot is completely on its knees - tc-equivalents of the WAust/China milk route are negative and Brazilian rounds are not much better.  Period interest nevertheless remain healthy for quality tonnage, with levels presently bid by major miners at some USD 14,500 for about 1.5 years on modern 180,000-tonners being a positive contrast to average daily spot earnings of less than USD 4000.

Aframax rates in the North Sea and Baltic have hovered around bottom levels the past week. The only exception has been Owners fixing out of the port of Primorsk in the 12-16 April window. Maintenance on two berths have limited the availability of tonnage meeting the current physical restrictions combined with ice restrictions. However, going forward we expect the market to remain soft as there is an abundance of available tonnage that needs to get fixed before rates will improve.  In the Mediterranean and Black Sea, we have seen the market moving sideways the past week as Owners take a stand in order to maintain current levels for a cross-Med run. Activity from Charterers has been stable, and although prompt ships have rolled over from last week, we have seen few ships ballasting into the area, resulting in a downward correction. In the week to come we expect Owners to maintain their position, as the market is expected to remain soft.

More downward pressure on rates across both basins this week. From the USG, Ultras are fixing in the high-teens and mid-teens for FH and TA, respectively. ECSA have seen some activity this week where Supras fixing around mid USD 13,000 for TA, while from Emed to Wafr rates are around USD 7,000. In the Pacific, the Indo coal rates have been falling especially on prompt dates, where Supras are facing USD 7k in front for rv to China at the time of writing. CIS rv paying owners in the mid 6k bss CJK delivery to SE Asia, while clinker trips from Vietnam to North China is trading around USD high 8k.

The VLCC market took a proper beating this week, trading in the mid ws30’s MEG/eastbound at the time of writing – barely covering OPEX. Although dramatic, it is not unusual for this time of year, and on a “positive” note, it probably can’t go much lower. Alas, we do not foresee a pick-up this side of the summer, although market players are full of optimism for second half 2019.

The Eastern VLGC market has tightened up significantly over the past few days, as there are almost no available vessels until the early parts of May. We see more and more inquiries for early May liftings already, although so far only QP and KPC have announced their cargo acceptances so far. Even though QP gave quite some delays to their term lifters, it seems it has no effect to the rather tight vessel situation. The market is now awaiting ADNOC and Aramco acceptances, and only after this, they will decide on their position and whether they will need to charter in or potentially relet their tonnage. The current Baltic (Ras Tanura to Chiba) is closing in on 900,000 per month yesterday, and with the overall tight market situation, we do expect further increase of rates, and T/C/E will probably pass the 1-million-dollar-mark shortly. Last time similar levels were discussed is back in February 2016. In the West, the market is equally tight. This is also somewhat fuelled by the current problems with Fog in the US Gulf area, which creates significant delays that in turn eat up much of the shipping length. Although there are quite some people off attending an on-going industry function in Houston this week, it does not seem this have affected the market activity too much. We have seen a few fixtures this week for both mid- and end May loading, both out of the Gulf and the East coast. Levels have been steadily moving upwards, and as per last done rates, the ships in the West is currently trading in the high USD 900’s per month, reflecting a premium of about 8-10% on the transpacific route.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: Mt Belvieu propane prices weakened Wednesday following a larger than expected build of 1.6 million barrels. Domestic production remains above 2 million barrels a day whilst exports were above 1 million barrels a day for the second week running. At the Houston IHS conference much of the talk has been about new US export capacity coming on at the end of this year and in 2020, aligning well with new US fractionation capacity. Both of which will be substantial. The belief is still that all of the new US propane to hit the water will find a home by pricing itself into the international market.

comment_type: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG： Qatar Petroleum released their May acceptances with some lifters experiencing 2-3 weeks’ delays, mainly for equal ratio cargoes which were nominated for early month lifting. QP is reportedly selling a 45 kt Propane cargo for 1st decade lifting at June CP plus around $10 premium, they may still be able to squeeze a full Propane spot cargo for end May or early June loading. The Baltic VLGC freight has soared by over $5 during the last few days (WOW) and is still climbing. With limited vessels open in the East until 1st decade May.  Traders with cargo length and not enough shipping, tends to resell their FOB tons to collect the premium instead of selling CFR delivery.  Saudi Aramco announced April CP over the weekend at $515 for Propane and $535 for Butane, up by $25 and $15 respectively. Since the April CP was announced, May CP has gained quickly and is $494 at the time of writing.  However the spread between May/June CP have widened from last week’s 20ish to $40. May FEI/CP also widened from previous -$8 to -$26, which reflects the front strength against forward length.    FAR EAST: The tightness in the front market didn’t see any relief during this week.  Although the Houston ship channel slowly started to resume to normal operation, lifters are still waiting for clearance on previous backlogs.  Limited or no sellers can commit cargoes with fixed arrival until the vessel has departed from US Gulf.  23kt Propane for 1H May arrival is bid at May FEI plus $48 while the offer is at $21 higher.  22+22 kt c3/c4 cargoes is in even shorter supply with buyer’s bidding at May CP plus $60 with no sellers to be seen.  23kt Propane for 2H May arrival is less tight  with value being about $25 less.  Off window discussions mostly ended up in deadlock.  Japanese and Korean importers are not willing to release AG origin cargoes without in return getting US origin cargoes back because of low inventory.  Very few trades was concluded within this week, as a consequence inquiries are outstanding ranging from 2h April to May delivery.  Indian IOC issued a buy tender for 22+22 kt c3/c4 with 2h May delivery into Ennore, and optional parcels for 15/15 kt or 20/20 kt delivered in June to Aug.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Eastern Market
text: MEG： The intermonth CP value is still in a heavily backwardated structure. April/May remains at $45-50 while May/June now stands at $15-20.  At time of writing, April Propane CP is traded at 507$, and butane stands at $20 higher. Cargoes which can make within April delivery are being favored and discussed at teens premium. Freight has soared to above $40, as plenty of vessels are lining up outside US and limited tonnage showing open in the AG gulf.    FAR EAST: Front market is extremely tight, with a handful of cargoes being delayed due to the Houston ship channel closure. On Wednesday 23kt propane for 2h April arrival was traded at Apr FEI plus $50, and a similar cargo for 1h May arrival was concluded at May FEI plus $40. Some traders have continue trying to arrange time swaps to secure tons with delivery within April.  Indonesia’s Pertamina have issued tenders to secure two split-ratio cargoes for 1h May delivery, while BPCL also tendered to buy similar cargos for 1h/mid-May delivery. Results of these are yet to be known.   Most Chinese importers are exploring cargos for 1h May arrival, even so there are still some prompt inquiries for April delivery. Sellers are hesitant showing offers because of heavy backwardations.  As MEG supply is short, Chinese players have turned to some other origins. Our shiptrack shows around 500k tons Iranian origin cargoes discharge into China within the month of March, which is the highest on record in the recent past. April volume is expected to be slightly smaller as less floating cargoes are available.

comment_name: Gas Market Weekly Comment - Western Market
text: The winter is over, the absolute price of propane is falling, and this combined with loading delays  is allowing the arbs and freights to reach the best levels in over a year. Delays in the US Gulf has caused near panic in Asia forcing premiums to FEI to sky rocket. The US is exporting roughly 2.5 million tons per month of LPG and out of this roughly 50 percent is going to Asia . Hence 15 day delays in loading translates into aproximately 750,000 mts per month into Asia and thus it is not hard to understand the large premiums being seen for second half May arrivals. The question going forward is, will arbs last at reasonable levels. Fog season will end but as stated before production is too strong and US propane must price to move. Already today propane is down to 45 percent of WTI and we expect it to drop further. Historically,  propane below 45 percent of WTI makes for a good Arb and frieght market.

The VLCC market took a turn for the worse this week, as activity slowed down in all areas and ships of all classes have been piling up. Those charterers dipping their feet in receive double digit offers, with tonnage offering initially below last done levels. Thus, we expect rates to drop further as the week progresses, and owners could find themselves trading at OPEX levels before long. At the time of writing, ws45 has been done on a ship older than 15 years for MEG/East, and modern tonnage will probably follow suit soon.

It has been fairly good activity in the West the last week, and finally the tonnage list for cargoes out of West Africa on natural dates is looking more healthy. Rates are still scraping the bottom of what Owners consider beneficiary compared to throwing anchor and waiting for better times, but at least now we could see a slight improvement going forward. In the MEG, on the other hand, there is not much positive signs for Owners going forward. The list of available tonnage is increasing, and even in a tight window for 20t crane ships, Owners didn’t manage to capitalize. Activity in the area still remains decent, but not to the extent where anything will happen rate wise. In the Black Sea, rates are coming off as well, with last done on TD6 at ws60. Not unexpected as the Turkish Strait delays are down to 3-4 days each way.

Aframax rates in the Nsea and Baltic took a big hit this week as activity slowed down and there was an abundance of available tonnage offering in on the few cargoes in the market. Rates have hit bottom for now with TCE nearly covering OPEX. We expect these markets to move sideways as we currently see very little support from surrounding markets suggesting any upwards turn in the near future. Although the unbalance between supply and demand in the Mediterranean and Black Sea continues with prompt open ships rolling over from last week, cargo activity has been healthy enough to see the market trade sideways. TD19 is currently at around ws90 levels, and we have seen a few ships fixing Fuel stems and leaving the market heading East. Congestion in the Turkish Straits is finally coming off, resulting in transit time has come down from 8 days mid last week to 3-4 days at the time of writing.

We expect this fixing trend to continue and more fixtures will be done in view of the upcoming industry event next week.  The bullish sentiment on freight from last week continues, as healthy shipping demand from the West is keeping the Eastern spot fleet availability tight. Last done deal in the MEG was done at very low $40 Baltic, and time of writing there are still a couple of uncovered cargos for last decade April loading. There is also an expectation of a few more requirements from Indian Charterers, and we expect the bullish sentiment on freight to continue into next month.

Despite wider uncertainty in the short term outlook of the cargo market due to oversupply, with some referencing output shutdowns as a consequence, multi-month charter rates remain buoyant.  Record imports persist into Europe not only from the US but also from Middle East and Africa which are struggling to find demand in the Middle East, China and the Far East. Despite the weak voyage length fundamentals spot levels this week have risen modestly off the latest floor and may signal the first signs of an upward trend.  Owners and Charterers will convene in Shanghai next week at the LNG19 conference with many discussions focusing the forward outlook which sees a variety of influencing factors, shut-ins, commissioning, summer cargo demand and yard prices. 2019 has plenty of variable elements to consider and it is this backdrop that appears to be fueling an array of forward views. The order-book grew again this week by 1 with the quoted price at 191M USD, a tick up from last done and likely to continue. In summary, short term fundamentals look weak but improving throughout the year with potential for huge volatility.

Even though rates have been lagging behind in the East, the week overall has shown a continued recovery in the Panamax market. A transatlantic round voyage currently yields about USD 8,000 per day, while a short fronthaul from the Continent yields about USD 15,500. In the East, a Pacific round voyage pays around the mid USD 7,000's. The BPI 4TC-index is up 94 points to 1056.

The week started slowly in the Atlantic with Greece off for holidays and after a positive last week in the USG, this week feels more uncertain with increased tonnage supply in the area, where Ultras has been fixing TA's around USD 16k. From ECSA Supras have obtained around 15k for TA round, while Mediterranean to West Africa is paying owners around USD 9k. In the Pacific, a softening feeling in Se Asia by mid-week. Supras fixing around USD 9k for Indo/China, while Nopac rv's is paying around high USD 8k. In Indian Ocean, owners are seeing around mid USD 9k for WCIndia to China, while MEG/ECIndia runs trading around high USD 10k.

Finally some good news again for the big ships after a series of setbacks including historically strong cyclone paralyzing major iron ore loading area West Australia, disrupting maybe as much as 8 million tons over 4 full days. Average daily earnings are still far too low to cover even operating expenses, but increased coal activity in Pacific combined with generally positive mineral volume developments in Atlantic give reason for cautious optimism. The worst of this year may be passed as Vale are expected to return for parts of their temporarily closed-down iron ore facilities. Underlying bright outlook plus improving paper levels give support to quite some period fixing, most recently exemplified by 181,000/16 done for 9-12 months at USD 13,400, 180,000/10 for 4-6 months at USD 13,000, and also 182,000/10 concluded at bci ave5tc + 8 pct basis 12-16 months, all to major players.

The VLCC market took a turn for the worse this week, as activity slowed down in all areas and ships of all classes have been piling up. Those charterers dipping their feet in receive double digit offers, with tonnage offering initially below last done levels. Thus, we expect rates to drop further as the week progresses, and owners could find themselves trading at OPEX levels before long. At the time of writing, ws45 has been done on a ship older than 15 years for MEG/East, and modern tonnage will probably follow suit soon.

More activity and positive sentiment this week, as rates have been increasing in both hemispheres. A transatlantic round voyage currently yields about USD 5,500 per day, while a short fronthaul from the Continent yields around low USD 13,000's. In the East, a Pacific round voyage pays around the USD 8,000's. The BPI 4TC-index is up 123 points for the week, currently at 962 points.

The spot LNG shipping market sentiment is holding relatively flat for another week, although there were quite a few requirements surfacing this week in both basins, but their impact has been rather minimal, as there are still enough prompt ships looking to be chartered. The Pacific rates have not moved this week whereas the Atlantic rates have been adjusted to correspond with the latest reported levels. However, there is an underlying firmer tone developing and the markets may well experience an upturn further out, as we are seeing Charterers looking to secure tonnage for multi-month or even multi-year period(s) with delivery later part of the year, and the availability list for such periods has seen reductions. LNG end-users were also heard looking at purchasing a few spot cargoes, which could be positive development for the shipping markets.

After a period with improving levels, rates again turned red this week. Mainly as a result of a lack of miners in the market. Average index value is presently at disappointing USD 5,000 level. However, there were some good news from Brazil, were operations at Brucutu mine is expected to resume. So far, the effect has been seen in rising dry-bulk shares and improved FFA values. The closure of the mine after the dam burst 2 months ago is estimated to have caused approximately 5 million tons loss in production.

The Atlantic market remained steady, with more cargo flow in ECSA/ USG, lacking FH. East Mediterranean-Continent areas slow with limited fresh cargoes on the market. Flat market in Asia with slightly weak sentiment. Indian ocean stable with good levels achieved in South Africa. Tess 58,000 fixed for a trip delivery South Africa redelivery Pakistan-WC India close to USD 12,000s plus around USD 200,000 ballast bonus.

Continued sparse activity in the West has allowed Charterers to pull rates even further down. The 1st decade in West Africa has been worked at a pedestrian pace with ships being picked off quietly and owners just content to cover cargoes closest to their dates. Meanwhile there has been a reversal of fortunes in the MEG with a flurry of action for first decade April dates and owners managing to wrestle back some control as the list has tightened.  The Turkish delays have slowly decreased, and this has allowed more fluidity in the availability for the Black Sea, TD6 has come off to ws70 at the time of writing.  The week ahead has a softer tone with still too many ships available and cargoes not seemingly increasing in volume.

At the time of writing the West market continues its upward trend. Vessel availability for April is relatively scarce for US Gulf and a West Africa cargo tender 18-20 April is seemingly pretty much down to the faith of one or two vessels, if that. We expect short term freight to continue strengthening and overhang of vessels available from April going into May will be reduced significantly.  In the East - Saudi April acceptances came out over the weekend where as expected most lifters got delayed (or even deferred into next month) due to upstream oil cuts. A logical effect to this would usually mean lack of shipping requirements as most cargo dates are now quite forward, but as shipping availability is becoming increasingly tighter in the East; some players have started to move for 2H April dates. Last done deal in the MEG was done in the mid/high USD 30s, and there are still a handful of uncovered cargos to be fixed for 2H April.

text: A build in US inventories when most market players expected a draw signaled an end to the domestic winter. There had been fog which reduced traffic in Houston ship channel for part of the week ending March 15th. This contributed to the 900,000 bbl build for the week. The fog season this year has been later and longer than previous years, and with more fog forecast for the weekend and Monday 25th March, we are not out of the woods yet. The reduced liftings from the US Gulf have maintained worldwide arbs. Domestic production is a shade below 2million barrels per day, and is only set to increase to new record levels throughout this year. The build coupled with a draw in US crude inventories has pushed Mt Belvieu propane as a percentage of WTI down to 46%, the lowest seen for quite some time. At this percentage of crude we expect the worldwide arbs to remain wide and demand to be strong. In South American markets seasonal imports continue to increase as winter nears.

The market for Aframaxes trading in the North Sea and Baltic came off significantly this week. Rates came under downward pressure due to lack of activity and tonnage building up. Everyone is now waiting to hear when ice restrictions in certain Baltic ports will be lifted. We expect this soft trend to continue. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea we have seen TD19 (cross-Med) drop to ws85 levels at the time of writing. Over the past week rate levels ex Black Sea have dropped from more than ws100 to sub-90 levels. On a lighter note, the current week started with a boost in activity as a steady flow of cargoes have come into the market decreasing the tonnage build up in the area and creating an optimistic vibe among Owners, who hope to see an upturn towards the end of the week, as there currently aren’t any obvious alternative markets to flee to.

With the March VLCC MEG program behind us the Owning community was looking forward to a sprout of activity for early April with ambition to push rates up in to the ws60 eastbound. However, activity has thus far been disappointing. Ws59 is last done for a MEG/China run, although still about USD 30k per day in t/c returns on a non eco modern ship - well above historic returns for time of year. USG activity has also halted, and a handful of Owners having ballasted their ships from the east on spec are nervously awaiting fresh export cargoes to take them back east.

text: MEG: April CP swap’s have seen volatility throughout this week with $10 up and down swings on daily basis, reflecting continued uncertainty in the front market and differing views with regard to future CP value.  April MEG liftings continue being traded at double digits premium to CP and still inquires remain outstanding. Spurred by demand from India and Indonesia especially.  Term lifters are still awaiting Saudi acceptances, which should come over the weekend, before taking additional decisions.  At the time of writing, April propane CP is traded at $488 and butane at around $20 higher.  FAR EAST: There is big a big gap in price between cargoes delivered in 1h April versus 2h April. This Thursday 23kt propane for 2h Apr was concluded at balance March FEI flat, and other bids for similar cargo are at April FEI plus $12.  However, the CFR market for 1h April delivery continue being very active, with bidding at April FEI +$34 while offering stands at April CP +$47, this equates to April FEI plus $60 at current values.  The delays of US origin tonnes saw no relief this week, causing further backwadation between 1st and 2nd half arrival cargoes.  India’s BPCL issued buy tenders totaling 85kt in total volume for April delivery. Indonesia’s Pertamina tendered to buy a 44kt split cargo for delivery in 1h April, the result is unknown at time of writing. FPC withdrew their buy tender for 22k or 44k propane for delivery 6-20 April as no suitable offer was received for this period.  A couple of propane and heavy propane cargos have been sold into China, with premium concluded reported to be above April CP +$40’s.  There are still outstanding inquires for 2h April delivery but buyer’s sentiment is weaker because of slow domestic distribution and eroding margins with surging costs.

FOB cargoes on sale across all basins, plus some short term requirements have kept things bit more busy this week, especially as we move towards the shoulder months. In the spot market, the scenery has however not changed significantly and the availability list yet remains long, giving Charterers plenty of options. Therefore, spot rates remain under pressure across all three basins. In the term market, however, interest from Charterers in securing tonnage towards autumn/winter has increased and especially for coverage from September onwards.  For a change, there were no new large LNGC  orders reported this week, but plenty activity on SSLNG, a segment we also follow closely here at Fearnleys.

text: This winter in the US has been deified by smaller than expected draws in US inventories. This week the 1.2 million barrel draw was again lower than expected. The reason behind these lower draws has been the domestic production which has only dipped under the 2 million barrels per day a few times. Even through very cold weather for a sustained amount of time in many parts of the US the production is just too great.  This very high production is only set to increase and exports will be expected to make up for this additional production, ie product will have to be priced to move. The recent fog delays have had a large part in pushing up delivered markets with high cash diffs in the East and West windows, and is set to continue through the week. Traders right now are trying to assess how long these premiums will continue, and if they can justify paying through netback value for US FOBs. A tender from Chile was heard to be won on a delivered basis at around 17cpg.

Average daily earning still well below operating costs, and owners keep bleeding - but nevertheless finally some bright spots for the big ships, and most players seem to believe the worst for 2019 is now past. Healthy iron ore and coal volumes from Australia absorb a number of early far east units, and west australia/china rates have improved by some 18 pct to come in at usd 5.50 pmt w-o-w. In Atlantic, the tendency is for fronthaul ore being loaded further north to compensate for ongoing Brazilian export problems, however freight levels paid remain weak.  Little period concluded for the modern large units at fixed rates as gap between available levels and forward expectation remain too wide, but for the smaller vintage ships the most recent is 171000 dwt built 2005 open India prompt done for 20-23 months at usd 9750.

There has been limited activity this week, partly due to a greek holiday and a lack of fresh orders along with a slimming tonnage list. Rates have been going down in both basins, but signs are showing that the grain levels will are looking positive for April dates from ECSA. transatlantic round voyage currently yields about USD 4,500 per day, while a short fronthaul from the continent yields around low USD 12,000. In the east, a Pacific round voyage pays around the USD 8,000's. The BPI 4TC-index is down 99 points for the week, currently at 839 points.

A more negative segment this week in Pacific, although seeing still Indo coal cargoes getting fixed at around  USD 12000 to China. Indian Ocean has improved with vessels fixing 12250+225k gbb Rbay to Feast and from WCI to China paying around USD 11000. In the Atlantic still relatively weak levels seen from continent with scrap cargo to Emed fixing around USD 7750. ECSA seen stronger levels with USD 13000 + 300k gob done for frontbaul and USD 15000 to Med.

The VLGC market in the West came back to life this week with several fixtures out of the US during first decade of April. A week or so back in time, 1-10 April seemed more-or-less done in terms of cargo enquiries, however, a spot FOB tender parallel to a couple of US East coast cargoes needing freight revived the market. Very high USD 50’s was still on the cards as of yesterday although owners are now trying to use the momentum to push freight back above the USD 60 per ton mark. 2nd decade April stems are already being shown, however, remains to be fixed. First half April looks to be controlled by one major owner and vessel overhang from March to April has been reduced from 4-5 VLGCs to abt 1-3 VLGCs. The market East of Suez was active last week for end March and very early April laycans and the market turned from somewhat negative to suddenly breaking USD 30 per ton again. Early April seems fairly tight on shipping, however, with ADNOC acceptances being delayed some 1-2 weeks and players expecting both delays and cuts from Saudi Aramco with regards to April cargoes, the inevitable question is how long this uptick with last.

The Vlcc market has this week been a bit ‘all-over-the-place’. One moment it has looked firm with steady rates being paid both in the Meg and also West Africa. The lack of steady demand ex Americas and particularly Usg has infused some doubt in the market and especially for those who have ballasted West on spec. It has therefore been too much of a gamble not to accept the rates offered on the few cargoes shown , and rates have taken a bit of a dip. Nothing dramatic so far but increased volumes for all the major Vlcc-routes required for rates to have any chance to hold at present levels.

As expected, Aframax rates in the Nsea and Baltic increased entering the fixing window in third decade of March. This firm sentiment looks to continue as Owners have the upper hand in the current fixing window. However, going forward there is more available tonnage coming open in the area and we expect rates to soften once 3rd decade cargoes get covered. In the Mediterranean and Black Sea on the other hand, we have seen rates come off this week due to low activity levels from Charterers side. Prompt ships are piling up in the area and we have seen TD19 (cross-Med) crumble down from WS 110 levels mid last week to WS 90 levels at time of writing. Fixtures ex Black Sea have dropped around 35 points from WS 135 to WS 100 levels over the last week. Unless Owners start ballasting their ships away from the area in order to try their luck in alternative markets, we expect freight levels in the Mediterranean and Black Sea to remain under pressure in the week to come as the current tonnage list still looks healthy.

Suezmaxes lost further ground over the past week as Charterers looked to cherry pick tonnage off market thus burying fixtures and managing to erode rates futher. Demand for fuel oil in the east has kept the med market ticking over and there are signs of some arbitrage enquiry in the north that could compliment the slim West Africa offerings.  TD20 has hit a low of ws 60 so far this week and TD6 has slipped down to ws 75 having had very limited action. There is still some pain to come for owners as the trend for the week ahead has a softer tone with just too many ships still available on lists.

text: MEG: It all started middle of the week, April CP moved from $460 to $490s. Tightness in the front market have pushed up the price. Saudi Aramco appear to have little to nothing when it come to spot availabilities till June. Term lifters are cautiously waiting for April lifting acceptances, also thinking about confirmed and possible future   US fog delays. The spread between Propane and Butane has narrowed a bit with anticipation that more US butane will come to East. There are however some uncertainties due to the weather.   FAR EAST: The Asian market has been quiet with the Tokyo conference being this week.  Nevertheless, in the window one Korean importer aggressively bid for 23kt propane for prompt 2h Mar delivery. No sellers appeared in the window until Thursday, to offer 23kt propane for 1h April, this show a premium of low 40s over April CP.  April CP gained strength from the tightness in front month, with April FEI less support. With expectation that ample supply from US will sail to east, Apr FEI/CP turned into negative again and traded at minus $8 at the time of writing.   Off window there are active inquiries from either China or SEA. But with slim margins in both residential and PDH petchem, importers might restrain their spot activities and cover volume on rigid demand basis. Indonesian Pertamina is reported to have awarded their last tender for 11/11 only arriving early April. Another noticeable phenomenon is more Iranian cargoes have been tracked sailing to China from Mar. So far we’ve seen around 300k tonnes is arriving/will arrive in first half period.

We’ve noticed a small increase in fixture activity from the past few weeks, but the charter levels are in line with shoulder season expectations. Shipping rates, both in the West and in the East were somewhat soft and we’ve logged a small reduction on the spot headliner rates. On a positive note there isn’t too much downside risk left in the spot market and «Owners» continues to be optimistic about 3Q and the winter to come. Vessel availability has come off slightly, but not enough to have an impact yet on spot rates. We kept LNG newbuild prices stable this week, but shipyards are reporting good interest in LNG slots.

Aframax rates in NSea and Baltic are currently under upward pressure. Moving into 3rd decade fixing window in Baltic, there will be a greater volume of cargoes compared to previous months. There is still a requirement for ice class tonnage, but the supply of available tonnage is thinner as more ice class vessels have left the area. On the back of this we expect NSea market to capitalize on a firmer Baltic market and we could see rates jump in the 15-20 March fixing window here. In Med and BlSea rates have continued to pick up the past week, especially ex BlSea where fixtures ex Novo and CPC to Med are currently at ws135 levels. While rate levels in alternative markets such as US have come off slightly, the steady flow of fresh cargoes coming in to the market in Med/BlSea have kept activity levels up. Owners are pleased to see TD19 currently at around ws112.50 levels, with expectations of a firm market in the days to come.

The smaller ships are continuing to improve, so we reiterate our view from last week that the bottom is in and that an upturn should materialize very shortly. The Capesize to Panamax market ratio is now at 58%, which is the lowest level since early 2016. Every time previously this ratio was at such low levels a market rebound followed.

The VLCC activity is up and so is the optimism among VLCC owners. After recent fall in rates, the trend has turned around and rates climbed back up. Contrary to last month where the activity USG-Cbs led the way we have seen MEG-activity leading the way. Thinner tonnage on the ground in MEG has also affected Wafr/East rates which have firmed in tandem with earnings for the Eco types hovering abt $40k/day. The jury is still out whether this firming trend is a mere ‘flash in the pan’ or sustainable.

Looking forward into next week we expect a steadier feel to the market to be the order of the day with the 2Q beckoning and more challenges ahead.

text: The Mt Belvieu market took Wednesday’s draw of 2 million barrels in US inventories in its stride. The arbs to Asia and Europe remain very strong, with high premiums in the respective windows. These have been pushing up US FOB offer levels. We could even see double figures for a March cargo if one becomes available. Fog in the US Gulf has played it’s part in delaying laycans, pushing up the prompt window premiums as vessels get delayed. Another 4 straight days of fog are expected over the weekend, potentially delaying more loadings. Terminals are doing their best to clear any backlog and mitigate as much fog risk as possible. A US Gulf Coast FOB tender for up to a cargo a month from May to December 2019 was released this week. With market participants agreeing that it was a good time to release a tender with wide arbs. It was a bit of surprise when an Eastern trader released another USGC FOB tender for a cargo per month from April to September 2019. In South America, Gasmar issued a tender to buy CFR into Chile for end April arrival. This marked the beginning of the demand season in the region as the Southern Hemisphere transitions into winter.

The VLGC market seems to have taken yet another breather both East and West this week, as most market players have been occupied in industry functions in Tokyo (this week), following the IP Week in London last week. In the West, a couple of cargo tenders has been put on the market, one FOB and one CFR, both for award later in the week, and is expected to attract some attention. Another FOB tender for a cargo out of West Africa is also expected. One vessel has been fixed on end March dates out of the US Gulf, and this might well be the final March-cargo to come on market. In the East, we have not recorded much activity. Some traders have been working on optimization however so far without much fixing activity. One cargo inquiry from one of the Indian companies attracted some interest, and a ship is currently on subs at levels at a slight premium to the current Baltic. The Baltic has followed the market activity very much and has been moving sideways since last week. The index is currently trading at levels around USD 11-13,000 per day depending on vessel type, which is some USD 4,000 per day lower than current trades in the Western markets.

The VLCC activity is up and so is the optimism among VLCC owners. After recent fall in rates, the trend has turned around and rates climbed back up. Contrary to last month where the activity USG-Cbs led the way we have seen MEG-activity leading the way. Thinner tonnage on the ground in MEG has also affected Wafr/East rates which have firmed in tandem with earnings for the Eco types hovering abt $40k/day. The jury is still out whether this firming trend is a mere ‘flash in the pan’ or sustainable.

Still positive development in the Pacific with Indo coal trips to WCI paying around USD 10500 and to China around USD 11000. Clinker runs from S.China to N.China is fixed around USD 10250, while Nopac rv is paying around USD 8250 to Seasia, while in Indian Ocean. The Atlantic market has not picked up the pace in the same way as the Pacific. From the Continent scrap runs to Emed are paying around USD 9000 and from Emed to Wafr owners are seeing around USD 7500. While from the USG vessels are seeing low teens for tct to Med and around mid teens for FH. From the ECSA front hauls are paying around USD 12000 + 200kgbb and to Cont/Med around USD 9000.

The Baltic Capesize index is now assessed below those of all the smaller segments. This is usually a strong sign that the bottom is in or at least very close. This coupled with seasonal tailwinds starting in March should result in an imminent market upturn for the big ships.

text: MEG: Saudi Aramco announced Mar CP at $490 and $520 respectively for propane and butane, up by $50 each, which is much higher than player’s expectation. The tightness on AG spot supply didn't get relieved and traders can scarcely squeeze out tons for resale. Apr CP swap is heavily backwardated, but slowly edged up at $466 at the time of writing. Apr C3/C4 spread has narrowed down from Mar at $20 at the time being.  FAR EAST: Tightness in 2h Mar extends into 1h Apr. The foggy weather in US continues and incurs further delays, which exert upward pressures on price in short term. On Wed a 23kt propane delivered in 1h Apr was traded at Apr FEI plus $15, which is $12$ higher than other bid. And we barely see any offers for this period even off window. 2h Apr is slightly at ease with expectation that the cargo will move smooth later on. Price of non-US origin is also hitting rooftops, with outstanding tenders from Indian and Indonesia for equal ratio cargoes delivered ranged from late Mar to Apr. Propane cargo within Mar arrival is reported done at low mid 40s into China, and premium of for 1h Apr arrival cargos hover over 40$. One North China petchem user has issued a private tender to secure one full propane cargo delivered in Apr. And other Chinese are actively inquired for propane or heavy propane cargo delivered in 1h Apr as well.

A much more positive outlook in most areas resulted in a strong increase in both hemispheres. Having been lagging slightly behind the general market, the North Atlantic has looked firmer and has increased the most. A transatlantic round voyage currently yields about USD 3,500 per day, while a short fronthaul from the continent yields about USD 12,000. In the east, a Pacific round voyage pays around the low USD 7,000's. The BPI 4TC-index is up 103 points to 752.

text: This winter in North America has been a monster. The cold weather started early and it has lasted long. None the less the propane production has been an even bigger monster. Averaging just over 2 million barrels a day, the question of whether the US could handle record exports and cold weather has been answered with a resounding YES. Export Terminals and mid-stream companies are gearing up with expansions, new fractionators, and new pipelines to handle the production going forward, but the question will no longer be is there enough product,  but where will the product go? This week US C3 inventories decreased by 1.2 million barrels which was less than expectations. This and declining freight rates has allowed the arb to widen to levels not seen in several months and is pointing towards stronger terminalling fees. It certainly seems that this who locked in terminalling under 6 cpg for 2019 are currently on the right side for now.

As expected, Aframax rates in the Baltic and North Sea increased this week. Quite a few vessels had left the area leaving charterers with fewer options to fix. This equipped owners with the opportunity to push for higher rates than last done. At the time of writing we expect the firm sentiment to continue, especially out of strategic ice restricted export areas. We have seen a steady flow of cargoes coming into the Mediterranean market the last few days. However, the increased activity has yet to be translated into firming rates as there is still an oversupply of tonnage. The past week we have seen TD19 drop to WS 85 levels. On the bright side we have seen an upturn in alternative markets such as North West Europe and USG/Caribs.

The brisk activity ex Usg for march has managed to pull the rates up for the other major VLCC-routes. Ships have ballasted on spec from the East towards Americas looking for increased tce’s which again has started to thin the lengthy tonnage-list for Meg and West Africa. Rates have corrected up , but one might argue that the latest sharp decrease in rates ex Meg and West Africa was A bit overdone. Therefore better balance of tonnage supply for the respective areas and  rates found support at present levels.

The market was on the way up at the end of last week, but to start this week there has been further weakness. There is a lot of period tonnage trying to find a home, and with a lack of spot cargoes this has pushed down the market and FFAs further.  However, we are still optimistic in the near term as seasonal factors should kick in soon and support the market.

Sporadic action has allowed tonnage lists to build and further erosion of rates across the board has been the flavour of the past week. It has been a slow decline rather than a collapse in levels which has allowed earnings to remain close to 20 k per day  in the Atlantic, there has been some notable fixing out of the Usg and this is one area that has shown some life, the WTI- Brent spread has been wide enough to allow imports into the ukcm and that is an attractive voyage for a select few.  Some owners have preferred to sit ships spot, seemingly satisfied to wait for the right voyage giving the best TCE returns rather than fixing less attractive options at lower money. Still further pain ahead for the foreseeable future but the Atlantic basin tonnage lists will need watching if Usg exports continue.

Due to increased coal demand in Asia, we recently reached USD 10,000 pd levels for RVs on Ultramaxes and larger Supramaxes. In the Indian Ocean, we recently saw USD 10,000 pd for a West Coast Indian salt trip into China. We saw USD 12,500 pd plus a USD 250,000 ballast bonus fixed on an Ultramax for ECSA trip to Singapore-Japan. Increased activity in USG  led to vessels obtaining USD 16,000 for FH.  The Mediterranean and Bsea markets remain slow with rates reported in the USD 7,000/8,000 pd range with clinker to Wafrica.

Owners ideas are currently starting with a $3 bss baltic, but there is also some available shipping length from traders that will add pressure to rates. Shipping availability for US loadings both in 2H March and 1H April currently looks slightly long and most therefore expect the West freight rates to come off slightly.

We are almost done and dusted with February and that also means the official end of the Northern Hemisphere “winter months”. From a market perspective there is little change, as the cargo demand has stayed relatively flat for a while now. There are however signs of improved cargo activity, which has in turn rippled into new shipping requirements for March and April. Still, LNGC spot rates remain under pressure, since the availability list is rather long and includes sublets that in general can fix at competitive levels to compensate for their reduced flexibility or period availability.  It’s IP week in London, and among other discussions, there are still a wide range of views on how the rest of the 2019 will pan out on commodity pricing. The only thing certain is that no one has a reliable crystal ball.  On the newbuilding side, it was another active week with Maran Gas ordering two more 174,000cbm LNGC newbuilds from DSME for late 2021 delivery. More to come next week?

A healthy week has passed in the Western hemisphere. Rates have stabilised in the high USD 50’s bss Houston/Chiba and seemingly first and second decade March is more or less covered by now. A cargo tender ex Angola is expected to draw some attention from various players. Second half March loaders ex USG have yet to surface, however, there should be more cargo enquiries on the horizon.   After a long dull period in the East, we finally see a more active market much due to healthy activity around 1st decade of March. Baltic seems to have reached its bottom and TCE is again back at above $300K/per month. The BLPG is currently trading in the high 20’s and trending upwards. The rebound also brings more demand from 2nd decade of March and keeps the market tight. Moreover, the Indians hasn’t come out yet with their March shipping demand despite the strong cargo demand. Once they do, its reasonable to think this will put further sparks into the market.

Amid the bearish sentiments circulating since the start of the month, we did see improvements in terms of shipping requirements this week.  Activity has picked up and mainly in the East of Suez. However, spot shipping rates are still under pressure as demand is unable to support the current number of vessels available. Furthermore, we have seen a continuous dip in the Far East LNG prices, which in turn continues to keep the West-to-East arbitrage opportunities low. Going forward, and as we are about to enter the “shoulder months” in the gas market, the market expects current shipping levels to remain relatively flat. However, as the current spot market is in favour towards the Charterers, we may start seeing more interest for multi-month requirements to cover the second half of the year and the next winter. On newbuildings, we understand that Maran Gas has exercised their option and has placed another order for a 174,000cbm MEGI with DSME. Reports indicate that the vessel will be delivered in the first half of 2021.

The Suezmax market has been a mix of bewilderment and an acceptance of reality as the continued slow pace of firm cargoes working has continued to sap owners of their resilience. WAfr saw a drip feed of cargoes for early March dates and rates have been somewhat voyage sensitive but TD20 has fallen to ws67.5 and earnings sub 20k/day. Delays in the Turkish straits have reduced but this has not really affected market rates significantly, TD6 has fallen away to ws87.5 and the potential to soften even further. The outlook unfortunately in the week ahead is for more of the same with a softer tone across the board prevailing.

Shipping activity in the East have been lackluster with very few enquiries to report. Most lifters ended up getting delayed for their March acceptances ex-ADNOC, and hence we are also seeing some additional shipping length from Traders in March. We are still awaiting final March acceptances from Aramco, which is usually needed to kick start activity. The Baltic VLGC Index, which has been moving downward for quite some time, turned around upwards last week and has continued in the same direction this week, although at baby steps. The latest freight levels equates to a time charter equivalent rate of around USD 250,000 per month. The Western VLGC market has not really come to life this week. A couple of fixtures done nevertheless, and done at levels, far above what has been concluded in the East. The levels done represent a T/C/E of around 500 to 550,000 dollars per month.

Another week with rates for the VLCCs under pressure and therefore corrected down somewhat more. There is however a feeling that there is support at present level and the ‘bottom’ may have been found. Those with modern ships, spurred by in influx of fresh business ex USG, have taken a slightly firmer stand. Therefore, WAfr/East rates may edge up slightly, though not yet done. MEG/East remains another story as the list is still overpopulated by ‘mature’ ladies or ex drydock. Therefore a turnaround here is probably a bit down the road and a very active start of the March program required.

After the return from holidays in the East rates in the Supra market started climbing this week. Indo/China coal rv is by mid-week paying owners around USD 8000 bss Spore delivery. In Indian Ocean, Rbay to Ag/WCI owners are looking at around USD 10k + 100k gbb, while ECI to China is paying around USD 5000. In the Atlantic some stronger rates has been seen, from USEC Supras to Cont seeing around USD 11000, to Emed via USG around USD 7000. From the Baltic to India, is paying around USD 11000. Further south in ECSA vessels fixing USD 10k+100k to Seasia and to Emed around USD 5500.

IOC terminal commissioning was hotly contended this week and is welcome demand and marks the opening of the first LNG Terminal on the East coast of India. This new arrival occurs just as OLT announces that the LNG Toscana Regasification Terminal in Italy is working at almost 100% after less than one year from the introduction of the new allocation mechanism via auction, a very clear indication that trade routes has shifted significantly. Signs of Spring can be seen in Europe which is welcome relief from the dark days of winter but offers less rest bite for owners. The position list could be described as blossoming but that doesn’t give correct connotations for its effect on the market and charter rates which continue to soften. Its weak across the board – all basins and all duration take a hit except for 3 years and longer. Its clear that the prompt market is being underpinned but lackluster demand but the bigger picture remains relatively stable, more LNG due to be produced, the only question mark here is will it be in time for winter 2019/2020. Second-hand prices and NB prices remain stable, for now, but ongoing discussions between the Korean yards could see a significant change in the ownership structure of the 1st tier LNG yards, which may impact NB prices and in turn Charter rates.

The first positive week in a while, as the rates increased in both basins after Chinese New Year. A transatlantic round voyage still pays shipowners around USD 2500, while a short fronthaul from the continent yields around USD 10,500. In the east, a transpacific round yields around USD 5,500. The BPI 4TC-index is up 58 points to 611.

Aframax rates in NSea and Baltic hovered around bottom levels the last week. Currently there is a more firm sentiment to the market as this week started on a very busy note. Quite a lot of the available tonnage have been fixed away. Charterers with cargoes in the current fixing window will face Owners asking for rates more than last done. In Med and BlSea we saw steady activity levels. Tonnage supply is still in Charterers favour with a number of ships still spot open. The market has moved sideways most of the week with a slight downward trend the last few days. We have seen more Aframax-moves from Med direction US. Owners are finding the US-markets more exiting, especially with Caribs/USG picking up to ws140 levels the past week. We expect the market to remain stable in the coming week. One to follow is how the alternative markets in the North and US play out.

Although we see few signs that the market is set to improve imminently, we are encouraged by the fact that the smaller size segments are livening up. If the last few days pace of market increase for the smaller segments continues for another week then the Capesize/Panamax market ratio will fall to levels that previously has signalled that a market upturn is close. The Chinese are back from holidays, and the latest steel PMI returned to expansion, so we are pretty certain that the market will start improving soon.

The activity for the VLCCs, particularly in the days prior to the Lunar New Year holidays, remained active but as the holidays started in earnest things slowed down worldwide. Ships in all categories remain in ample supply and hence charterers take it easy. Rates have been and are under heavy downward pressure with earnings dipping below USD 20k/day for even the most economical ships. The ‘last bastion’, the USG/East rates have also come down, shaving off abt USD 1 mill from last done levels. All in all, subdued and under pressure for now with few bright spots on the horizon.

A slow week as the market is awaiting the Chinese New Year celebration to come to an end. Rates have seen a slight downturn this week, with positive underlying signs emerging. A transatlantic round voyage currently yields around low USD 2000’s, while short front-hauls from the Continent pays shipowners on the low side of USD 10,000 per day. In the East, a transpacific round voyage pays about USD 4300. The BPI-Index is currently at 553 points.

Activity has been slow for Suezmaxes the past week, third decade dates in W.Afr were slow in showing and caused a slow decline in the rates as owners tried to secure business as close to their dates as possible. TD20 fell to ws70 and with a marked reduction in the Turkish Straits delays TD6 has steadied to ws95. Algerian barrels ex Arzew have kept the Med position list ticking over and sprinkling of cargoes in the North for East destinations have been welcome relief in an otherwise uninspiring market. A further softening of rates in the week ahead is on the cards, now is time for owners to tighten their belts in order to ride this trough out, Charterers are very much in the driving seat for now.

As expected, Aframax rates in the N.Sea and Baltic came under downward pressure this week. The downward correction was mainly due to lack of activity and a build-up of available tonnage in the area. As it will take some time to absorb the prompt available tonnage, we expect the market to stay soft till we reach 3rd decade fixing window. A rather quiet week in Med and Bl.Sea. Owners have been more reluctant to ballast away from the area in the back of seeing alternative markets taking a hit, with Carib-USG dropping around ws45 points and USG-TA dropping ws25-30 points in a week’s time. We have seen a slight downward trend on straight cross Med voyages while Bl.Sea stems continued to trade sideways. Expect the market to remain steady/soft in the coming week with the support of a healthy tonnage list.
The Owners with ships coming open in February will try hard to push freight upwards - Read more in the full report.

With the Chinese New Year celebrations taking place this week, the dry bulk market is as expected extremely quiet. Freight rates are presumably at the lowest for the year over all, and number of spot ships is increasing every day. On top of this, the dry bulk community is watching the developments in Brazil carefully, and what the actual consequences will be in terms of reduced output. Time being it is estimated that 40 million tons of iron ore pellets will be impacted, but this is an estimate only and the length of the period is unknown.

Very limited activity and information due to holidays in the East, with continued downward pressure by mid-week. Ultra from USG to India was fixed at ca USD 15k, direction E.Med was done at USD 6k. Smaller Supra from Brazil to China was covered close to USD 8k+bb. Grain runs from Bl.Sea to Cont was covered at tick over USD 4k and Ultra close to USD 6k. From Algeria to USEC, Supra was covered at USD 2k and similar trip from Canakkale to USEC at USD 3500. From MEG, vessels are fixing around USD 8k aps bss for tct to Bangladesh. Indo RVs have been paying in the USD 5500s aps bss to China and around USD 5k to India. Some period fixtures has been concluded lately, with a split rate discount for the first 30-40 days.

With Chinese New Year celebrations going on, the market has remained rather slow all over the field, although some ships are being fixed somewhat under the radar. Recent deals concluded in the West indicates a further drop in returns to some USD 12-13,000 per day for the transpacific route and about USD 14-15,000 per day on the transatlantic route. The position lists cannot be described as very long, and the largest Owners are close to being sold out for February loadings in the US Gulf. So, a handful of fixtures may enable the market to tighten. The Owners with ships coming open in February will try hard to push freight upwards, so if any cargoes left for Feb, we might see US/East freight rates back up towards the mid USD 50’s due to this shorter shipping length. As the US market is seeing more shipping availability for 1st half March, ships fixed for early March cargoes are currently trading at a discount to the ones loading during 2nd half February. In the East, the market is sliding sideways, with little or no action to report, and the Baltic index is currently returning levels below OPEX which establish a significant “premium” in the western market on some 18-20% depending on trading route.

LNG spot market activity remains muted as Lunar New Year festivities take place in most parts of Asia Pacific and with no arbitrage between the basins. Rates are continuing their descending trend on the back of limited requirements in all basins. In the East, availability keeps growing and although it would seem as a better place to be for an Owner, a few independent Owners are repositioning their open vessels to the Atlantic. In the West, availability is slowly growing as Independent Owners’ positions are joining the existing available sublets. But as a few projects will be commissioning cargoes during Q2, some more activity is indeed expected in the US Gulf. On other news, it is very encouraging for the LNG market to see another major US project getting its FID – Congratulations to the Golden Pass promoters. Yards may continue to be busy building LNG vessels. Second hand prices remain stable and there were no Newbuilding transactions recorded this week.  In the meantime, we wish everyone a Happy Lunar New Year!!

The shipping market continues to mark time and sentiment shifts to the downside. Pacific and Atlantic rate levels have continued their downward trajectory throughout the week despite the market seeing a pickup in vessel requirements, the impact on availability? Minimal as there are plenty of open ships.    Looking ahead, the market may see an upturn after the celebrations of Chinese New Year. Until then, the vessel availability list looks likely to continue to lengthen. In the Middle East, the odd requirement can be witnessed whilst in the Atlantic, portfolio players remain well serviced by vessels delivering into Europe, that said, there is interest from parties with specific needs. Turning to the Pacific, it looks mildly more optimistic for Owners, yet requirements fall short of the number of vessels sitting prompt and it’s probably fair to say idle time will mount up as requirements turn their focus to second half-Feb or even March.   Second hand prices remain flat as do New Build prices as we welcome two new high spec, fuel efficient vessels scheduled for delivery in 2021.
In the east of Suez market a range of vessels have been booked away, and in all likelihood the market has hit a short term floor - read more in the full report.

Another week of a relatively soft shipping market as the lack of intensity in trading activities has led to various project and trader-controlled vessels being available for sub-let. This is in addition to vessels being redelivered this and next month due to charterers not declaring the optional periods, where they had previously anticipated an active trading market in January. As a result the current sentiment is far from what most have predicted a couple of months ago.  Every fixture heard in the market recently seems to have been done at terms lower than the previous fixture as headline rates dropped approximately 70% since the peak levels established in November. As reported last week, the correlation between the LNG shipping and cargo market has been restored but It may not take long for vessel availability to drop significantly as soon as there is an uptick of trading activities. As project and trader-controlled vessels contribute to almost half of the available tonnage list, expect these ships to be the first to go, to be utilized by their own charterers when LNG trading and demand increases.
The spread between freight rates East and West continue to widen - read more in the full report.

We are half-way to January and it does feel like the shipping market has taken a breather. We are only seeing limited new activity, which together with a number of redeliveries East of Suez, has caused our short term availability to look rather long, especially in the Pacific. As a result, any new piece of shipping business has gained great interest from the Owners, which has consequently put pressure on rates. As a matter of fact, it is starting to look like the correlation between the LNG shipping and cargo market has restored, making it more challenging to see any change in the short term shipping sentiment without a boost in the cargo side first (more cargoes or better arb’s). Although we are in the winter months, we get the feeling that without a solid cold spike, the “shoulder month season” might be coming upon us sooner than expected. That said, as we have learned in the past, the tide can change very quickly in the world of LNG and the players who can move just before the tidal change, will usually get the best deals.  For a change, the shipyards had a rather quiet announcement week as no new LNGC orders were reported.
We are likely to see a further drop in the Baltic index, at least until the February acceptances starts coming out and fixing activity increases - read more in the full report.

The first proper trading week of 2019 is underway and although we’ve recorded a good number of fixtures so far this year, it hasn’t been enough the get the shipping market out of the softening trend we’ve seen through the holiday season. The shipping rates have come off and so has other elements such as the ballast bonus sentiment. This weakening can mostly be associated to an increase in availability, amongst which, some are sublets, which indicates that the underlying demand is also coming off. Although the spot market is coming off near term, the sentiment and Owners remain optimistic for 2019 and term rates for a 1yr and 3yrs TC’s are relatively stable.
In the West one LPG major’s market quote was concluded at a level more-or-less wiping out the rather established “west premium” for the Transatlantic route - read more in the full report.

While many of the market participants are still enjoying the Festive Period, market activity has just slowly started to pick up. A few fresh requirements, one from an Eastern Major, will keep things busy this week, but as vessel availability in the East is increased, it will not be a surprise if we witness a further correction on East of Suez rates as Charterers are focusing on February cargoes. In the Atlantic, availability is limited and consists mainly of portfolio sublet tonnage as activity remains muted and with the West to East arbitrage closed it will be interesting to see the next market direction here.
